## [ALBRECHT-SP-23] Practically-exploitable Cryptographic Vulnerabilities in Matrix
**Citation:** Martin R. Albrecht, Sofía Celi, Benjamin Dowling, Daniel Jones. "Practically-exploitable Cryptographic Vulnerabilities in Matrix." IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (S&P), 2023. DOI 10.1109/SP46215.2023.10351027.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/485.pdf
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/485.pdf
**Domain:** H

### What it does
This paper is a security analysis, not a mechanism proposal: it reports six practically-exploitable cryptographic vulnerabilities in Matrix, an open federated real-time-communication standard, and its flagship client Element (built on matrix-js-sdk and matrix-react-sdk). Matrix lets clients on different homeservers (accounts hosted by different, mutually untrusted federated servers) exchange end-to-end-encrypted messages; the analysis targets that end-to-end encryption layer against a malicious homeserver, in the setting where every device and user has completed out-of-band verification (the strongest protection the protocol offers) — the paper states this is the hardest, most interesting setting for an attacker, and that when verification has not been completed for even one device, impersonation becomes trivial regardless of the vulnerabilities reported here. All six attacks require the cooperation of a homeserver; the paper assumes a single homeserver throughout for simplicity.

Matrix's cryptographic core: pairwise device-to-device channels use Olm, an implementation of the Signal X3DH key-exchange protocol combined with the Signal Double Ratchet algorithm. Group/room messages use Megolm, a custom unidirectional ratchet built on top of Olm: a device creating a Megolm session distributes its session key to every other device over individual pairwise Olm channels, then symmetrically ratchets forward and signs each subsequent Megolm ciphertext with an Ed25519 key tied to that session. Devices that missed the initial key distribution (e.g., a newly added device) can request the session via the Key Request protocol, receiving it as a "forwarded" Megolm session over Olm; the Element user interface marks messages decrypted from forwarded sessions with a lower-trust warning than messages from sessions received directly.

The six vulnerabilities, each with the class of design flaw the paper attributes to it:
1. Trivial confidentiality break via homeserver control of room membership and device lists (design flaw): room-management messages that add users to a room, and a user's device list, are neither encrypted nor cryptographically authenticated even in end-to-end-encrypted rooms; a malicious homeserver can forge a room-join message or insert its own device into a target user's device list, causing legitimate devices to share future Megolm session keys directly with the attacker-controlled device or user.
2. Attack against out-of-band (SAS, short authentication string) verification (lack of domain separation): the verification protocol does not separate device identifiers from users' cross-signing master public keys in the same field; the paper implements an attack that gets a victim to cryptographically sign an attacker-controlled cross-signing identity, believing it belongs to their conversation partner, enabling a mallory-in-the-middle position over the victim's Olm (and therefore Megolm) channels.
3. Semi-trusted impersonation against Megolm authentication (implementation bug plus lack of specification guidance): matrix-js-sdk accepts m.forwarded_room_key messages from any device as long as the message is Olm-encrypted, regardless of whether the receiving device requested them and regardless of the sender's actual relationship to the claimed session, letting an attacker push an attacker-controlled Megolm session to a target device; the resulting messages carry the same UI trust warning as legitimately forwarded keys, so the attack reaches parity with, not below, the trust level of the honest Key Request protocol.
4. Trusted impersonation against Megolm (protocol confusion): building on vulnerability 3, an attacker creates a new inner Megolm session sent over the outer forged Megolm channel; the inner session inherits the forged sender identity but not its "forwarded" (lower-trust) status, so the resulting message displays with no warning at all, exceeding the trust level achievable through the legitimate Key Request protocol.
5. Impersonation escalated to a confidentiality break against server-side Megolm backups (implementation bug): by impersonating a trusted device during self-verification (chaining vulnerability 3), the attacker can respond to a victim device's SSSS (Secure Secret Storage and Sharing) request for the server-side Megolm-backup key with an attacker-chosen key; the victim device then encrypts its backup of every inbound Megolm session it holds under that attacker-controlled key, which the colluding homeserver can then decrypt, exposing the plaintext of every Megolm message the victim device has access to.
6. IND-CCA (indistinguishability under chosen-ciphertext-attack) break in symmetric Megolm Key Backups and SSSS (specification-level cryptographic issue): Matrix composes AES-CTR encryption with an HMAC-SHA-256 message authentication code (MAC) in an encrypt-then-MAC construction, but the initialization vector (IV) is not covered by the MAC. The paper constructs a standard IND-CCA distinguishing attack: querying an encryption oracle for a known plaintext, splicing its ciphertext body onto the challenge ciphertext's IV, and querying a decryption oracle on the spliced ciphertext (which still passes the MAC check) to recover the AES keystream and decrypt the original challenge.

### Measured results
This is a vulnerability-disclosure paper; its measured facts are which attacks the authors implemented and verified against the real Matrix specification and the Element/matrix-js-sdk codebase (specifically Element Web at commit #479d4bf, matrix-react-sdk at commit #59b9d1e, matrix-js-sdk at commit #4721aa1), not performance benchmarks.
- Vulnerability 1 (room-membership/device-list control): design-level flaw demonstrated by construction from the specification (no cryptographic protection exists by design for the affected message types); no separate proof-of-concept run count reported.
- Vulnerability 2 (out-of-band verification attack): "We implemented this attack and report that it succeeds in practice" against the target commits listed above; the paper further states the attack can plausibly run in parallel against both parties of a verification exchange, but does not report a separate measured trial for the parallel case.
- Vulnerabilities 3-5 (impersonation chain and backup-key confidentiality break): each is a working proof-of-concept implemented against the same commits, chained together as described above; the paper reports the chain succeeds but does not give a trial count, success rate, or timing.
- Vulnerability 6 (IND-CCA break on backups): the attack is constructed formally and the paper states it is exploitable only against symmetric Megolm Key Backups and SSSS in the abstract cryptographic sense; the authors explicitly state that in practice they do not know how to instantiate it against real Matrix, because (a) per-session keys limit the decryption oracle's scope to sessions the attacker already controls, and (b) a modified ciphertext will generally fail to parse as valid JSON before it reaches the decryption step, so it is characterized as theoretical only, not a demonstrated practical break.
- Disclosure timeline: reported to Matrix developers between 20 May 2022 and 6 July 2022; coordinated public disclosure on 28 September 2022, alongside the developers' first countermeasures. At the time of public disclosure, the out-of-band verification attack (vulnerability 2), the semi-trusted impersonation attack (vulnerability 3), the trusted impersonation attack (vulnerability 4), and the impersonation-to-confidentiality attack (vulnerability 5) were fixed; the room-membership/device-list attack (vulnerability 1) was not fixed by disclosure, though a per-room local setting was added to mitigate the device-list variant, and the IND-CCA fix (vulnerability 6) was deferred because the developers judged it not practically exploitable.
- CVEs assigned by the Matrix developers: CVE-2022-39250 (verification attack); CVE-2022-39246, CVE-2022-39249, CVE-2022-39257, and (found in their own ecosystem review of other clients) CVE-2022-39252, CVE-2022-39254, CVE-2022-39264 (semi-trusted impersonation and variants); CVE-2022-39248, CVE-2022-39251, CVE-2022-39255 (trusted impersonation); the impersonation-to-confidentiality break is covered by the same CVEs as the trusted impersonation attack.
- Deployment scale (context, from the paper's introduction, not an experimental measurement): matrix.org reported 28 million global visible accounts as of March 2021.
- Cryptographic parameter noted as a departure from standard guidance: Matrix truncates HMAC-SHA-256 output to 64 bits, versus the HMAC RFC's recommendation of at least 128 bits (no less than half the hash output) and no fewer than 80 bits.

### Parameters
- Analysis target versions: Element Web commit #479d4bf, matrix-react-sdk commit #59b9d1e, matrix-js-sdk commit #4721aa1.
- Cryptographic primitives used by Matrix, as documented and relied on by the attacks: AES-256 (256-bit keys) for AES-CTR and AES-CBC (with PKCS7 padding for CBC block splitting in Olm, Megolm, and the asymmetric Megolm backup scheme); HMAC-SHA-256 truncated to 64 bits for message authentication; HKDF-SHA-256 for key derivation; Ed25519 for Megolm session-authenticity signatures and cross-signing; X25519 for the SAS out-of-band-verification key exchange.
- Threat model parameter: single homeserver assumed throughout (stated as a simplification, not a claimed limit of the attacks' generality).

### Stated limitations
The out-of-band-verification attack (Section IV/V per the paper's own numbering) is explicitly stated not to work when a user verifies two of their own devices — a malicious homeserver cannot use this specific attack to compromise Olm connections between two devices belonging to the same user. The IND-CCA break on backups (vulnerability 6) is stated by the authors to be of only theoretical interest: they state they do not know how to instantiate it in practice against real Matrix, for the two structural reasons given above (oracle scope limited by per-session keys; ciphertext modification breaks JSON parsing before the decryption oracle can be reached). The paper's scope is explicitly restricted: it covers only the Matrix specification and the Element client (not other Matrix clients, some of which do not even use matrix-js-sdk, and which the authors state they did not investigate); it covers only authentication and confidentiality without requiring a client secret compromise, explicitly leaving forward secrecy, post-compromise security, and deniability out of scope, on the stated grounds that a protocol failing at the more fundamental goals makes these advanced properties moot for the purposes of this paper. The paper states that Matrix's specification does not enforce that messages inside "encrypted" rooms are actually encrypted, so unless a client is configured to reject all communication from unverified devices or rooms containing them, no cryptographic authentication guarantee holds regardless of whether the six reported vulnerabilities are fixed.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
- A federated group-messaging design in which a server (homeserver) controls room membership and device-list metadata needs that metadata itself to be cryptographically authenticated to end-to-end-encrypted-room participants, or a malicious server can silently insert an eavesdropping device without breaking any per-message cryptography — the paper's vulnerability 1 shows the absence of that authentication is sufficient by itself to break confidentiality.
- A key-forwarding mechanism (here, the Key Request protocol) that lets a device request a missing group-session key from another device needs the receiving side to enforce the same trust checks the sending side enforces; the paper's vulnerability 3 exists specifically because matrix-js-sdk enforces sharing restrictions when a device offers a key but not when a device receives one, so a design that only checks trust on the sending side does not achieve the trust level it appears to provide.
- Verification of message authenticity (checking cryptographic identity/signature bindings) must happen no later than message-decryption time, not at message-display time, when other parts of the system act on decrypted-but-undisplayed state; the paper's vulnerability 4/5 chain is enabled specifically because Element checks authenticity at display time, so protocol messages that silently update client state without ever being displayed bypass authentication entirely.
- Any identifier space shared between two logically distinct key types (here, device identifiers and cross-signing master public keys) needs explicit domain separation — a distinguishing tag or type field checked consistently everywhere the identifier is consumed — or an attacker can substitute one type of key where the other is expected, which is exactly how the out-of-band-verification attack achieves a mallory-in-the-middle position.
- An encrypt-then-MAC construction needs the MAC to cover every input that varies per ciphertext, including the initialization vector, or an adversary with encryption- and decryption-oracle access (achievable here via the legitimate key-forwarding and backup-upload protocol flows) can mix IVs across ciphertexts and break IND-CCA security; whether this is practically exploitable in a given deployment depends on whether an attacker can obtain oracle access broader than one session's worth and whether modified ciphertexts still parse as valid application-level data before reaching the MAC check.
- The system-wide guarantee that "out-of-band-verified means trustworthy" only holds if every participating device and user completes verification; the paper states that a client design must offer, and a deployment must enable, an explicit reject-unverified-devices setting, because otherwise the presence of even one unverified device or user in a room removes cryptographic authentication guarantees for everyone in it, independent of whether the six specific vulnerabilities here are fixed.

### Contradicts
None found. This paper does not claim to contradict any specific figure attributed to Matrix elsewhere in the corpus; it establishes that Matrix's end-to-end encryption, at the versions studied, fell short of both confidentiality and authentication against a malicious homeserver, which the authors state runs counter to Matrix's own advertised claim that end-to-end encryption is enabled by default and protects against untrusted third-party servers.

### References worth retrieving
- foundational: Matrix.org Foundation, "Client-Server API" (unstable) [1] — the specification under analysis.
- foundational: Matrix.org, "Olm: A Cryptographic Ratchet" [2] and "Megolm Group Ratchet" [3] — the specific protocol documents defining the mechanisms attacked.
- foundational: Marlinspike, "The X3DH Key Agreement Protocol" [5] and "The Double Ratchet Algorithm" [6] — the Signal-protocol foundations Olm is built on.
- attack/critique: Meredith, Balducci (NCC Group), "Matrix Olm Cryptographic Review" [7] — a prior third-party cryptographic audit of Olm, cited as prior work distinct from this paper's Megolm-focused and implementation-level findings.
- foundational: Bernstein, Duif, Lange, Schwabe, Yang, "High-speed High-security Signatures" [8] — the Ed25519 signature scheme Megolm and cross-signing rely on.
- competing/related formal analysis: cited formal-analysis works on Signal (the Double Ratchet / Signal protocol formal security analyses referenced in the paper's prior-work discussion) — relevant because Megolm shares architectural elements with Signal's Sender Keys group-messaging variant, and the paper states none of the existing formal analyses cover Olm or Megolm directly, marking this as an open problem the paper itself does not close.
- foundational: ALWEN-CRYPTO-20 (Alwen, Coretti, Dodis, Tselekounis, "Security Analysis and Improvements for the IETF MLS Standard for Group Messaging," ePrint 2019/1189) — cited in this paper's prior-work discussion as the comparable formal-security-analysis approach applied to MLS rather than Matrix; already a target in this corpus.

## [ALMEIDA-CSUR-25] Approaches to Conflict-free Replicated Data Types
**Citation:** Paulo Sérgio Almeida. "Approaches to Conflict-free Replicated Data Types." ACM Computing Surveys, 2025. DOI 10.1145/3695249.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.18220
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.18220
**Domain:** D

### What it does
A Conflict-free Replicated Data Type (CRDT) lets independent replicas of one data object accept local updates without coordinating with other replicas first, remain available under network partitions, and reach identical state on every replica that has received the same set of updates, whatever order those updates arrived in. The paper systematizes four families of CRDT design, comparing their message content, delivery-guarantee requirements, and state-size growth. Operation-based CRDTs propagate individual update operations: each replica runs a side-effect-free `prepare` step that turns an invoked operation into a message, and an `effect` step at every replica (including the origin) that applies the message to local state; this family needs causal-broadcast delivery — every message delivered at most once, and delivered only after every message it causally depends on. Pure operation-based CRDTs are a stricter version that require Tagged Causal Broadcast middleware to expose message timestamps and causal-stability notifications to the CRDT itself, so the CRDT logic never touches local state directly, only a partially ordered log (PO-Log) of received operations; a message is causally stable at a node when every message the node will later receive carries an equal or later logical timestamp, so no further concurrent operations remain to interleave with it, letting the PO-Log discard stable entries. State-based CRDTs instead propagate full or partial local state; correctness requires only that local state form a join-semilattice (a partially ordered structure with a defined merge, or join, operation for any two states) and that every state-mutating operation be an inflation — the state after the operation is greater than or equal to the state before it, under the semilattice order — so that repeated or reordered delivery of the same state never moves a replica backward; delivery need only be reliable and eventually complete (at-least-once, eventually), not ordered. Delta-state CRDTs keep the join-semilattice state model of state-based CRDTs but replace each mutator with a delta-mutator that returns a small delta-state instead of the full next state; a naive propagation algorithm accumulates deltas in a per-replica delta-buffer, joins each locally applied or received delta into both the buffer and the durable state, and periodically broadcasts and clears the buffer. The paper derives an optimal delta-mutator using Birkhoff's join-decomposition theorem from lattice theory: for a distributive lattice, every state has a unique irredundant join decomposition into join-irreducible elements, so the difference between two states can be computed exactly as the join of the elements in one state's decomposition that are not already below the other state, and the optimal delta-mutator is defined as this difference between the mutator's full-state result and the current state.

### Measured results
None. The paper is a systematization survey; it defines formal properties, derives algorithms, and cites deployed systems (Riak, Redis, AntidoteDB, SwiftCloud, Automerge, Yjs), but reports no experiment of its own, no benchmark, and no figure with stated node counts, message counts, or latency. The one specific number given about a cited deployment — "a list of over 40 applications using [Yjs]" — carries no experimental conditions (measurement date, counting method) and is not attributed to a primary measurement, so it is not usable as a quantitative result under this batch's rule 1.

### Parameters
Not applicable in the sense of tunable runtime parameters — the paper defines formal design-space choices rather than numeric parameters. Where later CRDT implementations expose a parameter (for example, a retention window for tombstones or causal-context compaction), this survey states the mechanism generally and does not fix a value.

### Stated limitations
Operation-based CRDTs are unsuitable for large weakly-connected systems prone to long partitions: the paper states each replica must retain every operation not yet delivered to every other replica, and this retained set grows linearly with partition duration, producing unbounded memory growth under a sufficiently long partition, and that two independent groups of operation-based replicas that evolved separately cannot be merged in realistic (non-full-history) implementations. Pure operation-based CRDTs cannot extract information from the CRDT's own state inside `prepare`, because `prepare` in this family never touches local state; this is stated as a strict limitation relative to the general operation-based model. State-based CRDTs carry a metadata component that grows linearly with the number of replicas in the causal context or replica-indexed map (for example, a counter represented as a map from replica id to integer, rather than a single integer), and this overhead cannot be amortized transparently across multiple CRDT objects the way operation-based middleware cost can — amortizing it requires explicitly nesting multiple CRDTs inside one container CRDT, which the paper states is a non-transparent refactoring cost. The naive delta-state propagation algorithm is stated to be too naive for practical use: the per-replica delta-buffer tends to grow back toward the size of the full state, for two identified reasons — deltas are re-propagated back to the replica they originated from, and a received delta-group is joined into the local buffer in full even where most of it duplicates already-held state. Server-based identity-collapsing techniques for scaling CRDT replica-id maps down when no client session is active are described as "not aware of these techniques having been described or if they have been used," marking that idea as unimplemented and unverified rather than a result. List-CRDT approaches using a pre-existing dense total order for element identifiers (Treedoc, Logoot, LSEQ) are stated to have identifiers whose size keeps growing over time. List-CRDT approaches that instead explicitly order small unique identifiers (Woot, Causal Trees, RGA, YATA) are stated to accumulate tombstones in state, addressed only by causal-stability-based removal.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Operation-based CRDTs and, more strictly, pure operation-based CRDTs require the messaging layer to supply causal broadcast: exactly-once, causally-ordered delivery to every replica. Pure operation-based CRDTs additionally require the messaging middleware to expose causal timestamps and per-node causal-stability notifications to the CRDT logic (Tagged Causal Broadcast), which is a stronger interface requirement than plain causal broadcast provides. State-based and delta-state CRDTs require only at-least-once, eventually-complete delivery with no ordering guarantee, but every operation-mutator in this family must be provably an inflation over the state's join-semilattice order, a property the implementer must establish per data type, not something the messaging layer can enforce. Named (non-anonymous) CRDTs of any family require every replica to hold a globally unique replica identifier; the paper states this as the only requisite for state-based CRDTs to support dynamic joining, leaving, and merging of independently evolved replica groups. Achieving the delta-state model's optimal (smallest) delta-mutator requires the CRDT's state lattice to be a finite distributive lattice, or reducible to one through finite quotient sublattices, so that Birkhoff's unique-irreducible-join-decomposition result applies; a state lattice without this structure cannot use the optimal-delta construction the paper derives. The inter-datacenter delta-propagation simplification (skipping general join-decomposition-based redundancy elimination) requires a small, fixed, fully-meshed set of replicas — the example given is one replica per datacenter — and requires tracking a version vector per replica to gate delivery on causal-dependency satisfaction.

### Contradicts
None found. The paper explicitly corrects two claims it identifies as widespread misconceptions rather than disagreeing with any specific paper in this corpus: that CRDTs are defined by having commutative operations (the paper states the more significant advance over prior optimistic replication, such as Lazy Replication, is supporting non-commutative operations under operation-based design), and that state-based CRDT mutators must be monotonic functions (the paper states the correct requirement is that mutators be inflations, which is what produces monotonic state evolution, not monotonicity of the mutator function itself).

## [ALVISI-SP-13] SoK: The Evolution of Sybil Defense via Social Networks

**Citation:** Lorenzo Alvisi, Allen Clement, Alessandro Epasto, Silvio Lattanzi, Alessandro Panconesi. "SoK: The Evolution of Sybil Defense via Social Networks." IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy, 2013. Pages 382-396 (as paginated in text, pp. 383-397). DOI 10.1109/SP.2013.33.
**Retrieved:** full text
**Source URL:** https://www.cs.cornell.edu/~lorenzo/papers/AlvisiSoK.pdf
**Domain:** F

### What it does
The paper unifies social-graph Sybil defense — distinguishing forged identities from genuine ones by analyzing the graph structure of a social network rather than by a central authority — under one framework and states which structural property that framework can safely rely on. It shows that four candidate structural properties of a social graph (node-degree distribution, network diameter, clustering coefficient, conductance) can each be defeated cheaply by an adversary who inserts identities via preferential attachment (an inserted node connects to existing node v with probability proportional to v's degree), except conductance, which the paper defines as the ratio of edges leaving a vertex set to the sum of degrees inside that set. It then reduces universal Sybil defense (SybilGuard, SybilLimit, SybilInfer, GateKeeper) to a random-walk membership test: an honest verifier and a candidate node each sample a random edge from a short random walk (length order log n, where n is graph size), and a match indicates same-graph membership with a probability derivable from the birthday paradox. The paper then reframes the goal from universal defense (classify every node in the network) to local defense, called Problem 1: given an honest seed node u, find the largest connected subset S containing u whose internal mixing time (the walk length after which a random walk lands on a uniformly random edge) is short and whose cut to the rest of the graph is sparse enough (at most o(|S|/mixing time) edges) that S can be found by a local algorithm without traversing the whole graph. It solves this with ACL (Andersen-Chung-Lang), a Personalized PageRank random walk with a jump-back probability alpha to the seed, approximated by a push-flow algorithm (APPR) with error parameter epsilon, then degree-normalized to rank every other node by trust from the seed's perspective.

### Measured results
| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| SybilLimit precision decays once attack edges exceed the theoretical bound | Preprocessed Facebook-New Orleans graph (63,392 nodes / 816,886 edges before preprocessing, reduced to 40,757 nodes / 632,597 edges by removing all nodes with degree below 5); attack-edge insertion probability p swept 0.01 to 0.10; SybilLimit configured with 1.5*sqrt(m) random walks of length 1.5*log(n) |
| Preprocessing removes 85%+ of nodes on WikiTalk | WikiTalk graph: 92,117 nodes / 360,767 edges raw, reduced to 13,069 nodes / 133,343 edges after removing degree-below-5 nodes |
| ACL tolerates denser attacks than SybilLimit: ACL at p=0.05 attack strength performs comparably to SybilLimit at p=0.01 | Facebook-New Orleans graph, attack strength p swept 0.01-0.10, ACL configured with alpha=10^-3, epsilon=10^-6 (10^-7 for DBLP), precision/recall averaged over 10 randomly chosen seeds |
| ACL achieves high precision at high recall without preprocessing on Facebook, DBLP, Epinions, WikiTalk; SybilLimit's precision degrades to varying degrees without preprocessing and performs poorly on DBLP even preprocessed | Four graphs: DBLP (718,115 nodes / 2,786,906 edges), Epinions (26,588 / 100,120), Facebook (63,392 / 816,886), WikiTalk (92,117 / 360,767); attack edge probability p=0.01 |
| Under a targeted-attachment attack (fixed number of attack edges g=50,000 connecting to honest nodes chosen at random until g edges obtained, then gamma=10,000 additional Sybil nodes added in a Barabasi-Albert scale-free topology), ACL and the Mislove community-detection algorithm are near-perfect and outperform GateKeeper, SybilLimit, SybilGuard | Facebook-New Orleans graph, g=50,000, gamma=10,000 |
| Under the RenRen-observed attack pattern (isolated Sybil nodes each connected via many attack edges rather than a single well-connected Sybil cluster), every tested defense performs close to random (0.5 probability that a random honest node ranks above a random Sybil node) | Facebook-New Orleans graph; measured probabilities: SybilLimit 0.45, SybilGuard 0.44, Mislove 0.34, GateKeeper 0.49, ACL 0.37 |
| Yang et al.'s RenRen heuristic (flag as Sybil any account whose friendship-acceptance rate is below 50% and whose clustering coefficient is below 1/100) identifies over 98% of Sybils with a false-positive rate under 0.5% | RenRen social network, as reported by Yang et al. and cited by this paper, not independently re-measured here |
| A conductance-based defense layer built on friendship-acceptance-rate monitoring bounds the fraction of edges a Sybil node can spend on attack edges without detection: at honest-acceptance probability p=0.10 and flag threshold T=0.50, each Sybil node must hold at least 7 links to other Sybil nodes per attack edge to avoid detection | Derived bound (Proposition 3): fraction of edges that may be attack edges is p(1-T)/(T-p); example values p=0.10, T=0.50 taken from Yang et al.'s RenRen thresholds |

### Parameters
- alpha (ACL jump-back probability to seed): set to 10^-3 in experiments; theory sets alpha = (10*mixing time)^-1 for a subset S
- epsilon (ACL/APPR approximation error, trading running time against precision, running time O(1/(alpha*epsilon))): 10^-6 for Facebook, Epinions, WikiTalk; 10^-7 for DBLP (chosen so every node in the attacked graph receives non-zero weight)
- SybilLimit random-walk count: 1.5*sqrt(m) walks (m = edge count)
- SybilLimit random-walk length: 1.5*log(n) (n = node count)
- Preprocessing threshold: nodes with degree below 5 are iteratively removed before running SybilLimit-family protocols
- Attack-edge insertion probability p: swept 0.01 to 0.10 across experiments
- Targeted-attachment attack: g (fixed attack-edge count) = 50,000; gamma (added Sybil node count) = 10,000; Sybil sub-topology generated by Barabasi-Albert preferential attachment

### Stated limitations
The paper states that the two assumptions underlying universal random-walk Sybil defense (honest-region mixing time of O(log n), and a sparse cut between honest and Sybil regions) do not hold in the measured graphs: preprocessing to raise mixing time removes over 85% of nodes on WikiTalk, and removed nodes are treated as Sybil by the protocol even though the paper states it is unclear how they can safely use or contribute resources. ACL solves only the local problem (finding one seed's community, Problem 1); the paper states that a universal Sybil defense for a community-structured network remains an open problem. ACL and every other tested random-walk method perform close to random-guessing (0.34-0.49 probability) against the RenRen-observed attack pattern of many isolated Sybil nodes each with several attack edges, rather than one well-connected Sybil cluster with few attack edges — the paper states this vulnerability to multiple-attack-edges-per-node is fundamental to conductance-based methods, following a proof by Yu et al. Multi-seed ranking merging (Cao et al.'s approach) has no proven theoretical guarantee even under all-honest seeds, because seeds near the honest/Sybil boundary can produce an adversarial probability distribution over Sybil nodes with unknown effect on the merged ranking. The friendship-acceptance-rate defense layer is stated to be circumventable by an adversary who issues friendship requests preferentially to other Sybil-controlled nodes.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
ACL requires each honest verifying node to hold, or be able to sample, a local view of the social graph reachable by random walk from itself; it does not require a global, centrally computed graph snapshot at query time, but the paper's own experiments compute walks over a fully materialized graph. ACL's guarantee (Theorem 3) is conditioned on the target subset S having a power-law degree distribution and a cut of size o(|S|/mixing-time of S) to the rest of the graph; a caller supplying a graph without these properties receives no proven guarantee. The ranking is seed-relative: it requires the caller to supply one honest seed per verifying viewpoint, and results do not merge across seeds without losing the proven guarantee (per the multi-seed discussion above). Any system consuming ACL's ranking to admit or reject identities must set alpha from an estimate of the target community's mixing time, which the paper does not show how to measure without already possessing a labeled honest/Sybil partition.

### Contradicts
Community-detection-based Sybil defense is often described as solved by this line of work; the paper itself states this is false in general — Mislove's greedy conductance-heuristic algorithm can be forced by an adversary using only two attack edges (from one honest node v to two Sybil endpoints) to admit an entire attacker-constructed Sybil chain deterministically. No other corpus entry directly disagrees with this paper's measurements as of this batch.

## [ALWEN-CRYPTO-20] Security Analysis and Improvements for the IETF MLS Standard for Group Messaging
**Citation:** Joël Alwen, Sandro Coretti, Yevgeniy Dodis, Yiannis Tselekounis. "Security Analysis and Improvements for the IETF MLS Standard for Group Messaging." CRYPTO, 2020. DOI 10.1007/978-3-030-56784-2_9.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://eprint.iacr.org/2019/1189.pdf
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2019/1189.pdf
**Domain:** H

### What it does
This paper gives a formal cryptographic security proof for TreeKEM, the group-key-agreement protocol at the core of the IETF's Messaging Layer Security (MLS, message-layer security) draft standard for secure group messaging (SGM). It defines continuous group key agreement (CGKA) as a standalone cryptographic primitive — a protocol that lets a dynamic set of users add members, remove members, and perform updates, where each update run by any one member produces a new shared secret ("update secret") that every other member can compute, while looking random to an outside attacker. The paper proves TreeKEM satisfies a formally defined but non-adaptive CGKA security notion, identifies a specific forward-secrecy weakness in the version of TreeKEM under standardization, and proposes and proves secure a modified TreeKEM that fixes it.

Mechanism (TreeKEM/ratchet trees). Group members occupy the leaves of a left-balanced binary tree (a binary tree built so that its left subtree is always a maximal full binary tree — every internal node in it has two children — and the remainder recurses on the right); every non-root node in the tree, internal or leaf, holds a public/private key pair for a public-key encryption (PKE) scheme, and every member knows the private keys on the direct path from its own leaf to the root. To perform an update, a member generates fresh key pairs for every node on its own direct path to the root, deriving each level's key pair and the next level's seed from the previous level's seed via a pseudorandom generator (PRG), then for every node on its co-path (the sequence of siblings of direct-path nodes) encrypts the information needed to derive the new keys under that co-path node's public key — or, if that node is "blank" (holds no key because of a prior add/remove that left a gap), under the public keys of every node in that node's "resolution," the smallest set of non-blank nodes covering all leaves beneath it. The seed value at the root, produced this way, is the new update secret; it is fed to a higher-level protocol (via a PRF-based pseudo-random-number generator, PRF-PRNG, plus a per-user forward-secure authenticated encryption with associated data, FS-AEAD, construction) that derives symmetric encryption keys for the actual chat messages. Adding a member fills the first blank leaf, or grows the tree by one leaf if none is blank; removing a member blanks that leaf's direct path and truncates trailing blank structure. The paper's central claim about efficiency, inherited from the MLS design rather than proved fresh here, is that an update's packet size can be made logarithmic in group size n by encrypting only along the co-path (order log n ciphertexts) rather than separately to every other member (order n ciphertexts), which is the entire motivation for using a tree rather than running a pairwise double-ratchet protocol (the two-party predecessor to TreeKEM, underlying Signal and applications built on it) between every pair of group members.

Forward-secrecy defect found and proved. After a member processes an update, it must retain the private keys it used to decrypt that update's ciphertexts, because those same keys are needed to process future updates encrypted along overlapping co-paths. The paper proves that corrupting (compromising the full local state of) any group member other than the one that ran a given update can therefore reveal that update's secret in full, because the corrupted member's retained keys are exactly the keys the update secret was encrypted under. The paper shows this failure is structural, not incidental: it requires, in the best case, a logarithmic number of additional updates by other specific members before a compromise for the older update secret to become unrecoverable, and a linear number in the worst case depending on update order; if the sibling (in the tree) of the update's initiator never performs its own update, that update secret is never forward secret at all.

Fix (Modified TreeKEM). The authors replace the standard PKE used at each tree node with a new primitive, updatable public-key encryption (UPKE), whose public and secret keys change with every encryption and decryption respectively, so that after a node's secret key is used to decrypt one update, the post-decryption (evolved) key no longer reveals the plaintext of that decryption. This closes the forward-secrecy gap because the retained key a corrupted member holds after processing an update no longer suffices to recover that update's secret. The paper instantiates UPKE from the Computational Diffie-Hellman (CDH) assumption in the random-oracle model, building on a construction by Jost, Maurer, and Mularczyk (cited as [15]) and a suggestion from Konrad Kohbrok on the MLS mailing list (cited as [16]), and proves the resulting Modified TreeKEM achieves the strongest ("optimal," per the paper's own CGKA definition and matching what the MLS specification aims for) forward secrecy and post-compromise security (PCS, the property that a compromised member's security is eventually restored once the compromise ends and normal protocol use, i.e., updates, continues) simultaneously, at close to no added computational or communication cost over unmodified TreeKEM.

Ordering assumption. Every security definition and proof in the paper assumes the delivery server that queues protocol messages for offline members delivers CGKA (group-key) messages in the same order to every member of a session — the server may still drop or delay messages, and may deliver in different orders to different sessions/pairs of users, but within one session's view all members eventually see the same total order of protocol messages. This assumption is taken directly from the MLS draft specification, where it is stated explicitly, and the authors note it can in principle be realized without a centralized delivery service, by using a public bulletin board such as a blockchain protocol.

### Measured results
This is a theory paper: its results are cryptographic security proofs (reductions to standard hardness assumptions) rather than empirical performance measurements, and no benchmarked latency, bandwidth, or throughput figures with experimental conditions (hardware, node counts, trial counts) appear in the paper.
- Theorem 1 (non-adaptive security of TreeKEM): given a PRG that is (t_prg, epsilon_prg)-secure (an adversary running in time at most t_prg distinguishes the PRG's output from random with advantage at most epsilon_prg) and a PKE scheme that is (t_cpa, epsilon_cpa)-CPA-secure (secure against chosen-plaintext attack under the same time/advantage parameterization), TreeKEM is a (t, c, n, P, epsilon)-secure CGKA protocol for each of the three safety predicates P studied (tkm — TreeKEM's own exact predicate; pcs — post-compromise security only; fsu — forward secrecy with updates), with epsilon = 2·c·n·(epsilon_prg + epsilon_cpa), where n is group size and c bounds the number of adversary queries; this is a reduction bound, not a measured number, and requires the reader to instantiate the underlying PRG and PKE security parameters to obtain a concrete numeric value.
- Theorem 2 (non-adaptive security of Modified TreeKEM): an analogous bound for the UPKE-based fixed protocol, likewise stated as a reduction (the paper defers the full statement's exact constants to the theorem text/appendix; the underlying UPKE construction (Theorem 3) is proved CPA*-secure under the CDH assumption over a group G in the random-oracle model, again as a reduction, not a benchmark).
- Communication complexity claims are structural, not measured: the paper states MLS/TreeKEM packet sizes can in certain circumstances degrade to Omega(n) (linear in group size) rather than the intended O(log n) (logarithmic), and that this degradation "can, in principle, continue indefinitely and/or reoccur in any session once the right conditions are created" — this is a claim of a worst-case complexity regime the protocol can enter under adversarial or unlucky update ordering, not a number from a run of the protocol, and the paper does not give a numeric threshold, node count, or reproduction condition beyond this qualitative description.
- The adaptive-security bound the paper sketches (applying a reduction technique of Jafargholi et al.) is explicitly characterized by the authors as requiring block-cipher keys of size on the order of n·log(n) bits to apply meaningfully, which they state is "practically speaking, unrealistic" — recorded here as the authors' own characterization of their bound's looseness, not as a claim this corpus should treat as a usable parameter.

### Parameters
- Tree shape: left-balanced binary tree (LBBT) on n members — defined recursively so the root's left subtree is a maximal full binary tree on the largest power of 2 not exceeding n, and the right subtree is an LBBT on the remainder.
- Security-definition parameters in Theorem 1/2: t (adversary running time), c (number of oracle/protocol queries the adversary makes), n (group size) — all left as free variables in the reduction rather than fixed to specific tested values.
- Adaptive-security bound (sketched, not the paper's main proved result): requires block-cipher key size of order n·log(n) bits to be meaningful, per the authors' own statement, which they characterize as impractical.
- UPKE instantiation: built from the CDH assumption over a group G, in the random-oracle model (Theorem 3).

### Stated limitations
The paper's proofs (Theorems 1 and 2, for both TreeKEM and Modified TreeKEM) hold only against a non-adaptive adversary — one that must announce every corruption at the start of the security game rather than choosing corruptions adaptively based on protocol messages observed so far. The authors state the restriction stems from commitment issues with PKE ciphertexts common in the cryptographic literature, and that removing it without an exponential loss in the security bound is an open problem; they sketch, but do not complete, a proof technique (adapted from Jafargholi et al.) toward adaptive security, and explicitly characterize the resulting bounds as "still quite far from usable in practice."

The global-ordering-of-delivery assumption (same order of CGKA messages seen by every group member) is not removed or weakened in this work; the authors state that removing it would require either significantly weakening the adversary in the security definition, or making larger changes to TreeKEM's construction that they suspect would be impractical for real-world use, drawing an analogy to how stronger two-party ratcheting protocols end up requiring hierarchical identity-based encryption (HIBE) with arbitrary depth.

The paper explicitly sketches an attack (Section 8.3) showing that even TreeKEM variants with local-state leakage only (no active/malicious-insider corruption) fail to achieve what the authors call "ideal security" in a fully arbitrary, unordered network model: when two siblings in the ratchet tree (Bob and Charlie, with Alice a third party) each process a concurrent update from a different party, a leaked state from one sibling can let an adversary recover a group key the honest protocol design did not expect that party to be able to compute; the paper states this generalizes to all TreeKEM variants it is aware of, including the Kohbrok fix used elsewhere in this paper (which fixes the case only when the two concurrent updaters' direct paths intersect the third party's path at the same node) and Causal-TreeKEM.

The paper explicitly states it does not construct or prove security for a complete secure-group-messaging (SGM) protocol — only for the CGKA primitive that TreeKEM implements — and lists provable full-SGM security, more accurate PKI (public-key infrastructure) modeling, protection against active/malicious-insider attackers, metadata protection against a corrupt delivery server, deniability, post-quantum instantiations, and fully decentralized SGM as open research directions the paper does not resolve.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
- Every group member must retain, for each node on its own direct path, the most recently generated private key, because processing future updates whose co-paths overlap that path requires it; a system layer that tries to erase keys more aggressively than TreeKEM's own update logic requires would break the protocol's own correctness, not just its forward secrecy.
- The delivery mechanism (an untrusted server or equivalent) must deliver CGKA protocol messages in the same order to every member of a session, though it may drop, delay, or reorder relative to other sessions; a system that cannot guarantee this consistent per-session total order is outside the model this paper's security proofs (Theorems 1 and 2) apply to. The paper states this ordering could in principle be supplied by a public bulletin board such as a blockchain protocol, rather than a single centralized server, but the paper does not construct or evaluate such a substitution.
- The paper's own Section 8.5 (Decentralization) states MLS "is defined to operate using untrusted but centralized server infrastructure" — specifically a key server (for retrieving other members' initial public keys) and a delivery server (for queuing and ordering protocol messages) — and that this centralization reflects the standardization working group's corporate/organizational orientation rather than a cryptographic necessity; the authors state that naive ways to implement both servers atop a blockchain exist, but that it is unclear how to do so while also minimizing metadata leakage, latency, and the cost of writing to the blockchain, and what security guarantee such a substitution would actually provide — they identify fully decentralized SGM as an open, unresolved research direction, not a solved problem.
- The public-key infrastructure (PKI) that supplies members' initial keys is treated in this paper as an idealized functionality (any user can request a fresh public key for any user ID, and the corresponding private key is available only to that ID); the authors state real MLS deployments require an out-of-band mechanism to authenticate a peer's long-term signing key before trusting any key server response, and that this out-of-band step is the actual root of trust for the whole system — the paper's formal proofs do not model or verify that step.
- Attack availability caveat relevant to composing this mechanism with a partition-tolerant or asynchronous delivery layer: the Section 8.3 sketch shows that removing the global-ordering assumption (i.e., substituting a fully arbitrary/unordered network) breaks the paper's own non-adaptive security proof for TreeKEM and, per the authors, for every TreeKEM variant they are aware of at the time of writing — a decentralized design that cannot guarantee consistent per-session delivery order needs a different CGKA construction than TreeKEM as analyzed here.

### Contradicts
None found against other entries in this batch. Within its own scope the paper's central finding directly contradicts an informal claim commonly made about TreeKEM/MLS at the time — that the draft protocol already achieved standard forward secrecy — by proving TreeKEM (pre-fix) achieves only a strictly weaker property the authors formalize as "forward secrecy with updates" (fsu), not full forward secrecy.

### References worth retrieving
- foundational: Alwen, Coretti, Dodis, "The Double Ratchet: Security Notions, Proofs, and Modularization for the Signal Protocol," EUROCRYPT 2019 [1] — the two-party CKA/FS-AEAD/PRF-PRNG modularization this paper's CGKA definition is explicitly modeled after.
- foundational: Jost, Maurer, Mularczyk, "Efficient Ratcheting: Almost-Optimal Guarantees for Secure Messaging," EUROCRYPT 2019 [15] — source of the updatable-encryption idea the Modified TreeKEM fix builds on.
- foundational: Marlinspike, Perrin, "The Double Ratchet Algorithm" [17] — the two-party predecessor protocol TreeKEM is designed to outperform for groups.
- foundational: Barnes, Beurdouche, Millican, Omara, Cohn-Gordon, Robert, "The Messaging Layer Security (MLS) Protocol," IETF Internet-Draft [3] — the standard under analysis.
- competing: Cohn-Gordon, Cremers, Garratt, Millican, Milner, "On Ends-to-Ends Encryption: Asynchronous Group Messaging with Strong Security Guarantees," ACM CCS 2018 [7] — a competing formal treatment of asynchronous group messaging security guarantees.
- competing: Cremers, Hale, Kohbrok, "Revisiting Post-Compromise Security Guarantees in Group Messaging," ePrint 2019/477 [9] — directly comparable analysis of PCS guarantees in group messaging.
- competing: Jafargholi, Kamath, Klein, Komargodski, Pietrzak, Wichs, "Be Adaptive, Avoid Overcommitting," CRYPTO 2017 [14] — source of the adaptive-security reduction technique this paper adapts and finds too loose to be practical.
- foundational: Mittra, "Iolus: A Framework for Scalable Secure Multicasting," ACM SIGCOMM 1997 [18] — early tree-structured group-key-management precedent cited in related work.
- foundational: Dodis, Fazio, "Public Key Broadcast Encryption for Stateless Receivers" [10]; Fiat, Naor, "Broadcast Encryption," CRYPTO 1993 [12] — foundational broadcast-encryption literature cited as background for tree-based group key distribution.
- competing (concurrent-CGKA line, superseded-by relative to this corpus's later entries): this paper's own Section 8.3 attack applies to "Casual-TreeKEM" [24], a citation not resolved in the excerpted bibliography portion above but referenced as a TreeKEM variant explicitly permitting concurrent updates — likely the direct predecessor problem addressed by ALWEN-EUROCRYPT-22 (CoCoA) and ALWEN-CRYPTO-23 (Fork-Resilient CGKA) elsewhere in this corpus.

## [ALWEN-CRYPTO-23] Fork-Resilient Continuous Group Key Agreement
**Citation:** Joël Alwen, Marta Mularczyk, Yiannis Tselekounis. "Fork-Resilient Continuous Group Key Agreement." CRYPTO, 2023. DOI 10.1007/978-3-031-38551-3_13.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/394.pdf
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/394.pdf
**Domain:** H

### What it does
This paper generalizes continuous group key agreement (CGKA — the primitive letting an evolving group of clients agree on a sequence of shared group keys, the basis of scalable end-to-end-encrypted group messaging) to a new primitive, Fork-Resilient CGKA (FR-CGKA), that lets clients process protocol messages ("packets") arriving in any order consistent with causality, not only the single fixed order every prior CGKA protocol required. A fork occurs when group members end up with diverging views of the group's event history, typically because a network or server outage let different subsets of members exchange packets independently for a period; once connectivity is restored, members must reconcile ("resolve") their divergent views into one agreed group state. The paper's stated goal is to remove the specific cryptographic obstacle that stops today's CGKA protocols — including the CGKA underlying the IETF's Messaging Layer Security (MLS) draft standard — from supporting the "natural fork resolution" pattern already used by systems like Matrix: gather the packets each side is missing, then run a deterministic state-resolution algorithm over the combined causal history. Every prior CGKA protocol deletes cryptographic secrets as soon as they are used to transition to a new epoch (a numbered version of the group's state), specifically to guarantee forward secrecy (FS — that a later state compromise cannot expose earlier communications); this deletion also makes it cryptographically impossible to reprocess a delayed packet describing an alternate, un-taken transition out of an already-abandoned epoch, which is exactly what fork resolution by replaying missed packets requires.

Formal model: the paper replaces "the client's current epoch" (the concept every prior CGKA authenticity/forward-secrecy definition is built around) with "the client's current view of the group's history," represented as a history graph — a directed tree of epochs where an edge from epoch E0 to E1 represents one group-modifying event (add, remove, or key update) turning E0 into E1. A client's local state is described via a "pebbled history graph": three kinds of markers (move, visited, key pebbles) placed on epoch nodes track, respectively, whether the client can still send/receive packets referencing that epoch, whether a packet transitioning out of that epoch has already been irreversibly processed (which forward secrecy requires), and whether the client still holds that epoch's symmetric group key. This pebbling abstraction is presented as a minimal, protocol-independent interface that a higher-level fork-resolution procedure can query to determine which missing packets a client can still process, without needing to know the underlying cryptographic state.

Two constructions are given. FREEK is a practical FR-CGKA protocol built on SAIK (a prior server-aided CGKA the paper cites as [AHKM22a], itself built on MLS/TreeKEM). Its core mechanism replaces standard forward-secrecy-by-deletion with a puncturable pseudorandom function (PPRF — a PRF whose key can be "punctured" on a chosen input, after which the key still evaluates the PRF everywhere except that input, and reveals nothing about the punctured output): the "init secret" a client retains for a parent epoch is now the key to a PPRF, and instead of deleting that secret entirely after deriving a child epoch's key (which would forbid processing any other, un-taken child epoch later), the client punctures the PPRF key only on the specific challenge tied to the epoch it actually transitioned into, preserving the ability to derive keys for other, still-unprocessed child epochs while still achieving forward secrecy for the one it already committed to. The challenge value that gets punctured is constructed from a cryptographic commitment to the new epoch's public state combined with half of the freshly generated "commit secret" (the paper states a naive alternative — punncturing on the commit secret directly, or on a random attacker-suppliable value — either leaks old secrets through the punctured key or opens a denial-of-service attack in which a malicious member front-runs an honest packet's challenge value to block a target from ever processing the honest packet). O-FREEK is a second, optimally secure FR-CGKA construction achieving the strongest security predicate the paper defines (every epoch is secure unless keeping it secure would be logically inconsistent with protocol correctness), built by extending a technique from prior work (cited as [ACJM20]) that uses hierarchical identity-based encryption (HIBE, a public-key encryption scheme whose secret keys form a tree-shaped hierarchy, where a key at one node can derive keys for all its descendants but reveals nothing about ciphertexts encrypted to non-descendant identities) restricted to a binary identity space (binary-tree encryption, BtPke), combined with an analogous hierarchical identity-based signature scheme (binary-tree signatures) for authenticity, and a puncturing mechanism built on top of BtPke to prevent two attack classes specific to the FR-CGKA setting: cross-fork attacks (in which a single retained secret key remains valid across multiple forked epochs simultaneously, so corrupting one member after it "moves on" from one fork branch still exposes secrets in a sibling branch it never officially left) and collusion attacks (in which an unpunctured shared secret, combined with a second corrupted member's independently retained key, jointly reconstructs a group key that neither compromise alone should expose).

### Measured results
This is a theory paper: its contributions are formal security definitions, two protocol constructions, and machine-checkable-style security proofs (game-based reductions), not empirical benchmarks. No experimental measurements — no node counts, wall-clock timings, message-size measurements from a running implementation, or comparable numeric performance figures with stated conditions — appear in the paper; the authors state FREEK is intended as "practical" and O-FREEK as having "only theoretical efficiency" (their own characterization, not a benchmarked figure), and no implementation or deployment is described.
- Structural complexity claim (context, not a new measurement of this paper): CGKA protocols in general reduce the O(n) communication and computation cost of pre-CGKA group-messaging protocols for operations like member removal or a forward-secrecy-refreshing update to O(log n), under mild assumptions about client online/offline behavior — a property informally called "fair-weather complexity." The paper attributes this comparison figure to prior work on pre-CGKA protocols (cited as [Fou23a, MP22, Wha23, HLA19]), not to a measurement of its own.
- Comparison to Matrix, DCGKA [WKHB21], and [CEST22] (stated as an existing-system property drawn from those works, not remeasured here): each already supports the natural-fork-resolution pattern this paper targets for CGKA, but none achieves CGKA's fair-weather logarithmic complexity — removing a group member requires O(n) download bandwidth per client in each of them, as does a single post-compromise-security (PCS) update.
- Comparison to distributed MLS (dMLS, an experimental Matrix-team modification of MLS cited as [Mat23b]): dMLS achieves the ability to process packets in any causality-respecting order (the same headline property FR-CGKA targets), but the paper states it does so "at the cost of seriously weakening forward secrecy," concretely because dMLS stores old secrets rather than deleting them — corrupting a client while it still holds a "move pebble" on an old epoch can reveal the epoch keys, and therefore the message contents, of every descendant epoch of that node, even ones the client has already logically "moved past." FREEK is designed specifically to avoid this: the paper states FREEK keeps those descendant-epoch keys secure.
- FREEK vs. its base protocol SAIK: the paper proves that when FREEK is restricted to operate as an ordinary CGKA (each member keeps only a single "current" move pebble, immediately discarding the old one on every transition, matching how SAIK behaves), FREEK achieves the identical CGKA security level as SAIK — the two become "almost equivalent" because FREEK's puncturing operations become vacuous once old pebbles are always deleted immediately.
- O-FREEK's security predicate is explicitly the optimal one (P = false in the paper's general predicate framework): every epoch is secure except where insecurity is logically forced by protocol correctness.

### Parameters
- The paper does not fix concrete numeric parameters (group sizes, key lengths, PPRF/HIBE security-parameter bit widths) anywhere in the main body; all constructions are described and analyzed asymptotically or via formal security-game reductions, with cryptographic primitives (PPRF, HIBE/BtPke, HIBS/BtSig, mmPKE — multi-message multi-recipient public-key encryption) treated as black boxes satisfying stated security properties (one-wayness with adaptive corruptions for the PPRF; RCCA, a relaxation of chosen-ciphertext security, plus one-wayness for mmPKE; unforgeability for the signature scheme).
- O-FREEK's BtPke puncturing structure: a client's secret key for parent epoch U, once it needs to be punctured on a descendant epoch V, is represented as a binary tree of height |V| (the number of epochs, i.e., the fork-branch depth, since the key was inserted into the client's state) — the paper does not give this as a numeric benchmark, but this height-scales-with-history-depth structure is the concrete mechanical basis for the paper's own characterization of O-FREEK as having "only theoretical efficiency," recorded here as a structural fact traceable to the construction rather than as the authors' bare assertion.

### Stated limitations
The paper states O-FREEK, despite achieving the strongest (optimal) security predicate defined, has only theoretical efficiency, in explicit contrast to FREEK, which is presented as the practical construction — no numeric threshold or benchmark is given for what makes O-FREEK impractical, only the structural fact (noted above) that its punctured keys scale with fork-branch depth.

FREEK's security predicate is explicitly weaker than optimal: the paper states this stems from certain secrets (the init secret and the MAC key) being shared among all group members rather than personalized per member, so an adversary that merely holds a move pebble for any one member on a parent epoch U — not necessarily the specific target member — gains enough shared secret material to help compromise a child epoch V, whereas the optimal predicate would require compromising the specific target member's own state on U.

The paper explicitly does not solve, and states as an open design question, how to choose which epoch a fork-resolving client should base its new current epoch on: the choice affects each member's transition cost, and constructing a long chain of resolution steps can destroy TreeKEM's normally logarithmic communication cost, degrading it to "super-logarithmic"; the authors state there is no one-size-fits-all solution, since different applications may want to minimize average transition cost versus minimizing cost for a subset of resource-constrained clients (e.g., IoT devices).

The example fork-resolution protocol given (Section 6) is explicitly presented as "a proof of concept" demonstrating that the pebbling abstraction and FR-CGKA together can support natural fork resolution, not as a complete or optimized fork-resolution system; the paper states it reuses an existing state-resolution algorithm from Matrix's specification (cited as [Fou23b]) rather than designing a new one.

The paper's related-work discussion states that prior concurrent-CGKA protocols (cited as [AAN+22b, AAN+22a, BDG+22, BMO+18]) support concurrent post-compromise-security updates only within a single epoch: once a client applies one or more concurrently generated updates, it enters a new epoch and can no longer process any other event still pertaining to the old epoch, including delayed packets — the paper characterizes this as "only a very limited type of fork resilience," which the FR-CGKA construction in this paper is designed to go beyond.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
- Any fork-resolution procedure built on FR-CGKA needs the underlying transport to guarantee only causality-respecting delivery per sender-receiver pair (packets from the same origin to the same destination arrive in the order sent) — the paper states an otherwise-unreliable network satisfying only this property already suffices to deliver packets in "arbitrary but causality respecting order," which is the exact class of delivery order FR-CGKA is designed to tolerate; a network that reorders even same-origin, same-destination traffic is not covered.
- A client must retain enough of its pebbled-history-graph state (move, visited, and key pebbles per known epoch) to determine which of its missing packets it can still process; deleting move or key pebbles is safe at any time (it only forgets keys the client no longer needs), but a visited pebble, once placed, can never be removed, because its presence records that a cryptographic secret required to reprocess that transition has already been irreversibly used or deleted — a client that discards this bookkeeping loses the ability to correctly determine which delayed packets remain processable.
- FREEK specifically requires the challenge value punctured into the PPRF key to be derived from a commitment to the new epoch's public state plus half the freshly generated commit secret, not from the commit secret alone and not from an unauthenticated value attached to the packet; the paper's own analysis shows that either alternative reopens either a forward-secrecy leak (through what a punctured PPRF key can reveal, notably for common Goldreich-Goldwasser-Micali/GGM-tree-based PPRF constructions) or a denial-of-service vector where a malicious member preempts an honest packet's challenge to block a target from ever accepting it.
- O-FREEK's optimal-security guarantee depends on every group member ratcheting (updating and puncturing) its own hierarchical key material at every epoch transition it processes, including transitions across fork branches; a client design that keeps a single long-lived key across multiple fork branches reopens the cross-fork attack the paper identifies, in which one retained secret key remains valid for decrypting or signing in more than one branch of a fork simultaneously.
- The paper's formal model treats an untrusted server or mailboxing service purely as an availability mechanism — the agreement, confidentiality, and authenticity guarantees of FR-CGKA do not rely on that server behaving correctly, honestly, or consistently, but a client still needs some delivery mechanism (server-relayed, peer-to-peer gossip, or otherwise) that eventually gets it the packets it is missing, since FR-CGKA's own guarantees say nothing about whether or when a given packet arrives.
- The paper's Section 1 explicitly frames FR-CGKA as the CGKA-level piece needed before a decentralized or federated messaging system (its own example: a group split across two host servers whose inter-server link goes down) can support scalable fork resolution — but the paper does not itself construct or evaluate a complete fork-resolution protocol beyond the Section 6 proof of concept, so a system adopting FR-CGKA still needs to supply its own state-resolution algorithm (the paper points to the Matrix specification's algorithm, [Fou23b], as one usable building block) and its own policy for which epoch to resolve onto (left as the unresolved design question noted above).

### Contradicts
None found against other entries in this batch. The paper's own comparison to dMLS ([Mat23b]) states that dMLS achieves causality-respecting packet processing only by weakening forward secrecy relative to what standard CGKA (and this paper's own FREEK) guarantees — this is presented as a design tradeoff the paper's authors identify in a competing system, not a disagreement about a measured figure.

### References worth retrieving
- foundational: Alwen, Coretti, Jost, Mularczyk, "Continuous Group Key Agreement with Active Security," cited as [ACJM20] — source of the hierarchical-identity-based-encryption technique O-FREEK extends for optimal CGKA security, and of the cross-fork-attack concept this paper generalizes to the fork-resilient setting; likely the closest prior formal definition of Fork-Resilience under a centralized delivery service that BeeKEM's Cross-Fork Security proof needs to be checked against.
- foundational: Alwen, Hartmann, Kiltz, Mularczyk, "Server-Aided Continuous Group Key Agreement," cited as [AHKM22a]/[AHKM22b] — SAIK, the base protocol FREEK is built on.
- foundational: Alwen, Coretti, Dodis, Tselekounis, "Security Analysis and Improvements for the IETF MLS Standard for Group Messaging," CRYPTO 2020, cited as [ACDT20] — this is ALWEN-CRYPTO-20, already a target in this corpus; the TreeKEM security baseline SAIK and this paper's FR-CGKA build on.
- competing: The Matrix.org Foundation, "Matrix Specification" [Fou23a] and "Matrix State Resolution" [Fou23b] — the natural-fork-resolution paradigm and state-resolution algorithm this paper adapts and compares against, at O(n) download bandwidth per removal/update rather than CGKA's O(log n).
- competing: Weidner, Kleppmann, Hugenroth, Beresford, DCGKA protocol, cited as [WKHB21] — a competing fork-tolerant group-key-agreement design using the natural-fork-resolution paradigm without CGKA's fair-weather efficiency; the direct predecessor line to BeeKEM per this corpus's brief.
