## [ALWEN-EUROCRYPT-22] CoCoA: Concurrent Continuous Group Key Agreement
**Citation:** Joël Alwen, Benedikt Auerbach, Miguel Cueto Noval, Karen Klein, Guillermo Pascual-Perez, Krzysztof Pietrzak, Michael Walter. "CoCoA: Concurrent Continuous Group Key Agreement." EUROCRYPT, 2022. DOI 10.1007/978-3-031-07085-3_28.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://eprint.iacr.org/2022/251.pdf
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2022/251.pdf
**Domain:** H

### What it does
CoCoA (COncurrent COntinuous group key Agreement) is a continuous group key agreement (CGKA) protocol — a protocol letting an evolving group of clients continuously derive a shared symmetric group key across a sequence of epochs, each epoch beginning when a member joins, leaves, or updates (refreshes) its own cryptographic key material — designed so that many members can update concurrently without the per-user communication cost this normally forces. CoCoA still relies on a centralized, untrusted delivery server that batches operations into synchronized rounds and forwards them, so it operates under the same total-ordering-of-delivery assumption as TreeKEM (the protocol underlying the IETF's Messaging Layer Security, MLS, draft standard) and other prior CGKA protocols; its contribution is handling many members updating within the same round efficiently, not removing the ordering requirement itself.

Mechanism. Members sit at the leaves of a ratchet tree — the same binary-tree structure TreeKEM uses, where each node holds a public/private key pair and a member knows the private keys on the path from its leaf to the root. In prior TreeKEM-family protocols, when several members submit concurrent update requests within one round, the delivery server accepts exactly one and rejects the rest, forcing the losers to retry. CoCoA's server instead attempts to apply every submitted update: if two or more updates target the same tree node in a round, the server arbitrarily picks one winner for that node, but every update still contributes progress elsewhere in the tree. The paper's proved result is that this merging strategy guarantees all previously compromised members recover full security (achieve post-compromise security, PCS — the property that a group's security is restored once a compromised member updates and communication continues normally) within at most ⌈log(n)⌉+1 rounds of such merged concurrent updates, regardless of how the server breaks ties, where n is the number of group members. To keep per-update packet size low despite concurrent merging, CoCoA is server-aided: rather than broadcasting one packet to be relayed unchanged to everyone (as plain TreeKEM does), the untrusted server actively computes an individualized packet tailored to each recipient, containing only the ciphertexts and public keys relevant to that member's own path in the tree; this requires new mechanisms (explicit signatures on protocol messages, and a parent-hash-based consistency check across members' partial views) to keep every member's partial view of the shared tree state consistent despite no member seeing the full tree, since the paper's security proof shows that undetected disagreement between members — for example, about tree membership — can lead to serious security failures.

Trade-off circumvented and its cost. A prior lower bound (Bienstock, Dodis, Rösler, cited as [BDR20]) shows that any concurrent-update mechanism completing in at most 2 rounds must incur communication cost at least linear in the number of concurrently updating members T, and Omega(n^2) total if all n members update concurrently within 2 rounds. CoCoA circumvents this specific bound by using up to ⌈log(n)⌉+1 rounds instead of 2, at which point every member's cumulative communication (sending and receiving) across the whole healing process is only order log(n)^2 (i.e., (log n) squared) ciphertexts, rather than growing linearly or worse in n or T. Unlike the "propose-and-commit" concurrency mechanism MLS adopted (in which committing to T concurrently proposed updates leaves the T members' tree paths blanked, degrading future commit-packet size toward linear in n until those blanks are later repaired), CoCoA's merge-based approach never blanks tree nodes during concurrent operation, so it does not degrade the cost of subsequent, later updates.

Security-model assumption. The paper's security proof holds against a "partially active" adversary: the adversary can adaptively leak any member's full local state (including random coins) at will and can send arbitrary, even malformed, messages as the untrusted server, but cannot forge protocol messages as an honest member because it never obtains members' signing keys through corruption. The authors state this is a common but strong assumption for this line of work, and explicitly identify proving CoCoA secure against a fully active adversary (one that can forge as a corrupted member) as an open question for future work.

### Measured results
This is a theory paper: its quantitative results are asymptotic communication-complexity bounds derived from the protocol's construction and proved via formal security reduction, not measurements from a running implementation on real hardware, node counts, or network conditions — no implementation, deployment, or benchmarked wall-clock/bandwidth figures are reported anywhere in the paper.

Table 5 (the paper's own comparison of CGKA protocols' communication complexity) gives Big-O bounds under a fixed comparison setting: a group of n members, t of which have been compromised, with the ratchet tree assumed fully unblanked at the start, comparing scenario (a) — the group knows it has been compromised but not which t members — against scenario (b) — the compromised set is publicly known, so only those t members must act:

| Protocol | Rounds to heal | Cumulative sender comm. (a) | Cumulative sender comm. (b) | Per-user recipient comm. (a/b) | Subsequent per-user update cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Original TreeKEM & variants [ACDT20, BBR+23, KPPW+21, Mat19] | n (a) / t (b) | n log(n) | t log(n) | n log(n) / t log(n) | log(n) |
| Propose-commit TreeKEM [BBR+23] | 2 | n^2 (uncoordinated) / n (coordinated) | t^2(1+log(n/t)) / t(1+log(n/t)) | n / t(1+log(n/t)) | up to n (a) / up to t(1+log(n/t)) (b), degraded by blanking |
| Bienstock et al. [BDR20] | 2 | n^2 / n | t^2(1+log(n/t)) / t(1+log(n/t)) | n (uncoordinated: n^2) / t(1+log(n/t)) | log(n) worst case, but only in a weak security model — matches propose-commit TreeKEM once strengthened to comparable PCS via tainting |
| Bidirectional channels [WKHB21] | 2 | n^2 | tn | n / t | n |
| CoCoA (this work) | ⌈log(n)⌉+1 | n·log(n)^2 | t·log(n)^2 | log(n)^2 (a) / log(n)·min(t,log(n)) (b) | log(n) |

Conditions for this table: ratchet-tree-based protocols assumed to start fully unblanked; "coordination" distinguishes whether concurrently updating members know of each other's in-flight updates (avoiding server-rejected packets) versus not; all non-O() entries in the last five columns are to be read as O(x) per the table's own note; the Bienstock et al. entry's uncoordinated-case recipient communication is separately stated as n^2 (case a) / t^2(1+log(n/t)) (case b).

Transition-from-fully-blanked-to-fully-unblanked-tree comparison (a stated worked example, not a separate experiment): TreeKEM needs n/2 rounds, with per-user recipient complexity (ciphertexts downloaded) of order n·log(n); the Bienstock et al. protocol unblanks the whole tree in 2 rounds at linear sender and recipient communication per user; CoCoA unblanks the tree in 1 round at linear sender cost but only logarithmic (order log(n)) recipient cost per user.

Per-round state a CoCoA user needs (a structural, derived figure rather than an experimental one): to process an update, a CoCoA user needs only order log(n) secret keys and about 2·log(n) public keys — far less than the full 2n−1 public keys in the shared ratchet-tree state — because the server delivers only individualized, per-recipient packets rather than the shared broadcast every prior TreeKEM-family protocol relies on.

Theorem 1 (correctness/robustness under encryption/signature security): if the encryption scheme CoCoA uses is IND-CPA-secure (indistinguishable under chosen-plaintext attack) and the signature scheme is UF-CMA-secure (existentially unforgeable under chosen-message attack), the stated robustness property holds; this is a reduction-based proof, not a numeric measurement, and the paper states the proof follows from corresponding results in prior work ([KPPW+21]) applied to the general public-key group-state-distribution (GSD) result in the random-oracle model.

### Parameters
- Group size n and number of compromised members t, treated as free asymptotic variables throughout; no concrete numeric group size is tested or benchmarked.
- Rounds to heal from compromise: exactly ⌈log(n)⌉+1 in the paper's proved worst case, though the paper states "typically fewer rounds" suffice in practice (not separately quantified).
- Per-user cumulative communication after full concurrent healing: order n·log(n)^2 total across all users (case a) or t·log(n)^2 (case b, only compromised users act), i.e. each acting user's own share is order log(n)^2.
- Per-user local knowledge requirement: order log(n) secret keys and order 2·log(n) public keys, versus the full 2n−1 public keys a member would need to track the entire shared ratchet tree in prior non-server-aided protocols.
- Security-parameter lambda: referenced only abstractly (`CGKA.Gen(1^lambda)` in the formal syntax) with no concrete bit-length instantiated or tested.

### Stated limitations
The paper's security proof (Theorem 1 and the surrounding security-model discussion) applies only to a "partially active" adversary that can adaptively leak any member's local state and send arbitrary server-side messages but cannot forge protocol messages, because it never obtains signing keys through corruption; the authors state extending the analysis to a "fully active" adversary — one that also compromises the ability to forge on behalf of corrupted members — is an important open question left for future work.

The lower bound the protocol circumvents ([BDR20]) applies only to protocols that complete concurrent healing within 2 rounds; the authors state their circumvention is achieved specifically by trading additional interaction (up to ⌈log(n)⌉+1 rounds instead of 2) for lower bandwidth, and explicitly frame this as a trade-off, not a free improvement: "we are paying a log(n) factor in sender communication in exchange for faster PCS that is independent from the number of compromised users" relative to non-concurrent pre-propose-and-commit TreeKEM, and "this comes at the cost of slower healing and a factor of log^2(n)... in sender communication cost" relative to propose-commit TreeKEM specifically when many members need to heal quickly.

Signature-key distribution is stated as an unavoidable Omega(n) communication cost independent of round count or concurrency: distributing n fresh signature verification keys (one per updating member) to every other group member inherently costs order n communication for each recipient, because every member must know every other member's current verification key to authenticate packets. The paper's mitigation — "lite updates," which refresh all of a member's secret key material except its signature key — is explicitly described by the authors as "not ideal from a security perspective," offered only as a practical way to avoid the cost of re-certifying signature keys (which the paper notes may require an external, slow process such as manual certificate authority issuance) on every key refresh.

The paper's own concluding comparison states CoCoA's bandwidth is not universally superior: it states CoCoA "seems to have a slightly worse efficiency than TreeKEM based protocols predating the propose-and-commit paradigm" when only a single member needs to heal (a case where CoCoA reduces to ordinary sequential TreeKEM-like behavior and grants immediate PCS to a lone updater, matching that baseline), and the stated bandwidth advantage of CoCoA's approach is conditional on "fast PCS... required for many users" concurrently.

The paper explicitly separates "corrupted parties known" (scenario b) from "corrupted parties unknown" (scenario a) as materially different costs throughout Table 5 and its surrounding discussion, and does not claim a mechanism for a group to determine which case applies in a real deployment — this determination is treated as an external input to the protocol, not something CoCoA itself resolves.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
- CoCoA still requires a stateful, synchronized-round delivery mechanism: the untrusted server "works in rounds, collects operations into batches and sends them out at the end of each round" (the paper's own formal definition, Section 2.1) — this is the same total-ordering-of-delivered-messages structure TreeKEM/MLS depends on, only batched rather than one-message-at-a-time; a fully asynchronous, unordered, or partition-tolerant delivery layer that cannot guarantee this per-round batching and consistent per-session delivery is outside what CoCoA's security proof covers.
- The delivery server must actively compute individualized, per-recipient packets rather than relaying one broadcast packet verbatim, because CoCoA members deliberately do not track the full shared ratchet-tree state; a deployment that wants to keep the delivery server as a "dumb" relay (as plain TreeKEM allows) cannot adopt CoCoA's bandwidth savings, since those savings specifically depend on server-side computation tailored to each recipient's partial view.
- Every group member must be able to verify every other member's signature-verification key; the paper states distributing n fresh signature keys costs at least order n communication per recipient regardless of round count, so any system layer that wants to avoid this floor needs a separate mechanism (the paper's own suggestion is "lite updates" that refresh all secret material except the signature key, explicitly presented as a security-availability trade-off, not a solution that removes the cost).
- The protocol's security proof assumes the adversary cannot forge protocol messages on behalf of corrupted members — that is, it assumes signing keys of corrupted members are not accessible to the adversary through the corruption model used in the proof; a deployment where an attacker can otherwise obtain or forge valid signatures (for example, via a compromised certificate authority or signing-key-extraction attack) is outside the threat model this specific security result covers, and the paper flags a fully active adversary as unresolved future work.
- CoCoA's consistency mechanism (parent-hash checks and explicit signatures across individualized packets) exists specifically because, unlike prior CGKA protocols where the majority of what one member uploads is downloaded by everyone, CoCoA's uploaded and downloaded communication for a given member diverge substantially — any composition with a different transport or storage layer needs to preserve the property that every member can independently verify its partial-tree view is consistent with the rest of the group, or the paper's stated attack surface (severe security failures from undetected member disagreement, e.g. about group membership) reopens.

### Contradicts
None found against other entries in this batch. Within the paper's own comparison, it explicitly contradicts an implicit assumption that concurrent CGKA updates must cost either the Bienstock-et-al.-style Omega(T) per-round communication or the propose-and-commit-style future-blanking penalty: CoCoA achieves neither, at the stated cost of needing up to log(n)+1 rounds rather than 2.

### References worth retrieving
- foundational: Bhargavan, Barnes, Rescorla, "TreeKEM: Asynchronous Decryption-Key Update for Secure Group Messaging," cited as [BBR18] — the original TreeKEM proposal, including its early (later-dropped) concurrent-conflict handling that this paper's CoCoA formalizes and analyzes.
- foundational: Alwen, Coretti, Dodis, Tselekounis, "Security Analysis and Improvements for the IETF MLS Standard for Group Messaging," CRYPTO 2020, cited as [ACDT20] — this is ALWEN-CRYPTO-20, already a target in this corpus; the non-concurrent TreeKEM security baseline this paper's Table 5 compares against directly.
- competing: Bienstock, Dodis, Rösler, "On the Price of Concurrency in Group Ratcheting Protocols," cited as [BDR20] — source of the Omega(T) / Omega(n^2) lower bound this paper explicitly circumvents by using more rounds; contains the closest direct comparison numbers (Table 5's "Bienstock et al." row).
- competing: Weidner, Kleppmann, Hugenroth, Beresford, "Key Agreement for Decentralized Secure Group Messaging with Strong Security Guarantees," cited as [WKHB21] — a decentralized, bidirectional-channel-based CGKA the paper compares directly in Table 5 (linear communication complexity, explicitly called "impractical" by this paper's authors "in the contexts we are interested in"); this is the DCGKA line that the brief identifies as BeeKEM's direct predecessor.
- competing: Weidner, "Group Messaging for Secure Asynchronous Collaboration," Master's thesis, cited as [Mat19] — Causal TreeKEM, which re-randomizes rather than overwrites node secrets to support a form of concurrency, but which the paper states "lacks forward secrecy and a complete security proof."
- competing: Klein, Pascual-Perez, Walter, Kamath, Capretto, et al., cited as [KPPW+21] — Tainted TreeKEM (TTKEM), the source of the security model and GSD (group-state-distribution) proof technique this paper's own Theorem 1 builds on, and a direct comparison point in Table 5.
- foundational: Alwen, Coretti, Jost, Mularczyk, "Continuous Group Key Agreement with Active Security," cited as [ACJM20] — source of the "ideal/real" CGKA security notion against fully active adversaries that this paper's own security model falls short of, explicitly marked as future work here.
- competing: Alwen, Hartmann, Kiltz, Mularczyk, "Server-Aided Continuous Group Key Agreement," cited as [AHKM22] — the server-aided CGKA line CoCoA's individualized-packet mechanism is built in the same spirit as; this is the SAIK protocol that ALWEN-CRYPTO-23 (Fork-Resilient CGKA) builds FREEK on top of, already a target in this corpus.
- foundational/critique: Cohn-Gordon, Cremers, Garratt, Millican, Milner, "On Ends-to-Ends Encryption: Asynchronous Group Messaging with Strong Security Guarantees," cited as [CCG+18] — the ART protocol, credited by this paper as initiating the study of logarithmic-complexity E2E group protocols and the CGKA research line generally.

- "the delivery server no longer blindly forwards packets, but instead actively computes individualized packets"

## [ALWEN-EUROSP-17] Towards Practical Attacks on Argon2i and Balloon Hashing
**Citation:** Joël Alwen, Jeremiah Blocki. "Towards Practical Attacks on Argon2i and Balloon Hashing." IEEE European Symposium on Security and Privacy (EuroS&P), 2017. DOI 10.1109/EuroSP.2017.47.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://eprint.iacr.org/2016/759.pdf
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2016/759.pdf
**Domain:** I

### What it does
The paper reduces the memory an attacker needs to evaluate a data-independent memory-hard function (iMHF) — a key-stretching function, used to slow brute-force password guessing, whose memory-access pattern does not depend on the secret input and so resists timing side-channel attacks — well below the memory the honest algorithm uses, for Argon2i-A (the Password Hashing Competition winner), Argon2i-B (the version proposed to the Internet Research Task Force as a password-hashing standard), and Balloon Hashing. An iMHF's evaluation corresponds to pebbling a directed acyclic graph (DAG) in which each node is a memory block and each edge is a data dependency: computing a node's label requires holding its parents' labels in memory. The attack, extending Alwen and Blocki's CRYPTO 2016 construction, computes a small depth-reducing set S of graph nodes such that deleting S from the DAG leaves only short paths; an attacker recomputes the values in S on demand instead of storing them, trading extra computation for a large memory reduction, at attack quality (the ratio of the honest algorithm's cost to the attack's amortized cost, where a ratio above 1 counts as a working attack) that grows with the number of memory blocks. The paper's own contribution is threefold: extending the theoretical attack to Argon2i-B (not previously analyzed), for which it proves attack quality Θ(N^0.2) by constructing a depth-reducing set of size Θ(N^(4/5)) that leaves a residual graph of depth N^(3/5) (N being the total number of memory-block computations, τ passes times σ table size); introducing heuristics — a smaller depth-reducing set construction and an "XOR compression" trick — that improve the attack's concrete efficiency even when the attacker's on-chip memory bandwidth is bounded; and simulating the attack on randomly sampled instances of all three algorithms to measure memory consumption for practical parameter ranges (up to 16-24 GB) and for varying limits on attacker parallelism. Cost is measured as energy complexity (an estimate of the physical energy an attack hardware implementation would consume), which the paper states tightly approximates area-time complexity for the class of attacks considered.

### Measured results
| Metric | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Argon2i-B attack quality at 1 GB, τ=6 passes | Reduces cost by a factor of 2 | Simulated attack on random Argon2i-B DAGs, memory parameter M=1GB, "paranoid" pass count from the IRTF proposal; 10 random graph samples per data point, results varying only in the 2nd-3rd significant digit across samples |
| Passes needed to defeat the attack at 1 GB | More than 10 passes (τ>10) required for the attack to fail against 1 GB Argon2i-B | Same simulation setup; compared against the IRTF proposal's own maximum recommended "paranoid" setting of 6 passes |
| Argon2i-B attack quality, minimal-memory recommended setting | Approximately 5 at 1 GB, approximately 9.3 at 16 GB | τ=1 pass, parameters chosen by the IRTF proposal's own stated selection procedure (maximize memory for a fixed time budget, which yields τ=1 in memory-rich/impatient-user settings) |
| Argon2i-A attack quality at τ=4 passes | Greater than 4 | Simulated attack, n and σ varied 2^17-2^24 nodes, τ∈{1,3,4}, compared directly against Argon2i-B under the same parameters (Figure 2) |
| Balloon Hashing (BH) vs Argon2i-B | BH attack quality increases faster with memory usage than Argon2i-B's at matched n and τ; BH is stated to be less resistant than Argon2i-B | Label size B=512 bytes for BH vs B=1024 bytes (Blake2b) for Argon2i-B; τ=1, n=2^24 gives M=8GB for BH vs M=16GB for Argon2i-B under equal node counts |
| Maximum attacker parallelism required | 1,324 cores for the hardest tested Argon2i-B instance (τ=1, M=16GB); 1,496 cores for the hardest Argon2i-A instance (same M, τ) | Across the full simulated parameter sweep, n∈{2^17,...,2^24}, τ∈{1,3,4,6,10,20} for Argon2i-B/BH, τ∈{1,3,4} for Argon2i-A |
| On-chip memory bandwidth required, worst case | About 2 TB/s (M=1GB, τ=1 pass); about 0.6 TB/s for 4-pass Argon2i-B at 1GB | Derived assuming 1.5 GB/s bandwidth needed per Blake2b compression-function core (extrapolated from an implemented 4-core, 8-thread Argon2i-B measurement of 5.8 GB/s aggregate [Biryukov, Dinu, Khovratovich, Table 4]); compared against then-current AMD Radeon R9 Fury (512 GB/s) and emerging Samsung HBM2 (>1 TB/s) hardware |
| Effect of bounding parallelism | Attack quality for Argon2i-B peaks near parallelism p=200 and can decrease beyond that point; for Argon2i-A quality rises almost monotonically with p, flattening at higher p | Fixed M=1GB (σ=2^20), p tested at {25,50,100,200,500,750,1000}, τ∈{1,4,7,10}, 10 random graph instances per configuration |
| Multi-lane Argon2i attack quality | Attack quality >1.18 against 4-lane Argon2i-B (τ=4, σ=2^17, p=4), versus no working attack (quality <1, specifically 0.89) against the equivalent single-lane 4-pass Argon2i-B at the same per-lane memory | Hand-selected attack parameters (gap=32, #layers=256, g=13,970); demonstrates the Argon2i multi-lane parent-selection rule (parents drawn across lanes) reduces resistance to this attack relative to running independent single-lane instances |
| iXOR (indegree-21, XOR-and-high-indegree hardening) attack quality | With the paper's added "XOR compression" heuristic, 3-pass iXOR and 6-pass Argon2i-B show roughly equivalent attack quality | iXOR = Argon2i-A modified to draw 20 additional random parents per node and XOR their labels before compression, modeling the Corrigan-Gibbs et al. hardening technique used in BH-Double-Buffer |

### Parameters
- Memory parameter σ (table size) and timing parameter τ (pass count): swept over n=στ ∈ {2^17, 2^18, ..., 2^24} and τ ∈ {1, 3, 4, 6, 10, 20} for Argon2i-B and BH; τ ∈ {1, 3, 4} for Argon2i-A.
- Compression-function output/label size B: 1024 bytes for Argon2i (Blake2b-based); 512 bytes for Balloon Hashing (except a 1344-byte variant using SHA3, not the one plotted).
- Attacker parallelism p, explicitly bounded in one experiment set: {25, 50, 100, 200, 500, 750, 1000} at fixed M=1GB; {25, 50, 100, 200, 500, 1000} in the fixed-runtime (n=2^24) variant.
- Assumed memory bandwidth per attacker compute core: 1.5 GB/s, taken as a reference point derived from an implemented Argon2i-B measurement of 5.8 GB/s on 4 cores.
- iXOR indegree: 21 (1 sequential parent plus 20 random parents), matching the original BH-Double-Buffer construction's indegree.
- Multi-lane example parameters: τ=4, σ=2^17, p=4 lanes (n=2^19).
- Number of random graph samples per data point: 10, with reported variation confined to the 2nd-3rd significant digit of measured attack cost.

### Stated limitations
The authors state their understanding of Argon2i-A and Argon2i-B security remains incomplete after this work, and list as open questions whether the attack on Argon2i-B can be further improved and whether a matching lower bound on Argon2i-B's energy complexity can be proved. They state the multi-lane attack result is not fully optimized: they conjecture attack quality on multi-lane Argon2i-A and Argon2i-B can be improved further with additional parameter and heuristic tuning, and explicitly leave this as future research rather than a result they establish. The paper notes it focuses its main simulation results on the single-lane variant of each iMHF because, combined with the "trivial" (independent-instance) approach to parallelism, single-lane constructions are more resistant to this attack than the Argon2i design's cross-lane parent-selection rule — meaning the headline attack-quality numbers understate the effect against the deployed multi-lane configuration. The authors state that prior observers (the Argon2 authors and others) had argued the original Alwen-Blocki attack does not threaten real-world Argon2 security because of large constants hidden in the asymptotic bounds and because a literal hardware implementation would need memory bandwidth beyond then-available technology; the current paper's stated purpose is to test, not assume, those objections, and it reports the concrete simulated numbers rather than asserting the asymptotic result alone.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A system choosing Argon2i-B (or another data-independent MHF) as a password-hashing or key-stretching primitive must select the pass count τ knowing that quality-2 or better memory-reduction attacks exist against low pass counts at practical memory sizes (e.g., τ=6 at 1GB), so the choice of τ trades directly against user-perceived latency: the paper states that increasing τ multiplies running time by τ, and that human users have limited tolerance for authentication delay (on the order of 1-2 seconds cited as the tolerance window in the source text). Any parameter-selection procedure for this class of MHF needs an explicit joint choice of memory σ and passes τ; the paper states the IRTF proposal's own selection procedure (fix memory first from available hardware, then pick the maximum τ affordable in the time budget) tends to produce τ=1 in memory-rich or impatience-constrained deployments, which the measured results show is the parameter region most vulnerable to this attack. A deployment relying on the multi-lane parallel Argon2i construction for throughput must account for the measured finding that cross-lane parent selection reduces attack resistance relative to running independent single-lane instances in parallel; choosing single-lane Argon2i and parallelizing across independent instances instead preserves the stronger resistance this paper measures. Any claim that a hardening technique (such as XOR-and-high-indegree) increases attacker cost needs re-verification under this paper's optimized attack, because the XOR-compression heuristic introduced here is shown to substantially reduce the naive cost increase that technique otherwise imposes.

### Contradicts
The paper contradicts the informal industry consensus, attributed in its own text to the Argon2 designers (Biryukov, Dinu, Khovratovich) and to Khovratovich and Aumasson, that the original Alwen-Blocki (CRYPTO 2016) attack "does not present a threat to the real world security of Argon2-B (or BH)" because of large asymptotic constants and infeasible hardware bandwidth requirements; this paper's simulated results show the attack reduces cost by a factor of 2 against Argon2i-B at 1 GB memory and τ=6 passes, within the IRTF proposal's own recommended parameter space, and states the IRTF proposal's security analysis had omitted this attack from consideration. No contradiction with another paper in this corpus was found (BIRYUKOV-EUROSP-16, the Argon2 paper itself, is the object of this critique rather than an independent measurement disagreement — see BIRYUKOV-EUROSP-16's entry for the corresponding attribution).

### References worth retrieving
- **Foundational**: J. Alwen, J. Blocki. "Efficiently computing data-independent memory-hard functions." CRYPTO, 2016. [AB16] (the attack this paper extends and simulates.)
- **Foundational**: C. Percival. "Stronger key derivation via sequential memory-hard functions." BSDCan, 2009. [Per09] (introduces memory-hard functions.)
- **Foundational/superseded-by**: A. Biryukov, D. Dinu, D. Khovratovich. "Argon2 password hash." Version 1.3, 2016. [BDK16] (the specification defining Argon2i-A/Argon2i-B; see BIRYUKOV-EUROSP-16.)
- **Foundational**: A. Biryukov, D. Dinu, D. Khovratovich, S. Josefsson. "The memory-hard Argon2 password hash and proof-of-work function." IETF Internet-Draft draft-irtf-cfrg-argon2-00, 2016. [BDKJ16] (the IRTF standardization proposal whose parameter-selection guidance this paper critiques.)

[CGBS16a], [CGBS16b] (the Balloon Hashing algorithm and its earlier XOR-and-high-indegree BH-Double-Buffer variant, both attacked in this paper.)

## [ALWEN-SCN-24] DeCAF: Decentralizable CGKA with Fast Healing
**Citation:** Joël Alwen, Benedikt Auerbach, Miguel Cueto Noval, Karen Klein, Guillermo Pascual-Perez, Krzysztof Pietrzak. "DeCAF: Decentralizable CGKA with Fast Healing." Security and Cryptography for Networks (SCN), 2024. DOI 10.1007/978-3-031-71073-5_14.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/629.pdf
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/629.pdf
**Domain:** H

### What it does
DeCAF is a continuous group key agreement (CGKA) protocol: a group of users maintains a shared, continuously updated key while going online only sporadically and having their protocol messages relayed by an untrusted server or, in the decentralized setting the paper targets, posted to an append-only data structure such as a blockchain. DeCAF replaces TreeKEM's key-replacement update with a secretly key-updatable public-key encryption (skuPKE) scheme: an update samples a pair of public and secret update information that transforms an existing key pair into a new one, rather than replacing it outright, so concurrent updates to the same ratchet-tree node can both be applied instead of one being dropped. Each user holds a path from their leaf to the root of a ratchet tree; an update re-randomizes every key on that path and encrypts the new path secrets to the resolution (the set of uncompromised, non-blanked descendants) of each co-path node, exactly as in TreeKEM, but using the update rather than replace operation of skuPKE. Because both concurrent updates to a node are retained instead of one being discarded, a corrupted user heals — has all their leaked secrets replaced by fresh, unknown-to-the-adversary material — after every corrupted user has issued one update and those updates have propagated through ⌊log(t)⌋ + 1 epochs, where t is the number of currently corrupted users, independent of the group size n and independent of which users happen to update. Add and remove operations follow the mechanism already standardized in Messaging Layer Security (MLS), which the paper states eases adoption.

### Measured results
No empirical measurement; all results are asymptotic communication-complexity bounds proved formally, not benchmarked on an implementation.

| Protocol | Concurrent updates | Epochs to heal t corruptions in group of n | Cumulative sender (upload) communication | Per-user recipient (download) communication | Sender cost of one update after healing |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| TreeKEM I (commit-only healing) | No | n | O(n log(n)) | O(n log(n)) | O(log(n)) |
| TreeKEM II (update-proposal healing) | Yes | 2 | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) |
| Causal TreeKEM (Weidner thesis, 2019) | Yes | n | O(n log(n)) | O(n log(n)) | O(log(n)) |
| Bienstock et al. (TCC 2020) | Yes | 2 | O(n²) | O(n²) | O(log(n))* — weak post-compromise security (PCS) only; matching PCS to the others needs O(n) cost after healing |
| Weidner, Kleppmann, Hugenroth, Beresford (CCS 2021, decentralized CGKA / DCGKA) | Yes | 2 | O(n²) | O(n) | O(n) |
| CoCoA (Alwen et al., EUROCRYPT 2022), centralized-server setting | Yes | log(n) | O(n log²(n)) | O(log²(n)) | O(log(n)) |
| CoCoA, decentralized setting (no server crafting per-user messages) | Yes | log(n) | O(n log²(n)) | O(n log(n)²) — loses its recipient-communication advantage | O(log(n)) |
| DeCAF (this paper) | Yes | log(t) | O(n log(n) log(t)) | O(n log(n) log(t)) | O(log(n)) |

Conditions common to every row: n is the group size, t is the number of corrupted users out of n (unknown to the protocol, which does not know its identity is corrupted), and all users are assumed to update every epoch — an assumption the authors state is required for TreeKEM I and Causal TreeKEM to reach the stated epoch counts, and that could be reduced for TreeKEM II, Bienstock et al., and Weidner et al. by an oracle-optimal, unrealizable choice of which users update. The concrete worked example in the paper: for t = 4 corrupted users prioritized left-to-right in the tree, CoCoA needs ⌈log(n)⌉ + 1 = 4 epochs to heal and DeCAF needs ⌊log(t)⌋ + 1 = 2 epochs.

### Parameters
- t: number of corrupted users, unknown to the protocol; the healing time is stated as a function of t, not of which users are corrupted.
- k: a block-batching parameter for the blockchain instantiation — the ratchet tree is updated only every k blocks, so a message referencing a given tree version can be included in any of the next k blocks. The paper states k should not be chosen larger than necessary, because only one update per k-block epoch counts toward healing (unless a corruption occurs strictly between two updates inside the same k-block window). No numeric value for k is given or tested; it is left as an implementation choice.
- Security-proof bound: with an IND-CPA-secure skuPKE instantiation and random-oracle-modeled hash functions, DeCAF is (O(εEnc · 2(nQ²)²), t, Q)-secure in the active-security CGKA game, where εEnc is the skuPKE encryption adversary's advantage, t is adversary running time, and Q is the number of oracle queries in the security game.

### Stated limitations
DeCAF's forward secrecy is stated as slightly weaker than TreeKEM's, because of a potential delay until other users receive and process a given update message — the paper does not quantify this delay. Every user must process every other user's updates (unlike CoCoA, where at most log(n) other updates matter to a given user), so DeCAF's download communication is larger than CoCoA's in the centralized-server setting; the authors state DeCAF and CoCoA are "incomparable" under a central server, with the choice depending on context, and DeCAF is preferable only once the decentralized setting is assumed. Recording every protocol message on a permissionless blockchain is stated as potentially expensive, because permissionless chains such as Bitcoin or Ethereum have slow block-arrival and confirmation times and a nontrivial per-transaction cost; the paper's proposed mitigation — posting only a hash of each block's messages on-chain and keeping the messages off-chain — is stated to lose the robustness property described below unless the data-availability problem is solved separately, which the paper does not address. Deleting outdated ratchet-tree secret keys for forward secrecy must, on a longest-chain (forkable) blockchain, wait until the relevant block is considered confirmed, or a user risks losing group access on a fork; the paper does not give a confirmation-depth value. The comparison to Causal TreeKEM notes that Causal TreeKEM's claimed post-compromise security guarantee — healing in n epochs, with corrupted users unaware of their own corruption — lacks a formal security proof in the source the authors cite (a 2019 master's thesis); DeCAF's own proof is formal.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
DeCAF requires an append-only, agreed-upon transcript of protocol messages available to every group member — instantiated in the paper as a blockchain, but the authors state a single central server suffices structurally, at the price of losing the properties below. The security proof requires an IND-CPA-secure skuPKE scheme (a concrete instantiation from the computational Diffie-Hellman assumption is given) and models the protocol's hash functions as random oracles. Achieving the three properties the paper attributes to the decentralized setting — resistance to server-driven splitting of the group into inconsistent views, resistance to a server censoring one party's messages indefinitely, and robustness to a single point of failure — requires that every protocol message actually be recorded on-chain rather than only hashed on-chain with the payload held off-chain; recording only a hash requires a separately solved data-availability problem that DeCAF does not supply. Preventing indefinite denial-of-service against one user's healing requires the underlying chain to guarantee liveness (a submitted transaction is included within a bounded number of blocks with high probability) and requires DeCAF's own concurrent-update support, because concurrent updates remove the incentive for other users to flood the mempool to keep one user's update out. Forward secrecy requires each user to delete superseded ratchet-tree secret keys, timed to blockchain finality: immediately on a chain with immediate finality, or only after confirmation depth on a longest-chain protocol — DeCAF does not specify what confirmation depth suffices.

### Contradicts
None found within this batch.

- foundational: Auerbach, Cueto Noval, Pascual-Perez, Pietrzak, "On the cost of post-compromise security in concurrent continuous group-key agreement," TCC 2023.
- irrelevant: X. Coin, "Elixxir architecture brief v2.0" (cited only as a prior example of blockchain-backed messaging, not a CGKA construction).

- "CoCoA requires ⌈log(n)⌉ + 1 = 4 epochs to recover, DeCAF only ⌊log(t)⌋ + 1 = 2"
- "in this setting it is outperformed by DeCAF in every aspect" (referring to the decentralized setting)
- "the number of epochs that it takes to heal depends on the number of corrupted parties, but not on relative update behaviour of users"

## [ALWEN-TCC-20] Continuous Group Key Agreement with Active Security
**Citation:** Joël Alwen, Sandro Coretti, Daniel Jost, Marta Mularczyk. "Continuous Group Key Agreement with Active Security." Theory of Cryptography Conference (TCC), 2020. DOI 10.1007/978-3-030-64378-2_10.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://eprint.iacr.org/2020/752.pdf
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2020/752.pdf
**Domain:** H

### What it does
The paper defines the strongest security notion proved to date, at time of publication, for continuous group key agreement (CGKA) — the primitive that lets a long-lived group of parties, each coming online only sporadically and relaying protocol messages through an untrusted server, agree on a continuously refreshed shared secret key — and gives three CGKA constructions meeting different levels of that notion. The definitions are stated as universal composability (UC) functionalities, so proved security holds when the CGKA protocol is used inside a larger system rather than only in isolation. Two prior simplifying assumptions are removed. The "cannot-inject assumption" had assumed the network adversary never forges a protocol message between a party's state compromise and its recovery; removing it means the definitions cover insider attacks, where an adversary uses one party's leaked state to author messages other parties accept. The "no-splitting assumption" had assumed an untrusted delivery service, when multiple parties propose changes concurrently, always picks one proposal and delivers it to everyone; removing it means the definitions cover an adversary that partitions the group into subgroups holding inconsistent, mutually unaware states. "Optimal security" means a produced key is judged insecure only when the protocol's own correctness trivially reveals it to the adversary, not through any modeling shortcut.

Three constructions are given, all built on the TreeKEM/TTKEM ratchet-tree design (each party occupies a leaf, updates a path to the root, and encrypts new secrets to the co-path's resolution) and formally proved to meet these definitions:
- P-Pas, for a passive-but-adaptive network adversary (permits reordering and dropping messages, forbids forged messages): built by replacing plain public-key encryption with hierarchical identity-based encryption (HIBE), so every ratchet-tree node's key is bound to an identity vector that changes with every operation, which prevents an adversary from re-using leaked state across a group split.
- P-Act, for an active-and-adaptive adversary: augments P-Pas with key-updating signatures (KUS), an analogous primitive for authenticating messages, and a hash-based mechanism ensuring any two parties who accept an injected message land in mutually consistent states; the tradeoff is that different honest parties may disagree on whether to accept the same injected message ("non-robust").
- P-Act-Rob, for an active-but-static adversary: replaces the hash mechanism with a non-interactive zero-knowledge proof (NIZK) attached to every message, proving message well-formedness, so that if any one honest party accepts a message, every honest party does ("robust"); the cost is that the proof is given only in the standard model against a static (non-adaptive) adversary, because the NIZK's use of common reference strings is incompatible with the random-oracle proof technique used for P-Pas and P-Act.

### Measured results
No implementation and no empirical measurement. The paper's results are asymptotic communication- and computation-complexity bounds derived by proof, not benchmarked figures — this entry records them as parameters, not measured facts.

### Parameters
- Fair-weather commit-message size: logarithmic in group size n for P-Pas, stated to hold "if the exact sequence of preceding operations" is favorable; the paper states the cost of the next operation ranges from Θ(log(n)) to Θ(n) depending on that sequence, and that under mild assumptions on participant online/offline behavior it stays in the O(log(n)) range. No numeric threshold for what counts as a favorable sequence is given.
- P-Pas computation cost: linear in group size n in the paper's simplified Appendix C description, because a processing party updates identity labels across the whole labeled tree (LT); the paper states this is not inherent and can be reduced to logarithmic in n by storing, per node, only the index at which the node was created (each identity vector is then a suffix of a global commit-history index) — this optimization is described but not separately re-analyzed for its effect on other costs.
- HIBE ciphertext size: if the HIBE scheme used has constant-size ciphertexts (the paper cites Lewko-Waters, TCC 2010, as an example), P-Pas has only constant blow-up over the underlying TTKEM protocol; otherwise message size grows with the number of commits sent without interaction (not with group size).
- HIBE encryption cost: often linear in HIBE identity-vector length, which equals the number of messages sent without interaction; the paper notes this could potentially be pre-processed for some HIBE schemes, trading commit cost for process cost, but does not evaluate this tradeoff.
- Security assumptions per protocol, stated as theorem hypotheses: P-Pas requires HIBE and public-key encryption (PKE) to be IND-CPA secure; P-Act requires HIBE and PKE to be IND-CCA secure and KUS to be existentially unforgeable under chosen-message attack (EUF-CMA secure); P-Act-Rob additionally requires a NIZK proof system and a common reference string.

### Stated limitations
The paper's own conclusion states all three constructions "scale sub-linearly in the number of parties and polynomially in the security parameter," and explicitly labels them "not practically efficient," offered as feasibility results rather than deployable protocols. P-Act-Rob's robustness proof holds only against a static adversary (one that commits to its corruption targets ahead of time), not the adaptive adversary the other two protocols withstand, because the NIZK's common-reference-string model is incompatible with the paper's adaptive-security proof technique. The paper's PKI model is described as "overly idealized": adding a party is assumed to always retrieve a key genuinely owned by that party, and a joining party has no means to verify that its welcome message actually came from the party claiming to send it, or that the group state it is joining is legitimate and fresh rather than fabricated — long-term identity key compromise and its recovery are stated as unaddressed. The active-setting definitions do not model a fully malicious PKI: a corrupted party cannot upload a self-generated public key without first corrupting an already-enrolled party and injecting an add proposal through that party's leaked state, which the paper states falls short of "full insider security" and is left as an open problem. The paper conjectures, but does not prove, that full UC security is impossible in the standard model (without a random oracle) while preserving logarithmic complexity; whether the paper's weaker restricted-environment UC notion is achievable in the standard model is left open. A named unresolved case ("security of detached nodes"): a party who joins a group and immediately removes the only party whose state was ever exposed can end up with a key the paper's own definition does not certify secure, because not all ancestor epochs of the new party's join point can be determined from available information; the paper conjectures that fixing this requires protocols that are inherently size-inefficient, without proof.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Security proofs are conditioned on a public-key infrastructure (PKI) functionality (F_pki) that is assumed idealized: correctly delivering the actual public key of the party requested, with no verification available to a joining party that its own welcome message came from a legitimate sender. Two of the three constructions (P-Pas, P-Act) are proved secure only in the random-oracle model, requiring every hash function in the deployed system to be treated as programmable (for full UC security) or non-programmable (for the weaker, restricted-environment variant) — the choice determines the strength of guarantee obtained. P-Act-Rob additionally requires a trusted setup providing every party a common reference string for its NIZK system. The paper's security definitions assume the environment issues at most one "Create Group" call per session (bounding the CGKA functionality to a single group's honest history tree, with the model's composability claims resting on that restriction) and, for the strongest composable statements, that the environment avoids corruption patterns causing the "commitment problem" — a restriction the paper states affects only composition guarantees, not the core security statement. The paper additionally requires (Section 9) that any group-communication mechanism update the entire group state on every operation, not just pairwise channels between the two directly involved parties, and gives a concrete attack showing pairwise-channel designs (as used by Signal) and key-homomorphic-encryption designs based on ElGamal-style additive keys both fail the paper's optimal-security notion for this reason.

### Contradicts
None found within this batch.

### References worth retrieving
- foundational: Alwen, Coretti, Dodis, Tselekounis, "Security analysis and improvements for the IETF MLS standard for group messaging," CRYPTO 2020 (introduces the CGKA primitive this paper extends).
- foundational: Alwen, Capretto, Cueto, Kamath, Klein, Pascual-Perez, Pietrzak, Walter, "Keep the Dirt: Tainted TreeKEM," ePrint 2019/1489 (source of the TTKEM protocol this work adapts for P-Pas).
- foundational: Bhargavan, Barnes, Rescorla, "TreeKEM: Asynchronous Decentralized Key Management for Large Dynamic Groups," 2018.
- competing: Cohn-Gordon, Cremers, Garratt, Millican, Milner, "On ends-to-ends encryption: Asynchronous group messaging with strong security guarantees," ACM CCS 2018 (introduces the ART protocol, first CGKA construction with O(log(n)) fair-weather complexity).
- foundational: Jaeger, Stepanovs, "Optimal channel security against fine-grained state compromise: The safety of messaging," CRYPTO 2018 (source of the key-evolving technique adapted to the group setting for P-Pas).
- foundational: Jost, Maurer, Mularczyk, "Efficient ratcheting: Almost-optimal guarantees for secure messaging," EUROCRYPT 2019 (two-party key-homomorphic-encryption approach the paper shows does not extend to optimal group security).
- attack/critique: Poettering, Rösler, "Towards bidirectional ratcheted key exchange," CRYPTO 2018 (two-party pairwise-channel approach the paper's Section 9.1 attack applies to).
- competing: Howell, Leavy, Alwen, "Wickr Messaging Protocol: Technical Paper," 2019 (deployed linear-complexity protocol cited as one of the practical systems this work's sub-linear constructions improve on asymptotically).
- foundational: Marlinspike, Perrin, "The Double Ratchet Algorithm," 2016 (two-party ratcheting primitive whose group generalization motivates CGKA).
- irrelevant: Facebook, "Messenger Secret Conversations technical whitepaper," 2016; WhatsApp, "WhatsApp encryption overview," 2017 — cited only as examples of deployed linear-complexity group messaging, not as CGKA constructions with their own comparison data.

### Verbatim extracts
- "all schemes scale sub-linearly in the number of parties and polynomially in the security parameter, thus — while not practically efficient — provide feasibility results"
- "an interesting open question is, whether the same level of security, while preserving logarithmic complexity, could also be achieved in the standard model"
- "the adversary can use leaked states of parties to inject messages that are processed correctly by some parties, but rejected by others"
- "our overly idealized and incorruptible PKI also separates our active setting... from true insider security"
- "we conjecture that protocols with such guarantee are inherently inefficient"

## [AMBATI-SACMAT-26] SoK: Self-Sovereign Digital Identities

**Citation:** Sushanth Ambati, Kainat Adeel, Jack Myers, Nikolay Ivanov. "SoK: Self-Sovereign Digital Identities." ACM Symposium on Access Control Models and Technologies (SACMAT), 2026. DOI: 10.1145/3750555.3811903.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.06896 (arXiv:2603.06896v2 [cs.CR], 11 Mar 2026)
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.06896
**Domain:** E

### What it does
This is a systematization of knowledge (a structured survey that classifies existing work rather than proposing a new mechanism) on self-sovereign digital identity (SSDI), a paradigm in which a user, rather than a service provider or a federated identity broker (such as Google or Facebook), holds their own authentication keys and data and presents them on demand as digital credentials. The paper follows a five-step method: it reviews eight prior surveys published 2018-2023 to establish what has already been systematized; it draws on 80 sources (active SSDI projects, peer-reviewed papers, standards-body reports, and privacy-advocacy manifestos) to distill six recurring adoption challenges; it structurally classifies 47 scientific publications proposing SSDI systems along five dimensions (system type, trust infrastructure, cryptographic technique, which of the six challenges each addresses, evaluation method); it evaluates 12 production-deployed SSDI systems along five self-sovereignty dimensions; and it synthesizes five forward-looking research frontiers from the first four steps.

The six challenges it identifies: (1) identity binding — establishing that one decentralized identifier (DID, a self-generated identifier not issued by any central authority) corresponds to one real-world individual or organization, addressed in the literature by credential-based binding (a trusted issuer such as a government or university attests to the correspondence), web-of-trust binding (peers vouch for one another across a social graph), or biometric binding (tying identity to a physical characteristic); (2) key management and protocol immaturity — users must generate, store, back up, rotate, and recover their own cryptographic keys with no central password-reset mechanism, and over 100 registered DID methods remain largely non-interoperable; (3) usability — the shift from username-and-password to key-based authentication and selective disclosure (revealing only specific attributes of a credential) imposes cognitive load unfamiliar to typical users; (4) oversight and regulation — legal frameworks such as GDPR's right to be forgotten assume a centralized party capable of deleting data, in tension with immutable ledger anchoring, and no single party exists for law enforcement to serve a subpoena on; (5) critical-mass adoption — a cold-start problem in which users will not adopt SSDI credentials until verifiers accept them, and verifiers will not integrate verification until enough users hold credentials; (6) single infrastructure dependence — the great majority of proposed systems anchor identity to one specific blockchain, so a consensus failure, a 51% attack, or a smart-contract vulnerability in that one chain endangers every identity anchored to it, a risk the paper calls meta-centralization because it exists at the ecosystem level even when the chosen chain is itself internally decentralized.

### Parameters
Not applicable — this is a literature systematization with no runnable mechanism or tunable parameter of its own. The classification scheme applied to the 47-paper corpus used five fixed dimensions (type, trust infrastructure, cryptographic technique, which of 6 challenges addressed, evaluation method) and the 12-deployment assessment used five fixed self-sovereignty dimensions (key control, permissionless issuance, portability, selective disclosure, revocation resistance), each scored fully / partially / not supported.

### Stated limitations
The paper states that the scientific literature it surveyed treats usability "as an afterthought or ignore[s] it entirely," with only 2 of 47 papers reporting any user study, and calls this "a critical gap" because "systems that are not evaluated with real users risk optimizing for the wrong objectives." Key recovery is stated as "arguably the most critical unsolved problem": social-recovery schemes (a quorum of trusted contacts restoring access) introduce their own trust assumptions and coordination overhead, and hardware-backed key storage (secure enclaves, hardware security modules) protects keys at rest but does not solve backup if the device is lost or destroyed. Sybil resistance (preventing one actor from registering multiple identities) has no solution accepted as satisfactory among the three surveyed approaches: credential-based binding reintroduces dependence on a centralized issuing authority, web-of-trust binding is vulnerable to collusion and has bootstrapping problems in sparse networks, and biometric binding is irreversible once compromised and raises privacy concerns. The paper's own real-world evaluation found every one of the 12 deployed systems makes at least one compromise against full self-sovereignty, government-backed systems in particular sacrificing permissionlessness and revocation resistance by design because governments require the ability to revoke a credential. GDPR's right-to-be-forgotten conflicts with immutable ledger anchoring, and the paper states the legal sufficiency of the common workaround (storing only hashes on-chain, personal data off-chain) "remains contested." The paper explicitly frames its five-dimension deployment assessment as "a first step" toward a sovereignty-assurance framework, not a completed one, and identifies formalizing such a framework as future work.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A credential-based identity-binding approach requires an external, already-trusted issuing authority (a government, university, or employer) willing to attest off-protocol that a given DID corresponds to a specific real-world entity; the protocol itself supplies no mechanism to establish that correspondence. A web-of-trust binding approach requires an existing social graph dense enough to avoid the bootstrapping failure the paper states occurs in sparse networks, and requires that colluding participants be detectable or economically discouraged elsewhere in the system, since the mechanism itself does not resist collusion. Key recovery via social recovery requires a quorum of contacts the user selects in advance to remain reachable and honest at the moment of recovery; hardware-backed key storage requires a physically available replacement device or backup channel, since the paper states it does not itself solve loss-of-device backup. Any mechanism anchoring identity to a single blockchain inherits that chain's consensus-failure and governance-crisis risk for every identity anchored to it, so avoiding this single-infrastructure dependence requires either a ledger-agnostic design or migration tooling across ledgers, for which the paper states "the current landscape falls far short" of existing cross-ledger interoperability standards. A design using zero-knowledge proofs for selective disclosure requires wallet software and verifier software to agree on a standardized proof format across DID methods, which the paper states does not yet exist.

### Contradicts
None found.

### References worth retrieving
- **Foundational:** Mühle, Grüner, Gayvoronskaya, Meinel. Survey identifying essential SSI components (DIDs, verifiable credentials, distributed ledgers) — one of the earliest SSI surveys, cited as an architectural-overview baseline this SoK extends with challenge- and deployment-level analysis.
- **Foundational:** Der, Jähnichen, Sürmeli. Early position paper on SSI opportunities and challenges, cited as anticipating several of this SoK's six challenges without a systematic survey methodology.
- **Competing:** Stokkink, Ishmaev, Epema, Pouwelse. "TrustChain"-style peer-to-peer SSDI system (paper [132] in this SoK's numbering) — one of only 4 of 47 surveyed systems avoiding blockchain dependency entirely; explicitly argued by its authors that a "truly self-sovereign" system should not depend on any single ledger, cited by this SoK as not having achieved significant adoption.
- **Competing:** Zaeem, Khalil, Lamison, Pandey, Barber. "On the usability of self sovereign identity solutions," University of Texas at Austin Center for Identity Technical Report 21-02, 2021 — one of the only empirical usability studies of SSDI found in the 47-paper corpus; source of the finding that users found onboarding confusing and expressed anxiety about losing private keys.
- **Attack-or-critique:** Giannopoulou — critical sociopolitical analysis questioning whether SSI decentralization empowers users or merely relocates power to different intermediaries, cited by this SoK as a sociopolitical-perspective survey it builds on.
- **Superseded-by:** none identified — this is itself the most recent (2026) SoK in the domain.

- "Key recovery is arguably the most critical unsolved problem."
- "the vast majority of SSDI proposals rely on a single blockchain or distributed ledger as their trust anchor."
- "only 3 of the 12 surveyed projects (25%) were fully operational."
- "adopting the SSDI label without delivering its core properties" (describing "sovereignty washing").
- "usability is a precondition for adoption, not a secondary concern."

## [AMPARORE-ARXIV-26] Range-Based Set Reconciliation via Range-Summarizable Order-Statistics Stores
**Citation:** Elvio G. Amparore. "Range-Based Set Reconciliation via Range-Summarizable Order-Statistics Stores." arXiv preprint, 2026. DOI 10.48550/arXiv.2603.19820.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.19820
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.19820
**Domain:** D

### What it does
The paper reduces the local computational cost of Range-Based Set Reconciliation (RBSR) by specifying the exact storage-backend interface RBSR needs and by building a concrete implementation of that interface. RBSR is a set-reconciliation protocol (introduced by Meyer, already in this corpus as the range-based set reconciliation citation) in which two replicas holding ordered sets compare a compact summary of each contiguous key range; a range where the summaries agree is skipped, a small mismatching range is sent as an explicit list, and a large mismatching range is split by rank into balanced child ranges and compared recursively. The paper defines a Range-Summarizable Order-Statistics Store (RSOS): an ordered-set data structure exposing five operations — `size()`, `Aggregate(l,u)` (returning the count and a composable summary of the range), `Rank(z)` (count of elements below a value), `Select(r)` (the element at a given rank), and `Enumerate(l,u)` (the ordered contents of a range) — plus `Insert` and `Delete`. RBSR needs exactly this bundle: range aggregation to compare ranges, rank/select to cut a range into equal-cardinality children without rescanning it, and enumeration to resolve small mismatches directly. The paper proves that an aggregate-augmented B+-tree, where every internal-node child pointer also stores the cached pair (subtree element count, subtree composable summary), realizes an RSOS: `Rank` and `Select` cost O(h), `Aggregate(l,u)` costs O(Bh) (O(h) under a bounded page fanout B), `Enumerate(l,u)` costs O(h+k) for k returned elements, and `Insert`/`Delete` cost O(Bh), where h = Θ(log_B n) is the tree height for n stored elements — because each of these operations touches at most one root-to-leaf path plus, for updates, at most one split/merge/redistribution per level. Composing this per-operation bound over a full reconciliation gives a total local responder-side cost of O(Qh) for Q queried ranges, at fixed split fanout b and enumeration cutoff t (derivation in the paper's appendix). The paper implements this design as AELMDB (Anti-Entropy Lightning Memory-Mapped Database), an extension of the LMDB storage engine that stores the aggregate metadata directly in B+-tree branch-page node prefixes — selected per-database via flags for entry count, key count, and a fixed-size additive hash-sum — rather than in a separate auxiliary tree, and integrates it with Negentropy, a deployed RBSR protocol implementation used in the Nostr protocol's NIP-77 relay-synchronization specification and explored for Waku Sync. AELMDB additionally implements a window-subrange optimization (`MDB_agg_window`) that caches the mapping from a stable outer query range to its absolute rank interval, so repeated nested subrange queries inside that outer range avoid re-deriving the mapping from scratch.

### Measured results
All measurements ran on one machine: an AMD 3700X CPU under Linux, LMDB file mmap size 2048 MiB, Negentropy protocol parameters held fixed at split fanout b=16 and explicit-enumeration cutoff threshold t=32, 10 repeated reconciliations per benchmark instance averaged into one reported value, each instance run in an isolated fresh process. Four backends were compared, all executing the identical Negentropy/RBSR protocol logic over the same synthetic reconciliation workloads, differing only in how the RSOS oracle was realized: an in-memory Vector reference; BTreeLMDB, a baseline that computes range aggregates and rank navigation through a separate auxiliary tree layered inside LMDB; AELMDB, the paper's in-tree aggregate design plus window-subrange caching; and NoWndAELMDB, an ablation of AELMDB with the window-subrange path disabled. Six synthetic scenario families were used (base_dense, base_sparse, scale_dense, scale_sparse, stress, stress_dyn), each with 8 parametrically scaled instances (i=1..8) varying the size of the in-slice intersection, in-slice symmetric difference, and out-of-slice context on both sides; in the stress_dyn family both the in-slice intersection and in-slice symmetric difference grow quadratically in i (4096·i^2 and 1024·i^2 respectively).

| Metric | Result | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Reconciliation time (T_rec), AELMDB vs. BTreeLMDB | AELMDB 4.69x faster on base_dense, rising to 13.98x faster on stress_dyn | Family-wise geometric mean of per-scenario ratios over the 8 instances per family, same 6 families above |
| Reconciliation time, AELMDB vs. NoWndAELMDB (window-subrange ablation) | NoWndAELMDB 1.08x to 1.27x slower than AELMDB across the 6 families | Same benchmark suite; isolates the contribution of the window-subrange cache alone, holding the in-tree aggregate design fixed |
| Resident memory (S_RSS), BTreeLMDB vs. AELMDB | Ratio rises monotonically from 1.06x (base_dense) to 1.36x (stress_dyn) | Linux RSS sampled via /proc/self/status immediately before and after each isolated bench run, so the reported figure is the memory increment attributable to the reconciliation run |
| Preparation time (T_prep, insertion cost), BTreeLMDB vs. AELMDB | BTreeLMDB 0.89x to 0.96x of AELMDB's time (i.e., BTreeLMDB inserts slightly faster) | Same suite; attributed to AELMDB propagating aggregate deltas along the full root-to-leaf path on every insertion |
| Disk usage (S_disk), BTreeLMDB vs. AELMDB | Nearly tied, reported as negligible difference | Same suite |
| Absolute stress_dyn instance-8 example | Vector T_rec 19.708 ms, BTreeLMDB T_rec 1197.161 ms, NoWndAELMDB T_rec 74.800 ms, AELMDB T_rec 62.927 ms (arithmetic means over the 8 instances in the family) | stress_dyn family, same hardware and protocol parameters as above |

The evaluation is explicitly scoped to single-machine, reconciliation-heavy workloads under one fixed protocol configuration; the paper states it does not characterize concurrent transactions, crash recovery, cold-cache behavior, or cross-engine portability, and reports no results for any of those conditions. All experiments verified computed reconciliation output against ground truth and confirmed byte-identical output across backends, so the reported speed and memory differences isolate storage-realization cost rather than reflecting different communication behavior.

### Parameters
- Negentropy split fanout b = 16 (paper states this is Negentropy's default value; held fixed across all backends in the evaluation, not varied).
- Explicit-enumeration cutoff threshold t = 32 (Negentropy default, held fixed, not varied).
- LMDB file mmap size: 2048 MiB, fixed for all benchmark runs.
- 10 repeated reconciliations per scenario instance, averaged into one reported value; no stated variance or confidence interval.
- Negentropy record identifier size: 256 bits; the composable summary is the modular sum of identifiers, mod 2^256, hashed with SHA-256 and truncated to the first 128 bits for the protocol-level comparison value.
- Six scenario families, each with 8 parametrically scaled instances (i = 1 to 8); exact per-family element-count formulas are given in the paper's Table 1 (for example, base_dense_i: 64i in-slice-shared elements, 4i in-slice-peer-only elements, 1000i out-of-slice-shared, 200i out-of-slice-peer-only).

### Stated limitations
The paper states a full end-to-end collision analysis of Negentropy's concrete comparison function (SHA-256 over the range aggregate, truncated to 128 bits) is outside its scope, and that this comparison rule is probabilistically sound rather than information-theoretically exact — a false SKIP can occur whenever two unequal ranges collide under the aggregate encoding or under hash truncation. The correctness proof for RBSR over RSOS (Proposition 4.1) is conditioned explicitly on an assumption that every SKIP decision is sound; the paper does not prove this assumption holds for Negentropy's concrete comparison function, only states the tradeoff exists. The evaluation is scoped to reconciliation-heavy, single-machine workloads and the paper states explicitly that it does not evaluate concurrent transactions, crash recovery, cold-cache behavior, or cross-engine portability, listing all four as left to future work. The RSOS abstraction and its bounds assume a bounded-page-size model (B = O(1) with respect to n) and O(1)-time aggregate-field combination; the paper does not state what happens to the derived bounds outside this model. Insertion (preparation) cost is higher for AELMDB than for the BTreeLMDB baseline in every tested scenario family (ratio 0.89x-0.96x, meaning BTreeLMDB is faster), attributed to AELMDB needing to propagate aggregate-delta updates along the entire root-to-leaf path on every write. The paper states the observed speedups are workload-dependent and that gains "will depend on workload characteristics, especially the balance between frequent reconciliation queries and the maintenance cost of aggregate metadata under updates," not a universal claim. The paper states an open question it does not resolve: how far the RSOS abstraction extends to comparison mechanisms other than homomorphic summary constructions, citing Meyer and Scherer's demonstration that RBSR can be realized using conventional (non-homomorphic) cryptographic hashes as a direction not covered by this paper's realization.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
RBSR over an RSOS backend requires the reconciling parties' data to be embedded in one totally ordered universe with a defined strict order relation, since every operation (Aggregate, Rank, Select, Enumerate) is defined over contiguous ranges of that order; Negentropy's concrete instantiation orders records lexicographically by (timestamp, 256-bit identifier), so any component storing data reconciled this way must expose that same ordering. The composable range summary requires the per-element contribution function ϕ to map into a monoid — an algebraic structure with an associative combining operation and an identity element — so that a range's summary can be computed by combining any partition of that range's sub-summaries; Negentropy's summary uses modular addition of 256-bit identifiers, which satisfies this by construction. The correctness of RBSR's SKIP decision (Proposition 4.1) requires that the protocol-level comparison function applied to two ranges' aggregates agrees only when the ranges are truly equal; a system substituting a different comparison rule (e.g., a smaller hash truncation) inherits a higher false-SKIP probability, a tradeoff this paper does not quantify for Negentropy's specific 128-bit truncation. Realizing an RSOS via the aggregate-augmented B+-tree construction requires the storage engine's tree to allow attaching fixed-size aggregate metadata to internal-node child pointers and to update that metadata along the insert/delete path; AELMDB does this by extending LMDB's on-disk branch-page format, so a different backend without an equivalent per-page metadata slot would need a separate auxiliary structure (as BTreeLMDB does), incurring the paper's measured 4.69x-13.98x reconciliation-time penalty. The window-subrange optimization requires the recursive reconciliation protocol to issue many queries against a stable, unchanging outer range; a protocol whose active-range set does not exhibit this locality pattern would not benefit from the measured 1.08x-1.27x speedup this component contributes.

### Contradicts
None found against other entries in this corpus. The paper explicitly draws a mechanism-level contrast, not a numeric contradiction, with AUVOLAT-SRDS-19 (Merkle Search Trees): it states Merkle Search Trees extend subtree-digest caching to ordered CRDT (Conflict-free Replicated Data Type) state by imposing a rigid, canonically derived tree representation of the data, whereas RBSR operates on logical ranges of an ordered set and drives its recursion by element order rather than by a predetermined canonical tree topology.

### References worth retrieving
- Foundational: Aljoscha Meyer, "Range-based set reconciliation," SRDS 2023 / arXiv:2212.13567 — already in this corpus's verified-seed list; the paper states this as "the most systematic generic treatment of the RBSR family" and the direct formal starting point for its own model.
- Foundational: Aljoscha Meyer, Konstantin Scherer, "Range-based set reconciliation without homomorphic hashing," preprint 2024 — shows RBSR realizable with conventional (non-homomorphic) cryptographic hashes over history-independent search trees; the paper states this broadens the protocol-level design space in a direction orthogonal to its own storage-layer contribution.
- Competing: Alex Auvolat, François Taïani, "Merkle search trees: Efficient state-based CRDTs in open networks," SRDS 2019 — already in this corpus as AUVOLAT-SRDS-19; cited as a comparison point that caches subtree digests but imposes canonical tree structure, unlike RBSR.
- Competing (sketch-based set reconciliation): Yaron Minsky, Ari Trachtenberg, Richard Zippel, "Set reconciliation with nearly optimal communication complexity," IEEE Transactions on Information Theory 49(9), 2003 — the characteristic-polynomial approach the paper contrasts against RBSR's range-refinement approach.
- Competing: Long Gong, Ziheng Liu, Liang Liu, Jun Xu, Mitsunori Ogihara, Tong Yang, "Space- and computationally-efficient set reconciliation via parity bitmap sketch (PBS)," Proc. VLDB Endow. 14(4), 2020 — stated to target low computational cost with near-information-theoretic-minimum communication, a direct alternative trade-off point to RBSR.
- Competing: Tomer Keniagin, Eitan Yaakobi, Ori Rottenstreich, "CertainSync: Rateless set reconciliation with certainty," Proc. ACM Meas. Anal. Comput. Syst. 9(2), 2025 — rateless set reconciliation without parameter estimation, another explicit alternative comparison point.
- Competing: Lei Yang, Yossi Gilad, Mohammad Alizadeh, "Practical rateless set reconciliation," ACM SIGCOMM 2024.
- Foundational (deployed protocol this paper builds on): Doug Hoyte and contributors, "Negentropy: Protocol specification, reference implementations, and tests," GitHub, 2024, and the Nostr NIP-77 specification for Negentropy-based relay synchronization.
- Foundational (data structure precedent): Zhuoyue Zhao, Dong Xie, Feifei Li, "AB-tree: Index for concurrent random sampling and updates," Proc. VLDB Endow. 15(9), 2022 — cited as evidence that aggregate metadata inside page-oriented search trees supports efficient sampling under updates, a precedent for AELMDB's design.
- Foundational (authenticated-index precedent, different goal): Feifei Li, Marios Hadjieleftheriou, George Kollios, Leonid Reyzin, "Dynamic authenticated index structures for outsourced databases," ACM SIGMOD 2006 — Embedded Merkle B-tree, cached-metadata-in-B-tree precedent built for authenticated query proofs rather than range reconciliation.
