## [ANAOBI-WWW-23] Will Admins Cope? Decentralized Moderation in the Fediverse
**Citation:** Ishaku Hassan Anaobi, Aravindh Raman, Ignacio Castro, Haris Bin Zia, Dami Ibosiola, Gareth Tyson. "Will Admins Cope? Decentralized Moderation in the Fediverse." Proceedings of the ACM Web Conference (WWW), 2023.
**Retrieved:** full text
**Source URL:** target record (registry/targets-deduped.json)
**Domain:** K

### What it does
The paper measures the moderation workload carried by Pleroma instance administrators in the Fediverse (a federation of independently operated servers exchanging posts through ActivityPub-style federation) and builds WatchGen, a classifier that predicts which federated instances an administrator will later apply a moderation policy against. Pleroma exposes federation policies: administrator-configured rule-action pairs that act on incoming posts, users, or entire remote instances (for example, rejecting all posts from a given remote instance, or tagging posts above a certain age). WatchGen extracts per-instance features (post volume, hate-word counts, URL counts, mention counts, prior policy actions) from each instance's public API and its federated peers' data, trains a classifier on instances that later had a policy applied against them, and outputs a ranked watchlist an administrator can act on before applying a policy manually.

### Measured results
| Metric | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Instances discovered by crawling distsn.org and the-federation.info, then federation-peer enumeration | 9,981 total instances found (2,407 Pleroma, remainder non-Pleroma such as Mastodon) | 16 Dec 2020 - 19 Oct 2021, metadata polled every 4 hours via each instance's public API |
| Instances with retrievable metadata | 1,740 of 2,407 Pleroma instances (72.28%) | Failure causes for the remaining 667: 65.1% non-existent domain, 17.9% HTTP 404, 6.4% HTTP 403 (private timeline), 4.5% HTTP 502, 1.3% HTTP 503, under 1% HTTP 410 |
| Instances exposing policy information | 93.2% of the 1,740, covering 94.2% of users and 94.5% of posts | Same dataset |
| Unique policy types observed | 49 | Same dataset |
| Instances still on default (unconfigured) policy set | 66.9% | Same dataset, end of measurement period |
| Instances managed by exactly one administrator | 71.6% of 1,633 instances that expose administrator information (93.8% of 1,740) | Total of 2,111 unique administrators observed |
| Post-to-administrator ratio for multi-administrator instances vs. single-administrator instances | 6:1 (more posts per added administrator on average) | Driven by a small number of instances, notably poa.st |
| Correlation of post growth to administrator-count growth | Spearman coefficient 0.19 (weak) | Growth measured per instance over the 10-month period; only 6.9% of instances added any administrator during the period |
| Aggregate post growth vs. administrator growth | 60.3% increase in posts, 35.6% growth in administrators | Same 10-month period, aggregate across all 1,740 instances |
| Policy volume difference tied to administrator growth | Instances that added administrators applied 1.5x more policies overall, 1.8x more `reject` policy actions, and received 4x more policies applied against them by other instances | Comparison is instances with administrator growth vs. instances without, same dataset |
| Average delay from federation to first policy application against a newly federated instance | 82.3 days | Computed from time between an instance's federation date and the date a `SimplePolicy` action was first applied against it; 55% of federations that predate the measurement window are excluded because their federation timestamp is unknown |
| Delay for "top 10" most-targeted instances vs. "bottom 10" least-targeted instances | 59.5 days (top 10) vs. 74.7 days (bottom 10) | Same delay metric, subset by number of policies received |
| Delay for specific controversial instances | gab.com: 19 days average; neckbeard.xyz: up to 98.4 days average | Same delay metric; neckbeard.xyz grew by 789.4k posts and kiwifarms.cc by 469.2k posts during the measurement window |
| Instances that delegate moderation to an account distinct from the administrator | 3.5% of the 1,740 instances (29 of 819 instances that expose moderator role information; a further 72 assign the moderator role to an account that is also an administrator) | Same dataset |
| Effect of having a dedicated (non-administrator) moderator | Instances with a dedicated moderator take 103 days on average to apply a `SimplePolicy` action after federation, vs. 111 days without one; 38% of instances with a dedicated moderator apply zero `SimplePolicy` actions, vs. 70% without one | Same dataset |
| WatchGen, global training pool, full 38-feature set (16 retained as most determinant), 80:20 train/test split, 5-fold cross-validated grid search over hyperparameters, sklearn | Random Forest: accuracy 0.92, precision 0.88, recall 0.68, F1 0.77 (best of 4 models tested); Logistic Regression F1 0.49; Multi-Layer Perceptron F1 0.53; Gradient Boosted Trees F1 0.71 | Predicting whether any policy will later be applied against a given instance by any other instance |
| WatchGen, global pool, excluding the two post-volume features (posts, transformed posts) | Random Forest F1 drops from 0.77 to 0.62 | Same task, isolating the contribution of post-volume features |
| WatchGen, time-windowed training (1 to 9 months of data, remainder held out as test) | Best F1 reached at month 5 for Gradient Boosted Trees and month 7 for Random Forest | Month 10 excluded for insufficient remaining test data |
| WatchGen, per-instance local model (each instance trains only on its own federated peers' data, first 8 months train / last 2 months test) | Mean F1 0.55 across instances; 42.6% of instances reach F1 >= 0.6; 8.3% of instances fall below F1 0.4 | Decentralized training variant, one independent model per instance, using Random Forest (the best global-model algorithm) |
| Relationship between local training-set size and local model performance | 65.4% of instances with F1 >= 0.6 have over 50,000 local posts; only 4.4% of instances with F1 < 0.6 have over 50,000 local posts | Same decentralized-training experiment |

### Parameters
- Data-collection window: 16 December 2020 to 19 October 2021 (10 months), metadata polled every 4 hours per instance.
- Logistic Regression: regularization parameter C tuned over {0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100, 1000}.
- Multilayer Perceptron: single hidden layer, hidden-layer size in {10, 50, 100}; activation function in {relu, tanh, logistic}; learning-rate schedule in {constant, invscaling, adaptive}.
- Random Forest: n_estimators in {5, 50, 250}; max_depth in {2, 4, 8, 16, 32, None}.
- Gradient Boosted Trees: n_estimators in {5, 50, 250, 500}; max_depth in {1, 3, 5, 7, 9}; learning rate in {0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100}.
- Feature set: 38 extracted features distilled by manual experimentation to 16 retained as most determinant (full list in the paper's Table 5, including post count, hate-word count from hatebase.org, URL count, mention count, hashtag count, and per-policy action counts).
- Global-model split: 80:20 train/test.
- Local-model split: first 8 months train, last 2 months test, per instance, using only that instance's federated peers as training data.

### Stated limitations
The authors state their delay metric is "a rudimentary proxy" for how long it takes an administrator to identify a problem, and that many unmeasured factors could explain the observed delay. WatchGen's global-pool variant assumes a central broker aggregating training data from all instances, which the authors state may be infeasible given the decentralized nature of the Fediverse; the local variant they test as an alternative shows a mean F1 of 0.55, a measured drop from the global model's 0.77, attributed to the reduced per-instance training-set size. The paper covers Pleroma instances only; the authors state as future work that they intend to extend the study to other Fediverse platforms, specifically Mastodon and PeerTube. The dataset excludes federations that predate the measurement window (55% of observed federations) from the delay analysis because their federation timestamp cannot be determined. The study observes only the policies administrators set and does not examine other administrator behavior, such as individual posts they author.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
WatchGen's global (central-broker) variant requires a component that can aggregate per-instance moderation-relevant metadata (post counts, hate-word counts, prior policy actions, user counts) across all participating instances into one training pool; this conflicts with a design in which no party holds a global view of instance activity. The local (decentralized) variant instead requires each instance to observe federation-relevant metadata only from its own federated peers, and produces materially worse prediction accuracy (F1 0.55 vs. 0.77) as a measured consequence of the smaller per-instance training set. Any system reusing the feature set needs instances to expose post content signals (hate-word matches via a wordlist such as hatebase.org, URL counts, mention counts) and prior policy-action history through a public API, the way Pleroma instances do. The predicted signal (whether an instance will later have a policy applied against it) is trained against administrators' actual historical policy decisions, so the mechanism reproduces existing administrator judgment rather than an independent measure of harm.

### Contradicts
None found.

### References worth retrieving
- Zia, Raman, Castro, Anaobi, De Cristofaro, Sastry, Tyson. "Toxicity in the decentralized web and the potential for model sharing." ACM SIGMETRICS, 2022. — foundational (same author group's prior study of toxicity in Pleroma, and of federation policies).
- Raman et al. "Challenges in the Decentralised Web: The Mastodon Case" (cited as ref [39] for Mastodon infrastructure and resilience). — foundational.
- Zignani, Gaito, Rossi. "Follow the 'Mastodon': Structure and Evolution of a Decentralized Online Social Network." ICWSM, 2018. — foundational (Mastodon social-graph structure, comparison point for a non-Pleroma Fediverse platform).
- Bielenberg et al. on Diaspora growth, topology, and server reliability (cited as ref [4]). — competing/comparison (a different decentralized social network's measured reliability and topology).
- Trautwein et al. on IPFS (InterPlanetary File System). — foundational (decentralized storage measurement, cited as a comparison decentralized-system study).
- Cheng et al. (ref [25]), cited for using random forest and logistic regression to predict whether a user will be banned, reducing moderator load. — competing (a centralized-platform ban-prediction classifier, directly comparable to WatchGen's task).

### Verbatim extracts

- "only 3.5% of instances have dedicated account(s) assigned the role of moderator."
- "Random Forest being the best performing model (f1=0.77)."
- "instances with multiple administrators have more posts, with a ratio of 6:1."

## [ANDERSON-CCGRID-06] The Computational and Storage Potential of Volunteer Computing
**Citation:** David P. Anderson, Gilles Fedak. "The Computational and Storage Potential of Volunteer Computing." IEEE/ACM International Symposium on Cluster Computing and the Grid (CCGrid), 2006. DOI 10.1109/CCGRID.2006.101.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://boinc.berkeley.edu/potential_ccgrid.pdf
**Source URL:** https://boinc.berkeley.edu/potential_ccgrid.pdf
**Domain:** C

### What it does
The paper measures the hardware capacity that "volunteer computing" — a deployment model where members of the public run client software on their own machines to contribute computing and storage to a project they do not administer — actually supplies, using logged measurements from the SETI@home project's host pool as of November 18, 2005. Each participating host runs the BOINC (Berkeley Open Infrastructure for Network Computing) client, which periodically benchmarks the host's central processing unit (CPU) speed via the Whetstone and Dhrystone synthetic benchmarks, measures installed random-access memory (RAM), swap space, total and free disk space on the volume it is installed on, and download network throughput measured during active file transfers, and reports these along with availability statistics to a scheduling server. The paper aggregates these per-host reports (217,551 hosts with data as of the measurement date, per the paper's own breakdown tables) into distributions and combines them into project-wide capacity estimates. The paper's central mechanism is a multiplicative capacity model: total usable floating-point computing power X is stated as the product of nine independently measured factors — host arrival rate, average host lifetime, average CPUs per host, average floating-point operations per second (FLOPS) per CPU, average CPU efficiency (fraction of CPU time actually available to the volunteer application net of other load), average on-fraction (fraction of time the client runs), average active-fraction (fraction of on-time during which the user's preferences permit computation or communication), the reciprocal of the average redundancy factor applied for fault tolerance, and the average per-project resource share when a host is attached to more than one project. An analogous multiplicative expression is used to estimate storage and network-transfer capacity from the corresponding measured factors.

### Measured results

All figures below are drawn from the SETI@home BOINC host pool, snapshotted November 18, 2005, restricted to hosts that had completed at least one unit of work in the prior two weeks. The breakdown tables in the paper sum to 217,551-217,552 hosts (Table 1: CPU-type breakdown totals 217,551; Table 5: hosts-per-user breakdown totals 217,552); the paper's own abstract separately rounds this to "about 200,000 hosts."

| Metric | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Total measured hosts | 217,551 (CPU-type breakdown) / 217,552 (hosts-per-user breakdown) | SETI@home BOINC pool, Nov 18 2005 snapshot, hosts active within the prior two weeks |
| Aggregate raw hardware FLOPS | 341,120 GFLOPS (≈341 TeraFLOPS) total, 1.568 GFLOPS/host average | Same host set, Whetstone/Dhrystone CPU benchmarks, all CPUs on a host benchmarked simultaneously |
| Sustained delivered processing rate | 95.5 TeraFLOPS | Same host set; raw 341 TFLOPS hardware capacity multiplied by the product of the five availability/efficiency/redundancy/share factors (measured product = 0.28) |
| Average RAM / swap per host | 806 MB RAM, 1.78 GB swap | Same host set; SETI@home itself uses about 32 MB RAM per host |
| Average network download throughput | 289 Kbps | Measured only during active file transfers, exponentially weighted average per host; upload not reported because SETI@home's upload files are too small to measure meaningfully |
| Average / total disk space | 60 GB total, 35 GB free average per host; 7.74 Petabytes total free disk space across the pool | Same host set; BOINC measures only the volume it is installed on, so this underestimates hosts with additional unmeasured volumes and can overestimate where multiple BOINC instances share one network volume |
| Storage access rate | 5.27 Terabytes per second (aggregate) | Derived from the same host set's per-host throughput and disk measurements, stated in the paper's conclusion as the pool's potential aggregate storage access rate |
| Host lifetime (churn) | Average 89.5 days | Measured as interval from host creation to last communication, restricted to hosts that had not communicated in at least one month; the paper states this measure "underestimates lifetime because it omits active hosts" |
| Host availability fractions | Mean on-fraction 0.81; mean connected-fraction 0.83; mean active-fraction 0.84; mean CPU efficiency 0.899 | Same host set, per-host BOINC-reported measurements averaged across the pool |
| Redundant-computing overhead | Effective computing power reduced "by a factor of slightly more than two" when using 2-way redundant task execution (assuming a low fraction of inconsistent results) | Stated as the general effect of the paper's described redundant-computing validation technique, not tied to a specific measured inconsistency rate |
| CPU multiplicity | 25% of hosts have 2+ CPUs; 2% have 4+ CPUs | Same host set |
| Operating system breakdown | Windows 86.8% of hosts / 90.0% of FLOPS; Linux 18,227 hosts (22,419 GFLOPS); Darwin 9,006 hosts (9,717 GFLOPS); SunOS 715 hosts | Same host set, Table 2 |
| Hosts per user | 1 host: 83,870 users (38.6% of total hosts); 2-10 hosts: 32,257 users (44.9%); 11-100: 1,217 users (11.7%); 101-1,000: 27 users (2.2%); 1,000+: 3 users (2.4%); largest 3 individual users held 2,179, 1,738, and 1,491 hosts respectively | Same host set, Table 5 |
| Deployment scale context (not this project, cited as general context) | On the order of 1 million hosts participate across all BOINC-based projects, GIMPS, distributed.net, Folding@home, Grid.org, and World Community Grid combined, versus an estimated 1 billion PCs in operation — about 0.1% participation | Stated as a general estimate for the volunteer-computing field as of the paper's writing, not a measurement of the SETI@home pool specifically |
| Data-intensive-application headroom | "Tens or hundreds of TeraFLOPS" of computing power remains available even at data rates R of 100 or 1,000 megabytes processed per 3.6×10^12 floating-point operations (one CPU-hour at 1 GFLOPS) | Derived from the same host set's combined CPU-speed and network-throughput distributions; the paper states this analysis omits server-side and ISP-backbone network saturation effects |

### Parameters
- Host inclusion window: hosts that completed work within the prior two weeks of the November 18, 2005 snapshot.
- Redundant computing factor: 2-way redundancy assumed in the capacity-reduction estimate ("slightly more than two" reduction), with escalation to a third instance only on result disagreement; no specific measured disagreement rate given.
- Default BOINC user-preference values reported as measured settings, each with its default alongside the measured average: "run if user active" (default No, 71.9% of users select Yes); active-hours restriction (default none, 3.3% of users set a range, average duration 12.41 hours); communication-hours restriction (default none, 0.8% of users set a range, average duration 12.18 hours); minimum connection interval (default 0.1 days, average setting 0.69 days); disk access interval (default 60 seconds, average setting 78.9 seconds); disk maximum used (default 100 GB, average setting 63.6 GB); disk maximum percent used (default 50%, average setting 42.6%); disk minimum free (default 0.1 GB, average setting 0.97 GB); per-project resource share (average 0.917 for SETI@home, with 16.8% of users also attached to other BOINC projects).

### Stated limitations
The paper states BOINC measures disk space only on the volume where the client is installed, so its per-host disk figures underestimate hosts with additional unmeasured volumes and can overestimate space where several BOINC installations share one network-accessible volume. The paper states the churn/lifetime measurement (89.5 days average) "underestimates lifetime because it omits active hosts," since it counts only hosts that had already gone a month without communicating. The paper states BOINC does not measure RAM or swap usage by other, non-BOINC applications on the host, so the capacity figures reflect installed hardware rather than what is actually free for a volunteer application to use at any given moment. The paper states its data-intensive-application analysis "omits some important factors: saturating lots of client network connections could swamp the outgoing server links, ISP backbone networks, and shared incoming links," and that addressing this "raises numerous research issues." The paper states it has about ten months of historical host data at the time of writing but that "the rapid change in the host pool makes it hard to derive meaningful conclusions from this data," so no longitudinal churn trend is reported, only the single-snapshot lifetime average. The paper states peer-to-peer communication between volunteer hosts (needed for large intermediate or replicated input files) is not yet supported by BOINC and is future work requiring separate measurement of peer-to-peer connectivity and bandwidth.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Requires that whatever component consumes this capacity estimate tolerate the redundancy overhead the paper describes as necessary for correctness: because "anonymously volunteered computers can't be trusted," the paper's own capacity model already discounts raw hardware capacity by a redundant-computing factor of slightly more than two, so any storage or computation layer built on this host population must either replicate the same validation technique (multiple independent hosts computing or holding the same unit, compared for agreement) or accept unvalidated results from untrusted volunteer hosts. Requires the consuming system to model per-host availability rather than assume durable presence: mean on-fraction 0.81, connected-fraction 0.83, active-fraction 0.84, and mean host lifetime 89.5 days (itself an underestimate) mean a storage or compute placement mechanism must plan for a host disappearing from the network on a timescale of roughly three months on average, and must not assume uninterrupted network reachability even while a host is on. Requires the consuming system to supply its own inter-host communication mechanism if it needs volunteer hosts to exchange data directly, since the paper states BOINC's architecture is entirely client-initiated communication with a central scheduling server (which the paper notes as an advantage for firewall and network-address-translation, NAT, traversal) and has no peer-to-peer transfer capability at the time of writing. Requires accounting for the fraction of a host's disk space and network throughput that its owner has reserved via BOINC's own preference settings (e.g., the default 50% maximum-disk-percentage and 100 GB maximum-disk-usage limits), since the measured averages already reflect these self-imposed caps rather than raw hardware totals.

### Contradicts
The target registry's own citation note for this key states the paper covers "more than 330,000 hosts." The retrieved full text's own breakdown tables (Table 1, Table 2, Table 5) sum to 217,551-217,552 hosts, and the paper's abstract independently rounds this to "about 200,000 hosts." No figure matching 330,000 appears anywhere in the retrieved text. The 330,000 figure in the registry's `why_needed` field is not supported by this paper and must not be carried into any downstream synthesis; the correct measured host count from the primary source is approximately 217,551-217,552 (as of the November 2005 snapshot), rounded by the paper itself to "about 200,000."

### References worth retrieving
- Sarmenta. "Bayanihan: Web-Based Volunteer Computing Using Java." Lecture Notes in Computer Science 1368, Springer-Verlag, 1998, pp. 444-461. — foundational (paper credits this work with articulating the volunteer-computing concept and its technical issues).
- Chien, Calder, Elbert, Bhatia. "Entropia: architecture and performance of an enterprise desktop grid system." Journal of Parallel and Distributed Computing 63, 2003, 597-610. — competing (a differently architected volunteer/desktop-grid deployment, studied for application speedup rather than raw capacity measurement).
- Germain, Neri, Fedak, Cappello. "XtremWeb: Building an Experimental Platform for Global Computing." 1st IEEE/ACM International Workshop on Grid Computing, 2000. — competing (another volunteer-computing platform studied for application speedup; shares an author, Fedak, with this paper).
- Litzkow, Livny, Mutka. "Condor - A Hunter of Idle Workstations." 8th International Conference on Distributed Computing Systems, 1988, pp. 104-111. — foundational (pioneered idle-workstation cycle-stealing; the paper explicitly contrasts Condor's trusted, migratable-task model against volunteer computing's untrusted, non-migratable model).
- Kubiatowicz et al. "OceanStore: An Architecture for Global-Scale Persistent Storage." ASPLOS, 2000. — foundational (cited as the type of long-term storage application for which the paper's measured host-churn statistics are directly relevant).
- Foster, Iamnitchi. "On Death, Taxes, and the Convergence of Peer-to-Peer and Grid Computing." 2nd International Workshop on Peer-to-Peer Systems, 2003. — foundational (source of the comparison data-processing ratios — 60 MB and 660 MB per CPU-hour for astrophysics applications — that this paper's data-intensive-application analysis is built against).
- Kondo, Taufer, Brooks, Casanova, Chien. "Characterizing and Evaluating Desktop Grids: An Empirical Study." IPDPS, 2004. — competing (an independent empirical measurement study of desktop-grid host availability, comparable in kind to this paper's own measurement).
- Gray. "Distributed Computing Economics." Microsoft Research Technical Report MSR-TR-2003-24, 2003. — foundational (cited as the paper's source for the incentive and participation-driver factors that determine host-pool growth, referenced in the paper's Section 3.1 discussion of host-count growth).

## [ANDONI-ARXIV-26] Efficient Algorithms for Adversarially Robust Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
**Citation:** Alexandr Andoni, Themistoklis Haris, Esty Kelman, Krzysztof Onak. "Efficient Algorithms for Adversarially Robust Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search." arXiv:2601.00272, 2026. DOI 10.48550/ARXIV.2601.00272.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/pdf/2601.00272
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.00272
**Domain:** B

### What it does
This paper gives algorithms that answer Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) queries correctly with high probability even when an adversary chooses both the searched dataset and every query adaptively, after seeing every prior answer — a threat model under which the paper shows ordinary randomized nearest-neighbor data structures can be forced to fail. The (c,r)-ANN problem (Definition 1.1) is: given a dataset S of n points in a metric space, a radius r, and an approximation factor c, build a data structure that, for a query point q, returns some point within distance c*r of q if any point within distance r of q exists, and otherwise may answer "no such point." Locality-Sensitive Hashing (LSH), the standard oblivious solution, groups points so that nearby points collide in the same hash bucket with higher probability than far points; a prior attack (Kapralov et al., 2024, cited but not reproduced in this corpus) is stated to show that an adaptive adversary needs only a number of queries polynomial in log(n) to learn enough about an LSH structure's internal hash functions to make it fail on a subsequent query.

The paper's adversarial-robustness model (Definition 3.1) is a game: the adversary picks the dataset S; the algorithm preprocesses S using private internal randomness the adversary cannot see; then, over Q rounds, the adversary picks each query using the full history of previous queries and answers, and the algorithm must answer correctly in every round with probability at least 1 - delta over its own randomness, for the run to count as delta-adversarially-robust. The dataset may also be updated (points added or deleted) obliviously, meaning the adversary fixes the update schedule in advance rather than adapting it to the algorithm's answers.

Three constructions are given, all working by preventing the adversary from learning the algorithm's internal randomness rather than by hiding the output (unlike the noise-adding techniques used for numeric estimation problems, which the paper states do not apply to search problems because the output must be an actual dataset point, not a perturbable number):
1. Fairness-based robustness (Theorem 1.2): building on prior work on "fair" ANN algorithms that select a valid answer uniformly at random from the qualifying candidates (Aumuller et al., 2022), the paper proves that any exact fair ANN algorithm is automatically adversarially robust, because uniform random selection is a form of statistical independence across queries that denies the adversary a learnable signal.
2. Search-to-decision via bucketing (Theorem 1.3): the search problem is reduced to a weak decision problem (does a point within r exist? does one within c*r not exist?) that can be solved by an oblivious LSH structure and then made robust with differential-privacy techniques (Hassidim et al., 2022) — maintaining Θ(sqrt(Q)) independent copies of the decision structure and combining their answers privately (via subsampled aggregation, avoiding a private-median step the prior framework needed). The dataset is partitioned into buckets of about sqrt(n) points each, a robust decider is run per bucket to find which bucket holds a qualifying point, and that bucket is then searched exhaustively for the final answer.
3. Concentric-annuli construction (Theorem 1.4): to remove the sqrt(n) floor the bucketing method imposes on query time, the (r, c*r) annulus around a query is split into several smaller concentric sub-annuli, the fair algorithm from construction 1 is run within each sub-annulus, and a counting argument guarantees at least one sub-annulus has low enough point density that the fair algorithm terminates quickly with probability at least 0.9; a differentially private selection step then picks a favorable sub-annulus to run the final (held-out) query on, without revealing which internal randomness the selection is based on to the adversary.

A separate "for-all" family of algorithms (Theorem 1.5 and Appendix D) targets a stronger, different guarantee: with probability at least 0.99, the built data structure answers every possible query correctly (not merely each of Q adaptively chosen queries with per-round failure probability delta), by discretizing the metric space into a covering and running enough independent LSH hash functions that a union bound over all points in the covering succeeds. This is stated to apply only to low-dimensional metric spaces, defined here as the regime d = O(sqrt(Q)), as opposed to the high-dimensional regime d = omega(sqrt(Q)) the fairness/privacy constructions target.

### Measured results
Every figure in this paper is a proved asymptotic bound over an abstract computational model, not an empirical measurement; there is no implementation, dataset, or run reported anywhere in the text. The bounds and the exact model conditions each depends on are:

| Result | Bound | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Standard oblivious LSH (baseline, not robust) | Query time O~(d * n^rho), space O~(n^(1+rho)) | d-dimensional metric space, n points, rho = rho(c) in (0,1) a constant fixed by the approximation factor c and the LSH construction; for the Hamming cube {0,1}^k with the best known construction, rho = 1/(2c-1) (Andoni and Razenshteyn, 2015) |
| Theorem 1.2 (fairness-based robustness) | Space O~(n^(1+rho(c)) * log(nQ)) bits; query time O~(d * (n^rho(c) + n(q,cr)/n(q,cr)+1... i.e. depends on the density ratio D) * log(nQ)) | n(q,r) is the count of dataset points within radius r of query q ("S-density"); query time depends on D = n(q,cr)/n(q,r), the ratio of far-ball to near-ball density around q, which the adversary can make arbitrarily large by constructing an adversarial dataset — this is stated as the construction's weakness |
| Theorem 1.3 (bucketing / search-to-decision) | Query time O~(d * n^(1/(2-rho))); space O~(sqrt(Q) * n^(2/(2-rho))); update time O~(d * n^(rho/(2-rho)) * sqrt(Q)); success probability at least 1 - Theta(delta) over Q queries | Same rho(c) as above; independent of dataset density (assumption-free), unlike Theorem 1.2; query time is always at least O(sqrt(n)) regardless of how close c pushes rho toward 0, which the paper states as this construction's limitation |
| Theorem 1.4 (concentric annuli) | Query time O~(d * n^beta) with probability at least 1 - delta, space O(sqrt(Q) * n^(1+beta)), update time O~(d * n^beta * sqrt(Q)), where beta = min over positive integers k of max(rho(c^(1/k)), 1/k) | For the Hamming hypercube specifically, rho(c) = 1/(2c-1) makes beta = Theta(log(log(c))/log(c)), which the paper states goes to 0 as c grows, unlike Theorem 1.3's exponent 1/(2-rho(c)), which does not |
| Theorem 1.5 (for-all guarantee, Hamming hypercube) | Space O~(d * n^(1+rho+o(1))); query time O~(d * n^rho); correctness on every possible query simultaneously with probability at least 0.99 | rho = 1/(2c-1); d-dimensional Hamming hypercube {0,1}^d specifically; the paper states this family's space complexity scales with an extra factor of d relative to the adaptive-adversary algorithms above, "making them intractable for high-dimensional metric spaces," and that these algorithms must be tailored per metric space rather than generalizing |
| Comparison to concurrent work (Feng et al., 2025) | Feng et al.'s algorithm: query time O(d * s * n^rho); space O(sqrt(Q) * s * n^(1+rho)); update time O~(d * n^rho * s * sqrt(Q)), where s = n(q,cr), the raw near-ball density (not a ratio) | The paper states its own Theorem 1.2 depends additively on the density ratio D (which is strictly smaller than Feng et al.'s s), and that this dependency does not affect the space complexity of its own algorithms (which grow only by an added factor of sqrt(Q)), whereas Feng et al.'s query time depends multiplicatively on s |

### Parameters
- n: dataset size (number of points).
- d: dimensionality of the metric space.
- c: the ANN approximation factor (c >= 1); larger c generally drives rho(c), and therefore query-time exponents, toward 0.
- r: the target radius defining a "near" neighbor; c*r is the radius defining the discard threshold.
- Q: the total number of adaptive queries the algorithm must remain robust against; several constructions' space costs scale with sqrt(Q).
- delta: the per-construction failure probability bound (adversarially-robust constructions) or, for the for-all family, the paper fixes a concrete constant success probability of 0.99 rather than a tunable delta.
- rho(c): the LSH quality exponent, metric-space- and construction-dependent; explicit closed form given only for the Hamming hypercube under the best known LSH construction, rho(c) = 1/(2c-1) (cited to Andoni and Razenshteyn, 2015).
- beta (concentric-annuli construction): beta = min_{k in positive integers} max(rho(c^(1/k)), 1/k), a derived quantity from rho and c, not an independently chosen parameter.
- Regime split: high-dimensional d = omega(sqrt(Q)) is where the fairness/decision/annuli constructions (Theorems 1.2-1.4) are the paper's contribution; low-dimensional d = O(sqrt(Q)) is where the for-all constructions (Theorem 1.5, Appendix D) apply instead.

### Stated limitations
Theorem 1.2's query time is stated to depend on the density ratio D between the c*r-ball and r-ball around a query, and the paper states the adversary can construct a dataset where this ratio is large, "severely degrading performance" — this is an explicit, named weakness of the fairness-only construction, not merely an unoptimized bound. Theorem 1.3's query time is stated to always be at least O(sqrt(n)) regardless of how favorable c is, which the paper calls not ideal given that oblivious LSH methods can push the query-time exponent arbitrarily close to 0 by increasing c. The for-all family (Theorem 1.5, Appendix D) is stated to have space complexity that scales by an extra factor of d, "making them intractable for high-dimensional metric spaces," a direct consequence of needing enough independent hash functions to union-bound over every possible query; the paper also states these for-all algorithms "lack the generality of their adaptive counterparts" because each is tailored to a specific metric space rather than working generically. The adversarial-robustness game defined here (Definition 3.1) treats updates to the dataset as oblivious — chosen in advance by the adversary, not adaptively based on the algorithm's answers — and the paper states it is "not concerned with robustness" against adaptively chosen updates, only queries. The conclusion states three explicit open questions the paper does not resolve: whether matching time/space lower bounds exist for robust ANN algorithms, whether the fairness-to-robustness link generalizes to estimation problems beyond search, and — stated directly — that "a practical implementation of our approach and the nuances it presents in a real system are also important avenues to investigate," meaning no implementation or systems-level evaluation exists in this paper.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Every construction requires the algorithm's setup-phase and per-query internal randomness to be genuinely private from the adversary (Definition 3.1 states the adversary "may know the code for A but not the specific instance of R_setup"); a real deployment must therefore supply a source of randomness the querying party (or anyone observing the querying party's queries and answers) cannot predict or reconstruct — the proofs give no robustness guarantee if this randomness leaks through a side channel the model does not account for. The bucketing and concentric-annuli constructions both require access to a differential-privacy composition and amplification toolkit (the Laplace mechanism, privacy amplification by subsampling, and adaptive/parallel composition theorems, all cited to prior differential-privacy literature and used, not re-derived, as noted in Appendix B) — a system adopting this mechanism needs a correct implementation of these DP primitives, since the robustness proof is built on their guarantees holding exactly. The fairness-based construction (Theorem 1.2) requires an existing exact fair ANN algorithm as a subroutine (cited to Aumuller et al., 2022) that returns a uniformly random valid neighbor, not merely the closest one, so a system without such a subroutine cannot use this construction directly. The bucketing and annuli constructions both require maintaining sqrt(Q) or more independent copies of an underlying LSH-based decision structure simultaneously, so a deployment must know (or bound) Q, the number of future adaptive queries it needs to remain robust against, in advance, since the space cost is stated as a function of Q rather than being unboundedly extensible. The for-all algorithms require the metric space to be discretizable into a bounded covering (explicit constructions given only for the Hamming hypercube and l_p spaces), so applying them to an arbitrary or unbounded metric space is out of scope as stated.

### Contradicts
None found against another entry in this batch. Section 2.1 states its own results differ from Feng et al. (2025), a concurrent and independent paper solving the same problem, in that Feng et al.'s query time scales multiplicatively with a raw near-ball density count while this paper's scales additively with a density ratio — an explicit, attributed disagreement in approach and bound shape between two papers on the same problem, not a contradiction discovered within this corpus.

### References worth retrieving
- Kapralov, Mousavifar, Ozgur (or coauthors), 2024, attack on standard LSH data structures under adaptive queries — attack (the motivating result this paper responds to; states an adaptive adversary needs only a polylogarithmic number of queries to defeat unmodified LSH).
- Feng, Feng, Li, Song, Woodruff, Zhang, "On Differential Privacy [robust ANN]," 2025 — competing (concurrent, independent solution to the same robust-ANN problem, compared directly in Section 2.1 and Table 1).
- Hassidim, Kaplan, Mansour, Matias, Stemmer, 2022 — foundational (the differential-privacy robustification-via-aggregated-copies framework this paper's bucketing and annuli constructions build on).
- Aumuller, Har-Peled, Mahabadi, Pagh, Silvestri, "Sampling a Near Neighbor in High Dimensions — Who is the Fairest of Them All?," ACM Transactions on Database Systems 47(1), 2022 — foundational (defines and studies the fair-ANN algorithms this paper's Theorem 1.2 invokes as a subroutine).
- Beimel, Kaplan, Mansour, Nissim, Saranurak, Stemmer, "Dynamic Algorithms Against an Adaptive Adversary: Generic Constructions and Lower Bounds," STOC 2022 — foundational (source of the cited lower bound that robust search algorithms for certain problems are inherently slower than oblivious ones).
- Andoni and Razenshteyn, "Optimal Data-Dependent Hashing for Approximate Near Neighbors," STOC 2015 — foundational (source of the explicit rho(c) = 1/(2c-1) LSH construction used as the concrete example throughout).
- Cherapanamjeri and Nelson, 2020 and 2024 — foundational (prior discretization/net-based techniques for for-all-guarantee ANN and robust distance estimation, which Appendix D's construction refines).
- Ben-Eliezer, Jayaram, Woodruff, Yogev, 2022b — foundational (formalized adversarial robustness for streaming algorithms; source of the adversarial-robustness game definition adapted here as Definition 3.1).
- Pham and Pagh, 2016, and Wei, 2022 — competing (Las Vegas LSH constructions with no false negatives, stated to remain vulnerable to adversaries who inflate their expected runtime, per Kapralov et al., 2024).

## [ANGEL-SP-18] PIR with compressed queries and amortized query processing
**Citation:** Sebastian Angel, Hao Chen, Kim Laine, Srinath T. V. Setty. "PIR with compressed queries and amortized query processing." IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy, 2018. Pages 962-979. DOI 10.1109/SP.2018.00062.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://eprint.iacr.org/2017/1142.pdf
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2017/1142.pdf
**Domain:** G

### What it does
This paper (the system is called SealPIR in the text, though the paper's own title does not use that name) makes single-server computational Private Information Retrieval (PIR) cheaper on two axes: the size of the query a client sends, and the per-query computation a server performs when many queries from the same client arrive together. Ordinary computational PIR built on Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE), of which the paper's baseline XPIR is an instance, requires the server to hold the database as a d-dimensional hyperrectangle of ciphertext-encrypted elements; the client's query, under the prior approach (Stern's protocol, which XPIR implements), must contain one ciphertext per candidate position along one dimension, so a database of n elements arranged with dimension d needs roughly the d-th root of n ciphertexts in the query. SealPIR replaces this multi-ciphertext query with a single compressed ciphertext plus a server-side procedure called EXPAND: using a technique built on ciphertext substitution (a property of the underlying FHE scheme, here the SEAL library's implementation of the Fan-Vercauteren, FV, encryption scheme), the server homomorphically expands the client's one compressed ciphertext back into the same d ciphertexts XPIR would have required, without the client ever having to send them explicitly. This shrinks client-to-server query bandwidth without changing what the server ultimately computes over. The second technique, probabilistic batch codes (PBC), lets a server answer several PIR queries from the same client (for a batch of k desired elements) using less total computation than running k independent single-element PIR queries. A PBC encodes the n-element database by replicating each element into w candidate positions ("buckets") chosen by w independent hash functions (a construction called Cuckoo hashing when the specific reverse-hashing allocation strategy of Cuckoo hashing is used to place elements into buckets), producing m = w times n total encoded elements across b buckets; to retrieve k desired elements, the client maps its k indices to b buckets using the matching consumer-side hashing procedure (this mapping can fail, returning an explicit failure marker, with a computable failure probability) and issues one PIR query per bucket rather than one per original element, and the server runs standard single-query PIR independently on each bucket.

### Measured results
All measurements on Microsoft Azure H16 server instances (16-core 3.6 GHz Intel Xeon E5-2667, 112 GB RAM) and F16s client instances (16-core, 2.4 GHz Intel Xeon E5-2673, 32 GB RAM), Ubuntu 16.04, compiled with Rust nightly 1.25, across three Azure data centers (West US, South India, West Europe). Each experiment run 10 times with averaged results; standard deviations reported as under 10% of the mean in every case. The paper reports hardware as multi-core (16-core) instances but does not state explicitly, for the microbenchmarks in Figure 9, whether the implementation used a single thread or multiple threads of that 16-core machine; this detail could not be verified from the text.

Microbenchmarks (Figure 9), 288-byte database elements, FHE ciphertext polynomial degree 2048 with 60-bit coefficient modulus, comparing XPIR (dimension d=2 and d=3) against SealPIR (d=2):

| Database size (n, elements) | Metric | XPIR d=2 | XPIR d=3 | SealPIR d=2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 65,536 | Client query generation (ms) | 13.83 | 4.98 | 3.37 |
| 1,048,576 | Client query generation (ms) | 55.14 | 12.74 | 3.37 |
| 65,536 | Query network size (KB) | 4,384 | 1,632 | 64 |
| 1,048,576 | Query network size (KB) | 17,536 | 4,064 | 64 |
| 65,536 | Server answer computation (s) | 0.21 | 0.27 | 0.13 |
| 1,048,576 | Server answer computation (s) | 2.12 | 2.52 | 2.01 |
| 65,536 | Answer network size (KB) | 256 | 1,824 | 256 |
| 1,048,576 | Answer network size (KB) | 256 | 1,952 | 256 |

Query size reduction over XPIR is 274 times at d=2 and 63 times at d=2-vs-d=3 comparison basis, for larger databases. SealPIR's EXPAND procedure adds 11% to 38% server CPU overhead relative to answering a query vector directly (no query compression), but keeps total server answer time comparable to XPIR at the same database size.

Response-time measurements deploying the PIR server in Azure US West and clients under four network conditions, retrieving one 288-byte element, compared against scp (secure copy, downloading the whole database) as a naive-PIR baseline: intra-datacenter (about 3.4 Gbps, measured with iperf), inter-datacenter (client in South India, about 800 Mbps), home network (client in South India, rate-limited to 20 Mbps via the Linux tc traffic-control utility, chosen to match the reported 18.7 Mbps mean US download speed from a cited Akamai report), and mobile network (client in South India, rate-limited to 10 Mbps via tc, chosen to approximate reported average US mobile carrier data speeds). At intra-datacenter bandwidth, scp gives the lowest response time; SealPIR is competitive with both XPIR variants except at the largest tested database size (2^22 elements), where SealPIR falls behind because its EXPAND optimization forces a small plaintext modulus at that size, increasing the number of plaintexts needed. At lower bandwidth (home and mobile conditions), SealPIR's lower network consumption yields up to a 42% reduction in response time relative to the compared schemes.

Throughput (Figure 11), server in Azure US West, 4 to 256 concurrent clients across South India and EU West, database of 2^20 elements of 288 bytes each, experiment designed so the server's CPU or WAN link (not the client or a specific inter-datacenter link) is the bottleneck: XPIR with d=2 saturates at 9 requests/second; SealPIR saturates at 7 requests/second (23% lower throughput than XPIR d=2 in this comparison); against XPIR with d=3, SealPIR achieves about 50% higher throughput. Both SealPIR and XPIR achieve more than 20 times the throughput of naive PIR via scp, because scp's bottleneck is network bandwidth rather than CPU.

Probabilistic Batch Code (PBC) benchmark (Figure 12), database of 2^20 elements, 288 bytes each, SealPIR (t=2^20) as the underlying single-query PIR library, comparing mPIR (SealPIR plus PBC with Cuckoo hashing, w=3 hash functions, b=1.5k buckets) against Pung's own multi-retrieval scheme, at batch sizes k = 16, 64, 256: at k=256, mPIR gives a 2.6 times reduction in server CPU cost for answering queries compared to Pung's scheme, and a 40.5 times reduction compared to running k independent single-query PIR instances. mPIR is 6 times more network-efficient (combined upload and download) than Pung's scheme at the measured batch sizes. mPIR's estimated Cuckoo-hashing failure probability is about 2^-40 for k > 200 (closer to 2^-20 for smaller k), lower than Pung's stated 2^-20 failure probability.

End-to-end case study porting SealPIR and mPIR into the Pung private-messaging system (256K simulated users, 32 real clients, remainder simulated by pre-populating the server database with random messages, closed-loop round-based operation), each client sending one message and retrieving k messages per round, k up to 256: at k=64, the modified system ("Pung+MS," using both mPIR and SealPIR) achieves 3.1 times the throughput, in messages per minute, of the original Pung implementation. Per-client network cost for one round at k=16 falls from 279 MB (original Pung) to 7.7 MB (Pung+MS), a reduction the paper states as over 36 times.

### Parameters
- FHE ciphertext polynomial degree N: 2048, with 60-bit ciphertext coefficient modulus q (SEAL uses q = 2^60 - 2^18 + 1; XPIR uses q = 2^61 - i times 2^14 + 1 for various i), chosen following XPIR's published security estimates based on the Albrecht-Player-Scott hardness analysis.
- Database element size: 288 bytes throughout the main evaluation, chosen to match the message size used by the Pung system in the case study.
- Plaintext modulus t: 2^23 as the default SealPIR setting (a larger t lowers network and computation cost but risks decryption failure from excess noise growth, so t is lowered in some experiments, e.g. to 2^20 for the PBC benchmarks, to guarantee correct decryption).
- XPIR packing parameter alpha: 14 elements packed per XPIR plaintext, chosen to have roughly the same effect as SealPIR's t=2^23 setting for 288-byte elements under the paper's security parameters.
- PIR dimension d: tested at d=2 and d=3 for XPIR; SealPIR evaluated at d=2 in the main comparisons.
- PBC parameters (Cuckoo-hashing variant): w=3 independent hash functions, b=1.5k buckets for a batch size of k, following prior empirical analysis of Cuckoo hashing failure rates cited from other work.
- Batch size k for multi-query PIR: tested at 1 (no amortization baseline), 16, 64, and 256.

### Stated limitations
The paper states that determining the exact failure probability and constant factors of Cuckoo hashing analytically remains an open problem in the literature it cites, so its own failure-probability figures (2^-40 for k > 200, 2^-20 for smaller k) are described as empirical estimates from prior work rather than proven bounds. The paper states that under a malicious (not merely semi-honest) server, the server controls where database elements are placed and so can deliberately place specific elements at index combinations that make GenSchedule always fail for a client requesting that combination, opening what the paper calls a "selective failure" attack analogous to one already known in single-query PIR; the paper states this requires additional mechanisms (making the client's externally visible reaction independent of query success or failure) to convert an information-leaking failure into a mere availability failure, but the paper does not implement or measure such a mechanism. The paper states SealPIR falls behind XPIR in response time specifically at the largest tested database size (2^22 elements) under high-bandwidth (intra-datacenter) conditions, because its EXPAND optimization there forces a smaller plaintext modulus and more plaintexts. The paper states, as future work rather than a solved problem, that CPU costs could be further reduced using a matrix-multiplication aggregation technique from prior work (Beimel et al.) not implemented in this paper, and that PBC bucket-allocation strategies studied here are drawn from online load-balancing literature (elements arriving one at a time) rather than from strategies specific to the offline setting (all elements available at once) that PBC actually operates in, leaving offline-optimized allocation as an open direction.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The client must already know, before issuing a query, which numeric index or indices in the database it wants; the paper states three alternative external mechanisms an application must supply to produce that index (a Bloom filter shared out of band, as in the Pung system; a PIR-by-keyword scheme; or the client independently simulating the server's Cuckoo-hashing placement given a shared pseudorandom seed), none of which SealPIR or the PBC construction itself provides. Multi-query batching (mPIR) requires the client and server to agree in advance on the batch size k and the hashing parameters (w, b) used to construct and consume the PBC; a client that does not know these parameters cannot correctly map its desired indices to buckets. The scheme's privacy guarantee (the server cannot tell which index was retrieved) holds under a semi-honest (honest-but-curious) server for the analysis given; the paper states that a fully malicious server breaks a distinct property (whether a client's chosen batch of indices can be retrieved at all) unless a system built on this scheme separately adds the selective-failure countermeasure described above. mPIR's failure mode (GenSchedule returning an explicit failure marker for a chosen index set) is visible to the client before any PIR query is issued, so a system relying on mPIR must have a defined recovery behavior (retry with different indices, retrieve fewer elements, or otherwise) built into its application logic, since the paper does not mandate a single response to a schedule failure.

### Contradicts
The prior-pass claim (recorded in the target-retrieval registry's rationale) that this paper reports a throughput of "102 MB/s" with no attached experimental condition is not supported anywhere in this paper's text: no figure or table in the paper states a MB/s throughput number at all. The paper's own throughput results are stated in requests per second (7 for SealPIR, 9 for XPIR d=2, both saturating at a 2^20-element, 288-byte-element database under a specific multi-client, multi-datacenter deployment) or in messages per minute (Pung case study), never in MB/s; the "102 MB/s" figure attributed to this paper should be treated as unverified against the primary source and possibly misattributed from a different PIR paper. No other cross-corpus contradiction found.

### References worth retrieving
- foundational: C. Aguilar-Melchor, J. Barrier, L. Fousse, M.-O. Killijian. "XPIR: Private information retrieval for everyone." PoPETs 2016 — the direct baseline this paper's every microbenchmark, response-time, and throughput comparison is measured against.
- competing: S. Angel, S. Setty. "Unobservable communication over fully untrusted infrastructure" (Pung), USENIX OSDI 2016 — the private-messaging system this paper modifies for its end-to-end case study; holds Pung's original custom multi-query PIR scheme this paper's mPIR is compared against.
- foundational: J. Stern. Untitled CPIR protocol referenced as "Stern's protocol" (Figure 1's source construction), cited as the basis for both XPIR and SealPIR's per-dimension query structure.
- foundational: A. Beimel et al. Matrix-multiplication aggregation technique for multi-query PIR, cited as an unimplemented future optimization for reducing SealPIR's CPU cost.
- competing: Y. Ishai et al. Subcube batch code construction, cited as the batch-coding approach underlying Pung's multi-retrieval scheme, against which the paper's own probabilistic batch code is compared in Figure 5.
- attack: M. R. Albrecht, R. Player, S. Scott. "On the concrete hardness of learning with errors." Journal of Mathematical Cryptology, 2015 — the hardness-estimation basis for this paper's and XPIR's choice of FHE security parameters.

- "This technique achieves up to 40× speedup over processing queries one at a time."
- "we can simultaneously reduce network costs by 36× and increase throughput by 3×."

## [ARREGUI-GARCIA-ARXIV-26] On the Effects of Decentralized Moderation on Network Robustness and Information Diffusion in Mastodon
**Citation:** Beatriz Arregui-García, Lucio La Cava, Anees Baqir, Andrea Tagarelli, Riccardo Gallotti, Sandro Meloni. "On the Effects of Decentralized Moderation on Network Robustness and Information Diffusion in Mastodon." arXiv preprint, 2026.
**Retrieved:** full text
**Source URL:** target record (registry/targets-deduped.json)
**Domain:** K

### What it does
The paper measures whether instance-level domain blocking in Mastodon (an administrator on one instance severing all federation with another instance) produces a stable network structure over time, and whether that structure changes how information spreads across the federation. The authors build a signed, directed, temporal graph over Mastodon instances: a positive edge records that at least one user on instance i follows at least one user on instance j (a static, time-invariant layer), and a negative edge records that instance i issued a domain block against instance j on a given day (a daily, time-varying layer). They test structural stability with a discrete-time Markov model over the nine possible directed-dyad sign states, checking whether the empirical distribution of dyad states matches the stationary distribution implied by the average daily transition matrix, at increasing aggregation windows. They then partition instances into a minority group m (instances that actively issue bans) and a majority group M (instances that are predominantly banned), and simulate information diffusion on the positive network with a hybrid contagion model: simple contagion (a discrete-time SIR process, each contact with an informed neighbor informs a susceptible node with probability beta) within a group, and complex contagion (a susceptible node adopts only once the fraction of informed neighbors exceeds threshold T) across the group boundary.

### Measured results
| Metric | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Governance-social interface size | 5,413 instances | Induced subgraph of instances present in both the inter-instance follow snapshot and the daily domain-block record; August 2023 to July 2024, one year |
| Daily domain block actions | Average approximately 4.5x10^4 per day; peak approximately 5.2x10^4 in August 2023; minimum approximately 3.6x10^4 in winter 2023-2024; stabilizing near 4.7x10^4 for the remainder | Same one-year window, aggregated across all instances in the interface |
| Unique moderating vs. moderated instances | Approximately 932 unique moderating instances; approximately 4,848 unique moderated instances | Same one-year window; both populations show continuous turnover, no fixed recurrent core |
| Fraction of active inter-instance links that are negative (blocks) | Approximately 16% during the initial months, declining to approximately 10% during the final four months | Same one-year window |
| Dyad-state persistence (9x9 directed-dyad sign-state transition matrix, daily) | Approximately 98.6% of dyads retain their state from one day to the next | Diagonal dominance of the average daily transition matrix |
| Frobenius distance between daily transition matrices | Maximum approximately 0.82, against a theoretical upper bound of sqrt(18) is approximately 4.24 for maximally divergent 9x9 row-stochastic matrices | Computed across all consecutive day pairs in the one-year window |
| Timescale at which dyad-state stationarity emerges (Kullback-Leibler divergence between predicted and observed motif-abundance distributions) | KL divergence decreases monotonically with aggregation-window size, approaching zero for windows exceeding approximately 20 days | Strict daily-resolution stationarity does not hold; only mesoscopic (multi-week) aggregation satisfies it |
| Timescale at which detailed balance (reversibility) is approximated | Windows of approximately two weeks or longer | Detailed balance fails at daily resolution |
| Within-group information diffusion, beta=1.0, gamma=1.0 (final attack rate, T-dependent) | Minority-to-minority final attack rate approximately 96%; majority-to-majority final attack rate approximately 80% | Simulated on the static network formed by averaging the daily moderation layer over one month combined with the time-invariant positive layer; beta is the SIR infection probability, gamma the recovery probability, both set to 1.0 as an upper bound on within-group contagion |
| Cross-group asymmetry | Minority-to-majority transmission (I^T_mM) remains robust over a broader range of thresholds T than majority-to-minority transmission (I^T_Mm), which declines faster as T increases | Same simulation, at T=0 both directions show substantial diffusion |
| Aggregate observables across the (beta, T) parameter space | Emissivity bias B_E negative across most of the parameter space, indicating the minority group is the more efficient emitter; receptivity bias B_R small in magnitude and non-monotonic; echo-chamber bias B_EC moderate under permissive contagion (low T) and approaches 1 under restrictive contagion (high T) | Full joint sweep of beta and T; B_E, B_R, and B_EC are aggregate observables computed from the four attack-rate scenarios per the formulas of Diaz-Diaz, San Miguel, and Meloni (2022) |
| Loose-moderation counterfactual (domain-block links reclassified as active positive connections) | Overall spread increases; minority-to-majority transmission eventually exceeds majority-to-minority transmission as more pathways open; emissivity bias B_E becomes more negative (minority's broadcasting advantage increases); receptivity bias B_R is higher in the baseline than in the loose scenario; echo-chamber bias B_EC is stronger in the baseline than in the loose scenario | Same simulation framework, with the moderation layer's negative edges treated as positive edges instead |

### Parameters
- Observation window: August 2023 to July 2024 (one year), daily-resolution domain-block records.
- SIR simple-contagion model: infection probability beta = 1.0 used as the primary reported condition (an upper bound on within-group contagion); joint sweep of beta also performed (Figure 6/7) but the range tested is not stated as discrete numeric values in the extracted text.
- Complex-contagion threshold T: swept over [0, 1].
- Diffusion-simulation network: static network built by averaging the daily moderation (negative) layer over a one-month window (chosen because it matches the approximately 20-day equilibrium timescale identified from the KL-divergence analysis), combined with the time-invariant positive (follow) layer.
- Degree-transition analysis: in-degree and out-degree values above 100 grouped into a single category to reduce fluctuation from the long tail of the distribution.

### Stated limitations
The authors state three limitations directly. First, the analysis operates exclusively at the instance level, aggregating follower relationships and moderation actions across all users within each instance, which may obscure individual-level heterogeneity. Second, the follow network is treated as a time-invariant backbone; the authors state this is justified by the differing timescales of the moderation and following processes but that it does not capture gradual evolution of social ties over longer timescales, and that incorporating temporal follow data would give a more complete picture of how the positive and negative layers co-evolve. Third, the contagion model captures only the simple/complex distinction between within- and cross-group transmission and does not account for the semantic content of information or heterogeneous receptivity of individual instances; the authors state that a content-aware diffusion model could yield more refined predictions of which information types are most affected by moderation boundaries.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The stationarity finding requires daily-resolution, longitudinal domain-block records per instance-pair over a period long enough to aggregate to multi-week windows (approximately 20 days for KL divergence to approach zero); a system that logs only current block state, without a dated history of block issuance, cannot reproduce this measurement. The information-diffusion simulation requires a positive (follow) topology and a moderation (block) topology defined over the same set of instances; the authors restrict analysis to the 5,413-instance intersection of two independently collected datasets because the two layers must be simultaneously observed on identical nodes for the signed-network construction to be well defined. The minority/majority partition (governance-active instances vs. predominantly banned instances) is derived from the empirical block-issuance data itself, so any mechanism intended to reproduce or predict this asymmetry needs the same block-issuance signal used here as ground truth.

### Contradicts
None found. This paper's minority/majority governance-asymmetry framing complements rather than contradicts ANAOBI-WWW-23's finding (same domain, different platform: Pleroma) that only a minority of instances (71.6% single-administrator, 3.5% with dedicated moderators) actively manage moderation workload.

## [ASTHANA-ICTIR-11] On the Feasibility of Unstructured Peer-to-Peer Information Retrieval
**Citation:** H. Asthana, Ruoxun Fu, Ingemar J. Cox. "On the Feasibility of Unstructured Peer-to-Peer Information Retrieval." 3rd International Conference on the Theory of Information Retrieval (ICTIR), 2011. DOI 10.1007/978-3-642-23318-0_13.
**Retrieved:** full text via http://www0.cs.ucl.ac.uk/staff/ingemar/Content/papers/2011/ICTIR2011B.pdf
**Source URL:** http://www0.cs.ucl.ac.uk/staff/ingemar/Content/papers/2011/ICTIR2011B.pdf
**Domain:** B

### What it does
The paper determines how many nodes an unstructured peer-to-peer network must query, and the resulting network traffic, to retrieve documents at a target accuracy, using a probably-approximately-correct (PAC, a formal framework in which a search returns a result that is correct with a bounded probability rather than deterministically) search model. A query is broadcast to z randomly selected nodes out of n total; each node holds an independently random subset of the document collection sized so its capacity, summed across all nodes, gives a total system storage R = m·r, where m is the number of unique documents and r is a document's average replication count. The probability of retrieving one specific document di, given it is replicated onto r nodes, is P(di) = 1 − (1 − r/n)^z. Retrieval accuracy for a query is defined as the overlap between the top-k documents an exhaustive search over the entire collection would return and the top-k documents the z-node PAC search returns, divided by k. The expected accuracy averaged over all queries, weighted by query popularity qj, is derived for three replication strategies: uniform (every document replicated the same number of times, independent of popularity), proportional (a document's replication count set proportional to its query popularity, ri = R·qi), and square-root (replication count proportional to the square root of popularity, ri = R·√qi / Σ√qi — following Cohen and Shenker's derivation of this as the strategy that minimizes expected search size for a fixed total storage budget R). The query-popularity distribution qi is modeled as a power law, qi = (1/c)·i^(−α), with the normalization constant c and exponent α fit from AOL query logs and a commercial search engine's logs, giving α in the range 0.8 to 1.0.

### Measured results

| Result | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Nodes queried for 90% top-1 accuracy, uniform replication | ~2,300 nodes | n=1,000,000 nodes, m=10,000,000,000 (10 billion) documents in the collection, each node indexes κ=1/1,000 (0.1%) of the collection |
| Communication cost per query, uniform replication | ~3 MB total (query broadcast plus responses from all queried nodes) | Same 2,300-node query fan-out; query message 300 bytes (conservative, accounting for TCP/IPv6 overhead, versus an estimated 60-byte raw average query of 2.5 terms/30 characters at 2 bytes/character); response 1 KB per node (top-10 results, ~800 bytes compressed to 10% plus TCP/IPv6 overhead rounding) |
| Aggregate network traffic, uniform replication | 3 GB/s, equal to about 0.065% of 2009 global internet traffic (~4,630 GB/s) | 1,000 queries/second across the 1,000,000-node network, same per-query cost of ~3 MB |
| Per-peer bandwidth for query answering | 0.69 KB/s download, 2.3 KB/s upload | 1,000,000 nodes answering 1,000 queries/s in aggregate, so each peer answers ~2.3 queries/s on average |
| Nodes queried and cost/query for α=0.8, 90% accuracy | Uniform: 2,300 nodes / 3.000 MB; proportional: 2,750 nodes / 3.575 MB; square-root: 1,650 nodes / 1.534 MB | Same n=1,000,000, m=10 billion documents, κ=1/1,000; proportional replication is worse than uniform at this α |
| Nodes queried and cost/query for α=1.0, 90% accuracy | Uniform: 2,300 nodes / 3.000 MB; proportional: 1,180 nodes / 1.534 MB; square-root: 780 nodes / 1.014 MB | Same configuration, α=1.0; square-root reduces bandwidth relative to uniform by about two-thirds at this α, about 50% at α=0.8 |
| Aggregate traffic range across replication strategies | 0.03% to 0.07% of global internet traffic | 1,000 queries/s, α swept 0.8 to 1.0, all three replication strategies from Table 1 |
| Local crawl time per peer | ~58 days per full crawl iteration | Each peer crawls its assigned 10 million documents (1/1,000 of a 10-billion-document collection) at 25% of a 200 KB/s average global internet connection speed (Akamai 2010 report), average document size 25 KB |
| Per-peer storage requirement | 5-10 GB disk, 500 MB memory (peak, for query answering with a Trie-based index) | Crawled data ~250 GB raw (10 million documents at 25 KB average), indexed to ~10 GB using term-frequency/position indexing typical of Lucene-class IR packages; noted lossy index compression can reduce index size 50-70% with minimal precision loss |

### Parameters
- Network size n: 1,000,000 nodes (justified by comparison to Gnutella, BitTorrent, and the Faroo commercial P2P search system's claimed user count).
- Collection size m: 10,000,000,000 (10 billion) documents (justified by 2011-era estimates that Google indexed ~20 billion documents, Bing and Yahoo ~12 billion).
- Query rate: 1,000 queries/second (compared against an estimated Google rate of 38,000 queries/second across ~150 million users; the paper states 1,000 queries/second corresponds to each of 1,000,000 nodes issuing ~4 queries/hour continuously, called an upper bound on realistic per-node query rate).
- Target expected accuracy: 90%.
- Per-node storage fraction κ = capacity/m: primary case 1/1,000 (0.1%), giving 5-10 GB local disk; a secondary parametric sweep in Figure 3b covers κ from 0 to 0.02 on a log-linear plot of nodes-queried versus κ.
- Power-law query-popularity exponent α: swept 0 to 1.6 in Figure 1 (fixed search size z=1,000) and Figures 2a/2b (search size swept 0-2,500 at fixed α=0.8 and α=1.0); the communication-cost analysis in Section 4 uses α=0.8 and α=1.0 specifically, values the paper states were measured from AOL query logs and a commercial search engine's logs.
- Query message size: 300 bytes (conservative estimate over a measured average of ~60 bytes, to account for TCP/IPv6 protocol overhead).
- Response size: 1 KB per node, for top-10 results only (justified by the stated finding that users rarely look past the top-10 search results).
- Character encoding assumption: 2 bytes/character (UTF-8 average).
- Node bandwidth for crawling: 25% of 200 KB/s average global internet connection speed (Akamai 2010 report), used during idle time.
- Section 2.2 parametric example (used to introduce the replication-strategy equations, not the main feasibility analysis): m=1,000,000 documents, n=10,000 nodes, κ=1,000 documents per node.

### Stated limitations
The square-root replication strategy is explicitly stated not to be the accuracy-maximizing policy, only the strategy that minimizes expected search size for a fixed storage budget under Cohen and Shenker's derivation; the paper states an accuracy-optimal replication policy is left for future work. The communication-cost analysis considers only bandwidth feasibility, not query latency; the paper states latency analysis, including the fact that an unstructured architecture need not wait for every queried peer to respond before showing partial results, "is part of our future research," not addressed in this paper. The paper's PAC framework covers only the search stage of retrieval, explicitly excluding the acquisition (crawling/indexing) stage from its formal accuracy model, though the crawl-time estimate (58 days per iteration) is given as a separate, informal calculation; the paper states this crawl duration "could degrade the freshness of results and decrease the relevance of documents" and proposes, without evaluating, a cloud-computing-assisted crawling scheme (Amazon EC2 servers funded by donations, distributing crawled fragments via BitTorrent) as a possible mitigation. The known-item search model underlying the core probability equation (Section 2) is stated to be adopted from prior work on file retrieval by exact filename match; the paper states general information retrieval is broader because query terms may match document content, not just a filename, making query-to-document matching more ambiguous — the paper's own extension to ranked top-k retrieval (Section 2.3, Equation 10) is presented as the mechanism that generalizes past this limitation, but the paper does not validate this extension against any real query log or document collection, only derives it analytically. All numeric feasibility results are derived from stated hardware, network, and document-size assumptions (200 KB/s average connection speed, 25 KB average document size, 1 KB compressed result size, etc.), not from a live deployment or a simulation using measured churn or real document/query traces.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Achieving the stated accuracy figures requires the query rate assumption (1,000 queries/second across 1,000,000 nodes) to hold; the per-query cost and per-peer bandwidth figures scale directly with both the query rate and the node-query fan-out z, so a system with a different member count or query rate needs the underlying equations (Equations 8-13) re-evaluated with its own n, m, and target accuracy, not the specific numbers reported here. The square-root and proportional replication strategies both require replication rate ri to be set from the query-popularity distribution qi (ri = R·qi for proportional, ri = R·√qi/Σ√qi for square-root) — this requires the system to observe or estimate per-document query popularity before choosing how many copies of a document to place, which the paper does not itself specify a mechanism for collecting. The accuracy model assumes each node's indexed subset and each query's target node subset are drawn independently at random from the full node population; a query-routing layer that biases node selection (by proximity, by prior contact, or by any non-uniform sampling) would invalidate the closed-form accuracy equations as stated. The crawl-time and per-peer-bandwidth figures assume nodes contribute crawling bandwidth during otherwise-idle time (25% of average connection bandwidth) and 5-10 GB of local storage; a system whose participants cannot supply this much idle bandwidth or storage would not achieve the stated crawl completion time or index coverage.

### Contradicts
None found within this paper's own claims. Against the prior-pass error the governing brief documents (a distributed search system's recall figures misattributed elsewhere as "1.2 million documents across 750 peers, 45-130 peers contacted"): this paper's own primary numbers are 10 billion documents across 1,000,000 nodes, with 780 to 2,750 nodes queried (depending on replication strategy and power-law exponent) to reach 90% accuracy, and a per-query communication cost of 1.0 to 3.6 MB — not the 6 MB figure sometimes associated with this line of work in secondary summaries; that 6 MB, 3-billion-document figure belongs to a different paper's stated bound (Li et al., cited here as reference [1], "On the Feasibility of Peer-to-Peer Web Indexing and Search," IPTPS 2003) and is not a number this paper states or derives.

### References worth retrieving
- foundational: J. Li, B. T. Loo, J. Hellerstein, F. Kaashoek, D. R. Karger, R. Morris, "On the Feasibility of Peer-to-Peer Web Indexing and Search," IPTPS 2003 (reference [1]; the paper this feasibility analysis is explicitly positioned against as an independent route to the same question, cited for the concern that multi-term-query bandwidth in structured, DHT-based approaches can be substantial).
- attack-or-critique: Y. Chawathe, S. Ratnasamy, L. Breslau, N. Lanham, S. Shenker, "Making gnutella-like p2p systems scalable," SIGCOMM 2003 (reference [2]; cited for further concerns about DHT bandwidth and churn).
- attack-or-critique: E. Sit, R. Morris, "Security considerations for peer-to-peer distributed hash tables," IPTPS 2002 (reference [3]; cited specifically for DHT susceptibility to adversarial attack, motivating the paper's preference for an unstructured architecture).
- competing: M. Zhong, J. Moore, K. Shen, A. L. Murphy, "An evaluation and comparison of current peer-to-peer full-text keyword search techniques," WebDB 2005 (reference [4]; a comparative evaluation of competing P2P full-text search techniques).
- foundational: Cohen, Shenker — the square-root and proportional replication-strategy derivation this paper directly builds on and extends to non-uniform PAC accuracy (already a corpus seed per BRIEF.md as the Cohen-Shenker square-root replication result; matches reference [10] in this bibliography — retrieve the exact citation to confirm venue/year against the corpus entry already held).
- foundational: Ferreira et al., the probabilistic-quorum-system model of P2P search this paper's Section 2.1 reviews as the origin of probabilistic search analysis (reference [9]).
