## [ASTHANA-PHD-14] PAC'nPost: A Peer-to-Peer Micro-blogging Social Network

**Citation:** Harshvardhan Asthana. "PAC'nPost: A Peer-to-Peer Micro-blogging Social Network." PhD thesis, University College London, 2014.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/1457379/1/Harshvardhan%20Asthana%20thesis%20-%20submitted.pdf (candidate URL from registry; local file matches title, author, and abstract)
**Source URL:** https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/1457379/1/Harshvardhan%20Asthana%20thesis%20-%20submitted.pdf
**Domain:** B

### What it does
PAC'nPost lets a node in an unstructured peer-to-peer network retrieve the short posts ("micro-blogs") of the users it follows, and search all published micro-blogs by keyword, without a central server and without directly contacting the nodes it follows. It builds on the probably approximately correct (PAC) search architecture, in which a node retrieves an item with a target accuracy by querying a fixed number z of random peers, provided the item has already been replicated onto a computable fraction of the network. The framework's problem is to replicate every newly created post onto enough nodes, fast enough, without flooding the network with copies (a mechanism the thesis calls rapid-yet-restrained dissemination) and without a central coordinator, given that microblog creation happens continuously and at a high rate rather than as a single one-off rumor.

Every node in the network periodically (every s seconds) sends a request to z randomly chosen peers, naming the list of user IDs it follows and the identifier of the latest post from each it has already retrieved. Each queried node answers by returning, from its own local storage, the most recent post from every followed user it has stored, plus its own most-recently-published post, plus the current contents of a small local structure called the transfer buffer. The transfer buffer holds a bounded number of recently encountered posts that the node has not yet decided to stop forwarding; a post the node chooses not to place in the buffer is permanently excluded from further forwarding by that node (called "stifling," borrowed from epidemic/gossip terminology). Buffer membership is decided per post with a probability that decays with the post's age, P(select) = e^(−t/β), where t is the post's age in seconds and β is a tunable "dissemination parameter" — a larger β keeps older posts eligible for forwarding longer, increasing both the post's final replication and each node's bandwidth. A post is eligible for buffer selection only during its first sr seconds after publication (a fixed replication window), after which no node will forward it further regardless of buffer decisions already made. When a post is first published, its origin node immediately sends it to z (or, in the bandwidth-optimized variant, a separate initial-seeding count zs) random peers, giving the post a head start on this stifling process before ordinary scheduled queries take over its spread.

Retrieval accuracy, µ, defined as the probability of finding a specific post by querying z random nodes given it has been replicated onto r of n total nodes, follows µ = 1 − (1 − r/n)^z, the same relation underlying the PAC search architecture cited from the thesis's own earlier ICTIR 2011 paper (Asthana, Fu, Cox). This equation determines the replication fraction r/n required for a chosen target accuracy at a chosen query fan-out z, and the thesis inverts it to compute the number of nodes queried needed for a required accuracy, or vice versa. Keyword search reuses the identical query mechanism: a query for a keyword is broadcast to the same z random peers, each of which searches its local micro-blog collection using the BM25 ranking algorithm and returns its own top-k ranked results, which the querying node merges by BM25 score into a single top-k list.

To decouple the replication rate from the query interval s (in the base design the two are coupled because replication happens only via ordinary scheduled queries), the thesis's Chapter 4 variant introduces a separate role, "replicators": at every iteration, a node is admitted into the replicator set with a probability that also decays with the age of its most-recent locally-stored post, e^(−(t−1)/δ) for parameter δ, and each replicator independently forwards its own transfer buffer contents to zr additional random nodes per iteration — mimicking the "eager push" primitive of classical gossip protocols while still using the transfer-buffer stifling mechanism to support many concurrent, independently-aged rumors (one per post) rather than a single global rumor.

Chapter 5 adds a two-step algorithm for detecting a trending keyword — one occurring in posts at an elevated rate — without any node having access to global post-creation statistics. Step one: on each scheduled query, each queried node reports the top-j most frequent keywords (by cumulative count) found in its local keyword-storage sets covering the most recent (s+t) iterations, where t is the number of consecutive iterations a keyword must appear in to count as trending; the querying node sums frequencies across the z responses. Step two: on the following scheduled query, the node asks the same z peers for the specific iteration numbers at which any keyword whose combined frequency exceeds w times the median frequency (w a system parameter) was observed; merging the returned iteration numbers lets the node compute a trending fraction σ — the proportion of the required t consecutive iterations in which the keyword was actually observed — and treat the keyword as trending once σ exceeds a threshold.

### Measured results

| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| Required replication rate r/n = 12% for 95% retrieval accuracy at z=25 nodes queried | Derived from µ = 1−(1−r/n)^z with µ=0.95, z=25 (analytical, not simulated) |
| Accuracy 95% on first request rises to 99.83% by second request and 99.99% by third request | Same accuracy formula, applied cumulatively across s=30-second scheduled requests, each independently sampling z=25 nodes |
| Retrieval accuracy 96.68% (mean), 0.15 std dev, at transfer-buffer size \|T\|=3, deterministic selection (DSel) | Network of 100,000 nodes, post creation rate 25 posts/sec, 10 simulations, each 600 iterations, TREC Microblog Tweets2011 corpus as post source, each node follows 35 random peers |
| Fixed-buffer retrieval accuracy ranges from 90.65% (\|T\|=1) to 99.49% (\|T\|=5) at n=10,000, and from 83.49% (\|T\|=1) to 98.78% (\|T\|=5) at n=100,000 | Post creation rate 25 posts/sec, z=25, s=30, 10 simulations per configuration, deterministic (DSel) buffer selection |
| At post creation rate 125 posts/sec, required buffer size for 95%+ accuracy rises to \|T\|=5 (n=10,000, 95.27%) and \|T\|=11 (n=100,000, 95.47%) | Same simulation setup, 10x the post creation rate |
| Posts reach 95% of final replication within 13-24 iterations depending on buffer size and network size | Iteration-to-95%-of-final-replication tables, same simulation configurations as above |
| Flexible (exponential-decay) buffer: β=5.1 gives 95.33% retrieval accuracy at n=10,000; β=14.8 gives 95.46% at n=100,000; corresponding replication 11.6% (n=10,000) and 12.6% (n=100,000), close to the theoretical 12% target | 10 simulations per (β, n) pair, 600 iterations each, z=25, s=30 |
| Keyword search accuracy is substantially lower than post-retrieval accuracy under local BM25 statistics (e.g., 84.97%@10 vs 95.46% post retrieval at n=100,000, β=14.8) but recovers to near the post-retrieval level (92.80%@10) when global BM25 statistics are made available to all nodes | Same 100,000-node simulation; local vs. global BM25 parameter comparison isolates the cause as parameter-estimation error from local-only statistics, not a fundamental search-architecture limit |
| Bounding transfer buffer at \|T\|max=25 (vs. unbounded) requires raising β from 14.8 to 15.7 to retain 95%+ post-retrieval accuracy (95.13% achieved), with keyword accuracy 84.98%@10 | n=100,000, mean buffer size otherwise ranges 1-15 posts and max buffer size 45-450 posts unbounded |
| Under heavy churn (mean session length 60 seconds, ~1,000 of 100,000 nodes joining/leaving per second, 50,000 active at a time), accuracy at β=15.7 falls to 92.53% post retrieval / 84.20% keyword@10; raising β to 17.3 restores 95.46% / 87.47% | n=100,000, \|T\|max=25, Poisson join arrivals balancing exponential exit rate |
| Massive-exit churn (80,000 to 10,000 active nodes) degrades accuracy only mildly; massive-join churn (10,000 to 80,000 active nodes) causes a sharp initial accuracy drop that recovers to near-baseline within about 60 seconds | n=100,000, β=17.3, \|T\|max=25, post creation rate 25/sec |
| Per-node upload+download bandwidth of 6.64 KB/sec (~17.2 GB/month) under the coupled (Chapter 3) design; aggregate network traffic 0.664 GB/sec at n=100,000, stated as 0.014% of measured 2009 global internet traffic (4,630 GB/s) | β=17.3 configuration (the churn-resilient one), 1 KB/post disk size, minimum 8 posts per request/response, ≥50% compression assumed, z/s=0.83 requests serviced per node per second |
| Analytically minimized total system bandwidth: 10.35 MB/iteration at n=10,000 (19.45% replication, z=16, s=60); 327.36 MB/iteration at n=100,000 (6.15% replication, z=49, s=60) | Bandwidth model B=Br+Bq+Be (Eqs. 4.1-4.3) with ct=64 bytes/contact, cn=8 bytes/peer-specifier, cb=1000 bytes/post, f=35 followers/node, α=2.5×10^-4 posts/node/iteration (10x Twitter's measured average of 4,600 tweets/sec across a 200-million-user base) |
| Non-uniform (power-law, γ=0.68) follower/posting-rate replication of high- vs. regular-popularity users' posts separately gives only marginal bandwidth reduction versus uniform replication (e.g., 9.46 MB vs 10.35 MB at n=10,000, p(h)=0.01α) | Top-1% of nodes assigned 20% of all follower edges and (in the tested split) up to 50% of post-creation probability; analytical optimum per Eqs. 4.1-4.3 applied separately to each population |
| Decoupled replicator-based design: e.g. zr=8.5, δ=0.66, zs=50, β=6.9 gives 95.54% post-retrieval accuracy at 21.28% replication and 9.21 MB bandwidth (n=10,000); zr=7.5, β=15.9 gives 95.85% accuracy at 6.57% replication and 307.32 MB bandwidth (n=100,000) | 10 simulations per configuration, 1,200 iterations each, TREC corpus, BM25 local statistics, z=16 (n=10,000) or z=49 (n=100,000), s=60 |
| Trending-keyword detection: with a keyword injected into y=5% of posts over t=10 consecutive iterations and j=2 (top-2 keyword-frequency pairs returned per query), 9,379 of 10,000 nodes (93.8%) reach trending fraction σ≥80%; extra bandwidth overhead 9.73% | n=10,000 nodes, β=5.1 (12% replication baseline), z=25, s=30, w=10, 10 simulations per (y,j) combination |
| Detecting 5 simultaneous trending keywords (rates 5%, 10%×3, 15%) requires j=3 to reach high σ for the least-frequent (5%) keyword (6,153/10,000 nodes at σ≥80%); at j=2 the 5% keyword is not detected by most nodes (1,064/10,000); bandwidth overhead reaches 37.73% at j=3 | Same n=10,000 base simulation configuration, 5 concurrent injected trending keywords over t=10 iterations |

All simulation results above ran the actual PAC'nPost node logic in a discrete-iteration simulator, not an emulated network testbed; no real-network deployment or wide-area measurement is reported anywhere in the thesis.

### Parameters
Target accuracy µ: fixed at 95% throughout ("the most important decision" the designer makes, per the thesis; a lower target trades directly against replication or query count). Nodes queried per request, z: 25 in the base design (Chapters 3, 5); optimized to 15-16 (n=10,000) or 45-51 (n=100,000) as a function of query interval s in the bandwidth-optimized design (Chapter 4). Query interval, s: 30 seconds (base design, chosen to resemble Twitter's user experience) or 60-120 seconds (bandwidth-optimized design). Replication window, sr: 30 seconds (time a post is allowed to spread before being deemed available for retrieval). Dissemination parameter β: swept from 4.9-15.0 across experiments depending on n and target accuracy; determines exponential post-selection-into-buffer probability e^(−t/β). Maximum transfer buffer size, |T|max: unbounded in initial experiments, then capped at 25 (Chapter 3) or 100 (Chapter 4, decoupled design). Post creation rate, α: 25 posts/iteration (10x an assumed Twitter baseline of 4,600 tweets/sec over 200 million users) as the default; 125 posts/iteration (50x-500x baseline depending on n) tested as a spike condition; also expressed as α=2.5×10^-4 posts/node/iteration for the bandwidth model. Followers per node, f: fixed at 35 uniformly, based on Kwak et al.'s reported 1.47 billion links over 41.7 million Twitter users; later relaxed to a power-law distribution with exponent γ=0.68 (top 1% of nodes hold 20% of all follower edges). Post size, cb: 1,000 bytes (500 UTF-8 characters at 2 bytes/character). Per-contact protocol overhead, ct: 64 bytes (empty TCP/IP packet). Per-followed-peer specifier cost, cn: 8 bytes. Per-node contributed disk: 1 GB, split 90% post storage / 10% index. Churn model: session lengths exponentially distributed with mean 60 seconds under the "heavy churn" test; Poisson-arrival joins balance exponential-exit departures, holding active population roughly constant at 50,000 of 100,000 total. Seeding parameter zs: 25-105 tested (Chapter 4), trading off against β for a fixed target replication. Replicator-selection parameter δ: 0.66 in the reported decoupled-design simulations. Replicator fan-out zr: 7-9 (n=10,000) or 7-8.5 (n=100,000) in the decoupled-design simulations. Trending-keyword parameters: t=10 consecutive iterations to qualify as trending, w=10 (frequency threshold multiplier over median), j=1-3 (number of keyword-frequency pairs returned per query), y=5%-15% (fraction of posts carrying the injected trending keyword in test scenarios).

### Stated limitations
The thesis states PAC'nPost provides no mechanism for a user to delete or recall a published post once it has spread; a "recall/delete mechanism" is listed as future work. It states that the fixed-capacity, first-in-first-out (FIFO) storage area at each node means older posts are eventually evicted and permanently lost from the network once no node retains a copy, and that "an archiving strategy needs to be considered" — no such strategy is designed or evaluated in the thesis. The two-step trending-keyword algorithm is stated to require significant additional bandwidth (up to 37.73% overhead in the tested multi-keyword configuration) when tuned to detect multiple simultaneous trending keywords, which the authors state is future work to reduce. The thesis states BM25 is not an optimal ranking function for very short documents (micro-blog posts sized like SMS messages, ~140 characters) because term-frequency weighting is largely uninformative at that length, and states that query-independent features (publisher popularity, follow-relationship distance) would be a better ranking signal — not implemented or evaluated, only proposed as future work. The thesis states the framework is vulnerable to two forms of content pollution: false-identity disinformation and spam; it states these malicious posts would not appear in a user's followed-post timeline (because that timeline is restricted to accounts the user follows) but could appear in keyword-search results, and states that no defense is implemented — a "system of complaints" is sketched as a possible future direction but explicitly noted to itself require a decentralized reputation mechanism whose complaint-submitter's own reliability must also be assessed, which the thesis states is unsolved and left as future work rather than designed. The trending-keyword mechanism's susceptibility to spam abuse (a spammer inserting the trending keyword into unrelated posts to be retrieved by searches on that keyword) is stated explicitly as a known, unaddressed vulnerability, also deferred to future work. The non-uniform (popularity-weighted) replication scheme is stated to yield only marginal bandwidth savings versus uniform replication, in contrast to distributed web search, because the thesis's own periodic-polling retrieval model requires every node to keep querying for both high- and low-popularity content on every cycle, which the authors state erodes the benefit non-uniform document distribution provides in a more static distributed-search setting. The system-bandwidth calculation for mobile devices (6.64 KB/sec sustained upload+download) is stated by the authors to be "currently not viable for a mobile phone," with the only proposed mitigation being to have a mobile app communicate through a separate always-on desktop node rather than the phone itself directly participating.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
PAC'nPost requires an underlying peer-sampling/membership service that supplies each node with a partial, near-uniformly-random view of the network and periodically refreshes that view by exchanging entries with other nodes; the thesis names Cyclon, the overlay management system of Jelasity et al., and Brahms as examples that could supply this, but does not itself implement or evaluate any of them, so the correctness of PAC'nPost's random-peer-selection assumption depends entirely on whichever such service is deployed beneath it. It requires every participating node to follow at least one other peer, because a node that follows nobody never issues the scheduled queries that also carry replication traffic via the transfer buffer; the thesis states that if a newly published post is seeded only to nodes that follow nobody, that post fails to replicate — an explicitly acknowledged (if "very unlikely") failure mode. The keyword-search accuracy measurement depends on a centralized "gold standard" database that mirrors every published post, used only for evaluation, not for production operation — a real deployment has no such oracle and cannot itself measure retrieval or keyword-search accuracy against ground truth. The bandwidth-optimized (decoupled) design and the trending-keyword mechanism both assume the underlying transfer-buffer/stifling mechanism from the base design already functions and is running on every node; the trending-keyword mechanism specifically piggybacks its extra request/response fields onto the already-scheduled query and therefore inherits every precondition (working peer-sampling service, non-empty follow lists, honest response content) that the base retrieval mechanism requires. Retrieval-accuracy measurement throughout assumes queried nodes answer truthfully and completely from their actual local storage; no experiment introduces a node that misreports its stored content, forges a keyword-frequency count, or omits available posts, so none of the measured accuracy or bandwidth figures characterize behavior under such a node.

### Contradicts
None found among the papers in this batch (W1-5). The thesis's own two-page WWW 2012 companion paper (Asthana and Cox, "PAC'nPost: A Framework for a Micro-blogging Social Network in an Unstructured P2P Network") is stated by the registry's own retrieval-justification note to be too short to state the mechanism in implementable detail; this thesis is the correct full-length source for citing PAC'nPost mechanism details and measured figures, and any prior citation of numeric results to the WWW 2012 paper alone should be checked against this thesis instead. The thesis's own claim that existing DHT-based peer-to-peer social networks (PeerSoN, eXO, Cuckoo, My3) "do not address how a keyword search across all published data could be performed" and "assume a tight-knit community of peers" is the thesis authors' characterization of those systems, not a verified fact from this batch — retrieving those papers directly would be needed to confirm or contradict it.

## [ATENIESE-CCS-07] Provable Data Possession at Untrusted Stores
**Citation:** Giuseppe Ateniese, Randal Burns, Reza Curtmola, Joseph Herring, Lea Kissner, Zachary Peterson, Dawn Song. "Provable Data Possession at Untrusted Stores." ACM Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS), 2007. DOI 10.1145/1315245.1315318.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.cs.jhu.edu/~ragib/sp10/p598-ateniese.pdf
**Source URL:** https://www.cs.jhu.edu/~ragib/sp10/p598-ateniese.pdf
**Domain:** C

Note: the retrieved document is the authors' full version, which itself states it is "the full version of the paper that appears in Proceedings of the 14th ACM Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS 2007)," and states one correction to the original proceedings version — the public-key parameter `e` was moved into the secret key after the authors found an error in the original security proof, which removes public verifiability from the main scheme (a restricted variant restoring public verifiability is given separately). Title and authors match the registry record.

### What it does
Provable Data Possession (PDP) lets a client that has stored a file at an untrusted remote server verify that the server still holds the complete, unmodified file, without the client retrieving the file or the server transmitting the file back. The client generates a proof request (a challenge) naming a small, randomly chosen subset of the file's blocks; the server computes a short response over exactly those blocks; the client checks the response against metadata it kept locally. Because the check touches only a sampled subset of blocks rather than the whole file, both server-side computation and the data transmitted per challenge are held constant, independent of file size, so long as the server actually holds every block requested.

The scheme is built from a homomorphic verifiable tag (HVT): a short, cryptographically unforgeable per-block credential that lets the server prove it holds one or more specific blocks without transmitting those blocks, and lets tags for multiple blocks be combined into one aggregate value that still checks against the corresponding aggregate of the underlying blocks. Setup: the client picks a public/secret key pair, computes one tag per file block (each tag bound to that block's position by a one-time index derived from a secret value and a global counter, preventing tag reuse across positions or files), and sends the file plus all tags to the server; the client then deletes its local copy and keeps only a small constant amount of key material. Challenge: the client picks a fresh random key for a pseudo-random permutation and sends a challenge naming how many blocks to sample (`c`) and the keys needed to derive which `c` block indices are being requested; the server locates those blocks and their tags, combines the requested tags into one aggregate value `T` and computes a second aggregate value `ρ` from the same blocks raised to a client-supplied random exponent; the client verifies the algebraic relation between `T` and `ρ` holds, which is possible only if the server actually possessed every one of the `c` requested blocks (in the paper's strong variant, S-PDP) or their sum (in the paper's efficient variant, E-PDP). The paper's key point of difference from the schemes it compares against is blockless verification: the server never returns the actual data, only an aggregate cryptographic value, so verification bandwidth stays constant regardless of block size or count.

Two constructions are given. S-PDP assigns each sampled block an independent pseudo-random coefficient before combining tags, which the paper states guarantees the server possessed each of the `c` requested blocks individually. E-PDP sets every coefficient to 1, reducing server and client computation to a single modular exponentiation each, at the cost of only guaranteeing possession of the sum of the requested blocks rather than each block individually; the paper argues this weaker guarantee is not a practical concern because a cheating server would need to precompute and store an astronomically large number of block-sum combinations to exploit the gap (for n=1,000 blocks and c=101 sampled per challenge, on the order of 10^140 stored values).

### Measured results

All measurements from the authors' own implementation of E-PDP, and comparison implementations of two other protocols the paper implemented for the comparison (B-PDP, the Deswarte et al./Filho et al. RSA-hash scheme; MHT-SC, David Wagner's Merkle-hash-tree-based suggestion). Hardware: Intel 2.8 GHz Pentium IV, 512 KB cache, 800 MHz EPCI bus, 1024 MB RAM, Red Hat Linux 9 kernel 2.4.22, OpenSSL 0.9.8b crypto library, 1024-bit RSA modulus, 4 KB file blocks, files stored on an ext3 filesystem on a Seagate Barracuda 7200.7 (ST380011A) 80 GB Ultra ATA/100 drive. Every reported result is the mean of 20 trials; the paper states results "varied little across trials" and does not report confidence intervals.

| Result | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Detection-probability example | For n=10,000 blocks with t=1% (100 blocks) deleted, sampling c=460 blocks (4.6% of n) gives detection probability >99%; c=300 gives >95% | Derived from the paper's closed-form probability bound (not a simulation), a function of n, t, c only |
| E-PDP proof time with sampling vs. all-blocks | 0.4 s at 99% confidence sampling vs. 1.8 s checking every block, for a 64 MB file | E-PDP implementation, on-disk (I/O included), 64 MB file, the confidence-level comparison in Fig. 4 |
| E-PDP disk-vs-memory overhead | E-PDP generates proofs (1.0 s) faster than the disk delivers data (1.8 s) for a 64 MB file when checking all blocks; sampling at 99% confidence adds about 0.04 s of I/O overhead over the in-memory-only time, for larger files | Same hardware, all-blocks and sampled configurations compared in memory vs. on disk |
| E-PDP vs. B-PDP and MHT-SC, challenge computation | E-PDP more than 185 times faster than B-PDP and more than 4.5 times faster than MHT-SC | 768 KB files, challenge (proof-generation) phase only, same hardware; the paper states these ratios grow arbitrarily large for larger files because B-PDP and MHT-SC scale linearly with file size while E-PDP's cryptographic cost grows only logarithmically |
| E-PDP pre-processing throughput | 162 KB/s | Client-side metadata (tag) generation only, excludes I/O to load data or transfer the file; linear in file size because E-PDP exponentiates every block |
| MHT-SC pre-processing throughput | 433 KB/s (average) | Same measurement protocol as above, for the Merkle-hash-tree comparison scheme |
| Concrete deployment example (not a separate measurement, a worked calculation from the derivation above) | 4 GB file (n=1,000,000 4KB blocks): tag storage overhead 128 MB at the server, client key material about 3 KB, per-challenge client-to-server message 168 bytes, per-challenge server-to-client response 148 bytes, c=460 blocks sampled to detect ≥1% deletion at >99% confidence | 1024-bit RSA modulus, S-PDP scheme, AES for the pseudo-random permutation, HMAC for the pseudo-random function, SHA-1 for the hash function |
| Server pre-computation cost to defeat E-PDP's weaker sum-only guarantee | On the order of 10^140 combinations to precompute and store | Worked example, n=1,000 blocks, c=101 blocks sampled per challenge, stated by the paper as intractable, offered as the argument that E-PDP's weaker guarantee is not exploitable in practice |

### Parameters
- File block size: 4 KB, chosen (per Fig. 6's measured pre-processing-vs-challenge tradeoff) to minimize server effort; the paper states the best balance occurs at "natural file system and memory block sizes of 4-64 KB."
- RSA modulus size: 1024 bits, used throughout all reported experiments.
- Sample size `c` (blocks queried per challenge): worked example uses c=460 for 99% confidence and c=300 for 95% confidence, both at t=1% of n deleted; general closed-form bound given as a function of n, t, and c (Section 5.1), with the paper noting detection probability at fixed `t`-as-a-fraction-of-n is achievable with `c` independent of the total block count n.
- Security parameters κ, ℓ, λ: defined as construction parameters for the pseudo-random function, pseudo-random permutation, and public-verifiability threshold respectively; the paper gives no single numeric default, deferring to standard cryptographic parameter sizes (e.g., ℓ=160 is used as a typical value in one computation-cost comparison).

### Stated limitations
The paper states E-PDP guarantees possession only of the sum of the requested blocks, not of each individual block, unlike S-PDP; it argues (not measures) that exploiting this gap requires a server to precompute and store a combinatorially infeasible number of block-sum values, and gives a numeric example (n=1,000, c=101) rather than a proof that no smaller feasible attack exists for all parameter choices. The paper states it leaves devising a publicly-verifiable PDP scheme with challenge and response sizes smaller than one file block as "an open problem" — the public-verifiability variant it does construct has communication cost "slightly larger r than the size of a file block," which the paper flags as worse than the main scheme's constant, sub-block-size communication. The paper states the KEA1-r (Knowledge of Exponent Assumption, RSA variant) cryptographic assumption underlies its main scheme's security proof, and separately gives an alternative construction avoiding that assumption at the stated cost of "a significant amount" of added network communication. The paper states client-side pre-processing throughput (162 KB/s) is the limiting performance factor for E-PDP overall, since challenge and verification are far cheaper; it offers two unmeasured mitigations — pre-processing is a one-time cost per file (unlike repeated challenges) and is "completely parallelizable" across files or, given shared key material, within a single file — without measuring parallelized throughput. The paper states its probabilistic detection guarantee applies only when the server has deleted or corrupted a fraction `t` of the blocks; detecting the loss of a small, fixed absolute number of blocks (rather than a fraction of n) requires proportionally larger `c` as n grows, which the paper's own bound formula implies but does not separately tabulate.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Requires the client to retain the full file (or reconstruct it) at Setup time in order to compute one tag per block before deletion, and requires the client to retain a small constant amount of secret key material (about 3 KB in the paper's 4 GB worked example) for the life of the stored file; losing that key material makes the client unable to issue or verify any future challenge. Requires the storage server to retain the tag set alongside the file: the paper's worked example adds 128 MB of tag storage for a 4 GB file (roughly 3.2% overhead), so any storage layer this mechanism sits on top of must accommodate that fixed per-file overhead in addition to the raw file bytes. Requires the client to be able to issue challenges specifying particular sampled block indices and receive a response tied to exactly those indices — this means the underlying storage or transport layer must let the verifying party address individual fixed-size blocks of a stored object by position, rather than only by whole-object retrieval; a storage layer that reshapes, recompresses, or re-chunks the object between Setup and Challenge without preserving block boundaries breaks the tag-to-block binding the scheme relies on (the paper does state the server may store the file however it likes, including compressed, provided it can still answer per-block challenges correctly). Provides only a possession check, not a retrievability guarantee: the paper explicitly separates its own scheme from proof of retrievability (POR), so any system requiring a proof that the client (or a third party) could actually reconstruct the full file from what the server holds needs POR or POR-equivalent verification (see ATENIESE-CCS-07's own Related Work discussion of Juels and Kaliski), not PDP alone. Detection is probabilistic over a deleted-block fraction: a system that must detect the loss of a small fixed number of blocks regardless of total file size needs to size `c` accordingly (per the paper's own formula), and PDP's guarantee for t below the sampling resolution is correspondingly weaker.

### Contradicts
None found against other entries in this corpus as currently extracted. The registry's own citation note (`why_needed`) states this paper's guarantee "does not necessarily prov[e] the client could reconstruct the whole file if some blocks were in fact lost" and calls out possession-versus-retrievability as a commonly conflated distinction — the retrieved full text confirms this directly, stating its schemes are a distinct, more restricted guarantee from proof of retrievability (POR) as introduced by Juels and Kaliski, whose POR scheme (per this paper's own related-work description) applies only to encrypted files and only to a number of queries fixed in advance, while this paper's PDP schemes apply to unencrypted, public data and place no bound on the number of challenges.

### References worth retrieving
- Juels, Kaliski. "PORs: Proofs of Retrievability for Large Files." (introduces proof of retrievability, POR — cited by this paper as comparable in scope but restricted to encrypted files and a pre-fixed query count). — competing (the stronger-guarantee, narrower-applicability alternative this paper is explicitly checked against).
- Golle, Jarecki, Mironov. (cited as [20] — introduces storage-complexity enforcement based on the n-Power Decisional Diffie-Hellman assumption, and describes David Wagner's Merkle-hash-tree suggestion, implemented in this paper as MHT-SC). — competing (direct performance-comparison baseline in this paper's own experiments, more than 4.5x slower than E-PDP at 768 KB).
- Deswarte, Quisquater, Saidane. (cited as [17], RSA-hash-based remote storage verification) and Filho, Barreto (cited as [19], the same protocol family) — implemented in this paper as B-PDP. — competing (direct performance-comparison baseline, more than 185x slower than E-PDP at 768 KB).
- Schwarz, Miller. "Store, Forget, and Check: Using Algebraic Signatures to Check Remotely Administered Storage." (cited as [40] — verifies m/n erasure-coded data across colluding sites using algebraic signatures). — competing (a scheme targeting erasure-coded, multi-site storage, directly relevant to this project's storage-encoding component; this paper states its file-access, server-computation, and communication complexity are all linear in the number of file blocks per challenge, and that its security is unproven).
- Sebe, Domingo-Ferrer, Martinez-Balleste, Deswarte, Quisquater. (cited as [41] — Diffie-Hellman-based remote file integrity checking). — competing (comparison scheme; this paper states it requires O(n) client storage and full-file server access per challenge, violating the outsourced-storage model this paper targets).
- Naor, Rothblum. (cited as [37] — introduces sub-linear authentication and proves one-way functions are necessary for efficient online checking). — foundational (the paper's security definitions and knowledge-extractor framing draw directly on this work).
- Aspnes, Feigenbaum, Yampolskiy, Zhong. "Towards a theory of data entanglement." (cited as [2] — an alternative undetectable-deletion-resistance technique via data entanglement). — competing (an alternative mechanism family to PDP for the same untrusted-storage integrity problem, achieving resistance to deletion by encoding cross-object dependencies rather than by challenge-response sampling).

### Verbatim extracts
- "E-PDP is 185 times faster than the previous secure protocol on 768 KB files"
- "the client can detect server misbehavior with probability greater than 99% by asking proof of possession for only 460 randomly selected blocks"
- "E-PDP generates proofs faster than the disk can deliver data: 1.0 second versus 1.8 seconds"
- "we leave as an open problem devising publicly-verifiable PDP schemes where the size of challenges and responses is less than the size of a single file block"
- "E-PDP only guarantees possession of the sum of the blocks... and not necessarily possession of each one of the blocks"

## [ATTIYA-PODC-16] Specification and Complexity of Collaborative Text Editing
**Citation:** Hagit Attiya, Sebastian Burckhardt, Alexey Gotsman, Adam Morrison, Hongseok Yang, Marek Zawirski. "Specification and Complexity of Collaborative Text Editing." ACM Symposium on Principles of Distributed Computing (PODC), 2016. DOI 10.1145/2933057.2933090.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.cs.technion.ac.il/~hagit/publications/podc16.pdf
**Source URL:** https://doi.org/10.1145/2933057.2933090
**Domain:** D

### What it does
The paper gives a formal correctness definition for a replicated list object — the abstraction underlying collaborative text editing, where each list element represents one inserted unit such as a character or line — and proves a worst-case lower bound on the memory any correct implementation must retain. Two specifications are defined over abstract executions consisting of insert, delete, and read operations and a visibility relation between them. The strong list specification requires a single global, transitive, irreflexive, total list order over all inserted elements such that every read returns exactly the elements visible to it and not yet deleted, in an order consistent with that one global order; this rules out an element deleted earlier resurfacing in a different relative order once its neighbors change. The weak list specification relaxes this: the list order is required to be acyclic only among the specific elements a given read returns, so orderings that involve an already-deleted element may form cycles without violating the specification, permitting more implementation behaviors (for example, two different reads observing "ab" and "ba" for the same pair of characters once an interleaving element between them has been deleted). Both specifications imply eventual consistency for protocols that additionally guarantee eventual visibility (every operation eventually becomes visible to all but finitely many future events). The paper reformulates the RGA (Replicated Growable Array) protocol using a timestamped-insertion (TI) tree — a tree data structure that never removes or modifies nodes, only adds them, so that convergence follows directly from set union being associative and commutative regardless of message-delivery order — and proves RGA implements the strong list specification. The paper's central negative result targets "push-based protocols," a formally defined class requiring that every insertion generates an outbound message immediately, every first-observed deletion of an element generates an outbound message immediately, and every operation observes every operation that happened-before it (Definition 13); this class is shown to contain both operation-based protocols (messages carry a description of the operation) and state-based protocols (messages carry full state), and to contain deployed eventually-consistent write-propagating protocols generally, under the assumption that sending a message does not itself change the sender's list state.

### Measured results
This is a formal-methods paper with no implemented system and no empirical benchmark; its results are theorems with proofs, not measurements from a run. The reported quantities are asymptotic bounds, each tied to a stated protocol class and a stated number of replicas:

| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| Metadata overhead of any push-based protocol satisfying the weak or strong list specification is Ω(D) | D = number of deletions in the execution; requires n ≥ 3 replicas; holds under causal atomic broadcast (proved via an information-theoretic encoding argument constructing 2^d distinct single-replica states from d-bit strings, for d = ⌊(D-2)/2⌋, forcing at least one state to require d bits) |
| Metadata overhead of RGA over an execution is O(D lg k) | D = number of deletions, k = number of operations in the execution; RGA is proved to satisfy the strong list specification (Theorem 1) |
| The Ω(D) lower bound extends to push-based client/server protocols, applying to the client's metadata overhead | n ≥ 3 replicas; proved by showing a broadcast protocol can simulate a client/server protocol via state machine replication (Proposition 10), then applying the D ≥ 4 lower-bound execution to the simulating protocol (Corollary 11) |

Metadata overhead is formally defined (Definition 11) as the ratio, at a given replica state, of the bit-size of internal (user-unobservable) metadata to the bit-size of the user-observable list contents at that state; the worst-case metadata overhead of a protocol is the largest such ratio over any replica state in any execution in the considered class.

### Parameters
- The lower bound (Theorem 5) requires n ≥ 3 replicas and D ≥ 4 deletions; below D = 4 no bound is stated.
- The lower-bound construction uses d = ⌊(D-2)/2⌋ as the encoded bit-string length, giving Ω(D) via 2^d distinct forced replica states.
- RGA's upper bound is stated as O(D lg k) with no numeric constant given; the paper states the gap between this O(D lg k) upper bound and the Ω(D) lower bound is left open.
- The broadcast model assumed is causal atomic broadcast: causal ordering, no duplicate delivery, and consistent global delivery order across replicas; the paper states its lower bound is strengthened, not weakened, by assuming this idealized broadcast "for free," since a weaker underlying network would only add further metadata cost to implement broadcast.

### Stated limitations
The lower bound applies only to the defined class of push-based protocols; the paper states that relaxing this restriction (protocols that do not send a message immediately upon every insertion or first deletion) is left for future work, so the bound does not, as proved, cover consensus-mediated or batching protocols outside that class. The gap between the Ω(D) lower bound and RGA's proved O(D lg k) upper bound is stated as unresolved — the paper does not claim RGA is asymptotically optimal, only that it is close. The weak list specification's applicability to the Jupiter protocol is stated as a conjecture ("we conjecture that Jupiter satisfies the weak specification"), not a proof. The paper states its specifications model only a flat list object and do not cover richer collaborative-editing systems such as shared structured documents (the paper cites XML editing as an example); it states the lower bound would still apply to such systems but that additional features might induce additional complexity beyond what is analyzed. The client/server extension (Corollary 11) is derived by simulation from the broadcast-model result rather than analyzed as a separate protocol class with its own network assumptions, and the paper states exploring client/server systems more directly is future work, noting only that some deployed client/server systems do not implement the strong specification and that this result suggests that relaxation does not, by itself, give those systems a complexity advantage over strong-specification protocols.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Any protocol this lower bound governs must supply causal broadcast at minimum — the paper's model requires that if send(m) happens-before send(m′), no replica receives m′ before m — and the paper's results are proved to hold even under the strictly stronger causal atomic broadcast (adding no-duplicate-delivery and a single consistent global delivery order across all replicas), so a system that only provides causal broadcast inherits the same Ω(D) floor without needing atomic broadcast. A push-based protocol, by the paper's Definition 13, must generate an outbound message immediately after every insertion and after every deletion that is the first observed deletion of its element; a design that defers or batches these outbound messages exits the class this lower bound is proved for, and the paper does not state what bound, if any, applies outside it. RGA's proof of the strong list specification depends on its state being representable as a strictly-growing set of tree nodes (never modified or removed once added) combined under set union, which is associative and commutative independent of delivery order; a component wishing to reuse RGA's convergence guarantee must preserve this append-only structural property and must not garbage-collect or mutate tree nodes outside the mechanism the paper analyzes. The client/server simulation result (Proposition 10) requires the underlying transport to satisfy causal atomic broadcast among the simulating replicas for the simulation to correctly reproduce the client/server protocol's executions.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus. The paper's own related-work section states that Treedoc and Logoot (cited comparison protocols) have worst-case metadata overhead linear in the number of deletions, consistent with — not contradicting — this paper's Ω(D) lower bound, and states that operational-transformation protocols storing a full update log have metadata overhead at least linear in the number of updates for the same reason.

### References worth retrieving
- Foundational: S. Burckhardt, A. Gotsman, H. Yang, M. Zawirski, "Replicated Data Types: Specification, Verification, Optimality," POPL 2014 — already in this corpus as BURCKHARDT-POPL-14; the paper states its own list specifications extend this framework with an added relation for element order, and that this paper's lower-bound proof strategy could not directly reuse that paper's simpler-data-type argument, requiring a new incremental decoding argument instead.
- Foundational: H. Attiya, F. Ellen, A. Morrison, "Limitations of Highly-Available Eventually-Consistent Data Stores," PODC 2015 — extends the Burckhardt et al. lower-bound proof strategy the current paper also could not directly reuse.
- Foundational (protocol proved correct here): the RGA (Replicated Growable Array) protocol, standard implementation cited from the collaborative-editing literature — reformulated and proved to satisfy the strong list specification in this paper.
- Competing: D. A. Nichols, P. Curtis, M. Dixon, J. Lamping, "High-latency, low-bandwidth windowing in the Jupiter collaboration system," UIST 1995 — the Jupiter protocol, conjectured (not proved) to satisfy only the weak list specification, and cited as underlying deployed public collaboration systems.
- Competing: Treedoc and Logoot (operational transformation / dense-identifier list CRDTs) — cited as implementing the strong list specification via a different tree-position-encoding approach than RGA, sharing RGA's linear-in-deletions worst-case metadata overhead.
- Competing: WOOT (graph-based list CRDT) — cited as a partial-list-order graph representation, contrasted with RGA's tree-traversal approach.
- Attack/critique: A. Imine, M. Rusinowitch, G. Oster, P. Molli, "Formal Design and Verification of Operational Transformation Algorithms for Copies Convergence," Theoretical Computer Science 351(2), 2006 — shown to demonstrate several OT protocols fail the TP1/TP2 transformation properties needed for guaranteed convergence.
- Foundational: C. A. Ellis, S. J. Gibbs, "Concurrency Control in Groupware Systems," SIGMOD 1989 — the paper this work explicitly follows in modeling collaborative editing as a replicated list object problem.

- "the worst-case metadata overhead of Rn_rga over executions with k operations and D deletions is O(D lg k)"
- "we conjecture that Jupiter satisfies the weak specification"
- "the class of push-based protocols contains...eventually consistent write-propagating protocols"
- "our lower bound applies for both weak and strong semantics"

## [AUERBACH-CRYPTO-25] Continuous Group-Key Agreement: Concurrent Updates without Pruning
**Citation:** Benedikt Auerbach, Miguel Cueto Noval, Boran Erol, Krzysztof Pietrzak. "Continuous Group-Key Agreement: Concurrent Updates without Pruning." CRYPTO, 2025. DOI 10.1007/978-3-032-01913-4_5.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/1035.pdf
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/1035.pdf
**Domain:** H

### What it does
The paper measures, by formal derivation over a defined random-operation model rather than by implementation, how badly TreeKEM's communication cost degrades under concurrent updates, and then gives a modified update-proposal mechanism, MLS-Cutoff, that removes that degradation for a bounded rate of concurrency. TreeKEM is the continuous group-key agreement (CGKA) construction inside the IETF's Messaging Layer Security (MLS) standard: each of N group members owns a leaf of a binary ratchet tree, each tree node holds a public/secret key pair, and a user updating their key material replaces the keys from their leaf to the root, encrypting each new secret to the public key of the sibling subtree not on their own path — costing log(N) ciphertexts when the tree is fully populated. Concurrent operation uses "propose and commit": several users each broadcast an update proposal (a fresh leaf public key only, no new group secret), and one user later commits, folding every pending proposal into a single new group state. A commit cannot deliver the new keys on a proposing user's path to that path's co-nodes without knowledge the committer lacks, so TreeKEM "blanks" (deletes the key pair of) every non-leaf node on a proposer's update path that is not also on the committer's own path; a blanked node's children absorb its in-degree, so a future commit reaching a blanked node must instead encrypt separately to each of its unblanked descendants, and this growth compounds as more blanks accumulate.

The paper's model, Experiment Exp-Prop-Com, fixes a group of size N = 2^n and, for t rounds, draws P users uniformly at random to each issue one update proposal, followed by C users drawn uniformly at random to each issue a commit (C − 1 of them committing to no proposals, when C > 1, to model proposals issued less often than every commit). The paper derives a closed-form lower bound on the expected commit size under this process (Theorem 4.2, below) and shows the blank rate at a tree node of sufficient depth converges, via the node's blank/populated state forming a Markov chain, to a stationary probability of P/(P+C).

MLS-Cutoff modifies only how proposals are applied to the tree, keeping every other MLS mechanism (authentication, tree-hash and parent-hash consistency checks) unchanged. When a user issues an update proposal, the proposal itself already re-keys the user's full path (unlike plain MLS, where a proposal carries only the new leaf key), but a receiving committer stops applying that re-keying icut steps before the root — the cutoff parameter, set to log(log(N)) — so nodes above the cutoff are never touched by ordinary proposals and stay populated unless two proposing users' paths happen to collide below the cutoff, in which case the tree is blanked from the collision point upward as in ordinary MLS.

### Measured results
No implementation and no real-world trace; every figure below is a bound proved over the paper's own randomized-operation model (Exp-Prop-Com), not a benchmark. The paper states explicitly that real-world CGKA operation-sequence data is not publicly available and that its model is a deliberate simplification chosen for tractability, not a claim of realism.

| Result | Statement | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| TreeKEM/MLS expected commit-cost lower bound (Theorem 4.2, informal) | E[Cost(t)] ≥ Ω(N · log₂(1 + P/(P+C))) | P proposals and C commits per round constant, t sufficiently large (paper's stated sufficient bound: t > 2N² log(N)), uniform random choice of proposing and committing users each round |
| Small-N refinement of the same bound | E[Cost(t)] ≥ log₂(N)/4 − log(N)/4 | Special case P = C = 1, stated as more informative than the general bound for small N |
| Exponent e = log₂(1 + P/(P+C)) at C = 1, varying P | e = 0.22 (P=1/5), 0.42 (P=1/2), 0.58 (P=1), 0.74 (P=2), 0.87 (P=5), 0.93 (P=10), 0.99 (P=50) | C = 1 throughout; for P < 1 the paper writes P = 1/c with C = c to keep P a rate rather than a per-round integer count |
| Consequence stated in prose | At P = C = 1 (one proposal per commit), expected commit cost is "already over √N"; at P = 50, exponent 0.99 puts cost "almost linear" in N | Same model; MLS's stated target group size is up to 50,000 members (N = 50,000), against which the paper judges neither "almost all updates sequentially" nor "commits become almost linear in N" as acceptable |
| Per-node blank probability | Stationary probability that a sufficiently deep tree node is blank converges to P/(P+C) | Derived from the node's blank/populated transitions forming a Markov chain under the same round process |
| MLS-Cutoff expected proposal/commit size (Lemma 5.2) | E[\|pmsg\|] ≤ E[\|cmsg\|] ∈ O(log(N)) | C = 1, P constant, t sufficiently large, cutoff parameter icut = log(n) = log(log(N)) for N = 2ⁿ |
| MLS-Cutoff expected ciphertext count, explicit form | E[\|CTXT\|] ≤ log(N) + (P(P−1) + 1)·log(N / log(N)) + 1 | Same conditions as Lemma 5.2, derived en route to it |

Context figures the paper cites, not measured by it: Signal caps group size at 1,000 users; MLS's design target is groups up to 50,000 users.

### Parameters
- N: group size, expressed as N = 2ⁿ throughout the analysis.
- P: number of update proposals issued per round, treated as a constant independent of N in every asymptotic result; the worked table above uses P values from 1/5 to 50.
- C: number of commit-only rounds separating proposal rounds (C = 1 means every round includes P proposals followed by one commit; C > 1 models proposals issued less often than commits).
- t: number of rounds run; results require t large enough for the round-level Markov chain to approach its stationary distribution — Theorem 4.2 states t > 2N² log(N) as a sufficient bound.
- icut: MLS-Cutoff's cutoff depth, the number of tree levels near the root left untouched by an ordinary proposal's re-keying; set to log(n) = log(log(N)) to obtain the O(log(N)) bound of Lemma 5.2 — no other value is analyzed.

### Stated limitations
The randomized-operation model is stated by the authors as a deliberate simplification, not a claim about real user behavior: real-world CGKA operation traces are stated to be unavailable, so the uniform-random proposer/committer model was chosen to make the lower-bound proof tractable and its intuition legible, not because it is thought to match deployment. Theorem 4.2's stated t > 2N² log(N) round threshold means the bound is a limiting/asymptotic statement about many rounds, not a bound on cost after any fixed number of operations. Experiment Exp-Prop-Com never removes users from the group, so it never models the blanking that removal itself introduces in either MLS or MLS-Cutoff; the paper argues informally, without proof, that MLS-Cutoff would clear such blanks faster than MLS because of its additional path re-keying on proposals, but does not extend Lemma 5.2 to cover removals. MLS-Cutoff's O(log(N)) bound holds only while P stays constant relative to N; the paper states that once concurrency becomes "massive" (proposals from a number of users linear in group size), a linear communication cost is inherent for any CGKA achieving fast post-compromise security (PCS) built from standard primitives, citing Bienstock, Dodis, Rösler (TCC 2020) — MLS-Cutoff's own worst-case complexity is stated to remain Ω(N), matching plain MLS, for this reason. The paper explicitly leaves evaluating MLS-Cutoff's performance "in more realistic models" — i.e., under non-uniform, potentially adversarial or coordinated operation sequences — as an open question for future work.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The security proof for MLS-Cutoff (Theorem 5.1) is conditioned on the underlying public-key encryption scheme being IND-CCA2 secure, the signature scheme being strongly existentially unforgeable under chosen-message attack (SEUF-CMA secure), and the protocol's hash and key-derivation functions and message authentication code being modeled as random oracles / ideal primitives, matching the assumptions of the MLS insider-security proof (Alwen, Jost, Mularczyk, CRYPTO 2022) that this proof is stated to closely follow. MLS-Cutoff requires the delivery service and every group member to run the same tree-hash and parent-hash consistency checks that MLS already uses, unmodified — the paper's stated design goal is that MLS-Cutoff changes only how the ratchet tree is blanked or populated by applying proposals, leaving every other MLS mechanism for authenticity and consistency intact, so that the modification is deployable inside the existing MLS wire format. Achieving MLS-Cutoff's O(log(N)) result requires the actual deployed proposal/commit rate to stay within the constant-P regime the paper analyzes; a deployment that lets update proposals scale with group size falls back to the Ω(N) worst case shared with plain MLS, so a rate-limiting or scheduling policy elsewhere in the system determines whether MLS-Cutoff's improvement is realized.

### Contradicts
This paper's Theorem 4.2 gives quantitative content — a specific exponent table and a stated "already over √N" figure at P = C = 1 — to a qualitative claim (that concurrent update proposals degrade TreeKEM's communication complexity) that ALWEN-SCN-24 (DeCAF) and ALWEN-TCC-20 state only asymptotically as the same Θ(n)/Θ(log(n)) split TreeKEM I versus TreeKEM II already carries; no numeric disagreement was found between this entry and those two.

### References worth retrieving
- foundational: Bhargavan, Barnes, Rescorla, "TreeKEM: Asynchronous Decentralized Key Management for Large Dynamic Groups," 2018.
- foundational: Alwen, Jost, Mularczyk, "On the insider security of MLS," CRYPTO 2022 (source of the insider-security notion and safety predicate MLS-Cutoff's Theorem 5.1 proves against, and of the proof technique the authors state they closely follow).
- foundational: Barnes, Beurdouche, Robert, Millican, Omara, Cohn-Gordon, "The Messaging Layer Security (MLS) Protocol," RFC 9420, 2023.
- competing: Alwen, Auerbach, Cueto Noval, Klein, Pascual-Perez, Pietrzak, Walter, "CoCoA: Concurrent continuous group key agreement," EUROCRYPT 2022 (the paper states CoCoA achieves logarithmic complexity in this setting by re-keying updaters' full paths, but at the cost of slower post-compromise security and no insider security).
- competing: Weidner, Kleppmann, Hugenroth, Beresford, "Key agreement for decentralized secure group messaging with strong security guarantees," ACM CCS 2021.
- competing: this corpus's ALWEN-SCN-24 (DeCAF, listed in the bibliography as AACN+24), directly comparable on concurrent-update communication complexity.
- foundational: Bienstock, Dodis, Rösler, "On the price of concurrency in group ratcheting protocols," TCC 2020 (source of the Ω(N) inherent-linearity result for CGKA achieving fast PCS from standard primitives, cited to justify MLS-Cutoff's own worst-case bound).
- foundational: Bienstock, Dodis, Garg, Grogan, Hajiabadi, Rösler, "On the worst-case inefficiency of CGKA," TCC 2022.
- foundational: Auerbach, Cueto Noval, Pascual-Perez, Pietrzak, "On the cost of post-compromise security in concurrent continuous group-key agreement," TCC 2023.
- attack/critique: Cremers, Günsay, Wesselkamp, Zhao, "ETK: External-operations TreeKEM and the security of MLS in RFC 9420," ePrint 2025/229.
- competing: Balbás, Collins, Gajland, "WhatsUpp with sender keys? Analysis, improvements and security proofs," ASIACRYPT 2023 (this corpus's BALBAS-ASIACRYPT-23).

## [AUVOLAT-SRDS-19] Merkle Search Trees: Efficient State-Based CRDTs in Open Networks
**Citation:** Alex Auvolat, François Taïani. "Merkle Search Trees: Efficient State-Based CRDTs in Open Networks." IEEE International Symposium on Reliable Distributed Systems (SRDS), 2019, pp. 1-10. DOI 10.1109/SRDS.2019.00032.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://hal.science/hal-02303490/document
**Source URL:** https://hal.science/hal-02303490/document
**Domain:** D

### What it does
A Merkle Search Tree (MST) lets two replicas holding large key-value sets or maps find exactly which entries differ by exchanging only the tree nodes on the paths to the differing entries, without either replica needing prior knowledge of the other's state or membership. It builds a balanced ordered search tree deterministically from a set of items so that any two replicas holding the same items always construct the identical tree, letting the standard Merkle-tree technique (hashing each node from its children's hashes, so a single root hash identifies the whole data set and matching subtree hashes prove matching subtree contents) apply directly to comparison and diffing. The construction assigns each item x to a tree layer using a collision-resistant hash function h_B(x) whose output is written in base B: the layer l(x) is the length of the longest all-zero prefix of h_B(x), so on average 1/B of items land at layer 1 or higher, 1/B^2 at layer 2, and so on, giving each layer's nodes an average out-degree of B and an expected tree depth of log_B(n) for n stored items (the probability of exceeding depth log_B(n) + c falls exponentially in c). Layer-0 items are leaves; layer-l items serve as the boundary values separating layer-(l-1) subtrees, so the tree is simultaneously key-ordered (unlike a hash-prefix tree, which destroys key order to stay balanced) and balanced only through hash-derived randomness, not through explicit rebalancing operations. Because assignment is a pure function of an item's hash, inserting the same set of items in any order converges to the same tree and the same root hash; this structural uniqueness also holds at every intermediate node, so comparing two trees can skip any subtree pair whose hashes match. Comparing tree f at one node against tree g at another exchanges O(d log_B(n)) messages, where d = |{x : f(x) ≠ g(x)}| is the number of differing items and n = max(|f|, |g|); each read, insert, or delete costs O(log_B(n)). The paper builds a causally-consistent distributed event store on top of MSTs — a grow-only set of timestamped events — reconciled through a gossip-based push-pull anti-entropy algorithm that periodically compares Merkle root hashes with a randomly sampled peer and descends into mismatching subtrees, requiring no causal-broadcast primitive and no per-node vector-clock bookkeeping.

### Measured results
The simulator is an actor-based Elixir implementation of about 2000 lines, publicly released, simulating a network of 1000 nodes (2000 in one scaling test) with synchronous communication rounds and no node crashes; events are generated with increasing timestamps at randomly chosen nodes. Three anti-entropy methods are compared under the identical gossip-based algorithm and event-dissemination workload: Scuttlebutt (vector-clock-based anti-entropy), MST (this paper's method, fixed at B=16), and MPT (Merkle Prefix Tree, a hash-prefix-tree competitor that discards key order but stays balanced through the same exponentially-decreasing hash-collision property). Entropy is a defined dissemination-consistency metric: the sum, over every message, of the binary entropy of the fraction of nodes that have received that message at a given simulation round; lower values mean more uniform diffusion.

| Scenario | Metric | Scuttlebutt | MPT | MST (this paper) | MST vs. Scuttlebutt |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Light load: 1000 nodes, 0.1 events/round network-wide, best configuration of each method | Bandwidth use (per round, average) | 1.3 MB | 0.51 MB | 0.44 MB | -66% |
| Light load, same configuration | Entropy (average per round) | 1.61 | 1.44 | 1.06 | -34% |
| Light load, same configuration | 99th-percentile delivery delay | 64 rounds | 56 rounds | 44 rounds | -31% |
| Heavy load: 1000 nodes, 1 event/round network-wide | Bandwidth use | 2.1 MB | 3.9 MB | 2.2 MB | roughly tied (MST +5% vs. Scuttlebutt) |
| Heavy load, 1000 nodes | Entropy | 15.4 | 26.9 | 17.5 | Scuttlebutt lower (better) |
| Heavy load, 1000 nodes | 99th-percentile delivery delay | 50 rounds | 100 rounds | 74 rounds | Scuttlebutt lower (better) |
| Heavy load: 2000 nodes, 1 event/round network-wide | Bandwidth use | 7.6 MB | did not terminate (message-count explosion) | 4.2 MB | MST substantially lower |
| Heavy load, 2000 nodes | Entropy | 14.9 | did not terminate | 21.0 | Scuttlebutt lower (better) |
| Heavy load, 2000 nodes | 99th-percentile delivery delay | 54 rounds | did not terminate | 88 rounds | Scuttlebutt lower (better) |

Theoretical (not simulated) per-anti-entropy-round traffic, from the paper's Table II: Scuttlebutt O(p+d), MST O(d log_B(n)), where p is the number of nodes ever having participated (past and present) and d is the number of items that differ. Dissemination time for both methods is given as 2λ log(m) for Scuttlebutt and 2λ log(m) log_B(n) for MST, where λ is network latency and m is the number of currently connected nodes. The paper derives an affine boundary between the two methods' bandwidth advantage as a function of node count p and event rate r, calibrated using two simulation configurations where the methods performed equally (p=1000, r=1, and a second unshown configuration at p=500, r=0.33); Figure 5 plots the resulting green/red advantage regions against the discrete experimental configurations actually run.

### Parameters
- Branching parameter B fixed at 16 for all MST and MPT experiments ("In our experiments, we fix B = 16").
- Network size: 1000 nodes for the primary experiments; 2000 nodes for the one scaling comparison, where the MPT run did not terminate.
- Event generation rates: 0.1 events per round network-wide (light-load scenario, Table IV/Figures 2 and 4) and 1 event per round network-wide (heavy-load scenario, Table V/Figure 3) — a 10x difference between the two scenarios.
- Scuttlebutt gossip fanout tested at 1, 2, 4; gossip interval tested at 1, 2, 4, 8 rounds.
- MST/MPT anti-entropy fanout fixed at 6; maximum simultaneous merges tested at 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8.
- No node joins, leaves, or crashes occurred in any reported simulation; the paper states this explicitly as a scope limit, not a tested condition.

### Stated limitations
The paper states its experimental evaluation was restricted to "a very narrow problem" — a grow-only event store, described as one of the simplest known CRDTs — and to a single, simple gossip-based reconciliation algorithm; it does not evaluate more complex CRDT types (sets supporting deletion, multi-value maps) empirically. For CRDT types that need causality tracking, the paper states its simple per-item construction would store causality metadata alongside every item, generating large quantities of redundant data, and proposes storing that metadata separately as unevaluated future work. No node joins, leaves, or crashes were simulated; the paper states it "conjectures" (its own word) that Scuttlebutt's vector-clock overhead becomes even worse in open networks with churn, since inactive nodes' vector-clock entries accumulate and are exchanged at every round, but this claim about churn is not itself measured in this paper. In the heavy-load scenario, MST does not achieve as low an entropy value as Scuttlebutt at either 1000 or 2000 nodes, meaning Scuttlebutt disseminates more uniformly under high event rates in the tested configurations; the paper's own overall assessment is that MST is efficient specifically under moderate-to-low event rates, not universally. Using MSTs as a secondary index over data distributed via a distributed hash table (DHT) is proposed but explicitly stated as unevaluated: "The feasibility of such an approach when many updates occur at many nodes has not yet been evaluated." The comparison-cost bound O(d log_B(n)) assumes constant-size keys and values in K and V; the paper does not state a bound for variable-size elements.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Every replica must use the same hash function and the same base-B assignment rule to place items into tree layers, and that hash function must be collision-resistant (the paper states the probability of two colliding strings is assumed negligible) and must project uniformly across values of size a power of B, since the layer-depth and balance guarantees derive directly from that uniformity; the paper cites SHA-512 as satisfying both properties in practice. The reconciliation protocol requires an anti-entropy transport capable of exchanging tree nodes identified by hash and does not require, and is stated to specifically avoid needing, a causal broadcast primitive — the paper positions this as the mechanism's advantage over delta-based CRDT approaches that need causal broadcast for correctness. Achieving the paper's O(log_B(n)) depth and O(d log_B(n)) comparison-cost bounds requires the branching parameter B to be fixed network-wide (all experiments here use B=16); the paper describes B as a tunable trade-off between shallower trees (larger B, fewer round-trips, more bytes per node) and smaller messages (smaller B), but gives no derivation of an optimal value. For applications needing causality tracking (deletion-supporting sets, multi-value registers), the paper states the base construction requires an external mechanism to store causality metadata separately from the per-item MST entries, since storing it inline would duplicate metadata across the tree; no such mechanism is specified or evaluated in this paper.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus at time of writing. AMPARORE-ARXIV-26, elsewhere in this corpus, characterizes this paper's Merkle Search Tree as "imposing a rigid, canonically derived tree representation of the data," contrasted with AMPARORE-ARXIV-26's own range-based reconciliation approach, which operates on logical key ranges rather than a predetermined tree topology — a mechanism-level distinction stated by the later paper, not a numeric disagreement.

### References worth retrieving
- Foundational: R. C. Merkle, "A digital signature based on a conventional encryption function," 1987 — the original Merkle hash-tree construction this paper generalizes.
- Foundational: M. Shapiro, N. Preguiça, C. Baquero, M. Zawirski, "Conflict-Free Replicated Data Types," Stabilization, Safety, and Security of Distributed Systems, Springer, 2011 — the CRDT concept this paper's construction targets.
- Foundational: P. S. Almeida, A. Shoker, C. Baquero, "Efficient state-based CRDTs by delta-mutation," arXiv:1410.2803, 2014 — the delta-CRDT line the paper positions its causal-broadcast-free approach against.
- Competing: R. van Renesse, D. Dumitriu, V. Gough, C. Thomas, "Efficient Reconciliation and Flow Control for Anti-entropy Protocols," LADIS 2008 — the Scuttlebutt vector-clock anti-entropy algorithm used as the primary empirical baseline in this paper's evaluation, with measured bandwidth, entropy, and delivery-delay figures directly compared against MST above.
- Competing: R. J. T. Goncalves, P. S. Almeida, C. Baquero, V. Fonte, "DottedDB: Anti-Entropy without Merkle Trees, Deletes without Tombstones," SRDS 2017 — cited as an extensively optimized vector-clock approach that, per this paper, still requires metadata linear in the total number of participants past and present.
- Competing / precedent: S. A. Crosby, D. S. Wallach, "Super-Efficient Aggregating History-Independent Persistent Authenticated Dictionaries," ESORICS 2009 — the first deterministic balanced Merkle-tree construction preserving key order using binary treaps; this paper's construction achieves the same properties with wider (B-ary) nodes for shallower trees.
- Foundational: R. Tamassia, N. Triandopoulos, "Efficient Content Authentication in Peer-to-Peer Networks," Applied Cryptography and Network Security, Springer, 2007 — a non-deterministic order-preserving balanced Merkle tree construction, cited as unfit for anti-entropy for that reason, and cited again as a direction to extend for the proposed DHT-secondary-index future work.
- Attack/critique target for comparison baseline used in this paper's own evaluation: the Merkle Prefix Tree (MPT) construction over hashed keys, as used by systems such as Dynamo — cited (via G. DeCandia et al., "Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store," 2007) as the standard approach this paper's key-order-preserving construction is designed to beat, and empirically shown in this paper's own Table IV/V to lose on bandwidth and entropy and to fail to terminate at 2000 nodes under heavy load.
- Foundational (tree-shaped CRDT limitation cited as motivating a possible MST application): M. Shapiro, "A comprehensive study of Convergent and Commutative Replicated Data Types," 2011, and N. Preguiça, J. M. Marques, M. Shapiro, M. Letia, "A Commutative Replicated Data Type for Cooperative Editing" (Treedoc), ICDCS 2009 — cited as having an identified balancing-limitation that an MST-based construction could address.
