## [AZARI-ACNS-25] Tighter Provable Security for TreeKEM
**Citation:** Karen Azari, Andreas Ellison. "Tighter Provable Security for TreeKEM." Applied Cryptography and Network Security (ACNS), 2025. DOI 10.1007/978-3-031-95761-1_20.
**Retrieved:** full text (source file has no explicit retrieval URL header; matched via title, authors, and abstract text)
**Source URL:** https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-95761-1_20
**Domain:** H

### What it does
The paper computes how many bits of concrete security TreeKEM — the ratchet-tree continuous group-key agreement (CGKA) construction inside the Messaging Layer Security (MLS) protocol — retains for group sizes and operation counts used in practice, by proving a tighter reduction than the prior best bound. TreeKEM's group members occupy the leaves of a binary tree; each commit re-keys the committing user's path to the root and produces ciphertexts encrypting new secrets to sibling subtrees, and the protocol's proof-theoretic security loss (how much an attacker's advantage against the whole protocol can exceed its advantage against the underlying encryption scheme) had previously been bounded only in terms that become vacuous — worse than a random guess — once realistic user counts and commit counts are substituted. The authors' method: define a "generalized selective decryption" (GSD) game specific to a public-key setting, which formalizes the encryption-chain structure TreeKEM produces (each ratchet-tree secret is itself encrypted under other tree secrets, forming a graph of encryption dependencies) and captures how a party's compromise reveals only the state reachable from it, and then prove security of that game directly for DHIES — the Diffie-Hellman Integrated Encryption Scheme, the only public-key encryption scheme currently standardized for use in MLS — in the random oracle model (ROM), rather than proving a generic bound for any IND-CPA-secure (indistinguishable under chosen-plaintext attack) scheme and specializing afterward, which is what produced the prior work's looser bound. The proof reduces GSD security to two underlying assumptions: eavesdropping (EAV) security of the private-key encryption component of DHIES, and hardness of the Diffie-Hellman problem in the group DHIES is instantiated over.

### Measured results
No implementation and no benchmark; every figure below is a numeric consequence of the paper's Theorem 1 security bound, evaluated at named parameter settings, not a measured runtime or bandwidth cost.

| Scenario | Group size / lifetime / commit rate | 128-bit parameters (this paper vs. prior [Klein et al., IEEE S&P 2021]) | 256-bit AES only | 256-bit parameters |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Large group, hourly commits, frequent updates (update proposals p bounded by p ≤ c·u, dominated by p) | ~10,000 users (u ≤ 2^14), 5-year session, one commit per hour (c ≤ 2^16) | 81 bits (this paper) vs. 64 bits (prior) | 95 bits (this paper) | 209 bits (this paper) vs. 192 bits (prior) |
| Few updates (proposals p ≤ c·log(u), so 3·c·log(u) + p ≤ 2^22) | Same group size and commit rate as above | 90 bits (this paper) vs. 82 bits (prior) | 104 bits (this paper) | 218 bits (this paper) vs. 210 bits (prior) |
| Very large group, one commit per minute, frequent updates (p ≤ c·u) | ~1,000,000 users (u ≤ 2^20), 50-year session, one commit per minute (c ≤ 2^25) | 60 bits (this paper) vs. 34 bits (prior) | 80 bits (this paper) | 188 bits (this paper) vs. 162 bits (prior) |

Conditions common to every row: 128-bit parameters use the MLS_128_DHKEMX25519_AES128GCM_SHA256_Ed25519 cipher suite (Curve25519 Diffie-Hellman group, 128-bit AES), assumed to give a 128-bit security level for both the Diffie-Hellman problem and the private-key encryption scheme, with adversary running-time-to-advantage ratio set to t/ε_EAV = t/ε_DDH = 2^128; 256-bit parameters use MLS_256_DHKEMP521_AES256GCM_SHA512_P521 (curve P-521, 256-bit AES) at a 256-bit security level, with the same running-time ratio set to 2^128. Add proposals are assumed rare relative to update proposals throughout.

Asymptotic form of the two bounds being compared, general (not tied to the numeric scenarios above): this paper's security loss is O(u·(c·log(u) + p)) reducing to EAV security of the private-key encryption scheme, plus O(c·log(u) + p) reducing to Diffie-Hellman hardness; when proposals are few (p < c·log(u)) these simplify to O(c·u·log(u)) and O(c·log(u)) respectively. The prior bound (Klein, Pascual-Perez, Walter, Kamath, Capretto, Cueto, Markov, Yeo, Alwen, Pietrzak, IEEE S&P 2021 — "Tainted TreeKEM") is O((c·log(u) + p)²), reducing to IND-CPA security of the public-key encryption scheme as a whole rather than splitting into a private-key EAV term and a Diffie-Hellman term. Here c is the number of commits, p is the number of add or update proposals, and u is the maximum number of users.

### Parameters
- DHIES construction: a group-generation algorithm G producing a Diffie-Hellman group (𝔾, q, g); a private-key encryption scheme Π_s used for the message payload; a key-derivation function family H_pk, modeled as a random oracle. No numeric group parameters beyond the two cipher-suite examples above (Curve25519 / 128-bit AES; P-521 / 256-bit AES) are evaluated.
- Theorem 1 bound: ε ≤ 2·u·(3·c·log(u) + p)·ε_EAV + 2·(3·c·log(u) + p)·ε_DDH + negl, where ε_EAV is the private-key scheme's EAV-security advantage bound and ε_DDH is the Diffie-Hellman decision problem's advantage bound, each paired with a running time t; the theorem holds for a single challenge query, and the paper states the proof extends to multiple challenge queries without a stated additional multiplicative loss (unlike the prior work's bound, which the paper states requires an additional multiplicative loss in the number of challenges under a hybrid argument to reach the multi-challenge case).
- GSD-graph parameter δ: the maximum in-degree in the generalized selective decryption graph the proof constructs; the general reduction to private-key encryption incurs a security loss of O(δ·N), reduced further to O(N) in Appendix B.4 for "a very specific set of schemes" the paper does not enumerate in the passage read.

### Stated limitations
The paper states, in relation to Alwen, Coretti, Dodis, Tselekounis's modular MLS-security reduction (CCS 2021), that even after substituting this paper's tighter TreeKEM bound into that reduction, the overall MLS protocol's proved security is not expected to reach a meaningful level, because that reduction's own loss (separate from TreeKEM's) is "very large (but polynomial)"; the authors state finding a tighter reduction for MLS as a whole remains "a crucial open problem." The result is proved specifically for DHIES, the one public-key encryption scheme currently standardized in MLS, and the paper does not state that the tighter bound transfers to a different public-key encryption scheme without re-proof. The bound is proved in the random oracle model, requiring the deployed key-derivation function to be treated as an ideal random function; the paper states it does not rely on random-oracle "programmability" in this work, but the analysis is not a standard-model result. The 60-to-95-bit security levels obtained even under this tighter bound are below the 128-bit or 256-bit nominal security level of the underlying primitives at the same parameter choice, so the paper's own numbers show the reduction still gives up security margin relative to the raw primitive strength, particularly in the largest-scale scenario (1,000,000 users, 50-year session, one commit per minute), where the 128-bit-parameter result is only 60 bits.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The bound requires the deployed CGKA construction to be exactly TreeKEM instantiated with DHIES for its public-key encryption component; the proof structure (splitting the security loss into an EAV-security term for the private-key encryption sub-component and a Diffie-Hellman-hardness term) does not apply as stated to a different combination of primitives. It requires whatever key-derivation function DHIES uses to be treated as a random oracle by the rest of the security analysis — a system substituting a concrete hash construction accepts the random-oracle idealization as a standing assumption, not a proved property of that construction. The numeric security levels in the table above are conditioned on assumed 128-bit or 256-bit security levels for the underlying Diffie-Hellman group and AES instantiation, at a stated adversary running-time-to-advantage ratio of 2^128; a deployment assuming a weaker concrete hardness for those primitives, or facing an adversary with a different running-time budget, gets a different bit count than the ones tabulated here, not these ones directly. Achieving the higher bit counts in the "few updates" scenario over the "frequent updates" scenario requires the deployment's actual ratio of add/update proposals to commits to fall in the p ≤ c·log(u) regime — a policy decision made by whatever component in the wider system decides how often users are permitted or required to issue update proposals per commit, not by TreeKEM itself.

### Contradicts
None found within this batch. This paper directly supersedes the concrete-bit-count comparison figures attributed to Klein, Pascual-Perez, Walter, Kamath, Capretto, Cueto, Markov, Yeo, Alwen, Pietrzak, "Keep the Dirt: Tainted TreeKEM," IEEE S&P 2021 (cited in-text as reference [12]) — any figure carried forward from that paper's security-loss bound for the scenarios above should be replaced with this paper's tighter numbers, cited to this entry.

### References worth retrieving
- foundational: Abdalla, Bellare, Rogaway, "DHIES: An encryption scheme based on the Diffie-Hellman Problem," 1998 (defines the encryption scheme this paper's bound is proved for).
- foundational: Klein, Pascual-Perez, Walter, Kamath, Capretto, Cueto, Markov, Yeo, Alwen, Pietrzak, "Keep the Dirt: Tainted TreeKEM, Adaptively and Actively Secure Continuous Group Key Agreement," IEEE S&P 2021 (the prior best bound this paper directly tightens and numerically compares against throughout).
- foundational: Alwen, Coretti, Dodis, Tselekounis, "Security analysis and improvements for the IETF MLS standard for group messaging," CRYPTO 2020.
- foundational: Alwen, Coretti, Dodis, Tselekounis, "Modular design of secure group messaging protocols and the security of MLS," ACM CCS 2021 (source of the modular MLS-security reduction into which this paper's tighter TreeKEM bound would be substituted).
- competing: Balbás, Collins, Gajland, "WhatsUpp with sender keys? Analysis, improvements and security proofs," ASIACRYPT 2023 (this corpus's BALBAS-ASIACRYPT-23).
- foundational: Barnes, Beurdouche, Robert, Millican, Omara, Cohn-Gordon, "The Messaging Layer Security (MLS) Protocol," RFC 9420, 2023.
- foundational: Bhargavan, Barnes, Rescorla, "TreeKEM: Asynchronous Decentralized Key Management for Large Dynamic Groups," Inria research report, 2018.
- foundational: Panjwani, "Tackling adaptive corruptions in multicast encryption protocols," TCC 2007 (an earlier source of the generalized selective decryption game this paper adapts to the public-key setting).
- attack/critique: Cohn-Gordon, Cremers, Dowling, Garratt, Stebila, "A formal security analysis of the Signal messaging protocol," IEEE EuroS&P 2017.
- foundational: Bellare, Rogaway, "Random oracles are practical: a paradigm for designing efficient protocols," ACM CCS 1993 (source of the random oracle model this paper's proof is stated in).

- "finding a tighter reduction for the MLS protocol as a whole is a crucial open problem"
- "we don't expect this to provide a meaningful level of security"

## [BACK-HASHCASH-02] Hashcash - A Denial of Service Counter-Measure
**Citation:** Adam Back. "Hashcash - A Denial of Service Counter-Measure." Self-published technical report, 1st August 2002.
**Retrieved:** full text via http://www.hashcash.org/papers/hashcash.pdf
**Source URL:** http://www.hashcash.org/papers/hashcash.pdf
**Domain:** I

### What it does
Hashcash lets a server force a client to spend a chosen amount of computation before the server accepts a request, so that a resource with no per-use charge (email delivery, an anonymous remailer, a TCP connection slot) cannot be consumed at unlimited rate by one sender. The paper defines a cost-function abstractly as a pair of routines: MINT, run by the client, which finds a token expensive to produce, and VALUE, run by the server, which checks the token cheaply. The hashcash construction of MINT is: given a service name string s that identifies the target service (a host name or an email address, so a token minted for one service cannot be replayed against another), pick a random string x, and search for an x such that a public hash function applied to (s, x) produces an output whose leading b bits match a fixed target (originally the hash of the service name, later simplified by Hal Finney and Thomas Boschloo to the fixed all-zero string, which the paper states halves verification cost). VALUE recomputes the hash of (s, x) once and checks the same b leading bits. Because the only known algorithm for finding such an x is brute-force search, and each trial hash independently has a 2^-b chance of matching a b-bit target, minting is expensive in the leading-bit count b while verification always costs exactly one hash evaluation, and this asymmetry is the whole rate-limiting effect. Hashcash is non-interactive (the client chooses its own random start value with no challenge from the server, so it works over one-way channels such as email) and trapdoor-free (the server holds no secret that lets it mint tokens more cheaply than a client can, unlike a known-solution client-puzzle scheme). The server keeps a database of spent tokens to reject reuse, bounded by embedding a timestamp in the service-name string so expired entries can be discarded. An interactive variant lets the server issue a challenge string and, combined with a keyed message authentication code sent to the client instead of stored server-side state, defends TCP connection-slot exhaustion (a hashcash-cookie, generalizing the syn-cookie) by requiring a computed token before the server commits any per-connection state.

### Measured results
None usable. The paper is a construction and classification paper; it states it "describes initial experience from experiments using hashcash" but reports no run count, hardware, wall-clock time, or deployment-scale figure for that experience anywhere in the retrieved text, so no number from it meets the experimental-conditions requirement.

### Parameters
- b: the number of leading bits of the hash output that must match the target (the work factor). The paper does not state a recommended numeric value of b for the non-interactive hashcash construction itself; it treats b as adjustable per deployment and, for the interactive variant, as dynamically adjustable by the server in response to measured CPU load (Section 4.1).
- Start-value length |x|: the paper states |x| must be long enough that the probability of two clients independently reusing the same start value is negligible, and states a specific bit length "should be enough even for a busy server," but the digit string for that recommended length is corrupted in the extracted text (a font-encoding artifact) and is not recorded here because it cannot be verified against the source PDF.
- Spent-token database retention: bounded by embedding a timestamp in the service-name string and discarding database entries once an expiry period elapses; the paper states the expiry period should account for clock inaccuracy, computation time, and transmission delay, without giving a numeric value.
- Time-lock-puzzle variant (an alternative fixed-cost, non-parallelizable cost-function the paper also presents, built on Rivest-Shamir-Wagner time-lock puzzles): the author recommends not deploying it with a modulus below 768 bits and states RSA moduli of 512 bits had by publication been factored by two independent groups; the author further suggests changing the public modulus "every hour or so," which the paper itself flags with "say," marking it as a suggestion rather than a derived or measured figure.

### Stated limitations
Hashcash's non-interactive form supplies no defense against a precomputation attack: an adversary with a year of spare compute can mint tokens in advance, all valid for one future date, and spend them in a burst on that date, an attack the interactive form is immune to because the server's challenge cannot be predicted in advance. The paper's proposed mitigation (mixing in a slowly changing, unpredictable public beacon value, such as a lottery result) is presented as a possible fix, not one the paper implements or measures. The double-spend database requires the server to hold state per accepted token until its embedded timestamp expires; the paper does not bound how large that database grows under high request rates. The paper states as an open problem that no known non-interactive, publicly auditable, fixed-cost (rather than probabilistic) cost-function exists with verification as cheap as hashcash's, and likewise states as open whether any non-parallelizable cost-function exists with verification cost in the same order of magnitude as a symmetric-key construct like hashcash. The interactive hashcash-cookie mechanism allocates connection slots in proportion to each client's available CPU resources, which the paper states biases outcomes toward clients with faster processors. The author's own assessment (attributed to Back, not a derived or measured claim) is that non-parallelizable cost-functions give only marginal added resistance to distributed denial-of-service compared with hashcash, because an attacker who already controls many network-connected nodes can have each node run the ordinary protocol independently rather than sub-dividing one puzzle, and that this equally defeats per-connection fairness throttling regardless of parallelizability.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A deployment needs a server-side store, keyed by spent token, that persists at least as long as the timestamp-derived expiry window it uses to reject double-spent tokens; without an accurate, loosely-synchronized clock across server and client, the timestamp-based expiry either rejects valid recent tokens or fails to bound database growth. The service-name string bound into each token must be chosen so that it is unique per protected resource (a specific host name, mailbox address, or connection identifier), or tokens minted against one resource can be replayed against another. Any component that wants graceful throttling under load (the paper's interactive hashcash and hashcash-cookie designs) needs a live measurement of current server CPU or connection-slot load, since the mechanism only produces fair, load-proportional degradation if the required bit count b is adjusted from that measurement. A hashcash-cookie deployment additionally requires a server-held symmetric MAC key shared across the server's own instances of the check, since the server sends a MAC of the connection state to the client instead of storing that state itself, and any component verifying the returned token must hold that same key.

### Contradicts
None found; this paper reports no experiment whose numeric result could disagree with another entry in this batch. Note for cross-paper composition: TAHERIBOSHROOYEH-ARXIV-22 (in this batch) builds a rate limiter on a different asymmetry -- a staked deposit plus a zero-knowledge membership proof and per-epoch nullifier -- rather than on a compute-cost asymmetry; the two are not measurements of the same mechanism and neither paper's numbers bear on the other's.

### References worth retrieving
- Dwork, Naor, "Pricing via Processing or Combatting Junk Mail," CRYPTO 1992 -- foundational (this paper states its author was unaware of Dwork and Naor's prior CPU-pricing proposal at the time hashcash was first published in 1997; retrieved in this batch as DWORK-CRYPTO-92).
- Juels, Brainard, "Client puzzles: A cryptographic countermeasure against connection depletion attacks," NDSS 1999 -- competing (a known-solution, trapdoor-possessing cost-function this paper compares against directly on verification cost, public auditability, and variance).
- Jakobsson, Juels, "Proofs of work and bread pudding protocols," CMS 1999 -- foundational (proposes reusing a cost-function's spent work for a second useful computation).
- Bernstein, "Syn cookies," published at cr.yp.to -- foundational (the mechanism hashcash-cookies generalizes with an added CPU cost).
- Rivest, Shamir, Wagner, "Time-lock puzzles and timed-release crypto," MIT/LCS/TR-684, 1996 -- foundational (source of the time-lock-puzzle-based fixed-cost, non-parallelizable cost-function this paper presents and evaluates as an alternative to hashcash).
- Dean, Stubblefield, "Using client puzzles to protect TLS," USENIX Security 2001 -- competing (the paper this one cites as the one deployed implementation of a client-puzzle system integrated into a real protocol, TLS).
- Clarke, Sandberg, Wiley, Hong, "Freenet: A distributed anonymous information storage and retrieval system," Designing Privacy Enhancing Technologies 2001 -- foundational (a system this paper states adopted hashcash to throttle publication floods).
- Dai, "b-money," 1998 -- foundational (this paper states hashcash was adopted as the minting mechanism in Dai's b-money electronic-cash proposal, a design later cited as a direct precursor to Bitcoin's proof-of-work).

### Verbatim extracts

- "efficiently-verifiable ... which consume just a single compression round"
- "reduces verification cost by a factor of 2"
- "a determined adversary may spend a year pre-computing tokens"
- "non-parallelizable cost-functions are of questionable practical value"

## [BALDUF-IMC-23] The Cloud Strikes Back: Investigating the Decentralization of IPFS
**Citation:** Leonhard Balduf, Maciej Korczyński, Onur Ascigil, Navin V. Keizer, George Pavlou, Björn Scheuermann, Michał Król. "The Cloud Strikes Back: Investigating the Decentralization of IPFS." ACM Internet Measurement Conference (IMC), 2023. DOI 10.1145/3618257.3624797.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.16203
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.16203
**Domain:** A

### What it does
The paper measures how much of a deployed content-addressed peer-to-peer file system, IPFS (InterPlanetary File System), runs on cloud infrastructure rather than on volunteer-operated machines. It does not propose a mechanism; it instruments four channels of the running IPFS network and reports the fraction of each channel that terminates on nodes hosted by a small number of commercial cloud providers. The four channels: the Kademlia distributed hash table (DHT) topology (who is a DHT server and where they are hosted), Bitswap and DHT message traffic (who generates and receives requests), content provider records (who hosts retrievable content), and entry points (HTTP gateways, DNSLink, and Ethereum Name Service (ENS) records that map human-readable names to content identifiers).

The authors crawl the DHT by sending crafted FindNode messages that sweep the address space, enumerating every node's k-buckets (its outbound DHT connections) to reconstruct a snapshot of the DHT graph. They separately capture Bitswap request traffic through a modified Go-IPFS node with an unbounded connection count that logs all incoming local-broadcast traffic, and DHT traffic through a modified Hydra-Booster (a Protocol-Labs-operated DHT accelerator) running 20 virtual peer IDs. They classify every observed IP address as cloud-hosted or not using the Udger IP-to-provider database, and geolocate every address using the MaxMind GeoLite2 database.

### Measured results
| Metric | Figure | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| DHT servers hosted in the cloud | 79.6% (20,300 of 25,510 average crawled nodes); non-cloud 18.6% (4,737) | Average-over-crawls, unique-nodes (A-N) counting method; 101 crawls, 2023-04-18 to 2023-05-26, twice daily |
| Same metric, alternative counting method | 39.9% cloud (34,375 addresses), 60.1% non-cloud (51,689) | Global-unique-IP (G-IP) counting method, matching the method of a prior 2022 study (Trautwein et al.); same crawl dataset |
| Top-3 cloud-provider share of DHT servers | 51.9% of nodes; single largest provider (Choopa) 29.3% (7,492 nodes) | A-N method, same crawl dataset |
| DHT peer-ID traffic centralization | Top 5% of peer IDs generate ~97% of DHT+Bitswap traffic | 290M messages total from Hydra-Booster (DHT) and Bitswap-monitor logs, August 2022–May 2023 |
| DHT IP traffic centralization | Top 5% of IPs generate ~94% of messages; cloud nodes alone generate ~85% of DHT traffic vs. ~15% for non-cloud | Same traffic logs; DHT vs. Bitswap broken out separately, Bitswap cloud share ~42% |
| Cloud share of raw IP population in traffic logs | 35% overall (lower than the 79% crawl figure because traffic logs include NAT-ed clients invisible to DHT crawls) | Same traffic logs |
| Cloud share of traffic volume by IP | ~93% overall, ~98% for download-related traffic; Amazon AWS alone 68%, AWS+Packet jointly 82% | Same traffic logs |
| Hydra-Booster (Protocol-Labs-operated) share of DHT traffic | 35% of all DHT traffic, 50% of download-specific DHT traffic, ~0% of advertisement traffic | Same traffic logs |
| Content providers by hosting class | NAT-ed 35.57%, cloud-based 45%, non-cloud (public IP) 18%, hybrid 0.58% | 5.6 million content identifiers (CIDs), provider records collected over 28 days, reachability-verified |
| Provider popularity concentration | ~1% of peers appear as providers in ~90% of provider records; of those, ~70% are cloud-based, NAT-ed peers appear in <8% | Same 5.6M-CID provider-record dataset |
| Content dependency on cloud | 95% of content has at least one cloud-based provider; for 91% of content, at least half its providers are cloud-based; 23% of content is served only by cloud-based peers; conversely 77% of content identifiers have at least one non-cloud provider | Same dataset |
| NAT-ed provider relay dependency | ~80% of NAT-ed providers use a cloud-hosted node as their circuit-relay | Same dataset |
| DNSLink gateway hosting | Only 20% of gateway IPs referenced by DNSLink records are non-cloud; 50% of gateway IPs are hosted by Cloudflare alone | One month of passive DNS data from SIE Europe, March 2023 |
| ENS-referenced content hosting | 82% of content referenced by Ethereum Name Service (ENS) records is hosted on cloud nodes; 60% of that content's providers are located in the US or Germany | 20.6k setContenthash() event-log records extracted via the Etherscan API from 16 known resolver contracts, of which 16.8k resolved to provider records and 9k to unique IPs |
| Node-removal resilience (random) | Largest connected component retains 96% of remaining nodes after removing 90% of nodes at random | One crawl snapshot, 2023-05-12, 24,414 total / 16,676 crawlable nodes treated as an undirected graph; 10 repetitions, 95% confidence interval reported |
| Node-removal resilience (targeted, highest-degree-first) | Graph fully partitions into singleton components after ~60% of nodes removed | Same snapshot and graph construction |
| Node out-degree | Bounded within a narrow band set by the Kademlia parameter k | Same crawl dataset |
| Node in-degree | 90th percentile below ~500; a small number of very-high-in-degree nodes exist, 8 of the top 10 hosted on Amazon AWS | Same crawl dataset |

### Parameters
- Kademlia bucket size k = 20 (used both for the closest-peers lookup and as the number of resolvers contacted during Provide()).
- DHT connection manager target: 600–900 open connections per node (a configurable, version-dependent default the paper notes "were changed between IPFS releases").
- Content retrieval terminates a DHT-based provider search after 20 providers are found or all resolvers are exhausted.
- Crawl cadence: at least twice per day over 101 total crawls; average crawl duration 5.0 minutes; connection timeout 3 minutes (the paper states the choice trades shorter duration for snapshot accuracy against longer timeout for completeness, citing prior crawler-accuracy literature).
- Hydra-Booster instrumentation: 20 virtual peer IDs co-located on one virtual machine.
- Content-identifier (CID) sampling: from raw Bitswap traces, CIDs are deduplicated and a fixed 200,000 sampled per day for the "daily sampled Bitswap CIDs" dataset.
- Provider-record collection window: 28 days, 5.6 million CIDs.

### Stated limitations
The authors state that Bitswap-broadcast-based content discovery reaches only one hop, so their undirected-graph resilience analysis (which treats all observed edges, including Bitswap, as bidirectional communication channels) does not guarantee that content stays equally available even when the graph stays connected; they state a more nuanced analysis of content availability under partition is "left for future work." They state they cannot confirm whether Hydra-Booster's proactive-cache-fill behavior (which generates outbound lookups for every uncached requested CID) was exploited as an intentional denial-of-service vector during the measurement period, only that the behavior creates that exposure. They state their crawl only captures DHT servers, which are nodes with a public IP, so NAT-ed DHT clients are invisible to the topology and cloud-share figures derived from crawling, and must be estimated separately from Bitswap/DHT traffic logs (which is why the crawl-based cloud share, 79.6%, differs from the traffic-log-based cloud share, 35%). They state that the crawl cannot directly observe incoming connections (in-degree), only infer it from presence in other peers' published buckets, which undercounts true in-degree. For the ethics statement, they state they do not attempt to map collected IP addresses back to personal identities and do not perform content lookups on collected CIDs.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
This is a measurement paper and defines no mechanism for another system component to depend on. Its results constrain claims a synthesis can make about deployed content-addressed storage: any claim that a Kademlia-DHT-based content-location layer is decentralized in practice must state which channel (topology, traffic volume, content-provider population, or entry points) the claim covers, because the four channels disagree by 15 to 60 percentage points in cloud share depending on which is measured and which counting methodology is used. A synthesis proposing to rely on DHT crawls alone to estimate real participant diversity must account for the paper's finding that counting methodology (unique-IP-across-crawls vs. average-unique-nodes-per-crawl) changes the measured cloud share by a factor of two (39.9% vs. 79.6%), because short-lived, IP-rotating non-cloud nodes are overcounted by the unique-IP method.

### Contradicts
No claim commonly attributed to this paper was found to be unsupported by its text.
Disagrees with WEI-NSDI-24 (Trautwein et al./Wei et al., the same lab's earlier and later IPFS measurement work) on cloud-node share of DHT participants: this paper's 79.6% (its own counting method) versus the 2022 study's under-3% and the same alternative-methodology re-derivation giving 39.9%. The paper attributes the entire disagreement to counting methodology and crawl frequency, not to a change in the network between measurement windows — see WEI-NSDI-24 entry for whether that paper's numbers corroborate or diverge further.

### References worth retrieving
- Trautwein, Raman, Tyson, Castro, Scott, Schubotz, Gipp, Psaras, "Design and evaluation of IPFS: a storage layer for the decentralized web," ACM SIGCOMM 2022 — competing/prior measurement, source of the disputed <3% cloud-node figure this paper re-derives and disputes.
- Henningsen, Florian, Rust, Scheuermann, IPFS DHT crawler and analysis (2019 dataset), cited as [31],[32] — foundational, source of the crawler used in this paper and of the earlier (lower) resilience-to-removal figures this paper improves on.
- Gervais, Karame, Capkun, Capkun, 2014 — cited as [29], attack/critique, address-set-recovery style analysis (see also BIP37 privacy work already in corpus).
- Xia, Wang, Yu, Liu, Luo, Xu, Tyson, "Challenges in decentralized name management: the case of ENS," ACM IMC 2022 — foundational, methodology this paper's ENS dataset extraction follows.
- Albert, Jeong, Barabási, "Error and attack tolerance of complex networks," Nature 2000 — foundational, scale-free-network resilience theory this paper's random/targeted removal analysis is framed against.
- Balduf, Henningsen, Florian, Rust, Scheuermann (cited as [5]) — foundational/self-citation, prior work on Bitswap-broadcast privacy from the same author group.

- "5% of the most active peerIDs are responsible for almost 97% of the traffic"
- "34375 (39.9%) addresses on cloud providers, and 51689 (60.1%) non-cloud addresses"

## [BALDUF-IMC-24] Looking AT the Blue Skies of Bluesky
**Citation:** Leonhard Balduf, Saidu Sokoto, Onur Ascigil, Gareth Tyson, Björn Scheuermann, Maciej Korczynski, Ignacio Castro, Michał Król. "Looking AT the Blue Skies of Bluesky." ACM Internet Measurement Conference (IMC), 2024. DOI 10.1145/3646547.3688407.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.12449
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.12449
**Domain:** J+K

### What it does
The paper measures whether Bluesky's decomposition of a social network into independently swappable components (identity, data hosting, feed aggregation, content moderation) actually produces provider diversity in practice, or re-concentrates around one operator per component instead.

Bluesky's architecture, as described by the paper, separates five roles. A Decentralized Identifier (DID) names each user, resolved to a DID Document that lists the user's current handle and the network endpoint of the Personal Data Server (PDS) holding that user's data. A PDS stores a user's repository, a signed, git-like append log of every action (post, like, follow, block) the user performs; a user can migrate their repository to a different PDS, including a self-hosted one, while keeping the same DID and social graph, by updating the endpoint field in their DID Document. Because polling every PDS individually for updates does not scale, a Relay aggregates repository updates from all known PDSes into one stream (the Firehose) and caches repository copies locally; Bluesky PBC (the company) operates the default Relay and Firehose at bsky.network, though the protocol does not require a single Relay. Feed Generators are services, operable by anyone, that consume the Firehose (or a subset of it) and produce a ranked list of post references implementing a particular feed-ranking algorithm; they can be self-hosted or run through a hosting platform. Labelers are accounts that attach machine-readable labels (for example "nudity" or a spoiler warning) to specific posts, accounts, or media; any account can register as a Labeler by publishing a service-information record in its own repository, and each user chooses, individually, which Labelers to subscribe to and how their client should react to a given label from that Labeler. The AppView is the component that collates data from across the network (consuming the Firehose) into the views a client displays (a user's timeline, a thread, search results); Bluesky PBC operates the only AppView the paper found in production use.

The paper's measurement methodology, for each component, is to enumerate the full population of operators of that component from Bluesky's own public data streams, then compute how concentrated that population is. Data sources: the Relay's sync.listRepos call for the full list of active user DIDs and their latest repo-commit version (queried weekly, March-April 2024); each user's DID Document (downloaded via Bluesky's centralized plc.directory service for the did:plc method, and via HTTPS .well-known lookups for the did:web method); a full snapshot of every user's repository content via the Relay's sync.getRepo endpoint; a continuous subscription to the Firehose from March 6 to April 30, 2024; the AppView's getFeedGenerator and getFeed endpoints for Feed Generator metadata and posts; and each Labeler's own public label-stream endpoint, listed in its DID Document.

### Measured results
| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| Dataset scale: 5,591,824 user DIDs found via weekly Relay queries (March-April 2024); 5,077,159 DID Documents downloaded from the centralized plc.directory service plus 6 more via did:web; 5,523,919 repositories downloaded over 10 days in April 2024; 279,289,739 Firehose events collected from 2024-03-06 to April 30 (99.78% repo commits, 0.19% identity updates, 0.02% handle updates, 0.01% tombstones); 43,063 Feed Generators discovered, with posts collected for 40,398 of them (93%) between 2024-04-16 and 2024-05-10, totaling 21,520,083 posts; 62 unique Labeler accounts identified as of 2024-05-01, of which 46 had a functional endpoint on repeated daily reconnection attempts and 36 had issued at least one label |
| Cumulative repository content since Bluesky's November 2022 launch, as observed through May 2024: 740 million likes, 225 million posts, 160.9 million follows, 77.9 million reposts, 10.8 million account-blocking operations | Full repository snapshot, April 2024 |
| Daily active users as of April 2024: consistently around 500,000, contributing approximately 3 million likes, 800,000 posts, and 300,000 reposts per day; daily active users fell by approximately 60,000 between March and May 2024 | Derived from the Firehose/repository timeline, compared against a stated 1 million daily active users for Mastodon and 245 million for Twitter/X (both figures cited to external sources, not measured by this paper) |
| Subdomain-handle concentration: of 5,077,159 FQDN handles extracted from DID Documents, 98.9% are subdomains of bsky.social, the platform's default free custodial domain | Full DID Document snapshot, March 2024 |
| Among the remaining 57,202 non-bsky.social handles, no single alternative operator hosts more than a few hundred: 256 FQDNs under swifties.social, 179 under tired.io, 133 under vibes.cool (the latter two both operated by the same third party, Skyname); 35 accounts use a personal github.io subdomain | Same DID Document snapshot |

### Parameters
The paper is a measurement study of a live deployed system, not a system with tunable design parameters. Its own methodological parameters (data-collection windows, not protocol settings) are:

| Parameter | Value used |
|---|---|
| User Identifier Dataset collection window | Weekly queries, March-April 2024 |
| DID Document snapshot window | One week, March 2024 |
| Repository snapshot collection window | 10 days, April 2024 |
| Firehose continuous subscription window | 2024-03-06 through 2024-04-30 |
| Feed Post collection window | 2024-04-16 through 2024-05-10, bi-weekly polling |
| Labeler reconnection check frequency | Daily |
| Random-sample verification of self-assigned language tags | Approximately 0.1% of tagged posts manually checked against actual post language |

### Stated limitations
The paper states it "deliberately omit[s] a deeper analysis of the social graph, as Bluesky does not introduce novel solutions in this regard," so no independent social-graph structural analysis comparable to Mastodon-instance studies is reported here. It states that it cannot distinguish, from the Feed Generator metadata alone, between a Feed Generator that is permanently deleted versus temporarily unavailable, and consequently excludes 4.3% of discovered Feed Generators lacking retrievable metadata from further analysis. It states Feed Generators differ in how much post history they retain (some impose duration or count limits), so the Feed Post Dataset cannot be assumed complete for any Feed Generator's full history predating the collection window. It states that user label-subscription preferences (which Labelers a given user follows, and how their client reacts) are not publicly visible, and that the authors deliberately made no attempt to infer them, for ethical reasons; so no measurement of Labeler adoption from the subscriber side is reported. It states that the Brazil user-migration event (following a 2024 court-ordered ban on Twitter/X in Brazil) fell outside the data-collection period, so its effect on Bluesky's growth curve is not captured in this paper's figures. It states explicitly that it is not clear how a user migration away from Bluesky PBC's centralized Relay and AppView would work in practice, and that network effects might prevent it regardless of the protocol's technical openness. It states that whether the current open Feed Generator and Labeler ecosystems remain economically viable and scalable as non-Bluesky-PBC-operated infrastructure (rather than as a thin layer atop Bluesky PBC's centralized Firehose and AppView) "remains to be seen," explicitly flagging this as unresolved rather than answered by the paper's data.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A component-diversity claim about Bluesky (or an architecture like it) requires specifying which component is meant, since this paper's own results diverge sharply by component: identity-handle hosting is stated as 98.9% concentrated in the platform operator's own free domain, Feed-Generator hosting-as-a-service is stated as 85.86% concentrated in one third-party platform (Skyfeed), while domain registrar choice among the small fraction of self-managed-domain users is comparatively less concentrated (top four registrars hold 50%) — a synthesis step that treats "Bluesky's decomposition produces diversity" as one true-or-false claim would need to average or otherwise combine these disparate per-component figures, which this paper does not do. Interpreting any Bluesky content-moderation measurement requires knowing that the official Bluesky Labeler's specific label values (for example !takedown) carry hardcoded client behavior that ordinary community Labelers' labels do not, so a labeling scheme built on this architecture must reserve some label namespace for platform-operator-only enforcement actions if it wants a takedown mechanism, since the paper states this exclamation-mark-prefixed namespace is "valid only when issued by the official Bluesky Labeler." Any system relying on this paper's Firehose-based full-network-visibility approach requires a client to sustain roughly 30 gigabytes per day of bandwidth per subscribed consumer, which sets a lower bound on the bandwidth cost of running an independent Relay, AppView, or comparable full-network-observing service without relying on Bluesky PBC's own infrastructure. The handle-ownership-verification mechanism for self-managed domains requires the domain owner to control DNS TXT records under an _atproto subdomain (used by 98.7% of measured self-managed handles) or, less commonly, a /.well-known/atproto-did HTTPS-served file (1.3%); a system reusing this verification approach inherits dependence on DNS or web-server control as the ownership-proof channel, with the associated registrar-level concentration this paper measures (50% of self-managed domains through four registrars).

### Contradicts
None found within this batch as a direct numeric disagreement. The paper's finding that identity-handle concentration (98.9% under one operator-controlled domain) coexists with comparatively higher registrar-level diversity among the remaining self-managed handles illustrates, within this single paper, that "decentralized identity" is not a single measurable quantity; a synthesis step should not cite this paper for one undifferentiated Bluesky "decentralization score." This paper cites La Cava, Greco, Tagarelli (the LACAVA-ANS-21 entry in this batch) directly, as reference [11], solely as an example of prior Fediverse-centralization measurement work in its related-work discussion of Mastodon; it does not reproduce or dispute LACAVA-ANS-21's specific structural figures.

- foundational: Kleppmann, Frazee, Gold, Graber, Holmgren, Ivy, Johnson, Newbold, Volpert, "Bluesky and the AT Protocol: Usable Decentralized Social Media," arXiv:2402.03239, 2024 — the protocol specification this measurement paper's architecture description (PDS, Relay, Firehose, AppView, Labeler) is drawn from.
- competing/independent-measurement: Raman, Joglekar, De Cristofaro, Sastry, Tyson, "Challenges in the decentralised web: The Mastodon case," IMC 2019 (reference [29]) — the direct Mastodon-architecture measurement precedent this paper's Bluesky study is modeled after and implicitly compared against; also the paper LACAVA-ANS-21 in this same batch was originally sought to update.
- competing: Balduf, Korczyński, Ascigil, Keizer, Pavlou, Scheuermann, Król, "The Cloud Strikes Back: Investigating the Decentralization of IPFS," IMC 2023 (reference [7]) — an earlier measurement study by an overlapping author set, on a different decentralized-storage system, measuring the identical general question (does a nominally decentralized system re-concentrate) for IPFS rather than Bluesky.

## [BARNES-RFC-23] The Messaging Layer Security (MLS) Protocol

**Citation:** Richard Barnes, Benjamin Beurdouche, Raphael Robert, Jon Millican, Emad Omara, Katriel Cohn-Gordon. "The Messaging Layer Security (MLS) Protocol." IETF RFC 9420, 2023. DOI 10.17487/RFC9420.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9420.html
**Source URL:** https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9420.html
**Domain:** H

### What it does
MLS establishes a shared symmetric group key for two to thousands of clients, with forward secrecy (a past key stays secret after a later compromise) and post-compromise security (PCS, a future key stays secret after a past compromise heals), at a per-change cost that grows with the logarithm of group size rather than linearly or quadratically.

The mechanism is a ratchet tree: a perfect binary tree (a complete balanced binary tree where every leaf sits at the same depth) with one leaf per group member. Each tree node holds a Hybrid Public Key Encryption (HPKE) keypair. The private key of any node is known only to members at leaf nodes descended from it — the tree invariant. To change the group's shared secret while excluding one member, a client encrypts fresh entropy once per node on that member's path to the root (the direct path), producing log(N) ciphertexts instead of N-1 pairwise ciphertexts, where N is group size.

State evolves as a linear sequence of epochs. In each epoch a set of authenticated members shares one epoch secret, from which further keys derive. A member proposes changes (add, remove, update) in a Proposal message; a Commit message applies a set of proposals and starts the next epoch, redistributing a fresh epoch secret over the updated tree so only current members can compute it; a Welcome message equips a newly added member with the state needed to join at that epoch. Two supporting roles sit outside the cryptographic core: an Authentication Service (AS) that lets members verify each other's credentials, and a Delivery Service (DS) that routes messages between participants. The protocol assumes the AS is trusted and treats the DS as largely untrusted — MLS is designed to keep group data confidential and correct even if the DS is compromised, and expects only reliable message delivery from it.

### Measured results
None. RFC 9420 is a protocol specification, not an experimental paper; it states asymptotic costs (see Parameters) but reports no measured latency, bandwidth, node counts, or throughput from any implementation or deployment.

### Parameters
| Parameter | Value / bound | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Cost of a group-key change excluding one member, sender-key baseline (pairwise) | O(N) computation and communication | N = group size; used to distribute a fresh sender key to each member individually |
| Cost of achieving PCS with plain shared sender keys | O(N²) key-update messages | to give every member post-compromise security via sender keys, without a tree |
| Cost of a group-key change via the ratchet tree (MLS) | O(log N) HPKE encryptions | perfect binary tree of depth d = log2(N), one ciphertext per node on the excluded member's direct path |
| Tree shape | perfect binary tree, 2^d leaves at uniform depth d, 2^(d+1) − 1 total nodes | fixed structural requirement, not a tuned parameter |

### Stated limitations
The document states its own security analysis is high-level and that a complete analysis is out of scope, deferring to citations in the companion architecture document (BEURDOUCHE-RFC-25). It states MLS provides no confidentiality protection for some messages and fields (Section 16.4), naming group metadata as an exposed category. It states an attacker able to observe messages in transit can learn group state, including potentially group membership, and can mount denial-of-service or selective-message-removal attacks against the group; it recommends carrying MLS messages over TLS or QUIC to mitigate this, placing that mitigation outside the protocol itself. It states the protocol places no requirement on how an implementation represents the ratchet tree internally, so a security or performance property of one representation cannot be assumed of another.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The Delivery Service must deliver a Commit and its accompanying Welcome message in a way that lets every recipient compute the same next epoch state; the specification does not itself provide agreement on which Commit is canonical when two members generate Commits concurrently from the same epoch. The document requires (MUST) that applications establish some way to resolve conflicting Commit messages for the same epoch, either by preventing the conflict from occurring or by a rule that selects one Commit as canonical among several sent in that epoch; it requires this resolution to minimize how long forked or stale group states are retained in memory, and to delete them promptly once no longer needed for forward secrecy. It requires that generating a Commit not modify the sender's own state before acceptance is known, and that a Welcome message not be delivered to a new joiner until its corresponding Commit is known to have been accepted. The protocol assumes an Authentication Service that group members trust to validate credentials; a compromised or misbehaving AS is treated as a distinct, separately analyzed failure mode from DS compromise. The tree invariant (a node's private key known only to leaves in its subtree) must be preserved by every path update, or the confidentiality argument for excluding a removed member fails.

### Contradicts
None found. This entry documents no measured claim, so it neither confirms nor conflicts with another corpus entry's measurements. It is the total-order-imposing baseline that BIENSTOCK-TCC-20, BIENSTOCK-TCC-22, and BARTUSEK-EPRINT-26 reason about, and that BeeKEM (already in corpus) states it removes.

### References worth retrieving
- Cohn-Gordon, Cremers, Garratt, Millican, Milner, "On Ends-to-Ends Encryption: Asynchronous Group Messaging with Strong Security Guarantees" (ART), DOI 10.1145/3243734.3243747 — foundational (the asynchronous ratcheting tree construction MLS's ratchet tree is based on)
- Cohn-Gordon, Cremers, Dowling, Garratt, Stebila, "A Formal Security Analysis of the Signal Messaging Protocol," EuroS&P 2017 — foundational (Double Ratchet analysis, the two-party baseline MLS generalizes)
- Beurdouche, Rescorla, Omara, Inguva, Duric, "The Messaging Layer Security (MLS) Architecture" (MLS-ARCH) — foundational (companion document; already a corpus target as BEURDOUCHE-RFC-25)
- Melara, Blankstein, Bonneau, Felten, Freedman, "CONIKS: Bringing Key Transparency to End Users," USENIX Security 2015 — foundational (key transparency referenced for AS credential handling)
- Bellare, Ng, Tackmann, "Nonces Are Noticed: AEAD Revisited," CRYPTO 2019 — foundational (the AEAD security definitions MLS's sender-data encryption scheme cites)

### Verbatim extracts
- "MLS assumes a trusted AS but a largely untrusted DS."
- "Applications MUST have an established way to resolve conflicting Commit messages for the same epoch."
- "requiring a number of key update messages that scales as the square of the group size"
- "costs that scale as the log of the group size"
- "A group has a single linear sequence of epochs."
- "in size ranging from two to thousands"

## [BARTUSEK-EPRINT-26] Fair-Weather No More: Guaranteed Efficiency in Secure Group Messaging

**Citation:** James Bartusek, Nir Bitansky, Yevgeniy Dodis, Rachit Garg, David J. Wu. "Fair-Weather No More: Guaranteed Efficiency in Secure Group Messaging." IACR Cryptology ePrint Archive, 2026. DOI unassigned.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1677.pdf
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1677.pdf
**Domain:** H

### What it does
The paper builds the first continuous group key agreement (CGKA — a primitive that maintains one shared secret among a changing group of users, where any member, not a central manager, may add or remove members or refresh keys) with a computation and communication cost per operation that is provably polylogarithmic in the group size in the worst case, not merely in the best case.

The construction routes CGKA through a new primitive the paper calls incremental distributed broadcast encryption (DBE — a scheme where each user samples an independent public/private keypair with no coordination, and any sender can encrypt one ciphertext that every user in a chosen set can decrypt with its own private key plus the other members' public keys). Incremental means a user's aggregated public key and each member's aggregated secret key can be updated to reflect one added or removed member without recomputing from the full membership. A CGKA scheme built directly on incremental DBE broadcasts a fresh group secret, encrypted under the current aggregated public key, on every Add, Remove, or refresh operation; this variant achieves post-compromise security (PCS — the group recovers a secure state through normal operations after an honest member's secret state was exposed) with every operation staying polylogarithmic, because the incremental update and the encryption both avoid touching all n members' keys.

Forward secrecy (FS — past group keys stay secret even after a current member's state is later exposed) needs a second primitive, updatable DBE, built in the random oracle model (a proof technique that treats a specified hash function as an ideal random function) on the same lattice assumption. Updatable DBE lets a sender implicitly rotate every receiver's secret key while sending one compact ciphertext, so a member who never sends an update is still protected against future compromise revealing past secrets. Add and Remove stay polylogarithmic in the updatable-DBE-based scheme; the one operation the paper does not make sublinear is a dedicated forward-secrecy-refresh operation, which is allowed to take time linear in group size and is the only such operation in the scheme.

### Measured results
None. This is a cryptographic construction and security-proof paper; every stated bound is asymptotic (a function of group size n and security parameter λ) under a stated hardness assumption, not a measured latency, bandwidth, or throughput figure from any implementation or deployment. The paper states its own lattice parameters are likely too large for a practical deployment without further optimization not attempted in this work.

### Parameters
| Parameter | Value / bound | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Computation and communication for Setup, Init, Add, Remove, PCRefresh, Process, in the PCS-only scheme | polynomial in the security parameter λ only, independent of group size n | under the decomposed Learning With Errors (decomposed LWE) assumption; the paper's Definition 6.5 formalizes "optimal efficiency" as a fixed polynomial p(λ) bounding every one of these operations |
| Add, Remove, and general operations in the FS-capable scheme | polylogarithmic in n, same lattice assumption plus random oracle model | forward secrecy added on top of the PCS-only construction |
| Forward-secrecy-refresh operation | linear in group size n | the single linear-cost operation in the FS-capable scheme; still produces a compact (sublinear-size) ciphertext |
| Per-party storage | linear in group size n (the group roster and every current member's public key) | stated as matching the standard MLS/CGKA literature model, where roster storage is required and not counted as a communication or computation cost |
| Underlying hardness assumption | decomposed LWE, parameterized by (n_lattice, m, q, σ̃) in the paper's lattice notation (distinct from CGKA group size n) | a falsifiable, plausibly post-quantum lattice assumption from prior work (Abram, Malavolta, Roy, CRYPTO 2025) |

### Stated limitations
The paper states the PCS-only construction achieves only passive security: the adversary may read honest members' secret states over time but cannot craft messages on their behalf or control message delivery order beyond dropping or delaying messages, matching the security model of Bienstock et al. (BIENSTOCK-TCC-22). It states security against active adversaries who forge or reorder messages is left to future work, though the authors argue informally that their scheme should resist drop and delay attacks. It states the lattice parameters needed for the current proof are likely too large for real-world use without further, unattempted optimization. It states, as its own explicit open problem, that no construction is known that achieves worst-case sublinear complexity for forward secrecy in computation, not merely communication — the FS-refresh operation stays linear-time in every construction in the paper. It reports, in an appendix, a concrete attack that breaks an aggressive sublinear-time variant of the updatable DBE scheme, offered as partial evidence that the linear-time FS-refresh is not easily removed by the paper's own technique. It states the paper's improvement is over the framework of Bienstock et al. (BIENSTOCK-TCC-22) and does not claim to remove that paper's black-box impossibility result — that result rules out sublinear worst-case CGKA built from public-key encryption used as a sealed component (its internal algebraic structure not accessed), and this paper's construction avoids that barrier by using the internal lattice structure of its encryption scheme directly, not by refuting the impossibility result.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The construction requires a common reference string (crs) sampled once at setup, shared by all group members. It requires each party to store the full current group roster and every other current member's public key, so any component using this CGKA must supply and keep that per-member public-key list current at every party. It requires message delivery to be honest, in the sense that the adversary cannot forge or actively tamper with the content of add, remove, or refresh messages — active-adversary security is explicitly not proved. Achieving forward secrecy requires periodically running the dedicated FS-refresh operation; because that operation costs communication and computation linear in group size, a system that wants both efficiency and up-to-date forward secrecy must decide how often to pay that linear cost, and the paper states the model is meaningful specifically where network bandwidth is far more expensive than local per-party computation, or where members run FS-refresh infrequently and accept a correspondingly weaker forward-secrecy guarantee between refreshes.

### Contradicts
None found against another corpus entry's measurement — this paper reports no measurements. It directly narrows, but explicitly does not refute, the impossibility scope of BIENSTOCK-TCC-22: that paper shows no CGKA built black-box from public-key encryption avoids Ω(n) worst-case communication, and this paper's own construction sidesteps that scope by using a non-black-box, structured lattice-based primitive (incremental and updatable distributed broadcast encryption) rather than generic public-key encryption. The paper states TreeKEM (the CGKA underlying RFC 9420/BARNES-RFC-23) does not achieve forward secrecy in general, citing Alwen, Coretti, Dodis, Tselekounis (CRYPTO 2020) as having demonstrated this, and reports that a cited independent experimental paper (Auerbach, Cueto Noval, Erol, Pietrzak, CRYPTO 2025) measured TreeKEM's communication complexity converging toward linear in a random-update scenario, reaching Ω(√n) at update-batch size d=1 and Ω(n^0.99) at d=50 — a measurement the present paper reports as a citation, not one it produced itself, so it is not usable in this evidence file as this paper's own measured result.

### References worth retrieving
- Bienstock, Dodis, Garg, Grogan, Hajiabadi, Rösler, "On the Worst-Case Inefficiency of CGKA," TCC 2022 — foundational (already a corpus target: BIENSTOCK-TCC-22; supplies the black-box impossibility result and the CGKA security model this paper adopts)
- Bienstock, Dodis, Rösler, "On the Price of Concurrency in Group Ratcheting Protocols," TCC 2020 — foundational (already a corpus target: BIENSTOCK-TCC-20)
- Alwen, Coretti, Dodis, Tselekounis, "Security Analysis and Improvements for the IETF MLS Standard for Group Messaging," CRYPTO 2020 — foundational (defines CGKA, RTreeKEM, and updatable public-key encryption; source of the claim that TreeKEM lacks forward secrecy)
- Alwen, Coretti, Dodis, Tselekounis, "Modular Design of Secure Group Messaging Protocols and the Security of MLS," ACM CCS 2021 — foundational (composition theorems combining CGKA with symmetric-key primitives for active-attacker security)
- Auerbach, Cueto Noval, Erol, Pietrzak, "Continuous Group-Key Agreement: Concurrent Updates Without Pruning," CRYPTO 2025 — competing (measures TreeKEM's average-case communication converging to near-linear; independent empirical/analytic result on the incumbent construction)
- Alwen, Brzuska, Govinden, Harasser, Tessaro, "Succinct PPRFs via Memory-Tight Reductions," CRYPTO 2025 — competing (the prior sublinear-communication CGKA from indistinguishability obfuscation, which this paper positions itself against on efficiency and post-quantum grounds)
- Cohn-Gordon, Cremers, Garratt, Millican, Milner, "On Ends-to-Ends Encryption: Asynchronous Group Messaging with Strong Security Guarantees," ACM CCS 2018 — foundational (source of the double-join attack this paper's incrementality property must resist)
- Barnes, Beurdouche, Robert, Millican, Omara, Cohn-Gordon, "The Messaging Layer Security (MLS) Protocol," RFC 9420, 2023 — foundational (already a corpus target: BARNES-RFC-23; the standardized TreeKEM-based protocol this paper's worst-case bound applies against)
- Alwen, Jost, Mularczyk, "On the Insider Security of MLS," CRYPTO 2022 — foundational (active-adversary security analysis in the TreeKEM paradigm, cited as the direction this paper's active-security extension would need)

- "achieves basic CGKA security ... and post-compromise security, but not forward secrecy"
- "the forward-secure refresh operation takes linear time in the group size"
- "the only linear-time operation in our new CGKA scheme is a special forward secrecy refreshing operation"
- "the per-party storage is linear in the group size"
- "We leave it as an open problem to achieve a truly (computation-wise!) sublinear CGKA scheme with forward secrecy"
- "our results show that computation costs scale linearly in practical scenarios even in the best-case scenario"

## [BENET-ARXIV-14] IPFS - Content Addressed, Versioned, P2P File System (DRAFT 3)
**Citation:** Juan Benet. "IPFS - Content Addressed, Versioned, P2P File System (DRAFT 3)." arXiv:1407.3561, 2014.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/abs/1407.3561
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/1407.3561
**Domain:** C

### What it does
The InterPlanetary File System (IPFS) lets any participating computer publish and retrieve files and other data structures by content — every unit of data is located by the cryptographic hash of its own bytes rather than by a server address — so that the same content can be served by any peer holding it, verified by any receiver without trusting the sender, and deduplicated automatically whenever two objects hold identical bytes. The system is a stack of seven sub-protocols, each independently swappable behind a defined interface, described bottom-up:

Identities: a node's identifier (NodeId) is the cryptographic hash of its public key, generated using S/Kademlia's proof-of-work identity-generation puzzle (a difficulty parameter requiring the hash to have a minimum number of leading zero bits), which raises the cost of an attacker minting many node identities. On connection, peers exchange public keys and verify each peer's claimed NodeId is the hash of the key it presents; a mismatch terminates the connection. Hash values throughout the system are stored in a self-describing "multihash" format (a header naming the hash function and digest length precedes the digest), so the choice of hash function can change over time without breaking compatibility.

Network: transport-agnostic; the paper recommends WebRTC DataChannels for browser connectivity or uTP/LEDBAT (Low Extra Delay Background Transport) elsewhere, with SCTP (Stream Control Transmission Protocol) available for reliability atop transports that lack it, ICE (Interactive Connectivity Establishment) for NAT (Network Address Translation) traversal, and optional per-message integrity (hash checksum) and authenticity (HMAC keyed to the sender's public key) checks. Addresses are stored in a self-describing "multiaddr" format that names the protocol stack used to reach a peer, so IPFS does not assume IP (Internet Protocol) reachability and can run over overlay networks.

Routing: peers locate other peers' network addresses and locate which peers can serve a given content-addressed object using a distributed hash table (DHT) that combines S/Kademlia's Sybil-resistant identity generation and disjoint-path lookups with Coral's design of storing peer references rather than the data itself at DHT-selected nodes. Objects of 1 KB or smaller are stored directly in the DHT as values; larger objects are represented in the DHT only by the NodeIds of peers who can serve them, retrieved by a `FindValuePeers` call, avoiding the storage and bandwidth cost of forcing "nearest" DHT nodes to hold data they may not need, a design property the paper attributes to Coral. The routing interface (`FindPeer`, `SetValue`, `GetValue`, `ProvideValue`, `FindValuePeers`) is stated as swappable for any component implementing it, e.g., a static hash table in a local, non-churning network instead of a DHT.

Exchange (BitSwap): a block-trading protocol modeled on BitTorrent but operating across all files a node holds rather than within one torrent's swarm — a node's `want_list` and `have_list` can be satisfied by blocks unrelated to any single file. Each pair of connected peers keeps a ledger of bytes sent and received; the debt ratio `r = bytes_sent / (bytes_recv + 1)` feeds a sigmoid function `P(send | r) = 1 − 1/(1 + exp(6 − 3r))` giving the probability a node sends a requested block to a debtor peer, so the willingness to send falls off as a peer's owed debt to the sender grows, described by the paper as providing leniency to established trust relationships and resistance to both freeloading and Sybil node creation. A node declining to send a block to a peer subsequently ignores that peer for a cooldown period (default 10 seconds) so the peer cannot simply retry to game the probabilistic decision. Ledgers are exchanged and compared when a connection activates; a mismatch resets the ledger to zero for both parties, discarding accrued credit or debt, which the paper notes a malicious node could exploit to erase its own debt (at the cost of also erasing any accrued trust). A node holding nothing its peers want seeks pieces its peers want at lower priority than its own wants, incentivizing caching and dissemination of rare pieces even when not immediately useful to the caching node.

Objects: content-addressed immutable objects form a Merkle directed acyclic graph (DAG) — a generalization of Git's object model in which any object's links to other objects are themselves cryptographic hashes embedded in the linking object, so tampering with any linked object changes its hash and is detected by whichever object refers to it. Each object carries an array of named links (each link naming a target hash and target size) plus an opaque data field whose format is entirely application-defined, so IPFS can transport arbitrary data structures — key-value stores, relational databases, linked-data triple stores, publishing systems, or blockchains — without needing to understand their internal format itself, while still being able to list an object's references, resolve string path lookups by walking the link table one component at a time, and recursively enumerate every object reachable from a root. There is no global root object; instead, every path begins with a specific object's hash, and the same descendant object is reachable via multiple equally valid paths rooted at any of its ancestors. Objects can be optionally wrapped for encryption or signing; an `EncryptedObject` or `SignedObject` frame changes the wrapped object's hash (defining a distinct object identity), and encrypted links make traversal past that point impossible without the corresponding decryption key, so a parent object can be encrypted under one key while a child is encrypted under a different key or left unencrypted.

Files: a Git-inspired object model of `block` (a variable-size chunk of data), `list` (a collection of blocks or other lists), `tree` (a collection of blocks, lists, or trees, used to model directories), and `commit` (a version-history snapshot of a tree) objects, layered on top of the general Merkle DAG. Because commits and their ancestor trees remain reachable through hash links, every prior version of a filesystem tree stays retrievable and the full change history is recoverable directly from the object graph, without a separate version-history store. Large files are split into blocks and lists using one of three interchangeable strategies the system offers rather than mandates: Rabin fingerprinting (as used in the Low-Bandwidth File System, LBFS) to choose content-defined block boundaries, the rsync rolling-checksum algorithm to detect which blocks changed between versions, or a user-supplied block-splitting function tuned to a specific file type.

Naming (IPNS, the InterPlanetary Name Space): because Merkle DAG objects are immutable, a mutable pointer scheme is layered on top so that new content can be found at a stable path. Every node is assigned the mutable namespace `/ipns/<NodeId>`; the node publishes an object to that path signed with its private key, and the object is itself published as an ordinary immutable IPFS object whose hash is then stored in the DHT as the value associated with the node's NodeId (`routing.setValue(NodeId, <object-hash>)`), so retrieving `/ipns/<NodeId>` means looking up that DHT value, fetching the referenced object, and checking its signature against the public key implied by the NodeId — this construction is drawn from the Self-Certifying File System (SFS) naming scheme. Because hash-based names are not memorable, the paper layers human-friendly naming on top: peer links (one user's namespace linking directly to another's, forming a web of trust), DNS TXT records mapping a domain name to an IPNS path, Proquint pronounceable encodings of a hash, and third-party name-shortening services analogous to DNS/URL shorteners today.

### Measured results
This paper reports no experiments, benchmarks, or deployment measurements of IPFS itself. Every performance-relevant number in the retrieved text is either a design parameter (e.g., the 1 KB DHT direct-storage threshold, the BitSwap sigmoid coefficients, the 10-second default ignore-cooldown) or a figure the paper attributes to a different, cited system: Kademlia's expected `⌈log2(n)⌉` lookup hops (e.g., stated as 20 hops for a 10,000,000-node network, attributed to Maymounkov and Mazières' Kademlia paper) and S/Kademlia's stated 0.85 lookup success rate at up to 50% adversarial nodes using disjoint-path lookups (attributed to Baumgart and Mies' S/Kademlia paper, matching this corpus's own already-verified S/Kademlia entry). Per Rule 1 of this extraction protocol, neither of these cited figures is recorded here as a result of this paper, because this paper did not produce them. The registry's own citation note for this key states that measured deployment behavior for IPFS is covered by a separate paper in this corpus (Trautwein et al., SIGCOMM 2022), not by this design document.

### Parameters
- DHT small-value storage threshold: objects ≤ 1 KB stored directly as DHT values; larger objects stored in the DHT only as peer references (NodeIds of peers able to serve the block).
- BitSwap sending-probability function: `P(send | r) = 1 − 1 / (1 + exp(6 − 3r))`, where `r = bytes_sent / (bytes_recv + 1)` is the debt ratio between two peers; the paper states this sigmoid "works in practice" but explicitly leaves broader exploration of the BitSwap strategy space as future work.
- BitSwap ignore cooldown after a declined send: default 10 seconds.
- S/Kademlia identity-generation difficulty: an integer parameter controlling the minimum number of leading zero bits required in a candidate NodeId's hash before it is accepted; no specific numeric value is given in this paper (the underlying scheme is cited to Baumgart and Mies).
- File-splitting strategy: not a fixed parameter but a choice among three interchangeable mechanisms (Rabin fingerprinting, rsync rolling checksum, or a user-supplied function), left to the application.

### Stated limitations
The paper states BitSwap's strategy-selection function (which peer to send to, and how much) is unexplored design space: "The exploration of the space of such strategies is future work," with the sigmoid function offered only as one choice that "works in practice." The paper states a token/currency-based BitSwap strategy is a natural extension but is deferred: "This can be implemented as a BitSwap Strategy, and will be explored in a future paper," and such a system would additionally require a global ledger to track currency ownership and transfer, which the paper does not design. The paper states BitSwap's ledger-reset-on-mismatch behavior is exploitable: "It is possible for malicious nodes to purposefully 'lose' the Ledger, hoping to erase debts," noting the mitigating factor that doing so also discards any trust the malicious node had accrued, and that a partner peer may treat the mismatch as misconduct and refuse to trade, without the paper specifying any protocol-level defense beyond that discretion. The paper states path-based lookups carry "considerable overhead" because each path component requires a DHT lookup, peer connection, and block retrieval, mitigated only by two unevaluated techniques (indefinite tree caching, since hash-addressed objects never change, and constructing a flattened tree that lists every object reachable from a root in one structure) rather than by a measured fix. The paper states object encryption is entirely optional and application-controlled, so IPFS's own content-addressing and deduplication properties do not by themselves provide confidentiality; a parent and child object can be encrypted under different keys or not at all, and traversal past an encrypted link fails without the corresponding key, meaning the same data uploaded unencrypted by two different users deduplicates while encrypted data generally will not (the paper does not measure this effect but the mechanism described implies it).

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Requires every participating node to provide local storage (disk or, for non-persistent caches, RAM) in which retrieved blocks are held, because "all blocks available in IPFS are in some node's local storage" and there is no other persistence layer; a node with no local storage cannot serve content it does not currently have live in a network buffer. Requires an explicit pinning operation for any object a node wants to guarantee will survive local garbage collection or cache eviction — the paper describes an object as durably available in the network only if some node pins it (optionally recursively, covering its descendants), so content whose only copies are held unpinned, transiently, by nodes that fetched it as a caching side effect is not guaranteed to persist; the mechanism supplies no default retention policy beyond what participants choose to pin. Requires the DHT/routing layer to remain reachable and correctly answer `FindValuePeers` queries for any large object to be locatable at all, since large objects are represented in the DHT only by peer references, not by their content; if no peer that both holds the object and has announced itself via `ProvideValue` is discoverable through routing, the object is unretrievable regardless of whether some node still holds its bytes. Requires BitSwap's debt-ratio incentive mechanism to be paired with a strategy that a deployment separately selects and tunes, since the paper's own default sigmoid is presented as an example rather than a specified, evaluated default. Requires the naming layer (IPNS) to depend on the same DHT/routing layer for its only mutable-state distribution path — publishing a new value at `/ipns/<NodeId>` means writing to the routing system's key-value store, so if routing is partitioned, degraded, or attacked (e.g., an eclipse or Sybil attack against the DHT), name resolution degrades along with it even though the underlying immutable objects remain independently fetchable by hash. Requires every consumer that verifies an IPNS record to independently confirm the signature against the public key implied by the claimed NodeId, since the mutable pointer itself carries no other authenticity guarantee.

### Contradicts
None found against other entries in this corpus as currently extracted.

International Conference on Parallel and Distributed Systems, 2007. — foundational (already verified in this corpus; source of the identity-generation puzzle and disjoint-path lookup mechanisms IPFS's routing layer is built on, and of the 0.85-success-at-50%-adversarial figure this paper cites but does not itself measure).
- Maymounkov, Mazières. "Kademlia: A peer-to-peer information system based on the XOR metric." IPTPS, 2002. — foundational (already verified in this corpus; base DHT design IPFS's routing layer extends).
