## [BIENSTOCK-TCC-22] On the Worst-Case Inefficiency of CGKA

**Citation:** Alexander Bienstock, Yevgeniy Dodis, Sanjam Garg, Garrison Grogan, Mohammad Hajiabadi, Paul Rösler. "On the Worst-Case Inefficiency of CGKA." Theory of Cryptography Conference (TCC), 2022. DOI 10.1007/978-3-031-22365-5_8.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://eprint.iacr.org/2022/1237.pdf
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2022/1237.pdf
**Domain:** H

### What it does
The paper proves that no continuous group key agreement (CGKA) protocol built by treating public-key encryption (PKE) as a sealed component — using only its encryption and decryption interface, never its internal algebraic structure — can guarantee communication cost below linear in group size n in the worst case, and that no single such protocol is simultaneously optimal on every sequence of group operations.

The proof introduces a new primitive, Compact Key Exchange (CKE): n users each independently and non-interactively broadcast a public key, and one designated sender encrypts a symmetric key into one ciphertext that all n users can decrypt with their own private key. The paper first proves CKE and CGKA are equivalent in worst-case communication complexity — a CGKA protocol with small worst-case ciphertexts implies a CKE scheme with small ciphertexts, and a CKE scheme with small ciphertexts implies a CGKA protocol with correspondingly small worst-case ciphertexts. It then proves a black-box separation: any CKE scheme built by treating PKE as a sealed component must produce ciphertexts of size Ω(n) (growing at least linearly with the number of receivers), by an attack that shows a ciphertext smaller than this bound cannot "embed" enough independent decryption trapdoors for all n receivers to be extractable. Composing the two results yields the paper's Ω(n) lower bound on CGKA's worst-case communication.

The lower bound targets a specific pattern of group operations the paper calls a bad sequence: some set of users add k new members and go offline (become passive), while the remaining active users execute rounds of state updates (refreshes) among themselves. Because post-compromise security (PCS — the requirement that once a user is removed or refreshes, all group secrets become independent of any secret material that user previously generated or leaked) forbids reusing key material the passive users received only from the users now updating, each such round must re-communicate fresh secrets to all k passive users, at communication cost Ω(k) per round, even amortized over the whole sequence.

### Measured results
None in the empirical sense — every reported figure is an asymptotic complexity bound derived by cryptographic proof and construction, not a measured runtime, message count, or deployment statistic.

| Result | Bound | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| CKE ciphertext size, black-box from PKE | Ω(n) | n = number of receivers; ciphertext produced by the one designated sender, non-adaptive passive adversary |
| CGKA worst-case communication per operation, black-box from PKE | Ω(n) | n = group size; holds for a specific "bad sequence" of adds followed by state-refresh rounds among the remaining active users; the paper states its bound already holds for fully synchronous, non-concurrent CGKA executions, distinguishing it from the concurrency-specific bound of Bienstock, Dodis, Rösler (TCC 2020) |
| Communication cost, single administrator (equivalent to classical multicast encryption) | O(log n), under the double-join-prevention property alone | the sole administrator is never removed and executes every operation, so a tree structure never needs to degrade |
| Communication cost, two administrators that can replace one another | jumps to Ω(n) | derived from the paper's own Ω(n) bound applied to a two-administrator scenario, under the double-join-prevention property alone (without the second, randomness-leakage-resilience property) |
| Communication cost, MLS "propose-and-commit" framework (draft-ietf-mls-protocol-14) | Ω(n) per commit, in the same bad-sequence pattern | shown by applying the paper's general result to a scenario where administrators repeatedly replace each other after an add of k users |

### Parameters
The paper's constructions and proofs are parameterized by the number of group members (n), the number of users added in one collective event (k), and the number of active users conducting rounds of updates (α) — none of these are tuned constants; they are variables the asymptotic bounds are stated in terms of. No concrete numeric parameter (key size, round count, timing) is given, consistent with this being a complexity-theoretic result.

### Stated limitations
The paper states its lower bound applies specifically to CGKA protocols making black-box use of PKE, and states explicitly that circumventing the bound with a strong primitive such as indistinguishability obfuscation (as used in prior multi-party non-interactive key exchange work) may be possible, though the authors describe finding a practical (non-black-box) construction that avoids the bound as "a challenging problem." It states its impossibility result targets the standard, strong form of post-compromise security in the literature, which bundles two properties — double-join prevention and resilience to randomness leakage — and that both properties individually already force the Ω(n) bound; it states, as an explicit open problem for future work, what efficiency guarantees are achievable if the randomness-leakage-resilience property is dropped and only double-join prevention is required. It states weakening PCS to assume randomness is always securely deleted after use (never leaked) permits trivial O(log n) protocols, such as Tainted TreeKEM without its tainting mechanism, but states most real-world implementations should not accept that level of trust. It states two further open problems: finding practical (non-PKE-black-box) building blocks that circumvent the bound, and identifying and forbidding all problematic operation sequences in a live protocol.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Any CGKA construction that wants to escape this paper's Ω(n) worst-case bound must not treat its underlying public-key encryption as a sealed black box — it must exploit PKE's internal algebraic structure directly, or substitute a non-black-box primitive, because the impossibility result covers every protocol that uses PKE only through its stated encrypt/decrypt interface. A system deploying a black-box-PKE-based CGKA (which the paper states covers all currently known practical protocols, including every TreeKEM variant and pairwise-Signal-based CGKA) must accept that some legitimate, non-adversarial sequence of adds followed by state refreshes forces Ω(n) communication in that round, and cannot assume amortization over a longer session avoids this cost, since the bound holds even amortized over the whole sequence. A deployment that wants to avoid the two-administrator degradation case must either accept only ever having one administrator (reducing to classical multicast encryption, achievable at O(log n)) or accept the Ω(n) cost once a second administrator with replacement rights is introduced. The bound's derivation assumes a non-adaptive, passive adversary and a common-reference-string model for CKE, which the paper states only strengthens (makes more general) the resulting impossibility, so a system facing a weaker or differently modeled adversary is not thereby exempted from the bound.

### Contradicts
None found against another corpus entry's measurement — no measured results exist to disagree with. This paper directly bounds the CGKA construction described by BHARGAVAN-HAL-18 (TreeKEM) and standardized in BARNES-RFC-23: it states TreeKEM protocols achieve O(log n) only in "fair-weather" conditions and degrade to Ω(n) worst-case, even amortized, once trees are forced to degrade by PCS requirements — consistent with, not contradicting, BHARGAVAN-HAL-18's own O(log n) fair-weather claim, since that paper never claims a worst-case bound. It states its own lower bound is proved by a method independent of, and not a strengthening or weakening of, the concurrency-specific lower bound in Bienstock, Dodis, Rösler (TCC 2020) — the two results hold under different conditions (this paper's bound needs no concurrency at all) and neither implies the other. BARTUSEK-EPRINT-26 (2026) states it narrows, without refuting, this paper's black-box impossibility result, by using a non-black-box lattice-structured primitive rather than PKE treated as a sealed component.

### References worth retrieving
- Bienstock, Dodis, Rösler, "On the Price of Concurrency in Group Ratcheting Protocols," TCC 2020, pp. 198-228 — foundational (already a corpus target: BIENSTOCK-TCC-20; the concurrency-specific lower bound this paper states is independent of its own)
- Alwen, Auerbach, Cueto Noval, Klein, Pascual-Perez, Pietrzak, Walter, "CoCoA: Concurrent Continuous Group Key Agreement," EUROCRYPT 2022 — competing (circumvents the TCC-2020 concurrency lower bound by accepting slower PCS recovery, per this paper's footnote 5)
- Alwen, Coretti, Dodis, Tselekounis, "Security Analysis and Improvements for the IETF MLS Standard for Group Messaging," CRYPTO 2020 — foundational (first formalizes CGKA, per this paper's citation [3])
- Alwen, Capretto, Cueto, Kamath, Klein, Markov, Pascual-Perez, Pietrzak, Walter, Yeo, "Keep the Dirt: Tainted TreeKEM, Adaptively and Actively Secure Continuous Group Key Agreement," IEEE S&P 2021 — competing (Tainted TreeKEM, the specific protocol this paper cites for its double-join-prevention-only trivial construction and its blanking/tainting technique)
- Bienstock, Dodis, Tang, "Multicast Key Agreement, Revisited," CT-RSA 2022 — foundational (shows the single-administrator case of CGKA reduces to classical multicast encryption, cited as reference [12] and directly used in this paper's "two administrators" argument)

- Cohn-Gordon, Cremers, Garratt, Millican, Milner, "On Ends-to-Ends Encryption: Asynchronous Group Messaging with Strong Security Guarantees," ACM CCS 2018 — foundational (the Asynchronous Ratchet Tree protocol this paper cites among TreeKEM-family constructions)
- Barnes, Beurdouche, Robert, Millican, Omara, Cohn-Gordon, "The Messaging Layer Security (MLS) Protocol," Internet-Draft draft-ietf-mls-protocol-14, 2022 — foundational (the MLS propose-and-commit framework this paper's lower bound is shown to apply to; the finalized version is already a corpus target, BARNES-RFC-23)

- "CKE with communication cost o(n) by the special user cannot be realized in a black-box manner from public-key encryption"

## [BIRYUKOV-EUROSP-16] Argon2: New Generation of Memory-Hard Functions for Password Hashing and Other Applications
**Citation:** Alex Biryukov, Daniel Dinu, Dmitry Khovratovich. "Argon2: New Generation of Memory-Hard Functions for Password Hashing and Other Applications." IEEE European Symposium on Security and Privacy (EuroS&P), 2016. DOI 10.1109/EuroSP.2016.31.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.cryptolux.org/images/0/0d/Argon2.pdf — note this URL serves the designers' own Argon2 specification document, "Argon2: the memory-hard function for password hashing and other applications," Version 1.3 (PHC release), dated March 24, 2017, authored by the same three designers. It is the maintained technical specification and security-analysis document for the algorithm the EuroS&P 2016 conference paper introduced, and is the exact candidate URL given for this citation key in the target registry; all figures below come from this document's own text, tables, and change log rather than from any secondary summary.
**Source URL:** https://www.cryptolux.org/images/0/0d/Argon2.pdf
**Domain:** I

### What it does
Argon2 is a memory-hard function (MHF): a key-stretching function designed so that computing it requires a large amount of memory, making brute-force password guessing on custom hardware (FPGAs, GPUs, ASICs) no cheaper per guess than on the memory-limited hardware a legitimate server uses. Argon2 fills a caller-specified amount of memory M with pseudo-random blocks, then performs T passes over that memory, where each new block is computed by a compression function G from a previous block and one or more reference blocks selected by an indexing function; the caller also sets a parallelism degree, splitting memory into that many lanes so multiple threads fill blocks concurrently, with cross-lane references allowed after the first column of blocks. Argon2 has two data-flow variants: Argon2d selects each block's reference index using the contents of previously computed data, so the access pattern depends on the secret input, giving strong resistance to a class of time-memory tradeoff attacks but exposing a data-dependent memory-access pattern (a timing side channel) that an adversary co-located on the same machine can observe; Argon2i selects reference indices independently of the data, using the compression function itself as a pseudo-random number generator in counter mode, so the memory-access pattern is public and reveals nothing about the input, at the cost of needing more passes to reach comparable tradeoff resistance. The compression function G is built by applying a permutation P (a modification of the Blake2b round function called BlaMka, which adds 32-bit multiplications to the modular additions to increase the latency of an ASIC's arithmetic circuit while preserving CPU-friendly pipelining) across pairs of 128-bit register groups, then shuffling and reapplying it, so an 8-register permutation P produces a compression function over a p^2-register block with two rounds. To resist the ranking-based time-space tradeoff attack (in which an adversary recomputes cheaply reconstructible blocks instead of storing them), the indexing function's reference-distance exponent (a tunable parameter called gamma in the reference-block-selection formula) is chosen to bound how large a memory reduction is achievable without a matching increase in time-area product, the metric used throughout this document to compare adversary cost against honest cost.

### Measured results
| Metric | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Memory-fill throughput | Both Argon2d and Argon2i fill 1 GB of RAM in a fraction of a second | Stated as a general performance claim in the introduction and Section 4.1, not tied to a single specific hardware configuration beyond the benchmark table below |
| Cycles per byte / bandwidth, Argon2d (1 pass) | 1.3 cpb / 2.5 GB/s at 1 thread; 0.9 cpb / 3.8 GB/s at 2 threads; 0.6 cpb / 5.4 GB/s at 4 threads; 0.6 cpb / 5.4 GB/s at 8 threads | Measured on an Intel Core i7-4500U (Haswell, 1.8 GHz, 4 physical cores), 1 GB memory filled, gcc 4.8.2 with `-m64 -mavx -std=c++11 -pthread -O3`, cycle counts read via the RDTSCP instruction |
| Cycles per byte / bandwidth, Argon2i (3 passes) | 4.7 cpb / 2.6 GB/s at 1 thread; 2.8 cpb / 4.5 GB/s at 2 threads; 2.0 cpb / 5.4 GB/s at 4 threads; 1.9 cpb / 5.8 GB/s at 8 threads | Same hardware and build configuration as above |
| Compression-function throughput (non-cryptographic prototype) | About 0.7 cycles per byte per core | Experimental prototype compression function performing simple XOR mixing, block sizes of 1024 bits or larger, used to justify the chosen block-size design rather than as a claim about the shipped Argon2 compression function |
| Ranking tradeoff attack, 1-pass Argon2d | Adversary can reduce memory by a factor of 3 while keeping the time-area product unchanged (memory reduction 1/4 gives computational penalty C(alpha)=20.2, depth penalty D(alpha)=5.5) | Ranking-method tradeoff algorithm applied to Argon2's own indexing function; full penalty table given for memory fractions 1/2 through 1/7 |
| Ranking tradeoff attack, 3-pass Argon2i | Memory reduction by a factor of 3 incurs a computational penalty of about 2^14 | Same ranking algorithm applied to the 3-pass Argon2i indexing function; the paper argues 2^14 Blake2b cores would occupy more chip area than 1 GB of RAM, bounding the adversary's further reduction |
| Memory-optimization ("no-use gap") attack on Argon2i v1.2.1 | Time-area product advantage about 3.5x for 1-pass Argon2i, about 4x for multi-pass (average-memory basis); about 5x and 2.7x respectively if peak memory is used in the calculation | Applies specifically to version 1.2.1's overwrite-based memory reuse; measured average memory-use fraction for 1-pass Argon2i, L1 ~= 0.15 (about 1/7 of memory used on average, versus 1/2 in a straightforward implementation) |
| Overhead of the v1.3 XOR-based fix | Performance difference of 5%-15% for memory requirements of 8 MB and higher, depending on operating system and hardware; concretely 1.61 cycles/byte (v1.2.1) versus 1.7 cycles/byte (v1.3) for 3-pass Argon2d | Both measured at 2 GB RAM, 4 threads, 1.8 GHz CPU running Ubuntu |
| Alwen-Blocki tradeoff attack applicability | Time-area advantage E <= M^(1/4)/36 for t>=3 passes; smaller than 1 (no adversary benefit) for M up to 2^20 (1 GB), and smaller than 2 for M up to 2^24 (16 GB) | Derived analytically from the Alwen-Blocki attack's own published time-area formula (2 T^(7/4) (5+t+ln T)/8), applied to Argon2's parameters; the document concludes this approach is not better than its own ranking attack at these memory sizes |
| Summary of best known tradeoff-attack factors (v1.3) | 1- and 2-pass Argon2i: time-area product reduced by 5x (low-storage attack); t>2-pass Argon2i: reduced by 3x (ranking attack); t-pass Argon2d: reduced by 1.33x (ranking attack) | Stated as the document's own summary across all attacks analyzed in its Security Analysis section |
| Indexing-function exponent gamma sweep | Minimum time-area product AT_gamma ranges from 0.78 (gamma=1) down to 0.59 (gamma=5); maximum memory-reduction threshold alpha_gamma ranges 3.2-4.38; chi-squared uniformity metric drops from 0.89 (gamma=1) to 0.09 (gamma=5) | Ranking method with sliding window applied for each gamma from 1 to 5 in steps of 0.1, evaluated over 0.01<alpha<1, with reference-distribution uniformity computed over 10 bins; gamma=2 selected as the integer value minimizing the adversary's time-area gain while keeping reasonably uniform block reference frequency |
| Application-level timing recommendations | Cryptocurrency mining: 0.1 s on a 2 GHz CPU, 1 core, using Argon2d with 2 lanes and 250 MB RAM. Backend server authentication: 0.5 s on 2 GHz/4 cores, Argon2d with 8 lanes and 4 GB RAM. Hard-drive-encryption key derivation: 3 s on 2 GHz/2 cores, Argon2i with 4 lanes and 6 GB RAM. Frontend server authentication: 0.5 s on 2 GHz/2 cores, Argon2i with 4 lanes and 1 GB RAM | Author-recommended settings for named use cases, not independently measured deployment data |

### Parameters
- Memory parameter M: user-controlled, no value stated to be insecure; recommended settings above range from 250 MB to 6 GB depending on application.
- Number of passes T: user-controlled, running time scales linearly with it; Argon2i is specifically recommended with 3 passes "to get rid entirely of the password in the memory" against memory-leak attacks.
- Degree of parallelism (lanes) d: user-controlled up to 2^24 threads, though the document states 8 threads already exhaust the bandwidth and computing power of its Haswell test machine; slice count l fixed at 4 in the reference design (values of l=8 or l=16 are noted as possible alternatives), chosen because the time-area penalty multiplier (1 - (p-1)/(p*l)) * (1 + (p-1)/l) stays between 1.05 and 3 for 2<=p,l<=10.
- Indexing-function reference-distance exponent gamma: set to 2 in the shipped design, selected from a swept range of 1 to 5 (step 0.1, restricted to integers for the final choice) to balance time-area-product resistance against uniformity of block-reference frequency.
- Salt length: 128 bits recommended as sufficient for all applications, reducible to 64 bits under space constraints.
- Tag (output) length: 128 bits recommended as sufficient for most applications including key derivation; longer tags recommended if longer keys are needed.
- Compression function: BlaMka, a modification of the Blake2b round function adding 32-bit (permutation P uses 64-bit in the appendix specification) multiplications to the modular additions; block size 1024 bytes (8192 bits) in the reference design.

### Stated limitations
The document states Argon2d does not overwrite memory and is therefore vulnerable to garbage-collector and similar memory-disclosure attacks, and states it is not recommended for settings where such threats are possible; Argon2i with 3 passes overwrites memory twice specifically to close this exposure, so that even if the entire working memory is disclosed after hashing completes, recovering the password requires the adversary to recompute two full passes. The authors state the compression function G is not claimed to be collision-resistant or preimage-resistant, relying instead on the attacker's lack of control over its inputs to make collisions unlikely; the proof of block distinctness (Theorem 1) is stated to depend on two explicit assumptions about the permutation P (that P(Z) XOR Z is collision-resistant and 4-generalized-birthday-resistant) that are not independently proved in this document. The document explicitly states it will be updated if better attacks are found against the Alwen-Blocki tradeoff strategy, describing that line of attack as "a subject of active research" rather than closed, and its conclusion states that further tradeoff-attack development specific to Argon2 remains future work and that Argon2's resistance to GPU cracking with low memory requirements "remains to be seen." The multi-lane parallelism construction is stated to admit a computable time-area penalty reduction of up to a factor of 3 (an adversary computing the last memory column sequentially with reduced memory), which the design's choice of l=4 is stated to be a deliberate trade against synchronization overhead rather than a claim of immunity to that reduction.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A system deploying Argon2 must choose between Argon2d and Argon2i (or a hybrid) based on whether the execution environment can leak timing information to an adversary: the document's own selection procedure directs the caller to pick Argon2i whenever side-channel observation is a viable threat, and either variant otherwise, meaning the calling system must characterize its own co-tenancy and physical-access threat model before parameter selection is possible. The recommended-parameters procedure requires the caller to supply, from outside this specification, the maximum thread count available per call, the maximum memory each call may use, and the maximum wall-clock time (in seconds) a call may take, then to search over the pass count T for the largest value fitting that time budget; Argon2 supplies no default for any of these three inputs; they must come from the deployment's own hardware and latency requirements. Argon2's proof of no block collisions (Theorem 1) depends on the mode-of-operation rule that a segment's first block never refers to the last block of any segment in the previous slice, so an implementation that alters the indexing rule without preserving that constraint invalidates the stated collision-freedom guarantee. The document states the memory-wiping option should be enabled at the call site "if side-channel attacks is a viable threat," meaning defense against the memory-disclosure attacks described above requires the caller to explicitly opt into a library-level feature rather than receiving it as a mode default.

### Contradicts
This document, describing itself as source [BDK16] in ALWEN-EUROSP-17, is the origin of the claim ALWEN-EUROSP-17 (Alwen, Blocki, EuroS&P 2017) directly disputes: this specification's own text states that its analytically derived time-area advantage for the Alwen-Blocki tradeoff attack "is not better than the ranking attack" for memory up to 16 GB, concluding that approach poses no practical threat at the memory sizes this document analyzes. ALWEN-EUROSP-17's simulated results show a concrete attack that reduces cost by a factor of 2 against Argon2i-B at 1 GB of memory and 6 passes — within the parameter space this document treats as safe — using heuristics (an improved depth-reducing-set construction and a bounded-parallelism analysis) this document's own analytic argument does not consider. See ALWEN-EUROSP-17's entry in this evidence file for the full measured comparison; the two documents disagree about the practical severity of the same underlying attack family at the same memory scale.

### References worth retrieving
- **Attack**: J. Alwen, J. Blocki. "Efficiently computing data-independent memory-hard functions." IACR Cryptology ePrint Archive. [1] (Already retrieved and extracted in this corpus as ALWEN-EUROSP-17; this document's Section 5.6 analytically engages this attack and concludes it is not superior to the ranking attack at practical memory sizes, a conclusion ALWEN-EUROSP-17's simulations dispute.)
- **Foundational**: C. Percival. "Stronger key derivation via sequential memory-hard functions." 2009. [15] (scrypt, the prior memory-hard password-hashing scheme this document positions Argon2 against, noting scrypt admits a trivial time-memory tradeoff.)

## [BIRYUKOV-FC-15] Proof-of-Work as Anonymous Micropayment: Rewarding a Tor Relay
**Citation:** Alex Biryukov, Ivan Pustogarov. "Proof-of-Work as Anonymous Micropayment: Rewarding a Tor Relay." Financial Cryptography and Data Security, 2015 (this file is the authors' extended version of the FC'15 paper). DOI: 10.1007/978-3-662-47854-7_27.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://eprint.iacr.org/2014/1011.pdf
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2014/1011.pdf
**Domain:** I

### What it does
The scheme rewards a Tor relay operator for providing improved service, using client-submitted proof-of-work as the unit exchanged instead of a measured-bandwidth currency or direct monetary payment. A relay operator selects a crypto-currency mining pool and a compatible proof-of-work algorithm, generates a ticket-signing key pair separate from its Tor identity keys, and publishes this choice in its relay descriptor. A client who wants improved service opens a circuit to that relay and sends a SUBSCRIBE message; the relay replies with a mining job (algorithm, per-share difficulty, job data). The client mines a share at that difficulty, generates a random value x and its hash H(x), and sends the share plus H(x) to the relay. The relay checks the share and forwards it to the mining pool, which credits the relay with a fraction of pool earnings once enough shares accumulate to solve a block at the pool's full difficulty. The relay then issues the client a partially blind signature over H(x), with the current calendar date as an included but non-blinded attribute; the tuple (signature, date, x, H(x)) is a priority ticket. The client later presents the ticket to the same relay (over the same anonymous circuit) to receive prioritized traffic scheduling for a fixed duration; the relay stores spent-ticket state only long enough for tickets to expire (the paper suggests 48 hours) to bound that state. Priority scheduling is implemented with a Hierarchical Token Bucket: bandwidth is split into a paid class and a free class in a tree, each class has a guaranteed rate and a ceiling rate it may temporarily borrow up to from unused sibling-class capacity, and higher-priority classes borrow first — a class with tickets can use its full ceiling when no other ticket-holding client contends, while the free class always retains its guaranteed floor rate. Because the client never transmits fiat or crypto-currency value directly to the relay, the relay's bandwidth-measurement mechanism is not part of the reward path — the paper's design goal states the scheme deliberately avoids any dependency on a secure bandwidth-measurement mechanism.

### Measured results
The paper does not run a network deployment or simulation; its numeric results are an analytical profitability calculation from measured mining-hardware hash rates and observed crypto-currency market prices, not a systems evaluation.

| Result | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| CPU hash rates measured on one machine | Blake-256 9.6 Mh/s, Groestl 1 Mh/s, HEFTY1 128 Kh/s, JHA 308 Kh/s, Keccak 5.2 Mh/s, Quark 300 Kh/s, Scrypt 40 Kh/s, Scrypt-N 20 Kh/s, Scrypt-Jane 360 h/s, SHA-256d 9.6 Mh/s, X11 360 Kh/s, X13 104 Kh/s | Intel Core i7-2760QM, 4 cores at 2.40 GHz, September 1, 2014 market snapshot averaged over multiple observations |
| Per-currency mining revenue at measured hash rate | Ranges from 0.008 cents/day (Bitcoin via SHA-256d) to 3.8 cents/day (CNotes via Quark, Smartcoin via X11) | Same hardware and date; several currencies (Blakecoin, Heavycoin, Yacoin, Marucoin) had no reported revenue (n/a) at that snapshot |
| Estimated electricity cost | 11 cents/day, with observed short spikes to 11 cents/day peak | Assumed 45 W maximum CPU power draw |
| Exit-relay income, single-relay-paid case | Top relay (consensus bandwidth 200,000 KB/s) about 500 USD/month; middle-tier relay (10,000 KB/s) about 25 USD/month | Assumes each client mines an equivalent of 3.8 cents per 24 hours, 1/24 of which accrues to the relay per 1-hour client session; only the Exit relay in the circuit is paid |
| Exit-relay income, higher mining-rate case | Top relay up to 1,600 USD/month | Same setup, assumed 11 cents per client per day |
| Exit-relay income, evenly-split-across-3-relays case | Top relay up to 160 USD/month (at 3.8 cents/day/client); relay becomes profitable above the operator's own hosting cost at 36 cents/day/client | Appendix A variant: client mines for all three relays on its circuit rather than the Exit relay alone |
| Hosting cost model | 25 EUR/month for consensus weight below 15,000; 40 EUR/month for weight 15,000-50,000; 70 EUR/month above 50,000; 2 EUR per additional TB beyond an included 10 TB | Rental prices from a named hosting-market listing (Hetzner server auction, 2014), used as the cost baseline against which income is compared |
| Population assumptions underlying all income figures | Of about 2,000,000 daily Tor clients, only 500,000 assumed to be real (non-botnet) users and thus eligible to mine; each mining session assumed to last 1 hour at 100% CPU | The authors explicitly label these "very rough estimates" because the true hardware, non-botnet fraction, and mining-willing fraction of Tor's client population cannot be observed |

### Parameters
Ticket validity/expiry: suggested 48 hours, to bound the size of the relay's spent-ticket record. Ticket date granularity: full calendar day, so that all tickets issued on the same day by a relay are mutually indistinguishable. Priority duration per ticket: a fixed interval of Δt seconds of prioritized cell transmission (value left unspecified). Assumed real fraction of Tor's daily client population: 500,000 of 2,000,000 (the remainder attributed to botnets, citing a 2014 report of a Tor client-count spike from the Mevade botnet). Assumed mining session length: 1 hour/day at up to 100% CPU, with the paper noting in its appendix that 25% CPU would be more realistic in practice.

### Stated limitations
The authors state their own income projections are "very rough estimates," because it is not possible to learn Tor users' actual hardware, the real (non-botnet) fraction of the client population, the number of users willing to mine, or the number of new users a Bittorrent-over-Tor use case might bring. The paper states a curious relay can learn a client's hash rate from repeated interactions and could use it to recognize returning clients across sessions, and separately that a relay learns that the same client returned the same day if that client pre-mines tickets for later use; the paper's suggested mitigation, unverified experimentally, is that a client randomizes its hash rate. The paper states a powerful miner could attempt to deny paid traffic to other clients on a relay by consuming all its priority-serving capacity, but classifies this as economically irrational because the miner earns more by contributing the same work to the mining pool directly. The scheme is stated as requiring, but not providing, an anonymous crypto-currency (Zerocoin cited) if genuine payment anonymity from mining-pool records rather than only from ticket-signature blinding were later desired; the paper describes this only as a possible future extension. The paper states that CPU mining of Bitcoin or established Altcoins is not profitable on its own in 2014 because the difference between coin value and electricity cost is negative for consumer hardware, which is the premise the whole reward scheme is built to route around by aggregating many clients' otherwise-unprofitable CPU cycles into a pool.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Requires the relay to hold or obtain a crypto-currency mining-pool account and requires that pool to accept proof-of-work shares of the difficulty the relay assigns to clients; the relay's earned coins never touch the client. Requires a partially blind signature scheme (the paper specifies a WI-Schnorr-based partially blind signature construction) under which the timestamp attribute is visible to the signer but the message (H(x)) is not, so the relay can bind an expiry date to a ticket without learning which client holds it. Requires the relay to retain a per-client-visible record of spent ticket hashes only for the ticket-validity window, to detect double-spending; this requires clients and relay to agree on ticket expiry and requires the relay's local clock to be trusted for the date attribute. Requires the underlying Tor circuit to already provide anonymous transport between client and relay for every protocol message (SUBSCRIBE, JOB, share submission, ticket issuance, ticket redemption) since the scheme supplies none of its own; it inherits whatever traffic-analysis exposure the anonymity layer has. Requires a traffic scheduler at the relay implementing at least two priority classes with borrowable ceiling rates (the paper specifies Hierarchical Token Bucket) so that a ticket confers a real, differentiated increase in transmission priority rather than only an accounting entry. Explicitly does not require any bandwidth-measurement or bandwidth-audit subsystem elsewhere in the system, and does not require a central bank or distributed banking quorum — a design goal the paper states to distinguish itself from BRAIDS, LIRA, and TEARS.

### Contradicts
None found. This paper is a design and analytical-cost paper with no independent measurement to reconcile against another source in this batch; its critique of TorPath (Sybil vulnerability despite the TorPath mechanism, and that circuit-assignment servers ignore relay bandwidth, weakening anonymity) is the authors' own analysis of a design cited but not itself in this batch. Its critique of TEARS-style banking, that TEARS still relies on a new distributed bank entity and on an external secure bandwidth-measurement mechanism, is the authors' characterization; JANSEN-HOTPETS-14 (TEARS itself, already extracted in this batch) confirms both properties in its own text, so this is not a contradiction but an independent, consistent reading of the same source.

### References worth retrieving
- Ghosh, Richardson, Ford, Jansen, "A TorPath to TorCoin: Proof-of-Bandwidth Altcoins for Compensating Relays," HotPETs 2014 — competing: proof-of-bandwidth alternative; this paper's own text identifies a stated Sybil vulnerability in TorPath's coin-minting and a centralization cost from its "assignment servers."
- Jansen, Hopper, Kim, "Recruiting new Tor relays with BRAIDS," CCS 2010 — foundational/competing: prior ticket-based scheme this paper explicitly adapts ideas from (partially blind ticket issuance) while removing its central-bank dependency.
- Jansen, Johnson, Syverson, "LIRA: Lightweight Incentivized Routing for Anonymity," NDSS 2013 — competing: prior lottery-based scheme sharing this paper's reliance-avoidance goals; cited as still needing external secure bandwidth measurement, unlike this paper.
- Jansen, Miller, Syverson, Ford, "From Onions to Shallots: Rewarding Tor Relays with TEARS," HotPETs 2014 — competing: distributed-bank e-cash alternative, the direct trust-model contrast already in this batch (JANSEN-HOTPETS-14).
- Miers, Garman, Green, Rubin, "Zerocoin: Anonymous distributed e-cash from bitcoin," IEEE S&P 2013 — foundational: the anonymous-currency extension this paper proposes integrating if genuinely anonymous payment is later wanted.
- Ron, Shamir, "Quantitative analysis of the full bitcoin transaction graph," FC 2013 — attack: cited as the class of Bitcoin-anonymity-defeating analysis this scheme's ticket construction is designed to remain inapplicable against, since shares carry only a relay's or pool's Bitcoin address, never the client's.
- Ngan, Dingledine, Wallach, "Building Incentives into Tor," FC 2010 — foundational: earlier Tor incentive-scheme survey/proposal, cited among the four incentive lines the paper's related-work section positions itself against.

"it should not rely on secure bandwidth measurement mechanisms"
"a curious relay can however learn the hash rate of a client"
"it is economically more reasonable for such miner to just earn shares"
"these are of course very rough estimates"

## [BIRYUKOV-SP-13] Trawling for Tor Hidden Services: Detection, Measurement, Deanonymization

**Citation:** Alex Biryukov, Ivan Pustogarov, Ralf-Philipp Weinmann. "Trawling for Tor Hidden Services: Detection, Measurement, Deanonymization." IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy, 2013. DOI 10.1109/SP.2013.15.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.cryptolux.org/images/2/25/Tor-HS-deanonymization.pdf
**Source URL:** https://www.cryptolux.org/images/2/25/Tor-HS-deanonymization.pdf
**Domain:** J

### What it does
The paper demonstrates three attacks against Tor hidden services (a Tor hidden service publishes a rendezvous descriptor to a small set of relays instead of a public IP address, so a client reaches it only through the Tor network). First, an attacker computes future rendezvous-descriptor identifiers and precomputes relay key pairs whose fingerprints land immediately after those identifiers on the fingerprint ring Tor uses to assign descriptor storage, then runs relays with those keys so the attacker's own relays become the hidden service's descriptor-storage points (hidden service directories, HSDirs). Injecting the relays into every second gap of the ring lets the attacker capture every descriptor published network-wide. Second, controlling a hidden service's rendezvous descriptor storage or its guard node lets the attacker count descriptor fetch requests, which the paper uses as a proxy for the number of distinct clients that used the hidden service in the counted period. Third, an attacker who additionally controls a Tor relay acting as a hidden service's entry guard (the fixed first hop of every circuit the hidden service builds) forces the hidden service to open a rendezvous circuit to an attacker-controlled rendezvous point; the rendezvous point sends a distinctive count of relay cells (50 padding cells) back down the circuit, and the guard node recognizes the resulting cell-count and timing signature on any circuit passing through it, which identifies the immediately preceding relay as the hidden service's own entry point and, when the guard is one hop from the hidden service's own machine, reveals its IP address directly.

### Measured results
| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| 59,130 descriptor publication requests, 58,389 descriptors fetched, 24,703 with unique public keys, ~1.5% encrypted | 50 Amazon EC2 instances running 1,200 Tor relay processes (24 relays per instance) for 25 hours, November 2012 |
| ~3% of hidden descriptors estimated missed | Verified against a 120-hidden-service sample from public sources; 4 relays from the sample were absent from the harvested set |
| 39,824 unique onion addresses collected, cost reduced to USD 57 | Second harvesting run, 58 EC2 micro instances, relays set to 0-1 Bytes/sec reported bandwidth to avoid attracting client traffic unrelated to the attack |
| Estimated botnet size 12,000-30,000 infected machines | Derived from descriptor-fetch counts of 1,408-4,977 requests/day for one hidden service (command-and-control channel), 13-29 July, capped at one fetch per 24 hours per machine because Tor caches descriptors for 24 hours |
| Silk Road: 15,185-19,284 descriptor requests/day; DuckDuckGo: 502-549 requests/day | Four consecutive days, 9-12 November 2012, measured by controlling one of each service's three responsible HSDir relays |
| Average gap between consecutive HSDir fingerprints on the ring: 10^44.8, minimum 10^42.16 | One randomly selected Tor consensus document, November 2012; finding a key fingerprint that falls in such a gap took a few minutes on a multi-core computer |
| Guard-identification attack: 8, 6, 5 correct identifications from ~36,000 rendezvous cells over 1h20m; second run: 5, 2, 1 correct identifications from ~16,000 rendezvous cells over 40 minutes | Two hidden services operated by the authors, attacker running one guard-adjacent (middle) relay and one rendezvous point |
| Cell-count traffic signature (3 cells up / 53 cells down) observed on 0 of 748,846 circuits examined | Circuits passing through one guard node the authors operated, used to establish the signature's false-positive rate |
| 90% probability of deanonymizing a long-running hidden service within 8 months, for EUR 8,280 (~USD 11,000) | Renting 23 relays of the EUR 45/month "EcoServer Large X5" class, each independently having ~0.6% average monthly probability of being chosen as one of a hidden service's three guards; combined chance per hidden service of 13.8% per guard-rotation attempt |

### Parameters
- Hidden service directory (HSDir) set size: 3 relays per descriptor replica, 2 replicas published, so 6 HSDirs total per hidden service.
- HSDir flag acquisition delay: 25 hours of consensus presence required before a relay is trusted as an HSDir.
- Consensus validity window: published hourly, fresh for 1 hour, valid for 3 hours total; clients fetch the next consensus in the interval (fresh-until + 45 min, valid-until − 10 min).
- Guard set size: 3 guards chosen initially; replaced only when fewer than 2 remain reachable; each guard's tenure is a random duration between 30 and 60 days.
- Maximum Tor relays per IP address admitted to the consensus: 2 (enforced by directory authorities; used in the attack by running additional "shadow" relays on the same IP that do not appear in the consensus until an active relay drops out).
- Attacker resource used for full-network descriptor harvesting: R = N / (12 × 2) IP addresses, where N is the number of HSDirs in the network (derived from the need to cover every second gap on the fingerprint ring, in two ring passes per day, with 2 relays per IP).

### Stated limitations
The paper's descriptor-count-based population estimates are approximate: multiple power cycles of one machine in a day overcount that machine, and the 24-hour descriptor cache means a machine that stays on for multiple days is undercounted. The authors state the guard-identification method proposed for encrypted introduction points cannot distinguish between hidden services once the full descriptor set for comparison is unavailable to the attacker. The authors state their proposed fixes are "nothing more than stop-gap measures" and that hidden services need a more complete redesign. The paper does not measure detection resistance of the attacker's own relays against countermeasures the Tor directory authorities might apply beyond the flag-assignment change already made in response to this work.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Any rendezvous/directory design that assigns responsibility for storing a lookup record deterministically from a public identifier (a fingerprint ring keyed by a hash of the identifier, here) gives an adversary who can compute future identifiers the ability to precompute keys that land adjacent to that identifier and, by running relays with those keys, capture the storage role before the legitimate publisher does. Any capacity- or reputation-gated onboarding delay (the 25-hour HSDir-flag wait, here) bounds only the attacker's setup latency, not the number of identities the attacker can eventually operate, when the identity-creation cost itself is close to free (running a Tor relay process). A guard-node or fixed-entry-hop mechanism that keeps the same relay as a client's or service's first hop for weeks concentrates all of that period's deanonymization risk onto whichever party operates that one relay; the risk is proportional to the probability of an adversary being selected in the guard-selection weighting, which this paper measures directly for one bandwidth class.

### Contradicts
None found. No other paper in this batch measures Tor hidden-service directory assignment or guard-selection probability directly; JOHNSON-CCS-13 and SUN-USENIXSEC-15 measure Tor circuit compromise from different adversary positions (autonomous-system-level and relay-operator-level traffic correlation, and BGP-level routing manipulation) and do not overlap with this paper's descriptor-harvesting or guard-identification figures.

### References worth retrieving
- foundational: Dingledine, Mathewson, Syverson. "Tor: The second-generation onion router." USENIX Security Symposium, 2004.
- foundational: Øverlier, Syverson. "Locating hidden servers." IEEE S&P, 2006.
- competing/related: Elahi, Bauer, AlSabah, Dingledine, Goldberg. "Changing of the Guards: A framework for understanding and improving entry guard selection in Tor." WPES 2012. (already a target in this batch: ELAHI-WPES-12)
- attack: Bauer, McCoy, Grunwald, Kohno, Sicker. "Low-resource routing attacks against Tor." WPES 2007.
- attack: Murdoch. "Hot or not: Revealing hidden services by their clock skew." ACM CCS 2006.
- attack: Zander, Murdoch. "An improved clock-skew measurement technique for revealing hidden services." USENIX Security Symposium 2008.
- foundational: Douceur. "The Sybil attack." IPTPS 2002.

- "we could have lost about 3% of hidden descriptors"
- "None of the circuit exhibited the trafﬁc pattern of 3 cells up the circuit and 53 cells down the circuit"
- "the probability to deanonymize a long-running hidden service... is more than 90%, for a cost of... USD 11,000"
- "the above suggestions are nothing more than stop-gap measures"

## [BLAKE-HOTOS-03] High Availability, Scalable Storage, Dynamic Peer Networks: Pick Two

**Citation:** Charles Blake, Rodrigo Rodrigues. "High Availability, Scalable Storage, Dynamic Peer Networks: Pick Two." Workshop on Hot Topics in Operating Systems (HotOS IX), 2003.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.usenix.org/legacy/events/hotos03/tech/blake.html
**Source URL:** https://www.usenix.org/legacy/events/hotos03/tech/blake.html
**Domain:** C

### What it does

The paper derives a lower bound on the per-node bandwidth a cooperative storage system needs to spend maintaining redundancy against membership turnover, so a designer can check whether a target combination of data scale, redundancy level, and host turnover rate is reachable with a given per-host bandwidth budget before building the system. The bound follows from a resource-usage model, not from an implementation.

The base model holds `N` identical hosts cooperatively storing `D` bytes of unique data with redundancy expansion factor `k` (replication factor or coding expansion), for `S = kD` bytes of total contributed storage. Hosts join at rate `α` and leave at rate `λ`, with `α = λ` holding the population size constant; average membership lifetime is `T = N/λ`. Every join requires downloading the joining host's assigned share of data, `S/N` bytes on average; every leave requires copying that departing host's `S/N` bytes to replacement hosts to avoid a permanent redundancy loss. Summing both directions gives total maintenance bandwidth `2S/T`, or per-node bandwidth `B/N = 2(S/N)/T` — twice the average per-host storage contribution divided by the average membership lifetime (Equation 1).

The model is then extended to separate transient disconnection from permanent departure using a membership timeout `τ`: a host is treated as still a member, and its data is not re-replicated, until it has been unreachable longer than `τ`. Delaying response to failure this way lengthens the effective average lifetime (`Tτ`) but also means only a fraction of members — the availability `a` — are actually serving data at any instant, so replacing `B` with `aτB` and re-deriving redundancy needed for a per-object unavailability target `ϵa` yields, for pure replication, `ka = log(ϵa) / log(1 - aτ) ≈ log(1/ϵa) / aτ` (Equation 2), and a resulting per-node bandwidth `Bτ/Nτ = (2D / (Nτ·aτ·Tτ)) · log(ϵa)/log(1-aτ)` (Equation 3). For erasure coding, where an object is split into `b` blocks stored with effective redundancy factor `kc` and reconstructed from any `m ≈ b` available blocks out of `kc·b` stored, the analogous redundancy factor is derived from the normal approximation to the binomial distribution as a function of `b`, `a`, and `σϵ` (the number of standard deviations of the normal distribution corresponding to the target availability, e.g. `σϵ = 4.7` for six nines) (Equations 4-5).

### Measured results

| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| Storing 1 TB of unique data at high availability is described as effectively infeasible with Gnutella-like participation and cable-modem-like bandwidth, per the derived model | model parameters `Nτ`, `aτ`, `Tτ` estimated from an original crawler-and-prober measurement of ~33,000 Gnutella hosts, conducted April 11-19, 2003, methodology adapted from Saroiu, Gummadi, Gribble (2002) with a crawler extended to capture the entire membership for a precise host-count estimate |
| Discriminating true departure from transient downtime (increasing the membership timeout τ) yields up to roughly a 30x reduction in maintenance bandwidth | same Gnutella trace, target: 1 TB unique data at 6 nines (99.9999%) per-object availability, replication-style redundancy, varying leave timeout from near 0 to 30 hours (Figure 2) |
| At large τ, erasure coding at b=15 fragments needs a redundancy factor of about 15 to match the availability that replication needs a redundancy factor of about 120 for — an 8-fold bandwidth saving from coding over replication on this trace | same Gnutella trace and target (6 nines, 1 TB unique data), b=15 fragments, comparing replication vs. erasure coding redundancy factors (Figure 3) |
| With coding, maintaining 1 TB of unique data at Gnutella-like participation requires about 75 Kbps per-node maintenance bandwidth while up, contributing about 500 MB of disk per host | same trace, coding at b=15, large τ |
| 5% of the 33,000 Gnutella hosts (about 6,000 hosts) provided 40% of total service time (29 of 72 total service-years) in a 3-day subset of the trace; average availability of that top-5% subset was about 40% | same Gnutella crawl/probe trace, 3-day subset used for the service-time-by-host-fraction measurement (Figure 4) |
| Restricting to the top 5% of hosts with a 1-day membership timeout reduces required bandwidth to about 30 Kbps per node per unique TB using coding — roughly a 1,000-fold improvement in maintenance bandwidth over the least favorable point (short timeout) in Figure 2 | same trace, admission-control scenario: top-5%-availability subset only, 1-day timeout, coding |
| Stricter admission control identifies a subset of 967 Gnutella hosts with 99.5% availability, exceeding measured enterprise availability from a cited prior study, at the cost of a 10-fold reduction in aggregate service time versus using all hosts | same Gnutella trace, admission-control analysis restricting to the most-available hosts |
| Disk capacity for a "typical" user grew roughly 8,000-fold from 1990 to a projected 2005 figure, while home/academic access bandwidth grew only about 50-fold over the same period (Table 1: disk 60 MB in 1990 to 0.5 TB in 2005; home bandwidth 9.6 Kbps in 1990 to 384 Kbps in 2005) | figures the paper states as "generous bandwidth estimates," a trend table constructed from historical/projected typical consumer hardware, not a controlled experiment |

### Parameters

| Parameter | Definition | Value(s) used |
|---|---|---|
| `k` | redundancy expansion factor (fixed baseline scenario, Figure 1) | 20 |
| Data scales examined (Figure 1) | total unique data stored | 1 TB, 50 TB, 1000 TB |
| Link saturation threshold (Figure 1) | fraction of link capacity maintenance alone may consume | 50% |
| `τ` (leave timeout) range examined (Figures 2-3) | delay before treating a disconnected host as departed | 0 to 30 hours |
| `σϵ` for six-nines availability | standard-deviation count in the normal approximation | 4.7 |
| `b` (erasure code fragments) | blocks per object | 15 (Figure 3 comparison) |
| Gnutella trace host count | distinct hosts crawled | ~33,000 |
| Gnutella trace duration | measurement window | April 11-19, 2003 (about 8 days) |
| Admission-control subset sizes examined | most-available host subsets | top 5% (~6,000 hosts), and a stricter subset of 967 hosts at 99.5% availability |

### Stated limitations

The model rests on explicitly stated simplifying assumptions the authors say are each conservative individually (each would require more, not less, bandwidth if relaxed): identical per-node space and bandwidth contribution across all hosts, when real nodes vary; a constant average join/leave rate, when the relevant bound for a probabilistic guarantee is the worst-case rate, not the average; independence of leave events, when the authors state network and machine failures are not truly independent and that true guarantees would need more redundancy than the model computes; and a constant steady-state population and total data size, when a shrinking population needs more bandwidth and a growing one cannot sustain the model's steady-state assumption indefinitely. The model also excludes query bandwidth entirely, counting maintenance bandwidth only, and the authors state their bandwidth estimate is therefore conservative relative to any real deployed system, which must also serve reads. The paper states the availability-and-redundancy analysis assumes a static data placement strategy — a fixed function from current membership to the set of replicas per block — and does not model dynamic re-placement policies. Admission control and load-shifting strategies are analyzed and found not to change the fundamental bandwidth-scale-dynamics tradeoff; the paper states this explicitly as a conclusion of Section 4.1, not merely as an unexamined possibility.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system

Any redundancy scheme relying on this paper's bandwidth bound requires an accurate, population-specific measurement of `N` (host count), `a` (fractional availability), and `T` (average membership lifetime) — the paper explicitly computes its own figures from an original Gnutella crawl rather than assuming a generic churn rate, and states the bound is only as good as those inputs. A system that wants the roughly 30x bandwidth saving from distinguishing transient disconnection from permanent departure needs a membership-timeout mechanism (`τ`) that defers re-replication until a host has been unreachable longer than that threshold, which in turn requires the system to track per-host last-contact time and to accept the corresponding increase in expected time-to-repair for genuinely departed hosts. Achieving the modeled improvement from admission control requires a mechanism that measures per-host availability over time and can refuse or deprioritize volatile hosts before assigning them data — the paper states this converts the design "into a garden variety distributed systems problem" of building storage from a smaller number of highly available collaborators, which is a structural consequence of restricting membership, not a property the paper claims comes free. Any comparison between replication-based and erasure-coded redundancy under this model requires knowing both the target per-object unavailability `ϵa` and the block-fragmentation parameter `b`, since the bandwidth advantage of coding over replication (measured at 8-fold on this trace) is a function of those two parameters, not a fixed ratio.

### Contradicts

None found within this batch on a shared measured quantity. This paper's central claim — that combining high redundancy guarantees, large data scale, and fast membership dynamics simultaneously overreaches available bandwidth "regardless of lookup" — is a critique of the premise that distributed hash table (DHT)-based lookup robustness by itself yields storage robustness; it does not report a number that conflicts with a number in another paper in this batch, since its Gnutella measurement (host count, availability distribution, service-time concentration) is on a different network from the Overnet measurements in BHAGWAN-IPTPS-03 and the trace-driven simulation results in BHAGWAN-NSDI-04 and CHUN-NSDI-06. Note for later cross-paper checking: CHUN-NSDI-06 (Carbonite) reports live PlanetLab repair-bandwidth measurements explicitly aimed at the same delayed-repair strategy this paper analyzes only by model: a later synthesis step should check whether Carbonite's measured bandwidth reduction from deferring repair on short departures is of comparable magnitude to this paper's roughly 30x figure derived analytically from the Gnutella trace, since the two are different methodologies (measured live system vs. an analytic bound applied to trace-derived parameters) answering a related but not identical question.

### References worth retrieving

- Bhagwan, Savage, Voelker, "Replication strategies for highly available peer-to-peer storage systems," UCSD Technical Report CS2002-0726, Nov 2002 — foundational (source of the normal-approximation coding-redundancy derivation this paper's Equations 4-5 build on)
- Bhagwan, Savage, Voelker, "Understanding availability," IPTPS 2003 — foundational (already in this corpus as BHAGWAN-IPTPS-03; source of the distinguishing-downtime-from-departure framing this paper adopts)
- Bolosky, Douceur, Ely, Theimer, "Feasibility of a serverless distributed file system deployed on an existing set of desktop PCs," SIGMETRICS 2000 — competing (the enterprise-availability figure this paper's 967-host, 99.5%-availability subset is compared against)
- Dabek, Kaashoek, Karger, Morris, Stoica, "Wide-area cooperative storage with CFS," SOSP 2001 — competing (a DHT-based storage system the paper's introduction cites as an example that hopes to inherit robustness from lookup)
- Rowstron, Druschel, "Storage management and caching in PAST," SOSP 2001 — competing (same category as CFS)
- Saroiu, Gummadi, Gribble, "A measurement study of peer-to-peer file sharing systems," MMCN 2002 — foundational (the prior study whose crawler methodology this paper's own Gnutella measurement is adapted from and extended)
- Weatherspoon, Kubiatowicz, "Erasure coding vs. replication: A quantitative comparison," IPTPS 2002 — competing (the erasure-coding-for-storage proposal this paper's Section 3.3 formula generalizes)

## [BOLDYREVA-PKC-03] Threshold Signatures, Multisignatures and Blind Signatures Based on the Gap-Diffie-Hellman-Group Signature Scheme
**Citation:** Alexandra Boldyreva. "Efficient threshold signature, multisignature and blind signature schemes based on the Gap-Diffie-Hellman-group signature scheme." Public Key Cryptography (PKC), 2003. DOI 10.1007/3-540-36288-6_3.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.iacr.org/archive/pkc2003/25670031/25670031.pdf
**Source URL:** https://www.iacr.org/archive/pkc2003/25670031/25670031.pdf
**Domain:** E

### What it does
This paper gives three extensions of the BLS signature scheme (Boneh, Lynn, Shacham; a signature scheme whose security relies on the Computational Diffie-Hellman, CDH, problem being hard while the related Decisional Diffie-Hellman, DDH, problem is easy in the same group — such groups are called Gap Diffie-Hellman, GDH, groups) that let a group of parties jointly produce or delegate signatures, and states a formal proof of security for each.

TGS, the threshold GDH signature scheme, lets any subset of more than t out of n parties jointly compute a valid BLS signature while no coalition of t or fewer parties can forge one or learn the secret key, tolerating up to t < n/2 malicious parties (an optimal fraction, matching the maximum any threshold scheme can tolerate while remaining both robust and secure). Key generation uses Gennaro, Jarecki, Krawczyk, and Rabin's distributed key generation (DKG) protocol, run interactively by all n parties with no trusted dealer, producing a Shamir (t,n)-threshold secret sharing of the BLS secret key x — a sharing in which any t or fewer shares reveal no information about x, and any t+1 shares reconstruct it via Lagrange interpolation. To sign a message M, each participating party i simply runs the base BLS signing algorithm on its own share x_i, producing a signature share sigma_i = H(M)^{x_i}, and broadcasts it — no interaction or zero-knowledge proof is needed at signing time. A designated combiner reconstructs the full signature as the product of t+1 shares raised to their Lagrange coefficients, sigma = product over the chosen set R of sigma_i^{L_i}. Robustness (the property that the protocol produces a valid signature even if up to t parties actively deviate) is achieved because each share's validity can be checked directly: the DKG protocol publicly broadcasts B_i = g^{x_i} for every party, so the combiner verifies each sigma_i against B_i using the DDH-tuple check before combining, and requests a fresh share or treats the party as malicious if the check fails. Share length does not grow with n. The scheme can be made proactive (periodically re-randomizing shares so an adversary's knowledge from one time period becomes useless in the next) using the general proactive secret sharing techniques of Herzberg, Jarecki, Krawczyk, and Yung, because TGS meets the three preconditions those techniques require: it is a discrete-log-based threshold scheme, its key generation implements Shamir sharing with publicly verifiable share commitments, and its signing protocol is simulatable.

MGS, the GDH multisignature scheme, lets an arbitrary subgroup L of players, decided at signing time rather than fixed in advance, jointly produce one constant-size signature that a verifier accepts as proof every member of L participated. Each player P_j with secret key x_j computes and broadcasts its own BLS signature share sigma_j = H(M)^{x_j} on the message; a designated combiner (any party can serve this role) multiplies the shares from the participating set to produce sigma = product of sigma_j; a verifier reconstructs the combined public key pk_L = product of the individual public keys g^{x_j} for j in L and checks the DDH tuple (g, pk_L, H(M), sigma). Verification and signature length are independent of the number of players in L, and — unlike the prior formalized multisignature scheme of Micali, Ohta, and Reyzin, which required the subgroup to be fixed before any signature share was computed and required three communication rounds — MGS requires no prior agreement on the signer set and is non-interactive (one round). Each signature share is exactly a standard BLS signature, so the same technique supports batch verification of separate BLS signatures on the same message under different public keys, using the same product-then-verify approach.

BGS, the blind GDH signature scheme, lets a user obtain a valid BLS signature on a message from a signer without the signer learning the message, and prevents the user from deriving more than one valid signature per completed protocol run. The user picks a random blinding factor r, sends M-hat = H(M) * g^r to the signer; the signer, without learning M, computes sigma-hat = (M-hat)^x and returns it; the user removes the blinding factor by computing sigma = sigma-hat * y^{-r}, which equals the standard BLS signature H(M)^x. The construction parallels Chaum's RSA-based blind signature protocol structurally.

### Measured results
None. This is a pure cryptographic-construction paper: every claim is a formal security theorem with an accompanying reduction proof (given in the paper's appendices), not an experimental measurement. The paper states no benchmark, implementation, node count, or runtime figure of its own. Where it discusses efficiency, it does so structurally — round counts, share-length independence from n, and dependence or independence of a value on the number of participants — not as measured numbers.

### Parameters
- (t, n)-threshold: the threshold signature scheme TGS tolerates any t < n/2 malicious parties, stated as the achieved bound, not a tested range; the paper calls this "an optimal result" for the threshold fraction a robust, non-interactive threshold scheme of this kind can tolerate.
- Signature/share/key sizes: not given as numeric byte counts in this paper. The paper does state, citing the BLS base scheme, that BLS signatures are "approximately 160 bits" in some GDH group instantiations — this figure is attributed to the base BLS paper, not measured here.
- Chosen-target CDH problem query bound: the blind-signature security definition parameterizes adversary advantage by q_t (queries to a "target" oracle) and q_h (queries to a "helper" signing oracle), with the forgery condition requiring the adversary to produce more valid signatures than helper-oracle queries (q_h < q_t); this is a security-definition parameter, not a numeric value chosen for an instantiation.

### Stated limitations
The paper states its threshold-signature security proof (Theorem 4.2) holds "in the random oracle model only" — an idealized model in which a hash function is treated as a public random function — because the underlying BLS base signature scheme's own security proof requires the random oracle model; the threshold construction inherits this dependency rather than removing it.

The paper states that its multisignature security model, following Micali-Ohta-Reyzin, does not address robustness by default: an adversary that has corrupted all but one signer can always deviate from the protocol to prevent a valid multisignature from being produced, and the paper states it does "not focus on the robustness property in this work," only sketching how robustness could be added.

The paper states that its comparison of subgroups in a multisignature is left to the application: a verifier may reject a valid multisignature because it disagrees with which subgroup L signed, and the paper explicitly states it does "not take this problem into account" in its formal analysis.

The paper's blind-signature security proof rests on a new, unproven computational assumption it introduces (the chosen-target CDH assumption) rather than reducing to the standard CDH assumption; the paper states only that it conjectures this new assumption holds "for all groups where the CDH problem is hard," not that this has been proved.

The paper explicitly leaves multisignature robustness, and the exact efficiency trade-offs of alternative threshold DKG protocols, outside its formal treatment, citing related open problems from Micali-Ohta-Reyzin (the composition-after-signing problem, which this paper's MGS explicitly resolves) as context rather than closing every open question in the area.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The threshold scheme TGS requires an underlying communication substrate providing both a broadcast channel and secure point-to-point channels among all n participants; the paper states this explicitly as its assumed communication model, and the distributed key generation protocol (DKG) it reuses from Gennaro-Jarecki-Krawczyk-Rabin depends on this channel structure for its own security guarantees.

Robust operation depends on every party's per-share public commitment (B_i = g^{x_i}) being available to whichever party performs signature-share combination, since the combiner's DDH-tuple check against B_i is what lets it detect and exclude an invalid share instead of silently producing a corrupted combined signature; a deploying system must make DKG's publicly broadcast commitments persistently available to the combiner role, not just to participants during key generation.

Proactivization requires layering the separate PSS (Proactive Secret Sharing) protocol from Herzberg-Jarecki-Krawczyk-Yung on top of TGS and requires periodic synchronized share-refresh rounds among all n parties; TGS alone does not provide forward security against an adversary that compromises different subsets of parties across multiple time periods without this addition.

The multisignature scheme MGS requires each verifier to know, and be given, the complete list of public keys for every player in the claimed signing subgroup L at verification time, since the combined public key pk_L is recomputed by the verifier as the product of the individual keys — the verifier cannot check a multisignature against an unlisted or partially specified signer set.

The multisignature security model requires that corrupted players prove knowledge of their secret key at public-key registration time (to prevent rogue-key attacks, where an adversary derives a public key mathematically related to an honest party's key without knowing a corresponding secret key); a deploying system must enforce a proof-of-possession or equivalent registration check, or the paper's security guarantee for MGS does not apply.

The blind signature scheme BGS requires the signer to hold the GDH secret key x and to compute exponentiations on demand as an online interactive party for every blind-signing request; the scheme provides no mechanism for a signer that is offline or whose key material is distributed (that composition — blind signing over a threshold-shared key — is not addressed in this paper).

### Contradicts
None found against other entries in this corpus. Within its own related-work discussion, the paper states its threshold scheme TGS tolerates t < n/2 malicious parties non-interactively, exceeding the threshold-DSS scheme of Gennaro et al. [GJKR96] (t < n/4, requiring substantial interaction) on both the tolerated fraction and interaction cost — this is the paper's own comparison, attributed to Gennaro et al.'s construction, not an independent measurement of Gennaro et al.'s paper.

### References worth retrieving
- Boneh, Dan; Lynn, Ben; Shacham, Hovav. "Short signatures from the Weil pairing." ASIACRYPT 2001, LNCS vol. 2248, Springer, 2001. — foundational (the base BLS signature scheme every construction in this paper extends; already in this corpus as BONEH-ASIACRYPT-01).
- Gennaro, Rosario; Jarecki, Stanislaw; Krawczyk, Hugo; Rabin, Tal. "Secure Distributed Key Generation for Discrete-Log Based Cryptosystems." (GJKR99, cited as the DKG protocol TGS's key generation reuses directly.) — foundational.
- Gennaro, Rosario; Jarecki, Stanislaw; Krawczyk, Hugo; Rabin, Tal. Threshold DSS signature scheme (GJKR96). — competing (the threshold-DSS scheme this paper directly compares against on tolerated threshold, interaction cost, and robustness technique).
- Shoup, Victor. Threshold RSA signature scheme (cited as [Sh]). — competing (compared directly on tolerated threshold, trusted-dealer requirement, and use of random-oracle zero-knowledge proofs for robustness).
- Micali, Silvio; Ohta, Kazuo; Reyzin, Leonid. "Accountable-subgroup multisignatures." (cited as [MOR].) — competing (the prior formalized-security multisignature scheme this paper's MGS directly improves on and whose stated open problem — signer-subgroup composition decided after signature shares are computed — this paper resolves).
- Bellare, Mihir; Namprempre, Chanathip; Pointcheval, David; Semanko, Michael. "The One-More-RSA-Inversion Problems and the security of Chaum's Blind Signature Scheme." (cited as [BNPS].) — foundational (the chosen-target-RSA-inversion proof technique this paper's chosen-target-CDH proof for BGS directly parallels).
- Chaum, David. RSA-based blind signature scheme (cited as [C]). — foundational (the original blind-signature construction BGS is structurally modeled on).
- Herzberg, Amir; Jarecki, Stanislaw; Krawczyk, Hugo; Yung, Moti. Proactive secret sharing protocol PSS (cited as [HJKY], [HJJKY]). — foundational (the general proactivization technique TGS is stated to be compatible with).

- "The signature generation protocol does not require interaction or any zero-knowledge proofs"
- "MGS scheme solves the open problem stated in [MOR]: it does not require a priori knowledge of a subgroup of signers"
- "We conjecture that the chosen-target CDH problem is hard for all groups where the CDH problem is hard."

- "we do not focus on the robustness property in this work"
