## [BOSHMAF-NDSS-15] Íntegro: Leveraging Victim Prediction for Robust Fake Account Detection in OSNs
**Citation:** Yazan Boshmaf, Dionysios Logothetis, Georgos Siganos, Jorge Lería, Jose Lorenzo, Matei Ripeanu, Konstantin Beznosov. "Íntegro: Leveraging Victim Prediction for Robust Fake Account Detection in OSNs." NDSS, 2015.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.ndss-symposium.org/ndss2015/integro-leveraging-victim-prediction-robust-fake-account-detection-osns
**Source URL:** https://www.ndss-symposium.org/ndss2015/integro-leveraging-victim-prediction-robust-fake-account-detection-osns
**Domain:** F

### What it does
Íntegro ranks accounts in an online social network (OSN) so that real accounts are placed above fake accounts in the ranked list even when fakes have deliberately friended real users who accept requests from strangers (victims), an adversary strategy that defeats prior ranking schemes relying purely on the assumption that fake accounts stay sparsely connected to real accounts. The mechanism has three stages.

First, a victim classifier trained with a random forest algorithm on low-cost, readily available profile features (friend count, photo count, feed-item count, account age, and similar attributes that require no expensive backend query) predicts, for every real account, the probability that it will accept friend requests from fakes (a vulnerability score). Second, every edge in the social graph is reweighted according to the vulnerability scores of its two endpoints: an edge incident to a predicted victim is assigned a low weight relative to edges between two accounts unlikely to be victims, using the formula w(vi, vj) that depends on the vulnerability scores p(vi) and p(vj) and two tuning constants alpha and beta. Third, trust (a numeric quantity, analogous to the trust used by prior random-walk-based rankers) is initialized on a set of manually verified trusted accounts (seeds) selected across communities detected by the Louvain method, then propagated through the weighted graph for omega = O(log n) iterations of power iteration (n is the number of nodes), and each account's degree-normalized trust after omega iterations becomes its rank; accounts are sorted by this rank in descending order.

Because edges into the fake region carry low weight whenever they pass through a predicted victim, the total amount of trust that can flow from the real region into the fake region is bounded by the sum of the weights on attack edges (edges directly joining a real and a fake account), called vol(E_a), regardless of how many attack edges exist — this is the mechanism's core robustness property, contrasted against prior schemes (SybilRank) whose bound instead grows with the raw count of attack edges.

### Measured results
| Result | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Íntegro production precision at Tuenti, lowest-ranked 20K accounts | 95% | deployment on Tuenti's daily-active-user graph, several million nodes, tens of millions of edges (exact counts masked per non-disclosure agreement), snapshot of 6 February 2014; 96.6% of nodes and 94.2% of edges in one giant connected component, evaluation restricted to that component |
| SybilRank precision, same interval | 43% | same graph and evaluation |
| Tuenti's existing user-based abuse-reporting system, hit rate | 5% | same deployment; assumes all fakes eventually get reported |
| Victim-classifier AUC (area under ROC curve), Facebook dataset | 0.70 (40% better than random) | 9,646 real users initially collected in 2011 who received friend requests from fakes, re-validated June 2013, reduced to 8,888 after excluding 7.9% disabled/deactivated accounts; 18 low-cost profile features; 10-fold cross-validation |
| Victim-classifier AUC, Tuenti dataset | 0.76 (52% better than random) | 60,000 real users who received friend requests from fakes, 50% victims, collected 10 February 2014 from live production cache; 14 low-cost profile features (fewer available fields than Facebook) |
| AUC sensitivity to training-set size | no significant AUC increase above 40,000 feature vectors | cross-validation on the Tuenti dataset |
| Ranking AUC under targeted-victim infiltration | Íntegro-RF sustained AUC > 0.92, at most 0.07 decrease as attack edges increased; SybilRank degraded toward ~0.7 | Facebook graph replaying 65 real socialbots' recorded infiltration (n=2,991 nodes, m=11,952 edges), timestamped attack edges added incrementally, averaged over at least 10 runs, 95% confidence intervals |
| Ranking AUC under random-victim infiltration | same pattern: Íntegro-RF AUC > 0.92, up to 30% relative improvement over SybilRank; SybilRank degraded toward ~0.7 | synthetic fake region of 3,068 fakes / 36,816 friendships (small-world graph model) attached to the second Facebook graph (6,136 real accounts, 38,144 friendships) by 35,306 random attack edges (n=9,204, m=110,266) |
| Distant-seed attack (attacker targets accounts k hops from all trusted seeds) | SybilRank slightly better than Íntegro for k<3; Íntegro better for k≥3 | Facebook graph, varying k from 1 to 5 |
| Random-seed attack (attacker victimizes randomly chosen trusted seeds) | ranking quality of both systems degrades as victimized-seed count rises from 1 to 100 | Facebook graph |
| Community detection on Tuenti GCC | 42 communities found in 5 Louvain iterations, modularity 0.83, largest community 220,846 nodes, 15 communities exceeding 50,000 nodes | Tuenti giant connected component after preprocessing |
| Fake-account rate in newly joined accounts (deferred by the design) | 6% of a 100-account random manual sample were fake; most successful single fake account had 103 victims | accounts that joined Tuenti in the 30 days before the 6 February 2014 snapshot |
| Estimated manual-inspection cost avoided | Tuenti's 5% hit rate would need 1,267 person-hours to discover 19,000 fake accounts via user reporting alone | stated comparison against Íntegro's deployment, given as a derived estimate rather than a separately measured quantity |
| Computational cost | O(n log n) end-to-end, where n = number of accounts | derived from an m = O(n) assumption justified by the platform-enforced friend-count caps (5,000 on Facebook, 1,000 on Tuenti); victim classification and trust propagation each independently cost O(n log n), community detection costs O(n), ranking/sorting costs O(n log n) |
| Theoretical security bound (Theorem 4.1) | number of fake accounts ranking similar to or higher than real accounts after O(log n) iterations is O(vol(E_a) log n) | assumes the real region is fast-mixing and the attacker establishes attack edges uniformly at random; proof given in a cited companion technical report, not reproduced in full in this paper |

### Parameters
| Parameter | Value used | Range tested / notes |
|---|---|---|
| Edge-weight exponent alpha | 0.5 (illustrative example) | governs how strongly a low vulnerability score suppresses edge weight |
| Edge-weight multiplier beta | 2 (illustrative example) | paired with alpha in the weighting formula |
| Propagation iterations omega | O(log n); worked example uses omega = ceil(log2(9)) = 4 | terminated early, before convergence to the graph's true mixing time, which the paper states is much larger than O(log n) for typical social networks |
| Trusted-seed count | minimum one seed per detected community; exact count in the Tuenti deployment set by available manual-verification resources | Tuenti evaluation manually verified 0.05% of nodes in each detected community as trusted |
| Feature count used by victim classifier | 18 features (Facebook), 14 features (Tuenti) | listed in Table I with per-dataset relative-importance (RI) scores; friend count has RI 100.0% (Facebook) and 84.5% (Tuenti) |
| Classifier training-set size (final) | 40,000+ feature vectors | AUC did not improve significantly beyond this size in cross-validation |

### Stated limitations
The authors state two design limitations inherited from SybilRank and similar power-iteration ranking schemes. First, Íntegro's design is stated to apply only to undirected social graphs, because directed graphs have a substantially smaller mixing time than their undirected counterparts, making short random walks unsuitable for robust ranking on directed graphs. Second, Íntegro defers ranking newly joined accounts because their sparse initial connectivity would otherwise place them at low rank and generate false positives; the authors measured that only 7% of new users active in the prior 30 days on Tuenti had more than 46 friends (versus a platform average of 254), and that 6% of a 100-account random sample of these deferred new accounts were fake. The authors explicitly state that handling this trade-off (excluding new accounts versus risking false positives against them) is an operational decision left to the platform operator, and note a vouching-based alternative exists in other published fake-account detection designs for admitting legitimate new users, without evaluating it themselves. The authors state Íntegro is not a standalone fake-account detection system but is intended to complement existing detection mechanisms; in the Tuenti deployment it operated alongside a separate feature-based detection system and the existing user-reporting system. The community-detection step explicitly does not rely on the assumption that fake accounts form tightly-knit communities among themselves — the authors state this assumption does not always hold and that fakes can evade community-based detection by keeping sparse connectivity among themselves, and Íntegro is designed to tolerate an attacker who befriends either real or fake accounts without restriction.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Íntegro requires a set of manually verified trusted accounts (seeds) distributed across the graph's detected communities; verification is performed by human analysts, and the paper states the number of seeds selectable is bounded by available manual-verification resources, with a stated minimum of one seed per detected community. It requires a community-detection step (the Louvain method, run before rate adjustment) over the full social graph to prevent inter-community sparsity from starving the trust-propagation process. It requires training data for the victim classifier consisting of real accounts already known to have accepted friend requests from fakes, plus a defined feature set of low-cost profile attributes that must be available for every account for the resulting feature vectors to be complete — the paper states 4 of the 18 Facebook features had no equivalent field in the Tuenti dataset. It requires the underlying graph to be undirected, per the stated limitation above. It requires an operational policy decision, external to the mechanism itself, on how to treat newly joined accounts during the deferral window, since the mechanism assigns them uninformatively low rank by design. Its security bound (Theorem 4.1) is proved only for an attacker establishing attack edges uniformly at random against a fast-mixing real region; the paper's own seed-targeting experiments show the bound's practical behavior changes under a resourceful attacker who instead targets accounts near or overlapping the seed set, with SybilRank slightly outperforming Íntegro at small attacker-to-seed distances (k<3).

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus. The paper explicitly disputes a property commonly assumed by community-detection-based fake-account approaches — that fake accounts necessarily form tightly-knit communities among themselves — citing evasion by sparse self-connectivity as a documented counter-strategy; this is a claim about other systems' assumptions, not about a specific paper in this corpus.

### References worth retrieving
- foundational: Q. Cao, M. Sirivianos, X. Yang, T. Pregueiro, "Aiding the Detection of Fake Accounts in Large Scale Social Networks" (SybilRank) [ref 13] — the direct comparison baseline throughout, using an unweighted power-iteration ranking with an O(n log n) bound growing with the raw count of attack edges rather than their total weight
- competing: G. Danezis, P. Mittal, "SybilInfer" [ref 18] — Bayesian-inference-based fake account probability assignment, O(n (log n)^2) time per trusted account, stated to provide no analytical worst-case bound on fakes outranking real accounts
- competing: H. Yu, M. Kaminsky, P. B. Gibbons, A. Flaxman, "SybilGuard" [ref 16], and H. Yu, P. B. Gibbons, M. Kaminsky, F. Xiao, "SybilLimit" [ref 17] — modified-random-walk detection, O(sqrt(m*n) log n) time in a centralized setting; SybilLimit already in this corpus as YU-SP-08
- competing: GateKeeper [ref 20] — flow-based detection improving on SumUp, requires balanced-graph assumptions, O(n log n) time per trusted account ("ticket source")
- competing: B. Viswanath et al., using Mislove's greedy local-community-expansion algorithm [ref 19] to partition real and fake regions — O(n^2) time, evadable by sparse intra-fake-region connectivity
- foundational: Y. Boshmaf, I. Muslukhov, K. Beznosov, M. Ripeanu, "The Socialbot Network: When Bots Socialize for Fame and Money," ACSAC 2011 [ref 7] — source of the timestamped-attack-edge Facebook dataset reused in the targeted-victim infiltration experiment
- foundational: Louvain method for community detection [ref 54] — the community-detection algorithm used for both seed selection and evaluation of the trust-propagation graph structure

### Verbatim extracts
"Íntegro resulted in up to an order of magnitude higher precision in fake account detection" — deployment result summary.
"Íntegro achieved 95% precision, as compared to 43% by SybilRank and 5% by Tuenti's user-based abuse reporting system" — the three-way production comparison.
"the number of fake accounts that rank similar to or higher than real accounts after O(log n) iterations is O(vol(Ea) log n)" — Theorem 4.1's statement.
"Íntegro's design is limited to only undirected social graphs" — stated limitation.
"Íntegro is not a stand-alone fake account detection system" — stated scope limitation.
"fakes can easily evade detection if they establish sparse connectivity among themselves" — stated limitation of community-detection-based approaches, motivating Íntegro's design choice not to rely on that assumption.

## [BOSWELL-ARXIV-24] Measuring NAT64 Usage in the Wild
**Citation:** Elizabeth Boswell, Stephen McQuistin, Colin Perkins, Stephen Strowes. "Measuring NAT64 Usage in the Wild." arXiv preprint (CoRR), 2024. DOI 10.48550/ARXIV.2402.14632.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.14632
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.14632
**Domain:** L

### What it does
NAT64 lets an IPv6-only host reach an IPv4-only destination by translating between the two address families at a middlebox, given a DNS64 resolver that synthesizes an IPv6 AAAA record from the destination's IPv4-only A record. This paper does not build NAT64; it measures how widely NAT64 and DNS64 are actually deployed on the public Internet and what reachability and latency cost crossing one imposes, using the RIPE Atlas measurement platform (a distributed network of volunteer-hosted measurement probes).

Detection method: four tests run from each probe. DNS Test 1 sends a DNS AAAA query for the reserved name `ipv4only.arpa` (RFC 7050); a working DNS64 resolver returns a synthesized AAAA record, while a plain IPv6-only host without DNS64 gets NXDOMAIN. DNS Test 2 repeats the same query against a second IPv4-only name (`time-c-b.nist.gov`), because the paper found some resolvers correctly synthesize a record for `ipv4only.arpa` specifically but not for other IPv4-only names. The Standard Prefix ping test sends an ICMPv6 ping to a fixed IPv4 target address encoded under the standard NAT64 prefix (`64:ff9b::/96`), run from every probe regardless of DNS-test outcome, to catch probes that can reach a NAT64 device without having received the prefix via DNS64. The Custom Prefix ping test repeats that ping using whatever non-standard prefix a probe's DNS Test 1 response supplied, and is also run on other probes in the same Autonomous System (AS, an internet routing domain) as a probe that received a non-standard prefix, to detect probes whose own configured DNS resolver is unaware of an available NAT64 device even though the network path has one. Passing tests sorts probes into two device categories: NAT64+DNS64 (fully working path-and-name-resolution pair) and NAT64-only (working translation path with no automatic AAAA synthesis, requiring the client to already know or construct the address).

Path characterization method: from the dual-stack probes identified as having working NAT64, the authors ran Paris traceroute (a traceroute variant tolerant of per-flow load balancing) to a fixed set of IPv4-only targets, once natively over IPv4 and once over IPv6 through the NAT64-synthesized address, and compared the two paths' success rate, hop count, count of non-responding ("missing") hops, and round-trip time (RTT).

### Measured results
| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| 224 probes (in 43 IPv6 ASes) found with any working NAT64 reachability, out of 6,154 probes that ran the tests (RIPE Atlas has approximately 12,000 probes total; not all participated) | Test window December 2022-January 2023, several weeks |
| DNS Test 1 pass rate 3.3% (201/6,154), fail 96.5%, inconclusive 0.2%; DNS Test 2 pass 0.7% (42), fail 99.2%; Standard Prefix ping pass 1.1% (66), fail 98.8% | Same test run |
| 36 probes passed both DNS tests (fully working DNS64); 18 of those (50%) also consistently passed the matching ping test and are classified NAT64+DNS64 (6 IPv6-only, 12 dual-stack) | Same test run |
| 326 probes failed one or both DNS tests but passed a ping test (reach a NAT64 device without functioning DNS64); 206 of these, after excluding 120 judged not actually intending NAT64 use, form the NAT64-only group | Same test run |
| Most common IPv6 AS among NAT64-capable probes: AS 6939 (Hurricane Electric), 145 probes; only 1 of those 145 could actually complete path measurements, because the deployment blocks outside traceroutes | Same test run |
| 27 of 34 probes with usable path-measurement data had a "local" NAT64 (probe's IPv4 AS, IPv6 AS, and the NAT64's AS all match); 7 had a "remote" NAT64 (path leaves the probe's own AS to reach the translator) | Recurring-traceroute dataset (see below) |
| Overall traceroute success rate: 87.94% of native IPv4 paths reached the target, versus 87.07% of NAT64 paths (0.87 percentage-point difference); 12.03% of unsuccessful IPv4 paths still reached the target's AS, versus 0.00% of unsuccessful NAT64 paths | 13,519 matched pairs of IPv4/NAT64 paths (both legs reaching the destination), drawn from a recurring-measurement set of 15,564 pairs from 34 probes to 14 IPv4-only targets (7 NTP servers, up to 11 RIPE Atlas anchors), hourly traceroutes over 41 hours |
| Missing (non-responding) hops: mean 16.52% of hops missing on IPv4 paths (SD 11.92, median 16.67%) versus mean 38.06% missing on NAT64 paths (SD 14.50, median 36.84%) | Same 13,519-pair dataset; 89.50% of specific missing-hop runs (mean; median 100.00%, SD 16.46%) recurred identically across two separate measurement periods for the two most successful targets, evidence the missing hops are caused by specific non-responding routers rather than random loss |
| Path length: mean 17.72 hops (SD 5.25, median 17.00) for IPv4, versus mean 20.99 hops (SD 6.10, median 21.00) for NAT64 — a 23.13% / 3.27-hop average increase | Same 13,519-pair dataset; remote-NAT64 paths averaged a 2.21-hop difference (5.08 hops after excluding one probe with a TTL-manipulating router that produced anomalously short IPv4 traceroutes), local-NAT64 paths averaged 3.45 hops; T-Mobile US prefixes (`2607:7700:0:x:0:y`) averaged 4.38 hops versus 2.49 for all other paths |
| RTT: mean 160.82 ms (SD 91.61, median 169.80 ms) for IPv4, versus mean 184.55 ms (SD 105.59, median 193.51 ms) for NAT64 — a 17.47% / 23.74 ms average increase | Same dataset; local-NAT64 RTT difference averaged 27.56 ms (1.34 ms after excluding the high-RTT T-Mobile prefixes), remote-NAT64 RTT difference averaged 1.22 ms; Pearson correlation between per-path RTT difference and hop-count difference = 0.29 (moderate) |

### Parameters
- Test window: several weeks, December 2022-January 2023; 6,154 participating probes out of RIPE Atlas's roughly 12,000.
- Detection tests: 4 (DNS Test 1 against `ipv4only.arpa`, DNS Test 2 against `time-c-b.nist.gov`, Standard Prefix ping to 91.201.7.243 encoded as `64:ff9b::5bc9:7f3`, Custom Prefix ping using each probe's own synthesized prefix).
- Preliminary traceroute round: 183 of 205 dual-stack NAT64-capable probes online (9 NAT64+DNS64, 14 NAT64-only usable after filtering); 3 UDP probe packets per hop (Paris traceroute); 18 IPv4-only targets (7 NTP servers, 11 RIPE Atlas anchors), chosen for geographic spread; raw yield 3,565 IPv4/NAT64 path pairs, reduced to 1,230 usable pairs (54 probes, 18 destinations) after excluding 2,320 traceroutes with no hop matching the NAT64 prefix (mostly targeting a non-ICMP-responsive Hurricane Electric deployment) and 15 other anomalies.
- Recurring traceroute round: 37 of the 54 usable probes still available; hourly traceroutes over 41 hours to 14 of the 18 targets (4 anchors had gone offline); final usable set 15,564 IPv4/NAT64 path pairs from 34 probes, after removing 5 probes' data (incomplete runs), the 41st hourly run, 6 unresponsive targets, and 1,076 pairs whose NAT64 leg never touched the NAT64 prefix.

### Stated limitations
The authors state they have no mechanism to detect a CLAT (customer-side NAT46, used in 464XLAT deployments) because CLAT translation hides IPv6 addresses on the path before they reach the measurement point, so the paper's results measure only standalone NAT64/DNS64 deployment and explicitly exclude 464XLAT. The authors state RIPE Atlas gives wide coverage of residential and operator networks but limited visibility into mobile networks, and note a wireless-testbed platform such as the discontinued MONROE would have given broader mobile-network visibility, which was unavailable to them. The authors state traceroute measurements do not directly reflect real application performance; they characterize traceroute-visible path properties (hop count, missing hops, RTT) as a proxy, not application-level latency or throughput, and state that further application-performance measurement is out of scope for this paper. The authors state their AS-assignment heuristic for locating a NAT64 device (matching the announced prefix's AS, or falling back to the last non-NAT64-prefixed hop's AS) can be indeterminate, in which case they default to assuming the NAT64 is in the probe's own IPv6 AS — a default that could misclassify some remote deployments as local. The authors state that one identified NAT64 device does not check the source address of translated packets, calling this a minor security concern because it could be used to hide the source AS of traffic; this is reported as an observed configuration issue in one deployment, not a general property of NAT64.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Any peer-reachability design that assumes IPv6-only clients can always reach IPv4-only destinations, or vice versa, through NAT64 needs to account for measured NAT64 deployment being rare among the probes tested (255 of 6,154, about 4.1%) — most tested networks have no detectable NAT64 path at all, so a design cannot assume a translator will be present on an arbitrary IPv6-only client's path. Where a NAT64 path does exist, a peer-to-peer transport or hole-punching layer that depends on stable, low round-trip-time paths needs to tolerate the measured average 23.13% longer hop count and 17.47% higher RTT relative to native IPv4, and needs to tolerate substantially reduced traceroute-level path visibility (a mean 38.06% of hops non-responding on NAT64 paths versus 16.52% on native IPv4), which affects any mechanism relying on path-hop diagnostics (e.g., a NAT-traversal probe that infers translator behavior from ICMP responses) rather than end-to-end reachability alone. A design that discovers NAT64 presence by relying solely on the RFC 7050 standard prefix-discovery DNS query needs to account for this paper's finding that this method alone is insufficient: the paper's four-test method found working NAT64-only paths on hosts that never received a synthesized AAAA record via that discovery mechanism, so a design that checks only for a synthesized address will undercount reachable translators. A design that treats "the NAT64 device is inside my own network" as a security or trust boundary needs to independently verify that assumption per deployment, since the paper found 7 of 34 measured cases used a translator outside the probe's own AS.

### Contradicts
None found.

### References worth retrieving
- competing: Hsu, A., Li, F., Pearce, P., Gasser, O., "A First Look At NAT64 Deployment In-The-Wild," arXiv:2311.04181, Jan 2024 — parallel, independently run RIPE Atlas NAT64 measurement study using ping/DNS/HTTP(S) methodology instead of traceroute; the paper states this work reports a similarly low NAT64 probe count. Should be retrieved to check whether its independent measurement agrees with or diverges from this paper's 224/6,154 figure.
- foundational: Chen, G., Cao, Z., Xie, C., Binet, D., "NAT64 Deployment Options and Experience," RFC 7269, IETF, 2014 — deployment-options reference this paper builds its test design against.
- foundational: Cheshire, S., Schinazi, D., "Special Use Domain Name 'ipv4only.arpa'," RFC 8880, IETF, 2020 — defines the reserved name used in DNS Test 1.
- foundational: Matthews, P., Beijnum, I.v., Bagnulo, M., "Stateful NAT64: Network Address and Protocol Translation from IPv6 Clients to IPv4 Servers," RFC 6146 (cited as reference [10]) — the NAT64 mechanism specification itself.
- competing: Lencse, G., Répás, S., "Performance analysis and comparison of the TAYGA and of the PF NAT64 implementations," TSP 2013 — small-scale controlled-testbed NAT64 implementation performance comparison, a direct precedent this paper positions itself against as testbed-only (not in-the-wild).
- competing: Llanto, K.J.O., Yu, W.E.S., "Performance of NAT64 versus NAT44 in the Context of IPv6 Migration," IMECS 2012 — competing controlled-network NAT64/NAT44/native-IPv6 performance comparison.
- foundational: Augustin, B. et al., "Avoiding traceroute anomalies with Paris traceroute," IMC 2006 — the traceroute variant this paper's measurement method uses.

### Verbatim extracts
"224 probes, in 43 networks, that can use NAT64 to access the IPv4 Internet"
"NAT64 paths are, on average, 23.13% longer, with 17.47% higher round-trip times"
"it is not sufficient to rely on the standard NAT64 prefix discovery procedure"
"NAT64 is a workable substitute to native IPv4, but impacts latency and reachability"
"only one of these probes is able to" [complete path measurements, due to blocked outside traceroutes]
"this is a minor security concern, as it can be used to hide the source AS"

## [BRIGHTID-WP] Universal Proof of Uniqueness (BrightID Whitepaper)
**Citation:** BrightID project (collective; not peer-reviewed). "Universal Proof of Uniqueness." Project whitepaper, 2020.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.brightid.org/whitepaper
**Source URL:** https://www.brightid.org/whitepaper
**Domain:** E

Note on source status: this document is a project whitepaper, not a peer-reviewed paper. No figure it states is a measured result from a described experiment; every number below is project-stated design intent or a description of a method used elsewhere, and is recorded as such.

### What it does
BrightID lets a person prove to an application that they are not already using another account under that same application, without a central authority verifying identity. It builds a social graph — a network of cryptographically signed connections between people — and runs a ranking analysis over that graph to distinguish people from duplicate accounts (Sybils).

The basic unit is a connection: two people cryptographically sign a record of having connected, and each person's device stores its own connection list (names and photos of connections), never uploaded to a BrightID node. A BrightID node stores only the graph structure (which BrightIDs are connected) and, separately, a mapping between per-application user identifiers and BrightIDs, one such mapping per registered "context" (a paired identifier system plus verification system an application registers, so a person can hold at most one verified identifier per context). Analysis runs a rank-based Sybil-detection algorithm over the graph — the paper states its research was partly based on SybilRank, which was tested by its original authors on the Spanish social network Tuenti by ranking users by likelihood of being a duplicate and handing the ranked list to human reviewers, who found more duplicates that way than through user reporting alone (a result the whitepaper cites, not one it measured). The paper states nodes are free to run different or combined ranking algorithms and to weigh them differently by context; applications choose which nodes and which resulting verifications to trust.

The graph analysis is anchored by seed groups: pre-selected trusted starting points from which the ranking algorithm's notion of trust or reachability propagates. Where the underlying analysis operates over groups rather than individual connections, a seed is a group of people rather than a single person, so a seed can persist even as individual membership changes. A prospective member of an existing group must connect to more than 50% of the group's current members to join (an additional invitation or authorization step can be layered on top of this base rule). A hierarchy of accountability governs seed status: any member of a seed group's parent or ancestor group can revoke that group's seed status, which cascades to revoke every descendant group's status as well; the whitepaper does not resolve who initially holds the power to grant seed status to a group with no existing parent, stating this as an open question. Independent auditors — members of other seed groups, not the one under review — make "audit" connections to people in a region and record baseline and follow-up rank measurements to judge whether a seed group's presence is actually improving verification outcomes there.

Nodes propagate signed operations (connections, group actions, flags) to each other by a gossip protocol. Time is divided into fixed periods split into an analysis phase and a synchronization phase: during synchronization, nodes exchange missing operations, order the frozen operation set, compute a running checksum, and reach consensus on that set before it is applied to the graph and the following analysis phase begins; some operation types (creating users, founding groups, flagging users, authorizing primary groups) are instead applied immediately rather than waiting for the next synchronization phase.

A user's signing key can be replaced through social recovery: at account setup, the user designates at least three existing connections as "trusted connections." To recover a lost or compromised key, the user reconnects to two of those trusted connections, each of whom sees the connection flagged as a recovery request and confirms which person is recovering; once two such confirmations are recorded, every node substitutes the new signing key for the old, which becomes permanently invalid. A user's private connection data (names, photos) can separately be password-encrypted and held by a trusted connection or in cloud storage, and is handed back to the user during recovery if a trusted connection holds a copy.

A reputation mechanism ("stars") is layered over verification: a verified user accumulates stars over time and by making connections to people who go on to become verified; making a connection stakes some of the connecting user's future stars, forfeited if the connected person fails to become verified within a stated period, with the resulting reward or penalty propagating a few steps through the graph and weakening at each step. An unstaked-connection option exists so a person under social pressure to connect can do so without financial stake or without the risk being visible to the other party, at the cost that an unstaked connection contributes nothing toward either party's verification.

### Measured results
The whitepaper reports no experiment of its own. Every quantitative or evaluative figure in the text is either a design threshold BrightID's own designers chose, or a result the paper attributes to somebody else's prior work, cited without the conditions needed to check it here:
- The whitepaper cites that the SybilRank algorithm, tested by its original authors on the Tuenti social network, produced a ranked list of suspected duplicate accounts that let human workers find more duplicates than user self-reporting did. No number of accounts, ranks, or duplicates found is given in this whitepaper; the citation points to a separate SybilRank source not retrieved in this batch.
- The design threshold for joining an existing group is stated as connecting to more than 50% of current group members; this is a design choice, not a measured optimum.
- The design threshold for account-key recovery is stated as two confirmations out of at least three designated trusted connections; this is likewise a design choice, not a measured optimum.
None of these figures carries an experimental condition (graph size, attacker fraction, run count) that would let a reader use it as a measured cost or a security bound.

### Parameters
- Trusted-connection set size for recovery: at least three designated at signup; two of them must confirm to complete a key-replacement recovery. Values are project defaults, not derived or measured.
- Group-join threshold: connection to more than 50% of a group's current membership, before any additional invitation or authorization requirement is layered on.
- Seed-group audit process: no numeric threshold is given for when an audited region's rank measurements count as "improvement"; the whitepaper leaves this a qualitative judgment for auditors.
- Time-period structure: nodes operate on periods split into an analysis phase and a synchronization phase; no concrete period length is stated.
- Star-propagation depth: rewards and penalties from a connection's outcome are stated to propagate "several steps" through the graph, weakening at each step; no concrete step count, decay function, or weighting formula is given.

### Stated limitations
Seed selection is stated to be especially important, and especially hard, during the network's rapid-growth phase, when subgraphs of genuine users may exist that are not yet well connected to the rest of the graph — such a subgraph can be indistinguishable, from the ranking algorithm's perspective, from a Sybil region an attacker constructed to resemble an honest one. The whitepaper states an open question it does not resolve: who holds the authority to grant seed status to a new top-level seed group with no existing parent group. The whitepaper states that an ineffective seed group (one whose presence does not measurably improve verification outcomes in its region) can itself indicate the seed group's use by an attacker to manufacture Sybils, but gives no automatic detection mechanism for this beyond manual auditor review. Verifications returned by an untrusted node are stated to need independent auditing by an application before being relied upon; the whitepaper does not describe an automatic mechanism that performs this auditing, only that applications and other nodes are able to compare verification responses across multiple nodes.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
An application that wants Sybil-resistant per-user verification must register a context (an identifier system plus a chosen verification method) with one or more BrightID nodes, and must independently decide which nodes' verification responses to trust — nothing in the base protocol enforces node honesty for a single-node context; the whitepaper states this is a centralization risk the application either accepts or mitigates by using multiple independent nodes and comparing their outputs. The Sybil-detection ranking algorithm needs at least one seed (a preselected trusted point or group in the graph) from which to propagate its trust computation, and the quality of the result depends on that seed set's placement relative to genuinely well-connected honest users, which the whitepaper states is unresolved during rapid growth. The gossip-and-consensus protocol requires every participating node to receive the full stream of signed operations (or enough of them, corrected during the synchronization phase, to reach the same frozen operation set) before applying the next graph state; a node that misses operations without later reconciling them during synchronization would diverge from the rest of the network, though the whitepaper does not analyze what happens under sustained partition. Social recovery requires the designated trusted connections to remain reachable and honest; the whitepaper states this method reduces the effectiveness of bribery attacks against a single user (accepting a bribe and then recovering removes the briber's leverage) but does not analyze collusion among the trusted connections themselves beyond stating the user is trusting them "to not collude."

### Contradicts
None found. The whitepaper does not itself use the term "GroupSybilRank" anywhere in the retrieved text; it names only "SybilRank" as the algorithm part of its research was based on. A synthesis citing this source for a "GroupSybilRank-style algorithm" is describing a characterization from elsewhere, not a term this primary source uses.

### References worth retrieving
- Cao, Sirivianos, Yang, Pregueiro, "Aiding the Detection of Fake Accounts in Large Scale Social Online Services" (SybilRank), USENIX NSDI 2012 — foundational (the ranking algorithm this whitepaper states its own research was partly based on, cited here by name and by its Tuenti evaluation).

"connecting to more than 50% of existing members"
"resulted in workers finding many more duplicates than through user reporting"
"trusted connections... to not collude to take over their account"

## [BUCHET-CCR-25] An Analysis of QUIC Connection Migration in the Wild
**Citation:** Aurélien Buchet, Cristel Pelsser. "An Analysis of QUIC Connection Migration in the Wild." ACM SIGCOMM Computer Communication Review, 2025. DOI 10.1145/3727063.3727066.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.06066
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.06066
**Domain:** L

### What it does
QUIC's connection-migration mechanism lets a client switch the IP address and/or port it uses for an already-established connection without a new handshake, so an in-progress transfer or session survives a network change (Wi-Fi to cellular, address rebinding behind a NAT, or a deliberate switch for tracking resistance). QUIC identifies a connection by Connection Identifiers (CIDs) carried in the packet header rather than by the IP/port 4-tuple TCP uses, so a packet arriving from a new address can still be matched to an existing connection as long as the CID is recognized. To migrate, an endpoint first announces spare CIDs to its peer via encrypted `NEW_CONNECTION_ID` frames sent at any point during the connection; once both sides hold at least one CID not previously used in cleartext headers, the client can send a `PATH_CHALLENGE` frame from the new address, and the server must echo it back in a `PATH_RESPONSE` to validate the new path before migration completes. Using a fresh CID on both sides (not just a new address) prevents an eavesdropper from linking the pre- and post-migration traffic by matching the CID visible in the cleartext packet header.

This paper does not modify QUIC; it measures how many real-world QUIC-speaking servers actually implement and permit this migration handshake, as opposed to how many merely speak QUIC. Method: (1) discover QUIC-capable IP targets via ZMap-based UDP scans of the full IPv4 address space on port 443, plus IPv6 targets seeded from a published responsive-address Hit-list and from DNS resolution of over 125 million domain names (Centralized Zone Data Service com/net/org zones plus the Tranco top-sites list); a reserved QUIC version-negotiation number is used to elicit a response that confirms QUIC support without completing a full handshake. (2) Map discovered IP addresses to domain names via forward DNS (A/AAAA records via MassDNS through a local Unbound resolver), to supply Server Name Indication (SNI) for TLS Client Hellos, since many hosts (especially behind CDNs) will not complete a handshake without SNI identifying the requested domain. (3) A custom stateful scanner (approximately 1,200 lines of Rust, built on Cloudflare's Quiche QUIC library, since the alternative quic-go library used by a prior study's scanner did not support migration at the time of writing) attempts a full QUIC handshake with HTTP/3 ALPN negotiation against each target, and where the server offers at least one spare CID, triggers a migration (new source port, same interface) and confirms success only on receipt of a valid `PATH_RESPONSE`; on success it also issues an HTTP request to capture the server's HTTP header. (4) Post-processing maps successful targets' IPs to Autonomous Systems (ASes, internet routing domains) via RouteViews BGP route data and to owning organizations via the CAIDA AS-to-Organization dataset.

### Measured results
Scans conducted in May 2024, run in parallel from two vantage points (VP1: cloud provider, western Europe; VP2: data center, North America); the paper reports only VP1 in the main text because the two vantage points' results did not differ meaningfully. Datasets: IPv6 Hit-list (4 May 2024), CZDS com/net/org zones (10 April 2024), Tranco list (25 April 2024), RouteViews BGP RIBs (17 May 2024), CAIDA AS-to-Organization mapping (1 May 2024).

| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| 12,024,542 IPv4 targets, 11,854 distinct ASes, responsive to UDP port 443 QUIC probing (full IPv4 address space scan, no SNI) | ZMap scan, VP1, May 2024 |
| 3,237,165 IPv6 targets, 3,288 ASes, responsive (seeded from Hit-list + DNS-derived addresses, no SNI) | Same scan round |
| 332,682 of the responsive IPv4 addresses (2,667 ASes) and 1,463,071 of the responsive IPv6 addresses (488 ASes) were mapped to at least one domain name and used with SNI | Domain resolution from over 125M CZDS+Tranco domain names via MassDNS |
| IPv4, no SNI: successful handshakes 591,848 (4.9% of targets, 52% of distinct ASes); successful same-interface migrations among those 474 (7.7% of handshake-succeeding targets, 2% of distinct handshake ASes) | Full-space IPv4 scan, no SNI |
| IPv4, with SNI: successful handshakes 230,889 (69% of targets, 84% of ASes); successful migrations 119,779 (52% of handshake-succeeding targets, 67% of ASes) | Domain-mapped IPv4 subset |
| IPv6, no SNI: successful handshakes 110,764 (3.4% of targets, 79% of ASes); successful migrations 1,281 (1.2% of handshake-succeeding targets, 6.8% of ASes) | Hit-list-and-DNS-seeded IPv6 scan, no SNI |
| IPv6, with SNI: successful handshakes 887,330 (61% of targets, 87% of ASes); successful migrations 693,461 (78% of handshake-succeeding targets, 53% of ASes) | Domain-mapped IPv6 subset |
| Of the 693,461 IPv6-with-SNI targets supporting migration, 654,598 (about 94%) belonged to a single organization, Hostinger | Same scan; the paper states other IPv6 providers "offer very little support" for migration by comparison |
| IPv4 responsive-address count is about 5 times the count Zirngibl et al. reported with a similar method in 2021, which was itself about 3 times the count Rüth et al. reported in 2018 | Cross-study comparison the authors draw against two specific prior scans, not a controlled replication |
| Cloudflare and Google: high QUIC-handshake and general responsiveness, but the paper states they "do not seem to support connection migration" among the top providers observed in the IPv4-with-SNI scan | IPv4-with-SNI top-provider breakdown (Figure 3b) |
| Top HTTP server headers among migration-successful targets: IPv4 with SNI — LiteSpeed (88k), AmazonS3 (439), Apache (187); IPv6 with SNI — LiteSpeed (620k), AmazonS3 (6.3k), nginx (2k); IPv4 no SNI — nginx (7.1k), JSP (1.3k), kittenx (642); IPv6 no SNI — nginx (884), gvs (134), JSP (75) | Server headers collected via the post-migration HTTP request, VP1 |

### Parameters
- Scan month: May 2024. Two vantage points: VP1 (cloud provider, western Europe, reported in main text), VP2 (data center, North America, results in appendix, described as "very similar" to VP1).
- IPv4 target discovery: full /0 address space, ZMap, UDP port 443.
- IPv6 target discovery: seeded from a published responsive-address Hit-list (4 May 2024) plus AAAA records resolved from the domain-name corpus; not exhaustive (IPv6 address space is not fully scannable).
- Domain corpus: over 125 million domain names from CZDS (com/net/org zones, 10 April 2024) and the Tranco top-sites list (25 April 2024); DNS resolution via MassDNS through a local Unbound server yielded 3M distinct IPv6 addresses and 6.2M distinct IPv4 addresses.
- Migration scanner: custom, approximately 1.2k lines of Rust, built on Cloudflare Quiche (quic-go was rejected because it lacked migration support at the time); tested against a controlled Cloudflare Quiche server under multiple configurations and against a handful of independently-verified Google/Cloudflare production servers before the wide scan.
- Migration performed: same network interface, different source port only (the paper states investigating true multi-interface or server-preferred-address migration is left as future work).
- Rate limiting applied to all scans per Internet-measurement best-practice guidance (Menlo Report); an opt-out prefix exclusion list was maintained from requests received via a published contact page hosted at both vantage points.
- Handshake success criterion: reception of a complete, valid TLS 1.3 Server Hello. Migration success criterion: reception of a valid `PATH_RESPONSE` frame after sending `PATH_CHALLENGE` from the new source port.

### Stated limitations
The authors state the scanner does not record server-advertised transport parameters that could explain non-migration, such as `disable_active_migration` or `preferred_address`, so the paper cannot attribute specific non-support cases to a specific declared server policy versus a network-path failure (load balancer misrouting, firewall blocking of the non-handshake `PATH_CHALLENGE` packet, or simple lack of implementation support) — the authors list all of these as plausible causes but state their current scanner cannot distinguish among them. The authors state the scanner was validated against a controlled Quiche deployment and a small number of independently-verified Google/Cloudflare servers, not against the full range of known QUIC implementations, so some migration-capable implementations using behavior the scanner does not anticipate may have been missed; they note the QUIC Interop Runner could broaden this coverage but did not, at the time of writing, fully support migration testing. The authors state the study measures migration on the same network interface with only a source-port change, not true multi-interface migration or migration to a server-preferred address, and list both as future work. The authors state the IPv4-with-SNI and CZDS/Tranco-derived target sets are biased toward popular websites and cloud providers, and separately cite prior work (Steger et al.) finding the IPv6 Hit-list itself biased toward ISP networks — both dataset-selection biases the authors flag as affecting who is represented in the with-SNI results, not measurement noise. The authors state successful handshakes obtained without SNI likely represent either misconfigured servers or servers not associated with any domain name, since HTTP/3 formally requires SNI when a server is identified by domain name.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A NAT-traversal or reachability design that depends on QUIC connection migration to survive an address change needs to account for measured migration support being far from universal even among servers that speak QUIC and pass a full TLS handshake: with SNI supplied (the condition closest to a normal client connecting to a named service), migration succeeded for 52% of IPv4 targets and 78% of IPv6 targets that had already completed a handshake — meaning roughly half of IPv4 QUIC servers and a fifth of IPv6 QUIC servers that a client can talk to at all will not support a mid-connection address change, so any design relying on migration for continuity needs a fallback path (new connection/new handshake) for the non-supporting majority or near-majority. A design specifically counting on migration for privacy against network-path observers (unlinking pre- and post-migration traffic) needs the presence of a spare, not-yet-used CID on both ends before migrating, which this paper's own mechanism description states is required to prevent an eavesdropper from linking the two paths by the visible CID — a precondition the scanner enforces operationally by requiring the server to have offered at least one additional CID before attempting migration. The measured concentration of IPv6 migration support in a single organization (94% of IPv6-with-SNI migration-successful targets belong to one hosting provider, Hostinger) means a decentralized reachability design cannot treat "IPv6 QUIC migration is broadly available" as a property of the IPv6 QUIC ecosystem generally; it is presently a property of a small number of large hosting operators' default configurations, not a general server behavior. A design needs a mechanism to detect migration support per-server at connection time (offer a CID and observe whether the server accepts a subsequent PATH_CHALLENGE) rather than assuming it, since this paper found no reliable way, short of an actual attempt, to predict from other server-visible information (organization, HTTP header) whether a given target supports migration, beyond the coarse observation that some providers (Cloudflare, Hostinger) are internally consistent (all-or-none) while others (AWS, OVH) are not.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus.

### References worth retrieving
- foundational: Zirngibl, J. et al., QScanner-based QUIC deployment measurement, 2021 (cited as reference [21]) — the prior study this paper's IPv4 responsive-address count (about 5x larger) is directly compared against, and the study whose QScanner tool (built on quic-go) could not be reused here because quic-go lacked migration support.
- foundational: Rüth, J. et al., 2018 QUIC deployment measurement (cited as reference [15]) — earlier baseline in the same responsive-address growth comparison (about 3x smaller than the 2021 figure).
- foundational: Gasser, O., Scheitle, Q., Foremski, P., Lone, Q., Korczyński, M., Strowes, S. D., Hendriks, L., Carle, G., "Clusters in the Expanse: Understanding and Unbiasing IPv6 Hitlists," IMC 2018 — source of the IPv6 responsive-address Hit-list this paper's IPv6 scan seeds from.
- competing/foundational: Govil, Y., Wang, L., Rexford, J., "MIMIQ: Masking IPs with Migration in QUIC," FOCI 2020 (cited as reference [7]) — a system proposal that uses QUIC migration specifically for IP-address-masking/privacy purposes, directly relevant to any privacy-tier design considering migration-based unlinkability, since this paper's measured low migration-support rates bound how broadly such a design could actually work today.
- foundational: Kosek, M., Doan, T. V., Granderath, M., Bajpai, V., "One To Rule Them All? A First Look at DNS over QUIC," PAM 2022 (cited as reference [10]) — methodological precedent for QUIC scanning technique this paper's target-discovery approach is based on.
- foundational: Le Pochat, V., Van Goethem, T., Tajalizadehkhoob, S., Korczynski, M., Joosen, W., "Tranco: A Research-Oriented Top Sites Ranking Hardened Against Manipulation," NDSS 2019 — source of the Tranco domain list used for SNI-mapping and IPv6 seeding.

## [BURCKHARDT-POPL-14] Replicated Data Types: Specification, Verification, Optimality
**Citation:** Sebastian Burckhardt, Alexey Gotsman, Hongseok Yang, Marek Zawirski. "Replicated Data Types: Specification, Verification, Optimality." ACM SIGPLAN-SIGACT Symposium on Principles of Programming Languages (POPL), 2014, pp. 271-284. DOI 10.1145/2535838.2535848.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/popl2014.pdf
**Source URL:** https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/2535838.2535848
**Domain:** D

### What it does
The paper gives a way to state, independent of any implementation, what a replicated data type must return, and a matching proof method for showing a concrete implementation meets that statement and for showing no correct implementation can use less memory. A replicated data type specification defines an operation's return value as a function of its operation context — the set of prior events that affect it, plus two relations over that set: visibility (vis, one event's effect is observed by another) and arbitration (ar, a total tie-breaking order used only when visibility does not settle a conflict). This replaces defining an operation's result as a function of an internal implementation state, which the paper states could not express conflict-resolution policies declaratively before this work. The paper gives four data types as worked specifications: a counter (ctr), whose read context need only count increments and decrements; a last-writer-wins register (intreg), whose read returns the value of the arbitration-maximal write among those not superseded by a visible later write; a multi-value register (mvr), whose read returns the set of all values written by writes that are pairwise concurrent (neither visible to the other) and not superseded; and an observed-remove set (orset), whose read context returns exactly the elements a for which some visible add(a) exists with no visible remove(a) that itself observed that same add — meaning a remove cancels only the specific add operations it was issued with knowledge of, so a concurrent add against a remove is decided in the add's favor. The paper's verification method, "replication-aware simulation," proves a concrete implementation meets a specification by associating each replica's local state (or each message in transit) with an abstract description of only the events that produced it, so correctness of a single-replica code path can be checked without reasoning about the whole distributed execution; a small number of "agreement properties" about a data type's messaging behavior are proved once for each broad implementation class (state-based or operation-based) and then reused across every implementation in that class. The paper's optimality method proves a lower bound on an implementation's worst-case metadata overhead (the ratio, at some read operation, between the size of the full internal object state and the size of just the client-observable value returned) by constructing an "experiment family": a set of black-box-distinguishable executions, each ending in a read whose surrounding operations force the internal state to encode enough information that a later black-box test sequence can reconstruct which execution occurred, which proves those internal states must be pairwise distinct and therefore requires enough bits to distinguish among them (Lemma 14: worst-case metadata overhead is at least floor(log_|Λ|(|Q|)) divided by the largest return-value size in the family, for an experiment family of size |Q| over an alphabet Λ). A store combining multiple objects, possibly of different data types, is specified by consistency axioms (constraints over the visibility and arbitration relations across the whole store, formulated in the style of weak shared-memory consistency models), and the paper proves that per-object correctness of each object's data-type implementation, plus a transport-layer guarantee, together imply the whole store satisfies the composed axioms — so store-level correctness does not require re-verifying each implementation jointly.

### Measured results
This is a formal-methods paper: verification proofs and asymptotic bounds, not an implemented or benchmarked system, so there is no run, hardware, or dataset to report. The paper's central quantitative results are the matched upper and lower bounds on worst-case metadata overhead (Figure 10), each proved, not measured, as a function of the number of replicas n and the number of update operations m (2 ≤ n ≤ m):

| Data type | Existing implementation's overhead | Any correct implementation's lower bound | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| Counter (ctr) | Θ-hat(n) | Ω-hat(n) | Matched — this implementation proved optimal |
| Observed-remove set (orset), optimized [Bieniusa et al. 2012] | Θ-hat(n log m) | Ω-hat(n log m) | Matched — this implementation proved optimal |
| Observed-remove set (orset), unoptimized [Shapiro et al.] | Θ-hat(m log m) | (same Ω-hat(n log m) bound applies) | Not matched — this implementation is not optimal |
| Last-writer-wins register (intreg) | Θ-hat(log m), assuming O(log m) timestamp encoding (satisfied by Lamport clocks) | Ω-hat(log m) | Matched — this implementation proved optimal |
| Multi-value register (mvr), new optimization discovered during this paper's optimality proof | Θ-hat(n log m) | Ω-hat(n log m) | Matched — this implementation proved optimal |
| Multi-value register (mvr), prior implementation [Shapiro et al.] | Θ-hat(n^2 log m) | (same Ω-hat(n log m) bound applies) | Not matched — this implementation is not optimal |

The paper's own asymptotic notation (Θ-hat, Ω-hat, O-hat) is defined precisely (Definition 12) in terms of limits over n, m to infinity with an unspecified multiplicative constant K; no numeric constant is given for any bound. Seven existing implementations of the four data types above were formally verified correct against the paper's specifications using the replication-aware simulation method; this is a proof result (each verified, yes or no), not a measured quantity.

### Parameters
Not applicable in the sense of runtime-tunable parameters — this is a specification and proof framework, not a deployable system with configuration knobs. The bounds in Figure 10 are stated as functions of two structural quantities of an execution: n (number of replicas that performed at least one update) and m (number of update operations across the whole execution), with the stated domain restriction n ≤ m ≤ 2 (executions with fewer updates than replicas are excluded from the asymptotic analysis, since the paper states it is interested in the regime where every replica is mutated). The lower-bound proof for the counter (Lemma 16) additionally requires m to be a multiple of (n-1) for its specific experiment-family construction; the orset lower-bound proof (referenced, not detailed in the retrieved excerpt) requires (m-1) to be a multiple of (n-1).

### Stated limitations
The paper states its optimality technique was applied only to state-based implementations (an implementation class where a message conveys the sender's whole local state) and that other implementation classes — including operation-based implementations, several of which the paper's own verification section formally proves correct — are left for future work with no metadata bound derived for them. The paper states it studied only four data types (counter, last-writer-wins register, multi-value register, observed-remove set) and that studying additional types, explicitly naming lists used for collaborative editing, is future work — a gap the corpus's ATTIYA-PODC-16 entry (co-authored by three of the same authors) directly addresses two years later. The paper states its execution model, while following the model used by replicated-data-type designers generally, abstracts away the concrete algorithms used by actual store implementations, including fail-over and session-migration protocols that let a client interact with multiple physical replicas under the illusion of one virtual replica; verifying those algorithms against this framework is stated as future work, not done here. The paper states its worst-case overhead metric does not capture optimizations whose benefit is invisible to a worst-case analysis, and that more detailed overhead metrics are a direction for future work.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Every consistency-axiom proof in the paper's store-composition result (Definition 20, Proposition 19) requires each object's data-type implementation to be independently proved correct against its own specification under some visibility witness, and requires the transport layer to satisfy a stated transport-layer specification (T-Any or a specific variant) matching that witness; the paper states axiom validity "most often depends on the transport layer specification," so a system substituting a weaker transport than the one an implementation was verified against cannot inherit that implementation's store-level correctness guarantee without redoing the transport-dependent half of the proof (Definition 21). The observed-remove set specification requires visibility information to reach the point of conflict resolution: a remove operation's effect depends on which prior add events it observed, so any storage layer implementing this specification must transmit or reconstruct the visibility relation between add and remove events, not merely a value. The last-writer-wins register's proved-optimal Θ-hat(log m) implementation requires a timestamp encoding of size O(log m); the paper states this bound is satisfied by Lamport clocks specifically, so a system wanting to match this proved-optimal bound needs a clock or timestamp mechanism no larger than logarithmic in the number of updates. The EVENTUAL consistency axiom (Figure 13) requires, for every event, that it not be invisible to infinitely many other events on the same object; establishing this for a real store requires the transport layer to guarantee eventual delivery, since the axiom is a constraint on the abstract visibility relation that a lossy or permanently partitioning transport cannot satisfy.

### Contradicts
None found. The paper's own comparison table (Figure 10) marks two existing implementations as provably non-optimal relative to its own derived lower bound — the original observed-remove set of Shapiro et al. at Θ-hat(m log m) against a Ω-hat(n log m) lower bound, and the original multi-value register of Shapiro et al. at Θ-hat(n^2 log m) against the same class of bound — which is a finding produced by this paper's own method, not a disagreement with another paper's measurement.

### References worth retrieving
- Foundational (data type this paper builds a proved-optimal implementation of): A. Bieniusa, M. Zawirski, N. Preguiça, M. Shapiro, C. Baquero, V. Balegas, S. Duarte, "An optimized conflict-free replicated set," INRIA Technical Report 8083, 2012 — the observed-remove set implementation this paper proves matches its Ω-hat(n log m) lower bound.
- Foundational (prior, non-optimal implementations this paper's bounds are compared against): M. Shapiro et al. work on the original observed-remove set and multi-value register implementations (cited via reference [32] and related entries in the paper's bibliography), shown by this paper's Figure 10 to have strictly higher worst-case metadata overhead than the newly proved-optimal alternatives.
- Foundational (extended version with full proofs): S. Burckhardt, A. Gotsman, H. Yang, M. Zawirski, "Replicated data types: specification, verification, optimality (extended version)," Microsoft Research technical report, 2013 — cited throughout the retrieved text as [12,§C] and [12,§A] for derivations and proofs omitted from the conference paper, including the intreg and mvr lower-bound proofs and standard-encoding definitions.
- Foundational (companion framework paper): S. Burckhardt, A. Gotsman, H. Yang, "Understanding eventual consistency," Microsoft Research Technical Report MSR-TR-2013-39, 2013.
- Foundational (this paper's own explicit forward pointer to the successor work already in this corpus): the paper's future-work section names studying "lists used for collaborative editing" as a direction, which ATTIYA-PODC-16 — already in this corpus, sharing four of this paper's five authors — directly undertakes, extending this paper's specification and lower-bound method to a list data type and proving an Ω(D) metadata-overhead lower bound in the number of deletions D.
- Foundational (weak shared-memory model basis for the store-level consistency axioms): M. Batty, S. Owens, S. Sarkar, P. Sewell, T. Weber, "Mathematizing C++ concurrency," POPL 2011, and M. Batty, M. Dodds, A. Gotsman, "Library abstraction for C/C++ concurrency," POPL 2013 — cited as the axiomatic shared-memory-model style this paper's store consistency axioms generalize to replicated stores.
- Foundational: B. Charron-Bost, "Concerning the size of logical clocks in distributed systems," Information Processing Letters 39(1), 1991 — a classical result on logical-clock size relevant to the last-writer-wins register's timestamp-encoding assumption.

## [CAI-CCS-14] A Systematic Approach to Developing and Evaluating Website Fingerprinting Defenses

**Citation:** Xiang Cai, Rishab Nithyanand, Tao Wang, Rob Johnson, Ian Goldberg. "A Systematic Approach to Developing and Evaluating Website Fingerprinting Defenses." ACM CCS, 2014. DOI 10.1145/2660267.2660362.
**Retrieved:** full text
**Source URL:** https://www.cse.buffalo.edu/~rniyanan/papers/tamaraw.pdf
**Domain:** G

### What it does
The paper defends against website fingerprinting attacks, in which an eavesdropper observing only encrypted traffic timing and packet sizes on a tunnel (SSL, Tor) infers which website a client visited, by presenting Tamaraw, a constant-rate padding defense, together with a methodology for measuring any defense's efficiency against the best possible attacker rather than against one specific classifier. Tamaraw sends traffic in both directions in fixed-size packets at fixed time intervals rho_out and rho_in (separate rates per direction, since outgoing web-request traffic is far less frequent than incoming page-content traffic); packet size is set to 750 bytes rather than the network's maximum transmission unit, chosen because most outgoing packets already fall near that size. Unlike its predecessor BuFLO, which pads total transmission time only up to a fixed cutoff tau (creating a tuning dilemma between coverage and overhead), Tamaraw pads the number of packets sent in each direction up to the next multiple of a padding parameter L, independent of any per-page time cutoff, so that many different web pages collapse to the same padded packet count and become indistinguishable to a classifier that observes only packet counts. The paper's ideal-attacker methodology treats two packet sequences as indistinguishable exactly when a defense makes their observable traces identical, giving an attack-independent upper bound on any classifier's accuracy, and separately proves lower bounds on the bandwidth overhead any defense must incur to reach a given security level under this ideal attacker. It also gives a closed-form method for converting a defense's measured closed-world accuracy (attacker chooses among n known sites) into an open-world true discovery rate (attacker must additionally rule out the entire rest of the internet), avoiding the need to run separate open-world experiments.

### Measured results
| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|

### Parameters
- Packet size: 750 bytes for Tamaraw (chosen to cover most outgoing packets without excess padding); MTU (1500 bytes) for BuFLO and for one tested Tamaraw configuration.
- rho_out, rho_in (packet-send interval, seconds/packet, one per direction): swept 0.005 to 0.16 s/packet in the Pareto-frontier search (Appendix Figure 4); chosen operating points rho_out=0.04, rho_in=0.012 (MTU packets) and rho_out=0.02, rho_in=0.006 (750-byte packets, halved to hold the same transmission rate at the smaller packet size). BuFLO's original configuration used rho_out = rho_in = 0.02.
- L (padding parameter, packets): incoming and outgoing packet counts each padded up to the next multiple of L; L=100 used throughout the reported Tamaraw evaluation.
- BuFLO's tau (time cutoff, seconds): tau=9 used in the matched-overhead comparison against Tamaraw (553 vs. 18 partitions at ~130% overhead); BuFLO configurations otherwise taken from Dyer et al.'s prior evaluation.
- K (dummy-packet run length signaling end of traffic): introduced as an implementation parameter for detecting stream end, but the paper's own analysis assumes client and proxy know when to pad rather than fixing a specific K.
- Classifier-distinguishability thresholds for the feature-sensitivity experiments (Section 3): 0.55 and 0.75 accuracy, used to define the minimum generator perturbation magnitude v at which a feature classifier can tell the two classes apart.
- Dataset sizes: 800 sites (Alexa top 800, closed-world security/overhead evaluation, one load per site); 100 sites (Alexa top 100, bandwidth/time overhead tuning and open-world evaluation, 70 loads per site); 400 sequences (bbc.co.uk repeated loads, feature-sensitivity experiments, 200 train / 200 test per class).

### Stated limitations
The paper states its causal packet-ordering constraint (a scheduled dummy packet is sent rather than reordering to send an already-ready real packet of the other direction) is a pessimistic implementation choice made to guarantee correctness, and that a practical implementation permitting reordering when the causal dependency allows it could achieve lower size and time overhead than the measured figures. It states that Tamaraw is not perfectly successful at hiding total transmission size against generators that substantially change that size (G1, G2, unique-packet-length generators), because the padding parameter L bins packet counts into ranges rather than eliminating the size signal entirely. It states its evaluation methodology derives an upper bound on attacker accuracy (via the ideal ambiguity-set attacker) rather than a demonstrated attack, so the reported closed-world epsilon-security values bound what any classifier, however powerful, can achieve, but do not represent a specific fielded attack's measured accuracy. It states the theoretical lower-bound framework in Section 5.1 covers only a specific class of attacker (AS attackers using ambiguity-set partitioning) and that the connection between Tamaraw's actual construction and this optimal-partitioning theory is only partial, since Tamaraw's partitions are fixed independent of the dataset rather than dataset-optimized as the theoretical construction requires.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Tamaraw requires a proxy or client-side component capable of enforcing fixed-rate, fixed-size packet transmission independently in each direction, and requires that component to determine, out of band from the padded stream itself, when the real data transfer for a page has ended (the paper flags this as non-trivial and assumes an oracle for it in its own simulation rather than solving it). The scheme requires the padding parameter L and the two rates rho_out, rho_in to be fixed system-wide constants shared by every client generating traffic under the defense, since Tamaraw's security guarantee (via the ambiguity-set partitioning bound in Section 6.2.1) depends on many different pages colliding onto the same padded packet-count bucket; a per-client or per-session choice of L would fragment the anonymity set the defense provides. The open-world performance conversion (Section 5.2) requires the defender or evaluator to supply a closed-world classifier's accuracy across the full candidate site set plus each site's real-world visit popularity (the paper uses Alexa page-views-per-million) as an input.

### Contradicts
None found within this batch. The paper's own headline framing ("website fingerprinting attacks are a paper tiger," attributed by the paper's introduction to prior critique work by Perry) is explicitly rejected by the paper's own undefended-baseline result (under 50% false discovery rate against the 100 most popular sites with no defense at all), which the paper states directly contradicts that claim.

### References worth retrieving
- Dyer, Coull, Ristenpart, Shrimpton. "Peek-a-Boo, I Still See You: Why Efficient Traffic Analysis Countermeasures Fail." IEEE S&P 2012 — foundational (source of BuFLO, the baseline defense Tamaraw extends and whose configurations Figure 1 reuses)
- Cai, Zhang, Joshi, Johnson. "Touching from a Distance: Website Fingerprinting Attacks and Defenses." ACM CCS 2012 — foundational (source of the Ca-DLevenshtein attack whose Tor overhead/security numbers this paper reuses in Table 1 and Figure 1, and of the packet-ordering-carries-information finding motivating the feature-based methodology)
- Liberatore, Levine. "Inferring the Source of Encrypted HTTP Connections." ACM CCS 2006 — foundational (source of the Jaccard-coefficient and Naive Bayes classifiers this paper's F1/F2 feature classifiers derive from)
- Panchenko, Niessen, Zinnen, Engel. "Website Fingerprinting in Onion Routing Based Anonymization Networks." WPES 2011 — competing (a prior attack/defense evaluation on Tor this paper's methodology is positioned against)
- Wang, Goldberg. "Improved Website Fingerprinting on Tor." WPES 2013 — competing (bbc.co.uk page-selection rationale for the feature-sensitivity dataset is cited to this paper)
- Perry. "A critique of website fingerprinting attacks." Tor Project blog, 2013 — attack/critique (source of the "paper tiger" characterization this paper's undefended-baseline result argues against)
- Luo, Zhou, Chan, Lee, Chang, Perdisci. "HTTPOS: Sealing Information Leaks with Browser-side Obfuscation of Encrypted Flows." NDSS 2011 — competing (a browser-side fingerprinting defense surveyed in Section 4)
