## [CAMENISCH-TRUST-16] Anonymous Attestation Using the Strong Diffie-Hellman Assumption Revisited
**Citation:** Jan Camenisch, Manu Drijvers, Anja Lehmann. "Anonymous Attestation Using the Strong Diffie-Hellman Assumption Revisited." International Conference on Trust and Trustworthy Computing (TRUST), 2016. DOI 10.1007/978-3-319-45572-3_1.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://eprint.iacr.org/2016/663.pdf
**Source URL:** https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-45572-3_1
**Domain:** E

### What it does
Direct Anonymous Attestation (DAA) lets a platform — a secure hardware element (a Trusted Platform Module, TPM) paired with a host computer — sign a message so a verifier is convinced an authorized secure element produced the signature, without the signature revealing which specific platform signed. This paper identifies proof errors in the qSDH-assumption-based (q-Strong Diffie-Hellman) DAA schemes standardized in TPM 2.0 and ISO, and constructs a repaired scheme.

The paper states three flaws in prior qSDH-based DAA schemes. First, the most efficient prior schemes use a simplified membership credential that is not proven existentially unforgeable under adaptive chosen-message attack, because their security proof issues a specially crafted credential only to a randomly chosen honest platform and then incorrectly assumes any forgery reusing part of an issued credential has a 1/q chance of reusing that specific one — a claim the paper states is false when no honest platform joins or when the adversary disregards credentials issued to honest platforms. Second, the zero-knowledge proof-of-knowledge these schemes use to prove possession of a credential proves knowledge of secret values a, b and the platform secret gsk, but never proves the required relation b = a * gsk holds between them, so a signature that passes verification cannot always be used to extract a genuinely valid credential — which the paper states blocks any unforgeability proof. Third, every existing security proof for these schemes uses an isomorphism from G2 to G1 (present only in type-1 and type-2 pairing settings), but the TPM 2.0 standard is deployed using type-3 pairings, where no such isomorphism exists, leaving the standardized scheme's security unproven in its actual deployment setting. The paper separately reports that Chen and Urian's LRSW-based DAA-with-attributes instantiation is forgeable outright by the trivial credential A=B=C=D=E_1=...=E_L=1 (the group identity element), which signs any attribute set.

The paper's repaired scheme, Pi_daa+, uses a BBS+ signature (a signature scheme on a vector of messages, introduced by Au, Susilo, Mu, SCN 2006) as the membership credential, and gives a new proof of knowledge of a BBS+ signature that runs entirely in group G1, avoiding the less efficient G2 and GT groups and their pairing operations during proof generation; verification needs two pairing operations, with the remainder of the computation in G1. As a side result the paper proves the BBS+ signature scheme itself existentially unforgeable under adaptive chosen-message attack in the type-3 pairing setting, without assuming an isomorphism between G2 and G1 — a proof the paper states did not previously exist, since the original BBS+ proof by Au et al. used the Eurocrypt version of the qSDH assumption, which does assume that isomorphism. The scheme adds support for signature-based revocation (revoking a platform from a prior signature, without knowing its secret key) via mandatory basenames — a per-verifier-context value B = H1(bsn) that the platform's pseudonym nym = B^gsk is computed from — required because a revocation-inequality check performed jointly between a corrupt host and its TPM could otherwise let the host learn B'^gsk for an adversarially chosen B', turning the TPM into a static Diffie-Hellman oracle; requiring bsn to be a hash of a public per-context string removes that leak in the random-oracle model. The scheme also supports attribute-carrying credentials, storing every attribute except the platform's own secret key on the host rather than the TPM, for efficiency, without weakening unforgeability under an honest-TPM, corrupt-host threat model.

### Measured results
| Scheme | TPM sign cost | Host sign cost | Est. sign time (ms) | Verify cost | Est. verify time (ms) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Chen-Feng [CF08] | 2 G1-exp, 1 GT-exp | 1 G1-exp, 2 G2-multi-exp, 1 GT-exp, 1 pairing | 50.1 | 1 G2-exp, 2 G3-multi-exp, 1 G5-multi-exp(T), 3 pairings | 172.7 |
| Chen [Che09] | 2 G1-exp, 1 GT-exp | 1 G1-exp, 1 G3-multi-exp(T) | 58.9 | 1 G2-exp, 1 G2-multi-exp, 1 G4-multi-exp(T), 1 pairing | 111.0 |
| Brickell-Li [BL10] | 3 G1-exp | 1 G1-exp, 1 G2-multi-exp, 1 GT-exp, 1 pairing | 45.7 | 1 G2-exp, 1 G2-multi-exp, 1 G4-multi-exp(T), 1 pairing | 111.0 |
| Chen-Plessl-Steedman [CPS10] | 3 G1-exp | 4 G1-exp | 8.8 | 2 G2-multi-exp, 4 pairings | 89.6 |
| This work (conference version) | 3 G1-exp | 1 G1-exp, 1 G2-multi-exp, 1 GT-exp, 1 pairing | 45.7 | 1 G2-exp, 1 G2-multi-exp, 1 G4-multi-exp(T), 1 pairing | 111.0 |
| This work (updated, journal version) | 3 G1-exp | 2 G1-exp, 2 G2-exp, 1 G2-multi-exp | 17.6 | 1 G2-exp, 1 G3-exp, 1 G5-multi-exp, 2 pairings | 60.2 |

Conditions: estimated running times computed by measuring the running time of the primitive operations (individual exponentiations and pairings, not full protocol runs) on the 256-bit Barreto-Naehrig (BN) pairing curve that the TPM 2.0 standard supports, each operation executed 100,000 times and averaged, using the IAIK ECCelerate library on a single thread of an Intel Core i5 4300u CPU; no multi-exponentiation optimization was used. Figures shown are for zero attributes (L=D=U=0), to make schemes with and without attribute support comparable; revocation-list checks are excluded from these numbers.

| Scheme | Credential size (bytes) | Signature size (bytes, no attributes) |
|---|---|---|
| Chen-Feng [CF08] | 97 | 1058 |
| Chen [Che09] | 65 | 259 |
| Brickell-Li [BL10] | 65 | 259 |
| Chen-Plessl-Steedman [CPS10] | 132 | 262 |
| This work (conference version) | 97 | 258 |
| This work (updated, journal version) | 97 | 324 |

Conditions: byte sizes computed for the same 256-bit BN curve using point compression, again excluding attribute contributions to allow comparison against schemes without attribute support. The paper's own stated conclusion from this table: the updated TPM-signing operation is as efficient as the fastest prior scheme and works entirely in G1; two LRSW-based schemes (CPS10, and the paper's own extended prior work CDL16b) have a faster host-signing operation, but this scheme is stated to be substantially faster than every prior qSDH-based scheme at both host signing and verification, at a small increase in credential size.

### Parameters
- Pairing type: type-3 (G1 not equal to G2, no efficient isomorphism between them), chosen because it allows the most efficient operations in G1 among the three pairing types the paper cites (type-1, type-2, type-3).
- Curve: 256-bit Barreto-Naehrig curve, the one specified by the TPM 2.0 standard, used for all benchmark figures above.
- L, D, U: total attribute count, disclosed-attribute count, and undisclosed-attribute count in a credential; set to zero in the efficiency comparison to isolate the base-scheme cost from attribute handling.
- Join-session concurrency bound: when the scheme uses extraction-by-rewinding instead of online-extractable proofs, the paper states the issuer must limit the number of simultaneous join sessions to be logarithmic in the security parameter, to avoid an exponential blow-up in the security proof's rewinding argument; no concrete bound is given, only the asymptotic requirement.

### Stated limitations
The paper states it remains future work to revisit the standards it identifies flaws in (TPM 2.0's DAA schemes) to eliminate those flaws and establish provable security in deployment. The fully anonymous signing option (an empty basename, bsn = bottom) supported by prior DAA schemes is not supported by this scheme, because it is required for the mandatory-basename fix that closes the static-Diffie-Hellman-oracle leak during revocation checks; the paper argues this does not reduce achievable privacy, since a platform can instead choose a basename it uses only once to obtain the same anonymity property. Extraction by rewinding, an alternative to the scheme's online-extractable proofs that would be more computationally efficient, is stated to require the issuer to cap simultaneous join sessions at a logarithmic bound in the security parameter to keep the security proof's running time from blowing up exponentially, and the paper states this instantiation's security proof holds only in a stand-alone setting, not under the universal-composability framework's composability guarantees, because that framework does not permit rewinding at all.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A verifier checking a non-revocation proof must supply a fixed, application-specific basename bsn for every verification context, since the platform's pseudonym is computed as a hash of that basename raised to the platform's secret key; a system that omits basenames (fully anonymous verification) is not supported by this scheme and must instead have platforms generate a single-use basename per signature to obtain equivalent anonymity. Signature-based revocation requires every verifier to hold the current revocation list of prior signatures and requires the platform, during signing, to prove in zero knowledge that its own secret key differs from the key underlying every revoked signature; this proof must be re-run by the platform for every entry on the revocation list at signing time, so the revocation list's size directly bounds signing cost, though the paper gives no measured figure for this cost as a function of list size. The DAA credential-issuing party (the issuer) must generate a BBS+ key pair honestly and issue credentials through the paper's Join protocol; the security proof assumes static corruption, meaning the adversary's set of corrupted parties is fixed before the protocol run begins, not adaptively during it. Attribute-carrying deployments must place every attribute except the platform's own secret key on the host rather than the TPM for the stated efficiency gain; the paper states this preserves unforgeability under an honest TPM with a corrupt host, but a system whose threat model instead assumes a corrupt TPM with an honest host would need a different attribute placement, which the paper does not analyze.

### Contradicts
The paper does not itself introduce the BBS+ signature scheme; it cites Au, Susilo, Mu (ASM06, SCN 2006) as the source of BBS+ and states its own contribution is a new proof that BBS+ is existentially unforgeable specifically in the type-3 pairing setting, without assuming an isomorphism between G2 and G1 — the paper labels this "a side-result of independent interest" within a paper whose primary construction is the DAA scheme Pi_daa+. A synthesis step citing this source as the origin of BBS+ itself, rather than as the source of its type-3 security proof, is not supported by this paper's own framing.

### References worth retrieving
- Au, Susilo, Mu, "Constant-size dynamic k-TAA," SCN 2006 — foundational (the original BBS+ signature scheme construction and its type-2 security proof, which this paper extends to type-3).
- Camenisch, Drijvers, Lehmann, "Universally composable direct anonymous attestation," (cited as CDL16b) — foundational (the security model, including its ideal functionality, that this paper extends to support attributes and signature-based revocation).
- Brickell, Camenisch, Chen, "Direct anonymous attestation," (BCC04) — foundational (the original DAA scheme designed for the TPM, based on strong-RSA, that this line of qSDH-based work replaces for efficiency).
- Brickell, Li, "Enhanced privacy ID from bilinear pairing," (BL11) — competing (the EPID scheme this paper's revocation extension is compared against, including the static-Diffie-Hellman-oracle leak the paper's basename requirement is designed to close).
- Chen, Urian, "DAA-A: direct anonymous attestation with attributes," (CU15) — competing (the prior attribute-carrying DAA scheme this paper both compares against in Table 1/2 and reports a forgery attack against, via the trivial all-identity-element credential).
- Chen, Plessl, Steedman, (CPS10) — competing (an LRSW-based DAA scheme with faster host-signing than this paper's qSDH-based scheme, per Table 1).

"the LRSW scheme is forgeable using the trivial credential"
"a side result... we have proven the BBS+ signature scheme to be secure in type-3 pairing settings"

## [CAO-NSDI-12] Aiding the Detection of Fake Accounts in Large Scale Social Online Services
**Citation:** Qiang Cao, Michael Sirivianos, Xiaowei Yang, Tiago Pregueiro. "Aiding the Detection of Fake Accounts in Large Scale Social Online Services." USENIX NSDI, 2012.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.usenix.org/system/files/conference/nsdi12/nsdi12-final22.pdf
**Source URL:** https://www.usenix.org/system/files/conference/nsdi12/nsdi12-final22.pdf
**Domain:** F

### What it does
SybilRank ranks the users of an online social network (OSN) by their likelihood of being a fake
account (Sybil), so that the operator can direct limited manual-inspection effort toward the
lowest-ranked accounts first, rather than relying only on user abuse reports.

The mechanism starts from a small set of trust seeds — accounts manually confirmed non-Sybil —
and distributes an initial amount of trust equally among them. It then runs power iteration (a
standard technique for repeatedly propagating a value across a graph by matrix multiplication) to
simulate a random walk: at each iteration, every node splits its current trust evenly among its
neighbors and sums what its neighbors send it. This is run for w = O(log n) iterations, where n
is the node count, and then stopped before the walk reaches its true stationary distribution — an
early-terminated random walk. Because Sybil accounts are assumed to connect to the honest region
through only a limited number of attack edges (edges between a Sybil and a non-Sybil user), that
narrow connection is a bottleneck: trust seeded in the non-Sybil region cannot yet spread
uniformly into the Sybil region within O(log n) steps, so non-Sybil users retain higher
degree-normalized trust (a node's trust divided by its own degree) than Sybil users at
termination. SybilRank ranks nodes by degree-normalized trust rather than raw trust, which the
paper states removes a Sybil's advantage from artificially inflating its own degree and gives
each non-Sybil node close to the same degree-normalized score, since after O(log n) power
iterations trust within the well-connected non-Sybil region approaches its own local stationary
distribution (trust proportional to degree).

Because a single well-connected OSN often contains multiple weakly-interconnected communities,
SybilRank additionally applies the Louvain community-detection method to partition the graph and
places multiple trust seeds inside each detected community (in the deployment, roughly 100 nodes
inspected total across communities in an 11-million-node graph), rather than seeding trust only
in one dominant community; this prevents communities distant from a single seed set from being
starved of trust and misclassified as Sybil. A final stage annotates ranked-list intervals with
the measured proportion of confirmed fakes within each interval (from manual sampling), letting
the operator choose where in the ranked list to spend inspection effort or how often to issue
CAPTCHAs, rather than relying on a single Sybil/non-Sybil cutoff, which the paper states no
social-graph defense can currently produce with an acceptable false-positive rate.

The paper proves (Theorem 1, full proof in a companion technical report not examined here) that
when an attacker establishes g attack edges at random into a fast-mixing (mixing time O(log n))
non-Sybil region, the total count of Sybils that rank above non-Sybil users, summed over the
whole network, is O(g log n) — a bound the paper states holds for any number of trust seeds.

### Measured results

| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| Deployed on the complete Tuenti social graph: 1,421,367,504 edges, 11,291,486 nodes, 11,216,357 in the giant connected component; 595 communities found via Louvain, 25 of them >100K nodes; ~100 nodes manually inspected total to pick trust seeds | Tuenti (Spain's largest OSN at the time), snapshot from August 2011 |
| Of the 2,000 lowest-ranked users manually inspected, 100% were confirmed fake | Same Tuenti deployment |
| Across the lowest 200K ranked users (sampled 100 users per 50K-user interval, up to 650K users disclosed), ~90% were confirmed fake, versus ~5% for Tuenti's existing user-abuse-report method — stated as an 18-fold efficiency increase | Same deployment; described by the authors as directly related to the precision metric from collaborative filtering |
| Fake proportion falls abruptly above the 200K mark: ~90% → ~50% → ~10% moving up the ranked list | Same deployment |
| Simulated ranking quality: at 1,500 attack edges into a 5,000-node Sybil region on the Facebook sample (regular-attack topology), a non-Sybil node still ranks above a random Sybil with 70% probability (area under the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve) | Facebook sample graph (10,000 nodes, 40,013 edges), 50 trust seeds, averaged over 100 runs |
| SybilRank outperforms SybilLimit, SybilInfer, Mislove's community detection (CD), GateKeeper, and EigenTrust on area under the ROC curve and on false positive/negative rates, across regular and scale-free attack structures on all 8 test graphs | 8 social graphs from Table 1 (sizes 7,115–18,772 nodes), Sybil region of 5,000 nodes with attack-edge count varied from a small value up to a value large enough to degrade all schemes; d=4 non-attack edges per Sybil; 20% fixed false-rate pivot for ROC comparisons; 100 runs averaged |
| EigenTrust has "at least 20% higher false positive and negative rates than SybilRank in most of the attack scenarios" | Same simulation setup |

| EigenTrust concentrates high degree-normalized trust near seeds (>9,400 of 10,000 non-Sybil nodes fall below trust value 2 at distance >2 hops); SybilRank keeps roughly uniform degree-normalized trust regardless of seed distance | Synthetic scale-free graph, regular attack with 10,000 attack edges, 5 seeds, total trust set to 2m |
| In a 5-community synthetic graph (one 2,000-node core plus four 2,000-node satellite communities linked to the core by 500 edges each, average degree 10), distributing 50 seeds across all communities (10 each) outperforms confining all 50 seeds to the core community, for SybilRank, EigenTrust, and Mislove's CD alike; SybilRank remains most accurate under both seeding strategies | Synthetic multi-community graph, attack edges varied 0–5,000 |
| Under a targeted attack (200 attack edges connected to the k non-Sybil nodes nearest a trust seed, k varied 1,000–10,000), all schemes degrade as k shrinks (attack edges concentrate nearer the seed); SybilRank degrades least but still degrades at small k | Facebook graph, 5,000-node regular-attack Sybil region |
| Hadoop/MapReduce prototype processes a 160-million-node synthetic scale-free graph in under 33 hours, with execution time increasing almost linearly with graph size across sizes from 10M to 160M nodes, using O(log n) power iterations | Amazon EC2 cluster of 11 m1.large instances (1 master, 10 slaves) |
| Mean random-walk length needed to reach a fixed total variation distance of 0.01 from the stationary distribution is much longer for confirmed Sybils than for random users in the same community (random-user walks mostly <100 steps) | 25 Louvain-detected Tuenti communities >100K nodes; 1,000 random users and 100 confirmed Sybils sampled per community |

### Parameters
- Power iterations w: set to O(log n); the paper does not report the specific integer used for the Tuenti deployment (11.2M-node graph) beyond the asymptotic form, stating only that measured Sybil random-walk lengths (Figure 11) exceeded the power-iteration count SybilRank actually used.
- Trust seeds K: 50 used in the main simulated comparisons (1 chosen from the top-10 highest-degree non-Sybil nodes, 49 random non-Sybil nodes); for schemes supporting only a single seed, 1 randomly chosen top-10-degree node is used for a fair comparison. In the Tuenti deployment, seeds are chosen per Louvain-detected community after manual verification of ~4 candidate nodes per community (25 communities >100K nodes).
- Attack-edge count g: varied per experiment; up to 1,500 (Facebook, regular attack) and up to 15,000 (synthetic scale-free graph) in the ranking-quality comparison; 10,000 in the seed-distance experiment; 0–5,000 in the multi-community experiment; 200 in the targeted-attack experiment.
- Non-attack (intra-Sybil) edges per Sybil, d: fixed at 4 in the main attack-strategy simulations; varied 4–40 in the EigenTrust-comparison experiment (Figure 7).
- Sybil region size: fixed at 5,000 nodes in all simulated attacks, described as chosen to "stress-test each scheme."
- ROC fixed false-rate pivot: 20%, used to compute the corresponding other false rate for comparison across schemes.
- Total variation distance for mixing-time measurement: 0.01, used to define the walk length compared between Sybils and random users in each Tuenti community.
- EigenTrust reset probability: 0.15, run to convergence (not early-terminated), following the cited EigenTrust paper's own setting.

### Stated limitations
The paper states SybilRank's central limitation is inherent to the open nature of OSNs: a fake
account that succeeds in befriending many real users accumulates trust and is ranked as non-Sybil,
which is why the fake proportion in the Tuenti-ranked list falls sharply above the 200K mark. It
states that no social-graph-based Sybil defense, including SybilRank, can currently produce a
binary Sybil/non-Sybil classification with an acceptable false-positive rate, so a fixed
ranked-list pivot cannot substitute for manual inspection — SybilRank instead reports the fake
proportion per ranked-list interval so an operator can allocate inspection effort. It states its
own security guarantee (Theorem 1) is derived under the assumption that attack edges are placed
uniformly at random by the Sybils, not under the more effective targeted-attack strategy of
placing attack edges close to trust seeds; the paper's own targeted-attack experiment (Section 6.5)
shows all schemes, including SybilRank, degrade as the targeting gets closer to the seed. It states
that whether real social networks' non-Sybil mixing time is truly O(log n), or has an unknown
larger constant factor, or grows faster than O(log n), is unresolved, citing two independent
measurement studies that found some social networks mix slower than expected; SybilRank's
robustness to this uncertainty is qualified, not eliminated — the paper states SybilRank does not
depend on the absolute mixing time value, only on the non-Sybil region mixing faster than the full
graph including Sybils, but concedes that using too few iterations relative to the true non-Sybil
mixing time risks starving trust to non-Sybil users poorly connected to any seed. For the Tuenti
deployment, the paper states it could not evaluate SybilRank with the same false positive/negative
and ROC metrics used in simulation, because manually labeling ground truth at Tuenti's scale was
infeasible, and states it could not disclose the exact fraction of network-wide fakes SybilRank
misses, citing confidentiality constraints. It states pre-processing (pruning extremely-high-degree
nodes' edges and deferring very recent accounts) was required before applying SybilRank to Tuenti
to control two identified sources of error — well-maintained high-degree fakes and low-connectivity
new honest accounts — meaning the deployed system is not the unmodified base algorithm.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Requires the operator to hold the complete social graph as an undirected graph, and requires an
initial manually verified set of non-Sybil trust seeds (drawn per detected community, not
globally) before the mechanism can run at all. Requires the non-Sybil region of the graph to be
well-connected, non-bipartite, and fast-mixing relative to the full graph including Sybils
(mixing time strictly less than that of the full graph), which is a property of the graph
structure that must be verified for a given deployment, not assumed by construction — the paper's
own Tuenti section measures an approximation of this gap rather than asserting it. Requires Sybils
to be limited in the number of attack edges they can form into the non-Sybil region; the paper
states this assumption can fail if fake accounts can cheaply befriend large numbers of real users,
and that the mechanism's accuracy specifically degrades for accounts that do so, regardless of any
other property of the account. Requires a downstream process (human review, or an automated
challenge such as a CAPTCHA) to consume the ranked list and its per-interval fake-proportion
annotations, because SybilRank itself produces a ranking and an approximate fake-density curve,
not an admission or suspension decision. Community detection (the paper uses the Louvain method)
must be re-run to identify the graph's community structure before seed placement, adding an O(m)
preprocessing cost (m = edge count) ahead of the O(n log n) trust-propagation and ranking cost.

### Contradicts
None found among the papers in this corpus. This entry corrects a claim commonly associated with
this line of work: SybilRank's security guarantee (Theorem 1) is stated only for the case where
attack edges are placed uniformly at random; the paper's own experiments (Section 6.5) show
detection accuracy is measurably worse under a targeted-attack placement strategy, so a categorical
claim that SybilRank bounds Sybil rank under any adversarial edge-placement strategy is not
supported by this paper.

## [CASH-CCS-15] Leakage-Abuse Attacks Against Searchable Encryption

**Citation:** David Cash, Paul Grubbs, Jason Perry, Thomas Ristenpart. "Leakage-Abuse Attacks Against Searchable Encryption." ACM CCS, 2015. DOI 10.1145/2810103.2813700.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://eprint.iacr.org/2016/718.pdf
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2016/718.pdf
**Domain:** G

### What it does
Searchable encryption (SE) lets a client store encrypted documents at a server and query them by keyword without revealing plaintext, at the cost of a defined leakage profile: information the server sees during upload and search even under the scheme's security proof. This paper builds attacks that recover a client's query keywords or plaintext content from that leakage alone, given a stated amount of auxiliary knowledge, without breaking any cryptographic primitive.

The paper defines four leakage profiles ordered by amount of information revealed, L1 (least) to L4 (most). L1 (query-revealed occurrence pattern) leaks, for each queried keyword, the set of document identifiers containing it (the access pattern), revealed only for queried terms. L2 (fully-revealed occurrence pattern) leaks the same occurrence sets for every term in the corpus, not only queried ones, but not the order of terms within a document. L3 adds the within-document order of first keyword occurrence. L4 leaks the full plaintext under a deterministic word-substitution cipher (every occurrence, not just first, visible).

The count attack (query recovery, targets L1) assumes the adversarial server additionally knows, for every keyword in a fixed vocabulary, the number of documents in the true corpus containing that keyword (`count(w)`). A keyword with a document-count value not shared by any other keyword is recovered immediately by matching the observed query's result-set size to that unique count. Remaining queries are recovered by iteratively comparing observed co-occurrence counts between pairs of queries against the co-occurrence counts computable from the known document set, eliminating candidate keywords whose co-occurrence count does not match; the process repeats until no further query is disambiguated. The attack needs no known queries and no numerical optimization, unlike the prior IKK attack (Islam, Kuzu, Kantarcioglu, NDSS 2012), which uses simulated annealing to match an observed co-occurrence matrix to a known one and requires some fraction of queries to be known in advance.

The generalized count attack extends this to two adversary-knowledge deficits. First, index padding (the client pads each keyword's document-count entry up to a multiple of an integer n, so multiple keywords may share a padded count): the attack tolerates false co-occurrences up to a bounded window and bootstraps candidate queries by brute-force guessing rather than requiring an initial unique-count match. Second, partial document knowledge (the server holds only a fraction of the true document set): the adversary estimates each keyword's true document count with a Hoeffding-inequality confidence interval computed from the known subset, and prunes candidate keywords whose interval excludes the observed query result size.

The plaintext recovery attacks (target L2 and L3) exploit a server that knows the plaintext of a small number of stored documents (known-document attack) or can insert chosen documents into the client's store (chosen-document, active attack). Under L3 (keyword order preserved), the server reads keyword hashes directly off the known plaintext's position-ordered ciphertext. Under L2 (keyword order randomized per document), a known document only narrows a keyword hash to the set of hashes appearing in that document; the chosen-document variant plants documents whose keywords are drawn to have maximally separated frequency ranks (computed from an auxiliary corpus, related or unrelated to the target), then matches observed hash frequency ranks in the client's uploaded data to the planted keywords' known ranks.

### Measured results

| Attack | Dataset | Conditions | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| IKK (reproduced) | Enron, 150 employees' sent mail, 30,109 docs, 50 MB on disk | 150 unique queries, 15% of queries known, vocabulary swept 500-6500 keywords, 25 trials (15 above 3500 keywords, since one 6500-keyword trial takes over 10 hours) | Recovery near-perfect at 500 keywords, falls with vocabulary size; performs poorly above 5000 keywords |
| Count attack | Enron, same setup | 10% of keywords queried, no known queries, vocabulary swept 500-6500 keywords, 25 trials | Outperforms IKK at every vocabulary size tested; worst trial at 6500 keywords failed to reconstruct only 5 of 650 keywords |
| IKK vs. count, known-query sensitivity | Enron, m=4500 keywords, 150 unique queries | 15% of queries known vs. 5% known | IKK recovers ~25% of queries at 15% known, drops to 0% at 5% known |
| Count attack under index padding | Enron and Apache "java-user" mailing list (2001-2011, ~38,000 emails, 244 MB on disk) | 5000 keywords, 10% queried, 25 trials (5 random paddings x 5 query transcripts) | Reconstruction unaffected up to index-size expansion of ~140% (Enron) / ~330% (Apache); at over 500% expansion, Enron attack still learns all keywords in half of trials; implementation fails completely above 700% expansion |
| Count attack under partial document knowledge | Enron, 500 keywords, 150 queries | Server knows 50-100% of true document set, 25+ trials (5 document subsets x 5 query transcripts) | Outperforms IKK at every knowledge level tested; below 99% document knowledge IKK performs quite poorly; at 50% knowledge the count attack's false-positive rate exceeds its recovery rate |
| Known-document plaintext recovery (L3) | Enron and Apache | Adversary knows 2 or 20 random documents, cumulative recovery rate over 10 selections per condition | In the Apache dataset, with only 2 known documents, 80% of all documents have 20% of their keywords exposed |
| Known-document plaintext recovery, non-random known document | Enron | Single company-wide announcement email, 500 recipients, 832 unique keywords | Average of 35% of indexed keywords recovered across every document in the corpus |
| Chosen-document attack, hash order unknown (L2) | Apache and Enron | 5000 keywords; two settings: 50/50 split of one dataset (server trains on half, client uploads the other half) and cross-dataset (Enron frequencies attack Apache and vice versa); documents of size k=0-20 keywords, 10 runs per setting for the 50/50 case | For the 50/50 split, error rate exceeds recovery rate above k≈19 keywords per planted document; cross-dataset recovery starts lower than 50/50-split recovery but its error rate is not worse, indicating consistent word-frequency rank across the two corpora |

### Parameters
- Vocabulary size (fixed per experiment, most common stemmed keywords after 200-stopword removal): swept 500 to 6500; typical value 5000.
- Fraction of queries known to the adversary (IKK only): 14-15% in the reproduced experiments, versus 0% for the count attack.
- Fraction of keywords queried: 10% in the main count-attack comparison.
- Padding multiple n (index-expansion factor): swept 1x to 8x (0% to 700% expansion).
- Fraction of true document set known to server: swept 50% to 100% in 10% increments.
- Hoeffding-inequality confidence parameter used in the partial-knowledge count attack: ε = sqrt(0.5 · n · log 40), giving a 95% confidence interval on a keyword's true document count.
- Chosen-document size k (keywords per planted document): swept 0 to 20.

### Stated limitations
The attacks require the server to already hold a leakage profile of L1 or greater and, for the count attack, explicit or statistical knowledge of the true document set's keyword-occurrence counts; a server with zero prior document knowledge and disjoint query and training corpora causes both the IKK attack and the count attack to fail completely (the paper's own tested "unknown documents" case). The generalized count attack under partial knowledge shows a sharp accuracy floor: below 60% document knowledge, tightening candidate pruning with confidence intervals performs worse than a coarser worst-case window, because the co-occurrence estimate is higher-dimensional and needs more samples than a single keyword-count estimate to reach comparable accuracy. The authors state active insertion under L3 is "obviously very damaging" and do not further analyze it, leaving its quantification to future work. The authors state a future statistical attack, not yet demonstrated, might succeed even in the disjoint-corpus setting or above 700% padding overhead. The authors state L1 is not proven safe in general: when a large fraction of possible keywords is queried, L1 leakage approaches L2 leakage in practical exposure.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A design using searchable encryption for network-hosted content must state, for its actual index construction, which of the four leakage profiles (L1-L4) it produces, since the attacks in this paper apply differently by profile: L1 requires the adversary already possess or estimate the true document-count-per-keyword to mount the count attack; L2 and L3 are vulnerable to known-document and chosen-document attacks with no separate count knowledge needed. Any content-addressed or peer-served index that lets an adversarial peer observe repeated queries against a corpus it also holds, even partially, supplies the exact precondition (partial document knowledge, observed access pattern) these attacks use; the paper's own experiments show partial knowledge as low as 50% is already exploitable via the confidence-interval attack. A scheme relying on per-query result-length hiding to defend against this must hide the count in a way immune to the padding attack's own bypass point: expansion above roughly 140-330% (dataset-dependent) is required before this paper's count attack degrades, and the paper's own implementation still partially recovers keywords up to 500% expansion.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus. The paper's own count attack strictly dominates the IKK attack (Islam, Kuzu, Kantarcioglu, NDSS 2012) on every metric tested in this paper, which corrects any claim that IKK represents the strongest available leakage-abuse attack against L1-leakage SE.

### References worth retrieving
- foundational: R. Curtmola, J. A. Garay, S. Kamara, R. Ostrovsky. "Searchable symmetric encryption: improved definitions and efficient constructions." ACM CCS, 2006.
- foundational: M. S. Islam, M. Kuzu, M. Kantarcioglu. "Access pattern disclosure on searchable encryption: Ramification, attack and mitigation." NDSS, 2012. (the IKK attack this paper directly extends)
- competing: D. Cash, S. Jarecki, C. S. Jutla, H. Krawczyk, M.-C. Rosu, M. Steiner. "Highly-scalable searchable symmetric encryption with support for boolean queries." CRYPTO, 2013.
- competing: D. Cash, J. Jaeger, S. Jarecki, C. S. Jutla, H. Krawczyk, M.-C. Rosu, M. Steiner. "Dynamic searchable encryption in very-large databases: Data structures and implementation." NDSS, 2014.
- attack: O. Goldreich, R. Ostrovsky. "Software protection and simulation on oblivious RAMs." Journal of the ACM, 1996. (ORAM, cited as the stronger but slower alternative to SE)
- competing: W. He, D. Akhawe, S. Jain, E. Shi, D. Song. "Shadowcrypt: Encrypted web applications for everyone." ACM CCS, 2014.
- competing: B. Lau, S. Chung, C. Song, Y. Jang, W. Lee, A. Boldyreva. "Mimesis aegis: A mimicry privacy shield." USENIX Security, 2014.

### Verbatim extracts
- "we present a characterization of the leakage profiles of in-the-wild searchable encryption products"
- "the count attack is not given any known queries"
- "worst trial the count attack failed to reconstruct only 5 of 650 keywords"
- "recovery rate drops from 85% to 65% at the first increment of added noise" (describing IKK's own result under co-occurrence noise, not this paper's count attack)
- "unless the server has access to 99% of the true document data, the IKK attack performs quite poorly"
- "80% of the documents will have 20% of their keywords exposed"
- "it is dangerous to attempt to protect queries on known document sets using SE schemes"

## [CASTRO-OSDI-02] Secure Routing for Structured Peer-to-Peer Overlay Networks
**Citation:** Miguel Castro, Peter Druschel, Ayalvadi Ganesh, Antony Rowstron, Dan S. Wallach. "Secure Routing for Structured Peer-to-Peer Overlay Networks." USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation (OSDI), 2002.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://people.mpi-sws.org/~druschel/publications/security.pdf
**Source URL:** https://people.mpi-sws.org/~druschel/publications/security.pdf
**Domain:** A

### What it does
This paper makes a structured peer-to-peer overlay (a network in which each node holds a small routing table and a lookup for a key is forwarded hop by hop toward the node or nodes responsible for that key) deliver a message to every correct replica root for a key with high probability, even when a bounded fraction of nodes actively try to prevent delivery. It decomposes the problem into three mechanisms, each closing one attack the paper demonstrates against overlays that lack it.

First, certified node-identifier (nodeId) assignment: a set of certification authorities (CAs), which can be offline and uninvolved in day-to-day operation, sign a certificate binding a node's randomly assigned nodeId to its public key and IP address. This stops an attacker from choosing a nodeId, which the paper shows otherwise lets an attacker place itself as the sole custodian of a target key's replicas or as every routing-table entry of a targeted victim.

Second, a constrained routing table alongside the normal proximity-optimized one: every constrained-table slot must hold the live nodeId numerically closest to a publicly computable point in the identifier space, a rule independent of network-measured proximity and therefore not manipulable by an attacker who intercepts or fakes proximity probes. The paper demonstrates that without this constraint, an attacker's routing-table updates propagate malicious entries faster than honest ones do, and derives that the fraction of faulty entries in a node's table after processing one further update is at least (1 − f)·f + f, strictly greater than the starting fraction f, so repeated updates push the faulty fraction toward one.

Third, secure message forwarding: a node routes a lookup using the fast proximity-aware table, then applies a routing failure test to the returned set of prospective replica roots. The test compares the average numerical distance between consecutive nodeIds in the sender's own neighbor set (call it µ_p) against the same statistic computed over the returned prospective root set (µ_rn), because faulty nodeIds cluster less densely than the full honest population would. The set is accepted (test returns negative) only if every certificate in it is valid and µ_rn ≤ µ_p × γ, where γ is a tunable threshold. If the test returns positive, or if no response arrives before a timeout, the sender falls back to redundant routing: it sends r message copies through r different members of its own neighbor set (a technique the paper calls neighbor set anycast for overlays, such as Pastry and Chord, whose replica roots cluster in one node's neighbor set rather than spreading uniformly over the identifier space), collects signed certificates from any node that reports the destination's root in its own neighbor set, and iterates up to three times to assemble the definitive replica set.

### Measured results

| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| Probability of routing to a correct replica root drops from near 1 at f=0 to 65% at f=10%, for N=100,000 nodes | Pastry, closed-form model σ ≈ (1−f)^(log_2b N), b=4, validated against simulation with error below 2% (Figure 3) |
| At f=20% and N=100,000, success probability is 65% with b=4 and 75% with b=6 (larger b reduces hop count at the cost of larger routing tables) | Same closed-form model applied to Pastry/Tapestry-style routing with varying base b |
| Chord (fixed b=1) reaches only 42% success at f=20%, N=100,000, under the same model | Same model, Chord's fixed digit base |
| Routing-failure-test minimum error rate α=β=0.0008 at γ=1.72 | Simulation, 100,000 random nodeIds, f=c=0.3 (fraction and collusion bound both 0.3), n=256 distance samples at sender, k=l=32 root-neighbor samples |
| Under a nodeId-suppression attack (attacker leaves the overlay to thin nodeId density near the sender or the root neighbor set), minimum achievable error exceeds 0.001 once c ≥ 0.2, even with 256 samples | Simulation, same 100,000-node setup, c=f swept |
| At γ=1.23, l=32, 256 samples, target false-negative rate β=0.001: false-positive rate α=0.12 without a nodeId-suppression attack and α=0.77 under a nodeId-suppression attack, at c=0.3 | Simulation, 100,000 nodeIds |
| Probability of reaching all correct replica roots via redundant routing with neighbor set anycast exceeds 0.999 for f ≤ 0.3 | Simulation and closed-form model, N=100,000, b=4, l=r=32 |
| Overall reliability target Σ > 0.999 achievable for f ≤ 0.18 with γ=1.8, l=16 (redundant routing invoked only 0.5% of the time when there are no faults); for f ≤ 0.25 with γ=1.58, l=32 (redundant routing invoked 0.4% of the time with no faults) | Simulation, N=100,000, two named parameter scenarios |
| Extra bandwidth for a negative routing-failure test: 5.6 KB with l=32, 2.9 KB with l=16 (message headers excluded) | Computed from message counts and PSS-R signature sizes: 1024-bit modulus nodeId certificates at 128 bytes each |
| Redundant routing, best case (all root neighbors gathered in one round): 22 KB extra bandwidth with l=32, 7 KB with l=16; under attack: fewer than 451 messages with l=32, f=0.25, fewer than 188 messages with l=16, f=0.18, with roughly 12 KB (l=32) or 1 KB (l=16) of additional bytes for nodeId lists | Same 100,000-node analytic setting, PSS-R 64-byte signed nonces |
| Checked iterative routing (rejected alternative): minimum hop-test error α=β≈0.35 at c=0.3, 256 samples; combining it with Pastry's constrained routing table improved end-to-end success from below 0.3 to 0.4 at c=0.3, N=100,000, b=4, l=32, but added 2.7 extra hops per route on average from false positives | Simulation, same 100,000-node setting |
| BFT-replica-group correctness: with r=32 replicas and f=0.2 (20% of overlay nodes compromised), probability that a given replica group of 32 has fewer than 1/3 faulty replicas is under 93%; combined with routing success this yields only 72% overall probability of correctly reaching a 32-node replica group at N=100,000 | Closed-form binomial-distribution calculation, cited as the reason the paper's own authors rejected a Lynch-Malkhi-Ratajczak-style full-BFT-replicated-overlay alternative |

The paper's own headline conclusion: the combination of certified nodeIds, constrained routing tables, and the routing-failure-test-plus-redundant-routing primitive "allow us to tolerate up to 25% malicious nodes while providing good performance when the fraction of compromised nodes is small" — stated as the paper's summary claim, distinct from and not identical to any single numbered figure above; treat it as the paper's own qualitative headline, not an additional independent data point.

### Parameters
- f: fraction of nodes in the overlay that are faulty/malicious.
- c: upper bound on the fraction of faulty nodes that can collude (c ≤ 1, and α, β are shown to depend on c but not on f directly).
- γ: routing-failure-test threshold controlling the tradeoff between false-positive rate α and false-negative rate β; values used in experiments range from 1.23 to 1.8 depending on target security level.
- l: neighbor set size (also root-neighbor-set size k in most experiments, k=l); values tested: 16, 32, 64, 128, 256 as sample counts, with l itself tested at 16 and 32 for the end-to-end scenarios.
- n: number of nodeId-distance samples the sender uses to compute µ_p; tested at 32, 64, 128, 256, with 256 used as the paper's primary operating point.
- b: digit base for the routing table (controls table size versus hop count); tested at b=4 (Pastry's typical default) and b=6; Chord is fixed at b=1.
- N: overlay size; tested at 1,000, 10,000, 100,000, and 1,000,000 for the base routing-success model, with 100,000 used for all routing-failure-test and redundant-routing simulations.
- r: number of redundant-routing message copies sent per lookup, set equal to l in the reported experiments.

### Stated limitations
The paper states explicitly that "the security and performance of our techniques was fully evaluated only in the context of Pastry; a full evaluation of the techniques in other protocols is future work" — the CAN, Chord, and Tapestry adaptations described are design sketches, not evaluated implementations. The paper states the routing failure test's own accuracy is undermined by a nodeId suppression attack it identifies as "unavoidable": an attacker can leave the overlay to thin nodeId density near the sender (raising the false-negative rate β) or near the destination root (raising the false-positive rate α), can alternate between the two, and the paper states honest nodes have no way of detecting which mode is in effect. The paper states two further routing-failure-test attacks — collecting certificates of departed nodes to inflate a set's apparent density, and mixing controlled and correct nodeIds within one prospective root set — and offers a mitigating certificate-confirmation protocol but does not fully close either. The paper states its own hop-test variant of checked iterative routing has a high minimum error (≈0.35) because it relies on a single density sample at each hop, and rejects the technique after finding no measurable improvement when combined with redundant routing, attributing the failure to iterative routes being less independent of one another than recursive routes. The paper states it does not have a model for the effect of proximity-manipulation attacks on the locality-aware (non-constrained) routing table, and states only a belief, not a proof, that such attacks are hard to mount for small f. The self-certifying-data reduction the paper proposes does not remove the need for secure routing when inserting new objects, verifying an object's absence, or handling node joins — the paper states these cases still require the full secure routing primitive.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The certified-nodeId mechanism requires an external certification-authority infrastructure whose public keys are distributed out of band (the paper suggests bundling them with node software, as browsers bundle root certificates), and requires a certificate-revocation or reissuance path for any node whose IP address changes, since the paper binds nodeId certificates to IP addresses specifically to block certificate-swapping among colluding attacker-controlled nodes. The constrained-routing-table mechanism requires that the overlay's routing table slots be defined by a public, verifiable function of node identifiers (a point p in the identifier space), which forecloses proximity as the sole neighbor-selection criterion for that table; a system wanting both proximity optimization and this defense must maintain two separate tables, as this paper does. The routing failure test requires every node in a neighbor or root-neighbor set to hold a valid nodeId certificate that the testing node can check, so it depends on the certified-nodeId mechanism as a precondition — the test's stated accuracy figures (the α/β values in the measured-results table) hold only once nodeIds are already unforgeable. Self-certifying data as a way to reduce reliance on secure routing requires an independent per-object integrity mechanism (a content hash or an owner signature) supplied by the application layer, since routing itself does not embed integrity checking; the mutable-object extension the paper sketches additionally requires a Byzantine-fault-tolerant replication algorithm run by the replica group holding the object.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus. Cross-reference: URDANETA-CSUR-11 (the survey citing this paper) restates several of these figures (the 0.77/0.12 false-positive pair, the 2.7-extra-hops figure, the Condie et al. 80%-poisoning figure attributed to a different paper) faithfully to the conditions given here; a downstream synthesis step should cite this entry, not the survey's paraphrase, for any of the numbers in the table above.

### References worth retrieving
- Sit, Morris. "Security considerations for peer-to-peer distributed hash tables." IPTPS 2002. — foundational, the attack taxonomy (node lookup, routing-table maintenance, network partitioning) this paper builds its threat model from, and the source of the iterative-routing idea this paper adapts and then rejects
- Douceur. "The Sybil attack." IPTPS 2002. — foundational, defines the Sybil attack this paper's certified-nodeId defense responds to

## [CASTRO-SOSP-03] SplitStream: High-Bandwidth Multicast in Cooperative Environments
**Citation:** Miguel Castro, Peter Druschel, Anne-Marie Kermarrec, Animesh Nandi, Antony Rowstron, Atul Singh. "SplitStream: High-Bandwidth Multicast in Cooperative Environments." ACM Symposium on Operating Systems Principles (SOSP), 2003.
**Retrieved:** full text
**Source URL:** target record (registry/targets-deduped.json)
**Domain:** L (also relevant to K, application-layer patterns: peer-assisted video)

### What it does
SplitStream distributes the forwarding load of live multicast (one source sending the same stream to many receivers) evenly across all participating peers, instead of concentrating it on a small set of interior tree nodes, so that every peer can be asked to forward only as much data as it receives. The source splits the content into k stripes (for example, k separately encoded portions of a video stream, produced by multiple description coding, or k erasure-coded blocks of a file). Each stripe is multicast over its own tree, built with Scribe (an application-level multicast system layered on the Pastry structured overlay: each node has a random nodeId, and a multicast tree for a group is the union of Pastry routing paths from each member to a pseudo-random groupId). SplitStream chooses each stripe's groupId (called the stripeId) so the k stripeIds differ in their most significant digit; because Pastry routes messages toward nodes sharing a longer prefix with the destination key, this forces the trees' sets of interior (forwarding) nodes to be disjoint by construction, so a node that forwards stripe i is necessarily a leaf, not an interior node, in every other stripe's tree. To bound a node's outbound bandwidth (its number of children across all trees, i.e., its forwarding capacity), a node that has reached its outdegree limit rejects one existing child (a "push-down") when a new child requests to join, favoring rejection of children in stripes that do not share a prefix with the node's own nodeId; the rejected child then either finds a new parent among its former siblings (recursively) or anycasts to a "spare capacity group" of nodes with unused forwarding capacity, located via a depth-first search over that group's own Scribe tree so the located parent is near the orphan in the underlying physical network.

### Measured results
| Metric | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Node stress during forest construction, 40,000-node overlay, GATech topology (transit-stub, 5,050 routers) | 16x16 config: max 2,971, mean 57.2, median 49.9; 16x18: max 1,089, mean 52.6, median 47.4; 16x32: max 663, mean 35.3, median 30.9; 16xNB (unbounded): max 472, mean 16.9, median 12; dxd: max 2,532, mean 42.1, median 36.6; Gnutella-derived bandwidth distribution: max 1,054, mean 56.7, median 54.2 | b=4, k=16 stripes, leaf-set size l=16, averaged over 10 randomly seeded GATech topologies; node stress = messages received per node |
| Link stress during forest construction, same setup | 16x16: max 5,893, mean 74.1, median 52.6, 99% of links used; 16xNB: max 1,804, mean 21.2, median 17, 94% of links used | Same conditions; results within about 10% higher on the Mercator topology (102,639 routers) and about 10% lower on the CorpNet topology (298 routers) |
| SplitStream forest construction vs. centralized server distributing the same file, 40,000 nodes | Maximum node stress during construction is 13.5x lower than a centralized server's node stress (which equals the client count, 40,000); maximum link stress is at least 6.8x lower than a centralized system | 16x16 configuration, GATech, 40,000 nodes |
| Multicast link stress comparison, 40,000 nodes, GATech, 16x16 configuration | SplitStream uses 98% of topology links (mean stress 20.5, max 1,411); IP multicast and centralized unicast use 43% of links (IP mean 16); Scribe uses 47% of links (mean 39.6, max 3,990) | Single multicast to all 40,000 nodes; average link stress on links SplitStream uses is 28% worse than IP multicast's, vs. 247% worse for Scribe |
| Multicast link stress comparison on other topologies | Average stress on links SplitStream uses is at most 13% worse than IP multicast on CorpNet and at most 37% worse on Mercator; Scribe's average link stress is 203% worse than IP multicast on CorpNet and 337% worse on Mercator | Same 40,000-node setup, same configuration |
| Delay penalty (RAD, ratio of average delay via stripe tree to average delay via IP multicast) | Increases as spare capacity decreases; RMD (ratio of maximum delays) peaked at 5.4 on GATech and 4.6 on CorpNet across the 16 stripes; without physical-network-proximity-aware routing, average RAD would be approximately 3.8 for 16xNB and higher for other configurations | 40,000 nodes, GATech and CorpNet topologies; delay measured per stripe as the ratio between stripe-tree delivery delay and IP multicast delivery delay |
| Resilience to a single random node failure, 40,000-node forest, GATech | Mean and median number of stripes lost per node is 1 for all configurations; worst-case ancestor failure: 16x16 max 6.8, mean 2.1, median 2; Gnutella-derived config max 7.2, mean 2.4, median 2; 16xNB max 1, mean 1, median 1 | Analysis of path node-disjointness from each node to each stripe's root |
| Catastrophic failure recovery | 2,500 of 10,000 nodes (25%) killed at t=10s; most nodes receive packets on at least 14 of 16 stripes after 30s (one failure-detection period); all nodes receive all stripes within less than 3 minutes; steady-state control overhead before failure is 1.6 messages/second/node | 10,000-node forest, 16x16 configuration, GATech, one data packet per second per stripe, Pastry leaf-set probing tuned for 1% loss rate with a 30s probing period, SplitStream heartbeats every 30s |
| High-churn performance | 99.5% of nodes receive at least 75% of stripes (12 of 16) almost all the time; average stripes received per node between 15 and 16 most of the time; control messages never exceed 4.5/second/node, consuming under 0.17% of a 1 Mb/s data stream's bandwidth | Replayed real Gnutella churn trace: 17,000 unique nodes monitored over 60 hours, 7-minute probing interval, average session time approximately 2.3 hours, 1,300 to 2,700 concurrently active nodes; SplitStream forest created 20 minutes into the trace, 16x20 configuration, GATech topology, one data packet per stripe every 10 seconds |
| PlanetLab live deployment | 72 SplitStream nodes (2 per host) on 36 PlanetLab hosts across the US and Europe; 4 hosts (8 nodes) killed between sequence numbers 32 and 50; 90% of packets received within 1 second delay, 5% experience delay over 2 seconds, maximum observed delay 11.7 seconds | 16x16 configuration, 320 Kbit/s stream, 20-Kbit packets with sequence numbers, one packet/second/stripe, TCP as transport (so lost packets incur retransmission delay), 30-second failure-detection period |

### Parameters
- Number of stripes k = 2^b, tied to the Pastry base parameter b; experiments used b=4, giving k=16 stripes.
- Pastry leaf-set size l=16.
- Node-degree configurations tested: 16x16 (desired indegree 16, forwarding capacity 16, spare capacity 0 beyond stripe-origination exemption), 16x18 (12.5% spare capacity), 16x32 (100% spare capacity), 16xNB (no forwarding-capacity bound), dxd (indegree equals forwarding capacity per node, with each node receiving its "home" stripe with probability 1 and each other stripe with probability 0.5), and a Gnutella-bandwidth-derived configuration (desired indegree = max(1, min(inbound_bandwidth/20 Kbps, 16)), forwarding capacity = min(outbound_bandwidth/20 Kbps, 32), assuming a 320 Kbps stream at 20 Kbps per stripe, sampled from measured Gnutella peer bandwidth distributions, yielding approximately 90% of nodes with desired indegree 16 and a mean spare capacity of 6.9 per node).
- Simulation topologies: GATech (5,050 routers, transit-stub, 10 transit domains averaging 5 routers each, 10 stub domains per transit router averaging 10 routers each, 10 random seeds averaged), Mercator (102,639 routers, 2,662 autonomous systems, hop count as delay proxy), CorpNet (298 routers, measured Microsoft corporate network, link delay = minimum measured delay over one month).
- LAN link delay: 1 ms.
- Implementation optimizations used in simulation: cycle-detection state maintained only at nodes whose parent does not share a longer prefix than the child (reduces construction overhead up to 40%); batched anycasts across multiple stripes per join (reduces anycast count up to 8x); depth-first anycast traversal that avoids revisiting a parent.

### Stated limitations
The correctness and complexity analysis (Section 4.5) assumes all nodes in the node set N join the forest simultaneously, that communication is reliable so all spare capacity is visible in the spare capacity group, and that nodes do not leave voluntarily or through failure; the authors state SplitStream includes mechanisms to handle violations of each assumption but that these mechanisms "may block some" of the guarantees the analysis provides. The bandwidth-bottleneck model assumes the bottleneck between two communicating nodes lies at the sender or receiver access link, not in the network interior; the authors state this does not hold universally and describe extending SplitStream (monitoring per-stripe arrival rate and re-parenting on shortfall) as future work, not implemented. Free-riding (a node that consumes forwarding capacity without contributing its own, cited by the authors as prevalent in Gnutella) is identified as an issue in open cooperative environments; the authors state that discouraging it, beyond local enforcement of the node-degree constraint, would need either a trusted execution platform or an incentive mechanism, and state this explicitly as "an interesting area of future work," not solved in this paper. The Mercator topology has no measured link-delay data, so delay-penalty (RAD/RMD) results are not reported for it. Anycast to the spare capacity group can fail to find a parent even when eligible capacity exists, if every candidate would create a routing cycle with the orphan; the paper's own mechanism to resolve this (finding and displacing a non-descendant leaf in the desired stripe tree) is described but its own success rate under this specific failure mode is not separately measured.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
SplitStream requires a structured peer-to-peer overlay with prefix-based routing (the paper uses Pastry) whose group-communication layer builds each multicast tree as the union of overlay routing paths from members to a group's rootId (the paper uses Scribe); the interior-node-disjoint property is obtained purely by choosing k groupIds that differ in their most significant digit, so it depends on the overlay's routing actually converging by shared key prefix, not by any separate scheduling step. Applications using SplitStream must supply content encoded so each stripe requires approximately equal bandwidth and so the content can be reconstructed from a sufficient subset of stripes (the paper names multiple description coding for streaming media and erasure coding for file data as the two encodings it is designed around); a stripe-splitting scheme without this redundancy property loses playable or reconstructible content whenever any stripe's tree is disrupted. The system needs each node's own nodeId to determine which one stripe it is obligated to forward (the stripe whose stripeId shares its nodeId's leading digit), so nodeId assignment must precede stripe-tree construction. Bounding a node's outbound bandwidth to its stated forwarding capacity is enforced only locally by each node's own SplitStream instance; the mechanism does not verify a node's claimed capacity or degree against any external check, so it requires participant honesty about capacity, or a separate incentive or trusted-execution mechanism supplied elsewhere, to resist a node that falsely advertises high spare capacity or refuses forwarding after joining.

### Contradicts
None found.

- Stoica, Morris, Karger, Kaashoek, Balakrishnan. "Chord: A scalable peer-to-peer lookup service for Internet applications." ACM SIGCOMM 2001. — foundational (Chord, cited as a comparable structured overlay to Pastry).
- Zhao, Kubiatowicz, Joseph. "Tapestry: An infrastructure for fault-resilient wide-area location and routing." UCB TR UCB//CSD-01-1141, 2001. — foundational (Tapestry, cited alternative overlay that Bayeux, a competing multicast system, is built on).

## [CHASE-CCS-19] SEEMless: Secure End-to-End Encrypted Messaging with less Trust

**Citation:** Melissa Chase, Apoorvaa Deshpande, Esha Ghosh, Harjasleen Malvai. "SEEMless: Secure End-to-End Encrypted Messaging with less Trust." ACM CCS, 2019. DOI 10.1145/3319535.3363202.
**Retrieved:** full text via candidate URL `https://eprint.iacr.org/2018/607.pdf`
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2018/607.pdf
**Domain:** E

### What it does
SEEMless lets a user detect whether the messaging provider serving her public key to her contacts is showing everyone the same key (non-equivocation), so a compromised or coerced provider cannot silently insert its own key for a man-in-the-middle attack, while also letting key changes take effect in well under a minute instead of the roughly one-hour delay the paper attributes to prior work. It formalizes a privacy-preserving verifiable key directory (VKD): a stateful directory that, at each discrete round (epoch), accepts a batch of username-to-public-key registrations and updates, and produces a short cryptographic commitment to the current directory state. A client queries the directory for a username and receives the current public key plus a proof that the key is bound to the published commitment, without the proof revealing anything about other users' keys (zero-knowledge, with a well-defined leakage function). The construction keeps two append-only zero-knowledge sets (aZKS) built on a Patricia trie: an "all" aZKS holding every version of every (username, key) pair ever issued, and an "old" aZKS holding retired key versions; verifying that a key is current means proving membership in "all" and non-membership in "old." Both aZKS root commitments are chained into a Merkle tree of per-epoch commitments (replacing the plain hash chain used by CONIKS), which the paper states shortens the audit-proof cost. A verifiable random function (VRF) hides which entry in the trie corresponds to which username by mapping the username to a pseudorandom label, so an observer of the tree structure cannot tell how many times a given user has updated her key without also holding a proof; SEEMless uses three VRF evaluations per query response (versus CONIKS's one) as the mechanism enforcing this stronger label-privacy property. Auditors — any party, not a privileged role — verify between consecutive epochs that the aZKS commitments were correctly appended to the Merkle tree and that both aZKS grew append-only; the paper states one honest auditor per adjacent epoch pair is sufficient for the non-equivocation soundness guarantee to hold. A persistent authenticated data structure ("Persistent Patricia Trie," PPTr) stores only the state of each tree node that actually changed at each epoch, rather than the whole tree, which the paper credits with letting the same construction run entirely in RAM at scales where CONIKS's implementation exhausted memory.

### Measured results
| Metric | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Server update time at 10M registered users | 0.28 s average | 1,000 new registrations and 1,000 key updates per epoch, batch inserted every 100k-user increment; Linux VM, 2.30GHz Intel Xeon E5-2673, 125GB RAM, 64GB JVM heap for server-side |
| aZKS commitment insertion into the epoch Merkle tree | 61 microseconds | After 10M server epochs have passed; cost estimated using the Patricia trie structure from CONIKS as an over-estimate |
| Offline per-request VRF computation cost | 1.3 ms (registration, 1 VRF call) to 2.5 ms (update, 2 VRF calls) | Computed between epochs, not counted against online update time; VRF built on Secp384r1 with Bouncy Castle, Icart's function for hashing to the curve, SHA-384 |
| CONIKS scalability limit in the same test harness | Heap exhaustion at ≈4.5M users | Same Linux VM/JVM configuration as the SEEMless server-update test; CONIKS's Java implementation could not proceed further with frequent epochs, attributed to repeated copying of its Patricia trie |
| Query proof generation/verification time at 10M users | SEEMless: 6.03 ms (server prove) / 10.51 ms (client verify); CONIKS: 2.01 ms / 3.47 ms | Averaged over 100 users, 10 trials each; VRF cost dominates (compute/prove/verify VRF averaged 1.3/1.9/3.4 ms over 5,000 trials, used as simulated constants); SEEMless needs 3 VRF proofs per query vs. CONIKS's 1 |
| Query proof size at 10M users | ≈8,600 bytes average (SEEMless); up to 3x that for CONIKS is stated as the expected ratio because CONIKS uses 1 authentication path vs. SEEMless's 3 | Includes username, public key, key commitment and opening, VRF proof, and Patricia-trie authentication path |
| KeyHistory bandwidth, 10 special users updating 10 times, 1M regular users (R), 1M epochs | SEEMless: ≈1.09 MB per fully-verifying user (vs. ≈1.03 MB at 100k epochs); CONIKS: ≈576.8 MB over the same span | Special users (S) update at regular intervals; regular users (R) register once per epoch as a load control |
| KeyHistory bandwidth, 20 updates over 5 months, 200k epochs fixed, |R|=1M | SEEMless: ≈2.01 MB total to verify full key history, verified in under 0.05 s (excluding VRF cost) | Includes username/key bytes (at least 1,000 bytes per update) sent for the user to verify used values |
| KeyHistory verification time, non-caching, at 100k epochs | CONIKS: over 349 s; SEEMless comparable figure not separately isolated in this row (see Figures 7-8 in source) | 10 special users, 1M regular users, 10 key updates by special users |
| KeyHistory verification time at 1M epochs | CONIKS: 3,495 s without VRF caching, 71 s with caching | Same experiment configuration, increased epoch count |
| KeyHistory verification time, 200k epochs fixed, varying update count | CONIKS: over 699 s without caching, over 14 s with caching (constant regardless of update count since CONIKS's cost is epoch-count-driven) | Same S/R population sizes |
| Client-side VRF cache size after 20 updates over 1M epochs | ≈2.8 KB | Derived from the paper's formula `[2i + 2^(floor(log i)+1) + log t - (floor(log i)+1)] x 32 bytes`, i = number of user updates, t = number of server epochs |
| Server-side VRF-proof cache for 10M users at 20 updates each | ≈28 GB | Caching the VRF proof for each of 10M users' latest key version |
| Server-side VRF-value+proof cache to answer Query without recomputation | 1.44 GB over 10M registered users | 3 x 48-byte VRF value per user (48 bytes = the VRF value size stated), current key only |
| Auditor bandwidth and time per adjacent-epoch audit | Less than 4.24 MB (upper bound, includes double-counted nodes), under 5 MB stated informally, verified in under 0.3 s | Simulated using the actual "all"/"old" aZKS hash-recomputation counts from the 10M-user experiment: under 47k new hashes (0.17 s) for "all," under 17k new hashes (0.05 s) for "old," plus leaf downloads (192 KB) and an upper bound on unchanged-subtree-root downloads (4.04 MB) |

### Parameters
- VRF construction: Secp384r1 elliptic curve, Bouncy Castle library, Icart's function for hashing to the curve, SHA-384, with the input hashed twice (`SHA384(0||input)` and `SHA384(1||input)`) and Icart applied to both hashes, because applying Icart once does not give an output indistinguishable from random.
- VRF value size: 48 bytes.
- VRF calls per operation: 1 for a new registration; 2 for a key update (one for the new key entering the "all" aZKS, one for the old key entering the "old" aZKS); 3 total per Query response in SEEMless versus 1 in CONIKS.
- Epoch length: not fixed by the construction; the paper's own experiments treat half-a-minute epochs as a realistic working assumption (525,600 minutes/year approximated by 1M epochs), and states the epoch length is not bounded by blockchain block time when a blockchain is used only for periodic root-commitment posting.
- Test scale range: up to 10M registered users for Query and server-update experiments; up to 1M "regular" users and 10 "special" users, up to 1M epochs, for KeyHistory experiments.
- Auditing granularity: one audit unit covers one pair of adjacent epochs; parallel auditors can each cover disjoint adjacent-epoch pairs.

### Stated limitations
The paper places specific trust assumptions on users and the surrounding system, listed under "Model Assumptions": it assumes the user's device can store her current secret key but may be lost or re-imaged, losing that secret; it assumes the user has some out-of-band way to authenticate to the service provider (a second factor, e.g., a text message or phone call), stated as already required by existing end-to-end encryption systems and therefore not an added attack surface; it assumes the server enforces access control on who may query whose key; and it assumes the user can recognize approximately when she last updated her key, to notice if the log lists updates she does not recognize. It assumes Alice, Bob, and the server keep approximately synchronized clocks. It assumes some external mechanism (a blockchain post, as in Catena, or a gossip protocol, as in CONIKS) exists so that different users' views of the current root commitment do not silently diverge; the paper explicitly leaves that mechanism outside SEEMless itself. The paper explicitly defers to future work: usability studies for the end-user interface exposing VKD verification, and storage optimizations such as moving inactive users' cached VRF values to disk rather than keeping them all in RAM. Server-side caching of every user's VRF proof (to avoid recomputing on Query) is stated to require ≈28 GB at 10M users with 20 updates each — an increasing, not bounded, cost as update counts grow, which the paper does not resolve inside this construction. The paper states Keybase's competing design assumes users hold multiple trusted devices and manage long-term cryptographic signature keys themselves, and states its own authors' judgment that "for an end user, it is incredibly difficult to manage keys" under that assumption — this is the paper's own stated opinion about a different system's user-facing usability, not a measurement.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A working SEEMless deployment needs at least one honest auditor examining every adjacent pair of epochs; the non-equivocation soundness guarantee is stated as conditional on that minimum, and auditing can be distributed arbitrarily across many independent parties without coordination since each adjacent-epoch check is independent. The system needs an external, out-of-band mechanism ensuring all clients' views of the current root commitment do not fork silently — SEEMless does not supply this itself; the paper names a blockchain post (as in Catena) or a gossip protocol (as in CONIKS) as options, and states client software must periodically interact with whichever mechanism is chosen (for a blockchain option, checking the chain at least as often as the "vulnerability window" the deployment is willing to tolerate, since a misbehaving server is caught only at the next post). The user's client software must persist her current key locally between sessions to detect equivocation, since the whole non-equivocation guarantee depends on the user's own device being the source of truth for what her key currently is; a device that never independently remembers this cannot detect a server showing a different party the wrong key. The system assumes the user or her software has an out-of-band, already-established authentication channel to the service provider (e.g., a second factor) independent of the VKD itself — SEEMless does not create or replace this channel. The server needs synchronized-enough clocks with clients to make epoch boundaries meaningful to all parties. Any component relying on SEEMless's stronger label-privacy property (hiding how many times a user has updated relative to CONIKS) inherits the added VRF cost (3x the VRF calls per query) as an explicit privacy/performance trade-off — a caller not needing that specific privacy property gets no benefit from paying this cost.

### Contradicts
None found against other entries in this corpus. Cross-reference: Parakeet (MALVAI-NDSS-23, same batch) presents its own reimplementation of this paper's aZKS construction and measures markedly worse persistent-storage numbers than SEEMless's own self-reported figures here (Parakeet reports ≈66 minutes, 47 storage accesses, to insert 100k users into a 300k-user set with a MySQL-backed persistent layer, versus this paper's RAM-only 0.28-second update-time figure at 10M users). This is not a contradiction of a shared measurement — the two papers measure different storage backends (SEEMless's own experiments run entirely in RAM; Parakeet's SEEMless reimplementation adds a MySQL persistence layer) and different operations, so the discrepancy reflects added persistent-storage cost, not a disputed figure for the same configuration. A reader combining the two entries should not average or directly compare these two sets of numbers as if they described the same experimental setup.

### References worth retrieving
- Melara, Blankstein, Bonneau, Felten, Freedman. "CONIKS: Bringing Key Transparency to End Users." USENIX Security 2015 (cited as [20]) — foundational; the direct predecessor this paper extends and benchmarks against throughout.
- Bonneau. "EthIKS: Using Ethereum to Audit a CONIKS Key Transparency Log." (cited as [3]) — competing; the paper states EthIKS weakens CONIKS's privacy guarantee and makes per-operation blockchain invocation "quickly infeasible" at scale — a specific cost claim worth independently verifying.
- Tomescu, Devadas. "Catena: Efficient Non-equivocation via Bitcoin." IEEE S&P 2017 (cited as [26]) — competing/complementary; the blockchain-commitment-posting mechanism this paper explicitly proposes integrating with for root-commitment consistency.

- Keybase.io, "Protocol Security Review" and "Managing Teams and Keys with Keybase" (cited as [15], [16]) — competing; the deployed auditable-key-directory system compared on user-key-management assumptions.
