## [CHU-JSAC-02] A Case for End System Multicast
**Citation:** Yang-hua Chu, Sanjay G. Rao, Srinivasan Seshan, Hui Zhang. "A Case for End System Multicast." IEEE Journal on Selected Areas in Communications, 2002.
**Retrieved:** full text
**Source URL:** target record (registry/targets-deduped.json)
**Domain:** L

### What it does
Narada distributes one-to-many data delivery (multicast) among participating end hosts rather than routers, so that no dedicated multicast infrastructure in the network is required. Each participating host implements membership management and packet replication itself. Narada builds the delivery structure in two steps rather than constructing trees directly. First, every member keeps a full list of all other group members (propagated by periodic refresh messages with a monotonically increasing sequence number, exchanged between mesh neighbors and gossiped along the mesh), and members probe random non-neighbor members to compute the utility of adding a direct link (a member's utility contribution is its relative decrease in delay to reach each other member if the link is added); a member adds a link when the expected utility gain exceeds a threshold scaled to group size and current neighbor count, and drops the link with lowest consensus cost (the maximum, across both endpoints' perception, of how many other members use that link as their next hop) when that cost falls below a matching threshold. This produces a richer connected graph, the mesh. Second, Narada runs a distance-vector routing protocol over the mesh (extended with a Border-Gateway-Protocol-like path-vector mechanism to avoid count-to-infinity, and a "Transient Forward" routing cost that keeps a departing member forwarding packets until routes reconverge) to compute, for each source, a reverse-shortest-path spanning tree over the mesh links; a member forwards a packet only if it arrived from that member's designated next hop toward the source, and forwards it onward to every neighbor that uses this member as its own next hop toward that source. For latency-and-bandwidth-sensitive applications such as video conferencing, Narada instead runs a shortest-widest-path variant that prefers the highest-bandwidth path and breaks ties by lowest latency, using exponentially smoothed and hysteresis-stabilized bandwidth and latency estimates obtained from periodic pings (every 200 ms) and passive bandwidth monitoring on each mesh link.

### Measured results
| Metric | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Internet testbed | About 20 hosts, including one behind ADSL and hosts in Asia and Europe; "Primary Set" = well-connected North American university hosts subset, "Extended Set" = all hosts including the more heterogeneous ones | Aggregated over runs across a two-week period, interleaving schemes and varying time of day to control for network-condition drift |
| Primary Set, 1.2 Mbps source rate, bandwidth by receiver rank | Sequential Unicast: nearly all receivers near source rate except rank 1; Narada: worst-performing receiver (rank 1) averages 1,150 Kbps, comparable to or better than Sequential Unicast due to Internet routing pathologies; Random: worst receiver (rank 1) averages about 600 Kbps with large variance | 25 independent runs per point, error bars show standard deviation across runs, not confidence in the mean |
| Primary Set, 1.2 Mbps, RTT by receiver rank | Sequential Unicast unicast-path RTT up to about 150 ms; Narada worst-case receiver RTT about 160 ms; Random worst-case receiver RTT about 350 ms | Same setup |
| Extended Set, 2.4 Mbps source rate | Apart from ranks 1-5 (least well-connected hosts), all members get at least 1.8 Mbps and RTTs under 250 ms on average with Narada; for ranks 1-5, Narada outperforms Sequential Unicast by exploiting Internet routing pathologies (e.g., two Taiwan machines, one poorly connected to North America, achieves much better performance by routing through the other) | Same experimental protocol (interleaved runs, 20 minutes each, statistics gathered after the first 4 minutes to allow overlay convergence) |
| Typical-run convergence time and stability | Overlay converges to a reasonably stable structure after about 4 minutes; mean bandwidth after 150 seconds is practically the full source rate; mean RTT after 150 seconds is about 100 ms; a transient congestion event at about 460 seconds causes a bandwidth dip and RTT spike, recovered in about 40 seconds via topology adaptation | Primary Set, 1.2 Mbps source rate, source host at UCSB, single representative run |
| Per-receiver RTT distribution across all receivers | Over 94% of RTT estimates below 200 ms; over 98% below 400 ms | Same Primary Set experiments, aggregated across receivers |
| Network resource usage (normalized to DVMRP tree resource usage) | Naive Unicast: 2.62 (Primary, 1.2 Mbps) / 1.83 (Extended, 2.4 Mbps); Random: 2.24 / 1.97; Narada: 1.49 / 1.31; Min-Span (minimum spanning tree, optimal, not achievable in practice): 0.85 / 0.83 | Internet testbed, final overlay tree at end of each experiment |
| Narada protocol overhead (non-data traffic bytes / data traffic bytes) | 10.79% (Primary, 1.2 Mbps) and 14.20% (Extended, 2.4 Mbps) average overhead; over 90% of this overhead is bandwidth-probe traffic (92.24% / 94.30%), remainder is routing and group-management traffic | Internet testbed, groups up to about 20 members |
| Physical link stress, 128-member group, Waxman topology (single representative run) | DVMRP: at most 1 on every link; naive unicast: one link reaches stress 127, several links above 16; Narada: no link exceeds stress 9, a 14-fold improvement over naive unicast | Packet-level discrete-event simulator, one randomly chosen source |
| Worst-case physical link stress vs. group size, three topology models (ASMap, Waxman, Mapnet), Narada | About 5-7 for group size 64; about 8-14 for group size 256 | 25 independent simulations per point, mean with 95% confidence intervals, fanout range <3-6> |
| Mean receiver delay vs. group size, three topology models | Group size 16: Random 70-80 ms, Narada 40-55 ms, DVMRP 25-30 ms; group size 256: Random 150-170 ms, Narada 70-105 ms, DVMRP largely independent of group size | Same simulation setup; ratio of Narada's mean delay to DVMRP's is less than 1.7 at group size 16 and less than 3.5 at group size 256 |
| Normalized resource usage (NRU) vs. group size, Waxman topology, relative to IP multicast | Group size 16: Narada about 1.3, Naive Unicast and Random about 1.6; group size 128: Narada about 1.9, Naive Unicast and Random about 2.4; NRU at most 1.9 across all three topology models at group size 128 | Same simulation setup |
| Simulated protocol overhead (routing and group management only, no bandwidth probes modeled) | About 2% at group size 64, about 4% at group size 128, at a 128 Kbps source rate; overhead is independent of source rate | Same simulation setup, 40-minute runs, routing-message exchange every 30s, performance probes every 10s |
| Simulation topologies | Waxman: 1,024 routers, 3,145 links (generated with the Georgia Tech random graph generator); ASMap: 1,024 routers, 3,037 links (from BGP routing-table data, random 8-12 ms link delays); Mapnet: 1,070 routers, 3,170 links (CAIDA Mapnet database, delays from geographic distance) | Group sizes up to 256 members, members attached to a random backbone router with 1-4 ms delay |

### Parameters
- Mesh maintenance: refresh-message timeout Tm (time without an update before a member is presumed dead or partitioned), probe-based partition-repair scheduling with a maximum queue-residency time T and per-cycle sleep period P (exact numeric values for Tm, T, P not stated in the extracted text as fixed constants; described as tunable per the pseudocode in the paper's Figure 5).
- Link-addition and link-dropping utility thresholds: scaled as a function of group size and each member's current neighbor count; the drop threshold is set less than or equal to the add threshold to ensure a dropped link is not immediately re-added, and the paper's partition-avoidance argument requires the drop threshold to stay below half the group size.
- Bandwidth/latency probing for conferencing customization: latency probes (pings) every 200 ms between mesh neighbors; bandwidth estimated by passive monitoring, exponentially smoothed, then discretized into bandwidth levels (example given: 512 Kbps and 1024 Kbps levels) with hysteresis to reduce oscillation.
- Internet testbed: about 20 hosts; Primary Set at 1.2 Mbps source rate; Extended Set at 2.4 Mbps source rate; each experiment run for 20 minutes, statistics collected after the first 4 minutes; results aggregated over runs across a two-week period.
- Simulation: fanout range <3-6> (minimum and maximum mesh neighbors per member) for all reported results; group sizes up to 256 members; routing-message exchange interval 30s; per-member performance-probe interval 10s; 25 independent runs per data point with 95% confidence intervals; simulation duration 40 minutes, with all members joining in the first 100 seconds and no further membership change afterward.

### Stated limitations
The authors state Narada's design, in which every member maintains full knowledge of every other group member, is a deliberate choice that "leads to the concern that the costs of maintaining such information may be prohibitively expensive for larger sized groups." They state three specific open issues for scaling beyond the tens-to-hundreds member range tested: overlay hop count (and thus delay) between members grows with group size; transient performance during member failure, departure, or congestion has not been investigated, only performance over longer timescales, and this could be a greater concern at larger group sizes because such events occur more frequently; and it is unclear whether active-measurement overhead and overlay-construction convergence time remain low as group size grows. The simulator does not model bandwidth, queuing delay, packet loss, or cross traffic, "because it is difficult to model Internet dynamics in a reasonable way in a simulator" and because modeling cross traffic would restrict simulation scalability; consequently the simulation's Protocol Overhead metric excludes bandwidth-probe cost, which the Internet experiments identify as over 90% of real overhead. The Internet experiments approximate IP multicast performance with a Sequential Unicast test (unicasting to each receiver independently, in the absence of the others) rather than measuring real IP multicast, because IP multicast deployment was too limited to evaluate directly; the same experiments do not measure link stress at all, because that requires accurate knowledge of physical paths between every member pair. The paper assumes a fail-stop failure model (once a member dies it stays dead, and its death is locally detectable by others) and does not address the bootstrap mechanism a joining member uses to learn of existing members, stating this is left to be application-specific. The authors state minimum spanning trees are optimal for network resource usage but that "it is not clear that they perform well from the application perspective," so this optimum is not adopted.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Narada requires each member to maintain a complete list of all other group members, updated through periodic refresh messages propagated along the mesh; the authors state this scales poorly and is a deliberate tradeoff for two properties: independence from any single non-failing external node (an out-of-band bootstrap mechanism is used only to let new members join, and its failure does not disrupt already-connected members) and the ability to reconnect the group even after simultaneous failure of a large fraction of members. The mesh-repair mechanism depends on a fail-stop failure model in which member death is locally detectable (via redundant probes to a member that stops sending refresh messages) and permanent; a system where failed members can silently return or where failure is not locally detectable is outside the assumptions the partition-repair analysis relies on. The distance-vector data-delivery layer requires periodic routing-update exchange between mesh neighbors (containing path-vector information to avoid count-to-infinity) and depends on the mesh remaining connected; if the mesh is partitioned, per-source trees computed over it are also partitioned until the mesh-repair mechanism (Section III-A.3) restores connectivity. Bandwidth-aware routing (the conferencing-application customization) requires each mesh link to carry ongoing passive bandwidth measurement and periodic active pings, so a deployment without those measurement primitives cannot use the shortest-widest-path routing variant and falls back to static or latency-only metrics, which the paper states yields degraded performance for applications needing both bandwidth and latency guarantees. The reported delay and resource-usage advantages over DVMRP-based IP multicast are measured relative to a testbed of real, uncontrolled Internet paths and a fail-stop member model; the authors do not measure performance under Byzantine (arbitrarily malicious, not just failed) member behavior, so nothing in this paper establishes resilience of the utility-based link-selection or mesh-repair mechanisms against a participant that reports false performance information.

### Contradicts
None found.

### References worth retrieving
- Deering. "Multicast Routing in Internetworks and Extended LANs." — foundational (DVMRP, the IP-multicast baseline this paper compares Narada against throughout).
- Ratnasamy, Handley, Karp, Shenker. "Application-level multicast using Content-Addressable Networks." — competing (coordinate-space-addressed overlay multicast, an alternative design family to Narada's mesh-then-tree approach, cited directly in the related-work comparison).
- Zhuang, Zhao, Joseph, Katz, Kubiatowicz. "Bayeux." — competing (address-space-based scalable multicast, contrasted directly with Narada's performance-based neighbor selection).
- Francis. "Yoid: Your Own Internet Distribution." — competing (direct-tree-construction overlay multicast, contrasted directly against Narada's two-step mesh approach).
- Pendarakis, Shi, Verma, Waldvogel. "ALMI: An Application Level Multicast Infrastructure." — competing (centralized overlay-multicast control, explicit architectural contrast to Narada's fully decentralized design).
- Chawathe. "Scattercast: An Architecture for Internet Broadcast Distribution as an Infrastructure Service." PhD thesis. — competing (proxy/infrastructure-based multicast, and source of Gossamer, the other mesh-then-tree protocol the paper cites as similar to Narada).
- Banerjee, Bhattacharjee, Parthasarathy. "A Protocol for Scalable Application Layer Multicast" (Nice project). — competing (hierarchy-based overlay multicast achieving better scaling than Narada, cited directly as a scaling alternative).
- Jain, Mahajan, Wetherall, Borriello, Gribble. "Scalable self-organizing overlays" (Kudos). — competing (two-level hierarchy multicast, cited as achieving better scaling properties than Narada).
- Wang, Crowcroft. "Bandwidth-delay Based Routing Algorithms." — foundational (source of the shortest-widest-path routing algorithm Narada's conferencing customization is built on).
- Floyd, Handley, Padhye, Widmer. "Equation-based Congestion Control" (TFRC). — foundational (the rate-controlled UDP transport protocol used on each overlay link in Narada's conferencing customization).

## [CHUN-NSDI-06] Efficient Replica Maintenance for Distributed Storage Systems

**Citation:** Byung-Gon Chun, Frank Dabek, Andreas Haeberlen, Emil Sit, Hakim Weatherspoon, M. Frans Kaashoek, John Kubiatowicz, Robert Morris. "Efficient Replica Maintenance for Distributed Storage Systems." USENIX Symposium on Networked Systems Design and Implementation (NSDI), 2006.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.usenix.org/conference/nsdi-06/efficient-replica-maintenance-distributed-storage-systems
**Source URL:** https://www.usenix.org/conference/nsdi-06/efficient-replica-maintenance-distributed-storage-systems
**Domain:** C

### What it does

The paper defines a replica-maintenance algorithm, Carbonite, that keeps stored objects durable (recoverable after disk failure) at close to the minimum bandwidth a system that could perfectly distinguish permanent disk failure from transient disconnection would spend, without needing to make that distinction itself. It separates durability (an object's bytes are recoverable somewhere in the system) from availability (a get returns the object immediately); an object can be durable but not currently available if its only surviving copy sits on a node that is temporarily unreachable. The paper argues durability is cheaper to provide and a sufficient goal for many wide-area applications, distinct from availability.

Carbonite's core rule: for each object it is responsible for, a node counts currently-available replicas; whenever that count drops below a target replication level `rL`, it enqueues creation of new replicas to bring the count back to `rL`. It differs from prior distributed-hash-table (DHT) systems in one respect: rather than forgetting a replica the moment it becomes unavailable, Carbonite remembers which node held each replica and reintegrates that replica back into the tracked set the moment the node returns, instead of discarding the returned copy and treating a new node as replacing it. Because a returned replica counts again, a node experiencing repeated transient failures does not force new-replica creation as long as at least `rL` replicas remain counted (available or recently failed-but-remembered) — the system builds up a working surplus of tracked replicas without needing to measure or assume a value for `a`, the average fraction of time a node is available. A Chernoff-bound argument shows the surplus needed for the probability of a spurious repair to become exponentially small is on the order of `2·rL/a` replicas — the paper calls this a rough estimate, not a value Carbonite computes or targets explicitly; Carbonite arrives at approximately this surplus as an emergent behavior of the reintegrate-on-return rule, without ever computing `a`.

The choice of `rL` is separated from ordinary steady-state durability by modeling replica count as a continuous-time Markov birth-death process: replicas are lost at rate proportional to how many exist (each independently at rate `λf`, the per-disk permanent-failure rate) and are created at repair rate `µ`, which depends on per-node access-link bandwidth and how much data each node stores. The ratio `θ = µ/λf` bounds the number of replicas the system can sustain in steady state regardless of how high `rL` is set: at `θ < 1` the system cannot maintain even its starting replication level and settles into a "best-effort" mode where raising `rL` further has no effect, because replacement cannot keep pace with loss. Object placement scope — how many other nodes may hold a copy of data from a given failed node — trades off repair speed against blast radius: a large scope spreads repair work (and hence the bytes any single node must copy after a failure) across more access links, cutting repair time roughly in proportion to scope size, but with random placement across a large scope, essentially every possible replica set combination gets used, so any simultaneous failure of `rL` disks somewhere in the system is likely to destroy some object; a small scope concentrates objects onto fewer replica sets, making any given `rL`-disk failure less likely to hit one, but destroying more objects when it does — the paper states the expected number of objects lost during a large failure event is identical between the two strategies, only the variance differs.

| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| PlanetLab trace: 632 hosts, 21,255 transient failures, 219 disk failures, over the period March 1, 2005 - February 28, 2006 | CoMon monitoring data (uptime-counter resets detect reboots; unreachability timing pinpoints failure onset) supplemented with PlanetLab Central reinstall event logs to identify true disk failures |
| Transient host downtime: median 1,208 s, mean 104,647 s, 90th percentile 14,242 s; any-failure interarrival: median 305 s, mean 1,467 s, 90th percentile 3,306 s; disk-failure interarrival: median 54,411 s, mean 143,476 s, 90th percentile 490,047 s | same 632-host, 1-year PlanetLab (CoMon+PLC) trace (Table 1) |
| Estimated mean time between failures per single disk: 2.23 years (λf ≈ 0.439 disk failures/year); estimated replica creation rate µ ≈ 3 disk copies/year; θ = µ/λf ≈ 6.85 | derived from Table 1's average disk failure interarrival (39.85 hours across ~490 average concurrent nodes), assuming 150 KB/s per-node access-link bandwidth (PlanetLab's imposed cap) and 500 GB unique data per node at rL=3 (1.5 TB stored per node) |

### Stated limitations

Carbonite's design assumes disks fail independently of each other, on the reasoning that geographically distributed drives from different manufacturers are unlikely to share a failure cause; the paper states its own year-long PlanetLab trace showed correlated failures caused by coordinated software reinstalls, a direct violation of the independence assumption the model relies on, and reports the measured 44% overhead figure despite this violation rather than after removing it. The simulator models unlimited per-node disk capacity and assumes all network paths are independent (no shared bottlenecks) and that any available node is reachable from every other node, which the paper states is "occasionally not the case on PlanetLab," citing a separate source for that observation, though it also cites existing masking techniques as a possible mitigation not evaluated here. Large placement scope is stated to increase per-node monitoring traffic and to limit scalability, and separately to increase the probability that any single simultaneous rL-node failure destroys some object (even though the expected total number of objects lost across many such events is unchanged relative to small scope) — the paper frames this as a genuine open tradeoff, not a solved one. The timeout mechanism is stated to help only when node downtime is reliably shorter than node/disk lifetime; past a certain length, increasing the timeout further both saves bandwidth and reduces durability, because it delays the point at which real disk failures begin repair. The paper explicitly narrows its scope to immutable data and states that naming and locating data are outside the scope of the work (naming) or only indirectly relevant (locating, as it can affect replica-placement policy choices).

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system

Carbonite requires each node to maintain per-object soft state recording the current set of nodes (available or recently failed) holding each replica it is responsible for, and requires this state to fail over to a successor node when the responsible node itself fails — the paper states this monitoring state is "soft" and can be transferred relatively transparently, in contrast to the hard state of the replica location pointers a directory-based system (e.g., the paper's OceanStore/Bamboo-based prototype) must maintain, which do require durable tracking. Achieving the paper's measured near-oracle bandwidth cost requires the reintegration mechanism specifically: a system that discards a returned replica and only tracks exactly rL replicas (the "Cates" comparison point, approximating DHash/PAST/OpenDHT) is measured at close to double the oracle's bandwidth on the same trace, so any system claiming Carbonite-level efficiency must implement reintegration, not merely extra redundancy. Reducing repair time via larger placement scope requires a monitoring mechanism scaled to that larger scope; the paper's own prototype work found this needed different solutions for consistent-hashing systems (a Merkle-tree-based synchronization protocol adapted to skip already-known-missing objects) versus directory-based systems (a heartbeat multicast tree with O(log N) out-degree, propagating node liveness rather than per-object liveness), so a design that adopts large scope must also adopt one of these two monitoring mechanisms or an equivalent, since naive periodic key-list exchange or all-pairs probing is stated to scale as N² and is called infeasible at scale. Choosing rL and evaluating whether a bandwidth budget is feasible requires an estimate of the deployment's true λf (per-disk permanent-failure rate) and achievable per-node repair bandwidth µ, since θ = µ/λf sets a hard ceiling on sustainable replication level regardless of how rL is configured — a system operating below θ=1 cannot be helped by raising rL at all.

### Contradicts

None found within this batch as a direct numeric conflict. The paper explicitly states it reaches a different conclusion than BLAKE-HOTOS-03 (Blake and Rodrigues) despite analyzing a related feasibility question: Blake and Rodrigues concluded wide-area storage on unreliable nodes cannot hold large amounts of data, based on an analysis of continual membership turnover, while this paper attributes the difference to considering "a relatively stable system membership where data loss is driven by disk failure" rather than continual churn — both figures are as each paper states them and are not measuring the same population or the same failure regime, so this is a difference in modeled scenario, not an empirical disagreement.

## [CHYSTIAKOV-ARXIV-25] Cartesian Merkle Tree

**Citation:** Artem Chystiakov, Oleh Komendant, Kyrylo Riabov. "Cartesian Merkle Tree." arXiv preprint, 2025. arXiv:2504.10944.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/pdf/2504.10944
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.10944
**Domain:** D

### What it does
A Cartesian Merkle Tree (CMT) authenticates set membership and non-membership with a Merkle root while keeping the tree structure independent of insertion order. It achieves this by combining three properties in one node set: a binary search tree ordered on key `k`, a min-heap ordered on a priority `p`, and a Merkle hash `mh` at every node (not only at leaves). The priority of an element is computed deterministically from its key by a hash-derived function `p = PH(e)`, rather than chosen at random as in a classical Cartesian tree (treap). Because priority is a deterministic function of the key, the same key set always produces the same tree shape regardless of insertion order, so the structure is history-independent. Each node's Merkle hash is `mh = H(entry || leftChildMH || rightChildMH)`, with the two child hashes sorted in ascending order before hashing and a missing child treated as hash 0. Insertion places a new node by the binary-search-tree rule on `k` and then rotates it upward while its priority exceeds its parent's, restoring the heap property (mirroring standard treap insertion) and recomputing Merkle hashes along the rotation path. Removal marks the target node's priority as negative infinity and rotates it downward until it is a leaf, then detaches it, recomputing hashes along the path. An inclusion proof carries a `prefix` (the key and sibling Merkle hash of each ancestor up to the root) and a `suffix` (the target node's two child hashes); a verifier reconstructs the accumulator hash bottom-up and compares it to the known root. A non-membership proof instead returns the key of the node whose position would immediately have held the absent key, plus that node's own inclusion path, and the verifier confirms the returned node is genuinely present and that the search rules place the absent key nowhere else.

### Measured results
Benchmarks measure Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) gas cost of the Solidity reference implementation's Insert and Remove functions, compared against a Solidity Sparse Merkle Tree (SMT) implementation with its `value` field removed so both structures occupy the same number of storage slots per node. Trees were populated with 100, 1,000, 5,000, and 10,000 randomly ordered elements, using two hash functions, Keccak256 and Poseidon.

| Operation | Hash | Elements | Min Gas | Avg Gas | Max Gas |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Insert (CMT) | Keccak256 | 100 | 97,593 | 187,682 | 301,113 |
| Insert (CMT) | Keccak256 | 10,000 | 97,593 | 303,871 | 552,723 |
| Insert (CMT) | Poseidon | 100 | 148,017 | 599,943 | 1,246,860 |
| Insert (CMT) | Poseidon | 10,000 | 148,017 | 1,140,019 | 2,773,845 |
| Insert (SMT) | Keccak256 | 100 | 102,125 | 248,063 | 667,958 |
| Insert (SMT) | Keccak256 | 10,000 | 102,125 | 339,509 | 877,732 |
| Insert (SMT) | Poseidon | 100 | 136,354 | 471,704 | 903,027 |
| Insert (SMT) | Poseidon | 10,000 | 136,366 | 765,205 | 2,155,222 |
| Remove (CMT) | Keccak256 | 100 | 41,917 | 129,109 | 259,680 |
| Remove (CMT) | Keccak256 | 10,000 | 41,917 | 244,545 | 522,075 |
| Remove (CMT) | Poseidon | 100 | 92,329 | 430,727 | 1,071,617 |
| Remove (CMT) | Poseidon | 10,000 | 92,341 | 982,465 | 2,437,679 |
| Remove (SMT) | Keccak256 | 100 | 35,029 | 131,847 | 224,916 |
| Remove (SMT) | Keccak256 | 10,000 | 35,029 | 237,191 | 374,284 |
| Remove (SMT) | Poseidon | 100 | 35,029 | 284,457 | 466,242 |
| Remove (SMT) | Poseidon | 10,000 | 35,029 | 590,051 | 864,656 |

At 10,000 elements, average Insert gas for CMT with Keccak256 (303,871) is lower than SMT with Keccak256 (339,509) at the same size; average Remove gas for CMT with Keccak256 (244,545) is higher than SMT with Keccak256 (237,191). The paper states operation time complexity is O(log n) for insert, update, and removal, and states the trade-off against SMT as a Merkle proof size "at worst two times larger than SMTs" — this ratio is stated, not shown as a measured table entry in the retrieved text.

### Parameters
- Hash function `H` for Merkle hashing and priority derivation `PH`: instantiated in benchmarks as Keccak256 or Poseidon; the paper states `PH` "can be any deterministic algorithm."
- Dataset sizes tested: 100, 1,000, 5,000, 10,000 elements, chosen "to show how data size impacts performance."
- Storage layout: SMT comparison implementation had its `value` field removed so CMT and SMT nodes occupy the same number of storage slots, to keep the gas comparison fair.

### Stated limitations
The paper states a related structure, the Sparse Merkle Tree, cannot exceed a tree depth of 97 because of EVM stack limitations, and states its collision-free element count is bounded near 2^50 (about 1.12x10^15) by the birthday-problem argument. This bound is stated for SMT in the background section, not asserted as a CMT limitation in the retrieved text — no equivalent explicit bound is stated for CMT's own maximum size in this text. The Incremental Merkle Tree family (background comparison, not CMT itself) is stated to require an off-chain service to reconstruct the tree for proof generation and cannot be used independently on-chain.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A verifier must know the current Merkle root and trust the deterministic priority function `PH` used to build the tree; if a party inserting elements could choose `PH` outputs adversarially, the history-independence property (same key set implies same tree shape regardless of insertion order) would not hold, since the whole point of deriving `p` from `k` deterministically is to remove insertion-order and priority-choice freedom. Proof verification (Algorithm 5) requires the verifier to walk a `prefix` list of ancestor keys and sibling hashes and a `suffix` pair of the target's own child hashes, recomputing hashes bottom-up with the two-child ordering rule (children sorted ascending before hashing) — any implementation must reproduce that exact ordering and concatenation or verification fails. Non-membership proofs require the verifier to independently check that the returned "nonExistenceKey" node's position under the binary-search-tree and min-heap ordering rules is consistent with the claimed absence, not merely that some hash matches.

### Contradicts
None found.

### References worth retrieving
- iden3, "Sparse Merkle Tree" (technical documentation, 2024) — foundational, the structure CMT is directly compared against in the benchmarks.
- DL Solarity, "Cartesian Merkle Tree Solidity Implementation" (GitHub, 2025) — foundational, the reference implementation the benchmarks were run against.
- DL Solarity, "Sparse Merkle Tree Solidity Implementation" (GitHub, 2025) — competing, the comparison implementation used in the gas benchmarks.
- DL Solarity, "Cartesian Merkle Tree Circom Circuit" (GitHub, 2025) — foundational, the zero-knowledge-proof-compatible circuit implementation.

- "the only trade-off being a Merkle proof size at worst two times larger than SMTs"
- "if p is deterministically derived from k, then the same key will always produce the same point"
- "reaching depths of 97 or more is currently infeasible due to limitations within the EVM stack"

## [COHEN-IPTPS-03] Incentives Build Robustness in BitTorrent
**Citation:** Bram Cohen. "Incentives Build Robustness in BitTorrent." Workshop on Economics of Peer-to-Peer Systems, presented at IPTPS 2003. May 22, 2003.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://bittorrent.org/bittorrentecon.pdf
**Source URL:** https://bittorrent.org/bittorrentecon.pdf
**Domain:** I

### What it does
BitTorrent redistributes the upload cost of serving a file from a single host to the set of concurrent downloaders, by having every downloader upload pieces of the file it already holds to its peers while it continues downloading pieces it lacks. This removes the requirement that hosting a file with an unbounded number of downloaders needs unbounded upload capacity at one machine.

A file is published by placing a small static .torrent file (containing the file's length, name, per-piece SHA1 hashes, and the address of a tracker) on an ordinary web server, and starting at least one seed, a peer that already holds the complete file. The tracker is a lightweight coordination point reached over HTTP: a downloader reports what file it wants and what port it listens on, and the tracker replies with a list of other peers downloading the same file, drawn at random rather than through any peer-selection heuristic that would bias the resulting connection graph toward a structured or power-law shape. Peers connect directly to each other over these tracker-supplied addresses; the tracker never routes file data itself.

Each file is divided into fixed-size pieces (a quarter megabyte in the deployments described), and each piece is further divided into 16-kilobyte sub-pieces for pipelined transfer over TCP, with a fixed number of sub-piece requests (five) kept outstanding at any time to keep the TCP connection saturated. A peer reports to every connected peer which pieces it currently holds, and only reports a piece as held once its SHA1 hash has been checked. Piece download order follows four combined rules. Once a sub-piece of a given piece has been requested, all remaining sub-pieces of that same piece are requested next, ahead of sub-pieces from any other piece, so that complete pieces finish quickly. Subject to that priority, a peer downloads whichever piece is held by the fewest of its own peers ("rarest first"), which keeps rare pieces from disappearing when the peers holding them leave, and keeps every peer's held-piece set useful to upload to others. At the very start of a download, before a peer has anything to upload, pieces are instead selected at random rather than by rarity, because a rare piece is more likely to be held by only one peer and so download more slowly than a piece obtainable in parallel sub-piece chunks from many peers. Near the end of a download, once every remaining needed sub-piece is already requested from some peer, a peer additionally requests all remaining sub-pieces from every peer that has them ("endgame mode"), and cancels the redundant in-flight requests as each sub-piece arrives, to avoid a single slow peer stalling completion.

Upload allocation among peers is governed by a choking algorithm run independently by each peer. Choking is a temporary refusal to upload to a given connected peer; it does not close the connection, so the choked peer can resume receiving without renegotiation. A peer always unchokes a fixed number of other peers (four, by default), chosen by highest current download rate received from them, recomputed once every ten seconds, a period the author states is long enough for TCP to ramp a new transfer up to its available capacity. Current download rate is calculated as a rolling 20-second average, rather than a long-term cumulative total, because bandwidth availability is stated to shift quickly as other transfers start and stop. Independent of that four-way rule, one additional connection is always unchoked regardless of its current download rate, called the optimistic unchoke, and which connection holds that role rotates every third recompute period (30 seconds); this lets a peer discover whether an otherwise-unused connection would in fact yield a better download rate than the currently favored ones, in the same role that always cooperating on the first move plays in a repeated prisoner's-dilemma strategy. If a peer receives no data for over a minute from a peer it was formerly downloading from, it marks that peer as having "snubbed" it and stops uploading to it except via the optimistic-unchoke slot; because this can produce more than one concurrent optimistic unchoke, it speeds recovery when a peer's download rate has collapsed. Once a peer has finished downloading and has no download rate left to measure, it instead prioritizes uploading to peers to which it has the best upload rate, to keep utilizing upload capacity productively.

### Measured results
| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| At a real large deployment of a single file over 400 megabytes, the number of complete downloaders ("seeders") reached at least 1,000 at one point in time | Field observation from one real BitTorrent deployment (figure 1 in the source), no controlled experiment; the paper states the actual number of completed downloads over the full period was "probably several times" 1,000, without giving a number |
| The largest known real-world BitTorrent deployments, as of the paper's writing (2003), had over 1,000 simultaneous downloaders | Field observation, unspecified file(s) and time period, no measurement methodology given |
| Tracker bandwidth overhead is about one-thousandth of total bandwidth used in a deployment, expected to fall to about one ten-thousandth with unspecified future protocol extensions | Field estimate from real deployments, no methodology, hardware, or run count given; the ten-thousandth figure is a stated expectation, not a measurement |
| Simply having peers announce their held-piece sets produces "less than a tenth of a percent" bandwidth overhead while reliably utilizing all available upload capacity | Stated as a general property of the piece-announcement protocol, no experimental setup, dataset, node count, or run count given |

None of these figures come with node counts, topology, dataset composition, or run counts sufficient to reproduce them; the paper is a design and mechanism description supported by informal field observation of real deployments, not a controlled experiment.

### Parameters
| Parameter | Value used | Tested range |
|---|---|---|
| Piece size | "typically a quarter megabyte" | Not otherwise specified |
| Sub-piece size | "typically sixteen kilobytes" | Not otherwise specified |
| Pipelined outstanding sub-piece requests | "typically five" | Not otherwise specified |
| Default number of unchoked peers | Four | Not otherwise specified |
| Choking-decision recompute interval | Ten seconds | Justified as long enough for TCP to reach full transfer capacity; not otherwise varied |
| Optimistic-unchoke rotation interval | Thirty seconds (every third ten-second recompute period) | Justified as enough time for upload to reach capacity, download to reciprocate, and download to reach capacity in turn; not otherwise varied |
| Download-rate averaging window used for choking decisions | Rolling 20-second average | Contrasted against a former implementation that used long-term net transfer totals, stated to have performed worse; no quantitative comparison given |
| Snub threshold | No data received from a peer for over one minute | Not otherwise specified |

### Stated limitations
The paper states that erasure codes had been suggested by other work as a technique for the piece-verification and distribution problem, but that BitTorrent's much simpler fixed-piece SHA1-hash approach "has proven to be workable" instead, without a quantitative comparison of the two approaches. It states that for deployments with a single seed whose upload capacity is well below that of the aggregate downloaders, and for deployments where the original seed is eventually taken offline, a piece can become completely unavailable if rarest-first replication does not spread it in time; the paper presents rarest-first as reducing but does not claim eliminating this risk. It does not report a formal robustness or fairness analysis of the choking algorithm; the claim that seeking pareto efficiency through tit-for-tat "tend[s] to have" properties of full resource utilization, consistent download rates, and resistance to non-contributing peers is presented as a consequence of a cited general economic argument, not as a property proven or measured for BitTorrent specifically. The paper does not model or measure adversarial peer behavior (for example peers that upload junk data, or coordinate to defeat the choking algorithm); it addresses only unmodified good-faith peer behavior under high churn.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
BitTorrent's choking mechanism requires a bidirectional TCP connection between any two peers exchanging pieces, since choking blocks only the upload direction while leaving the same connection able to resume downloading without renegotiation. It requires the tracker to supply peer lists chosen at random rather than through a structured peer-selection rule, since the paper attributes BitTorrent's churn robustness to the resulting random-graph topology and explicitly attributes the fragility of power-law peer graphs (produced by many other peer-selection algorithms) to their vulnerability to segmentation after modest churn. It requires a piece-integrity check (the per-piece SHA1 hash from the .torrent file) to exist before a peer is willing to advertise or serve that piece to others, since the reported piece set doubles as the input that both piece selection (rarest-first) and choking-partner selection operate on. It requires a mechanism outside the wire protocol (the choking algorithm is stated to not be part of the BitTorrent wire protocol itself) to select which unchoked peers to reciprocate with, meaning any peer-selection or reputation input other than recent observed download rate would have to be added at that separate layer, not the protocol itself. The rarest-first piece-selection policy requires each peer to know, from its own connected peers' advertised piece sets, which pieces are locally rare; this signal comes from the same piece-announcement messages the choking algorithm's traffic accounting does not use, so a peer that withheld its held-piece set from others to preserve privacy would prevent both the choking algorithm's income signal to it, since others would not know to reciprocate, and rarest-first's ability to protect that peer's pieces from disappearing.

### Contradicts
None found. No other entry in this batch reports figures for BitTorrent's choking algorithm or tracker overhead.

### References worth retrieving
- competing: M. Castro, P. Druschel, A.-M. Kermarrec, A. Nandi, A. Rowstron, A. Singh, "SplitStream: High-bandwidth content distribution in cooperative environments," IPTPS 2003 — a tree-structured alternative distribution approach cited by Cohen as not utilizing the upload capacity of leaf nodes, the direct architectural alternative BitTorrent's mesh-based piece exchange is implicitly compared against.
- foundational: A.-L. Barabási, "Linked: The New Science of Networks," Perseus Publishing, 2002 — cited as the source for the claim that random graphs have good robustness properties, underlying the paper's argument for the tracker's random peer selection.
- attack/critique context: E. Adar, B. A. Huberman, "Free riding on Gnutella," First Monday 5(10), 2000 — cited as establishing the general peer-to-peer fairness problem BitTorrent's tit-for-tat choking is designed to solve; also cited directly by VISHNUMURTHY-P2PECON-03 in this batch for the same freeloading motivation.
- foundational: P. Maymounkov, D. Mazières, "Kademlia: A peer-to-peer information system based on the XOR metric," IPTPS 2002 — cited only for the observation that real deployments experience very high peer churn (peers connecting for minutes to a few hours), not for any mechanism BitTorrent reuses.

- "The current scaling bottleneck (which hasn't actually been reached) appears to be the bandwidth overhead of the tracker."
- "Currently that's about a thousandth the total amount of bandwidth used"
- "Ten seconds is a long enough period of time for TCP to ramp up new transfers to their full capacity."
- "30 seconds is enough time for the upload to get to full capacity, the download to reciprocate"

## [COHEN-SIGCOMM-02] Replication Strategies in Unstructured Peer-to-Peer Networks

**Citation:** Edith Cohen, Scott Shenker. "Replication Strategies in Unstructured Peer-to-Peer Networks." ACM SIGCOMM, 2002. DOI 10.1145/633025.633043.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.csl.mtu.edu/cs6461/www/Reading/Cohen02.pdf
**Source URL:** https://www.csl.mtu.edu/cs6461/www/Reading/Cohen02.pdf
**Domain:** B

### What it does
The paper determines how many copies of each data item a peer-to-peer (P2P) network should hold, given a fixed total storage budget, to minimize the number of nodes a blind random search must probe before finding an item. It models search as random probing: a search draws nodes uniformly at random and stops when one holds a copy of the queried item, so the expected number of nodes probed for item i (the expected search size) is inversely proportional to the fraction of total system capacity allocated to item i. Node capacity per peer is fixed at rho copies; total system capacity is R = n*rho for n nodes; item i receives p_i = r_i/R of that capacity, where r_i is its copy count. The paper proves that among all allocations lying between two named baselines, "Uniform" (equal copies per item, independent of demand) and "Proportional" (copies proportional to query rate q_i), every allocation strictly between them has a strictly lower expected search size than either baseline, and both baselines produce the identical expected search size m/rho (m = number of distinct items), independent of the query distribution. It then derives the allocation that minimizes expected search size: Square-root allocation, p_i proportional to sqrt(q_i), and gives three distributed algorithms that converge to it without any node needing to know the global query-rate distribution.

### Measured results
| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| Gain factor of Square-root over Uniform/Proportional scales as: constant for skew w<1, logarithmic in m for w=1, polynomial in m for 1<w<2, linear in m for w>2 | Derived analytically (Table 1) for truncated Zipf-like query distributions on m items, query rate of the i-th most popular item proportional to i^-w |
| Maximum gain factor of the optimal two-item allocation over Uniform or Proportional is 2 | Analytic result for m=2 items, rho=1 |
| Square-root allocation's expected search size (ESS) is 30%-50% of Proportional's/Uniform's ESS for larger m | Two query distributions built from Boeing Web proxy logs: top-m URLs weighted by request count, and top-m hostnames weighted by number of distinct requesting users |
| Under the hostname distribution, the maximum search size required by Square-root is within a factor of 2 of the minimum possible (achieved by Uniform), while Proportional requires a substantially larger maximum search size | Boeing proxy log hostname distribution, m=1000 locatable items |
| Sibling-number-memory (SNM) distributed replication algorithm converges to Square-root allocation faster than path replication and is insensitive to delay between a search and follow-up copy creation; path replication converges more slowly and can fluctuate when queries arrive in bursts or copy-creation delay is large relative to query rate | Simulated network of 10,000 nodes, tracking the fraction of nodes holding a copy of one item over time; searches stop after finding k copies, k in {1, 5}; fixed copy lifetime; queries at fixed intervals; some runs add delay between search and follow-up copy generation (Figures 6-7, no numeric summary table given in text) |

### Parameters
- rho: per-node capacity (number of item copies/keys a node can hold); held symbolic throughout the analysis, set to 1 in the two-item numeric example (Figure 1B)
- ℓ (lower bound on p_i, from r_i >= 1): ℓ = 1/R
- u (upper bound on p_i, from r_i <= n): u = rho^-1 = n/R
- Truncated-search parameter L (maximum search size before a query is declared insoluble): failure probability bounded by 2^-C when p_i >= C/(rho*L); the paper sets C = O(log L) so failure probability is polynomially small in L
- fs (fraction of soluble queries) / (1-fs) (fraction of insoluble queries): used to weight the combined cost fs*A_q(p) + (1-fs)*L(p); swept in the hostname-distribution figure (0%, 25%, 50%, 75%, 100% soluble)
- Zipf skew parameter w: swept across w<1, w=1, 1<w<2, w=2, w>2 in the analytic gain-factor table
- Simulation: 10,000 nodes; k (copies to find before stopping search) in {1, 5}; fixed copy lifetime duration (value not stated numerically in the retrieved text); queries issued at fixed intervals

### Stated limitations
The analysis assumes an adaptive termination search mechanism (search stops once the query is resolved) and states that a different question -- replication without adaptive termination -- is addressed elsewhere (reference [7], Kangasharju/Ross/Turner). The distributed replication algorithms are proved to converge to Square-root allocation only under a stated deletion-process assumption: copy lifetimes are independent of the item's identity and survival probability is non-increasing with age; the paper states this assumption is violated by Least Recently Used (LRU) and Least Frequently Used (LFU) eviction, though satisfied by First In First Out (FIFO), fixed lifetime durations, and random deletion. Path replication is stated to have a convergence weakness: the number of copies created per search can overshoot or undershoot the fixed point by a large factor when queries arrive in bursts or when the delay between a search and its follow-up copy creation is large relative to the query rate, and the paper states this issue can occur even for a large number of nodes. The paper states an open issue: how the proposed distributed algorithms behave in more realistic settings than the model and simulations cover.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The distributed replication algorithms require that copy deletion be independent of which item is stored and of that item's access pattern -- an eviction policy that instead prunes least-recently-used or least-frequently-used copies breaks the fixed point the algorithms converge to, because it makes deletion rate depend on query rate. Path replication and sibling-number memory both require the requesting node, after a successful search, to know which item was found, so it can create new copies of that specific item at randomly selected nodes; the number of new copies created (path replication: the search size; sibling-number memory: an estimator built from recorded sibling-copy counts and ages) is a function of the search outcome for that item. Probe memory requires every node to record, per item, the count and combined search-size total of every probe it has seen for that item within a recent time window, and requires nodes to aggregate this bookkeeping across the nodes on a search path. The two-tier optimal policy (mixing Square-root with a Uniform floor) requires designating a subset of permanent-copy nodes per item that never evict that copy except on going offline, coordinated with a maximum search size L chosen jointly with that floor.

### Contradicts
None found against other entries in this batch. The paper's own numbers push back against the common attribution of "Proportional replication is close to optimal" -- the paper states Proportional is one of the two worst points among the family of allocations it studies (Lemma 3.1, Theorem 3.1), matched only by Uniform.

### References worth retrieving
- Lv, Cao, Cohen, Li, Shenker. "Search and replication in unstructured peer-to-peer networks." ICS 2002. -- foundational (already in corpus as the companion implementation paper; this paper's [9])
- Kangasharju, Ross, Turner. "Optimal content replication in P2P communities." Manuscript, 2002. -- competing (addresses replication without adaptive termination, a variant this paper explicitly excludes)
- Ratnasamy, Francis, Handley, Karp, Shenker. "A scalable content-addressable network." SIGCOMM 2001. -- foundational (structured-overlay contrast)
- Stoica, Morris, Karger, Kaashoek, Balakrishnan. "Chord: A scalable peer-to-peer lookup service for internet applications." SIGCOMM 2001. -- foundational (structured-overlay contrast; already in corpus as STOICA-SIGCOMM-01)
- Rowstron, Druschel. "Storage management and caching in PAST, a large-scale, persistent peer-to-peer storage utility." SOSP 2001. -- competing (alternative storage-replication design)
- Zhao, Kubiatowicz, Joseph. "Tapestry: An infrastructure for fault-tolerant wide-area location and routing." UCB/CSD-01-1141, 2001. -- foundational
- Kleinrock. "Queueing Systems, Volume II: Computer Applications." Wiley-Interscience, 1976. -- foundational (source of the capacity-assignment optimization the Square-root proof reuses)
- Vaidya, Hameed. "Scheduling data broadcast in asymmetric communication environments." ACM/Baltzer Wireless Networks 5, 1999. -- foundational (source of the same optimization problem in a broadcast-scheduling context)

## [COHNGORDON-CCS-18] On Ends-to-Ends Encryption: Asynchronous Group Messaging with Strong Security Guarantees
**Citation:** Katriel Cohn-Gordon, Cas Cremers, Luke Garratt, Jon Millican, Kevin Milner. "On Ends-to-Ends Encryption: Asynchronous Group Messaging with Strong Security Guarantees." ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS), 2018. Pages 1802-1819. DOI: 10.1145/3243734.3243747.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://eprint.iacr.org/2017/666.pdf (version 2.3, March 2020 — the paper's own posted revision)
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2017/666.pdf
**Domain:** H

### What it does
Asynchronous Ratcheting Trees (ART) let a group of message-application users derive a shared symmetric group key without requiring any two members to be online at the same time, while giving the group Post-Compromise Security (PCS — from the paper's own earlier definition, the guarantee that a party recovers a secret channel after a key compromise once that party takes a further protocol step, without needing to detect the compromise first). ART builds the group key from a binary tree of Diffie-Hellman (DH) key pairs, one leaf per group member. Each internal node's secret is the DH combination of its two children's secrets (a group element mapped back to an integer via a function the paper calls ι, so the combined value itself becomes usable as a new DH secret at the next level up); the tree root's secret, called the tree key, derives the current stage key by hash-chaining it with the previous stage key, and the stage key is the group's shared symmetric key.

A group creator who is the only party online generates a fresh DH key pair for every other member's leaf directly (using a one-round authenticated key exchange run against each future member's published prekeys, so the creator alone can compute the whole tree even though nobody else has connected yet), then broadcasts every public key in the tree. Any later member computes the tree key by combining their own leaf secret with the public keys along their copath (the sibling nodes on the path from a leaf to the root), needing only O(log n) DH exponentiations for a group of n members. To achieve PCS, a member updates by drawing a fresh leaf secret, recomputing every node secret on the path from that leaf to the root, and broadcasting the updated public keys on that path; any other member combines the broadcast updates with their own copath knowledge to recompute the same new tree key. Because only path nodes change, an update costs the updater O(log n) exponentiations and every other member O(log n) exponentiations to process it, rather than the O(n) a fully re-run group key exchange would need.

### Measured results

**Asymptotic comparison (Table 1), derived, not measured, comparing ART against two deployed designs at group size n, sender/other split for setup and steady-state ("ongoing") operation:**

| Design | Setup exponentiations (sender / other) | Ongoing exponentiations (sender / other) | Ongoing symmetric encryptions (sender / other) | Ongoing bandwidth (sender / other) | PCS |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sender Keys (WhatsApp, Facebook Messenger group mode) | O(n) / O(n) | 0 / 0 | 1 / 1 | O(1) / O(1) | No |
| Pairwise Signal (Apple iMessage, Signal's own app) | O(n) / O(n) | O(n) / O(1) | n-1 / 1 | O(n) / O(1) | Yes |
| ART (this paper) | O(n) / O(log n) | O(log n) / O(log n) | 1 / 1 | O(log n) / O(log n) | Yes |

**Implementation benchmark:** ART implemented in Java, compared against pairwise Signal-style Double Ratchet channels, both using 32-byte messages (sized to carry an AES-256 key), on a 2016 MacBook Pro (3.3 GHz Intel Core i7, 16 GB RAM), averaged over four runs. Reported directly in text: setup and per-message sending both complete in a few milliseconds for a group of 10, and on the order of one second for a group of 1,000. Bandwidth: ART's per-message outgoing bytes stay below pairwise Signal's at every measured group size from roughly 10 to 1,000 participants (Figure 7a, read from the log-log plot; the paper states no closed-form numeric values beyond the qualitative comparison). Setup wall-clock time: ART is consistently slightly slower than pairwise channels at the same group sizes but follows the same asymptotic growth curve (Figure 7b); the paper attributes ART's higher constant factor to the tree creator's linear (not logarithmic) initiator-side work, versus pairwise's quadratic effort spread evenly across all members.

**Formal verification:** a Tamarin model (unbounded number of parties, protocol instances, and group members) verifies that an agent's initial derived group key stays secret provided no group member the agent believes is present has been compromised; the model check completes in approximately 15 minutes on what the paper describes only as "a modern desktop," without further hardware specification.

### Parameters
| Parameter | Value used | Range tested / notes |
|---|---|---|
| Group size (implementation benchmark) | 10 to 1,000 members | Log-scale sweep, Figure 7 |
| Message size | 32 bytes | Chosen to carry one AES-256 key |
| Benchmark hardware | 2016 MacBook Pro, 3.3 GHz Intel Core i7, 16 GB RAM | Single machine, no distributed network measurement |
| Runs averaged | 4 | Stated variance attributed to Java JIT compiler behavior, not derived |
| Tamarin verification time | ~15 minutes | Single run, "modern desktop," no further specification |

### Stated limitations
The paper explicitly places four problems out of scope and names why: sender-specific authentication (proof of which specific group member sent a message under the shared key) is not provided, because ART omits per-sender signature keys by design choice, so any group member can produce a message indistinguishable in origin from any other member's; malicious-insider security for subsets of a group (m < n honest members) is not addressed, deferred to prior GKE work by Abdalla, Chevalier, Manulis, and Pointcheval; executability under concurrent, conflicting key updates (two members updating simultaneously) is not solved — the paper offers two informal mitigations (a short grace window accepting messages under a stale key, or transport-layer rejection of out-of-order updates) but states a complete solution is an open research question; transcript agreement (all members agreeing on the ordered list of sent and received messages) is not covered. A malicious group creator can silently add an undetected eavesdropper to a newly created group, an attack the paper considers out of scope on the grounds that any group member could republish plaintext regardless of protocol design. Asynchronous group creation carries a stated security cost: if the creator is compromised during the initial creation phase before any other member has come online, all resulting stage keys stay insecure until every group member has independently performed at least one key update; the paper documents this explicitly as an increased requirement captured in its formal freshness predicates, not something ART eliminates. The bandwidth comparison found that ART's true byte count over the network can exceed pairwise channels' when broadcast is implemented via server-side fanout, because every recipient receives and processes a full logarithmic-size update rather than the constant-size message pairwise delivery sends per recipient; ART's advantage is lower per-agent sending latency, not lower total network bytes. The Java implementation and Tamarin proof are stated deliverables, but the paper does not benchmark against the Sender Keys design at all, stating this omission directly on the grounds that Sender Keys does not achieve PCS and so is not a comparable security target.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
ART requires a one-round authenticated key exchange protocol (used by the group creator to derive each future member's leaf secret from that member's published prekeys) but states no specific structural requirement on that sub-protocol beyond it being a strong one-round Authenticated Key Exchange (AKE). It requires every group member to maintain a persistent local view of the DH tree's public-key structure (its own copath) between sessions, since a member computes the tree key from its own leaf secret combined with copath public keys, not from any message content alone. It requires reliable broadcast of updated public keys to the whole group after every member update — the paper's own stated mitigations for concurrent updates (a grace-period buffer, or transport-layer rejection of stale updates) require either a relaxation of key-freshness guarantees or an ordering-enforcing transport layer, meaning the choice of transport directly trades off availability against key-lifetime exposure. It assumes an untrusted server may only reorder or drop messages, never forge signed or MAC-authenticated update messages, since ART authenticates the initial group-setup message with a digital signature and every subsequent update with a MAC. It does not authenticate individual senders within an update (no per-sender signature key), so any system layering identity attribution or accountable messaging on top of ART must supply that separately; the paper flags this explicitly as future extension territory (Section 8), not a built-in property. It assumes DH-group hardness (the paper's PRF-ODH assumption) as its sole computational hardness basis and offers no post-quantum variant.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus.

### References worth retrieving
- Cohn-Gordon, Cremers, Garratt. "On post-compromise security." IEEE CSF 2016. — foundational (source of the PCS definition ART targets; already a target in this corpus as COHNGORDON-CSF-16)
- Cohn-Gordon, Cremers, Dowling, Garratt, Stebila. "A formal security analysis of the Signal messaging protocol." — foundational (formal treatment of the two-party ratchet ART's group case extends; already a target as COHNGORDON-EUROSP-17)
- Kim, Perrig, Tsudik. "Tree-based group key agreement." ACM TISSEC. — foundational (the synchronous tree-DH group key agreement line ART generalizes to asynchronous operation)
- Facebook. "Messenger Secret Conversations (Technical Whitepaper Version 2.0)." 2017. — competing (deployed Sender Keys design, the direct comparison target in Table 1)
- WhatsApp. "WhatsApp Encryption Overview." 2016. — competing (deployed Sender Keys design)
- Rösler, Mainka, Schwenk. "More is less: on the end-to-end security of group chats..." 2018. — attack (contemporaneous vulnerability findings against WhatsApp, Signal, and Threema group operations, cited in this paper as concurrent work)
- Farb, Lin, Kim, McCune, Perrig. "SafeSlinger..." 2013. — competing (synchronous secure-group-credential-exchange design directly contrasted against ART's asynchronicity)
- Green, Miers. "Forward secure asynchronous messaging from puncturable encryption." — foundational (alternative forward-secrecy mechanism for the asynchronous setting)
- Abdalla, Chevalier, Manulis, Pointcheval. "Flexible group key exchange..." — foundational (subset-security GKE line the paper defers malicious-insider handling to)

## [COHNGORDON-CSF-16] On Post-Compromise Security
**Citation:** Katriel Cohn-Gordon, Cas Cremers, Luke Garratt. "On Post-Compromise Security." IEEE Computer Security Foundations Symposium (CSF), 2016. DOI: 10.1109/CSF.2016.19.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://eprint.iacr.org/2016/221.pdf (extended version, v1.4, October 2019 — the paper's own posted revision of the CSF 2016 paper)
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2016/221.pdf
**Domain:** H

### What it does
This paper defines Post-Compromise Security (PCS): the guarantee that Alice regains a security guarantee about communication with Bob even though Bob's secrets have already been compromised by an adversary, without Alice needing to detect that the compromise occurred. Before this paper, standard Authenticated Key Exchange (AKE — a protocol by which two parties derive a shared session key and confirm each other's identity) security definitions ruled out any guarantee once a party's long-term key was learned by an adversary, on the informal argument that a party who knows a long-term key can run every computation the true owner could run and so cannot be distinguished from the true owner. The paper's counterargument: this informal impossibility proof does not account for a session that runs after the compromise and generates fresh, uncompromised secret state — if that later session's fresh state is what future authentication relies on, the original long-term-key compromise is no longer sufficient to sustain an impersonation.

The paper distinguishes two compromise strengths. Weak compromise gives the adversary temporary use of long-term-key operations (for example, temporary control of a Hardware Security Module, a device that performs signing without exposing the key itself) without ever learning the key value; total compromise gives the adversary the long-term key value itself. For weak compromise, the paper proves (Theorem 11) that an ordinary signed Diffie-Hellman (DH) challenge-response protocol already achieves PCS: because the adversary never learns the signing key, once the adversary's temporary hardware access ends, the adversary cannot forge new signatures, so a session run after access ends is secure. For total compromise, the paper proves an outright impossibility for protocols with no persistent state (Theorem 14: no stateless protocol is secure in the paper's KE-PCS model), because a stateless protocol's only secret inputs are the compromised long-term key and fresh session randomness, both of which the adversary can supply itself. To achieve PCS under total compromise, the paper defines a generic transformation from any three-message AKE protocol π into a stateful protocol π† that maintains synchronized secret state ("intermediate secrets") between the two parties across sessions and derives each new session key by mixing in that evolving state; it proves that if π is secure in a strong existing AKE model (ΩAKE∩ISM), the transformed π† is secure in a still-stronger model (ΩAKE) that additionally captures PCS. The paper further proves a companion impossibility (Theorem 19): no correct one-round protocol secure in its PCS model can be post-network robust, meaning any one-round PCS protocol is vulnerable to a denial-of-service attack in which a network adversary permanently prevents two parties from ever again establishing matching session keys, because rejecting a forged message under attack necessarily desynchronizes the parties' persistent state. The paper's full transformation (given as a two-round protocol) is built specifically to resist this failure mode, remaining "post-network robust" even after an adversary with temporary network control interferes.

### Measured results
None. This is a formal-methods paper: its results are definitions, security-model constructions, and theorems with proofs (all proofs given in the paper's appendices), not empirical measurements. No implementation, simulation, or benchmark is reported. The two structural (not empirical) results load-bearing for later composition analysis are Theorem 14 (no stateless protocol achieves PCS under total compromise, unconditionally, for any protocol structure) and Theorem 19 (no one-round protocol that achieves PCS under total compromise can also resist network-level denial of service, unconditionally).

### Parameters
Not applicable — no experiment or implementation is reported. The paper's formal models are parameterized by a set of adversary queries Q (create, send, corrupt, randomness, session-key, and others defined in the paper's Table 2) and a freshness predicate F restricting which query sequences count as valid attacks; the exact predicate clauses making up each named model (eCKw, eCKw-PCS, ΩAKE∩ISM, ΩAKE, KE-PCS) are given precisely in the paper's Table 3, and any downstream use of these models must copy that predicate exactly rather than approximate it, because the difference between predicate clauses is what separates a satisfiable model from an unsatisfiable one (Theorem 14 is exactly the statement that the KE-PCS predicate is too permissive for any stateless protocol to satisfy).

### Stated limitations
The paper's first (weak-compromise, HSM-based) construction assumes only a signature interface to the long-term key — the abstract operation "sign with this key" and nothing else — and the authors state explicitly that most real Hardware Security Modules expose a wider operation set (they cite the PKCS#11 standard as an example), so extending the result to a general key-storage interface, including Diffie-Hellman-style key-derivation operations of the form (chosen exponent)^(stored key), is left as future work, described by the authors as needing care because the interaction between such an interface and DH session-key computation is subtle. The paper considers only necessary conditions demonstrated by one concrete protocol (the signed DH challenge-response of their Figure 4); deriving general necessary or sufficient conditions on protocol structure for achieving PCS under weak compromise is left open, with the sole stated partial result that the signature must cover some freshly generated data. The paper does not address zero-round-trip (0-RTT) protocols like Axolotl/Double Ratchet, which send a first message before any round-trip completes; the authors state as an open question how the ratcheting mechanism's necessity for 0-RTT operation interacts with the security goals of PCS. The generic stateful-protocol transformation targets only signature-based, three-message input protocols; the paper does not claim the transformation's applicability to arbitrary starting protocols outside that message-count and authentication-type assumption.

**Case-study limitation findings — protocols the paper shows fail to achieve PCS, with the specific mechanism of failure:**
- OPTLS (a since-superseded signature-free TLS 1.3 handshake proposal, also matching Google's early QUIC design): the server signs a temporary public key together with a validity period, and that pre-signed key then functions as a standing credential — an adversary with only temporary access to the server's signing key can issue a fake pre-signed key that remains valid and usable for impersonation after the adversary's HSM access is revoked, so the protocol does not achieve PCS even though it separately provides forward secrecy through its ephemeral DH exchange, and this failure persists even if the signing key is held in a Trusted Platform Module (TPM).
- TextSecure/Axolotl (the ratcheting predecessor to Signal's Double Ratchet, as deployed in the discontinued TextSecure messaging app): each user device stored a full copy of the user's long-term identity key but ran an independent, unshared Axolotl ratchet chain per device; an adversary who learned a user's long-term identity key could register a new device under that identity, and other users would accept the new device as legitimate purely on the strength of the correct identity key, so an adversary could keep impersonating a user by registering fresh devices even after the user's genuine devices had completed an honest key-refreshing session that should, under PCS, have locked the adversary out. The paper states it remains unclear whether Axolotl's ratcheting in TextSecure provided any security benefit over a plain strong AKE protocol beyond reducing round trips, though a separately cited earlier analysis (Frosch et al., "How Secure is TextSecure?") found an unrelated unknown-key-share attack and did not itself examine post-compromise security.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The paper's core PCS-achieving construction under total compromise requires persistent, synchronized secret state shared between the two communicating parties across sessions ("intermediate secrets"), so any system adopting it must provide durable per-peer storage that survives between sessions, not just within one session; a fully stateless implementation cannot satisfy PCS under total compromise by Theorem 14, unconditionally, regardless of what other mechanism is layered around it. Robust operation under network interference (post-network robustness) requires at least two message rounds, by Theorem 19 — any system requiring both PCS-under-total-compromise and resistance to network-level denial of service cannot use a one-round handshake, and this trade-off cannot be resolved by adding cryptographic strength, only by adding a round. The weak-compromise (HSM) construction requires that the long-term signing key never leave the isolated hardware boundary in any form — the security proof depends specifically on the key being usable only through a black-box sign operation, so any code path or backup procedure that exports the raw key value invalidates the guarantee entirely, converting a weak compromise into a total one. A system using the paper's key-refreshing transformation must ensure state updates are explicitly tied to successful peer authentication; the paper states that a state update performed without authenticating the peer first risks the deletion of a secret value still needed to communicate with the legitimate peer, which is exactly the flaw the paper's own "robustness" definition is built to rule out. Multi-device deployments must share ratchet/session state across a user's devices, not merely share the long-term identity key per device independently — the TextSecure case study demonstrates that per-device long-term-key copies without shared session state reopens the exact impersonation vector PCS is meant to close.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus. This paper's own case studies contradict a claim commonly associated with TextSecure/Axolotl and its descendant the Double Ratchet — that ratcheting alone delivers post-compromise security — by showing the specific multi-device implementation TextSecure shipped did not achieve PCS despite using a ratchet; the paper is explicit that this is a fact about the specific multi-device architecture deployed, not a claim that ratcheting mechanisms cannot achieve PCS (Signal's later Double Ratchet, evaluated in COHNGORDON-EUROSP-17 in this corpus, is the two-party protocol built to close this gap).
