### Parameters

| Parameter | Definition | Value used |
|---|---|---|
| `n` | total storage nodes (identified with shards for protocol description) | `n = 3f+1` |
| `f` | maximum Byzantine (malicious) nodes tolerated | up to `n/3` (rounded down) |
| Matrix dimensions (RedStuff) | primary x secondary sliver split before encoding | `[f+1, 2f+1]` |
| Storage overhead (RedStuff) | ratio of stored data to original blob size | 4.5x |
| Storage overhead (classic 1D erasure coding, e.g. Storj/Sia-style at n=3f+1) | same ratio | 3x |
| Storage overhead (full replication, at 10^-12 durability target) | same ratio | 25x |
| Recovery cost (RedStuff) | bandwidth per node to recover one lost sliver | O(\|blob\|/n) |
| Recovery cost (1D erasure coding) | same | O(\|blob\|) |
| Shard count (both production networks) | total shards, distributed across storage nodes | 1,000 |
| Approximate node count (both production networks) | storage node committee size | ~100 (95 mainnet, 101 testnet, at the observation date) |
| Deployment codebase | erasure coding library used in production | reed-solomon-simd (replaced an earlier RaptorQ implementation after a reported vulnerability) |
| Blockchain control-plane implementation | consensus/state-machine-replication substrate used | Sui |
| Client evaluation instance | testnet measurement hardware | AWS m5d.8xlarge, 10 Gbps bandwidth, 32 vCPUs, 128 GB RAM, US East (N. Virginia) |

### Stated limitations

The paper states that a naive symmetric `[f+1, f+1]` matrix encoding would double the replication cost relative to its chosen asymmetric `[f+1, 2f+1]` design, and that its actual design "achieves the minimum replication cost at the expense of a slightly more structured recovery procedure" — the 4.5x overhead is stated as a deliberate, explained trade rather than an incidental cost. The metadata-distribution optimization described in the write protocol (encoding metadata with a 1D `(f+1)`-out-of-`n` scheme to reduce metadata storage from quadratic to linear system-wide overhead) is stated as not yet deployed: "our production deployment currently forgoes this optimization and stores the metadata in full on every node," meaning the measured production system carries a metadata-storage cost higher than the protocol as fully designed would. The paper's own comparison table (Table 1) prices "classic ECC" systems (Storj, Sia) at a flat 3x overhead figure derived from the encoding construction at `n=3f+1`, while the paper's own related-work discussion separately cites Storj's actual deployed configuration (29-of-80 Reed-Solomon) as producing a 2.75x replication factor — these are two different numbers for the same comparison system within the same paper, and the paper does not reconcile the gap between the idealized 3x figure used for the headline comparison and the 2.75x figure it separately reports for Storj's real deployment. The paper states classic erasure-coded systems such as Storj have "a key limitation" in their inability to efficiently heal lost parts, relying on users to reconstruct and re-encode the full file — this is presented as the specific gap RedStuff's self-healing property closes, not as a universal property of all erasure coding. Shard-recovery measurements on mainnet (epochs 17 and 20) are drawn from real operational incidents, not a controlled experiment, and the paper states these durations (17-64 hours per multi-shard recovery event) as observed outcomes without stating a target service-level bound the system is designed to meet.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system

RedStuff requires an external, black-box blockchain substrate that accepts a concurrent transaction set and outputs a single total order of state updates without indefinite censorship; the paper states this abstraction, not a specific consensus algorithm, is what RedStuff needs, and any state-machine-replication protocol meeting it would suffice (the deployed system uses Sui). The 2D encoding's recovery mechanism requires per-sliver vector commitments (the deployment uses Merkle trees) so a recovering node can verify a returned symbol against what the original writer committed to — without this, a Byzantine node returning a substituted symbol during recovery would not be detectable. Achieving the stated O(blob/n) recovery cost requires the requesting node to be able to reach at least `f+1` other nodes holding the relevant row/column symbols; if fewer than `f+1` honest nodes are reachable (a partition, or an adversary exceeding the `f` threshold), sliver recovery as described does not complete. The epoch-change mechanism requires the underlying blockchain to make committee and shard-assignment state available and immutable at each epoch boundary, since shard-transfer versus shard-recovery decisions and the count of shards each node is currently responsible for are read directly from on-chain state. The system's Byzantine-fault-tolerance guarantee (data survives loss of up to 2/3 of shards, continues accepting writes with up to 1/3 of shards unresponsive) requires the `n = 3f+1` / adversary-controls-at-most-`f` assumption to hold in the deployed committee; the paper's adversarial model further assumes every pair of honest nodes has a reliable, authenticated channel and an asynchronous network that eventually delivers messages within an epoch (though it may drop messages across an epoch boundary), which downstream availability guarantees are conditioned on.

### Contradicts

The commonly-cited figures "storage overhead 3.5x for Walrus against Storj's 1.75x" are not supported by this paper's own text: the paper states Walrus/RedStuff's overhead as 4.5x, not 3.5x, and states Storj's actual deployed replication factor as 2.75x (from its 29-of-80 Reed-Solomon configuration), not 1.75x. Neither of the previously-circulated figures traces to this primary source; both must be treated as unverified until a different source is found that supports them. Within this paper itself, note a smaller internal inconsistency worth flagging for a synthesis step: Table 1 prices "classic ECC" systems generically at 3x overhead (the theoretical minimum at `n=3f+1` for one-dimensional Byzantine-fault-tolerant erasure coding), while the related-work section separately states Storj's actual deployed system achieves 2.75x — a real deployment reporting a lower overhead than the paper's own idealized comparison baseline for the same system category. No other paper in this batch (BENET-FILECOIN-17, BHAGWAN-IPTPS-03, BHAGWAN-NSDI-04, BLAKE-HOTOS-03, CHUN-NSDI-06) reports a storage-overhead or recovery-bandwidth figure for Filecoin, Storj, Sia, or Arweave that conflicts with this paper's figures; BENET-FILECOIN-17 reports no measured overhead figure for Filecoin at all (see that entry), so this paper's own Filecoin comparison numbers (1.5-hour seal, 3-hour sealed read) are the only source for those figures within this batch and are themselves cited from Filecoin's own network-performance documentation rather than independently measured here.

### References worth retrieving

- Rashmi, Shah, Kumar, "Enabling node repair in any erasure code for distributed storage," IEEE ISIT 2011 — foundational (the general node-repair framework RedStuff's two-dimensional structure draws on, alongside the Twin-code framework)
- Marina, Velkoska, Paunkoska, Baleski, "Security in Twin-code framework," ICUMT 2015 — foundational (Twin-code, the crash-tolerant efficient-recovery framework RedStuff explicitly adapts to the Byzantine setting)
- Nazirkhanova, Neu, Tse, "Information dispersal with provable retrievability for rollups," ACM AFT 2022 — competing (Semi-AVID, described as the most closely related prior work; cannot achieve Write Completeness without full data reconstruction, making it expensive for epoch change)
- Cachin, Tessaro, "Asynchronous verifiable information dispersal," IEEE SRDS 2005 — competing (AVID; the paper argues AVID's verifiability machinery is unnecessarily constraining for this problem)
- Al-Bassam, Sonnino, Buterin, Khoffi, "Fraud and data availability proofs: Detecting invalid blocks in light clients," FC 2021 — foundational (data-availability-sampling approach used by Celestia, cited as a related two-dimensional Reed-Solomon-coding system with a different retention model — full replication for about a month, versus Walrus's arbitrarily long retention)
- Storj Labs, "Storj: A decentralized cloud storage network framework," 2018, and "Understanding file repair in a distributed network," 2026 — competing (source of the corrected 2.75x replication-factor figure and the stated inability-to-efficiently-heal-lost-parts limitation)
- Vorick, Champine, "Sia: Simple decentralized storage," Nebulous Inc. whitepaper, 2014 — competing
- Williams, Diordiiev, Berman, Raybould, Uemlianin, "Arweave: A protocol for economically sustainable information permanence," Arweave yellow paper DRAFT-1, 2019 — competing (source of the Proof-of-Access mining/full-replication design this paper measures against directly)
- Douceur, "The Sybil attack," IPTPS 2002 — attack (cited for the Sybil-attack risk in full-replication systems where storage nodes might falsely claim to hold multiple copies)
- Fisch, "PoReps: Proofs of space on useful data," IACR ePrint 2018/678 — foundational (Filecoin's proof-of-storage construction, cited as the source of Filecoin's resource-intensive sealing/proving latency)

## [DAVIDSON-POPETS-18] Privacy Pass: Bypassing Internet Challenges Anonymously
**Citation:** Alex Davidson, Ian Goldberg, Nick Sullivan, George Tankersley, Filippo Valsorda. "Privacy Pass: Bypassing Internet Challenges Anonymously." Proceedings on Privacy Enhancing Technologies (PoPETs), 2018 (3):164-180. DOI 10.1515/popets-2018-0026.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://petsymposium.org/popets/2018/popets-2018-0026.pdf
**Source URL:** https://petsymposium.org/popets/2018/popets-2018-0026.pdf
**Domain:** I

### What it does
Privacy Pass lets a client redeem one unlinkable anonymous token per rate-limited action, obtained in a batch of N tokens after passing a single challenge (a CAPTCHA in the deployed case), so a server can rate-limit or gate repeated access without learning which of the client's earlier challenge-passes any later redemption corresponds to. The mechanism is a verifiable oblivious pseudorandom function (VOPRF): an oblivious PRF is a two-party protocol letting a client obtain F_k(x) for a server-held key k without revealing x to the server, and "verifiable" means the client also gets a proof that the server used the same key k it committed to. The client generates N random token values t_1...t_N, computes T_i = H1(t_i) for a hash-to-curve function H1, blinds each with a random exponent r_i to get a blinded token, and sends the batch to the server together with proof of having passed the challenge. The server signs each blinded token under its own private key and produces one non-interactive zero-knowledge proof (a batched discrete-log-equality, or DLEQ, proof) that every signature in the batch used the same private key, rather than one DLEQ proof per token; the client verifies this single batched proof and unblinds each signed token to recover N usable (t_i, W_i) pairs, where W_i = the PRF evaluation F_k(t_i). To redeem a token later, the client presents an unspent pair (t, W) together with a MAC computed over request-binding data R using a key derived from W; the server recomputes F_k(t) from its own key, checks that t has not been redeemed before, and verifies the MAC to confirm the client actually holds a validly signed token, without either side ever having linked this redemption to the earlier signing session that produced it. This unlinkability follows from the OPRF's message-hiding property (the server never saw t or T_i unblinded during signing) plus the one-more-token security property, which the paper proves under a standard hardness assumption and which guarantees a client holding l signed tokens cannot construct l+1 valid ones. Key rotation invalidates old tokens: the server periodically retires old signing keys and clients must obtain fresh tokens under a key still on the server's accepted-key list, which the paper recommends keeping to about 2-3 concurrently accepted keys to limit how far the user base is split across key-specific anonymity sets.

### Measured results

| Condition | Result |
|---|---|
| Cryptographic microbenchmarks, NIST P-256 elliptic curve, JavaScript client / Go server implementation, N tokens per batch swept at N = 5, 10, 15, ..., 100, 100 repeated trials per N | Client: token generation (GenToken + Blind) = 120 + 64N ms; DLEQ verification = 220 + 110N ms; total signing request = 340 + 180N ms; total redemption request = 57 ms (constant, independent of N). Server: signing = 0.04 + 0.20N ms; DLEQ proof generation = 0.32 + 0.55N ms; total signing = 1.48 + 0.87N ms; total redemption = 0.8 ms (constant) |
| Message size overhead, same benchmark setup, N tokens per batch | Signing request (client to edge): 57 + 63N bytes; signing response (edge to client): 295 + 121N bytes (about double the request size because the JavaScript client compresses elliptic-curve points but the Go server does not, to avoid making the client perform expensive point decompression); redemption request: 396 bytes (constant); for N = 30, total additional communication load stated as under 6 KB |
| Cloudflare production deployment, browser extension released 8 November 2017, figures averaged over a 7-day window ending 28 November 2017 (20 days after release) | Chrome users: 8,499; Firefox users: 3,489 (excludes manually-installed copies). Cloudflare accepted 1.6 trillion requests per week on average, of which 780 billion came over the Tor network. 1.04% of all requests globally were served a CAPTCHA challenge, versus 17% of Tor-network traffic — stated by the authors as evidence of disproportionate challenge exposure for Tor users |
| Same deployment window, redemption-phase operating load | Redemption phases peaked at 2,000 per second globally and 200 per second for Tor users; 515 million requests globally contained a Privacy-Pass clearance cookie, of which 34.5 million (22.58% of Tor-originated requests) came from the Tor network |
| Same deployment window, median request/response sizes | Tor-user request/response sizes: 700-800 bytes / 5-6 KB; median CAPTCHA submission and response sizes: under 1 KB — the paper notes these figures differ slightly from the controlled benchmarks above because they include Cloudflare-specific data not modeled in the benchmark harness |
| Token-batch size deployed in production vs. server-supported maximum | Cloudflare issues N = 30 tokens per solved challenge in the initial deployment, chosen as a balance of usability, performance, and token-hoarding risk, though the server supports up to N = 100; the paper states this upper bound of 100 means accumulating 1,000,000 tokens for a denial-of-service stockpile would require a minimum of 10,000 CAPTCHA solutions |

### Parameters
- Elliptic curve: NIST P-256.
- Token batch size N: benchmarked at N = 5, 10, 15, ..., 100 in 5-token increments; deployed value N = 30; server-enforced maximum N = 100.
- Key rotation interval: the paper recommends short rotation periods "such as 3-4 days" to bound how long a stockpiled token batch of signed tokens remains redeemable.
- Number of concurrently accepted signing keys: recommended at 2-3, to limit the degree to which multiple active keys split the anonymity set of token holders into smaller, more identifiable groups.
- Threat/security model: security proofs are given in the random oracle model, and one-more-token security is stated to follow from "a standard assumption" without the paper stating that assumption's name at the point cited in the main text (developed in the paper's Section 5.4.3 proof).

### Stated limitations
The paper states its protocol does not defend against a monster-in-the-middle (MitM) adversary during the signing phase: because tokens carry no client-binding metadata (by design, to avoid deanonymization via that metadata), a MitM that intercepts a client's completed-challenge signing request can substitute its own blinded tokens and receive signed tokens without having solved the challenge itself; the paper's stated mitigation is only that this requires a renewable source of challenge solutions to exploit repeatedly, not a cryptographic fix. Token accumulation ("farming") is stated as a residual risk enabling stockpiling for a denial-of-service attack; the paper's countermeasures are operational limits (the 100-token signing cap, and key rotation on the order of days) rather than a protocol-level prevention. Token exhaustion is stated as possible: an embedded sub-resource that repeatedly triggers redemption can drain a client's stored tokens; the paper's mitigation (rate-limiting redemptions per URL, tracked client-side) is described as reducing rather than eliminating the attack, and a stronger fix (blacklisting URLs after one redemption attempt) is stated as "not implemented at time of writing." The paper states a structural anonymity limit shared with all such registration-based systems: early-adopter clients belong to a small anonymity set, and a server that signs tokens for very few clients (or immediately after a key rotation) can narrow a later redemption to one of a small number of possible signers; the paper states this makes the scheme, like Tor itself, "only really effective when the number of users is quite large." The paper explicitly states its threat model does not defend against a verifier (the edge/CDN) colluding with the token issuer to break unlinkability, nor against a client that shares its tokens with other parties — both are named directly by the target registry's citation as out of scope, and correspondingly this paper's security proofs (Section 5, unlinkability and one-more-token security) are stated relative to an honest-but-possibly-curious single verifier-issuer, not a colluding pair. Double-spending protection is stated to require each service to implement its own redemption-index check (a hash table or Bloom filter over spent tokens); the paper does not measure the storage or lookup cost of this index at Cloudflare's request volume, only recommends it be present.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The protocol requires the server to run and maintain a signing key, publish a small, low-churn list of currently accepted verification commitments (2-3 keys recommended) so clients whose tokens were signed under a recently-rotated-out key can still redeem before those tokens expire, and requires some out-of-band or globally-consistent channel for distributing key-rotation updates; the paper suggests "beacons or other globally visible and consistent locations, such as the Tor consensus" for this, but states the initial deployment instead updates commitments directly inside the browser extension. It requires the calling application (the "challenge" the client must first pass) to supply the actual work-based anonymity guarantee: Privacy Pass tokens are only as scarce as the challenges that produce them, so the mechanism composes with any challenge type (the paper's deployment uses a CAPTCHA) but supplies no scarcity of its own. It requires the redeeming server to maintain a double-spend index across every previously redeemed token value t, and the paper states each service's own redemption index must be separate from every other service's, since services must "use their own private keys for signing tokens so that tokens cannot be spent multiple times across different services." It requires the client to be able to store unspent token pairs locally between the signing and redemption phases (the browser extension's local storage in the deployed case) and to track, per domain, whether a token has already been spent, since the paper's own mitigation for the token-exhaustion attack depends on this per-domain spend tracking being available and enforced client-side.

### Contradicts
None found.

### References worth retrieving
- Jarecki, S., Kiayias, A., Krawczyk, H., "Round-optimal password-protected secret sharing and T-PAKE in the password-only model." — foundational (originates the oblivious PRF and DLEQ-proof-based verifiable OPRF construction this paper adapts directly, including the batched DLEQ-proof extension)
- Henry, R., Goldberg, I., "Formalizing anonymous blacklisting systems." — competing (formalizes multiple anonymous blacklisting/whitelisting approaches for the same Tor-CAPTCHA-denial problem, including blind-RSA-based designs and "Nymble-like" trusted-third-party designs the paper explicitly declines to adopt because they require an extra trusted party)
- Henry, R., Goldberg, I., "Batch proofs of partial knowledge." — foundational (source of the batching technique the paper's batched DLEQ proof adapts, cited as showing batch verification is possible for this proof family)
- Liu, Z., Liu, Y., Winter, P., Mittal, P., et al., "TorPolice: ..." — competing (a privacy-preserving access-control mechanism for Tor-originated connections, contrasted as narrower in scope than this paper's general browser-based solution)
- Lofgren, P., Hopper, N., "BNymble: More anonymous..." — competing (a Nymble-family anonymous-blacklisting system using a trusted third party, part of the design space the paper positions itself against)
- Chaum, D., "Blind signatures for untraceable payments." — foundational (originates the blind-signature primitive the paper's VOPRF-based token scheme is compared against as a heavier-weight alternative construction)
- Papadopoulos, D., Wessels, D., Huque, S., et al., "..." (elliptic curve verifiable random functions) — foundational (cited as closely related work in constructing elliptic-curve verifiable random functions, informing the paper's own VOPRF construction choices)

## [DAVIDSON-POPETS-23] FrodoPIR: Simple, Scalable, Single-Server Private Information Retrieval
**Citation:** Alex Davidson, Goncalo Pestana, Sofia Celi. "FrodoPIR: Simple, Scalable, Single-Server Private Information Retrieval." Proceedings on Privacy Enhancing Technologies (PoPETs), 2023. DOI 10.56553/POPETS-2023-0022.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://eprint.iacr.org/2022/981.pdf
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2022/981.pdf
**Domain:** G

### What it does
FrodoPIR lets a client download one item from a server-held database, at a server-chosen index, without revealing to the server which index the client read. The server cannot distinguish a query for index i from a query for any other index. The construction splits into an offline phase and an online phase. In the offline phase the server derives a pseudorandom Learning-With-Errors (LWE) matrix A (dimension n times m, from a lambda-bit seed) and multiplies it by the database (arranged as an m by omega matrix D) to produce a public parameter matrix M = A times D; the client independently derives the same A from the published seed and, per future query, samples a secret vector and computes preprocessed values that do not depend on which index will later be queried. Because this preprocessing is client-independent (the server does the same work once no matter how many clients query later) and query-independent (the client does the same work once no matter which index it will later query), a single offline computation amortizes across every client and every query. In the online phase the client picks the actual query index, adds a small correction to one entry of its preprocessed vector, and sends the modified vector; the server computes one vector-matrix multiplication against its database and returns the result; the client subtracts its own secret to recover the requested item. Security rests on the Matrix-LWE assumption: an adversary given the query vector cannot distinguish which index was targeted.

### Measured results
All computation measured single-threaded on an Amazon EC2 t2.2xlarge (8 CPU cores, 32 GB RAM), except Table 7 which uses a c5n.2xlarge to match a comparison paper's hardware. Database elements are 1 KB (w = 2^13 bits) unless stated otherwise. Security parameter n = 1774 (conservative setting for 2^52 client queries at 128-bit security) unless stated otherwise.

Non-amortized performance by database size (Table 6, 1 KB elements, single client, single server, lattice dimension n = 1774):

| log2(m) items | Client download, offline (KB) | DB preprocessing (s) | Client query (KB, online) | Server response (KB, online) | Server response time (ms) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 16 | 5682 | 104.6 | 256 | 3.203 | 45.0 |
| 17 | 5682 | 206.3 | 512 | 3.203 | 94.5 |
| 18 | 5682 | 429.1 | 1024 | 3.203 | 188.4 |
| 19 | 6313 | 936.4 | 2048 | 3.556 | 417.9 |
| 20 | 6313 | 1895.2 | 4096 | 3.556 | 825.4 |

Server response size grows less than 3.6 times the original 1 KB element across all measured database sizes, versus 128 times for SOnionPIR and 320 times for PSIR at the same 2^20-element database size, comparison run on the same t2.2xlarge hardware with each client making 500 queries.

Financial cost, at $0.09 per GB of server-to-client transfer and $0.0464 per CPU hour (AWS on-demand pricing, August 2022): offline database preprocessing for a 2^20-element database costs slightly above 1 US cent (a one-time, globally amortizable cost); the online per-query cost is about 0.001 cent at the largest measured database size.

Comparison against Spiral (Menon and Wu) on a shared c5n.2xlarge instance, single-threaded, at three database shapes (Table 7):

| Database shape | Metric | Spiral | FrodoPIR |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2^20 items x 256 B | Query size | 14 KB | 4 MB |
| 2^20 items x 256 B | Response size | 20 KB | 912 B |
| 2^20 items x 256 B | Server computation time | 1.37 s | 0.16 s |
| 2^20 items x 256 B | Throughput | 196 MB/s | 1.56 GB/s |
| 2^18 items x 30 KB (FrodoPIR extrapolated from 2^16 items for memory reasons) | Server computation time | 17.69 s | 4.27 s |
| 2^18 items x 30 KB | Throughput | 434 MB/s | 1.76 GB/s |
| 2^14 items x 100 KB | Server computation time | 4.58 s | 0.89 s |
| 2^14 items x 100 KB | Throughput | 358 MB/s | 1.76 GB/s |

FrodoPIR wins on computation throughput at every measured shape; Spiral wins on response-size-to-element ratio and bandwidth when elements are large (30 KB or 100 KB).

Reducing the LWE dimension n from 1774 to 1572 or 1288 (Table 10, log2(m) = 16 and 20, same t2.2xlarge hardware): bandwidth (client download) falls by more than 11% at n = 1572 and by 27% at n = 1288, relative to n = 1774, at both database sizes; client derivation of the matrix A falls by about 20% at the smaller dimensions.

Applied worked example, Google SafeBrowsing-style URL blocklist checking, using a single 2^18-element, 1 KB-element database shard with the parameters of Table 5 at m = 2^18, on the same t2.2xlarge instance (Table 8): offline client download 180 KB, database preprocessing 28.6 s, online client query 1024 KB, online server response 0.1 KB, online server response time 5.223 ms.

Comparison against the two-server PIR constructions of Kogan and Corrigan-Gibbs (dpfPIR, ooPIR) and against the non-private baseline, all scaled to 1 billion users, using each scheme's stated per-query latency to derive server counts (Table 9):

| Indicator | Non-private | dpfPIR (2-server) | ooPIR (2-server) | FrodoPIR (1-server, estimated) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Servers needed for 1B users | 143 | 9047 | 1348 | 9778 |
| Latency (ms) | 90 | 122 | 91 | 90 |
| Client running time (s/month) | 0.5 | 0.8 | 8.0 | 1272.0 |
| Online communication (MB/month) | 3.0 | 3.6 | 9.0 | 539.7 |
| Max client storage (MB) | 4.5 | 4.5 | 26.1 | 30.69 |

FrodoPIR's server count and per-client monthly bandwidth are both worse than the two-server schemes in this specific comparison; the paper attributes this to the SafeBrowsing usage pattern (many small, frequent queries against a large database) rather than to a general FrodoPIR weakness, and states this comparison, unlike Table 7, is not a favorable case for FrodoPIR's design.

### Parameters
- LWE modulus q = 2^32 (fixed across all reported parameter sets, chosen to match 32-bit unsigned integer arithmetic).
- LWE dimension n: 1774 used as the primary conservative setting (128-bit security for up to 2^52 client queries); 1572 and 1288 tested as less conservative alternatives (Table 10) trading security margin for bandwidth.
- Plaintext modulus rho: 2^10 for database sizes m <= 2^18, 2^9 for m > 2^18 (Table 5).
- Number of tolerated queries before matrix A must be re-derived, l (script-l): 2^52 in the primary parameter sets.
- Error distribution chi: uniform ternary.
- Element size w: 1 KB (2^13 bits) in the main experiments (Section 6); 256 B, 30 KB, and 100 KB tested in the Spiral comparison (Table 7).
- Per-client number of preprocessed queries c: 500, fixed across the amortization comparisons with SOnionPIR and PSIR.
- Improvement factor kappa = (log(rho) times m) / (n times log(q)): reported as 13.0 to 187.6 across the five parameter rows of Table 5, rising with m.

### Stated limitations
The paper states the main limitation of FrodoPIR is that online client query size grows linearly in the database size m, unlike SOnionPIR and PSIR whose online query sizes grow more slowly; at m = 2^20, the client query reaches 4 MB. A second stated limitation is that the server's transformed database representation is roughly 3 times the size of the original database. The paper states this can be mitigated (query size, not the 3x storage factor) by sharding the database into s parallel instances, at the cost of a client download that grows by a factor of s and a public-parameter download per shard. The paper states it does not provide a fully optimized implementation: it explicitly excludes computational optimizations such as sub-cubic matrix multiplication and query batching, leaving them as unexplored future work. The paper states it does not evaluate the "DoublePIR" optimization of concurrent work (Henzinger et al.) applied to FrodoPIR, though it states the underlying observation should apply. The paper states its security analysis assumes a semi-honest (not malicious) server, and that no attack against the specific Matrix-LWE variant used is currently known, but does not prove none exists.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The client must know, before the online phase, the specific numeric index it wants to query; the paper states elsewhere (Section 7, referring to Kogan and Corrigan-Gibbs) that mapping a real-world key (such as a URL hash) to that index requires a separate mechanism the client downloads out of band, distinct from the FrodoPIR protocol proper. The scheme requires an offline phase before any query: the client must download the server's public parameters (the seed and matrix M) before making its first query, so a client cannot query cold. Database updates require the server to redistribute updated public parameters for whichever shard changed, and require every client to re-run preprocessing for that shard before it can query updated data; this couples update frequency to client-side computational and bandwidth allowance. The security guarantee (128-bit, against up to 2^52 or 2^32 queries depending on chosen n) decays as the server answers more queries against the same matrix A, and the server must eventually resample A to reset the guarantee; the paper assumes, under its semi-honest model, that the server does this resampling honestly. The scheme provides no defense if multiple non-colluding servers are required elsewhere in a design: it is explicitly single-server, so a system relying on FrodoPIR cannot also assume the multi-server non-collusion property that dpfPIR and ooPIR rely on.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus at time of writing. The paper's own Table 9 comparison contradicts an unqualified claim that FrodoPIR is cheaper than multi-server PIR in general: for the SafeBrowsing workload specifically, FrodoPIR uses more servers, more client compute time per month, and more monthly bandwidth than the two-server dpfPIR and ooPIR schemes of Kogan and Corrigan-Gibbs. The general throughput and financial-cost advantage claimed in Sections 6.1-6.2 holds against single-server stateful competitors (SOnionPIR, PSIR) under the amortized multi-client comparisons, not against multi-server schemes.

### References worth retrieving
- foundational: A. Henzinger, M. M. Hong, H. Corrigan-Gibbs, S. Meiklejohn, V. Vaikuntanathan. "One server for the price of two: Simple and fast single-server private information retrieval" (SimplePIR/DoublePIR), Cryptology ePrint 2022/949 — concurrent work using the same LWE mechanism; not yet in this corpus.
- competing: M. H. Mughees, H. Chen, L. Ren. "OnionPIR: Response efficient single-server PIR" — this is the SOnionPIR baseline compared against in Figures 6-7.
- competing: S. Patel, G. Persiano, K. Yeo. "Private stateful information retrieval" (PSIR) — the second single-server baseline compared against.
- competing: S. J. Menon, D. J. Wu. "SPIRAL: fast, high-rate single-server PIR via FHE" — the Table 7 comparison target for large database elements.
- competing: H. Corrigan-Gibbs, A. Henzinger, D. Kogan. "Single-server private information retrieval with sublinear amortized time" (CHKPIR), EUROCRYPT 2022 — the sublinear-online-time comparison in Section 6.2.
- competing: D. Kogan, H. Corrigan-Gibbs. Two-server PIR constructions (dpfPIR, ooPIR) for SafeBrowsing, cited as [54] — source of the Table 9 comparison numbers and the usage-model assumptions (query rate, update rate) FrodoPIR's SafeBrowsing example reuses.
- foundational: E. Boyle, N. Gilboa, Y. Ishai. "Function secret sharing: Improvements and extensions" — underlies distributed-point-function PIR-by-keyword approaches discussed as an alternative to FrodoPIR's index-based model.
- attack: M. R. Albrecht, R. Player, S. Scott. "On the concrete hardness of learning with errors" — the lattice-hardness estimator FrodoPIR's security parameters are derived from.

- "the server response size compared with the original 1KB data element" grows "< 3.6× overhead."
- "SOnionPIR (128×) and PSIR (320×)" response-size overhead at the same database size.
- "Clearly, FrodoPIR involves heavier usage costs compared to all known solutions" (SafeBrowsing comparison).

## [DHAMDHERE-IMC-12] Measuring the Deployment of IPv6: Topology, Routing and Performance
**Citation:** Amogh Dhamdhere, Matthew Luckie, Bradley Huffaker, kc claffy, Ahmed Elmokashfi, Emile Aben. "Measuring the Deployment of IPv6: Topology, Routing and Performance." ACM Internet Measurement Conference (IMC), 2012. DOI 10.1145/2398776.2398832.
**Retrieved:** full text via users.caida.org PDF
**Source URL:** https://users.caida.org/~amogh/papers/ipv6-IMC12.pdf
**Domain:** L

### What it does
The paper compares the IPv6 network's topology, routing dynamics, and data-plane performance against IPv4's, at a point when IPv6 deployment was still small, to determine whether the IPv6 network was converging toward the structure of the mature IPv4 network or remaining a separate, immature overlay. It builds historical topology snapshots by collecting BGP AS-path data from Route Views and RIPE RIS, applying a majority-filtering method (five samples of AS paths over a three-week window, keeping only paths seen in the majority of samples) to remove backup and transient links, repeated every three months, producing 56 IPv4 snapshots and 36 IPv6 snapshots spanning 1998-2011 (IPv4) and 2003-2011 (IPv6). It classifies AS business type using the authors' own prior algorithm and AS-to-AS business relationships (customer/provider/peer) using Gao's algorithm. For routing dynamics it processes BGP update streams from five networks that reported both IPv4 and IPv6 data throughout the study period (AT&T, Hurricane Electric, NTT-America, Tinet, IIJ), filtering out update bursts caused by monitor session resets using a method from prior work. For performance it runs its own active measurement: fetching a same-origin-AS webserver object of at least 10,000 bytes over both IPv4 and IPv6, alternating protocol, three fetches per server, from five vantage points, then comparing fetch time and RTT.

### Measured results
| Metric | Result | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Topology growth model | AS-count and AS-link growth both fit linear-then-exponential curves, with the inflection around 2008; exponents 0.13 (ASes) and 0.16 (AS links) for the post-2008 exponential phase | BGP topology snapshots, 1998-2011 (IPv4) / 2003-2011 (IPv6), majority-filtered as described above |
| Single-player dominance | Hurricane Electric (HE) appeared in 20% to 95% of IPv6 AS paths depending on vantage point; in 2012, HE was added to between 20% and 50% of paths where IPv4 and IPv6 paths for the same pair of endpoints differed | five BGP vantage points providing both IPv4 and IPv6 data since 2003 (Table 1); percentages vary by which vantage point is used |
| Path congruence | only 40-50% of AS-level paths toward dual-stacked origin ASes were identical between IPv4 and IPv6 at time of measurement; up to 95% could become identical if IPv6-capable ASes established IPv6 peerings matching their existing IPv4 peerings | AS-path comparison for dual-stacked origin ASes across the same BGP vantage points, October 2011 snapshot referenced for the "same AS for each VP" figure |
| Performance vs. path congruence | 79% of paths had IPv6 performance within 10% of IPv4 (or better) when the forward AS-level path was identical between protocols; only 63% had comparable performance when the AS-level paths differed | active measurement, five vantage points (a state network in New York, a research network and a commercial ISP in Japan, a commercial network and an enterprise customer in the Netherlands), objects ≥10,000 bytes, three fetches per server alternating protocol, five-second gap between measurements, filtered to exclude measurements with >10% standard error of mean download time (95% confidence) or IPv4/IPv6 object-size mismatch >1%; final dataset 544 dual-stack ASes (233 enterprise/customer, 106 small transit providers, 10 large transit providers, 195 content/access/hosting providers) |
| Relative fetch-time distribution | of paths tested, roughly 5% had IPv6 faster and 21% had IPv4 faster by more than 10% when the AS-level path differed between protocols; 37% were within 10% of each other on the same path, 10% differed by more than 10% on the same path | same active-measurement dataset as above, per Figure 14's four-way breakdown (same-path/different-path × IPv4-faster/IPv6-faster) |
| Reachable-AS-link overlap | 60-70% of IPv4 AS-path links toward dual-stacked origins were already present in the IPv6 topology, without any new BGP peering session being required | same BGP topology dataset, snapshot referenced in Figure 15 |

### Parameters
| Parameter | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Topology snapshot window | 5 AS-path samples over 3 weeks, majority-filtered, one snapshot every 3 months | Section 2, "BGP topology data" |
| Object-size threshold for performance fetches | ≥10,000 bytes, to escape TCP slow start | Section 2, "Performance data" |
| Fetches per webserver | 3, alternating IPv4/IPv6 sequentially, ~5 s gap between measurements | Section 2, "Performance data" |
| Filtering threshold for performance data | excluded if standard error of mean download time >10% at 95% confidence, or IPv4/IPv6 object sizes differ by >1% | Section 2, "Performance data" |
| Webservers tested per origin AS | up to 3, drawn from the Alexa top 1-million list | Section 2, "Performance data" |
| Active-measurement tools | scamper's `tbit` (page fetch with TCP SACK/timestamps negotiated, full packet trace) and `traceroute` | Section 2, "Performance data" |

### Stated limitations
The authors state that Route Views/RIPE RIS BGP data is known from prior work to inadequately expose the complete Internet topology, missing a significant fraction of peering and backup links at the edge; they mitigate this by focusing on customer-provider links, which they argue dominate the collected data, and note that any counts derived from this data are at worst lower bounds. They state they cannot determine, from the data available, why IPv6 deployment lags at the network edge, and offer a lack-of-incentive explanation as a conjecture rather than a measured finding. They state that a single dominant player (Hurricane Electric) can significantly skew graph-theoretic metrics such as average AS-path length computed over the IPv6 topology, which the reader must account for when comparing IPv6 topology statistics to IPv4's. Future work stated: continued periodic release of topology/routing data, measurement of whether deployment accelerated after World IPv6 Launch (June 2012, after this paper's writing), a quantitative organization-level adoption model, and extension of performance measurement to loss, fragmentation, and reordering causes beyond RTT.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A design that assumes an IPv4 and an IPv6 path between the same pair of ASes traverse the same intermediate networks cannot rely on that assumption for this paper's measurement period: only 40-50% of such paths were identical, so protocol-specific routing decisions (congestion control tuned to one protocol's path characteristics, or a latency budget derived from one protocol) cannot be transferred to the other protocol without checking path congruence first. A design relying on the IPv6 topology having redundancy or path diversity comparable to IPv4's must account for the observed single-player dominance: Hurricane Electric's presence in up to 95% of measured IPv6 AS paths (from some vantage points) means many nominally distinct IPv6 routes share one transit AS, so IPv6 path diversity computed by naive AS-path counting overstates independence relative to a design that needs disjoint failure domains.

### Contradicts
None found. This paper corroborates rather than contradicts CZYZ-SIGCOMM-14's performance-methodology citation (Nikkhah et al.) and states its own performance result (79%/63% path-congruence split) is a confirmation, not a contradiction, of that prior work.

### References worth retrieving
- **Foundational** — Amogh Dhamdhere, Constantine Dovrolis. "Twelve Years in the Evolution of the Internet Ecosystem." IEEE/ACM Transactions on Networking, 19(5), 2011. — source of the AS business-type classification algorithm and majority-filtering method this paper reuses.
- **Foundational** — Lixin Gao. "On Inferring Autonomous System Relationships in the Internet." IEEE/ACM Transactions on Networking, 9(6), 2001. — source of the AS relationship (customer/provider/peer) classification algorithm this paper reuses.
- **Competing** — Mehdi Nikkhah, Roch Guérin, Yiu Lee, Richard Woundy. "Assessing IPv6 through web access: a measurement study and its findings." CoNEXT 2011. — the performance-measurement methodology this paper follows and confirms (also cited by CZYZ-SIGCOMM-14).
- **Foundational** — Matthew Luckie. "Scamper: a scalable and extensible packet prober for active measurement of the Internet." IMC 2010. — the tool used for the active `tbit`/traceroute measurements.
- **Foundational** — Ahmed Elmokashfi, Amund Kvalbein, Constantine Dovrolis. "BGP churn evolution: A perspective from the core." IEEE/ACM Transactions on Networking, 20, 2011. — churn-normalization method the routing-dynamics section applies.
- **Attack or critique** — H. Chang, W. Willinger. "Difficulties Measuring the Internet's AS-Level Ecosystem." Annual Conference on Information Sciences and Systems, 2006. — one of several sources this paper cites as documenting BGP-collector topology bias.
- **Attack or critique** — Y. He, G. Siganos, M. Faloutsos, S. V. Krishnamurthy. "A Systematic Framework for Unearthing the Missing Links: Measurements and Impact." NSDI 2007. — cited alongside the above for the same missing-links critique of public BGP data.

### Verbatim extracts

"79% of paths we observed had IPv6 performance within 10% of IPv4"
"only 40-50% of AS paths are currently identical in IPv4 and IPv6, up to 95% of AS paths could be identical"
"the exponents for ASes and AS links are 0.13 and 0.16, respectively"

## [DICURSI-BIGDATA-24] A Herd of Young Mastodonts: the User-Centered Footprints of Newcomers After Twitter Acquisition

**Citation:** Francesco Di Cursi, Chiara Boldrini, Andrea Passarella, Marco Conti. "A Herd of Young Mastodonts: the User-Centered Footprints of Newcomers After Twitter Acquisition." IEEE International Conference on Big Data, 2024. DOI 10.1109/BigData62323.2024.10825038.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.16383
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.16383
**Domain:** J

### Scope note

The registry record for this key states its purpose as measuring "where a large wave of new users actually settled inside the fediverse's instance topology" after the Twitter exit event. The retrieved full text does not measure this. Its own data collection is explicitly instance-agnostic: a snowball sample of 2,000 Mastodon users and their contacts, gathered by following user-to-user reply, mention, and boost interactions starting from one seed account, without tracking or reporting which Mastodon instance (server) each user belongs to. The paper's actual subject is whether Mastodon users who joined after the Twitter acquisition form Dunbar-model ego networks (personal social circles of bounded size, seen in offline human relationships and in prior centralized-platform studies), not how newcomers distributed themselves across instances. The instance-redistribution question the registry record describes is covered by three other papers this paper cites in its related-work section (He et al., Raman et al., Zignani et al., listed below); their instance-level findings are attributed to them, not measured by this paper, and are not independently verified full-text evidence in this entry.

### What it does

The paper tests whether Mastodon (a federated Twitter-like microblogging network, part of the "Fediverse" of platforms built on the ActivityPub protocol) users who joined after Elon Musk's acquisition of Twitter form personal social circles matching Dunbar's ego network model, the same layered structure of relationship intimacy previously found in offline human relationships and in centralized platforms such as Facebook and Twitter. An ego network is built around one user (the ego) and the other users that ego communicates with directly (alters), grouped into nested circles by contact frequency: from a closest "super-support clique" contacted about every 5 days, out through wider circles to an "active network" of roughly 150 people contacted at least once a year, the number known as Dunbar's number. The authors collected 2,000 Mastodon users and their direct communications (replies, mentions, and boosts, i.e. reposts) through snowball sampling via the public Mastodon API, starting from one long-active user on the main instance mastodon.social, then applied a Meanshift clustering algorithm (a non-parametric method that groups data points by iteratively moving them toward the nearest region of high density) to each user's annual contact frequencies with their alters, to find how many social circles that user's contacts naturally group into and how large each circle is.

### Measured results

| Measurement | Figure | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Collected dataset size | 1,999 ego users; 130,492 total alters; 71,272 active alters (contacted at least once a year); 973,217 directed links; 2,932,049 total user-to-alter interactions | Snowball sample via public Mastodon API, capped at 2,000 users, all in one connected component, collection window January-March 2024, activity observed through December 31, 2023 |
| Toot (post) volume collected | 3,965,007 total toots; 2,626,141 directed (replies, mentions, boosts); 1,321,860 undirected; 1,043,683 replies; 1,663,551 boosts | Same dataset |
| User growth after the Twitter acquisition | Cumulative registered-user count more than quadruples after the acquisition date; users still active on a given day ("alive users") grow roughly 3x over the same period; post-acquisition daily active users producing at least one social toot stabilizes around 500 | Measured over the full observation window, October 2016 to December 2023, daily granularity |
| User-type composition | Of the collected users, 20.21% (404) were active both before and after the acquisition ("Aficionados"), 3.05% (61) only before ("Others1"), and 76.74% (1,534) only after ("Others2") | Same dataset, classified by activity window relative to the Twitter acquisition date |
| Post-acquisition user retention | Of roughly 1,500 users in the post-acquisition-only group, more than half remain active (posting) for at least 300 days from their first toot; only about 500 of those 1,500 remain regularly active by the middle of the observed lifespan window; only a small fraction reach more than 400 days | Lifespans aligned to each user's own first-toot date, not calendar date |
| Ego network size, unfiltered (all alters) | Mean 434.69 alters per ego, median 164.5 | All alters regardless of contact frequency, full 1,999-ego dataset |
| Ego network size, active alters only | Mean 153.53, median 50.0, close to Dunbar's number of about 150 for the mean | Alters contacted at least once a year, after filtering relationships shorter than 6 months and single-contact alters |
| Number of social circles per ego (Meanshift clustering output) | Mode 4 circles, mean 4.76, median 4.0; a substantial share of egos also cluster into 3 or 6 circles | Applied to the 1,534-user "Others2" (post-acquisition, active) subgroup used for the ego-network analysis |
| Ego network size by number of circles found | 1 circle: mean size 1.1 (72 egos); 2 circles: 6.76 (67 egos); 3 circles: 20.92 (186 egos); 4 circles: 45.78 (325 egos); 5 circles: 77.05 (235 egos); 6 circles: 146.27 (189 egos), the configuration whose size matches Dunbar's approximately-150 figure | Same clustering output, active-alter counts only |
| Scaling ratio between adjacent circles | Frequently close to 3, matching the "canonical" scaling ratio reported in Dunbar's offline model; the ratio between the two outermost circles is higher than 3 in every configuration (for example 5.91 between the 6th and 5th circles in the 6-circle group) | Computed from Table VI's per-circle alter counts across the 3-, 4-, 5-, and 6-circle egos |
| Annual contact frequency by circle | Outermost circle's average contact frequency is stable across egos with different numbers of circles (roughly 35-84 contacts per year depending on group), while additional inner circles show progressively higher frequency | Same circle-grouped dataset |
| Relationship duration by circle | Outermost circle's average bond length is similar across groups (about 191-238 days), while inner circles that appear only for egos with more circles show shorter average duration in the 4-6-circle configurations (as low as about 97-99 days for some innermost circles) | Same dataset, measured in days from first to last observed contact within the observation window |

### Parameters

- Snowball sample cap: 2,000 collected users, starting from one seed user active since 2016-2017 on mastodon.social.
- Alter-inclusion filter: an alter-ego relationship is retained only if it started more than 6 months before the observation end date (2023-12-31), the pair had at least 2 contacts, and the annual contact frequency exceeds 1 (i.e., more than once a year).
- Observation end date fixed at 2023-12-31 for all collected timelines, regardless of collection date (January-March 2024).
- Meanshift clustering bandwidth: not given a fixed numeric value in the paper; described as automatically optimized by standard library tooling (cited as scikit-learn) rather than set manually.
- User-type classification threshold: users are split into three categories by whether their activity falls before, after, or on both sides of the Twitter acquisition date; the "Others2" (post-acquisition only) group, 76.74% of the sample, is the one used for the ego-network analysis in Section VII.

### Stated limitations

The authors state their sample's ego networks are smaller than Dunbar's canonical model predicts (median 50 active alters against a canonical ~150), and attribute this to the short observation window of about 1.5 years rather than to a structural difference from offline or other online social networks, since 6-circle egos in their data do reach the canonical ~150 figure. They state the scaling ratio between the two outermost circles is higher than the canonical ratio found closer to the ego, and attribute this specifically to the short observation window making the lowest-frequency (about once-a-year) outermost relationships hard to characterize reliably in this time frame. They state single-contact alters are discarded because a contact frequency cannot be reliably computed from one observed interaction, which the paper does not quantify as a fraction of the discarded population. They state the study is a single snapshot and plan to replicate it later to test whether circle sizes converge toward the canonical values as the platform and its users' relationships mature, and to extend the analysis to Bluesky, a separate decentralized social network. They state that not all users who join after a migration event remain active, observing that user growth outpaces "alive"-user growth throughout the post-acquisition period.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system

None as a positive system mechanism — this is a measurement and social-network-structure study, not a protocol proposal. The methodological requirement worth noting for anyone using this paper's figures: the ego-network circle-size results are drawn only from the post-acquisition-only user subgroup (1,534 of 1,999 collected users) after the 6-month-duration and 2-contact-minimum filters, so the reported mean of 153.53 active alters and the per-circle sizes in Tables V-IX describe that filtered subgroup, not the full unfiltered dataset (whose unfiltered mean is 434.69).

### Contradicts

None found within this corpus regarding this paper's own measured content. The registry's stated reason for retrieving this paper (instance-level redistribution of migrating users) is not supported by anything measured in the full text; that question is addressed, per this paper's own related-work summary and not independently verified here, by He, Zia, Castro, Raman, Sastry, Tyson, "Flocking to Mastodon: Tracking the great Twitter migration," ACM Internet Measurement Conference 2023, and by Raman, Joglekar, Cristofaro, Sastry, Tyson, "Challenges in the decentralised web: The Mastodon case," ACM IMC 2019 — both listed below as references worth retrieving directly, since the specific instance-concentration percentages this paper attributes to them must be checked against their own full text before being used as evidence.

### References worth retrieving

- He, Zia, Castro, Raman, Sastry, Tyson, "Flocking to Mastodon: Tracking the great Twitter migration," ACM Internet Measurement Conference, 2023 — competing/foundational, highest priority; this paper's related-work section states He et al. found 20% of new Mastodon profiles were created before Twitter's decline began, that users favor popular instances while smaller instances retain more active users, and that migration is driven substantially by users following the same people (their followees) to the same instances — none of these figures are independently confirmed here and must be retrieved from He et al. directly.
- Raman, Joglekar, Cristofaro, Sastry, Tyson, "Challenges in the decentralised web: The Mastodon case," ACM Internet Measurement Conference, 2019 — competing/foundational, highest priority; this paper's related-work section attributes to Raman et al. a finding that 5% of instances hold 90% of users and 94% of toots (posts), that the same small number of commercial hosting providers host many instances, and that outages in 10 instances could remove 60% of global toot volume — retrieve directly to verify before use.
- Zignani, Quadri, Galimberti, Bertoli, Rossi, cited in this paper as "Zignani et al." studying decentralization's impact on user behavior across Mastodon instances — foundational/independent-measurement; this paper attributes to it a finding that 35-40% of users link to other instances but only 10% link to instances in a different country, and per-instance degree-distribution exponents from 2.1 to 3. The full citation for reference [25] was not captured in the extracted bibliography text through reference [24]; retrieve by title search on "Zignani decentralization Mastodon" to obtain the exact venue and year.
- La Cava, Greco, Tagarelli, "Discovering the landscape of decentralized online social networks through Mastodon," SEBD 2022 — foundational (instance-level network topology, clustering, and small-world properties of the Mastodon instance graph).
- La Cava, Greco, Tagarelli, "Information consumption and boundary spanning in decentralized online social networks: the case of Mastodon users," Online Social Networks and Media 30, 2022 — foundational (instance-level content-consumption and boundary-spanning behavior).
- Arnaboldi, Conti, La Gala, Passarella, Pezzoni, "Ego network structure in online social networks and its impact on information diffusion," Computer Communications 76, 2016 — foundational (the ego-network methodology this paper applies, previously validated on centralized platforms).
- Dunbar, Arnaboldi, Conti, Passarella, "The structure of online social networks mirrors those in the offline world," Social Networks 43, 2015 — foundational (the canonical online/offline ego-network correspondence this paper tests for Mastodon).
- Toprak, Boldrini, Passarella, Conti, "Harnessing the power of ego network layers for link prediction in online social networks," IEEE Transactions on Computational Social Systems 10(1), 2022 — foundational (methodology precedent for the circle-extraction pipeline this paper follows).

### Verbatim extracts

## [DIMAKIS-TIT-10] Network Coding for Distributed Storage Systems
**Citation:** Alexandros G. Dimakis, P. Brighten Godfrey, Yunnan Wu, Martin J. Wainwright, Kannan Ramchandran. "Network Coding for Distributed Storage Systems." IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, 2010. DOI 10.1109/TIT.2010.2054295.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/abs/cs/0702015 (arXiv preprint cs/0702015v1, 2 Feb 2007; earlier version of the work later published as the cited 2010 IEEE Transactions on Information Theory article — see Contradicts)
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/cs/0702015
**Domain:** C

### What it does
A regenerating code lets a distributed storage system replace a lost fragment of an erasure-coded file by downloading less data than either full-file reconstruction or standard Maximum-Distance-Separable (MDS) erasure-code repair requires. An MDS code stores a file of M bytes as n fragments of M/k bytes each, any k of which reconstruct the file; when a fragment is lost, the paper's first construction, called Optimally Maintained MDS (OMMDS), lets a replacement node ("newcomer") connect to the n−1 other surviving fragment-holders and download exactly M/k bytes total in the extreme case demonstrated (k=7, n=14: 0.27M bytes, a 73% reduction from downloading the whole file). OMMDS is proved (Proposition 2) to be the minimum bandwidth achievable by any scheme that keeps fragments at MDS size.

The paper's second and main construction, the Regenerating Code (RC), relaxes the requirement that fragments stay at MDS size. A newcomer connects to exactly k existing fragment-holders (the minimum possible) and downloads αM/k bits from each, where α is a free parameter. Theorem 1 gives the minimum feasible α (called α_c) below which reconstruction is information-theoretically impossible for any code, and shows that at α = α_c a linear network code exists — and randomized linear network coding across the storage nodes succeeds with probability approaching 1 as the finite-field size grows — that lets any k-subset of nodes reconstruct the file. This makes fragments larger than MDS fragments by a factor β_RC = k²/(k²−k+1), so a data collector reconstructing the full file downloads β_RC times the file size instead of exactly the file size.

### Measured results
| Result | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| OMMDS newcomer download vs. naive full-file download | 0.27M bytes; 73% reduction | k=7, n=14 (the k value used in the DHash++ system), newcomer connects to n−1=13 surviving nodes |
| RC newcomer download vs. naive; vs. OMMDS | 0.16M bytes; 84% less than naive, 39% less than OMMDS | k=7, newcomer connects to k=7 nodes |
| RC maintenance-bandwidth reduction vs. Hybrid (one full replica + (n,k) erasure code) | up to 25% lower bandwidth for equal availability, or more than 3 orders of magnitude lower unavailability at equal bandwidth | PlanetLab trace (527 days, 303 nodes, f=0.017 fraction failed/day, mean availability a=0.97), k=7; simulation using the analytical availability/bandwidth model of Rodrigues and Liskov (IPTPS 2005) |
| RC vs. Hybrid, larger k | benefit grows; RC better than Hybrid in every trace tested | k=14, same four traces |
| RC vs. Hybrid on the least stable trace | RC can be very slightly worse than Hybrid | Gnutella trace (2.5 days, 1,846 nodes, f=0.30/day, a=0.38), k=7 |
| Reduction in unavailability and bandwidth vs. Hybrid | 100× lower unavailability using about 58× less bandwidth for a 1 GB file | PlanetLab trace, target unavailability 0.01 |
| RC read-time overhead β_RC | 14% extra data transferred to reconstruct a file at k=7; 7.1% at k=14; 3.1% at k=32 | β_RC = k²/(k²−k+1), asymptotically approaches 1 as k grows |

The four availability traces used for the bandwidth/unavailability simulations: PlanetLab (527 days from Jan 2004, 303 nodes, f=0.017, a=0.97), Microsoft PCs (35 days from Jul 6 1999, 41,970 nodes, f=0.038, a=0.91), Skype superpeers (25 days from Sep 12 2005, 710 nodes, f=0.12, a=0.65), Gnutella (2.5 days from May 2001, 1,846 nodes, f=0.30, a=0.38). A node is considered permanently failed after a 1-day timeout with no response; f is the fraction of nodes failing permanently per day under that timeout, a is the mean fraction of non-permanently-failed nodes that are reachable at a given time.

### Parameters
- k: number of fragments needed to reconstruct the file (values tested: 7, 14, and, for the read-overhead calculation only, 32)
- n: total number of fragments (n = k·R for redundancy factor R)
- α: bits stored per fragment as a fraction of M/k; minimum feasible value α_c = (1/k) · 1/(1 − 1/k + 1/k²)
- β_RC = k²/(k²−k+1): storage/read overhead factor for Regenerating Codes relative to an MDS fragment
- β_MDS = (n−1)/(n−k): repair bandwidth overhead factor for OMMDS, approaching 1/(1−R) as k,n→∞ at fixed rate R=k/n
- f, a: per-trace permanent-failure rate and mean node availability, both derived from the four traces at a fixed 1-day failure-detection timeout
- Newcomer connects to exactly k nodes for the RC scheme (the minimum possible number, fixed by the authors to simplify the construction) and to n−1 nodes for OMMDS

### Stated limitations
The paper reports availability only, not durability, following the same restriction in the Rodrigues-Liskov methodology it compares against. Disk space used is not reported for any scheme except OMMDS, because bandwidth is treated as the more constrained wide-area resource; the paper states disk usage is proportional to bandwidth for every other scheme evaluated. The bandwidth-count model charges for permanent node failure only, not for node joins, unlike some designs it cites. The model assumes node availability is independent across nodes, an admitted simplification. The f/a estimates are stated as possibly biased: nodes returning after transient failures longer than the timeout are not reincorporated in this model (which would inflate the measured f), and uniform-random node selection in practice favors more-available, less-failure-prone nodes than the trace average, which the authors state is unlikely to affect the relative ranking of schemes but do not rule out. RC has a per-read overhead (β_RC extra bytes transferred) that can outweigh its maintenance-bandwidth savings when files are read frequently and k is small; the authors state RC is likely to be a net win specifically for archival or backup storage, where files are large and infrequently read.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A newcomer generating a replacement fragment must be able to connect simultaneously to k (RC) or n−1 (OMMDS) other fragment-holders and receive coded data from each; this requires those holders to be locatable and reachable at repair time, which the paper does not itself provide (it assumes an underlying distributed storage substrate such as OceanStore, Total Recall, or DHash++ supplies node discovery). The RC construction requires linear network coding capability at storage nodes: fragments must be produced as linear combinations over a finite field, and the field must be large enough for randomized coding to succeed with high probability, which the proof states can be driven arbitrarily high by increasing field size but does not quantify a concrete field size or coding-computation cost. The system must track which k or n−1 nodes a newcomer connects to and treat all data collectors symmetrically (any k nodes suffice), which requires every fragment-holder to be able to serve fragment data on demand for repair, not only for read.

### Contradicts
The retrieved text is the 2007 arXiv preprint (cs/0702015v1), not the final 2010 IEEE Transactions on Information Theory version the registry citation names. This preprint does not use the terms "Minimum-Storage Regenerating (MSR)" or "Minimum-Bandwidth Regenerating (MBR)" anywhere in the text; it presents two named schemes, OMMDS (MDS-size fragments, higher repair bandwidth — the construction later literature calls the MSR point) and RC (fragments larger by factor β_RC, minimum bandwidth for a newcomer connecting to exactly k nodes — the construction later literature calls the MBR point), and proves a single feasibility bound (Theorem 1) rather than presenting a full storage-versus-bandwidth tradeoff curve with two labeled extremes. Any claim that this text states the MSR/MBR framework by name is not supported by the retrieved text; the framework is a later restatement of these same two constructions found in follow-on papers. No other entry in this batch disagrees with this paper's figures.

### References worth retrieving
- Rodrigues, Liskov, "High availability in DHTs: Erasure coding vs. replication," IPTPS 2005 — competing; supplies the Hybrid scheme and the evaluation methodology this paper's Section V directly extends, and its more pessimistic conclusion about erasure-code practicality is the one this paper's results are checked against
- Weatherspoon, Kubiatowicz, "Erasure coding vs. replication: a quantitative comparison," IPTPS 2002 — competing; reported an order-of-magnitude bandwidth reduction from erasure coding, a different scenario the paper cites for context
- Bhagwan, Tati, Cheng, Savage, Voelker, "Total Recall: System support for automated availability management," NSDI 2004 — foundational; one of the deployed systems whose design motivates the paper's redundancy problem
- Dabek, Kaashoek, Karger, Morris, Stoica, "Wide-area cooperative storage with CFS," ACM SOSP 2001 — foundational; a deployed erasure-coded storage system the paper cites as motivating context
- Ahlswede, Cai, Li, Yeung, "Network information flow," IEEE Trans. Info. Theory 46(4), 2000 — foundational; origin of network coding, the technique the paper applies to storage repair
- Dimakis, Prabhakaran, Ramchandran, "Ubiquitous Access to Distributed Data in Large-Scale Sensor Networks through Decentralized Erasure Codes," IPSN 2005 — foundational; the authors' own prior application of network coding to distributed storage in a sensor-network setting

### Verbatim extracts
- "Regenerating Codes can reduce maintenance bandwidth use by 25% or more compared with the best previous design"
- "if α < α_c then reconstruction at some data collector who connects to k storage nodes is information theoretically impossible"
- "RC has a small constant factor overhead compared with Ideal Erasure codes, while Hybrid has a rather large but only additive overhead"
- "the same 1 GB can be maintained with 100× lower unavailability using about 58× less bandwidth"
