## [DZIEMBOWSKI-CRYPTO-15] Proofs of Space
**Citation:** Stefan Dziembowski, Sebastian Faust, Vladimir Kolmogorov, Krzysztof Pietrzak. "Proofs of Space." CRYPTO, 2015. DOI 10.1007/978-3-662-48000-7_29.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://eprint.iacr.org/2013/796.pdf
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2013/796.pdf
**Domain:** C

### What it does
A proof of space (PoS) lets a party (the prover) convince a second party (the verifier) that the prover is persistently dedicating a specified amount of disk storage, without the verifier ever transferring or storing that amount of data itself. The protocol has two phases. In the initialization phase, the verifier sends the description of a hash function to the prover; the prover uses it to label every node of a directed acyclic graph chosen for having high "pebbling complexity" (defined below), where each node's label is the hash of its children's labels, builds a Merkle hash-tree over all labels, and sends only the tree's root hash (a single L-bit value) to the verifier. In the execution phase, run any number of times later, the verifier picks a small set of random node positions and asks the prover to open the corresponding labels; the prover answers by revealing the label and its Merkle-tree authentication path, and the verifier checks the path against the previously stored root. The prover can only answer efficiently if it stored the full labeling; a prover that discarded most of the labeling must either keep a large residual fraction of them or recompute from scratch at high time cost at every execution.

The security argument reduces cheating-prover storage to a graph-pebbling game: placing a "pebble" on a graph node models an algorithm holding that node's label in memory, and a pebble can be placed on a node only once its parent nodes are pebbled. A graph family has pebbling complexity Ω(f,g) if any successful pebbling strategy that starts with fewer than f initial pebbles held between rounds must, during a further pebbling execution, use at least g simultaneous pebbles or make at least g total pebbling moves. The paper constructs two explicit graph families achieving different pebbling-complexity guarantees (Theorems 1 and 2) and uses each to instantiate the protocol above, giving two proof-of-space constructions with different storage/time tradeoffs for a cheating prover, formalized in Section 3.2's (N0, N1, T)-security model: a cheating prover is defeated unless it either retains N0 bits of storage between the initialization and execution phases, or retains up to N1 bits and spends T oracle queries during a single execution.

### Measured results
This is a theoretical-cryptography paper with formally proved asymptotic bounds, not an empirical measurement study; there is no implementation, simulation, or benchmark on real hardware. All "results" below are proved complexity bounds, stated with the theorem's own conditions, not measured figures.

| Construction | Security guarantee (Theorem 3) | Communication (initialization) | Prover computation (initialization) | Verifier computation (initialization) | Communication (execution) | Verifier computation (execution) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Eq. (7), graph family of Theorem 1 (max in-degree 2) | (c1·N/log N, c2·N/log N, ∞)-secure: cheating prover must use Ω(N/log N) storage indefinitely, regardless of time spent, for constants c1, c2 > 0 | O(γ log²N) | 4N (i.e., Θ(N) hash evaluations) | O(γ log²N) | O(γ log N) | O(γ log N) |
| Eq. (8), graph family of Theorem 2 (max in-degree O(log log N)) | (c3·N, ∞, c4·N)-secure: cheating prover must use Θ(N) storage (almost as much as the honest N), or else Θ(N) time per execution, for constants c3, c4 > 0 | O(γ log N log log N) | O(N log log N) | O(γ log N log log N) | O(γ log N) | O(γ log N) |

γ is the statistical security parameter (number of random challenge positions the verifier checks). N is the storage size in L-bit blocks the honest prover dedicates. Prover computation during execution is stated as 0 (constant, independent of N) in both constructions, once the labeling is stored. The initialization time for the prover, I, is proved Θ(N) for the first construction and O(N log log N) for the second; the paper states I must be at least linear in N for any such protocol, so the first construction meets that lower bound exactly.

The graph construction of Theorem 1 draws on the Paul-Tarjan-Celoni (1976/77) graph family with mᵢ = 2ⁱ sources/sinks and nᵢ = Θ(i·2ⁱ) nodes; for a target size N, the largest such graph with nᵢ ≤ N gives mᵢ = Θ(N/log N), the source of the N/log N storage bound. The graph of Theorem 2 combines random bipartite expander graphs, superconcentrators, and dense-long-path graphs of Erdős, Graham and Szemerédi (1975), constructed by a randomized algorithm with polynomial expected running time that succeeds with probability at least 1 − 2^(−Θ(N/log N)).

### Parameters
- N: storage size dedicated by the honest prover, in L-bit blocks
- L: random-oracle output length, stated as needing to be set large enough that finding a collision (roughly 2^(L/2) oracle queries) is infeasible; the paper gives L = 512 with a bound of 2^(L/3) total oracle queries across the experiment as "a conservative choice" — the paper's own words, not this extraction's judgment
- γ: statistical security parameter, controls the number of random challenge positions Θ(γ) checked in each execution
- d: maximum in-degree of the pebbling graph — 2 for the Theorem 1 construction, O(log log N) for the Theorem 2 construction
- (N0, N1, T): the security model's three adversary bounds — storage retained between phases, storage retained during a single execution (N1 ≥ N0), and oracle-query budget during execution
- ε: a tunable slack parameter trading verifier efficiency against the tightness of the storage bound (set to c1/(2 log N) for the first construction, c4/2 for the second)
- τ: a threshold constant (0 < τ < 1) below which the second construction's Ω(0, [S0 < τN]·max{N, N²/S1}) pebbling-complexity bound applies

### Stated limitations
The security proof does not reduce to the plain random-oracle model; it needs an added assumption (Section 3.1) that the set of hash outputs a bounded-storage cheating prover can write down without re-querying is well-defined at every time point, because the standard "ex post facto" argument used for related pebbling-based proofs cannot be applied when the adversary is allowed unbounded queries during initialization. The authors state this additional assumption is "a bit unsatisfactory" and identify removing it, using techniques for proving random oracles incompressible, as future work. The paper explicitly notes it does not claim its storage-tracking set SH exists for every possible cheating prover strategy, only that an equivalent prover obeying the assumption exists with almost the same parameters and advantage. A simpler PoS built by storing sorted outputs of a random function is noted to achieve only weak security because of time-memory tradeoffs for inverting random functions or permutations (inversion in √N time and space for permutations, N^(2/3) for general functions), which is why the paper does not use that simpler construction. A related primitive, proof of storage / proof of retrievability, is stated as not qualifying as a PoS because the verifier there must send at least |F| bits to the prover during setup, violating the polylogarithmic-communication goal.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The construction requires a cryptographic hash function modeled as a random oracle, with output length L chosen large enough that no party (including any adversary) can find collisions within the total query budget of the deployment; in practice this needs instantiation with a concrete hash function such as SHA3, which the paper notes carries only heuristic (not reduction-based) security. The verifier must be able to sample and remember one Merkle-tree root hash per prover per commitment period, and must issue random challenge queries during each execution phase — the protocol supplies no mechanism for choosing when to challenge, only that repeated challenges over time make the proof "persistent." The scheme assumes the prover has random access to its stored labeling during execution; if the prover cannot hold the full N-block labeling, it must either retain a large residual fraction (Θ(N) or Θ(N/log N), depending on construction) or recompute at Θ(N) or higher time cost per execution — the system built on top of this primitive must decide what storage threshold and time budget count as a passing prover, since the theorem gives asymptotic bounds with unspecified constants, not concrete disk-size or millisecond figures. The paper's Spacecoin application (cited, not itself part of this paper) uses this PoS to gate mining: a miner runs initialization once for N bits of space, then answers per-round execution challenges cheaply — that composition requires whatever consensus layer sits above the PoS to bind one completed initialization (one committed Merkle root) to one accepted unit of space per identity, a binding this paper does not itself provide or analyze.

### Contradicts
None found within this batch. The paper's own related-work discussion states that its "collapsed" single-phase variant (running initialization and execution together) is essentially the same construction independently proposed as a Proof of Secure Erasure by Karvelas and Kiayias (SCN 2014) and by Ateniese et al. (SCN 2014); those two papers give a security proof directly in the random oracle model without this paper's added assumption, because a Proof-of-Secure-Erasure security argument does not need the "ex post facto" strengthening this paper's persistent PoS argument requires.

## [ELAHI-WPES-12] Changing of the Guards: A Framework for Understanding and Improving Entry Guard Selection in Tor

**Citation:** Tariq Elahi, Kevin Bauer, Mashael AlSabah, Roger Dingledine, Ian Goldberg. "Changing of the Guards: A Framework for Understanding and Improving Entry Guard Selection in Tor." ACM WPES, 2012. Pages 43-54. DOI 10.1145/2381966.2381973.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://cypherpunks.ca/~iang/pubs/cogs-wpes.pdf
**Source URL:** https://cypherpunks.ca/~iang/pubs/cogs-wpes.pdf
**Domain:** J

### What it does
The paper measures how much of a Tor client's exposure to a malicious entry guard (a fixed relay a client uses as its long-term first hop) comes from ordinary relay churn versus from Tor's own scheduled guard rotation. The authors build COGS (Changing Of the Guards), a Tor-client path-selection simulator built on Tor's own source code (version 0.2.2.33), that replays real hourly consensus documents and relay descriptors from the live Tor network and simulates guard selection and rotation for tens of thousands of clients under configurable adversary and parameter settings, then logs which simulated clients have a malicious relay in their currently active guard list at each hour. A client is counted as compromised the instant any malicious relay appears in the first N online entries of its guard list (N being the client's configured number of guards), because the authors treat even brief exposure as potentially security-relevant.

### Measured results
| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| Guard relay uptime/downtime statistics: median guard down time 3 hours, median guard up time 20 hours (mean 42.17h down, 156.7h up); general relay population median down 10 hours, median up 4 hours (mean 45h down, 19.82h up) | Tor Metrics Portal consensus data, April-November 2011, relays present throughout the period |
| Fraction of active guard lists compromised increases monotonically over an 8-month simulated period, both with and without guard rotation, with guard rotation producing a markedly higher compromise curve that peaks around late May and then reaches a steady state | COGS simulation, 80,000 simulated clients, malicious relay bandwidth fixed at 100 weighted bandwidth units (WBU, approximately top 20% of guard bandwidth), introduced one hour into the simulation, guard-only flag, April-November 2011 real consensus replay |
| With standard 30-60-day guard rotation, a client is expected to see 12 to 24 unique guards over 8 months (average 17); without rotation, minimum 3 guards per client | Derived from Tor's guard-list size (3) and the 30-60-day rotation window over the 8-month simulation period |
| With guard rotation, mean number of guards seen per client rises to 19; without guard rotation, mean rises only to 5 (versus a minimum of 3) | Same COGS simulation, client guard-exposure log over April-December 2011 |
| Increasing guard list size (1, 2, 3, 5, 10 guards) increases compromise rate when guard rotation is on; with guard rotation off, guard list sizes above 3 initially show lower compromise, an effect the authors observe does not persist over time as guards fail and get replaced | Same COGS simulation, independent runs per guard-list-size setting |
| Only about 9% of guards remained part of the Tor network for the full 8-month study period; median guard longevity 1,371 hours (~57 days) | Guard longevity CDF computed from the same April-November 2011 consensus data |
| Median guard bandwidth across all consensuses in the 8-month period peaked at 113 WBU; a client with 3 or more guards always exceeds this bandwidth on average, while 5% of single-guard clients fall below it | Same dataset, guard bandwidth statistics (min 40, median 67, mean 68.31, max 113 WBU) |
| Tor with 1 guard versus 3 guards: 1-guard clients experience 60% worse expected circuit bandwidth 50% of the time, but 25% more average guard-list bandwidth the other 50% of the time | Same COGS simulation, expected circuit performance measured with and without guard rotation across guard-list sizes |
| Compromise rate increases with adversarial bandwidth (tested at 10, 100, and 1,000 WBU) but not linearly | Same COGS simulation, adversarial-bandwidth sweep, April-July 2011 window |

### Parameters
- Simulated client population: 80,000 clients per run, chosen by increasing the sample size until the resulting compromise-rate distributions stabilized according to the Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance test.
- Simulation period: April 2011-November 2011 (8 months), chosen for relatively stable network bandwidth and a consistent consensus format version.
- Simulation granularity: 1 hour, matching consensus document publication frequency.
- Malicious relay: introduced 1 hour after simulation start (after clients already hold honest guards, establishing what the authors describe as a conservative, lower-bound compromise-rate estimate), assigned only the guard flag (not exit, to avoid confounding selection probability), bandwidth held constant at 100 WBU for most experiments (varied to 10 and 1,000 WBU in one sweep), representing approximately the top 20% of guard bandwidth.
- Guard list size tested: 1, 2, 3 (Tor default), 5, and 10 guards, with and without guard rotation.
- Guard rotation window (Tor's default parameter at the time of this study): guards are dropped between 30 and 60 days of age.
- Client model: constant population (no churn of clients themselves, only of relays), clients simulated as always online (stated as a worst-case assumption relative to real intermittently-connected clients).

### Stated limitations
The authors state they did not vary the guard rotation period itself in this paper and explicitly leave a rotation mechanism independent of relay stability and network characteristics to future work. They state it is "unclear how to best model the client behaviour" for join/leave dynamics and adversary insertion timing, and describe this as an open research problem outside this paper's scope; they used a fixed client population with the adversary entering after all clients already hold guards, and state that "counterintuitive properties" they observed (larger guard lists reducing compromise rates when rotation is off) "may not hold for other conditions" of client and adversary modeling. They state it is unclear whether low-bandwidth guards, despite rarely being solely responsible for a client's active list bandwidth, provide load-balancing or relay-diversity security benefits, and cite this as an avenue for future investigation. They state their choice to model the adversary as a single high-bandwidth relay (rather than many low-bandwidth relays with equivalent total bandwidth) relies on an equivalence result from Murdoch and Watson (PETS 2008) rather than on an independent derivation in this paper.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Any capacity-ordered relay-selection mechanism that keeps a client's first hop fixed for a multi-week tenure (Tor's guard-flag design, measured here) requires the tenure length itself to be treated as a tunable security parameter with a measured trade-off against performance, because this paper measures that increasing the number of guards a client rotates through over a fixed period directly increases the number of relays capable of compromising that client, while reducing rotation frequency or guard-list size directly reduces average circuit bandwidth. A mechanism that selects relays for a persistent role in proportion to self-reported or measured bandwidth (Tor's bandwidth-weighted guard selection) requires that a small set of injected high-bandwidth malicious relays be assumed at least as effective as many low-bandwidth ones at equal aggregate bandwidth, an assumption this paper adopts from prior work rather than independently testing. A design relying on relay uptime/downtime stability to justify a long-lived special role (the entry-guard role, justified by relays' longer up-times and shorter down-times relative to the general relay population, measured here in Table 1) still exhibits enough natural churn that a persistent adversary is guaranteed eventual appearance in every client's guard list given sufficient elapsed time, independent of any scheduled rotation mechanism.

### Contradicts
None found. This paper's finding that guard rotation contributes more to compromise risk than natural churn alone is consistent with, and is cited as support for, the guard-compromise-dominates finding in JOHNSON-CCS-13 (which measures median guard-compromise time of 50-60 days against median exit-compromise time under 2.5 days, on the live Tor network rather than in simulation); no numeric figure in this batch contradicts another entry.

### References worth retrieving
- foundational: Wright, Adler, Levine, Shields. "Defending Anonymous Communications against Passive Logging Attacks." IEEE S&P 2003. (introduces "helper nodes," the predecessor of entry guards)
- foundational: Wright, Adler, Levine, Shields. "The predecessor attack: An analysis of a threat to anonymous communications systems." ACM TISSEC 7(4), 2004.
- foundational: Øverlier, Syverson. "Locating Hidden Servers." IEEE S&P 2006. (proposes entry guards for onion routing)
- attack: Bauer, McCoy, Grunwald, Kohno, Sicker. "Low-Resource Routing Attacks against Tor." WPES 2007. (Sybil attack replacing honest guards via inflated self-reported bandwidth)
- attack: Borisov, Danezis, Mittal, Tabriz. "Denial of service or denial of security?" ACM CCS 2007. (selective DoS attack interaction with entry guards)
- foundational (equivalence result used as a simulation assumption): Murdoch, Watson. "Metrics for security and performance in low-latency anonymity networks." PETS 2008.
- competing/related: Edman, Syverson. "AS-awareness in Tor path selection." ACM CCS 2009.
- attack: Danezis, Syverson. "Bridging and Fingerprinting: Epistemic Attacks on Route Selection." PETS 2008.

### Verbatim extracts

- "guard rotation increases the visibility of each client on average to 19 guards"
- "only about 9% of guards remained part of the Tor network for the entire 8-month duration"
- "Tor with one guard offers the least likelihood of compromised guard lists"
- "we did not vary guard rotation periods in this paper"
- "it is unclear how to best model the client behaviour"

## [ELLIS-SIGMOD-89] Concurrency Control in Groupware Systems

**Citation:** C.A. Ellis, S.J. Gibbs. "Concurrency Control in Groupware Systems." ACM SIGMOD, 1989. Pages 399-407. DOI 10.1145/67544.66963.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/67544.66963
**Source URL:** https://doi.org/10.1145/67544.66963
**Domain:** D

### What it does
The dOPT algorithm (distributed Operational Transformation) lets every participant in a real-time multi-user editing session apply their own edits to their local replica immediately, without acquiring a lock, while still converging every replica to the same final state once all edits have propagated. It achieves this by rewriting a received operation against operations already applied locally that the sender had not yet seen, so that operations applied in different orders at different sites still produce the same result. Each site holds a replicated site object (an application data structure, for example a character string), a request queue, a request log of executed operations, and a state vector with one counter per site recording how many operations from that site have been executed locally. When a user acts, the local site executes the operation immediately, assigns it a priority, and broadcasts a request tuple (originating site id, the originating site's state vector at generation time, the operation, its priority) to every other site. A receiving site compares the incoming request's state vector to its own: if the sender's state vector is not yet dominated by the receiver's own state (the sender still has unseen predecessor operations to receive), the request is queued and deferred (Case I); if the two state vectors are equal, the operation executes unmodified (Case II); if the receiver has executed operations the sender had not yet seen when it generated the request, the receiver scans its own log for those extra logged operations and applies a transformation function to the incoming operation for each one, then executes the transformed operation (Case III). The transformation step is defined by a transformation matrix T, one entry T_uv per ordered pair of operators (u, v) in the system, each entry a hand-written function that computes a corrected operation from two conflicting operations and their priorities so that applying operation A followed by transformed operation B produces the same site-object state as applying B followed by transformed A. For a text editor with two operators, insert[X; P] (insert character X at position P) and delete[P], the paper gives the four transformation-matrix entries explicitly: insert-insert, delete-delete, insert-delete, and delete-insert. Tie-breaking between two operations at the same position uses a priority value; the paper shows a naive priority equal to the site identifier alone diverges (a three-site worked example produces the string "xyz" at one site and "zxy" at another) and replaces it with a priority defined as the list formed by concatenating an operation's largest same-position predecessor's priority with the site's own identifier, comparing two such priority lists element by element from the first list position where they differ.

### Measured results
None. The paper is a theoretical/algorithmic contribution with a worked numerical example (the three-site insert scenario in Figure 4) used to illustrate correctness and a failure mode, not a benchmark. It reports no runtime, message-count, node-count, or throughput figures, and the retrieved text describes no evaluation section, testbed, or performance measurement of any kind. It states qualitative operational guidance for its GROVE implementation: system quiescence (resetting the growing log) "should be enforced periodically (e.g., once per minute) and when the system falls quiet for an extended period of time (e.g., ten seconds)" — the paper gives no derivation for these two numbers and does not label them as measured; they read as suggested defaults.

### Parameters
- Number of sites N: assumed constant for the algorithm as presented (assumption A1); the paper states an extension to a varying site count is possible and defers it to end of section 4, then does not give it in the retrieved text.
- Quiescence interval: suggested "once per minute" as a periodic trigger and "ten seconds" of inactivity as an idle trigger for resetting the request log; stated as example values, not derived or measured.
- Priority: for the text-editing instantiation, a list formed by concatenating an operation's highest-priority same-position predecessor in the local log with the originating site's own identifier; compared element-by-element, longer list wins ties, giving temporal successors placement to the left of predecessors in the string.
- Transformation matrix size: m x m, where m is the cardinality of the operator set O; the text-editing example instantiates 4 of the m^2 entries (insert-insert, delete-delete, insert-delete, delete-insert) for m=2 operators.

### Stated limitations
The algorithm as specified assumes a constant number of sites (assumption A1), exactly-once and error-free message delivery (assumption A2), and that a message cannot be executed before it is generated (assumption A3); the paper states the second assumption "should be satisfied by the communications protocols so we take it as given," meaning dOPT itself supplies no reliable-delivery mechanism. The request log grows without bound during a session and must be scanned both to calculate a new operation's priority and to transform incoming operations, so the paper states the system needs periodic quiescence (all sites confirmed to have executed all outstanding requests) to reset the log to empty; detecting quiescence is stated to be "equivalent to the well known distributed consensus problem." The paper's own worked example (Figure 4, three sites, priority-by-site-ID) demonstrates that using the site identifier alone as an operation's priority causes divergent final states between two sites (one produces "xyz," the other "zxy") when three insertions at the same position race in different orders relative to each other; the fix (the priority-list scheme) is proposed and given a sketched, not complete, proof — the paper states "the details of the full proof are beyond the scope of this paper." The proof sketch itself explicitly excludes some cases: it states "we have not discussed the case involving insertions at different positions" (argued not to need priority numbers) and "we have also not discussed cases involving deletion" (argued to often commute). Stated future work: generalizing the characterization of the transformation matrix beyond the two-operator text example, and extending the correctness proof to hypertext and other groupware data models — meaning the paper's own correctness argument is proved only for the character-string insert/delete case, not proved in general for an arbitrary operator set.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Every operator pair (u, v) in the application's operator set O needs a hand-specified transformation function T_uv before dOPT can run over that data model; the paper gives no automatic or general method for deriving T from an operator definition, so a system adopting dOPT for a different data structure than a character string must independently design and prove correct a new transformation matrix. The algorithm requires the communications layer to guarantee each message is received exactly once and without error (assumption A2, taken as given rather than provided by dOPT). It requires each site to replicate the full site object locally, since operations execute against a local copy immediately, before any global ordering is established. It requires a way to detect global quiescence (equivalent to distributed consensus, per the paper) to bound the log's growth, meaning the rest of the system must supply a consensus or barrier mechanism dOPT itself does not define. The priority-list scheme requires every site to compare priorities using the same element-by-element list-comparison rule and to compute an operation's priority from the correct predecessor entry in its own local log at the moment of generation, so all sites must apply an identical, deterministic priority-calculation procedure for convergence to hold.

### Contradicts
The paper's own abstract states the algorithm's "overall structure is independent of the semantic information," but the algorithm's central mechanism (the transformation matrix T) is a set of hand-written functions, one per operator pair, each function embedding operation-specific semantics (for example, incrementing or decrementing a text position); only the algorithm's control structure (request queue, state-vector comparison, log scan) is semantics-independent, not the transformation step it depends on. None found against other entries in this corpus.

### References worth retrieving
- Lamport, "Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events in a Distributed System," CACM 21(7), pp. 558-565, 1978 — foundational, supplies the partial-order (happened-before) definition dOPT's precedence property is built from.
- Bernstein, Goodman, Hadzilacos, "Concurrency Control and Recovery in Database Systems," Addison-Wesley, 1987 — foundational, the database serializability framework the paper contrasts its non-serializable correctness criterion against.
- Grief, Seliger, Weihl, "Atomic Data Abstractions in a Distributed Collaborative Editing System," POPL 1986 — competing, a locking-based ("tickle locks") concurrency-control approach for collaborative editing the paper argues against.
- Stefik, Foster, Bobrow, Kahn, Lanning, Suchman, "Beyond the Chalkboard: Computer Support for Collaboration and Problem Solving in Meetings," CACM 30(1), pp. 32-47, 1987 — competing, source of the dependency-detection concurrency-control approach the paper compares against and of the WYSIWIS interface concept.
- Sarin, Grief, "Computer-Based Real-Time Conferences," Computer 18(10), pp. 33-45, 1985 — competing, source of the reversible-execution (optimistic, undo-based) concurrency-control approach the paper compares against.
- Cohen, Fish, Kraut, Leland, "Quilt: A Collaborative Tool for Cooperative Writing," ACM SIGOIS, pp. 30-37, 1988 — competing, a transaction-based non-real-time groupware editor the paper contrasts with GROVE's real-time model.

### Verbatim extracts

- "the algorithm is fully distributed, and resilient to site failure"
- "The final string at this site is zxy which is inconsistent with the xyz at node 3."
- "Quiescence should be enforced periodically (e.g., once per minute)"
- "Detection of quiescence is equivalent to the well known distributed consensus problem"
- "the details of the full proof are beyond the scope of this paper"

## [ENGELBART-ANRW-26] QUIC as Multiplexing Layer in WebRTC
**Citation:** Mathis Engelbart, Fabian Willi Fromwald, Jörg Ott. "QUIC as Multiplexing Layer in WebRTC." Applied Networking Research Workshop (ANRW), 2026. DOI 10.1145/3822163.3827919.
**Retrieved:** full text via conference slide deck (talk slides, presented July 19, 2026)
**Source URL:** https://doi.org/10.1145/3822163.3827919
**Domain:** L

### Note on source form
The retrieved text is an OCR transcript of the presentation slide deck, not the paper's typeset body text — each slide's bullet text repeats across consecutive extracted "pages" as the deck was captured frame-by-frame. Two of the deck's graphs (a bandwidth/latency time series on slide 3, and a four-panel delay/rate comparison on slide 10 spanning 5 Mbit/s at 10, 25, and 50 ms one-way delay) present numeric results only as plotted curves; the OCR text carries axis labels and scenario parameters but not the plotted data values themselves, so no specific latency or throughput number from those two figures can be recorded under Rule 1 of this extraction. Everything below is restricted to what the slide text states outright.

### What it does
The paper proposes replacing WebRTC's two separate transport stacks — (S)RTP (Secure Real-time Transport Protocol, for media) over UDP with SRTP's own congestion control, and SCTP (Stream Control Transmission Protocol, for data channels) over UDP with SCTP's own congestion control — with a single QUIC connection that carries both. RTP packets are carried using RoQ (RTP over QUIC, IETF draft-ietf-avtcore-rtp-over-quic), which encapsulates an RTP packet inside a QUIC datagram frame behind a flow identifier used to multiplex multiple RTP flows on one QUIC connection. Data-channel traffic is carried by a new protocol the authors propose, "Data Channels over QUIC" (draft-engelbart-quic-data-channels), and a further draft (draft-engelbart-multiplex-roq-qdc) defines how RTP and Data Channel traffic multiplex onto one QUIC connection, using flow identifiers or QUIC stream types to distinguish them. Because both traffic classes now share one QUIC connection, they share one congestion controller and one bandwidth estimate instead of running two independent ones that the deck states must otherwise be coordinated through "Coupled Congestion Control." The deck states congestion control can be implemented at the QUIC layer using an existing real-time algorithm (GCC, SCReAM, or NADA), and that using such a controller for real-time media over QUIC requires a QUIC packet-receive-timestamp extension (draft-ietf-quic-receive-ts) so the sender can compute one-way delay the way RTCP feedback does today. Scheduling policy is stated as: media encoders are configured to produce data at their allocated rate and are prioritized on the QUIC connection so they are delivered at low latency without consuming the full available bandwidth, while data-channel traffic (not necessarily rate-based, e.g. a file transfer) dynamically yields bandwidth to media when media is under its target rate and consumes the remainder when media is at or under target.

### Measured results
The authors built two implementations for comparison: a baseline WebRTC application (Pion WebRTC for the peer connection, Gstreamer for media) streaming video while sending data over a data channel, and an alternative using the same bandwidth-estimation algorithm implementation over a QUIC transport (quic-go). Both were evaluated across a matrix of bandwidth and delay scenarios using Linux network namespaces and `tc-netem` for traffic shaping, including a stated point of 5 Mbit/s at 10 ms, 25 ms, and 50 ms one-way delay. No numeric latency, throughput, or fairness value from these runs is stated as text in the retrieved slides — the results appear only as time-series and delay/rate plots, so none is usable as a recorded figure under Rule 1. The deck's stated qualitative conclusions, attributed to the authors and not independently verified here, are: RTP and Data Channels can be multiplexed over one QUIC connection; a real-time congestion controller such as GCC can be integrated into QUIC using the receive-timestamp extension; and multiplexing can resolve the bandwidth-unfairness problem that arises when RTP and Data Channel traffic run independent congestion controllers over separate UDP flows.

### Parameters
| Parameter | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Test bandwidth points (deck slide 10) | 5 Mbit/s, at 10 ms / 25 ms / 50 ms one-way delay | scenario labels on the delay/rate comparison figure |
| Congestion-control algorithms named as QUIC-layer options | GCC, SCReAM, NADA | slide 6 |
| Implementation components | Pion WebRTC, Gstreamer, quic-go; Linux network namespaces + `tc-netem` for bandwidth/delay shaping | slide 8 |

No numeric parameter values (target bitrate, buffer size, pacing rate) beyond the bandwidth/delay test points above are stated in the retrieved text.

### Stated limitations
The retrieved slide text carries no discussion, limitations, or future-work section distinct from the three-line conclusion; a slide deck of this form typically omits the caveats a full paper states in prose, so any limitation not listed among the three conclusion bullets above is unverified from this source and would need the accompanying ANRW 2026 paper text, not just the talk slides, to check.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A WebRTC peer wishing to use this multiplexing scheme needs both peers' QUIC stacks to support the packet-receive-timestamp extension (draft-ietf-quic-receive-ts) before a real-time congestion controller such as GCC can run at the QUIC layer, because that extension is what lets the sender compute one-way delay the way RTCP receiver reports do in today's separate-stack WebRTC. The scheme also needs an agreed multiplexing protocol on both peers (draft-engelbart-multiplex-roq-qdc, itself an unpublished Internet-Draft the paper states as still in progress) before RTP and Data Channel flows can share one QUIC connection; a peer implementing only RoQ or only Data Channels over QUIC, without the multiplexing draft, cannot use this scheme. Because media and data now share one congestion-controlled connection, the scheduling policy described (prioritize media, let data channels yield or consume the remainder) must be implemented by whatever component multiplexes the two traffic classes onto QUIC streams or datagrams — an implementation that does not prioritize media traffic on the shared connection loses the low-latency delivery property the paper states this design is meant to provide.

### Contradicts
None found.

### References worth retrieving
- **Foundational** — IETF draft-ietf-avtcore-rtp-over-quic (RoQ). — the RTP-in-QUIC encapsulation this design is built on.
- **Foundational** — IETF draft-ietf-quic-receive-ts. — the packet-receive-timestamp extension the design states is required for real-time congestion control over QUIC.
- **Competing** — the coupled-congestion-control approach to the same RTP/Data-Channel unfairness problem, referred to on slide 3 as the alternative the field has otherwise pursued instead of QUIC multiplexing; the specific citation for this alternative is not given in the retrieved slide text and needs the full paper to identify.
- **Foundational** — Google Congestion Control (GCC), SCReAM, NADA — the three named real-time congestion-control algorithms the deck states can run at the QUIC layer; none is cited with a specific reference in the retrieved slide text.

## [EPPSTEIN-SIGCOMM-11] What's the Difference? Efficient Set Reconciliation without Prior Context

**Citation:** David Eppstein, Michael T. Goodrich, Frank Uyeda, George Varghese. "What's the Difference? Efficient Set Reconciliation without Prior Context." ACM SIGCOMM, 2011. DOI 10.1145/2018436.2018462.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.ics.uci.edu/~eppstein/pubs/EppGooUye-SIGCOMM-11.pdf
**Source URL:** https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/2018436.2018462
**Domain:** D

### What it does
The Difference Digest lets two hosts, each holding a set of keys, compute both one-sided set differences (the keys each holds that the other lacks) in a single round of communication, with communication cost proportional to the size of the symmetric difference rather than to the size of either set, and without either host knowing the difference size beforehand. It achieves this with two components: an Invertible Bloom Filter (IBF) that encodes a set into a small table supporting cell-by-cell subtraction between two IBFs, and a Strata Estimator that predicts the difference size before encoding so the sender can size the IBF correctly. An IBF is a table of n = alpha*d cells (alpha >= 1, d an estimate of the difference size), each cell holding three fields: idSum (the exclusive-or, XOR, of every element ID hashed into that cell), hashSum (the XOR of a second, independent hash of each such element ID, used as a checksum), and count (the number of elements hashed into that cell). Encoding an element hashes it to hash_count distinct cell indices and XORs its ID into idSum, XORs its checksum hash into hashSum, and increments count at each of those cells. Subtracting one IBF from another is done cell-by-cell: idSum values are XORed together, hashSum values are XORed together, and count values are subtracted (which can go negative). Because a common element hashes to the same cells in both IBFs, XORing its ID into idSum twice cancels it, so after subtraction, a cell contains information only about elements in the symmetric difference. A cell is "pure" when it holds exactly one such element: count equals +1 or -1, and the paper shows the hashSum field is needed to confirm purity because a count of 1 alone can be produced by a coincidental combination of multiple elements. Decoding repeatedly finds a pure cell, reads off the encoded element ID from idSum, removes that element from every cell it hashes to (by further cell-by-cell subtraction), and repeats until no pure cells remain; if all elements of the difference are recovered this way, decoding succeeds, otherwise decoding fails and the two hosts must retry with a larger IBF. The Strata Estimator builds a hierarchy of independently sampled, fixed-size IBFs (one "stratum" per hierarchy level), each stratum sampling a geometrically shrinking, hash-selected subset of the universe of possible keys, so that summing the decoded difference counts across strata gives an estimate of the total difference size using space proportional to the logarithm of the key universe size. A Hybrid Estimator variant augments the least-selective strata with a single Min-wise sketch (a set-similarity estimator built from k random permutation-minimum hash values) in the same space budget, to improve accuracy for large differences without sacrificing the Strata Estimator's accuracy for small ones. The KeyDiff service implements this as a generic Linux service over TCP with three calls: add a key, delete a key, and diff against a named remote host, and it maintains several precomputed IBFs of different fixed sizes in parallel, updated incrementally as keys are added or removed, so the correctly sized IBF can be selected once the difference-size estimate is known rather than built during the diff call itself.

### Measured results
Every dataset was generated as pairs of sets containing keys from a universe of all 32-bit values (12 bytes allocated per IBF cell: 4 bytes each for idSum, hashSum, and count); the first set SA was chosen randomly without replacement, the second set SB copied a random subset of SA, and each reported point was computed from 100 file pairs (an experiment counted as successful only if the entire set difference was recovered), except where a table states otherwise.

| Result | Conditions | Value |
|---|---|---|
| IBF decoding success independent of total set size | Sets of 100, 1K, 10K, 100K, 1M keys; IBF with 50 cells; deltas 0-50 | Deltas up to 25 decode with extremely high probability regardless of set size; deltas of 45-50 fail to decode at any set size |
| Optimal hash_count for small deltas | Sets of 100 keys, deltas 0-50, IBF with 50 cells, hash_count 2-6, 1,000 trials per configuration | hash_count=4 decodes 100% of trials for deltas under 30; hash_count=3 gives ~98% success for deltas 15-25 and 92% at 30, but is best above delta 30 |
| Minimum space overhead for 99% decode success | Sets of 100K elements, varying IBF cells as a proportion of delta, IBF cells/delta ratio measured | Deltas below 200 need at least 50% overhead; overhead reaches an asymptote beyond delta 1,000; hash_count=3 has lowest overhead for deltas above 200, hash_count=4 for deltas below |
| Strata Estimator scaling factor for 99% non-underestimation | hash_count=4, 80 cells per stratum, various strata sizes tested from 10 to 160 cells | Scaling factor of 1.39 needed at 80 cells per stratum; overhead drops sharply from 10 to 40 cells, diminishing returns after 80 |
| Strata vs. Min-wise estimator accuracy, equal space (15.3 KB) | Sets of 100K elements, deltas 10 to 100K; Strata: 16 strata x 80 cells; Min-wise: 3,840 4-byte hashes | Min-wise overhead 1.35 down to 1.0 for deltas beyond 2,000, but 1st-percentile Min-wise estimate is 0 (infinite overhead) for all deltas below 200; Strata requires 1.33-1.39 correction across the same range, 1.0-1.33 for small deltas |

| Data transmission vs. prior work | Sets of 100K elements; Difference Digest recovers 100% of the difference with 99% reliability, Approximate Reconciliation Trees (ART) recovers 95% with 99% reliability, CPISync (Characteristic Polynomial Interpolation) configured with foreknowledge of difference size | Difference Digest and CPISync need an order of magnitude less bandwidth than ART for deltas up to 4,000 (4% of set) and 10,000 (10% of set) respectively; CPISync uses ~10 bytes/element in the difference versus IBF's average 24 bytes/element |

Strata (16x80 cells): add 4.224 us, server compute 0.021 ms. Hybrid (7x80 cells + 2,160 hashes): add 4.319 us, server compute 0.023 ms |

### Parameters
- Universe size U: all 32-bit values in the evaluation (u = 2^32); IBF cell fields sized 4 bytes each for idSum, hashSum, count (12 bytes/cell total).
- hash_count (number of cells each element hashes into): tested 2 through 6; paper recommends 3 for estimated differences above 200, 4 for smaller estimated differences, based on the measured decode-success and overhead results above.
- IBF sizing factor alpha (cells allocated per unit of estimated difference d): rule of thumb given is to size the phase-2 IBF at twice the phase-1 estimate ("twice the estimate found in the first phase") to cover both estimator under-estimation and decoding overhead.
- Strata Estimator cells per stratum: 80 cells per stratum used in the reported configuration, chosen because overhead reaches diminishing returns beyond 80 cells (Figure 8).
- Number of strata: floor(log2(d_max)) where d_max is the largest anticipated difference; 16 strata used for a d_max of 100K in the Strata-vs-Min-wise comparison; 7 strata plus 2,160 Min-wise hashes used in the Hybrid Estimator configured for a d_max around 2,000 (floor(log2(2000)) = 10, reduced to 7 to reallocate space to Min-wise).
- Scaling/correction factor applied to the raw estimator output to keep 99% of estimates at or above the true difference: 1.39 for the pure Strata Estimator at 80 cells/stratum; 1.45 for the Hybrid Estimator; a further scale of 1.25 to 2.3 applied in the second phase per the paper's configuration guideline.

### Stated limitations
The IBF decoding procedure can fail outright: the paper states decoding succeeds only "with high probability," and Figure 5/6/7 quantify failure directly — for example no IBF completely decodes at deltas of 45-50 with only 50 cells, and deltas below 200 require at least 50% space overhead over the difference size to reach 99% decode success. The Strata Estimator and IBF-based reconciliation as described assume both hosts use the same hash functions and agree on hash_count and cell counts in advance; the paper's model section states the method assumes SA and SB "are stored at two distinct hosts" with no discussion of more than two parties. The paper states no protection against or analysis of an adversarial or non-cooperating peer: the retrieved text contains no discussion of malicious key insertion, hash-function manipulation, or adversarial exploitation of the peeling-decode process (the failure modes GADUREK-SEA-26, elsewhere in this corpus, analyzes directly). CPISync is stated to require either foreknowledge of the difference size or an "interactive approach" at "greater computation and latency costs" when that size is unknown; the paper's own benchmark configured CPISync with foreknowledge, so the reported CPISync latency numbers are a best case. ART (Approximate Reconciliation Trees) is stated to recover only some, not all, of the difference in general, and the paper's own bandwidth comparison against ART used the arbitrary standard of 95% recovery with 99% reliability, calling ART's apparent bandwidth advantage at large deltas "misleading" for that reason. The precomputed-IBF approach that gives low diff-time latency requires maintaining multiple fixed-size IBFs in parallel per key, so every add or delete operation touches all of them; the paper states this adds 3.858 to 31.320 microseconds of latency per key update, depending on how many parallel IBFs are precomputed, as the cost of the fast diff path.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Both hosts must agree in advance on the two hash functions Hc (checksum hash) and Hk (cell-index hash) and on the hash_count parameter, since decoding correctness depends on identical elements hashing to identical cell indices at both ends. The application must supply keys as fixed-size identifiers that fit the idSum XOR field (32-bit keys in the evaluation); the paper does not address variable-length elements in the retrieved text. A system deploying this for online reconciliation needs to maintain the IBF (and, for fast diff latency, multiple precomputed IBFs at different sizes) incrementally as keys are added or removed, since the paper's own measurements show building an IBF at request time from a stored list, rather than maintaining it online, costs seconds of server compute time (3,957.847 ms per response with 1M keys, no precomputation) versus tens of microseconds when precomputed. Because the Strata Estimator needs floor(log2(d_max)) strata sized to the anticipated maximum difference, the system must have some prior estimate of the plausible range of difference sizes to size the estimator; the paper does not describe a mechanism for handling a difference larger than the estimator was provisioned for beyond retrying with a larger structure. Decoding requires the peeling process to find at least one pure cell at each step; a system layering this over adversarial peers would need an external integrity check, since the paper's decode procedure trusts that a count of +-1 combined with a matching checksum indicates a genuine single element.

### Contradicts
None found against other entries in this corpus. GADUREK-SEA-26 (also in this corpus) analyzes an adversarial-input failure mode of IBF peeling decode that this paper does not consider; the two do not contradict each other, since this paper's decode-success measurements (Figures 5-7) are all against randomly generated, non-adversarial set differences, and GADUREK-SEA-26 addresses a different, adversarial threat model.

### References worth retrieving
- Byers, Considine, Mitzenmacher, Rost, "Informed content delivery across adaptive overlay networks," SIGCOMM 2002 — competing, source of Approximate Reconciliation Trees (ART), one of the three baselines this paper benchmarks against.
- Minsky, Trachtenberg, Zippel, "Set reconciliation with nearly optimal communication complexity," IEEE Trans. Info. Theory 49(9), 2003 — competing, source of Characteristic Polynomial Interpolation (CPISync), the other primary baseline; this paper states CPISync needs O(d^3) decode time via Gaussian elimination versus its own O(d).

Knowledge and Data Engineering 23, 2011 — foundational, an earlier application of IBFs by the same authors, cited as prior IBF use before whole-IBF subtraction was introduced in this paper.
- Byers, Luby, Mitzenmacher, Rege, "A digital fountain approach to reliable distribution of bulk data," SIGCOMM 1998 — foundational, source of Tornado codes, which this paper states its IBF encoding is structurally similar to (uniform random hashing versus Tornado's non-uniform degree distribution).

- Karpovsky, Levitin, Trachtenberg, "Data verification and reconciliation with generalized error-control codes," IEEE Trans. Info. Theory 49(7), 2003 — foundational, cited in the coding-theoretic framing of set reconciliation.

## [EVERSPAUGH-USENIXSEC-15] The Pythia PRF Service
**Citation:** Adam Everspaugh, Rahul Chatterjee, Samuel Scott, Ari Juels, Thomas Ristenpart. "The Pythia PRF Service." USENIX Security Symposium, 2015. Pages 547-562.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.usenix.org/system/files/conference/usenixsecurity15/sec15-paper-everspaugh.pdf
**Source URL:** https://www.usenix.org/system/files/conference/usenixsecurity15/sec15-paper-everspaugh.pdf
**Domain:** I

### What it does
Pythia is a network service that evaluates a pseudorandom function (PRF, a keyed function whose output is indistinguishable from random to anyone without the key) on a client's behalf, so a client can harden a low-entropy secret such as a password without storing the PRF key itself and without letting an offline attacker who steals the client's database brute-force the secret. The service introduces a partially oblivious PRF (PO-PRF): the client's PRF input splits into a tweak t, which the client reveals to the server in the clear, and a message m, which stays hidden from the server through cryptographic blinding. The server evaluates F_kw(t, m) = e(H1(t), H2(m))^kw, using an admissible bilinear pairing e over three prime-order groups G1, G2, GT and two hash-to-group functions H1, H2 modeled as random oracles; kw is an ensemble key derived as kw = HMAC(msk, K[w]) from a server-held master secret key msk and a per-client table entry K[w]. The client blinds m by sending x = H2(m)^r for a random exponent r, the server returns y = x^kw together with a proof pi that the same discrete logarithm relation holds between a public commitment p_w = g^kw and the pair (x, y), and the client checks the proof, then unblinds by computing y^(1/r) to recover F_kw(t, m). Revealing t to the server, while hiding m, is what lets the server rate-limit or flag repeated queries against a specific account or key selector without learning the password or message being hardened. The construction supports key rotation: because kw is HMAC-derived from a table entry K[w], the server can issue a compact update token that rolls previously computed PRF outputs forward to a freshly generated K[w] without the client needing to resubmit every prior message, and rotating the entire master secret msk works the same way, one compact update token per active ensemble. An unblinded variant exists for deployments that do not need message privacy: the client sends m directly and the server computes H3(t‖m) using a single elliptic-curve group instead of a pairing, at the cost of losing message secrecy but keeping verifiability and key rotation.

### Measured results

| Condition | Result |
|---|---|
| Group operation and hashing microbenchmarks, Barreto-Naehrig 254-bit prime-order pairing curves (BN-254, ~128-bit security), mean of 10,000 operations, EC2 c4.xlarge, Python line_profiler | Group op: G1 5.7 microseconds, G2 6.7 microseconds, GT 9.8 microseconds; exponentiation: G1 175, G2 572, GT 1145 microseconds; hashing (64-byte input): G1 77, G2 210 microseconds; one pairing operation: 1005 microseconds |
| Per-operation server/client computation cost for a single PRF evaluation, three protocol variants: UNB (unblinded, ZK-proof-verified), BLS (unblinded, BLS-signature-verified), PO (partially oblivious, the full Pythia protocol) | Server Sign: 0.3 / 0.3 / 1.5 ms; server Prove: 0.5 / 0.3 / 2.5 ms; client Blind: -/-/0.3 ms; client Unblind: -/-/1.2 ms; client Verify: 0.9 / 2.0 / 4.0 ms. Server-side Table lookup 1.2 ms, Rate-limit update 0.9 ms, shared across variants |
| End-to-end client-server latency including TLS, LAN setting (client and server in same AWS EC2 availability zone), 1,000 requests averaged with 100 warmup requests, cold/hot/no-proof connection variants | UNB: 7.0 / 3.8 / 2.4 ms; BLS: 7.9 / 4.9 / 2.4 ms; PO (full Pythia): 14.9 / 11.8 / 5.2 ms; ping RTT in this setting: 0.1 ms |
| Same latency measurement, WAN setting (server in EC2 US-West California, client at University of Wisconsin-Madison) | UNB: 389 / 82 / 80 ms; BLS: 392 / 85 / 80 ms; PO: 403 / 96 / 84 ms; ping RTT in this setting: 82 ms — cold-connection cost is dominated by four TLS/TCP setup round trips, not by PRF computation |
| Maximum throughput, autobench distributed load-testing tool, two clients in the same AWS region as the server, all connections cold (no TLS session resumption, no HTTP KeepAlive), compared against a static HTTPS page baseline | Static page baseline: 2,200 connections per second; UNB and BLS: 1,400 cps; PO (full Pythia): 1,350 cps, on a single EC2 c4.xlarge instance (8 virtual CPUs, 2.9 GHz Intel Xeon, 15 GB RAM, SSD storage) |
| Per-entry storage for the ensemble pre-key table K, MongoDB, measured as the average of 100,000 entries | 195 bytes per entry (two 32-byte values plus database overhead and indexes); scales to under 20 GB for 100 million clients |
| Rate-limiting record storage per distinct tweak, MongoDB, hour-granularity rate limits, assumed maximum throughput of 2,000 requests/second | 144 bytes per entry including overhead and indexes; total rate-limiting storage never exceeds 1 GB under this assumed load, because entries are purged after each rate-limiting period expires |
| Bulk key-rotation benchmark: client simulator with MongoDB and mongoengine, 100,000 database entries, one key-update token requested from Pythia and applied to every entry | Under 1 ms per entry; full rotation of 100,000 entries completed in under 97 seconds; authors state that assuming linear scaling, 1 million users would complete in under 17 minutes |
| Example tiered rate-limiting policy implemented in the prototype: at most 10 queries per hour per account, at most 300 per month | Stated consequence: guessing a random 4-digit PIN under this policy would take 1.4 years in expectation |

### Parameters
- Pairing curve: Barreto-Naehrig 254-bit prime order curves (BN-254), chosen to provide approximately 128 bits of security.
- Security parameter n for symmetric key lengths: the paper states a typical choice of n = 128.
- Server stack: nginx web server, uWsgi application gateway, Django backend module implementing PRF-Srv in Python, MongoDB for the key table and rate-limiting records, Relic cryptographic library (C) with a Python wrapper.
- Test hardware: Amazon EC2 c4.xlarge instance, 8 virtual CPUs (Intel Xeon, third generation, 2.9 GHz), 15 GB RAM, SSD storage, Ubuntu 14.04; LAN client also a c4.xlarge instance; WAN client an Intel Core i7 3.4 GHz at University of Wisconsin-Madison.
- Example rate-limiting policy tested: tiered limit of 10 queries per hour per account and 300 per month, at hour-granularity expiry.
- Password-onion login latency budget used in the paper's worked example: T = 300 ms.

### Stated limitations
The paper states a formal proof of security for the full one-more pseudorandomness notion is deferred to the full version of the paper and is not obtained within this paper for every claimed property; only one-more unpredictability (sufficient for applications where the PRF output is used as an unforgeable credential rather than stored, such as the brainwallet application) is proved in the paper's own appendix. The paper's PO-PRF construction relies on a new, unproven-in-prior-literature hardness assumption the authors introduce, a one-more bilinear computational Diffie-Hellman assumption, stated as "to the best of our knowledge this assumption is new." The rate-limiting mechanism depends entirely on the tweak t being learned by the server; the paper's own related-work analysis states that any oblivious-PRF or blind-signature variant that also hides t "does not allow granular rate limiting" because the server cannot verify that a query's tweak matches the one it was told, so attackers can bypass rate limits by lying about which account a blinded query targets. The client-side denial-of-service risk: because Pythia performs per-tweak rate limiting, an attacker who can associate a specific tweak with a target user gains a vector for locking that user out; the paper states this is mitigated in the brainwallet application only because Bitcoin addresses are not directly usable as the tweak. The forward-secrecy guarantee from key rotation is explicitly conditioned on the old key and update token being completely erased after rotation; the paper does not measure or verify this erasure occurring on real storage media. The paper's WAN latency figures (389-403 ms cold) are dominated by TLS/TCP connection setup, not by Pythia's own computation, and the paper states straightforward engineering fixes (TLS session resumption, QUIC, or a custom UDP protocol) were not implemented or measured in this evaluation, only proposed.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Pythia requires the client to already possess a per-client key selector w (an "ensemble" identifier) established through an out-of-band Init call, and requires that selector, together with a server-held table entry K[w], to be treated as long-term state the server must retain and be able to update; loss of this table by the client or corruption at the server changes which PRF outputs subsequently verify. It requires the tweak t to be chosen by the client such that it is exactly the granularity at which the calling application wants rate limiting applied (the paper's example uses a per-account salt as t), because the server can rate-limit only at the granularity of distinct tweak values it observes, not at any finer or coarser grain. It requires an authenticated channel or process for the client to request key rotation (the paper's Reset call takes an authtoken) to prevent an attacker from forcing a spurious rotation that discards a legitimate client's stored ensemble key. It requires whatever system stores the client's own PRF-derived values (the paper's password-onion example) to track a version marker per stored entry so it knows whether that entry has already received a pushed key-update token, since updates can run concurrently with normal logins rather than under a database lock. The construction assumes the decisional bilinear Diffie-Hellman-family hardness assumption holds in the chosen pairing group and that H1, H2 behave as random oracles; a system substituting a non-pairing-friendly group or a different hash construction cannot reuse the stated security proof.

### Contradicts
None found.

## [FAGIN-PODS-01] Optimal Aggregation Algorithms for Middleware
**Citation:** Ronald Fagin, Amnon Lotem, Moni Naor. "Optimal Aggregation Algorithms for Middleware." ACM PODS, 2001 (journal version J. Comput. Syst. Sci. 66, 2003). Pages 102-113 (PODS extended abstract). DOI 10.1145/375551.375567.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/pdf/cs/0204046
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/pdf/cs/0204046
**Domain:** B

### What it does
The Threshold Algorithm (TA) finds the k objects with the highest combined score across m ranked attribute lists while reading as few list entries as possible, and its stopping rule is provably the earliest a correct algorithm can stop on every possible input, not only on average or in the worst case over a probability model.

Mechanism: each of m attributes has a separate list of all N objects sorted by that attribute's score, descending. Two list-access primitives are defined: sorted access (read the next entry in a list, in score order) and random access (look up a named object's score in a given list directly). TA proceeds in rounds. In each round it takes one sorted-access step in every list in parallel; whenever an object is newly seen in any list under sorted access, TA performs a random access to every other list to obtain that object's score in every attribute, computes its combined score with a fixed monotone aggregation function t (for example min or average), and keeps a running set of the k highest-scoring objects seen so far. After each round, TA computes a threshold value tau = t(x1, ..., xm), where xi is the score of the last object seen under sorted access in list i — the best possible combined score any object not yet seen could have. TA halts as soon as at least k seen objects have combined score at least tau, and returns those k objects. Correctness follows because monotonicity of t guarantees no unseen object can beat any returned object's score once the halting condition holds.

A cost model is defined so results can state a real-valued middleware cost: s sorted accesses and r random accesses cost s*cS + r*cR for positive constants cS and cR that are the same for every algorithm compared. "Instance optimality" is defined relative to a class of algorithms A and a class of databases D: algorithm B is instance optimal over A and D if, for every algorithm A in A and every database D in D, cost(B,D) = O(cost(A,D)) with a constant independent of the database.

Two variants remove or bound random access. NRA (No Random Access) never performs random access; it tracks, for each partially-seen object, an upper bound and a lower bound on its combined score from the attribute values seen so far, and halts once k objects' lower bounds all exceed every other object's upper bound. CA (Combined Algorithm) mixes h sorted-access steps with one random-access step per round, trading the two access costs against each other.

### Measured results
This paper contains no experiment, testbed, dataset, or empirical run; every quantitative claim is a proved worst-case bound over an abstract cost model (sorted-access cost cS, random-access cost cR, m attribute lists, k requested outputs), not a measurement, so no entry here carries node counts, hardware, or trial counts because the paper reports none. The bounds and the model parameters they depend on are:

| Result | Bound | Model conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Naive algorithm (read every list fully) | Linear middleware cost in database size N | Any m, any monotone aggregation function t |
| Fagin's Algorithm (FA), independent list orderings | O(N^((m-1)/m) * k^(1/m)) middleware cost, with high probability | m sorted lists, N objects, list orderings pairwise probabilistically independent |
| TA optimality ratio, algorithms making no "wild guesses" (never returning an object never seen), t monotone | at most m + m(m-1) * cR/cS, matched by a lower bound of the same value (Theorem 9.1) | Class D = all databases; class A = correct algorithms with no wild guesses |
| TA optimality ratio, t strictly monotone, unrestricted algorithms (wild guesses allowed) | c*m^2 for a constant c depending on cR/cS (Theorem 6.5); no algorithm beats ratio m/2 (Theorem 9.3) | Class D = all databases; t strictly monotone |
| NRA optimality ratio | exactly m, both upper bound (Theorem 8.5) and matching lower bound (Theorem 9.5, t strict) | Class A restricted to algorithms making no random access at all |
| CA optimality ratio, t = min, distinctness property | at most 4m + k (general monotone) or 5m (t = min specifically), against a lower bound of m/2 (Theorem 9.4) | Database class restricted to the "distinctness property" (no two objects tie in a list); CA parameter h fixed |
| TA buffer size | independent of database size N (Theorem 4.2) | TA need only retain the current top-k objects and the last-seen entry per list |

### Parameters
- m: number of sorted attribute lists (equivalently, number of scored attributes per object). Treated as a fixed constant in the optimality theorems; the optimality ratio for TA scales linearly or quadratically in m depending on the theorem.
- k: number of top objects requested. Treated as fixed; buffer size and the additive term in TA's cost bound scale with k.
- cS, cR: per-access costs for sorted and random access respectively, positive real constants. No numeric values are given; every bound is stated symbolically in terms of the ratio cR/cS.
- theta (threshold approximation parameter, theta > 1): TA_theta halts once k objects have score at least tau/theta, trading exactness for fewer accesses; the paper proves TA_theta remains instance optimal for theta > 1 under the no-wild-guess assumption but not under the strict-monotonicity assumption of Theorem 6.5.
- h (CA parameter): number of sorted-access steps performed per single random-access step in the Combined Algorithm; no numeric value recommended, only that CA's optimality ratio is proved as a function of m for the h used in Theorem 8.9/8.10.

### Stated limitations
The paper states outright that finding good heuristics for which list to advance next under sorted access is an open problem, and warns that a specific published heuristic (Guntzer, Balke, and Kiessling's "Quick-Combine") is demonstrably not instance optimal despite good average-case behavior. The authors list unresolved questions explicitly in Section 11: for which aggregation functions TA is "tightly" instance optimal (optimality ratio exactly matching the lower bound) is open in general; whether other algorithms in the same restricted classes are tightly instance optimal is open; and efficient data structures for NRA and CA "in cases of interest" are left for future work. The cost model itself ignores internal computation cost of computing field values, counting only list-access cost. No claim is made about distributed or networked deployment: the model is a single middleware system with local access to m lists, not a client contacting remote nodes.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
TA requires the existence of a component that can perform sorted access to each of the m ranked lists in parallel and, on demand, random access to any list to fetch a named object's score in that list. A distributed implementation therefore requires each participant holding a scored list to answer a random-access lookup for an arbitrary object identifier, not only serve entries in sort order — this is a stronger interface requirement than a simple ranked-iterator. The aggregation function t must be fixed and monotone (non-decreasing in every argument) for TA's correctness proof (Theorem 4.1) to hold; a non-monotone combining rule (e.g., one with feedback or context-dependence) is out of scope. NRA removes the random-access requirement but still needs every list to support ordered sequential access to completion or to the point where bounds separate the top k from the rest, and it returns objects' membership in the top k without necessarily returning their exact combined score in every case (the paper notes this as an explicit tradeoff, not a defect). The cost model assumes cS and cR are constants known to (or at least identical across) the comparison of algorithms; if per-node random-access cost varies by network distance, the plain middleware-cost bounds would need re-derivation, which this paper does not attempt.

### Contradicts
None found. The paper is compared against no other entry in this batch.

### References worth retrieving
The extracted text renders every bibliography citation marker as a bare "[?]" placeholder — the reference list itself did not survive PDF-to-text extraction in this copy, so no citation strings can be quoted or classified from this file. The related-work section (Section 10) names, in running prose rather than as bibliography entries, three papers worth retrieving by name search: Nepal and Ramakrishna (an algorithm equivalent to TA under a weaker optimality notion) — foundational/competing; Guntzer, Balke, and Kiessling (two papers: "Quick-Combine," a heuristic variant of TA compared empirically against FA, and a second paper defining "Stream-Combine" for the no-random-access case) — competing; Natsev et al. (generalizes the sorted-list-join scenario to arbitrary joins) — foundational.

### Verbatim extracts
"TA is essentially optimal ... for all of them" (aggregation functions), "not just in a high-probability worst-case sense, but over every database."
"TA requires only bounded buffers, whose size is independent of the size of the database."
"Halt as soon as you know you have seen the top k answers."
"the optimality ratio of TA is at most m + m(m − 1)cR/cS."
"NRA ... is tightly instance optimal" with ratio "m."
