## [FELDMANN-CSUR-21] Survey on Algorithms for Self-Stabilizing Overlay Networks
**Citation:** Michael Feldmann, Christian Scheideler, Stefan Schmid. "Survey on Algorithms for Self-Stabilizing Overlay Networks." ACM Computing Surveys, 2021 (publication date given on the document itself as January 2020). DOI 10.1145/3397190.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://schmiste.github.io/csur20.pdf
**Source URL:** https://schmiste.github.io/csur20.pdf
**Domain:** A

### What it does
This survey classifies distributed algorithms that let an overlay network (a graph of logical links among peers, each link a path through the underlying physical network) recover a specified target topology starting from any initial graph, including one corrupted by faults, without central coordination. A protocol satisfying this is called self-stabilizing, defined by two properties the survey states explicitly: convergence (from any system state, the protocol reaches a legitimate state matching the target topology) and closure (once in a legitimate state, the protocol stays there). The survey runs no experiments of its own; every quantitative result below is a runtime or work bound the survey states as proved in the paper it discusses, not a measurement the survey authors performed.

The survey identifies four local graph operations — Introduce, Forward, Merge, Invert — as the building blocks every self-stabilizing overlay protocol in its taxonomy composes: Introduce sends a node's own reference to one of its two known neighbors, connecting them; Forward relays a held reference to another neighbor and drops the local copy; Merge collapses two references to the same node into one; Invert reverses the direction of a link from explicit (a stored reference) to implicit (a reference in transit). The survey states a proof that Introduce, Forward, and Merge alone suffice to convert any weakly connected graph into any strongly connected target graph, and that adding Invert makes the four sufficient to reach any weakly connected target graph, and further states these four are also individually necessary, since each performs an operation none of the other three can (Introduce is the only edge-creating operation, Forward the only node-separating operation, Merge the only edge-removing operation, Invert the only operation that can render a node unreachable from another).

The survey classifies self-stabilizing overlay designs by target topology: linearization (sorted lists and the de Bruijn graph), metrical graphs (line and circular metrics, general and special metrics under local or global probing, Euclidean metrics), and expanders (skip graphs, random graphs, and a general Transitive Closure Framework that derives a self-stabilizing protocol for any locally checkable target topology). For skip graphs specifically, the survey describes SKIP+ as the first self-stabilizing scalable design in this line: SKIP+ distinguishes stable edges (already part of the skip graph structure from a node's local view) from temporary edges (forwarded toward a neighbor for which they would be more relevant), and every node continuously runs three rules — create reverse edges, forward temporary edges, and locally close and sort neighbors by identifier. The survey states SKIP+'s own paper proves convergence from any weakly connected graph to a skip graph in O(log^2 n) rounds, and that a single join or leave event requires polylogarithmic work. The survey states HSKIP+ (Feldotto, Scheideler, Graffi, 2014) is "an improved version" of SKIP+ that "reduces the stabilization time in practice and needs less work for single join or leave events," without stating a numeric bound for either improvement.

### Measured results
This survey states no measurement of its own; every bound below is a theorem the survey reports as proved in the cited primary paper.

| Result stated by the survey | Source |
|---|---|
| SKIP+ converges from any weakly connected graph to a skip graph in O(log^2 n) rounds; a single join or leave event requires polylogarithmic work | Jacob, Richa, Scheideler, Schmid, Täubig (cited as [25], the SKIP+ paper) |
| The Transitive Closure Framework converges to any locally checkable target topology in at most D(n) + log n + 1 rounds, where D(n) is the maximum distance from any non-detector node to its nearest detector node | Cited as [9] |
| The Transitive Closure Framework yields an O(log n)-time self-stabilizing algorithm for the SKIP+ topology specifically, which the survey states is optimal because any self-stabilizing algorithm requires time at least the diameter of the network in its legitimate state | Same source, applied to SKIP+ |
| A generalized edge-flip rule ("k-Flipper") transforms any d-regular connected graph into a connected d-regular Θ(d)-expander using O(dn) applications of a Θ(d^2 n^2 log(1/ε))-Flipper operation, for d ∈ Ω(log n) | Cited as [39] |
| The Finite Departure Problem (a node leaving the system permanently, entering an "exit" state) cannot be solved by any self-stabilizing protocol using only local control — an oracle is required | Cited as [Theorem 7.2, referencing [18]] |
| The Finite Sleep Problem (a node leaving temporarily, entering a "sleep" state reachable again by a later message) can be solved by local control protocols alone | Same source, [18] |

### Parameters
This survey states no parameters of its own; the bounds above are stated in terms of n (node count), d (target graph degree), and D(n) (a topology-specific detector-distance function), each defined by its cited source.

### Stated limitations
The survey states, in its own concluding section, four open problems it identifies as unresolved across the entire self-stabilizing-overlay literature it surveys, not limited to any one paper: (1) upper and lower bounds on the total work (edges inserted, changed, or removed during convergence) are known for very few topologies, in contrast to the more developed literature on convergence time; (2) transient behavior during convergence is not well understood — the survey states a node's degree "may temporarily raise significantly, far beyond the maximum initial or final node degree" even for topologies that are degree-bounded once stable, and designing algorithms that also bound degree during convergence is stated as an open question; (3) no general theory connects the convergence time or work of a self-stabilizing protocol to "how far" the initial topology is from the target, a property the survey calls locality; (4) the survey states explicitly, in its own words, that research on churn-tolerant overlays and research on self-stabilizing overlays "has been largely independent" of each other, so no general result in this survey's own scope bounds how much concurrent join/leave activity a self-stabilizing protocol can tolerate while still converging. Separately, the survey states that monotonic searchability (a guarantee that once a search for a target node succeeds, every later search for the same target also succeeds) is not satisfied by the straightforward routing algorithm for a self-stabilizing sorted list, and that the general protocol achieving monotonic searchability across a wide range of target topologies can force a search for a non-existent node to traverse up to Ω(n) hops before terminating.

This survey's own bibliography and text contain no mention of bandwidth or node-capacity heterogeneity anywhere except in the title of the single reference it cites for HSKIP+ itself. No self-stabilizing overlay design published in the window this survey covers is presented by the survey as improving on, or even revisiting, HSKIP+'s specific property of ordering routing by node bandwidth. This is a negative finding, not a claim that no such design exists elsewhere in the literature — it states only that this survey, read in full, does not surface one.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The model underlying every protocol in this survey assumes a static node set: the survey states node departures are only addressed as a separate, later-developed extension (Section 7.2), and that termination of the self-stabilization process may not be reached if the node set changes during convergence, citing a proof of this in the surveyed literature. Every protocol in this survey's basic model assumes fair message receipt (every message sent is eventually processed) and weakly fair action execution (an action enabled in all but finitely many states is executed infinitely often), with no bound placed on message propagation delay or relative node execution speed — the model is explicitly asynchronous. Every protocol assumes node identifiers are correct and uncorrupted in the initial state and are manipulated only by comparison, storage, and transmission (never recomputed or reassigned) — a self-stabilizing overlay protocol in this survey's model cannot repair a corrupted node identifier itself and requires an external mechanism (a failure detector or an identifier-assignment scheme) to guarantee identifier correctness before the protocol begins. A protocol solving the Finite Departure Problem specifically requires an oracle, per Theorem 7.2 — no purely local protocol can guarantee that a permanently departing node's references are fully purged from the system, so any system requiring that guarantee must supply an oracle mechanism the survey's local-primitive protocols do not provide on their own.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus. This entry supplies a negative finding relevant to the brief's HSkip+ evaluation: this survey, forward-mined specifically to check for a post-2014 design dominating HSkip+ on bandwidth-heterogeneous routing, does not identify one.

### References worth retrieving
- Jacob, Richa, Scheideler, Schmid, Täubig. "Skip+: A self-stabilizing skip graph." — foundational, the design HSkip+ improves on (Skip+ itself is already a brief-mentioned mining seed but not yet a keyed corpus entry)
- Feldotto, Scheideler, Graffi. "HSkip+: A self-stabilizing overlay network for nodes with heterogeneous bandwidths." P2P 2014. — foundational (already read per brief §7 as HSKIP+)
- Awerbuch, Scheideler. "Towards a scalable and robust DHT." Theory of Computing Systems 45(2), 2009. — competing, cited as related work on scalable robust overlay design
- Aspnes, Shah. "Skip graphs." ACM TALG 3(4), 2007. — foundational, the deterministic-skip-graph family SKIP+ and HSKIP+ both descend from
- Godfrey, Shenker, Stoica. "Minimizing churn in distributed systems." SIGCOMM CCR. — foundational for churn-tolerant overlay design, cited in the survey's own open-problems section as a body of work disconnected from self-stabilization research
- Rhea, Geels, Roscoe, Kubiatowicz. "Handling churn in a DHT." — foundational, same churn-tolerance line the survey states is disconnected from self-stabilization research
- Unnamed reference [56] on the first monotonic-searchability protocol for the sorted list. — foundational
- Unnamed reference [57] on the generic monotonic-searchability protocol applicable across topologies. — foundational, defines the Ω(n)-hop worst case for non-existent-node search
- Unnamed reference [38] on a specialized monotonic-searchability protocol for the perfect skip graph. — competing / superseding for that specific property against SKIP+'s reliance on additional edges for local checkability
- Unnamed reference [18] introducing the Finite Departure Problem and Finite Sleep Problem formalism and the oracle-necessity proof (Theorem 7.2). — foundational
- Unnamed reference [33], a universal protocol for the Finite Departure Problem applicable across self-stabilizing protocols. — foundational / superseding for the node-departure problem generally
- Unnamed reference [55], showing the Finite Departure Problem solvable without an oracle under a relay-based interconnection model. — competing / superseding for the specific oracle-necessity result under a different model

### Verbatim extracts
- "SKIP+ transforms any weakly connected graph ... into a skip graph after O(log^2 n) rounds"
- "An improved version of the self-stabilizing SKIP+ graph is HSKIP+ ... which reduces the stabilization time in practice and needs less work"
- "Any self-stabilizing solution for the FDP has to rely on an oracle"
- "this line of research has been largely independent of research on self-stabilizing algorithms" (churn tolerance vs. self-stabilization)
- "the degree of a node may temporarily raise significantly, far beyond the maximum initial or final node degree"
- "Search requests may traverse up to Ω(n) hops until termination when searching for non-existent nodes"

## [FISCH-EUROCRYPT-19] Tight Proofs of Space and Replication
**Citation:** Ben Fisch. "Tight Proofs of Space and Replication." EUROCRYPT, 2019. DOI 10.1007/978-3-030-17656-3_12.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://eprint.iacr.org/2018/702.pdf
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2018/702.pdf
**Domain:** C

### What it does
A proof of space (PoS) lets a prover convince a verifier it is persistently storing at least a specified amount of data, through a compact commitment plus cheap spot-check challenges (defined identically to DZIEMBOWSKI-CRYPTO-15). This paper's contribution is closing the gap, called the space gap ε, between the storage N an honest prover actually uses and the storage (1−ε)N a cheating prover can get away with while still passing verification; a PoS is "arbitrarily tight" if ε can be driven toward zero by a construction parameter without inflating the degree of the underlying graph (only the number of stacked layers grows, as O(log(1/ε))).

The construction, Stacked Depth-Robust Graphs (Stacked DRGs), builds on the stacked bipartite-expander PoS of Ren and Devadas (TCC 2016): a graph of O(log(1/ε)) layers, each n nodes, where each layer individually is a depth-robust graph (DRG) — a graph in which any subgraph on a stated fraction of the nodes (the paper analyzes 80%) retains a long directed path (length Ω(n)) — and bipartite-expander edges connect consecutive layers. The prover labels every node with a hash of its parents' labels (as in the generic graph-labeling PoS), commits to the labels of each layer with a vector commitment (e.g. a Merkle tree), and stores only the final layer's labels, deleting earlier layers as computed. Deleting an ε fraction of the final layer's stored labels forces the prover to recompute nearly all labels in the earlier layers to answer future challenges, because the expander edges between layers make each later layer's labels depend on a spreading fraction of nodes in every earlier layer; since each layer is itself depth-robust, that recomputation costs Ω(N) sequential steps. This is what makes the space gap tight and, unlike the Ren-Devadas base construction, resistant to parallel-execution cheating (a prover running many computations at once cannot substitute time for storage).

A second construction, ZigZag DRGs, adapts Stacked DRGs into a proof of replication (PoRep): a publicly verifiable proof that the prover holds several independently generated, individually retrievable copies (replicas) of a specific input file, not merely one copy referenced multiple times. Each layer is the union of a DRG and a constant-degree non-bipartite expander graph, and the direction of the inter-layer expander edges alternates layer to layer (the "zig-zag"), so dependencies that were computed forward in one layer become recoverable backward in the next. Each layer's labels encode the data of the previous layer using a key derived from that layer's own DRG edges. This makes decoding the original data from any replica fast and parallelizable, at the cost of roughly double the number of layers versus the plain PoS variant, whereas the direct PoRep application of the base Stacked-DRG construction makes data extraction as expensive as generating the replica in the first place.

### Measured results
All figures below are proved asymptotic or concrete-parameter bounds from the paper's own analysis, not measurements from an implementation; the paper contains no benchmark on real hardware or running system.

| Result | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Space gap of this paper's Stacked-DRG PoS | ε (arbitrarily small, tunable) | O(log(1/ε)) layers; degree d fixed independent of ε; underlying DRG only required to retain Ω(n) depth in subgraphs on 80% of nodes |
| Proof size of this paper's construction | O(d/ε) | d = degree of the depth-robust graph used per layer; this is stated as asymptotically optimal for any pebbling-based PoS with an ε space gap |
| Concrete instantiation | 10 layers achieve a 1% space gap, using degree 8+d graphs | d = degree of the chosen DRG; 80%-subgraph depth-robust property; result of the paper's own tightened analysis |
| Ren-Devadas (2016) stacked-expander PoS space gap | at least 1/2 | practical parameter regime (γ > 0.6 needs degree ≥ 40 graphs, so practically ε < 1/3 to keep proof sizes reasonable); not secure against parallel attacks |
| Dziembowski et al. (2015, this batch's DZIEMBOWSKI-CRYPTO-15) space gap | at least 1 − 1/512 | as stated by this paper's related-work analysis of that construction |
| Pietrzak (2018) depth-robust-graph PoS, concrete degree/proof-size cost | degree 2,760·log N required for a 1/2 space gap on N 32-byte data blocks; proof size ≥ 26 MB at λ=10-bit security and N=2^30; degree 19,310·log N and λ=60 layers needed for a 1/10 space gap, giving proof size ≥ 1 GB | figures attributed by this paper to the concrete analysis in Alwen, Blocki, Pietrzak's "Sustained space complexity" (reference [6] in this paper's bibliography); not independently re-derived here |
| Proof-size comparison, Stacked DRGs with Butterfly-graph connectors (Cecchetti, Miers, Juels PIE construction) vs. this paper's expander-graph connectors | Butterfly-connector proof queries proportional to 5·log(n)·λ/ε; expander-connector proof queries proportional to 11λ/ε | α=0.80, ε=0.01; Butterfly variant is already 5× larger for kilobyte-size data and 15×–20× larger for gigabyte- or terabyte-size data |
| Merkle vector-commitment storage overhead the prover can trade for read cost | deleting hashes on the top k levels of the Merkle tree saves a factor 2^k in storage; at k=7 this is under 1% storage overhead, costing at most 128 additional hashes/reads to re-derive a path | stated for the honest prover's vector-commitment bookkeeping, not the core PoS storage |

### Parameters
- N: total space (in blocks) the honest prover commits to store
- ε: target space gap; the fraction of storage a cheating prover might save and still pass verification, tunable toward zero
- 𝓁 (number of layers): O(log(1/ε)) for the Stacked-DRG PoS; roughly double that for the ZigZag PoRep variant, to maintain the same space-gap guarantee while enabling fast extraction
- d: degree of the depth-robust graph within each layer, fixed independent of ε (the paper's concrete construction uses a degree-8 Chung random bipartite graph for the inter-layer edges)
- Depth-robustness threshold: analyzed concretely at (n, 0.80n, Ω(n)) — any subgraph on 80% of a layer's nodes retains an Ω(n)-length path
- λ: cryptographic/statistical security parameter, drives the number of challenge queries per layer
- δ: a challenge-query tuning parameter; the paper shows total proof queries across all layers can be held to O(1/δ), giving overall proof complexity O(d/ε)
- k (Merkle-tree pruning depth): free parameter trading storage for extra hash computation during path reconstruction; the paper's own example sets k=7

### Stated limitations
The Ren-Devadas base construction this paper builds on is stated to not be proven secure against a graph-labeling adversary in the random oracle model generally, only against a pebbling-modeled adversary; this paper's own construction is stated to close that gap by additionally proving security against parallel pebbling attacks, from which security in the random oracle model follows. The paper states that constructions of depth-robust graphs achieving arbitrarily small α (i.e., very strong depth robustness) exist in theory but are "purely theoretical and not viable in practice," which is why this paper deliberately targets a construction needing only a weak, fixed 80%-subgraph depth-robustness property instead. The direct PoRep application of the plain Stacked-DRG PoS (without the ZigZag modification) is stated to make data extraction "as inefficient as replica generation," meaning recovering the original file from a replica costs as much sequential computation as producing that replica did — the paper's stated reason for introducing the separate ZigZag construction. The paper's own analysis of a compression-robust encoder graph (the Cecchetti-Miers-Juels PIE construction, discussed in comparison) demonstrates a counterexample where compression-robustness alone does not imply proof-of-space security, because data labels can sometimes be recomputed out of topological order using an inverse pseudorandom-permutation decoding path rather than needing genuinely sequential recomputation — the paper states this is a specific caveat about a competing definition, not a limitation of its own Stacked-DRG or ZigZag constructions. The paper notes an incompletely optimized proof-size tradeoff at one point in the ZigZag analysis ("here does not yet optimize this tradeoff"), without further elaboration on what the achievable optimum would be.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The Stacked-DRG PoS requires a cryptographic hash function (used as the graph-labeling function) and a vector-commitment scheme such as a Merkle tree, with the verifier retaining only the O(polylog(N))-size commitment root, not the data itself. For a PoRep built on this PoS to guarantee ε-rational replication (the property that storing k independently-generated replicas is the storage-minimizing strategy up to an ε loss), the paper states it needs the composed scheme to be simultaneously a tight proof of space and a proof-of-retrievable-commitment (PoRC) — a component this paper defines separately (Section 2.1) and does not itself argue can be substituted by an arbitrary proof-of-storage scheme without re-verifying that composition. A prover instantiating this PoS must be able to compute the full graph labeling once (initialization time is not stated as reduced from linear in N; the earlier Dziembowski-family result already showed initialization is at least linear in N), and must have persistent storage for the final layer's labels between the initialization and every later execution round; the protocol assumes the verifier issues challenge queries and enforces a wall-clock timing bound on responses, since soundness against a prover that discarded labels and recomputes them on demand depends on that computation being provably too slow to complete within the challenge window. For the ZigZag PoRep specifically, a system consuming the extracted data must be able to run the decoding procedure layer by layer, in parallel, recovering each earlier layer from the one after it using per-node keys derived from within-layer DRG edges — this requires the replica-holding party to retain every layer's labels in the ZigZag topology, not just the last layer, which is a storage-shape assumption distinct from the plain Stacked-DRG PoS.

### Contradicts
None found within this batch that directly disagree in a measured figure. The paper's own comparison table implicitly disputes the practicality claims made for the Dziembowski-Faust-Kolmogorov-Pietrzak (2015) and Pietrzak (2018) depth-robust-graph constructions: this paper states those constructions, while asymptotically sound, require degree and proof-size parameters that are not "concretely practical" (specific figures: 26 MB to 1 GB proof sizes at stated security levels), a stronger and more specific claim than either of those papers' own framing of their results as asymptotically efficient. This is presented here as this paper's own comparative analysis, attributed to it, not independently re-verified against DZIEMBOWSKI-CRYPTO-15's own text in this extraction.

### References worth retrieving
- Ren, Devadas, "Proof of space from stacked expanders," TCC 2016 — foundational; the stacked bipartite-expander construction this paper directly extends by replacing line graphs with depth-robust graphs
- Fisch, "PoReps: Proofs of space on useful data," ePrint — foundational; defines the ε-rational replication security notion this paper's PoRep construction targets, and the PoRep syntax (Setup/Preproc/Replicate/Extract/Prove/Poll/Verify) this paper reuses
- Alwen, Blocki, Pietrzak, "Sustained space complexity" — foundational; source of the concrete degree/proof-size figures this paper cites for Pietrzak's depth-robust-graph PoS as impractical at stated security levels
- Pietrzak, "Proofs of Catalytic Space," ePrint 2018/194 — competing; an independently proposed depth-robust-graph PoS this paper compares against on space gap and concrete parameter cost
- Cecchetti, Miers, Juels, "PIEs: Public incompressible encodings for decentralized storage" — competing/concurrent; an independent construction (publicly incompressible encodings, using Butterfly-graph connectors instead of expander connectors) this paper compares proof size against directly (5×–20× larger, by the figures above) and analyzes for a counterexample to its compression-robustness security property
- Abusalah, Alwen, Cohen, Khilko, Pietrzak, [et al.], "[Beyond Hellman's Time-Memory Trade-Offs...]" — competing; the random-function-table PoS revival this paper's related work cites as having a large asymptotic space gap (1 − 1/(64 log N))
- Dziembowski, Faust, Kolmogorov, Pietrzak, "Proofs of Space," CRYPTO 2015 — foundational; the original PoS construction (this batch's DZIEMBOWSKI-CRYPTO-15) that this paper's stacked-DRG construction improves on for space-gap tightness
- Protocol Labs, "Proof of replication," 2017, https://filecoin.io/proof-of-replication — competing/application; the deployed system whitepaper motivating this paper's formal treatment, cited in the registry's own why_needed as lacking this paper's security proof
- Boneh, Bonneau, Bünz, Fisch, "Verifiable delay functions," CRYPTO 2018 — foundational; introduces the verifiable-delay-function primitive this paper's related-work section discusses as an alternative simple PoRep basis with impractical O(N²) initialization time

- "data extraction is as ineﬃcient as replica generation"
- "showing that just 10 layers achieve a PoS with a 1% space gap"

## [FORD-EUROSPW-17] Proof-of-Personhood: Redemocratizing Permissionless Cryptocurrencies
**Citation:** Maria Borge, Eleftherios Kokoris-Kogias, Philipp Jovanovic, Linus Gasser, Nicolas Gailly, Bryan Ford. "Proof-of-Personhood: Redemocratizing Permissionless Cryptocurrencies." IEEE European Symposium on Security and Privacy Workshops (EuroS&PW), 2017. DOI 10.1109/EUROSPW.2017.46.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://infoscience.epfl.ch/record/228239
**Source URL:** https://doi.org/10.1109/EUROSPW.2017.46
**Domain:** E

### What it does
Proof-of-personhood (PoP) lets a person prove they control exactly one cryptographic identity token, tied to one physical body, without disclosing who they are — a basis for Sybil resistance (defense against one attacker registering many identities) that does not depend on spending computation (proof-of-work) or capital (proof-of-stake). The paper builds PoP on the pseudonym party (Ford and Strauss, 2008): a real-world, in-person gathering, organized by any set of volunteers acting as organizers, at which every attendee receives exactly one PoP-token by the end of the event.

The security model is an anytrust assumption: attendees trust only that at least one organizer, and at least one of the organizers' independent servers (a conode, jointly forming a collective authority or cothority), is honest and not colluding with the rest — the specific honest party need not be known in advance. Before the party, organizers fix its place, date, start and end times, a barrier time after which no new PoP-tokens are issued, and a token expiration date, publish these in a configuration file, and run dry-run tests without real attendees. Organizers also select an independent group of observers to record video of the event for transparency and later dispute resolution. Each attendee generates a fresh key pair locally, then derives an ephemeral public key specific to this party by hashing the configuration file into an elliptic-curve point H and computing X' = H^x from the attendee's private key x using Ed25519; this ephemeral key, not the attendee's ordinary public key, is what gets bound to the PoP-token, so using the ephemeral key elsewhere does not compromise the attendee's other-service anonymity. At the party, attendees enter during a fixed window (departure remains free at any time for safety); once the barrier time arrives, no further entry is allowed, and organizers form a line where each organizer individually confirms every attendee's personhood, records the attendee's ephemeral public key, and marks the attendee with a physical ink stamp — visual confirmation that prevents an attendee from returning to the front of the line for a second token. After all organizers have confirmed an attendee, the attendee proceeds to a separate room with no path back to re-enter the confirmation line. At the party's end, the conodes collectively sign a party transcript containing a hash of the recorded video and the full list of attendee public keys; each attendee's PoP-token is the triple of their ephemeral public key, their ephemeral private key, and this attendee-public-key list from the transcript.

To authenticate a PoP-token to an online service without revealing which attendee it belongs to, the paper proposes a linkable ring signature scheme (Liu et al., 2004): the token holder signs a challenge message within a service-specific context, producing both a signature and a verification tag; the service checks the signature against the full anonymity set of attendee public keys in the party transcript, then checks whether the resulting tag already exists in its own database. A first use is accepted and its tag stored; a repeat use of the same token against the same service produces the same tag and is rejected, preventing one PoP-token from creating more than one account per service, without ever revealing which attendee's key produced either signature.

PoPCoin is the paper's proposed cryptocurrency application: a minting pool is formed from attendees who authenticate their PoP-token to a set of trusted servers within a stated validation window (the paper's example: one week) after the party. In the simple variant, the system substitutes proof-of-stake's minter-selection step with a random draw over the PoP-token-holding minting pool, using RandHound (a distributed protocol producing scalable, unbiasable, publicly verifiable randomness run by the last N minters against Byzantine adversaries) to pick the next minter every M minutes; a minter caught extending two chains is punished, which the paper states resolves proof-of-stake's nothing-at-stake problem (the incentive to build on every competing chain since doing so costs nothing). A second variant instead extends ByzCoin (a Bitcoin-like cryptocurrency using collective signing, CoSi, to reduce Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerance's message overhead), replacing ByzCoin's proof-of-work-based sliding share window of size W with PoP-token-based membership, so the consensus group of the last W blocks' minters runs RandHound to select the next window member and then continues as ByzCoin's leader-based collective-signing protocol.

### Measured results
The paper describes a design and a real-world deployment vision; it reports no benchmark, simulation, or measured deployment result of its own (no party was run and measured as part of this work). Its only comparison against a competing scheme is qualitative: the paper states the Proof-of-Individuality (PoI) project, which uses virtual video-based pseudonym parties plus Ethereum smart contracts, has three disadvantages relative to this paper's physical-pseudonym-party approach — it needs a separate mechanism to confirm a submitted video is an actual live stream rather than a recording; it depends on Ethereum's security and in turn on Ethereum's proof-of-work foundation, so it cannot alone bootstrap a secure cryptocurrency; and it adds implementation complexity from that Ethereum dependency. No figure accompanies any of these three points; each is a design comparison, not a measurement.

### Parameters
- Party timing parameters: place p, date d, start time t_start, end time t_end, barrier time t_barrier (after which no new tokens are issued), and token expiration date t_exp — every value is fixed per-party by the organizers, with no numeric example given in the paper.
- PoPCoin block interval M: the period, in minutes, after which minters repeat the minting selection process; no concrete value is given, only the variable name.
- ByzCoin sliding window size W: the number of most recent blocks whose minters form the active consensus group; no concrete value is given.
- RandHound participant count N: the last N minters run RandHound to produce the randomness selecting the next minter; no concrete value is given.
- PoPCoin token-authentication validation window: the paper's own illustrative example is one week, explicitly marked as an example ("e.g., one week"), not a derived or measured requirement.

### Stated limitations
The paper states PoPCoin is envisioned to begin as a small local cryptocurrency (comparable to community currencies such as Ithaca Hours, BerkShares, and the Leman), with a pseudonym party held roughly every few months, before any larger-scale federation across independent local groups is attempted; the paper offers no evidence such federation is technically solved, describing it as a future step contingent on the initial local experiment succeeding and gaining traction. Scaling PoP-token issuance to prevent one person from obtaining tokens at two simultaneous parties in different regions is proposed to rely on physical travel infeasibility (the paper's example: traveling from Europe to the US west coast within a few hours), which the paper states depends on the parties' relative timing and geographic separation rather than on any cryptographic guarantee. The paper states the PoI project's video-based virtual pseudonym party does not provide the same security properties as an in-person physical pseudonym party, specifically because confirming a submitted video is a genuine live stream and not a pre-recording is an unsolved requirement for that competing approach; this paper's own physical-party design is presented as avoiding that specific problem by requiring physical co-presence, not as having solved video-liveness verification itself.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Running one pseudonym party requires a set of volunteer organizers, each operating an independent server (conode) that together form a collective authority, and requires at least one organizer and at least one conode among them to be genuinely honest and non-colluding for the anytrust security assumption to hold; the specific honest party need not be identified in advance, but its existence is a precondition the protocol does not itself enforce or detect. The party additionally requires an independently selected group of observers to record video for transparency, and the paper leaves the process of independently selecting both organizers and observers as external to the protocol it specifies. Every attendee must generate their key pair locally, on their own device, before the party, and must derive their party-specific ephemeral public key from the published configuration file using the paper's Ed25519-based hash-to-point construction; a service that authenticates PoP-tokens must obtain and hold the party transcript (published by organizers on trusted servers) to validate a token's origin and expiration date, and must independently maintain its own per-service database of linkable-ring-signature tags to detect a repeated use of the same token. The PoPCoin minting mechanisms require RandHound's distributed randomness generation to be run by a live, cooperating subset of current minters (the last N, or the current window's W minters in the ByzCoin variant) at each selection round, and require a punishment mechanism external to the paper's own description to be enforceable against a minter caught extending two chains, for the stated resolution of the nothing-at-stake problem to hold in practice.

### Contradicts
None found.

### References worth retrieving
- Ford, Strauss, "An offline foundation for online accountable pseudonyms," Workshop on Social Network Systems, 2008 — foundational (the original pseudonym-party construction this paper's PoP mechanism is built directly on).
- Liu, Wei, Wong, "Linkable spontaneous anonymous group signature for ad hoc groups," ACISP 2004 — foundational (the linkable ring signature scheme this paper's PoP-token authentication mechanism uses to prevent one token from creating multiple accounts per service).
- Kogias, Jovanovic, Gailly, Khoffi, Gasser, Ford, "Enhancing Bitcoin security and performance with strong consistency via collective signing," USENIX Security 2016 — foundational (introduces ByzCoin and CoSi, both directly used by this paper's second PoPCoin construction).
- Proof of individuality project (cited as an online resource, consulted October 2016) — competing (the video-based virtual pseudonym-party alternative to this paper's physical-party design, with three stated disadvantages relative to it).
- Douceur, "The Sybil attack," IPTPS 2002 — foundational (the attack this paper's proof-of-personhood mechanism, and Sybil-resistance mechanisms generally, are designed to resist).
- Nakamoto, "Bitcoin: A peer-to-peer electronic cash system," 2008 — foundational (the proof-of-work "one CPU one vote" minting principle this paper's PoPCoin proposes to replace with a "one PoP-token one vote" principle).

### Verbatim extracts
"we assume an anytrust model in which attendees trust only that at least one organizer"
"marking the attendee with an ink stamp"
"the reliance on Ethereum introduces a non-negligible amount of complexity"
"forks cannot occur by accident"

## [FORD-USENIX-05] Peer-to-Peer Communication Across Network Address Translators
**Citation:** Bryan Ford, Pyda Srisuresh, Dan Kegel. "Peer-to-Peer Communication Across Network Address Translators." USENIX Annual Technical Conference, General Track, 2005.
**Retrieved:** full text via arXiv mirror
**Source URL:** https://www.brynosaurus.com/pub/net/p2pnat.pdf (arXiv:cs/0603074)
**Domain:** L

### What it does
The paper documents "hole punching," a technique that lets two clients each behind their own NAT (Network Address Translator) establish a direct peer-to-peer session, for both UDP and TCP, using a well-known rendezvous server only to introduce the two clients and never to carry their traffic afterward. Both clients first establish an active UDP or TCP session with a rendezvous server S. S records, for each client, the client's private endpoint (the (IP address, port) pair the client reports using itself, taken from a field in the registration message body) and its public endpoint (the (IP address, port) pair S observes the message arriving from, taken from the packet's own IP/UDP or IP/TCP headers). To connect, client A asks S for help reaching client B; S replies to A with B's public and private endpoints and simultaneously forwards A's public and private endpoints to B over S's existing session with B. Each client then sends packets — UDP datagrams, or for TCP, simultaneous outgoing connection attempts — to both of the other client's reported endpoints (public and private) and locks onto whichever endpoint elicits a valid response first. Sending the first outbound packet toward the peer's public endpoint is what "punches a hole" in the sender's own NAT: it creates a NAT session entry for that destination, so a return packet from the peer is no longer "unsolicited" from the NAT's point of view and is forwarded inward. For TCP, the API obstacle is that the Berkeley sockets API does not normally allow one local port to both listen for inbound connections and originate multiple outbound connection attempts; the paper's answer is to set `SO_REUSEADDR` (and, on BSD systems, `SO_REUSEPORT`) on every socket bound to that port, letting the same local TCP port back a listen socket and several concurrent outbound connect() attempts.

### Measured results
| Metric | Result | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| UDP hole punching compatibility | 310 of 380 reported data points (82%) showed the NAT consistently translating the client's private endpoint to the same public endpoint | volunteer-submitted "NAT Check" client-program results, 68 NAT vendors plus 8 operating systems' built-in NAT, self-selecting non-random sample |
| UDP hairpin translation support | 80 of 335 data points (24%) supported hairpin translation | same NAT Check dataset, hairpin-specific subset (feature added to NAT Check later than the base test) |
| TCP hole punching compatibility | 184 of 286 data points (64%) showed consistent private-endpoint translation and no RST response to unsolicited inbound SYNs | same NAT Check dataset, TCP-specific subset |
| TCP hairpin translation support | 37 of 286 data points (13%) supported hairpin translation for TCP | same NAT Check dataset |
| Per-vendor UDP hole-punch compatibility (highest to lowest among vendors with ≥5 data points) | Belkin, Cisco, SMC, 3Com: 100%; Linksys: 98% (45/46); Netgear: 84% (31/37); Windows built-in: 94% (31/33); ZyXEL: 78% (7/9); Linux built-in: 81% (26/32); FreeBSD built-in: 78% (7/9); D-Link: 76% (16/21); Draytek: 12% (2/17) | Table 1, same NAT Check dataset |
| Corroborating large-ISP result | of the top three consumer NAT router vendors observed on one large ISP's network, representing 86% of NATs seen, all three vendors currently produced NATs compatible with UDP hole punching | cited as a separate, independent corroborating result reported to the authors by the ISP; no vendor names, sample size, or measurement date given in the paper |

### Parameters
| Parameter | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| NAT Check UDP probe payload | ping-like request/response between client and 3 well-known servers (servers 1, 2, 3), each at a distinct public IP | Section 6.1.1 |
| NAT Check TCP unsolicited-SYN test wait | server 3 waits up to 5 s for its own inbound connection attempt to the client to resolve, then signals server 2 to proceed and continues waiting up to 20 s total | Section 6.1.2 |
| Retry policy on failed outbound connect (TCP hole punching, step 4) | retried after a short delay (paper states "e.g., one second"), up to an application-defined maximum timeout | Section 4.2 |
| Sockets API options required for TCP hole punching | `SO_REUSEADDR` on all sockets bound to the shared local port; `SO_REUSEPORT` additionally required on BSD-derived systems | Section 4.1 |
| NAT Check dataset size | 380 total data points across 68 hardware vendors and 8 operating systems; only 335 include UDP hairpin results and only 286 include any TCP results, because hairpin and TCP testing were added to NAT Check after data collection had already begun | Section 6.2 |

### Stated limitations
The authors state NAT Check's volunteer-submitted dataset is drawn from a "self-selecting" community and therefore does not constitute a random sample or necessarily represent the true distribution of NATs in common use. They state three specific testing-protocol limitations: NAT Check does not obfuscate the IP addresses it transmits in message payloads, so it cannot detect or protect against the small number of NATs known to blindly rewrite IP-address-shaped byte sequences found in application payloads; NAT Check's hairpin translation test may under-report support because it assumes a NAT that permits hairpin traffic does not separately filter that traffic as if it were arriving from the untrusted public side, an assumption the authors state they later realized may not hold for all NATs; and NAT Check cannot detect NATs that behave consistently for a single client behind them but degrade to symmetric-NAT behavior (or worse) once two or more clients on the same private network use the same local port concurrently, because reliably testing for that behavior requires running NAT Check on two client hosts simultaneously. The paper states multi-level NAT scenarios in general require hairpin translation for hole punching to fully succeed, and states hairpin translation support was rare among tested NATs (24% UDP, 13% TCP) even though the scenarios requiring it were also comparatively rare at the time of writing.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Hole punching requires a rendezvous server reachable by both peers before the peers can establish a direct session, and that server's role ends once the hole is opened — it never carries session traffic, unlike the relay-server alternative the paper contrasts it with (see DUARTE-ABAKOS-20's measured throughput collapse for a relay path under bandwidth constraint). The mechanism requires the NAT to be a "cone" NAT — consistently mapping one private (IP, port) pair to the same public (IP, port) pair across sessions — and fails when the NAT is "symmetric," assigning a different public mapping per destination; the paper states 82% (UDP) and 64% (TCP) of the tested population met this requirement, so roughly one-fifth of UDP participants and over one-third of TCP participants in a design targeting that same population cannot be reached by unmodified hole punching. Because A's first message toward B's private endpoint may reach an unrelated host that happens to hold the same private IP address (NATs commonly assign private addresses from the same default DHCP pool), any application built on this mechanism must authenticate every inbound message — by an application-specific credential, a cryptographic token, or at minimum a nonce pre-arranged through the rendezvous server — to filter out such stray traffic, rather than trusting that a message arriving on the punched session is necessarily from the intended peer. Multi-level NAT topologies (a shared ISP-operated NAT layered with per-customer consumer NATs) additionally require hairpin translation support in the shared NAT layer, measured present in only 24% (UDP) / 13% (TCP) of tested devices, so a design that must support multi-level NAT cannot assume hairpin support is available and needs a fallback (such as the relay-server path) for that case.

### Contradicts
None found. DUARTE-ABAKOS-20 measures the same connection-reversal-plus-hole-punching mechanism this paper defines and reports comparably low overhead, not a disagreement.

### References worth retrieving
- **Foundational** — Rosenberg, Weinberger, Huitema, Mahy. "STUN - Simple Traversal of User Datagram Protocol (UDP) Through Network Address Translators (NATs)." RFC 3489, 2003. — defines the cone/symmetric NAT terminology this paper's Section 5.1 relies on, and the protocol used for NAT-behavior classification in corroborating studies.
- **Foundational** — Rosenberg. "Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE)." Internet-Draft, 2003 (later RFC 5245). — protocol built on hole punching for offer/answer session negotiation.
- **Competing** — Guha, Takeday, Francis. "NUTSS: A SIP-based approach to UDP and TCP network connectivity." SIGCOMM Workshops, 2004. — a more complex TCP hole-punching approach the paper states requires the rendezvous server to spoof source IP addresses and requires client raw-socket access, contrasted with this paper's own approach requiring neither.
- **Competing** — Biggadike, Ferullo, Wilson, Perrig. "NATBLASTER: Establishing TCP connections between hosts behind NATs." ACM SIGCOMM Asia Workshop, 2005. — the paper states this uses similar spoofing/raw-socket tricks to NUTSS to handle bad NAT behaviors this paper's own technique does not attempt to work around.
- **Competing** — Eppinger. "TCP connections for P2P apps: A software approach to solving the NAT problem." CMU-ISRI-05-104, 2005. — the paper states NatTrav implements an asymmetric TCP hole-punching procedure, contrasted with this paper's symmetric procedure (Section 4).
- **Foundational** — Holdrege, Srisuresh. "Protocol complications with the IP network address translator." RFC 3027, 2001. — the paper states this is where UDP hole punching was first mentioned, in section 5.1.
- **Attack or critique** — Duarte, Cardoso, de Mello, Borges. "Beware: NAT Traversal is a Simple and Efficient Approach to Open Firewall Holes." Abakós, 2020. — states the exploitable side effect of this paper's own mechanism: any internal host can use hole punching to open a firewall hole for an unauthorized service (already in this batch, DUARTE-ABAKOS-20).
- **Foundational** — Francis, Gummadi. "IPNL: A NAT-extended Internet architecture." SIGCOMM 2002. — one of several architectural alternatives the paper states would decouple host identity from location, contrasted with hole punching's no-upgrade-required property.

### Verbatim extracts
"about 82% of the NATs tested support hole punching for UDP, and about 64% support hole punching for TCP"
"punches a hole in A's NAT for a new UDP session"
"applications must therefore authenticate all messages in some way to filter out such stray traffic"
"Support for hairpin translation is much less common"
"hole punching works consistently and robustly for both TCP and UDP communication"

## [FREEDMAN-NSDI-04] Democratizing Content Publication with Coral
**Citation:** Michael J. Freedman, Eric Freudenthal, David Mazières. "Democratizing Content Publication with Coral." USENIX/ACM NSDI, 2004.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.usenix.org/legacy/event/nsdi04/tech/full_papers/freedman/freedman.pdf
**Source URL:** https://www.usenix.org/legacy/event/nsdi04/tech/full_papers/freedman/freedman.pdf
**Domain:** A

### What it does
CoralCDN lets any web publisher offload traffic spikes onto a peer-to-peer network of volunteer proxy caches, without the publisher operating any infrastructure beyond a URL-naming convention. A client requests a "Coralized" URL (an ordinary URL with `.nyud.net` appended to the hostname); a Coral DNS server (dnssrv) resolves it to a nearby volunteer HTTP proxy (CoralProxy); the proxy serves the object from its local cache, or fetches it from another Coral node caching the object, or as a last resort fetches it once from the origin server and then caches it for subsequent requests network-wide. The mechanism that finds nearby proxies and nearby cached copies is Coral, a distributed sloppy hash table (DSHT): a key-value indexing structure related to a distributed hash table (DHT) but designed to let many values be stored under one key without concentrating request traffic on the few nodes closest to that key.

Coral's routing layer assigns every node a 160-bit identifier (the SHA-1 hash of its IP address) and every key a 160-bit identifier, using the same exclusive-or (XOR) distance metric as Kademlia. Unlike Kademlia, a Coral lookup does not always jump to the numerically closest known node; instead it corrects only `b` bits of the target identifier per hop (the paper uses b=1), deliberately lengthening the average path so that no small set of nodes closest to a heavily requested key receives every request for that key — a congestion pattern the paper calls tree saturation, borrowed from shared-memory interconnection network research.

A Coral put (insertion) proceeds in two phases. In the forward phase, the inserting node routes progressively closer to the key's identifier, stopping early if it reaches a node that is simultaneously full for that key (holding `l` values whose time-to-live, TTL, is at least half the new value's TTL) and loaded for that key (having received more than a maximum leakage rate `γ` requests for that key in the past minute). In the reverse phase, the node walks back up the stack of contacted-but-not-full-or-loaded nodes, in order of increasing distance from the key, and stores the value at the first one that accepts it. This ensures a few nodes retain long-lived values close to the key (kept fresh by the trickle of γ requests per minute that do get through) while the bulk of copies scatter across increasingly distant nodes.

Coral nodes additionally organize into a hierarchy of clusters based on round-trip-time (RTT): a node belongs to one DSHT at each of several levels, where a level-i cluster's members have pairwise RTTs below that level's diameter threshold. A lookup and DNS-based proxy discovery query the fastest (lowest-level-number, tightest-RTT) cluster first, falling through to slower clusters only if the fast cluster has no answer, so both latency and the chance of finding a network-nearby cached copy improve without a global coordinator assigning cluster membership.

### Measured results
| Metric | Figure | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Aggregate synthetic client request rate generated | 99.6 requests/sec, ~32,800 Kbit/sec cumulative download rate, "almost two orders of magnitude greater than the origin web server could handle" | 166 PlanetLab machines (geographically distributed, mainly North America and Europe), origin an unmodified Apache server behind a 384 Kbit/sec upstream DSL line serving 12 distinct 41 KB files; each client requests one of 4 web pages (3 embedded images each) after a random 0-180 second startup delay, for 30 minutes |
| Origin-server load reduction | 15 requests hit the origin server in the first minute (for 12 unique files, 3 redundant due to simultaneous startup); after 8-10 minutes, files were replicated at nearly every server and few requests went past a proxy's local cache | Same 166-node experiment |
| End-to-end client latency (50th / 96th percentile), all nodes | Single-level 0.79s / 9.54s; multi-level 0.31s / 4.17s; multi-level+traceroute 0.19s / 2.50s | Same 166-node experiment; single-level = one global (level-0) cluster only; multi-level = 3-level hierarchy with RTT thresholds infinity/60ms/20ms |
| End-to-end client latency (50th / 96th percentile), Asian nodes only | Single-level 2.52s / 8.01s; multi-level 0.04s / 4.16s; multi-level+traceroute 0.03s / 1.75s | Same experiment, subset of 5 nodes in Hong Kong (2), Taiwan, Japan, Philippines |
| Coral internal get-operation latency | Multi-level system 2-5x faster than single-level up to the 80th percentile; single-level becomes faster after the 98th percentile under heavy packet loss because the multi-level hierarchy incurs extra timeouts traversing levels | Same 166-node experiment |
| Cluster formation | Level-1 (60ms threshold) world map: distinct regional clusters, largest Eastern U.S. (70 nodes), Western U.S. (37 nodes), Europe (19 nodes); level-2 (20ms threshold) U.S. map: 16 distinct clusters including California (22 nodes), Northeast Corridor (29 nodes, North Carolina to Massachusetts), 3 separate non-singleton clusters within the San Francisco Bay Area corresponding to measured RTT variation | Snapshot taken 30 minutes into the same 166-node experiment (network allowed to stabilize before client load began) |
| Load balancing of a single hot key | Closest node received 106 put RPCs in the first minute, settling to 83 put RPCs/minute in steady state, against a derived prediction of γ·(2^b−1)·⌈log n⌉ = 108 RPCs/minute; far-side nodes (differing from the key in their most significant bit) received zero put RPCs; most-loaded node for get requests received 27 RPCs in the first minute, then traffic dispersed as the key propagated | 494 nodes (3 Coral instances per each of the 166 PlanetLab hosts), single level-0 cluster only, all nodes issuing back-to-back put/get requests for the same key at their maximum non-concurrent rate (average 400 pairs/sec per node, ~12 million put/get requests/minute aggregate, only a fraction reaching the network because satisfied gets are served locally once a node holds the key) |

### Parameters
- Node/key identifier space: 160 bits; node ID = SHA-1 hash of the node's IP address.
- Routing correction per hop, b = 1 bit (stated as the value used in the paper's experiments; the mechanism is parameterizable).
- Full-node threshold l = 4 values stored per key with TTL at least half the new value's TTL.
- Leakage rate γ = 12 requests per key per minute per node before a node reports itself "loaded" for that key.
- Cluster hierarchy: 3 levels, RTT diameter thresholds infinity (level-0, global), 60 ms (level-1), 20 ms (level-2).
- Network stabilization period before load experiments began: 30 minutes (with a stated 5-minute clustering period as the tunable that sets this).
- DSHT routing-table size: logarithmic in the number of nodes in that DSHT (inherited from the Kademlia-style XOR-metric routing table).
- Derived closest-node request rate under the two-phase insertion algorithm: γ·(2^b−1)·⌈log n⌉ requests per minute (proof sketch given in the paper, for a perfectly balanced identifier tree).
- CoralProxy caching: no explicit eviction policy tested (paper states no objects were evicted from CoralProxy caches during the reported experiments; adaptive TTL-based eviction is noted as "not yet implemented").

### Stated limitations
The authors state the paper does not address CoralCDN's security properties, most importantly the integrity of cached data; they state a solution is future work and would need three components: preventing honest nodes from caching invalid data (a possible approach is embedding self-certifying pathnames in Coralized URLs, which the authors note "requires server buy-in"), enabling nodes to trace and exclude data originating from known-compromised nodes, and preventing clients from being directed to malicious proxies (which they state "requires client buy-in"). They state CoralCDN "may require some additional abuse-prevention mechanisms, such as throttling bandwidth hogs," which are not implemented in the reported system. They state a race condition can cause CoralCDN to issue multiple simultaneous requests to the origin server at the start of a flash crowd, which they attribute to the store operation lacking test-and-set semantics, and propose (without implementing) an extension to store transactions to return status information as a fix. They state DNS-redirection proxy assignment does not yet account for proxy heterogeneity (current load, available bandwidth), leaving room for a feedback-based allocation policy. They state Coral's network measurement, based on traceroute-like DNS-time probing, is "somewhat constrained" relative to centrally managed commercial content-distribution networks, because Coral nodes lack Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) feeds and operate under tight latency limits to avoid delaying DNS replies during probing, and because Coral's design assumes no single node knows the identity or network location of every other node in the system. They state CoralCDN offers less aggregate storage capacity than commercial content-distribution networks because cache management is fully localized per node, offsetting this by design for a far larger number of participating machines and vantage points. The paper's related-work comparison to CoDeeN notes CoralCDN does not permit HTTP POST operations or SSL tunneling, a scope restriction rather than a measured failure.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A DSHT client-facing application that needs the load-avoidance property depends on the underlying node-identifier space being large and effectively randomly distributed (Coral uses the SHA-1 hash of a node's IP address as its 160-bit identifier), because the tree-saturation-avoidance proof and the measured request-rate result at the closest node both assume the routing table's logarithmic-hop structure holds; irregularities in node-ID distribution are stated to increase the closest node's load "slightly" above the derived bound. Any application relying on Coral's cluster hierarchy for latency-optimized data placement requires an RTT-probing mechanism operating within DNS-reply time constraints (dnssrv's probes must complete before a DNS response is due), so a deployment context that cannot tolerate active per-query network probing at resolution time cannot use this mechanism as described. The get-side load balancing (retrieving one of several redundant stored values) requires the requesting application to handle multiple, possibly inconsistent, returned references itself — CoralProxy does this by fetching from multiple sources in parallel — so a component consuming Coral's DSHT abstraction must be designed for soft-state, multi-valued lookups rather than the single-authoritative-value semantics a conventional DHT-backed key-value store provides. The security discussion states that any content-integrity guarantee for cached data is not provided by the DSHT itself; a system layering trust or authenticity requirements on top of Coral needs to supply its own mechanism (the paper suggests, but does not build, self-certifying pathnames or a web-of-trust encoding using cluster membership).

### Contradicts
None found regarding a claim commonly attributed to this paper. The target registry's why_needed note characterizes Coral as optimizing "for round-trip-time-measured network proximity over identifier closeness" — the paper text supports the stronger and more precise claim that Coral does not attempt to route to the identifier-closest node at all when doing so would concentrate load (the b-bit-at-a-time correction rule and the full/loaded early-termination condition), which is a deliberate departure from Kademlia's direct-routing goal rather than a network-proximity substitution for it; DNS-level proxy selection is the part of the system that uses measured RTT for proximity, a separate mechanism (Section 3.1) from the DSHT's own identifier-space routing rule (Section 4.1).

### References worth retrieving
- Maymounkov, Mazières, "Kademlia: A peer-to-peer information system based on the XOR metric" (cited as [17]) — foundational (already in corpus per BRIEF section 7); Coral's routing table and XOR distance metric are stated to be "based on Kademlia."
- Dabek, Kaashoek, Karger, Morris, Stoica, "Wide-area cooperative storage with CFS" (cited as [5]) — competing, a DHT-based file system requiring strict read/write consistency, contrasted against Coral's relaxed-consistency directory-service approach.
- Rowstron, Druschel, "Storage management and caching in PAST" (cited as [27]) — competing, same strict-consistency DHT-storage category as CFS.
- Zhao, Huang, Stribling, Rhea, Joseph, Kubiatowicz, Tapestry (cited as [35]) — foundational/competing, the DHT whose relaxed-consistency directory-service routing (caching a pointer at each hop during insertion) Coral's flexible clustering is compared against as providing "similar latency-optimized lookup."
- Pai, Wang, Park, Pang, Peterson, "The dark side of the web: An open proxy's view" (CoDeeN) (cited as [23]) — competing, the open-proxy CDN system compared point-by-point against CoralCDN's design goals in Section 7.
- Ratnasamy, Francis, Handley, Karp, Shenker, CAN (cited as [25]) — foundational, listed among traditional key-based routing layers Coral's approach is contrasted with.
- Stoica, Morris, Liben-Nowell, Karger, Kaashoek, Dabek, Balakrishnan, Chord (cited as [31]) — foundational (already in corpus per this batch, STOICA-SIGCOMM-01), listed among traditional key-based routing layers.

## [FREIRE-PKC-13] Non-Interactive Key Exchange
**Citation:** Eduarda S.V. Freire, Dennis Hofheinz, Eike Kiltz, Kenneth G. Paterson. "Non-Interactive Key Exchange." Public Key Cryptography (PKC), 2013. DOI: 10.1007/978-3-642-36362-7_17.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://eprint.iacr.org/2012/732.pdf (full version of the PKC 2013 paper)
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2012/732.pdf
**Domain:** H

### What it does
Non-Interactive Key Exchange (NIKE) lets two parties, each holding only the other's public key, compute a shared symmetric key with no protocol messages exchanged between them at the time of computation. The canonical instance, from Diffie and Hellman's original paper: Alice holds public key g^x and private key x, Bob holds public key g^y and private key y, in a group G of prime order p with generator g; each computes g^(xy) independently and hashes it together with both parties' identities to derive the shared key. This paper's contribution is not a new NIKE scheme in isolation but a systematic security-definition and construction-relationship study built on the earlier Cash-Kiltz-Shoup (CKS) formal model for NIKE.

The paper defines a NIKE scheme as three algorithms plus an identity space and a shared-key space: CommonSetup (produces system parameters), NIKE.KeyGen (produces one identity's public/secret key pair from those parameters), and SharedKey (takes one party's own identity and secret key plus a second party's identity and public key, and outputs the shared key or a failure symbol). It defines four security models differing only in which oracle queries an adversary may make against a challenger: CKS-light (the simplest — exactly two honest users, no corruption, a single test query), CKS (the original Cash-Kiltz-Shoup model — arbitrary honest and corrupt user registration and reveal queries, but no extract queries against honest users' secret keys and no honest-reveal queries), CKS-heavy (adds extract and honest-reveal queries, but only a single test query), and m-CKS-heavy (the paper's preferred model — the same expanded query set as CKS-heavy but with unlimited test queries). All four models operate in what the paper calls the dishonest key registration (plain/bare PKI) setting: an adversary may register any public key of its own choosing under any identity, and the model does not assume the Certificate Authority checks that a submitted public key is new or that the registrant knows the corresponding private key. The paper proves (Theorem 1) that all four models are polynomially equivalent to one another, with explicit reduction-loss factors given for each direction of implication, meaning a scheme's security proved in the simplest model (CKS-light) automatically implies security in the strongest model (m-CKS-heavy), at a stated multiplicative security loss.

The paper gives two concrete NIKE constructions meeting the CKS-light definition (and hence, by the equivalence theorem, the m-CKS-heavy definition): a Random-Oracle-Model scheme (NIKE_fac) proved secure under the factoring assumption, built in the group of signed quadratic residues; and a standard-model scheme (NIKE_dbdh-2) proved secure under a variant of the Decisional Bilinear Diffie-Hellman assumption for asymmetric pairings, combining a weak Programmable Hash Function with a chameleon hash function so the security proof's simulator can handle shared-key queries between one honestly generated and one adversarially chosen public key. The paper also gives a generic transformation converting any CKS-light-secure NIKE scheme, combined with a strongly one-time-secure signature scheme, into a Key Encapsulation Mechanism (KEM) proved secure against Indistinguishable-under-Chosen-Ciphertext-Attack (IND-CCA): the KEM's public/secret key pair is a NIKE key pair, a ciphertext is a freshly generated NIKE public key from the sender together with a one-time signature binding it to the intended recipient's identity, and the encapsulated key is the NIKE shared key the two public keys jointly determine.

### Measured results
None — this is a formal cryptography paper. Its quantitative content is derived security-reduction bounds and construction-efficiency figures stated directly by the authors from their own constructions, not measured by experiment, benchmark, or implementation. Two derived (not measured) figures the paper states explicitly:
- Model-equivalence reduction loss (Theorem 1, derived): going from the m-CKS-heavy model down to the simplest CKS-light model loses a multiplicative factor of q_T · q_H² in the security reduction, where q_T is the number of test queries and q_H the number of register-honest-user queries an adversary makes; the paper attributes this loss to the hybrid-argument proof technique used to establish the bound and states it as an open problem whether a tighter relation between the models can be proved, or proved impossible.
- Concrete key size (stated by the authors as a computed example, not a benchmark): at the 128-bit security level, using Barreto-Naehrig (BN) pairing-friendly curves with point compression, the standard-model pairing-based NIKE scheme's public keys consist of 768 bits plus one element from the chameleon-hash range space; the derived KEM built from this NIKE scheme has public keys consisting of an identity string, two group elements (one in each of the pairing's two source groups G1 and G2), and one chameleon-hash key, with ciphertexts additionally carrying a one-time-signature verification key and signature. The paper states this KEM's decapsulation cost is two bilinear-pairing evaluations (one to check public-key validity, one to compute the shared value) and describes the resulting KEM as comparable in performance to the Boyen-Mei-Waters (2005) direct-chosen-ciphertext-security scheme, without giving a numeric benchmark for either.

### Parameters
Not applicable as a tested range — the paper reports proved security bounds and one illustrative parameter choice, not a swept experimental study. The one concrete parameter given: 128-bit security level, BN curves, point compression, yielding the 768-bit-plus-one-chameleon-element public key size stated above; the paper does not state this is the only or a required choice, only an example computed for illustration.

### Stated limitations
The paper's standard-model factoring-based NIKE construction (a variant of NIKE_fac transported out of the Random Oracle Model) requires an additional assumption the authors state explicitly does not hold in their own default security model: that the adversary registers only valid public keys. The authors state this scheme therefore does not strictly meet their own stated security definitions in the plain (dishonest key registration) setting, and would require validity to be enforced through some external interactive registration protocol — for instance, a proof of correctness of the public key submitted at registration — that the paper does not itself construct. The paper flags an error in prior work it builds on: it states that Cash, Kiltz, and Shoup's claim that the basic (unhashed) Diffie-Hellman NIKE scheme is secure under the Strong Diffie-Hellman assumption is problematic, because the security reduction needs two Decisional Diffie-Hellman (DDH) oracles (one per party sharing the challenged key) while the Strong DH assumption supplies only one; this paper's own factoring-based construction is offered as a way to avoid needing a gap assumption to patch that gap, in a different group (signed quadratic residues) than the CKS-analyzed scheme. The paper's own concluding section states three explicit open problems it does not solve: constructing a pairing-free NIKE scheme secure in the standard model (called particularly challenging in the RSA/factoring setting, for the same public-key-validity-checking reason the paper's own standard-model factoring scheme falls short of the full plain-setting definition); constructing an identity-based NIKE scheme provably secure in the standard model, beyond the Random-Oracle-Model schemes cited from prior work, noting that starting from an Identity-Based Encryption (IBE) scheme is not straightforwardly reversible because IBE private-key generation is typically randomized; and defining a security model and constructing a three-party NIKE scheme based on the Joux protocol, for which the paper states no security model or adversarially-robust construction currently exists. The paper states directly that the unhashed basic Diffie-Hellman NIKE scheme (shared key g^(xy) with no hash of identities) is completely insecure in the paper's own default (dishonest key registration) setting even though it is provably secure under the Decisional Diffie-Hellman assumption in the weaker honest-key-registration (HKR) setting, giving the explicit attack: an adversary registers an honest party Alice's own public key g^x as if it were the adversary's key, then queries for the shared key between itself and another honest party Bob, immediately obtaining Alice and Bob's actual shared key g^(xy) — a homomorphic-key attack the paper states also applies to Bernstein's earlier NIKE scheme.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Achieving the paper's default (plain, dishonest-key-registration) security model requires no assumption whatsoever about the Certificate Authority's registration checks — no proof of possession or knowledge of the private key is assumed — which the paper states is deliberately a stronger, more realistic assumption than models that assume such checks; a system layering identity binding or other guarantees on top of a NIKE scheme proved secure only in the weaker honest-key-registration (HKR) setting must independently add its own registration-time validity checking, or inherits the full-break homomorphic-key attack the paper demonstrates against the unhashed Diffie-Hellman scheme in the plain setting. The NIKE-to-KEM (and onward to public-key encryption) conversion requires a strongly one-time-secure signature scheme as a separate component and requires that scheme's verification key be bound into every ciphertext; the resulting KEM's IND-CCA security proof works specifically by having the reduction respond to a decapsulation query with a NIKE corrupt-reveal query, so the security of the composed system is bounded by, and cannot exceed, the security of the underlying CKS-light NIKE scheme against corrupt-reveal queries. The paper's pairing-based standard-model NIKE construction requires every public key submitted by any party (honest or adversarial) to satisfy a publicly checkable well-formedness condition, verified by two bilinear-pairing evaluations at each SharedKey computation — any system deploying this construction must perform that check at share-computation time, not merely at registration time, since the model allows an adversary to submit malformed keys directly rather than only through a registration step. NIKE provides no forward-secrecy property by its nature: the paper states explicitly that because the primitive is non-interactive (no fresh per-session randomness is exchanged), one cannot hope to obtain any forward-security guarantee from NIKE alone, so any system requiring forward secrecy must obtain it from a different, session-fresh mechanism composed around the NIKE-derived shared key, not from NIKE itself.

### Contradicts
This paper contradicts a specific security claim made in prior work within the same technical line: it states that Cash, Kiltz, and Shoup's claim that the basic (unhashed) Diffie-Hellman NIKE scheme is secure under the Strong Diffie-Hellman assumption is "problematic," because the stated reduction needs two DDH oracles while the Strong DH assumption supplies only one — the paper identifies this as a specific proof gap in a named prior result, not a report of a different measured outcome. No contradiction found against any other paper in this corpus.

### References worth retrieving
- Cash, Kiltz, Shoup. "The Twin Diffie-Hellman Problem and Applications" (source of the CKS security model for NIKE). — foundational (the paper this work's entire model taxonomy starts from and extends; the paper flags a specific proof problem in this source's Strong-DH security claim)
- Bernstein. [Elliptic-curve NIKE scheme and sketch of a NIKE security model]. — foundational (earliest efficient concrete NIKE construction; the paper shows the same homomorphic-key attack that breaks the unhashed Diffie-Hellman scheme in the plain setting also applies to Bernstein's scheme)
- Dupont, Enge. [ID-based NIKE security model, analysis of the Sakai-Ohgishi-Kasahara scheme]. — foundational (identity-based NIKE line; source of one of the two ROM schemes this paper's stated open problem — a standard-model ID-based NIKE — aims to move beyond)
- Paterson, Srinivasan. [ID-based NIKE security model refinement, connections to Identity-Based Encryption]. — foundational (the other ROM ID-based NIKE analysis the paper's open problem targets; also the source of the ID-based NIKE-to-IBE connection this paper's own NIKE-to-PKE result parallels)
- Gennaro, [et al.] [Hierarchical ID-based NIKE protocols]. — foundational (hierarchical extension of the ID-based NIKE line)
- Boyen, Mei, Waters. "Direct chosen ciphertext security from identity-based techniques." ACM CCS 2005. — competing (the KEM this paper's own derived KEM construction is directly compared against for performance)
- Hofheinz, Kiltz. "The group of signed quadratic residues and applications." CRYPTO 2009. — foundational (source of the algebraic group and proof techniques this paper's own factoring-based ROM construction, NIKE_fac, builds on)
- Boyd, Cliff, Nieto, Paterson. "One-round key exchange in the standard model." — foundational (the paper's stated route from its NIKE-to-PKE conversion to a one-round Authenticated Key Exchange protocol secure in the standard model)
- Cremers, Feltz [or the general interactive-AKE model line the paper positions NIKE's definitions against] — foundational (the paper explicitly contrasts NIKE-specific definitions with heavier interactive-AKE security models, e.g. Canetti-Krawczyk and Bellare-Rogaway style models cited in its related work)
