## [FRIEDMAN-JEMS-01] The Social Cost of Cheap Pseudonyms

**Citation:** Eric J. Friedman, Paul Resnick. "The Social Cost of Cheap Pseudonyms." Journal of Economics & Management Strategy, 2001. DOI 10.1162/105864001300122476.
**Retrieved:** full text
**Source URL:** https://sites.google.com/site/econfriedman/cheap-pseudonyms
**Domain:** F

### What it does
The paper proves that in a system where identity changes are free, no equilibrium strategy for a repeated cooperation game sustains substantially more cooperation than a strategy that distrusts every newcomer, once a small non-vanishing rate of mistaken or malicious defection exists. It models the game as an infinite sequence of periods in which M active players are matched uniformly at random into pairs to play a prisoner's dilemma; a fraction alpha of players exit at the end of each period and are replaced by new entrants; every player observes the complete public history of past pairings and actions before choosing an action; and any player may discard its identifier and re-enter as an indistinguishable newcomer at zero cost. The paper compares four strategy classes: a localized punishment strategy usable only when identities are fixed, a public grim trigger strategy that punishes the whole population after any single defection, a public forgiving trigger strategy that punishes for a finite number of periods, and a paying-your-dues (PYD) strategy in which an entrant unconditionally cooperates while a compliant veteran defects against the entrant with a computed probability. It then defines two further mechanisms outside the base game: a monetary entry fee paid on each identity change, and a once-in-a-lifetime identifier issued through a blind-signature protocol with a trusted intermediary, which lets a player commit to non-persistent identity without revealing it to anyone, including the intermediary.

### Measured results
The paper reports no simulation or empirical data; every result below is a proven bound on the equilibrium payoff function V(s), the average per-player, per-period expected payoff under strategy vector s, under the stated parameter conditions.

| Result | Conditions (from the paper's propositions) |
|---|---|
| Full cooperation is sustainable, V(LPS) = 1 | Identities fixed (cannot be changed); exit rate alpha <= 1/2; localized punishment strategy (LPS): cooperate with a newcomer or a veteran who complied last period, defect against a veteran who deviated last period |
| Full cooperation is sustainable with free identity changes, V(PGTS) = 1 | Free identity changes allowed; alpha <= 1/2; no trembles or malicious players (probability of error epsilon = 0); public grim trigger strategy (PGTS): defect forever once any defection has ever occurred |
| PGTS collapses to zero cooperation, V(PGTS) = 0 | Free identity changes; any epsilon > 0 (trembles or malicious players present) |
| Fixed-identity cooperation is near-total, V(LPS) >= 1 - 2*epsilon | alpha < 0.3, M > 1, epsilon < 0.1; player identifiers cannot change |
| Paying-your-dues equilibrium payoff, V(PYD) = 1 - alpha/(2-alpha) - O(epsilon) - O(1/M) | alpha < 0.3, epsilon < 0.1, M > 11, and the computed dues-probability q-hat(alpha, epsilon, M) <= 1 (automatically satisfied when alpha < 0.24 or epsilon < 0.05) |
| Stable value (population M to infinity, then epsilon to 0) lower bound, SV >= 1 - alpha/(2-alpha) | Free identity changes; impersistent identities; PYD strategy |
| No equilibrium exceeds the PYD stable value | alpha < 0.3; a threshold beta > 0 exists such that for any target value v > 1 - alpha/(2-alpha) - beta, there is an epsilon-bar such that for all epsilon < epsilon-bar and M > beta/epsilon, no equilibrium reaches v (Proposition 3) |
| Once-in-a-lifetime identifiers restore full cooperation even with heterogeneous player payoffs, SV = 1 | Trusted (or blind-signature-mediated) intermediary issues at most one committed identifier per player per arena; LPS extended to treat regular (non-committed) identifiers as untrustworthy |

At alpha near zero, the PYD equilibrium's per-player net loss (relative to full cooperation) is between 0.5 and 1 unnormalized utility unit, computed from the payoff matrix in which mutual cooperation pays 1 and mutual defection pays 0 to each player.

### Parameters
- alpha: fraction of the M active players who exit (and are replaced by entrants) at the end of each period; propositions require alpha < 0.3, and full cooperation under fixed or free identifiers with epsilon = 0 further requires alpha <= 1/2.
- M: number of active players per period; propositions require M > 1 (Proposition 1), M > 11 (Proposition 2), and M > beta/epsilon for a threshold beta (Proposition 3, no numeric value for beta given).
- epsilon: probability a player trembles (plays the opposite of its intended action) or, equivalently, the fraction of malicious players; propositions require epsilon < 0.1; the paper takes the limit epsilon to 0 after M to infinity when defining the stable value SV.
- q-hat(alpha, epsilon, M): the PYD veteran's computed probability of defecting against a compliant entrant, given in closed form in the text; required to satisfy q-hat <= 1, automatically true for alpha < 0.24 or epsilon < 0.05.
- Entry fee F: no numeric value derived or recommended; the paper states only that F must be large enough to deter the wealthiest player type from deviating, which then excludes some lower-value players from participating, and that standard price-discrimination remedies do not apply to this setting.

### Stated limitations
The paper states its model does not determine the reliability of player-reported feedback (whether players report negative outcomes honestly), citing this as a separate, unaddressed problem beyond the scope of the analysis. It states that redistributing collected entry fees back to players breaks the model's assumption that player exit is exogenous, and that redistribution also fails when player expected lifetimes are heterogeneous, since some players know in advance they will not remain long enough to recoup a fee. It states that when players have heterogeneous valuations of money or heterogeneous game payoffs, any fixed entry fee or PYD dues level that deters the highest-value deviator simultaneously excludes some lower-value players from participating, and that this exclusion problem has no standard solution in the entry-fee literature the authors are aware of. It states that the once-in-a-lifetime identifier protocol remains vulnerable to a timing attack in which the intermediary correlates the appearance of a new committed identifier in the game with the most recent identifier request, unless players hold an acquired identifier for a randomized delay before using it. It states that a person can still acquire multiple once-in-a-lifetime identifiers for one arena by using other people's true identities to request them, and that this is deterred, not prevented, once a robust cryptographic infrastructure exists.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The equilibrium results require a public history mechanism that every player can observe before acting: each pairing and each action taken must become common knowledge, either through direct interaction monitoring or explicit feedback collection: the model equates this to the environment's ability to publish a complete play history. The once-in-a-lifetime identifier mechanism requires a system-wide or per-arena intermediary — trusted not to reveal identity mappings, or cryptographically prevented from learning them via blind signatures — that enforces a strict one-committed-identifier-per-player-per-arena limit, and requires each player to hold a pre-existing private key tied to a true identity, usable to sign the blinded certificate request. The PYD mechanism requires an exogenous source of variability in the entrant count each period (the paper assumes each player independently loses its identifier with probability epsilon) to prevent strategies that condition punishment on the literal count of new identifiers appearing; a deploying system must supply this randomness or an equivalent.

### Contradicts
None found. No other paper in this batch measures or restates this paper's specific equilibrium bounds.

### References worth retrieving
- Ellison. "Cooperation in the prisoner's dilemma with anonymous random matching." Review of Economic Studies, 1994 — foundational (source of the public forgiving trigger strategy this paper builds on and reverses the limit order against)
- Kandori. "Social norms and community enforcement." Review of Economic Studies, 1992 — foundational (prior work on reputation transfer this paper contrasts with, since here reputation transfer is a player-controlled strategic variable)
- Milgrom, North, Weingast. "The role of institutions in the revival of trade: the law merchant, private judges, and the champaign fairs." Economics and Politics, 1990 — foundational (prior reputation-transfer model without player control)
- Tadelis. "What's in a name? Reputation as a tradeable asset." American Economic Review, 1999 — competing (models reputation as a tradeable name where skill, not performance, is the underlying signal)
- Watson. "Starting small and renegotiation." Journal of Economic Theory, 1999 — competing (alternative slow-start equilibrium approach to newcomer trust)
- Nowak, Sigmund. "A strategy of win-stay, lose-shift that outperforms tit-for-tat in the prisoner's dilemma game." Nature, 1993 — foundational (evolutionary behavior of the prisoner's dilemma under trembles, cited to motivate modeling errors)
- Kreps, Milgrom, Roberts, Wilson. "Rational cooperation in the finitely repeated prisoner's dilemma." Econometrica, 1982 — foundational (shows small numbers of atypical players can dramatically change the equilibrium set)

"A single tremble or malicious player causes mass defection in future periods"
"the intermediary never learns what identifier A is using"
"this remains an equilibrium with full participation and full cooperation, unlike entry fees"

## [FURUTANI-TIFS-23] Interpreting Graph-Based Sybil Detection Methods as Low-Pass Filtering

**Citation:** Satoshi Furutani, Toshiki Shibahara, Mitsuaki Akiyama, Masaki Aida. "Interpreting Graph-Based Sybil Detection Methods as Low-Pass Filtering." IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security, 2023. DOI 10.1109/TIFS.2023.3237364.
**Retrieved:** full text
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.10835
**Domain:** F

### What it does
The paper explains, in one shared mathematical structure, why five previously separate propagation-based Sybil-detection methods (CIA, SybilRank, SybilWalk, SybilSCAR, SybilBelief) succeed or fail on a given graph, by showing each one is a specific instance of graph signal low-pass filtering. A graph signal is a real number assigned to every node (here, a reputation score); a shift matrix (the paper considers the random-walk Laplacian, the augmented normalized Laplacian, the maximum-degree-normalized Laplacian, and the Bethe-Hessian matrix, each derived from the graph's adjacency and degree structure) defines a graph-specific Fourier basis via its eigenvectors, ordered from low frequency (eigenvectors correlated with large-scale community structure) to high frequency (eigenvectors correlated with local noise). Graph filtering multiplies the graph-Fourier-transformed input signal by a filter kernel function h(lambda) evaluated at each eigenvalue lambda, then transforms back; a low-pass kernel keeps low-frequency (community-informative) components and suppresses high-frequency (noisy) ones. The paper derives that each existing method corresponds to one specific (shift matrix, filter kernel) pair — for example, SybilRank uses the random-walk Laplacian with kernel (1-lambda)^Gamma, and CIA uses the same Laplacian with kernel (1-alpha)/(1-alpha(1-lambda)) — and that a method's detection accuracy is governed by two independently checkable properties: whether its filter kernel actually attenuates high-frequency eigenvalues relative to low ones, and whether its shift matrix's low-frequency eigenvectors are informative about the true community split (measured via spectral clustering's Normalized Mutual Information against ground truth). Using this framework, the authors introduce SybilHeat: a new method using the heat kernel h(lambda)=e^(-s*lambda) (a kernel with no lower bound on attenuation, so larger scaling parameter s removes more high-frequency content) paired with a regularized Laplacian shift matrix with regularization parameter tau set to the graph's average degree, which the paper shows analytically resembles the best-performing shift matrix (the Bethe-Hessian) in eigenvector informativeness. Computing the exact filtered output requires full eigendecomposition, costing O(N^3) for N nodes; the paper substitutes a Chebyshev polynomial approximation of order K, reducing the per-query cost to O(K|E|) where |E| is the edge count, making SybilHeat's output computable without eigendecomposition.

### Measured results
| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| Detection accuracy (AUC, probability a random Sybil ranks above a random benign node) of all six methods (CIA, SybilRank, SybilWalk, SybilSCAR-C, SybilBelief, SybilHeat) rises with community strength |c_in - c_out|/2 (the gap between within-community and between-community edge probability); SybilBelief achieves the best accuracy in the theoretically detectable region but drops sharply below the detectability threshold; SybilHeat performs second-best in the detectable region and best (tied with SybilWalk and SybilSCAR-C) in the undetectable region | Synthetic graphs: Stochastic Block Model (SBM) and Degree-Corrected SBM (DCSBM), N=1,000 nodes, k=2 communities, average degree d_ave=5, degree-heterogeneity parameter theta_i=1 for SBM and theta_i drawn from Uniform(3,7) for DCSBM, 10% of each community's nodes labeled, averaged over 100 runs; the vertical detectability threshold follows the conjectured bound (c_in-c_out)/2 > sqrt((c_in+c_out)/2) |
| Random-walk-based methods (CIA, SybilRank, SybilWalk) perform worse on DCSBM (degree-heterogeneous) graphs than on SBM graphs, attributed to lower community detectability of their shift matrices' low-frequency eigenvectors on degree-heterogeneous graphs | Same synthetic setup, spectral-clustering Normalized Mutual Information measured directly for each shift matrix as a separate diagnostic (not the detection AUC itself) |
| Under label noise (a fraction epsilon <= 0.5 of training labels flipped), SybilBelief is most robust, SybilHeat is second and nearly as robust as SybilBelief for epsilon <= 0.1, and CIA/SybilRank degrade fastest; SybilSCAR-C is less noise-robust than SybilWalk despite sharing the same filter kernel form (1/lambda), because SybilSCAR-C's shift matrix has low- and high-frequency eigenvalues clustered close together on sparse graphs | Same synthetic SBM/DCSBM setup, N=1,000, k=2, d_ave=5, c_out=0.5, theta_i=1 (SBM) or Uniform(3,7) (DCSBM), noise fraction epsilon swept, averaged over 100 runs |
| On real social networks, detection AUC at epsilon=0.0/0.1/0.2 noise: karate club (34 nodes/78 edges) 0.80/0.58/0.54 (CIA), 0.95/0.66/0.56 (SybilRank), 0.99/0.78/0.61 (SybilWalk), 0.97/0.72/0.55 (SybilSCAR-C), 1.0/0.93/0.53 (SybilBelief), 0.99/0.79/0.52 (SybilHeat); dolphin network (62/159) 0.97/0.78/0.71, 0.96/0.76/0.61, 1.0/0.97/0.77, 0.99/0.82/0.70, 1.0/0.97/0.78, 1.0/0.93/0.74; football (115/613) 0.78/0.69/0.55, 0.82/0.73/0.59, 0.88/0.77/0.59, 0.89/0.79/0.60, 0.91/0.82/0.61, 0.89/0.80/0.60; political blogs (1,224/33,430) 0.75/0.70/0.63, 0.97/0.96/0.92, 0.75/0.77/0.75, 0.97/0.93/0.84, 0.97/0.96/0.90, 0.98/0.98/0.96 | Four real graphs (largest connected component used in each case), half of the graph's communities designated benign region and half Sybil region, max(3, floor(0.1*N)) nodes labeled per side, SybilHeat parameter scale s=8, CIA restart alpha=0.85, SybilRank iterations Gamma=floor(log N), SybilSCAR residual prior theta=0.5; SybilSCAR-D excluded for unstable convergence |
| Detection performance for all methods degrades on sparse graphs relative to dense graphs of the same modularity, because fewer low-frequency eigenvalues remain isolated from the high-frequency bulk on sparse graphs | Synthetic SBM comparison: dense case N=3,000/k=2/d_ave=20/c_out=1 versus sparse case N=3,000/k=2/d_ave=5/c_out=1, spectral distributions of each shift matrix plotted directly (not detection AUC) |

### Parameters
- Filter kernel forms (Table I in the source): CIA h(lambda)=(1-alpha)/(1-alpha(1-lambda)) on the random-walk Laplacian L_rw; SybilRank h(lambda)=(1-lambda)^Gamma on L_rw; SybilWalk h(lambda)=1/lambda on the augmented normalized Laplacian L_aug; SybilSCAR-C h(lambda)=1/lambda on the maximum-degree-normalized Laplacian L_max; SybilSCAR-D h(lambda)=1/lambda on L_rw; SybilBelief an ideal low-pass filter on the Bethe-Hessian matrix H(r)
- SybilHeat filter kernel: heat kernel h(lambda)=e^(-s*lambda); scaling parameter s=8 used in the reported experiments (larger s attenuates high-frequency components more strongly, no stated tested range beyond this single value)
- SybilHeat shift matrix: regularized Laplacian L_tau = I - D_tau^(-1/2) A D_tau^(-1/2), regularization parameter tau set equal to the graph's average degree d_ave, following a cited prior recommendation
- Chebyshev polynomial approximation order K: used to reduce SybilHeat's per-computation cost from O(N^3) (full eigendecomposition) to O(K|E|); specific K value used in experiments not given in the retrieved text
- CIA restart parameter alpha: 0.85
- SybilRank iteration count Gamma: floor(log N)
- SybilSCAR residual prior probability theta: 0.5
- Synthetic-graph parameters: N=1,000, k=2 communities, average degree d_ave=5, theta_i=1 (SBM, homogeneous degree) or theta_i ~ Uniform(3,7) (DCSBM, heterogeneous degree); 10% of each community's nodes labeled; all synthetic results averaged over 100 runs
- Real-graph labeling: max(3, floor(0.1*N)) nodes labeled per side (benign/Sybil), using the largest connected component of each of 4 named benchmark community-detection graphs
- Community detectability threshold used as the reference boundary: (c_in - c_out)/2 > sqrt((c_in + c_out)/2) for SBM, per a cited conjecture; an analogous DCSBM-specific bound is used for the degree-heterogeneous case

### Stated limitations
The paper states its own theoretical framework builds directly on a prior work by the same authors that covered only two methods (CIA and SybilBelief) and could not explain performance differences arising from degree heterogeneity or modularity differences between graphs; this paper extends that coverage to five methods but the extension is still confined to methods expressible as a linear shift-matrix/filter-kernel pair, so it does not by construction cover nonlinear detection methods. The paper states explicitly that SybilHeat's own performance could likely be improved further by a different filter kernel or shift matrix than the ones chosen, meaning the paper itself does not claim SybilHeat as an optimum, only as one point satisfying the two derived necessary conditions. It states, citing existing studies, that learning node features and edge weights (as opposed to relying purely on labeled-node reputation propagation over an unweighted graph) would further improve detection performance, which SybilHeat as presented does not do. SybilSCAR-D is excluded from the empirical comparison because the paper found its convergence unstable, a limitation of that specific baseline method rather than of the paper's own proposed method. The theoretical detectability threshold used throughout (equation 3, and its DCSBM analogue) is stated as a conjecture from a cited prior paper, not a proof, though the paper's own empirical spectral-clustering results are consistent with it.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Every method covered by this framework, including SybilHeat, requires a set of pre-labeled benign nodes and, for methods other than SybilRank and CIA (which use only one label type each), a set of pre-labeled Sybil nodes as well; the paper's own experiments assume these labels arrive already correct except in the explicit noise-robustness tests, and do not address how a deployed system obtains them. The framework's guarantee that low-frequency eigenvectors carry community-structure information holds only in the graph regime the paper analyzes (SBM or DCSBM-generated, or empirically similar real graphs) above the stated detectability threshold; below that threshold the paper's own results show SybilBelief's accuracy collapses sharply, so a system relying on it needs an independent estimate of whether its deployment graph is in the detectable regime. SybilHeat's Chebyshev approximation requires the shift matrix (the regularized Laplacian) and the average degree d_ave to be computable from a graph the caller supplies in full, since tau is set from that same average-degree statistic; a system that cannot expose global degree statistics, or that only has a partial or streaming view of the graph, cannot use this scaling rule as given. The paper's stated computational-cost improvement (O(K|E|) versus O(N^3)) presumes the caller can perform repeated sparse matrix-vector multiplications against the full edge set, meaning a system embedding SybilHeat needs the entire graph materialized somewhere it can run that computation, not merely local per-node views.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus as of this batch regarding the paper's own reported figures. This paper reframes, rather than contradicts, GONG-TIFS-14 (SybilBelief) and its family: it derives that SybilBelief's strong noise robustness and strong detectable-region performance follow mathematically from its filter kernel being an ideal (hard cutoff) low-pass filter, while its collapse below the detectability threshold follows from the same kernel discarding all high-frequency information, including the marginal signal that remains available in weakly modular graphs; GONG-TIFS-14 itself did not identify this shared cause and reported the individual behaviors as separate empirical observations. This is a structural explanation building on GONG-TIFS-14's numbers, not a factual contradiction of them, since GONG-TIFS-14's own datasets and community-structure sweep are consistent with the pattern this paper attributes to filter-kernel shape.

## [GAO-CNS-18] SybilFuse: Combining Local Attributes with Global Structure to Perform Robust Sybil Detection
**Citation:** Peng Gao, Binghui Wang, Neil Zhenqiang Gong, Sanjeev R. Kulkarni, Kurt Thomas, Prateek Mittal. "SybilFuse: Combining Local Attributes with Global Structure to Perform Robust Sybil Detection." IEEE Conference on Communications and Network Security (CNS), 2018. DOI 10.1109/CNS.2018.8433147.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/pdf/1803.06772
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/pdf/1803.06772
**Domain:** F

### What it does
SybilFuse ranks nodes in a social network by likelihood of being a Sybil identity, combining two information sources that prior work used only separately: local per-node and per-edge attributes, and global graph structure. It trains local classifiers on node- and edge-level features to produce local trust scores, then propagates those scores through the graph using a weighted variant of two established structure-propagation mechanisms — random walk and loopy belief propagation (LBP, an iterative message-passing inference procedure on graphical models that can produce approximate marginal probabilities even when the graph contains cycles). Because the propagation weights come from the trained local classifier's confidence rather than being fixed a priori, the method is designed to remain effective when the graph-structural assumptions ("strong trust network," "fast-mixing honest region") that prior structure-only defenses require do not hold.

Mechanism: (1) local trust score computation — extract discriminative node features from available account attributes (in the paper's own Twitter evaluation, since only structural data was accessible, three purely structural proxy features were used: the fraction of a node's incoming follow requests it accepts, the fraction of its outgoing follow requests that get accepted, and its local clustering coefficient), train a Support Vector Machine (SVM) classifier with a Radial Basis Function (RBF) kernel on a small labeled sample, and output the classifier's probabilistic confidence as each node's local trust score; edge trust scores use a default constant (0.9 in the paper's experiments) to model homophily (the tendency of connected accounts to resemble each other) when edge-level features are not separately extractable from the available data. (2) weighted score propagation — feed the local scores as either a weighted random walk (SF-RW) or a weighted loopy belief propagation pass (SF-LBP) over the full graph, so a node's final score integrates its own local signal with the local signals of everything structurally connected to it. (3) output — either threshold the final scores (a threshold obtained via cross-validation on training data) to produce a binary Sybil/benign label, or rank all nodes ascending by score so a human analyst reviews the most-suspicious accounts first.

### Measured results
| Experiment | Conditions | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Robustness to local-classifier error, synthetic network | Preferential-attachment-generated benign (1,000 nodes) and Sybil (500 nodes) regions, average degree 10 in each region, 1,000 attack edges, simulated local trust scores sampled in [0.1, 0.9] at controlled false-positive/false-negative rates (0.5 decision threshold), edge trust scores fixed at default 0.9 | With node trust scores: for FPR = FNR <= 0.3, both SF-RW and SF-LBP achieve >0.98 accuracy and Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC). With edge trust scores (1 benign + 1 Sybil trusted seed, node scores 0.9/0.1 for seeds, 0.5 default elsewhere): >0.92 accuracy and AUC under the same error bound. Performance improves as classifier error falls, as attack-edge count falls, and as Sybil-node count rises; SF-LBP consistently outperforms SF-RW across all tested settings |
| Labeled real-world Twitter network, moderate scale | 8,167 nodes, 54,146 edges after converting a directed follower network from [Yang et al., WWW 2012] to undirected by keeping only bidirectional edges; ground truth: 7,358 verified benign, 809 Sybil nodes; SVM trained on 50 benign + 50 Sybil randomly sampled nodes; edge scores default 0.9 | Sybil nodes emit 40,010 attack edges total (49.5 per Sybil on average); 53.4% of Sybils are isolated (connect only to benign nodes), emitting 37.0% of attack edges; 41.2% of Sybils form one largest connected component (42.8% of attack edges); 5.4% form small connected groups (20.2% of attack edges); 5,546 benign nodes (75.4% of all benign nodes) are "victims" (benign nodes directly connected to a Sybil) |
| Sybil-ranking performance, same 8,167-node network | Compared against SVM alone, SybilRank (SR), CIA, SybilBelief (SB), SybilSCAR (SS), Integro (INT), Integro with a hypothetical perfect victim predictor (INT-PF), four ensemble combinations, and random guessing (RG); ranking evaluated as fraction of true Sybils among the top-K ranked nodes | SF-RW's average fraction-of-Sybils improvement over SR, CIA, INT is 44.8, 16.2, 54.3 percentage points respectively. SF-LBP's average improvement over RG, SVM, SR, CIA, INT, SB, SS is 85.7, 57.5, 85.9, 57.4, 95.5, 36.5, 13.4 percentage points respectively; SF-LBP achieves >98% Sybil coverage up to the top 400 ranked nodes. INT's victim predictor achieved 18.3% precision, 19.6% recall on this network, and INT-PF (perfect victim prediction) performed only slightly better than random guessing, because Integro's edge-downweighting formula suppresses score propagation through victims, and 75.4% of benign nodes here are victims |
| Composition of top-500 ranked nodes by Sybil type | Same network; Sybils categorized as isolated, in the largest connected component (LCC), or in other small connected groups | SVM ranks isolated Sybils best (74.6% of all Sybils it surfaces are isolated); global structure-based methods rank LCC Sybils best (71.2% SR, 66.4% CIA, 62.4% SB, 71.6% SS of surfaced Sybils are LCC members); SF-LBP performs best at ranking both isolated and LCC Sybils simultaneously |
| Large-scale labeled Twitter network | 21,297,772 nodes, 265,025,545 edges after undirected conversion, from a Twitter follower-network snapshot [Kwak et al., WWW 2010]; ground truth obtained by re-crawling every account via Twitter's API: 145,156 (0.7%) suspended (labeled Sybil), 1,911,482 (9.0%) deleted (excluded, status unknown), remainder active (labeled benign); local-score SVM trained on 3,000 benign + 3,000 Sybil sampled nodes; same three structural features as the smaller network | Network modularity of the benign/Sybil partition: 0.0042 (modularity >0.3 is the threshold Clauset et al. state indicates real community structure, so this partition is not a detectable community by that standard); 77,917 connected components in the Sybil region, 50% of Sybils isolated, 45% forming the largest connected component, remainder in small (<20-node) groups; the largest-connected-component-plus-benign partition has modularity only 0.0046; 18,414,469 total attack edges, averaging 127 attacked benign nodes per Sybil; 90% of attack edges concentrate on 3% of benign nodes (hypothesized to be celebrity accounts that follow back indiscriminately) |
| AUC on the large-scale Twitter network | Same 21M-node network, same compared methods | SR 0.57, CIA 0.80, INT 0.48, INT-PF 0.54, SB 0.74, SS 0.74, SF-RW 0.81, SF-LBP 0.85 |
| Sybil-ranking fraction on the large-scale Twitter network, top 1K nodes | Same network | SF-LBP's improvement over SR, CIA, INT, INT-PF, SB, SS: 54.8, 46.5, 55.1, 55.1, 55.1, 53.9 percentage points respectively (one reported figure of 55.1% appears against three different baselines) |
| Ground-truth check against Twitter's own suspension policy | Manual review of the top-100 nodes ranked by SF-LBP on the large-scale network | 71 were already suspended by Twitter; of the 29 still-active accounts, 24 (82.8% of the 29) showed spam/low-quality-profile characteristics consistent with being Sybil but had evaded Twitter's own detection, 3 were judged genuinely benign, 2 were inconclusive due to protected account settings |

The paper's own robustness experiment (synthetic network) does not compute an accuracy figure for SF-RW specifically, stating that random-walk-based final scores are "typically very low" in absolute terms, making a fixed threshold unreliable; only AUC is reported for SF-RW in that experiment.

### Parameters
| Parameter | Value used | Range/notes |
|---|---|---|
| Basic synthetic network size (robustness experiment) | 1,000 benign, 500 Sybil nodes, average degree 10 in each region, 1,000 attack edges | held as the "basic setup" while one factor was varied at a time |
| Local classifier error rate (FPR = FNR), synthetic robustness experiment | swept 0 to 0.4 | 0-0.4 |
| Edge trust score default | 0.9 | fixed across all experiments; used to "model homophily" wherever edge features could not be extracted |
| Node trust score for trusted seeds (edge-score experiments) | 0.9 (benign seed), 0.1 (Sybil seed), 0.5 (default, all other nodes) | one benign + one Sybil seed sampled per run |
| SVM kernel | RBF, via LIBSVM | fixed |
| Training-set size, moderate Twitter network | 50 benign + 50 Sybil nodes, randomly sampled | fixed |
| Training-set size, large-scale Twitter network | 3,000 benign + 3,000 Sybil nodes, randomly sampled | fixed |
| Victim-predictor training set (Integro comparison) | 50 victims + 50 non-victims, Random Forest | fixed |
| Modularity threshold for "significant community structure" (cited from Clauset et al.) | 0.3 | used as an external reference point, not tuned |

### Stated limitations
Existing structure-only Sybil defenses that SybilFuse compares against are stated by the authors to require assumptions the large-scale Twitter measurement directly shows are violated: a "strong trust network" (limited attack-edge count) and, for two of them, a fast-mixing benign region implying a well-connected giant community. The paper's own modularity measurement (0.0042, rising to only 0.0046 even restricted to the largest Sybil connected component) is presented as direct evidence the benign and Sybil regions on this real Twitter graph cannot be treated as separable communities, which the authors state is why prior structure-only methods perform poorly there. Integro's victim-prediction approach is stated to degrade toward random-guess performance even under a hypothetical perfect victim predictor once the true victim fraction is large (75.4% here), because its edge-downweighting formula then suppresses propagation broadly rather than selectively. The authors state that a strategic adversary aware of SybilFuse's specific local features could evade the local classifier by mimicking benign local statistics, but argue (without a corresponding experiment) that doing so requires denser Sybil-to-Sybil connectivity that then becomes more detectable by the structure-propagation stage; they state periodic retraining of local classifiers is advisable to track evolving attack behavior, without measuring an optimal retraining interval. Ground truth is bounded by Twitter's own detection policy: nodes not suspended by Twitter are labeled benign by default, and the authors' own manual audit of the top-ranked-but-still-active accounts found 82.8% of a 29-account sample showed Sybil-like characteristics, meaning the paper's own accuracy figures against this ground truth likely undercount true Sybil detection since some labeled "benign" nodes are actually undetected Sybils. Deleted accounts (9.0% of the large network) were excluded from training and evaluation because the authors could not determine whether deletion was user- or platform-initiated. The paper cites (Liu et al., ACM CCS 2015) that gradual movement of attack edges over time defeats seed-propagation-based defenses like SybilInfer and SybilRank under a churn attack requiring the attacker to know the trusted seed locations and for those locations to remain stable over an attack window; the authors argue but do not experimentally demonstrate that SybilFuse resists this because it does not propagate exclusively from fixed trusted seeds.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Requires a source of local, per-node (and ideally per-edge) attribute data sufficient to train a supervised classifier; when such attributes are unavailable, as in the paper's own Twitter evaluations, the method falls back to purely structural proxy features (accepted-request ratios, clustering coefficient) and a constant default for edge scores, which is a degraded configuration of the method rather than its intended input. Requires a labeled training sample of both benign and Sybil nodes (50+50 or 3,000+3,000 in the paper's experiments) obtained from some ground-truth source external to the algorithm itself — the paper's own ground truth comes from Twitter's platform-level suspension decisions, an external, centrally-operated classifier the paper's method is itself layered on top of. Requires the ability to periodically re-run and retrain, since the authors' own discussion states resistance to both social churn and strategic feature-mimicking depends on the system administrator refreshing trusted seeds or retraining classifiers on a schedule the paper does not specify. Places no requirement on graph fast-mixing or on a bounded count of attack edges, unlike the structure-only defenses (SR, SB, SS) it compares against — this is the paper's central claimed structural advantage, evidenced by its performance holding up on a network the authors show fails the fast-mixing and strong-trust-network assumptions those other methods require.

### Contradicts
The target-registry's description of this paper (used to select it for retrieval) states it was evaluated "on a Tuenti dataset" — the retrieved full text contains no mention of Tuenti anywhere; its two labeled evaluation networks are both derived from Twitter data (an 8,167-node network built from Yang et al.'s WWW 2012 spammer-network crawl, and a 21-million-node network built from Kwak et al.'s WWW 2010 Twitter crawl). This is a mismatch between the registry's prior description and the paper's actual content, not a mismatch of the retrieved file's identity (title and authors both match the registry entry exactly).

Beyond that, none found among other entries in this corpus. This paper's own re-implementation-free citation of prior methods' reported assumptions (strong trust network, fast mixing) is consistent with, not contradictory to, WEI-INFOCOM-12's explicit statement of the same two assumptions for SybilDefender.

## [GHOSH-HOTPETS-14] A TorPath to TorCoin: Proof-of-Bandwidth Altcoins for Compensating Relays
**Citation:** Mainak Ghosh, Miles Richardson, Bryan Ford, Rob Jansen. "A TorPath to TorCoin: Proof-of-Bandwidth Altcoins for Compensating Relays." Workshop on Hot Topics in Privacy Enhancing Technologies (HotPETs), 2014.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://dedis.cs.yale.edu/dissent/papers/hotpets14-torpath.pdf
**Source URL:** https://dedis.cs.yale.edu/dissent/papers/hotpets14-torpath.pdf
**Domain:** I

### What it does
TorPath lets the participants of one Tor (The Onion Router, an anonymity network that routes traffic through a multi-relay circuit so no single relay learns both a client's identity and its destination) circuit jointly generate cryptographic proof of how much end-to-end goodput (successfully delivered payload throughput) that specific circuit carried, without any centralized bandwidth authority, so that proof can back the minting of a companion currency (TorCoin) proportional to measured transfer rather than to a self-report. The construction has two layers. TorPath first replaces Tor's directory servers with a decentralized group of assignment servers that assemble a circuit (one client plus an entry, middle, and exit relay) for each client through a three-stage protocol: in Group Initialization, clients and relays each submit a temporary public key onion-encrypted (successively encrypted in layers, one per assignment server, so no single server can read the innermost content alone) under all assignment servers in the forming consensus group; in Verifiable Shuffle, the consensus group jointly and verifiably permutes each column of the resulting key matrix using the Neff shuffle (a shuffle whose correctness -- that the output is a permutation of the input without revealing the permutation -- any observer can verify), so each output row becomes one anonymous circuit's four temporary keys with no single participant learning which real identity holds which key; in Path Lookup, each participant learns only the IP address of its immediate circuit neighbor by a second onion-encrypted, shuffled exchange, so a client learns only its entry relay and each relay learns only its adjacent circuit member. Each assigned circuit receives a Circuit Identifier formed from the hash of the shuffle matrix and the circuit's row index. TorCoin then runs a proof-of-bandwidth protocol on top of an assigned circuit: every m Tor packets, each of the four circuit participants commits to a fresh temporary hash value, the values accumulate into a shared blob as they pass from client to exit relay and back, and once the blob is fully formed and signed by all four participants using their circuit-specific temporary keys, the client checks whether a hash of the assembled blob has enough low-order zero bits to count as a mined coin (a Bitcoin-style proof-of-work check, applied to a value that could only have been assembled by all four participants having actually forwarded traffic to each other, rather than to arbitrary computation); because each of the four contributions is revealed only after all parties have committed to their own hash first, no strict subset of the four participants can reconstruct the blob on their own to mint coins without the others' cooperation. A valid coin's sequence number must be exactly one more than the last coin recorded from that circuit's identifier on the blockchain (Bitcoin's distributed, append-only transaction ledger, reused here to prevent a coin from that circuit being claimed twice), and is capped by a fixed, publicly known per-circuit coin limit. The mined coin is split with one third of its value paid to each of the three relays via the standard Bitcoin transfer protocol.

### Measured results
| Measurement | Conditions |
|---|---|
| Per-round TorCoin protocol packet overhead: 1,752 bytes total, broken into a first client-to-entry packet of 34 bytes, entry-to-middle of 66 bytes, middle-to-exit of 98 bytes, exit-to-middle return of 324 bytes, middle-to-entry return of 518 bytes, and entry-to-client return of 712 bytes | Measured by simulating message passing through a set of relays using the Python Twisted framework, with keys, hashes, and signatures assumed uniformly 32 bytes each; described by the authors as "Preliminary Results," with no stated relay count, run count, or real-network deployment. |
| TorCoin protocol overhead as a fraction of Tor traffic: approximately 5% when the packet-count interval m is 10 or more | Derived from the 1,752-byte per-round overhead against a standard Tor cell size of 514 bytes, so one round trip of 6 cells (entry-middle-exit and back) carries 514 x 6 = 3,084 bytes of base traffic; this is an arithmetic derivation from the simulated overhead figure and the fixed Tor cell size, not an independently measured network run. |

### Parameters
- m (the number of Tor packets between successive rounds of TorCoin proof-of-bandwidth generation): the paper states m greater than or equal to 10 yields roughly 5% overhead, and states m can be tuned in further experimentation to trade transmission efficiency against incentive granularity for relay operators; no other specific value is tested or recommended.
- Consensus-group quorum size: given only as an illustrative example ("if there are 10 assignment servers in the network, we might require at least 6 of them to participate"), not a value the paper adopts as a recommendation.
- Consensus-group size n (number of clients gathered before a shuffle proceeds): stated as configurable, trading a larger anonymity set against longer circuit-assignment wait time; no numeric value given or tested.
- Per-circuit TorCoin mint limit (the cap on coins any one assigned circuit may mine): stated to exist and to be recorded in the blockchain for verification, with no numeric value given.
- Assumed key/hash/signature length in the overhead measurement: 32 bytes.
- Standard Tor cell size used in the overhead derivation: 514 bytes.

### Stated limitations
The paper states the Neff shuffle used for circuit assignment is complex and requires several rounds of communication among assignment servers, and states this cost is tolerated only under the unverified expectation that assignment servers will number fewer than 10 and be well-provisioned; the paper offers a workaround (using conventional Tor circuits immediately, then transitioning to TorCoin circuits once assigned) for latency-sensitive users rather than a measured latency figure. TorPath's circuit-assignment mechanism is stated to be incompatible with the deployed Tor network because it requires route assignment and access control that ordinary Tor relays and directory servers do not implement, though the authors state a single physical machine could run both a standard Tor relay and a TorPath/TorCoin service simultaneously. The Neff shuffle applied per-position can assign the same physical relay to more than one position (for example, both entry and middle) on the same circuit; the authors state this should be rare with a reasonable number of participating relays and consider it no worse than Tor's existing risk of one operator controlling multiple relays on a circuit by chance, and explicitly defer building any detection mechanism for it to future work. The paper explicitly states that Bitcoin's transaction layer offers only limited payment anonymity and that this limitation is inherited unmodified by TorCoin, presenting Zerocoin, Mixcoin, and CoinShuffle only as candidate, unimplemented fixes to that separate problem. The design as specified always assigns three fresh relays per circuit rather than persisting a stable entry relay across circuits (Tor's actual practice, adopted for a different reason -- limiting a client's cumulative exposure to malicious entry relays over time); the authors sketch a persistent-entry-relay variant of the assignment matrix but state it comes at the cost of a higher chance of forming an all-colluding circuit, without giving a numeric bound on that increase.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Verifying that a claimed TorCoin corresponds to real bandwidth transfer requires a reader to hold the full public consensus log of shuffle matrices produced by assignment servers, since a Circuit Identifier is checked against that log and the four temporary public keys it names; a system without persistent access to that log cannot independently audit a coin. Assignment-server honesty is assumed only in majority: the adversary model states the design tolerates a minority of assignment servers being controlled by an adversary, with the rest merely honest-but-curious (they follow the protocol but may try to infer private information from what they see), and the anonymity and coin-integrity guarantees are stated to hold conditional on that majority assumption. The mechanism assumes that at most half of the temporary keys across the network belong to colluding participants, under which condition the paper computes that only 1/16 (1/2^4, since a circuit has four positions) of assigned circuits are fully colluding and able to mint coins for zero genuine bandwidth transfer; a higher colluding fraction was not analyzed by the paper and would raise this fraction. The mining check itself requires that the underlying transport reliably deliver each of the four onion-forwarded commit/reveal messages per round in order, since a message lost or reordered on the forward or return path prevents the blob from being validly formed and signed by all four participants. Anything reading TorCoin balances for a reward or reputation purpose downstream must treat coin possession as proof of goodput on one specific, now-identified circuit at mint time, not as a general, ongoing measure of a relay's capacity or honesty, since the mechanism produces no per-relay aggregate score, only per-circuit, per-round proofs.

### Contradicts
None found within this paper's own claims; the authors describe their own overhead figures explicitly as preliminary and simulated, not as a production measurement, so no later paper's field measurement of TorCoin overhead should be read as confirming or refuting a claim this paper does not make. No other entry in this batch reports a comparable bandwidth-backed incentive currency to compare numerically.

### References worth retrieving
- Nakamoto, "Bitcoin: A peer-to-peer electronic cash system," 2008 -- foundational (the base blockchain and proof-of-work construction TorCoin's mining and double-spend-prevention protocol adapts).
- Jansen, Johnson, Syverson, "LIRA: Lightweight Incentivized Routing for Anonymity," NDSS 2013 -- competing (a prior Tor incentive scheme this paper argues can partition the anonymity set by traffic speed and relies on a trusted central bank for coin assignment, both properties TorCoin is designed to avoid).
- Moore, Wacek, Sherr, "Exploring the potential benefits of expanded rate limiting in Tor: Slow and steady wins the race with Tortoise," ACSAC 2011 -- competing (a prior incentive scheme, Tortoise, this paper argues may compromise client anonymity by making traffic identifiable).
- Jansen, Hopper, Kim, "Recruiting new Tor relays with BRAIDS," CCS 2010 -- competing (a prior relay-recruitment incentive scheme cited among the unsatisfactory prior designs this paper responds to).
- Snader, Borisov, "EigenSpeed: secure peer-to-peer bandwidth evaluation," IPTPS 2009 -- competing (a peer-reported bandwidth measurement scheme this paper contrasts against for relying on self-reporting rather than proof of transfer).
- Neff, "A verifiable secret shuffle and its application to e-voting," CCS 2001 -- foundational (the Neff shuffle, the specific verifiable-shuffle algorithm TorPath uses to assign circuits).
- Jansen, Miller, Syverson, Ford, "From onions to shallots: Rewarding Tor relays with TEARS," HotPETs 2014 -- competing (a contemporaneous alternative Tor relay-reward scheme by an overlapping author set, cited by this paper for extended discussion of incentive-system requirements and tradeoffs).
- Miers, Garman, Green, Rubin, "Zerocoin: Anonymous distributed e-cash from Bitcoin," IEEE S&P 2013 -- competing (cited as a candidate, unimplemented fix for the Bitcoin transaction-anonymity limitation this paper inherits).
- Ruffing, Moreno-Sanchez, Kate, "CoinShuffle: Practical decentralized coin mixing for Bitcoin," HotPETs 2014 -- competing (cited as a second candidate, unimplemented fix for the same Bitcoin transaction-anonymity limitation).
- Karame, Androulaki, Capkun, "Two Bitcoins at the price of one? double-spending attacks on fast payments in Bitcoin," IACR ePrint 2012/248 -- attack (cited for the double-spend risk TorCoin's blockchain-based sequence-number check is designed to prevent).

## [GILBOA-EUROCRYPT-14] Distributed Point Functions and their Applications
**Citation:** Niv Gilboa, Yuval Ishai. "Distributed Point Functions and their Applications." EUROCRYPT, 2014. DOI: 10.1007/978-3-642-55220-5_35.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.iacr.org/archive/eurocrypt2014/84410279/84410279.pdf
**Source URL:** https://www.iacr.org/archive/eurocrypt2014/84410279/84410279.pdf
**Domain:** G

### What it does
A distributed point function (DPF) splits a point function P_{x,y} — the function that returns y at input x and returns the all-zero string everywhere else — into two keys k0 and k1, such that evaluating each key alone reveals nothing about x or y, and evaluating both keys at any input x' and taking the exclusive-or (XOR) of the two results reproduces P_{x,y}(x'). A key generation algorithm Gen(x, y) produces the pair (k0, k1); an evaluation algorithm Eval(k_b, x') returns one server's share of P_{x,y}(x').

The construction builds a binary tree of depth ceil(log|x|) over the domain of x. Each level of the tree replaces a random portion of the key with a pseudorandom generator (PRG) seed, compressing the key by close to a square root at each level, with the two parties' seeds correlated so that the two evaluation paths cancel to zero everywhere except at the single leaf corresponding to x. The recursion needs only a one-way function (which implies a PRG), not public-key cryptography.

Two-server computationally private information retrieval (PIR): a user who wants bit i of an n-bit database held identically by two non-colluding servers generates DPF keys for the point function that is 1 at index i and 0 elsewhere, sends one key to each server, and each server returns the XOR of its share function over every database bit; the user XORs the two one-bit answers to recover the target bit. The same construction gives two-server private keyword search (membership test against a word set) and non-interactive "PIR writing" (updating one entry of a database secret-shared between two servers without revealing which entry).

### Measured results
No experimental implementation is reported. All figures are derived analytically from the recursive construction.

| Quantity | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Key size (asymptotic bound) | roughly 8*kappa*\|x\|^(log_2 3) bits | kappa = PRG seed length, \|x\| = domain bit-length of the point function input, |y| = 1 |
| Key length, exact (recursion depth minimizing key size) | \|x\|=20: 1,298 bytes; \|x\|=40: 5,000 bytes; \|x\|=80: 18,906 bytes; \|x\|=160: 61,943 bytes | Table 1, |y| = 1, recursion depth chosen to minimize key size (depths 2, 4, 5, 6 respectively) |
| Key length, worst case (depth fixed at ceil(log\|x\|)) | \|x\|=20: 4,513 bytes; \|x\|=40: 20,003 bytes; \|x\|=80: 72,941 bytes; \|x\|=160: 241,256 bytes | Table 1, same |x| values, recursion depth fixed at Proposition 1's ceil(log\|x\|) rather than the depth minimizing key size |
| 2-server CPIR communication complexity | 2*m(b, log n, 1) + 2 bits total, where m is the maximum DPF key size for a domain of size n | n = database size in bits; single-bit answer per server (Theorem 2) |
| 2-server CPIR query complexity (using the DPF construction) | O(kappa * (log n)^(log_2 3)) | kappa = PRG seed length; answer complexity 1 bit per server (Corollary 2) |
| Server-side computational cost, naive | n * \|k_b\| pseudorandom bits | evaluating the DPF separately at every one of n domain points |
| Server-side computational cost, tree-optimized | fewer than n + 2*sqrt(n) pseudorandom bits | reusing the PRF tree so each internal node's children are computed once and shared across leaf evaluations |
| Private keyword search query length | O(kappa * nu * log_2 3) bits, answer length 1 bit per server | nu = keyword bit-length; two non-colluding servers, single communication round, no error probability (Theorem 3) |

### Parameters
- kappa: PRG seed length, set by the choice of one-way function; no default value stated, only its role in the key-size formula.
- Recursion depth l: either chosen to minimize key size (exact column of Table 1) or fixed at ceil(log2 |x|) (Proposition 1's bound); the paper reports both and states the fixed-depth bound is "somewhat pessimistic."
- |y|: output length of the point function; Table 1 and most theorems are given for |y| = 1 (binary answers), with the general case handled by an extension (Section on "a more efficient implementation is possible").

### Stated limitations
The paper proves a matching lower bound rather than stating an open engineering gap: any two-server PIR protocol with information-theoretic (not merely computational) secrecy and sublinear-size queries and short answers cannot exist, citing a linear lower bound from Chor, Goldreich, Kushilevitz, and Sudan (reference 8 in this paper's bibliography); this is why the DPF-based CPIR construction relies on a computational (one-way-function) assumption rather than achieving information-theoretic privacy. The paper also proves the converse direction, Theorem 5: any two-server CPIR protocol with sublinear query length and binary answers implies the existence of a one-way function, so the computational assumption cannot be removed.

The paper states, without giving a full proof, that a naive amortization technique is deferred to a "full version" for the case of evaluating a DPF once for every nonzero entry of a database (footnote, computational cost discussion). No implementation, benchmark, or wall-clock timing is reported anywhere in the text.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Two servers that do not collude with each other; the secrecy proof (Theorem 2, Definition 2) is stated for exactly two non-colluding servers holding an identical copy of the database, and the security argument fails if the same party controls both servers or observes both queries.

A one-way function must exist in the deployment's cryptographic setting; if it is only a standard (not exponentially hard) one-way function, the resulting DPF and CPIR scheme achieve standard (polynomial-time) security rather than the stronger exponential-hardness guarantee (Theorem 1).

Both servers must hold byte-identical copies of the database at query time, since the reconstruction algorithm M XORs the two servers' per-bit answers computed over the same n-entry database (Definition 2); a query answered against divergent copies does not reconstruct correctly.

The client must generate a fresh key pair per query (or reuse one for repeated identical queries, which the paper flags as the useful case for the single-bit-answer feature); nothing in the construction supports a third party regenerating a lost key pair.

### Contradicts
None found.

### References worth retrieving
- **Foundational:** B. Chor, O. Goldreich, E. Kushilevitz, M. Sudan, "Private Information Retrieval," Journal of the ACM 45(6), 1998 — the linear lower bound this paper's Theorem 5 relies on.
- **Foundational:** B. Chor, N. Gilboa, "Computationally Private Information Retrieval," STOC 1997 — the 2^O(sqrt(log n)) query-length protocol this paper improves on.
- **Competing:** C. Cachin, S. Micali, M. Stadler, "Computationally Private Information Retrieval with Polylogarithmic Communication," EUROCRYPT 1999 — an earlier polylogarithmic single-server CPIR under a different (Phi-hiding) assumption.
- **Competing:** E. Kushilevitz, R. Ostrovsky, "Replication is NOT Needed: SINGLE Database, Computationally-Private Information Retrieval," FOCS 1997 — single-server CPIR alternative avoiding the two-non-colluding-server requirement.
- **Competing:** C. Gentry, Z. Ramzan, "Single-Database Private Information Retrieval with Constant Communication Rate," ICALP 2005 — competing single-server construction with constant-rate communication.
- **Foundational:** M. Freedman, Y. Ishai, B. Pinkas, O. Reingold, "Keyword search and oblivious pseudorandom functions," TCC 2005 — prior keyword-search protocol this paper's Theorem 3 improves on.
- **Foundational:** R. Ostrovsky, V. Shoup, "Private information storage," STOC 1997 — the "PIR writing" problem this paper's construction also solves.
- **Foundational:** R. Ostrovsky, W. E. Skeith III, "Private Searching on Streaming Data," Journal of Cryptology 20(4), 2007 — the streaming model the keyword-search extension supports.

### Verbatim extracts
- "each of k0 and k1 hides x and y" (Abstract).
- "the length of each query is polylogarithmic in the database size n" (Abstract).
- "This analytical bound is somewhat pessimistic" (Section 1, on the 8*kappa*|x|^log_2(3) key-size formula).
- "computation of each server on a database of size n roughly corresponds to producing n pseudorandom bits" (Section 1).
- "a two-server CPIR protocol with query length o(n) and binary answers. Then a one-way function exists" (Theorem 5).

## [GOLD-ARXIV-23] G-Rank: Unsupervised Continuous Learn-to-Rank for Edge Devices in a P2P Network

**Citation:** Andrew Gold, Johan Pouwelse. "G-Rank: Unsupervised Continuous Learn-to-Rank for Edge Devices in a P2P Network." arXiv preprint, 2023. DOI 10.48550/ARXIV.2301.12530.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.12530
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.12530
**Domain:** K

### What it does
G-Rank ranks search results inside a peer-to-peer (P2P, no central server) network without any centrally trained model, using only records each peer already holds locally plus records received by gossip from other peers. Every peer keeps a clicklog: a local, append-only list where each row holds the querying peer's node ID, the query term, the ranked results returned for that query, and the item the peer clicked. When a peer issues a query, it first checks its own clicklog for the term; if the term has not been seen, it falls back to matching the term against local file metadata (title, artist, genre tag). If the term has been seen before, results are ranked by the number of clicks each candidate item has accumulated across all clicklog entries the peer holds (its own and gossiped-in ones), weighted by a per-peer-pair similarity score. Peers discover each other only through gossip: receiving a clicklog update from peer B exposes peer A to every node ID appearing in B's log, so the same message that carries ranking evidence also carries topology information. Gossip is pull-based and solicited: a peer sends a request message to one peer at a time and that peer replies with some or all of its clicklog; nodes cannot refuse an incoming request. New results ranked equal in score are additionally tie-broken so that items whose metadata matches the query term always outrank items that match only through clicklog click history with no metadata match, which is stated to blunt query-bombing (an adversary manufacturing spurious query-click pairs).

The similarity score between peer i and peer j, written S_i(n_j), is computed as (kappa_t + kappa_m^2) / kappa_u, where kappa_t is the count of query terms both peers have in their top-K query sets, kappa_m is the count of results both peers have clicked for shared queries, and kappa_u is the count of the union of clicked results between the two peers; the raw score is then normalized to [0,1] by dividing by the maximum score in the peer's list. Squaring kappa_m makes the score fall away faster than linearly as two peers' click behavior diverges, which the authors intend to speed re-clustering away from a peer whose behavior has started to diverge. An isolation constant F, tested at F=0 and F=1, sets a floor added to every similarity weight before it multiplies a candidate item's click count in the final ranking score R_i(Q) = sum over peers of (click_count_k * (S_i(n_j) + F)); at F=0 a peer with zero similarity to the querying peer contributes nothing, and at F=1 every gossiped-in clicklog entry contributes with equal minimum weight regardless of similarity.

### Measured results
All figures below come from one simulated network of 100 peers, initialized so each peer holds 10% of a 256-release Creative-Commons music catalog (approximately 26 items per peer) drawn from the PandaCD label, indexed by 39 unique genre tags used as the query-term vocabulary. Every experiment (baseline and each adversarial variant) was run twice, once at isolation constant F=0 and once at F=1. Adversarial simulations bootstrap 10 malicious peers (or, in the Epic Sybil case, 75 of the 100 peers) at simulation time step t=2500 (25% through the run) and trigger their attack at t=5000.

| Experiment | Condition | Measured outcome |
|---|---|---|
| Baseline (no adversary) | 100 peers, F=0 and F=1, no attackers | Per-peer distance to the globally optimal ranking (positional edit distance between a peer's local ranking and the ranking by global click count) drops sharply early in the run and approaches near-zero for effectively all peers and query terms. |
| Baseline (no adversary) | Same setup | Median fraction of queries for which the single globally most-clicked item for that term appears in a peer's top-ranked results grows slowly at first, then approaches 100% as gossip accumulates; the Epic Sybil Attack run is the only case in the paper where this fraction does not reach 100% by the end of the simulation. |
| Targeted Sybil Attack | 10 sybil peers, each issues 100 queries on one chosen term at attack time, always clicking the lowest-ranked result, then waits to be gossip-pulled | Rankings measurably deviate from optimality after the attack; peers at F=0 are affected more slowly than at F=1. |
| Clicklog Inflation Attack | 10 malicious peers, 1000 queries each (10x the Targeted Sybil count) at attack time, results chosen at random rather than always-lowest-ranked | Produces faster divergence from optimal rankings than the Targeted Sybil Attack, under otherwise identical peer count and network setup. |
| Epic Sybil Attack | 75 of 100 peers are adversarial (a network supermajority), each performing 100 queries choosing the lowest-ranked item, same bootstrap/attack timing as the Targeted Sybil Attack | Ranking quality degrades faster and further than any other tested condition; is the only condition in which the top-item-inclusion metric fails to reach 100% by simulation end. Post-attack rankings remain more accurate than at simulation start in every adversarial condition tested, including this one. |
| Push vs. Pull gossip | 10 malicious peers running the Targeted Sybil Attack, but malicious peers push unsolicited clicklog messages to up to 2 peers each while benign peers push to at most 1 peer, versus the default pull scheme where a peer requests from exactly 1 peer it chooses | Push-based dissemination produces faster convergence toward optimal rankings before the attack, and correspondingly faster and deeper divergence immediately after the attack, than the pull-based scheme used in the other experiments. |
| Gossip message size | All simulations, message size measured as clicklog data transferred per gossip exchange | Mean gossip message size grows quickly early in the run then its growth rate falls off as peers become mutually aware; message size is stated to rarely exceed 600 kB. Each clicklog row is stated to be approximately 600 bytes. |
| Isolation constant F | F=0 vs. F=1, all adversarial experiments | Setting F=0 (discount peers with zero measured similarity entirely) produces a smaller negative effect on rank-distance from adversarial clicklog entries than F=1 (weight every gossiped entry with at least the floor weight F), but neither setting prevents the network from converging toward a single degraded ranking under the Targeted Sybil or Clicklog Inflation attacks. |

The paper reports no wall-clock or bandwidth-per-second figures beyond the gossip message size above, and explicitly declines to report computation time because it depends on implementation language and each device's hardware.

### Parameters
Network size: 100 simulated peers, fixed across every experiment. Catalog: 256 music releases, 39 unique tag values used as the full query vocabulary. Initial per-peer library: 10% of the catalog (approximately 26 items), assigned uniformly at random. Bootstrap gossip at peer join: a randomly selected existing peer shares a randomly sampled subset of its own clicklog; each new peer starts with up to 44 entries (its own 39 initial query-click pairs plus up to 5 gossiped-in entries). Adversary count: 10 malicious peers in every adversarial experiment except Epic Sybil, which uses 75. Adversary bootstrap time: simulation tick t=2500 (25% through the run). Attack trigger time: t=5000. Targeted Sybil query volume per attacker: 100 queries on one chosen term, always clicking the lowest-ranked result. Clicklog Inflation query volume per attacker: 1000 queries, results chosen at random. Push vs. Pull fan-out: malicious peers push to up to 2 peers, benign peers push to at most 1. Isolation constant F: tested at 0 and 1 (no intermediate values reported). Gossip cadence: a hybrid scheme guaranteeing every peer receives at least one gossip update per simulation tick, combined with a per-peer probability p = 1/|N| of performing a query-then-gossip action at a given tick. Evaluation cadence: one evaluation round every 100 queries. Random noise injection into ranking: 50% of queries have two randomly selected result-list positions swapped, stated as a mechanism to avoid ranking plateaus (not varied as an experimental parameter; held fixed at 50% throughout).

### Stated limitations
The paper states that G-Rank does not correct for query misspellings or typos, though it states this could potentially be integrated. The click model used to generate simulated user behavior is described as simplified: simulated peers select the top-ranked item except when two items tie in score, in which case the lower item ID is chosen as a fixed tiebreaker; the authors cite this as a simplification relative to modeling real click noise. The paper states that a "global optimal ranking" used as the comparison baseline throughout the evaluation is only computable inside the simulation, where a global observer can aggregate all peers' state; the authors state explicitly that in a live deployed network this global optimum is not feasibly observable, so the reported distance-to-optimum figures are simulation-only quantities without a deployed-network analogue. The similarity-clustering mechanism (Section 3D) is stated to be a "fuzzy non-parametric" first version, and the authors state that more explicit self-clustering methods, such as outlier detection by distance from cluster centroids, are left to future work. The paper reports no measurement of computation time or CPU/energy overhead, stating this is highly dependent on implementation language and per-device hardware. The paper tests only two values of the isolation constant F (0 and 1), not a swept range. The dataset (256 releases, 39 tags) and network size (100 peers) are both small relative to a production P2P deployment; the paper draws conclusions from this single scale and does not report a scaling experiment across larger peer counts or catalogs.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Peer discovery in G-Rank is not supplied by any separate mechanism: a peer becomes aware of another peer's existence only by receiving a clicklog gossip message naming that peer's node ID, so the ranking mechanism and the topology-discovery mechanism share one message type and G-Rank cannot be deployed without some initial bootstrap peer supplying a first clicklog sample to a joining node. The pull-based pattern (a peer requests an update from one chosen peer, and that peer must reply) requires an underlying transport that supports one-to-one request/response messaging between peers that already know each other's addresses; it does not specify NAT traversal or peer-address resolution, leaving that to whatever transport layer carries the gossip messages. Every peer's clicklog and click history is transmitted in full or in part to any peer that requests it and is not stated to be access-controlled, encrypted for a specific recipient, or filtered by requester identity in the design tested here; a component supplying peer identity or access control would need to sit below this mechanism, since G-Rank has none of its own beyond the derived similarity score. Ranking quality depends on receiving enough distinct, honest clicklog entries per query term; a term with too few observed click events falls back to unranked or noisy metadata matching, so the mechanism requires either a warm network with substantial query history or an explicit cold-start supplement for the first queries on a new term. The mechanism assumes malicious peers can be pull-gossiped from and cannot be selectively excluded once discovered; any Sybil-resistance or peer-admission control the surrounding system supplies determines how many malicious node IDs can enter a given peer's known-peer list, which directly bounds the volume of poisoned clicklog data the ranking model can be forced to absorb.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus regarding G-Rank's own reported figures. HEGEDUS-ECMLPKDD-19 (reference [29] in this paper's own bibliography) independently compares gossip-based and federated decentralized training for a different task (matrix-factorization recommendation, not learn-to-rank) and is a useful adjacent data point on gossip-based decentralized learning convergence, but it does not measure G-Rank and no direct figure-for-figure conflict exists between the two papers in this corpus.

### References worth retrieving
- Ormándi, Hegedűs, Jelasity, "Gossip learning with linear models on fully distributed data," Concurrency and Computation: Practice and Experience 25.4, 2013 — foundational (origin of the gossip-based distributed model-training paradigm this paper builds on)
- Hegedűs, Danner, Jelasity, "Decentralized recommendation based on matrix factorization: A comparison of gossip and federated learning," ECML PKDD, 2020 — competing (already in this corpus as HEGEDUS-ECMLPKDD-19; direct gossip-vs-federated comparison on an adjacent recommendation task)
- Li, Mingyu, et al., "Bringing Decentralized Search to Decentralized Services," 15th USENIX OSDI, 2021 — competing (a decentralized search system to compare against)
- Lai, Ziliang, et al., "Decentralized search on decentralized web," arXiv:1809.00939, 2018 — competing
- Parreira, Josiane Xavier, et al., "Efficient and decentralized pagerank approximation in a peer-to-peer web search network," VLDB, 2006 — foundational (decentralized PageRank approximation, the closest prior ranking-without-a-central-index mechanism)
- Cheng, Alice, Eric Friedman, "Manipulability of PageRank under sybil strategies," 2006 — attack (analysis of Sybil manipulation of a ranking algorithm, the closest prior attack analysis to G-Rank's own Sybil-resistance claims)
- Fung, Clement, Chris JM Yoon, Ivan Beschastnikh, "The limitations of federated learning in sybil settings," RAID 2020 — attack (Sybil attacks specifically against federated learning, the competing decentralized-training paradigm this paper argues against)
- Aberer, Karl, et al., "An architecture for peer-to-peer information retrieval," SIGIR 2004 Workshop on P2P IR — foundational

### Verbatim extracts
"the network converges towards a single set of rankings that it appears unable to escape from"
"G-Rank is susceptible to sybil and spam attacks, though its relative resilience... is notable"
"the size of each gossip message rarely exceeds 600 kB"
"each clicklog row entry is approx. 600 bytes in size"
"nodes cannot refuse update requests and only send request messages to a single node"
"in a live network the global optimum may not be feasibly observable"
"push-based gossip schemes result in faster convergence at the expense of faster divergence"
