## [GUPTA-NSDI-04] Efficient Routing for Peer-to-Peer Overlays
**Citation:** Anjali Gupta, Barbara Liskov, Rodrigo Rodrigues. "Efficient Routing for Peer-to-Peer Overlays." Proceedings of the First USENIX/ACM Symposium on Networked Systems Design and Implementation (NSDI), 2004.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.usenix.org/legacy/event/nsdi04/tech/gupta/gupta.pdf
**Source URL:** https://www.usenix.org/legacy/event/nsdi04/tech/gupta/gupta.pdf
**Domain:** A

### What it does
The paper achieves lookup completion in one or two overlay hops, instead of the O(log n) hops typical structured overlays require, by having every node hold a routing table proportional in size to the total membership n (one hop) or a smaller fixed fraction of it (two hop). It builds both schemes on a 128-bit circular identifier ring, the same ring topology Chord uses, and relies on Chord's proven correctness for maintaining each node's immediate successor and predecessor.

One-hop scheme: the ring is divided into k contiguous slices; the slice leader is the ring successor of the numeric midpoint of the slice's identifier range. Each slice is further divided into units, each with its own unit leader chosen the same way. When a node detects a membership event (a neighbor joining or leaving), it reports the event to its slice leader. Slice leaders batch events for tbig seconds, then exchange batched event lists with every other slice leader, so bandwidth spreads unevenly across time rather than synchronizing on one instant. A slice leader forwards its slice's collected events to its unit leaders after a further twait-second batching delay; unit leaders piggyback that information on ordinary keep-alive messages exchanged with neighbors once per second, and each node relays the information one direction (predecessor-to-successor or the reverse) so no node retransmits data it has already received from the other direction, eliminating redundant propagation. A completed lookup, if it fails because the routing entry used is stale, is retried against the last valid successor pointer, so lookup correctness depends only on successor/predecessor pointers being correct, exactly as in Chord; the full membership table is an optimization on top of that correctness base, not a requirement for it.

Two-hop scheme: each slice leader additionally selects a group of l nodes from every other slice (group size chosen randomly, or by proximity so its members are spread across network locations) and forwards routing information about one such group to the corresponding remote slice leader, who disseminates it slice-wide the same way as one-hop event data. Each node thereby holds full routing information for its own slice and partial information (l candidate forwarding nodes) for every other slice, ordered by measured network distance. A lookup for a key outside the node's own slice is sent to the closest known forwarding node in the key's slice; that forwarding node holds full information about its own slice and completes the lookup in a second hop.

### Measured results

| Result | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Per-node upstream bandwidth, one-hop scheme, n=10^5 | Ordinary node 3.84 kbps; unit leader 7.36 kbps upstream / 3.84 kbps downstream; slice leader ~35 kbps upstream | Analytic model, m=10 bytes per event, v=20 bytes protocol overhead per message, k slices and u units-per-slice computed from the derived formulas |
| Per-node upstream bandwidth, one-hop scheme, n=10^6 | Ordinary node 38.4 kbps; unit leader 73.6 kbps upstream / 38.4 kbps downstream; slice leader ~350 kbps upstream | Same model and parameters, n=10^6 |
| Aggregate bandwidth overhead vs. theoretical zero-overhead broadcast | ~20% at n=10^5, dropping to ~2% at n=10^6 | Analytic model; overhead attributed entirely to per-message protocol overhead (v), since the scheme itself never sends redundant event information |
| Per-node bandwidth, two-hop scheme, n=10^8, 20,000 events/s, l=15 | Slice leader 1.6 Mbps upstream / 800 kbps downstream; unit leader 1 kbps upstream / 530 bps downstream; ordinary node 530 bps both directions | Analytic model, m=10 bytes, v=20 bytes, l=15 forwarding-group size per remote slice |
| Query failure rate, one-hop, coarse-grained simulation, varying inter-slice communication interval | Failure rate rises from about 0.2% (10 s interval) toward about 1% (100 s interval); at the analytically-derived interval of 23 s, observed failure rate is about 0.4%, lower than the 1% conservatively predicted analytically | 20,000-node system, mean join rate 2 nodes/s, mean leave rate 2 nodes/s, exponentially distributed node lifetime, query rate 1 query per node per second, uniform random new-node and query placement, synchronous round-based simulator, no slice-leader failures or packet loss modeled, 50 slices with 5 units per slice |
| Query failure rate, two-hop, same sweep | Lower than the one-hop scheme at every tested interval, and less sensitive to interval length than the one-hop scheme | Same 20,000-node coarse-grained simulation; bandwidth-optimal slice count of 7, 60 units per slice |
| Query failure rate, one-hop, steady state, fine-grained simulation | Settles at about 0.2% after roughly the first 10 minutes; after one re-routing attempt, about 0.01% (1 in 10^4 queries); 99.99% of queries satisfied within two or fewer hops | 2,000-node system simulated in p2psim, 10 slices, 5 units per slice, first 300 s all-nodes-join burst, then Gnutella-measured churn rate of 24 membership events/minute |
| Query failure recovery after a mass-crash event | Query success returns to a reasonable rate about 50 s after the crash; full stabilization to pre-crash failure rate takes about 350 s further, driven by slice-leader-failure recovery; recovery is sensitive to query rate — at 1 lookup per 10 s the system does not stabilize below 2% failure for the full 50,000 s simulation, while at 2 lookups per second it stabilizes within 300 s | 2,000-node p2psim simulation, 10 slices, 5 units per slice, 45% of nodes crashed simultaneously (randomly chosen) at simulated time t=8000 s |
| Aggregate system bandwidth around a mass-crash event | About 300 kbps before the crash, settling to about 180 kbps roughly 150 s after (lower steady state reflects reduced system size after the crash); bandwidth returns to expected levels faster than query-failure rate does, because stale routing-table entries are only corrected by being "re-discovered" through failed lookups | Same 2,000-node, 45%-crash p2psim experiment |
| Average spike bandwidth vs. crash size | Grows approximately linearly with the fraction of nodes crashed in the burst | Same p2psim setup, crash fraction swept from small values up to 45%, bandwidth averaged over the ~50 s settling window in each case |

### Parameters
- Identifier space: 128-bit circular ring (Chord-style).
- Hierarchy depth: 3 levels (slice, unit, node), stated as chosen to trade off propagation delay against per-node load at upper levels; no other depth was evaluated quantitatively.
- Derived slice count k and units-per-slice u: computed by minimizing slice-leader upstream bandwidth, k = sqrt(r·m·n / (4·v)), u = sqrt(4·v·n / (r·m·(ttot − twait − tdetect)^2)), where r is event rate, m=10 bytes (event description size), v=20 bytes (per-message protocol overhead).
- Event timers (chosen so tsmall = tbig for minimum bandwidth): tbig = 23 s (slice-leader-to-slice-leader batching interval, used in the one-hop-scheme bandwidth analysis) — a separate, later analysis for the fault-tolerance target of f=1% at n=10^8 and r=20,000 events/s derives tbig=40 s, twait=1 s, tsmall=30 s, leaving about 4 s for join/leave detection; unit size implied by that choice is 60 nodes, with 25 units fixed per slice, giving an expected slice size of 1,500 and k = n/1,500 slices.
- Query-failure target f: 1% (used to derive the timer values above); the coarse-grained simulation shows this target is conservative — the observed failure rate at the derived 23 s interval is 0.4%, not 1%.
- Two-hop forwarding-group size l: 15, chosen for a system of n=10^8.
- tdetect (keep-alive-miss detection delay): 3 s, to account for a missed keep-alive plus a few confirmation probes.
- Coarse-grained simulation: n=20,000, join/leave rate 2 nodes/s each, query rate 1/node/s, inter-slice communication interval swept 10-100 s.
- Fine-grained (p2psim) simulation: n=2,000, 10 slices, 5 units/slice, churn rate 24 events/minute (taken from Saroiu-Gummadi-Gribble's 2002 Gnutella measurement study), query rate 1/node/s (varied to 1 per 10 s in the recovery-sensitivity test).
- Inter-host latencies for both simulations: derived from Internet measurements among 1,024 DNS servers (King methodology, Gummadi-Saroiu-Gribble IMW 2002); the paper states results are largely topology-independent because lookup latency itself was not measured and inter-node latency is over an order of magnitude smaller than the propagation timeouts used.

### Stated limitations
The analytic bandwidth and failure-rate model excludes slice- and unit-leader failure overhead, on the stated grounds that such failures are rare, and excludes message loss, message delay, and proximity-probe overhead, on the stated grounds that these are small relative to the system's other time constants — none of these three exclusions is measured or bounded quantitatively in the paper. The one-hop scheme is stated not to require or use network-proximity information for routing, and the two-hop scheme's exploitation of proximity is limited to choosing a low-latency first-hop forwarding node; the paper explicitly separates this from a further possible optimization (proximity-aware dissemination trees for propagating membership events within a slice) that it states it did not implement, calling it future work in Section 6. Caching and load-balancing via cached lookup-path segments, which prior peer-to-peer systems exploited, is stated to be usable by the two-hop scheme but not by the one-hop scheme, since the one-hop scheme has no intermediate forwarding step to cache at; the paper states it was "investigating" how to obtain a similar benefit for the one-hop scheme, unresolved at time of writing. The paper explicitly frames its own system as trading materially higher bandwidth than the proven Liben-Nowell et al. lower bound on routing-maintenance cost, in exchange for lower lookup latency; it does not claim to be bandwidth-optimal. The Kelips comparison in Related Work states that at 10^5-10^6 nodes Kelips' O(sqrt(n)·log^3(n)) convergence time reaches over an hour, causing a large fraction of routing entries to go stale — this is presented as a critique of a competing system, not a property of the paper's own design.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The scheme requires an underlying ring identifier structure with proven successor/predecessor maintenance (the paper explicitly reuses Chord's protocol and its correctness proof for this layer) — any substitute ring-maintenance layer would need an equivalent correctness guarantee for the one-hop and two-hop failure-recovery arguments to hold. Slice leaders and unit leaders bear materially higher bandwidth than ordinary nodes (35-350 kbps upstream at 10^5-10^6 nodes for the one-hop scheme's slice leaders, versus single-digit kbps for ordinary nodes), so the system needs a way to identify well-provisioned nodes to serve those roles — the paper proposes an explicit "supernode" designation at join time, mirroring a cited prior mechanism, but does not itself specify or measure that selection mechanism's cost or accuracy. Both schemes assume node identifiers and query targets are distributed uniformly at random around the ring; the failure-rate analysis explicitly depends on this uniformity assumption. The recovery-from-crash results show query throughput itself is part of the repair mechanism — stale routing entries are corrected only by lookups that hit them and detect the staleness — so a deployment with very low background query rate needs an explicit mechanism (the paper suggests artificially inserted queries) to bound recovery time after a leader failure; the paper measured that a query rate of 1 per 10 s failed to stabilize below 2% failure for the full 50,000 s simulation window while 2 lookups/s stabilized within 300 s, at n=2,000. The two-hop scheme's proximity-based forwarding-node selection requires nodes to be able to probe or measure latency to remote-slice candidate nodes.

### Contradicts
None found — no other entry in this corpus reports a conflicting bandwidth or failure-rate figure for one-hop or two-hop DHT routing under matching conditions. This paper's own Related Work section states its design trades away the Liben-Nowell et al. proven bandwidth lower bound in exchange for lower latency; that lower bound is a structural consequence from a different paper, not a contradiction discovered here.

### References worth retrieving
- foundational: I. Stoica, R. Morris, D. Karger, F. Kaashoek, H. Balakrishnan, "Chord: A Scalable Peer-to-peer Lookup Service for Internet Applications," ACM SIGCOMM 2001 (already in corpus as STOICA-SIGCOMM-01; the ring-maintenance layer this paper's correctness proof is inherited from).
- competing: I. Gupta, K. Birman, P. Linga, A. Demers, R. van Renesse, "Kelips: Building an efficient and stable P2P DHT through increased memory and background overhead," IPTPS 2003 (directly compared in Related Work; O(sqrt(n)·log^3(n)) convergence time contrasted against this paper's one/two-hop schemes).
- competing: A. Mizrak, Y. Cheng, V. Kumar, S. Savage, "Structured superpeers: Leveraging heterogeneity to provide constant-time lookup," IEEE Workshop on Internet Applications, 2003 (an alternative two-hop scheme where all queries route through slice-leader-equivalent nodes and ordinary nodes exchange no state; directly contrasted against this paper's two-hop design in Related Work).
- competing: J. R. Douceur, A. Adya, W. J. Bolosky, D. Simon, M. Theimer, "Reclaiming space from duplicate files in a serverless distributed file system," ICDCS 2002 (a constant-hop-count design assuming smaller peer dynamics and tolerating lossy search, cited as a lower-dynamics predecessor).
- foundational: R. Rodrigues, B. Liskov, L. Shrira, "The design of a robust peer-to-peer system," 10th SIGOPS European Workshop, 2002 (the earlier single-hop DHT design by an overlapping author set, assuming corporate-scale peer dynamics; this paper's stated point of departure).
- competing: R. Mahajan, M. Castro, A. Rowstron, "Controlling the cost of reliability in peer-to-peer overlays," IPTPS 2003 (analytic bandwidth-maintenance-cost model for Pastry's O(log N)-state, O(log N)-hop design, offered as the contrasting point on the state/hop tradeoff).
- foundational: D. Liben-Nowell, H. Balakrishnan, D. Karger, "Analysis of the evolution of peer-to-peer systems," PODC 2002 (proves the lower bound on routing-maintenance bandwidth that this paper's design explicitly exceeds in exchange for lower latency).
- foundational: A. Rowstron, P. Druschel, "Pastry: Scalable, decentralized object location, and routing for large-scale peer-to-peer systems," IFIP/ACM Middleware 2001 (the O(log N)-state, O(log N)-hop design used as the maintenance-cost comparison point via Mahajan et al.).

- "our complete membership description can be seen as an optimization to following successor pointers"

## [GUPTA-SIROCCO-20] Resource Burning for Permissionless Systems
**Citation:** Diksha Gupta, Jared Saia, Maxwell Young. "Resource Burning for Permissionless Systems." SIROCCO 2020 (invited paper). DOI 10.1007/978-3-030-54921-3_2.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.04865 (arXiv:2006.04865v1)
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.04865
**Domain:** F

### What it does
This is a survey and position paper, not a paper reporting a new measured mechanism; it defines a
general framework, restates published cost bounds from four application domains, and states five
open problems. No number in this entry is a new result of this paper — each cited bound below
belongs to the paper it cites, and this entry records only what Gupta, Saia, and Young report
about it.

Resource burning is defined as verifiable consumption of a resource, where both the amount
consumed and the identifier (ID) that consumed it are computationally easy to check, done solely
to force an entity to prove distinct provenance before receiving an identity or performing an
action. The paper generalizes proof-of-work (the resource is computation) to any tunable
resource: CAPTCHAs (the resource is human effort spent solving a puzzle), proof-of-space (the
resource is storage), and resource testing (the resource is exclusive access to a wireless
channel, verified by demanding an echoed response on a randomly chosen channel that an
adversary controlling multiple identities on one radio cannot cover). The paper explicitly
excludes proof-of-stake from this category: proof-of-stake measures an already-held resource
(a cryptocurrency balance) rather than consuming one, and requires that stake be globally
knowable, which the paper states restricts its use mainly to cryptocurrency systems.

The paper's general model: identifiers are good (single real user, follows protocol) or bad
(adversary-controlled); a single adversary controls all bad identifiers and can schedule their
joins and departures adversarially, view good identifiers' messages before acting, but cannot
predict a good identifier's private random bits in advance. The adversary spends resources at
rate T (adversarial spending rate: total adversary cost over system lifetime divided by
lifetime); good identifiers collectively spend at algorithmic spending rate A. For churn
problems, JG denotes the join rate of good identifiers and PG the posting rate of good
identifiers (both defined the same way, as a count over system lifetime divided by lifetime).
The paper models resource-burning defense as a two-player zero-sum game between an attacking
adversary and a defending algorithm, and derives that at Nash equilibrium the algorithm's
expected utility is Θ(−f(0)) when the adversary sets T to its own advantage, for defense-cost
function f.

### Measured results
This paper contains no original experiments. It reports cost bounds proved or conjectured by
other cited work, organized by the domain in which the resource is burned.

| Domain | Resource burned | Cost bound reported | Source cited |
|---|---|---|---|
| Blockchain identifier generation (GenID: static set of identifiers, at most an O(α) fraction adversarial in the final set) | computation | latency 3 rounds, Õ(n²) bits sent per good identifier, O(1) burned cost per good identifier | Aspnes, Jackson, Krishnamurthy (cited [11]) |
| GenID, alternate construction | computation | latency Θ(n) rounds, Õ(n²) bits sent per good identifier, Õ(1) burned cost per good identifier | Andrychowicz, Dziembowski (cited [10]) |
| GenID, randomized leader election | computation | expected latency Θ(ln n / ln ln n) rounds, Õ(n) bits sent per good identifier, burned cost Θ(ln n / ln ln n) per good identifier | Hao et al. (cited [67]) |
| GenID, most recent | computation | expected O(1) latency, O(n) bits sent per good identifier, O(1) burned cost per good identifier | Aggarwal et al. (cited [4]) |
| DefID (GenID under churn: at most O(α)-fraction bad identifiers at any time) | computation | algorithmic spend rate O(JG + T), no additional assumptions | Gupta, Saia, Young (cited [58]) |
| DefID, improved | computation | algorithmic spend rate O(JG + √(T·JG)), subject to two assumptions on good-identifier join-rate stability across epochs (an epoch is defined as the time for the good-identifier fraction to change by 3/4), stated to be supported by real-world data | Gupta, Saia, Young (cited [59,60]); matching lower bound obtained for a large class of algorithms in [59] |
| Distributed hash table (DHT), conjectured | computation | Õ(√(T·JG) + JG), a conjectured extension of the DefID bound with a logarithmic-factor increase from group membership | This paper's own conjecture (Section 4.2), not proved |
| Application-layer distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) defense | bandwidth/computation | no conjectured closed-form bound; stated as an open problem | This paper (Open Problem 4) |
| Review spam | human classification time | conjectured Õ(T^(2/3) + PG) | This paper's own conjecture (Section 6.1), derived from a "preliminary analysis," not proved |

The paper additionally cites two real-world resource-consumption figures, without deriving them:
Bitcoin's May 2020 annual energy consumption at 57.92 terawatt-hours (compared to Bangladesh's
annual electricity consumption), Ethereum's at 7.9 terawatt-hours (compared to Angola's), and an
estimated 150,000 human-hours per day spent solving CAPTCHAs in 2012 (citing separate prior
sources [39], [114], [137]).

### Parameters
- α: the fraction of a burnable resource the adversary is assumed to control. The paper states α must be a small constant (often below 1/3 or 1/4) in settings requiring correctness guarantees, and may be any constant bounded away from 1 in settings requiring only performance guarantees. The permissionless-DHT open problem (Problem 3) is stated to assume α < 1/3.
- T (adversarial spending rate), A (algorithmic spending rate), JG (good-identifier join rate), PG (good-identifier posting rate): all defined as a total cost or count over the system lifetime, divided by that lifetime; no numeric value is given for any of them, they are the free variables the cited cost bounds are stated in terms of.
- Puzzle/challenge difficulty x: the model assumes an identifier can be issued a challenge of any difficulty x requiring consumption of x units of the chosen resource; no specific tuning rule for x is given as settled, and several cited works (Mankins et al., Wang and Reiter, Noureddine et al.) are described as offering different, unresolved approaches to setting it.

### Stated limitations
The paper states it is not known whether the GenID costs it cites can be reduced further for the
general problem or for an "almost-everywhere" variant (where an o(1) fraction of identifiers need
not learn the final set), and that no lower bound exists yet for the general GenID problem. It
states that extending the DefID matching lower bound (currently proved only for "a large class of
algorithms") to all algorithms is an open problem. Current DefID solutions depend on a
committee — a small identifier set with a good majority — coordinating resource burning, and the
paper states that "additional work is required" to decentralize this coordination for use in a
DHT (distributed hash table). It states DefID's majority-of-good-identifiers guarantee at the
network level is insufficient by itself for group-based DHT constructions, which additionally
require a minority of bad identifiers inside every individual group, and that maintaining this
per-group property under continual identifier shuffling "incurs large bandwidth costs" not yet
minimized jointly with resource-burning cost — stated as an explicit open problem (Open Problem 3).
It states no conjectured cost bound exists yet for application-layer DDoS defense (Open Problem 4)
because request cost heterogeneity breaks the direct analogy to DefID's uniform join/departure
events, leaving "a tight upper bound... an interesting direction for future work." The review-spam
conjecture is stated to follow only from "a preliminary analysis," not a proof. Proof-of-stake is
stated to require that each identifier's stake be globally knowable, restricting its applicability
mainly to cryptocurrency systems even setting aside other unresolved concerns the paper reports as
an attributed quote from a named researcher.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A resource-burning defense requires a means to verify both that the claimed resource was consumed
and which identifier consumed it — the paper's own definition makes this a hard requirement, not
an implementation detail. Requires the resource's cost to be arbitrarily tunable per identifier
(a challenge of difficulty x consumes x units), which the paper states holds naturally for
computation, memory, and bandwidth, and requires an explicit adjustment scheme (puzzle difficulty
or challenge probability) for CAPTCHAs. The DefID and DHT bounds require an assumption of
bounded, epoch-to-epoch-stable good-identifier join-rate behavior to reach the improved
O(JG + √(T·JG)) bound; absent that assumption, only the weaker O(JG + T) bound applies. Applying
DefID-style bounds to a DHT requires a committee mechanism — a small identifier group with a
built-in good majority — to issue and validate resource-burning challenges, and the paper states
this committee functionality itself still needs to be decentralized for a permissionless DHT.
The review-spam conjecture requires an available classifier that labels each post as spam or
legitimate with a fixed, known error probability, supplied by a component outside this paper's
scope (the paper cites classification accuracy near 90% from a separate work, [110], as existing
infrastructure this conjecture assumes).

### Contradicts
None found among the papers in this corpus. This paper explicitly distinguishes itself from
proof-of-stake mechanisms, which it classifies as not resource burning because they measure
rather than consume a resource — a definitional statement, not a disagreement with a measured
result elsewhere in this corpus.

## [GYONGYI-VLDB-04] Combating Web Spam with TrustRank
**Citation:** Zoltán Gyöngyi, Hector Garcia-Molina, Jan Pedersen. "Combating Web Spam with TrustRank." VLDB, 2004. Pages 576-587. DOI 10.1016/B978-012088469-8.50052-8.
**Retrieved:** full text via http://www.vldb.org/conf/2004/RS15P3.PDF
**Source URL:** http://www.vldb.org/conf/2004/RS15P3.PDF
**Domain:** F

### What it does
TrustRank ranks web pages (or, at the granularity actually used in the evaluation, whole web sites) by an estimate of how unlikely each is to be spam, so a search engine can filter or demote spam without manually checking every page. A human evaluator (the oracle) checks a small set of pages directly and assigns a good/bad label. TrustRank then propagates trust from the labeled good pages along the outgoing hyperlinks of the web graph, using the same iterative computation as PageRank but restarted at each step toward the seed set instead of toward the whole graph. A page many hyperlink hops from every good seed page receives a low score even if it has high ordinary PageRank.

Mechanism, in the two steps a reader would implement: (1) seed selection — rank all sites by "inverse PageRank," a bias-free damped random walk run backward along inlinks so that sites with many outlinks to high-PageRank sites are ranked first, since such sites are efficient starting points for reaching much of the good web in a few hops; take the top-ranked few thousand sites, filter out sites absent from major web directories (this removes sites that mimic a directory's structure to inflate their own score), and have a human evaluator label a fixed budget of the highest-ranked remaining sites as good or bad; keep only the good ones as the seed set. (2) trust propagation — run the same power-iteration update as biased PageRank, t* = alpha_B * T * t* + (1 - alpha_B) * d, for M_B iterations, where T is the web's row-normalized link transition matrix and d is the seed set represented as a uniform probability vector over the labeled good sites (zero elsewhere). Two variant propagation rules were also defined but not implemented in the reported experiment: trust dampening (each hyperlink hop multiplies the passed trust score by a constant beta < 1) and trust splitting (a page with trust score T(p) and out-degree omega(p) passes T(p)/omega(p) along each outgoing link, so pages with many outgoing links pass less trust per link).

### Measured results
All experiments run on the site-level graph obtained by collapsing the full set of pages crawled and indexed by AltaVista as of August 2003 into 31,003,946 sites (individual pages sharing a fully qualified host name become one site); 13,197,046 of these sites (over one third) are unreferenced and receive the same minimal static score under every method tested.

| Experiment | Conditions | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Seed selection | Inverse PageRank with alpha_I = 0.85, M_I = 20 iterations, on the 31,003,946-site graph; top 25,000 by inverse-PageRank score, directory-filtered down to about 7,900, of which the top 1,250 were manually evaluated by the paper's first author acting as oracle | 178 sites selected as the good seed set S+ |
| Evaluation sample construction | 31,003,946 sites ranked by PageRank, split into 20 buckets each holding 5% of total PageRank mass (bucket 1 = 86 highest-PageRank sites, bucket 20 = 5,000,000+ lowest); 50 sites sampled at random per bucket | 1,000-site sample; oracle-usable subset of 748 sites: 563 reputable, 37 web-organization, 13 advertisement (all three counted "good," 613 total), 135 spam ("bad"); 252 sites dropped as unusable (22 personal-page hosts, 35 aliases, 56 empty, 96 non-existent, 43 unclassifiable) |
| TrustRank vs. PageRank, bucket-level spam concentration | TrustRank computed with M_B = 20 iterations, alpha_B = 0.85, the 178-site seed set; PageRank computed with M = 20, alpha = 0.85 on the same graph; buckets defined per method to hold equal counts | Top 5 TrustRank buckets contain almost no spam; PageRank's bad-site fraction peaks at 50% in buckets 9-10; PageRank bucket 2 already shows about 20% bad sites |
| Bucket-level demotion | Same TrustRank/PageRank run as above, on the 748-site evaluable sample | Spam sites starting in PageRank bucket 2 are demoted by 7 buckets on average (landing near TrustRank bucket 9); good sites in PageRank bucket 16 are promoted by about 1 bucket on average |
| Pairwise orderedness (fraction of sample pairs where the higher-trust page is not the worse one) | 748-site sample, pairs built cumulatively from the top 100 to all 748 top-PageRank sites; compared against Ignorant Trust (score 1/2 to all but the 5 seeds overlapping the sample) and against plain PageRank | TrustRank pairwise orderedness reaches about 0.95 at 500 sample sites and stays above both baselines across every sample size tested |
| Precision/recall at TrustRank-bucket thresholds | Threshold delta swept over the 17 TrustRank-bucket boundaries on the 748-site sample | At threshold = TrustRank buckets 1-10: precision 0.86, recall 0.55; over the full 748-site sample (threshold = 0): precision 0.82 (= 613/748), which is also the sample's baseline good fraction |
| M-step trust function (toy 7-page example, not the AltaVista graph) | Trust score = 1 if reachable from a random 3-page seed in <= M hops from Figure 2's 7-node example graph | M=1: pairwise orderedness 19/21, precision 1, recall 3/4. M=2: 1, 1, 1. M=3: 17/21, 4/5, 1 |
| Ignorant trust function (toy example) | Same 7-page example, random seed set of size L=3, score 1/2 for unlabeled pages | Pairwise orderedness 17/21 over 42 ordered pairs; precision 1, recall 1/2 at threshold 1/2 |

A separate synthetic-graph comparison of inverse PageRank against a second seed-selection scheme ("high PageRank") is reported only in a cited technical report (Gyöngyi and Garcia-Molina, "Seed selection in TrustRank," Stanford tech report 2004), not reproduced with numbers in this paper; the paper states only the qualitative conclusion that inverse PageRank was "slightly better."

### Parameters
| Parameter | Value used | Range tested |
|---|---|---|
| alpha_I (inverse PageRank decay factor, seed selection) | 0.85 | not varied; cited as the standard value from the original PageRank paper |
| M_I (inverse PageRank iterations) | 20 | not varied; stated as sufficient for convergence of relative site ordering |
| alpha_B (TrustRank decay factor) | 0.85 | not varied |
| M_B (TrustRank iterations) | 20 | not varied |
| L (oracle invocation budget / seed pool manually evaluated) | 1,250 sites examined, yielding 178 good seeds | not varied in the main experiment |
| Site-count reduction before oracle evaluation | 25,000 top inverse-PageRank sites -> ~7,900 after directory filtering -> 1,250 manually checked | not varied |
| Evaluation sample size | 1,000 sites (748 usable) | not varied |
| Number of PageRank/TrustRank buckets | 20, later merged to 17 (buckets 17-20 combined because they hold only the 13M+ zero-inlink sites) | not varied |
| Trust dampening factor beta | defined symbolically (beta < 1); no numeric value used in the reported AltaVista experiment | not tested numerically |

### Stated limitations
The paper works at site granularity, not page granularity, purely to reduce computation; the authors state the same methods apply equally at either granularity but do not report page-level results. Using the paper's first author as the sole oracle "raises the issue of bias in the results," which the authors acknowledge as their only practical option given the unavailability of a search-engine spam expert with time to spare. TrustRank "is unable to effectively separate low-scored good sites from bad ones," because a site with no inlinks (over 13 million of the 31 million sites) carries no information a link-propagation method can use. The authors state that trust dampening and trust splitting were proposed but their interplay was not explored experimentally and is left as future work, and that seed selection could be made iterative (reconsidering which pages to send to the oracle based on prior oracle answers) rather than done in one batch, also left to future work.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Requires a directed link graph over the items to be ranked (the paper uses web hyperlinks; any analogous directed graph would substitute) and requires that "good" nodes point predominantly to other good nodes (the "approximate isolation" assumption) — TrustRank's demotion of spam depends on spam sites lying multiple hops from every seed, so a spam item with a direct or short-hop link from a seed page defeats the metric for that item. Requires a fixed, small, human-vetted seed set assembled before propagation runs; the paper's own seed-selection heuristic (inverse PageRank plus a directory-membership filter) is itself vulnerable to being gamed by any actor that can mimic a listed directory's link structure, which is exactly why the authors added the directory filter after observing spam pollution in their unfiltered candidate list. Requires re-running the human-oracle labeling step whenever the seed set needs to change, since nothing in the mechanism updates seed membership automatically. Does not require edge weights or any signal beyond the existence of a hyperlink.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus. Not itself contradicted by any paper in this batch; it is cited by LAS-EPRINT-26 among related trust-propagation approaches only in a general list, without comparison figures.

### References worth retrieving
- foundational: L. Page, S. Brin, R. Motwani, T. Winograd, "The PageRank citation ranking: Bringing order to the web," Stanford tech report, 1998 — the base random-walk formulation TrustRank biases.
- foundational: T. Haveliwala, "Topic-sensitive PageRank," WWW 2002 — the custom static-score-distribution-vector technique TrustRank's biasing reuses.
- competing: S. Kamvar, M. Schlosser, H. Garcia-Molina, "The EigenTrust algorithm for reputation management in P2P networks," WWW 2003 — a PageRank-style algorithm for peer reputation in peer-to-peer networks, cited as the closest peer-to-peer analogue.
- competing (efficiency): S. Kamvar, T. Haveliwala, C. Manning, G. Golub, "Extrapolation methods for accelerating PageRank computations," WWW 2003.
- attack/critique-adjacent: J. M. Kleinberg, "Authoritative sources in a hyperlinked environment," Journal of the ACM 46(5), 1999 — the hub/authority framework the paper references when discussing directory-clone spam that inflates hub scores.

### Verbatim extracts
- "we can effectively filter out spam from a significant fraction of the web, based on a good seed set of less than 200 sites."
- "more than one third of the sites (13,197,046) were unreferenced."
- "we manually evaluated the top 1,250 (seed set S) and selected 178 sites."
- "for the 500 top-PageRank sample sites TrustRank receives a pairwise orderedness score of about 0.95."
- "if the threshold delta is set...precision is 0.86 and recall is 0.55."
- "the baseline precision score for the sample X is 613/(613+135) = 0.82."
- "there is virtually no spam in the top 5 TrustRank buckets."
- "spam sites in PageRank bucket 2 got demoted seven buckets on average."

## [HALE-SSR-26] Benchmarking of the Amortized Post Quantum Combiner for MLS
**Citation:** Britta Hale, Xisen Tian, Lee Wang. "Benchmarking of the Amortized Post Quantum Combiner for MLS." Security Standardisation Research (SSR), Lecture Notes in Computer Science, 2026. DOI 10.1007/978-3-032-19567-8_5.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-19567-8_5
**Source URL:** https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-19567-8_5
**Domain:** H

### What it does
The Amortized Post-Quantum (APQ) combiner reduces the bandwidth, compute time, and memory cost of adding post-quantum protection to Messaging Layer Security (MLS), a continuous key agreement (CKA) protocol that ratchets keys forward through a tree-structured key encapsulation mechanism (KEM) called TreeKEM. This paper is an independent implementation and benchmark of the APQ combiner draft (Tian, Hale, Mularczyk, Joël, draft-ietf-mls-combiner), extending the proof-of-concept implementation of GREENE-EPRINT-25 with a second combiner mode and a head-to-head comparison against the X-Wing hybrid KEM.

The mechanism runs two MLS sessions in parallel with identical membership: a traditional session B (classical KEM and digital signature algorithm (DSA)) and a post-quantum (PQ) session A. Every epoch in session B advances by a Partial Commit (traditional KEM and DSA only). Periodically, a Full Commit advances session A using a PQ KEM, exports a PQ secret from A's key schedule, and injects it into B as a pre-shared key (PSK) proposal that B commits, mixing PQ entropy into B's key schedule via a key derivation function (KDF). Two modes are tested: PQ/T Confidentiality-Only (session A signs with a traditional DSA, so only confidentiality against a quantum adversary is PQ-protected) and PQ/T Confidentiality+Authenticity (session A signs with a PQ DSA, so authenticity is also PQ-protected, propagating into the authenticated-encryption-with-associated-data (AEAD) keys B derives). A partial commit does not update the PQ material, so a quantum break during a run of Partial Commits reduces the effective post-compromise-security (PCS) window to the interval between Full Commits, while forward secrecy (FS) is still achieved on every Partial Commit because each commit still ratchets the traditional key material forward.

The implementation extends OpenMLS (Rust) with the RustCrypto crypto-provider, adding ML-KEM and ML-DSA (the NIST-standardized post-quantum KEM and signature algorithms) via new RustCrypto and HPKE (Hybrid Public Key Encryption) crate integrations. It deviates from the draft by omitting the APQMLSInfo bookkeeping extension and by using OpenMLS's export_secret rather than the epoch_secret (unavailable via the OpenMLS API) as the PSK source; the authors state both differences have negligible effect on the measurements because APQMLSInfo is a small fixed-length byte string and the two secret types are the same size.

### Measured results
All tests ran a two-party MLS session (not scaled to larger group sizes; the paper argues the two-party case is the worst case for per-participant overhead amortization since MLS's tree-based scaling improves with group size) for 500 epochs, each epoch advanced by one empty commit from a single party. Timing figures are the average of 10 runs of the full 500-epoch test via the Rust Criterion microbenchmarking tool. Message-size and memory figures are totals across the 500-epoch run; memory was measured with the Rust Hotpath profiling tool. Hardware: a MacBook Pro with an Apple M2 Max (ARM CPU/GPU), 64 GB RAM, macOS Ventura.

Baseline (single, uncombined MLS sessions), total time over 500 epochs at 3 security levels (Low/Medium/High): traditional Edwards-curve ciphersuites (T-Ed-AES, T-Ed-Cha) ran faster than the lowest-security PQ ciphersuites, but at the 256-bit security level both PQ Confidentiality-Only (PQ-C-H, 3.353 s) and PQ Confidentiality+Authenticity (PQ-CA-H, 2.422 s) ciphersuites outperformed their traditional counterparts (T-EC-AES-H 5.244 s); PQ-CA-H ran 23% faster than PQ-C-H. Elliptic-curve traditional ciphersuites (T-EC-AES) ran roughly 4 times slower than Edwards-curve traditional ciphersuites (T-Ed-AES/T-Ed-Cha) within the traditional class.

Baseline message size, totaled over 500 epochs: PQ ciphersuites produced several orders of magnitude more bytes than traditional counterparts (e.g., low security: T-Ed-AES-L 0.24 MB vs. PQ-C-L 1.40 MB vs. PQ-CA-L 1.62 MB; high security: T-Ed-AES-H 0.24 MB vs. PQ-C-H 6.15 MB vs. PQ-CA-H 8.75 MB).

Baseline peak memory: classical ciphersuites capped at 1.2 MB peak regardless of security level; PQ ciphersuites' peak memory rose with security level, from 1.3 MB (PQ-C-L) to 1.8 MB (PQ-CA-H). Total (cumulative, 500-epoch) memory showed a larger gap: 235% higher for PQ-C-L versus T-EC-AES-L at low security, rising to 750% higher for PQ-CA-L versus T-Ed-AES-H comparison at higher security (the paper's own comparison pairing).

APQ amortization tests, Full:Partial commit ratios of 1:1, 1:10, 1:50, 1:100 (plus 1:2 and 1:5 in the X-Wing comparison), across the same 500-epoch, two-party, 10-sample-averaged setup, at three security levels for both modes:
- Total runtime: in all combinations except H-CA-L and H-C-X, APQ's total runtime exceeded the runtime of running the PQ component alone, even at 1:100 — because Partial Commits dominate the count and hit the traditional-ciphersuite component repeatedly, so APQ's per-epoch cost skews toward the traditional ciphersuite's cost, and for medium/high security levels that traditional component (P384-based KEM and DSA, or Ed448) was itself slower than its paired PQ component.
- Message size and memory: amortization behaved as expected in every configuration. At a 1:1 ratio, total message size approximately equaled the sum of running the two solo sessions separately. At ratios of 1:10 and beyond, message size dropped exponentially, converging toward the solo traditional session's magnitude; at ratios beyond 1:50, this reached a 94% cumulative message-size reduction relative to a single MLS session running the PQ ciphersuite alone, and up to an 85% reduction in total memory usage.
- Diminishing returns: efficiency gains from lowering the ratio flattened past 1:50 for all APQ modes, converging to a floor set by the slower of the two component ciphersuites.

Head-to-head against the X-Wing hybrid KEM combiner (a single-session hybrid that must invoke ML-KEM768 on every commit), at matched security levels, over the same 500-epoch protocol: APQ's Confidentiality-Only variant (H-C-X) overtook X-Wing in total runtime at a 1:2 Full:Partial ratio, with speedups from 26% (at 1:5) up to roughly 50% (diminishing, past 1:50). The Confidentiality+Authenticity variant (H-CA-X, which also carries ML-DSA65 signatures that X-Wing does not provide) overtook X-Wing's runtime only at a 1:5 ratio, still despite providing an authenticity property X-Wing lacks; its runtime floor approached the solo traditional Ed25519 ciphersuite's runtime. Message size and total memory for H-C-X overtook X-Wing starting at 1:2; for H-CA-X starting at 1:5.

### Parameters
| Parameter | Value(s) tested |
|---|---|
| Group size | 2 (fixed; paper argues this is the worst case for amortization) |
| Total epochs per test | 500, single empty commits from one party per epoch |
| Timing samples | 10 runs of the 500-epoch test, averaged, via Criterion |
| Full:Partial commit ratios (general amortization tests) | 1:1, 1:10, 1:50, 1:100 |
| Full:Partial commit ratios (X-Wing comparison) | 1:1, 1:2, 1:5, 1:10, 1:50, 1:100 |
| Combiner modes | PQ/T Confidentiality-Only, PQ/T Confidentiality+Authenticity |
| Security levels | Low, Medium, High (ML-KEM512/768/1024 paired with matched traditional and, for Conf+Auth, ML-DSA44/65/87) |
| PQ algorithms | ML-KEM (all three NIST parameter sets), ML-DSA (all three NIST parameter sets) |
| Hardware | Apple M2 Max, 64 GB RAM, macOS Ventura |
| Optimal amortization ratio (stated) | approximately 1:50 |

### Stated limitations
The implementation omits the APQMLSInfo bookkeeping extension defined in the draft standard, and substitutes the export_secret for the epoch_secret as the PQ-to-traditional PSK source because the epoch_secret is not exposed by the OpenMLS API; the authors state both deviations have negligible measurement impact but do not measure that claim directly. Timing measurements exclude network transmission entirely — they measure cryptographic-operation cost only, with no packets sent across a network, so end-to-end latency in a real deployment is not represented. All commits in every 500-epoch run are issued by a single party for measurement clarity, which the authors state differs from normal operation where commits are distributed across group members. Testing is limited to a two-party group; the paper argues, but does not measure, that larger groups would only improve APQ's relative performance because of MLS's logarithmic tree-based scaling. The APQ combiner's total runtime exceeding its solo-PQ-session runtime in most configurations is left only partially explained; the authors identify the traditional ciphersuite component as the cause but state that testing alternative traditional-ciphersuite implementations across other crypto-providers and crypto-libraries to resolve the remaining discrepancy is left to future work. The underlying APQ draft standard was still under active discussion (GitHub and mailing-list) at the time of writing, so full-fidelity testing against a finalized, fully compliant implementation is deferred to future work.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Requires maintaining two parallel MLS sessions with identical membership at all times, exactly as in GREENE-EPRINT-25; any membership-management component must apply every Add/Remove to both sessions. Requires the delivery/ordering layer to carry two independent commit streams (traditional and PQ) plus the PSK Proposal message that ties a Full Commit's PQ secret into the traditional session, at a cadence the application selects. A partial-commit-only period narrows the PQ post-compromise-security window to the gap between Full Commits, so a component that needs PQ PCS bounded below a target interval must fix the Full:Partial ratio no coarser than that interval allows; this paper's own data show ratios beyond 1:50 buy diminishing returns in bandwidth and memory while widening that PQ PCS gap, so the ratio choice is a direct trade against PQ PCS latency, not a free efficiency gain. The Confidentiality-Only mode leaves the traditional-session signatures as the sole binding on message authenticity, so an attacker with both a quantum computer and access to one session participant's traditional signing key can forge session-internal non-repudiation (a niche threat model distinct from external quantum authenticity, per the authors' own footnote). Requires an OpenMLS-compatible crypto-provider exposing ML-KEM and ML-DSA operations; the specific runtime and memory numbers are tied to the RustCrypto provider on Apple M2 Max hardware, and the authors' own data show large runtime variation between traditional-ciphersuite choices (Edwards-curve versus NIST-curve KEMs and DSAs) at matched security levels, so a different crypto-provider or CPU architecture is not guaranteed to reproduce the reported floors.

### Contradicts
Independently measures the same APQ combiner mechanism as GREENE-EPRINT-25 but reports contrary detail on the sign of the runtime benefit: this paper's amortization data show APQ's total runtime exceeding the solo-PQ-session runtime in most tested configurations (all except H-CA-L and H-C-X), which the authors describe as counter to the intuition that APQ reduces PQ cost relative to a PQ-only session; GREENE-EPRINT-25 by contrast reports APQ configurations running consistently faster than a PQC-only baseline (30-50% runtime advantage) at every group size tested. The two papers are not measuring the same baseline (GREENE-EPRINT-25 compares APQ against a PQC-only MLS session across group sizes 2-100 on an AMD FX-6300; HALE-SSR-26 compares APQ against both a solo-PQ session and a solo-traditional session, fixed at group size 2, on an Apple M2 Max, and additionally varies ciphersuite security level), so the two results are not a like-for-like disagreement, but both cannot be summarized as "APQ is faster than PQ-only" without stating which traditional-ciphersuite pairing and hardware the claim rests on.

### References worth retrieving
- X. Tian, B. Hale, M. Mularczyk, Joël, "Amortized PQ MLS Combiner," IETF Internet-Draft draft-ietf-mls-combiner-02, Oct. 2025 — foundational (the draft standard this paper implements and benchmarks)
- N. Greene, B. Hale, "Making post quantum key exchange efficient: An implementation with the MLS protocol," ePrint 2025/1881 — foundational (the prior implementation this paper extends; retrieved in this batch as GREENE-EPRINT-25)
- M. Barbosa, D. Connolly, J. D. Duarte, A. Kaiser, P. Schwabe, K. Varner, B. Westerbaan, "X-Wing: The Hybrid KEM You've Been Looking For," ePrint 2024/039 — competing (the hybrid-KEM combiner this paper directly benchmarks against, in Section 4.3)
- R. Mahy, "Messaging Layer Security Ciphersuite using XWing Key Exchange Mechanism," IETF Internet-Draft draft-mahy-mls-xwing-00, Mar. 2024 — competing (standardizes the X-Wing ciphersuite compared here)
- K. Kohbrok, "Phnx-im/hpqmls" (PheonixIM), GitHub — competing (a simultaneous, independent APQ combiner implementation the paper distinguishes itself from by providing formal performance benchmarking rather than interoperability testing)
- D. Sikeridis, P. Kampanakis, M. Devetsikiotis, "Post-Quantum Authentication in TLS 1.3: A Performance Study," NDSS 2020 — competing (independent PQ-overhead measurement in a different protocol, cited as consistent prior evidence that PQ signatures/ciphertexts are orders of magnitude larger than traditional counterparts)
- C. Paquin, D. Stebila, G. Tamvada, "Benchmarking post-quantum cryptography in TLS," PQCrypto 2020 — competing (independent PQ-in-transport-protocol benchmark)
- J. Alwen, S. Coretti, Y. Dodis, Y. Tselekounis, "Security Analysis and Improvements for the IETF MLS Standard for Group Messaging," CRYPTO 2020 — foundational
- W. Beullens, "Breaking Rainbow Takes a Weekend on a Laptop," CRYPTO 2022 — attack (post-quantum signature scheme cryptanalysis, relevant to PQ algorithm selection)
- W. Castryck, T. Decru, "An Efficient Key Recovery Attack on SIDH," EUROCRYPT 2023 — attack (post-quantum KEM cryptanalysis)

## [HALKES-NETWORKING-11] UDP NAT and Firewall Puncturing in the Wild
**Citation:** Gertjan P. Halkes, Johan A. Pouwelse. "UDP NAT and Firewall Puncturing in the Wild." IFIP Networking, 2011. DOI 10.1007/978-3-642-20798-3_1.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://opendl.ifip-tc6.org/db/conf/networking/networking2011-2/HalkesP11.pdf
**Source URL:** https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-642-20798-3_1
**Domain:** L

### What it does
This paper measures how often two Network Address Translator (NAT) boxes or firewalls, of unknown and possibly differing behavior, can be made to accept a direct UDP connection from each other using UDP hole punching, a technique in which each peer sends an outbound packet toward the other so that the intervening NAT or firewall opens a path for the reply. The paper classifies a NAT or firewall's outbound-mapping behavior into three categories: Endpoint-Independent Mapping (EIM, the NAT reuses the same external IP and port for a given internal IP and port no matter which remote host is contacted), Address-Dependent Mapping (ADM, a new external mapping per remote IP address), and Address-and-Port-Dependent Mapping (APDM, a new external mapping per remote IP-and-port pair); ADM and APDM are collapsed into one category, A(P)DM, because the experiment used only single endpoints per host. Filtering behavior (whether inbound packets are accepted at all) is classified as Endpoint-Independent Filtering (EIF, any external source may reach the mapped port) or Address(-and-Port)-Dependent Filtering (A(P)DF, only a host the internal side has already contacted may reach it). The measurement software, built into the Tribler BitTorrent client and deployed to real users' machines over two trials, has each peer self-determine its own NAT/firewall type by comparing the external address and port reported back to it by different communication partners (rather than using STUN, a centralized address-discovery protocol) and by checking whether a direct connection request from a remote peer arrives before or after a rendez-vous-mediated reverse connection request. A third peer already connected to both endpoints acts as a rendezvous server, relaying each side's address to the other so both can attempt simultaneous outbound packets, and this rendezvous role does not require the relaying peer itself to be directly connectable.

### Measured results
| Result | Condition |
|---|---|
| 21% of peers are directly connectable (EIM-EIF: no NAT-imposed mapping change, no filtering) | Trial 1, 907 peers, 646 peers for which a NAT/firewall type conclusion could be drawn |
| 52% of peers are EIM-APDF (endpoint-independent mapping, address-and-port-dependent filtering), the largest single category | Trial 1, same 646-peer subset |
| 11% of peers are behind an A(P)DM NAT (mapping changes per remote host), the type the paper calls the largest obstacle to connectability, because it can only connect to EIM-EIF and EIM-ADF peers | Trial 1, same 646-peer subset |
| 79% of peers are not directly connectable without a NAT-traversal mechanism | Trial 1, same 646-peer subset, restated in Section 6 as an aggregate finding |
| A further 64% of all peers can potentially set up connections between themselves through rendezvous-mediated UDP hole punching (the EIM-A(P)DF population), reducing the population that cannot connect at all to about 15% | Trial 1, restated in Section 6 and the Conclusions |
| More than 80% of hole-punching attempts between eligible peer pairs succeed | Trial 1 abstract-level summary figure, drawn from the pairwise success-rate breakdown below |
| Peers classified EIM-EIF still show only an 85% pairwise connection success rate against each other, attributed to a minority of peers with persistently poor connectability, plausibly caused by link saturation | Second-trial dataset: 15,545 connections between 841 peers for which both endpoints' NAT/firewall type were known |
| Connections between EIM-ADF and EIM-A(P)DF peer pairs succeed slightly more often than EIM-EIF-to-EIM-EIF pairs, but the paper states this is not statistically significant | Same 15,545-connection dataset; only 36 peers in the trial were classified EIM-ADF |
| Connections to and from EIM-APDF peers succeed slightly less often than EIM-EIF-to-EIM-EIF pairs | Same 15,545-connection dataset |
| First-attempt connections from an A(P)DM peer to an EIM-ADF peer succeed in approximately 41% of cases, attributed to Triangle Inequality Violation (TIV) — the direct packet arriving after, rather than before, the rendezvous-relayed reverse packet that opens the remote firewall hole | Same 15,545-connection dataset |
| Injecting UDP side traffic in a local test environment against newly acquired NAT routers produced packet-loss rates of 50% or more, or router crashes, on some routers; TCP side traffic on the same routers produced no more than 5% packet loss | Separate local reproduction test, not the field trial; routers described only as "newly acquired," no count or model list given |
| Mapping/firewall hole timeout: many NAT/firewalls use a timeout of one minute or less when only a single request-reply packet pair is exchanged; when an initial handshake precedes the delayed-reply probe, the timeout shifts to markedly longer values, with a large fraction of peers showing a 180-second timeout, matching the Linux kernel default | Timeout probe sent from a pre-programmed IP address and port at several delay values simultaneously from different source ports; small number of EIM-ADF NAT/firewalls excluded from this measurement because their behavior could distort the result |

The paper states no exact numeric labels for the per-pair connection success rates beyond those given in prose (the source figure, Table 1, is a colored bar matrix without printed percentages for every cell); only the specific percentages called out in the text above (85%, approximately 41%) are usable as numbers.

### Parameters
- Trial 1: 907 peers, no immediate retry on a failed connection attempt, ran several weeks, log data sent to a central collection server.
- Trial 2: 1,531 peers, up to three retries on a failed connection attempt, ran several weeks, used a less intrusive reporting method that the paper states biased the sample toward peers with unfiltered Internet connections — for this reason the paper uses Trial 1 for the market-share (NAT/firewall type distribution) result and the combined 15,545-connection dataset (drawn from peers with both endpoints classified) for the pairwise success-rate result.
- New-connection cooldown enforced during the experiment: 5 minutes, to prevent a closed connection's still-open mapping from producing a false first-attempt success.
- Recommended keep-alive interval, derived from the timeout measurement: send at least every 55 seconds, assuming several messages are exchanged within the first 30 seconds of a mapping's life, because some NAT/firewalls extend the timeout only after observing more than a single request-reply exchange.

### Stated limitations
The paper states its sample is likely biased toward home users rather than corporate users, because P2P file-sharing software use is typically discouraged in a corporate environment, and that home users tend to use less professional network equipment "more prone to misbehaviour," which may reduce the reported connection success rates below what a more diverse population would show. The paper states it did not implement a mechanism to distinguish Address-Dependent Filtering (ADF) from Address-and-Port-Dependent Filtering (APDF) in the live client, though it collected data (A(P)DF-to-A(P)DM connection attempts) that could later distinguish them, because the two categories account for only a small fraction of peers and the paper judged the software complexity not worth the benefit. The paper states it could not discount packet loss on saturated links, mapping-table exhaustion in some older router models, or other unidentified points of packet loss as causes of below-100% success rates among nominally compatible peer pairs, and states it did not have access to older router or modem models to test this directly. The local packet-loss reproduction test used only "newly acquired" NAT routers, which the paper states may behave differently, and possibly more resiliently, than the router population actually deployed among the trial's peers.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A design relying on this paper's rendezvous mechanism needs a third peer already holding an established connection to both endpoints that want to connect, so a directly-connectable-peer population (this paper measures it at 21% of the total in Trial 1) must exist for rendezvous relaying, or another means of introducing peers to a shared connected third party. NAT/firewall type self-classification depends on receiving consistent address/port reports from multiple independent communication partners, so a peer with too few prior connections cannot yet classify itself and the classification is stated to be probabilistic, not certain, in the presence of "behavioural subtleties" the paper documents in some NAT implementations. The paper's connection-setup protocol depends on a direct connection request being sent before, or nearly simultaneously with, a rendezvous-relayed reverse connection request, and unpredictable one-way-delay ordering between the two paths (attributed to a Triangle Inequality Violation between direct and relayed paths) is stated to determine whether the very first attempt at an asymmetric peer pair succeeds, so a system depending on first-attempt success for A(P)DM-to-EIM-ADF pairs cannot assume it above roughly 41%. Any system relying on the measured mapping timeouts must send periodic keep-alive traffic at intervals no longer than about 55 seconds per this paper's data, or a NAT/firewall mapping will close and require a fresh hole-punching exchange.

### Contradicts
None found. The paper's own numbers are internally two-sided: the abstract's rounded "approximately 64%... more than 80%" summary corresponds to the more granular breakdown in Section 5.2 and Section 6 (85% for EIM-EIF pairs, approximately 41% for A(P)DM-to-EIM-ADF first attempts), which are lower than the abstract's rounded floor for specific peer-type pairs; a reader citing only the abstract figure would understate the variance the paper itself reports across NAT/firewall type combinations.

### References worth retrieving
- Audet, Jennings, "Network Address Translation (NAT) Behavioral Requirements for Unicast UDP," RFC 4787, 2007 — foundational (the BEHAVE RFC this paper's NAT-type classification is built against and cites for the expected industry convergence toward EIM behavior).
- Ford, Srisuresh, Kegel, "Peer-to-peer communication across network address translators," USENIX, 2005 — foundational (the paper cited for recognizing NAT-imposed connectability loss as a P2P problem).
- Guha, Francis, "Characterization and measurement of TCP traversal through NATs and firewalls," IMC, 2005 — competing (measures TCP-side NAT traversal, the counterpart study to this paper's UDP-side measurement).
- Roverso, El-Ansary, Haridi, "NATCracker: NAT combinations matter," ICCCN, 2009 — foundational (source of the more extensive NAT-behavior subdivision this paper simplifies for its own experiment).
- Liu, Pan, "The impact of NAT on BitTorrent-like P2P systems," P2P, 2009 — competing (measures NAT's effect on an existing deployed P2P system, a comparison point for this paper's connectability figures).
- Hätönen, Nyrhinen, Eggert, Strowes, Sarolahti, Kajo, "An experimental study of home gateway characteristics," IMC, 2010 — competing (independent measurement of home NAT/gateway timeout behavior, cited as corroborating this paper's single-packet-versus-handshake timeout difference).
- Noh, Baccichet, Girod, "Experiences with a large-scale deployment of Stanford peer-to-peer multicast," Packet Video Workshop, 2009 — foundational (a deployed P2P system cited for connectability context).

### Verbatim extracts
- "approximately 64% of all peers are behind a NAT box or firewall which should allow hole punching to work" (Abstract).
- "more than 80% of hole punching attempts between these peers succeed" (Abstract).
- "even peers classified as EIM-EIF only show an 85% success rate" (Section 5.2).
- "the first connection attempt does succeed in approximately 41% of the cases" (Section 5.2).
- "over three quarters of the peers on the Internet (79%) are not directly connectable" (Section 6).
- "keep-alive message should be sent at least every 55 seconds" (Section 7).

## [HANDSHAKE-WP-18] Handshake: A Decentralized, Permissionless Naming Protocol Compatible with the Domain Name System
**Citation:** Handshake project (collective; whitepaper unattributed to named individuals in the retrieved copy). "Handshake: A Decentralized, Permissionless Naming Protocol Compatible with the Domain Name System." Project whitepaper (not peer-reviewed), 2018.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://handshake.org/files/handshake.txt
**Source URL:** https://handshake.org/files/handshake.txt
**Domain:** E

### What it does
Handshake replaces the trusted-Certificate-Authority root of web security by giving each fully-qualified top-level name (TLD) a blockchain-recorded owner and an associated certificate, so a client can check a name-to-certificate binding against chain state instead of trusting one of a fixed set of Certificate Authorities. The scope is narrower than Namecoin's whole-namespace ledger: Handshake secures only the root-zone level (the TLD), and delegates everything below a TLD to existing DNS infrastructure operated by that TLD's owner. A miner-run proof-of-work chain orders registration events, so a name claimed earlier is provably prior to a later, conflicting claim by a different party. Because an infinite number of short, desirable strings could otherwise be registered for free by one party, the chain requires the coin native to it as a scarcity input: a party places a coin-denominated bid to acquire a name, and the whitepaper states the bid amount is permanently destroyed from the circulating supply rather than transferred to a seller, so registering a name has a real resource cost enforced by supply reduction. Verification without running a full copy of the chain (Simplified Payment Verification, SPV) depends on an authenticated data structure the whitepaper calls the Flat-File Merkle Tree (FFMT): a base-2 Merkle trie stored directly in append-only flat files rather than layered on a general-purpose database, from which a full node emits compact Merkle inclusion or exclusion proofs for a given name. Existing TLD holders (Verisign for .com/.net, PIR for .org, Afilias, ICANN, Namecoin, Keybase, and others named in the text) are allocated a share of the initial coin supply redeemable by submitting a Domain Name System Security Extensions (DNSSEC) proof of control over the corresponding legacy TLD, and an SPV client falls back to a hardcoded or dynamically queried ICANN root zonefile for any TLD not yet claimed on the Handshake chain.

### Measured results
The whitepaper presents implementation benchmarks of its own authenticated data structure; because this document is a project whitepaper and not independently peer-reviewed, every figure below is recorded as project-stated design intent per the registry classification for this key, not as an independently verified measurement.

| Project-stated figure | Conditions given in the text |
|---|---|
| FFMT insertion over 50x faster than Ethereum's base-16 Patricia trie; over 500x faster than Google's Sparse Merkle Tree (used in Certificate Transparency) | Comparison is the project's own benchmark of its "initial FFMT implementation" against the two named alternative structures; no shared hardware, dataset, or run count stated for the two baselines |
| FFMT proof size comparable to a compressed Sparse Merkle Tree proof, and roughly 4x smaller than a base-16 trie proof | Same benchmark context as above; "comparable" and the 4x figure are not accompanied by absolute byte sizes |
| Sparse Merkle Tree insertion required at least 1.2 million rounds of hashing for a typical batch of 5,000 leaves | Stated as the project's own benchmark of the Google Sparse Merkle Tree baseline, without heavy caching |
| 500-leaf FFMT insertion batches averaged roughly 100-150 ms near peak capacity; committing (fsync) a batch of 44,000 accumulated leaf values averaged 400-600 ms | Benchmark run on one consumer laptop: Intel Core i7-7500U at 2.70 GHz with an NVMe PCIe SSD; total benchmark inserted 50,000,000 leaves of 300 bytes each in batches of 500, with periodic commits of 44,000 values; no run count or variance given |
| Alternative data structures examined and rejected: "many" unnamed structures had proof sizes "frequently exceeding 1-3 kilobytes" | No structures are individually cited for this figure beyond the two named comparisons (Ethereum trie, Google Sparse Merkle Tree) |

### Parameters
- Block interval: 5 minutes, stated as the target the FFMT's measured commit times (400-600 ms for 44,000 leaves) must fit inside.
- Per-block tree-update cap: a maximum of 600 tree updates per block, stated as an added fail-safe bound giving predictable worst-case insertion cost.
- Proof-of-work function: Hashcash-derived, combining SHA3 and BLAKE2b; the whitepaper states this combination is chosen because SHA3 is under-represented in existing proof-of-work hardware, to reduce the advantage of hardware built for other chains.
- Coin allocation to the free and open source software community: approximately 70% of total initial coin supply (stated once as "around 70%" and elsewhere itemized to 68.0%).
- Coin allocation to legacy naming-infrastructure stakeholders redeemable via DNSSEC proof: ICANN 24,480,000 coins; Namecoin 10,200,000 coins; PIR (.org) 3,400,000 coins; Afilias 3,400,000 coins; Verisign (.com/.net) 6,800,000 coins; Keybase, Inc. 0.25% of total supply; Handshake reserved-names pool (over 80,000 names) 2.5% of total supply; TLD holders generally 2.5% of total supply, distributed evenly.
- Initial coin valuation stated in the text: 7.5% of total supply valued at $136,000,000 in the initial distribution round described.

### Stated limitations
The whitepaper's own Disclaimers section states no guarantee is provided for the naming and auction system's functionality, including renewal availability, fees, or block availability in general, and no guarantee of coin supply, coin value, or name value. It states that transaction formats are not guaranteed to remain valid past one year, and that pre-signed transactions should not be presumed permanently valid. Trademark holders, not the protocol, are stated to be responsible for managing their own renewals and registrations. The chain's own root-zone security is stated to depend on the proof-of-work function, and the document states the resulting protocol is "not usable in practice without proper SPV proofs," meaning the raw consensus construction alone is stated as insufficient without the compact-proof mechanism described. The text states that specialized proof-of-work hardware can produce hardware monopolies, calling this "an acceptable risk" without a quantified bound. It states that no known proof-of-stake system was, at time of writing, sufficiently decentralized and resilient to fraudulent SPV proofs to serve as a substitute for proof-of-work in this design. The document opens by stating it is "not a prescriptive document" describing "the approach," rather than a specification.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A client that wants root-zone security without a full copy of the chain needs an SPV resolver capable of verifying FFMT inclusion and exclusion proofs; the whitepaper states the protocol is unusable without this. For every TLD not yet claimed by its legacy holder, an SPV client is stated to require either a hardcoded ICANN root zonefile snapshot or a live query path to ICANN's own root servers as fallback, so a Handshake-only client cannot resolve unclaimed legacy TLDs without also trusting one of those two ICANN-derived sources. Legacy TLD holders reclaiming a name on Handshake are stated to need a valid DNSSEC proof chain rooted in the two IANA-controlled root Key Signing Keys, so the mechanism inherits a dependency on IANA's DNSSEC root operations for that one-time claim step, even though ordinary Handshake-chain operation afterward does not require it. Sybil resistance for name registration depends on the native coin's bid-and-destroy auction, so any component that lets a party register a name without a coin-denominated, destroyed bid removes the scarcity mechanism the whitepaper states is necessary to prevent single-party namespace monopolization.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus batch. Retrieved via the project's own site rather than an independent archive; the retrieval note in the target registry classifies every number in this entry as project-stated, not independently measured, and this entry preserves that qualifier throughout.

### References worth retrieving
- foundational: Satoshi Nakamoto, "Bitcoin: A peer-to-peer electronic cash system" — underlying UTXO and proof-of-work construction Handshake extends.
- competing: Blockstack whitepaper (blockstack.org/whitepaper.pdf) — a full-namespace blockchain-secured naming system the text discusses and contrasts on SPV name verification (the "SNV" protocol).
- competing: Ethereum Yellow Paper (ethereum.github.io/yellowpaper) and Ethereum Name Service documentation (ens.domains) — the base-16 Merkle Patricia trie the FFMT benchmark is compared against, and a competing name-binding system on a general-purpose chain.
- competing: Google Trillian / Certificate Transparency Sparse Merkle Tree (github.com/google/trillian; IACR ePrint 2016/683) — the second data structure the FFMT benchmark is compared against.
- attack/critique: OpenNIC FAQ (wiki.opennic.org) — cited as prior work on an alternative DNS root zone, contrasted for its reliance on a still-centralized root operator.
- foundational: William Vickrey, auction-theory paper cited as [vickrey] (jstor.org/stable/2977633) — theoretical basis for the auction mechanism's incentive design.
- foundational: MES16 covenants paper, Financial Cryptography 2016 (fc16.ifca.ai/bitcoin/papers/MES16.pdf) — the covenant construction the naming-transaction state machine is built on.
- attack/critique: "Shattered" SHA-1 collision demonstration (shattered.io) — cited in the context of choosing hash functions for the proof-of-work and Merkle structure.

### Verbatim extracts
- "Users use the native token (coin) to register TLDs which are pinned to a specific certificate as the identity."
- "When a name is auction and sold, the coins are permanently destroyed from the system."
- "A Hashcash proof-of-work function using SHA3 and blake2b is used."
- "resulted in over a 50x speedup over Ethereum's Base-16 Trie and over a 500x speedup"
- "A typical insertion of 5,000 leaves required at least 1.2 million rounds of hashing"
- "the 500-value insertions themselves averaged roughly 100-150ms"
- "No guarantees are provided for transaction formats past one year."
- "no guarantees are provided with regards to functionality of the naming and auction system"
