## [HOLLAND-POPETS-22] RegulaTor: A Straightforward Website Fingerprinting Defense
**Citation:** James K. Holland, Nicholas Hopper. "RegulaTor: A Straightforward Website Fingerprinting Defense." Proceedings on Privacy Enhancing Technologies (PoPETs), 2022(2):344-362. DOI: 10.2478/popets-2022-0049.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://petsymposium.org/popets/2022/popets-2022-0049.pdf
**Source URL:** https://petsymposium.org/popets/2022/popets-2022-0049.pdf
**Domain:** G

### What it does
RegulaTor defends a Tor circuit against website fingerprinting (WF), a traffic-analysis attack in which a passive local eavesdropper between the client and the Tor entry node observes the sequence of packet sizes and timings and classifies which page the client is loading. RegulaTor exploits an observed common pattern in web-page loads: a large initial burst ("surge") of download data followed by decay, driven by the browser first requesting a base page and then requesting many embedded objects whose responses arrive in a decaying rate over time. It reshapes both download and upload traffic to always follow this generic decaying-surge shape, so page-specific volume and timing information is masked, without a machine-learned model and without per-page tuning.

The download-side mechanism: RegulaTor first sends the initial 10 real download packets at a constant, unmodified rate, so the TLS handshake and circuit build finish normally and no artificial surge starts before real data exists. It then begins a decaying surge at rate R packets/second, where the instantaneous target sending rate at time t seconds after the surge began is R * D^t (D is a decay constant, D < 1, so the rate decays exponentially). Real packets in the send queue are sent at the target rate; when the queue is empty a dummy packet is sent instead, up to a total padding budget of N dummy packets drawn uniformly at random from (0, N) at the start of each page load (once the N-packet budget is used, no more dummy packets are sent, though real packets may still be delayed to match the target rate). If the queue of waiting real packets exceeds a threshold T times the current target rate, a new surge is triggered (the surge-time counter resets) to avoid excess queuing delay when the real page data genuinely needs high bandwidth. If a real packet has been delayed more than a cap of C seconds, it is sent immediately regardless of the schedule.

The upload-side mechanism: RegulaTor pads upload traffic at a constant rate until the initial download surge begins to arrive (covering the client's initial page request), then schedules upload packets at rate (download rate) / U, where U is a fixed ratio; because upload sequences are typically small in volume, sending upload dummy packets at this pace costs little bandwidth while removing upload-side timing information. Any upload packet delayed more than C seconds is sent immediately.

Two operating points are tuned by the authors using the Tree-Structured Parzen Estimator (TPE) hyperparameter-search technique (via the Python `hyperopt` library), optimizing a weighted combination of latency overhead, bandwidth overhead, and the Tik-Tok attack's accuracy against the resulting defended traces: RegulaTor-Light (favoring lower overhead) and RegulaTor-Heavy (favoring stronger defense).

### Measured results

| Result | Figures | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Closed-world accuracy, undefended | Tik-Tok 97.0%, Deep Fingerprinting (DF) 98.4%, CUMUL 97.2% | Table 3; DF-CW dataset: 95 sites, 1,000 instances each, collected by Sirinam et al. in 2016 via tor-browser-crawler on ten low-end machines visiting Alexa Top 100 homepages 1,250 times each, batched 25-per-site per round to control long/short-term variance, corrupted traces discarded |
| Closed-world accuracy, WTF-PAD | Tik-Tok 94.2%, DF 92.4%, CUMUL 59.4% | Table 3, same dataset, default WTF-PAD (`normal_rcv`) parameters, authors' original code |
| Closed-world accuracy, FRONT-1700 | Tik-Tok 78.2%, DF 77.5%, CUMUL 31.6% | Table 3; Ns=Nc=1700, Wmin=1, Wmax=14 |
| Closed-world accuracy, FRONT-2500 | Tik-Tok 66.0%, DF 69.8%, CUMUL 17.1% | Table 3; Ns=Nc=2500, Wmin=1, Wmax=14 |
| Closed-world accuracy, RegulaTor-Light | Tik-Tok 34.8%, DF 23.3%, CUMUL 20.8% | Table 3; R=260, D=0.860, T=3.75, N=2080, U=4.02, C=2.08 |
| Closed-world accuracy, RegulaTor-Heavy | Tik-Tok 25.4%, DF 19.6%, CUMUL 16.3% | Table 3; R=277, D=0.940, T=3.55, N=3550, U=3.95, C=1.77 |
| Closed-world accuracy, Tamaraw | Tik-Tok 10.1%, DF 9.9%, CUMUL 17.0% | Table 3; rho_out=0.04, rho_in=0.012, L=100; Tao Wang's implementation; included as an example of a high-theoretical-strength but high-overhead defense |
| Closed-world defense overhead on DF-CW | Tamaraw: 36.9% latency / 196% bandwidth; WTF-PAD: 0% / 54.0%; FRONT-1700: 0% / 81.0%; FRONT-2500: 0% / 119.0%; RegulaTor-Light: 8.9% / 48.3%; RegulaTor-Heavy: 6.6% / 79.7% | Table 4; latency overhead = additional time to send the last real packet of the defended trace versus the undefended trace, divided by undefended sending time; bandwidth overhead = dummy packets sent divided by real packets in the undefended trace |
| Open-world precision-tuned Tik-Tok F1-score | WTF-PAD 0.870, FRONT-2500 0.625, RegulaTor-Heavy 0.135 (lower is more effective defense) | open-world dataset DF-OW: 40,716 traces from Alexa Top 50,000 (excluding the top 100 used in DF-CW), collected via tor-browser-crawler on ten low-end machines, one visit per site; open-world test set composition favored the attacker, with 9,500 of 29,500 test traces from the monitored class |
| Generalization to KNN dataset (RegulaTor-Heavy parameters tuned on DF-CW, reused unmodified) | Tik-Tok accuracy 17.8%, 5.1% latency overhead, 77.3% bandwidth overhead; FRONT-2500 comparison: Tik-Tok accuracy 44.9%, 98.3% bandwidth overhead | KNN dataset: Wang et al., 2020, 50 websites x 10 pages x 20 samples = 10,000 total samples; only closed-world traces used |
| Generalization to GE dataset, unadjusted RegulaTor-Heavy | Tik-Tok accuracy 11.3%, 15.1% latency overhead, 39.6% bandwidth overhead | GE (Goodenough) dataset, Pulls, 2014, 100 websites x 90 instances, average 5,663.9 packets per trace versus 2,100.9 for DF-CW and 1,807.6 for KNN |
| Generalization to GE dataset, volume-adjusted RegulaTor-Heavy | Tik-Tok accuracy 5.2%, latency overhead 2.9%, bandwidth overhead 82.9% | initial surge rate R scaled by 2.431x (relative traffic-volume increase) to R=673, padding budget N scaled to 8,030; comparison FRONT tuned to match FRONT-2500 bandwidth (padding budget 2,830 both directions) achieved Tik-Tok accuracy 43.4% at 45.8% bandwidth overhead |
| Real-world pluggable-transport deployment | Tik-Tok accuracy 11.6%, latency overhead 13.9%, bandwidth overhead 78.2% | PT dataset: 100 Alexa Top 100 websites x 100 samples, collected over one month (August 2021), via a Tor bridge running WFPadTools (Obfsproxy-based) as the pluggable transport, compared against a "dummy" pluggable transport baseline; initial surge rate raised to 356 and padding budget to 4,564 based on 10-sample-per-site average trace length of 2,697.2, other RegulaTor-Heavy parameters left unchanged |

### Parameters
Six tunable parameters (Table 1): R (initial surge rate, packets/second), D (packet-sending decay rate per second, D < 1), T (surge threshold ratio, triggers a new surge when the waiting-packet queue exceeds T times the current target rate), N (padding budget in packets, the maximum dummy packets sent per page load, with the actual count drawn uniformly at random from (0, N) each load), U (download-to-upload packet-rate ratio, upload packets sent at rate = download rate / U), C (delay cap in seconds, a delayed packet beyond this cap is sent immediately).

Values used: RegulaTor-Light: R=260, D=0.860, T=3.75, N=2080, U=4.02, C=2.08. RegulaTor-Heavy: R=277, D=0.940, T=3.55, N=3550, U=3.95, C=1.77. Both sets were found via Tree-Structured Parzen Estimator hyperparameter search, minimizing a weighted loss combining latency overhead, bandwidth overhead, and Tik-Tok attack accuracy on the RegulaTor-defended DF-CW dataset; the search space's exact bounds are stated to be detailed in an appendix not reached in this extraction pass.

Cross-dataset parameter transfer: R and N were rescaled proportionally to the ratio of the target dataset's average trace length to DF-CW's average trace length (2.431x for the GE dataset); D, T, U, C were left unchanged and reported to generalize regardless of traffic volume.

### Stated limitations
The paper states it did not test RegulaTor against an attacker who links a defended packet sequence to a web site using information from a series of page loads on that site, rather than a single page load in isolation, and states this "task may be easier for an attacker able to use information about multiple web pages on the same website"; this is left explicitly for future work.

The paper states RegulaTor's choice of surge parameters depends on the traffic volume of the undefended sequence: if the surge size is too small relative to real traffic volume, latency increases unnecessarily as data waits behind an undersized surge budget; the paper's own generalization test (GE dataset) shows unadjusted parameters raise latency overhead from roughly 6.6-8.9% to 15.1% when applied to a dataset with roughly 2.7x the packet volume of the tuning dataset, and states that some occasional data collection is needed to re-estimate relative traffic volume when moving RegulaTor to a new site population.

The paper notes RegulaTor's parameters were tuned specifically against the Tik-Tok attack, while WTF-PAD and FRONT in the same comparison used only their original authors' default parameters (not re-tuned against Tik-Tok), and states this may give RegulaTor "a slight advantage against Tik-Tok" in the closed-world comparison — a caveat on the paper's own headline comparison, not an external critique.

The paper reports that CUMUL's accuracy against RegulaTor-Light (20.8%) was not necessarily lower than CUMUL's accuracy against FRONT (compared figures not fully separated in this extraction), and attributes this to CUMUL deriving most of its features from a cumulative-sum trace representation that FRONT's early-burst obfuscation disturbs more than RegulaTor's shape-preserving approach does — stated as a case where RegulaTor's advantage over FRONT does not hold uniformly across attacks.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Both the client and the entry-side proxy (in the paper's implementation, a Tor bridge running a pluggable transport) must run the RegulaTor scheduler in lockstep: the upload-side schedule is derived from the observed download-side sending rate (rate = download rate / U), so the proxy's download pacing must be visible to, or coordinated with, the client's upload pacing logic.

The defense pads traffic only between the client and the first relay in the circuit (the entry node or bridge); the paper states this keeps the real-world bandwidth cost of padding low because Tor's overall capacity is limited chiefly by exit-node availability, not entry-node link capacity — a system reusing this design should not extend padding further into the circuit expecting the same bandwidth-cost argument to hold, since that argument depends specifically on entry-side padding.

The threat model assumes a passive local eavesdropper who observes packet sizes and timing but does not decrypt or tamper with traffic; results are reported for both a closed-world attacker (limited to a fixed monitored-site set) and an open-world attacker, and the paper states the open-world test set favored the attacker by using an unrealistically high monitored-to-unmonitored ratio (9,500 of 29,500 traces monitored) relative to real-world browsing.

Deploying RegulaTor against a new site population requires estimating that population's typical page traffic volume in advance (via a small sample collection) so R and N can be rescaled; the paper's real-world pluggable-transport deployment collected only 10 samples per site to perform this rescaling, which it states was sufficient.

### Contradicts
None found.

### References worth retrieving
- **Competing:** J. Gong, T. Wang, "Zero-delay lightweight defenses against website fingerprinting" (FRONT), USENIX Security 2020 — the primary comparison target throughout, described in this paper as "the best published deployable defense" prior to RegulaTor; holds FRONT's own reported overhead and accuracy figures.
- **Competing:** X. Cai, R. Nithyanand, T. Wang, R. Johnson, I. Goldberg, "A systematic approach to developing and evaluating website fingerprinting defenses" (Tamaraw), ACM CCS 2014 — the strong-but-impractical-overhead baseline.
- **Competing:** K. P. Dyer, S. E. Coull, T. Ristenpart, T. Shrimpton, "Peek-a-boo, I still see you: Why efficient traffic analysis countermeasures fail," IEEE S&P 2012 — WTF-PAD's predecessor line, the other lightweight-defense comparison baseline.
- **Competing:** W. De la Cadena et al., "TrafficSliver: Fighting website fingerprinting attacks with traffic splitting," ACM CCS 2020 — a traffic-splitting defense discussed as protecting against a different (guard-node-only) attacker, explicitly not defending against the local eavesdropper this paper's threat model uses.
- **Competing:** S. Henri, G. Garcia-Aviles, P. Serrano, A. Banchs, P. Thiran, "Protecting against website fingerprinting with multihoming," PoPETs 2020 — a second traffic-splitting defense discussed as not protecting against local attackers who see outgoing traffic.
- **Attack:** M. S. Rahman, P. Sirinam, N. Mathews, K. G. Gangadhara, M. Wright, "Tik-Tok" — the primary attack this defense is tuned against (cited as reference [38] in this paper's own numbering; full citation not reached in this extraction pass but referenced throughout as the strongest attack).
- **Attack:** J. Hayes, G. Danezis, "k-fingerprinting: A robust scalable website fingerprinting technique," USENIX Security 2016 — kFP, cited for the KNN dataset origin.
- **Foundational:** J. Bergstra, R. Bardenet, Y. Bengio, B. Kegl, "Algorithms for hyper-parameter optimization," NeurIPS 2011 — the Tree-Structured Parzen Estimator technique this paper uses for RegulaTor parameter tuning.
- **Attack/critique:** X. Cai, X. Zhang, B. Joshi, R. Johnson, "Touching from a distance: Website fingerprinting attacks and defenses," ACM CCS 2012 — cited as the paper that defeated earlier application-level object-reordering defenses.

## [HU-SP-21] Merkle²: A Low-Latency Transparency Log System

**Citation:** Yuncong Hu, Kian Hooshmand, Harika Kalidhindi, Seung Jin Yang, Raluca Ada Popa. "Merkle²: A Low-Latency Transparency Log System." IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (S&P), 2021. DOI 10.1109/SP40001.2021.00088.
**Retrieved:** full text via candidate URL `https://eprint.iacr.org/2021/453.pdf`
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2021/453.pdf
**Domain:** E

### What it does
Merkle² lets a transparency log publish a new digest every second while keeping both the cost a data owner pays to check her own entries and the cost an auditor pays to check the whole log's integrity independent of how many digests have been published since the owner last checked, so a system does not have to trade short publication intervals (low latency for detecting a wrongly-served entry) against growing per-check cost as time passes. Prior designs split into two families: prefix trees (leaves ordered lexicographically by key, as in CONIKS), which support efficient lookup of a specific entry's current value but force a data owner to check every published digest because states in different epochs carry no defined relationship to each other; and chronological trees (leaves ordered by time of append, as in Certificate Transparency), which let an owner check only the newest digest against an old one via an efficient extension proof, but do not support efficient lookup by key. Merkle² nests the two: the outer structure is a chronological tree ordered by append time, and every internal node of that chronological tree — not just the leaves — is itself the root of an inner prefix tree covering all entries appended up to that point, so each data block ends up stored in O(log n) prefix trees, one per level on the path from its chronological leaf to the chronological root, where n is the number of entries. A lookup for a key locates it via the prefix trees, giving CONIKS-style key-indexed retrieval; monitoring compares only the latest chronological root against the last root the owner or auditor has already checked, using an extension proof over the chronological tree, and does not touch intervening epochs' prefix trees at all. Appending a new entry in the naive version of this structure would require rebuilding O(log n) prefix trees from scratch each time; the paper's "pre-build" technique instead maintains each prefix tree incrementally in the background before it becomes the append target, at the cost of fixing a maximum chronological tree height (and hence a maximum log capacity) in advance. A data owner needs to verify only two proofs ever, in the paper's design: a first-value proof at enrollment and, from then on, only the current-epoch monitoring proof — because monitoring proofs can be cached and skipped for prefix-tree branches already checked, an owner who has checked before does not have to re-download the intervening structure to catch up after being offline.

### Measured results
| Metric | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Users supported per server machine, 1-second epoch | Merkle²: 8×10⁶ users; stated as 100x more than CONIKS at the same epoch length | Single Amazon EC2 r5.2xlarge instance, prototype in Go (≈800 LoC server, ≈200 LoC auditor, ≈450 LoC client library, ≈600 LoC verification daemon, ≈2400 LoC core data-structure library); SHA-3 hash, Ed25519 signatures, LevelDB persistent storage; chronological tree height capped at 31 (supports up to 2^31 ID-value pairs) |
| Users supported per server machine, 1-hour epoch | CONIKS supports 2x more users than Merkle² | Same hardware and workload assumptions; attributed to CONIKS's cheaper append/lookup dominating when monitoring cost (Merkle²'s comparative advantage) becomes less relevant at long epochs |
| Append time, last 100 appends, 2^20 ID-value pairs already in system | CONIKS: 3 ms; Merkle²: 151 ms | Merkle² measured with the pre-build strategy; each append touches 31 prefix trees (one per chronological-tree level up to the height-31 cap) |
| Append time comparison to AAD (bilinear-accumulator-based log) | AAD "significantly slower" than both Merkle² and CONIKS even with 32-entry batching; AAD's own paper benchmarks only up to 2^13 = 8,192 ID-value pairs | AAD figures taken from AAD's own paper and repository, not independently re-run — the authors state their own EC2 setup could not run AAD (public-parameter generation alone reported to take over 20 hours), and AAD's original benchmarks used a more powerful r4.16xlarge instance |
| Monitoring cost, ID owner, CONIKS vs. Merkle² | CONIKS latency grows linearly with epochs monitored: 1.29 ms (1 epoch) to 88.03 ms (1000 epochs); Merkle²: 2.33 ms (1 epoch) to 2.32 ms (10 epochs), independent of epoch count | 2^20 ID-value pairs in the CONIKS system; latency in milliseconds, Table II of the source |
| Monitoring message size, ID owner | CONIKS: 2.1 KB (1 epoch) to 2.1 MB (1000 epochs); Merkle²: 22.9 KB (1 epoch), 21 KB (10 epochs) | Same setup, Table III of the source |
| Estimated monthly monitoring cost, 1-second epoch, CONIKS-style | ≈5.4 GB downloaded and ≈3.8 minutes of verification time per data owner per month | Derived arithmetic from the paper's own measured 1000-epoch figures (2.1 MB / 88 ms per 1000 epochs), extrapolated to 2,592,000 epochs/month at 1-second epochs — not a direct 1-month measurement |
| Owner monitoring cost in Merkle² for the same monthly workload | 22.9 KB, independent of epoch count | Same derivation; the paper states Merkle²'s per-owner monitoring proof does not grow with the number of epochs elapsed |
| Auditor cost | Merkle²: 0.25 ms latency, 654 bytes per epoch; CONIKS: 0.22 ms, 370 bytes per epoch | Table II/III; stated that Merkle² auditors become "as lightweight as" CONIKS auditors once there are 28 or more appends between epochs |
| Certificate-transparency-style auditor bandwidth comparison to ECT | ECT: ≈9.5 GB/day; Merkle²: ≈1.9 KB/day | Derived from a stated real-world rate of 5,002,599 certificates appended per day (cited external statistic, not measured here) and ECT's stated 2 KB-per-append auditor cost (from ECT's own paper); Merkle²'s figure computed as log(10⁹) x 32 bytes x 2 |
| Memory usage at 2^20 ID-value pairs | Merkle²: ≈22 GiB RAM; CONIKS (persistent-structure variant): ≈6.3 GiB RAM; AAD: 263 GiB RAM plus 64 GiB for public parameters | 256 appends fixed per epoch; chronological tree height capped at 31; AAD's figure taken from AAD's own paper, not re-measured |
| Lookup latency/size, master key vs. latest value, 10⁶ ID-value pairs | Merkle² master-key lookup: 1.62 ms / 3.8 KB; latest-value lookup: 2.31 ms / 9.8 KB; CONIKS lookup: 1.28 ms / 1.6 KB | Table II/III; master-key lookup cheaper because it needs fewer non-membership proofs due to the forest design's largest chronological subtree typically covering the master key |
| Public-key-transparency application throughput scenario | Merkle² outperforms CONIKS at short epoch intervals (e.g., 1 second); CONIKS outperforms Merkle² when the epoch interval reaches ≈1 hour, because appends/lookups then dominate over monitoring cost | Derived workload: 200 appends/second for 1 billion users, 42 emails/user/day, 62% of emails needing a key lookup (Enron email dataset statistic) — 26 lookups/user/day; 10⁶ ID-value pairs inserted before benchmarking, external usage statistics cited, not independently verified by this paper |

### Parameters
- Hash function: SHA-3 (128-bit security level target).
- Signature scheme: Ed25519, stated as the only public-key operation in the system.
- Chronological tree height cap: 31, chosen to support the pre-build strategy; bounds total log capacity at 2^31 ID-value pairs and means each append touches 31 prefix trees.
- Persistent storage backend: LevelDB.
- VRFs (verifiable random functions) are explicitly not implemented, because the paper states privacy is not its focus — this is a deliberate scope exclusion, not a measured limitation.
- Baseline systems compared: CONIKS (both the original design and the authors' own persistent-data-structure-optimized "CONIKS*" variant), AAD (bilinear-accumulator-based transparency log), and ECT (chronological+prefix-tree hybrid for certificate transparency); AAD and ECT figures are taken from their own papers/repositories, not re-run on the authors' hardware.
- Asymptotic cost table (Table I) parameters: n = number of log entries, λ = AAD's security parameter, E = number of epochs elapsed, P = number of appends between epochs.
- Test-scale range: up to 2^20 ID-value pairs for microbenchmarks; up to 10⁶ ID-value pairs for end-to-end system evaluation and application scenarios.

### Stated limitations
The paper states directly, under "Limitations and future work," that Merkle² cannot outperform CONIKS when the epoch interval is long, because at long intervals append and lookup cost (which are more expensive in Merkle² than in CONIKS) dominate over monitoring cost (Merkle²'s comparative advantage); the crossover in the paper's own certificate/email-workload experiments occurs around a 1-hour epoch interval. The paper states it leaves improving append and lookup efficiency to future work, naming two unimplemented directions: a two-server split where one server pre-builds large future prefix trees while another serves current requests from smaller cached trees, and batching lookup proofs across users with a proxy layer to reduce server bandwidth. The paper states memory usage is a concern because data is replicated across the nested tree structure (Merkle² measured at ≈22 GiB vs. CONIKS's ≈6.3 GiB at the same 2^20-entry scale), and states an unimplemented optimization — skipping storage of prefix trees associated with chronological tree right children, which the paper says are not needed — is left to future work. The pre-build strategy requires fixing a maximum chronological tree height (31 in this implementation) in advance, which caps the total number of ID-value pairs the log can ever hold at 2^31; the paper does not describe a mechanism for extending capacity beyond a chosen height without redeployment. The paper explicitly declines to compare against Google Key Transparency's newer design because it is "still in its early stages" with "no protocol detail or implementation available for benchmarking" — this is a stated evidentiary gap, not a claim that the design underperforms.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The construction assumes the server picks the maximum chronological tree height (and thus maximum log capacity) before deployment, since the pre-build technique that keeps append cost bounded depends on the height being fixed in advance; a component needing unbounded future capacity must plan a height large enough in advance or accept a redeployment when the cap is reached. Concurrency control requires the server to serialize appends against each other (two concurrent appends may touch the same prefix tree), enforced in the prototype by having the server issue a position number to the user and reject the append if the corresponding signature is not returned within a short time bound; lookups and monitoring can run concurrently with appends because the hashes they need were already computed in past epochs. The soundness of an owner's monitoring shortcut (checking only the latest digest, skipping intervening epochs) depends on the owner having verified at least a first-value proof once at enrollment and having cached the resulting prefix-tree branch checks; a system that discards this cached state between sessions forces the owner back to a from-scratch check. Any external mechanism relying on Merkle²'s auditor cost advantage needs auditors who checked the log recently enough that the number of appends since their last check exceeds the paper's measured 28-append break-even point against CONIKS-style per-epoch digest fetching — below that append count, the paper's own data shows CONIKS's simpler per-epoch fetch is not meaningfully more expensive. The system assumes an Ed25519 key infrastructure for the one public-key operation it performs (append confirmation signing) and a SHA-3 hash function for all tree-node commitments; substituting either changes the paper's stated 128-bit security-level target and none of the reported performance numbers were measured under an alternative choice.

### Contradicts
This paper makes a specific claim about SEEMless (CHASE-CCS-19, same batch) worth flagging for cross-reference: it states SEEMless "relies on strong auditors to monitor the append-only property of the Persistent Patricia Trie, which still incurs a super-linear cost on the auditors" — an asymptotic-complexity characterization, not a disputed measured figure. This does not contradict SEEMless's own reported measured numbers (under 4.24 MB and under 0.3 s per adjacent-epoch audit at 10M users, per the CHASE-CCS-19 entry in this corpus) — a cost can be super-linear in an asymptotic sense while still being small in absolute terms at the specific scale SEEMless measured. A reader combining these two entries should treat the asymptotic classification and the absolute measured numbers as compatible, not conflicting, claims. No other paper in this corpus was found to directly contradict a measured figure in this entry.

## [HUANG-ATC-12] Erasure Coding in Windows Azure Storage
**Citation:** Cheng Huang, Huseyin Simitci, Yikang Xu, Aaron Ogus, Brad Calder, Parikshit Gopalan, Jin Li, Sergey Yekhanin. "Erasure Coding in Windows Azure Storage." USENIX Annual Technical Conference (ATC), 2012.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.usenix.org/system/files/conference/atc12/atc12-final181_0.pdf
**Source URL:** https://www.usenix.org/system/files/conference/atc12/atc12-final181_0.pdf
**Domain:** C

### What it does
A Local Reconstruction Code (LRC) reduces the number of fragments a storage system must read to reconstruct one unavailable data fragment, while keeping storage overhead close to a standard Reed-Solomon erasure code. A (k, l, r) LRC divides k data fragments into l equal-size groups, computes one local parity per group from only that group's fragments, and computes r global parities from all k data fragments; total fragment count is n = k + l + r, giving storage overhead n/k = 1 + (l+r)/k. Reconstructing a lost data fragment reads only the other fragments in its own group plus that group's local parity — for the paper's (6,2,2) example, 3 fragments instead of the 6 a (6,3) Reed-Solomon code needs for the same task, because Reed-Solomon parities are each computed from all data fragments and cannot narrow the read to a subgroup.

Because LRC parities are not Maximum-Distance-Separable (MDS — the property that any k of n fragments suffice to reconstruct the original k), not every combination of up to l+r simultaneous failures is recoverable; the paper's coding-equation construction (Section 2.2.1) is chosen specifically to achieve the Maximally Recoverable (MR) property — decoding every failure pattern that is information-theoretically decodable, given the fixed choice of which fragments feed which parities, even though some patterns (e.g., losing all data fragments of one group plus that group's local parity, leaving only the two global parities to cover multiple lost data fragments) remain undecodable by construction, not merely unimplemented.

Windows Azure Storage (WAS) deploys the coding scheme inside its append-only stream layer: an extent is written as three full replicas, sealed once it reaches 1–3 GB and stops being written, then erasure-coded asynchronously and lazily in the background by the Stream Manager, after which the three full replicas are deleted. Every fragment of one coding group is placed in a distinct fault domain, so a single-fault-domain outage cannot take out more fragments than the code's stated fault tolerance assumes are independent.

### Measured results
| Result | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Mean Time To Failure (MTTF), from the paper's Markov reliability model | 3-replication: 3.5×10⁹ years; (6,3) Reed-Solomon: 6.1×10¹¹ years; (6,2,2) LRC: 2.6×10¹² years | M=400 storage nodes, S=16 TB per node, B=1 Gbps network bandwidth per node, repair traffic throttled to ε=0.1 of bandwidth, detection-and-triggering time T=30 minutes, independent-failure assumption; (6,2,2) LRC repair cost C=3.6 (average fragments read to repair any single fragment), decodability ratio of 4-simultaneous-failure patterns pd=86% |
| Reconstruction cost reduction at fixed 1.5x storage overhead | Reed-Solomon (6,3) needs 6 fragments to reconstruct one lost data fragment; (12,4,2) LRC needs 3 — a 50% reduction | both codes at 1.5x storage overhead; comparison restricted to parameter sets whose Markov-model MTTF is at least that of 3-replication, over the 20-fault-domain cap of WAS clusters |
| Storage overhead reduction at fixed reconstruction cost | Reed-Solomon (6,3) at reconstruction cost 6, 1.5x overhead; (12,2,2) LRC at the same reconstruction cost 6, 1.33x overhead | same constraint set as above |
| Small (4 KB) I/O reconstruction latency, production cluster | Direct read 91 ms; Reed-Solomon (12,4) reading k=12 of 15 remaining fragments 305 ms; LRC (12,2,2) reading 6 fragments 166 ms (vs. 151 ms for Reed-Solomon reading an over-provisioned k+1=13) | production WAS cluster under heavy load, one 1 Gbps network interface card per storage node; comparison is (12,4) Reed-Solomon vs. (12,2,2) LRC, both at 1.33x storage overhead — (12,3) Reed-Solomon is excluded because its reliability falls below 3-replication |
| Large (4 MB) I/O reconstruction latency and bandwidth, production cluster | Direct read 99 ms; Reed-Solomon (12,4) reading 12 fragments 893 ms (9× slower than direct); LRC (12,2,2) 418 ms | same production cluster, light-load condition already shows this gap; "aggressive" over-reading (reading more than the minimum fragment count) helps small-I/O latency but hurts large-I/O latency, because large I/O is bottlenecked by network/disk bandwidth rather than by the slowest single straggler |
| Decoding-only latency (excluding fragment transfer) | Reed-Solomon 13.2 μs per 4 KB fragment; LRC 7.12 μs | same production measurement context; the paper states this difference is orders of magnitude smaller than fragment-transfer time and therefore does not affect the overall latency comparison |
| Cost reduction motivating erasure coding generally | over 50% storage cost reduction vs. 3-replication, reported as halving data-center footprint and power draw for that fraction of storage | company-reported general benefit statement, not a controlled comparison; not decomposed by code choice |

### Parameters
- (k, l, r): LRC construction parameters — k data fragments split into l equal groups each producing one local parity, plus r global parities computed from all k data fragments; deployed production parameter set for storage cost 1.33x is (12, 2, 2), yielding n=16 total fragments
- Fault-domain cap: 20, the maximum fragment count considered in the paper's parameter sweep, set by the number of fault domains available per WAS storage cluster ("storage stamp")
- Reliability-model inputs: M (storage node count) = 400, S (storage per node) = 16 TB, B (network bandwidth per node) = 1 Gbps, ε (fraction of bandwidth allowed for repair traffic) = 0.1, T (failure detection + repair-trigger time) = 30 minutes
- Extent size at which an append-only extent is sealed and becomes eligible for erasure coding: 1 GB to 3 GB
- Replica count before erasure coding: 3 full copies, deleted once erasure coding of the sealed extent completes successfully

### Stated limitations
LRC is not Maximum-Distance-Separable, so it needs strictly more total parity fragments than an MDS code offering the same fault tolerance would need in principle; the paper states this explicitly as the reason LRC "requires higher storage overhead for the same fault tolerance" relative to Reed-Solomon. LRC is optimized specifically for reconstructing lost data fragments, not lost parity fragments: reconstructing a global parity in the (12,2,2) deployed configuration needs as many as 12 fragments, the same cost a plain Reed-Solomon reconstruction would need, and the paper states this tradeoff is deliberate because parity loss (triggered only by disk, node, or rack failure) happens off the critical path of serving client reads, unlike data-fragment reads. The Markov reliability model in Section 3.1 assumes independent failures; the paper states correlated failures do occur in practice and that the model "can be readily extended" to add non-adjacent-state transitions to capture them, but does not itself report a correlated-failure analysis or its resulting MTTF figures. The comparison to alternative modern storage codes (Weaver, HoVer, Stepped Combination) is stated to hold specifically for WAS's design goal of fast data-fragment reconstruction; the paper concedes those codes reconstruct lost parities more efficiently than LRC does. Aggressive over-reading (fetching more fragments than the minimum and taking the first arrivals) is stated to help hide slow-fragment latency for small I/O but to actively worsen latency for large I/O, because large-I/O reconstruction is bandwidth-bound rather than straggler-bound — a mechanism-dependent limitation, not a universal one. Techniques that read from more fragments but transfer less data per fragment (the paper cites two specific systems for this alternative) are stated, per those systems' own reported numbers, to achieve only around 20–30% I/O and bandwidth savings, "much" less than LRC's reduction, which the paper offers as its comparison rather than an independent re-measurement in this paper.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Every fragment belonging to one coding group must be placed in a distinct fault domain; the reliability figures in Table 1 and the correlated-failure caveat both depend on this placement holding, since a shared fault domain across group members would violate the model's independence assumption and invalidate the stated MTTF. The stream layer must support an asynchronous, off-the-critical-path background process (the Stream Manager) that scans sealed extents and schedules erasure coding without blocking client writes, and must keep the three full replicas available and undeleted until the coded fragments are validated (the paper states failed erasure-coding operations are aborted, leaving the full replicas intact, and are retried later). On-demand reconstruction for a client read requires a coordinator node capable of reading the minimum needed fragment set (3 of 16 for the deployed (12,2,2) configuration reconstructing a data fragment) with low enough latency to meet customer service-level agreements; the paper's own production measurements show this becomes bandwidth-bound rather than straggler-bound for large I/O, so the network capacity per storage node (1 Gbps in this deployment) directly bounds achievable reconstruction latency. Detecting failures and triggering repair within a bounded time T is required for the reliability model's repair-rate terms (ρ₆ through ρ₉) to hold at the stated values; the paper sets T=30 minutes as the dominant term in single-failure repair rate, meaning any system adopting this scheme needs a failure-detection subsystem operating on that timescale to reproduce the stated MTTF.

### Contradicts
None found within this batch. The paper's own comparison in Section 6 states that prior deployed erasure-coded storage systems at Facebook and Google "do not explore alternative erasure coding designs other than Reed-Solomon codes," positioning this as a gap this paper closes rather than a disagreement with a specific prior measurement.

### References worth retrieving
- Huang, Chen, Li, "Pyramid Codes: Flexible Schemes to Trade Space for Access Efficiency in Reliable Data Storage Systems," IEEE NCA 2007 — foundational; the authors' own prior code family that LRC is stated to be "a critical improvement over"
- Gopalan, Huang, Simitci, Yekhanin, "On the Locality of Codeword Symbols," Allerton 2011 — foundational; cited as the paper studying in detail the "fundamental contention between parity reconstruction and data fragment reconstruction" that this paper's Section 3.4 references but does not itself derive
- Hafner, "Weaver codes: Highly fault tolerant erasure codes for storage systems," USENIX FAST 2005 — competing; storage overhead ≥2x by this paper's own figures, directly compared in Figure 6
- Hafner, "HoVer Erasure Codes for Disk Arrays," DSN 2006 — competing; directly compared in Figure 6, stated to offer "many trade-off points better than Reed-Solomon" but inferior to LRC overall
- Greenan, Li, Wylie, "Flat XOR-based erasure codes in storage systems: constructions, efficient recovery, and tradeoffs" (Stepped Combination codes), IEEE MSST 2010 — competing; directly compared in Figure 6, stated to not achieve the same storage/reconstruction tradeoffs LRC does
- Dimakis, Godfrey, Wu, Wainwright, Ramchandran, "Network Coding for Distributed Storage Systems," IEEE TIT 2010 — competing; this batch's DIMAKIS-TIT-10, cited under the "read from more fragments but less data from each" alternative-repair-bandwidth-reduction family
- Khan, Burns, Plank, Pierce, Huang, "Rethinking Erasure Codes for Cloud File Systems: Minimizing I/O for Recovery and Degraded Reads," USENIX FAST 2012 — competing; cited as reporting only ~20–30% I/O/bandwidth savings from the partial-data-per-fragment repair approach, the figure this paper's related work explicitly contrasts against LRC's larger reduction
- Ford, Labelle, Popovici, Stokely, Truong, Barroso, Grimes, Quinlan, "Availability in Globally Distributed Storage Systems," USENIX OSDI 2010 — foundational; source cited for the independent-vs-correlated-failure modeling extension and for the claim that transient errors account for over 90% of data-center failure events

## [HUGENROTH-USENIXSEC-21] Rollercoaster: An Efficient Group-Multicast Scheme for Mix Networks
**Citation:** Daniel Hugenroth, Martin Kleppmann, Alastair R. Beresford. "Rollercoaster: An Efficient Group-Multicast Scheme for Mix Networks." USENIX Security Symposium, 2021.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.usenix.org/system/files/sec21-hugenroth.pdf
**Source URL:** https://www.usenix.org/system/files/sec21-hugenroth.pdf
**Domain:** H

### What it does
Rollercoaster delivers a message to every member of a group at latency that grows logarithmically in group size, over a mix network, while preserving the mix network's metadata-privacy guarantees. A mix network delays and reorders messages at each relay (mix node) so an observer of network traffic cannot correlate a message's arrival with its departure; this paper builds on Loopix, a mix-network design in which every user's client generates payload messages, decoy drop messages, and decoy loop messages at independent Poisson-process rates, and every relay adds an exponentially-distributed random delay to each message it forwards, so that traffic volume and timing carry no signal.

Sending a message to a group of m members by having the sender unicast to each member individually (naive sequential unicast) takes the sender's fixed payload-sending rate lambda_p, so total delivery time to the last recipient grows linearly, O(m), because the sender's own rate is the bottleneck and every one of the m copies passes through it before the last one leaves. Rollercoaster instead forms a distribution tree: after the source sends the message to its first recipient, every node that already holds the message becomes a further sender, so the set of nodes holding the message multiplies by a branching factor k+1 at every tree level, and the number of levels needed to cover m recipients is L = ceil(log_{k+1}(m)). Each node computes its position in this tree deterministically from a single shared nonce via a GenSchedule algorithm, so no additional coordination messages are needed beyond the nonce itself. Rollercoaster requires no modification to the underlying Loopix protocol and adds only a 16-byte header (recording message source, sender, and role) inside the existing Sphinx packet format Loopix already uses.

A fault-tolerant variant (RC-FT) detects when a node assigned to forward the message in the tree is offline (the source detects a missing acknowledgment after a timeout) and reassigns that node's children to another already-informed node, so a single offline forwarder degrades delivery to its subtree rather than blocking it. This variant assumes the original source node stays connected and acts honestly for the duration of message distribution; the paper proves this assumption formally in its extended appendix.

An optional protocol extension, MultiSphinx, modifies a small, bounded number of mix nodes so a single input message can be split into a small fixed number p of output messages inside the mix layer (p-restricted multicast) rather than only at the endpoint nodes of the distribution tree, further lowering the payload-sending rate each client needs to sustain — relevant because a mobile device's radio incurs a fixed energy cost each time it wakes from idle to send, so fewer, larger message batches save battery relative to many small ones at the same total data volume.

### Measured results
All measurements come from a deterministic, single-machine, reproducible Python simulator (not a real network), because the authors state Loopix's real-network performance was already established in the original Loopix paper and simulation lets them eliminate external interference (unrelated network congestion, CPU contention) and gather far more results per unit of computation; no cryptographic operations are actually performed in the simulator (justified by Loopix's own finding that queuing and per-hop delay dominate total message latency, with crypto and network transmission time being negligible by comparison). The simulator was validated by reproducing a latency-distribution figure from the original Loopix paper. The final evaluation ran 276 independent simulations totaling more than 992,160 hours of simulated node time in under 209 hours of CPU core time (a 4,500x simulated-to-real speedup). Fixed simulation parameters throughout: 16 users per provider, client rates lambda_p = lambda_d = lambda_l = 2/s, per-hop mix delay rate lambda_mu = 3/s (overall client sending rate lambda = 6/s, satisfying Loopix's suggested lambda/lambda_mu >= 2 ratio), a 3-layer mix network with 3 mix nodes per layer, 10 ms simulation tick granularity, 24-hour simulated time span per configuration. Application traffic is modeled as a Poisson process, one message sent on average every 30 seconds by an online group member, with an 80/20 participation-inequality split (20% of users generate 80% of messages).

All-online scenario, average message latency reduced from unicast to Rollercoaster (k = p = 2), group size 128: 34.9 s to 7.0 s; group size 256: to 8.3 s. At group size 128, 99th-percentile latency dropped from 75.6 s (unicast) to 12.3 s (Rollercoaster), 90th percentile from 60.8 s to 9.9 s. Overall, for group size 128, the paper's summary states a 5x speedup in mean latency (34.9 s to 7.0 s) and a reduction in 99th-percentile latency from 75.6 s to 12.3 s.

Fault-tolerance scenario, offline behavior modeled from the Device Analyzer smartphone-usage dataset (traces filtered to n=27,790 total, n=25,618 with connectivity information, n=20,117 covering at least 48 hours, n=2,772 with no gap over 12 hours; the paper notes this dataset is more than five years old and is used only to derive archetype online/offline behavior models, not as a live measurement). Three connectivity models were built at 65% (matching the dataset), 80%, and 88% mean online time. At 65% online, group size 128, without fault tolerance the 99th-percentile latency exceeded 10,000 s; with the fault-tolerant variant (RC-FT), 99th percentile fell to under 21.9 s (90th percentile 18.0 s), compared to 103.3 s (99th percentile) / 61.9 s (90th percentile) for unicast under the same offline model.

Multiple-groups scenario: 128 users distributed across 1 to 16 groups (every user a member of every group), at both 100% and 80% online — the number of group memberships had little measured impact on Rollercoaster's latency.

Message-burst scenario: group size 128, burst sizes b of 1 to 32 messages sent at once, at 100% and 80% online — Rollercoaster (fault-tolerant variant) tolerated much larger bursts than unicast before send-queue growth degraded latency; both schemes showed queue-growth-driven latency increases at b=32, with the effect appearing at a higher burst size for p-restricted multicast than for plain Rollercoaster.

p-restricted multicast (MultiSphinx) scenario: group size 128, 80% online, increasing the branching factor k alone (holding p=1) had negligible or negative effect on mean latency; increasing k and the multiplication factor p together allowed a reduced client sending rate lambda (with lambda_mu decreased proportionally to preserve the lambda/lambda_mu >= 2 ratio, which increases per-hop delay) while maintaining comparable latency — reported as a heatmap over lambda/1 through lambda/16 and k=p from 1 to 16, without a single summary percentage.

Asymptotic comparison (analytical, not simulated): naive sequential unicast has latency O(m) and zero packet-size overhead; naive mix-node multiplication has latency O(1) but packet-size overhead O(m) (because a single input packet must carry m-1 payloads and headers); Rollercoaster achieves latency O(log m) with O(1) packet-size overhead (Table 2).

### Stated limitations
Group membership is assumed fixed and known to all members for the duration of a message distribution; the problems of group formation and of adding or removing members are explicitly left for future work. The fault-tolerant variant assumes the message's original source node remains connected and behaves honestly throughout distribution; the paper states this assumption is used in its formal proof (given in an appendix of the extended paper) rather than relaxed or tested against a dishonest or disconnecting source. The threat model assumes trust among group members: the scheme provides no unlinkability or unobservability guarantee against an attacker who compromises or colludes with a group member, only against outsiders. A naive mix-node-multiplication alternative (rejected in favor of Rollercoaster) is shown to leak the exact group size to a corrupt or even merely observing multiplication node, and the paper explains why cover traffic mitigation for that alternative would require bandwidth scaling with the largest supported group size — this is presented as the reason the naive design was not used, not as a residual property of Rollercoaster itself. MultiSphinx, the optional mix-node-splitting extension, is stated to weaken the assumption Sphinx normally relies on (that every input message to a mix node is independent); if an adversary corrupts a p-restricted multiplication node, that adversary gains a chance to correlate which two output messages came from the same input, a partial reduction in anonymity relative to unmodified Loopix, described but not quantified with an attack success rate in the retrieved text. Receiver anonymity and unlinkable group membership (hiding membership even from other members, or hiding which specific member received a message) are explicitly left for future work; the paper's own guarantee is membership unobservability against outsiders only. The evaluation is entirely simulation-based; the authors state they rely on the pre-established real-network performance of Loopix rather than re-measuring on a real network or with a black-box network simulator such as Shadow, and no live-deployment or adversarial-network experiment is reported. The Device Analyzer connectivity dataset used for the fault-tolerance evaluation was, at time of writing, more than five years old, and the paper uses it only to derive behavioral archetypes for a synthetic connectivity model rather than as a direct current measurement. Related-work comparisons name Vuvuzela's cover-traffic-based design as reaching call-setup delays up to 10 minutes and message latency over 30 seconds, which the authors state they consider too large for the collaborative-application target this paper sets (this is the paper's own comparative judgment about a different system, included here as an attributed statement, not as this paper's own measured result).

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Requires an underlying Loopix-model mix network already deployed and correctly parameterized (fixed per-client Poisson rates for payload, drop, and loop messages; per-hop exponential delay; a layered mix topology with providers as user entry points); Rollercoaster is a layer on top of this network and supplies no mix-network mechanism of its own. Requires every group member to be able to compute the same deterministic distribution-tree schedule from one shared nonce (the GenSchedule algorithm), so key distribution or group setup must supply that nonce to every member before a multicast begins. Requires a fixed, mutually known group membership at message-send time; a system that needs dynamic add/remove of members mid-session is not covered. The fault-tolerant variant requires an acknowledgment-and-timeout mechanism between a forwarding node and its parent, and its correctness proof depends on the message's original source remaining online and honest; a design that cannot guarantee source availability for the duration of one multicast round does not meet this precondition. The optional MultiSphinx extension requires modifying a subset of mix nodes to support message multiplication with a fixed small factor p, which is a change to the underlying Sphinx/Loopix relay software, not merely client-side logic — a deployment unable to modify relay behavior can use only the base Rollercoaster scheme (k branching among endpoints), not MultiSphinx's added mix-layer splitting. The scheme's metadata-privacy guarantee (sender-recipient unlinkability, online unobservability, membership unobservability) inherits directly from Loopix's own guarantees against a global active adversary; a deployment that weakens or omits the underlying Loopix decoy-traffic and delay parameters correspondingly weakens Rollercoaster's guarantees, since Rollercoaster adds no independent anonymity mechanism beyond the distribution-tree structure and the MultiSphinx header.

### Contradicts
None found.

## [HULSING-CCS-19] The SPHINCS+ Signature Framework

**Citation:** Daniel J. Bernstein, Andreas Hülsing, Stefan Kölbl, Ruben Niederhagen, Joost Rijneveld, Peter Schwabe. "The SPHINCS+ Signature Framework." ACM CCS, 2019. DOI 10.1145/3319535.3363229. (Note: the target registry's author field lists Hülsing, Butin, Gazdag, Rijneveld, Mohaisen — those are the authors of a different document, reference [31] in this paper's own bibliography, an IETF/RFC-track hash-based-signatures draft, not this CCS paper. Title, venue, year, and DOI in the retrieved text all match the target record exactly; only the author field in the registry entry is misattributed.)
**Retrieved:** full text via candidate URL `https://eprint.iacr.org/2019/1086.pdf` (full version, dated September 23, 2019)
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2019/1086.pdf
**Domain:** E

### What it does
SPHINCS+ produces a digital signature scheme that needs no persistent record of which keys it has already used (stateless), built entirely from hash-function security assumptions (no lattice or pairing assumption), so a signer can reuse the same long-term key pair on multiple machines or after restoring from backup without risking a forgery from key reuse — a failure mode that stateful hash-based schemes such as XMSS or LMS suffer if their usage counter is ever rolled back or duplicated. It generates a large virtual tree of one-time signing keys (a hypertree, split into d layers of Merkle trees, each of height h/d), addresses a leaf key pseudorandomly by hashing the message together with the signer's secret seed, and never needs to track which leaf was used before because a new message picks a fresh pseudorandom leaf with overwhelming odds of avoiding collision. Instead of a single-use one-time signature scheme signing the message digest directly, SPHINCS+ replaces it with a new few-time signature scheme the authors call FORS (forest of random subsets), which the authors state gives better size/speed trade-offs than the plain hash-to-obtain-a-leaf-index approach used by SPHINCS. The framework's second contribution is an abstraction called a tweakable hash function — a hash function parameterized by a public "tweak" value distinct per tree position — which lets the paper's security reduction treat every internal hash call generically and derive a single unified security bound, rather than re-deriving security for each hash-function instantiation choice from scratch. The framework offers two families of tweakable-hash-function instantiations, "robust" and "simple": robust achieves security in the standard model plus a quantum random oracle model (QROM) argument for compact public parameters, while simple gives up that formal guarantee for smaller code and faster execution. Signing is deterministic by default — the per-message randomizer R is derived from a secret PRF key and the message, with no external entropy source needed — but the framework supports an optional additional randomness input (OptRand) to counter side-channel attacks that exploit deterministic signing.

### Measured results
| Comparison | SPHINCS+ instantiation and parameters | Cycles: keypair / sign / verify | Bytes: sig / public key / secret key | Conditions |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| vs. SPHINCS-256 | Haraka, robust, n=192, h=51, d=17, b=7, k=45, w=16 | 1,254,968 / 29,015,002 / 2,739,770 | 30,696 / 48 / 96 | SPHINCS-256 baseline: 2,868,464 / 50,462,856 / 1,672,652 cycles, 41,000/1,056/1,088 bytes (SUPERCOP-reported, 3.5GHz Intel Xeon E3-1275 V3 Haswell); SPHINCS+ is stated as 25% shorter signatures and 1.7x faster signing than SPHINCS-256, both guaranteeing security for up to 2^50 signatures under the same key; SPHINCS+ figures are the median of 100 runs on the same Haswell CPU, gcc-5.4 -O3 -march=native -fomit-frame-pointer -flto |
| vs. Gravity-SPHINCS (robust) | Haraka, robust, n=192, h=66, d=22, b=8, k=33, w=16 | 1,257,826 / 38,840,268 / 3,467,192 | 35,664 / 48 / 96 | Gravity-SPHINCS baseline (parameter-set L): 30,729,044,392 / 32,564,796 / 625,752 cycles, max sig 35,168 bytes, pk 32, sk 1,048,608 bytes (SUPERCOP, 3.1GHz Intel Xeon E3-1220 V3); this SPHINCS+ instance has slightly larger signatures and slightly slower signing than Gravity-SPHINCS, attributed to a top-layer caching mechanism Gravity-SPHINCS uses that inflates its secret-key size and key-generation time |

### Parameters
- Hypertree height h and layer count d: search-selected per target instantiation (examples above range h=51 to h=66, d=9 to d=22); h is not free — the paper's parameter-search script iterates h from `s-8` to `s+20` where `s = log2(max signatures)`, and requires `h % d == 0`.
- FORS parameters b (height of each FORS tree) and k (number of FORS trees): search-selected together with the target forgery-probability bound; example values k=29 to k=49, b=7 to b=12.
- Winternitz parameter w: fixed to 16 or 256 in the exploration script; all reported benchmark instantiations use w=16, which the paper states is chosen for a "reasonable trade-off between signing time and signature size."
- Hash-function output length n: 192 or 256 bits in the reported comparisons (also 128-bit variants in the NIST table); larger n raises security level and signature size together.
- Tweakable hash function instantiation choice: robust (SHA-256, SHAKE256, or Haraka; needs a QROM argument for compact public parameters) or simple (same three hash-function choices, no such proof); Haraka-based instantiations cannot reach as high a security level as SHA-256/SHAKE256 because of a generic meet-in-the-middle collision attack on Haraka's internal state, with classical complexity 2^128.
- Maximum signatures per key pair: parameter sets are generated for a target maximum (e.g., 2^50 for the SPHINCS-256 comparison, 2^64 for all NIST-submitted instantiations) — the maximum is a design input to the parameter search, not a fixed constant of the framework.
- Message-randomization input R: derived deterministically as `R = PRF(SK.prf, OptRand, M)`; OptRand can be set to a fixed public value (fully deterministic signing) or to fresh randomness (probabilistic signing, stated as a side-channel countermeasure) — this is a configurable choice, not a fixed value.

### Stated limitations
The paper states that all its benchmarked schemes — SPHINCS+, SPHINCS-256, Gravity-SPHINCS, Picnic — "do not reach the performance of, e.g., lattice-based signature schemes like Dilithium, Falcon, or qTESLA," and states these symmetric-primitive-only schemes are "mainly interesting for applications without strong latency requirements, such as offline code signing or certificate signing," not applications with strict latency needs. The paper states a general rule of thumb for the whole hash-based-signature design space: "a linear decrease in signature size comes with an exponential decrease in signing speed" — smaller signatures cannot be obtained without an exponential signing-time cost within this framework. The robust tweakable-hash construction's proof of compact-public-parameter security depends on a quantum random oracle model (QROM) assumption; the paper characterizes this as "slightly stronger" than the assumptions needed for other constructions, and states this assumption is unneeded if one is willing to accept exponential-size public parameters instead. The "simple" instantiation drops that formal QROM guarantee for smaller code and higher speed, so choosing simple over robust is stated as an explicit security-versus-performance trade-off, not a strict improvement. Verification speed for SPHINCS+ is stated to be structurally slower than Gravity-SPHINCS because SPHINCS+ requires tweakable-hash calls at every node rather than plain hashing. LowMC v3, the symmetric primitive Picnic2's competitive performance relies on, is stated by the authors as "not [having] been intensively studied," with earlier LowMC versions shown by cited prior work not to meet their claimed security levels — the paper flags this as an open question about Picnic2's assumptions, not a property of SPHINCS+ itself.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A verifier must have access to and trust the public parameters (a public seed, or a larger public-parameter structure depending on the robust/simple construction choice) associated with a given public key; the security reduction is stated relative to those parameters being generated as specified, not arbitrarily. The deterministic default signing mode requires the signer to hold a secret PRF key (SK.prf) and secret seed (SK.seed) with confidentiality equivalent to the signing key itself — compromise of either breaks the unforgeability argument the same way a stolen private key would for a conventional scheme; no additional live entropy source is required to sign, which the paper's own design of `R = PRF(SK.prf, OptRand, M)` establishes as a difference from a nonce-based scheme like ECDSA that fails catastrophically on repeated or predictable per-signature randomness. A system embedding SPHINCS+ must pick a maximum-signature bound in advance (as a parameter-search input) — the paper's own search script takes `maxsigs` as a configuration constant, and instantiations are tuned to a chosen ceiling (2^50 in one comparison, 2^64 for the NIST submissions); a deployment issuing signatures indefinitely without such a planned ceiling is outside what this paper's parameter derivations cover. A system choosing a hash function for the tweakable-hash instantiation must independently trust that hash function's security (SHA-256, SHAKE256, or Haraka) at the target security level; Haraka-based instantiations are stated to be unable to reach the highest security levels reachable with SHA-256 or SHAKE256, because of the generic meet-in-the-middle attack noted above — a system requiring the highest formally provable security level should not select Haraka. Systems requiring fast verification at scale (e.g., verifying many signatures per second) should weigh SPHINCS+'s tweakable-hash-per-node verification cost against alternatives; the paper's own Picnic2 comparison shows SPHINCS+ verification nearly 50 times faster in that specific comparison, but the Gravity-SPHINCS comparison shows the opposite ordering, so verification speed is stated to depend on which competing scheme and parameter set is being compared, not a fixed universal ranking.

### Contradicts
None found against other entries in this corpus — no other paper in this batch measures hash-based post-quantum signature performance. Note: the paper's own text corrects a claim commonly attributed to SPHINCS-256 (128-bit post-quantum security) — the paper states this figure ignored a tightness gap in the original proof and that a later attack reduced the actual figure to below 190 bits classical / 95 bits post-quantum; a reader citing "SPHINCS-256 achieves 128-bit post-quantum security" without this correction would be citing a claim this very paper says does not hold.

## [IDE-ARXIV-25] Personhood Credentials: Human-Centered Design Recommendation Balancing Security, Usability, and Trust

**Citation:** Ayae Ide, Tanusree Sharma. "Personhood Credentials: Human-Centered Design Recommendation Balancing Security, Usability, and Trust." arXiv preprint arXiv:2502.16375, 2025. DOI: 10.48550/ARXIV.2502.16375.

**Domain:** E

### What it does
This paper does not propose a cryptographic mechanism; it produces empirical, user-facing design requirements for personhood credentials (PHCs — credentials that let an individual prove to a digital service that they are a distinct human without revealing further identifying information) through two methods: a competitive analysis of 15 deployed personhood/identity-verification systems across six categories (behavioral filters such as CAPTCHA and reCAPTCHA; biometric systems such as World ID and Humanode; social-graph systems such as BrightID; social-vouching systems such as Proof of Humanity; decentralized-oracle cryptographic-proof systems such as DECO and CANDID; government-based ID systems such as India's Aadhaar, Estonia's e-ID, and Japan's My Number Card; plus ID.me and Civic Pass), and a semi-structured interview study with 23 participants (10 from the US, 12 from the EU/UK) plus a quantitative post-survey on their preferences.

The competitive analysis used a two-reviewer UI/UX evaluation protocol: two members of the research team independently signed up for and used each system, scoring it against a fixed set of questions (how intuitive the verification process is, how effectively the platform gives feedback during registration, how the platform manages user data, and what privacy risks the platform exposes), then reconciled scores through qualitative coding of recurring themes. Where a system could not be directly accessed (Estonia's digital ID, Civic, China's social credit system), the team reconstructed its workflow from published white papers and documentation rather than direct use, and states this distinction explicitly.

The interview study recruited participants aged 18 or older residing in the US or EU/UK through social media posts and the CloudResearch and Prolific crowdsourcing platforms, each compensated a $30 Amazon e-gift card for a 90-minute session, preceded by a 5-participant pilot round used to revise the interview protocol. Each 90-minute session had five parts: current digital-identity-verification practices, perception of PHCs before and after an explanatory video, six application scenarios (financial service, healthcare, social media, LLM application, government service, employment background check) with concrete credential examples for each, a design-sketching session where participants proposed interface solutions to concerns raised earlier, and a closing quantitative post-survey on credential-type, issuer, and architecture preference per scenario, with multiple selections allowed per question.

### Measured results

| Quantity | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Interview sample size | 23 participants (10 US, 12 EU/UK) | Semi-structured interviews, October 2024, IRB-approved, preceded by a 5-participant pilot round |
| Age distribution | 61% aged 25-34, 22% aged 35-44 | Same 23-participant sample |
| Education | 87% held a Bachelor's degree, 65% held a graduate degree | Same 23-participant sample |
| Technical background | 65% had a technology background, 48% had a computer-science background | Same 23-participant sample |
| Compensation and duration | $30 Amazon e-gift card per participant, roughly 90 minutes ("hour-and-a-half") per interview | Same 23-participant sample |
| Competitive-analysis corpus size | 15 apps across 6 categories, 5 of the 15 centralized (primarily government-based) | Two independent UI/UX reviewers per system, three systems (Estonia's digital ID, Civic, China's social credit system) reconstructed from documentation rather than direct use due to limited access |
| Credential and issuer preference per scenario | Reported per-scenario (financial, healthcare, social media, LLM, government, employment) as multiple-selection percentages in Figures 4a/4b and Figure 5; government-issued ID most preferred across scenarios except social media and LLM applications, where phone number then iris scan were most preferred for the LLM scenario; government entities most trusted issuers overall, followed by nonprofit organizations, with private companies more accepted specifically for social media and LLM scenarios | Post-survey, same 23-participant sample, self-reported preference not validated against an independent outcome measure |
| BrightID and World App user-review counts collected as competitive-analysis data sources | Worldapp: 1,523 reviews (documentation plus Google Play Store); BrightID: 328 reviews (documentation plus Google Play Store) | Cited as a corpus size for the competitive-analysis data sources table, not as an experiment the authors ran themselves |

No inferential statistics (no significance tests, no confidence intervals) are reported; all quantitative results are descriptive counts and percentages from a 23-person convenience sample plus documentation review of 15 systems, and the paper states this explicitly as a limitation.

### Parameters
Not applicable in the sense of a tunable cryptographic or protocol parameter; the paper's design outputs are qualitative recommendations. Its proposed tiered-verification design implication defines four levels with named example mechanisms: Level 1 (Low Sensitivity) — email or phone verification; Level 2 (Medium Sensitivity) — physical ID; Level 3 (High Sensitivity) — biometric fusion, e.g. facial recognition plus voice print; Level 4 (Very High Sensitivity) — multi-factor PHC, e.g. biometrics plus social-graph verification plus physical ID. These levels are a proposed design, not a measured or validated scale.

### Stated limitations
The paper states its own recruitment "resulted in limited diversity in educational backgrounds and age groups," restricting the generalizability of its findings, since it notes younger or differently-educated participants might show different technology preferences and expectations. It states participants without prior knowledge of PHCs responded based only on an explanatory video rather than hands-on use of a working system, and that their responses "might differ" given an interactive prototype instead — the paper states future work will build such a prototype. Separately, in its design-implications discussion, the paper states that current approaches to PHC issuance share "a fundamental limitation": a chicken-and-egg signal failure in which an ecosystem of PHC issuers will not emerge without systems that consume PHCs, and systems will not adopt PHCs without a broad base of issuers already existing; it cites, as evidence this is a live rather than solved problem, that despite industry coalitions pursuing decentralized identity credentials for at least seven years, digitally signed state IDs in the US are available only in California. From the competitive analysis: BrightID's account-recovery process was found tedious with unclear rules, illustrated by a cited user review stating that failing to set up recovery connections in advance forces creating an entirely new account; Proof of Humanity was found to lack any option to correct or update a mistaken submission; Idena's flip-test validation was found challenging for new users because it requires constructing a meaningful story within a strict time limit; World App's Google-Drive-based backup flow was found to confuse users about what access they were granting and to create recovery failures for users who never completed the backup step.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A tiered or multi-factor personhood-verification design, as the paper's own recommendation, requires the rest of the system to let a user or a relying party select among data sources of different sensitivity per transaction context, since participants expressed a clear preference against a single fixed verification method applied uniformly across financial, healthcare, social-media, and government scenarios. Portable, cross-platform personhood credentials, per the paper's own recommendation, require an interoperable cryptographic credential format (the paper names the W3C Verifiable Credentials data model and the DIF Universal Resolver as candidate standards) plus a zero-knowledge-proof mechanism, so a credential issued once can be verified by a different platform without recontacting the original issuer. A periodic or risk-triggered re-verification design (the paper's "dynamic multi-factor" recommendation) requires the issuing system to track time since last verification or to detect elevated-risk activity, and requires a user-facing prompt flow the paper does not itself specify in protocol terms. A decentralized, cross-industry issuance ecosystem, per the paper's own proposed architecture, requires a permissioned blockchain (the paper names Hyperledger Fabric) plus cross-chain interoperability protocols (the paper names Polkadot and Cosmos) plus smart contracts encoding compliance rules jointly set by industry and government issuers — none of which is validated in this paper beyond being a proposed architecture; the paper reports no implementation or measurement of this architecture.

### Contradicts
None found.

### References worth retrieving
- **Competing:** Kleros, "Proof of Humanity" documentation — the social-vouching PHC system directly evaluated in this paper's competitive analysis (Table 5); this paper adds an independent usability critique (no correction option for mistaken submissions, public linkage of wallet address to submitted photo/video) not present in Kleros's own documentation.
- **Competing:** World ID / Worldcoin documentation — the biometric (iris-scan) PHC system evaluated in this paper's competitive analysis; this paper's finding that the onboarding flow under-explains data handling and that Google-Drive-based backup confuses users is an independent usability measurement against the vendor's own claims.
- **Competing:** BrightID documentation — the social-graph PHC system evaluated in this paper; independent finding (drawn partly from Google Play Store reviews) that users find it difficult to build the social connections BrightID's graph-based scoring requires.
- **Competing:** Humanode documentation — biometric (face) PHC system on a dedicated blockchain, evaluated as more operationally complex (node setup and validation) than the other biometric systems reviewed.
- **Foundational:** DECO (Chainlink Labs) and CANDID (IC3 research team) — decentralized-oracle cryptographic-proof-of-attribute systems using zero-knowledge proofs against TLS session data or held credentials; both flagged in this paper for a shared risk (deanonymization via repeated use of the same attribute proof across services for CANDID; response-substring exploitation for DECO).
- **Foundational:** W3C Verifiable Credentials data model, DIF (Decentralized Identity Foundation) Universal Resolver — the interoperability standards this paper's portability recommendation is built on.

- "we conducted competitive analysis, and semi-structured online user interviews (N=23)."
