## [JOHNSON-CCS-13] Users Get Routed: Traffic Correlation on Tor by Realistic Adversaries

**Citation:** Aaron Johnson, Chris Wacek, Rob Jansen, Micah Sherr, Paul Syverson. "Users Get Routed: Traffic Correlation on Tor by Realistic Adversaries." ACM CCS, 2013. DOI 10.1145/2508859.2516651.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.freehaven.net/anonbib/cache/ccs2013-usersrouted.pdf
**Source URL:** https://www.freehaven.net/anonbib/cache/ccs2013-usersrouted.pdf
**Domain:** J

### What it does
The paper measures how quickly a realistic passive adversary deanonymizes a Tor user (Tor is a low-latency onion-routing anonymity network that hides a user's address from the destination by relaying traffic through three volunteer-operated relays: guard, middle, exit). Deanonymization by traffic correlation occurs when the same party observes traffic both entering the network at the guard and leaving it at the exit and links the two observations as the same flow. The authors build a Monte Carlo path simulator, TorPS, that replays historical Tor consensus data (the hourly list of active relays and their properties) and five modeled user-behavior traces through Tor's actual path-selection algorithm, then measures, for each simulated user, the probability distribution over time until a hostile party occupies both the guard and exit position on a circuit (relay adversary) or observes both path segments as a carrier of network traffic without running any relay (network adversary: an autonomous system, an Internet exchange point, or an organization operating several exchange points).

### Measured results
| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| More than 80% chance of full deanonymization within 6 months; median time to full compromise always under 70 days, across all five user models | Relay adversary running one guard relay (83.3 MiB/s) and one exit relay (16.7 MiB/s), 5:1 guard-to-exit bandwidth ratio, simulated October 2012-March 2013, TorPS Monte Carlo simulation |
| Median time to compromised guard: 50-60 days; median time to compromised exit: under 2.5 days | Same adversary and period; guard compromise dominates because clients rotate exits far more often than guards |
| Median rate of fully compromised streams: 0.25%-1.5%, varying by user behavior model | Same adversary and period |
| BitTorrent user model: exit compromise at median time under 6 hours, median rate over 12% | Same adversary; BitTorrent trace creates 6,768 streams/week over 118 ports versus 2,632 streams/week over 2 ports for the Typical model |
| Doubling adversary bandwidth roughly halves time to first compromise; at 200 MiB/s, 50% probability of full compromise within 30 days; at 10 MiB/s, under 10% probability of ever compromising a user | Typical user model, adversary bandwidth varied 10-200 MiB/s, same simulated period |
| Adversary entering the network 2 months into the simulation (12/1/2012) still fully compromises the user with ~70% probability over the remaining 4 months, versus ~70% probability for an adversary present from the outset over the full 4 months compared | Typical user model, same simulation infrastructure |
| Worst-case client origin: 45.9% (Typical), 64.9% (IRC), 76.4% (BitTorrent) of samples use a compromised stream within 1 day against a single AS adversary; over 98% compromised within 3 months for all models | 50,000 Monte Carlo simulations per behavior, clients placed at 5 AS origins (4 German, 1 Italian) identified as popular Tor client ASes by Edman and Syverson (2009), January-March 2013 |
| Best-case client origin: IRC users exposed at 44 days median; 38% (BitTorrent) and 44% (Typical) of users still compromised within 90 days despite over 50% evading compromise for the full period | Same AS-adversary simulation, best-case client origin selected by smallest area under the compromise-time CDF |
| Best-case standalone IXP compromises 3.7% of samples within 30 days; best-case IXP organization (a single entity administering multiple exchange points) compromises 12.4% in the same period | 19 identified IXP organizations administering 90 distinct Internet exchange points (IXPs), Typical user model, same simulation period |
| Congestion-Aware Tor (CAT, an alternative path-selection algorithm) shows only a minor reduction in time to first compromise but a markedly larger increase in the total fraction of streams compromised, relative to standard Tor | Relay adversary at 83.3/16.7 MiB/s, Typical user model, congestion profiles built from a Shadow-simulated virtual Tor network (Tor version 0.2.3.25) run until the median Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance between repeated congestion traces fell below 5% |
| Linear regression converting adversary relay bandwidth to consensus selection weight: r² = 0.71 for guard relays, r² = 0.69 for exit relays | Regression fitted against relays in the consensuses spanning the simulation period |

### Parameters
- Adversary bandwidth allocation: 5:1 guard-to-exit ratio, selected after testing 1:1, 2:1, 5:1, 10:1, and 50:1 splits of 100 MiB/s (5:1 maximized the probability of compromising at least one stream over the 6-month test period and was adopted for all subsequent experiments).
- Baseline adversary relay bandwidths in the main experiments: 83.3 MiB/s guard, 16.7 MiB/s exit (from the 5:1 split of 100 MiB/s).
- User models: Typical (2,632 streams/week, 205 unique IPs, ports 80/443), IRC (135 streams/week, 1 IP, port 6697), BitTorrent (6,768 streams/week, 171 IPs, 118 ports), WorstPort (Typical traffic on port 6523, second-least exit capacity excluding rejected ports), BestPort (Typical traffic on port 443, highest exit capacity).
- Simulation window: October 2012-March 2013 for relay-adversary experiments; January-March 2013 for network-adversary experiments, using 50,000 Monte Carlo samples per behavior model.
- Client AS origins: the 5 most popular client ASes identified by Edman and Syverson (2009) — AS3320, AS3209, AS3269, AS13184, AS6805 (4 German, 1 Italian); Chinese ASes excluded because Tor was subsequently blocked in China.
- CAT congestion threshold: a circuit is dropped from use for new streams once the mean of its last 5 round-trip-time congestion measurements exceeds 0.5 seconds.
- Guard expiration parameter cited from Tor's own configuration history: minimum guard expiration time was 30 days at the time of this study and was increased to 60 days in Tor version 0.2.4.12-alpha partly in response to this paper's finding that guard expiration accelerates compromise.

### Stated limitations
The authors state they consider only a passive end-to-end correlating adversary and explicitly exclude circuit clogging, network latency attacks, active traffic alteration by the adversary beyond running relays, and adversarial bridges (Tor entry points not listed in the public consensus) from their adversary model. They state a "comprehensive evaluation of all potential threats against Tor is beyond the goals of this paper." They state their five user-behavior traces are "limited and somewhat artificial," each built from only 20 minutes of recorded activity replayed on a schedule. They state historical relay-congestion data does not exist for the study period, so CAT's congestion profiles are synthetic (from a separate Shadow simulation) rather than drawn from the same historical period as the relay-adversary experiments. They state hidden services and bridges are not considered. They identify, but explicitly place outside their adversary model and leave unresolved, an active attack in which an adversary already on a circuit degrades the response time of circuits it has not compromised to bias congestion-aware clients toward re-selecting compromised circuits.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A capacity-weighted relay-selection mechanism that keeps a client's entry point fixed for tens of days (Tor's guard rotation, measured here at a 30-60 day tenure) concentrates deanonymization risk on whichever party is chosen during that tenure, so any design reusing guard-style fixed-entry selection must treat the guard-rotation interval as a directly load-bearing security parameter, not a performance-only tuning knob — this paper measures that increasing it from 30 to 60 days was adopted by the Tor Project specifically to increase time to first compromise. A path-selection algorithm that reacts to observed network conditions (Congestion-Aware Tor's round-trip-time measurement) requires that congestion measurement itself be resistant to adversarial manipulation, because a relay under adversary control can manufacture apparent congestion on circuits it does not control to bias client circuit selection toward relays it does control; this paper identifies that requirement as unmet and out of scope for its own security model. A traffic-correlation-resistant overlay routed above the transport layer requires knowledge of the underlying autonomous-system and Internet-exchange-point topology to reason about correlation risk, because two Tor relays chosen for AS-level diversity can still share a network-level adversary if traffic from both traverses the same exchange point or the same multi-exchange-point-owning organization.

### Contradicts
The paper states its results show Tor users are "far more susceptible to compromise than indicated by prior work" that modeled adversaries as independent per-AS entities rather than as adversaries who might operate several ASes or exchange points simultaneously; that prior-work estimate is not evaluated as a specific figure in this batch. No other paper in this batch measures Tor guard-compromise or exit-compromise timing, so no cross-paper numeric contradiction exists in this batch. This paper's guard-compromise-dominates-exit-compromise finding is consistent with, and cites, Elahi et al.'s (ELAHI-WPES-12) argument that guard selection is the primary bottleneck to full deanonymization.

- competing: Wang, Bauer, Forero, Goldberg. "Congestion-aware Path Selection for Tor." Financial Cryptography and Data Security (FC), 2012. (the CAT algorithm this paper evaluates)
- competing/related measurement: Wacek, Tan, Bauer, Sherr. "An Empirical Evaluation of Relay Selection in Tor." NDSS 2013.

## [JOHNSON-POPETS-17] PeerFlow: Secure Load Balancing in Tor
**Citation:** Aaron Johnson, Rob Jansen, Nicholas Hopper, Aaron Segal, Paul Syverson. "PeerFlow: Secure Load Balancing in Tor." Proceedings on Privacy Enhancing Technologies (PoPETs), 2017(2):74-94. DOI 10.1515/popets-2017-0017.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://petsymposium.org/popets/2017/popets-2017-0017.pdf
**Source URL:** https://petsymposium.org/popets/2017/popets-2017-0017.pdf
**Domain:** I

### What it does
PeerFlow assigns each relay in the Tor anonymity network a voting weight proportional to the traffic it actually carries, so that Tor clients route traffic across relays roughly in proportion to real capacity — the load-balancing function — while bounding how much a dishonest relay can inflate its own weight relative to the traffic it truly relays, which is the security function. Tor clients pick relays for each three-hop circuit (guard, middle, exit) with a probability proportional to the relay's consensus weight; a relay carrying a disproportionate share of circuits gains a disproportionate ability to observe or manipulate client traffic and, when it colludes with the other relays on a circuit, to deanonymize the client with a first-last correlation attack. PeerFlow computes weight from peer measurement rather than either self-report or the centralized probe design TorFlow uses: a subset of relays (the largest fraction `µ` of relays by capacity in each circuit position, `µ=0.75`), called measuring relays, each keep an application-layer byte count of traffic exchanged with every other relay while occupying that position, over a measurement period whose length depends on the measured relay's inferred bandwidth. A relay's inferred total traffic `ρ` is derived from these peer byte-counts and reported to the Directory Authorities as an estimate, with two protections against manipulation: (1) a "liar" check comparing a relay's self-reported capacity against what its peers measured, trimming the fraction `λ` of highest-disagreement measurements; (2) calibrated Laplace-distributed noise (differential privacy, parameters `δnoise`, `ϵnoise`) added to protect the link-level privacy of which relay pairs exchanged how much traffic, since raw peer measurements would otherwise reveal circuit-level traffic patterns. A relay whose measured traffic falls below its previously-inferred capacity beyond a threshold (`ϵdec`) is placed in "probation," a weight-reduction penalty, unless it sends compensating dummy traffic. Weight changes are further bounded across successive voting periods by a maximum per-period increase factor `ϵinc = 0.25`, limiting how fast an adversary can ramp up an inflated weight even if a single measurement period is gamed.

### Measured results
Three separate empirical studies, each with its own setup:

**TorFlow liar and selective-DoS attack (Table 1).** Implemented in Tor and the authors' own Shadow discrete-event network simulator plug-in (2128 lines of code) modeling TorFlow's Python bandwidth-scanning scripts, on a private simulated Tor network of 498 relays, 4 directory authorities, 7500 clients, and 1 bandwidth authority. One arbitrarily chosen exit relay (300 Mbit/s access link) ran 3 baseline (honest) trials and 6 attack trials combining a liar attack (falsely reporting 125,000 KB bandwidth) with a selective denial-of-service attack (forwarding traffic only for TorFlow's known measurement circuits, dropping all other traffic). Median goodput fell from 22.5 MiB/s (baseline) to 0.2 MiB/s (attack) while median consensus weight share rose from 7% to 11% — a measured bandwidth-inflation factor of 177 (ratio of consensus-weight-per-bandwidth-unit between attack and baseline conditions).

**EigenSpeed framing attacks (Tables 2 and 3), analytical, using the real Tor consensus of 2015-04-31 23:00 (5589 relays with positive selection probability) as input data, not a live or simulated network run.** In the "increase framing" attack (Table 2), varying the number of trusted relays from 280 (5% of honest relays) to 1677 (30%), an adversary using at most 3% of total network bandwidth could push each targeted honest relay's "increase metric" above 0.2 (exceeding EigenSpeed's suggested threshold `∆=0.1`), framing between 112 relays (at 30% trusted) and 1118 relays (at 10-20% trusted) using between 447 and 558 added adversarial relays. In the "targeted liar" attack (Table 3), reporting a false bandwidth 15 to 100 times the honest load-balanced rate let malicious relays obtain 7.4x to 28.1x weight inflation while keeping their liar and increase metrics below the honest non-trusted relays' own values, reaching adversary weight shares of 48.5% to 98.2% of the network across the four trusted-relay-fraction settings tested.

**PeerFlow load-balancing evaluation (Shadow simulation), a private Tor network configuration built from Tor Metrics 2014-09 data at approximately 1/12 scale: 4 directory authorities, 498 relays, 7,500 clients, 1,000 servers, run for 5 virtual hours per experiment (first 2 hours discarded as bootstrapping), 3 repeated experiments per model, comparing an Ideal model (fixed weights set to true configured capacity), the authors' TorFlow simulator plug-in, and a PeerFlow prototype (1222 lines of code, forked from Tor 0.2.5.10, without probation implemented).**

| Metric | Ideal | TorFlow | PeerFlow |
|---|---|---|---|
| Median per-relay-second goodput | 199.0 KiB/s | 0.1 KiB/s | 30.1 KiB/s |
| Third-quartile per-relay-second goodput | 960.3 KiB/s | 729.5 KiB/s | 683.0 KiB/s |
| Median aggregate network goodput | 483.7 MiB/s (SD 10.2) | 437.9 MiB/s (SD 11.3) | 427.4 MiB/s (SD 11.8) |
| 75th-percentile relay bandwidth utilization | ≤61% | ≤43% | ≤49% |
| 320 KiB download, 3rd-quartile completion time | 2.00 s | 1.51 s | 1.44 s |
| Weight inaccuracy (avg. \|log10(true relative capacity / relative weight)\|) | n/a | 1.02 (SD 0.244) | 0.428 (SD 0.0381) |
| Weight imprecision (SD/mean of weight across consensuses) | n/a | 0.288 (SD 0.213) | 0.217 (SD 0.0814) |

Per-experiment result stability was checked with the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic against the pooled distribution: maximum KS 0.0604 for per-relay goodput, 0.393 for aggregate goodput, 0.0628 for utilization, 0.0461 for download times.

**PeerFlow speed and efficiency, using CollecTor historical Tor network data from the January 31, 2015, 00:00 consensus and January 2015 extra-info descriptors, 5917 relays after excluding those with zero selection probability or incomplete byte histories.** At `µ=0.75`, this yields 400 measuring guards, 749 measuring middles, and 145 measuring exits. Estimated measurement-time distribution across relays weighted by capacity: 25th percentile 11.5 hours, 50th percentile 27.7 hours, 75th percentile 70.7 hours; 96.8% of capacity-weighted relays measured within 14 days, with the remainder (low-capacity relays) requiring longer, reducible to a maximum of 316.4 hours (13.2 days) by raising the minimum bandwidth thresholds for Fast (100 KB/s to 250 KB/s) and Guard (250 KB/s to 625 KB/s) flags by 150%. Reporting bandwidth overhead to Directory Authorities: 119.6 bytes/second average per Bandwidth Authority (using the same January 2015 consensus, 4-byte statistics, `O(mn)` total traffic for `m` measuring and `n` measured relays). Dummy-traffic overhead from probation avoidance, from 3 Shadow runs per `ϵdec` setting on the 498-relay network described above: at `ϵdec=0.05` (trusted fraction `τ=0.05`), median 14 and maximum 75 relays in probation per second, averaging 2.38 KiB/s (SD 0.677) total dummy traffic across the network; at `ϵdec=0.95` (`τ=0.30`), median and maximum 1 and 10 relays, averaging 0.00328 KiB/s (SD 0.00385) — small relative to the 428.0 MiB/s median network-wide PeerFlow goodput measured in the load-balancing evaluation above.

**PeerFlow's proven security bound (Theorem 1, analytical, not measured):** for an adversary controlling voting-weight fraction `α` below trimming threshold `λ=0.256`, with measuring-relay weight fraction `µ=0.75`, per-period increase cap `ϵinc=0.25`, and noise-loss parameter `ϵloss=0.01`, the worked numerical example gives an advantage factor `γ=4.52` at `α=0` (an adversary's relative consensus weight share can exceed its relative true-traffic share by at most this factor, or else it is pushed into probation). The paper states achieving even this bounded factor requires the adversary to either send traffic in only one direction (client-side or destination-side only, without relaying any real Tor traffic — "highly observable") or to concentrate its traffic exchange on a minority-weight subset of measuring relays (also observable to Directory Authorities and clients).

### Parameters
- `µ` (measuring-relay population fraction): 0.75, used throughout the deployed-scale analysis.
- `λ` (trim fraction for disagreeing measurements): 0.256, used in the Theorem 1 numerical example.
- `ϵinc` (max per-period weight-increase fraction): 0.25.
- `ϵdec` (probation-trigger decrease threshold): varied experimentally at 0.05, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 0.95 (Table 6); paired in the text with trusted-fraction values `τ` from 0.05 (giving `ϵdec=0.90`) to 0.30 (giving `ϵdec=0.2`) for `µ=0.75`.
- `δnoise` (traffic amount covered by differential privacy): 1 MiB.
- `ϵnoise` (differential privacy guarantee): 0.1.
- `ϵerr` (targeted fraction of traffic added as noise): 0.1.
- `qerr` (probability noise exceeds targeted fraction): 0.1.
- `ϵloss` (accuracy loss from taking the max of noisy values): 0.01.
- `τ` (trusted relay weight fraction per position), used in the EigenSpeed attack analysis at 5%, 10%, 20%, 30% of honest relays.
- EigenSpeed's own suggested thresholds, evaluated (not chosen by this paper): liar-metric threshold `L=10^-5`, increase-metric threshold `∆=0.1`; the paper's attacks push both metrics past these suggested values.

### Stated limitations
The bounded advantage factor `γ` in Theorem 1 is a worst-case bound the adversary can approach only by adopting an attack pattern the paper states is "highly observable" (one-sided traffic with no real relaying, or traffic concentrated on a minority-weight subset of measuring relays) — the paper does not claim these observable patterns go undetected, only that the mechanism does not itself block them beyond the stated bound. Probation was not implemented in the PeerFlow prototype used for the load-balancing (§7) evaluation; the authors measured only when probation would trigger and the compensating dummy-traffic cost separately (§8.2), so the load-balancing goodput and download-time results do not include probation's effect on relay behavior. The private Shadow network used for evaluation is built at approximately 1/12 the scale of the public Tor network from a single month's data (2014-09), and aggregate goodput distributions varied enough across repeated runs of the same model that the maximum Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic reached 0.393 for that specific metric, the paper's own signal of higher variance for that measurement. The paper explicitly declines to benchmark EigenSpeed in the load-balancing comparison, citing that it is not deployed in practice and that the vulnerabilities detailed in the paper's own §4 make its future adoption unlikely — this is the paper's stated reason, not an independently measured deployment fact. The measurement-time analysis (§8.1) is a projection from historical byte-history data onto PeerFlow's measurement-period procedure, not a live deployment measurement — relays with low observed capacity (below Tor's stated Fast and Guard bandwidth flag thresholds) have measurement times exceeding 14 days under the analyzed parameters, addressed only by proposing (not deploying) a 150% increase to those flag thresholds. The authors state possible future improvements to PeerFlow include improving scalability and further reducing the adversary's residual ability to inflate weight, implying the current bound is not considered final by the authors themselves.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
PeerFlow requires a functioning Directory Authority infrastructure that collects, trims, and aggregates peer-submitted measurement statistics into consensus weights, and that runs the probation and per-period weight-increase-cap logic — a design with no analogous centralized aggregation point cannot apply this mechanism as specified. It requires each relay in the "measuring" subset (the largest `µ` fraction by capacity per circuit position) to keep application-layer byte counts of every other relay it directly interacts with while occupying guard, middle, or exit position, which requires the transport layer to expose per-peer, per-position byte accounting at the relay — a relay implementation lacking this instrumentation cannot supply PeerFlow's measurement input. Peer measurements themselves must be treated as privacy-sensitive: raw measurement data would reveal which relay pairs exchanged how much traffic, so any composition of this mechanism with a client-anonymity requirement needs its own differential-privacy noise-injection step (parameterized by `δnoise`, `ϵnoise`) before publishing aggregated statistics — omitting this step reopens a traffic-pattern side channel. The security bound (Theorem 1) is stated only for an adversary whose voting-weight fraction stays below the trim threshold `λ`; a design that lets a single adversarial coalition exceed `λ` loses the bound "even without any trusted relays," per the paper's own statement, meaning some other component (for example a Sybil-resistance mechanism controlling how much aggregate weight one identity can acquire) must keep any single adversarial coalition under `λ` for this bound to hold at all. The mechanism assumes voting-weight periods and measurement periods are tracked and enforced consistently across all Directory Authorities and relays — the per-period increase cap `ϵinc` and the probation state both depend on comparing a relay's current-period statistics against its own prior-period state, requiring durable per-relay history, not just current statistics.

### Contradicts
This paper's measured attack against TorFlow (177x bandwidth inflation factor, Table 1) directly supports and quantifies observations made by Bauer et al. [7] and Thill [31] that TorFlow's design is vulnerable to relays recognizing and preferentially serving measurement circuits — the paper states it "confirms this observation by implementing and experimentally testing the attacks," rather than contradicting prior work. No other paper in this corpus was found to report Tor bandwidth-measurement or EigenSpeed figures to compare against. This paper is the direct evidentiary source for the honest-bandwidth-reporting attack surface that BRIEF.md's open-problem list (item 10) identifies as unaddressed by HSkip+'s bandwidth-ordering assumption: PeerFlow's peer-measurement design is one published mitigation for that attack surface, bounding (not eliminating) an adversary's achievable weight inflation via the factor `γ` under the stated conditions, rather than assuming honest self-report as HSkip+ does.

### References worth retrieving
- **[26]** Mike Perry, "TorFlow: Tor network analysis," HotPETs — foundational, defines the currently-deployed bandwidth-scanning system this paper attacks.
- **[28]** Robin Snader, Nikita Borisov, "EigenSpeed: Secure peer-to-peer bandwidth evaluation" — foundational/competing, the peer-measurement predecessor system this paper analyzes and attacks in §4.
- **[27]** Robin Snader, "Path Selection for Performance- and Security-Improved Onion Routing" (thesis) — foundational, source of the `∆=0.1` threshold this paper's EigenSpeed attacks are evaluated against and of the eigenvector-computation stopping criterion (10^-10 change in vector norm) this paper reuses.
- **[7]** Bauer, McCoy, Grunwald, Kohno, Sicker, "Low-resource routing attacks against Tor," ACM WPES 2007 — foundational/attack, the original observation of TorFlow's liar-attack vulnerability that this paper implements and measures.
- **[31]** Fabrice Thill, "Hidden Service Tracking Detection and Bandwidth Guessing Attacks" (thesis) — attack, source of the selective-DoS technique against TorFlow's fixed measurement-circuit endpoints that this paper implements and measures.
- **[24]** Johnson, Wacek, Jansen, Sherr, Syverson, "Users get routed: traffic correlation on Tor by realistic adversaries" — foundational, the first-last correlation deanonymization attack this paper's threat model is built to defend against.
- **[19]/[20]** Jansen, Bauer, Hopper, Dingledine and Jansen, Geddes, Wacek, Sherr, — foundational, Shadow-based Tor experimentation methodology this paper's evaluation relies on.
- **[21]** Jansen, Hopper, "Shadow: Running Tor in a box for accurate and efficient experimentation" — foundational, the network simulator this paper's entire empirical evaluation (§3, §7, §8) is built on.
- **[8]** Biryukov, Pustogarov, Weinmann, "Trawling for Tor hidden services: Detection, measurement, deanonymization," IEEE S&P 2013 — attack/critique, cited for the general problem of relays detecting and favoring measurement probes.
- **[13]** Cynthia Dwork, "Differential privacy" — foundational, the privacy definition underlying PeerFlow's noise-injection mechanism (`δnoise`, `ϵnoise` parameters).
- **[12]** Dingledine, Mathewson, Syverson, "Tor: The Second-Generation Onion Router" — foundational, defines the Tor network this entire paper analyzes.

## [KAASHOEK-IPTPS-03] Koorde: A Simple Degree-Optimal Distributed Hash Table

**Citation:** M. Frans Kaashoek, David R. Karger. "Koorde: A Simple Degree-Optimal Distributed Hash Table." IPTPS, 2003. DOI 10.1007/978-3-540-45172-3_9.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://pdos.csail.mit.edu/papers/koorde:iptps03/koorde.pdf (candidate URL from registry; local file matches title/authors/abstract)
**Source URL:** https://pdos.csail.mit.edu/papers/koorde:iptps03/koorde.pdf
**Domain:** A

### What it does
Koorde is a distributed hash table (DHT) that answers a lookup for a key by contacting a number of nodes proportional to log n (n being the number of nodes in the system) while each node stores state about only a constant number of other nodes, by combining Chord's ring identifier space and join/stabilization protocol with a de Bruijn graph used for forwarding. A de Bruijn graph on a b-bit identifier space connects each node m to two other nodes, 2m mod 2^b and 2m+1 mod 2^b (written m∘0 and m∘1): each edge corresponds to shifting one new bit into m's identifier while dropping its top bit. Looking up key k from node m proceeds by repeatedly shifting the bits of k into the current address one at a time; after b such shifts, the address equals k, and the de Bruijn graph guarantees this path exists using only the two-neighbor forwarding rule, so a complete de Bruijn graph answers any lookup in exactly b hops with 2 neighbors per node.

Real deployments populate only a sparse subset of the 2^b possible identifiers, so most de Bruijn nodes are "imaginary" (unoccupied). Koorde simulates the complete-graph path across this sparse ring: each real node m keeps its Chord successor (the next real node clockwise) and one de Bruijn pointer d, defined as the real predecessor of the imaginary node 2m. A lookup step advances a simulated position from imaginary node i to imaginary node i∘topBit(k) by first jumping via the de Bruijn pointer d (a jump near address 2m) and then walking forward along successor pointers until reaching the real predecessor of the target imaginary node, correcting for the fact that the sparse population may place another real node between m.d and the exact target. Each node checks, on receiving the query, whether it truly is the predecessor of the current imaginary target; if not, it forwards along its successor pointer until a node that is. With only the single de Bruijn pointer d, a lookup takes an expected 2b successor hops plus b de Bruijn hops; maintaining one extra pointer (d's successor, for 3 pointers total per node) reduces the expected successor-hop cost per de Bruijn step to 1, giving expected total routing cost 2b. Choosing the simulated starting imaginary node's low-order bits to already match the high-order bits of the key (rather than starting from m's own identifier) reduces the number of hops needed from O(b) (where b is the full identifier-bit-length, e.g. 160 for a typical hash) to O(log n) with high probability, because the distance in identifier space from m to its successor exceeds 2^b/n^2 with high probability, leaving only the top 2·log n bits of the address needing correction.

Koorde generalizes to a base-k de Bruijn graph, connecting each node to k nodes instead of 2 (node m to km, km+1, ..., km+(k−1)), trading routing-table size (degree k) for hop count (O(log_k n)) along the same curve as the generic degree/hop-count lower bound. At k = O(log n), Koorde additionally becomes fault-tolerant: each node maintains a Chord-style successor list of O(log n) nodes (rather than a single successor) so that under independent node failure with probability 1/2, at least one list entry survives with high probability, guaranteeing routing remains possible by following live successor pointers. The equivalent backup for the de Bruijn direction cannot be built as a simple "predecessor list," because predecessor pointers can point at nodes that have begun but not completed Chord's join protocol, which would make lookups incorrect; instead, node m looks up the predecessor p of 2m−x (with x = O(log n / n) chosen so Θ(log n) real nodes fall in the interval [2m−x, 2m] with high probability) and retrieves p's Chord successor list to obtain O(log n) redundant candidates for the de Bruijn pointer, at the practical cost of needing an estimate of n (obtainable from the observed distribution of a node's own successors).

### Measured results
None. The paper is entirely analytical: every quantitative claim is a proven lemma or an asymptotic (big-O) bound, not a measured figure from an implementation or simulation run. No node count, topology, dataset, or hardware configuration is used to produce any number in this paper. The paper states an implementation exists as part of the Chord software distribution but reports no measurement from it.

### Parameters
Identifier space size: 2^b, where b is the number of bits in a node/key identifier (b set by the output length of the hash function used; not itself numerically fixed in the paper). Base of the de Bruijn graph, k: tunable from 2 (constant-degree Koorde) up to O(log n) (fault-tolerant Koorde); k=2 gives degree 2 and O(log n) hops, k=O(log n) gives degree O(log n) and O(log n / log log n) hops. Successor-list length for fault tolerance: O(log n) entries (adopted directly from Chord's successor-list mechanism). Per-node de Bruijn pointer set for fault tolerance: O(log n) candidate predecessors of 2m, obtained via a lookup offset by x = O(log n / n) from 2m. Minimum pointer state for the non-fault-tolerant base scheme: 3 pointers per node (successor, de Bruijn pointer d, and d's successor).

### Stated limitations
The paper proves (Lemma 2.2) that any network in which nodes fail independently with probability 1/2 requires some nodes to have degree Ω(log n) to stay connected with constant probability, and states that this generalizes to a network partition, treated as failure of every node on the other side. Because base Koorde has constant degree, the paper states explicitly that base Koorde "cannot be fault tolerant against nodes failing with constant probability," and fault tolerance is recovered only by moving to the degree-O(log n) variant, which gives up the constant-degree property. The paper states it is an open question (unresolved as of this paper) whether a system exists that is simultaneously degree-optimal and constant-factor load-balanced: Chord's load-balancing technique (each physical node emulating O(log n) virtual nodes) can be applied to Koorde but increases per-node state and maintenance overhead by a logarithmic factor, which the authors state undoes the optimal-degree property for both Koorde and Viceroy. The paper states it does not know whether Koorde can self-stabilize the way Chord does (Chord can quickly reconstruct all finger-table entries from successor pointers alone after churn; the paper states "it is unclear whether Koorde can similarly self-stabilize"). The authors state in the introduction that they "mostly ignore" two DHT performance measures — proximity/delay-aware routing and resilience against malicious (as opposed to simply failing) nodes — due to page limit, so the paper makes no claim about Koorde's behavior against an adversarial (as opposed to independently failing) node population. The fault-tolerant de Bruijn-pointer construction requires an estimate of n (total node count), which the paper states is "easy to achieve in practice" via the distribution of a node's successors but does not analyze or measure the accuracy of that estimate.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Koorde requires Chord's ring-maintenance machinery to already exist and function correctly: node identifiers placed on a consistent-hashing ring, a working join protocol, and (for the fault-tolerant variant) Chord's successor-list stabilization protocol, since the paper states Koorde reuses these directly rather than defining new ones. The de Bruijn forwarding step requires that each node's successor pointer be correct at query time, because the correction step (walking forward along successors when the de Bruijn pointer's target node is not the true predecessor of the current imaginary node) depends on successor-pointer accuracy; a system running Koorde therefore inherits every precondition Chord's stabilization protocol requires for successor-pointer correctness under churn. Achieving the reduced O(log n)-hop variant (Section 3.3) requires that the gap in identifier space between a node and its successor exceed 2^b/n^2 with high probability, which holds only under the assumption that node identifiers are placed independently and uniformly at random on the ring (the same assumption Chord's own analysis makes); a non-uniform identifier assignment (for example, one chosen adversarially, or one derived non-randomly for application reasons) is not covered by this bound. The fault-tolerant degree-O(log n) construction requires every participating node to be able to estimate n, the total node count, from local information (the distribution of its own successors); a system that cannot support this local estimate cannot use the fault-tolerant variant as specified.

### Contradicts
None found among the papers in this batch (W1-5). The paper's Lemma 2.1 (degree d implies Ω(log_d n) hops) is a general lower bound applicable to any structured overlay with maximum degree d, so any other structured-overlay paper in the corpus reporting O(log n) hops at O(log n) degree (e.g., Kademlia) is consistent with, not contradicted by, this bound. This paper's own statement that the Viceroy DHT provides "constant expected degree" but a high-probability degree bound of O(log n) — with "fault tolerance... not discussed in the Viceroy paper" — is this paper's characterization of Viceroy, not an independent measurement of it; retrieving the Viceroy paper directly would be needed to verify or contradict that characterization.

### References worth retrieving
- Stoica, Morris, Karger, Kaashoek, Balakrishnan, "Chord: A Scalable Peer-to-peer Lookup Service for Internet Applications," SIGCOMM 2001 — foundational (Koorde's ring, join protocol, successor-list, and stabilization mechanism are all inherited directly from Chord).
- Maymounkov, Mazières, "Kademlia: A Peer-to-peer Information System Based on the XOR Metric," IPTPS 2002 — competing structured overlay, already in corpus per BRIEF.md.
- Ratnasamy, Francis, Handley, Karp, Shenker, "A Scalable Content-Addressable Network," SIGCOMM 2001 — competing structured overlay, O(d·n^(1/d)) hops at degree d.
- Rowstron, Druschel, "Pastry: Scalable, Distributed Object Location and Routing for Large-scale Peer-to-peer Systems," Middleware 2001 — competing structured overlay.
- Malkhi, Naor, Ratajczak, "Viceroy: A Scalable and Dynamic Emulation of the Butterfly," PODC 2002 — competing structured overlay; this paper states Viceroy achieves constant expected degree but O(log n) high-probability degree and does not analyze fault tolerance — a comparison figure to verify directly.
- Saia, Fiat, Gribble, Karlin, Saroiu, "Dynamically Fault-tolerant Content-addressable Networks," IPTPS 2002 — competing/attack-resilient overlay; reports O(log^3 n) per-node state, O(log n)-hop lookups requiring O(log^3 n) messages, log N-fold data replication, and O(log^3 N)-node metadata distribution to tolerate an adversary killing any half of the nodes while disconnecting only an ε fraction of survivors — the strongest adversarial-fault-tolerance figure this paper cites from another source.
- Liben-Nowell, Balakrishnan, Karger, "Analysis of the Evolution of Peer-to-Peer Systems," PODC 2002 — foundational; defines network "half-life" and proves every node must learn about Ω(log n) other nodes per half-life for connectivity, and bounds Chord's actual maintenance traffic at O(log^2 n) per node per half-life.
- Fraigniaud, Gauron, "The Content-addressable Network D2B," CNRS Université de Paris Sud TR 1349, 2003 — competing de Bruijn-graph-based DHT, explicitly contrasted: D2B modifies node identifiers to force a de Bruijn graph and achieves only high-probability O(1) out-degree, versus Koorde's unmodified-identifier exact construction; D2B's technical report is stated to not address concurrent joins.
- Hildrum, Kubiatowicz, Rao, Zhao, "Distributed Object Location in a Dynamic Network," SPAA 2002 — related structured-overlay/routing work cited for de Bruijn-style ideas applied to DHTs, concurrent with this paper.
- Karger, Lehman, Leighton, Levine, Lewin, Panigrahy, "Consistent Hashing and Random Trees," STOC 1997 — foundational (the consistent-hashing scheme Koorde inherits via Chord).

## [KALODNER-WEIS-15] An Empirical Study of Namecoin and Lessons for Decentralized Namespace Design
**Citation:** Harry A. Kalodner, Miles Carlsten, Paul Ellenbogen, Joseph Bonneau, Arvind Narayanan. "An Empirical Study of Namecoin and Lessons for Decentralized Namespace Design." Workshop on the Economics of Information Security (WEIS), 2015.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.econinfosec.org/archive/weis2015/papers/WEIS_2015_kalodner.pdf
**Source URL:** https://www.econinfosec.org/archive/weis2015/papers/WEIS_2015_kalodner.pdf
**Domain:** E

### What it does
Namecoin gives a blockchain-secured directory that maps arbitrary user-chosen names to values, satisfying decentralization, security, and human-readable names at once (the three properties jointly conjectured impossible before Bitcoin, called Zooko's triangle). A miner majority weighted by computing power runs the same consensus protocol as Bitcoin over a forked chain, so every participant reads the same name-to-value mapping without a central directory operator. Registration uses three chain-recorded operations. NAME_NEW posts a hash commitment of the desired name from a controlled address, hiding the plaintext name so no other party can observe and register it first. After 12 or more confirmed blocks, NAME_FIRSTUPDATE reveals the name and nonce and attaches the first value; a block-chain validator checks the nonce and name hash against the earlier commitment. NAME_UPDATE, taking a prior NAME_FIRSTUPDATE or NAME_UPDATE output as input, serves three purposes depending only on where the transaction sends its output: sending to the same address with an unchanged value renews the name, sending to the same address with a new value updates the record, and sending to a different address transfers control. Ownership of a name is bound to control of the private key of a special coin (0.01 NMC in this design), so transferring the name and transferring a payment can be combined in one atomic transaction with three outputs: name plus payment to the seller, and change back to the buyer, so that either both legs settle or neither does. Names lapse if not renewed within a fixed window; a lapsed name returns to the pool available to any new NAME_NEW claim.

### Measured results
| Measurement | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Registered .bit names, snapshot | ~120,000 (196,023 active names counted separately in the value-uniqueness pass; 119,624 counted in the resolution pass) | Namecoin block chain as crawled at time of writing (2015); two separate counting passes in the paper use slightly different name-activity filters |
| Fraction squatted | at least 76% of .bit domains | Names whose value string occurs 10 or more times across the chain are classified as squatted; 34,361 unique values found among 196,023 active names |
| Domains resolving to any IP/hostname | 9,354 of 119,624 .bit domains | Only names carrying a JSON value with a DNS-style record are counted as resolving |
| Domains serving real, non-duplicate, non-squatter content | 745 -> 455 (dedup) -> 278 (non-error) -> 222 (>=15 words) -> 28 (unique, not mirroring an ICANN-TLD site) | Funnel from the 9,354 resolving domains: HTTP GET on port 80 to the front page only, 5,374 responsive; 4,629 of the 5,374 owned by 3 squatters and removed first |
| Lower bound on secondary-market transfers (atomic) | 14 transactions total (6 detected by the three-output heuristic, of which 5 overlapped with an independent implementation-quirk heuristic that separately found the same 14) | Full transaction history of the Namecoin chain to date of writing; atomic transfer defined as a single transaction moving both a name and its associated payment |
| Upper bound on squatter-to-regular-user transfers | approximately 250 transactions, stable across the tested range | Squatter threshold n swept from 5 to 25 (a value counted as squatted if it recurs n or more times); transfer counted only where a name's value moves from a squatter-associated value to a non-squatter value and an info/email field does not merely persist unchanged |
| Registration availability by name length | 1-character: 100% taken; 2-character: 100% taken; 3-character: 58.61% taken; 4-character: 1.00% taken; 5-character: 0.02% taken | Combinatorial universe of all possible names of each length computed from the Namecoin domain-name specification (bibliography entry [7]); percentage is share of that combinatorial universe already registered |
| Expiration window | 12,000 blocks originally, raised by hard fork in March 2012 to 36,000 blocks (~250 days) | Applies chain-wide; a name unmentioned in any NAME_FIRSTUPDATE/NAME_UPDATE for 36,000 blocks returns to the available pool |
| Merged-mining hash power | Namecoin holds approximately one-third of Bitcoin's hash rate, including merge-miners | Measured against Bitcoin's contemporaneous hash rate at time of writing; stated as providing resilience to a 51% attack while noting a sufficiently large Bitcoin mining pool could still carry it out |

### Parameters
- NAME_NEW confirmation wait before NAME_FIRSTUPDATE: 12 or more blocks, to let the commitment reach chain consensus before reveal.
- Special name-holding coin value: 0.01 NMC, unspendable as ordinary currency while attached to a name.
- Per-transaction fee (at time of writing): 0.005 NMC, set in client software.
- Historical network fee on NAME_FIRSTUPDATE: nonzero originally, decayed to a value that rounds to 0 by block 85,585; the paper states this was designed to deter early bulk registration while making later registration cheap.
- Expiration window: 12,000 blocks (original) then 36,000 blocks (~250 days) after a March 2012 hard fork.
- Squatting-detection threshold used for the headline figure: value recurs 10 or more times (paper states no definitive threshold exists and sweeps 5-25 for the transfer-upper-bound figure).
- Content-inclusion threshold for "real content": page carries 15 or more words, after removing duplicate mirrors and error/default pages.

### Stated limitations
The domain-content survey queried only the front page of each domain over port 80/HTTP; sites resolving only on subdomains or only over HTTPS are excluded, and content reachable only through in-page links is not counted, so the 28-domain figure is a lower bound on non-trivial unique content by the authors' own statement. Detecting non-atomic name transfers in general is stated as not possible with the available chain data, because Namecoin's client sends updated names to a new address by default, making an ordinary value update indistinguishable on-chain from a change of owner; only the squatter-to-non-squatter subclass is detectable, and that bound is explicitly conservative (an upper bound, not a count). The paper states its economic-mechanism analysis assumes a "decentralized algorithmic agent" capable of running pricing and buy-back logic without addressing the practical feasibility of implementing such an agent. Losing the private key controlling a name loses that name irrecoverably; the paper treats this as a structural cost of any ownership-based (non-expiring) naming scheme, distinct from Namecoin's actual fixed-expiration design.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A consuming application needs continuous access to a synchronized copy of the Namecoin block chain to resolve a name, because the mapping lives only in chain state, not on any server the application can query directly. Renewal is a proof obligation on the holder: a name goes back to the available pool automatically after 36,000 blocks (~250 days) without an on-chain NAME_UPDATE citing a still-valid prior UPDATE/FIRSTUPDATE, so any naming layer building on this mechanism needs its own reminder or automated-renewal process external to the chain protocol, since the protocol supplies none. Front-running resistance during registration depends specifically on the two-phase commit-then-reveal design (NAME_NEW then NAME_FIRSTUPDATE): a system that lets a value be observed and copied before commitment is confirmed reopens front-running, which the paper states is exploitable by any node observing the peer-to-peer network before a commitment is bound to a signing address. Atomic name-for-payment exchange depends on both the name and the payment being representable as inputs/outputs of the same underlying transaction format (as Namecoin's Bitcoin-derived script does); a naming system whose payment rail is a separate ledger cannot reproduce this specific mechanism without a cross-chain atomic-exchange protocol.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus batch.

### References worth retrieving
- foundational: Satoshi Nakamoto, "Bitcoin: A peer-to-peer electronic cash system" (bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf) — underlying consensus and transaction-script mechanism Namecoin forks.
- foundational: "Domain name specification," Namecoin wiki, 2015 — defines the combinatorial name universe used for the length-availability table.
- competing: J. Bonneau, J. Clark, E. Felten, J. Kroll, A. Miller, A. Narayanan, "On decentralizing prediction markets and order books," WEIS 2014 — cited as prior evidence that decentralized algorithmic agents can implement complex market logic; relevant comparison for any algorithmic-pricing primary market.
- attack/critique: Wikipedia, "Domain name front running" — cited as evidence front-running is already a live problem in conventional DNS registrar services, motivating the commit-reveal design.
- foundational: Roger Dingledine, Nick Mathewson, Paul Syverson, "Tor: The second-generation onion router," 2004 — cited for the .onion resolution target type observed in .bit domain records.

## [KAMVAR-WWW-03] The Eigentrust Algorithm for Reputation Management in P2P Networks

**Citation:** Sepandar D. Kamvar, Mario T. Schlosser, Hector Garcia-Molina. "The Eigentrust Algorithm for Reputation Management in P2P Networks." ACM WWW, 2003. DOI 10.1145/775152.775242.
**Retrieved:** full text
**Source URL:** https://nlp.stanford.edu/pubs/eigentrust.pdf
**Domain:** F

### What it does
EigenTrust assigns every peer in a peer-to-peer file-sharing network a single global trust value derived from the network's entire transaction history, then biases file-download source selection toward high-trust peers to reduce downloads of inauthentic files. Each peer i keeps a local trust value for peer j equal to the peer's own count of satisfactory transactions with j minus its count of unsatisfactory transactions. These local values are normalized per row so each peer's outgoing trust sums to 1, producing a row-stochastic matrix C. A peer forms a wider opinion by asking its acquaintances for their opinions weighted by its trust in them; iterating this process (multiplying by C-transpose repeatedly) converges to a vector independent of the peer that started it. That converged vector is the left principal eigenvector of C, and its entries are the global trust values. Convergence is guaranteed only if C is irreducible and aperiodic; the paper enforces this by mixing a constant fraction a of the probability mass at every iteration into a fixed distribution p over a small set of pre-trusted peers designated at network creation, which also accelerates convergence and defeats malicious collectives that would otherwise trap the iteration in a closed cluster. Global trust values are computed without central storage: each peer computes its own value from values reported by peers who have interacted with it, using O(1) local state per peer under limited average interaction. In the secure variant, a peer's trust value is instead computed by M separate score-manager peers located by hashing the peer's identifier into M coordinate spaces of a distributed hash table (the paper names CAN or Chord); a majority vote across the M managers' reported values overrides individual malicious managers who report false results, and a peer cannot learn or influence its own score because it cannot choose its own coordinate in the DHT.

### Measured results
| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| Global trust computation converges (residual under a stopping threshold) in fewer than 10 iterations | Simulated network of 1,000 peers, measured after 100 query cycles |
| With no reputation system, malicious peers drive inauthentic downloads up to roughly 87% of all downloads at 40% malicious population (Threat Model B); with EigenTrust active, inauthentic downloads stay around 10% regardless of malicious fraction from 0% to 70% | Simulated network: 63 good peers (3 pre-trusted) plus malicious peers scaled from 0% to 70% of total population, standard settings of Table 1 (power-law topology, TTL=7, 30 simulation cycles of 50 query cycles each, 5 runs averaged, results averaged over the last 10 query cycles) |
| Baseline inauthentic-download rate with zero malicious peers present is 5%, attributed to good peers' own file-labeling and sharing mistakes | Same simulated network, 0% malicious peers |
| Malicious peers forming a mutual-high-trust collective (Threat Model B) do not raise their global trust significantly when pre-trusted peers are present; results are close to the independent-malicious-peer case (Threat Model A) | Same base network and settings, up to 70% malicious population organized as a chain of mutual trust assignments |
| Malicious peers that camouflage by returning authentic files in f% of downloads (Threat Model C) achieve peak network damage at f=50%, producing 28% inauthentic downloads network-wide; raising f above 20% costs more authentic uploads than it gains in inauthentic downloads | Simulated network of 53 good peers (3 pre-trusted) and 20 type-C malicious peers, f swept 0% to 90% in steps of 10%, standard Table 1 settings |
| A two-role division of labor (Threat Model D: type-D malicious peers build trust by uploading only authentic files, then hand that trust to type-B peers who upload only inauthentic files) reaches 5,000 inauthentic downloads for about 400 authentic uploads by malicious peers, versus over 1,000 authentic uploads needed under the single-role camouflage strategy (Threat Model C) for the same inauthentic-download count | Simulated network of 63 good peers (3 pre-trusted) and 40 malicious peers (39% of network) split across 10 configurations from 40 type-B/0 type-D to 5 type-B/35 type-D |
| Deterministic download-source selection (always pick the single highest-trust responder) concentrates almost all system load on one peer; probabilistic selection (download probability proportional to trust value) balances load while achieving comparable suppression of inauthentic downloads | Simulated network of 20 good peers, no malicious peers, standard Table 1 settings |
| Under a virus-style threat model where a malicious peer sends one infected file per 100 requests and an authentic file otherwise (Threat Model F), the paper states EigenTrust does not eliminate the infected copies, because the 10% of download traffic reserved for peers with zero trust (the "unknown" pool for newcomers) continues to reach the malicious peer | Same simulation framework; no separate quantitative figure is given for this threat model beyond the qualitative description |

### Parameters
- Local trust value s_ij: satisfactory transaction count minus unsatisfactory transaction count between peer i and peer j
- Normalized local trust c_ij: max(s_ij, 0) divided by the sum over j of max(s_ij, 0); falls back to the pre-trusted distribution p_j when peer i has no positive experience with anyone
- Mixing constant a (fraction of probability mass injected into pre-trusted distribution p each iteration): used in Algorithm 2/3, value not given as a single fixed number in the main text — described as "some constant less than 1"
- Pre-trusted peer count in simulations: 3 (out of a network of 60-63 total peers across experiments)
- Probability that a peer with global trust value 0 (a newcomer/unknown peer) is still selected as a download source: 10%
- Number of score managers M per peer (secure variant): parameterized, not fixed to one value in the paper
- Network topology: power-law graph modeled on measured Gnutella structure
- Content distribution: Zipf distribution over 20 content categories, per-peer file counts and category interest drawn from a prior measurement study of real P2P networks
- Simulation settings (Table 1): 60 good peers, 42 malicious peers (base setting, varied per experiment), 3 pre-trusted peers, 2 initial neighbors for good peers, 10 initial neighbors for malicious and pre-trusted peers, query TTL 7, 30 simulation cycles of 50 query cycles each, results averaged over 5 experiment runs
- Good peer inauthentic-file-return rate baseline: 5% (models honest labeling/sharing mistakes)

### Stated limitations
The paper states the scheme is not secured "in the traditional sense": the secure score-management protocol only makes the probability small that a peer can misreport a score undetected, and refers the full argument to a separate technical report rather than proving it in this paper. Choosing which peers to designate as pre-trusted is stated to be "an interesting research area" left outside the paper's scope; the algorithm's guarantee of convergence and collective-breaking depends on no pre-trusted peer belonging to a malicious collective, a condition the paper does not show how to verify. Under the Sybil attack threat model (an adversary creating unbounded new identities, discarding each after one bad transaction), the paper states this exploits the 10% traffic share reserved for peers with no track record, and states the attack is countered only by adding an entry cost to new identities (e.g., a computational puzzle or CAPTCHA), a mechanism outside EigenTrust itself. Under a low-rate virus-distribution threat model, the paper states directly that EigenTrust does not eliminate the infected files it lets through, and adds that no reputation system existing at the time claims to fully eliminate corrupt files. The paper states that if a single malicious collective exceeds 40% of the network, that collective can influence global trust value assignment during computation under the majority-vote secure scheme, though the paper's own inauthentic-download experiments assume trust values are computed correctly and do not model this case.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
EigenTrust requires a pre-existing, small, out-of-band-designated set of pre-trusted peers whose trustworthiness is assumed rather than derived from the algorithm itself; the paper suggests network designers or founders fill this role but gives no verification procedure. It requires a functioning distributed hash table (CAN or Chord are named) to locate each peer's score managers by hashing its unique identifier, and depends on that DHT's own churn-handling (state handoff on departure, data replication) to keep score-manager assignments available; EigenTrust supplies no independent mechanism for this. It requires every peer to observe and locally record its own per-transaction outcomes (satisfactory or not) with every peer it has downloaded from, since local trust values are the raw input the whole aggregation is built from. It requires an entry-cost mechanism from elsewhere in the system (a computational puzzle or CAPTCHA) to bound Sybil identity creation, since the paper states this is outside what EigenTrust itself provides. The global trust computation assumes limited average peer-to-peer interaction density to keep the per-iteration computation and message count low; the paper notes that a network of unusually active peers requires artificially capping how many local trust values each peer reports to preserve this.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus as of this batch. Note for later composition checking: this paper's local trust values are derived purely from file-authenticity outcomes of direct transactions and its threat models (A through F) do not include an adversary who selectively targets which honest peers to connect to (targeted attachment), which VISWANATH-SIGCOMM-10 and ALVISI-SP-13 show is the more damaging attack model for social-graph-based Sybil defenses; EigenTrust is not itself a social-graph defense (it aggregates transaction-history trust, not a social graph), so this is a domain distinction, not a contradiction.

### References worth retrieving
- Aberer, Despotovic. "Managing Trust in a Peer-2-Peer Information System." ACM CIKM 2001 — foundational (prior P2P local-trust-value approach)
- Cornelli, Damiani, De Capitani di Vimercati, Paraboschi, Samarati. "Choosing Reputable Servents in a P2P Network." WWW 2002 — foundational/competing
- Douceur. "The Sybil Attack." IPTPS 2002 — attack (defines the Sybil attack this paper's Threat Model E targets)
- Ratnasamy, Francis, Handley, Karp, Shenker. "A scalable content-addressable network" (CAN). ACM SIGCOMM 2001 — foundational (DHT substrate for secure score management)
- Stoica, Morris, Karger, Kaashoek, Balakrishnan. "Chord." ACM SIGCOMM 2001 — foundational (alternative DHT substrate)
- Beth, Borcherding, Klein. "Valuation of trust in open networks." ESORICS 1994 — foundational (earlier transitive-trust model, described as differing in approach)
- Page, Brin, Motwani, Winograd. "The PageRank Citation Ranking." Stanford technical report 1998 — foundational (random-surfer probabilistic model this paper's global trust vector is analogized to)
- Saroiu, Gummadi, Gribble. "A Measurement Study of Peer-to-Peer File Sharing Systems." MMCN 2002 — foundational (source of the file-count and sharing-behavior distributions used in the simulation's content model)

"the pre-trusted peers are essential to this algorithm, as they guarantee convergence and break up malicious collectives"
"this is a threat scenario that is not addressed by EigenTrust"
"EigenTrust greatly reduces – but does not completely eliminate – corrupt files"

## [KANARIS-ARXIV-23] Mass Adoption of NATs: Survey and experiments on carrier-grade NATs
**Citation:** Orestis Kanaris, Johan Pouwelse. "Mass Adoption of NATs: Survey and experiments on carrier-grade NATs." arXiv:2311.04658, 2023. DOI 10.48550/ARXIV.2311.04658.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/pdf/2311.04658
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.04658
**Domain:** L

### What it does
This paper surveys techniques for establishing a direct peer-to-peer connection through a Network Address Translator (NAT), then tests one of them (the IPv8 network overlay's built-in NAT-penetration routines) between real Dutch mobile carriers on live 5G connections. A Carrier-Grade NAT (CGNAT) is a NAT operated by an Internet Service Provider (ISP) itself, translating many customers' local addresses to a shared pool of public IPv4 addresses, distinct from a home NAT that translates one household's devices; a CGNAT means the last NAT hop between a mobile device and the public Internet is outside the user's control and cannot be reconfigured through port-mapping protocols the way a home router can. The paper classifies NATs by two axes carried over from STUN (Session Traversal Utilities for NAT) and RFC 4787: mapping behavior — Endpoint-Independent Mapping (EIM, one external IP:port per internal IP:port regardless of destination) versus Endpoint-Dependent Mapping (EDM, a new external mapping per destination) — and, within STUN's four legacy categories (full-cone, restricted-cone, port-restricted-cone, symmetric), maps full-cone and both restricted-cone types to EIM and symmetric NAT to EDM. For two peers each behind an EIM NAT, the paper describes address discovery through a synchronizer/rendezvous server (the STUN role) followed by a coordinated simultaneous outbound packet exchange (puncturing) opening each side's NAT. For a peer behind an EDM NAT whose external port cannot be predicted, the paper describes brute-forcing the 65,535 possible ports, and computes that at the Netherlands' stated median download/upload speeds (~128 Mbps down, ~40 Mbps up) and a minimum encoded packet size (8-byte UDP payload plus 84 bytes of Ethernet-level overhead), a sender can transmit approximately 57,000 packets per second, so scanning all 65,535 ports against one fixed destination port takes a little over 1 second. When both peers are behind EDM NATs, neither's external port is known in advance, so the paper models the two-sided brute force as choosing a source-port/destination-port pair from 65,535² ≈ 4.29 billion combinations, and instead of exhaustive search proposes a birthday-paradox-style probabilistic attack: each side fires packets across many ports simultaneously, relying on the same collision-probability argument behind the birthday paradox (any pair among many packets can collide, not one packet against one fixed target) to find one matching pair far faster than exhaustive brute force. The paper also covers hairpinning (both peers behind the same CGNAT contact each other by routing through the CGNAT's own translation table via a discovered external address) as a fallback when direct puncturing fails, and pwnat, a technique using spoofed Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) messages to attempt to elicit an initial contact from a NATed peer without a third-party rendezvous server, which the paper's own analysis argues cannot work when a NATed client must respond to a spoofed ICMP Echo Request whose original query identifier it does not know.

### Measured results
| Result | Condition |
|---|---|
| A two-sided brute-force port scan between peers each behind an Endpoint-Dependent-Mapping (symmetric) NAT is estimated at roughly 21 hours (4,294,836,225 combinations ÷ ~57,000 packets/second) | Derived, not measured: based on the Netherlands' stated median connection speed (~128 Mbps down / ~40 Mbps up) and a minimum 8-byte UDP payload with 84 bytes of Ethernet overhead per packet |
| A birthday-paradox-style probabilistic port collision reaches 50% success after approximately 54,000 packets sent (under a second at the same connection speed), and 99.9% success after approximately 170,000 packets (a little over 3 seconds), both figures the paper attributes to a cited prior calculation, not its own derivation | Cited from references [20], [21]; conditioned on the same assumed Netherlands median connection speed |
| A live mobile-carrier NAT-traversal test using IPv8 (Tribler's overlay protocol) succeeded in establishing and holding a UDP connection between 3 of 4 tested Dutch mobile carriers (T-Mobile, Lebara, Vodafone) and failed for the fourth (Lyca Mobile), attributed to Lyca operating a Symmetric (EDM) NAT that IPv8's built-in puncturing could not penetrate | Two Android phones each on a different carrier's 5G connection running Kotlin-ipv8, plus one computer running the JVM version of IPv8; overall stated as a 75% NAT-penetration success rate across the 4 carriers tested |
| No packet loss was observed in the successful cross-carrier connections; some received packets carried invalid public keys and could not be decoded | Same live 4-carrier, 5G experiment |
| A large Dutch ISP with 25 million customers, each averaging 33,000 connections per day, would generate a per-address-and-port data-retention log of approximately 425 terabytes | Derived arithmetic example the paper gives for the storage cost of port-level data retention under CGNAT, not a measurement of an actual ISP's retained log volume |
| Google's own reported statistic: 41.93% of Google's users had adopted IPv6 as of April 23, 2023 | Cited from an external Google statistics page, 11 years after IPv6's launch, not measured by this paper |

### Parameters
- Live experiment: 4 Dutch mobile carrier SIM cards (Lyca Mobile, Lebara, T-Mobile, Vodafone), each device on 5G, running Kotlin-ipv8 on Android and the JVM build of IPv8 on one computer, exchanging preset UDP messages and holding the punctured mapping open for the whole experiment duration (duration not stated as a number).
- Assumed connection speed for the brute-force and birthday-paradox timing estimates: ~128 Mbps download, ~40 Mbps upload, described as the Netherlands' median Internet speed at the time of writing, cited to an external source.
- Assumed packet size for the throughput derivation: minimum 8-byte UDP payload, 84 bytes total Ethernet-level packet overhead, giving ~57,000 packets per second at the assumed connection speed.
- Port space per NAT side: 65,535 possible ports (2^16 − 1), giving 65,535² ≈ 4,294,836,225 combinations for the two-sided brute-force case.
- Router connection-table ceiling cited as a practical bound on the birthday-paradox approach: some routers (the paper names the Juniper SRX 300 as an example) cap active connections at 64,000, which the paper notes is close to the ~54,000-probe count needed for 50% collision probability.

### Stated limitations
The paper states pwnat "can mainly work in cases where only one of the parties is behind a NAT, not both," and gives a mechanical reason: the NATed client does not know the external query identifier a spoofed ICMP reply would need to carry, so the client's response (an ICMP Time Exceeded packet) reaches the far NAT with no matching mapping entry and is discarded by most NAT implementations. The paper states hairpinning — both peers behind the same CGNAT contacting each other via their externally discovered addresses — is "not always" supported by CGNAT implementations, leaving relaying as the only remaining option when both puncturing and hairpinning fail. The paper states full IPv6 rollout, the solution it calls ideal for eliminating CGNAT, "won't be realized soon," citing Google's 41.93% IPv6-adoption figure as evidence of a long remaining transition. The 21-hour and sub-4-second timing figures for brute-force and birthday-paradox puncturing are derived arithmetic under one assumed national-average connection speed, not measurements against real routers under load; the paper itself flags that "some routers max out at 64,000 active connections," meaning the derived timing estimates may not hold once a real router's connection-table ceiling is reached during a scan. The live 4-carrier experiment tested reachability and a fixed message exchange only; the paper reports no measurement of latency, throughput, or repeated trials, and reports only a single pass/fail outcome per carrier pair rather than a success rate over multiple attempts.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Two-sided EIM-to-EIM puncturing, as described here, requires a synchronizer or rendezvous server both peers can reach, to exchange externally observed addresses and coordinate a simultaneous outbound packet from each side; the paper states both peers must initiate communication at the same time, so the mechanism further needs a shared clock or synchronization signal between the two sides. Brute-force and birthday-paradox puncturing against an Endpoint-Dependent-Mapping (symmetric) NAT require sending large volumes of probe packets in a short window, so a system that adopts this technique needs to tolerate, or explicitly rate-limit against, the router-side connection-table exhaustion the paper itself identifies as a practical ceiling (as low as 64,000 entries on some tested-elsewhere hardware) before the probability estimates in this paper hold. Any system that wants a peer's address discovery to work through a CGNAT depends on either CGNAT hairpinning being enabled by the operator (which the paper states is inconsistent across CGNAT deployments) or a fallback relay being available for the case where hairpinning fails. The comparison of NAT categories in this paper depends on the classification scheme in RFC 4787 and the STUN specification, so a system implementing this paper's decision logic needs the same NAT-type detection this paper assumes as an input, not something it supplies itself.

### Contradicts
None found against another entry in this batch. Table II (percent unstated) reports a 3-of-4-carrier, and prose separately states a "75% success rate of NAT penetration across the four different Dutch carriers tested" — both figures agree with each other and are recorded consistently above.

### References worth retrieving
- Y. Liu, L. Chang, J. Pan, "On the performance and fairness of BitTorrent-like data swarming systems with NAT devices," Computer Networks 59, 2014 — foundational (source of the claim that NATed BitTorrent peers are disfavored and can degenerate into client-server interaction, cited in this paper's introduction).
- G. Halkes, J. Pouwelse, "UDP NAT and Firewall Puncturing in the Wild," (cited here as STACS 98, 2011, though this is the same paper as HALKES-NETWORKING-11 in this corpus, whose verified venue is IFIP Networking 2011) — foundational (predecessor field measurement of UDP hole-punching success from the same research group, already retrieved in this corpus).
- B. Ford, P. Srisuresh, D. Kegel, "Peer-to-peer communication across network address translators," USENIX Annual Technical Conference, 2005 — foundational (cited for the claim that NAT vendors will likely improve hole-punching support as major P2P applications like Voice-over-IP and gaming protocols become more common).
- S. Guha, P. Francis, "Characterization and measurement of TCP traversal through NATs and firewalls," IMC, 2005 — competing (independent NAT-traversal measurement study for TCP, the counterpart to this paper's UDP-focused treatment).
- W.-K. Jia, "PFQDN: SDN- and DNS-assisted transparent communications among behind-NAT networks," IEEE Systems Journal 17(2), 2023 — competing (a Software-Defined-Networking- and Domain-Name-System-assisted alternative approach to behind-NAT connectivity, published the same year).
- Diego Madariaga et al. — competing (measures mobile-operator quality of service via ICMP round-trip time, jitter, and packet loss; the discussion section states this paper's own future work would use similar packet-loss measurements to infer NAT types across mobile operators).
- O. Maennel et al., extended-addressing proposal (cited as reference [12], 2008) — competing (an alternative to CGNAT that repurposes 10 bits of the TCP/UDP port field to extend the IPv4 address space by limiting each host to 64 ports, discussed in Section VII as an alternative to CGNAT).
