## [KARAMSHUK-INFOCOM-15] ISP-friendly Peer-assisted On-demand Streaming of Long Duration Content in BBC iPlayer

**Citation:** Dmytro Karamshuk, Nishanth Sastry, Andrew Secker, Jigna Chandaria. "ISP-friendly Peer-assisted On-demand Streaming of Long Duration Content in BBC iPlayer." IEEE INFOCOM, 2015. DOI 10.1109/INFOCOM.2015.7218393.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/abs/1504.03536
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/1504.03536
**Domain:** K

### What it does, and what the measurement actually is
This paper does not measure a live peer-assisted deployment. BBC iPlayer, in the trace period studied, delivered every byte from traditional content-delivery-network (CDN) servers; the paper states this explicitly ("although iPlayer is currently an over-the-top streaming service using traditional CDNs"). The authors instead built an event-driven trace-driven simulator: session start times, session durations, and per-session bitrates come from a real month-long log of iPlayer accesses, but every peer-to-peer transfer, every server-offload decision, and every reported traffic-gain figure is a simulation output computed by replaying that real access log through a hypothetical peer-assisted delivery policy, not a byte actually observed moving between two clients. Any figure below drawn from this paper describes what a peer-assisted iPlayer would have saved under the stated simulation assumptions, evaluated against real user arrival and departure patterns, not what a deployed peer-assisted iPlayer measurably saved.

The simulator's mechanism: each content item (a TV or radio episode) forms its own swarm; a user session is assigned to the swarm for its item, its serving Internet Service Provider (ISP), and its streaming bitrate (peers are additionally partitioned into up to nine bitrate tiers matching iPlayer's real encoding ladder). At each simulated session start, the simulator checks whether another concurrent session in the same content/ISP/bitrate swarm has already streamed at least 10% of the item's duration; if so, that peer is assumed able to serve the new session from its own buffered content, and the transfer is counted as peer-to-peer rather than server traffic. The 10% threshold is derived from an assumed 18.7 Mbps average download bandwidth against the streamed bitrates (762 Kbps or 1500 Kbps), so that a serving peer needs to have watched only 4-8% of an item's duration to have buffered enough content to satisfy a joining peer's immediate playback need. Peer availability follows an "online while you watch" rule: a peer is assumed to remain available to upload only while it is actively playing the content, motivated by a proposed digital-rights-management mechanism (buffered content is decoded by the player only upon a server-issued permission, refreshed by periodic heartbeats, so a peer that stops watching stops being able to serve) that the paper describes but does not build or test. Peer-to-peer assignment is assumed to be centrally managed by the delivery system, following the same managed-swarming design pattern the paper attributes to Akamai's NetSession. The paper defines traffic gain as G = 1 − Ts/Tu, where Ts is total server-to-client bytes transferred and Tu is total content bytes watched; G = 0 means no offload occurred and G approaching 1 means server traffic was nearly eliminated by peer-to-peer transfer.

### Measured results
Dataset: a trace of BBC iPlayer accesses in London, September 2013 — 2.2 million users, 1.3 million distinct IP addresses, 15.9 million sessions (the paper's abstract rounds this to "over 2 million users" and "a month-long trace"; the introduction separately states "almost 16 Million sessions"). Every figure below is a simulation output computed by replaying this trace through the mechanism above, not a directly observed peer-to-peer transfer volume.

| Result | Value | Simulated condition |
|---|---|---|
| Traffic gain, single highly popular item ("Bad Education," >100K sessions in Sep. 2013) | over 90%, largely unaffected by ISP-splitting or bitrate-splitting | swarms localized per top-5 ISP, split further by bitrate |
| Traffic gain, unpopular item (~1K sessions) | below 20% in at least one top-5 ISP | ISP-localized, bitrate-split swarm |
| Traffic gain across the full content corpus, per top-5 ISP | above 50% for every one of the top 5 ISPs; up to 88% system-wide on average | daily simulation runs, ISP-localized swarms |
| Traffic gain, single popular item, with bitrate stratification vs. without | ISP-1: 0.92 without / 0.88 with; ISP-2: 0.92/0.87; ISP-3: 0.91/0.86; ISP-4: 0.86/0.78; ISP-5: 0.77/0.67 (all simulated Gsim; corresponding theoretical Gtheo values from the analytical model tracked within ~0.03-0.07 of each Gsim) | Table III, per-ISP, most popular bitrate (1500 Kbps) |
| Share of sessions on the top two bitrate tiers | 74% (paper's summary) / "over 70%" (body text) of sessions | full trace |
| Share of sessions with a nonzero difference between session max and min bitrate | 35% (so 65% of sessions hold one constant bitrate throughout) | full trace |
| Effect of the "online while you watch" assumption when relaxed to "online while downloading, then depart" | traffic gain for the most popular item studied falls to less than half its "online while you watch" value, dropping to near 30% for a top-5 ISP | download bandwidths of 10, 50, and 100 Mbps tested; peer uploads only for min(watch duration, download-completion time) rather than the full watch duration |
| Effect of a minimum-swarm-size requirement m | gain drops considerably as m rises, for the medium-popularity item tested (similar pattern reported for other items) | single-item simulation, m swept as a parameter |
| Content-item popularity skew in the trace | top 10% of items account for over 80% of trafic and sessions | full content corpus |
| ISP traffic-share concentration | top-5 ISPs together account for over 70% of trafic (any of users, IPs, sessions, or bytes); top 2 ISPs each ~24%, next two 17% and 11% | full trace |
| Content bundling: share of item combinations with a positive traffic-gain delta | 5-15% of 2-item combinations; 9-26% of 7-item combinations | all possible bundle combinations up to size 7, per ISP |
| Content bundling: average positive delta gain, when positive | does not exceed 5-7% even for large bundles | same |
| Historic caching (k most recently watched items cached locally and made available to peers): traffic-gain improvement | +3-12% with a single cached item (the last watched); gains grow with larger k; unlimited-size caches improve gain by less than 2% beyond a cache capped at k=10, because 80% of users watch 10 or fewer episodes total and average unlimited-cache occupancy stays below k=5 | per-ISP simulation, k swept from 0 to 10 |
| Historic caching: swarm capacity increase factor | roughly 10x on average versus the no-caching baseline, including for previously unpopular-content swarms | same |
| Historic caching combined with a minimum-swarm-size constraint m | up to 20% higher gain than the no-caching case at the same m; gain exceeds 50% for all top-5 ISPs even at m=10, reaching 78% for the largest ISP | per-ISP simulation, m and k both applied |

### Parameters
Simulated bandwidth for buffering-threshold calculation: average download bandwidth b = 18.7 Mbps (cited to an Ofcom UK broadband-speed report). Peer-ready threshold: a concurrent peer counts as able to serve a joining session once it has streamed at least 10% of the content item's duration. Bitrate tiers: content mapped to the closest of nine maximum bitrates in iPlayer's real encoding ladder (480, 762, 796, 800, 816, 1500, 2800 Kbps and others named as "other" in the trace). Content items studied in detail: "Bad Education" (over 100K sessions, September 2013), "Question Time" (~10K sessions), "What's to Eat" (~1K sessions). ISP scope: the top 5 ISPs by session count. Alternative peer-availability bandwidths tested for the "online while downloading" sensitivity check: 10, 50, and 100 Mbps. Cache size k swept from 0 to 10 recently watched items; an unlimited-cache condition was also tested. Minimum-swarm-size parameter m swept as an independent variable in Figures 2c and 7c (specific value range not given as text in the extracted source beyond m=10 being reported explicitly).

### Stated limitations
The authors state iPlayer, as measured, is not itself a peer-assisted system; every peer-to-peer transfer and every gain figure in the paper is a simulation output driven by a real access-pattern trace, not an observed transfer. The paper states the "online while you watch" peer-availability model is an assumption paired with a proposed enforcement mechanism (buffered content decoded only on a server-issued, heartbeat-renewed permission) that the paper describes conceptually but does not implement or test; the authors state ensuring this in practice is "straightforward" in a streaming (as opposed to selfish-download, BitTorrent-like) setting, presented as the authors' own judgment. The authors state peer assignment to swarms is assumed to be centrally managed, "similar to NetSession and other managed swarming techniques," and do not evaluate a decentralized peer-discovery mechanism. The bundling analysis explicitly states it assumes altruistic users willing to contribute bandwidth and local storage to distribute content items they may never themselves watch, and states the model does not account for the additional bandwidth required to download and share the larger bundled objects; the authors state that even their reported positive bundling deltas (up to 5-7%) could be reduced further by these unmodeled factors. The paper states its bitrate-stratification finding (two bitrates covering 70%+ of sessions, so splitting swarms by bitrate barely reduces effective swarm size) and its ISP-concentration finding may generalize to other countries with similarly concentrated ISP markets (the authors name Verizon and Comcast in the United States as an example), but this generalization is presented as the authors' own conjecture, not as a measurement made in this paper. The paper states the bundling technique's ineffectiveness and the caching technique's effectiveness are contingent on the already-high content availability the "online while you watch" model produces at this trace's scale, not established as general properties independent of that scale.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A design reusing this "online while you watch" peer-availability model requires an enforcement mechanism ensuring a peer that stops watching also stops being counted as available to serve, since the reported traffic gains collapse by more than half once peers are permitted to depart immediately after their own download completes (the "online while downloading" sensitivity test). The paper's own proposed enforcement path (heartbeat-gated decode permission tied to digital rights management) requires the client to hold decrypted content only transiently and requires the server to remain in the loop issuing per-session permissions, which is a centralized dependency any decentralized redesign would have to replace with an equivalent liveness signal. Swarm assignment by content item, ISP, and bitrate tier simultaneously requires a central or trusted component to know, for every active session, which ISP a peer is on and which bitrate it is streaming, since the simulator performs this partitioning directly; a system without a trusted network-topology or ISP-membership oracle would need a separate mechanism to approximate ISP-local peer discovery. The measured effectiveness of historic caching (a roughly 10x swarm-capacity increase from caching just the 10 most recently watched items) requires client devices to retain decrypted or re-servable copies of recently watched content after playback ends, which is a storage and re-distribution commitment beyond simply buffering the content currently being watched, and which interacts with the same digital-rights-management dependency named above. The minimum-swarm-size sensitivity results establish that any component supplying swarm formation must guarantee some minimum concurrent-peer floor per content/ISP/bitrate partition, since gain "drops considerably" once that floor rises, meaning content with too few simultaneous viewers in a given partition falls back to full server delivery regardless of the peer-assistance mechanism's other properties.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus. The paper's own comparison points are external to this corpus: it states its 88% peak system-wide gain sits between the 70% figure the authors cite for Akamai's NetSession deployment and the 87% figure the authors cite for a Conviva-based US-wide video-on-demand study, and states that Conviva's own reported gain fell from 87% to 13% once peer swarms were restricted to same-ISP, same-city peers — a substantially steeper ISP-localization penalty than this paper's own simulated ISP-friendly gains (which stayed above 50% per top-5 ISP). Neither the NetSession nor the Conviva paper is present in this corpus to verify that comparison directly.

### References worth retrieving
- Menasche, de A Rocha, Li, Towsley, Venkataramani, "Content availability and bundling in swarming systems," IEEE/ACM Transactions on Networking 21(2), 2013 — foundational (the infinite-server-queue swarm model and the bundling framework this paper directly extends)
- Zhao, Aditya, Chen, Lin, Haeberlen, Druschel, Maggs, Wishon, Ponec, "Peer-assisted content distribution in Akamai NetSession," ACM IMC 2013 — competing (the deployed managed-swarming system this paper's central-assignment assumption is modeled after, and the source of the cited 70% traffic-offload and 18% same-AS figures)
- Balachandran, Sekar, Akella, Seshan, "Analyzing the potential benefits of CDN augmentation strategies for internet video workloads," ACM IMC 2013 — competing (the Conviva-trace study whose 87%-to-13% ISP-localization penalty this paper compares itself against)
- Huang, Wang, Li, Ross, "Understanding hybrid CDN-P2P: why Limelight needs its own Red Swoosh," ACM NOSSDAV 2008 — foundational (prior hybrid CDN-P2P feasibility study by an overlapping author)
- Han, Kim, Chung, Kwon, Kim, Choi, "Bundling practice in BitTorrent: What, how, and why," ACM SIGMETRICS Performance Evaluation Review 40, 2012 — competing (reports bundled content is more available among BitTorrent seeders, a finding this paper's bundling section contrasts its own negative result against)

## [KEIZER-CSUR-24] A Survey on Content Retrieval on the Decentralised Web

**Citation:** Navin V. Keizer, Onur Ascigil, Michał Król, Dirk Kutscher, George Pavlou. "A Survey on Content Retrieval on the Decentralised Web." ACM Computing Surveys 56(8), Article 198, 2024. DOI 10.1145/3649132.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/10192317/1/3649132.pdf (candidate URL from registry; local file matches title, authors, and abstract)
**Source URL:** https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/10192317/1/3649132.pdf
**Domain:** B

### What it does
The survey classifies published and deployed mechanisms for locating and retrieving content on a decentralized web — one whose control, governance, and management are not concentrated in a single organization — into three functional layers: search engines (finding content by keyword), name registries (mapping human-readable names to content identifiers), and decentralized file systems (storing and serving the content itself, addressed by a hash-derived content identifier rather than a location). It builds a systematization framework around these three layers, each analyzed along a common set of properties: how content enters the system (curation, registration), how it is organized for lookup (indexing, resolution), how results are prioritized (ranking), how the mechanism defends itself (security, privacy), and how participants are paid for the work of maintaining it (incentives). The survey states its scope covers both peer-reviewed research proposals and running industry projects, and explicitly separates the two because industry projects generally implement complete but narrow-focus systems while research proposals generally implement one mechanism in isolation without a full deployment.

The survey's own definitional content, usable directly as fact: a peer-to-peer (P2P) network is unstructured when nodes form connections without an imposed topology (easy to build, resilient to churn, but requiring query broadcast or random walk to find content because no node can be told in advance where a given item is stored) or structured when the overlay topology is fixed by a protocol rule, most commonly a distributed hash table (DHT), in which a variant of consistent hashing assigns responsibility for each key to a specific peer and any peer can retrieve a value in a bounded number of steps (stated as usually O(log n) hops, where n is the network's peer count) — at the cost of requiring topology maintenance that is both less robust under high churn and exposed to attacks that are harder to mount against an unstructured overlay. Content identifiers (CIDs) on the decentralized web achieve verifiability without a trusted third party through one of two self-certifying constructions: hashing the content itself (so any recipient can hash the retrieved bytes and check the result against the claimed identifier), or hashing a public key whose corresponding private key signs the content (so the signature, not the content hash, proves authenticity, which allows the underlying bytes to change while the identifier stays fixed to that key). The survey states Zooko's triangle as a stated tradeoff among three naming properties — human-readability, security (a verifiable binding between name and content), and decentralization (no trusted party performs the binding) — of which any naming scheme can have at most two simultaneously; hash-based CIDs satisfy security and decentralization but not human-readability, motivating decentralized name-registries (Section 5) that attempt to add human-readable names on top via a blockchain-recorded mapping.

### Measured results
This survey performs no experiment of its own; every quantitative figure it states is drawn from a cited primary source and, per BRIEF.md rule 3, is recorded here as the survey's own reporting of that source's finding — a later reader who wants to cite the underlying number should retrieve the cited paper directly rather than cite this survey for it.

| Result (as reported by this survey, sourced from the cited work) | Conditions stated by the survey |
|---|---|
| Almost 80% of peers in the InterPlanetary File System (IPFS) DHT are hosted in commercial cloud data centers, and 95% of content stored on IPFS has at least one cloud-hosted provider | Attributed to Balduf, Korczyński, Ascigil, Keizer, Pavlou, Scheuermann, Król, "The Cloud Strikes Back: Investigating the Decentralization of IPFS," IMC 2023 |
| A Sybil-based censorship attack on IPFS succeeds once 20 or more Sybil peers are placed as the closest peers (by Kademlia's XOR distance metric) to a target content identifier, letting them intercept and ignore provider-record lookups for that identifier | Attributed to Sridhar, Ascigil, Keizer, Genon, Pierre, Psaras, Rivière, Król, "Content Censorship in the InterPlanetary File System," NDSS 2024; the survey states Sybil peer identifiers can be generated by brute force to achieve this placement |
| Only a few thousand URLs are registered in the Ethereum Name Service (ENS), and 98% of ENS names identify blockchain (e.g., cryptocurrency exchange) addresses rather than URLs, despite recent browser-extension support for ENS resolution | Attributed to Xia, Wang, Yu, Liu, Luo, Xu, Tyson, "Challenges in Decentralized Name Management: The Case of ENS," IMC 2022 |
| Namecoin, an early blockchain-based name registry, is characterized as "dysfunctional" by an independent measurement study, in contrast to ENS, whose registered-name count is reported to be rising | Attributed to Kalodner, Carlsten, Ellenbogen, Bonneau, Narayanan, "An Empirical Study of Namecoin and Lessons for Decentralized Namespace Design," WEIS 2015 (survey reference [92]) |
| DHT-based content resolution in IPFS, while bounded at O(log n) hops, accumulates enough cumulative round-trip time per hop to create a measurable performance bottleneck, which motivated IPFS's later addition of centralized, cloud-hosted content indexers that resolve a lookup in a single round trip | Attributed to Trautwein, Raman, Tyson, Castro, Scott, Schubotz, Gipp, Psaras, "Design and Evaluation of IPFS: A Storage Layer for the Decentralized Web," SIGCOMM 2022 |

No node count, topology, or hardware configuration for any of the above figures is repeated in the survey text beyond what is quoted here; obtaining the full experimental conditions for any of these five findings requires retrieving the cited paper directly.

### Parameters
The survey states no tunable numeric parameter of its own (it defines no mechanism, only classifies existing ones). It does report specific configuration facts about deployed systems as descriptive, not experimental, content: in IPFS's Kademlia DHT, provider records for a content identifier c are stored at the 20 peers whose peer IDs are closest to c by XOR distance, and a get() operation returns provider records from those 20 closest peers — this is stated as IPFS's fixed replication-factor design choice, not a result of a parameter sweep.

### Stated limitations
The survey states that, to the best of its authors' knowledge, no existing project achieves full decentralization across all of search engine, name registry, and file-system layers simultaneously ("decentralised search on decentralised data") — every industry project or research proposal it reviews retains at least one centralized component (a centralized crawler, a centralized index store, a centralized gateway, or a permissioned or hybrid resolution path). It states that most decentralized search-engine research proposals address only one search component (typically indexing or index storage) in isolation and have not addressed ranking, curation-based governance, or a full end-to-end system; it states this explicitly as an open issue ("Complete Systems," Section 4.7.2) rather than a solved problem understated elsewhere. It states that claims of superior privacy or security for decentralized search "have not been shown in practice, as new attacks may arise in a new infrastructure," and calls for dedicated security analyses rather than treating decentralization itself as a security guarantee. It states that decentralized name-registries built on blockchains have not addressed key-loss, key-compromise, or key-revocation handling, and that threshold-signature-based ownership verification (multiple keys required to control a name) has not been implemented in the blockchain-based systems it surveys, in contrast to prior peer-to-peer social/personal naming literature that has considered the problem. It states that decentralized file systems exhibit "a trend toward centralisation" driven by three separate pressures — performance (DHT lookup latency, addressed by adding centralized cloud-hosted indexers), content-moderation requirements (addressed by a single company, Protocol Labs, centrally curating a public "bad bits" blocklist that other IPFS operators may or may not consult), and reliability — and states that little is known about the moderation process used to build that blocklist or about how widely other node operators actually apply it. It states that privacy for both content readers and content providers in decentralized file systems has been "mostly overlooked" by currently deployed systems, and that the strongest published defense it reviews (Backes, Goldberg, Kate, Toft's threshold-cryptography DHT query-privacy scheme) "requires significant overhead to content retrieval," presenting an unresolved performance/privacy tradeoff. It states that mutable (updatable) content is fundamentally in tension with hash-of-content addressing, because any content change necessarily changes a content-hash-derived identifier; the survey's stated partial mitigation (hash-of-public-key naming, as in IPNS) solves identifier persistence but not the separate problem of guaranteeing that a lookup on a persistent name returns the current version rather than a stale cached one, which the survey states remains an open problem even with version-number suffixes, because a reader has no way to know what the current version number actually is without an out-of-band source.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
As a survey, this paper does not itself impose requirements on a system built to its recommendations, but its classification of the mechanisms it reviews makes explicit several composition requirements a designer must satisfy to use them. Content-addressed storage (self-certifying CIDs) requires that any component providing a "current version" or "latest state" abstraction over that storage supply its own separate identifier-to-version mapping, because the survey states the content-hash-derived identifier itself cannot serve this role: a content hash changes on every update, so name persistence for mutable content requires layering a public-key-based naming scheme (or an external name-registry) on top of raw content addressing. Kademlia-DHT-based provider-record storage (as used by IPFS) requires that the DHT's key space have peer identifiers distributed independently and unpredictably of any single actor's control, because the Sybil-based censorship attack the survey cites (Sridhar et al.) succeeds specifically by placing enough attacker-controlled peer IDs near a target content identifier's XOR-distance neighborhood; a system adopting unmodified closest-20-peer provider-record storage inherits this precondition and its associated attack surface. Privacy-preserving retrieval via double-hashing (using hash(CID) rather than CID as the DHT lookup key, per Michel) requires that only parties who already know the plaintext CID be able to compute the lookup key, which in turn requires the CID itself to have reached the requester through some channel outside the DHT lookup being protected — the survey does not describe such a channel, so a system adopting this mechanism must supply one. NAT (Network Address Translation) traversal via a relay peer with a public IP (as IPFS implements) requires that some fraction of the network's participants hold public, reachable IP addresses to serve as relays, since the survey states this is how IPFS bootstraps communication between two NAT'ed peers, using standard hole-punching once a relay is found.

### Contradicts
None found among the papers in this batch (W1-5); this survey does not measure any system in this batch directly and states no figure that conflicts with the entries above. Internally, the survey's own description of "early P2P networks surviving on altruism" before "eventually fail[ing] to reach their full potential, partially due to the absence of incentives" is presented without a specific measured citation attached to the failure claim in the passage itself (Section 3.3) — this is the survey's own unattributed generalization and should not be treated as a measured fact from a specific paper without checking reference [119] (Krishnan, Smith, Telang, cited nearby) directly.

### References worth retrieving
- Balduf, Korczyński, Ascigil, Keizer, Pavlou, Scheuermann, Król, "The Cloud Strikes Back: Investigating the Decentralization of IPFS," IMC 2023 — independent measurement, holds the 80%-cloud-peers/95%-cloud-provider IPFS centralization figures cited above; retrieve for full methodology and node/content sample sizes.
- Sridhar, Ascigil, Keizer, Genon, Pierre, Psaras, Rivière, Król, "Content Censorship in the InterPlanetary File System," NDSS 2024 — attack paper, holds the 20-Sybil DHT-censorship attack and its proposed detection/mitigation mechanisms in full.
- Xia, Wang, Yu, Liu, Luo, Xu, Tyson, "Challenges in Decentralized Name Management: The Case of ENS," IMC 2022 — independent measurement, holds the ENS URL-count and 98%-blockchain-address figures in full, plus other stated ENS security/squatting findings.

- Trautwein, Raman, Tyson, Castro, Scott, Schubotz, Gipp, Psaras, "Design and Evaluation of IPFS: A Storage Layer for the Decentralized Web," SIGCOMM 2022 — foundational/independent measurement of IPFS performance, source of the DHT-resolution-latency-bottleneck finding.

## [KEIZER-MOBIHOC-20] Rewarding Relays for Decentralised NAT Traversal Using Smart Contracts
**Citation:** Navin V. Keizer, Onur Ascigil, Ioannis Psaras, George Pavlou. "Rewarding Relays for Decentralised NAT Traversal Using Smart Contracts." ACM MobiHoc, 2020. DOI 10.1145/3397166.3412799.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/10108564/
**Source URL:** https://doi.org/10.1145/3397166.3412799
**Domain:** L

### What it does
This paper supplies unreachable peers (those behind a Network Address Translator, NAT, that ordinary hole punching cannot traverse) with a relay path staffed by other network participants, using an Ethereum smart contract to enforce that a relay is compensated in proportion to the service it actually delivers, without a centralized relay operator. The mechanism has three parts. First, Proof of Timely Relay (PoTR): a client C selects two relay nodes for one relay session, a working relay R_A that forwards the actual data and a check node R_C used only for verification. A peer P sending data to C sends the payload through R_A and, at the same time, sends a hash of the data chunk plus a transmission-start timestamp to R_C, which forwards that hash-and-timestamp to C separately; C compares the hash-and-timestamp report against what R_A actually delivered to detect added delay, altered data, or dropped packets, without trusting R_A's own report of its performance. Second, a smart contract deployed on the Ethereum blockchain records a negotiated agreement between C and R_A — a minimum Quality-of-Service (QoS) threshold (drawn from latency, packet-drop rate, or throughput), an evaluation-interval length, a deposit from C that funds the relay credit, a payment-rate function mapping observed QoS to a payment amount, and a timeout duration — and both C and R_A submit a mutual trust score (1 for satisfactory, 0 otherwise) to the contract when the agreement terminates; the contract releases payment to R_A and returns the remaining deposit to C only once both trust scores are recorded, so refusing to submit a score blocks payment for both sides and creates an incentive for both parties to participate honestly in scoring. Third, a reputation system built from the trust-score history stored on-chain: any node can query the blockchain for another node's prior transaction count, trust scores, contract duration, and QoS scores, and each node applies its own local scoring policy over these historic values to rank candidate relays before contracting one, rather than relying on a globally computed or centrally published reputation number.

### Measured results
| Result | Condition |
|---|---|
| A 1:4:5 weighted combination of QoS score, trust score, and duration score outperformed every single-metric scoring policy (trust-only, QoS-only, duration-only) and random relay selection, at every tested malicious-node percentage in the network, measured as the ratio of malicious relays picked to total relays picked | PeerSim simulator, 100,000 simulated nodes, malicious-node percentage varied from 10% to 100% in the reported figure, historic transaction counts drawn from a Zipf distribution with a higher exponent for malicious nodes than for honest nodes (modeling malicious nodes as having fewer prior transactions on average), neighbor sample size k=5 per simulation cycle |
| Using more historic transactions in the combined 1:4:5 scoring function reduced the malicious-pick ratio up to a point (roughly 10-20 transactions), beyond which the ratio began rising again, attributed to averaging over a period long enough to lose sensitivity to a relay's current behavior | Same 100,000-node PeerSim simulation, combined 1:4:5 scoring function, malicious-node percentages of 10%, 20%, and 30% reported, transaction-count window swept from 0 to 150 |
| The reputation system stabilized to a malicious-pick ratio under 10% within 5 simulation cycles from inception (no prior transaction data), and after the maliciousness of some nodes was redistributed at cycle 20 and again at cycle 40, restabilized within 10 cycles to a malicious-pick ratio slightly above the pre-redistribution level | Same 100,000-node simulation, 40% of nodes malicious, all nodes starting with zero transaction history, an unsatisfactory relay remembered as unsatisfactory for one round before being eligible again |
| Smart-contract gas costs measured per function, on a private Ganache virtual blockchain (not the Ethereum public mainnet), Solidity implementation, priced using Ethereum Gas Station GWEI/GAS estimates and the USD/ETH conversion rate as of April 2020: deploy contract 1,738,464 gas ($1.34-$2.68 depending on transaction speed); start relay agreement 231,292 gas ($0.18-$0.36); terminate agreement (client side) 48,440 gas ($0.04-$0.07); terminate agreement (relay side) 78,980 gas ($0.06-$0.12); timeout 62,281 gas ($0.05-$0.10); submit trust score (client) 65,173 gas ($0.05-$0.10); submit trust score (relay) 95,970 gas ($0.07-$0.15); extend relay agreement 34,219 gas ($0.03-$0.05) | Private virtual blockchain (Ganache), Remix IDE for contract interaction, gas priced at slow/medium/fast transaction speeds using April 2020 GWEI/GAS and USD/ETH rates |
| The paper concludes overall client contract cost is approximately $0.40-$0.60 and relay cost approximately $0.10-$0.20, excluding the one-time, rarely repeated contract-deployment cost | Derived from the per-function gas-cost table above, assuming a client stays with a trusted relay over time rather than repeatedly re-contracting |
| Prior research (cited, not measured in this paper) found hole punching succeeds 60% of the time for TCP and 80% of the time for UDP | Cited to reference [19], Srisuresh, Ford, Kegel, RFC 5128, 2008 — an external figure, not a result of this paper's own experiment |
| Estimated fraction of NAT-behind nodes in two deployed P2P networks, cited from external sources: at least 86.8% of Bitcoin nodes and 52.2% of IPFS (InterPlanetary File System) nodes | Cited to references [6] (Henningsen et al., "Mapping the Interplanetary Filesystem," 2020) and [20] (Wang and Pustogarov, "Towards Better Understanding of Bitcoin Unreachable Peers," 2017) — external figures, not measured in this paper |

### Parameters
- PeerSim simulation network size: 100,000 nodes, each with a boolean maliciousness flag; all nodes act as both client and relay.
- Neighbor sample size per discovery cycle: k=5.
- Combined scoring function ratio found best-performing: 1:4:5 (QoS:trust:duration).
- Trust score values: binary, 1 (satisfactory) or 0 (unsatisfactory); a node scored 0 does not go negative, to remove any advantage from leaving and rejoining with a new identity.
- Smart contract negotiated parameters per agreement: minimum QoS promise (from latency, packet-drop rate, or throughput), evaluation-interval time, deposit amount, payment-rate function parameters, timeout duration — none given fixed numeric defaults in the paper; the paper states these should be application-specific and leaves their concrete selection to the developer or to future work.
- Payment-rate function: proposed as a negative exponential function of QoS score, with the paper stating it leaves the specific function parameters and further exploration to future work.

### Stated limitations
The paper states the system requires network synchrony — constant blockchain monitoring by both parties — as a drawback of using the smart contract as a mediating trusted third party, and simplifies its own analysis by assuming all nodes maintain a stable connection to the Ethereum blockchain. The paper states the payment-rate function is left largely unspecified: "due to space limitations we leave the further details of the payment rate functions for the future work." The dishonest-scoring attack (a node scoring another dishonestly to reduce a competitor's reputation) is analyzed only qualitatively; the paper states there is "no direct loss" for scoring dishonestly under the current design and explicitly defers "further exploration of this mechanism and trade-off for future work." Peer discovery — how an unreachable client actually locates nearby candidate relay nodes before applying the reputation scoring — is stated as unimplemented: the paper lists flooding, location-based server registration, and application-level anycast as options and states "further details of this is left for future work." The paper's cost evaluation was run on a private virtual blockchain (Ganache), not Ethereum mainnet, and the reported USD costs are pinned to April 2020 Ether-to-USD conversion rates and gas-price estimates, which the paper does not claim generalize to other periods. The paper states relay selection under the proposed system, in the best case, should outperform centralized relay solutions in latency, but reports no direct latency measurement against a centralized-relay baseline — the claim is stated as a design goal in Section 3, not validated as a measured result in Section 5.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The Proof of Timely Relay mechanism requires the client to have simultaneous, independent contact with two separate relay-capable nodes for every relay session — a working relay and a check node — so a network with too few reachable, relay-capable nodes near a given client cannot supply the second, independent verification path this mechanism depends on. The smart-contract payment-release logic requires both parties to submit a trust score before either receives its settlement, so a system adopting this mechanism must accept that an unresponsive party blocks payment until the stated timeout duration elapses, at which point only the calling party's payment is settled and the unresponsive party automatically receives a negative trust score. The reputation system requires an append-only, publicly queryable transaction ledger (a blockchain) recording every past agreement's negotiated parameters and both parties' trust scores, so any system without persistent, tamper-evident, publicly readable transaction history cannot reproduce this reputation mechanism as described. Because gas costs are incurred per on-chain function call, the paper's cost model assumes clients contract with the same relay repeatedly over time rather than renegotiating per transfer; a usage pattern with frequent relay switching would incur the deployment- and agreement-setup gas costs more often than this paper's cost estimate assumes. The threat model assumes malicious actors are rational (motivated by resource gain, principally bandwidth oversubscription, rather than by an intent to damage the network at a loss to themselves); the paper's own security analysis states this assumption explicitly and does not evaluate the system against an irrational or purely destructive adversary.

### Contradicts
None found against another entry in this batch. The hole-punching success figures this paper cites (60% TCP, 80% UDP, attributed to RFC 5128) are external citations, not this paper's own measurement, and are not compared against HALKES-NETWORKING-11's own field-measured hole-punching success rates in this entry; a synthesis step that wants a single hole-punching success figure should compare RFC 5128's cited numbers against HALKES-NETWORKING-11's directly measured rates rather than treating them as the same measurement.

- Bryan Ford, Pyda Srisuresh, Dan Kegel, "Peer-to-Peer Communication Across Network Address Translators," USENIX Annual Technical Conference, 2005 — foundational (the paper this one cites for the general NAT-traversal problem framing).
- P. Srisuresh, B. Ford, D. Kegel, "State of Peer-to-Peer (P2P) Communication across Network Address Translators (NATs)," RFC 5128, 2008 — foundational (source of the cited 60% TCP / 80% UDP hole-punching success figures).
- Mainak Ghosh, Miles Richardson, Brian Ford, Rob Jansen, "A TorPath to TorCoin: Proof-of-Bandwidth Altcoins for Compensating Relays," HotPETs, 2014 — competing (an alternative cryptocurrency-based incentive scheme for relay bandwidth, cited in Related Work as a prior approach this paper distinguishes itself from).

- William B. Norton, Jonas Simanavicius, "A Blockchain-backed Internet Segment Routing WAN (SR-WAN)," 2019 — competing (a smart-contract-based bandwidth-sharing system for routing, cited as related work).

## [KENIAGIN-SIGMETRICS-25] CertainSync: Rateless Set Reconciliation with Certainty
**Citation:** Tomer Keniagin, Eitan Yaakobi, Ori Rottenstreich. "CertainSync: Rateless Set Reconciliation with Certainty." Proceedings of the ACM on Measurement and Analysis of Computing Systems (SIGMETRICS), 2025. DOI 10.1145/3727110.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.08314
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.08314
**Domain:** D

### What it does
CertainSync reconciles two sets held by two participants — recovers their symmetric difference (the elements each side holds that the other does not) — with probability 1 of success and without either side estimating the symmetric difference size beforehand, unlike prior IBLT-based reconciliation schemes (Invertible Bloom Lookup Table — a fixed-size array of cells, each holding a count, an XOR of inserted keys, and an XOR of inserted key hashes, that supports listing back the inserted elements by repeatedly locating a cell holding exactly one element) whose listing step succeeds only with a probability that depends on a size estimate supplied in advance. Participant 1 builds an IBLT over its set using a "d-decodable rateless matrix" — a matrix defining which cells each element maps to, whose leading i-row submatrix is guaranteed to support successful listing whenever the symmetric difference size is at most i, for every i up to d — and transmits the matrix's rows as IBLT cells in order, in rounds. After each round, participant 2 subtracts its own IBLT (built with the same rows) from the received cells and tries to list the resulting symmetric-difference IBLT; if listing does not fully succeed, participant 2 requests more rows rather than guessing a target size, and stops requesting once listing succeeds. The scheme provides three interchangeable rateless matrix constructions differing in decoding-row growth pattern: EGH (initials of Eppstein, Goodrich, and Hirschberg, from a group-testing method built on the Chinese Remainder Theorem), OLS (Orthogonal Latin Square — an n-by-n grid construction used because two such grids can be superimposed with each symbol-pair appearing exactly once), and Extended Hamming (rows built from a parity-check matrix used in error-correcting codes). Because the reconciliation guarantee's communication cost grows with the universe size (the count of all possible elements, not just those held by either side), the paper adds UniverseReduceSync, which first hashes every element into a smaller reduced universe using a per-round salt agreed between participants, runs CertainSync inside that reduced universe, and repeats in further rounds with a smaller residual difference whenever the reduced-universe hashing produced a collision that hid an unresolved pair.

### Measured results
| Result | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Decoding accuracy vs. communication overhead, small symmetric difference | At |Δ| = 3, CertainSync EGH, CertainSync Extended Hamming, and Rateless IBLT reach listing success probability 1 at the lowest, comparable communication overhead; CertainSync OLS and Difference Digest need close to double that overhead | Universe size n = 10^6, 10 independent trials per scheme, receiver set = full universe, sender set built by removing |Δ| random elements from receiver's set, 192-bit (24-byte) IBLT cells (8-byte counter, 8-byte xorSum, 8-byte checkSum) across all compared schemes |
| Decoding accuracy vs. communication overhead, medium symmetric difference | At |Δ| = 100, Rateless IBLT is most efficient, CertainSync EGH close behind; CertainSync OLS and Difference Digest need roughly 10x the overhead of the former two to reach probability 1 | Same setup, n = 10^6 |
| Decoding accuracy vs. communication overhead, large symmetric difference | At |Δ| = 1000, Rateless IBLT converges to success probability 1 as cell count approaches 1.35·|Δ|; CertainSync OLS is comparable at lower probabilities; CertainSync EGH needs about 4x Rateless IBLT's overhead; Difference Digest is worst, near CertainSync EGH's overhead | Same setup, n = 10^6 |
| Communication overhead vs. universe size, small difference | At |Δ| = 3, Rateless IBLT and CertainSync EGH/Extended Hamming grow near-constantly with n and need the least overhead; CertainSync OLS grows proportional to ⌈√n⌉; Difference Digest is worst due to sending a size-estimator first | n swept 10^3 to 10^7, |Δ| = 3, 10 trials per point |
| Communication overhead vs. universe size, near OLS's bound | At |Δ| = 30, approaching OLS's theoretical maximum |Δ_max| = ⌈√1000⌉ = 32 for the minimal tested n = 1000 | n swept 10^3 to 10^7, |Δ| = 30 |
| Rateless IBLT baseline overhead (measured, cited to Yang, Gilad, Alizadeh 2024) | Between 1.35·|Δ| and 1.72·|Δ| bits on average, converging to 1.35·|Δ| for larger |Δ| | Simulation matching the same |Δ| sweep, n = 10^6, confirming Rateless IBLT's O(|Δ|) complexity is independent of n |
| CertainSync EGH scaling with |Δ| | Comparable overhead to Rateless IBLT up to |Δ| = 100, then linear growth (O(|Δ|^2) theoretical), becoming the worst scheme at |Δ| > 1000 among those compared, needing about 4x Rateless IBLT's overhead there | Same n = 10^6 sweep |
| CertainSync OLS scaling with |Δ| | Worse than CertainSync EGH for |Δ| ≪ ⌈√n⌉ = 1000 because of its ⌈√n⌉-dependence; overtakes EGH in overhead-efficiency as |Δ| approaches 1000, and its incremental (per-added-element) overhead exceeds Rateless IBLT's near |Δ|_max = ⌈√10^6⌉ = 1000 | Same n = 10^6 sweep |
| Graphene overhead (measured, cited to Ozisik et al. 2019, their Eq. 3) | Up to 20% above its own true minimum cost for small |Δ|, converging to O(|Δ|) for larger |Δ| | Same |Δ| sweep, n = 10^6 |
| UniverseReduceSync vs. CertainSync communication overhead over time | UniverseReduceSync EGH consistently needs the least overhead, unaffected by the collision-threshold parameter δ tested at δ = 1 and δ = 100; CertainSync EGH consistently needs the most, also unaffected by δ; UniverseReduceSync OLS's overhead decreases as δ rises from 1 to 100 | 15-minute window from a 60-minute real Ethereum Sepolia testnet trace of two non-peered Geth/Prysm nodes' transaction pools (TxPools), collected November 27, 2024; symmetric difference size ranged roughly 700-950 transactions across the 15 minutes; UniverseReduceSync cells: 8-byte counter + 32-byte xorSum + 32-byte checkSum = 576 bits; CertainSync cells: 3 x 8-byte fields = 192 bits |
| Ethereum TxPool composition observed | Queued transactions stayed close to the configured cap of 1024; pending transactions stayed around 5000, against a configured cap of 5120 | Same Sepolia testnet trace, Geth client 1.14.11-stable-f3c696fa, default txpool.globalslots = 1024, txpool.globalqueue = 5120, txpool.lifetime = 3 hours, observed over the full 60-minute collection window |

### Parameters
- IBLT cell size in the schemes-comparison experiments (Section 5): 192 bits (three 8-byte fields: counter, xorSum, checkSum), held fixed across all compared schemes for fair comparison.
- IBLT cell size in the Ethereum blockchain experiments (Section 6): CertainSync uses 192-bit cells (8-byte reduced-hash fields); UniverseReduceSync uses 576-bit cells (32-byte original-hash fields), because UniverseReduceSync's xorSum/checkSum carry full 256-bit transaction hashes while CertainSync's carry 64-bit reduced hashes.
- Universe size n: swept 10^3 to 10^7 for the universe-size experiments; fixed at n = 10^6 for the accuracy and scalability experiments; n = 2^256 for raw Ethereum transaction hashes before universe reduction.
- Symmetric difference size |Δ|: swept 1 to 10^4 for scalability experiments; fixed at 3, 100, and 1000 for the three accuracy panels; 700-950 in the live Ethereum trace.
- Collision threshold δ (UniverseReduceSync): tested at δ = 1 and δ = 100; the reduced universe size is derived as n_r = ⌈m(m-1)/(2δ)⌉, where m = |S1| + |S2| upper-bounds the union size.
- Number of trials: 10 independent trials per scheme per configuration in the synthetic (non-blockchain) experiments, averaged.
- Rateless-matrix decodability bound d: EGH is (d+1)-decodable for the tested d; OLS is ⌈√n⌉-decodable; Extended Hamming is fixed at 3-decodable, so its maximum recoverable symmetric difference size |Δ|_max = 3 regardless of n.
- Maximum symmetric difference size supported: EGH — n (unbounded up to universe size); OLS — ⌈√n⌉; Extended Hamming — 3 (stated as the reason Extended Hamming is inapplicable to UniverseReduceSync, whose whole purpose is handling variable, potentially larger differences).

### Stated limitations
The paper states as future work, not solved here: constructions for CertainSync beyond EGH, OLS, and Extended Hamming, drawn from combinatorial or recursive designs; reconciliation of more than two sets at once (multi-party set reconciliation) with the same certainty guarantee; and measurement of total reconciliation time (as opposed to communication-overhead bits) against baseline schemes under real-world conditions including high network churn — the paper explicitly did not measure wall-clock reconciliation time or churn effects. CertainSync OLS and CertainSync EGH each have a construction-specific regime where they are markedly less efficient than Rateless IBLT (OLS for |Δ| far below ⌈√n⌉, EGH for |Δ| above roughly 100-1000 depending on n), so no single CertainSync construction dominates across all symmetric-difference-size ranges — the paper frames this as construction choice depending on expected |Δ| range (Table 2), not as a solved unified scheme. UniverseReduceSync introduces possible hash collisions between elements in the reduced universe, which the basic CertainSync framework does not have, and requires multiple synchronization rounds (unbounded, collision-dependent) instead of CertainSync's exactly one round; the paper labels this trade-off explicitly in Table 3 rather than resolving it. UniverseReduceSync also requires parametrization (the collision threshold δ) and an estimation step for the reduced universe size, which is exactly the class of complexity CertainSync itself was designed to avoid.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Both participants must independently construct their own IBLTs using the identical rateless matrix (same construction type and same row ordering) before any subtraction step is meaningful, since the symmetric-difference IBLT is obtained only by subtracting two IBLTs built under the same element-to-cell mapping. The receiving participant must be able to attempt listing after each round and to signal "send more rows" or "stop" back to the sender — the protocol is inherently interactive (round-based), not a one-shot cell transmission, which requires a return channel from the participant that already holds the full universe (or superset) to the one sending IBLT cells. The paper's core experiments (Section 5) assume a "typical case" where one participant's set is a superset of the other's, simplifying symmetric-difference computation to element removal; Section 6 (the Ethereum experiments) states this simplifying assumption is not used there, indicating the general two-arbitrary-sets case is handled by the framework but was validated in the arbitrary-overlap form only on the blockchain workload, not in the controlled Section 5 experiments. UniverseReduceSync requires both participants to derive the same per-round hash salt from an agreed pseudorandom number generator, so the two sides must already share a synchronized seed or generation protocol before any reduced-universe round runs; without that shared salt, the two sides would hash elements into different reduced universes and no valid difference could be computed. The Fully Sync Verifier step in UniverseReduceSync reads the sign of the IBLT counter in each pure cell to determine which side an element originated from, so the underlying IBLT counter field must be able to go negative (subtraction, not just addition) — a plain non-negative counter representation would not support this verification step.

### Contradicts
None found — no other entry in this batch measures IBLT-based reconciliation communication overhead against this experimental setup. Note for cross-corpus checking: this paper's baseline figures for Rateless IBLT (Yang, Gilad, Alizadeh, ACM SIGCOMM 2024) — overhead between 1.35·|Δ| and 1.72·|Δ| bits, converging to 1.35·|Δ| — are cited from that paper's own theoretical result, not independently re-derived by Keniagin et al., so a future entry for Yang et al. should confirm this figure against the primary source before it is treated as doubly-verified.

## [KERANEN-RFC-18] Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE): A Protocol for Network Address Translator (NAT) Traversal
**Citation:** Ari Keränen, Christer Holmberg, Jonathan Rosenberg. "Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE): A Protocol for Network Address Translator (NAT) Traversal." IETF RFC 8445 (obsoletes RFC 5245), 2018. DOI 10.17487/RFC8445.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8445
**Source URL:** https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8445
**Domain:** L

### What it does
This document specifies a procedure two network agents (endpoints, called L and R) use to discover which pair, among many possible pairs of network addresses, actually lets them exchange UDP (User Datagram Protocol) traffic directly or through a relay, without either agent knowing in advance what kind of Network Address Translator (NAT) or firewall sits in its path. Each agent first gathers candidates: a host candidate is a transport address (an IP address and UDP port) taken directly from a local network interface; a server-reflexive candidate is the address a Session Traversal Utilities for NAT (STUN) server observes as the public-side translation of that interface's address, learned by sending the STUN server a Binding request and reading the mapped address the server reports back; a relayed candidate is an address allocated on a Traversal Using Relays around NAT (TURN) server, obtained by sending that server an Allocate request, which returns both a relayed address and (in the same response) a server-reflexive address. A fourth type, a peer-reflexive candidate, is discovered only later, when a connectivity check itself arrives from a source address neither side had previously listed. Each agent exchanges its complete candidate list with the other agent over a signaling channel outside ICE's own scope (for example, Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) offer/answer exchange), forms every possible local-candidate/remote-candidate pair, assigns each pair a priority, sorts the pairs into a per-stream ordered list called a checklist, and works down the checklist sending a STUN request from the local candidate to the remote candidate of each pair (a connectivity check) — a pair whose check receives a valid STUN response becomes a valid pair, and one or more valid pairs are then nominated for the actual data exchange between the client acting as controlling agent and the other acting as controlled agent.

The candidate priority (Section 5.1.2.1) is computed as `priority = (2^24) * (type preference) + (2^8) * (local preference) + (2^0) * (256 - component ID)`, where type preference is an integer from 0 to 126 that must be identical for every candidate of the same type and different across types (the RFC's recommended values are 126 for host, 110 for peer-reflexive, 100 for server-reflexive, 0 for relayed), local preference is an integer from 0 to 65,535 distinguishing multiple candidates of the same type (set to 65,535 when only one interface address exists), and component ID is an integer from 1 to 256 identifying a sub-stream (for example, Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) is component 1, Real-time Transport Control Protocol (RTCP) is component 2, when the two are not multiplexed onto one component). The candidate-pair priority (Section 6.1.2.3), used to sort the checklist, is `pair priority = 2^32 * MIN(G,D) + 2 * MAX(G,D) + (G>D ? 1 : 0)`, where G is the priority of the candidate offered by the controlling agent and D is the priority of the candidate offered by the controlled agent — this formula gives an identical pair priority to both agents regardless of which one computes it, because MIN and MAX do not depend on which side is which, up to the tie-breaking term that always favors the controlling agent's higher contribution.

### Measured results
This document is a normative protocol specification, not an experimental study; it reports no dataset, testbed, or trial with sample size, and every number in the sections below is a specified default or a formula parameter, not a measured outcome. The RFC does state two derived (not measured) bandwidth estimates as illustrative arithmetic:

| Figure | Basis | Condition |
|---|---|---|
| One STUN request/response pair for a basic voice call is a 20-byte request and a 28-byte response | Stated protocol-message sizes, not measured | Basic voice-only IPv4 VoIP deployment, one STUN transaction pair each for RTP and RTCP, for both caller and callee (4 transactions per call total) |
| A system of 1 million users, each making 4 calls in a busy hour, requires an aggregate STUN bandwidth of 1.7 Mbps | Arithmetic derivation from the per-transaction message sizes above, multiplied out per user and per call | Stated as "a very small number (relatively speaking)"; the RFC gives no measurement of an actual deployment's traffic |
| In a network with 100% BEHAVE-compliant NATs (per RFC 4787 and RFC 5382), TURN relay traffic volume for data relay is exactly zero | Stated as a logical consequence of the protocol's candidate-priority ordering, not a measurement | Idealized network condition; the RFC states real TURN traffic volume "is highly dependent on network topologies, and can and will vary over time" |
| Congestion from unpaced gathering and connectivity checks "has proven to be a problem in deployments that did not utilize pacing," with access links becoming congested as endpoints send checks as fast as possible | Stated as an observed deployment problem, cited without a specific deployment name, dataset, or numeric congestion figure | No further condition given; not attributable to a specific measured trial |

### Parameters
- Default candidate-pair checklist-set limit: 100 candidate pairs, configurable, imposed specifically to bound the STUN amplification attack described in Section 19.5.1.
- Recommended type-preference values: 126 (host), 110 (peer-reflexive), 100 (server-reflexive), 0 (relayed); each MUST be a distinct integer in 0-126 per type, identical within a type.
- Local preference range: 0-65,535; set to 65,535 when only one candidate of a type exists.
- Component ID range: 1-256 (component 1 = RTP or the only component, component 2 = RTCP when not multiplexed).
- Candidate priority: strictly a positive integer between 1 and 2^31 − 1, unique per candidate for a data stream.
- Ta (STUN/TURN transaction pacing interval): default 50 ms during gathering and connectivity checks; agents MAY negotiate a different value, and both agents MUST use the higher of the two proposed values; regardless of the per-agent Ta, all concurrent transactions from all agents on one implementation MUST NOT be sent more often than once every 5 ms in aggregate.
- RTO (STUN retransmission timeout) during gathering: `RTO = MAX(500 ms, Ta * Num-Of-Cands)`, where Num-Of-Cands is the count of server-reflexive and relay candidates being gathered.
- RTO during connectivity checks: `RTO = MAX(500 ms, Ta * N * (Num-Waiting + Num-In-Progress))`, where N is the total number of checks to perform and Num-Waiting/Num-In-Progress are checklist-set state counts that change per transaction; RTO MUST NOT be set below 500 ms regardless of formula.
- Keepalive interval Tr: SHOULD be 15 seconds; agents MAY use a larger value but MUST NOT use a value smaller than 15 seconds; keepalives are sent only on the pair(s) actually selected for data, only if no other traffic has crossed that pair within Tr seconds.
- STUN Voice Activity Detection (VAD) comfort-noise keepalive interval (illustrative, not normative): a packet every 15-20 seconds during silence, contrasted against a packet every 20-30 ms during active voice.

### Stated limitations
The RFC states ICE does not eliminate the need for STUN and TURN servers to be provisioned and reachable; it only reduces TURN's traffic volume toward zero as the fraction of BEHAVE-compliant NATs in the deployment approaches 100%, and states real-world TURN usage "is highly dependent on network topologies, and can and will vary over time." The RFC states ICE increases session-establishment time compared to a naive single-address attempt, as an explicit cost of the pacing that avoids network congestion: "The penalty of these improvements is that ICE increases session establishment times." The RFC's own security analysis (Section 19.1) states that probing for candidates and exchanging them "reveals the source addresses of the client and its peer to any on-network listening attacker" or to any attacker able to observe the negotiation channel, and that some revealed addresses (for example, a VPN user's local-interface server-reflexive address) may be sensitive; the RFC leaves mitigation of this exposure to the higher-layer ICE usage or to implementation-specific controls over which interfaces generate candidates, rather than solving it within ICE itself. The RFC states classic STUN's NAT-type discovery/classification process (as used before ICE) is "error prone," and ICE avoids that specific failure mode by testing connectivity directly rather than classifying NAT type — but this substitution is stated as ICE's own design choice, not as a claim that ICE eliminates every failure mode the RFC's own Security Considerations section documents (false-invalid, false-valid, false-peer-reflexive-candidate, and false-valid-on-false-candidate attacks are all analyzed as live threats mitigated, not eliminated, by STUN short-term credentials and secured candidate-exchange signaling). Section 19.1 also states that from the types of candidates a peer supplies and the timing characteristics of the resulting connectivity checks, the peer "might be able to determine characteristics of the local network" and "probe the local network," an information-exposure channel the RFC documents without providing a countermeasure for.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
ICE itself supplies no mechanism for exchanging candidates between the two agents; it depends on a separate signaling channel (the RFC names SIP offer/answer as the typical example) that both agents can already reach, and the RFC states explicitly that "ICE is not intended for NAT traversal for the signaling protocol, which is assumed to be provided via another mechanism." The RFC requires, not merely recommends, that all endpoints send periodic keepalives (STUN Binding Indications, at intervals no smaller than 15 seconds) on every candidate pair carrying data, because NAT/firewall UDP bindings are not permanent — a system embedding ICE must budget for this continuous background traffic for the lifetime of every active session, not only during setup. Server-reflexive and relayed candidate discovery depends on the availability of at least one reachable STUN server and, for relayed candidates and Allocate-request authentication, a TURN server holding a long-term credential the client already possesses; a deployment offering only STUN, with no TURN server available, cannot produce a relayed candidate and falls back to whatever host and server-reflexive candidates connectivity checks can validate. STUN Binding requests used for server-reflexive candidate discovery are unauthenticated by design (Section 19.3), so a system relying on ICE for its NAT traversal inherits an attack surface in which a compromised DNS resolution, an on-path observer on a shared network segment, or a compromised STUN server can inject a false server-reflexive candidate; the RFC's own mitigation for this is that peer-reflexive candidates (learned only from a successful connectivity check, and generally prioritized above server-reflexive candidates) still let the session succeed even if server-reflexive discovery is fully disrupted, provided at least one of the peer's own candidates was independently reachable.

### Contradicts
None found. This RFC's stated keepalive-interval default (15 seconds) and HALKES-NETWORKING-11's independently measured recommendation (send keepalives at least every 55 seconds, based on the shortest observed NAT mapping timeout in that paper's field trial) describe different quantities under different methods — this RFC's figure is a specified conservative protocol default chosen without a stated empirical derivation, while HALKES-NETWORKING-11's figure is a measured upper bound on interval safety drawn from real NAT/firewall timeout behavior in the field — and a synthesis step selecting a keepalive interval should cite HALKES-NETWORKING-11's measured figure over this RFC's unmeasured default when the two are compared, because only the former traces to an experimental measurement.

### References worth retrieving
- Rosenberg, Mahy, Matthews, Wing, "Session Traversal Utilities for NAT (STUN)," RFC 5389, 2008 — foundational (ICE's connectivity checks are STUN transactions; the whole priority/error-response machinery this RFC extends is defined here).
- Mahy, Matthews, Rosenberg, "Traversal Using Relays around NAT (TURN): Relay Extensions to Session Traversal Utilities for NAT (STUN)," RFC 5766, 2010 — foundational (defines the Allocate/Refresh transactions and relayed-candidate mechanism ICE's relayed candidates depend on).
- Rosenberg, Weinberger, Huitema, Mahy, "STUN - Simple Traversal of User Datagram Protocol (UDP) Through Network Address Translators (NATs)," RFC 3489, 2003 — superseded-by (classic STUN, whose NAT-type-classification brittleness this RFC's Section 18.3 explicitly contrasts itself against; superseded within the STUN line by RFC 5389).
- Audet, Jennings, "Network Address Translation (NAT) Behavioral Requirements for Unicast UDP," RFC 4787, 2007 — foundational (the "BEHAVE" compliance standard this RFC states ICE performs best against, and whose 100%-compliance condition it uses for the TURN-traffic-volume-zero illustrative claim).
- Daigle, IAB, "IAB Considerations for UNilateral Self-Address Fixing (UNSAF) Across Network Address Translation," RFC 3424, 2002 — foundational (the framework this RFC's Section 18 IAB Considerations explicitly answers point by point, including this RFC's own argument that ICE is a Bilateral, not Unilateral, Self-Address-Fixing protocol).
- Petit-Huguenin, Nandakumar, Keränen, "Session Description Protocol (SDP) Offer/Answer procedures for Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE)," draft-ietf-mmusic-ice-sip-sdp-21, work in progress as of this RFC's publication — foundational (the specific signaling-layer candidate-exchange mechanism this RFC assumes but does not itself define).
- Perumal, Wing, Ravindranath, Reddy, Thomson, "TCP Candidates with Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE)," RFC 6544 — foundational (extends ICE, defined here only for UDP, to TCP transport).

## [KLEIN-SP-21] Keep the Dirt: Tainted TreeKEM, Adaptively and Actively Secure Continuous Group Key Agreement
**Citation:** Joël Alwen, Margarita Capretto, Miguel Cueto, Chethan Kamath, Karen Klein, Ilia Markov, Guillermo Pascual-Perez, Krzysztof Pietrzak, Michael Walter, Michelle Yeo. "Keep the Dirt: Tainted TreeKEM, Adaptively and Actively Secure Continuous Group Key Agreement." IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (S&P), 2021. DOI 10.1109/SP40001.2021.00035.
**Retrieved:** full text
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2019/1489.pdf
**Domain:** H

### What it does
Tainted TreeKEM (TTKEM) is a Continuous Group Key Agreement (CGKA) construction: a protocol by which a group of parties who are not necessarily online at the same time derive a shared secret group key and refresh it over time, so that a group messaging protocol built on top gets forward secrecy (an old key stays secure even after a later state leaks) and post-compromise security (a party that leaked its state recovers security after it next updates). Parties are arranged as leaves of a binary tree; the secret value of the root is the group key, and each internal node's secret is derived from its two children (the "parents" in the paper's inverted edge direction, since edges point from leaves to root). A party updates by generating a new secret for its own leaf and re-deriving every node on the path from that leaf to the root, then sending the new public keys along that path, encrypted, to the rest of the group — a message of size logarithmic in group size for a balanced tree. Adds and Removes change tree membership. TreeKEM's existing mechanism for handling adds/removes overwrites ("blanks") nodes on the affected path; TTKEM instead marks such a node "tainted" by the identifier of the party who caused the taint, without overwriting its key, and every use of a tainted node's key requires XOR-ing in a fresh value contributed by the tainting party. A node is fully healed ("untainted") only once every tainted node in the subtree it roots has itself been overwritten by an Update, not merely once any single Update has touched it — this is the mechanical difference from blanking, where any leaf refresh anywhere under a blanked node "unblanks" it. Group membership changes and key updates are ordered and confirmed through an untrusted delivery server that all parties send operations to; the server can withhold delivery but cannot forge or read secrets.

### Measured results
| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| TTKEM asymptotically cheaper (fewer per-update ciphertexts) than both TreeKEM variants compared, at larger group sizes | Simulated groups of 2^3 to 2^15 members, trees of size 2^i initialized at 2^(i-1) members, 10·2^i Update/Remove/Add operations sampled at an 8:1:1 ratio (ratio taken from R. Barnes's IETF MLS mailing-list TreeKEM-with-blanking simulation); compared against two hand-built TreeKEM bounds — "TKEM" (executes operations one by one, no forced Update after each Commit, more efficient than real TreeKEM) and "TKEM commit" (forces an extra Update after every Add/Remove, less efficient than real TreeKEM); real TreeKEM lies between the two |
| At small group sizes (below roughly 2^7), all three protocol variants perform comparably; TTKEM's advantage appears only asymptotically | Same simulation, "administrator" scenario: 1 administrator per group under 128 members, 1 per 64 members above that, administrators chosen uniformly at random to perform Adds/Removes, sampled uniformly for removed users and update authors |
| Same qualitative result (small-group parity, TTKEM better at larger groups) under uniformly random assignment of who performs Adds/Removes, and under both uniform and Zipf-distributed choice of which member issues Updates | Same simulation parameters, "no administrator restriction" scenario |
| Fully untainting a TTKEM tree from an initial state with only the creator's path untainted requires total communication cost (⌊n/2⌋ − 1)·log(n) ciphertexts | n = group size; every second member updates once; order of updates is irrelevant because any non-creator update costs log(n) ciphertexts regardless of order |
| Fully unblanking the equivalent TreeKEM tree costs at least n·(log(n) − 2) + 2 ciphertexts, roughly twice the TTKEM cost | Proved as Lemma 1, order-dependent for blanking unlike tainting |
| Security-loss reduction for TTKEM: quasipolynomial ≈ (Q·n)^2·log(n) in the Standard Model | n = upper bound on group size, Q = number of Init/Update/Remove/Add queries the adversary issues; derived via the piecewise-guessing framework of Jafargholi et al. (CRYPTO 2017) |
| Security-loss reduction for TTKEM in the Random Oracle Model: polynomial, O((nQ)^2) | Same n, Q definitions; stated in Table 1 alongside comparable figures for ART (Ω((nQ)^n), Standard Model, selective/passive only) and TreeKEM (Ω((nQ)^n), Standard Model, selective/passive only) |

### Parameters
- Group sizes simulated: 2^3 to 2^15 members.
- Operation sequence length: 10·2^i for a tree of size 2^i.
- Operation-type ratio (Update:Remove:Add): 8:1:1, matching the ratio Richard Barnes used in an IETF MLS mailing-list simulation of TreeKEM with blanking.
- Administrator density: 1 administrator per group for groups under 128 members; 1 administrator per 64 members for larger groups.
- Update-author distribution tested: uniform at random, and Zipf-distributed (used to model that message-sending activity per individual follows Gibrat's law, which implies a Zipf distribution of activity level, citing Rybski et al., PNAS 2009, and Gabaix, QJE 1999).

### Stated limitations
The paper proves security only against a "partially active" adversary: one that can arbitrarily reorder or withhold delivery-server messages but cannot forge messages using a corrupted party's secret keys or otherwise deviate from the protocol using stolen key material. Security against a fully active adversary — one that can also inject or alter messages using leaked keys — is stated as open; the authors cite this as "the subject of ongoing research." The construction assumes a pre-existing public-key infrastructure through which a party initializing a group already knows every invitee's public key; the paper treats this key-distribution problem as orthogonal to CGKA and does not address it. The paper's simulations start from a fully healed tree (no blanks or taints) and separately analyze only the cost of reaching that healed state from group creation; they do not simulate a mixed steady-state workload that interleaves initialization with ongoing operations. The authors state they cannot conclude TTKEM is more efficient than TreeKEM in every setting, only in the distributions of operations tested (administrator-driven adds/removes, or Zipf-distributed update authorship). One additional inefficiency is stated but not resolved: when a group member returns online after a long absence and must process a large backlog of operations, there is "still room for improvement," potentially through server-side batching, which the paper does not design.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Requires an untrusted delivery server that every party sends Update/Add/Remove operations to and that enforces a single global order on those operations across all group members — when two parties submit conflicting operations concurrently, the server's ordering decision is what each party's confirm/reject response is built from. The server can prevent communication (withhold delivery) but the protocol's confidentiality guarantee does not depend on the server being honest about content. Requires a pre-existing mechanism, external to this protocol, by which any prospective group initiator already holds the public key of every invitee — the paper explicitly assumes this infrastructure exists rather than building it. Requires parties to process delivered operations in the order the server assigns; a party's local state becomes inconsistent with the group's if it processes operations out of that order. Requires that this order be enforced at least strongly enough to define a linear or partial order the safety predicate can reason over — the paper's security proof is stated for a specific ordering/confirmation protocol (send to server, wait for confirm-or-reject, update or discard local state accordingly) and would need re-derivation for a delivery model without server-mediated ordering (for example, a partition-tolerant broadcast).

### Contradicts
None found.

### References worth retrieving
- Foundational: Cohn-Gordon, Cremers, Garratt, Millican, Milner, "On Ends-to-Ends Encryption: Asynchronous Group Messaging with Strong Security Guarantees," ACM CCS 2018 (introduces ART, the CGKA predecessor TTKEM is compared against).
- Foundational: Alwen, Coretti, Dodis, "The Double Ratchet: Security Notions, Proofs, and Modularization for the Signal Protocol," EUROCRYPT 2019 (two-party CKA modularization TTKEM's group generalization builds on).
- Foundational: Alwen, Coretti, Dodis, Tselekounis, "Security Analysis and Improvements for the IETF MLS Standard for Group Messaging," CRYPTO 2020 (introduces rTreeKEM and the "strong FS" notion Table 1 compares against; source of the passive-adaptive quasipolynomial-loss proof sketch for TreeKEM).
- Foundational: Bhargavan, Barnes, Rescorla, "TreeKEM: Asynchronous Decentralized Key Management for Large Dynamic Groups," May 2018 (the original TreeKEM design document).
- Foundational: Barnes, Beurdouche, Millican, Omara, Cohn-Gordon, Robert, "The Messaging Layer Security (MLS) Protocol," IETF Internet-Draft draft-ietf-mls-protocol-09, 2020.
- Competing: Alwen, Coretti, Jost, Mularczyk, "Continuous Group Key Agreement with Active Security," TCC 2020 (achieves optimal forward secrecy including against some fully active adversaries — stronger active-security model than this paper's).
- Foundational: Jafargholi, Kamath, Klein, Komargodski, Pietrzak, Wichs, "Be Adaptive, Avoid Overcommitting," CRYPTO 2017 (the piecewise-guessing framework the security-loss bound is derived from).
- Foundational: Cremers, Hale, Kohbrok, "Efficient Post-Compromise Security Beyond One Group," ePrint 2019/477.
- Foundational: Jost, Maurer, Mularczyk, "Efficient Ratcheting: Almost-Optimal Guarantees for Secure Messaging," EUROCRYPT 2019.
- Foundational: Weidner, "Group Messaging for Secure Asynchronous Collaboration," Master's thesis, University of Cambridge, 2019 (cited elsewhere in this corpus as the O(n) DCGKA construction BeeKEM supersedes).
