## [KLEPPMANN-AFP-18] OpSets: Sequential Specifications for Replicated Datatypes
**Citation:** Martin Kleppmann, Victor B. F. Gomes, Dominic P. Mulligan, Alastair R. Beresford. "OpSets: Sequential Specifications for Replicated Datatypes." Archive of Formal Proofs, 2018. Extended version also at arXiv:1805.04263.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.04263
**Source URL:** https://www.isa-afp.org/entries/OpSets.html ; https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.04263
**Domain:** D

### What it does
OpSets (Operation Sets) give a way to state precisely which final states a replicated data structure — a data structure held as a separate copy on each of several nodes and updated independently — is allowed to reach after a set of concurrent edits, going beyond the weaker guarantee that copies merely converge to agreement without saying what they agree on. A node holds an OpSet: a set of immutable operation records, each carrying a globally unique, totally ordered identifier (an identifier can be a Lamport timestamp — a pair of a locally incrementing counter and a node identifier, compared first by counter then by node identifier, so any node manufactures a fresh identifier without coordinating with any other node). Two nodes exchange operations as messages and merge OpSets by plain set union, which is commutative, associative, and idempotent, so applying the same operations in a different arrival order or with duplicates or reordering still yields the same OpSet. An interpretation function reads an OpSet and produces the current state of the data structure by applying every operation once, strictly in ascending identifier order, starting from a fixed initial state; because this function is pure (deterministic, no side effects) and depends only on the OpSet's contents, any two nodes holding the same OpSet compute the same state regardless of the order operations physically arrived in. On top of this mechanism the paper specifies composable datatypes — maps, sets, lists, text (a list of characters), graphs, and trees — as a single relation-based object graph: an element relation E holding (operation-id, object-id, key, value) tuples and a list-order relation L holding predecessor-successor pairs, with each insert-after or assign operation adding or overwriting tuples in E or L. A concurrent-move operation on trees is specified as a redefinition of the assign operation: an assign whose target value is already an ancestor of the destination object is dropped (this alone prevents cycles), and an assign that would give an object two parents instead first removes any existing tuple in E referencing that value (this preserves the one-parent-per-node tree invariant) — evaluating this precondition at interpretation time, not at the time the operation was generated, is what lets concurrent moves resolve deterministically without acquiring a lock.

### Measured results
This paper reports no runtime performance measurements, no simulation, and no deployment data — its results are machine-checked mathematical theorems, not measured figures, so no entry in the four-rules sense (a number with experimental conditions) applies. The stated results are: (1) the OpSet list specification, formally proved in Isabelle/HOL (a proof assistant for machine-checked mathematics), rules out interleaving of two users' concurrently inserted character sequences at the same position — the merged result contains one user's whole sequence immediately followed by the other's, never an interleaving of the two; (2) the RGA (Replicated Growable Array) list CRDT is proved, in Isabelle/HOL, to satisfy this no-interleaving list specification; (3) the Logoot and LSEQ list CRDTs are proved not to satisfy it, and the paper additionally reports informally observing this interleaving anomaly occurring when running open-source implementations of Logoot and LSEQ, without stating how many trials, what input, or on what platform — this observation is not a quantified measurement and is recorded as unusable for the schema's Measured Results table; (4) the OpSet list specification is proved, in Isabelle/HOL, to be strictly stronger than the "Astrong" collaborative-text-editing specification of Attiya et al. (PODC 2016) — every algorithm satisfying the OpSet list specification also satisfies Astrong, but Astrong permits character interleaving that the OpSet specification forbids; (5) the tree-with-atomic-move specification is proved never to produce a cycle and never to give a node two parents, for arbitrary concurrent move operations, without requiring any lock or globally synchronized coordination step.

### Parameters
None in the empirical sense — the paper defines no tunable numeric parameter (no buffer size, timeout, replication factor, or similar). The one structural choice stated is the total order used for operation identifiers: the paper uses Lamport timestamps (counter, node-id pairs) ordered lexicographically by counter then by node identifier, and states this is one sufficient choice among possible schemes for generating unique, totally ordered identifiers without coordination.

### Stated limitations
A naive OpSet interpretation that recomputes the full data-structure state by replaying every operation in order from the initial state on each read "may exhibit poor performance," in the paper's words, because a node may need to reapply the same operations repeatedly; the paper states more efficient algorithms can be developed and shown to satisfy the specification (as it does for RGA) but does not itself supply or measure such an algorithm for the tree-with-move datatype. The paper explicitly does not resolve which of two symmetric outcomes a conflicting concurrent tree move should produce beyond "the move operation with the greater ID determines the item's final location" — an arbitrary, ID-based tie-break, not a semantically motivated choice. Practical implementation details of a JavaScript CRDT built around the OpSet model are stated to exist but are stated to be "beyond the scope of this paper," so no implementation or deployment evidence for that system is given here. The paper states an unproved hypothesis, not a result: that a commutative (rather than sequential-replay) tree-move CRDT can be derived from the OpSet specification in the paper, usable for a distributed peer-to-peer file system — labeled explicitly as future work. A second unproved hypothesis is stated: that materialized-view-maintenance techniques from database theory could be applied to make OpSet interpretation incremental rather than full-replay; also labeled future work, with no supporting proof or benchmark in this paper.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The specification requires every operation to carry a globally unique identifier from a total order, generated locally without any node needing to coordinate with any other node to obtain it; a system supplying only per-node monotonic counters without a tie-breaking node identifier would not satisfy the uniqueness requirement. It requires the underlying transport to guarantee, at minimum, eventual reliable delivery of every operation to every node — the paper explicitly tolerates arbitrary reordering, duplication, and transient loss of messages (with retransmission assumed for lost messages, "e.g. using TCP"), but a message that is permanently lost and never retransmitted leaves the receiving node's OpSet permanently short of an operation the sender applied, which the specification does not detect or repair. It requires the interpretation function to be pure: deterministic and free of side effects, computing its result from the OpSet's contents alone — any operation whose effect depends on wall-clock time, on random input, or on state outside the OpSet breaks the convergence guarantee the whole approach rests on. The specification does not require, and explicitly contrasts itself against, an atomic broadcast or total-order broadcast protocol (which the paper states is equivalent to solving distributed consensus and requires communication with a quorum of nodes to make progress) — a system built on OpSets must not require quorum availability to accept a local write, and any consensus layer placed underneath would defeat the property the paper is built to provide (local, always-available reads and writes even while a node is offline or partitioned). For the tree-move specification specifically, every node must apply the assign-based move interpretation over the full OpSet each time state is computed, evaluating the ancestor-cycle precondition at interpretation time rather than caching a stale precondition computed when the operation was first generated — a system that evaluates the precondition once, at generation time, and caches the result would reintroduce the possibility of cycles that this specification is built to rule out.

### Contradicts
The paper's own Theorem 1 contradicts a claim commonly associated with the Astrong specification of Attiya et al. (PODC 2016): Astrong is often treated as a sufficient correctness condition for collaborative text editing, but the paper proves algorithms satisfying Astrong (including Logoot and LSEQ) can still interleave two users' concurrent insertions into an unreadable jumble, so satisfying Astrong alone does not rule out this failure mode. Cross-reference within this corpus: KLEPPMANN-PAPOC-19 (a companion paper by the same authors) restates and extends this same interleaving result in a shorter form and states which algorithms are and are not subject to it; the two entries should be read together, not treated as independent confirmations, since PAPOC-19 draws on the same underlying analysis. None found — no measurement in this batch's other entries speaks to CRDT specification correctness.

### References worth retrieving
- competing (the specification this paper proves its own is strictly stronger than): Attiya, Burckhardt, Gotsman, Morrison, Yang, Zawirski, "Specification and Complexity of Collaborative Text Editing," ACM PODC, 2016.
- competing (proved not to satisfy the no-interleaving list specification): Weiss, Urso, Molli, "Logoot: A Scalable Optimistic Replication Algorithm for Collaborative Editing on P2P Networks," IEEE ICDCS, 2009.
- competing: Weiss, Urso, Molli, "Logoot-Undo: Distributed Collaborative Editing System on P2P Networks," IEEE Trans. Parallel Distrib. Syst. 21(8), 2010.

- competing (tree CRDT for a filesystem, resolves move conflicts via a global lock, giving up full asynchrony): Najafzadeh, Shapiro, Eugster, "Co-Design and Verification of an Available File System," VMCAI, 2018.
- competing: Najafzadeh, "The Analysis and Co-Design of Weakly-Consistent Applications," PhD thesis (full move-conflict argument this paper's tree specification responds to).
- foundational: Shapiro, Preguiça, Baquero, Zawirski, "A Comprehensive Study of Convergent and Commutative Replicated Data Types" (CRDT survey), INRIA Technical Report 7506, 2011.
- foundational: Shapiro, Preguiça, Baquero, Zawirski, "Conflict-Free Replicated Data Types," SSS, 2011.
- foundational (Burckhardt et al.'s operation-context formalism, which this paper positions itself against): Burckhardt, Gotsman, Yang, Zawirski, "Replicated Data Types: Specification, Verification, Optimality," ACM POPL, 2014.
- foundational (this paper's own prior Isabelle/HOL verification framework, reused here): Gomes, Kleppmann, Mulligan, Beresford, "Verifying Strong Eventual Consistency in Distributed Systems," Proc. ACM Program. Lang. (PACMPL) 1(OOPSLA), 2017.
- competing (Operational Transformation algorithm proved to satisfy a weaker text-editing specification, Aweak): Nichols, Curtis, Dixon, Lamping, "High-Latency, Low-Bandwidth Windowing in the Jupiter Collaboration System" (Jupiter OT algorithm), referenced via Attiya et al.'s conjecture, completed by Wei et al.

## [KLEPPMANN-ARXIV-20] Byzantine Eventual Consistency and the Fundamental Limits of Peer-to-Peer Databases
**Citation:** Martin Kleppmann, Heidi Howard. "Byzantine Eventual Consistency and the Fundamental Limits of Peer-to-Peer Databases." arXiv preprint arXiv:2012.00472, 2020.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.00472
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.00472
**Domain:** D+H

### What it does
Byzantine Eventual Consistency (BEC) is a correctness condition for a replicated database that a system can guarantee while tolerating an unbounded number of Byzantine-faulty replicas (replicas that may deviate from the protocol in arbitrary, possibly colluding ways), which makes any system meeting it immune to Sybil attacks (an adversary joining many fake peers) without proof-of-work or centrally controlled peer admission — because tolerance does not depend on any bound on the faulty fraction. BEC requires three properties of every correct replica: it applies its own generated updates immediately (self-update); any update one correct replica applies is eventually applied by every correct replica (eventual update); and two correct replicas that have applied the same set of updates reach the same state regardless of application order (convergence). The paper proves a necessary-and-sufficient theorem: a fault-tolerant BEC algorithm exists for a given set of transactions and invariants (predicates a database state must satisfy, such as a non-negative balance or a foreign-key constraint) if and only if those transactions are invariant-confluent (I-confluent) with respect to every invariant — meaning that whenever two transactions are executed concurrently by different replicas, each individually preserving an invariant, applying both together (in either order, since I-confluent transactions' updates commute) still preserves the invariant. The construction proceeds in two layers. First, Byzantine causal broadcast delivers messages to every correct replica in an order consistent with causal dependency, implemented by having each replica sign its messages, reference the hashes of its own causal predecessors in each message (forming a directed acyclic graph over delivered messages, since a cycle would require a hash collision), and periodically reconcile with peer connections by exchanging the hashes of "heads" (delivered messages with no known successor) and walking backward through the predecessor graph to discover and request every message the peer lacks — vector clocks are explicitly ruled out for this role because a faulty replica can hand two correct replicas different messages carrying the identical vector timestamp, making them believe falsely that their message sets already agree. Second, a replication algorithm layered on top of this broadcast applies each delivered update only if it passes a per-invariant safety check (for example: a foreign-key deletion is unsafe unless the referencing tuple's insertion causally preceded it) and only if any deletion in the message targets a tuple whose insertion the same message causally follows — a correct replica drops any update failing these checks rather than corrupting its own state, even though a faulty replica may have broadcast it.

### Measured results
| Result | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Round trips per reconciliation, naive algorithm (Algorithm 1) | Grows linearly with the number of updates accumulated since the last reconciliation (up to roughly 35-40 round trips at 100 updates) | In-memory single-process prototype simulating a message-passing network, 4 replicas each generating updates at a constant rate, every replica pair periodically reconciling, average over 600 reconciliations (100 per distinct replica pair) per data point, eager-send lines of the protocol disabled so all exchange happens via periodic reconciliation |
| Round trips per reconciliation, optimized algorithm (Algorithm 2, Bloom-filter-assisted) | Constant at 1.03 round trips on average regardless of the number of accumulated updates; 96.7% of reconciliations complete in one round trip, 3.2% in two, 0.04% in three or more | Same 4-replica prototype and 600-reconciliation averaging; Bloom filters configured at 10 bits per entry and 7 hash functions |
| Network bytes transmitted per reconciliation, Algorithm 2 vs. theoretical optimum | Approximately 1 kB per reconciliation above a hypothetical optimal algorithm that transmits only new update content with no metadata | Same prototype; each update assumed 200 bytes (excluding predecessor hashes), each hash 32 bytes (SHA-256), each request/response message carrying 100 bytes of fixed overhead (e.g. TCP/IP headers and signatures), Bloom filters at 10 bits per element |
| Network bytes transmitted per reconciliation, Algorithm 1 vs. optimum | More than double the theoretical optimum | Same prototype and cost model; attributed to Algorithm 1 sending many separate "needs" messages containing hashes and responding in many small unbatched messages rather than one batched response |

### Parameters
- Fault-tolerance definition used for the main theorem: an algorithm is called fault-tolerant if it can commit a transaction after receiving responses from up to r-2 of r replicas (tolerating one crashed or unreachable replica); the paper states the theorem also holds for algorithms tolerant of more faults, and uses the weaker one-fault definition because it makes the impossibility result stronger.
- Bloom filter configuration in the evaluation: 10 bits per entry, 7 hash functions (not stated as swept — this is the single configuration the round-trip and byte figures above were measured under).
- Assumed per-update size for the bandwidth cost model: 200 bytes, excluding predecessor hashes.
- Assumed hash size: 32 bytes (SHA-256).
- Assumed fixed per-message overhead: 100 bytes.
- Number of replicas in the evaluation: 4 (not swept).
- Averaging: 600 reconciliations per data point, 100 between each distinct pair of the 4 replicas.
- Byzantine agreement replica counts cited from prior work, for contrast (not this paper's own result): typical Byzantine agreement requires at least 3f+1 replicas to tolerate f faults; some require 5f+1; this can be lowered to 2f+1 assuming synchrony and digital signatures; Upright separates crash faults u and Byzantine faults r and uses 2u+r+1 replicas; Zeno makes progress with f+1 replicas but safety requires fewer than one-third of replicas Byzantine-faulty.

### Stated limitations
The main theorem requires that correct replicas form a single connected component in the graph of replicas and network links (Figure 1); if two correct replicas can communicate only through faulty replicas, no algorithm can guarantee data exchange between them, since the adversary can always block that path (an eclipse attack) — the paper states connecting each replica to every other is the simplest way to satisfy this, but calls "how can we best ensure correct replicas form a connected component" an open question in its conclusion, since full connectivity is expensive at scale. The evaluation ran only with all replicas correctly following the protocol; the paper states it believes adding faulty replicas would not fundamentally alter the results (this is an unmeasured belief, not a reported measurement, and must not be recorded as a figure) because faulty replicas could alter the shape of the predecessor graph, e.g. producing more concurrent updates than there are replicas. CPU and memory use of the prototype were not measured; the paper states this is left for future work. The paper could not compare its algorithms against Depot, a prior system tolerating arbitrary Byzantine faults, because the available Depot publications did not describe its algorithm in enough detail to reproduce it. The theorem's proof assumes an asynchronous system (no bound on message delay) but the paper states it also holds for partially synchronous systems in which delay is only temporarily unbounded. The paper explicitly does not resolve Bitcoin's proof-of-work electricity cost, because it shows a cryptocurrency's payment transactions are not I-confluent with respect to a non-negative-balance invariant (two concurrent debits from the same account can jointly violate the invariant even though each alone would not), so a cryptocurrency requires a Sybil countermeasure beyond what this result can remove. Two further open questions are stated without answer: how to formalize the process (given only informally in Table 1) of checking whether an update is safe with respect to an invariant, and whether the equivalence "solvable without coordination in a non-Byzantine system if and only if immune to Sybil attacks in a Byzantine one" holds in general.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Every replica must hold a distinct private key for digital signatures, with every other replica's corresponding public key known to it; every message must be signed by its sender, and a recipient discards any message with an invalid signature — a deployment without this signing infrastructure cannot use the algorithm, since it relies on signatures to prevent a faulty replica from impersonating a correct one. Pairwise network links between replicas must eventually deliver a sent message provided neither endpoint crashes (retransmission of lost messages is assumed available, e.g. via TCP), and replicas need a timer capable of triggering periodic actions (retransmission, reconciliation) without requiring synchronized or exact clocks. The construction requires a collision-resistant cryptographic hash function (the paper names SHA-256 as meeting this) because the predecessor graph's acyclicity, and the whole causal-delivery mechanism, depends on no two distinct messages sharing a hash. Applying BEC to a specific application requires that application's designer to determine which of its transactions and invariants are I-confluent, using rules like those in Table 1 (e.g. a foreign-key deletion is unsafe unless the deleted tuple's insertion causally precedes it in the message graph) — a transaction set found not to be I-confluent with respect to some invariant needs a separate Byzantine-consensus mechanism for just that portion, since the paper's theorem proves no fault-tolerant BEC algorithm can preserve a non-I-confluent invariant under arbitrary Byzantine faults. The reconciliation algorithm depends on each replica durably storing, per remote peer identity, the "heads" recorded at the end of the last successful reconciliation with that peer (via StoreHeads), so the optimized Algorithm 2's constant-round-trip performance requires persistent per-connection state across reconciliation rounds, not just per-message state.

### Contradicts
None found — no other entry in this batch measures Byzantine causal broadcast reconciliation cost. Cross-reference: this paper's I-confluence necessary-and-sufficient theorem for Byzantine systems extends I-confluence as originally defined for non-Byzantine systems by Bailis et al.; a claim that I-confluence alone was already known to be necessary and sufficient in a Byzantine-fault setting before this paper would be a claim this paper does not support — the paper states its own theorem is the extension.

### References worth retrieving
- foundational (I-confluence's original, non-Byzantine definition and proof): Bailis, Fekete, Ghodsi, Hellerstein, Stonebraker, "Coordination Avoidance in Database Systems" (or the extended version cited for I-confluence detail), VLDB, 2014 — cited in this paper as reference [6]/[7]; retrieve exact citation.
- competing (prior system tolerating arbitrary Byzantine faults, not directly comparable due to insufficient published algorithmic detail): Mahajan et al., "Depot: Cloud Storage with Minimal Trust," ACM TOCS / OSDI, cited as references [43, 45, 46] in this paper's numbering.
- competing (similar causal-broadcast algorithm to this paper's Algorithm 1, in an arbitrary-Byzantine-fault model): "OldBlue" — cited as reference [74]; retrieve full citation.
- competing (detects and bans misbehaving replicas via cryptographic proof plus trusted hardware, contrasted with this paper's no-trusted-component approach): van der Linde et al., cited as reference [40]; retrieve full citation — relevant as a competing design for Byzantine causal consistency worth comparing trust assumptions against.
- attack/negative-result (proves no Byzantine-tolerant system can enforce fork-causal or stronger consistency in an always-available, one-way convergent system): Mahajan et al., cited as reference [44]; retrieve full citation.
- foundational (CALM theorem, coordination-freedom for monotonic programs, directly underlies I-confluence's relationship to coordination-avoidance): Hellerstein, Alvaro, cited as references [5, 32] for the CALM theorem; retrieve full citations.
- competing (non-Byzantine causally consistent system avoiding coordination, whose Byzantine variant this paper's BEC is stated to generalize): Lloyd, Freedman, Kaminsky, Andersen, "Don't Settle for Eventual: Scalable Causal Consistency for Wide-Area Storage with COPS," ACM SOSP, 2011 — cited as reference [41].
- foundational (source of CRDTs / strong eventual consistency, which this paper builds on): Shapiro, Preguiça, Baquero, Zawirski, cited as reference [65] for strong eventual consistency; likely "Conflict-Free Replicated Data Types," SSS, 2011 (already retrieved for KLEPPMANN-AFP-18).
- foundational (source of Byzantine reliable broadcast without causal ordering, cited as a partial building block this paper's algorithm improves on): Drabkin et al., cited as reference [25]; retrieve full citation.

## [KLEPPMANN-CONEXT-24] Bluesky and the AT Protocol: Usable Decentralized Social Media

**Citation:** Martin Kleppmann, Paul Frazee, Jake Gold, Jay Graber, Daniel Holmgren, Devin Ivy, Jeromy Johnson, Bryan Newbold, Jaz Volpert. "Bluesky and the AT Protocol: Usable Decentralized Social Media." ACM DIN Workshop, CoNEXT, 2024. 9 pages. DOI 10.1145/3694809.3700740.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.03239 (candidate URL list target; text on disk matches the DIN '24 extended version)
**Source URL:** https://doi.org/10.1145/3694809.3700740
**Domain:** J+K

### What it does
The AT Protocol (Authenticated Transfer Protocol) separates social-media hosting into independently replaceable roles so a user can move between providers without losing their username, posts, or social graph. Each user account holds one repository: a signed, append-only collection of records (posts, likes, follows) encoded in DAG-CBOR (a restricted, compact form of the Concise Binary Object Representation). A Personal Data Server (PDS) hosts a set of repositories, exposes them over an HTTP API, and pushes a WebSocket stream of new and deleted records. A Relay crawls known PDSes, verifies the cryptographic proofs on each update, holds its own replica of every repository, and merges the per-PDS streams into one public stream called the firehose. An App View consumes the firehose and computes derived views specific to one social mode (like counts, reply threads, follower sets, timelines) that a client queries indirectly through the user's own PDS. Labelers and feed generators consume the firehose independently and produce, respectively, content-judgment labels and ranked post-ID lists that a client or App View applies as opt-in filters, so ranking and moderation policy are not fixed inside the App View. A repository's records form a Merkle Search Tree (a Merkle tree structure that stays balanced under arbitrary insertion and deletion order); the tree's root hash is signed after every change, which lets any party prove a record is or is not present in a given repository without holding the whole repository. Identity is a Decentralized Identifier (DID), an immutable URI that resolves to a DID document stating the user's current handle, PDS URL, and signing public key; a human-readable handle is a DNS name and is proved to correspond to a DID by a bidirectional link (a DNS TXT record or a `/.well-known/` HTTPS response naming the DID, plus the DID document naming the handle back). The paper defines two DID methods: `did:web`, which resolves via HTTPS to a domain the identity is permanently tied to, and `did:plc`, the protocol's own method, in which the DID is the truncated SHA-256 hash of the initial DID document and later versions are valid only if signed by the key authorized in the immediately preceding version, verified through a chain returned by a directory server.

### Measured results
| Figure | Conditions |
|---|---|
| Over 10 million registered users | Growth from invite-only launch in February 2023 to the paper's writing, roughly 20 months, counted by Bluesky Social PBC's own registration records |
| Real-time single-server mirror of every user repository cost US$153/month | Measured in July 2024, when Bluesky had 6 million users; figure covers repository storage and inbound bandwidth for fetching records from PDSes; excludes compute for building and serving summary indexes; cited to a third-party operator's own report (Newbold, ref. [43]), not an experiment run by this paper's authors |
| "Tens of thousands" of custom feeds created | No date or measurement method given beyond this count; not usable as a precise figure |
| Farcaster per-user storage cost approximately $5 USD/year in Ethereum-equivalent currency | Stated as a comparison figure from Farcaster's own fee schedule (ref. [30]), at the time of writing, not independently measured by this paper |

No latency, throughput, or failure-rate experiment is run by the authors themselves; the paper is an architecture description with one third-party cost citation, not an evaluation study.

### Parameters
- Post length limit: 300 characters of text, up to four images, plus short-form video (Bluesky app-level lexicon parameter, not an AT Protocol parameter)
- DID hash truncation for `did:plc`: SHA-256 hash of the initial DID document, truncated to 120 bits, base32-encoded
- Scuttlebutt comparison parameter cited from related work: default follow-graph crawl depth of three hops

### Stated limitations
The protocol currently supports only public content; the authors state they are investigating mechanisms for private blocking actions but have not built them. Direct messages are handled by a centralized service operated by Bluesky Social PBC, with decentralization stated as a future plan, not a current property. The PLC directory server is a single point that can omit valid DID document versions or fail to respond, and can choose which fork to serve if two correctly signed successor DID documents exist for the same DID; the authors state a future version will use an append-only transparency log to mitigate this, which does not exist yet. Signing keys are held custodially by the PDS operator for ordinary users, so a compromised or malicious PDS operator holds the keys needed to forge repository updates on that user's behalf; the protocol places no requirement on how a PDS authenticates its users. `did:web` identity security depends on trusting the domain's web hosting provider and the certificate authorities that authenticate its HTTPS endpoint. The authors state that most of the indexing infrastructure is currently run by one company, though they argue this does not make the system centralized because repositories are public and re-indexable by anyone.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A Relay requires every PDS to serve a WebSocket stream of signed repository updates and to accept periodic re-crawl requests as a fallback when the stream is interrupted; without a re-crawl fallback, deletions and additions made during a network interruption are missed. An App View requires a Relay's firehose as its only input and does not itself crawl PDSes; a new social mode built on the protocol needs a new App View but can reuse the same PDSes and Relay. Handle verification requires DNS or HTTPS control over a domain and requires the App View performing verification to defend against DNS cache poisoning, optionally with DNSSEC (Domain Name System Security Extensions); the paper states this defense as a should, not as implemented. `did:plc` requires a directory server that returns the full version history for a DID so that clients can verify the unbroken signature chain themselves; the directory's honesty is not required for basic integrity, only for availability and fork-choice, per the paper's own analysis. Blocking enforcement requires block records to be public, because every App View must be able to read who blocks whom in order to drop disallowed interactions; a design that keeps blocks private would remove the App View's ability to enforce them under the mechanism this paper describes.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus at the time of writing. Note for cross-paper checking: SECKIN-ARXIV-25 measures Bluesky's user and network growth through February 2025 and should be checked for growth-rate figures against this paper's "10 million users in 20 months" figure, since the two papers cover different measurement windows (this paper: through October 2024; SECKIN-ARXIV-25: through February 2025).

### References worth retrieving
- foundational: Auvolat, Taïani, "Merkle Search Trees: Efficient State-Based CRDTs in Open Networks," SRDS 2019, DOI 10.1109/srds47363.2019.00032 — defines the Merkle Search Tree structure the repository uses
- foundational: Sporny, Longley, Sabadello, Reed, Steele, Allen, "Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs) v1.0," W3C Recommendation, 2022 — the DID standard atproto's identity layer implements
- foundational: Laurie, "Certificate Transparency," ACM Queue 12(8), 2014, DOI 10.1145/2668152.2668154 — the append-only log design the authors cite as the intended future mitigation for PLC directory fork attacks
- competing: Henshaw-Plath (fiatjaf), "Pivoting Protocols, from SSB to Nostr," 2023 — Nostr's relay-based architecture, directly contrasted in this paper's related work
- competing: Srinivasan, "Farcaster: A Decentralized Social Network," 2023, and Farcaster Team, "Farcaster Architecture," 2024 — blockchain-anchored identity and storage-fee comparison system
- competing: Lemmer-Webber, Tallon, Shepherd, Guy, Prodromou, "ActivityPub," W3C Recommendation, 2018 — the Mastodon federation protocol this paper compares against on server lock-in and reply-thread consistency
- competing: "Scuttlebutt Protocol Guide," 2023, and Karlsson, "Launch of the PZP protocol and the future of Manyverse," 2024 — the peer-to-peer, key-on-device predecessor and its stated successor protocol addressing multi-device key loss
- attack/critique: Erin, "queer.af domain suspended without warning," 2024 — cited as a real instance of Mastodon-style server-loss risk to a user's social graph

- "it was possible to maintain a real-time copy of all user repositories on a single server for US$153 per month"
- "Any new version of the DID document is only valid if it has been signed by the key in the previous version"
- "there are no guarantees of anything [...] to use Nostr one must embrace the inherent chaos"
- "Fees are currently collected centrally by the Farcaster team"

## [KLEPPMANN-ONWARD-19] Local-First Software: You Own Your Data, in Spite of the Cloud
**Citation:** Martin Kleppmann, Adam Wiggins, Peter van Hardenberg, Mark McGranaghan. "Local-First Software: You Own Your Data, in Spite of the Cloud." ACM SIGPLAN International Symposium on New Ideas, New Paradigms, and Reflections on Programming and Software (Onward!), 2019. DOI 10.1145/3359591.3359737.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.inkandswitch.com/local-first/
**Source URL:** https://www.inkandswitch.com/local-first/ ; https://doi.org/10.1145/3359591.3359737
**Domain:** D

### What it does
This paper states seven requirements — "ideals" — that the authors argue software must meet to give users both real-time collaboration and full ownership of their data, and argues that Conflict-free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs — data structures whose concurrent updates on different replicas always merge to the same result without central coordination) are a mechanism that can satisfy several of the seven simultaneously. This is a requirements and position paper drawing on qualitative prototype experience, not a mechanism paper proposing a new algorithm; nothing in the schema's "Requirements it places on the rest of the system" section should be read as this paper mandating an implementation choice, only as the property set an implementer must reach. The seven ideals, each defined by contrast with the "cloud app" architecture in which a remote server holds the authoritative copy and every client copy is a subordinate cache: (1) No spinners — the software responds to input without a network round trip, because the primary copy of the data lives on the local device and synchronization happens in the background; (2) work is not trapped on one device — data synchronizes across every device a user works from, not merely stored on one; (3) the network is optional — the application functions fully offline, reading and writing the local copy, and reconciles with other devices only when a connection later becomes available; (4) seamless collaboration — multiple users edit the same document, matching or exceeding the simultaneous-editing experience of a centralized cloud app, without requiring a central server to mediate; (5) the long now — data and the software needed to read it remain accessible indefinitely, independent of whether the vendor that produced the software continues to operate; (6) security and privacy by default — a local-first design avoids the large centralized data store that concentrates every user's data behind one company's access controls, and can add end-to-end encryption so an assisting server holds unreadable ciphertext; (7) user retains ultimate ownership and control — the user is not restricted in copying, exporting, or otherwise using their own data by a provider's terms of service or API surface. The paper surveys eleven existing technologies and application categories (plain files with email attachments, Google Docs, Trello, Pinterest, Dropbox, Git plus GitHub, thin web clients, thick mobile clients, backend-as-a-service platforms such as Firebase, and CouchDB) against these seven ideals and states that none satisfies all seven; the paper's own conclusion from this survey is that CRDTs, used as the client-side data layer with a synchronization mechanism to move updates between devices, are the technology class it identifies as capable of jointly satisfying the collaboration ideal (4) alongside the offline and multi-device ideals (2, 3) without requiring a central authoritative server.

### Measured results
Server-to-server round-trip time between geographically distributed AWS datacenters, presented as a bound on the fastest possible cloud-app response latency, is cited from a separate paper (Bailis, Davidson, Fekete, Ghodsi, Hellerstein, Stoica, "Highly Available Transactions: Virtues and Limitations," VLDB 2014) and not independently re-measured here; the network-latency numbers behind Figure 1 belong to that source paper, not to this one, and must not be recorded as this paper's own measured result. Beyond that cited figure, this paper reports no quantitative benchmark of CRDT performance, network cost, or user-study statistics; its own empirical content is qualitative field experience from three internally-built prototypes (Trellis, a Kanban board; PixelPusher, a collaborative drawing tool; PushPin, a mixed-media canvas), tested by regular use within a five-person development team and individual usability sessions with approximately ten external users (professional designers, product managers, and software engineers), explicitly run without a formal evaluation methodology ("we did not follow a formal evaluation methodology, but rather took an exploratory approach"). No trial count, task list, or outcome metric is reported for these usability sessions, so no number from them meets this schema's bar for a measured result with experimental conditions; only their qualitative findings are recorded below, each clearly attributed to the authors' informal observation rather than to a quantified experiment.

### Parameters
None — this paper defines no tunable system parameter, benchmark configuration, or numeric threshold of its own.

### Stated limitations
The authors state their prototype findings are "somewhat subjective," collected without a formal evaluation methodology, from a five-person internal team plus roughly ten external testers, so the findings below are field observations, not controlled-experiment results. CRDTs (specifically the Automerge library used in the prototypes) accumulate a complete change history, including every character-by-character text edit, which the paper states created measured performance and memory/disk problems in real use (e.g. using PushPin for actual sprint planning); the paper states this history cannot easily be truncated because a collaborator might reconnect after months away and need to merge from that earlier point forward, and that this remained a major area of ongoing, unresolved work at the time of writing. CRDT algorithms by themselves specify only how to merge data, not how updates physically reach other users' devices; the paper states network communication "remains an unsolved problem" in their prototypes, having tried WebRTC, manual file-copying via Dropbox and USB drives, IPFS, and eventually the Hypercore peer-to-peer libraries from the Dat project. Peer-to-peer NAT traversal (routing around network address translation so two devices behind separate home routers can connect directly) is stated to be unreliable, varying by the specific router and network topology in use, and the P2P technologies used in the prototypes are stated to be "nowhere near production-ready." A purely peer-to-peer design without any server creates a "closed-laptop problem": if one user shares a document and closes their laptop before a second user comes online, the two never connect, so the paper concludes servers retain a role as "cloud peers" — non-authoritative supporting nodes for backup, discovery, bridging to traditional APIs, and burst compute — rather than being eliminated. The paper states unresolved, open research questions rather than solved problems for: access permissions for shared documents beyond an unguessable secret URL; algorithms and programming models for branching, forking, and rebasing a document's edit history among collaborators (most CRDT research assumes all collaborators immediately apply edits to one shared version, which the paper states does not match practical needs); and how differing application versions with differing data schemas can safely interoperate absent a central authoritative schema server. The paper's own qualitative finding is that Automerge's default, generic conflict-resolution policy was sufficient across all three prototypes and no case requiring application-specific merge semantics was identified — but the paper explicitly labels this a hypothesis ("we hypothesise that this is the case generally") awaiting further research, not a proven general result.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
For the seamless-collaboration ideal to hold without a central server, the paper's prototype experience found that merge behavior needs to operate at a fine granularity that accounts for a datatype's own semantics — its example is that Automerge positions two users' concurrent insertions into the same array position deterministically, whereas a line-oriented tool like Git treats the same situation as a manual-resolution conflict — so a synchronization layer that treats a document as an undifferentiated byte blob rather than a structured, datatype-aware CRDT will reintroduce the manual-merge burden the ideal is meant to remove. Achieving the offline and multi-device ideals together requires the application's data layer to keep a full local, independently readable and writable copy at every device, with synchronization handled as a background process rather than as a precondition for any read or write — an architecture where any operation blocks on reaching a server does not meet ideal 1 or 3 regardless of how fast that server responds when reachable. Achieving the long-now (longevity) ideal requires that both the data format and the software needed to interpret it remain usable independent of any single vendor continuing to operate a backend service; the paper's own recommendation is to favor durable, well-documented formats (plain text, JPEG, PDF, or, per the US Library of Congress's guidance which the paper cites, XML, JSON, or SQLite) precisely because these do not depend on a specific company's servers to remain interpretable. Realizing the security/privacy ideal with an assisting server in the loop requires end-to-end encryption at the application layer, so that any server holding a copy of the data holds only ciphertext it cannot read — the paper names this as necessary specifically because it foresees the server role persisting (as a "cloud peer" for backup, discovery, and bridging) rather than disappearing.

### Contradicts
The paper's own findings section explicitly narrows a claim that might otherwise be attributed to it: it does not claim CRDTs require a peer-to-peer network layer — the paper states plainly "CRDTs do not require a peer-to-peer networking layer; using a server for communication is fine for CRDTs" — and frames the move toward peer-to-peer transport as motivated specifically by the longevity ideal (outliving any single vendor's backend), not as a property CRDTs themselves demand. A claim sometimes attributed to this paper — that conflict resolution in collaborative CRDT-based software requires application-specific merge logic — is contradicted by the paper's own finding across all three prototypes, where the generic default resolution policy in Automerge was found sufficient and no case requiring customized semantics was identified (stated as a hypothesis for further testing, not a proof). None found regarding disagreement with other entries in this batch.

### References worth retrieving
- foundational (source of the AWS inter-datacenter round-trip latency figure reproduced as this paper's Figure 1 — not independently measured here, must be retrieved and cited separately before being treated as verified): Bailis, Davidson, Fekete, Ghodsi, Hellerstein, Stoica, "Highly Available Transactions: Virtues and Limitations," VLDB, 2014.
- foundational (the CRDT implementation underlying all three prototypes described here): "Automerge," https://github.com/automerge/automerge (project repository, cited as reference [1] in this paper).
- foundational (peer-to-peer networking stack used for PixelPusher and PushPin's transport layer, after WebRTC and IPFS were tried and set aside): Dat Project, "dat:// — a peer-to-peer protocol," https://datproject.org/ (cited as reference [46]); and Buus, "Hypercore," https://github.com/mafintosh/hypercore (cited as reference [35]).
- competing (server-centric CRDT deployments the paper explicitly distinguishes its own client-side focus from): Shukla, "Azure Cosmos DB: Pushing the Frontier of Globally Distributed Databases," 2018 (cited as reference [115]); also cited in the same footnote: Redis CRDTs, Riak, Weave Mesh, SoundCloud's Roshi, Facebook's OpenR.
- foundational (source of the earlier measurement of modern software input-to-display latency that motivated ideal 1, "No Spinners"): McGranaghan, "Slow Software," 2018, cited as reference [95] — retrieve for the "measured the performance of modern software" claim this paper references but does not itself re-derive.
- competing (an alternative CRDT/causal-history construction referenced in the paper's technology discussion): Baboulevitch, "Data Laced with History: Causal Trees & Operational CRDTs," 2018 (cited as reference [25]).

### Verbatim extracts

- "many technologies satisfy some of the goals, but none are able to satisfy them all"
- "we did not follow a formal evaluation methodology"
- "users surprisingly rarely encounter conflicts in their work"
- "CRDTs do not require a peer-to-peer networking layer; using a server for communication is fine"
- "NAT traversal... is unreliable depending on the particular router or network topology"
- "it can't easily be truncated because it's impossible to know when someone might reconnect"
- "we hypothesise that this is the case generally"

## [KLEPPMANN-PAPOC-19] Interleaving Anomalies in Collaborative Text Editors
**Citation:** Martin Kleppmann, Victor B. F. Gomes, Dominic P. Mulligan, Alastair R. Beresford. "Interleaving Anomalies in Collaborative Text Editors." Workshop on Principles and Practice of Consistency for Distributed Data (PaPoC), co-located with EuroSys, 2019. DOI 10.1145/3301419.3323972.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://martin.kleppmann.com/papers/interleaving-papoc19.pdf
**Source URL:** https://doi.org/10.1145/3301419.3323972 ; https://martin.kleppmann.com/papers/interleaving-papoc19.pdf
**Domain:** D

### What it does
This paper states the precise condition under which several published collaborative-text-editing algorithms garble concurrent insertions into an unreadable character-by-character jumble, and gives a fix for one of those algorithms. The full anomaly occurs when two users concurrently insert text sequences at the same position in a document (for example, one user typing " Alice" and another typing " Charlie" both immediately after "Hello"): a merging algorithm exhibiting the anomaly can interleave the two sequences arbitrarily, character by character, rather than keeping each user's insertion as one unbroken run. Logoot and LSEQ (two published text-editing CRDTs — Conflict-free Replicated Data Types, structures whose concurrent updates merge deterministically without coordination) exhibit the full anomaly because both assign each inserted character a position identifier drawn from a dense ordered set (conceptually a rational number between the identifiers of its left and right neighbors; concretely a path through a tree with the same effect), and when two users insert into the same gap without knowledge of each other's insertion, each spreads its own characters' identifiers across that gap independently, so the merged order interleaves the two runs arbitrarily. RGA (Replicated Growable Array, a different text-editing CRDT) does not exhibit the full anomaly — the paper cites its own prior mechanized Isabelle/HOL proof of this — because RGA anchors each inserted character to the single character immediately preceding it at insertion time rather than to a dense-identifier gap, so a sequentially typed run of characters (each anchored to the one before it) is never split apart by a concurrent insertion elsewhere. RGA does exhibit a lesser variant: if two runs of characters inserted by the same user, at different times, are both anchored to the same preceding character (which happens when a user inserts once, moves the cursor back to the same anchor point, and inserts again), and a third user's concurrent insertion is also anchored to that same character, all insertions sharing an anchor are ordered only by a timestamp comparison, so the third user's whole run can land between the first user's two runs — three merge outcomes become possible instead of the intended one, though no single run's internal character order is ever broken. The paper adds a clause to Attiya et al.'s Astrong specification of collaborative text editing (clause 1(d): for any two sets of concurrent insertions occupying the same document interval, either every element of one set precedes every element of the other in the merged result, or vice versa — never a mix) that rules out the full interleaving anomaly, which the original Astrong specification permits. The paper's fix for RGA's lesser anomaly extends each insertion operation's data from a triple (character, timestamp, reference-character-timestamp) to a 4-tuple that adds e — the set of timestamps of every other insertion sharing the same reference character at the moment this insertion was performed — then orders two insertions sharing a reference character by comparing the minimal timestamp in the "difference" of their two e-sets (the earliest timestamp at which the two insertions' causal histories diverged, rather than each insertion's own single timestamp), which the paper states groups every operation from one continuous editing session together, ahead of or behind every operation from a different, concurrent session.

### Measured results
This paper is a specification and mechanism paper reporting no benchmark, latency, or throughput figures — its evidentiary content is a demonstrated empirical observation and a set of formally stated conditions, not a quantified performance result. It reports one qualitative empirical observation, without a trial count, input size, or measured rate: the authors "performed tests with open source implementations of Logoot and LSEQ... and observed this interleaving anomaly occurring in practice," and separately released the underlying research data as a public dataset (DOI 10.17863/CAM.37617); because this observation carries no stated experimental conditions (no count of test runs, no input text length, no environment), it does not meet this schema's bar for a recordable measured figure and is reported here only as an attributed qualitative claim, not as data.

### Parameters
None — the paper defines no tunable numeric parameter. The one structural quantity it introduces is the per-insertion timestamp-set e used in the RGA fix, whose size the paper states is expected to be small in practice ("there are normally not many operations with the same reference character, regardless of the length of the document"), offered as an unmeasured expectation, not a derived or measured bound.

### Stated limitations
The claim that RGA satisfies the paper's own strengthened specification (Astrong plus clause 1(d)) once the 4-tuple fix is applied is stated explicitly as a conjecture, not a proof: "we conjecture that applying this construction to RGA results in a CRDT without interleaving... A formal proof of this conjecture is left for future work." The fix increases memory and network bandwidth used by the algorithm because of the added per-operation timestamp set e; the paper gives no measured overhead figure for this increase, only the unmeasured expectation noted above. The paper states, but does not prove, that Treedoc and WOOT (two other published text-editing CRDTs) do not suffer from either the full or the lesser interleaving anomaly — this is stated as an unproven conjecture ("we conjecture that Treedoc and WOOT do not suffer from either anomaly, but we leave a rigorous proof of this claim for future work"), so neither algorithm should be treated as verified interleaving-free on this paper's authority. The lesser RGA anomaly requires a specific, uncommon editing pattern (inserting a document, or part of one, in an order other than strict left-to-right) to manifest at all; the paper's own worst-case example — typing an entire document from back to front, causing every character to anchor to the document head and be ordered only by timestamp, permitting arbitrary character-level interleaving — is stated to be "unlikely to occur in realistic editing scenarios," while the paper still argues it is a case formal consistency models must account for.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Ruling out the full interleaving anomaly under the paper's revised specification (clause 1(d)) requires the merge algorithm to preserve, for every pair of concurrently inserted sequences occupying the same gap, a total group ordering between the two sequences as wholes — an algorithm that assigns identifiers to individual characters independently of which other characters were inserted in the same user action does not have the information needed to satisfy this clause, since nothing in a single character's identifier records which run it belongs to. The RGA fix requires every insertion operation to carry, in addition to its own timestamp and its reference character's timestamp, the full set of timestamps of every other insertion that shared the same reference character at the moment this insertion was made — this is additional state that must be transmitted and stored per operation, not derivable after the fact from the document's final character sequence alone, so a wire format or storage layout designed only around the original RGA triple cannot be retrofitted with this fix without a schema change. The fix's total ordering of concurrent insertions sharing a reference character depends on comparing timestamps for set membership (t1 in e2, or the minimal element of a set difference), which requires a total order over timestamps to be well-defined system-wide — the paper notes Lamport timestamps have already replaced Roh et al.'s original custom S4Vector datatype in subsequent RGA presentations, and this paper's fix is stated in terms of that same timestamp abstraction, so any timestamp scheme used must supply a total order, not merely a partial causal order.

### Contradicts
None found as an internal contradiction. This paper functions as a shorter, standalone restatement of a result also presented at greater length in KLEPPMANN-AFP-18 (OpSets) by the same authors: the full interleaving anomaly, Logoot and LSEQ's susceptibility to it, RGA's freedom from the full anomaly, and the revised Astrong specification (Theorem 1-3 material in the OpSets paper) are the same underlying findings, with this paper adding the previously unpublished lesser RGA anomaly and its conjectured fix, which OpSets (AFP-18) does not contain. A claim commonly attributed to RGA — that it fully solves the interleaving problem CRDTs face — is contradicted by this paper's own finding: RGA avoids the full anomaly but is shown here to still permit the lesser anomaly under non-sequential insertion patterns.

- foundational (RGA, the algorithm this paper's fix modifies): Roh, Jeon, Kim, Lee, "Replicated Abstract Data Types: Building Blocks for Collaborative Applications," J. Parallel Distrib. Comput. 71(3), 2011.

- competing (exhibits the full interleaving anomaly; cited via its interleaving-of-data GitHub issue/Stack Overflow thread as independent confirmation): Weiss, Urso, Molli, "Logoot: A Scalable Optimistic Replication Algorithm for Collaborative Editing on P2P Networks," IEEE ICDCS, 2009 (full citation to retrieve; this paper cites Logoot via [21],[22], not fully reproduced in the visible bibliography excerpt).
- competing (conjectured, not proved, free of both anomalies): Oster, Urso, Molli, Imine, "Data Consistency for P2P Collaborative Editing" (WOOT), ACM CSCW, 2006.

## [KLEPPMANN-PAPOC-22] Making CRDTs Byzantine Fault Tolerant

**Citation:** Martin Kleppmann. "Making CRDTs Byzantine Fault Tolerant." 9th Workshop on Principles and Practice of Consistency for Distributed Data (PaPoC), co-located with EuroSys, 2022. 8 pages. DOI 10.1145/3517209.3524042.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://martin.kleppmann.com/papers/bft-crdt-papoc22.pdf
**Source URL:** https://martin.kleppmann.com/papers/bft-crdt-papoc22.pdf
**Domain:** D+H

### What it does
Adapts operation-based CRDTs (Conflict-free Replicated Data Types, data structures that let independent replicas apply updates in any order and reach the same state without coordination) to keep Strong Eventual Consistency when some replicas are Byzantine-faulty (deviate arbitrarily from the protocol, whether by bug or by intent). Strong Eventual Consistency has three requirements: eventual delivery (an update delivered at one correct replica is eventually delivered at all correct replicas), convergence (correct replicas that delivered the same set of updates hold equivalent state), and termination. The mechanism has two parts.

First, every update is identified by the cryptographic hash of its own byte-string encoding, and every update carries the hashes of its direct causal predecessors (updates it causally depends on), not the transitive closure. Updates and predecessor hashes form a directed acyclic graph (DAG), stored in full by each node, resembling a Git commit history without merge commits: after concurrent updates, the DAG simply has multiple heads (updates that are not yet a predecessor of any other update). Two nodes compare the hashes of their current heads; if equal, the two nodes have delivered identical update sets, because the head hashes transitively cover every update reachable from them. If the heads differ, a graph traversal locates the missing parts and each side sends the other only those. A Byzantine node can add arbitrary vertices and edges to the DAG, including updates that reference nonexistent predecessor hashes, but a correct node simply never delivers an update whose dependency cannot be resolved; this cannot prevent two correct nodes from eventually delivering the same update set, assuming hash collisions are computationally infeasible.

Second, operation identifiers are derived from the same hash rather than from a per-node sequence number. A per-node counter fails under Byzantine nodes because a faulty node can equivocate: emit two distinct updates carrying the same declared sequence number and send one to each of two correct nodes (demonstrated in the paper's Figure 1, where nodes p and q end up with identical version vectors after delivering different updates from Byzantine node r, defeating version-vector-based reconciliation). Using the update's own hash as its identifier removes this failure because a Byzantine node cannot alter the numbering without changing the hash, so duplicate identifiers become computationally infeasible to produce. When an update contains multiple operations needing multiple identifiers, each is the update hash concatenated with an integer 1, 2, ... local to that update.

For CRDTs whose operations require validity conditions beyond bare uniqueness (for example, RGA (Replicated Growable Array) requiring a deletion to reference a previously inserted, still-existing element, or WOOT/YATA requiring insertion operations to reference valid predecessor/successor elements), the paper gives a rule for making the accept/reject decision replica-independent: define `before(u)` as the set of updates transitively reachable through the predecessor hashes of update u. Two nodes with different total delivered-update sets `Up` and `Uq` still compute the identical `before(u)` for the same u, because `before(u)` depends only on u's own causal history. Basing the validity decision solely on `before(u)` guarantees every correct node reaches the same accept/reject verdict for u, which is what Section 2.4 shows is otherwise not guaranteed (a state-dependent validity check can accept an update at one correct node and reject it at another, causing divergence even under eventual delivery). An alternative for monotonic existence conditions (elements can be created but never destroyed, i.e. deletions retain tombstones) is to delay delivery of a dependent update until the referenced element's creating update has itself been delivered, which also preserves convergence.

### Measured results
None. The paper states no experiment, testbed, implementation, or performance measurement. Section 5 states explicitly that measuring the performance impact is left to future work.

### Parameters
None numeric beyond a size estimate given as an example, not a measured result: with up to three concurrent heads and 256-bit hashes, the set of all updates a node has delivered can be summarized in under 100 bytes regardless of the total update count or node count, citing the mechanism's prior source (Kleppmann and Howard, arXiv:2012.00472) rather than presenting it as newly measured here.

### Stated limitations
The paper conjectures, without proof, that hash-based unique identifiers plus the `before(u)`-restricted validity rule suffice to guarantee convergence for CRDTs in general; a detailed proof for particular CRDT algorithms is explicitly left to future work. The paper does not demonstrate the techniques are effective for any specific CRDT algorithm; that demonstration is left to future work. The paper does not address message authentication as a requirement: it states that if authentication (attributing an update to the node that generated it) is desired, updates can additionally be signed, but this is not necessary for Strong Eventual Consistency and is not analyzed further. The mechanism assumes hash collisions are computationally infeasible; it does not defend against an adversary that can produce collisions. Eventual delivery still requires that every pair of correct nodes can communicate, directly or indirectly through other correct nodes — a Byzantine node on every path between two correct nodes can block their communication, and no mechanism in the paper resolves that case. Byzantine nodes can degrade performance by generating a large number of concurrent updates (inflating the head count) or updates with many predecessor hashes, without breaking correctness; no bound or defense against this degradation is given. The hash-as-identifier scheme increases storage cost relative to short sequence-number identifiers; the paper suggests, without designing or measuring, a compression scheme that recomputes hashes on demand instead of storing them all.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Every node must store the complete DAG of updates it has delivered (all vertices and edges), not a summary, since validity and delivery decisions read the full causal history of an update through `before(u)`. The system needs a way to encode each update as a byte string before computing its hash, and operation-based CRDT implementations must follow the generator/effector split (an operation is generated without side effects, then applied through a separate effector function) because the update's hash-derived identifier is only known after encoding, and the effector, not the generator, is what needs the identifier. The transport layer must support pairwise exchange of head-hash sets and DAG-traversal-based reconciliation of missing updates between any two nodes; no upper bound is placed on how many Byzantine nodes may be present, so the reconciliation protocol must not depend on quorum votes or a bound such as fewer than one-third or one-third Byzantine, unlike Byzantine reliable broadcast. Any CRDT with validity conditions beyond identifier uniqueness needs its accept/reject rule rewritten to depend only on `before(u)`, or on monotonic existence with delayed delivery; a CRDT that inspects mutable replica state outside `before(u)` when deciding validity is not covered by the proof sketch given. The mechanism assumes a cryptographic hash function collision-resistant against the deployment's adversary and, if update authorship matters, a signature scheme layered on top — neither is designed in this paper.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus.

### References worth retrieving
- foundational: Kleppmann and Howard. "Byzantine Eventual Consistency and the Fundamental Limits of Peer-to-Peer Databases." arXiv:2012.00472, 2020. (Source of the DAG reconciliation algorithm and the proof that Byzantine nodes cannot prevent correct nodes from delivering the same update set; this paper builds directly on it.)
- competing: Auvolat and Taïani. "Merkle Search Trees: Efficient State-Based CRDTs in Open Networks." SRDS 2019. (State-based CRDT counterpart tolerating any number of Byzantine nodes, described in this paper as the state-based analog of its operation-based approach.)
- competing: Chai and Zhao. "Byzantine Fault Tolerance for Services with Commutative Operations." IEEE SCC 2014. (Requires 3f+1 replicas to tolerate f Byzantine nodes; contrasted in this paper as unusable in open peer-to-peer systems because of Sybil-attack vulnerability.)
- competing: van der Linde, Leitão, Preguiça. "Practical Client-side Replication: Weak Consistency Semantics for Insecure Settings." VLDB 2020. (Different goal: ensures correct causal-dependency reporting via trusted servers and rational-client assumptions, rather than tolerating arbitrary causal-dependency claims.)
- competing: Jacob, Beer, Henze, Hartenstein. "Analysis of the Matrix Event Graph Replicated Data Type." IEEE Access, 2021. (A DAG-based CRDT the paper cites as already tolerating an arbitrary number of Byzantine nodes, structurally similar to this paper's hash graph.)
- foundational: Bracha. "Asynchronous Byzantine agreement protocols." Information and Computation 75(2), 1987. (Byzantine reliable broadcast, the stronger and more expensive property this paper's eventual-delivery requirement deliberately avoids needing.)
- foundational: Douceur. "The Sybil Attack." IPTPS 2002. (Cited as the reason 3f+1-style protocols cannot be deployed in open peer-to-peer systems.)
- foundational: Gomes, Kleppmann, Mulligan, Beresford. "Verifying strong eventual consistency in distributed systems." OOPSLA 2017. (Source of the Strong Eventual Consistency correctness definition used throughout this paper.)

## [KLEPPMANN-TPDS-17] A Conflict-Free Replicated JSON Datatype

**Citation:** Martin Kleppmann, Alastair R. Beresford. "A Conflict-Free Replicated JSON Datatype." IEEE Transactions on Parallel and Distributed Systems, 2017. DOI 10.1109/TPDS.2017.2697382.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/pdf/1608.03960
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/pdf/1608.03960
**Domain:** D

### What it does
Lets independent replicas modify a JSON document (arbitrarily nested maps, ordered lists, and registers holding primitive values) concurrently, offline, and merge every replica back to the same state with no coordination and no lost input, using a CRDT (Conflict-free Replicated Data Type, a data structure whose concurrent updates are constructed to commute so any delivery order produces the same result). Each replica applies a mutation to its own local copy immediately, generates an operation describing that mutation, and asynchronously broadcasts the operation to other replicas; no operation can fail once performed locally, unlike systems such as Bayou that allow tentative transactions to later be rolled back.

Every operation is assigned a unique identifier that is a Lamport timestamp: a pair `(c, p)` where `p` is the identifier of the generating replica (for example, a hash of its public key) and `c` is a per-replica counter incremented for every operation the replica generates, so `c` is compared as an integer. When a replica receives an operation with a counter value greater than its own stored counter, it advances its local counter to that value; this guarantees any operation causally caused by an earlier operation has a strictly greater counter, and only concurrent operations can share a counter value. Ties between concurrent operations with the same counter are broken by comparing replica identifiers, producing a total order over all operation identifiers.

Every operation carries an explicit `deps` field, the set of Lamport timestamps of its direct causal dependencies. A replica buffers an incoming remote operation and applies it (APPLY-REMOTE) only once every identifier in its `deps` set is already present in the replica's own set of applied operation identifiers; delivery need not arrive in causal order over the network, because the replica enforces the ordering itself before application. List elements form a linked structure: each element has a unique identifier (the identifier of the insertion operation that created it), and local state maps each identifier to the identifier of the following element (`next`). A deletion never removes an element from this linked structure; it clears the element's presence set (the set of operations that assert the element exists) to empty, marking it a tombstone, so ordered position is preserved even after deletion and a concurrent operation referencing a deleted element can make its presence set non-empty again. Maps and registers use the same presence-set mechanism: a key or register value is considered absent when its presence set is empty. Because assignment to a register is not globally serialized, concurrent assignments to the same register from different replicas leave all concurrently assigned values present simultaneously rather than picking one as a winner, preserving every user's input; nested lists and nested maps compose recursively by the same rule (an insertion or assignment can target a position inside an already-nested structure).

A "cursor" identifies a position in the document as a path of alternating map keys and list-element identifiers from the document root, so a cursor can be transmitted between replicas and used to locate the same logical position even after concurrent edits change the surrounding structure.

### Measured results
None. The paper states, in its own conclusion, that it is a formal semantics only: a practical implementation and its performance characteristics are explicitly deferred to follow-on work. No implementation, benchmark, message-size figure, or memory-overhead figure for this algorithm appears anywhere in the text. The paper cites Attiya et al. [31] as having independently analyzed metadata overhead for collaboratively edited lists and provided a correctness proof of the RGA (Replicated Growable Array) algorithm, but does not itself reproduce or report that analysis's figures, and RGA is a component this paper builds its list semantics on, not a separately measured baseline in this paper.

### Parameters
None with numeric values; the algorithm is presented as operational semantics (inference rules), not as a system with configuration parameters.

### Stated limitations
The paper is scoped to formal semantics of the JSON CRDT; a practical implementation and measurement of its performance are deferred to follow-on work. The supported operation set is insertion, deletion, and assignment; the authors state a move operation (reordering list elements or relocating a subtree) and an undo operation would be useful but are not defined here. Tombstones (deleted-element markers) are retained forever in this design; the authors state garbage collection of tombstones is required to prevent unbounded growth of the data structure and is left to future work. The authors state the "no input is ever lost" design principle produces merged states that can surprise application programmers unfamiliar with concurrent semantics (their Figure 6 example), and that further work is needed on understanding programmer expectations and on a possible schema language to express, for example, that a numeric field should behave as a counter rather than a plain register. The liveness property (every replica eventually processes every operation) is stated as an assumption, not proved in the paper; the authors assert it "can usually be provided in practice" because network interruptions are of finite duration, without a supporting measurement. Lamport-timestamp causal dependency sets (`deps`) are defined in the paper as the full set of an operation's causal-history timestamps; the paper notes a real implementation would need a more compact representation of causal history than storing the full set, without specifying one.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Every replica needs a transport that eventually delivers every generated operation to every other replica; delivery order across the network need not be causal, but the replica must buffer any operation whose `deps` are not yet all locally applied and apply it only once they are — so the replica-side apply logic, not the network, is what enforces causal order. Each replica needs a stable, comparable replica identifier (the paper suggests a hash of the replica's public key) and a monotonically increasing local counter, and must advance that counter upon receiving any operation with a higher counter value, to keep Lamport timestamps globally unique and causality-respecting. The system must retain tombstones for every deleted list element or map key indefinitely unless a separate garbage-collection mechanism (not defined in this paper) is added, so storage grows monotonically with the number of insert/delete operations ever issued, not with the current document size. Because concurrent assignments to the same register are all retained rather than resolved to one winner, any component consuming the document (the client application) needs its own policy for choosing among multiple concurrently present register values or presenting them to the user. The mechanism assumes every operation reaches every replica eventually (fair-loss, retry-based delivery); it does not itself provide encryption, authentication, or defense against a replica that forges another replica's Lamport timestamp or fabricates false causal dependencies.

### Contradicts
Its own target-registry justification (`why_needed` in `registry/targets-deduped.json`) states this paper carries "message-size measurements against Operational Transformation and other CRDTs" — the paper contains no such measurements; it is a formal-semantics paper with no implementation or evaluation, and the authors explicitly defer performance measurement to follow-on work. Any claim citing this paper for Automerge's measured memory or message-size cost is not supported by this text and needs a different, later source. None found against other entries in this corpus.

### References worth retrieving
- foundational: Attiya, Burckhardt, Gotsman, Morrison, Yang, Zawirski. "Specification and Complexity of Collaborative Text Editing" (cited as [31], analyzes metadata overhead of collaboratively edited lists and proves RGA correctness).
- foundational: Shapiro, Preguiça, Baquero, Zawirski. "Conflict-free replicated data types." SSS 2011 (cited as [3], origin of the CRDT concept this paper composes).
- competing: Attiya et al.'s RGA (Replicated Growable Array) as compared to WOOT, Treedoc, Logoot, LSEQ for ordered-list CRDTs — none of which support nesting, per this paper's related work.
- competing: Burckhardt, Gotsman, Yang, Zawirski. "Cloud types for eventual consistency" (cited as [35], composable cloud arrays and entities, an alternative composition framework without ordered lists).
- competing: Baquero, Almeida, Lerche (cited as [32]) and Almeida et al. (cited as [33]) on nested-map CRDT semantics and delta mutations, the closest prior work on composition this paper extends.
- foundational: Lamport. "Time, clocks, and the ordering of events in a distributed system." (cited as [42], source of the Lamport timestamp mechanism used for operation identifiers.)
- competing: DeCandia et al., Dynamo (cited as [37]) — multi-value register conflict handling left to application code, contrasted against this paper's structured merge.

"will report on its performance characteristics in follow-on work."
