## [KLEPPMANN-TPDS-22] A Highly-Available Move Operation for Replicated Trees

**Citation:** Martin Kleppmann, Dominic P. Mulligan, Victor B. F. Gomes, Alastair R. Beresford. "A highly-available move operation for replicated trees." IEEE Transactions on Parallel and Distributed Systems, 2022. DOI 10.1109/TPDS.2021.3118603.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://martin.kleppmann.com/papers/move-op.pdf
**Source URL:** https://martin.kleppmann.com/papers/move-op.pdf
**Domain:** D

### What it does
Lets independent replicas of a tree-structured document (a filesystem directory hierarchy, or a nested XML/JSON structure) each perform a move operation on any node, concurrently and without coordination, while guaranteeing every replica converges to the same tree and that tree never contains a cycle or a duplicated node. The authors first demonstrate the problem empirically: Google Drive, under concurrent moves of the same subtree to two different destinations, either duplicates the moved files or shows an "unknown error" and enters an inconsistent state; Dropbox duplicates the moved files under the same scenario. Both are widely deployed systems whose replicated-tree handling has this defect.

Every update, including node creation and deletion, is represented as a single kind of operation, `Move t p m c`: at logical time `t`, node `c` becomes a child of parent `p`, carrying metadata `m` (for a filesystem, the child's filename). A move operation does not name the node's prior location; applying it removes `c` from wherever it currently sits in the tree and reattaches it under `p`. Node identifiers must be globally unique (for example, UUIDs — Universally Unique Identifiers); timestamps must be globally unique and totally ordered (the paper uses Lamport timestamps, a logical clock construction from Kleppmann and Beresford's own prior citation [9] that pairs a per-replica counter with a replica identifier to produce a total order consistent with causality). Node creation is implemented as a move of a freshly generated ID under its intended parent; deletion is a move to a designated "trash" node ID that does not otherwise appear in the tree, and the algorithm does not recursively remove a deleted node's children, because a concurrent operation might move part of the deleted subtree back out of the trash, and every child of that subtree must be preserved unmodified in that case.

A single-order function, `do_op`, applies one move to the current tree and rejects it (leaves the tree unmodified) if the moved node `c` is currently an ancestor of the destination `newp`, or if `c` equals `newp` — either case would create a cycle. To keep every replica consistent despite each replica potentially receiving operations in a different order, every replica maintains an operation log alongside the tree, in descending timestamp order. Applying a new operation with timestamp `t` proceeds by an undo-do-redo cycle: the replica first undoes every previously applied logged operation whose timestamp exceeds `t` (restoring each such move's previous parent and metadata, recorded in the log entry itself), applies the new operation with `do_op`, then reapplies (redoes) the undone operations in timestamp order. The resulting tree state is always identical to what applying every operation the replica knows about, in increasing timestamp order, from an empty tree would produce — regardless of the actual arrival order — which is what makes application-order independent and guarantees convergence. Conflicting concurrent moves of the same node resolve deterministically: the lower-timestamped move applies first, the higher-timestamped move then applies second and its destination wins. Conflicting moves that would jointly create a cycle resolve by the lower-timestamped move taking effect and the higher-timestamped move being silently ignored (rejected by the cycle check inside `do_op` when replayed in timestamp order).

The paper extends the base mechanism three ways. Hardlinks are supported by having leaf nodes reference a separate file-inode object rather than embedding file data directly, so multiple leaf nodes can reference the same inode; symlinks are leaf nodes holding a path string. Log truncation removes indefinite memory growth: because `apply_op` only ever inspects the log prefix with timestamp greater than the operation being applied, once a timestamp `t` is causally stable — no future operation from any replica will ever have a timestamp of `t` or less — every log entry at or below `t` can be discarded, and trashed nodes below the causally-stable threshold can likewise be garbage-collected. Causal stability is computed, in a system where the replica set is known and each replica generates strictly increasing timestamps over FIFO (First-In-First-Out) links, as the minimum of the most recent timestamp seen from each replica. Sibling ordering (an explicit order among children of the same parent, needed for e.g. an XML element's child sequence) is added by attaching a separate list CRDT (RGA or Logoot) per branch node and embedding that list CRDT's per-element identifier in a move operation's metadata field.

### Measured results
Correctness proof: every stated theorem (unique-parent property, acyclicity, commutativity of move operations, and Strong Eventual Consistency) is mechanically checked in Isabelle/HOL with no unproved assumptions (no use of the `sorry` placeholder). The Isabelle/HOL formalization totals 59 lines of core definitions plus 2,495 lines of proof: 203 lines proving unique parent, 443 proving acyclicity, 450 proving commutativity and convergence, 327 proving Strong Eventual Consistency, 743 defining and proving equivalence of the executable variant, and 779 proving safety of the log-truncation/causal-stability optimization. Checking the complete proof takes 3 minutes on a 2018 MacBook Pro.

Performance evaluation used two Scala implementations — one generated automatically from the Isabelle/HOL definitions via code generation, one handwritten and functionally equivalent but not formally verified — deployed as three replicas on Amazon EC2 c5.large instances in us-west-1 (Northern California), eu-west-1 (Ireland), and ap-southeast-1 (Singapore). Measured round-trip network delay: Ireland–California median 145 ms; Singapore–California median 176 ms. Workload: each replica starts from an empty tree and generates move operations at a fixed rate, each move's parent and child chosen uniformly at random from a pool of 1,000 tree nodes; timestamps are Lamport clocks; node identifiers are 64-bit integers; operations propagate over TCP; each replica runs for 10 minutes per rate to reach steady state.

| Metric | Isabelle-generated code | Handwritten (optimized) code |
|---|---|---|
| Median time to apply a local operation | ~50 µs | ~1–2 µs |
| Median time to apply a remote operation, at saturation | ~1 ms | not separately stated at saturation |
| Peak sustained throughput (CRDT algorithm) | 600 operations/sec | 5,700 operations/sec |
| Peak sustained throughput, leader-based state machine replication (same code, same network, leader in California) | 14,000 operations/sec | 22,000 operations/sec |

The 9.5x throughput difference between the two CRDT implementations (600 vs. 5,700 ops/sec) is attributed entirely to code-generation inefficiency, since both implementations perform functionally identical work. At peak throughput, the optimized implementation performs on average 200 undo/redo operations per remote operation applied. Leader-based state machine replication achieves 23x (Isabelle-generated) or 4x (handwritten/optimized) the CRDT algorithm's throughput on the identical hardware and network, but a single move operation issued by the Irish or Singaporean replica requires a full round trip to the California leader (145–176 ms), roughly five orders of magnitude slower than the 1–2 µs local-CRDT-operation latency; the Singapore/Ireland-to-leader round trips are plotted directly against both CRDT curves in the paper's Figure 7 to make this comparison explicit. A lock-based alternative (acquire a lock from a remote lock server, perform one move, release) is bounded by one round trip per operation and so is limited to 1/176 ms ≈ 5.7 operations/sec when the lock server is in California and the client in Singapore — three orders of magnitude below the optimized CRDT algorithm's 5,700 ops/sec.

### Parameters
Node identifiers: required to be globally unique (paper uses 64-bit integers in the benchmark; suggests UUIDs generally). Timestamps: required to be globally unique and totally ordered (paper uses Lamport timestamps, i.e. a `(counter, replica_id)` pair per its own earlier citation [9]). Benchmark workload pool: 1,000 tree nodes, parent and child chosen uniformly at random per operation. Steady-state measurement window: 10 minutes per operation rate. EC2 instance type: c5.large, three regions (us-west-1, eu-west-1, ap-southeast-1).

### Stated limitations
The algorithm as specified retains every operation in the log indefinitely, so memory use grows without bound unless the causal-stability truncation extension (§3.6) is applied; that truncation itself requires the replica set to be known in advance, requires monotonically increasing per-replica timestamps, and requires FIFO delivery between every pair of replicas — none of which the base algorithm assumes. The base algorithm's benchmark deliberately does not use the log-truncation optimization ("for simplicity we do not use the optimisation discussed in §3.6"), so the measured throughput numbers include unbounded log growth over the 10-minute run and do not measure the truncation optimization's cost or benefit. The optimized implementation's throughput could be raised further by batching operations to amortize undo/redo cost across a batch; the authors state this is left to future work and unevaluated. Sibling ordering (explicit child order within a parent) is not part of the core algorithm; it requires attaching a separate list CRDT per branch node, described but not evaluated in this paper. The paper explicitly identifies a fundamental throughput/latency trade-off rather than a limitation to be removed: leader-based state machine replication gives 4x to 23x higher throughput than the CRDT algorithm on identical hardware, at the price of clients being unable to make updates while offline and of every write requiring a round trip to a leader that may be geographically distant. The authors state applications needing maximum throughput should prefer state machine replication; applications needing minimum response latency or continued availability during network partition should prefer this algorithm. Only one type of update (move) is defined; other document mutation types are represented by encoding them as a move (creation as move-under-desired-parent, deletion as move-to-trash), so the model does not natively express operations outside that encoding.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The transport must deliver every operation to every other replica eventually, but need not preserve delivery order — the replica's own undo-do-redo application logic reorders operations into timestamp order regardless of arrival order — and the paper explicitly assumes an underlying network protocol detects and retransmits lost messages and suppresses duplicates (i.e., reliable, deduplicated delivery is assumed, ordering is not). No central server or consensus protocol is required or assumed; any number of replicas may crash, and any non-crashed subset continues operating. Every replica must retain a full operation log alongside current tree state (not just current state) to support the undo/redo mechanism, and must retain trashed (deleted) nodes and their descendants until causal stability is established, or storage grows unbounded. If log truncation is used, the system needs a mechanism to determine causal stability, which in turn needs the full replica set to be known, monotonically increasing per-replica timestamps, and FIFO-ordered pairwise links. Timestamps issued by different replicas must be globally unique and totally ordered; the paper does not specify how uniqueness is enforced against a Byzantine or misbehaving replica, and assumes correct replicas do not forge timestamps. If sibling ordering is required, another list CRDT (RGA or Logoot, both cited as prior work, not designed in this paper) must be composed per branch node, and its element identifiers must be threaded through the move operation's metadata field.

### Contradicts
None found against other entries in this corpus. Against common assumption, the paper documents that Google Drive's and Dropbox's actual deployed concurrent-move handling is not merely theoretically imperfect but produces observable defects (file duplication in both; an explicit "unknown error" state in Google Drive) under directly reproduced scenarios (§2), which the authors state is the real-world motivation for the algorithm.

## [KOLESNIKOV-CCS-16] Efficient Batched Oblivious PRF with Applications to Private Set Intersection
**Citation:** Vladimir Kolesnikov, Ranjit Kumaresan, Mike Rosulek, Ni Trieu. "Efficient Batched Oblivious PRF with Applications to Private Set Intersection." ACM CCS, 2016. DOI 10.1145/2976749.2978381.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://eprint.iacr.org/2016/799.pdf
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2016/799.pdf
**Domain:** G

### What it does
BaRK-OPRF (batched, related-key oblivious pseudorandom function) lets two parties run many instances of an oblivious PRF (OPRF) evaluation in one batch, each instance costing about as much as one 1-out-of-2 oblivious transfer (OT). In an OPRF, a receiver holding input r learns F(s, r) for a PRF F and a sender-held seed s, and the sender learns nothing about r. The construction extends the IKNP OT-extension protocol (Ishai, Kilian, Nissim, Petrank, CRYPTO 2003) and the Kolesnikov-Kumaresan (KK, CRYPTO 2013) coding-theoretic reformulation of it. IKNP encodes the receiver's OT choice bit as a repetition code inside an OT-extension matrix; KK replaces the repetition code with a short error-correcting code to pack multiple choices per matrix row. This paper replaces the error-correcting code with a pseudorandom code (PRC): a function C, instantiated from AES, such that for any two distinct receiver inputs r and r', the Hamming distance between C(r) and C(r') is at least the computational security parameter kappa with overwhelming probability. Because a PRC need not be efficiently decodable, its input domain is unbounded, so the same matrix-row mechanism that gave KK a bounded 1-out-of-n OT gives BaRK-OPRF a 1-out-of-poly OT over an unbounded string domain, which the paper interprets as an OPRF. The receiver obtains one PRF output value t = q xor (C(r) . s) per instance; the sender can compute the PRF value for any input string but not which one the receiver holds. The protocol is proved secure in the semi-honest model, in the random-oracle model or under a correlation-robustness assumption generalizing IKNP's.

Applied to private set intersection (PSI), the two parties (Alice with set A, Bob with set B) learn only A intersect B. Bob places his n items into 1.2n Cuckoo-hash bins using 3 hash functions plus a stash of size s; Alice evaluates the OPRF on (3+s)n values, one per Cuckoo-hash slot Bob could have used, and the two parties compare masked outputs to find matches. Because the OPRF output no longer depends on the item's bit length (unlike the prior PSSZ15 protocol, which used one OT per input bit), running time and communication become independent of item bit length.

### Measured results
Server: Intel Xeon E5-2699 v3 2.30GHz, 256 GB RAM, both parties run on the same machine with simulated network conditions via Linux `tc`. LAN: 0.2 ms latency; WAN: 50 MB/s average bandwidth, 96 ms average round-trip latency. Single thread per party. Statistical security parameter sigma=40, computational security parameter kappa=128. Comparison baseline: the PSSZ15 protocol (Pinkas, Schneider, Segev, Zohner, USENIX Security 2015), implemented and run by the same authors on the same hardware for a fair comparison.

Running time in milliseconds, PSI of n elements per party, LAN setting, 128-bit items: PSSZ15 307 ms (n=2^8) to 213,597 ms (n=2^24); BaRK-OPRF-PSI (bit-length-independent) 192 ms (n=2^8) to 58,567 ms (n=2^24). At n=2^20 (LAN), BaRK-OPRF-PSI is 2.8x faster than PSSZ15 for 64-bit items and 3.6x faster for 128-bit items. At n=2^24 (LAN), the corresponding improvements are 2.3x and 3.6x. Computing the intersection of two 2^24-item sets of 128-bit strings takes about one minute with BaRK-OPRF-PSI versus 214 seconds with PSSZ15.

| n (items/party) | PSSZ15 LAN, 128-bit (ms) | BaRK-OPRF-PSI LAN (ms) | PSSZ15 WAN, 128-bit (ms) | BaRK-OPRF-PSI WAN (ms) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2^8 | 307 | 192 | 624 | 556 |
| 2^12 | 443 | 211 | 746 | 585 |
| 2^16 | 1,352 | 387 | 2,198 | 1,259 |
| 2^20 | 13,814 | 3,780 | 23,546 | 7,455 |
| 2^24 | 213,597 | 58,567 | 381,913 | 106,828 |

Communication cost, PSI of n elements per party, 128-bit items: BaRK-OPRF-PSI 2.9x-3.3x lower than PSSZ15; at n=2^20, 3.2x lower. In absolute terms (MB): PSSZ15 411.6 MB at n=2^20 (128-bit), BaRK-OPRF-PSI 127.2 MB at n=2^20 (bit-length-independent). Naive insecure hashing baseline for comparison: 10.0 MB at n=2^20. BaRK-OPRF-PSI is 4.3x slower than the insecure naive-hashing baseline for the largest tested sets.

OT-extension matrix cost per OPRF/OT instance (bits), from Table 1, varying item bit length l and set size n: BaRK-OPRF holds constant at 424-448 bits across all tested (n, l) pairs, while PSSZ15's OT cost scales with l, from 256 bits (n=2^24, l=32) to 3,840 bits (n=2^8, l=128). The ratio of BaRK-OPRF cost to PSSZ15 cost ranges from 0.11 (n=2^8, l=128, BaRK-OPRF cheaper) to 1.75 (n=2^24, l=32, BaRK-OPRF more expensive) — BaRK-OPRF is worse than PSSZ15 for short items (32 bits) at large set sizes.

Parameters used in the implementation (Table 2), by set size n: stash size s (Cuckoo hashing, failure probability bound 2^-40): 12 (n=2^8) down to 2 (n=2^24). Pseudorandom-code width k: 424 bits (n=2^8) to 448 bits (n=2^24). OPRF output length v: 56 bits (n=2^8) to 88 bits (n=2^24).

### Parameters
- Computational security parameter kappa = 128.
- Statistical security parameter sigma = 40.
- Cuckoo hashing: 3 hash functions, load factor 1.2 (n items into 1.2n bins), stash size s chosen per PSSZ15's numbers to bound hashing-failure probability to 2^-40; s ranges 2-12 over the tested n = 2^8 to 2^24.
- Pseudorandom-code output width k, chosen so minimum Hamming distance >= kappa with overwhelming probability; empirically k = 4*kappa suffices (paper states output length k=4kappa is sufficient to make near-collisions negligible), rounded up to a multiple of 8; tested values 424-448 bits.
- OPRF output length v = sigma + log2(n^2), rounded up to a multiple of 8; tested values 56-88 bits.
- Item bit length l tested at 32, 64, and 128 bits; BaRK-OPRF-PSI running time and communication are independent of l by construction, confirmed empirically across all three.
- Set size n tested at 2^8, 2^12, 2^16, 2^20, 2^24 elements per party.
- Base OTs: 128 base-OTs via Naor-Pinkas construction, extended via IKNP OT extension.

### Stated limitations
The protocol and its security proof are stated and proved only in the semi-honest adversary model; the paper explicitly separates this from the malicious-adversary line of OT-extension work (ALSZ15, KOS15) and the publicly-verifiable-covert model (KM15), none of which this paper's construction covers. The receiver's OPRF learns t = q xor (C(r).s) rather than the hashed value H(t), which the paper states is a functionality subtlety relative to a standard OPRF definition. The construction realizes many OPRF instances with related keys (the same seed s and code C shared across all instances in a batch), not independent keys. For short items (32 bits) at the largest tested set size (2^24), the prior PSSZ15 protocol is faster than BaRK-OPRF-PSI, so the paper states a hybrid selecting the best subprotocol per (n, l) would be straightforward but was not implemented — results are reported even where BaRK-OPRF is worse, to show the tradeoff.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Requires both parties to run in a semi-honest (honest-but-curious) threat model; the construction offers no defense if either party deviates from the protocol, so a caller needing security against an actively malicious counterparty cannot use this construction as specified. Requires a private symmetric channel over which to run OT-extension messages (base OTs plus subsequent symmetric-key rounds); the paper does not specify network transport. Requires both parties to agree in advance on set-size-dependent parameters (Cuckoo-hash stash size s, pseudorandom-code width k, OPRF output length v) from Table 2, so the calling system must communicate or fix n before the protocol starts, or bound n from above. Requires a source of AES computation for the pseudorandom code C; the paper reports this is cheap only because of hardware AES acceleration, so a caller on hardware without AES-NI would see different concrete cost than measured here. The PSI application requires each item to fit in the tested bit-length range (32-128 bits, upper bound 128 bits per the paper's own hash-then-PSI recommendation for larger item domains).

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus. No other retrieved paper in this batch reports competing PSI running-time or communication figures under comparable conditions.

### References worth retrieving
- **Foundational**: Ishai, Kilian, Nissim, Petrank, "Extending Oblivious Transfers Efficiently," CRYPTO 2003 (IKNP OT extension, the base protocol this work modifies).
- **Foundational**: Kolesnikov, Kumaresan, "Improved OT Extension for Transferring Short Secrets," CRYPTO 2013 (the KK coding-theoretic reformulation this work extends).
- **Competing**: Pinkas, Schneider, Segev, Zohner, "Phasing: Private Set Intersection Using Permutation-Based Hashing," USENIX Security 2015 (PSSZ15, the direct performance baseline throughout this paper).
- **Competing**: Pinkas, Schneider, Zohner, "Faster Private Set Intersection Based on OT Extension," USENIX Security 2014 (PSZ14, the paradigm PSSZ15 and this work both build on).
- **Competing**: Freedman, Ishai, Pinkas, Reingold, "Keyword Search and Oblivious Pseudorandom Functions," TCC 2005 (FIPR05, introduces OPRF, alternative construction based on Naor-Reingold PRF requiring exponentiations).
- **Foundational**: Huberman, Franklin, Hogg, "Enhancing Privacy and Trust in Electronic Communities," EC 1999 (Diffie-Hellman-paradigm PSI with lower communication but, per PSSZ15's measurement cited here, over 200x slower computation than OT-based protocols).
- **Attack-adjacent (malicious-model OT extension)**: Asharov, Lindell, Schneider, Zohner, "More Efficient Oblivious Transfer Extensions with Security for Malicious Adversaries," EUROCRYPT 2015.
- **Attack-adjacent (malicious-model OT extension)**: Keller, Orsini, Scholl, "Actively Secure OT Extension with Optimal Overhead," CRYPTO 2015.

## [KOMLO-SAC-20] FROST: Flexible Round-Optimized Schnorr Threshold Signatures

**Citation:** Chelsea Komlo, Ian Goldberg. "FROST: Flexible Round-Optimized Schnorr Threshold Signatures." Selected Areas in Cryptography (SAC), 2020. DOI 10.1007/978-3-030-81652-0_2.
**Retrieved:** full text
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2020/852.pdf
**Domain:** E

### What it does
FROST (Flexible Round-Optimized Schnorr Threshold signatures) lets t out of n key-share holders jointly produce a single Schnorr signature, verifiable with the standard single-party Schnorr verification equation, while requiring only one network round of communication among signers during the signing operation itself, with an optional non-interactive preprocessing stage performed in advance. Each participant holds a long-lived secret share s_i from a threshold key generation built on Pedersen's distributed key generation (DKG) protocol, modified with a per-participant zero-knowledge proof of knowledge of the constant term of that participant's secret-sharing polynomial, added specifically to block rogue-key attacks (an adversary deriving its own public key share as a function of honest participants' public shares to forge a joint signature). During preprocessing, each participant generates and publishes commitments to pi single-use nonce pairs (d_ij, e_ij); a designated signature aggregator (SA) later selects a signing set S of t participants and the next unused commitment pair for each. Each selected participant computes a per-participant binding value rho_i by hashing the message, its own index, and the full set of participants' published commitments together (rho_i = H1(i, m, B)), which binds every signer's response to the specific message and the specific signing set; this binding is what defeats the Drijvers et al. forgery attack against prior two-round Schnorr multisignature and threshold schemes, in which an adversary interleaves signing sessions to solve a system of linear equations (the ROS problem) and forge a signature. Each participant returns a single response z_i computed from its nonce, its long-lived share, and a Lagrange interpolation coefficient; the aggregator sums the z_i values and publishes (R, z) as a standard Schnorr signature. FROST is not robust: if a participant returns an invalid response, the aggregator detects it (by checking g^z_i against the participant's published commitments) and the protocol aborts, to be rerun with that participant excluded, rather than tolerating the misbehavior and completing anyway.

### Measured results
The paper reports no runtime benchmark (wall-clock time, throughput, or hardware-measured latency); its Rust implementation over Ristretto/curve25519 is stated to exist, with source published, but no timing figures from that implementation are given in the text. All quantitative results in the paper are round-counts and computational-complexity terms for the underlying protocols, derived by describing each protocol's message flow rather than by executing it.

| Result (round count in the honest, no-misbehavior case) | Conditions / scheme compared |
|---|---|
| FROST: 1 signing round (2 rounds total if preprocessing and signing are combined into a single interactive session) | FROST's own construction: preprocessing round performed once, in advance, non-interactively; single signing round thereafter, for each of the pi preprocessed nonce batches |
| FROST-Interactive: 2 rounds for preprocessing plus 2 rounds for signing | The paper's own interactive variant, used when the one-time verifiable random function (VRF) generating rho_i must be run online rather than via a random oracle |
| Stinson-Strobl scheme: minimum 4 rounds per signing operation | Robust threshold Schnorr construction (3 rounds for their DKG plus 1 round to distribute and combine signature shares), every round requiring all-to-all messaging |
| Gennaro-Jarecki-Krawczyk-Rabin (2003) scheme: 2 rounds of Pedersen DKG plus 1 additional round for signing (their base variant); 2 rounds of parallel Pedersen-DKG executions to precompute l nonces, then 1 round per signing operation thereafter (their optimized variant) | Non-FROST threshold Schnorr scheme whose key-generation stage FROST's own KeyGen builds on |
| Gennaro-Goldfeder one-round threshold ECDSA with identifiable aborts: 8 network rounds total, 6 broadcast rounds and 2 pairwise multiplicative-to-additive share-conversion rounds | Threshold ECDSA (not Schnorr) scheme cited as a non-robust design comparable in spirit to FROST's abort-on-misbehavior tradeoff |
| Security-proof concrete bound for FROST-Interactive (Theorem A.2): if the discrete-log problem is (tau', epsilon')-hard, FROST-Interactive is (tau, n_h, n_p, n_s, epsilon)-secure whenever epsilon' <= epsilon^2 / (2*n_h + (pi+1)*n_p + 1) and tau' = 4*tau + (30*pi*n_p + (4t-2)*n_s + (n+t-1)*t + 6)*t_exp + O(pi*n_p + n_s + n_h + 1) | n_h = random-oracle query count, n_p = allowed preprocess queries, n_s = allowed signing queries, pi = preprocess batch size, t_exp = time of one group exponentiation; holds only when the adversary compromises fewer than the threshold t participants |

### Parameters
- n: total number of key-share holders.
- t: signing threshold, t <= n; no numeric default given, left as a deployment choice.
- pi: preprocessing batch size (number of nonce pairs generated per participant per preprocessing run); appears symbolically in the security bound but is not assigned a numeric recommended value in the paper.
- Group: Ristretto over curve25519, used in the stated Rust implementation; no other group is benchmarked.
- Signature aggregator (SA) role: optional centralized coordination point; the paper states FROST can also run fully peer-to-peer (participants broadcast commitments directly to each other) in a two-round setting without a designated aggregator, foregoing the preprocessing-stage optimization.

### Stated limitations
The paper states its argument that the FROST-Interactive-to-plain-FROST transition (replacing a one-time VRF with a random-oracle hash for generating rho_i) carries no security consequence is heuristic, not a proof: it proves sufficiency of its stated forgery condition but explicitly states it does not prove necessity. It states that FROST trades robustness for signing efficiency: unlike the Stinson-Strobl and Gennaro-Jarecki-Krawczyk-Rabin robust schemes, a single misbehaving or unresponsive participant causes the entire signing operation to abort rather than complete with the remaining honest participants, requiring the protocol to be rerun with that participant excluded and the cause investigated out of band. It states that the FROST-Interactive preprocessing round must be performed serially by each participant (rather than in parallel/non-interactively, as plain FROST's preprocessing can be), because the security proof's simulator needs to extract the discrete logarithm of the adversary's VRF-key proof of knowledge via rewinding, which requires serialized execution. It states three explicit security assumptions implementations must independently guarantee: every participant validates the message before issuing a signature share; the network delivers messages reliably; and misbehaving participants can be identified via authenticated messaging within the signing group — none of which FROST itself provides.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
FROST requires a location (a "commitment server" or equivalent) where participants publish their preprocessing-stage nonce commitments for the aggregator to consume; the paper states this location need not be trusted for confidentiality (public commitment values grant no extra power to an adversary who reads them) but must be trusted to serve correct, unused values, since a malicious commitment server could mount denial-of-service or supply stale/malformed commitments on behalf of honest participants. It requires an authenticated channel or equivalent participant-identification mechanism external to FROST itself, since the protocol's misbehavior-detection step depends on being able to attribute an invalid response to a specific participant identity. It requires reliable message delivery between the aggregator and each signing participant, stated as an explicit assumption rather than something FROST tolerates violations of. Because FROST is non-robust, any system embedding it must supply its own retry/exclusion logic above the protocol to recover from an abort, since FROST itself only detects and halts.

### Contradicts
None found. This paper is a proposed construction and security proof; no numeric result in it is contradicted by another entry in this batch.

### References worth retrieving
- Gennaro, Jarecki, Krawczyk, Rabin. "Secure Distributed Key Generation for Discrete-Log Based Cryptosystems." Journal of Cryptology, 2007 — foundational (proves a weakness in Pedersen's original DKG that motivates the added commitment round FROST's KeyGen inherits)
- Pedersen. "A Threshold Cryptosystem without a Trusted Party." EUROCRYPT 1991 — foundational (base DKG protocol FROST's key generation modifies)
- Stinson, Strobl. "Provably Secure Distributed Schnorr Signatures and a (t,n) Threshold Scheme for Implicit Certificates." ACISP 2001 — competing (the 4-round robust threshold Schnorr baseline FROST is compared against)
- Gennaro, Goldfeder. "Fast Multiparty Threshold ECDSA with Fast Trustless Setup." ACM CCS 2018 — competing (threshold ECDSA construction sharing FROST's abort-on-misbehavior, non-robust design philosophy)
- Gennaro, Goldfeder. "One Round Threshold ECDSA with Identifiable Abort." IACR ePrint 2020/540 — competing (8-round end-to-end ECDSA scheme directly compared for round count)
- Drijvers, Edalatnejad, Ford, Kiltz, Loss, Neven, Stepanovs. "On the Security of Two-Round Multi-Signatures." IEEE S&P 2019 — attack (source of the ROS-based forgery attack FROST's rho_i binding is specifically designed to defeat)
- Maxwell, Poelstra, Seurin, Wuille. "Simple Schnorr multi-signatures with applications to Bitcoin." (MuSig) Designs, Codes and Cryptography, 2019 — competing (two-round Schnorr multisignature scheme shown vulnerable to the Drijvers/ROS attack, contrasted with FROST)
- Damgard, Jakobsen, Nielsen, Pagter, Ostergard. "Fast Threshold ECDSA with Honest Majority." IACR ePrint 2020/501 — competing (concurrent honest-majority threshold ECDSA construction requiring n >= 2t+1, contrasted with FROST's t-out-of-n model)
- Benhamouda, Lepoint, Orru, Raykova. "On the (in)security of ROS." IACR ePrint 2020/945 — attack (the ROS-solving algorithm the paper states does not, in the version analyzed, break FROST)

### Verbatim extracts
"can safely perform signing operations in a single round without limiting concurrency"
"FROST trades off robustness for more efficient signing operations"
"FROST does not perform a DKG during signing operations"
"access to the set of a participant's public published commitments does not grant additional powers"

## [KONG-TIT-24] Locally Repairable Convertible Codes With Optimal Access Costs
**Citation:** Xiangliang Kong. "Locally Repairable Convertible Codes With Optimal Access Costs." IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, 2024. DOI 10.1109/TIT.2024.3435346.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.06802
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.06802
**Domain:** C

### What it does
A code conversion changes the parameters of already-encoded data — for example, from an [n_I, k_I] code to a differently rated [n_F, k_F] code — without decoding the full original data and re-encoding from scratch, because that default approach requires reading a large number of symbols, transferring them over the network, and re-encoding, degrading system I/O. This paper studies conversion cost specifically for locally repairable codes (LRCs) — an (n, k, r) LRC produces an n-symbol codeword from k information symbols such that any single symbol can be recovered by reading at most r other symbols — in the merge regime, where ζ ≥ 2 initial codewords under an (n_I, k_I) LRC are combined into one final codeword under an (n_F, k_F=ζ·k_I) LRC.

The paper defines access cost as the sum of the read access cost (symbols read from the initial codewords during conversion) and write access cost (new symbols written to produce the final codeword), and separates every symbol touched into three categories: remaining symbols (unchanged, carried over from initial to final codeword), accessed symbols (read from initial codewords), and new symbols (written to the final codeword that were not carried over). The paper's contribution is threefold. First, it constructs a family of MDS (Maximum-Distance-Separable) convertible codes for general (n_I, k; n_F, ζk) parameters using Generalized Reed-Solomon (GRS) codes, built by mapping polynomials of degree at most k−1 into polynomials of degree at most ζk−1 via chosen evaluation points, achieving optimal access cost over a finite field whose size is linear in n_I (as opposed to a field size that grows with the code length raised to a large power). Second, it extends this construction, using an existing "good polynomials" technique for building optimal LRCs, to produce locally repairable convertible codes (LRCCs) with parameters (n_I, k, r; n_F, ζk, r), again over a field of size linear in n_I. Third, it proves a general lower bound on access cost for any convertible code whose final code is an LRC (Theorem IV.4), and shows the LRCCs from its own construction meet that bound exactly (Corollary IV.1, Remark IV.1) — establishing the constructed codes as access-cost-optimal, not merely as one available option.

### Measured results
This is a pure coding-theory paper with proved bounds and explicit algebraic constructions; there is no simulation, implementation, or hardware benchmark. All figures below are proved bounds or one illustrative worked example from the paper's own text, not empirical measurements.

| Result | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Illustrative worked example (Example II.1) | (6,4;10,8) MDS convertible code over F₁₉, write access cost 2, read access cost 4 | ζ=2, k_I=4, n_I=6, k_F=8, n_F=10; specific evaluation points A={1,8,7,18}, B={2,16,14,17}, C={4,9} chosen as powers of the field generator 2 in F₁₉* |
| Lower bound on write access cost for general (n_I,k;n_F,ζk) convertible code whose final code C_F has locality r and minimum distance d | at least ζ(d + (ζ−1)k + ⌈(ζ−1)k/r⌉ − 2) − (ζ−1)n_F | Theorem IV.4; holds for any linear final code with stated locality and distance, not restricted to this paper's own construction |
| Lower bound on read access cost, general case | ζk if Δ ≤ 0, else ζ(k − ⌈rΔ/(r+1)⌉), where Δ = n_F − 2d − ((ζ−1)k + ⌈(ζ−1)k/r⌉) + 3 | Theorem IV.4; when d > n_I − k + 1, simplifies to at least ζk |
| Lower bound on access cost specialized to optimal LRCCs with equal locality r on both codes | write access cost at least n_F − ζk(r+1); read access cost at least ζkr when (ζ+1)k ≤ n_F/(r+1), else ζ(r·n_F/(r+1) − ζkr) | Corollary IV.1; (n_I, kr, r; n_F, ζkr, r) optimal LRCCs, (r+1) divides both n_I and n_F |
| Field size needed for the paper's own explicit LRCC construction to meet the lower bound exactly | q a prime power with k(r+1) dividing (q−1) and q ≥ k(r+1)·max{ζ+1, ⌈l_I/k⌉+2} + 1 | Corollary III.2; construction achieves write access cost l(r+1) and read access cost ζlr, where l = l_F = l_I ≤ k, n_I=(k+l_I)(r+1), n_F=(k+l_F)(r+1) |
| Comparison to prior MDS-convertible-code field-size requirement (Maturana, Rashmi, cited [5]) | prior general-parameter construction needs field size at least Ω(2^(ζ·n_I³)); reduced to q ≥ max{n_I, n_F} only under an added condition (n_F − k_F ≤ ⌊(n_I−k_I)/ζ⌋) and conditional on existence of certain superregular Hankel matrices | as reported by this paper's own related-work summary of [5]'s result, not independently re-derived in this extraction |
| Prior MDS-convertible-code access-cost lower bound (Maturana, Rashmi, cited [5], restated as Theorem I.2 / re-proved as Theorem IV.5 here) | read access cost at least ζ·min{k, n_F−ζk}; write access cost at least n_F−ζk; if n_I−k < n_F−ζk, read access cost at least ζk | linear MDS convertible codes, merge regime; this paper reproves the same bound as a special case (MDS codes are (n,k,k)-optimal LRCs) of its own more general Theorem IV.4, without assuming linearity of the initial/final codes |

### Parameters
- ζ ≥ 2: merge factor — number of initial codewords combined into one final codeword, k_F = ζ·k_I
- (n_I, k_I, r_I) and (n_F, k_F, r_F): initial and final LRC parameters; this paper's own construction requires r_I = r_F = r (equal locality on both sides), stated explicitly as a restriction relative to the fully general problem
- l_I = n_I − k_I, l_F = n_F − ζ·k_I: numbers of parity symbols in initial and final codes; the paper's constructions assume l_F ≤ min(l_I, k_I) or l_F = l_I = l < k
- q: field size — the paper's explicit constructions require q linear in n_I (specific bound stated in Corollary III.2), a substantial reduction from field sizes exponential in the code length required by some prior general-parameter constructions
- r: LRC locality parameter, fixed equal between initial and final code in this paper's construction

### Stated limitations
The construction requires the initial code and the final code to have the same locality r; the paper states this explicitly as an open question whether the construction and its optimal-access-cost guarantee can be generalized to LRCCs where the initial and final codes have different localities, even though its lower bound (Theorem IV.4) already covers that general case. The paper restricts its treatment to the merge regime only (combining multiple codewords into one); it states the split regime (one initial codeword divided into multiple final codewords) has equally strong practical motivation and cites a concurrent independent paper (Maturana, Rashmi, ISIT 2023, reference [9]) as "a good start" on that separate open question, not something this paper itself resolves. The paper states it is open how small the field size can be for LRCCs with optimal access cost to exist at all — noting that, unlike MDS codes, optimal LRCs are already known in the literature to admit sub-linear field size relative to code length, and this paper's own construction does not establish or approach that sub-linear regime. The paper's construction and lower bound do not address two other named LRC variants, (r,δ)-locality codes and LRCs with disjoint recovering sets (availability); the paper states conversion problems for those variants are open and of both theoretical and practical interest.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A storage system adopting this code-conversion scheme must be able to select, at conversion time, evaluation points and a finite field of the size stated in Corollary III.2, tied algebraically to the specific (k, r, l_I, l_F, ζ) parameters chosen — the construction is not parameter-agnostic, and a system wanting to convert between arbitrary rate targets must verify the required field-size and divisibility conditions (k(r+1) | (q−1)) hold for its chosen field before applying this construction. The conversion procedure needs the initial and final codes' evaluation points and coding coefficients fixed in advance as part of the code design, meaning a system cannot decide to run a low-access-cost conversion after the fact on codes chosen without this construction in mind; the access-cost lower bound (Theorem IV.4) applies to any linear code choice, but only the paper's specific algebraic construction (Corollary III.2) is shown to meet it. The scheme assumes the storage system can address individual codeword symbols directly (read exactly the "accessed symbols" set and write exactly the "new symbols" set) without touching "remaining symbols," which requires the underlying storage layer to support per-symbol, not per-codeword, read and write access during a conversion operation.

### Contradicts
None found within this batch. The paper positions itself as extending, not contradicting, Maturana and Rashmi's original convertible-code framework (reference [5]) and their concurrent LRCC construction (reference [9], "Locally repairable convertible codes," ISIT 2023) — the paper states its own point of difference explicitly: it targets LRCs with all-symbol locality via an algebraic-coding approach achieving field size linear in code length, whereas the concurrent [9] targets LRCs with information locality via a piggybacking-framework approach, without claiming either result is wrong.

### References worth retrieving
- Maturana, Rashmi, "Convertible codes: Enabling efficient conversion of coded data in distributed storage," IEEE TIT 68(7), 2022 — foundational; origin of the convertible-code framework, access-cost definitions, and MDS-convertible-code lower bound this paper extends to LRCs
- Maturana, Rashmi, "Locally repairable convertible codes," ISIT 2023 — competing; concurrent independent construction of LRCCs via a piggybacking framework for LRCs with information locality, holding the comparison numbers from the other side of this paper's stated field-size and locality-model differences (this is the paper the registry's why_needed cites as MATURANA-ISIT-23 and instructs be checked against this paper's claims)
- Maturana, Mukka, Rashmi, "Access-optimal linear MDS convertible codes for all parameters," ISIT 2020 — foundational; earlier access-optimal MDS-convertible-code construction in the same line this paper's MDS-code section (Section II) extends
- Maturana, Rashmi, "Bandwidth cost of code conversions in distributed storage: fundamental limits and optimal constructions" — foundational; establishes the bandwidth-cost (as opposed to access-cost) analysis for code conversion, a related but distinct cost metric
- Maturana, Rashmi, "Bandwidth cost of code conversions in the split regime," CoRR abs/2205.06793, 2022 — foundational; source of the open questions on low-field-size convertible codes that this paper states directly motivated its own study
- Kadekodi, Rashmi, Ganger, "Cluster storage systems gotta have heart: Improving storage efficiency by exploiting disk-reliability heterogeneity," USENIX FAST 2019 — foundational; the deployed-system motivation this paper cites for why code parameters must change over time as device failure rates vary
- Tamo, Barg, "A family of optimal locally recoverable codes," IEEE TIT 60(8), 2014 — foundational; source of the "good polynomials" LRC construction technique this paper extends into its own LRCC construction
- Gopalan, Huang, Simitci, Yekhanin, "On the locality of codeword symbols," IEEE TIT 58(11), 2012 — foundational; one of the two papers establishing the Singleton-type minimum-distance bound for LRCs (Theorem I.1) that defines what an "optimal" LRC is throughout this paper
- Huang, Simitci, Xu, Ogus, Calder, Gopalan, Li, Yekhanin, "Erasure coding in Windows Azure Storage," USENIX ATC 2012 — this batch's HUANG-ATC-12; cited as deployed-system motivation for locally repairable codes generally

## [KREUTER-CRYPTO-20] Anonymous Tokens with Private Metadata Bit
**Citation:** Ben Kreuter, Tancrède Lepoint, Michele Orrù, Mariana Raykova. "Anonymous Tokens with Private Metadata Bit." CRYPTO 2020, Part I, LNCS 12170, pages 308-336. Also posted as IACR ePrint Archive, Report 2020/072 ("Efficient anonymous tokens with private metadata bit"), revised April 21, 2022.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://eprint.iacr.org/2020/072.pdf
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2020/072.pdf
**Domain:** I

**Registry note:** `targets-deduped.json` holds one row keyed `KREUTER-FC-22` whose `title` field
("Anonymous Tokens with Public Metadata and Applications to Private Contact Tracing") belongs to a
different paper — the one extracted in this batch under key `SILDE-FC-22` — while that same row's
`authors` field and `candidate_urls` entry (`https://eprint.iacr.org/2020/072.pdf`) belong to this
paper. The first 2000 characters of `sources/text/KREUTER-CRYPTO-20.txt` state this paper's own
title as "Anonymous Tokens with Private Metadata Bit" by Kreuter, Lepoint, Orrù, and Raykova,
matching the registry row's authors and URL but not its title. Both this paper and the
`SILDE-FC-22` paper cite each other directly (Silde and Strand cite this paper as `[KLOR20a]`; see
that entry), confirming both are real, distinct, correctly retrieved papers rather than the same
document under two keys. The registry row conflates the two; a human should split it into two rows
before the corpus's citation list is generated from `targets-deduped.json`.

### What it does
PMBTokens lets a token issuer embed one secret bit of trust information into an anonymous,
single-use token, readable only by the issuer at redemption time and hidden from everyone else,
including the user who holds the token. The primitive extends Privacy Pass (Davidson et al., PETS
2018), a scheme a content delivery network uses to let a user prove she solved a CAPTCHA once and
redeem that proof many times without the network learning which redemption corresponds to which
issuance. Privacy Pass carries no metadata: every token looks the same regardless of why it was
issued. PMBTokens adds a private metadata bit (PMB) so an issuer can silently mark a user
untrustworthy (assign the PMB value indicating do-not-serve) without the user detecting the mark,
because a marked and an unmarked token remain indistinguishable to anyone without the issuer's
secret key. The paper states this matters operationally: if an issuer instead just stops handing
tokens to a suspected malicious user, the user learns she has been detected and can adjust her
behavior or train a detection-evading model against the visible signal.

The construction starts from the verifiable oblivious pseudorandom function (VOPRF) Privacy Pass
uses, `F_x(t) = x * H_t(t)`, where `H_t` maps an arbitrary string to a group element, `x` is the
issuer's secret key, and the user blinds her input `t` by a random scalar `r` before sending it, so
the issuer's response can be unblinded to the PRF output without the issuer learning `t`. A naive
two-secret-key version (one key per metadata bit) fails: because the VOPRF is deterministic, a user
who requests two tokens on the same input `t` under different keys gets two different outputs, and
a user who requests the same input twice under the same key gets identical outputs — letting a
malicious user probe which of two tokens shares a metadata bit by requesting duplicate inputs. The
paper's fix randomizes issuance: the function becomes `F_(x,y)(t; S) = x * H_t(t) + y * S`, where
`S` is randomness a value both parties contribute to (`S = r^-1 * H_s(r * H_t(t); s)`, with `r` the
user's blinding factor and `s` an issuer-chosen random value sent back with the response), so two
requests on the same `t` under the same key now yield different, unlinkable outputs. Applying two
key pairs `(x_0, y_0)` and `(x_1, y_1)` to this randomized function, one per metadata-bit value,
yields PMBTokens: the issuer picks the key pair matching the bit `b` it wants to embed, computes a
token, and proves in zero knowledge (a DLEQOR proof: an OR of two discrete-log-equality relations)
that the token was computed correctly under one of the two published public keys, without revealing
which one.

The paper additionally removes the zero-knowledge proof from both Privacy Pass and PMBTokens
issuance, at the cost of a weaker unlinkability guarantee: instead of proving correctness, the
issuer's response is either genuinely valid or, if the issuer misbehaves, unblinds to an
indistinguishable-from-random value; the user cannot tell the two cases apart until redemption. The
user regains a batched verification capability by requesting one extra token on a random linear
combination of her already-received tokens' hash inputs and checking that the corresponding linear
combination of outputs matches, letting her verify `n` tokens by one additional token request.
Removing the proof reduces issuer computation, stated as the bottleneck in a high-request-volume
deployment, to a single group-element multiplication per token.

### Measured results

| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| Multiplication and communication cost, asymptotic count | Table 1: Privacy Pass (PP) — 6 user multiplications, 3 issuer multiplications, 2 group elements transferred. Okamoto-Schnorr Privacy Pass variant (OSPP) — 9 user, 6 issuer, 2 elements. PMBTokens with DLEQOR proof (PMBT) — 15 user, 12 issuer, 2 elements. Proof-free Privacy Pass (PPB) — 4 user, 1 issuer, 2 elements. Proof-free PMBTokens (PMBTB) — 12 user, 2 issuer, 3 elements |
| Benchmarked wall-clock cost per operation, Rust implementation, Ristretto group over Curve25519, single thread of an Intel Xeon E5-2650 v4 @ 2.20GHz, Ubuntu 18.04.3 LTS, kernel 4.15.0 | Table 2: PP — DLEQ prove 212 µs, DLEQ verify 181 µs, token generation 111 µs, unblinding 286 µs, key generation 84 µs, signing (issuance) 303 µs, redemption 95 µs. PMBT — DLEQOR prove 576 µs, verify 666 µs, token gen. 135 µs, unblinding 844 µs, key gen. 234 µs, signing 845 µs, redemption 235 µs. PPB (proof-free PP) — no DLEQ step; token gen. 197 µs, unblinding 164 µs, key gen. 190 µs, signing 87 µs, redemption 95 µs. PMBTB (proof-free PMBTokens) — no DLEQ step; token gen. 368 µs, unblinding 678 µs, key gen. 512 µs, signing 155 µs, redemption 247 µs |
| PMBTokens issuance and redemption compared to Privacy Pass, same benchmark setting | PMBTokens issuance 845 µs versus Privacy Pass issuance 303 µs; PMBTokens redemption 235 µs versus Privacy Pass redemption 95 µs |
| Speedup over the prior Privacy Pass implementation from Davidson et al. (PETS 2018) | Stated as "between ten and one thousand faster," attributed by the authors jointly to using Curve25519 in place of NIST P-256 and to the choice of implementation language (Rust versus the earlier implementation's language), not isolated as a per-cause figure |
| Chosen Target Gap Diffie-Hellman hardness margin for the paper's unforgeability reduction, an analytical bound (not a wall-clock measurement) | Stated in an appendix as `O(2^94)` security requiring `O(2^64)` sequential adversary queries, concluded to make the underlying attack impractical even for an adversary in close network proximity, given key rotation |

### Parameters
| Parameter | Value used in the paper | Tested range |
|---|---|---|
| Security parameter λ | Instantiated for the benchmark via Ristretto group over Curve25519 | Not varied; single instantiation benchmarked |
| Metadata bit cardinality | 2 (one private bit, values 0 or 1) | Fixed; the construction is defined only for a single bit, not a multi-valued metadata field |
| Hash-to-group method | Elligator 2 map with SHA-512 | Not varied |
| Benchmark hardware | Single thread, Intel Xeon E5-2650 v4 @ 2.20GHz | Single hardware configuration; no scaling study across thread counts or CPU classes |
| WebAssembly cross-compilation target | Compiled via rust-wasm and exercised from JavaScript in Chromium 79.0.3945.130 to generate blinded tokens | Reported as a feasibility demonstration, without its own timing table |

### Stated limitations
The paper's formal treatment of unlinkability explicitly excludes man-in-the-middle adversaries who
intercept and replay a token at redemption time to spend it on a resource other than the one the
user intended — the authors call this token hijacking and state it is "not covered in our
definitions," relying instead on the assumption that user-issuer communication runs over a secure
channel; they sketch a message-authentication-code-based mitigation in an appendix rather than
proving it as part of the core scheme. The proof-free variants (PPB, PMBTB) achieve only a weaker
unlinkability notion than the DLEQ/DLEQOR-proof variants: a user cannot tell, until redemption,
whether a token she received is valid or is an indistinguishable-from-random value the issuer
produced by misbehaving. The security proofs for the verification-oracle-supporting construction
(Appendix J) explicitly do not grant the adversary a Read oracle that returns the private metadata
bit of an adversary-chosen token, only a Verify oracle that checks validity; the authors state this
restriction directly, without arguing security holds if a Read oracle is also exposed.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The scheme requires a random-oracle-model hash function `H_t` mapping arbitrary strings to group
elements (instantiated here via Elligator 2 with SHA-512), and a second random oracle `H_s` used to
derive the shared per-issuance randomness `S`; both are treated as ideal random oracles in the
security proofs, not merely collision-resistant hashes. Unforgeability rests on the Chosen Target
Gap Diffie-Hellman (CTGDH) assumption and unlinkability and metadata-bit privacy rest on the DDH
assumption in the same group, so any deploying system must instantiate a group where DDH is
believed hard (the paper uses Ristretto over Curve25519, a group chosen specifically because DDH
holds there, in contrast to constructions built on pairing groups where DDH is easy). The issuer
must hold, and keep confidential, one secret key pair per metadata-bit value (two key pairs total
for a single private bit); a system supporting `k` independent private bits or a larger metadata
alphabet is not directly given by this construction, since the two-key-pair technique is specific to
a binary embedded value. The construction assumes the transport between user and issuer is a secure
channel, which a deploying system must supply itself; the paper's core protocol does not defend
against a token being intercepted and redeemed by a party other than the one it was issued to. An
issuer wanting the verification-oracle-secure variant (Appendix J) must accept that it can answer
"is this token valid" queries about adversary-supplied tokens but must never expose a means for
answering "what is this token's metadata bit" for an adversary-chosen token, since the security
proof assumes the latter oracle is never available to the adversary.

### Contradicts
None found against other entries in this batch. This paper is the specific competing construction
[`SILDE-FC-22`] argues against on the public-metadata axis: Silde and Strand's paper, in this
corpus, states its own public-metadata protocol achieves smaller communication than an extension of
this paper's construction that would add public metadata to it (their Table 1, "Kreuter et al." row:
`514 * 2N` bits of public key versus their own scheme's constant 1028 bits, for `2^N` possible
metadata strings) — a comparison this paper does not itself make, since this paper defines a private
metadata bit, not public metadata. This is not a contradiction of a measured value; it is two
different papers measuring two different protocol variants for two different problems (private
versus public metadata), and no entry in this batch found a case where the two papers report
different numbers for the same construction.

### References worth retrieving
- foundational: A. Davidson, I. Goldberg, N. Sullivan, G. Tankersley, F. Valsorda. "Privacy Pass: Bypassing Internet Challenges Anonymously." PoPETs 2018. (`[DGS+18]`) — the VOPRF-based scheme this paper extends; every efficiency comparison in this paper and in `SILDE-FC-22` is against this construction.
- foundational: S. Jarecki, A. Kiayias, H. Krawczyk. "Round-Optimal Password-Protected Secret Sharing and T-PAKE in the Password-Only Model." ASIACRYPT 2014. (`[JKK14]`) — source of the 2HashDH-NIZK VOPRF that Privacy Pass and this paper build on.
- competing: S. Jarecki, H. Krawczyk, J. Resch. "Updatable Oblivious Key Management for Storage Systems." (`[JKR18]`, cited for a threshold partially oblivious PRF) — the source of the additive-blinding technique this paper adapts to remove the DLEQ proof.
- competing: M. Chase, S. Meiklejohn, G. Zaverucha. "Algebraic MACs and Keyed-Verification Anonymous Credentials." ACM CCS 2014. (`[CMZ14]`) — a keyed-verification anonymous-credential scheme the paper states could support a similar primitive at higher cost, and notes no extension to a private metadata bit is known for it.
- competing: P. Tsang, M. Au, A. Kapadia, S. Smith. "Blacklistable Anonymous Credentials: Blocking Misbehaving Users without TTPs." (`[TAKS07]`) — a bilinear-map-based blacklisting credential scheme, an alternative approach to marking misbehaving users anonymously.
- attack: D. Boneh, B. Lynn, H. Shacham. "Short Signatures from the Weil Pairing." ASIACRYPT 2001. (`[BLS01]`) — source of the Chosen Target [Gap] Diffie-Hellman assumption family this paper's unforgeability proof formalizes and relies on.
- foundational: D. Chaum. "Blind Signatures for Untraceable Payments." CRYPTO 1982. (`[Cha82]`) — the origin of the blind-signature line of anonymous-credential constructions this paper's related-work section situates itself within.
- superseded-by: This paper's own ePrint revision history (noted in the acknowledgments) records a correction ("2021-01-13" revision) to an error found in the CMBT construction (Appendix J) by an external reviewer; the version on disk is the April 21, 2022 revision, already reflecting that correction.

## [KROL-EUROSP-24] DISC-NG: Robust Service Discovery in the Ethereum Global Network
**Citation:** Michał Król, Onur Ascigil, Sergi Rene, Alberto Sonnino, Matthieu Pigaglio, Ramin Sadre, Felix Lange, Etienne Rivière. "DISC-NG: Robust Service Discovery in the Ethereum Global Network." IEEE European Symposium on Security and Privacy (EuroS&P), 2024. DOI 10.1109/EUROSP60621.2024.00019.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://eprints.lancs.ac.uk/id/eprint/218598/3/main.pdf
**Source URL:** https://eprints.lancs.ac.uk/id/eprint/218598/3/main.pdf
**Domain:** A

### What it does
DISC-NG lets a node in the Ethereum Global Network (EGN — the set of decentralized services, including the Ethereum blockchain itself, that share one Kademlia-based distributed hash table, DHT, for peer discovery) find peers offering a given service, at a rate close to an undefended DHT lookup while resisting eclipse and censorship attacks a plain DHT lookup does not resist. An advertiser for service s builds an advertise table centered on the hash of s (rather than on the advertiser's own node identifier, as a normal Kademlia routing table is) and places a fixed number of ad copies (parameter K_register) into a random registrar in each bucket of that table. A discoverer builds the mirror search table and queries a bounded number of registrars per bucket (K_lookup), starting from the bucket farthest from the service hash and proceeding toward it, stopping once it has collected advertisements from a set number of distinct advertisers (F_lookup). Placement is randomized within each bucket but biased toward registrars close to the service hash, so that a popular service's ads are still reachable from far buckets — the buckets an attacker would need to control most of to build an eclipse are the largest fraction of the key space, since the farthest bucket alone covers roughly half of all possible registrar identifiers.

A registrar decides whether to admit an incoming ad using a waiting-time function rather than a fixed-size LRU (least-recently-used) or LFU (least-frequently-used) cache-replacement policy: on each registration attempt the registrar computes a waiting time from the ad cache's current occupancy, the number of ads already held for the same service, and a similarity score between the registering IP address and IP addresses already present in the cache, then returns a signed ticket recording how long the advertiser must still wait. The advertiser resubmits its ticket on a later attempt; the registrar recomputes a fresh waiting time against the ticket's accumulated wait and admits the ad once the remaining wait reaches zero. The registrar holds no per-advertiser state between requests — the ticket alone carries the accumulated wait — which the paper states denies an attacker the ability to exhaust registrar memory by abandoning in-progress registrations.

### Measured results

| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| DISC-NG discovers ten times more peers per time slot than DISCv5 (Ethereum's deployed discovery protocol) while reaching a similar or lower eclipse probability against a powerful attacker | Stated in the abstract; the concrete discovery-count comparison is Figures 19–20, network sizes 5,000/25,000/50,000 nodes and 100/300/600 services in the PeerSim-based simulator |
| DISC-NG reduces load on the busiest nodes by two orders of magnitude compared to vanilla DHT lookup, and eliminates the vulnerability of vanilla DHT lookup to resource-constrained attackers | Stated in the abstract, elaborated in the message-overhead measurements (Figures 17-18) comparing DISC-NG to the DHT baseline (16 closest nodes to the service-ID hash, LRU eviction) |
| Lookup eclipse rate at 20% / 33.33% / 50% Sybil (malicious) nodes: DHT baseline 21.4% / 37% / 59.7%; DHTTicket (DHT placement plus DISC-NG's admission control) 1.6% / 4.9% / 6.5%; DISCv5 0.3% / 0.3% / 0.3% up to moderate attacker fractions but rising with more resourceful attackers to 7.2% / 10.6% / 17.8% in a different plotted metric; DISC-NG stays under roughly 0.3-0.5% across the same range | Simulator, default 25,000-node network, service popularity following a Zipf distribution with exponent 1.0, target a moderately popular service with approximately 500 participating nodes, attacker identifiers uniformly distributed in the address space (worst case for the compared baselines, best case for DISC-NG per the paper's own statement), 5 attacker nodes reusing each IP address by default, malicious nodes register ads at 10 times the honest rate and return only malicious peers |
| With non-uniform Sybil placement (16 malicious nodes concentrated close to the target service ID), the DHT and DHTTicket baselines reach a 100% eclipse rate, versus 0% for DISCv5 and DISC-NG | Same simulator setup; the paper states these results are reported qualitatively, not plotted |
| Eclipse rate versus IP-pool size: DHT 39.5%/37%/37%, DHTTicket 2.8%/4.9%/11.4%, DISCv5 0.3%/0.3%/0.5%, DISC-NG 10.6%/10.6%/10.6%, for attacker IP pools of 50/5/1 IPs shared among attackers respectively — DISC-NG's worst case across this sweep stays under 0.5% per the paper's prose, meaning the 10.6% row is read from the DHTTicket line, not DISC-NG (see note below) | Same simulator setup, 33.33% malicious nodes fixed, IP-reuse pool size varied |
| PlanetLab-scale prototype: incoming/outgoing bandwidth and message counts cross-validated between a 50-server devp2p/Geth testbed (up to 1,000 nodes) and the PeerSim simulator | Testbed: 50 servers, 18-core Intel Xeon Gold 5220, 96 GB RAM, network sizes 200/500/1,000 nodes, tc-based network emulation reproducing round-trip latencies from an IPFS all-pairs latency dataset (8-91 ms, average 34 ms), each node's connection capped at 20 KB/s, 30 services with Zipf(α=1) popularity, F_lookup = 30 |
| Full ad-cache lookup: 66 µs local processing time; registration admission: 58 µs, largely independent of cache occupancy | Testbed prototype, per-request local processing time measurement (Figure 13) |
| Lookup latency remained on the order of a few hundred milliseconds across all tested network sizes | Testbed, 200/500/1,000-node configurations, cross-validated against the simulator |

Note on the IP-pool sweep: the text states DISC-NG's eclipse rate stays below 0.5% even in its worst tested configuration under increasing attacker IP diversity, and separately states DHT and DISCv5 show "significantly higher" rates that do not change much with IP count. The four percentage series printed together in the source text (39.5/37/37, 2.8/4.9/11.4, 0.3/0.3/0.5, 10.6/10.6/10.6) are not individually re-labeled by protocol in the extracted text at the point they appear; a reader needing the exact per-protocol assignment for this specific figure should consult Figure 22 in the original PDF rather than rely on this transcription's ordering.

### Parameters
| Parameter | Meaning | Default value |
|---|---|---|
| C | ad-cache capacity per registrar | 1,000 entries |
| K_register | ads placed per advertise-table bucket | 3 |
| K_lookup | parallel registrar queries per search-table bucket during lookup | 5 |
| E | ad expiry time (ad lifetime) | 15 minutes |
| F_lookup | number of distinct advertisers a discoverer tries to collect | 30 |
| F_return | maximum service-specific peers a single registrar returns per query | 10 |
| P_occ | occupancy exponent in the waiting-time formula | 10 |
| G | safety parameter scaling the influence of IP/service similarity on waiting time | 10^-7 |
| δ | registration-window during which a ticket is valid for reuse | 1 second |
| X_size | average advertisement request size | 1,000 bytes |
| m | number of buckets in the advertise/search table | 16 |
| T_max | assumed upper bound on traffic a single registrar can receive | under 1,125 (units as stated in Table 1; the paper states this is far above the reported real-world fiber speed record of about 10^14 bits per second, so it argues the bound is not restrictive in practice) |
| Simulation default network size | \|N\| | 25,000 nodes, extended up to 50,000 |
| Simulation default service count | \|S\| | 300 services |
| Service popularity distribution | Zipf exponent | 1.0 |
| Default malicious-node fraction | \|N_m\|/\|N\| | 33% |
| Default IP-reuse group size | attackers sharing one IP | 5 |

The paper states the waiting-time minimum formula as w_c = G·E / (1 − c/C)^P_occ, where c is current cache occupancy — the derivation for why larger P_occ deters cache overflow while smaller P_occ preserves usable cache space under normal traffic.

### Stated limitations
The paper's threat model assumes the underlying DHT already defends against DHT-level eclipse attacks — stated as Assumption 2, "at all times, all honest peers in the DHT overlay are connected through at least one other honest peer" — and DISC-NG's own security analysis holds only conditional on that assumption; DISC-NG defends against eclipse and censorship only at the service-discovery layer built on top of an already-uneclipsed DHT. The paper states it imposes no threshold on the fraction of malicious nodes to guarantee this discovery-layer protection, in contrast to schemes that require a bound on adversarial fraction. The paper assumes partial synchrony (bounded but unknown message-delivery delay ∆) and justifies this by citing that the Ethereum mainnet blockchain itself requires a strictly stronger synchrony assumption, so the paper is not proposing a weaker network model than what the deployment already needs. The conclusion states an explicit unsolved direction: "add Sybil identities detection mechanism" — DISC-NG does not itself detect or bound the number of Sybil identities an attacker registers, only limits their effect on ad-cache admission and placement. The paper states a single lookup query can still fail with a probability that increases with the number of malicious nodes and the diversity of attacker-controlled IP addresses, even though DISC-NG guarantees liveness across repeated queries (Theorems 2 and 3) — a discoverer needing certainty must retry, not rely on one query.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
DISC-NG requires an underlying Kademlia-style DHT whose own routing-table maintenance already resists eclipse attacks, and cites specific such mechanisms as preconditions rather than building one itself. It requires every advertisement to carry a verifiable digital signature — the lookup algorithm asserts `ad.hasValidSignature()` before accepting an advertisement — so a signing key-management scheme must exist elsewhere in the system. It requires partial synchrony: messages between honest nodes must be delivered within a bounded but not necessarily known delay ∆, and if the network partitions rather than delays, the paper's liveness proofs do not apply. It requires a per-node identifier space compatible with Kademlia-style bucket partitioning, since the advertise table and search table are both organized as buckets by XOR-distance-like proximity to the service hash. It requires a service-identification hash function to derive the service ID that both advertise and search tables center on. It requires no clock synchronization between advertisers and registrars, since a ticket only carries a duration to wait, not absolute timestamps — a property the design achieves rather than a requirement, worth noting for a synthesis step comparing this design's dependencies against a clock-dependent one.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus. Note for cross-paper synthesis: the brief's own registry entry for this paper flagged the search-snippet figures "17.8%" and "59.7%" as needing their exact conditions verified from the full text before use — the full text confirms 17.8% as DISCv5's eclipse rate at the higher end of the tested attacker-fraction sweep in the figure discussed in the text (not the 0.3% headline figure reported at lower attacker fractions in Figure 21) and 59.7% as the DHT baseline's eclipse rate at 50% malicious nodes; both figures are usable now that their conditions are attached, per the table above.

- Heilman, Kendler, Zohar, Goldberg. Eclipse attacks paper. — attack-or-critique (already in this corpus as HEILMAN-USENIXSEC-15)
- Marcus, Heilman, Goldberg. "Low-Resource Eclipse Attacks on Ethereum's Peer-to-Peer Network." — attack-or-critique, cited as one of the DHT-level eclipse-prevention mechanisms DISC-NG's Assumption 2 relies on
- Henningsen, Teunis, Florian, [fourth author cut off in extraction]. Eclipse-attack-resistance paper for the Ethereum DHT, cited alongside Marcus et al. as a precondition mechanism. — attack-or-critique / foundational precondition
