## [LACAVA-ANS-21] Understanding the growth of the Fediverse through the lens of Mastodon
**Citation:** Lucio La Cava, Sergio Greco, Andrea Tagarelli. "Understanding the growth of the Fediverse through the lens of Mastodon." Applied Network Science 6, 2021. DOI 10.1007/S41109-021-00392-5.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.15473
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.15473
**Domain:** J

### What it does
The paper builds an up-to-date crawled dataset of the Mastodon instance-to-instance follow network and uses it to measure the topological structure of that network and how the structure changed over roughly three years, compared against an earlier published Mastodon dataset. It does not measure the distribution of user accounts across instances (how many users each instance hosts); the measured object throughout is a directed graph whose nodes are Mastodon server instances and whose edges are aggregated follow relationships between users of one instance and users of another.

Data was collected by a purpose-built crawler using only the public, authenticated Mastodon REST API, starting from a seed list of instances obtained from the instances.social tracker (approximately 900 of about 1,100 candidate instances granted the crawler an authentication token). From the timelines of these seed instances the crawler discovered approximately 81,000 seed users, then performed a breadth-first search over the user-follow graph, discovering new users and instances as it traversed. Collected edges were anonymized by hashing at collection time, so the raw dataset cannot be traced back to individual identities; no scraping outside the authenticated API was performed, so instances that declined to grant an authentication token contribute no data beyond what other instances' users reveal about them.

Three network models are derived from the same underlying crawled user-follow graph, all as directed graphs of instances rather than of individual users: the Instances network (edges exist between two instances if any user of one follows any user of the other, restricted to instances known to be Mastodon), the Online-Instances network (the subgraph restricted to instances currently reported online by the tracker sites), and the Expanded-Instances network (the same graph but including edges to and from instances belonging to other Fediverse platforms besides Mastodon, discovered incidentally because Mastodon's follow-listing API does not distinguish the platform of a followed or following account).

Instance status (Mastodon versus another platform, online versus offline) is determined by cross-referencing the crawled instance identifiers against two independent third-party tracker websites, instances.social and fediverse.party, rather than being inferred from the crawl itself.

### Measured results
| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| Crawl produced 27,989,557 raw detected links; after de-duplication, approximately 1.4 million unique users and 18 million unique links, covering 16,282 instances of any Fediverse platform | Single crawl, November-December 2020, breadth-first search seeded from ~81,000 users across ~900 authenticated Mastodon instances |
| Merging the instances.social and fediverse.party trackers gives 9,433 known Mastodon instances total (online plus offline) and 1,193 known-online Mastodon instances | Third-party tracker data, cited "as reported in Table 1" of the paper, no date given beyond the crawl period |
| Restricting the census to instances shared between both tracker websites, rather than their union, reduces the online-instance count by 16.4% (to 997) and the overall count by 86.5% (to 1,276) | Same tracker-comparison dataset |
| The crawl intercepted (found data for) 6,960 of the 9,433 known Mastodon instances (73.8%), and 1,116 of the 1,193 known-online instances (93.5%) | Same crawl and tracker-comparison window |
| The dataset is stated to double the earlier state-of-the-art in currently-online instance count: this paper's 1,116 online instances found versus 548 reported by the earlier dataset (Zignani et al., mid-2017 to early-2018) | Direct comparison stated in the paper's own summary figure; the earlier dataset totaled 4,015 overall Mastodon instances versus 6,960 here |
| Instances network in-degree distribution: first quartile 91.5, median 202, mean 331, third quartile 413, non-outlier maximum 878; 21 instances have in-degree above 880, up to a maximum of 4,685 | Instances network, 6,960 nodes, crawled November-December 2020 |
| The top-5 instances by degree, in-degree, and out-degree are the same five in all three rankings: mastodon.social, pawoo.net, mastodon.xyz, octodon.social, and mstdn.io; mastodon.social is top-1 by every degree type | Same Instances network |
| In-degree CCDF: 50% of instances have in-degree at least 200; this drops to 20% around in-degree 600 and below 4% for the outlier instances | Same Instances network |
| Instances network structural summary: 6,960 nodes, 216,504 edges, reciprocity 65.1%, density 0.004, average degree 41.966 | Same crawl |
| Comparison against the earlier (Zignani et al.) network of 4,015 nodes and 95,221 edges: this paper's Instances network is +73% in node count and +127% in edge count; reciprocity is 8% lower, density is 33% lower, average degree is 37% higher, average path length and diameter are unchanged (2.340 and 5 respectively in both networks), degree assortativity is 5-13% more negative | Comparison of this paper's crawl (Nov-Dec 2020) against the previously published Zignani et al. dataset (2017-2018) |
| Restricting to online-only instances (Online-Instances network) versus the full Instances network: node count falls 84% (to 1,115 nodes), edge count falls 65% (to 75,046 edges), reciprocity rises 8% (to 70.6%), density rises roughly 14x (to 0.06), average degree more than doubles (to 87.074), average path length falls 13% and diameter falls 20% | Same crawl, subgraph restricted to instances reported online at collection time |
| Instance-ranking similarity across network variants, via Kendall's tau and Fagin's intersection metric on PageRank scores: Expanded-Instances vs. Instances, tau = 0.953; Online-Instances vs. Instances, tau = 0.899; Instances vs. the three-years-earlier network, tau = 0.626 (lower than the other comparisons, attributed to the temporal gap) | PageRank computed independently on each network variant, ranking correlation computed over the shared node set between each pair |

The paper reports negative degree assortativity (disassortative mixing, i.e., high-degree instances tend to connect to low-degree instances rather than to each other) as a consistent feature across every network variant tested (Instances: -0.253 to -0.274 depending on edge-direction treatment; Online-Instances: -0.284 to -0.290; the three-years-earlier network: -0.287 to -0.291), and states this distinguishes Mastodon's instance-level topology from well-known centralized social networks, which the paper states typically show positive assortativity, citing prior literature for that centralized-network baseline rather than measuring it directly in this paper.

### Parameters
| Parameter | Value used | Range tested |
|---|---|---|
| instances.social "dead" threshold | An instance is classed dead if inactive at least two weeks | Fixed value from the third-party tracker's own definition, not varied by the authors |
| instances.social "down" threshold | An instance is classed down if not currently reachable but was live within the preceding two weeks | Fixed value from the third-party tracker's own definition, not varied |
| Fagin's intersection metric top-k cutoff | Computed at k = 10, 50, 100, 500, 1,000 | These five values are the range tested; no single value is presented as the recommended default |
| Crawl duration / collection window | Approximately one month (November-December 2020 for the main crawl) | Not varied; single collection run |

### Stated limitations
The paper states the crawl's coverage of non-Mastodon Fediverse instances is necessarily partial, because such instances and users were discovered only incidentally through Mastodon-instance API responses, and the paper explicitly hedges its own Expanded-Instances findings on this basis: "although we detected non-Mastodon users and instances through Mastodon ones, and hence this knowledge of the Fediverse might be partial." It states it could not determine the online/offline status of instances in the earlier (Zignani et al.) comparison dataset at the time that dataset was itself created, so the paper's own claim of Mastodon reaching structural stability rests partly on a hypothesis ("we hypothesize that...Mastodon reached its stability") rather than on data available for both time points. It states explicitly that it does not analyze the content of posts or user-level social contents at all; only follow-relationship structure was collected and analyzed, and studying users' behavior and roles within and across instances is stated as the authors' planned next research stage, not something this paper addresses. The paper does not measure or report the number of user accounts hosted by each instance, or any resource-concentration metric (Gini coefficient, Nakamoto coefficient, HHI, or similar) over instance sizes; its concentration-adjacent findings (instance centrality via PageRank, core-decomposition inner-most-core sizes) measure structural position in the follow graph, not population share.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Reproducing or extending this paper's Instances-network measurements requires an authenticated Mastodon API token from each instance to be crawled, since the authors state they deliberately excluded any instance that declined to grant a token rather than scraping it by other means; a study that instead scrapes public HTML would collect a different, non-directly-comparable instance population. Comparing a new crawl's structural statistics against this paper's reported values requires matching the same graph granularity (instance-to-instance aggregated follow edges, not user-to-user edges), since the paper's own Table 3 versus Table 7 versus Table 8 comparisons show density, degree, and reciprocity shift substantially between the full Instances network, the Online-Instances subgraph, and the three-years-earlier dataset purely from differences in which instances are included, independent of any real change in the platform. Any downstream claim about "Mastodon's degree of centralization" sourced to this paper must specify whether it means the instance-level follow-graph topology (what this paper measures, e.g., disassortative mixing, PageRank concentration in a persistent small set of instances) or the distribution of user accounts across instances (what this paper does not measure); conflating the two would misattribute a user-population-concentration claim to this paper's evidence.

### Contradicts
The paper's own stated motivation for retrieval in this batch (per the target registry's why_needed field) was to determine whether Raman et al.'s 2019 instance-concentration figures held, worsened, or improved as the Fediverse grew. This paper does not perform that comparison: it cites Raman, Joglekar, De Cristofaro, Sastry, Tyson, "Challenges in the Decentralised Web: The Mastodon Case" (IMC 2019) only once, as reference [7] in a list of prior Mastodon-focused studies, and never discusses or reproduces any of that paper's specific findings or figures in its body text. The paper's own point of comparison throughout is Zignani, Gaito, Rossi's 2018 ICWSM dataset and findings, not Raman et al.'s. A claim that this paper confirms, refutes, or updates Raman et al.'s concentration figures is not supported by this paper's text and must not be attributed to it.

### References worth retrieving
- foundational (comparison baseline used throughout this paper): Zignani, Gaito, Rossi, "Follow the 'mastodon': Structure and evolution of a decentralized online social network," ICWSM 2018 — the paper this entry's every "earlier network" comparison figure is measured against; already implicitly retrieved in substance via this paper's Table 7/8 reproductions, but the original paper's own text was not separately read in this pass.
- competing/independent-measurement (named directly in the batch's retrieval rationale but not analyzed by this paper): Raman, Joglekar, De Cristofaro, Sastry, Tyson, "Challenges in the Decentralised Web: The Mastodon Case," IMC 2019 — holds the instance-concentration figures this paper was expected, but found not, to update; still worth retrieving directly for those figures.
- competing: Zignani, Quadri, Gaito, Cherifi, Rossi, "The Footprints of a 'Mastodon': How a Decentralized Architecture Influences Online Social Relationships," IEEE INFOCOM Workshops 2019 — reports per-instance footprint statistics (degree distribution, clustering coefficient) for the top 10 Mastodon instances, a finer-grained companion result to this paper's top-5-by-degree finding.
- foundational: Zulli, Liu, Gehl, "Rethinking the 'Social' in 'Social Media': Insights into Topology, Abstraction, and Scale on the Mastodon Social Network," New Media & Society 22(7), 2020 — qualitative moderator-interview study cited as finding horizontal (inter-instance) rather than within-instance growth, a claim this paper's structural results are consistent with but did not directly test.
- foundational: Varol, Ferrara, Davis, Menczer, Flammini, "Online human-bot interactions: Detection, estimation, and characterization," ICWSM 2017 — source of the ~15% Twitter bot-prevalence figure this paper's related-work section contrasts against a cited ~5% Mastodon bot figure from Zignani et al.

## [LANGLEY-SIGCOMM-17] The QUIC Transport Protocol: Design and Internet-Scale Deployment
**Citation:** Adam Langley, Alistair Riddoch, Alyssa Wilk, Antonio Vicente, Charles Krasic, Dan Zhang, Fan Yang, Fedor Kouranov, Ian Swett, Janardhan Iyengar, Jeff Bailey, Jeremy Dorfman, Jim Roskind, Joanna Kulik, Patrik Westin, Raman Tenneti, Robbie Shade, Ryan Hamilton, Victor Vasiliev, Wan-Teh Chang, Zhongyi Shi. "The QUIC Transport Protocol: Design and Internet-Scale Deployment." ACM SIGCOMM, 2017. DOI 10.1145/3098822.3098842.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://research.google/pubs/pub46403/
**Source URL:** https://doi.org/10.1145/3098822.3098842
**Domain:** L

### What it does
QUIC is a transport protocol that reduces the round trips needed to start an encrypted connection and lets an ongoing connection survive a change in the client's IP address or port, by running entirely in user-space over UDP (User Datagram Protocol) instead of inside the kernel as TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) does. A traditional HTTPS connection requires a TCP handshake (1 round trip) followed by a separate TLS (Transport Layer Security) handshake (1-2 more round trips) before any application data moves; QUIC merges transport and cryptographic setup into one handshake. On a first-ever connection to a server, QUIC completes in one round trip (1-RTT): the client sends a client hello, learns the server's public credentials (a server config and certificate), and on repeat connections to the same server can reuse those cached credentials to send encrypted application data in its very first packet, with zero added round trips (0-RTT) beyond the first packet's transit time — provided the client still holds a valid cached server config and a valid source-address token (a server-encrypted blob attesting the client's validated IP address from a prior handshake). Every QUIC connection carries a 64-bit Connection ID that identifies it independently of the underlying IP address and port pair; because Connection ID rather than the traditional (source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port) tuple identifies the connection, a NAT (Network Address Translator) rebinding a client's mapped external port, or a client itself changing IP address, does not by itself break the connection — the packet still carries the same Connection ID, so the server continues to recognize it. The paper distinguishes this passive survival of address changes ("QUIC endpoints simply elide the problem of NAT rebinding by using the Connection ID to identify connections") from client-initiated connection migration, an active protocol feature for a client to move a connection to a new path on purpose, which the paper states was, at time of writing, "a work in progress with limited deployment." QUIC multiplexes multiple independent byte streams within one connection and applies loss detection and congestion control at the connection level rather than per-stream, so a lost packet on one stream does not stall delivery of data already available on another stream (eliminating the head-of-line blocking that arises when HTTP/2 multiplexes streams over one underlying TCP connection, where TCP's own in-order delivery guarantee blocks all streams behind one lost segment). QUIC encrypts most of its packet header, leaving only the fields a receiver needs to route and decrypt a packet (flags, Connection ID) unencrypted, explicitly to prevent middleboxes (network equipment that inspects or rewrites protocol fields, positioned between endpoints) from depending on and thereby freezing ("ossifying") any other transport-layer signal.

### Measured results
| Result | Condition |
|---|---|
| An estimated 7% of Internet traffic is QUIC | Google's global deployment measurement, cited in the abstract, no further breakdown given |
| QUIC reduces Google Search Latency by 8.0% (mean) for desktop users and 3.6% (mean) for mobile users | Randomized experiment, QUIC experimental group (QUICg) vs. TLS/TCP control group (TCPg), equal population sizes; search results gathered December 12-19, 2016; over 1 billion samples; QUIC version 35 |
| QUIC reduces YouTube Video Latency (time from pressing play to playback start) by 8.0% (mean) for desktop, 5.3% (mean) for mobile | Same experimental framework; video playback results gathered January 19-26, 2017; over 1 billion samples; QUIC version 35 |
| QUIC reduces YouTube Video Rebuffer Rate by 18.0% (mean) for desktop, 15.3% (mean) for mobile | Same framework and measurement window as Video Latency above |
| Search Latency reduction by percentile (desktop): 0.4% at 1st percentile, 1.3% at 5th, 1.4% at 10th, 1.5% at 50th, 5.8% at 90th, 10.3% at 95th, 16.7% at 99th; (mobile): -0.6% at 1st, -0.3% at 5th, 0.3% at 10th, 0.5% at 50th, 4.5% at 90th, 8.8% at 95th, 14.3% at 99th | Same December 2016 desktop/mobile experiment; negative values indicate QUIC performed worse than TCP at that percentile |

| About 88% of QUIC connections from desktop clients achieve a 0-RTT handshake (at least a 2-RTT latency saving versus TLS/TCP); the mobile YouTube app achieves 0-RTT on only 65-68% of connections | Same December 2016/January 2017 measurement windows; the 20-percentage-point mobile reduction is attributed roughly half to IP-address changes invalidating the cached source-address token when mobile users switch networks, and half to mobile clients reaching a different data center (with a different server config) than the one their cached credentials were issued by |
| More than 20% of all measured connections have a minimum Round-Trip Time (RTT) greater than 150 ms; 10% have a minimum RTT greater than 300 ms | Distribution gathered from video-playback connections; the paper states the distribution for search connections is similar |
| Average TCP retransmission rate (used as a network-loss proxy) across all RTTs: 0% at the 50th percentile, 2% at the 80th, 8% at the 90th, 18% at the 95th, averaged in 10 ms RTT buckets | Video-playback connections, measurement window not separately stated for this figure beyond "these results were gathered from video playbacks" |

| QUIC's initial server CPU utilization was approximately 3.5 times that of TLS/TCP for serving YouTube traffic; after optimizing cryptography (a hand-optimized ChaCha20 cipher), packet reception (asynchronous kernel packet reception via a memory-mapped ring buffer), and internal state handling (cache-efficient rewrites), CPU utilization was reduced to approximately 2 times that of TLS/TCP | Measured on Google's production server fleet serving YouTube traffic; no separate sample size or measurement window stated for this specific figure |
| In a wide-scale reachability test of UDP payload sizes from 1200 to 1500 bytes in 5-byte increments, unreachability rose sharply once total packet size (QUIC payload plus UDP and IP headers) exceeded the 1500-byte Ethernet Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU); the paper chose 1350 bytes as QUIC's default payload size based on this data | Chrome's experimentation framework, approximately 25,000 Chrome instances per tested packet size, sending UDP packets to an echo server and waiting for a response; data collected over 28 days in January 2014 |
| QUIC is successfully used by 95.3% of video clients that attempt to use it; 4.4% cannot use it (QUIC or UDP blocked, or path MTU too small — manually inspected and found common in corporate networks/enterprise firewalls, with no case of an entire Internet Service Provider (ISP) blocking QUIC or UDP observed); the remaining 0.3% are in networks detected as rate-limiting QUIC/UDP traffic (via elevated packet loss and reduced bandwidth at peak hours), down from 1% measured in June 2015 after Google contacted the affected network operators | Video-playback metrics gathered in November 2016 (the 0.3% figure) and a separate measurement from June 2015 for the earlier comparison point |
| Experimenting with XOR-based Forward Error Correction (single-packet-loss recovery via parity), the paper measured a statistically insignificant impact on Search Latency and an increase in both Video Latency and Video Rebuffer Rate; separately, the benefit of an FEC scheme recovering from a single packet loss per group was limited to under 30% of loss episodes | One week of data collected in March 2016 for the loss-epoch distribution figure; FEC was removed from QUIC in early 2016 following these results |
| A production Cubic congestion-control bug fix reduced QUIC's own retransmission rates by about 30%, QUIC's CPU utilization by about 17%, and TCP's retransmission rates (on the same servers) by about 20% | Production deployment measurement, specific dates and sample sizes not given beyond the citation to an internal 2015 presentation |
| Investigating TCP video connections limited by the client's advertised receive window (not the sender's congestion window) found this affected 4.6% of examined connections, most limited to a 64 KB maximum receive window (about 45 MTU-sized packets), attributed to absent TCP window scaling; QUIC's default initial flow-control limit is 15 MB per connection | One week of TCP video-connection data collected in March 2016 |

### Parameters
- QUIC protocol version used for all reported experiments unless otherwise noted: version 35.
- Default QUIC UDP payload size: 1350 bytes, chosen from the packet-size reachability experiment above (unreachability rises sharply above 1450 bytes of total packet size against a 1500-byte Ethernet MTU).
- Connection ID size: 64 bits.
- Default initial connection-level flow-control (receive window) limit advertised by a QUIC client: 15 MB.
- TLS/TCP-side QUIC-discovery delay: when racing a QUIC connection against a fallback TLS/TCP connection on a repeat visit to a known-QUIC origin, the client delays initiating the TLS/TCP attempt by up to 300 ms, preferring QUIC if it succeeds first.
- Congestion control: both QUIC and the TCP comparison group use a paced variant of the Cubic algorithm.
- 0-RTT handshake success precondition: the client must hold both a valid cached server config (the server's credentials) and a valid cached source-address token (a server-encrypted attestation of the client's IP address from a prior successful handshake) for the specific origin and data center being contacted.

### Stated limitations
The paper states client-initiated connection migration — actively moving an established connection to a new network path — was, at time of writing, "a work in progress with limited deployment," distinct from and more limited than QUIC's passive tolerance of NAT rebinding via the Connection ID. The paper states QUIC "may perform worse than TCP" on networks with high bandwidth (over 100 Mbps) and/or very low RTT (a few milliseconds), attributed to client CPU limits and/or client-side OS or application scheduler inefficiencies, though it states these conditions are "outside typical Internet conditions." The paper states applications that pre-warm connections in the background before the user's action requires them (as the YouTube app does) receive no measurable benefit from QUIC's 0-RTT handshake, because the handshake latency was already hidden; it further states some applications, such as web browsers, "cannot always pre-warm connections since the server is often unknown until explicitly indicated by the user." The paper states QUIC's server CPU cost remains roughly twice that of TLS/TCP even after the described optimizations, and states this higher cost "will remain" even though further reductions (for example, general kernel bypass) are believed possible. The paper states it does not know whether protocol bits QUIC exposes, other than the one bit that triggered the documented October 2016 middlebox incident, have been ossified by other middleboxes, and states explicitly "we do not have a method to answer this question at Internet scale." The paper states networking (specifically handshake latency) "contributes to well under 20% of Search Latency and Video Latency," so QUIC's transport-level gains bound only a fraction of end-to-end application latency regardless of further transport optimization.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
QUIC's 0-RTT handshake requires the client to have completed at least one prior successful handshake with the specific server (or, more precisely, the specific data center's server configuration) it is reconnecting to, and to still hold both the cached server config and a still-valid source-address token from that prior handshake; a client reconnecting to a server it has never contacted, or whose cached credentials have expired or been invalidated by an IP-address change, falls back to a 1-RTT handshake instead. The paper states QUIC's passive survival of NAT rebinding depends on the receiving endpoint continuing to recognize packets by Connection ID alone, independent of the observed source IP and port — a requirement that composes only with a design in which nothing else in the system re-derives session identity from the network-layer address tuple. Because most of the QUIC packet header is encrypted, any network operator or middlebox that needs to classify, prioritize, or otherwise act differently on QUIC traffic must do so using only the deliberately small set of fields the protocol leaves unencrypted, and the paper's own middlebox incident (Section 7.5) demonstrates that any such external dependency on an unencrypted field is fragile to a protocol-side change the middlebox operator was not consulted on in advance. QUIC's server-side deployment requires an operator willing to accept roughly double the CPU cost per connection compared to TLS/TCP (after the optimizations described), and requires an unencrypted (fallback) TLS/TCP path already exists for clients or paths where the QUIC handshake fails, since the paper's own discovery mechanism (Section 3.8) depends on a TLS/TCP fallback whenever QUIC is blocked or its handshake packet exceeds the path's MTU.

### Contradicts
None found against another entry in this batch. The paper's own reported Search Latency reduction at the 1st and 5th percentiles for mobile users is negative (-0.6% and -0.3%), meaning QUIC performed measurably worse than TLS/TCP for the fastest connections in that population, a result stated directly in Table 1 alongside the paper's overall positive-mean framing rather than in tension with it.

### References worth retrieving
- S. Radhakrishnan, Y. Cheng, J. Chu, A. Jain, B. Raghavan, "TCP Fast Open," ACM CoNEXT, 2011 — competing (the paper's Section 8 gives a direct, mechanism-level comparison: TCP Fast Open limits first-round-trip client data to what fits in a TCP SYN segment, which QUIC does not, and works only for repeat connections to the same server IP, which QUIC's origin-based 0-RTT handshake does not require).
- W Michael Petullo, Xu Zhang, Jon A. Solworth, Daniel J. Bernstein, Tanja Lange, "MinimaLT: Minimal-Latency Networking Through Better Security," ACM CCS, 2013 — competing (a contemporaneous protocol with a similar 0-RTT handshake and encrypted multiplexed tunnel; the paper states MinimaLT additionally prevents linkability of a connection across an IP-address migration, a privacy property QUIC did not have at time of writing and which the paper states was "under consideration as QUIC evolves at the IETF").
- B. Ford, "Structured Streams: A New Transport Abstraction," ACM SIGCOMM, 2007 — foundational (the paper states QUIC's design is closest to Structured Stream Transport, sharing a channel identifier, monotonically increasing packet numbers, encrypted transport header, and lightweight streams).
- E. Rescorla, "The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3," IETF Internet Draft, 2017 — competing/superseded-by (the paper states TLS 1.3, partly inspired by QUIC's own handshake protocol, now provides equivalent latency benefits to QUIC's homegrown cryptographic handshake, and that IETF standardization work would replace QUIC's original handshake with TLS 1.3).

## [LAS-EPRINT-26] De-SyRIS: A Decentralized Sybil-Resistant Identity System without a Trusted Credential Issuer
**Citation:** Michal Ľaš, Ivan Homoliak, Juraj Mariani. "De-SyRIS: A Decentralized Sybil-Resistant Identity System without a Trusted Credential Issuer." IACR ePrint Archive, 2026.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1723
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1723
**Domain:** F

### What it does
De-SyRIS assigns each human a single decentralized identity resistant to mass fake-account creation (Sybil attack) without any party centrally issuing or vouching for that identity. It combines two independent Sybil-resistance signals so that defeating one alone does not defeat the system: facial-biometric uniqueness checking, and zero-knowledge (a cryptographic proof that a statement is true without revealing the data that makes it true) social-graph analysis proving an entity is reachable from an externally reputable entity through a chain of privately-held connections.

Mechanism, registration: a user's device captures a facial scan, signs it with a Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) manifest (cryptographically signed metadata proving when, on what device, and by what application media was captured) to counter synthetic images, and sends scan plus manifest to a Trusted Execution Environment (TEE, a hardware-isolated region of a processor that keeps code and data confidential even from the machine's own operating system) running under Oasis ROFL (a stateless verifiable-compute layer producing an on-chain-verifiable attestation for each computed result). Inside the TEE the system verifies the manifest's freshness and originating application, runs liveness checks, extracts a biometric embedding, and matches it against an encrypted embedding database that only TEEs holding valid remote-attestation quotes can query. A first-time match produces "full" registration; a collision with an existing embedding produces "limited" registration, requiring the new account to collect community endorsements — each already-fully-registered user may issue exactly one endorsement — before it is promoted to full status. The signed TEE result is submitted to the Oasis Sapphire confidential smart-contract chain, which records the embedding hash and reputation state.

Mechanism, connection establishment: two users meeting in person photograph each other, sign the photos with C2PA manifests, and submit them to a TEE, which matches each fresh photo against the counterpart's stored embedding and, on success, computes a connection commitment CC_AB = H(min(ID_A,ID_B) || max(ID_A,ID_B)) so the commitment value is identical regardless of which party computed it. A relayer batches these commitments into an on-chain Merkle tree; users may bypass the relayer and submit directly if the relayer censors them.

Mechanism, social-graph verification (avoids ever exposing the graph itself, which the paper's own related-work section flags as the metadata-leakage failure of public-graph systems such as BrightID and Circles): an entity constructs a recursive zero-knowledge proof (ZK Random Walk) by proving its connection to the previous entity in a path and appending its own identity and reputation score, then forwarding the extended proof to the next hop. A valid path must have length O(log n) (n = number of entities in the network) and accumulate enough reputation along the way to include at least one externally-reputable entity. To prove a path has no repeated entity (a cycle) without revealing which entities are on it, each entity inserted into the path is added to a Bloom filter (a fixed-size bit array that support membership queries with possible false positives but never false negatives) carried forward with the proof; path-distinctness between multiple submitted paths is checked by a pairwise bitwise-AND of their Bloom filters — fewer than 2k set bits in the intersection (k = number of hash functions) indicates the paths are very likely fully disjoint. Once an entity has gathered the required O(log n) mutually disjoint paths, it aggregates them into a single ZK Proof of Paths, submitted to the smart contract, which verifies it and grants non-Sybil status plus an increment to the entity's own accumulated (intrinsic) reputation — letting entities who have proved themselves reduce dependence on externally-reputable anchors over time. State (reputation, connections) changes only at fixed epoch boundaries (3-7 days), requiring re-proof each epoch to stay verified.

### Measured results
| Experiment | Conditions | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Social-graph entity-verification simulation | 100 simulated entities, 30 epochs, three synthetic graph topologies (Holme-Kim, Watts-Strogatz, Kleinberg small-world), two trust-distribution modes (spread: reputation drawn from a normal distribution up to a capped maximum, applied to a percentage of entities; seeded: fewer entities set to the maximum reputation) | In the Holme-Kim model, spread mode needs 15%-30% of entities holding external reputation before verification propagates through the network; seeded mode needs 8%-10%. The paper states the Watts-Strogatz and Kleinberg models are "unsuitable due to weak connectivity" for this test, without a numeric propagation figure for them. |
| ZK Random Walk / ZK Proof of Paths circuit performance (proof-of-concept, Plonky2 scheme, "l" = path length) | Single-machine proof-of-concept implementation; the walk implementation used a simple nullifier array, not the Bloom-filter design described in the mechanism section | ZK Random Walk (linear circuit, per-recursion-depth): compile 1.56s, circuit size 8KB + l x 4.2MB, prove time 328.56ms, verify time 4.44ms, proof size 124KB. ZK Random Walk (cyclic, single self-referential circuit): compile 2.39s, size 8.4MB, prove 630.27ms, verify 4.68ms, proof 130KB. ZK Proof of Three Paths: compile 1.25s, size 16.9MB, prove 1.58s, verify 7.19ms, proof 143KB. ZK Proof of Six Paths: compile 2.65s, size 33.8MB, prove 2.82s, verify 12.41ms, proof 149KB. |
| Bloom filter sizing for path-distinctness checking (worked example, not a simulation sweep) | Path length 10, filter size 4096 bits, 3 hash functions | False-positive rate approximately 0.05%; false-negative rate approximately 0.01% |

The paper states explicitly that "a more detailed analysis is needed to evaluate the algorithm's effectiveness in preventing Sybil entities from obtaining verification" — the 100-entity simulation measures verification reachability under an honest population, not resistance to an adversarial one.

### Parameters
| Parameter | Value used | Range tested |
|---|---|---|
| Path length for a valid ZK Random Walk / ZK Proof of Paths | O(log n) | not numerically fixed; scales with network size n |
| Epoch duration | between 3 and 7 days | stated as adjustable by "the system's intended strictness"; no specific value tested in the simulation |
| Endorsements required to promote a limited registration to full | "a specific endorsement threshold" | not numerically stated in the retrieved text |
| Endorsements one fully-registered user may issue | 1 | fixed, not varied |
| C2PA manifest freshness window, registration | example given: no older than one hour | not varied |
| C2PA manifest freshness window, connection establishment | example given: no older than 10 minutes | not varied |
| Bloom filter size / hash-function count (path-distinctness check) | 4096 bits, 3 hash functions, for path length 10 | not swept; one worked example only |
| Simulation network size | 100 entities | not varied |
| Simulation epoch count | 30 | not varied |

### Stated limitations
The system does not natively support key recovery or revocation; the authors propose, as unimplemented future work, routing recovery through trusted peers in the social graph instead of a centralized authority. The social-graph attack-resistance mechanism has no defense against an attacker who acquires k distinct attack edges (connections) into the honest region by using real, highly reputable identities as gateways to legitimize a large Sybil cluster; the paper states this outright as an open weakness, not merely a theoretical one. The system currently has no mechanism to penalize an entity for connecting indiscriminately with unknown (possibly Sybil) entities, which the authors say is "essential" future work. Entities can censor others by refusing to forward path proofs for them; the paper argues this has "statistically negligible impact" given the required multiplicity of paths but does not measure that claim numerically. Facial biometric registration depends on C2PA for anti-forgery, and the authors state that "since support for the C2PA standard in smartphones is not yet very widespread, it can theoretically be omitted," which the authors say reduces the registration-time defense to social-graph analysis alone. Merkle-proof persistence for zero-knowledge verification requires historical roots to remain available on-chain, and managing that root-availability buffer "without introducing centralized relayer dependencies remains a significant smart contract engineering challenge," per the authors. The reputation-threshold-for-a-valid-path setting is currently a fixed value derived from the maximum achievable intrinsic reputation with no external reputation; the authors state dynamic, network-adapting thresholds are future work. Community-endorsement-based correction of biometric false positives is stated by the authors to risk endorsements being "coerced" or otherwise obtained improperly, and the underlying facial-embedding quality and endorsement mechanism are called ongoing priorities, not solved problems.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Requires at least one operational TEE deployment (the paper specifies Oasis ROFL/Sapphire specifically) that can produce a remotely-attestable computation result; the paper's own discussion section states this is a live risk, not a design abstraction — it cites the 2025 SGX WireTap DRAM-bus-interposition attack (Seto et al., CCS 2025) as the reason the Integritee TEE-based project was discontinued, and states "Intel will not patch [it] as it assumes physical security," concluding that "the secure functioning of TEEs in decentralized environments remains an open question." Requires an encrypted, centrally-hosted (though TEE-gated) database of biometric embeddings reachable by every registering or connecting TEE instance — the paper labels this database "a centralized but encrypted repository," which is a centralization point in storage even though access is cryptographically gated. Requires at least a small externally-supplied reputation signal ("external reputation") injected into a minority of the entity population from outside the protocol, since the protocol's own intrinsic-reputation accumulation only functions once an entity has already completed at least one successful path proof — the system cannot bootstrap Sybil resistance from zero externally-supplied trust. Requires an on-chain relayer (or a fallback direct-submission path with degraded unlinkability) to batch connection commitments into the public Merkle tree; a permanently unavailable or fully compromised relayer forces users onto the direct-submission path, which the paper states "sacrifices some unlinkability." Requires that in-person meetings between connecting entities are not systematically fabricated at scale, since the whole social-graph Sybil-resistance claim rests on the assumption that establishing many mutual connections with honest entities is difficult for an attacker; the paper does not measure how difficult, only asserts it.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus regarding measured figures. On attribution: the target-registry's own description of this paper states its purpose is partly to determine "whether the trusted-execution-environment manufacturer becomes a new trusted party" — the retrieved text answers this only partially: it identifies Intel SGX and Oasis specifically as the deployed hardware/platform trust base and states outright that TEE security "remains an open question" in decentralized settings, but it does not analyze whether Intel or Oasis Labs becomes a systemic single point of trust comparable to World Network's Orb hardware manufacturer (which the paper's own related-work section criticizes on exactly that basis).

### References worth retrieving
- foundational: George Danezis, Prateek Mittal, "SybilInfer: Detecting sybil nodes using social networks," NDSS 2009 — cited as a social-graph analysis precedent.
- competing: BrightID, whitepaper, 2022 — public-graph proof-of-authority-blockchain social identity network; the paper states its public connection graph "risks metadata leakage," a criticism De-SyRIS's Bloom-filter/ZK design is built to avoid.
- competing: Circles ("money for a multipolar world"), whitepaper, 2024 — transitive-trust Universal Basic Income protocol with the same public-graph metadata-leakage property the paper criticizes.
- competing: World Network (Worldcoin/Orb), cited in text as [42] — proprietary iris-scanning hardware device (the Orb) for proof-of-human credentials; the paper calls the Orb "a centrally manufactured device that creates an adoption bottleneck and introduces assumptions about centralized hardware trust," the direct alternative-mechanism comparison for the biometric half of De-SyRIS.
- competing: Maria Borge, Eleftherios Kokoris-Kogias, Philipp Jovanovic, Linus Gasser, Nicolas Gailly, Bryan Ford, "Proof-of-Personhood: Redemocratizing Permissionless Cryptocurrencies," IEEE EuroS&PW 2017 — synchronized-pseudonym-party approach to Sybil resistance without biometrics or a social graph.

## [LAZAR-OSDI-18] Karaoke: Distributed Private Messaging Immune to Passive Traffic Analysis
**Citation:** David Lazar, Yossi Gilad, Nickolai Zeldovich. "Karaoke: Distributed Private Messaging Immune to Passive Traffic Analysis." USENIX OSDI, 2018.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://people.csail.mit.edu/nickolai/papers/lazar-karaoke.pdf
**Source URL:** https://people.csail.mit.edu/nickolai/papers/lazar-karaoke.pdf
**Domain:** G

### What it does
Karaoke hides which pairs of users communicate over text messaging from an adversary that controls the network and some fraction of the system's servers, at latency close to an order of magnitude lower than prior metadata-private designs (Vuvuzela, Stadium) at the same user count. Communication happens in fixed-length rounds. Each user sends and receives one message per round through a "dead drop," a location identified by a server and a per-round pseudorandom identifier; two users share a dead drop by prior agreement on a shared secret, and a user with no active conversation sends cover traffic to a randomly chosen dead drop. N servers are arranged in a full mesh and organized into l sequential layers; each message is onion-encrypted under the public keys of a client-chosen random path of servers, one per layer, so a message cannot be read until it has passed the honest servers on its path. Each layer decrypts one onion layer of every message it holds and re-orders the messages before forwarding, so a server's output order does not correlate with its input order (a parallel mixnet structure). At the final layer, the server holding a dead drop swaps the two messages addressed to it, so the server does not learn which of the two users sent which message.

To supply the noise messages that differential privacy requires without paying the cost of verifying every server actually sent its assigned noise, Karaoke uses two techniques. Optimistic indistinguishability lets the protocol assume, in the common case, that no messages are lost, revealing no information to the adversary; a client can detect precisely when a message it sent was lost (by checking a Bloom filter, described below) and only then does correlated information get revealed, so clients can switch to an idle mode after a detected loss to bound the number of future rounds in which loss-driven leakage can occur. Efficient noise verification lets each server generate noise messages independently and prove those messages were not later discarded, without a verifiable shuffle proof for every message: each server computes a Bloom filter (Bloom, 1970) over all ciphertexts it received during a round and sends this filter to every other server. If a server's own generated ciphertexts all appear in every other server's Bloom filter, it can conclude its noise was not dropped, without any server having to reveal which ciphertexts in its filter were noise versus real user traffic. The Bloom filter is deliberately imprecise (10% false-positive rate as configured) rather than a precise inclusion proof, because a false positive only costs slightly more noise, not a privacy violation.

Karaoke's privacy guarantee is stated as computational differential privacy: for any pair of users, the probability the adversary's observations are consistent with the pair having communicated is within a multiplicative factor e^epsilon and additive factor delta of the probability the observations are consistent with the pair not communicating.

### Measured results
Hardware: Amazon EC2 c5.9xlarge instances (36 Intel Xeon 3.0 GHz cores, 72 GB memory, 10 Gbps links) for the primary experiments; c4.8xlarge instances used additionally to match the instance type used by the Vuvuzela and Stadium papers for direct comparison. All server VMs placed in the same data center; 100 ms round-trip network latency added via `tc qdisc` to simulate a realistic geographically distributed deployment (the paper states this approximates US-to-Europe round-trip time). An additional coordinator VM starts each round and injects probe messages to measure round-trip latency. Millions of simulated users are generated as extra first-layer messages produced directly by servers (pre-generated before the round starts), not by launching that many client VMs. Unless stated otherwise, 80% of servers are assumed honest, which the paper's parameter selection translates into a 14-layer path length; Bloom filters are tuned to a 10% false-positive rate.

Prototype: approximately 4,000 lines of Go (compiled with Go 1.11); onion decryption implemented in native amd64 assembly via Go's NaCl library; gRPC over TLS for server-to-server communication, using streaming and batched RPCs over multiple TCP connections.

End-to-end latency versus number of users (Figure 6), 100 Karaoke servers, 3 Vuvuzela servers (Vuvuzela's own paper reports its latency does not improve with more servers), Stadium at 100 servers with chain length 9, Vuvuzela and Stadium figures as reported in their own papers:

| Users | Karaoke (c5) | Karaoke (c4) | Vuvuzela | Stadium |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2M | 6 s | 6 s | 10 s | 68 s |
| 4M | 6 s | 8 s | ~37 s (interpolated) | — |
| 6M | 7 s | 10 s | — | 136 s |
| 8M | 8 s | 16 s | ~55 s | — |
| 16M | 27-28 s | 35-39 s | — | — |

At 2M users, Karaoke achieves 5x lower latency than Vuvuzela and 8x lower latency than Stadium (on the weaker c4 instance type, matching the instance type used in the Vuvuzela/Stadium papers). At 16M users, Karaoke achieves 10x lower latency than Stadium. The paper attributes Karaoke's better scaling with user count to only a fraction of Karaoke servers handling each additional user's messages (versus every Vuvuzela server handling every message) and to Karaoke's marginal per-message cost being onion decryption and bandwidth rather than Stadium's per-message zero-knowledge proof.

Scaling by adding servers (Figure 7): with a fixed ratio of 25,000 users per server, latency across N = 50, 60, 80, 100, 150, 200 servers stays in the 6-12 second range and decreases slightly as server count grows, because more servers require less noise per server for the same privacy target (Figure 5's relationship).

Effect of honest-server fraction (Figure 8), fixed at 2M users and 100 servers: required path length l rises and end-to-end latency rises as the assumed honest fraction falls from 90% toward 30%. The paper states latency is acceptable for text messaging down to 60% assumed-honest, and states Karaoke "would not be a good fit" below 30% assumed-honest, without giving a latency figure for that point in the extracted text.

Ablation of Karaoke's two core techniques, both isolated at fixed workloads: (1) without optimistic indistinguishability, each server would need to add approximately 320,000 noise messages per server per round for the same privacy level, and end-to-end latency at 2 million users rises from 6.8 s to 31 s. (2) without Bloom-filter noise verification (substituting verifiable shuffles as in Stadium), at 6 million users and 100 servers each Stadium-style server spends 6 s generating a verifiable shuffle and 2 s verifying one at each hop, versus 250 ms for Karaoke's Bloom filter generation and checking at each hop; substituting verifiable shuffles into Karaoke's own 14-hop path would add roughly 2 minutes of latency (8 s per hop across 14 hops).

Parameter selection (§6.1): target epsilon = ln(4), delta = 10^-4, after 10^8 communication rounds of which 245 rounds are assumed to encounter message loss during a sensitive conversation. At the deployed configuration of N=100 servers, h = floor(0.8N) = 80 honest servers, route length l=14, each server generates a mean of N^2*lambda1 + N^2*lambda2 = 25,000 noise messages per round (from Figure 5, delta=10^-4 fixed, over the 10^8-round/245-loss composition).

Network-loss measurement (§7.6): probing one Karaoke server every 2 minutes for one day from 100 RIPE Atlas vantage machines distributed globally, 3 ping packets per probe spaced 1 second apart. 71,194 total probe results: 70,106 received all 3 responses, 991 received 2, 60 received 1, 37 received 0 (a complete connectivity loss). Complete losses clustered into bursts across 8 distinct machines (7 machines with one burst, 1 machine with two bursts). The paper extrapolates roughly 9 message-loss events per 100 days, or about 33 per year, per client, which it states is about an order of magnitude below the 245-round loss budget the chosen (epsilon, delta) parameters were designed to tolerate.

### Parameters
- Round-based communication; round length not stated as a fixed number of seconds in the extracted text (latency figures above are the measured per-round completion times under load).
- N = 100 servers in the primary deployment configuration (also tested 50-200 in the server-scaling experiment).
- Honest-server fraction h/N = 80% assumed in the default configuration (tested down to approximately 30-90% in the honest-fraction experiment).
- Path length (number of mix layers) l = 14 at 80% assumed-honest; l varies with the assumed honest fraction per Figure 8 (exact l values at other honest fractions not given as a table in the extracted text).
- Differential-privacy target: epsilon = ln(4), delta = 10^-4, over 10^8 rounds with a budget of 245 rounds of tolerated message loss during a sensitive conversation.
- Bloom-filter false-positive rate: 10%.
- Noise messages generated per server per round at N=100, h=80, l=14: approximately 25,000 (N^2*lambda1 + N^2*lambda2).
- Simulated network latency between servers: 100 ms round-trip, added via `tc qdisc`, to approximate a US-Europe geographic deployment.

### Stated limitations
Karaoke does not provide fault tolerance: it requires all servers to be online for a round to complete, and the paper states handling server outages and denial-of-service attacks is left to future work. Karaoke does not hide that a given user is using the system at all — an adversary observing a connection to a Karaoke server learns the user is a Karaoke user, though the paper states it hopes a large user population makes this fact alone less identifying. Karaoke makes no availability guarantees and states defending against denial-of-service attacks is future work. If an adversary compromises a user's own computer, Karaoke provides no privacy guarantee for that user's communications. Karaoke assumes clients already know the public keys of all servers and assumes users can establish a shared secret and initiate a conversation out-of-band; the paper states a complete system would need a separate "dialing" protocol (citing its own prior work, Alpenhorn) to perform that bootstrapping, and that bootstrapping protocol would add its own bandwidth and latency cost not accounted for in these measurements. Message loss is the primary channel through which information leaks; loss can come from an active attack or from a network outage long enough that TCP cannot recover, and the paper states it expects users to avoid sensitive conversations over highly unreliable network paths. The measured 33-events-per-year loss rate is drawn from probing one specific Karaoke deployment over RIPE Atlas for one day, an approximation, not a controlled adversarial measurement.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Requires every server on a message's chosen path to participate honestly in decrypting and re-shuffling within its assigned layer; a message cannot be decrypted by an adversary who does not control every server on its path, but the overall privacy guarantee assumes a globally known, fixed set of N servers with h of them honest, so the system needs a mechanism (not supplied by this paper) to establish and distribute that server set and its public keys to every client before a round can run. Requires synchronous rounds across all N servers — a round only completes once every server has finished processing its layer — so any deployment needs a coordination mechanism to start rounds and detect a stalled server, which the paper states is unhandled (no fault tolerance). Requires TCP-level reliable delivery between client and server within a round; momentary packet loss is tolerated but an extended outage causes the client to miss the round, which the privacy analysis treats as a bounded, budgeted event (245 rounds) rather than an unbounded one. Requires an out-of-band channel supplying the initial shared secret (dead-drop schedule) between two users who wish to communicate; Karaoke provides no mechanism for this itself. Requires the adversary to be unable to break the underlying cryptographic primitives (standard cryptographic hardness assumption) and requires computational, not information-theoretic, differential privacy as a consequence of relying on cryptography for the onion encryption.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus for the measured latency figures themselves. Karaoke's own comparison figures for Vuvuzela and Stadium are stated as drawn from those papers' own reported numbers, not independently re-measured by this paper on the same hardware for those two systems (only Karaoke's own c4/c5 comparison is apples-to-apples).

### References worth retrieving
- **Foundational**: J. van den Hooff, D. Lazar, M. Zaharia, N. Zeldovich, "Vuvuzela: Scalable Private Messaging Resistant to Traffic Analysis," SOSP 2015 (the direct latency baseline throughout this paper; only 3 servers used because Vuvuzela's own reported performance does not improve with more servers).
- **Competing**: N. Tyagi, Y. Gilad, D. Leung, M. Zaharia, N. Zeldovich, "Stadium: A Distributed Metadata-Private Messaging System," SOSP 2017 (the other direct latency baseline; uses per-message zero-knowledge verifiable-shuffle proofs, which this paper's ablation measures as materially slower than Karaoke's Bloom-filter approach).
- **Competing**: A. Kwon, H. Corrigan-Gibbs, S. Devadas, B. Ford, "Atom: Horizontally Scaling Strong Anonymity," SOSP 2017 (processes each message at hundreds of servers, latency 30 minutes to several hours per this paper's characterization).
- **Competing**: A. M. Piotrowska, J. Hayes, T. Elahi, S. Meiser, G. - **Foundational**: C. Dwork, A. Roth, "The Algorithmic Foundations of Differential Privacy," Foundations and Trends in Theoretical Computer Science 9(3-4), 2014 (the differential-privacy framework Karaoke's guarantee is stated in).
- **Foundational**: I. Mironov, O. Pandey, O. Reingold, S. Vadhan, "Computational Differential Privacy," CRYPTO 2009 (the specific relaxed definition — computational, not information-theoretic — that Karaoke's cryptography-based construction achieves).
- **Attack**: G. Danezis, "Statistical Disclosure Attacks: Traffic Confirmation in Open Environments," IFIP SEC 2003 (traffic-analysis attack class this paper's threat model is designed to resist).
- **Attack**: S. J. Murdoch, G. Danezis, "Low-Cost Traffic Analysis of Tor," IEEE S&P 2005 (part of the traffic-analysis literature this paper cites as ruling out Tor-based systems for its threat model).
- **Superseded-by direction (self)**: D. Lazar, Y. Gilad, N. Zeldovich, "Yodel: Strong Metadata Security for Voice Calls," SOSP 2019 — the same authors' own follow-on targeting sub-second latency (evidence-file key LAZAR-SOSP-19).
- **Foundational (own prior work)**: D. Lazar, N. Zeldovich, "Alpenhorn: Bootstrapping Secure Communication Without Leaking Metadata," OSDI 2016 (the out-of-band "dialing" protocol this paper states a complete deployment would need alongside Karaoke).

## [LAZAR-SOSP-19] Yodel: Strong Metadata Security for Voice Calls
**Citation:** David Lazar, Yossi Gilad, Nickolai Zeldovich. "Yodel: Strong Metadata Security for Voice Calls." ACM SOSP, 2019. DOI 10.1145/3341301.3359648.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://people.csail.mit.edu/nickolai/papers/lazar-yodel.pdf
**Source URL:** https://people.csail.mit.edu/nickolai/papers/lazar-yodel.pdf
**Domain:** G

### What it does
Yodel hides which pairs of users are on a voice call from an adversary that controls the network and compromises some servers, at latency low enough to carry a voice conversation, by avoiding a public-key operation per network hop for every message. Users route voice packets through a mixnet of N servers arranged so that each message passes through a client-chosen circuit, a fixed sequence of servers established once with public-key cryptography and then reused for many messages using only symmetric-key cryptography, unlike Karaoke (this same author group's prior system), which performs a public-key operation at every hop for every message.

Two mechanisms make circuit reuse safe against a network-observing, server-compromising adversary. Self-healing circuits let a circuit survive without leaking metadata when a user's network briefly drops: because a server would otherwise be able to notice "no message arrived on this circuit this round" and infer whose circuit it is, each server that would have relayed a real message instead relays a server-generated cover message on any round where the client fails to send one, so from an observing server's point of view a circuit always carries traffic whether or not its owning client is actually connected. Guarded circuit exchange addresses the separate problem of connecting two users to a shared circuit without one of them revealing, by connecting or not connecting to a given circuit endpoint, whether a call attempt succeeded: each user maintains two circuits, one dedicated to background cover traffic and one for an actual call partner (buddy); if a call setup message is lost, the user still has a safe circuit endpoint to connect to (either the cover circuit or the buddy circuit) without revealing to the server whether the call attempt succeeded.

Circuit setup (establishing the public-key-encrypted onion layers for a fresh circuit for the next round) proceeds in the background, using a separate small pool of CPU cores from the pool handling the current round's message relay, so the two phases do not compete for the same resources within a round. Noise circuits (server-generated cover circuits with no real user behind them) are created during setup in a volume derived from the assumed fraction of honest servers and the desired failure probability, following the same noise-generation-and-Bloom-filter-verification approach as Karaoke. Yodel relies on an external metadata-private messaging system (the paper uses its own prior systems, Alpenhorn for out-of-band dialing and Karaoke for circuit-endpoint exchange) for users to first tell each other which circuit to connect to.

### Measured results
Hardware: Amazon EC2 c5.9xlarge instances (Intel Xeon 3.0 GHz, 36 cores, 72 GB memory, 10 Gbit/s link) per server. On each server, 30 of 36 cores were dedicated to circuit-messaging relay for the current round and the remaining 6 cores to circuit setup for the next round. Deployment: 100 servers evenly distributed across 5 Amazon data centers (Virginia us-east-1, Ireland eu-west-1, London eu-west-2, Paris eu-west-3, Frankfurt eu-central-1), chosen to minimize inter-server latency while maximizing independent trust zones. Measured weekly-average round-trip latency between Virginia and Frankfurt (the highest-latency pair): 90 ms; between European server pairs: 15-40 ms. Millions of simulated users were generated as extra circuits created by servers during circuit setup (2 circuits per simulated user), excluding the cost of generating those circuits' setup onions (a cost that in a real deployment would fall on clients, not servers). Two real users ran the Yodel voice client from Boston (maximum measured round-trip latency to a Yodel server: 90 ms), using Alpenhorn for out-of-band dialing and Karaoke (on separate servers) for circuit exchange, to measure real end-to-end latency and throughput. Baseline configuration for all experiments except the trust-assumption sweep in §6.3: servers assumed honest with 80% probability, requiring 15-hop circuits; target failure probability 10^-8, which required approximately 3,700 noise circuits generated per server per round at a 100-server deployment. Relative standard deviation of each reported data point: 6% or less.

One-way voice-packet latency versus number of users, 100 servers, two audio codecs (Figure 10): with the LPCNet neural vocoder, latency stays under 1 second up to 5 million users (990 ms at 5 million users), rises to 1.4 seconds beyond 5 million users (at which point the paper states the system "would need more servers to support voice calls for that user load"), and beyond 8 million users inter-server packet loss made sustained voice-call throughput with LPCNet difficult. With the standard Opus codec at its lowest-quality setting (5x more bandwidth per call than LPCNet), 100 servers supported 1 million voice calls at 965 ms latency; Opus supports fewer simultaneous users than LPCNet at the same server count because of its higher bandwidth requirement.

Circuit setup latency versus number of users, 100 servers, 6 of 36 cores dedicated to setup (Figure 11): under 40 seconds at 8 million users. The paper states rounds start every 5 minutes, so setup completes with margin at every tested user count.

Scaling by adding servers, fixed per-server user ratio (Figure 12): at 25,000 users/server and 50,000 users/server ratios, latency rises slightly from 50 to 200 servers because per-server noise-circuit count scales with server count (at 200 servers each server creates 4x as many noise circuits as at 50 servers, for the fixed 80%-honest / 15-hop security target). At the 50,000-users/server ratio and 200 servers (10 million users), one-way latency is 848 ms.

Effect of trust assumption (path length) on latency, 100 servers, 2 million users (Figure 13): latency increases linearly with path length. At 100% assumed-honest servers (adversary controls only the network, no servers), path length 2 suffices, giving approximately 100 ms one-way latency. At the paper's baseline 80%-honest assumption, path length 15 is required. Under an assumption matching Herd's single-honest-first-hop model, Yodel needs 9 layers, giving approximately 450 ms latency at 2 million users and 100 servers — compared against Herd's own reported 200 ms for North American users at 10 million users and 1,000 servers, which the paper states comes with a weaker privacy guarantee than Yodel's (elaborated in the paper's discussion, not reproduced here as a number).

Server bandwidth (Figure 14), 100 servers, varying user count: average per-server transmit bandwidth reaches approximately 3 Gbit/s at 5 million users with LPCNet. The measured per-server bandwidth tracks closely to the analytically computed minimum bandwidth needed just to carry the raw audio (2 calls per user divided across servers, no security overhead), which the paper attributes to circuit messaging adding no bandwidth overhead from onion encryption and only a small overhead from inter-user checksums. The prototype could not sustain over 4.6 Gbit/s per server across the real internet without significant packet loss, which limited the Opus configuration to 1.75 million users on 100 servers.

Cost estimate (not an experimental measurement, a derivation from a 2016 published bandwidth-pricing figure): the paper cites a 2016 reported price of approximately $4,000/month for a 10 Gbit/s U.S.-to-Europe link and computes from it that Yodel's bandwidth could be funded by charging users under $1/year; this is a derived estimate from an external, unverified-by-this-pass pricing source, not a measurement this paper performed.

Fault tolerance (§7, stated as a limitation, not a headline result): at the evaluated 15-hop configuration, if 2% of servers are unavailable, approximately 30% of messages are lost.

### Parameters
- N = 100 servers in the primary evaluation (also tested 50-200 in the server-scaling experiment).
- Honest-server-probability assumption: 80% in the default configuration, swept from 100% down through configurations tested in Figure 13 (exact intermediate percentages for each tested path length not given as a table in the extracted text beyond the 80%/100% and Herd-comparison points).
- Path length (hop count): 15 hops at the 80%-honest baseline; 2 hops at 100%-honest; 9 hops when matching Herd's single-honest-hop trust assumption.
- Target failure probability: 10^-8.
- Noise circuits generated per server per round at N=100, 80%-honest, 15 hops: approximately 3,700.
- Round interval: 5 minutes.
- CPU allocation per server: 30 of 36 cores to current-round circuit messaging, 6 of 36 cores to next-round circuit setup.
- Audio codecs tested: LPCNet (low-bitrate neural vocoder, 1.6 kb/s per the codec's own citation) and Opus (standard VoIP codec) at its lowest-quality, highest-compression setting; Opus used 5x the bandwidth of LPCNet in this configuration.
- One-way inter-server delay used in the paper's own accounting of the 990 ms figure: 45 ms per hop across 15 hops in the synchronous-batch design.

### Stated limitations
Yodel's own stated most significant limitation is latency: 990 ms one-way exceeds the ITU G.114 recommendation of at most 400 ms for interactive telephone-quality calls, and the paper states this would make fast, interruption-heavy conversation difficult, while asserting (based on the authors' own use, not a controlled study) that longer, less-interrupted conversations remained usable. Noise generation per server scales linearly with the number of servers in the deployment, which the paper identifies as a bottleneck at deployments of several thousand servers (citing Tor's approximately 6,000-server scale as the comparison point); the paper states it believes the overhead stays low at deployments of hundreds of servers, based on Figure 9 and the §6.2 server-scaling measurement, but does not measure a several-thousand-server deployment. Fault tolerance is bounded: at the evaluated 15-hop configuration, 2% of servers being unavailable causes about 30% of messages to be lost, so the paper states Yodel is useful only when few servers are simultaneously down. Geographic latency is architecturally coupled across all users: because total latency is approximately the hop count times the maximum one-way latency between any two servers in the deployment, adding a server in a new region to reduce latency for users in that region raises latency for every other user in the system; the paper's own worked example is that adding an Australian server to the evaluated US/Europe deployment would raise end-to-end latency for all users from 990 ms to about 3 seconds. The paper states this coupling is inevitable given an anonymity set defined as all connected users in the system. Sybil circuit creation (an attacker creating many circuits to mount denial of service) is identified as a risk the paper suggests mitigating with existing mechanisms such as subscriptions or proof-of-work, explicitly stating that fully solving the problem needs further research, not addressed by this paper's own construction.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Requires an external metadata-private messaging channel to bootstrap each call: the evaluation itself used Alpenhorn (this author group's own prior OSDI 2016 system) for out-of-band dialing and Karaoke (this author group's own prior OSDI 2018 system) for circuit-endpoint exchange, running on separate servers from the Yodel mixnet; Yodel supplies none of this bootstrapping itself. Requires synchronous rounds across the full server deployment, the same coordination requirement as Karaoke; a circuit's self-healing property depends on every server on its path relaying either a real message or a cover message every round, which requires all N servers to remain reachable and processing rounds in lockstep for the low-loss operating regime the fault-tolerance figures describe. Requires the deployment's server set and path lengths to be fixed in advance around a target honest-fraction assumption (15 hops for 80% honest in the evaluated configuration); changing the assumed honest fraction changes the required path length and therefore the latency, so the system needs an externally supplied, trusted estimate of the fraction of compromised servers before path length can be chosen. Requires geographic co-location of the server deployment's regions to keep per-hop latency low; because total latency scales with the worst-case inter-server round-trip time, any component that needs to add servers in a new geographic region to improve locality for a subset of users instead raises latency for the whole population, so a caller cannot use per-region latency optimization without a global redesign. Requires an independent Sybil-resistance mechanism (not supplied by this paper) to bound the number of circuits an attacker can create for denial of service.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus for its own measured figures. The paper's comparison to Karaoke (8 seconds latency, 0.24 kbit/s throughput per user, at 4 million users) and to Herd (200 ms for North American users at 10 million users, 1,000 servers) are cited from those systems' own papers, not independently re-measured by this paper on the same hardware, so those specific comparison numbers should be checked against LAZAR-OSDI-18's own entry rather than treated as this paper's own measurement.

- **Foundational (self)**: D. Lazar, N. Zeldovich, "Alpenhorn: Bootstrapping Secure Communication Without Leaking Metadata," OSDI 2016 (the out-of-band dialing protocol used in this paper's own live-user evaluation).

- **Competing**: A. Kwon, H. Corrigan-Gibbs, S. Devadas, B. Ford, "Atom: Horizontally Scaling Strong Anonymity," SOSP 2017.
