## [LIU-PACMHCI-25] Understanding Decentralized Social Feed Curation on Mastodon
**Citation:** Yuhan Liu, Emmy Song, Owen Xingjian Zhang, Jewel Merriman, Lei Zhang, Andrés Monroy-Hernández. "Understanding Decentralized Social Feed Curation on Mastodon." Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction (CSCW), 2025. DOI 10.1145/3757688.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.18817
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.18817
**Domain:** K

### What it does
The paper reports a two-part interview study of Mastodon users and, from the first part's findings,
builds and tests braids.social, a prototype web client that lets a user compose one unified feed from
three of Mastodon's existing API-exposed feeds by setting a priority level per source, without any
server-side or platform-supplied ranking model.

Part one: eleven participants (P1–P11) gave 60-minute interviews about their existing Mastodon feed
use — which of the platform's built-in feeds (home, local, federated) they read, how they choose a
home server, and what third-party tools they already use to filter content.

Part two: braids.social is a Flask (backend) and React (frontend) web client that authenticates to a
user's Mastodon account over OAuth 2.0 with read-only permissions, then calls three existing Mastodon
API endpoints — Home Timeline, Public (with the `local` parameter), and Trending Status — each
returning 40 posts per call. Each source is assigned a priority level (None, Low, Medium, High
Priority) by the user through a slider. The client merges the returned posts into one display list,
placing posts from a higher-priority source above posts from a lower-priority source, while posts
within a single source's fragment retain that source's original chronological order. Each displayed
post carries a badge showing which source it was drawn from — "Users you follow," "Hashtag you
follow," "Trending post," "Local post," or "Prioritized account" — assigned once, from the first
source the post was seen in, to avoid a post carrying two badges when duplicated across sources. A
separate control lets a user pin up to a small number of specific accounts, on any Mastodon instance,
to always surface regardless of follow status. Ten of the eleven part-one participants (P12–P21) then
used braids.social in a further 60-minute session, completing three assigned feed-configuration tasks
and reporting on the experience.

### Measured results
This is a qualitative interview study; it reports no throughput, latency, message-count, or
scalability figures. The only reported figures are counts of participant responses within the fixed
interview sample:

| Finding | Count | Condition |
|---|---|---|
| Preferred Mastodon's chronological (non-algorithmic) feed order | 8 of 11 part-one participants | Open-ended interview question comparing chronological and algorithmic feeds |
| Switched their home server at least once | 3 of 11 part-one participants (P2, P3, P7) | Self-reported over the course of platform use, no fixed time window given |
| Preferred third-party Mastodon clients over the official app | 7 of 11 part-one participants | Self-reported client choice |
| Set "Home feed" (Following Content) to High priority and other sources to None/Low/Medium in braids.social | 9 of 10 part-two participants (all but P18) | Free configuration during the unstructured part of the part-two session, recorded in Table 1 |
| Given the task "make one source show roughly twice as many posts as another," chose the High/Low priority-level pair | 7 of 10 part-two participants | Task 3 of the assigned configuration tasks; the remaining 3 chose High/Medium |

Table 1 in the paper lists each of the 10 part-two participants' (P12–P21) chosen priority level
(None/Low/Medium/High) for each of the four source categories (Following Content, Local Posts,
Trending Posts, Accounts) during their free-form session with braids.social; it is a record of stated
individual preferences, not an aggregate measurement with a denominator beyond n=10.

### Parameters
| Parameter | Value used | Range tested |
|---|---|---|
| Posts retrieved per API call | 40, fixed, per source per request | Not varied |
| Priority levels per source | 4 discrete levels: None, Low, Medium, High Priority | Not varied; participants report difficulty distinguishing Medium from adjacent levels |
| Feed sources merged | 3 (Following Content = Home Timeline API, Local Posts = Public API with local parameter, Trending Posts = Trending Status API) plus a separate "Prioritized accounts" pin list | Fixed set; not varied |
| Interview sample size | 11 (part one), 10 of the same 11 (part two) | Not varied; the paper states this is a limitation |
| Authentication scope | OAuth 2.0, read-only | Not varied |

### Stated limitations
The authors state the findings are limited by small sample size, and that Mastodon users are, by
their own account, "generally more concerned about algorithmic transparency, anti-corporation, and
privacy than traditional social media users," so the sample may not generalize even within Mastodon's
own user base. Recruitment ran through Google Forms and Zoom, which the authors say may have
deterred some Mastodon users from participating. The authors state findings on Mastodon feed curation
may have limited generalizability to other decentralized platforms — PeerTube, Pixelfed — whose users
form different strong-tie/weak-tie interaction patterns, and separately that Mastodon's ActivityPub
protocol differs in decentralized architecture and information flow from AT Protocol and Farcaster,
so results may not transfer to platforms built on those protocols without adaptation. Participants in
the braids.social session reported difficulty precisely interpreting what distinguishes the "Medium"
priority slider setting from "Low" or "High"; the authors state they leave to future work "the optimal
level of granularity" for the slider affordance. The authors did not test whether user attitudes
toward machine-learning-based curation would shift if applied by a non-profit, ad-free operator,
stating this as an open question.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
braids.social is built entirely as a client against Mastodon's existing, unmodified server-side API;
it requires no protocol change and no new server-side capability beyond what the Home Timeline,
Public, and Trending Status endpoints already expose. It requires the home server to run the Trending
Status endpoint (the paper notes this is itself a server-side re-ranking of the federated feed by
popularity and time, so braids.social's "Trending Posts" source already depends on one piece of
algorithmic ranking computed off-client). It requires OAuth 2.0 read-only account access; no write or
posting capability is used. The client performs no local storage or persistence of the merged feed
across sessions beyond what is described; each session's badge assignment and fragment ordering are
recomputed from whatever the three API calls return at request time, so the merge mechanism requires
no cross-session state and no coordination between multiple client instances of the same user.

### Contradicts
None found. No claim about message counts, scalability, or attack resistance is made or misattributed
to this paper in the reviewed corpus.

### References worth retrieving
- **Raman, Joglekar, De Cristofaro, Sastry, Tyson, "Challenges in the decentralised web: The mastodon case," IMC 2019** — competing/foundational measurement study of Mastodon's deployed network, cited [64].
- **Zhang, Zhao, Wang, Johnston, Chalhoub, Ross, Liu, Tinsman, Zhao, Van Kleek et al., "Trouble in Paradise? Understanding Mastodon Admin's Motivations, Experiences, and Challenges," PACM HCI (CSCW2) 2024** — competing qualitative study on Mastodon governance/moderation, cited [81]; overlapping authorship with ZHANG-ARXIV-25 in this corpus.
- **Anaobi, Raman, Castro, Bin Zia, Ibosiola, Tyson, "Will Admins Cope? Decentralized Moderation in the Fediverse," WWW 2023** — foundational measurement of Mastodon moderation labor, cited [2].
- **La Cava, Greco, Tagarelli, "Understanding the growth of the Fediverse through the lens of Mastodon," Applied Network Science 2021** — foundational network-growth measurement, cited [48].
- **La Cava, Greco, Tagarelli, "Information consumption and boundary spanning in Decentralized Online Social Networks: The case of Mastodon users," Online Social Networks and Media 2022** — foundational measurement of cross-instance information flow, cited [49].
- **Zignani, Gaito, Rossi, "Follow the 'mastodon': Structure and evolution of a decentralized online social network," ICWSM 2018** — foundational structural measurement, cited [83].
- **He, Gordon, Popowski, Bernstein, "Cura: Curation at Social Media Scale," PACM HCI (CSCW2) 2023** — competing curation-tool system, cited [39].
- **Feng, Koo, Tan, Bruckman, McDonald, Zhang, "Mapping the Design Space of Teachable Social Media Feed Experiences," arXiv 2024** — competing/foundational feed-curation design work, cited [29].
- **Jeong, Sheth, Tahir, Alatawi, Bernard, Liu, "Exploring platform migration patterns between twitter and mastodon," arXiv/ICWSM 2023** — foundational migration measurement, cited [43].

"nine out of ten participants (except P18) put the following content...as a high priority" (line 556-557).
"seven out of ten participants set the categories to high and low priority" (line 605-606).
"Our findings indicate that while visual cues and real-time feedback improved transparency" (line 643).
"our findings are limited by the small sample size" (line 717).
"limited generalizability across other decentralized platforms with different interaction dynamics" (lines 728-729).

## [LOCHER-HOTNETS-06] Free Riding in BitTorrent is Cheap
**Citation:** Thomas Locher, Patrick Moor, Stefan Schmid, Roger Wattenhofer. "Free Riding in BitTorrent is Cheap." Proc. 5th ACM Workshop on Hot Topics in Networks (HotNets-V), 2006. Pages 85-90.
**Retrieved:** full text via http://conferences.sigcomm.org/hotnets/2006/locher06free.pdf
**Source URL:** http://conferences.sigcomm.org/hotnets/2006/locher06free.pdf
**Domain:** I

### What it does
BitThief is a BitTorrent client that completes downloads of complete files while uploading no data at all, defeating BitTorrent's tit-for-tat admission mechanism through the single non-reciprocal admission path that mechanism leaves open: optimistic unchoke. BitTorrent divides participants into seeders, who hold the complete file and upload to all requesters in round robin, and leechers, who upload only to peers that reciprocate, except that every leecher periodically unchokes one neighbor for free (optimistic unchoke) so that newly joined peers with nothing to share can start downloading. BitThief exploits this path three ways. First, it opens far more simultaneous connections than the reference client (up to 500, against a reference-client default of 80), which raises the number of seeder round robin slots and leecher optimistic-unchoke slots it can occupy at once; download rate rises linearly with the number of open connections because remote peers act independently of how many connections the requester holds, except that a second connection from the same IP address is refused by the reference client and by Azureus. Second, it re-announces to the tracker far more often than the reference client's roughly 1800-second interval, starting at a configurable short interval and backing off exponentially to once every 30 minutes, to acquire more peer addresses faster. Third, in place of the reference client's rarest-first piece selection, BitThief requests a random missing piece from whichever peer unchokes it, so no unchoke period goes unused. BitThief never announces any pieces to remote peers and never chokes or unchokes any remote peer, so every peer it contacts treats it as a peer that has just started downloading.

### Measured results
| Condition | Result |
|---|---|
| 7 torrents (170 MB-798 MB; A-G), unrestricted BitThief (permitted to download from seeders and leechers), reference client v4.20.2 permitted up to 500 connections for fair comparison, 3 runs per client per torrent, over the public Internet | BitThief completed every torrent. On torrents A, B, F, BitThief was on average slightly faster than the reference client (reference client uploaded 232 MB on torrent A, 129 MB on torrent B in one run). On torrents E and G (few seeders, many leechers), BitThief took roughly 4x longer than the reference client, which itself uploaded over 3.5 GB. |
| Same 7 torrents, BitThief restricted to download only from leechers (seeders excluded), 3 runs, same conditions | All downloads finished. Average download time increased relative to the seeders-permitted case. On torrent C, where only 15% of peers were leechers (so BitThief could use less than one sixth of available peers), BitThief took roughly 5x longer than the reference client, which was permitted to use both seeders and leechers. |
| Controlled private-network testbed: one private tracker, a configurable number of reference clients as seeders/leechers, one BitThief instance, scenario with a single slow seeder | BitThief started 9 minutes after three reference clients but caught up, and all four clients finished at roughly the same time. |
| Same torrent (359 MB on TorrentLeech, a sharing community requiring a minimum upload ratio; 350 MB on Mininova, an open public tracker), 3 BitThief runs per site | Mininova runs (531 seeders, 303 leechers reported): 32, 32, 37 minutes. TorrentLeech runs (24 seeders, 1 leecher reported): 7:25, 7:08, 7:08 minutes -- more than 4x faster despite roughly 33x fewer reported peers, because community peers upload more broadly to protect their upload ratio. |
| Block-contribution distribution across peers for the same torrent, BitThief connected to 309 peers on Mininova and 349 on TorrentLeech | On TorrentLeech (community), contribution across peers was more balanced. On Mininova (open), only a small number of peers supplied a large fraction of all blocks. |
| Sharing-ratio manipulation on TorrentLeech, by sending fabricated upload totals in tracker announcements (the tracker does not verify announced upload/download totals) | BitThief attained a reported sharing ratio of 1.4 on TorrentLeech without uploading any data. |
| Garbage-piece exploit from a prior paper (Liogkas et al., IPTPS 2006), reimplemented and tested against the reference client and Azureus | Answering all subpiece requests for a piece with random data caused both clients to ban the sending IP address once hash verification failed. Withholding exactly one subpiece per piece (so blame could not be pinned on the sender alone) still fooled the reference client, but Azureus tracked which peer supplied the most subpieces of a failing piece, reserved the remaining requests for that peer, and banned the IP once requests went unanswered. The authors conclude uploading garbage in any tested form does not improve download performance. |

### Parameters
- Tracker-reported peer list size: default 50 addresses per announcement; protocol maximum requestable is 200, but most trackers observed trimmed the response to 50 regardless of the requested count.
- BitThief simultaneous connection limit used in experiments: up to 500 (reference client's is 80 by default; raised to 500 for the fair-comparison experiments via --min_peers 500 --max_initiate 500 --max_allow_in 500).
- Tracker re-announce interval: reference client follows the tracker-supplied interval (observed near 1800 s); BitThief starts at a configurable shorter interval and backs off exponentially to a ceiling of 1800 s (once every 30 minutes).
- Piece-availability announcement: BitThief announces an empty piece list at connection setup and never updates it; announcing any percentage below 100% did not change measured performance, but announcing 100% caused remote peers to treat BitThief as a seeder and refuse to send it any pieces.

### Stated limitations
The paper's controlled-testbed experiment illustrating recovery from a slow seeder is described by the authors as an idealized case because no additional leechers joined the swarm during the run. BitThief as built does not implement collusion among multiple free-riding instances, does not use the distributed (DHT-based) tracker protocol, and does not perform a Sybil attack of presenting multiple fake identities to the same remote peer, though the authors state this would be straightforward to add given multiple IP addresses and would plausibly double the achievable download rate. The authors state that faking whole pieces by finding SHA-1 hash collisions to defeat per-piece integrity checking is computationally infeasible with then-current techniques and storage. The authors state that a mechanism combining tit-for-tat with an efficient bootstrap allowance for newly joined peers (who have nothing to share yet) remains an open problem, which they name as future work rather than solved in this paper.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
For an incentive mechanism to withstand this attack, it cannot rely solely on a reciprocity check triggered only by past upload behavior, because BitThief supplies zero upload and still receives service through the optimistic-unchoke and seeder round robin paths, which are unconditional by design. Any defense that closes this path must either meter or price the optimistic-unchoke slot itself, or supply new peers with reciprocity credit from some other source, since the bootstrap problem (new peers have nothing to reciprocate with) is the reason the unconditional path exists in the first place. A tracker-side or community-side ratio-enforcement layer requires the tracker to verify announced upload/download totals against independent evidence (for example, corroboration from receiving peers), because self-reported totals in the announce message are accepted without verification in the deployed protocol and can be fabricated by a client that never transfers the claimed bytes. A per-peer integrity/ban mechanism such as Azureus's blame-single-supplier logic requires the receiving client to track, per remote peer, which subpieces of a not-yet-hash-verified piece it supplied, so that a failed hash check can be attributed to a specific peer rather than diffused across a piece's several suppliers.

### Contradicts
The paper's own framing distinguishes its finding from Jun and Ahamad [9], who define free riding as contributing considerably less than other peers and propose a tit-for-tat-oriented fix; this paper's authors state they instead demonstrate downloads with strictly zero upload, a stronger claim than reduced contribution. No other paper in the current evidence file's W3-5 batch reports free-riding numbers under the same connection-count and torrent-size conditions to compare directly; SIRIVIANOS-IPTPS-07 in this batch reports an independent free-riding construction and its completion-rate figures should be compared against BitThief's at the level of "peer-set size used" rather than at the level of a shared torrent, since the two papers use different torrents and swarm compositions.

### References worth retrieving
- Adar, Huberman, "Free Riding on Gnutella," First Monday 5(10), 2000 -- foundational (earliest measurement of free riding in a P2P file-sharing network).
- Douceur, "The Sybil Attack," IPTPS 2002 -- foundational (defines the multi-identity attack the paper explicitly notes BitThief could add).
- Liogkas, Nelson, Kohler, Zhang, "Exploiting BitTorrent For Fun (But Not Profit)," IPTPS 2006 -- competing/foundational (the closest prior work; implements three individual selfish exploits including the garbage-piece exploit this paper reimplements and extends by combining attacks).
- Jun, Ahamad, "Incentives in BitTorrent Induce Free Riding," P2PECON 2005 -- competing (argues BitTorrent's tit-for-tat is insufficient using a weaker definition of free riding; proposes an iterated-prisoner's-dilemma-based fix).
- Andrade, Mowbray, Lima, Wagner, Ripeanu, "Influences on Cooperation in BitTorrent Communities," P2PECON 2005 -- foundational (measures sharing-ratio enforcement effects in communities; this paper's community exploit builds directly on that measurement).
- Grolimund, Meisser, Schmid, Wattenhofer, "Havelaar: A Robust and Efficient Reputation System for Active Peer-to-Peer Systems," NetEcon 2006 -- competing (proposed reputation-based incentive mechanism for P2P systems).
- Vishnumurthy, Chandrakumar, Sirer, "KARMA: A Secure Economic Framework for P2P Resource Sharing," P2PECON 2003 -- competing (currency-based incentive mechanism for P2P resource sharing).
- Tamilmani, Pai, Mohr, "SWIFT: A System with Incentives for Trading," P2PECON 2004 -- competing (alternative incentive mechanism for content trading).

### Verbatim extracts
- "we present BitThief, a free riding client that never contributes any real data"
- "opening more connections increases download speed linearly"
- "BitThief only requires roughly 5 times longer than the official client"
- "we now have a sharing ratio of 1.4 on TorrentLeech without ever uploading a single bit"
- "uploading random garbage, in any way, does not improve performance"

## [LOO-IPTPS-04] The Case for a Hybrid P2P Search Infrastructure
**Citation:** Boon Thau Loo, Ryan Huebsch, Ion Stoica, Joseph M. Hellerstein. "The Case for a Hybrid P2P Search Infrastructure." IPTPS, 2004. DOI 10.1007/978-3-540-30183-7_14.
**Retrieved:** full text via http://www.huebsch.org/papers/IPTPS04.pdf
**Source URL:** http://www.huebsch.org/papers/IPTPS04.pdf
**Domain:** B

### What it does
The mechanism routes a query to query broadcast (query flooding) or to a distributed hash table (DHT) depending on whether the sought item is popular or rare, so the network avoids both the high response-time cost query broadcast incurs for rare items and the high publishing bandwidth a DHT incurs for popular items. A DHT-based search publishes a copy of each document's identifier into an inverted index (a posting list per keyword) stored across the DHT, then answers a query by routing to the nodes holding each keyword's posting list and computing a distributed join across those lists; this gives complete recall in the absence of node failure but the publishing cost scales with how many documents contain each keyword, so a query on a keyword with a large posting list (the paper's example is a query for "Britney Spears") is expensive to keep indexed. Query broadcast, in contrast, needs no publishing step and finds popular items quickly because many nodes hold a copy, but performs poorly for rare items because few nodes can answer within a hop-limited flood. The hybrid scheme organizes ultrapeers (Gnutella supernodes that perform query processing on behalf of leaf nodes) into a DHT overlay. Each ultrapeer identifies items likely to be rare from its leaf nodes' traffic and selectively publishes only those into the DHT, using the heuristic that an item returned in a small query-result set is rare; a query is first sent by conventional query broadcast, and if too few results return within a timeout, the query is reissued as a DHT lookup.

### Measured results
Live Gnutella network measurement: a modified LimeWire client instrumented to log all Gnutella traffic, run as ultrapeer or leaf node, deployed on 30 PlanetLab ultrapeers. Network crawl on 11 October 2003 (around noon Pacific time), 45 minutes, from 30 ultrapeers in parallel, measured network size of approximately 100,000 nodes and approximately 20 million files. 700 distinct queries taken from Gnutella query traces, replayed from each of the 30 ultrapeers at three different times (giving 700 x 30 x 3 total query instances), to compute recall (fraction of results returned by one node relative to the union of results from all 30 nodes, itself a lower bound on total available results). Findings: 41% of all queries received 10 or fewer results; 18% of queries received no results. For queries returning a single result, average first-result latency was 73 seconds; for queries returning 10 or fewer results, average first-result latency was 50 seconds; for queries returning more than 150 results, average first-result latency was 6 seconds. Taking the union of results across all 30 ultrapeers instead of a single node's results reduces the fraction of queries with 10 or fewer results from 41% to 27%, and reduces the fraction with zero results from 18% to 6% — described as a lower-bound estimate because the 30-node union itself underestimates total network results. Distributed-join bandwidth comparison: replaying 70,000 Gnutella queries against a 700,000-file sample collected from the same 30 ultrapeers, queries returning 10 or fewer results required shipping on average 7 times fewer posting-list entries via a DHT distributed join than the average across all queries. Connection-lifetime (churn) measurement: two leaf nodes and two ultrapeers monitored over 72 hours. Average connection lifetime: leaf nodes 58 minutes, ultrapeers 93 minutes (ultrapeers 1.5x longer). Median connection lifetime: leaf nodes 13 minutes, ultrapeers 16 minutes. Excluding leaf nodes with lifetimes under 10 minutes raised the average remaining leaf-node lifetime to 106 minutes. Preliminary hybrid-system deployment: multiple hybrid clients (the paper's summary states 50 ultrapeers) deployed on PlanetLab as Gnutella ultrapeers, each also running a DHT-based search engine built on PIER (a peer-to-peer relational query engine over DHTs). Query results for queries returning fewer than 20 results were published into the DHT at a rate of approximately one file per 2-3 seconds per node; publishing bandwidth overhead was 3.5 KB per file without Join Indexes (an index technique storing the filename redundantly with each posting-list entry) and 4 KB per file with Join Indexes. Leaf queries returning no result within 30 seconds via Gnutella were re-issued to the PIER-based DHT search, which returned a first result in 10-12 seconds (with and without Join Indexes respectively); average first-result latency for these same queries under Gnutella alone was 65 seconds, so the hybrid approach reduced latency by about 25 seconds for that class of query. The hybrid deployment reduced the fraction of queries receiving no results in Gnutella by 18% (a smaller reduction than the 66% lower-bound figure from the earlier union-of-30-ultrapeers measurement), which the authors attribute to the deployment only republishing files that had already appeared as query results, not proactively republishing all rare files, and to the small number of participating ultrapeers limiting coverage. With Join Indexes, each query's routing cost was dominated by shipping the PIER query itself, approximately 850 B; the plain distributed-join algorithm without Join Indexes incurred a 20 KB overhead per query.

### Parameters
- Ultrapeer fan-out observed in the crawl: most ultrapeers supported either 30 or 75 leaf nodes (older LimeWire ultrapeers: 75 leaf nodes, 6 ultrapeer neighbors; newer: 30 leaf nodes, 32 ultrapeer neighbors).
- Republishing threshold for the hybrid scheme: query results with fewer than 20 total results were republished into the DHT.
- Re-query timeout: 30 seconds before a Gnutella leaf query with no result is reissued via the DHT.
- Publishing rate achieved: approximately 1 file published per 2-3 seconds per node.
- Query-instance corpus: 700 distinct queries x 30 ultrapeers x 3 replay times.

### Stated limitations
The authors state the deployment "should be seen as a strawman," because a full hybrid infrastructure would require upgrading all existing Gnutella clients, and their PlanetLab deployment did not do this. The selective-publishing heuristic (republish items seen in small result sets) misses rare items that have never previously been queried and found; the authors state this explicitly and note that proactive publishing of leaf nodes' full rare-item lists would be needed to close that gap, left to future work. The paper states as future work a plan to quantify how increasing the query-broadcast search horizon (larger time-to-live) affects overall system load, rather than measuring it in this paper. The paper states as future work a plan to study the tradeoff between the DHT re-query timeout and query workload, rather than optimizing it here. The connection-lifetime measurement is stated by the authors to be a lower bound on true session lifetime, because a node may change which neighbors it is connected to during a single Gnutella session without the measurement detecting a new session.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The hybrid scheme requires ultrapeers to participate in both a query-broadcast overlay and a DHT overlay simultaneously, and requires each ultrapeer to observe the result-set size of every query it forwards, so it can apply the small-result-set heuristic to decide what to publish. It requires a query-execution path capable of falling back from one search mechanism to the other within a bounded timeout (30 seconds in the deployment measured), which requires the query originator or its ultrapeer to track outstanding queries across that interval. The DHT side requires an inverted-index publishing pipeline (posting lists keyed by keyword) and a distributed-join execution engine (PIER, in this deployment); Join Indexes trade higher publishing bandwidth (4 KB/file versus 3.5 KB/file) for lower per-query bandwidth (850 B versus 20 KB), so which index variant is preferable depends on the query-to-publish ratio of the deployment. The DHT-side stability recommendation (only index ultrapeers, and only after a minimum uptime) requires the overlay to have a way to detect a node's session age before admitting its published data as authoritative.

### Contradicts
The paper describes an apparent conflict with an earlier Gnutella measurement study (Chawathe, Ratnasamy, Breslau, Lanham, Shenker, SIGCOMM 2003) that found most file downloads are for highly replicated items; the authors resolve this as measuring a different quantity, download requests (successful queries only) versus query result-set sizes (including queries that returned few or no results), not as a factual disagreement. None found against other entries in this evidence corpus.

### References worth retrieving
- Chawathe, Ratnasamy, Breslau, Lanham, Shenker, "Making Gnutella-like P2P Systems Scalable," ACM SIGCOMM 2003 — competing measurement of Gnutella workload popularity, download-request-based rather than query-result-based.
- Gummadi, Dunn, Saroiu, Gribble, Levy, Zahorjan, "Measurement, Modeling and Analysis of a Peer-to-Peer File-Sharing Workload," SOSP-19, 2003 — competing measurement showing a flatter-than-Zipfian popularity distribution.
- Huebsch, Hellerstein, Lanham, Loo, Shenker, Stoica, "Querying the Internet with PIER," VLDB 2003 — foundational; the distributed-join query engine this paper's DHT side is built on.
- Li, Loo, Hellerstein, Kaashoek, Karger, Morris, "On the Feasibility of Peer-to-Peer Web Indexing and Search," IPTPS 2003 — foundational; source of the "back-of-the-envelope" posting-list-bandwidth calculation this paper cites to motivate selective publishing.
- Balakrishnan, Kaashoek, Karger, Morris, Stoica, "Looking Up Data in P2P Systems" — foundational, general DHT lookup framing.

### Verbatim extracts
"41% of queries that receive 10 or fewer results, and 18% of queries that receive no results"
"queries that return 10 or fewer results require shipping 7 times fewer posting list entries"
"average connection lifetimes of leaf and ultrapeer nodes are 58 minutes and 93 minutes"
"our deployment should be seen as a strawman"
"the hybrid approach would reduce the latency by about 25 seconds"

## [LUBY-RFC-11] RaptorQ Forward Error Correction Scheme for Object Delivery

**Citation:** Michael Luby, Amin Shokrollahi, Mark Watson, Thomas Stockhammer, Lorenz Minder. "RaptorQ Forward Error Correction Scheme for Object Delivery." IETF RFC 6330, August 2011. DOI 10.17487/RFC6330.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6330
**Source URL:** https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6330
**Domain:** C

### What it does
RaptorQ recovers a block of data from any sufficiently large set of received encoding symbols, so a sender can produce as many redundant symbols as needed on the fly and a receiver can reconstruct the original data after losing an arbitrary subset of transmitted symbols, without a retransmission round trip. The sender divides a source object of length F octets into Z source blocks, each source block into K source symbols of T octets each. An encoder run once per source block builds an intermediate block from the K source symbols using a fixed pseudo-random generator (1024 shared random numbers, specified in the RFC) and produces encoding symbols, each identified by an Encoding Symbol ID (ESI): ESI values 0 through K-1 reproduce the original source symbols unchanged (the code is systematic), and ESI values K and above are repair symbols computed from the intermediate block. The receiver collects encoding symbols carrying (Source Block Number, ESI) pairs from any mix of source and repair symbols and, once it holds a mathematically sufficient set, recovers the intermediate block by solving a linear system over octets (Gaussian-elimination-style rank reduction), then reconstructs any still-missing source symbols. Large source blocks are additionally split into N sub-blocks of sub-symbols to bound working-set memory during encoding and decoding; the sub-symbols of a symbol's position across all N sub-blocks concatenate to form that symbol.

### Measured results
| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| Decoder fails to recover the source block on average at most 1 in 100 times | Receiver holds exactly K' encoding symbols (K' = extended source symbol count), ESIs chosen independently and uniformly at random from the possible range, for every K' value in the RFC's systematic-index table |
| Decoder fails on average at most 1 in 10,000 times | Receiver holds K'+1 encoding symbols, same random-ESI condition, same K' range |
| Decoder fails on average at most 1 in 1,000,000 times | Receiver holds K'+2 encoding symbols, same random-ESI condition, same K' range |

These three figures are mandatory conformance requirements the RFC places on any compliant decoder (Section 5.8), not a measurement of one specific implementation; the RFC states its own reference decoder (Section 5.4) meets them.

### Parameters
- K'_max (maximum source symbols per source block): fixed at 56403 (Section 5.1.2); source blocks otherwise range from 1 to 56403 source symbols.
- T (symbol size): 16-bit unsigned integer, must be less than 2^16 octets, and must be a multiple of the symbol alignment parameter Al.
- Z (number of source blocks): 8-bit unsigned integer, so at most 256 per object.
- F (transfer length of the object): 40-bit unsigned integer, at most 946,270,874,880 octets; the RFC states this ceiling follows arithmetically from the T, K'_max, and Z limits above (symbol-size ceiling times per-block symbol ceiling times block-count ceiling).
- N (number of sub-blocks per source block): 16-bit unsigned integer, chosen so sub-symbol size stays at or above a target lower bound SS while remaining a multiple of Al.
- Encoding and decoding parameters (K, K', T, Z, N, Al) must be identical between encoder and receiver; construction rules for deriving them from F and T are given in Section 4.4.1.2, not left to implementation choice.

### Stated limitations
The RFC states RaptorQ provides no source authentication or corrupted-packet detection on its own: a single corrupted repair-data packet accepted as legitimate can cause the decoder to reconstruct an object that is entirely corrupted and unusable, and the RFC recommends (not requires) an appended SHA-256 hash checked post-decode, a digital signature over that hash, and a packet-authentication protocol (TESLA, RFC 4082) to detect and discard corrupted packets on arrival. The RFC also flags that FEC parameters obtained out-of-band in a session description are a separate attack surface: a forged or corrupted session description causes receivers to apply the wrong decoding parameters, and the RFC recommends source-authenticated session descriptions as the mitigation.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The transport must deliver each encoding symbol tagged with its Source Block Number and Encoding Symbol ID, since decoding depends on knowing which ESI each received symbol carries. Encoder and decoder must share the object-level Common FEC Object Transmission Information (F, T) and the scheme-specific parameters (Z, N, Al) before decoding starts; these are derived once from F and T by the fixed construction rules in Section 4.4.1.2 and are not negotiated per packet. The scheme assumes symbols may arrive out of order, be duplicated, or be lost, but places no requirement on delivering symbols in ESI order. It supplies no confidentiality, integrity, or authenticity: a system built on RaptorQ must supply corruption detection (for example a hash check) and source authentication itself if a single forged repair symbol must not be able to corrupt the whole decoded object.

### Contradicts
None found.

### References worth retrieving
- Shokrollahi, Luby. "Raptor Codes." Foundations and Trends in Communications and Information Theory, Vol. 6, No. 3-4, 2011 — foundational (fuller theory treatment of the code family RaptorQ extends).
- Luby, Shokrollahi, Watson, Stockhammer. "Raptor Forward Error Correction Scheme for Object Delivery." RFC 5053, October 2007 — foundational (RaptorQ's direct predecessor, RFC 6330 states RaptorQ supports larger source blocks and better coding efficiency than this).
- Luby. "LT codes." Annual IEEE Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science, pp. 271-280, November 2002 — foundational (the original rateless/fountain code construction RaptorQ descends from).
- Luby, Vicisano, Gemmell, Rizzo, Handley, Crowcroft. "The Use of Forward Error Correction (FEC) in Reliable Multicast." RFC 3453, December 2002 — foundational (context for why FEC is used for object delivery rather than retransmission).

### Verbatim extracts
"on average the decoder will fail to recover the entire source block at most 1 out of 100 times"
"K'_max denotes the maximum number of source symbols that can be in a single source block"
"the RaptorQ code supports source blocks with between 1 and 56403 source symbols"
"The use of even one corrupted packet... may result in the decoding of an object that is completely corrupted and unusable"

## [LUO-ARXIV-25] Unveiling Ethereum's P2P Network: The Role of Chain and Client Diversity

**Citation:** Jiahao Luo. "Unveiling Ethereum's P2P Network: The Role of Chain and Client Diversity." arXiv preprint, 2025. DOI 10.48550/ARXIV.2501.16236.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.16236
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.16236
**Domain:** J

### What it does
The paper measures how many peers discoverable in Ethereum's peer-to-peer overlay (devp2p, the protocol stack combining a node-discovery layer, the RLPx encrypted-transport layer, and application sub-protocols) are actually reachable and configuration-compatible with a mainnet full node, and separates that measurement from the underlying causes: node-discovery protocol non-compliance and multi-chain (fork and sidechain) fragmentation of the shared discovery table. The authors deploy five instrumented Geth (Go Ethereum, the reference full-node client) instances that log every discovery-protocol message (Ping, Pong, FindNode, Neighbors) and RLPx handshake (Hello, Status) they send or receive, store the decoded messages in a database, and classify every discovered peer into one of three categories: no sub-protocol exchange attempted, sub-protocol exchange attempted but incompatible, or fully compatible. The tool additionally tracks each peer's self-reported client software identifier and version string from the RLPx Hello message, which lets the authors attribute specific protocol deviations (message counts, disconnect reasons, IP-address bugs) to specific client implementations and versions rather than to the network as a whole.

### Measured results
| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| 743,739 unique peers discovered, classified as 674,945 (90.8%) Class A (no sub-protocol exchange), 17,707 (2.4%) Class B (exchanged, incompatible), 51,087 (6.9%) Class C (fully compatible) | 5 instrumented Geth v1.14.0 full-node instances, Ubuntu 22.04, 1 Gb/s bandwidth, 256 GB RAM, 64 cores each; measurement window approximately May 2024 based on the reported daily message-rate chart |
| Over 8 billion messages collected; FindNode and its prerequisite Ping constitute ~91% of the total (3,735M Ping, 39M Pong, 3,996M FindNode, 172M Neighbors, 78M discovery-layer Disc, 366M RLPx Hello, 127M eth Status, all in millions) | Same deployment, full measurement period |
| ~2.64 million connection attempts/hour and ~16.9 million node-discovery attempts/hour | Same deployment; connection attempts capped at 10 per peer per minute to avoid overwhelming the network |
| 7,934 of 743,739 peers (1.07%) reported a private or fallback IP address in the discovery Ping message; 98.65% of those set it to 127.0.0.1, 0.44% to 0.0.0.0; only 156 of the 7,934 completed an RLPx sub-protocol exchange, predominantly running Besu (28.21%), Geth (23.72%), or OpenEthereum (18.59%) among that small reachable subset | Same deployment; attributed to a UPnP-NAT fallback bug, acknowledged and fixed by Besu (PRs #6225, #6439) and Reth developers during the study |
| 78.4 million Disconnect messages captured; reasons: Useless peer 41.58%, TCP sub-system error 31.39%, Disconnect requested 22.93%, Too many peers 2.84%, Breach of protocol 1.03%, all others under 0.3% each | Same deployment, "most recent measurement phase" |
| Compared to Kim et al. (2018): Useless-peer disconnects rose from under 1% to 41.58%, and Too-many-peers disconnects fell from 90% to 2.84% | Same dataset compared against the cited 2018 prior measurement (not independently re-verified by this author) |
| 92.12% of Breach-of-protocol disconnects were issued by Nethermind clients; the top 2 Nethermind builds (v1.25.4+20b10b35 and v1.26.0+0068729c) accounted for 41.7% and 26.8% of all breach disconnects respectively | Same dataset, Nethermind client-version breakdown of breach disconnects, 1,861 Nethermind peers examined |
| Of over 4 billion FindNode requests sent (>99.99% outbound), ~5% received a Neighbors response; 172.2 million Neighbors messages captured from 74,041 unique peers (average 2,285 replies/peer); 73.24% of individual Neighbors responses contained the specification-compliant 16 nodes, 26.01% contained fewer, and ~26% of requests timed out (Geth's default 1.5-second timeout when fewer than 16 nodes are received) | Same deployment |
| Node-count-per-response by client: Geth sends 12 then 16 nodes across two messages (spec-compliant, two-message split); Besu sends 13 nodes 71.89% of the time; Nethermind sends 12 nodes 16.64% of the time; Bor (Polygon's Geth fork) sends only 6, 9, or 10 nodes 87-90% of the time | Same deployment, per-client Neighbors-length distribution table across Geth, Erigon, Besu, Nethermind, bor, and reth |
| Sub-protocol prevalence: eth-68 on 78.05% of peers, snap-1 on 76.73%, eth-66 on 63.29%, eth-67 on 58.35%, older/other sub-protocols under 8% each | Same 74,041+ peer sample |
| Only 24.5% of all discovered peers run the correct current Ethereum mainnet configuration (network ID 1, specific genesis hash, specific fork ID); this is down from a previously reported 54.5% (Kim et al., not independently re-measured here); consequently only 19% of eth-68-supporting peers hold the proper mainnet configuration; 12.6% of mainnet-network-ID peers run pre-Cancun-upgrade (before 13 March 2024) fork identifiers | Same dataset, chain-parameter distribution measurement |
| Dial-attempt scaling: at 1,000,000 attempts, 53,685 unique peers found (29.51% unreachable, 57.42% incompatible, 13.07% fully compatible); at 500,000,000 attempts, 527,957 unique peers found (88.96% unreachable, 8.57% incompatible, 2.47% fully compatible); average of 947 connection attempts needed per successfully-reached live peer | Same deployment, 5-point dial-attempt sweep from 1 million to 500 million attempts |

### Parameters
- Node-discovery bucket size increased from the devp2p-specified 16 entries to 1,048,576 to widen the local routing table.
- Neighbors-message size capped at the specification's 16-node maximum to avoid amplification.
- Concurrent node-discovery tasks increased from Geth's default of 3 to 1,000, reducing time-to-connect-to-5,000-nodes from ~4 days to ~10 hours in the authors' own configuration.
- Dial-scheduler source count increased from 1 to 50, giving ~100 dials/second/node.
- Connection attempts throttled to a maximum of 10 per peer per minute network-wide.
- DHT (distributed hash table) refresh interval reduced from the default 5 minutes to 10 seconds.
- Geth's own default FindNode/Neighbors timeout: 1.5 seconds when fewer than 16 nodes are received (a Geth-internal parameter the paper measures the consequences of, not one the authors set).
- Measurement infrastructure: 5 Geth v1.14.0 instances, Ubuntu 22.04, 1 Gb/s bandwidth, 256 GB RAM, 64 cores per instance; MongoDB storage capped at 64 GB memory use; bandwidth usage self-limited to 1 Gbps and outbound transaction-request replies limited to half of received requests, stated as ethical/network-impact bounds rather than tuned experimental variables.

### Stated limitations
The paper does not report an aggregate, network-wide client-implementation market-share figure (e.g., "Geth holds X% of all Ethereum nodes"); every client-attribution figure in this paper is conditional on a specific narrow subpopulation — the 156 reachable peers with the private-IP bug, the 1,861 Nethermind peers examined for breach disconnects, or the per-client Neighbors-response-length table — and none of these subpopulations is presented as representative of the full peer population's client composition. Readers requiring an overall client-share concentration figure for Ethereum are not served by this paper; that number is not present in the retrieved text. The authors state "the full extent of these issues on overall network stability remains unclear" regarding the private-IP and peer-scoring bugs they identify. The paper's own comparison figures against Kim et al. (2018) are stated as taken from that prior study, not independently re-derived by this paper's own methodology on the earlier dataset, so the two measurements are not a controlled before/after comparison under identical instrumentation. The paper does not evaluate mobile or light-client peers, nor does it measure bandwidth or latency costs of the diversity-driven inefficiencies it identifies (it measures connection-success rates and disconnect/timeout counts, not throughput or user-facing latency).

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A shared node-discovery table (a single DHT serving Ethereum mainnet, Ethereum testnets, and unrelated EVM-compatible chains such as Polygon and BNB Smart Chain simultaneously, as measured here) requires an expensive per-candidate handshake (TCP connection, encryption, protocol Hello/Status exchange) before a peer's chain membership can be determined, so any design reusing a shared discovery layer across multiple independent chains or forks inherits a connection-success rate that falls as the number of incompatible chains sharing that layer grows — measured here at 2.47% fully compatible after 500 million dial attempts, down from 13.07% at 1 million attempts. A discovery protocol whose per-message size is capped by the underlying transport's datagram limit (UDP's 1,280-byte practical limit here, constraining Neighbors responses to 12-16 entries depending on IPv4 versus IPv6 addressing) requires every participating client implementation to agree on the exact node count per response, because this paper measures that implementations disagreeing on that count each other's messages does not error cleanly but instead produces timeouts (Geth waiting its full 1.5-second timeout for the fewer-than-16-node responses that Besu, Nethermind, and Bor send). A liveness/heartbeat message field used to populate address or scoring data (the discv4 Ping message's fromIP field feeding Geth's DHT bucket-ordering and Besu/Nethermind's peer-scoring) requires validation against the transport-layer source address, because this paper measures multiple client implementations (Geth via its UPnP-NAT fallback, CoreGeth, and its ETCMC fork) propagating unverified private/loopback addresses from that field into peer records.

### Contradicts
The paper's title and framing invite the expectation of an overall Ethereum client-market-share concentration figure, but no such aggregate figure appears in the retrieved text — a claim of "Ethereum node client concentration measured by Luo 2025" citing a specific percentage split across Geth/Nethermind/Besu/Erigon for the whole network would not be supported by this paper's own reported tables and must not be carried forward from this entry. No other paper in this batch measures Ethereum P2P network structure, so no cross-paper numeric contradiction exists in this batch.

## [MALKHI-PODC-02] Viceroy: A Scalable and Dynamic Emulation of the Butterfly

**Citation:** Dahlia Malkhi, Moni Naor, David Ratajczak. "Viceroy: A Scalable and Dynamic Emulation of the Butterfly." ACM PODC, 2002. DOI 10.1145/571825.571857.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.wisdom.weizmann.ac.il/~naor/PAPERS/viceroy.pdf
**Source URL:** https://www.wisdom.weizmann.ac.il/~naor/PAPERS/viceroy.pdf
**Domain:** A

### What it does
Viceroy locates data in a distributed hash table (DHT) while every server keeps a constant number of outbound links, so a server join or departure changes a constant number of links in expectation regardless of how many servers are in the network. It achieves this by having each server emulate one node of a butterfly network — a fixed interconnection pattern in which nodes are arranged in levels and each non-leaf node at level L connects down to two nodes at level L+1 and up to one node at level L-1.

Each server picks two values at join time: an identifier drawn independently and uniformly from the real interval [0,1), fixed for the server's lifetime, and a level, a positive integer chosen by a local estimation procedure (below). Three link sets connect servers: a general ring linking each server to its ring successor and predecessor by identifier order; a level ring linking servers that share the same level; and butterfly links — each server's "left down" link goes to the first level-L+1 server clockwise from its own identifier, its "right down" link goes to the first level-L+1 server clockwise from identifier + 1/2^L, and its "up" link goes to the first level-L-1 server clockwise from its own identifier.

A server estimates the network size n locally, without any global count, by taking the reciprocal of the ring distance to its immediate successor (1/d(s, succ(s))) as an estimate n0, then draws its level uniformly from [1, floor(log n0)]. This keeps level assignment self-adjusting to local density without communicating n to any server.

Lookup for target identifier x, starting at server y, runs in three phases: follow up-links to a level-1 root server; descend butterfly links, at each level-L server moving to the right-down link if the target is at ring distance >= 1/2^L and to the left-down link otherwise, until reaching a server with no further down link or one that overshoots the target; then traverse the general ring (clockwise or counter-clockwise) to the closest server to x. An improved third phase ("hopping," Section 7) interleaves level-ring links with ring links instead of stepping server-by-server, so the worst-case path length becomes logarithmic with high probability rather than only in expectation.

A background "bucket" mechanism (sketched, not fully specified) partitions the ring into contiguous groups of Theta(log n) servers each and reassigns levels within a bucket so every level from 1 to log n has at least one and at most a constant number of representatives per bucket, which bounds the largest number of incoming links any single server can receive.

### Measured results
None. The paper is a theoretical construction with worst-case and expected-case bounds proved as theorems; it contains no implementation, simulation, or empirical measurement. Every quantitative claim below is an asymptotic bound with a proof, not a measured figure, and is reported here as a stated bound, not a measurement, per Rule 1.

Stated asymptotic properties, each proved for a Viceroy network holding n servers, under the paper's own assumptions (see Requirements below):
- Out-degree of every server: 7 total (5 used in the simple, non-hopping lookup variant) (Theorem 6.6).
- Expected in-degree: O(1); largest in-degree: O(log n) with high probability, over the randomness of identifier and level choice (Theorem 6.6).
- Lookup path length (dilation): O(log n) in the worst case, with high probability, using the improved ("hopping") third-phase routing of Section 7 (Theorem 7.3). The simple lookup variant (Section 6) achieves O(log n) dilation only in expectation, not with high probability, because the ring-traversal third phase can pass through as many as O(log^2 n) servers in the worst case.
- Load per server (fraction of all-pairs lookups passing through a given server): expected O(log n / n); maximum over all servers, O(log^2 n / n) with high probability (Theorem 6.4).
- Join or leave cost: a constant number of link changes in expectation, and O(log n) link changes with high probability, per join or leave event.
- Bucket-mechanism overhead: a server leaving causes at most O(1) other servers to change level; a bucket reshuffle (triggered once every (c-1) log n steps for a paper-unspecified constant c) touches O(log n) servers, giving amortized O(1) per join/leave.

Table 1 (reproduced from the paper, comparing dilation / congestion / linkage cost against the schemes it cites): Chord — log n / (log n)/n / log n. Tapestry — log n / (log n)/n / log n. Content Addressable Network (CAN) with d dimensions — d*n^(1/d) / d*n^(1/d-1) / d. Kleinberg-style Small Worlds — log^2 n / (log^2 n)/n / O(1). Viceroy is the paper's proposed alternative to this table, trading Small Worlds' O(1) linkage cost for O(log n) dilation and O(log n) linkage cost at constant, not logarithmic, out-degree.

### Parameters
- Server identifier: drawn uniformly and independently from the continuous interval [0,1); in practice, a fixed number of random bits sufficient to make identifier collisions implausible (exact bit count not stated as a number, left to implementation).
- Level: integer in [1, floor(log n0)], n0 the server's local size estimate; redrawn only when floor(log n0) changes, per a footnote optimization, not on every join/leave elsewhere in the network.
- Bucket size: Theta(log n) servers; a bucket merges with a neighbor when its size drops below log n and splits when its size exceeds c*log n, for an unspecified constant c bounding the diversity property (at most c servers per level per bucket).
- Out-degree: fixed at 7 (2 down, 1 up, 2 ring — general successor/predecessor, 2 level-ring — next/prev on level); only 5 of the 7 links are used by the simple (non-hopping) lookup.

### Stated limitations
The paper explicitly excludes concurrent joins and leaves and server failures from its model: it assumes multiple join and leave operations do not overlap and that servers never fail, and refers the reader to a separate paper (Lynch, Malkhi, Ratajczak, IPTPS 2002) for concurrency and failure handling. It does not address load hotspots — repeatedly requested identifiers overloading the servers along the corresponding lookup paths — though it states in a footnote that standard replica-placement mechanisms could be adapted to the DHT framework without demonstrating this. It assumes joins and leaves are independent of server identifiers, so the active server set stays randomly distributed on the ring; a correlated join/leave pattern is outside the analysis. It does not specify how a client or a joining server obtains the address of any already-active server (bootstrap discovery is out of scope). The bucket mechanism that bounds maximum in-degree is only sketched, not fully specified or analyzed to the same rigor as the base construction, by the authors' own statement.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
- Requires that any server able to compute another server's identifier can open a connection to it; the paper treats connection establishment as a primitive and does not specify addressing, transport, or NAT traversal.
- Requires non-overlapping join/leave events (a serialization or locking discipline elsewhere in the system) for the join/leave algorithms and their O(1)-expected-link-change bound to apply as proved; concurrent joins/leaves are explicitly out of scope and left to a different mechanism.
- Requires a failure-free server population for the bounds as proved; crash tolerance is not part of this construction.
- Requires the level-selection procedure's local density estimate (1/d(s, succ(s))) to be accurate, which in turn requires identifiers to remain uniformly distributed on the ring — violated if join/leave is correlated with identifier choice (e.g., an adversary choosing identifiers to cluster in one region).
- Requires a separate bootstrap mechanism to supply a joining server or client with the address of one already-active server.
- Requires a separate mechanism (unspecified) to handle hotspots if uneven query popularity across identifiers is expected, since the load bound (Theorem 6.4) is an average over a uniform query distribution.

### Contradicts
None found. No other paper in this corpus's current batch measures Viceroy independently.

- Foundational: B. Y. Zhao, J. D. Kubiatowicz, A. D. Joseph, "Tapestry: An infrastructure for fault-tolerant wide-area location and routing," UC Berkeley TR UCB/CSD-01-1141, 2001.
- Competing: S. Ratnasamy, P. Francis, M. Handley, R. Karp, S. Shenker, "A scalable content-addressable network," SIGCOMM 2001 — the constant-degree CAN alternative directly compared in Table 1.

- Foundational: G. Pandurangan, P. Raghavan, E. Upfal, "Building low-diameter p2p networks," FOCS 2001.
- Foundational: W. Pugh, "Skip Lists: A probabilistic alternative to balanced trees," Communications of the ACM 33(6), 1990.

## [MALKOV-TPAMI-20] Efficient and robust approximate nearest neighbor search using Hierarchical Navigable Small World graphs
**Citation:** Yu. A. Malkov, D. A. Yashunin. "Efficient and Robust Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search Using Hierarchical Navigable Small World Graphs." IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence 42(4), 2020 (preprint arXiv:1603.09320, 2016). DOI 10.1109/TPAMI.2018.2889473.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.09320
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.09320
**Domain:** B

### What it does
Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW) finds the approximate K nearest neighbors of a query vector in a stored set of vectors, at a query cost that scales logarithmically with the number of stored elements rather than linearly, by searching a multi-layer proximity graph greedily from the top layer down. Each stored element is assigned an integer maximum layer at insertion, drawn from an exponentially decaying probability distribution controlled by a normalization parameter mL; the assignment needs no separate shuffling step, because the randomness comes from the layer draw itself. Within each layer, elements are connected into a proximity graph approximating a Delaunay graph (the graph in which two points are connected if their Voronoi cells touch), with fewer, longer-range connections at the upper layers and denser, shorter-range connections at the bottom layer. A search starts at a fixed entry point on the top layer and greedily moves to whichever connected neighbor is closest to the query (the "zoom-in" phase) until it reaches a local minimum in that layer; the local minimum is then used as the entry point into the next lower layer, and the process repeats until a search of the bottom layer (layer zero) returns the final result set. Insertion runs the same greedy-descent search on each layer down to the newly assigned element's own maximum layer, then applies a neighbor-selection heuristic to pick which of the search's candidate closest elements become the new element's graph connections; the heuristic examines candidates from nearest to farthest and connects to a candidate only if that candidate is closer to the element being inserted than to any already-connected candidate, which keeps well-separated clusters connected to each other (Section 3, Fig. 2) rather than only connecting to the single nearest cluster. Each element's connection count per layer is capped (parameter Mmax, with a separate cap Mmax0 for the bottom layer); when a capped element gains a new connection, its existing connections are re-pruned by the same heuristic.

### Measured results
Search-quality claims are stated as approximate K-nearest-neighbor recall against a controllable search-width parameter ef; the paper defines no single fixed "accuracy" figure independent of ef and dataset. Complexity: search and insertion both scale as O(log(N)) in expectation for datasets where the average node degree in the true Delaunay graph is bounded by a constant independent of dataset size N, a condition the paper states holds for random Euclidean data but which the authors say is not established for other spaces; insertion (construction) time for the whole index therefore scales as O(N log N). Comparison against the flat (non-hierarchical) NSW baseline (nmslib 1.1 "sw-graph" implementation): on a d=8 random hypercube dataset with 10-NN search at fixed recall 0.95, HNSW's query-time scaling with dataset size was not worse than logarithmic and outperformed NSW at every dataset size tested, on a Core i5 2400 CPU, single thread. On general (non-Euclidean, non-metric) datasets from a prior comparison study, repeated with the same nmslib test scripts: on the "wiki-8" dataset (2M elements, 8-dimensional Jensen-Shannon-divergence topic histograms, 10-NN search, distance-computation count rather than CPU time used to avoid confounding by implementation), HNSW's improvement over flat NSW reached almost three orders of magnitude, the largest margin of any dataset tested, on a dataset the authors state was NSW's weakest case. Comparison against open-source Euclidean K-approximate-nearest-neighbor (K-ANNS) algorithms (FLANN 1.8.4, Annoy, VP-tree, FALCONN 1.2) using the ann-benchmark testbed, single thread, on a 4-socket Xeon E5-4650 v2 server with 128 GB RAM, GCC 5.3 with -Ofast: HNSW is reported to outperform all rivals "by a large margin" on SIFT (1M points, d=128, brute-force query time 94 ms), GloVe (1.2M points, d=100, cosine similarity, BF 95 ms), CoPhIR (2M points, d=272, BF 370 ms), and DEEP (1M points, d=96, BF 60 ms); on 30M random d=4 points (BF 590 ms) HNSW is reported slightly faster than Annoy at high recall and clearly ahead of the remaining baselines; no single numeric recall-versus-latency figure is stated in the extracted text outside the plotted curves (Fig. 13). Construction-time and thread scaling: on a 10M-point SIFT dataset (d=128, M=16, efConstruction=100), build time was measured on two CPUs (a 4-socket Xeon E5-4650 v2 with 40 cores total, and a 6-core/12-thread Core i7-6850K) across 0-40 threads (Fig. 9), showing construction time falling with added threads with no measurable loss of index quality (specific minute values are read from a plot, not a table, and are not extracted here). At efConstruction=100 on the 4-socket Xeon server, a reasonable-quality 10M-SIFT index was built in 3 minutes. Comparison against Facebook's Faiss product-quantization (PQ) library on a 200M-point subset of the 1B SIFT dataset, on the same 4-socket Xeon E5-4650 v2 / 128 GB RAM server (Table 3): HNSW with M=16, efConstruction=500 built in 5.6 hours and used 64 GB peak runtime memory; HNSW with M=16, efConstruction=40 built in 42 minutes and used the same 64 GB; Faiss configuration 1 (OPQ64, IMI2x14, PQ64) built in 12 hours using 30 GB; Faiss configuration 2 (OPQ32, IMI2x14, PQ32) built in 11 hours using 23.5 GB. The paper states HNSW used significantly more RAM than Faiss but achieved higher accuracy, higher query speed, and faster index construction on this comparison (Fig. 15); the query-time-versus-dataset-size scaling for HNSW on this 200M-point run deviated from pure logarithmic scaling, which the authors attribute to the dataset's relatively high dimensionality.

### Parameters
- M (number of established connections per element per layer, the algorithm's one construction parameter left for the user to tune): reasonable range 5 to 48; smaller M favors lower recall targets and lower-dimensional data, larger M favors high recall and high-dimensional data; M is proportional to the index's memory consumption.
- Mmax0 (maximum connections per element at the bottom, zero, layer): setting it equal to M produces a strong performance penalty at high recall; the paper's simulations find 2*M a good default, with values above that degrading performance and increasing memory use without benefit.
- mL (normalization factor for the exponentially decaying layer-assignment distribution): the paper's suggested default is 1/ln(M) ("Autoselect" in the figures), determined empirically rather than derived from a formula given in the extracted text.
- efConstruction (candidate-list size used during index construction, controlling construction-time recall): the paper states it must be large enough to reach K-ANNS recall close to 1 during construction (0.95 is stated as sufficient for most use cases); larger values give little additional performance benefit but significantly increase construction time; efConstruction=100 was used for the 10M-SIFT construction-time measurement, and efConstruction=500 vs 40 for the two 200M-SIFT/Faiss comparison configurations.
- ef (candidate-list size used at query time, controlling the search-time recall/latency tradeoff): tuned per query; no single default value is stated, since it is the mechanism by which the query-time recall/latency point is chosen.
- extendCandidates (heuristic option, default false; stated as useful only for extremely clustered data) and keepPrunedConnections (heuristic option to keep a fixed number of connections per element), both parameters of the neighbor-selection heuristic (Algorithm 4).

### Stated limitations
The authors state that the search always starts from the top layer's single fixed entry point, and that this structure cannot be distributed by the same techniques used for the flat NSW graph, because congestion concentrates at the small number of high-layer elements; they describe partitioning data across cluster nodes as a workaround, but state that under partitioning the total parallel throughput of the system does not scale well with the number of nodes. The authors state that the theoretical O(log N) complexity derivation assumes an exact Delaunay graph with node degree bounded by a constant independent of dataset size, a condition they can confirm empirically only for low-dimensional data (their empirical check uses d=4); for high-dimensional data (e.g., d=128) they state that the average Delaunay-graph degree scales exponentially with dimensionality, making the same empirical check infeasible at reachable dataset sizes, and that further analytical work is needed to know whether the resilience result generalizes to higher dimensions. The paper states that M is the one construction parameter still requiring user selection with no auto-tuning method offered, and lists as future work inferring M automatically, testing at full 1-billion-point scale, and adding support for element update and removal, which the version described here does not support.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The search algorithm requires a fixed, designated entry point for the top layer of the graph; any system serving queries with HNSW must know or discover this entry point before it can start a search, and the entry point is updated whenever an inserted element's randomly drawn layer exceeds the current top layer. Distributing this index across separate machines (relevant for a decentralized deployment across untrusted peers, open problem 2 in the governing brief) is a problem the authors state their approach does not solve, because search congestion at the top layer defeats the flat-NSW technique for distribution, and the stated workaround (partitioning data across nodes) is stated not to scale its aggregate query throughput with added nodes. The paper's evaluated construction and query pipeline assumes a stable stored vector set for the duration of a query burst; it offers construction-time parallelism across threads with no measured index-quality loss, but does not evaluate concurrent insertion and deletion, which the authors state is unsupported by the version tested.

### Contradicts
None found against other entries in this corpus.

### References worth retrieving
- Malkov, Ponomarenko, Logvinov, Krylov, "Approximate nearest neighbor algorithm based on navigable small world graphs," (reference [26]) — foundational; the flat NSW algorithm HNSW is built on top of and is compared against throughout this paper's evaluation.
- Naidan, Boytsov, Nyberg, "Permutation search methods are efficient, yet faster search is possible," VLDB Proceedings 8(12), 2015 — competing; source of the general-metric-space test suite (Section 5.3) on which flat NSW performed poorly and against which HNSW is compared.
- Harwood, Drummond, "FANNG: fast approximate nearest neighbour graphs," CVPR 2016 — competing/parallel; the paper notes FANNG uses a similar neighbor-selection heuristic, published shortly after this paper's first preprint.
- Muja, Lowe, "Scalable nearest neighbor algorithms for high dimensional data," (FLANN) — competing baseline used directly in the Euclidean-space comparison (Section 5.2).
- Andoni, Razenshteyn, "Optimal Data-Dependent Hashing for Approximate Near Neighbors," STOC 2015 (FALCONN) — competing baseline, locality-sensitive hashing for cosine similarity, used directly in the comparison.
- Jegou, Douze, Schmid, "Product quantization for nearest neighbor search," and Babenko, Lempitsky, "Efficient indexing of billion-scale datasets of deep descriptors" — foundational to the Faiss product-quantization comparison baseline (Section 5.4), the state-of-the-art class for billion-scale settings the paper positions itself against.
- Boytsov, Naidan, "Engineering Efficient and Effective Non-metric Space Library," Similarity Search and Applications, 2013 — foundational; the nmslib library HNSW is implemented inside and evaluated through.
