## [MALVAI-NDSS-23] Parakeet: Practical Key Transparency for End-to-End Encrypted Messaging

**Citation:** Harjasleen Malvai, Lefteris Kokoris-Kogias, Alberto Sonnino, Esha Ghosh, Ercan Öztürk, Kevin Lewi, Sean Lawlor. "Parakeet: Practical Key Transparency for End-to-End Encrypted Messaging." NDSS, 2023.
**Retrieved:** full text via candidate URL `https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/081.pdf`
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/081.pdf
**Domain:** E

### What it does
Parakeet lets a message provider prove it serves each user the one true public key it committed to, so a client can detect a provider that hands different keys to different people for the same username (server equivocation), without the client trusting the provider or a blockchain. The system separates two roles. A verifiable key directory (VKD) run by the identity provider (IdP) stores every username-to-public-key mapping and commits to it with a compact cryptographic digest each round (epoch); a client who queries it receives the current key plus a proof it belongs to the committed digest. Parakeet's VKD instantiates the ordered zero-knowledge set (oZKS) primitive over a compressed Merkle Patricia Trie, storing only the current state of each tree node rather than a new node copy at every epoch, which the paper states is what makes the storage cost bounded rather than growing with the number of epochs. Separately, a small committee of witness servers cross-checks the IdP's per-epoch digest through a consistency protocol: the IdP broadcasts a signed notification of the new digest, each witness verifies an append-only audit proof against the previous digest and signs a vote, and once a quorum of votes is collected they aggregate into a certificate that any client can check without contacting every witness. The consistency protocol runs without a leader and without an external blockchain, which the paper states is why its throughput does not degrade when witnesses crash. To bound storage growth from an always-appending tree, Parakeet adds a two-phase compaction mechanism: at a tombstone epoch, entries eligible for eventual deletion are marked (not removed); only after a further compaction epoch are tombstoned entries actually deleted; auditors check that only sufficiently old entries are tombstoned and only tombstoned entries are deleted, and a client that wants deletion-soundness must query its own key history at least once between a tombstone epoch and the following compaction epoch.

### Measured results
| Metric | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Verify notification (consistency protocol) | 68.70 ms mean, 1.50 ms std | Single core, witness machine (AWS t3.medium, 2 vCPU/1 physical core, 4 GB RAM, 2.5 GHz Intel Xeon Platinum 8259CL); committee of 4 witnesses; notification batch of 1,024 updates, 64 bytes each; mean/std over 10 runs |
| Create vote | 0.02 ms mean, 0.00 ms std | Same setup as above |
| Verify certificate | 0.16 ms mean, 0.01 ms std | Same setup as above; certificate = 3 votes combined (2f+1 with f=1 for a 4-witness committee) |
| Create notification (IdP side) | 47.12 ms mean, 9.30 ms std | AWS t3.2xlarge (8 vCPU, 32 GB RAM), same 4-witness/1,024-batch/64-byte setup, 10-run mean/std; measured by subtracting server-side publish cost from total publish+notify cost |
| Verify vote | 0.07 ms mean, 0.00 ms std | Same IdP-side setup |
| Aggregate certificate | 0.00 ms mean (below measurable resolution), 0.00 ms std | Same IdP-side setup |
| VKD storage | ≈4.5 GB at 5 million users, linear growth | 100,000-user insertion batches, MySQL-backed storage, local Docker container |
| Projected VKD storage at 1 billion users | ≈850 GB | Extrapolated linearly from the 4.5 GB / 5-million-user measurement, not independently measured at that scale |
| Publish time, 100k-user batch on existing 500k-user VKD | ≈19 minutes total, 12 minutes of which is MySQL writes | Parakeet's VKD, MySQL storage layer with caching |
| SEEMless comparison: insert 100k users into 300k-user set | ≈66 minutes total; 51 minutes writing to persistent storage, 7 minutes reading, 47 persistent-storage accesses | Authors' own reimplementation of SEEMless's append-only zero-knowledge set (aZKS), same caching optimizations as their Parakeet oZKS implementation, same MySQL/Docker setup |
| End-to-end maximum throughput | ≈800 updates/s at latency below 3.5 s | WAN testbed on AWS t3.medium across 5 regions (N. Virginia, N. California, Sydney, Stockholm, Tokyo); baseline: 10 honest witnesses, batch size 1,024, update size 64 bytes; each point averaged over 3 independent runs, 5-minute client run |
| Throughput vs. witness count | ≈flat across 10, 20, 50 witnesses at fixed batch size 1,024 | Same WAN testbed; authors attribute the flat curve to the IdP, not witness count, being the bottleneck |
| Throughput vs. batch size | 100 updates/s at batch 2^5; 350 updates/s at batch 2^7; ≈800 updates/s at batch 2^10 and above | Same WAN testbed, 10 witnesses, 64-byte updates; batch 2^5 keeps latency under 800 ms |
| Throughput under crash-faults | Unaffected by 1 or 3 crash-faults out of 10 witnesses | Same WAN testbed; 3 is stated as the maximum crash-faults tolerable in this configuration; no Byzantine-fault (only crash-fault) benchmark is reported |
| First-year storage projection, SEEMless-style construction | ≈27 TB in year one; ≈21.4 TB/year steady-state per the multi-year chart | Derived (not directly measured) from an assumed 2 billion existing WhatsApp keys, ≈10 million daily key updates, one epoch per day, 64-byte node states; authors' own arithmetic, labeled as a worst-case estimate |
| First-year storage, Parakeet oZKS construction | ≈2.2 TB (1.1 TB base, doubled for concurrent-proof-generation node retention) | Same assumed WhatsApp-scale workload and node-state size; stated as roughly an order of magnitude smaller than the SEEMless-style projection |
| Five-year storage projection | SEEMless-style: growing to ≈110.9 TB; Parakeet: ≈3.4 TB | Same assumed workload, chart data (Figure 13) |
| Comparable throughput requirement for WhatsApp-scale deployment | ≈120 updates/s, derived from ≈2 billion monthly active users, ≈0.66 billion average downloads over five years, ≈3 devices/browsers per user | Authors' own derivation, not a measurement of an actual WhatsApp deployment; Parakeet's measured 800 updates/s is stated as exceeding this by "over 6x" |

### Parameters
- Byzantine fault model: 3f+1 total witnesses tolerate up to f Byzantine (arbitrary) failures; a quorum is any 2f+1 witnesses; network is assumed fully asynchronous (messages may be arbitrarily delayed and reordered but are eventually delivered).
- Benchmark baseline configuration: 10 honest witnesses, batch size 1,024 updates, update size 64 bytes (32-byte key + 32-byte value), committee size 4 for the microbenchmarks specifically.
- Tested batch-size range: 2^5 through 2^15 updates per batch.
- Tested witness-count range: 10, 20, 50 witnesses (throughput measured flat across this range).
- Tested crash-fault range: 0, 1, 3 crashed witnesses out of a 10-witness committee (3 stated as the maximum tolerable in that configuration).
- Node-state size for storage arithmetic: 64 bytes (32-byte hash output + 32 bytes of parent/child metadata).
- Signature scheme: ed25519-dalek, 32-byte public/private key pairs.
- Storage/transport implementation: Rust, tokio for async networking, RocksDB for persistence (unless otherwise specified), TCP for point-to-point channels.

### Stated limitations
The paper states that evaluating Byzantine (as opposed to crash) fault behavior for BFT-style protocols "is still an open question" and explicitly limits its crash-fault benchmark to crash faults only — no measurement of behavior under actively malicious (Byzantine) witnesses is reported. The compaction mechanism requires a client to come online and check its own key history at least once between each tombstone epoch and the following deletion epoch; a client that does not do so cannot detect a wrongful deletion, which the paper states as a minimal but real additional assumption compared to a pure append-only construction. The append-only base construction (before compaction) is stated to conflict with a right to full account-data deletion, which the paper mentions has relevance to "right to be forgotten" regulation. The 850 GB projected figure at 1 billion users is an extrapolation from a 5-million-user measurement, not a direct measurement at that scale. The throughput ceiling is attributed to the IdP being the system bottleneck (not the witness count), but the paper does not report the throughput ceiling of the IdP itself under further load, nor push witness count high enough to find where network overhead becomes the bottleneck — it states only that this crossover is "expected" to occur eventually.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Every client of the directory must independently obtain a small server commitment for each epoch from an out-of-band source it trusts to be consistent across all clients — Parakeet supplies this itself via its witness quorum-certificate mechanism, but any component depending on Parakeet must be able to reach that witness quorum (a majority of 2f+1 out of 3f+1 witnesses) rather than trusting the IdP alone. At least one honest auditor must check each update for correctness every epoch for the non-equivocation soundness proof to hold; the paper's model assumes such an auditor exists (it can be any of the witnesses, executed as part of their normal protocol step) but the proof is void with zero honest auditors. Compaction's security depends on every client periodically running the KeyHistory check on its own key at least once per tombstone-to-deletion interval; a component that never re-queries an inactive user's key cannot detect that user's data being wrongly deleted. The protocol assumes bounded clock drift among witnesses is sufficient for f-fault tolerance deductions in the asynchronous model (the paper references bounded-clock-drift reasoning without giving a numeric bound). The system assumes the IdP and witnesses each hold a durable private signing key and that key compromise of the IdP is out of scope — Parakeet detects equivocation but does not itself prevent a compromised IdP from producing internally consistent but wrong data before compromise is discovered by another means. Deployment at the paper's benchmarked scale assumes access to persistent storage with fast random writes (RocksDB or MySQL in the reported configuration); the SEEMless-style comparison measurement shows that a naive append-only construction becomes storage-write-bound at a few hundred thousand users, so a system layering key transparency at billions-of-users scale needs the oZKS-style bounded-storage construction Parakeet supplies, not the plain append-only aZKS from SEEMless.

### Contradicts
None found against other entries in this corpus. Note for cross-reference: this paper positions itself as directly extending and superseding the storage and consistency limitations of SEEMless (CHASE-CCS-19 in this batch); see that entry's own reported figures for the comparison numbers this paper's Figure 5/6/12/13 measurements were built to contrast with. This paper also names Merkle² (HU-SP-21 in this batch) only in its bibliography — it does not benchmark against Merkle² directly and states no comparison figures against it in the retrieved text.

## [MANGIPUDI-EPRINT-26] Auditable Continuous Group Key Agreement
**Citation:** Easwar Vivek Mangipudi, Maddie Gorman, Sasha Levinshteyn. "Auditable Continuous Group Key Agreement." IACR Cryptology ePrint Archive, 2026. DOI not stated in source.
**Retrieved:** full text
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1710.pdf
**Domain:** H

### What it does
Auditable CGKA (Au-CGKA, where CGKA is Continuous Group Key Agreement, the key-refresh mechanism underlying Messaging Layer Security, MLS, RFC 9420) lets a designated auditor committee recover the encryption key of any past epoch of an end-to-end encrypted group chat, for compliance audits, while every ordinary group member checks at admission time that recovery will actually be possible for that epoch, so a broken escrow is refused before the epoch is accepted rather than discovered only when an audit later fails. In each MLS epoch a single member, the committer, rotates the group's keys through the standard TreeKEM update path and posts a commit message to a public, append-only log kept by the delivery service. Au-CGKA adds three objects to that commit: a commitment c_root binding the epoch's root secret e_se, an escrow ciphertext holding N Shamir secret shares of e_se — one per auditor-committee member — encrypted under each auditor's post-quantum public key, and a zero-knowledge proof (a STARK, Scalable Transparent Argument of Knowledge — a proof system requiring no trusted setup) that the escrow ciphertext decrypts to a valid Shamir sharing of the same value c_root commits to. Every member derives the epoch secret itself through the ordinary MLS key schedule and checks it against c_root; a mismatched escrow is rejected at admission by any honest member that performs the check. Recovery is per-epoch independent: any threshold t of the N auditors can jointly decrypt their shares and reconstruct e_se for one target epoch without touching any other epoch's escrow. The auditor committee stays offline except when an audit is requested. The proof's only in-circuit work is the escrow's well-formedness and the commitment opening; the MLS key schedule and the TreeKEM update path are not encoded in the circuit, which keeps the proof's cost independent of group size.

### Measured results
| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| Au-CGKA commit-message overhead: fixed 5,637 B added to the MLS base update-path bytes, falling from 97% relative overhead at update-path depth h_e=4 to 44% at h_e=10 to 23% at h_e=20 | Apple M5 Pro (48 GB), auditor committee N=5, threshold t=3, ML-KEM-768; MLS base update-path sizes 5,808 B / 12,816 B / 24,496 B at h_e = 4 / 10 / 20 (group sizes 16 / 1,024 / ~1,048,576, since group size n = 2^h_e); each figure the arithmetic mean of five runs |
| Per-commit committer cryptography outside the proof system: 0.031 ms at every depth | Same hardware and parameters; dominated by the N=5 committee encryptions; excludes the MLS signature, which the prototype does not perform |
| 3-of-5 audit cost: 93 µs, independent of which epoch is audited | Same hardware, N=5, t=3 |
| STARK proof: 1.38 s to prove, 0.17 s to verify, 15.31 MB proof size, constant across all measured group sizes | Same hardware; group size swept h_e = 4 to 20 (16 to ~1,048,576 members); relation contains no term indexed by update-path depth, so cost is O(N) in committee size and O(1) in group size by construction; across the full h_e = 3..20 sweep, measured prove time spans 1.37-1.49 s, a spread the paper attributes to run-to-run and thermal drift rather than depth |
| General-purpose zkVM (zero-knowledge virtual machine) comparison: SP1 zkVM proves the same relation in 30.0 s (~22x slower than the custom STARK backend) but produces a constant 1.21 MiB recursively compressed proof (~12x smaller) that verifies in ~27 ms | Same operating point (group size 1,024, N=5), SP1 proving shard-parallel across all 18 CPU cores (same core count as the custom-backend figures), guest program running 1.97 million RISC-V cycles because SP1 lacks ML-KEM hardware precompiles; times are means of five runs; flat across the full depth sweep because the guest's work does not depend on the tree |
| Zero-knowledge soundness bound: ε_ZK ≤ 2^-299 against the hiding FRI (Fast Reed-Solomon IOP of Proximity) commitment | Stated as Lemma 11 of the paper, a computational guarantee, not a measured figure |

### Parameters
- Auditor committee size N = 5, threshold t = 3, held constant through every reported measurement (a 3-of-5 threshold scheme).
- Encryption for the MLS update path and the escrow's Module-LWE-based post-quantum public-key encryption: ML-KEM-768 throughout.
- FRI query count derived from the target security level: n_q = 156 at branching factor l_b = 2, chosen so n_q · l_b ≥ 2·(128+24+4), leaving 135 quantum bits of security after the knowledge-soundness charge, against the paper's own 2^21 event-class bound.
- Published commitment truncated to l_pub = 16 lanes, giving a 64 B commitment (the paper separately reports a 32 B stand-in digest width used as a placeholder in the reference implementation).
- Group-size sweep: update-path depth h_e from 4 to 20, corresponding to group sizes 16 to approximately 1,048,576 (2^20) members.
- Measurement basis: each reported figure is the arithmetic mean of five runs at the operating point, and of three runs per depth in the sweep, on a verified-idle Apple M5 Pro with 48 GB RAM.

### Stated limitations
The auditability guarantee holds only for epochs an honest member admits: if every member of a group colludes, the group can accept an epoch whose escrow holds a value different from the actual epoch secret, and no check performed from the log alone can detect this, because an admission check cannot recompute a secret it does not itself hold. The paper states this case is explicitly out of scope. The auditor committee's long-term decapsulation keys are not erasable — each auditor must retain its key indefinitely because an audit may be requested arbitrarily far in the future — so adaptive corruption of an auditor unavoidably exposes that key; the paper's secure-erasure model treats this key, alone among all protocol secrets, as persistent rather than erasable. The scheme deliberately trades forward secrecy against the auditor committee for recoverability: a coalition of t auditors assembled at any point in time can recover every past epoch, and no later rekeying operation removes that ability. The construction does not authenticate or verify the TreeKEM update path itself — the escrow's correctness is proven, but "the auditor recovers the epoch keys but obtains no independent account of how they were distributed" — group-management authentication is left to a complementary mechanism (TreeSync, cited as orthogonal). Reported figures exclude the MLS signature, which the prototype does not implement. The custom STARK backend's security levels are conditional on an assumption the paper labels (A3') and on the ethSTARK conjecture underlying the FRI commitment row, both unproven cryptographic conjectures rather than proofs. Absolute timings are stated as single-machine research-prototype figures that "drift by a few percent with sustained load."

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Requires a public, append-only log maintained by a delivery service that every commit message is posted to, and against which any member or third party can check an escrow's proof without trusting the committer or the server — the paper's stateless verification model needs this log and nothing else. Requires the underlying protocol to be MLS-shaped: a TreeKEM update path producing an epoch root secret through the standard RFC 9420 key schedule, since the escrow commits to that specific value without re-deriving it in-circuit. Requires an auditor committee of N designated parties, fixed at deployment, whose public keys under a post-quantum Module-LWE-based encryption scheme are known to every committer at commit time; recovery requires any t of these N to come online and jointly decrypt. Requires every group member to enforce the secure-erasure discipline already required by ordinary MLS — deleting each ephemeral secret (path secrets, node secrets, rotated HPKE secrets, the sharing randomness, individual Shamir shares, the STARK witness) immediately once no longer needed — because the paper's adaptive security proof holds specifically in this secure-erasure model and a party that fails to erase exposes more than the model accounts for. Requires the auditor committee's long-term decapsulation keys to be protected against compromise for the full retention period the deployment cares about, since these keys are never erased and their exposure at any point recovers every past epoch's secret. Does not require or provide any mechanism for detecting a fully colluding group; a caller relying on Au-CGKA for compliance against an adversarial group, not merely an adversarial network, needs an additional mechanism outside this protocol.

### Contradicts
None found.

## [MANKU-USITS-03] Symphony: Distributed Hashing in a Small World
**Citation:** Gurmeet Singh Manku, Mayank Bawa, Prabhakar Raghavan. "Symphony: Distributed Hashing in a Small World." USENIX Symposium on Internet Technologies and Systems (USITS), 2003.
**Retrieved:** full text via OCR of https://www.usenix.org/legacy/publications/library/proceedings/usits03/tech/manku.html PDF (the committed text extraction at sources/text/MANKU-USITS-03.txt is corrupted — the source PDF uses a custom font-encoding table that maps to unreadable glyphs under every extraction path tried, including a second extraction library; the file at sources/pdf/MANKU-USITS-03.pdf was rendered to page images at 300 dpi and read with Tesseract OCR to recover this entry. A reader who needs to check the extraction against the original should re-run OCR on that PDF, not re-read the committed .txt.)
**Source URL:** https://www.usenix.org/legacy/publications/library/proceedings/usits03/tech/manku.html
**Domain:** A

### What it does
Symphony gives every node in a wide-area distributed hash table a lookup latency of O(k^-1 log^2 n) hops (n = network size, k = long-distance links per node) while letting each node choose k independently at run time, including changing it after the network has grown or shrunk. Every node places itself at a uniformly random real-numbered position on a ring covering the interval [0,1) that wraps around, and manages the segment of the ring between its own position and its immediate predecessor's — the mechanism a hash key resolves to a manager through: an m-bit hash key K resolves to the node managing the segment containing K/2^m, with no relationship required between m and the link count. Each node holds two short links, one to each ring neighbor, plus k long-distance links. To create a long-distance link, a node draws a random offset x from the probability density p_n(x) = 1/(x ln n) for x in [1/n, 1] — a harmonic distribution, the source of the protocol's name — and establishes a link to whichever node currently manages the ring position x away from itself in the clockwise direction. Routing forwards a lookup for target x along whichever of a node's links (short or long) minimizes the clockwise (unidirectional variant) or absolute (bidirectional variant) ring distance to x; greedy forwarding of this form is inherited from Kleinberg's small-world construction, which the paper extends from k=1 to general k=O(1) links.

Because no node knows the exact current network size n, each node instead estimates n through an Estimation Protocol: it contacts s other existing nodes, uses the ring-distance to each to infer a local density estimate, and averages. Long-distance links are drawn using this estimate n-hat in place of the true n. A re-linking option lets a node periodically re-draw its long links as its estimate of n changes; the paper's own experiment (Sections 4.2–4.3) finds re-linking gives only marginal improvement, because increasing the raw number of links from 1 to 2 already dominates the achievable latency reduction.

1-Lookahead adds no new links: each node additionally exchanges its own neighbor list with each of its direct neighbors, piggybacked on routing traffic or keep-alives, so a lookup can jump two hops using knowledge of a neighbor's neighbor without an extra round trip.

Fault tolerance replicates a node's content onto its f successor nodes along the ring (direct connections maintained with all f), rather than by maintaining backup long-distance links — a design choice the paper states is motivated by its own link-deletion experiment (Section 4.8), which finds that removing short (ring) links isolates nodes while removing long links only lengthens routes. A lookup remains satisfiable as long as no run of f consecutive successor nodes fails simultaneously.

### Measured results
All results are from simulation, not a deployed network; the paper states no node count, hardware, or churn model beyond what is given per experiment below.

| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| Increasing links per node from 1 to 2 reduces average latency substantially; each further addition gives diminishing returns | Networks of 2^5 to 2^15 nodes, unidirectional and bidirectional routing compared, 1 to 7 long links per node (Figure 3) |
| Bidirectional routing (forward along whichever link minimizes absolute rather than clockwise-only distance) improves average latency by roughly 25% to 30% over unidirectional routing | Same sweep as above |
| Average latency with k=4 long links, bidirectional routing, 1-Lookahead: 7.6 hops | Network of 2^15 nodes |
| Average latency with k=4 links, bidirectional routing, 1-Lookahead, drops to 4.4 hops when k=log n links used instead | Network of 2^15 nodes |
| 1-Lookahead reduces average latency by roughly 40% | Applied on top of small-k networks, exact k and n given as the 2^15-node, k=4 case above |
| Choice of s=3 neighbors for the Estimation Protocol: average latency is relatively insensitive to s in the range tested | Expanding networks, s swept (Figure 5); the paper states larger s improves the n-estimate itself but has "insignificant" effect on latency, so all subsequent experiments in the paper fix s=3 |
| Join/leave cost: O(log^2 n) messages, with the constant factor under 1 — 20 messages to establish k=4 long links | Network of size 2^14 (Figure 8) |
| Dynamic 100,000-node network: average lookup latency stayed below 5 hops throughout | log n neighbors per node, node lifetime drawn from an exponential distribution of mean 0.5 hours, sleep time mean 23.5 hours, node pool grown linearly to 100,000 over 24 hours, held steady for 24 hours, then shrunk to zero over the final 24 hours (72 hours total simulated) |
| Random-uniform long-link selection (instead of the harmonic distribution) does not scale: path length grows as O(sqrt(n/k)) | Comparison sweep against Symphony's harmonic-distribution links, network size 2^15 (Figure 11) |
| Removing a random fraction of long-distance links only slowly increases average latency; removing the same fraction of short (ring) links causes lookup failure by isolating nodes | 16,000-node network with log n long-distance links per node, fraction of links deleted swept from 0% to 100% (Figure 10) |
| Comparison table at n=2^15 nodes: Symphony with k=4 (bidirectional, 1-Lookahead) uses 10 average TCP connections and reaches average latency 7.56; with k=27 links, 56 connections and latency 3.75. CAN (10 dimensions) uses 20 connections, latency 14.14. Chord uses 30 connections, latency 7.50. Viceroy uses 10 connections, latency 15.00. Pastry (4-bit digits) uses 56 connections, latency 3.75; (2-bit digits) 22 connections, latency 7.50. Tapestry (4-bit digits) uses 56 connections, latency 3.75. | All figures for a single network size, 2^15 nodes, taken from the paper's own Table 1, itself constructed from the closed-form latency/degree formulas each protocol's own paper states, not from a live comparative simulation |

### Parameters
- k (long-distance links per node): no fixed value; the paper's headline recommendation is k=4 with bidirectional routing and 1-Lookahead for latency near 7.6 hops at 2^15 nodes, treated as a per-node tunable that may vary across nodes and over time, not a network-wide constant.
- s (neighbors sampled by the Estimation Protocol): fixed at 3 for every experiment after Section 4.1, chosen because larger s does not measurably improve latency although it improves n-estimate accuracy.
- f (successor nodes holding replicated content for fault tolerance): stated as "a small value ... less than ten should suffice, assuming independent failures and short recovery times" — the paper gives no derivation or measurement for this figure and it should be treated as an unmeasured recommendation, not a derived or tested parameter.
- Probability density for long-link target selection: p_n(x) = 1/(x ln n) for x in [1/n, 1], zero otherwise — the continuous form of Kleinberg's discrete harmonic distribution.
- TCP connections per node: 2k + 2 (two short links plus k long links, each counted as one connection), or 2k + 2 + f when fault-tolerance replication connections are included.

### Stated limitations
The paper states network proximity is not incorporated into how long-distance links are placed: "we would have to embed the set of participating hosts onto a circle, taking network proximity into account. We expect this to require a fair amount of engineering," described as work in progress at time of publication, not solved by the mechanism the paper describes. The paper states an unexplained bimodal distribution in per-node message load when 1-Lookahead is used, and reports it as an open question the authors are still investigating. The dynamic-network experiment models only two node states (alive and asleep) drawn from exponential distributions and does not model heterogeneous or long-tailed real-world lifetime distributions; the paper states real deployments would show more variable lifetimes. The paper does not evaluate behavior under adversarial or malicious nodes — every experiment assumes a cooperative population.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Symphony requires every node to be assigned a uniformly random real-numbered ring position at join time; the paper does not specify a Sybil-resistant or otherwise controlled identifier-assignment mechanism, so an external component must supply honest random-identifier assignment if the deployment needs one. The protocol requires each node to obtain an estimate of the current network size n (via the Estimation Protocol, which itself requires contacting s=3 existing nodes) before it can draw long-distance link targets from the harmonic distribution; a bootstrap mechanism to reach an existing node is assumed but not specified. Fault tolerance requires the ring's short-link structure to remain intact — content replication runs only across a node's f ring successors, so any mechanism that disrupts the ring ordering (identifier reassignment, aggressive churn) directly threatens data availability, per the paper's own finding that short-link deletion, not long-link deletion, causes lookup failure. The protocol assumes cooperative, non-adversarial nodes throughout; no mechanism in the paper limits how many identities a single physical node may register or defends the harmonic-distribution link-selection procedure against a node that reports a false network-size estimate to bias where its long links land.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus.

### Verbatim extracts

## [MARCUS-EPRINT-18] Low-Resource Eclipse Attacks on Ethereum's Peer-to-Peer Network
**Citation:** Yuval Marcus, Ethan Heilman, Sharon Goldberg. "Low-Resource Eclipse Attacks on Ethereum's Peer-to-Peer Network." IACR Cryptology ePrint Archive, 2018/236.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://eprint.iacr.org/2018/236.pdf
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2018/236
**Domain:** A

### What it does
The paper isolates a victim node from every other participant on Ethereum's peer-to-peer network, using only two attacker-controlled machines, each with one IP address, and without controlling any path the victim's traffic travels (an off-path attack). It exploits the deployed geth (Go Ethereum) client's node-discovery protocol, a modification of Kademlia in which every node holds a persistent on-disk database (`db`) of every node it has ever contacted plus a short-term, memory-only routing table (`table`) that is empty on every reboot and rebuilt from the `db` through a seeding process.

Three separate attacks are presented. Connection monopolization exploits the absence, before geth 1.8.0, of any limit on unsolicited incoming TCP connections: the attacker waits for the victim to reboot and immediately opens incoming connections from many self-generated node identities (ECDSA key pairs, free to generate) until every one of the victim's connection slots is filled. Table poisoning exploits the fact that the mapping from a node identifier to its target routing-table bucket, `logdist`, is a public deterministic function (a SHA3 hash distance, inherited from Kademlia's public distance metric) with no secret salt: the attacker generates node identities that map to the router table's most heavily weighted buckets, inserts them into the victim's persistent `db` before the attack (via ping/pong bonding, refreshed at least once every 24 hours so entries do not expire), and then, at the instant of the victim's reboot, floods pings from those pre-registered identities so they fill the empty `table` before the victim's own seeding process or its `lookup(self)` call can insert legitimate node identifiers from the `db`. A third attack manipulates the victim's local clock: because query/response freshness is checked only via a timestamp with a 20-second tolerance window, forcing the victim's clock more than 20 seconds out of sync with the network causes it to reject legitimate messages and empty its `db`, then to accept only attacker messages carrying matching (attacker-controlled) timestamps.

### Measured results
| Attack | Result | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Connection monopolization, victim in New York | Eclipsed 49/50 tests (98%) | N=1000 attacker node IDs, two attacker machines (New York, 60 Mbps upload; Boston, 22 Mbps upload), victim online 1 day before attack, geth v1.6.6, maxpeers=25 |
| Connection monopolization, victim in Singapore | Eclipsed 43/53 tests (81%) | Same N=1000 attacker IDs, two attacker machines in New York with upload speeds 140 kbps-1 Mbps |
| Table poisoning, victim in New York, 33 days uptime | Eclipsed 34/51 reboots (66%); victim failed to seed at all in 19/51 reboots (37%), of which 18/19 (94%) succeeded as eclipses; victim's outgoing connections were fully attacker-controlled in 49/51 tests (96%) | 272 crafted attacker node IDs (n=17 buckets targeted), two attack machines (Boston 22 Mbps, New York 42 Mbps), geth v1.6.6, maxpeers=25, victim `db` held 25,580 nodes (near the full ~24K-node network as of Aug 2017 per ethernodes.org) |
| Table poisoning, victim in Singapore, 1 hour uptime | Eclipsed 44/50 reboots (88%) | Same attack machines and node-ID set, victim `db` size 7,000 nodes, maxpeers=25 |
| Time to craft one attacker node ID mapping to a specific bucket | Full 272-ID set (17 buckets) generated in under 15 minutes | MacBook Pro, Intel Core i5 2.9 GHz, 16 GB RAM, 5 runs averaged |
| Lookup-table storage for scaling the table-poisoning attack to arbitrary victims | ~67 MB for µ=16 (2^16 buckets) | Derived from a coupon-collector calculation, ECDSA private keys 64 bytes each |
| Expected nodes retained in a 4096-slot routing table after inserting N=25,000 node IDs | 168 nodes | Derived from the skewed logdist distribution (bucket i receives a node with probability 1/2^(i+1)), confirmed experimentally on a node run for 27 days from a New York data center; bucket 245 filled in 3.2 days, bucket 246 in 2.5 days |
| geth client share of the observed Ethereum network at the time of the time-manipulation experiment | 130 geth clients vs. 64,374 non-geth clients (by unique IP, port) connected to the victim | Single instrumented victim node, count over the timing-attack experiment window |

### Parameters
- maxpeers = 25 (default, geth v1.6.6, used for all reported experiments).
- Outgoing TCP connection cap: floor((1+maxpeers)/2) = 13, by default (pre-1.8.0).
- Post-countermeasure incoming-connection cap (Countermeasure 1, live in geth 1.8.0): floor(maxpeers/3) = 8.
- Kademlia-derived routing table: 256 buckets pre-1.8.0 (reduced to 17 in geth 1.8.0 "in recognition of the fact that most of the lower-number buckets are empty"), bucket capacity k=16.
- `db` eviction: nodes older than 1 day (no last-pong response) are evicted once per hour.
- Table eviction on new-node insertion: pings the oldest bucket entry; pre-1.8.0, if that ping is unanswered, the new node replaces it.
- Table eviction on failed lookup: a node is removed after more than 4 failed findnode responses.
- Timestamp freshness tolerance exploited by the time-manipulation attack: 20 seconds.
- Countermeasure 2 as implemented in geth 1.8.0 (partial, not the paper's full recommendation): at most 2 nodes per /24 IP subnet per bucket, at most 10 nodes per /24 subnet in the whole table.
- Attack scaling parameter n=17 buckets targeted, yielding 16 x 17 = 272 crafted node IDs, chosen because a victim's table under normal operation was observed to hold only "a few hundred nodes" even after days online.

### Stated limitations
The authors state their attacks require the victim to reboot, and list causes: outages, power failures, host-OS attacks, "packet of death" crashes, DDoS-induced resource exhaustion, or ordinary client software updates; they quote the prior Bitcoin eclipse-attack authors' statement that "the security of the peer-to-peer network should not rely on 100% node uptime." They state the table-poisoning attack, as described, is "tailor made for a particular victim," so scaling it to attack many victims simultaneously would need a precomputed lookup table (which they construct and size at ~67 MB) rather than per-victim crafting. They state their measured success rates undercount honest-network interference: in the 33-day experiment, the attack failed in 15 of 49 tightly-measured non-seeded reboots because honest nodes made unsolicited incoming connections to the victim before the attacker filled all slots, a race condition inherent to the fact that geth (even after Countermeasure 1) still permits some honest incoming connections. They state a residual vulnerability after their own recommended Countermeasure 2 (one-to-one IP-to-key mapping) is only partially implemented in geth 1.8.0: with the partial subnet-based limit, an attacker restricted to /24-subnet limits can still associate up to 10 node IDs per IP address with a victim's table, which "does not raise the bar for attackers quite as high as we had hoped." They state Countermeasures 3 and 4 (making the node-ID-to-bucket mapping and the self-lookup target non-public via a locally-random secret) were not adopted in geth 1.8.0, so the public-mapping vulnerability those countermeasures would close remains open post-patch. They state Countermeasure 7 (replacing timestamp-based freshness with nonces) was not implemented because it breaks backward compatibility with the existing RLPx v4 packet format. They state a residual "low-resource eclipse attack" (Section VI-C) that combines the clock-manipulation attack with table poisoning can succeed with very few attacker node identities and can circumvent most of their proposed countermeasures, because a victim whose clock has been skewed empties its own `db` and rejects legitimate neighbor messages, eliminating the protective effect Countermeasures 3-6 depend on.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A Kademlia-derived node-discovery layer that (like Ethereum's) does not require the "well-formedness" property of iterative content lookup — because content is replicated at every node rather than discovered by address — gains no benefit from keeping the node-ID-to-bucket distance mapping public, and a public mapping is what both the table-poisoning attack and, per the related-work section, the Steiner/Kohnen/Locher-family Kademlia-DHT eclipse attacks exploit; a system reusing Kademlia's routing-table structure without needing public-distance lookups should salt the distance function with a per-node local secret (the paper's Countermeasure 3) before any deployment claim of eclipse resistance is made. A node-identity scheme that allows unlimited free identity generation on one IP address (unlimited ECDSA key generation, as in pre-1.8.0 geth) requires a separate binding mechanism — the paper recommends a cryptographically-verified one-to-one IP-to-key mapping, proved by a signed pong response — before any k-bucket-style routing table can resist identity-flooding from a single physical machine; a subnet-count heuristic alone (2 per /24 per bucket, 10 per /24 total, as partially adopted in geth 1.8.0) leaves an attacker up to 10 identities per IP address, which the paper states is insufficient. Any client using timestamp-based freshness for its discovery-protocol UDP messages requires either a tight and enforced clock-synchronization guarantee or a nonce-based challenge-response scheme (Countermeasure 7) instead, because a timestamp check alone is defeated by manipulating the victim's own local clock (e.g., via NTP) rather than by any network-path attack.

### Contradicts
None found regarding a claim commonly attributed to this paper.
Provides direct primary-source support for the "deployed-Kademlia identity-forgery attack" characterization used by the target registry's why_needed note for this key; no numeric disagreement with another corpus entry was found in the reviewed text.

### References worth retrieving
- Maymounkov, Mazières, "Kademlia: A peer-to-peer information system based on the XOR metric," IPTPS 2002 — foundational (already in corpus per BRIEF section 7).
- Heilman, Kendler, Zohar, Goldberg, "Eclipse Attacks on Bitcoin's Peer-to-Peer Network," USENIX Security 2015 (cited as [23]) — foundational, the Bitcoin-eclipse-attack paper this work's Ethereum attack is modeled after and repeatedly compared against.
- Apostolaki, Zohar, Vanbever, "Hijacking Bitcoin: Routing Attacks on Cryptocurrencies," IEEE S&P 2017 (cited as [17]) — competing/related attack, a BGP-level eclipse mechanism contrasted with this paper's off-path, low-resource approach.
- Steiner, En-Najjary, Biersack (cited as [43]) — competing, prior Kademlia-DHT content-eclipse attack whose goal (isolating a content item) is explicitly contrasted with this paper's goal (isolating a node); the paper states [43]'s countermeasures (adopted in eMule 0.49a) are the model for its own Countermeasure 2.
- Kohnen, Leske, Rathgeb, "Conducting and Optimizing Eclipse Attacks in the Kademlia Peer-to-peer Network" (cited as [27]) — attack/critique, shown by this paper to circumvent the eMule-style subnet countermeasures using only a logarithmic number of IP addresses via Kademlia's iterative lookup, a mechanism this paper argues does not apply to Ethereum.
- Locher, Mysicka, Schmid, Wattenhofer (cited as [29]) — attack/critique, another Kademlia table-poisoning attack in the same family as [43],[27].
- Singh, Ngan, Druschel, Wallach, "Eclipse Attacks on Overlay Networks: Threats and Defenses" (cited as [40]) — foundational, an early general eclipse-attack paper for structured overlays.
- Gervais, Karame, Wüst, et al. (cited as [21]) — competing/attack, on eclipse attacks' role in optimal double-spending and selfish-mining strategies.
- Urdaneta, Pierre, Van Steen, "A Survey of DHT Security Techniques" (cited as [44]) — foundational survey (already flagged as a priority bibliography in BRIEF section 4.4).

## [MATURANA-TIT-22] Convertible Codes: Enabling Efficient Conversion of Coded Data in Distributed Storage

**Citation:** Francisco Maturana, K. V. Rashmi. "Convertible Codes: Efficient Conversion of Coded Data in Distributed Storage." IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, 2022. DOI 10.1109/TIT.2022.3155972.
**Retrieved:** full text (text on disk carries the earlier working title "Convertible Codes: Efficient Conversion of Coded Data in Distributed Storage"; author list, DOI, and content match the registry record)
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.13119
**Domain:** C

### What it does
Code conversion changes the redundancy parameters of data already stored under an erasure code, from an initial [n_I, k_I] code to a final [n_F, k_F] code, without decoding back to the original data and re-encoding from scratch. The paper defines the access cost of a conversion as the total count of coded blocks read or written during the conversion, and restricts its analysis to the merge regime, where multiple initial stripes (each a group of n_I coded blocks produced from k_I original data blocks) combine into fewer, larger final stripes, formally k_F = lambda * k_I for an integer lambda >= 2. A convertible code is a paired construction of the initial and final generator matrices, chosen jointly so that a conversion can compute each final stripe's parity blocks directly from a small subset of the initial stripes' existing parity blocks by linear combination, rather than by reading every data block and full-encoding again. The paper proves a lower bound on access cost achievable by any linear, maximum-distance-separable (MDS, meaning any k of the n coded blocks in a stripe suffice to reconstruct the original k data blocks) convertible code in the merge regime, then gives two explicit families of constructions (Hankel-I and Hankel-II, built from submatrices of a superregular Hankel array, a triangular array of field elements in which every submatrix is guaranteed invertible) that meet this lower bound while using a polynomial rather than exponential field size.

### Measured results
This is a theoretical paper: every reported figure is a proven bound or a worked numeric example under that bound, not an experimental measurement. No simulation, prototype, or deployment evaluation appears in the text.

| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| Access cost of conversion is at least r_F + lambda * min(k_I, r_F); at least r_F + lambda * k_I if r_I < r_F | Theorem 8, proven for all linear MDS (n_I, k_I; n_F, k_F = lambda * k_I) convertible codes in the merge regime; r_I = n_I - k_I and r_F = n_F - k_F are the initial and final parity-block counts |
| Worked example: naive re-encoding accesses 24 blocks per final stripe; the access-optimal convertible code accesses 12 | (n_I=14, k_I=10; n_F=24, k_F=20), lambda=2; the paper states this as a 50% reduction in access cost |
| Worked example: converting a [k_I+1, k_I] single-parity-check code by merging two initial stripes into one final [2k_I+1, 2k_I] stripe drops access cost from 2*k_I (naive re-encoding) to 2 blocks | Example 1, lambda=2, single-parity-check code (XOR-parity), n_I = k_I+1, n_F = k_F+1 |
| Hankel-I construction meets the access-optimal lower bound whenever r_F <= floor(r_I / lambda), at field size q >= max(n_I - 1, n_F - 1) | Merge regime, linear MDS convertible codes; field size matches the maximum field size already required by a plain [n_I,k_I] or [n_F,k_F] Reed-Solomon code, so the paper states no field-size penalty is incurred for this range |
| Hankel-II construction meets the access-optimal lower bound whenever r_F <= r_I - lambda + 1, at field size q >= k_I * r_I | Merge regime, linear MDS convertible codes; wider r_F coverage than Hankel-I at a larger field size |
| Worked example of Hankel-I: (n_I=9, k_I=5; n_F=12, k_F=10) built from a superregular Hankel array of size n_F - 1 = 11 | Illustrates the field size q=11 = max(n_I-1, n_F-1) with n_I-1=8, n_F-1=11 |
| Worked example of Hankel-II: (n_I=7, k_I=4; n_F=10, k_F=8) | Illustrates a case outside Hankel-I's r_F range that Hankel-II covers |

### Parameters
- lambda (merge factor, k_F = lambda * k_I): integer, lambda >= 2; the paper's theory and both Hankel constructions are stated for this range.
- r_I, r_F (initial and final parity-block counts, r_I = n_I - k_I, r_F = n_F - k_F): free parameters bounding which construction (Hankel-I or Hankel-II) applies and at what field size.
- s (number of groups the r_I initial parity encoding vectors are split into, in the general Hankel-based sequence of constructions): ranges over {lambda, lambda+1, ..., r_I}; s = lambda recovers Hankel-I, s = r_I recovers Hankel-II.
- Field size q: q >= max(n_I - 1, n_F - 1) for Hankel-I; q >= k_I * r_I for Hankel-II; the paper states this as an explicit field-size-versus-r_F-coverage tradeoff, with intermediate s values interpolating between the two.

### Stated limitations
The paper restricts every proof to the merge regime, k_F = lambda * k_I with lambda an integer at least 2; it states going beyond the merge regime to general parameter regimes as its first listed direction for future work, meaning the access-cost lower bound and both Hankel constructions carry no proven guarantee outside this regime. The paper optimizes only access cost, defined as block count touched; it states that network bandwidth, disk input/output, and CPU consumption are related but separate resource costs it does not bound, and explicitly notes its access-optimal constructions reduce these other costs but are not proven optimal for them. The general high-field-size construction of Section V is stated to require a field size that grows too large for practical use, which motivates the lower-field-size Hankel constructions, but those Hankel constructions cover only the r_F ranges bounded above (not every r_F value at every field size).

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Both endpoints (n_I, k_I) and (n_F, k_F) must be fixed and known to the code construction in advance for the access-optimal guarantee to apply as proven; the paper's own "Handling a priori unknown parameters" discussion shows the Hankel sequence can be built to stay access-optimal across a bounded family of possible final parameters (k_F' = lambda' * k_I, n_F' = r_F' + k_F', 0 <= r_F' <= r_F, 2 <= lambda' <= lambda) chosen at construction time, so a system that wants flexibility across multiple possible future targets must enumerate that family up front rather than discover the target parameters after the fact. The conversion procedure reads specific parity blocks from the initial stripes identified by the construction and computes final parity blocks by linear combination over the finite field, so the storage system must be able to address and read individual coded blocks (not only fully-reconstructed data) and must apply linear operations over the same field the code was built over. The MDS property and the access-cost lower bound are both proven only for linear codes, so a non-linear or non-MDS encoding scheme receives no guarantee from this paper's results.

### Contradicts
None found.

### References worth retrieving
- Rashmi, Shah, Gu, Kuang, Borthakur, Ramchandran. "A solution to the network challenges of data recovery in erasure-coded distributed storage systems: A study on the Facebook warehouse cluster." USENIX HotStorage, 2013 — foundational (measured repair-bandwidth motivation for reducing conversion cost).
- Kadekodi, Rashmi, Ganger. "Cluster storage systems gotta have HeART: improving storage efficiency by exploiting disk-reliability heterogeneity." USENIX FAST, 2019 — foundational (the paper the abstract cites for the 11%-44% storage-space-reduction motivation for redundancy adaptation; that figure is attributed to this source, not measured by MATURANA-TIT-22 itself).
- Sathiamoorthy, Asteris, Papailiopoulos, Dimakis, Vadali, Chen, Borthakur. "XORing elephants: Novel erasure codes for big data." VLDB Endowment, 2013 — competing (also in this corpus as SATHIAMOORTHY-VLDB-13, a locally repairable code rather than a convertible code).
- Rashmi, Shah, Kumar. "Optimal exact-regenerating codes for distributed storage at the MSR and MBR points via a product-matrix construction." IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, 2011 — foundational (also in this corpus as RASHMI-TIT-11; the repair-bandwidth-optimal code family this paper's access-cost framework parallels).
- Tamo, Wang, Bruck. "Access versus bandwidth in codes for storage." IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, 2014 — competing (states access cost and bandwidth cost as generally distinct optimization targets, directly relevant to this paper's stated limitation that it optimizes access cost only).
- Papailiopoulos, Dimakis. "Locally Repairable Codes." — competing (also in this corpus as PAPAILIOPOULOS-TIT-14; a different mechanism for reducing the block count touched during repair).

"the optimal access cost is (λ + 1)rF = 12, which corresponds to savings in access cost of 50%"
"the access-optimal convertible codes... also reduce the total network bandwidth, disk IO, and CPU overhead"
"an important future direction is to go beyond the merge regime considered in this paper"

## [MAYOR-P2P-13] On Unstructured Distributed Search over BitTorrent
**Citation:** William Mayor, Ingemar Cox. "On Unstructured Distributed Search over BitTorrent." IEEE P2P, 2013. DOI 10.1109/P2P.2013.6688715.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/1420897/1/Mayor_Billy.pdf
**Source URL:** https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/1420897/1/Mayor_Billy.pdf
**Domain:** B

### What it does
The mechanism lets a BitTorrent node discover a torrent's participants through unstructured probabilistically-approximately-correct (PAC) search over tracking data, instead of through a centralized tracker or a structured distributed hash table (DHT), so torrent discovery survives the failure or attack of both of those. PAC search finds a target document (here, a torrent's tracking data, meaning its infohash together with the list of nodes believed to hold it) by having the querying node contact z nodes sampled uniformly at random from the network and asking each whether it locally indexes the document; the probability of success is P(d_i) = 1 - (1 - r_i/n)^z, where n is the network size and r_i is the number of nodes that index the document. Because most BitTorrent torrents are held by too few nodes for this formula to give a workable success probability directly on torrent participation, the paper adds a protocol modification: every node, on receiving any query for a torrent, records the querying node in a local index entry for that torrent's infohash, regardless of whether the query succeeds. A search is now successful if it finds any node indexing the torrent's tracking data, not only a node directly participating in the torrent, so every query issued for a torrent increases that torrent's tracking-data replication r_i by up to z nodes, even if the query itself failed to find a participant. A torrent's original author can bootstrap this replication by issuing r(0) dummy queries at publication time, before any real querying node has searched for it.

### Measured results
Live-network distribution measurement: 13 public BitTorrent trackers periodically scraped from 1 May to 3 July 2012 (64 days), observing 1.6 million distinct torrents (m) across 5.4 million distinct nodes (n), nodes identified by IP address. The observed node-count-per-torrent distribution follows a power law (fitted line 0.6x^-0.6 on log-log axes, Figure 1); 25% of all torrents were found on only 1 node, 76% on 10 or fewer, only 2% on more than 100 nodes; torrent replication ranged from 0 to 21,445 nodes, mean 27, median 3. Under this measured distribution, achieving P(d_i)=0.8 with z=100 queried nodes requires 86,214 nodes of replication (1.6% of the 5.4M-node network); with z=500, the required replication is 17,354 nodes; only 9 of the 1.6 million observed torrents met or exceeded that 17,354-node level. Overhead analysis (analytical, not measured on a live deployment): under stated packet-size assumptions (TCP/IP overhead 64 B/packet, BitTorrent handshake 68 B, 4 B length prefix, 20 B infohash, 6 B per returned node), for z=100, u=100 queries/hour, n=5,000,000, churn rate c=0.06/hour, the upper-bound download cost of a query is 6.8 KB when 1 result is returned and 8.8 KB when 100 results are returned. A node's response-side bandwidth is estimated at 39 bits/sec download and between 22 and 198 bits/sec upload, based on an observed average query rate of q=1.33 searches/node/hour from a cited prior measurement study. A node's local index reaches 1 GB after 289,184 hours (about 33 years) of continuous operation at an average received-request rate of 133 requests/hour. Simulation study: three separate simulation sets, each on a modeled network of 5,000,000 nodes with one observed torrent, run under a fluid churn model (seeding time exponentially distributed with rate gamma; downloading time bounded by an exponentially distributed patience with rate theta, subject to a 10%-of-file-per-hour download cap and 1%-of-file-per-hour upload cap per node), z=100 fixed, each simulation run to a 5% confidence-interval stopping criterion or a minimum trial count, whichever is greater. (1) Constant participation (a departing participant immediately replaced): at 10 constant participants, average query-success probability 14.26% (average 8 repeated queries to reach success); at 1000 constant participants, average success probability 87% on the first query, over 450 simulated hours. (2) Fixed participation with no replacement and no new queries: success probability declined by between 11.55 and 28.51 percentage points over 450 hours for participation levels of 1000, 100, and 10 nodes; stabilizing this decline would require an estimated 181, 46, and 15 dummy requests per hour respectively at those three participation levels. (3) Fluid query-rate model (peaking at 10,000, 1,000, or 100 simultaneous participants): average success probability 99.06% for the 10,000-peak torrents, 78.61% for the 1,000-peak torrents, 25.68% for the 100-peak torrents; even the worst-performing curve (100-peak) required an average of only 6 repeated queries before success.

### Parameters
- z (nodes queried per search attempt): discussion and simulations use z=100 as the working value; the paper's Figure 2 relates required query rate u to z at fixed target success probabilities P(d)=0.5, 0.7, 0.9, showing success probability is more sensitive to z than to u.
- n (network size): 5,000,000, taken from the 64-day measurement study.
- c (network churn rate): 0.06 per hour (6% of nodes leave and are replaced hourly), derived from a cited prior study's estimate of 8.06 hours average download time and 8.42 hours average seed time (16.48 hours total residence, so 1/16.48 ≈ 6%/hour); the paper states this may be an overestimate of churn because it does not account for nodes downloading multiple torrents.
- u (query rate for a torrent, queries/hour): example values of 50 and 100 used in the analytical discussion; at u=100, z=100, P(d_i)=0.96; at u=50, P(d_i)=0.81; at z=50 (u held at 100), P(d_i)=0.57.
- r(0) (author bootstrap replication): example target minimum success probabilities of P(d)=0.1 requires r(0)=5,265; P(d)=0.5 requires r(0)=34,538 (costing the authoring node about 4.5 MB of upload at the paper's per-query cost figure).
- gamma (fluid-model seeding-time rate) = 0.01(6 repeating) per hour in the simulation; theta (download-patience rate) = 0.025 per hour; lambda (node arrival-time rate in the peak-participation simulation) = 0.0(3 repeating) per hour.

### Stated limitations
The authors state that node identification by IP address means the study cannot distinguish nodes behind network address translation (NAT) from each other, and cannot distinguish nodes that share a reallocated IP address over time, both of which the authors state cause the reported node counts to be an undercount; they state they assume this impacts the reported figures only slightly, without a derivation. The overhead and replication analysis in Sections 4-5 assumes network churn removes a constant proportion of nodes every hour; the paper states this is a simplification later relaxed only in the Section 6 simulations, which use a fluid churn model instead. The paper explicitly leaves two mechanisms unbuilt and files them as future work: adaptively selecting the query size z based on a torrent's popularity, and adaptively triggering dummy queries so a torrent's tracking-data replication is kept high enough for a target success probability, rather than only at publication time. The index-eviction problem (removing tracking-data entries that have become stale or wrong because the recorded node no longer holds the torrent) is analyzed only qualitatively; the paper states three candidate strategies (least-recently-used eviction, periodic-ping health checks, and fixed-age eviction) and states that evaluating them is left as future work. The paper positions PAC search as a complement to existing torrent-discovery mechanisms, not a replacement.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The mechanism requires every node to be reachable for direct point-to-point query and response (a node sending its torrent infohash to z randomly sampled peers and receiving either an empty response or a list of participant/indexer nodes), so it requires a random-peer-sampling capability at the network layer that can select z peers close to uniformly at random from the full node population; the paper assumes this sampling primitive exists (citing Kademlia and Brahms in its bibliography as prior mechanisms for it) without evaluating one itself. The bootstrap mechanism requires the torrent's authoring node to be willing to issue r(0) dummy queries at publication time and to bear that node's own upload bandwidth for doing so; the analysis assumes this authoring node is honest and cooperative, since a torrent whose author does not bootstrap replication and that has too few natural participants (the paper's own measurement shows 76% of torrents have 10 or fewer participants) is not shown to become discoverable without it. The replication model (Equation 3) treats query rate u as an external, uncontrolled input to the system; achieving a target discovery probability for an unpopular torrent requires either an out-of-band mechanism to raise u (participants issuing dummy queries) or accepting the lower probability, and the paper does not specify what triggers a participating node to start or stop issuing dummy queries beyond noting it as a future-work direction.

### Contradicts
None found against other entries in this evidence corpus. Within the paper, the authors address an apparent tension between their own 64-day measurement (most torrents held by very few nodes) and a cited prior study (Gummadi et al., SOSP 2003) reporting that most downloads are of highly replicated items, resolving it as the two studies measuring different things: torrent-count distribution here versus download-request distribution there.

### References worth retrieving
- Maymounkov, Mazières, "Kademlia: A Peer-to-Peer Information System Based on the XOR Metric," IPTPS 2002 — foundational; cited as a structured-P2P alternative to the tracker/DHT mechanisms this paper works around, and already in the corpus per the brief's "already verified" list.
- Cohen, Shenker, "Replication Strategies in Unstructured Peer-to-Peer Networks," ACM SIGCOMM CCR 2002 — foundational; the square-root-replication result this brief already treats as verified, cited here for its PAC-search framework.
- Asthana, Fu, Cox, "On the Feasibility of Unstructured Peer-to-Peer Information Retrieval," ECIR 2011 — foundational; source of the accuracy framework (P(d_i) formula, Equation 1) this paper applies to BitTorrent.
- Terpstra, Kangasharju, "BubbleStorm: Resilient, Probabilistic, and Exhaustive Peer-to-Peer Search," ACM SIGCOMM CCR 37(4), 2007 — competing exhaustive probabilistic search mechanism.
- Bortnikov, Gurevich, Keidar, Kliot, Shraer, "Brahms: Byzantine resilient random membership sampling," Computer Networks 53(13), 2009 — foundational; a Byzantine-resilient implementation of the random-peer-sampling primitive this paper's z-node query step assumes.
- Timpanaro, Cholez, Chrisment, Festor, "BitTorrent's Mainline DHT Security Assessment," NTMS 2011 — attack; cited as showing the widely deployed BitTorrent DHT allows passive monitoring and node removal by malicious nodes, motivating this paper's unstructured alternative.
- Sit, Morris, "Security Considerations for Peer-to-Peer Distributed Hash Tables," IPTPS 2002 — attack; foundational DHT-security critique cited alongside the Mainline DHT assessment.
- Qiu, Srikant, "Modeling and Performance Analysis of BitTorrent-Like Peer-to-Peer Networks," ACM SIGCOMM CCR 34(4), 2004 — foundational; source of the fluid churn model used in this paper's Section 6 simulations.
- Guo, Chen, Xiao, Tan, Ding, Zhang, "A Performance Study of BitTorrent-Like Peer-to-Peer Systems," IEEE JSAC 25(1), 2007 — foundational; source of the average query rate (q=1.33 searches/node/hour) and download/seed duration figures this paper's bandwidth estimate is built on.
- Dán, Carlsson, "Power-Law Revisited: Large Scale Measurement Study of P2P Content Popularity," IPTPS 2010 — independent measurement corroborating the power-law torrent-popularity distribution this paper measures.

## [MAZZOCCA-COMST-25] A Survey on Decentralized Identifiers and Verifiable Credentials

**Citation:** Carlo Mazzocca, Abbas Acar, A. Selcuk Uluagac, Rebecca Montanari, Paolo Bellavista, Mauro Conti. "A Survey on Decentralized Identifiers and Verifiable Credentials." IEEE Communications Surveys & Tutorials, 2025 (arXiv preprint 2024). DOI 10.1109/COMST.2025.3543197.
**Retrieved:** full text
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/pdf/2402.02455
**Domain:** E

### What it does
The survey documents Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs, a W3C-standardized identifier scheme independent of any centralized registry) and Verifiable Credentials (VCs, a W3C-standardized data model for cryptographically signed claims) as the two components of Self-Sovereign Identity (SSI, an identity model giving the identity owner direct control over their own identity data rather than a third party). A DID resolves to a DID Document, a JSON-LD document holding the subject's public keys, service endpoints, and authentication parameters, published through a Verifiable Data Registry (VDR), the paper's general term for whatever system stores and serves DID Documents, most commonly a distributed ledger. Resolution of a DID method-specific identifier to its DID Document happens through a universal resolver, an interface that dispatches to a method-specific DID adapter, so a verifier need not implement every DID method itself. A VC is issued by an issuer to a holder's DID, presented to a verifier as a Verifiable Presentation (VP) bound to a challenge/nonce to block replay, and verified against the issuer's public key retrieved from the VDR; the holder proves control of the credential by signing with the private key corresponding to the DID inside it. The paper catalogs nine threat categories against this architecture (key/credential compromise, credential-validity drift, several privacy-linkage threats, and man-in-the-middle/replay) each with a corresponding mitigation drawn from the cited literature, compares five open-source implementation toolkits (DIDKit, IOTA Identity Framework, Hyperledger Aries, Microsoft Entra Wallet Library, Veramo) on language, credential format, proof types, and VDR backend, and reviews VC revocation mechanisms, principally the W3C's bitstring-based "Revocation List 2020," in which each bit position corresponds to one credential's revocation status.

### Measured results
This is a survey; the authors ran no experiment, implementation benchmark, or simulation of their own, and no throughput, latency, or scalability figure in the paper is a measurement performed by these authors. The one concrete numeric example in the paper is illustrative, drawn from the cited W3C Revocation List 2020 specification rather than measured by this paper's authors: a bitstring covering revocation status for a credential population, at 16 KB uncompressed, compresses to 135 bytes via ZLIB, attributed to the property that most credentials remain valid so most bits share a value and compress well. No sample size, credential-population size, or bit-density condition is stated for this figure, so it is recorded here only as an illustrative example from the cited specification, not as an independently reproducible measurement.

### Parameters
The paper states no protocol parameters with numeric defaults of its own (it is not proposing a new mechanism); it reports parameters others' systems use as descriptive facts:
- DID types per the DID specification: Anywise (usable with an unbounded set of parties), Pairwise (known only to the subject and one counterparty, reducing cross-context correlation), N-wise (known to exactly N parties, generalizing Pairwise at N=2).
- Revocation List 2020 bitstring: one bit per credential index; bit=1 denotes revoked, bit=0 denotes valid; compressed with ZLIB before distribution.
- Table IV (implementation comparison) records categorical, not numeric, parameters per toolkit: DIDKit (Rust core, JSON-LD/JWT credential formats, RSA/EdDSA/ECDSA/EIP712/JWS2020 proof types, no built-in key/wallet management, SD-JWT selective disclosure); IOTA Identity Framework (Rust/Node.js, JWT format, EdDSA/ECDSA proof types, Stronghold key management, Tangle-based VDR, SD-JWT and Zero-Knowledge Selective Disclosure); Hyperledger Aries (Python/JavaScript/Go/.NET, JSON-LD format, BBS+/EdDSA proof types, Indy Ledger VDR, SD-JWT, described as steepest learning curve of the five); Microsoft Entra Wallet Library (Android/iOS only, JWT format, EdDSA/ES256K/ECDSA P-256 proof types, Azure Key Vault key management, SD-JWT); Veramo (JavaScript, JSON-LD/JWT format, EdDSA/ECDH/ECDSA proof types, selective disclosure through a plugin interface).

### Stated limitations
The paper states that W3C's DID and VC standards do not specify how a VDR must be implemented, leaving DLT choice, indexing, and access-control design entirely to each deployment. It states that DID method specifications vary in format, completeness, information density, and versioning across implementations, which it identifies as an open interoperability problem, not a solved one. It states that only one revocation mechanism (Revocation List 2020) is close to W3C standard status at the time of writing, and that only one other work in the literature it surveyed (its own authors' prior EVOKE paper) proposes an efficient alternative revocation mechanism, specifically for IoT (Internet of Things) networks; it states the scalability of current revocation approaches in high-throughput or constrained-device settings remains underexplored. It states DID key rotation, the mechanism for recovering from a compromised private key by publishing a new public key signed with the old one, reduces but does not eliminate the vulnerability window between compromise and detection, and that frequent rotation introduces its own usability burden. It states that granting a third party (a DID controller distinct from the DID subject) authority to manage a DID document introduces an impersonation risk if that controller generates a new key pair and substitutes it into the document, and that robust authorization/auditing mechanisms to detect unauthorized DID Document modification are called for but not yet standardized. It states selective disclosure (revealing only a subset of a VC's claims) does not by itself prevent a verifier from linking repeated presentations of the same credential to one individual, and that Pairwise DIDs reduce, without eliminating, that linkage risk.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The architecture requires a VDR that is available whenever a verifier needs to resolve a DID or check an issuer's public key; the paper states verifiers can reduce live-lookup dependence by locally caching the public keys of issuers they already trust, but this is described as a mitigation, not a removal, of the availability requirement. It requires a functioning DID method adapter registered with the universal resolver for every DID method a verifier might encounter, since the universal resolver itself only dispatches to method-specific adapters rather than resolving any method natively. It requires a revocation-status distribution channel (a registry, a bitstring endpoint, or equivalent) that both issuers and verifiers can reach, since a VC's stated validity period alone does not account for early revocation due to loss of privilege. It requires each identity owner to hold and operate a digital wallet capable of managing private keys, constructing VPs, and performing key rotation, placing key-management and backup obligations onto the end-user device or an escrow service the paper describes only as a named mitigation option (Trusted Third Party Key Recovery), not a specified mechanism. It requires an out-of-band accountability layer (Know-Your-Customer / Anti-Money-Laundering–style verification) wherever regulatory identity screening is required, since the paper states DID/VC privacy preservation and regulatory screening are in tension and unresolved by the DID/VC data model itself.

### Contradicts
None found within this batch. As a survey, this entry synthesizes claims from other primary sources rather than reporting independent measurements that could conflict with them; any disagreement would be between the survey's cited sources, not measured by this paper's own authors.

### References worth retrieving
- Sabadello. "A universal resolver for self-sovereign identifiers." Decentralized Identity Foundation, 2017 — foundational (defines the universal-resolver mechanism the survey's DID resolution architecture depends on)
- Alizadeh, Andersson, Schelen. "Performance Analysis of Verifiable Data Registry Solutions for Decentralized Identifiers." IEEE CSDE 2022 — competing (the survey cites this for VDR implementation choices but does not itself report the performance figures; retrieving it directly supplies the measured VDR comparison this survey lacks)
- Krul, Paik, Ruj, Kanhere. "SoK: Trusting Self-Sovereign Identity." PoPETs 2024 — competing (a parallel SoK on SSI trust assumptions and threat coverage, useful for cross-checking this survey's threat taxonomy)
- Ernstberger, Lauinger, Elsheimy, Zhou, Steinhorst, Canetti, Miller, Gervais, Song. "SoK: Data Sovereignty." IEEE EuroS&P 2023 — competing (parallel SoK covering decentralized identity, decentralized access control, and policy-compliant decentralized computation)
- Mazzocca, Acar, Uluagac, Montanari. "EVOKE: Efficient revocation of verifiable credentials in IoT networks." USENIX Security 2024 — foundational (this survey's own authors' prior work, the only cited efficient-revocation alternative to Revocation List 2020; contains the actual measured revocation-mechanism figures this survey only summarizes)
- Zhang, Krol, Sonnino, Zhang, Riviere. "EL PASSO: efficient and lightweight privacy-preserving single sign on." PoPETs 2021 — attack/critique (source of the "linked unlinkability" mitigation cited against cross-presentation correlation, Threat 6)
- Khan, Luo, Zhang, Ullah, Amin, Qadri, Heyat, Ruby, Wang, Ullah, Li, Leung, Wu. "A Survey on X.509 Public-Key Infrastructure, Certificate Revocation, and Their Modern Implementation on Blockchain and Ledger Technologies." IEEE COMST 2023 — foundational (surveys the PKI revocation mechanisms, OCSP and CRLs, that Revocation List 2020 is positioned against)
- Alzahrani. "An Information-Centric Networking Based Registry for Decentralized Identifiers and Verifiable Credentials." IEEE Access 2020 — competing (the non-DLT alternative VDR architecture the survey names as an alternative to blockchain-based registries)
