## [MISLOVE-HOTOS-03] POST: A Secure, Resilient, Cooperative Messaging System

**Citation:** Alan Mislove, Ansley Post, Charles Reis, Paul Willmann, Peter Druschel, Dan S. Wallach, Xavier Bonnaire, Pierre Sens, Jean-Michel Busca, Luciana Arantes-Bezerra. "POST: A Secure, Resilient, Cooperative Messaging System." Proceedings of HotOS IX, USENIX Association, 2003. Pages 61-66.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.usenix.org/legacy/events/hotos03/tech/full_papers/mislove/mislove.pdf
**Source URL:** https://www.usenix.org/legacy/events/hotos03/tech/full_papers/mislove/mislove.pdf
**Domain:** L

### What it does
POST delivers messages (electronic mail, instant messages, news, calendar and whiteboard updates) between users without a dedicated server, by storing every message once in a peer-to-peer store and telling the recipient where to find it. POST is built on Pastry, a structured peer-to-peer overlay in which every node and every stored object holds a 160-bit identifier from the same numeric space, and a message can be routed to the node whose identifier is numerically closest to a given key. Two services layer on Pastry: PAST, a distributed hash table that stores each object's replicas at the k nodes whose identifiers are numerically closest to the object's handle (a 160-bit key), and Scribe, a multicast system that builds a tree from Pastry routes joining every subscriber to one rendezvous node per group.

A user creates a message and inserts it, encrypted, into the shared store; the insertion produces a handle. POST's event-notification service then sends the recipient a small signed, encrypted message containing that handle and the decryption key, delivered to the contact address recorded in the recipient's identity block (itself a signed, mutable record stored in PAST under the hash of the user's public key). The recipient's client reads its own metadata log — a chain of content-hash blocks, each linked to the previous one and signed only by its single owner — to track which messages have arrived, without any other party being able to insert or alter log entries undetected. Message bodies are stored once system-wide through convergent encryption: the store computes Hash(X) over the plaintext X, uses that hash as the symmetric encryption key, and stores the ciphertext at the handle Hash(Encrypt_Hash(X)(X)); because the same plaintext always produces the same ciphertext and handle, POST stores only one copy of any message body inserted independently by multiple senders, even before any of those senders authorize a given recipient to read it — decryption still requires knowledge of the plaintext hash.

For a recipient who is not online when a message arrives, the paper states the sender delegates the notification-delivery obligation to a set of k randomly selected nodes, but does not describe the mechanism further, citing lack of space. Message delivery itself does not depend on the recipient being online: the message body is durably stored in PAST (replicated at k nodes) at insertion time, and the recipient retrieves it, together with the queued notification, whenever its own daemon next comes online and polls or receives the delegated notification.

To bound the network scope over which any one message is replicated, POST groups nodes into organizational overlays nested inside one global overlay: documents inserted by a member of an organization replicate only among that organization's own nodes, rather than across the entire global Pastry ring, while retrieval still works from anywhere in the global overlay. The paper states this construction in outline and omits its mechanism, again citing lack of space.

### Measured results
None. The paper is a HotOS (Hot Topics in Operating Systems) position paper describing a system design; its final section states that prototype implementations of POST and ePOST (the email application built on POST) exist and are "currently under experimental evaluation," and that calendaring and instant-messaging applications are "underway," but no quantitative result — no message count, node count, latency, storage overhead figure, or replication-factor measurement — appears anywhere in the text. Any figure attributed to this paper for delivery latency, storage overhead, or replication behavior is not supported by this text.

### Parameters
- Replication factor: denoted k throughout (the number of nodes holding a replica of each PAST-stored object); no numeric value is given in this paper. The system is stated to tolerate up to k-1 faulty or unreachable nodes in any replica set without loss of data or service.
- Notification delegation set size for offline recipients: also denoted k random nodes; no numeric value given, and the delegation mechanism itself is not described (cited as omitted for space).
- Log clustering parameter M: consecutive log records are stored together in clusters of M records on a single node, to reduce the cost of walking the log; no numeric value is given.
- No parameter in this paper carries an experimentally chosen value; every one is presented symbolically.

### Stated limitations
The paper states that determining an appropriate replication factor and appropriate assumptions about the fraction of faulty nodes in a given deployment requires further analysis and experimentation, and cites a prior study of peer-to-peer file systems in enterprise settings as evidence that "modest levels of replication can yield high availability," without itself supplying that measurement. Storage overhead per message is stated to be higher in POST than in a conventional server-based email system, because of the k-way replication PAST performs, an effect the authors say is partly offset by the single-copy property of convergent encryption removing duplicate attachment storage, and further offset by using otherwise-idle desktop disk space; erasure coding is cited as a further possible reduction that "we have not yet explored." Convergent encryption is stated to be vulnerable to a known-plaintext attack: an adversary who can guess a message's plaintext can confirm the message's presence in the store (though not who inserted it, and not who else references it, since metadata referencing a message is itself encrypted); the authors recommend prepending random bits before convergent encryption for small, highly structured, or otherwise predictable content. Single-writer logs are stated to be the only supported mechanism for mutable state, adopted specifically to avoid the cost and complexity of a general Byzantine fault-tolerant replicated state machine; the authors state this is not flexible enough for every cooperative application and that a separate line of work at LIP6 was investigating additional Byzantine fault-tolerant mechanisms for multi-writer mutable state, unresolved at the time of writing. Objects stored in PAST are assumed non-deletable throughout the design, which the paper states requires available disk space in the system to be always increasing and to exceed total storage demand. The paper states it remains an open question whether decentralized email of this kind will be sufficient to displace existing server-based email infrastructure.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The mechanism requires a trusted certificate authority that signs a binding between each user's unique name (for example, an email address) and their public key, and separately issues the node-identifier certificates Pastry's secure routing depends on to resist adversarial node placement; POST assumes this authority exists and may set policy (for example, requiring each user's node identifier to be bound to a live IP address) to force resource contribution. Every user is assumed to trust exactly one node, their own "trusted node," with their private key; no other node in the system is trusted by that user. The durability of any stored message depends on the failure independence of the k nodes holding its replicas and on a replication factor chosen relative to the actual node failure rate in the deployment, neither of which this paper measures; the organizational-overlay construction is offered specifically so that failure-independence assessment can be scoped to nodes under one administrative domain rather than the global overlay. The event-notification and metadata-log mechanisms both depend on Pastry's secure routing service (cited to Castro, Druschel, Ganesh, Rowstron, Wallach, OSDI 2002) to resist a malicious node intercepting or misdirecting a lookup; POST does not reimplement that defense itself. The offline-delivery mechanism (notification delegated to k random nodes) is asserted but its correctness properties, including what happens if some delegated nodes are themselves offline or faulty, are not specified in this text.

### Contradicts
None found. No other paper in this batch reports a directly comparable delivery-latency or storage-overhead figure for a store-and-forward peer-to-peer messaging design, and this paper reports no measured figures of its own to be contradicted.

### References worth retrieving
- Rowstron, Druschel, "Pastry: Scalable, distributed object location and routing for large-scale peer-to-peer systems," IFIP/ACM Middleware 2001 — foundational, the structured overlay POST is built on.
- Rowstron, Druschel, "Storage management and caching in PAST, a large-scale, persistent peer-to-peer storage utility," ACM SOSP 2001 — foundational, the storage layer POST uses directly.
- Castro, Druschel, Ganesh, Rowstron, Wallach, "Security for structured peer-to-peer overlay networks," OSDI 2002 — foundational, supplies the secure-routing defense POST's durability and notification guarantees depend on.
- Castro, Druschel, Kermarrec, Rowstron, "SCRIBE: A large-scale and decentralized application-level multicast infrastructure," IEEE JSAC 20(8), 2002 — foundational, the multicast/rendezvous layer POST's notification service uses.
- Stoica, Morris, Karger, Kaashoek, Balakrishnan, "Chord: A scalable peer-to-peer lookup service for Internet applications," ACM SIGCOMM 2001 — competing structured overlay, cited as an alternative POST states it "could easily be layered on."
- Dabek, Kaashoek, Karger, Morris, Stoica, "Wide-area cooperative storage with CFS," ACM SOSP 2001 — competing storage system built on Chord, offered as an alternative to PAST.
- Kubiatowicz et al., "OceanStore: An architecture for global-scale persistent store," ASPLOS 2000 — competing system; Section 6 states OceanStore separately explored peer-to-peer email storage and POST claims lower complexity via single-writer logs.
- Zhao, Kubiatowicz, Joseph, "Tapestry: An infrastructure for fault-resilient wide-area location and routing," UC Berkeley TR UCB/CSD-01-1141 — competing structured overlay, offered as an alternative substrate.
- Muthitacharoen, Morris, Gil, Chen, "Ivy: A read/write peer-to-peer file system," OSDI 2002 — foundational, the source of the single-writer content-hash-chained log design POST's metadata mechanism is stated to be inspired by.
- Castro, Liskov, "Practical Byzantine fault tolerance," OSDI 1999 — foundational, the general Byzantine-fault-tolerant replicated state machine approach POST's single-writer logs are designed to avoid the cost of.
- Kangasharju, Ross, Turner, Syrjala, Digeon, "Peer-to-peer e-mail," submitted for publication, November 2002 — competing, cited as a prior serverless email proposal sharing ePOST's goals but limited to email and not interoperable with existing infrastructure.
- Weatherspoon, Kubiatowicz, "Erasure coding vs. replication: A quantitative comparison," IPTPS 2002 — competing storage-redundancy mechanism, cited as an unexplored reduction to POST's replication overhead.
- Bolosky, Douceur, Ely, Theimer, "Feasibility of a serverless distributed file system deployed on an existing set of desktop PCs," ACM SIGMETRICS 2000 — foundational/independent-measurement, source of the "modest levels of replication can yield high availability" claim this paper cites without reproducing the measurement.
- Douceur, Adya, Bolosky, Simon, Theimer, "Reclaiming space from duplicate files in a serverless distributed file system," ICDCS 2002 — foundational, source of the convergent-encryption technique POST's message store uses.

## [MISLOVE-NSDI-08] Ostra: Leveraging Trust to Thwart Unwanted Communication
**Citation:** Alan Mislove, Ansley Post, Peter Druschel, P. Krishna Gummadi. "Ostra: Leveraging Trust to Thwart Unwanted Communication." USENIX NSDI, 2008.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.usenix.org/legacy/event/nsdi08/tech/full_papers/mislove/mislove.pdf
**Source URL:** https://www.usenix.org/legacy/event/nsdi08/tech/full_papers/mislove/mislove.pdf
**Domain:** F

### What it does
Ostra bounds the rate at which a sender can push unwanted communication (spam, unsolicited
messages, unsolicited shared content) to other users, in proportion to that sender's number of
trust links, without classifying message content and without requiring a single strong identity
per user.

Ostra assigns a credit balance to each link of a trust network (a graph in which an edge
represents a relationship costly to form and maintain, such as a mutual social-network
connection), not to each user identity. Each link's balance B stays within a range [L, U] with L
≤ 0 ≤ U. To send a message, the sender obtains a signed token along the path from sender to
receiver in the trust network: obtaining the token raises the lower bound L on each link along
that path by one unit, reserving capacity. When the receiver classifies the message, if marked
unwanted, one credit transfers from sender to receiver along each link of the path, permanently
lowering the sender-side link's balance and raising the receiver side's; if marked wanted, the
reservation is undone and no credit moves. A link whose balance reaches L blocks further
sends across it until the balance recovers. Because the total credit summed over all links is
conserved at every operation (Table 1: join, wanted send, unwanted send, and decay each leave
total system credit at 0), colluding users cannot manufacture additional sending capacity by
creating more identities — they can only redistribute the fixed credit among themselves, and any
message that reaches a victim outside their group must still cross at least one real link into
the honest region of the trust graph.

Two auxiliary mechanisms prevent legitimate users from becoming permanently blocked. First,
credit balances decay toward 0 at a constant fractional rate d per unit time, absorbing the
natural imbalance between credit a well-behaved user earns (by receiving unwanted messages) and
loses (by occasionally sending a message someone else classifies as unwanted). Second, a
non-owned overflow account C with no upper bound lets a user who has accumulated too much
credit (from being targeted) deposit it, freeing her links to receive further messages; deposited
credit still decays, so system-wide credit does not grow. A timeout T resets an unclassified
message's reservation as though it had been marked wanted, preventing indefinite credit lock-up
from dropped messages or long receiver absence.

A decentralized variant (Section 7) removes the assumption of a trusted central site that holds
the full trust graph. Each user runs an agent holding her own link balances; route discovery
combines a Bloom filter (a probabilistic set-membership structure) advertising each user's
two-hop neighborhood for short paths with landmark routing (a small set of well-known reference
nodes with published hop-distances) for longer paths. Authorization and classification messages
propagate along the discovered path, and each forwarding node has an incentive to relay
correctly because a node that drops a message is penalized (has its own outgoing credit
lowered) by its predecessor after timeout T.

### Measured results

| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| At 1% of the network as attackers (4,096 of the network), each legitimate user receives 0.22 unwanted messages/week (≈12/year) | YouTube-derived trust network, 446,181 users, 1,728,938 symmetric links; L=-3, U=3, d=10%/day; attackers vary 1 to 4,096 (0.0002%–1% of network); each good user sends 2 messages, each attacker sends 500 |
| Unwanted messages received scales linearly with the proportion of attackers, matching the analytic bound d·L·D+S | Same YouTube-derived network and parameters; three traffic models compared: Random, Proximity (destination distribution matching the measured email trace), and YouTube (single high-degree, 1,376-link target account) |
| Increasing the maximum credit imbalance per link L increases unwanted messages received | Same network; L varied from 1 to 100 |
| At 30% false-positive rate for classifying legitimate messages as unwanted, only a small proportion of messages are blocked, in the messaging-system model (Random/Proximity) | Same network |
| At 64% false-classification rate, ~40% of messages cannot be sent, in the content-sharing model (YouTube, single shared target account) | Same network |
| Min-cut analysis: proportion of user pairs (out of 3,000 randomly sampled) whose min-cut is not adjacent to either endpoint decreases as the lower of the two users' degrees increases, meaning better-connected users are less exposed to link-exhaustion attacks | YouTube-derived trust network, uniform link weight of 1 |
| Email-trace destination selection: 93% of messages sent to a friend or friend-of-friend, versus an expected 14% under random destination selection | 100-day anonymized email trace, 2 institutes, ~200 researchers; extracted social network of 150 users linked by ≥3 emails exchanged, covering 13,978 emails |
| Message delay under credit-bound throttling with L=-3, U=3: send delayed 0.38% of the time (avg 2.2h) at 2h avg. classification delay; 0.57% of the time (avg 6.1h) at 6h avg. classification delay; receive delayed 1.3% of the time in both cases (avg 4.1h and 16.6h respectively) | Same email trace; 95% of the trace's 1,003,819 received messages were randomly discarded to simulate removing junk mail (administrators estimated ~95% of incoming mail was junk); >98% of delayed receive-messages concentrated on 3 users |
| Bloom-filter routing: >90% of users' Bloom filters smaller than 4 kilobytes; with 765 landmark users (0.16% of population), remaining users can route to >89% of the network | Preliminary analysis on the same YouTube-derived trust network; unrouteable users mostly single-link, weakly connected |
| Degree-distribution comparison: YouTube power-law coefficient 1.66 (Kolmogorov-Smirnov goodness-of-fit 0.12), LinkedIn coefficient 1.58 (goodness-of-fit 0.05) | Maximum-likelihood fit; used to argue YouTube's graph structure is comparable to a genuine trust network like LinkedIn's despite YouTube not itself meeting Ostra's link-cost requirement |

### Parameters
- L (lower credit bound per link): tested 1 to 100 in the sensitivity experiment (Figure 9); L=-3 used as the conservative operating point in the main evaluation.
- U (upper credit bound per link): U=3 used in the main evaluation; U=L in magnitude by symmetry in the examples given.
- d (daily credit decay rate): 10% per day used in the main evaluation; the paper states d must be "high enough to cover the expected imbalance but low enough to prevent considerable amounts of intentional unwanted communication," with no derivation of the 10% figure beyond the trace-based sensitivity result.
- T (classification timeout): stated only as "typically on the order of days," no specific value derived or tested.
- Attacker population: varied 1 to 4,096 nodes (0.0002% to 1% of a 446,181-node network) in the sensitivity experiment; 512 attackers (≈0.1%) used as the default elsewhere.

### Stated limitations
The paper states the YouTube social network used for evaluation does not strictly meet Ostra's
own requirement of non-trivial cost to form and maintain a link, because YouTube subscription
links cost nothing to create; the authors substitute it because genuine trust networks such as
LinkedIn cannot be crawled for privacy reasons, and justify the substitution only by a
degree-distribution similarity argument, not by directly measuring Ostra's performance on a real
trust network. The authors state this substitution may cause the YouTube-based results to
understate Ostra's real-world performance, because some YouTube accounts reach degree 20,000+ while real trust
networks are bounded by human relationship-maintenance capacity (cited as 150–200). No
communication trace at the same scale as the social network was available; traffic patterns are
inferred from a 200-person, 100-day internal email trace, not measured on the evaluation network
itself. The centralized design requires a trusted entity to hold the complete trust network and
credit state; systems without any trusted component, such as SMTP-based email, require the
decentralized design of Section 7, which the paper describes as a preliminary sketch validated
only by a bloom-filter/landmark routing feasibility measurement, not an end-to-end evaluation.
Ostra requires that joining be by invitation from an existing user, restricting deployment to
"invitation-only" social networks. Ostra depends on receivers actively classifying messages as
wanted or unwanted; the paper acknowledges this is a burden and only sketches (without measuring)
implicit-feedback alternatives such as inferring classification from delete/archive/reply
actions. A user whose account password is compromised can still be drained of credit by an
attacker sending through it, bounded by the account's own per-link limits, not prevented.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Requires an underlying trust network in which link formation and maintenance carries a real,
non-zero cost to the participant, so that no user can cheaply create an unbounded number of
identities or links; the paper states this property explicitly does not hold for the YouTube
graph it evaluates against. Requires the trust network to be connected, so that a path exists
between any two user identities. Requires either a single trusted party holding the complete
trust network and credit state (centralized design), or — for the decentralized variant — a
route-discovery layer supplying Bloom-filter neighborhood advertisements and landmark-based
long-path routing, plus every forwarding node maintaining per-link balance state and honoring
signed authorization/classification/timeout messages from its neighbors. Requires receivers to
supply a wanted/unwanted classification for each received communication (or allow a timeout to
default it to wanted); the mechanism does not function without this feedback channel. Requires
new users to be introduced by an existing Ostra user at join time, which the rest of the system's
account-creation flow must supply. Does not require, and explicitly avoids requiring, a single
strong per-user identity — multiple identities per person are tolerated because sending capacity
is a property of trust links, not of identities.

### Contradicts
None found among the papers in this corpus.

### References worth retrieving
- H. Yu, M. Kaminsky, P. B. Gibbons, A. Flaxman. "SybilGuard: Defending against Sybil attacks via social networks." SIGCOMM 2006 — foundational (the random-route/attack-edge model Ostra's credit-conservation argument parallels)
- J. Douceur. "The Sybil Attack." IPTPS 2002 — foundational (defines the Sybil attack Ostra's multiple-identity analysis addresses)
- S. Garriss, M. Kaminsky, M. J. Freedman, B. Karp, D. Mazières, H. Yu. "RE: Reliable Email." NSDI 2006 — competing (a prior trust-based anti-spam system for email)
- M. Walfish, J. Zamfirescu, H. Balakrishnan, D. Karger, S. Shenker. "Distributed Quota Enforcement for Spam Control." NSDI 2006 — competing (quota-based rather than trust-link-based spam bound)
- A. Mislove, M. Marcon, K. P. Gummadi, P. Druschel, B. Bhattacharjee. "Measurement and Analysis of Online Social Networks." IMC 2007 — foundational (source of the structural claims about social-graph density used to argue link-attack resistance)
- P. F. Tsuchiya. "The Landmark Hierarchy: A New Hierarchy for Routing in Very Large Networks." SIGCOMM 1988 — foundational (landmark routing technique reused for decentralized path discovery)
- B. H. Bloom. "Space/time trade-offs in hash coding with allowable errors." CACM 1970 — foundational (Bloom filter used for local-neighborhood route discovery)
- M. Cha, H. Kwak, P. Rodriguez, Y.-Y. Ahn, S. Moon. "I Tube, You Tube, Everybody Tubes." IMC 2007 — foundational (source describing the YouTube dataset structure)

- "malicious, colluding users can pass credits only between themselves"
- "each user can produce unwanted communication at a rate of no more than d∗L+S"
- "the YouTube social network does not meet Ostra's requirements, because there is no significant cost"

## [MUGHEES-CCS-21] OnionPIR: Response Efficient Single-Server PIR
**Citation:** Muhammad Haris Mughees, Hao Chen, Ling Ren. "OnionPIR: Response Efficient Single-Server PIR." ACM CCS, 2021. DOI 10.1145/3460120.3485381.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://eprint.iacr.org/2021/1081.pdf
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2021/1081.pdf
**Domain:** G

### What it does
OnionPIR retrieves one entry from a server-held database without revealing to the server which entry was requested (single-server private information retrieval, PIR), while keeping the amount of data the client must download close to the size of the entry itself. In single-server PIR, the database of N entries is treated as an array; a basic protocol has the client send an encrypted query vector of N ciphertexts, one per database position, each homomorphically encrypting 1 at the target index and 0 elsewhere, and the server homomorphically computes the dot product of the query vector against the plaintext database and returns the encrypted result. Because N ciphertexts is too large to send directly, prior schemes reduce request size with hierarchical (multi-dimensional hypercube) queries and query compression (packing many query bits into one ciphertext, as in the prior system SealPIR), at the cost of a large response: the server's homomorphic dot-product computation in the second dimension of the hypercube multiplies together large ciphertexts, and this multiplication's noise growth forces the use of a large ciphertext modulus, which inflates the size of the encrypted response the client must download to on the order of 100 times the size of the underlying plaintext entry, independent of database size.

OnionPIR controls this noise growth using a technique from fully homomorphic encryption bootstrapping literature adapted to PIR: it replaces the second-dimension ciphertext-ciphertext multiplication with an "external product," a ciphertext-plaintext-style operation between a regular BFV ciphertext and an RGSW ciphertext (RGSW is a homomorphic-encryption ciphertext format designed for this operation). An external product decomposes one operand into small digits before multiplying, which grows the result's noise far more slowly than a direct ciphertext-ciphertext product, so the response can be encrypted under a much smaller ciphertext modulus while remaining decryptable, directly shrinking the response's byte size. A single query ciphertext is decomposed into RGSW form and expanded into the individual per-index selection ciphertexts server-side using a homomorphic "ciphertext expansion" procedure, so the client sends only a logarithmic number of query bits rather than one ciphertext per hypercube row.

Stateful OnionPIR extends this with a precomputation ("offline") phase, following the framework of Patel et al.'s stateful PIR: the client downloads compact helper information (subset sums over c partitions of the database, each partition of size k) ahead of time, cached as local client state; at query time (the "online" phase), the client combines its held state with a lightweight per-query request to retrieve the target entry using far less server computation per query than the stateless scheme, at the cost of periodically refreshing the state offline. Patel et al.'s original scheme requires the client to download the entire database once during the offline phase, which makes its amortized response size scale with the whole database. OnionPIR's stateful variant instead uses a technique the paper calls PBSR (partition-based subset retrieval), built on a homomorphic evaluation of a Benes copy network (a routing network built from a sequence of 2x2 switches, each a multiplexer selecting one of two inputs) to combine batched PIR retrieval of the needed subset sums with the copy-network routing homomorphically, so the offline phase downloads only the small helper data rather than the whole database, at a stated cost of doubling the per-query response size relative to stateless OnionPIR.

### Measured results
Hardware: Amazon EC2 t2.2xlarge instance, 32 GB RAM, 8 CPU cores with AVX enabled. Implementation built on Microsoft SEAL, a homomorphic-encryption library, with the paper's own implementation of RGSW ciphertexts and external products added on top. Batched PIR was not implemented; its offline-phase computation cost is simulated rather than measured, and this simulation applies only to the stateful-OnionPIR offline-phase figures (all other reported figures are direct measurements). Each non-simulated result is the average of 10 runs. Monetary cost is computed, not separately measured, from Amazon EC2's published on-demand rates as of the paper's writing (July 2021): one cent per CPU-hour and nine cents per GB of internet traffic.

Parameters: polynomial degree n = 4096, ciphertext coefficient modulus q = 124 bits, plaintext modulus t = 60 bits, giving a ciphertext expansion factor F = 4.2x; SEAL's default noise standard deviation and secret-key distribution; the Albrecht et al. LWE (learning with errors) hardness estimator rates these parameters at approximately 111 bits of computational security. Comparison baseline SealPIR uses n = 2048, q = 60 bits (115 bits of security by the same estimator), t = 12 bits, giving expansion factor F = 10. Each database entry is fixed at 30 KB; at n=4096/t=60-bit, one OnionPIR ciphertext holds 30 KB of plaintext, versus 3 KB per ciphertext in SealPIR (so a 30 KB entry there is split across 10 chunks). Database sizes tested: N = 2^16, 2^18, 2^20, 2^24 entries.

Stateless OnionPIR versus SealPIR, per-query cost, Table 3, at four database sizes (2^16 to 2^24 entries):

| N | Response size (KB) SealPIR | Response size (KB) OnionPIR | Request size (KB) SealPIR | Request size (KB) OnionPIR | Total compute (s) SealPIR | Total compute (s) OnionPIR | Server cost (US cents) SealPIR | Server cost (US cents) OnionPIR |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2^16 | 3,200 | 128 | 32 | 64 | 26.1 | 24.9 | 0.034 | 0.008 |
| 2^18 | 3,200 | 128 | 32 | 64 | 101.9 | 101.1 | 0.055 | 0.029 |
| 2^20 | 3,200 | 128 | 32 | 64 | 403.1 | 400.9 | 0.139 | 0.112 |
| 2^24 | 3,200 | 128 | 64 | 64 | 6,448.4 | 6,416.2 | 1.818 | 1.792 |

Response size is 128 KB for OnionPIR versus 3,200 KB for SealPIR at every tested database size, a 25x reduction, for a fixed 30 KB entry (giving OnionPIR's stated 4.2x expansion factor over the 30 KB plaintext, against SealPIR's approximately 100x). Server computation time is nearly identical between the two schemes and scales linearly with database size at both: about 1.7 hours (6,416-6,448 s) at N=2^24 for either scheme. Request size: OnionPIR's request size is fixed at 64 KB regardless of database size; SealPIR's is smaller (32 KB) up to N=2^20 but grows past N=2^24 and, per the paper's own stated extrapolation (not in the table), reaches 64 KB at 16 million entries and about 512 KB at 1 billion entries — a database size not directly measured in Table 3. Server monetary cost is dominated by network traffic at small N (where OnionPIR is stated to be orders of magnitude cheaper because of its smaller response) and converges toward computation-dominated, near-equal cost between the two schemes at large N; at N=2^16 OnionPIR's cost (0.008 cents) is about 4x lower than SealPIR's (0.034 cents), and at N=2^20 (one million entries) OnionPIR's cost is 19% lower.

Stateful OnionPIR versus stateless OnionPIR versus Patel et al.'s stateful scheme, Table 4, same four database sizes, subset-partition parameter c fixed at 500 for both stateful OnionPIR and Patel et al.; subset size k for stateful OnionPIR set per database size to 8 (N=2^16), 16 (N=2^18), 16 (N=2^20), 64 (N=2^24); Patel et al.'s k set to sqrt(N)/2 per that scheme's own paper.

| N | Stateful OnionPIR total response (KB) | Patel et al. total response (KB) | Stateful OnionPIR total request (KB) | Patel et al. total request (KB) | Stateful OnionPIR total compute (s) | Patel et al. total compute (s) | Stateful OnionPIR cost (cents) | Patel et al. cost (cents) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2^16 | 256 | 7,132 | 75.1 | 34 | 13.7 | 0.1 | 0.006 | 0.061 |
| 2^18 | 256 | 18,928 | 87.3 | 36 | 29.5 | 0.4 | 0.010 | 0.162 |
| 2^20 | 256 | 66,114 | 88.8 | 40 | 50.1 | 0.8 | 0.016 | 0.567 |
| 2^24 | 256 | 1,009,832 | 131.0 | 64 | 287.6 | 3.1 | 0.081 | 8.668 |

Stateful OnionPIR reduces computation by 1.8x to 22x over stateless OnionPIR across the tested database sizes (larger reduction at larger N), at a stated cost of doubled per-query response size (128 KB stateless to 256 KB total stateful) and a 1.1x-2x increase in request size. Compared to Patel et al., stateful OnionPIR's amortized response size is 27x to 3,900x smaller (256 KB fixed versus up to 1,009,832 KB at N=2^24, because Patel et al.'s offline phase downloads the entire database). Patel et al.'s own computation is smaller than stateful OnionPIR's (its offline phase requires no public-key computation, and the paper states it chose a larger subset size k for Patel et al. specifically to reduce that scheme's online computation), but stateful OnionPIR's monetary cost is 10x to 107x lower than Patel et al.'s across the tested sizes because of the response-size difference.

Comparison to other single-server PIR systems, cited from those systems' own reported figures, not independently re-measured on this paper's hardware except where stated: XPIR (Aguilar-Melchor et al.) takes about 383 seconds of server computation to retrieve a 30 KB entry from a 1-million-entry database (slightly less than OnionPIR's own measured cost for a comparable configuration) but has a 17 MB request size and about 100x response overhead. SealPIR reduces request size to 32 KB via query compression but keeps about 100x response overhead, matching XPIR on that metric. Two concurrent 2021 systems are compared: Park and Tibouchi's construction achieves 16x response overhead but more than doubles computation cost relative to SealPIR; Ali et al.'s scheme, measured by this paper's authors for a 60 KB entry from a 1-million-entry database (a size chosen because Ali et al.'s scheme performs best at multiples of 20 KB and OnionPIR at multiples of 30 KB, so 60 KB is used as the common comparison point), takes about 900 seconds of computation, 357 KB response size, and 119 KB request size, versus OnionPIR's own measured 800 seconds, 256 KB response size, and 64 KB request size for the same 60 KB-entry, 1-million-entry configuration.

### Parameters
- Polynomial degree n = 4096 (SEAL BFV scheme parameter).
- Ciphertext coefficient modulus q = 124 bits.
- Plaintext modulus t = 60 bits.
- Resulting ciphertext expansion factor F = 4.2x.
- Computational security level: approximately 111 bits, per the Albrecht et al. LWE estimator.
- Database entry size: fixed at 30 KB throughout the main evaluation (60 KB used only in the direct comparison against Ali et al.'s scheme, which performs best at multiples of 20 KB).
- Database sizes N tested: 2^16, 2^18, 2^20, 2^24 entries.
- Stateful-PIR partition count c = 500 (both stateful OnionPIR and the Patel et al. baseline, at every tested N).
- Stateful-PIR subset size k for stateful OnionPIR: 8, 16, 16, 64 at N = 2^16, 2^18, 2^20, 2^24 respectively (paper states this was chosen for a good computation/request-size trade-off, not derived from a closed-form rule).
- Stateful-PIR subset size k for Patel et al. baseline: sqrt(N)/2 at every N, per that scheme's own original paper's recommendation.
- Hypercube dimensionality d = 2 in all existing protocols the paper discusses, including this one (paper states this is what "all existing protocols" use, not a value this paper varies).

### Stated limitations
Batched PIR (serving multiple queries from a single client more efficiently in one round) was not implemented; the paper states OnionPIR can be extended to support batched queries and that batched querying is used inside the stateful PBSR construction, but its offline-phase computation cost in the reported tables is simulated, not measured on the actual system. The paper explicitly separates this from all other reported figures, which are measured. Batched PIR generally is stated to be inapplicable in many real scenarios because a client often has only one query to make at a time. Stateful OnionPIR only applies to a static database; the paper states supporting updates to the database under the stateful framework is an open direction, not solved here. Removing the public-key operations from stateful PIR's online phase entirely, without requiring the offline phase to be rerun after every query, is stated as a promising future direction, not achieved by this construction — the cited alternative construction (Corrigan-Gibbs and Kogan) that has a very cheap online phase requires rerunning its offline phase after every single online query, which the paper states makes its overall cost worse than stateless PIR despite the cheap online step. Symmetric-key doubly-efficient PIR with preprocessing (Canetti et al., Boyle et al.) only supports a single client per preprocessed database copy, which the paper states does not match the public-database model of PIR (many clients querying one shared database) without the server storing a separate preprocessed copy per client; the public-key variant of doubly-efficient PIR requires obfuscation, which the paper states makes it impractical currently. Oblivious RAM (ORAM), a related primitive providing access-pattern privacy, is stated as solving a different problem because conventional ORAM constructions serve only a single client against a private database, and prior extensions of ORAM to multiple clients require inter-client communication, a trusted proxy, or per-client-scaling computation.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Requires the server to hold the full plaintext database and perform O(N) homomorphic operations (a dot product across all N entries, or the hypercube-decomposed equivalent) per stateless query, so server-side compute cost scales linearly with database size regardless of which entry is requested; a caller needing sub-linear per-query server computation must use the stateful variant or an orthogonal preprocessing scheme, which this paper states requires either a static database (stateful OnionPIR) or an unsolved efficient-online-phase problem (Corrigan-Gibbs/Kogan-style constructions). Requires the client and server to agree in advance on the homomorphic-encryption parameters (polynomial degree n, moduli q and t) sized to the deployment's target database entry size, since the paper's own comparison shows entry-size mismatches change which scheme is more efficient (OnionPIR is tuned for 30 KB-multiple entries, Ali et al.'s scheme for 20 KB-multiples). Requires the client to generate and hold local state (c subset sums of size k) for the stateful variant, refreshed via a periodic offline phase that itself costs response bandwidth (128 KB per offline round in the measured configuration) and compute; a caller using the stateful mode must schedule and pay for this refresh independently of individual queries. Provides single-query, single-server privacy only against a database held by one honest-but-curious server; the paper does not analyze or claim resistance to a malicious server that deviates from the protocol, and multi-server PIR variants (requiring non-colluding servers) are treated as a separate, not-implemented, family in this paper's own related-work discussion.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus. No other retrieved paper in this batch measures single-server PIR response size or computation under comparable conditions.

### References worth retrieving
- **Competing (primary baseline)**: Sebastian Angel, Hao Chen, Kim Laine, Srinath T.V. Setty, "PIR with Compressed Queries and Amortized Query Processing," IEEE S&P 2018 (SealPIR — the direct performance baseline throughout Table 3 and the request-size discussion).
- **Competing**: Carlos Aguilar-Melchor, Joris Barrier, Laurent Fousse, Marc-Olivier Killijian, "XPIR" (cited via its response-overhead and computation figures compared directly against OnionPIR: ~383 s compute, 17 MB request, ~100x response overhead at 1M entries).
- **Competing**: Sarvar Patel, Giuseppe Persiano, Kevin Yeo, "Stateful PIR" (the stateful-PIR framework this paper's stateful OnionPIR extends and directly compares against in Table 4; introduces the offline/online split and the download-entire-database-in-offline-phase design this paper's PBSR construction avoids).
- **Competing (concurrent)**: Jeongeun Park, Mehdi Tibouchi, construction on external products improving response overhead to 16x at more than double SealPIR's computation cost.
- **Competing (concurrent)**: Asra Ali, Tancrede Lepoint, Sarvar Patel, Mariana Raykova, Phillipp Schoppmann, Karn Seth, Kevin Yeo, "Communication-Computation Trade-offs in PIR," IACR ePrint 2019/1483 (directly measured by this paper's authors for a head-to-head comparison: 900 s compute, 357 KB response, 119 KB request at 60 KB entries / 1M entries, versus OnionPIR's 800 s / 256 KB / 64 KB in the same configuration).
- **Foundational**: Eyal Kushilevitz, Rafail Ostrovsky, the original hypercube-representation single-server PIR blueprint this paper's Section 3 traces the field's request-size techniques back to.
- **Foundational**: Christian Cachin, Silvio Micali, Markus Stadler, phi-hiding-assumption PIR with O(log^4 N) request size and O(log^d N) response size.
- **Foundational**: Craig Gentry, Zulfikar Ramzan, communication-efficient PIR generalizing the Cachin et al. approach, O(log^(3-o(1)) N) request size.
- **Attack/critique**: Radu Sion, Bogdan Carbunar, observation that early number-theoretic single-server PIR schemes perform slower in practice than downloading the entire database at bandwidths of a few hundred Kbps, because of O(N) big-integer modular exponentiations on the server.
- **Foundational**: Eyal Kushilevitz's original blueprint is separately foundational to the multi-server line via Benny Chor, Oded Goldreich, Eyal Kushilevitz, Madhu Sudan's information-theoretic multi-server PIR — the first multi-server construction, O(sqrt(N)) request size with two servers.
- **Foundational (stateful, two-server)**: Henry Corrigan-Gibbs, Dmitry Kogan, two-server stateful PIR with amortized sub-linear computation, plus a single-server FHE variant the paper states is much less efficient because it must rerun its offline phase after every online query.
- **Related primitive, not a competitor**: Discussion of ORAM (oblivious RAM) extensions to multi-client access, cited as having limitations (inter-client communication, a trusted proxy, or per-client-scaling computation) that keep them from substituting for PIR.

## [NASRULIN-BRAINS-22] MeritRank: Sybil Tolerant Reputation for Merit-Based Tokenomics
**Citation:** Bulat Nasrulin, Georgy Ishmaev, Johan Pouwelse. "MeritRank: Sybil Tolerant Reputation for Merit-Based Tokenomics." IEEE BRAINS, 2022. DOI 10.1109/BRAINS55737.2022.9908685.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/pdf/2207.09950
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.09950
**Domain:** F

### What it does
MeritRank computes, for each node in a decentralized system, a personalized (per-viewer) reputation score for every other node from a feedback graph of recorded contributions, so that a token-based or reward-based system can allocate rewards proportional to actual contribution rather than to token stake, while bounding — not eliminating — the reputation gain an attacker can extract by creating fake identities (Sybil nodes). Every peer i maintains its own subjective view Gi = (Vi, Ei, wi) of the global feedback graph, built by gossip propagation of feedback edges; the paper does not require any peer's view to be globally consistent, only that subjective views converge as more data propagates. A reputation score Ri(Gi, j) is computed by a peer i for a target node j over i's own subjective graph, using one of three underlying propagation algorithms: Personalized PageRank (PPR, a random walk that periodically restarts at a fixed seed node), Personalized Hitting Time (PHT, a random walk that measures the expected number of steps to first reach a target node from the seed), or MaxFlow (MFW, network-flow-based trust aggregation across all paths from seed to target).

Because feedback aggregation without restriction lets an attacker's Sybil gain grow unboundedly (the paper cites Seuken and Parkes as establishing this when all peer feedback is taken into account without restriction), MeritRank instead targets Sybil tolerance: bounding the attacker's gain — the ratio between the reputation the attacker's Sybil nodes accumulate with fake (Sybil) edges present versus with them removed — by a constant c, rather than driving the ratio to 1 (full Sybil resistance, achievable only by degenerate mechanisms such as pure direct reciprocity that discard indirect feedback entirely). Three decay mechanisms lower this bound. Transitivity decay reduces a node's reputation as a function of its distance (number of hops) from the seed node in the propagation graph, directly targeting serial attacks (an attacker chains many Sybil nodes to reach the seed). Connectivity decay reduces reputation for nodes reachable through fewer than a threshold t of distinct paths (edge- or intermediary-independent connections), targeting parallel and cycle attacks (an attacker attaches multiple Sybil nodes through one or few intermediary edges, or forms cyclic Sybil structures to trap random walks). Epoch decay reduces the weight of older contributions over time, implemented either as decay applied directly to computed reputation values or as decay applied to the underlying graph edge weights.

### Measured results
All experiments used a feedback graph derived from the MakerDAO governance forum (a decentralized autonomous organization built on Ethereum), covering all recorded forum interactions (replies, likes, posts, proposal votes) from 24 June 2019 to 26 May 2022, 153 weekly epochs. Each interaction was converted to work units using the SourceCred MakerDAO project's existing weighting convention (e.g., one like on a post contributes four work units), then compressed into a feedback graph where edge weight w(i,j) is the cumulative work-unit value of feedback from user i to user j. By epoch 153 the feedback graph held 2,057 nodes and 35,853 edges; peak activity was epoch 149, adding 1,528 new edges. A single seed node outside the graph stayed connected, with equal weights, to whichever 10 nodes were most reputable at each epoch. A 20-epoch grace period preceded every attack simulation, after which one of the top-10 most reputable nodes was selected as the attacker. Two attack patterns were simulated: a single Sybil attack (attacker adds a chosen number of Sybil nodes once, then exits) and a repeated Sybil attack (attacker adds new, zero-reputation Sybil nodes every epoch for the rest of the run). Each figure reporting a varying parameter was averaged over 10 simulation runs; the paper states the standard error across runs was small enough not to be visible on the plots.

| Result | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Attacker's gain, single Sybil attack, minimal transitivity decay (alpha=0.05) | 1.5 to 2.5 (algorithm-dependent) | 50 Sybil nodes, algorithms PPR / PHT / MFW compared |
| Attacker's gain, single Sybil attack, as alpha rises to 0.95 | decreases for all three algorithms | 50 Sybil nodes; alpha=0 excluded because it prevents random-walk termination |
| Attacker's gain, single Sybil attack, varying Sybil node count (1 to 100) | does not grow significantly except for MFW | fixed transitivity decay alpha=0.4 |
| Attacker's gain, repeated Sybil attack | consistently higher than single-attack gain across all three algorithms, most pronounced for MFW | 153 epochs, varying alpha and Sybil-nodes-per-epoch (1 to 100) |
| Sybil tolerance ranking across algorithms | PHT lowest attacker gain; PPR worse than PHT (vulnerable to cycle attacks via random-walk restarts); MFW worst (aggregates trust additively across all paths) and more computationally expensive | both single and repeated attack scenarios |
| Connectivity decay effect, no decay (beta=0) | attacker's gain grows sub-linearly with Sybil-node count | reputation algorithm PHT, transitivity decay fixed at alpha=0.05, connectivity threshold t=1 |
| Connectivity decay effect, beta=1.0 | attacker's gain eliminated entirely (reputation of Sybil nodes reachable through one intermediary drops to zero) | same configuration |
| Combined transitivity+connectivity decay | attacker's gain limited to 1.5 | both coefficients set to 0.3, 50 Sybil nodes added per epoch, algorithm PHT |
| Epoch decay effect on attacker's gain | minimal impact; gain stays consistently high with only minor fluctuation regardless of decay value or whether decay is applied to reputation values or to graph weights | repeated Sybil attack, 50 Sybil nodes per epoch, alpha fixed at 0.05 |
| Retention Index (top-100 overlap before/after decay) | connectivity decay preserves highest overlap across all decay values; transitivity decay declines linearly with alpha; epoch decay drops sharply at gamma=0.1 (63% retained) then stabilizes near 50% retained at gamma=1.0 | PHT algorithm, top 100 nodes, 153-epoch MakerDAO graph, no attack present |
| Mean Proportional Deviation, positive component | direct neighbors of the seed gain up to 7x their baseline reputation at alpha=1.0 (transitivity decay); a similarly large deviation occurs under epoch decay; connectivity decay stays comparatively flat after an initial rise | no attack present, averaged over 10 runs, algorithm PHT |
| Mean Proportional Deviation, negative component | transitivity decay at alpha=1.0 drives all non-seed-neighbor reputations to -1 (complete nullification); connectivity decay affects a smaller, sparsely connected subset (23% of MakerDAO nodes have 0 or 1 incoming connections) | same conditions |

### Parameters
| Parameter | Value used | Range tested |
|---|---|---|
| Transitivity decay coefficient alpha | primary tests at 0.05 and 0.4; sensitivity swept | 0.05, 0.2, 0.4, 0.8, 0.95 (0 excluded, prevents random-walk termination) |
| Connectivity decay coefficient beta | 0 to 1.0 | full unit interval swept in Figure 8/9 |
| Connectivity threshold t | 1 | fixed at 1 throughout (targets nodes reachable through exactly one intermediary) |
| Epoch decay coefficient gamma | 0 to 1.0 | full unit interval swept, tested against both decay-on-reputation and decay-on-weights variants |
| Number of Sybil nodes (single attack) | 1, 10, 20, 50, 100 | swept |
| Number of Sybil nodes per epoch (repeated attack) | 1, 10, 20, 50, 100 | swept |
| Grace period before attack | 20 epochs | fixed, not varied |
| Seed connections | fixed to top 10 most reputable nodes, equal weights | not varied |
| Sybil tolerance bound c (Definition IV.4) | combined transitivity+connectivity decay achieves 1 <= c <= 2 in the tested configuration | c=1 stated as full Sybil resistance, theoretically achievable only by degenerate mechanisms (e.g., pure direct reciprocity / Tit-for-Tat) that discard indirect feedback |

### Stated limitations
The paper states, citing Seuken and Parkes, that Sybil tolerance is not achievable at all (the attacker's gain becomes unbounded) if a reputation mechanism takes all peer feedback into account without restriction, which is the underlying reason decay mechanisms are necessary rather than optional. The paper states that full Sybil resistance (c=1) is achievable only by mechanisms that severely limit the reputation system's utility, citing direct-reciprocity schemes such as Tit-for-Tat that ignore indirect feedback and collaboration entirely — MeritRank explicitly accepts c>1 in exchange for retaining indirect feedback. The paper states epoch decay does not enhance Sybil tolerance in its tested repeated-attack scenario and can be counterproductive: an attacker who maintains at least one attack edge and adds a new Sybil node every epoch keeps cumulative gain unaffected by epoch decay, regardless of whether decay is applied to reputation values or to edge weights. All three decay mechanisms degrade informativeness (defined as how well decay preserves the original reputation ranking and values of honest, non-attacked participants) even in the complete absence of any Sybil attack; transitivity decay in particular inflates the reputation of nodes near the seed by up to 7x at maximum decay while driving reputation for more distant honest nodes toward -1 relative deviation. The paper states its results on informativeness are graph-dependent: the MakerDAO top-100 nodes are densely connected and highly active (about 60% active in at least half of all epochs), so the measured informativeness preservation may not generalize to a network whose most reputable nodes are less consistently active. The paper explicitly states no assumption is made about the allocation mechanism that consumes MeritRank's reputation scores, beyond that higher reputation is more likely to receive equal-or-larger reward, and states that a detailed treatment of allocation-mechanism properties is out of scope. Future work is stated as exploring alternative decay heuristics to better balance the tolerance/informativeness trade-off and further investigating epoch decay's counterproductive behavior.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
MeritRank requires a gossip protocol (external to the reputation mechanism itself) that propagates feedback-graph updates (new edges, weight changes) between peers, and each peer's reputation computation operates only over that peer's own subjective, possibly stale or incomplete view of the graph — the mechanism does not require or produce global agreement on the graph state. It requires at least one fixed seed node whose identity and trustworthiness are established outside the mechanism (the experiments fix the seed as external and connect it to the top 10 currently most-reputable nodes); the propagation algorithms (PPR, PHT, MFW) all compute scores relative to this seed, so seed selection is a precondition the paper does not itself resolve. Reputation scores are explicitly subjective per viewer, meaning no consuming component may treat a node's MeritRank score as a single global, agreed-upon value shared across all peers — an allocation mechanism built on top of it must accept per-seed, per-viewer scores as input, and the paper explicitly declines to specify or evaluate any particular allocation mechanism (it only assumes higher reputation implies equal-or-greater expected reward). Because Sybil tolerance under this design is a bounded-gain property (c >= 1), not full Sybil resistance, a consuming component cannot assume Sybil nodes receive zero reputation; the tolerance bound depends on which decay parameters are chosen, which in turn trades off directly against preserving accurate rankings for honest participants, so the choice of decay parameters is a policy decision the mechanism exposes rather than resolves.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus. This paper's Sybil-tolerance formalism (Definition IV.4, bounding attacker's gain by a constant c >= 1 rather than requiring c = 1) is consistent with — not a dispute of — SybilLimit's and Íntegro's per-attack-edge bounding results elsewhere in this corpus; MeritRank bounds a reputation-inflation ratio under a feedback-aggregation model, while SybilLimit and Íntegro bound a count of accepted or highly ranked Sybil identities under a social-graph acceptance model, and the paper does not claim equivalence between these formalisms.

### References worth retrieving
- foundational: S. Seuken, D. C. Parkes, [cited for the impossibility result that Sybil tolerance cannot be achieved if a reputation mechanism accounts for all peer feedback without restriction] [ref 33]
- competing: PPR (Personalized PageRank) — cited as a widely used reputation propagation baseline, shown here to be more vulnerable to cycle-based Sybil attacks than PHT
- competing: MaxFlow-based trust aggregation (MFW) — shown here to have the weakest Sybil tolerance of the three algorithms tested and higher computational cost
- foundational: SourceCred MakerDAO project — the work-unit weighting convention (e.g., 4 work units per like) that the paper's feedback-graph construction directly reuses
- competing: Tit-for-Tat direct reciprocity, cited via BitTorrent's use of it — the degenerate case achieving full Sybil resistance (c=1) by discarding indirect feedback entirely

### Verbatim extracts
"a reputation mechanism is Sybil-Tolerant if... the attacker's gain is bounded by some constant c" — Definition IV.4, the formal Sybil-tolerance criterion.
"if the feedback from all peers is taken into account, Sybil tolerance is not achievable" — attributed to Seuken and Parkes.
"epoch decay fails to address repeated Sybil attacks effectively" — stated experimental finding.
"a combination of transitivity decay and connectivity decay achieves a desirable level of Sybil tolerance while preserving higher informativeness" — stated conclusion.
"direct neighbors of the seed node experience an average increase in their reputation scores by a factor of 7" — measured informativeness distortion at maximum transitivity decay.
"we do not make any specific assumptions about the allocation mechanisms" — stated scope limitation on the allocation layer.

## [NEAGUE-ARXIV-25] Semantica: Decentralized Search using a LLM-Guided Semantic Tree Overlay
**Citation:** Petru Neague, Quinten Stokkink, Naman Goel, Johan Pouwelse. "Semantica: Decentralized Search using a LLM-Guided Semantic Tree Overlay." arXiv:2502.10151, 2025.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/pdf/2502.10151
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.10151
**Domain:** B

### What it does
Semantica routes a search query to the peer most likely to hold a semantically matching document, without any peer holding a global index of where documents reside. It builds a semantic overlay network (a peer topology in which peers with similar content connect to each other) by embedding each peer's documents with a pre-trained large language model (LLM, a language model trained on large text corpora) and organizing peers into a prefix tree (trie) keyed on those embeddings, in place of the exact-key hashing a distributed hash table (DHT) uses.

Tree construction: peers join sequentially at a root node; a leaf node that exceeds a capacity of L = 50 users runs 2-means clustering on the member embeddings and splits into two child nodes, each peer reassigned to the child whose centroid its embedding is closest to. A peer whose distance to the two child centroids differs by less than a threshold delta is cloned into both children (soft clustering), so a peer near a cluster boundary keeps neighbors on both sides of the split. One peer per split-node acts as custodian, storing that split's centroids and the network addresses of the corresponding child nodes, chaining custodians from root to leaf so a joining peer can descend the tree without a global index.

Each peer maintains a "known-users" list (peers reachable through proximity in the same or a nearby leaf) and derives from it a "closest-users" list of its n_cu most cosine-similar peers. Peers refine this list through neighbor-expansion rounds: a peer queries a random member of its known-users list for peers closer to itself in embedding space, repeating for a fixed number of rounds or until the list stabilizes.

Query resolution (chain-hopping): a query (itself an embedding) is sent to the peer whose embedding is closest to it. If that peer lacks a matching document, it forwards the query to the known-users-list neighbor with the highest cosine similarity to the query, repeating up to a maximum hop count. The paper assumes perfect local search — a peer holding the queried document returns it with 100% reliability, and a peer lacking it reports so with 100% reliability — and states this assumption is made to keep local search out of scope, so the reported accuracy measures routing, not local retrieval.

### Measured results

| Metric | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Closest-user recall at initialization (before any expansion round) | Semantica > 5 (absolute count out of a possible 50) vs. random-baseline ~0.4 | AOL4PS dataset filtered to 6,978 users with >=1 co-occurring document; ground truth = each user's global top-50 cosine-similarity peers over the whole dataset; delta in {0, 5e-4, 1e-3} tested |
| Closest-user recall after 10 expansion rounds | Semantica ~35 (delta=0.001) or ~30 (delta=0.0005) vs. random-baseline ~5 | same setup; random baseline = same known-users list size as the delta=0.001 configuration before expansion, but randomized membership, run through the identical expansion-round algorithm |
| Closest-user recall after 20 expansion rounds | "almost all" required users, i.e. >40 of 50, for every delta value tested | same setup |
| Clone count per user | median 1, mean 1.32, std 0.64 at delta=0.001; mean 7.45, std 8.08 at delta=0.005 | AOL4PS, full delta sweep from 0 to 5e-3 given in the paper's Table II; ~5,100 of 6,980 users have zero clones at delta=0.001 |
| Two-hop document-retrieval rate | Semantica 12.75% vs. <6% for random-query baseline and for graph-diffusion (personalized-PageRank-style) baseline at any tested teleportation/alpha value | AOL4PS, query chain-hopping vs. Giatsoglou et al.'s graph-diffusion algorithm on a Barabasi-Albert graph with matched mean degree (m=104, chosen to match Semantica's mean known-users count of ~208); delta=0.003, 10 expansion rounds for Semantica; gap between Semantica and the alternatives narrows as the query-hop/query-count budget rises toward 200-600 |
| Graph-diffusion alpha ordering | alpha=1.0 > alpha=0.9 > alpha=0.5 > alpha=0.1 in retrieval accuracy | same setup; higher alpha means less diffusion, so the paper's own result is that adding diffusion degrades retrieval accuracy relative to the plain random-graph chain-hop baseline |
| Minimum-hop-distance shift to nearest document holder | Semantica's tree shifts many documents from a distance greater than 1 to a distance of exactly 1, at the cost of shifting some documents from distance 2 to distance 3 (occasionally 4-5), and makes some documents completely unreachable (disconnected subgraphs) | comparison of a Semantica-built directed graph (delta=0.001, 10 expansion rounds) against a Barabasi-Albert random graph with matched mean degree (m=86) |
| Abstract-level headline figures | "up to ten times more semantically similar users" found; "more than two times the number of relevant documents" retrieved at same network load | These are the paper's own summary of the closest-user-recall and document-retrieval experiments above, not separate measurements |

Dataset: AOL4PS, 187,521 websites accessed by 12,907 users over three months of 2006, 1,339,101 total queries; filtered to users with at least 30 unique documents in history, then to the 6,978 users sharing at least one document with another user; each user's documents split into a 10-document test set and a training set used to compute the user's mean document embedding via BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers).

### Parameters
- Leaf capacity before split: L = 50 users.
- Soft-clustering clone threshold: delta, swept over {0, 1e-6, 5e-6, 1e-5, 5e-5, 1e-4, 5e-4, 1e-3, 3e-3, 5e-3} for the clone-count measurement; {0, 5e-4, 1e-3} for the recall-vs-expansion-rounds measurement; delta=0.003 used for the document-retrieval experiment.
- Expansion rounds: swept from 0 to 20 for the recall experiment; 10 rounds fixed for the document-retrieval and hop-distance experiments.
- Closest-users list size n_cu: not given a fixed numeric value in the excerpted sections; the comparison graphs are built to match Semantica's own resulting mean known-users count (~208 in the retrieval experiment, giving Barabasi-Albert m=104; ~86-average-degree in the hop-distance experiment, giving Barabasi-Albert m=86).
- Maximum query hops (chain-hopping): swept from 2 to 600 queries/hops in the retrieval-accuracy comparison.
- Embedding dimensionality: 768 (BERT), held constant and not varied.
- Graph-diffusion teleportation/alpha values compared: 0.1, 0.5, 0.9, 1.0.

### Stated limitations
The paper assumes perfect local search (100% true-positive and true-negative retrieval on a peer's own document set) and states this is a deliberate scope exclusion, not a claim that local search is solved. It assumes users have document overlap (co-occurrence) with at least one other user and validates this only on the AOL4PS dataset; it does not test datasets without such overlap. At delta = 0 (no cloning), the authors report expansion rounds do not improve recall, because same-leaf peers then share identical neighbor lists and querying them returns redundant information — cloning is required for expansion rounds to work at all in this design. The tree provides no re-balancing mechanism for peer departures; the authors state that without one, sustained churn could leave leaf nodes badly depopulated and degrade the tree toward its worst-case O(N) height (versus average-case O(log N)), negating the claimed complexity advantage — and state this re-balancing is out of scope for the paper. Custodian departure makes that custodian's centroid data unavailable, with no backup-custodian election implemented (described as a potential extension, not built). The experiments do not rank retrieved results; the authors state ranking could be done locally by the querying peer via cosine similarity but did not implement or measure it. At high hop/query budgets (up to 200-600), the tree-structured graph's advantage over a random comparison graph narrows and the authors state the random graph eventually overtakes it, because some documents become entirely unreachable in the tree-derived graph due to disconnected subgraphs.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
- Every peer must be able to compute or obtain an embedding for its own documents (locally via an LLM, or via an external embedding service) and for each incoming query, in a shared embedding space, before this mechanism can route anything.
- The mechanism assumes perfect local search at each peer: the rest of the system must supply an exact-match or near-exact local retrieval routine over each peer's own stored documents, since Semantica's measured accuracy is routing accuracy layered on top of an assumed-perfect local answer.
- The overlay depends on out-of-band bootstrap discovery of at least one root peer (via a bootstrap server, a public DHT, or a known reference address); this mechanism does not itself solve peer discovery for a cold-started network.
- The custodian scheme requires each split-node's centroid and address data to be held reliably by a designated peer with no replication built in; any component relying on this tree for routing must tolerate lookups failing for a period after a custodian departs, or must supply its own custodian-replication mechanism, since none is built here.
- The mechanism requires peer document sets to overlap; a corpus of purely disjoint per-peer documents (no shared interest signal) does not fit the design's stated operating assumption and was not evaluated.
- Recall performance depends on soft-clustering (a nonzero delta) being enabled together with expansion rounds; a deployment that disables cloning to save the modest per-user duplication cost also disables the mechanism by which expansion rounds improve recall.

### Contradicts
None found against other entries in this corpus. Note for synthesis: the paper's own graph-diffusion comparison (Giatsoglou et al., personalized-PageRank-style diffusion) shows diffusion degrading retrieval accuracy relative to a no-diffusion baseline at every tested alpha, which is presented as confirming, not contradicting, the diffusion paper's own reported alpha ordering.

### References worth retrieving
- **Crespo & Garcia-Molina, "Semantic Overlay Networks for P2P Systems," AP2PC 2004** — foundational: the original semantic-overlay-network concept this paper extends with LLM embeddings in place of an unspecified similarity function.
- **Giatsoglou, Krasanakis, Papadopoulos, Kompatsiaris, "A Graph Diffusion Scheme for Decentralized Content Search Based on Personalized PageRank," ICDCSW 2022** — competing: the query-mechanism baseline directly benchmarked against Semantica's chain-hopping, with disagreeing conclusions about the value of diffusion.
- **Tang, Xu, Dwarkadas, "Peer-to-Peer Information Retrieval Using Self-Organizing Semantic Overlay Networks," SIGCOMM 2003** — foundational/competing: an earlier self-organizing semantic overlay cited as already showing "low latency and high accuracy... comparable to centralized approaches," a claim worth checking directly since Semantica's motivation rests partly on it.
- **Tay et al., "Transformer Memory as a Differentiable Search Index" (DSI), NeurIPS 2022** — foundational: the trie-based "Semantically Structured Identifiers" approach this paper's tree design is explicitly modeled after.
- **Neague, Gregoriadis, Pouwelse, "De-DSI: Decentralised Differentiable Search Index," 2024** — foundational (same author group): a prior decentralization step over DSI that this paper states still requires periodic online learning to update its index, a limitation this paper claims to remove.
- **Li, Loo, Hellerstein, Kaashoek, Karger, Morris, "On the Feasibility of Peer-to-Peer Web Indexing and Search," IPTPS 2003** — this is the "standing bound" paper named in BRIEF.md section 8, item 1; the brief already flags it as needing a check for whether anything has overturned its ~6 MB/query bound at web scale — worth cross-referencing against Semantica's per-query communication figures.
- **Maymounkov & Mazieres, "Kademlia," IPTPS 2002** — foundational: the DHT baseline this paper contrasts its trie-based approach against for exact- versus semantic-key routing (already in corpus per BRIEF.md section 7).
- **Stoica et al., "Chord," SIGCOMM 2001 / TON 2003** — foundational: cited as the other classical DHT baseline for exact-key routing.

- "Semantica can retrieve more than two times the number of relevant documents given the same network load."
