## [POST-NSDI-11] Bazaar: Strengthening User Reputations in Online Marketplaces

**Citation:** Ansley Post, Vijit Shah, Alan Mislove. "Bazaar: Strengthening user reputations in online marketplaces." USENIX NSDI, 2011.
**Retrieved:** full text
**Source URL:** https://www.usenix.org/legacy/event/nsdi11/tech/full_papers/Post.pdf
**Domain:** F

### What it does
Bazaar bounds the amount of monetary fraud any user of an online marketplace can commit, regardless of how many identities that user controls, by computing a network flow value between buyer and seller instead of summing feedback counts. Every successful transaction between two identities creates or strengthens an undirected weighted link between them in a "risk network," where the weight equals the aggregate monetary value of past successful transactions between that pair. Before a transaction proceeds, the marketplace operator asks Bazaar for the maximum flow (the greatest total weight that can be routed via any combination of paths, limiting each edge to its own weight, the standard graph max-flow value) between the buyer and seller in the risk network; if that value is below the proposed transaction amount, the transaction is flagged as potentially fraudulent. If the transaction proceeds, Bazaar selects a set of paths between buyer and seller whose combined weight covers the transaction amount and temporarily lowers each path's weight by its assigned share of that amount, placing that credit "on hold" until feedback arrives. Positive buyer feedback restores the held weight and adds a new direct link (of the transaction's value) between buyer and seller; neutral feedback or a timeout restores the held weight without adding a link; negative feedback makes the reduction permanent, since a fraudulent seller's own risk-network links are what get depleted. Because the max-flow value across any network cut is bounded by that cut's total weight, a set of colluding or Sybil identities can defraud non-malicious users only up to the total weight of the links crossing the cut between the malicious identities and the rest of the network — a bound independent of how many identities the malicious party splits itself into or how much fictitious feedback it manufactures among its own identities. New users bootstrap by having real-world friends grant "virtual" starter links (at the friend's own reputational risk) or by depositing money in escrow with the marketplace operator, which then creates links of that value to random other users. To make max-flow computation tractable, Bazaar builds a "multi-graph": a series of nested subgraphs G_0 (the full risk network), G_1, G_2, ... where G_i keeps only edges of weight at least k^i for a configurable base k (suggested value 2); a flow query starts at the sparsest graph containing the needed weight and only descends to denser graphs as required, since Bazaar only needs to confirm the flow value exceeds a threshold, not compute its exact value.

### Measured results
| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| Crawled dataset: 8,874,521 items of buyer-to-seller feedback across 3,168,455 distinct United-Kingdom users, spanning 5 eBay auction categories (Clothes, Collectibles, Computing, Electronics, Home/Garden), average prices £8.90-£21.31 | eBay.co.uk, 90-day feedback window (eBay's own retention limit), collected by breadth-first-search web scraping starting from one user, restricted to UK-located users and 5 named categories |
| Raising the link-weight threshold from £1 to £20 discards about 80% of risk-network links while the largest strongly connected component still contains most of the remaining nodes; for some categories the largest SCC does not fragment until the threshold passes £100 | Same eBay crawl, per-category risk networks built from positive-feedback transaction links |
| Multi-graph max-flow verification is 1.92x to 2.86x faster than single-graph max-flow, with per-category average query times of 6.29s (Clothes), 1.18s (Collectibles), 1.66s (Computing), 1.41s (Electronics), 5.34s (Home/Garden) versus 18.0s/2.53s/3.78s/2.71s/11.6s single-graph | 1,000 randomly selected user pairs per category, transaction amounts drawn from the observed auction-price trace, multi-graph base k=2, measured on a 2.83 GHz Intel Xeon machine |
| Multi-graph storage overhead is 221%-283% relative to a single graph, but 4.44-18.4 MB absolute, across 12-14 graph levels | Same 5 per-category risk networks, k=2 |
| At the Clothes category's average query time (6.29s), one server core completes 13,736 max-flow calculations per day; the trace's peak daily auction volume in that category was 80,846, implying a minimum 6-core server; concurrent-access conflicts on the same link occurred in 0.0165% of cases in that category | Same Clothes-category risk network and query set |
| No more than 5% (range 1.11%-4.68% across the 5 categories) of genuinely non-fraudulent transactions are incorrectly flagged as potentially fraudulent | Simulation using 80% of the crawled feedback to build the risk network, remaining 20% replayed as transactions, restricted to users with at least 5 observed transactions in the 90-day window, 10 runs per data point with different random seeds, no malicious users injected |
| Aggregate fraud a malicious user can conduct before all further transactions are flagged is empirically bounded by (and matches, within measurement noise) the total value of that user's prior non-fraudulent transactions (the y=x line) | Same simulation setup with 1% of users randomly designated malicious (following a cited prior study's methodology), each malicious user tested against randomly selected counterparties |
| Bazaar would have flagged 29.9%-42.6% (36.0% overall, £164,791.55) of all auctions that resulted in negative feedback in the 90-day trace as potentially fraudulent before they occurred | Same 90-day, 5-category eBay trace, computed from each seller's aggregate positive versus negative feedback value rather than from the live simulation |

### Parameters
- Multi-graph weight-threshold base k: suggested value 2 (each graph level keeps only edges of weight at least k^i)
- Feedback timeout T: configurable; used-value not stated as a specific number of days in the retrieved text
- Malicious-user fraction in the fraud-bound simulation: 1% of users, following a cited prior study's methodology
- Minimum observed-transaction count for a user to be included in the fraud-detection simulation: 5 transactions in the 90-day window
- Train/test split for simulation: 80% of feedback used to build the initial risk network, 20% replayed as simulated transactions
- Number of simulation runs per data point: 10, with different random seeds
- Purchase-time imputation: for the 45.4% of auctions lacking a recorded purchase time (fixed-price, multi-buyer auctions), a delay is subtracted from the feedback time, drawn from the observed delay distribution of auctions where both times are known
- Hardware for max-flow timing measurements: single machine, 2.83 GHz Intel Xeon processor

### Stated limitations
The paper states protecting sellers from fraudulent buyers is left to future work, noting this is partly mitigated because marketplace operators typically let sellers verify payment before shipping. It states that decentralizing the risk network (removing the requirement that the marketplace operator holds full knowledge of all transactions) is an open research question and future work, and that it does not know of any decentralized online marketplace to motivate a concrete design. It states a targeted-attack vector exists in which an attacker who has already accumulated legitimate transaction links can purchase a target seller's goods and give deliberately negative feedback to damage that seller's own outgoing links, though it argues Bazaar raises the cost of this attack relative to existing feedback systems because the attacker must first accumulate non-fraudulent transaction history. It states that a compromised user account lets an attacker conduct fraud up to that account's own Bazaar-bounded limit, an attack not unique to Bazaar but still bounded, unlike under unbounded feedback-based reputation. It states that if a malicious identity is the sole link between two otherwise-connected malicious identities and the rest of the network, the max-flow bound can be lower than the raw sum of that identity's prior successful transactions, because cut capacity, not link count, determines the bound. Multi-graph max-flow queries that fail (no sufficient-weight path set exists) must traverse every graph level and take longer on average than queries that succeed and can terminate early; the paper reports that treating queries running longer than 2 seconds as failures in the Computing category would misclassify only 5.5% of eventually-successful queries while lowering the average query time from 1.66s to 0.70s, an optimization not applied in the reported headline results.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Bazaar requires the marketplace operator to hold complete, authoritative knowledge of every transaction and its outcome (buyer identity, seller identity, monetary amount, and eventual feedback), because the risk network and its max-flow computation are built and queried centrally by that operator; the paper states explicitly that decentralizing this knowledge is unsolved. It requires a feedback channel from buyer to marketplace operator with three outcomes (positive, negative, neutral) plus a configurable timeout T that resolves silence to the neutral case. It requires the ability to place transaction weight "on hold" atomically at the time a transaction is authorized, meaning the operator's transaction-processing pipeline must call into Bazaar's flow computation before finalizing a sale, not asynchronously afterward. It assumes link weights are non-negative and that a transaction's value is fully known at authorization time, since the flow-reduction bookkeeping charges an exact monetary amount to specific paths. The bootstrapping mechanism assumes some new users have existing marketplace users willing to vouch for them via virtual links, or that the operator is willing to hold user funds in escrow; a system lacking either path leaves new users with zero max-flow to everyone and every one of their transactions flagged. It assumes rational-actor incentive alignment for honest feedback: the paper's own reasoning for why buyers report truthfully depends on the buyer's own links being at stake, meaning it does not defend against buyers who have no remaining stake in their own risk-network position.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus as of this batch. Note for later composition checking: Bazaar's core guarantee (fraud bounded by cut value, not identity count) depends on the operator's full-network view; this composes poorly with any anonymity or partial-visibility tier that hides identities' transaction graphs from a shared computation point, since the max-flow computation cannot be run over information the operator does not hold.

### References worth retrieving
- Douceur. "The Sybil Attack." IPTPS 2002 — foundational (defines the Sybil attack that Bazaar's cut-based bound targets)
- Mislove, Post, Gummadi, Druschel. "Ostra: Leveraging trust to thwart unwanted communication" — foundational (the paper's own prior link-credit mechanism, applied here to marketplace transactions rather than message delivery, per the target-record's classification)
- Danezis, Mittal. "SybilInfer: Detecting Sybil Nodes using Social Networks" — competing
- Yu, Gibbons, Kaminsky, Xiao. "SybilLimit" — competing
- Yu, Kaminsky, Gibbons, Flaxman. "SybilGuard" — competing
- Tran, Min, Li, Subramanian. "Sybil-Resilient Online Content Voting" — competing (source of the 1% malicious-user-fraction methodology this paper reuses)
- Mislove, Marcon, Gummadi, Druschel, Bhattacharjee. "Measurement and Analysis of Online Social Networks" — foundational (source of the dense-core observation this paper's multi-graph design builds on)
- Chau, Pandit, Faloutsos. "Detecting fraudulent personalities in networks of online auctioneers" — competing (graph-based auction fraud detection)
- Pandit, Chau, Wang, Faloutsos. "NetProbe: a fast and scalable system for fraud detection in online auction networks" — competing
- DeFigueiredo, Barr. "TrustDavis: A Non-Exploitable Online Reputation System" — competing
- Ghosh, Mahdian, Reeves, Pennock, Fugger. (reputation/mechanism-design paper, full title not visible in the retrieved bibliography fragment) — competing
- Ford, Fulkerson. "Maximal flow through a network" — foundational (max-flow algorithm baseline)
- Goldberg, Rao. "Flows in Undirected Unit Capacity Networks" — foundational (alternative max-flow algorithm considered and rejected as too costly)

## [QUELLE-PLOSONE-25] Bluesky: Network topology, polarization, and algorithmic curation
**Citation:** Dorian Quelle, Alexandre Bovet. "Bluesky: Network topology, polarization, and algorithmic curation." PLOS ONE, 2025. DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0318034.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.17571
**Source URL:** https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0318034
**Domain:** K

### What it does
The paper measures the deployed Bluesky network — a decentralized microblogging system built on the
AT Protocol — using complete user repository data pulled directly from the network rather than a
platform-supplied API export. Because Bluesky is decentralized, any party holding a user's decentralized
identifier (DID) can retrieve that user's repository: the authors first queried the centralized DID PLC
directory (a lookup service mapping each DID to the network address of that user's personal data server,
PDS) to resolve each user's PDS address, then queried that PDS directly for the user's repository
contents (posts, likes, reposts, follows, blocks, feed creations). Starting from a seed list of 5.28
million user IDs posted publicly by a Bluesky contributor in March 2024, they recursively expanded the
dataset by extracting data for every user referenced within already-downloaded data, repeating until no
new users were found, and stored the result in a relational database with one table per interaction type.

The paper characterizes four interaction layers, each treated as a distinct directed graph on the same
user set: Followership (persistent, edge exists until explicitly removed, does not by itself indicate
agreement), Replies (non-persistent, edge per reply within a thread), Reposts (non-persistent, equivalent
to a Twitter retweet, indicates willingness to redistribute content to one's own followers), and Likes
(non-persistent, indicates topical interest but does not itself redistribute content to followers). It
separately measures Bluesky's user-generated "custom feed" mechanism, in which any user can publish a
feed generator ranging from simple keyword/regex matching to machine-learning-based ranking, which other
users can then subscribe to or like; a feed's rank in Bluesky's own feed-discovery surface is driven by
its like count, which the paper measures as a proxy for adoption.

### Measured results

| Finding | Figure | Conditions |
|---|---|---|

| Custom feeds created | 39,639 | Same dataset, by 18,352 distinct active users who created at least one feed |
| Users who liked at least one custom feed | 139,033 of 5,000,000 (~2.8%) | Same dataset; these users liked feeds a combined 295,902 times |
| Mean likes received per feed | 2.128 (σ=5.932, max 1,799) | Distribution over all 39,639 feeds (Table 3) |
| Mean feeds created per feed-creating user | 2.161 (σ=13.931, max 1,828) | Distribution over the 18,352 feed-creating users (Table 3) |
| Mean feeds liked per feed-liking user | 14.783 (σ=156.641, max 16,132) | Distribution over the 139,033 feed-liking users (Table 3) |
| Total interaction-table row counts | Follows 149,650,293 / Posts 206,346,303 / Likes 771,009,280 / Reposts 81,655,778 / Blocks 8,357,905 / Feeds 39,639 | Full dataset, Feb 2023-May 2024 (Table 5) |
| Unique users per interaction type | Follows 3,844,491 / Posts 2,339,109 / Likes 2,581,744 / Reposts 1,197,330 / Blocks 479,427 / Feeds 18,352 | Same dataset (Table 5) |

| Stance shift on Israel-Palestine conflict, month before vs. after Oct 7, 2023 | Neutral posts 82.86% -> 37.98%; Oct 2023: pro-Israel 33.01% vs pro-Palestine 28.99%; final observed month: pro-Israel 20.74% vs pro-Palestine 39.00% | Daily post-stance classification (1,000 posts manually labeled by authors, 1,000 more labeled by Appen.com crowdworkers, used to train/validate the classifier applied to the 1.3 million-post subset) |

### Parameters
| Parameter | Value used |
|---|---|
| Seed user-ID list size | 5.28 million (posted publicly by a Bluesky contributor, March 26, 2024) |
| Final analyzed user count | 5,000,000 |
| Repository resolution path | DID -> DID PLC directory -> PDS network address -> per-user repository query |
| Crawl expansion rule | recursive: any user referenced in already-downloaded data is added and queried, repeated to fixed point |
| Observation window | February 2023 (platform launch) to May 20, 2024 |
| Stance-classification training data | 1,000 posts labeled by the authors + 1,000 labeled by Appen.com crowdworkers, drawn from the 1.3 million-post Israel-Palestine subset |
| Political-domain bias source | Media Bias/Fact Check (MBFC) ratings |
| Clustering-coefficient normalization | ratio against a configuration-model random graph with the same per-node degree sequence |

### Stated limitations
The paper carries no section titled "Limitations." In the Discussion, the authors state that only a
small minority of users have liked a feed despite the availability of almost 40,000 feeds, describing
feed-mechanism adoption as limited relative to the platform's user base. They state that Bluesky's
predominantly left-leaning political composition does not imply uniformity of opinion on every issue,
evidenced by the measured Israel-Palestine stance split, and state as an open question for future work
whether issue-specific polarization on the platform reflects healthy debate or the same affective
polarization and political sectarianism documented on Twitter and Facebook, without resolving that
question themselves. They note the Followership network shows the steepest post-opening activity
decline, which they attribute to new users following platform-suggested profiles without further
engagement, stated as an interpretation rather than a directly measured cause.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The measurement method itself depends on two properties of the AT Protocol's decentralization design:
a centralized DID-to-PDS directory (DID PLC) must be queryable to resolve any user's data-hosting
location, and each user's personal data server must serve that user's repository to any requester who
holds the user's DID, with no access control gating repository reads. Both properties are what make the
"complete repository" crawl possible without the platform operator's cooperation; a design that added
per-repository read authorization would break this measurement method as constructed. The custom-feed
mechanism requires no coordination beyond each feed generator computing its own ranking (by whatever
method its creator chooses) and users individually subscribing or liking; feed adoption as measured here
is a pure demand-side signal — the paper found no server-side promotion in this dataset was analyzed as
an amplification factor, since Table 3 measures like counts directly rather than any impression
metric. The measured near-power-law degree distributions (Table 1) and above-baseline clustering
coefficients across all four interaction layers place a requirement on any component whose performance
assumes uniform user degree or Erdos-Renyi-like structure: such assumptions do not hold for Bluesky's
observed graph, at any of the four interaction-layer definitions used here.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus.

### References worth retrieving
- **Kleppmann, Frazee, Gold, Graber, Holmgren, Ivy et al., "Bluesky and the AT Protocol: Usable Decentralized Social Media"** — foundational protocol description, cited [1]; describes the feed-generator "marketplace of algorithms" design this paper measures adoption of.
- **Failla, Rossetti, "'I'm in the Bluesky Tonight': Insights from a Year Worth of Social Data," arXiv** — competing independent measurement of the same platform, cited [6]; comparison numbers on Bluesky's network structure from a separate dataset.
- **Zignani, Gaito, Rossi, "Follow the 'mastodon': Structure and evolution of a decentralized online social network"** — competing measurement of the sibling Fediverse platform, cited [7]; already flagged from LIU-PACMHCI-25 and POLINSKI-CCR-24.
- **Aliapoulios, Bevensee, Blackburn, Bradlyn, De Cristofaro, Stringhini et al., "An early look at the Parler..."** — competing measurement of an alternative decentralized-adjacent social platform, cited [8].
- **Jeong, Jiang, Tan, Bernard, Liu, "BlueTempNet: A Temporal Multi-network Dataset of Social..."** — foundational, a competing/companion dataset paper on Bluesky, cited [28].
- **Cinelli, De Francisci Morales, Galeazzi, Quattrociocchi, Starnini, "The echo chamber effect on social media"** — foundational for the polarization-measurement methodology, cited [42].
- **Gehl, Zulli, "The digital covenant: non-centralized platform governance on the mastodon social network"** — foundational/competing governance study of the sibling Fediverse platform, cited [34].

## [RAMAN-IMC-19] Challenges in the Decentralised Web: The Mastodon Case

**Citation:** Aravindh Raman, Sagar Joglekar, Emiliano De Cristofaro, Nishanth Sastry, Gareth Tyson. "Challenges in the Decentralised Web: The Mastodon Case." ACM Internet Measurement Conference (IMC), 2019. DOI 10.1145/3355369.3355572.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.05801
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.05801
**Domain:** J+K

### What it does
The paper measures how independent, federated server operation in a deployed decentralized social network (Mastodon, a microblogging platform built on the ActivityPub federation protocol, where each independently run server is called an instance) produces concentration despite no central operator, and quantifies how much of the network's connectivity and content availability a small number of instance or hosting-provider failures can remove. The authors built three datasets by polling each instance's public API every five minutes over 15 months for metadata (user counts, toot counts, federation subscriptions, online status), crawling the full post history (toots) of every instance reachable in May 2018, and scraping follower relationships to build both a user-level follower graph and a derived instance-level federation graph (an edge from instance A to instance B exists if at least one user on A follows a user on B). They then run node-removal simulations on these graphs: iteratively strip the highest-ranked instances or hosting providers (Autonomous Systems, the routing-visible network blocks instances are hosted within) and measure the size of the largest connected component (LCC, the largest set of nodes still mutually reachable) and the number of disconnected components after each removal round. They separately simulate three toot-replication strategies — no replication (a toot exists only on its home instance and is fetched on demand), subscription-based replication (a toot is copied to every instance that has at least one user following its author, matching Mastodon's own caching behavior but assuming, unlike Mastodon, a global index such as a Distributed Hash Table so replicas remain discoverable), and random replication onto n randomly chosen instances — and measure toot availability under the same removal rounds.

### Measured results

| Quantity | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Unique instances indexed | 4,328 | From mnm.social instance directory, snapshots every 5 minutes, April 11 2017 to July 27 2018; 3.1% run the Pleroma server software, which federates with Mastodon over the same ActivityPub protocol |
| Total instance-metadata data points | ~500 million | Same 15-month, 5-minute-interval collection |
| Instances crawled for toots | 1.75K (of 4,328) | May 2018; instances filtered to those online at crawl time; 21.3% of all instances observed across the full 15-month cycle went offline and never returned |
| Public toots collected | 67 million, from 239K unique users | May 2018 crawl, 10 threads across 7 machines; covers 62% of the toot population reported by instance metadata (20% of the missing 38% were set private, the remainder hosted on instances that blocked crawling) |
| Follower graph size | 853K user accounts, 9.25M follower links | Crawled July 2018 from the 239K users who had tooted at least once; 87.9% of account names unique to one instance, 8.3% on two, 3.8% on three or more |
| Instance downtime distribution | ~half of instances under 5% downtime; 4.5% of instances up 99.5% of the time (covering 44% of toots); 11% of instances inaccessible more than half the time | 5-minute-granularity polling over the 15-month cycle; outages counted only when an instance later returns (persistently dead instances excluded) |
| Median daily downtime by instance size | <10K toots: 12%; 100K-1M toots: 0.34%; >1M toots: 2.1% | Same 5-minute polling; correlation between toot count and downtime measured at -0.04 |
| Mastodon vs Twitter average downtime | Mastodon 10.95% vs Twitter 1.25% | Twitter data via pingdom.com probing every minute, Feb-Dec 2007, when Twitter was roughly 1.5 years old (comparable age to the Mastodon snapshot) |
| Certificate-authority outage, single day | 105 instances down simultaneously on 2018-07-23, removing nearly 200K toots; responsible for 6.3% of all observed outages | Caused by simultaneous 90-day expiry of Let's Encrypt certificates issued together; Let's Encrypt used by >85% of instances |
| AS-wide outages | 6 ASes observed to fail; largest single event (AS9370, Sakura) removed 97 instances and 3.89M toots at once; most frequent (AS12322, Free SAS) failed 15 times, removing 9 instances each time; cumulative effect of all 6: temporary removal of 4.98M toots and 41.5K user accounts, under 1% of all observed failure events | Failure defined as all instances hosted in one AS becoming unavailable simultaneously; only ASes hosting >=8 instances counted, to avoid mistaking coincidence for AS failure |
| Outage duration distribution | 98% of instances go down at least once; 25% unavailable for at least 1 continuous day; of those, 21% last exactly around 1 day and 7% last over a month; 14% of all users unable to reach their instance for a full day at least once; worst single day (2017-04-15) made 6% of all global toots unavailable | Same 15-month polling window |
| Social-graph resilience to user removal | Without removal, 99.95% of users in the LCC; removing the top 1% highest-degree users (by follower count) drops the LCC to 26.38% of all users | Iterative removal of the top 1% remaining highest-degree nodes per round from the 853K-user follower graph |
| Twitter social-graph comparison | Twitter's 2011 graph: 95% of users in LCC with no removal; removing top 10% of users still leaves 80% in the LCC | 2011 Twitter follower dataset (Leskovec and Mcauley), same age-matched comparison logic as the downtime comparison |
| Federation-graph (instance-level) resilience to instance removal | Linear decay of LCC size as top N instances removed, ranked by users hosted or toots posted | Iterative top-N removal on the instance federation graph GF (instances as nodes, an edge when at least one follower link crosses between them) |
| Federation-graph resilience to AS removal | Before removal, 92% of instances and 96% of users in a single LCC; removing the top 5 ASes (by number of instances hosted: OVH SAS, Scaleway, Sakura Internet, Hetzner Online, GMO Internet, together hosting 42% of all instances) produces a 49% reduction in LCC size, leaving an LCC covering only 45% of instances and 66% of users | Iterative top-N AS removal on GF; ranking by users hosted instead of instances hosted shatters GF into 272 components after 5 removals, versus 139 components when ranked by instances hosted, because the top 5 ASes by users cover only 20% of instances but 85% of users, while the top 5 by instance count cover 42% of instances and 33.6% of users |
| Toot availability, no replication | Removing top 10 instances (ranked by toot count): 62.69% of all toots become unavailable; removing top 10 ASes: 90.1% of toots become unavailable | Simulation on the 67M-toot dataset; a toot counted unavailable once its sole hosting instance is removed |
| Toot availability, subscription-based replication | Removing top 10 instances: only 2.1% of toots unavailable (vs. 62.69% with no replication); removing top 10 ASes: 18.66% unavailable (vs. 90.1%) | Same removal simulation, assuming a global index (such as a Distributed Hash Table) makes every existing replica discoverable from any surviving instance |
| Toot availability, random replication vs subscription replication | After removing 25 instances: subscription-based replication reaches 95% availability; random replication with just n=1 extra copy reaches 99.2% availability | Random replication tested at n = {1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 9} random target instances per toot, compared against subscription-based and no-replication baselines, same removal simulation |
| Subscription-replication skew | 9.7% of toots receive zero replicas (their author has no followers on other instances); 23% of toots receive more than 10 replicas (authored by popular users) | Measured over the same 67M-toot dataset under the subscription-based replication rule |
| Hosting concentration | Top 3 ASes host 62% of all global users; Amazon alone hosts >30% of all users while used by only 6% of instances; Cloudflare hosts 31.7% of toots across 5.4% of instances | Instance IP addresses mapped to AS via MaxMind, same 4,328-instance dataset |
| Country concentration | Japan hosts 25.5% of instances and 41% of users; the US hosts 21.4% of instances; France hosts 16% of instances but only 9.2% of users | Same instance dataset, geolocated via MaxMind |
| Content-generation concentration | 78% of instances produce under 10% of their own toots on their federated timeline (i.e. rely on toots relayed from other instances); 5% of instances produce zero home toots; correlation between an instance's own toot volume and how often its toots get replicated elsewhere: 0.97 | Measured from the federated timeline composition of every instance in the toots dataset |

### Parameters
LCC-removal simulations proceed in rounds removing the top 1% of remaining nodes per round for the user follower graph, and top-N instances or top-N ASes (N swept from small values up to several hundred/800+ instances and up to 20+ ASes) for the instance federation graph. Random-replication factor n tested at {1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 9} extra copies per toot. Ranking criteria varied across three axes for instance removal (number of users hosted, number of toots posted, number of instances hosted) and for AS removal (number of instances hosted, number of users hosted).

### Stated limitations
The dataset captures a moving target: because measurement infrastructure was deployed progressively, the exact time windows of the instance, toot, and follower datasets differ slightly, though the authors state this does not affect the analysis. The toot dataset covers only 62% of the toot population that instance-reported metadata indicates exists; the missing 38% is split between toots marked private (about 20%) and toots on instances that blocked crawling (the remainder), and the authors state they therefore avoided deeper semantic content analysis and confined themselves to instance-level activity. It is impossible to determine whether two accounts with the same name on different instances belong to the same person, so the authors treat every per-instance account as a separate graph node. The authors cannot confirm the exact cause of most instance unavailability, nor determine which operators run load balancers or replicated back-ends behind their instance. AS-wide removal is presented explicitly as a rare, worst-case theoretical scenario rather than a routine failure mode, though six such events were observed within the 15-month measurement window. The random and subscription replication simulations assume every toot is treated as equally important, though the authors note more recent toots are in practice more important; they also assume a global index (e.g. a Distributed Hash Table) exists to make any surviving replica discoverable, a mechanism Mastodon does not currently implement, since Mastodon's own subscription-based caching keeps replicas visible only to users local to the caching instance. The random replication strategy as tested does not weight replica placement by an instance's available storage; the authors state this is a practical concern for a real deployment. Future work stated by the authors: a longitudinal study of the same issues over a longer period, mitigations for malicious bots, an evaluation of Mastodon's existing instance-blocking mechanism and its effect on the social graph, and a study of alt-right community migration onto Mastodon-derived forks such as Gab.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A replication mechanism intended to improve content availability under instance or AS failure requires a global index reachable from any surviving instance, because a replica that exists only on instances that also fail, or that is invisible outside the instance that cached it (Mastodon's current subscription-cache behavior), does not restore availability; the paper's own subscription-replication figures assume such an index and are not achievable under Mastodon's actual current caching visibility. A component performing follower-graph-driven (subscription-based) replication inherits the skew of the underlying social graph: because popular authors' followers cluster on the same small set of popular instances, subscription-based replica placement concentrates replicas on exactly the instances most likely to be targeted or to fail together in an AS-wide event, and any resilience analysis of that replication strategy must account for this correlated placement rather than assuming independent replica locations. A capacity-ordered or hosting-diversity mechanism placed above the federation layer needs per-instance hosting-provider (AS) information, since AS-level co-location, not merely instance count, determines how much connectivity a single correlated failure can remove. Any content-location or discovery mechanism relying on the federation subscription graph for reachability must tolerate a linear (not catastrophic) degradation under ordinary instance-count removal, but should expect a step-function collapse in reachability specifically when removal is concentrated on a small number of hosting providers with disproportionate user share, since the paper measures a materially worse component-count outcome (272 vs. 139 components after removing 5 ASes) when providers are ranked by user share rather than by instance count.

### Contradicts
None found.

- A. Braunstein, L. Dall'Asta, G. Semerjian, L. Zdeborová, "Network dismantling," Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 113(44), 2016 — foundational (cited as explanation for the federation graph's more uniform degree distribution producing linear rather than catastrophic decay).

## [RASHMI-TIT-11] Optimal Exact-Regenerating Codes for Distributed Storage at the MSR and MBR Points via a Product-Matrix Construction

**Citation:** K. V. Rashmi, Nihar B. Shah, P. Vijay Kumar. "Optimal Exact-Regenerating Codes for Distributed Storage at the MSR and MBR Points via a Product-Matrix Construction." IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, 2011. DOI 10.1109/TIT.2011.2159049.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/abs/1005.4178 (arXiv:1005.4178v2, 20 Jan 2011)
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/1005.4178
**Domain:** C

### What it does
A regenerating code repairs a failed storage node by downloading a fraction of the data stored at each of several helper nodes rather than the entire file, reducing the total repair-time network traffic below what full-file download requires. An [n, k, d] regenerating code stores a file across n nodes so that any k nodes reconstruct the whole file, and any d of the remaining n-1 nodes serve as helpers that each transmit beta symbols (beta <= alpha, where alpha is the number of symbols stored per node) during repair, for a total repair bandwidth of d*beta. The paper targets exact-regeneration: the replacement node's content is bit-for-bit identical to the failed node's original content, not merely equivalent for later data-reconstruction. It gives a product-matrix framework in which each stored node's content is a fixed linear function (row of an encoding matrix Psi applied to a product of two smaller matrices) of the source symbols, and proves this framework yields explicit codes meeting the cut-set bound (Theorem 1 of prior work, restated as equation 2: B <= sum over i=0..k-1 of min(alpha, (d-i)*beta)) at the Minimum Bandwidth Regenerating (MBR) point for every feasible [n, k, d], and at the Minimum Storage Regenerating (MSR) point for every [n, k, d] with d >= 2k-2. Unlike prior exact-regenerating constructions, n is a free parameter independent of d, so the number of storage nodes can be chosen and later changed without being tied to d+1.

### Measured results
This is a theory paper: every reported figure is a proven achievability or non-achievability bound, not an experimental measurement.

| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| Cut-set bound: B <= sum_{i=0}^{k-1} min(alpha, (d-i)*beta) | Equation (2), general [n,k,d] regenerating code, proven in prior work [4],[5] via network-coding cut-set analysis, restated here as the target this paper's constructions must meet with equality |
| MSR point parameters: alpha = B/k, beta = B/(k*(d-k+1)) | Equation (3), obtained by minimizing alpha first, then beta |
| MBR point parameters: beta = 2B/(k*(2d-k+1)), alpha = 2dB/(k*(2d-k+1)) | Equation (4), obtained by minimizing beta first, then alpha |
| Product-matrix MBR construction achieves the cut-set bound with equality (exact-regeneration) for all feasible [n, k, d] | New result of this paper; no restriction to n = d+1 |
| Product-matrix MSR construction achieves the cut-set bound with equality (exact-regeneration) for all [n, k, d >= 2k-2] | New result of this paper |
| Field size sufficient for the product-matrix MBR code: any q >= 2n | Stated as a sufficient (not claimed minimal) field size; smaller fields may work with careful choice of the encoding matrix Psi |
| Field size sufficient for the product-matrix MSR code: any q >= n^2 | Same caveat, sufficient not claimed minimal |
| Prior, non-achievability result cited: exact-regeneration at the MSR point is not achievable for any [n, k, d <= 2k-3] when beta=1 | Attributed to reference [14] (Shah, Rashmi, Kumar, Ramchandran), not proven or re-derived in this paper; cited as context bounding how far d can be lowered |
| Simpler restated prior code: exact-regeneration at the MSR point for [n=d+1, k, d >= 2k-1] (the 'MISER' code) | This paper gives a simplified product-matrix description of a code originally constructed in references [6],[7]; this is not the new d >= 2k-2 result above and remains restricted to n=d+1 |

### Parameters
- alpha (symbols stored per node): free parameter; at the MSR point, alpha = B/k (Equation 3); at the MBR point, alpha = 2dB/(k(2d-k+1)) (Equation 4).
- beta (symbols downloaded per helper node during repair, beta <= alpha): free parameter; at the MSR point, beta = B/(k(d-k+1)); at the MBR point, beta = 2B/(k(2d-k+1)).
- d (repair degree, count of helper nodes contacted, k <= d <= n-1): this paper's new MSR construction requires d >= 2k-2; the earlier restated MISER code requires d >= 2k-1 with the added restriction n = d+1; the MBR construction has no lower bound on d beyond the general k <= d <= n-1 requirement.
- n (total storage nodes): free parameter, independent of k and d, for both of this paper's new constructions (stated as the paper's principal advance over prior work, which fixed n = d+1).
- Field size q: q >= 2n suffices for the MBR construction; q >= n^2 suffices for the MSR construction; both stated as sufficient conditions that a careful choice of Psi may lower further, not as proven-minimal values.
- Encoding matrix Psi: can be chosen as a Vandermonde matrix, which the paper states makes encoding, data-reconstruction, and regeneration operations largely identical to standard Reed-Solomon code operations.
- Striping: the presented codes divide the message into stripes corresponding to beta=1 per stripe, so encoding and repair operate identically and independently per stripe.

### Stated limitations
The new MSR construction is proven only for d >= 2k-2; the paper does not claim or prove achievability for 2k-3 >= d >= k under exact-regeneration with finite beta, and cites a separate non-achievability proof (reference [14]) that the cut-set bound cannot be met at d <= 2k-3 with beta=1. The paper's own stated field-size requirements (q >= 2n for MBR, q >= n^2 for MSR) are sufficient conditions, not proven lower bounds; the paper states smaller fields "may often" work with a cleverly chosen Psi but does not characterize when. The simplified restatement of the prior [n=d+1, k, d>=2k-1] MISER code remains confined to n=d+1, a restriction this paper's own new constructions remove only for the MBR point (all d) and MSR point (d>=2k-2), not for that restated variant.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Repair and reconstruction both require linear operations over a fixed finite field Fq of the stated minimum size (2n for MBR, n^2 for MSR); a system layer that cannot perform field arithmetic at that size, or that needs to change n after code deployment beyond what the fixed field size supports, falls outside the construction as given. A failed node's repair connects to exactly d helper nodes chosen from the remaining n-1 nodes and downloads beta symbols from each; the guarantee of exact-regeneration (bit-for-bit identical content) requires all d helpers to be simultaneously reachable and to supply their beta symbols each, so a repair that can reach fewer than d live helpers at once receives no guarantee from this construction. The encoding matrix Psi must satisfy specific structural conditions (given above the paper's Theorem 2 and Theorem 4, for MBR and MSR respectively) for the exact-regeneration property to hold; an arbitrary or adversarially chosen Psi is not guaranteed to work, so code setup requires verifying or constructing Psi (for example as a Vandermonde matrix) according to those conditions.

### Contradicts
None found.

### References worth retrieving
- Dimakis, Godfrey, Wu, Wainwright, Ramchandran. "Network Coding for Distributed Storage Systems." IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, vol. 56, no. 9, 2010 — foundational (introduces regenerating codes and proves the cut-set bound, equation 2, that this paper's constructions meet with equality).
- Shah, Rashmi, Kumar, Ramchandran. "Explicit Codes Minimizing Repair Bandwidth for Distributed Storage." IEEE Information Theory Workshop, 2010 — foundational (the MISER code this paper gives a simplified product-matrix description of, in Appendix A, for [n=d+1, k, d>=2k-1]).
- Suh, Ramchandran. "Exact-Repair MDS Codes for Distributed Storage Using Interference Alignment." IEEE ISIT, 2010 — foundational (extends the MISER code to repair non-systematic/parity node failures exactly; also reused by this paper's simplified restatement).
- Shah, Rashmi, Kumar, Ramchandran. "Interference Alignment in Regenerating Codes for Distributed Storage: Necessity and Code Constructions." IEEE Transactions on Information Theory (submitted, arXiv:1005.1634) — attack/critique (proves the non-achievability of exact-regeneration at the MSR point for d <= 2k-3 with beta=1, the boundary this paper's own construction stops short of).
- Cullina, Dimakis, Ho. "Searching for Minimum Storage Regenerating Codes." Allerton, 2009 — foundational (computer-search identification of exact-regenerating MSR codes at specific small parameters, prior to this paper's general construction).
- Wu, Dimakis, Ramchandran. "Deterministic Regenerating codes for Distributed Storage." Allerton, 2007 — foundational (early explicit, non-exact regenerating code construction cited as prior work establishing achievability of the storage-repair-bandwidth tradeoff under functional regeneration).
- Papailiopoulos, Dimakis. "Locally Repairable Codes." — competing (also in this corpus as PAPAILIOPOULOS-TIT-14; trades a different repair-cost metric, locality, against the repair-bandwidth metric this paper optimizes).

"the MSR point can be achieved for all parameters satisfying d≥ 2k− 2"
"any field of size 2n or higher suffices" (MBR); "any field of size n2 or higher suffices" (MSR)
"the MSR point is not achievable for any [n, k, d≤ 2k− 3] with β = 1"

## [RAWAT-DLT-24] Accelerating Prolly Trees: Simplified Chunking for Rapid Updates

**Citation:** Abhimanyu Rawat, Tarun Kumar Vangani, Hanno Cornelius, Vanesa Daza. "Accelerating Prolly Trees: Simplified Chunking for Rapid Updates." Distributed Ledger Technologies Workshop (DLT), CEUR-WS, 2024.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://ceur-ws.org/Vol-3791/paper8.pdf
**Source URL:** https://ceur-ws.org/Vol-3791/paper8.pdf
**Domain:** D

### What it does
Lets a distributed system store a large key-value dataset as a content-addressed, ordered tree (a prolly tree, a portmanteau of "probabilistic" and B-tree, first introduced by Noms) that supports Merkle-tree-style verification (a change to one key-value pair changes the tree's root hash) plus B-tree-style ordered range access, while restructuring only a small, bounded portion of the tree on each individual insertion, deletion, or update — instead of the cascading rechunking that the paper attributes to prior prolly-tree designs (Dolthub, Canvas/okra, IPLD).

The tree's shape is content-defined: a node at level 0 stores one key-value pair and is hashed with SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit output); a node is promoted ("boundary node" status) to the next level up when its hash's rightmost hexadecimal digits fall below a fixed threshold. Because promotion depends only on a node's own content hash, any two participants building the same underlying key-value data independently produce the identical tree — the property that content-addressing gives for reconciliation and verification. The paper models the process as Q equally sized hash-value segments, giving each node an independent probability `P_b = 1/Q` of becoming a boundary node, and derives the expected tree height for N total nodes as `H ≈ log_Q(N)` from that probability. A "bucket" or "chunk" is the run of non-boundary nodes at one level between two consecutive boundary nodes; each boundary node stores the rolling Merkle hash of all nodes in its own chunk, so a chunk's contents can be compared or verified as a single hash without inspecting every node in it.

The paper's specific contribution is an Anchor Node placed at the rightmost end of every level, rather than at the left end as in the Canvas/okra design, and absent entirely from the Dolthub and IPLD designs per the paper's characterization of them. The Anchor Node is always treated as a boundary node by construction and functions as a running accumulator for whichever nodes at that level have been inserted most recently but have not yet triggered a boundary-node promotion elsewhere. Because new insertions land at the right edge of the structure and the Anchor Node absorbs their effect on the Merkle hash chain, a sequential insertion updates only the Anchor Nodes on the path from the insertion point up to the root, leaving every previously-formed chunk elsewhere in the tree untouched; a random (non-sequential) update instead touches only the one chunk directly containing the updated key, and its rolling hash update propagates only as far up as that chunk's own boundary node.

Update proceeds in three steps, given as explicit algorithms (Algorithm 3): `SearchPosition` descends from the root, at each internal node following the child whose key range could contain the target key, then moves left along the leaf level until it finds the target key's position; the update (insertion, deletion, or value modification) is applied at that position; `UpdateHashes` then recomputes the Merkle hash of the node's own chunk, and if that chunk's boundary node's hash itself changes, recursively finds and updates the next boundary node up, continuing until a level's hash is unaffected or the root is reached. The paper states this recomputation touches a maximum of two chunks for insertion in the common case. Deletion removes the node from every level it appeared at and updates the affected chunk's Merkle hash; the paper states deletion carries probability `1/b` (where `b` is the chunking factor, i.e. the expected chunk size implied by the threshold `Q`) that the deleted node's removal causes its chunk to merge with an adjacent chunk.

The design supports batch insertion: multiple key-value pairs inserted together are treated as a pre-formed miniature subtree grafted into the larger tree at the insertion point, between two existing boundary nodes, avoiding the restructuring that inserting the same pairs one at a time would otherwise trigger. The design also supports subtree segmentation: because tree height is deterministic given the data (per the `H ≈ log_Q(N)` model) rather than dependent on insertion history, any chunk can function as a self-contained, independently comparable subtree — the paper states this is useful for lightweight clients (it gives Internet-of-Things blockchain clients as the example) that cannot hold the full tree.

### Measured results
Benchmark hardware: a 13th Gen Intel i7-13700H (20 cores), 64 GB RAM, 1 TB M.2 SSD, Ubuntu 22.04 LTS. Compared against the publicly available benchmark codebases of Dolthub (`dolthub/dolt`) and Canvas/okra (`canvasxyz/okra`), both real-world deployed prolly-tree implementations (Canvas uses libp2p as its network layer in production). Canvas's tree-initialization figures in Table 1 (marked with an asterisk in the paper) are taken directly from Canvas's own publicly posted figures because Canvas's benchmark codebase does not itself support tree-initialization benchmarks; the Dolthub and the paper's own "Proposed" tree-creation and all insertion figures were directly executed by the authors.

### Parameters
Hash function: SHA-256, applied to each level-0 node's key-value content and to each higher-level node's own re-hashed content. Boundary-node threshold: the promotion criterion is stated as the node's hash's rightmost hexadecimal digit(s) falling below a predefined threshold; the specific numeric threshold value used for the benchmarked implementation is not given in the paper. `Q`: the number of equally sized segments the hash-value space is divided into for the height model, related to the threshold but not given a specific numeric value in the paper. Expected height formula: `H ≈ log_Q(N)` for N total nodes. Boundary-node probability: `P_b = 1/Q`. Chunking factor `b`: referenced in the deletion-triggered chunk-merge probability `1/b` but not given a numeric value in the paper. Entry counts tested: 1,000; 100,000; 1,000,000; 10,000,000; and (for creation only) 17,000,000 for Dolthub and Proposed; Canvas creation figures are reported only at 65,536 and 16,777,216 (taken from Canvas's own published data, not independently run by these authors).

### Stated limitations
The mechanism by which two prolly trees are compared to compute their difference, and the difference-calculation methodology itself, is explicitly stated to fall outside the scope of this paper; the authors state they provide sample execution code and a brief explanation in an appendix rather than a full treatment. The paper's model for expected tree height (`H ≈ log_Q(N)`) rests on two explicitly stated assumptions — uniform distribution of the hash function's output across its range, and independent selection of each node as a boundary node — neither of which is separately verified or measured in the paper; both are standard cryptographic-hash assumptions asserted, not tested. The Canvas tree-initialization figures used for comparison in Table 1 are taken from Canvas's own previously published figures rather than independently re-executed, because the authors state Canvas's own benchmark codebase does not support tree-initialization benchmarks; those specific rows are therefore not run on the same hardware as the Dolthub and Proposed rows in that table, unlike the insertion figures in Table 2, which were executed on the stated hardware for all three implementations. The authors state future work intends a multi-threaded version of the design to reduce operation time further, implying the benchmarked implementation is single-threaded. No comparison against Merkle Search Trees (MST, Auvolat and Taïani) is run empirically in this paper; MST is discussed only in the related-work section as a structurally similar but distinct design (chunking driven by leading zero count in the hash rather than trailing-digit threshold, and MST explicitly preserves transaction order, which the paper contrasts with prolly trees' content-addressable, non-lexicographic order).

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Every participant reconstructing or verifying the same key-value dataset must use the identical hash function (SHA-256, as used here) and the identical boundary-node threshold/`Q` parameter, because chunk boundaries and therefore the entire tree shape are derived deterministically from node-content hashes — two participants using different thresholds produce different, non-comparable trees for the same underlying data. The mechanism assumes the hash function's output is uniformly distributed and that each node's boundary-node status is drawn independently, which is what makes the height model and chunk-size distribution hold; a hash function or dataset that violates this assumption (for example, adversarially crafted keys engineered to bias hash outputs) is not analyzed in this paper, and no defense against such an adversary is given. The transport or storage layer must be able to address and retrieve individual chunks/subtrees independently, since subtree segmentation and lightweight-client use depend on a chunk being separately fetchable and separately verifiable via its own boundary node's rolling Merkle hash, without requiring the full tree. Cross-referencing MEYER-TR-24 in this same corpus: that paper states prolly trees are explicitly not "clamping-invariant" (its term for the property that two structurally different but same-content trees produce identical results when restricted to an arbitrary subrange), because a prolly tree's chunk boundaries are set by a rolling-hash window over consecutive items and clamping an arbitrary range changes which items fall inside that window, changing the resulting boundaries; a range-based set-reconciliation protocol requiring clamping-invariance (as MEYER-TR-24 defines it) cannot be composed directly with this prolly-tree design without an additional adaptation neither paper supplies.

### Contradicts
None found against other entries in this corpus on measured figures. The paper's related-work section (§5) characterizes the Dolthub, Canvas, and IPLD prolly-tree designs as all subject to "similar complexities in tree restructuring due to random updates or insertions" and states each insertion requires certain parts of those trees to update their hashes — these are the authors' own characterizations of competing systems' designs based on reading their published descriptions, not benchmarked against this paper's own measurements of those systems' restructuring cost (the paper measures Dolthub's and Canvas's total insertion/creation time, not their restructuring scope per operation), so a reader should treat the restructuring-scope claim as an architectural comparison, not a directly measured one.

### References worth retrieving
- competing: Auvolat, Taïani. "Merkle search trees: Efficient state-based CRDTs in open networks." SRDS 2019. (Cited as [19]; the structurally closest alternative n-ary Merkle tree design, using leading-zero-count-based promotion rather than trailing-digit threshold; already flagged by MEYER-TR-24 elsewhere in this corpus and worth retrieving to check this paper's characterization of MST's order-preservation property directly.)
- foundational: Boodman. "Prolly trees: Probabilistic B-trees." Noms documentation, 2021 (cited as [9], the original prolly-tree introduction this paper's design extends).

"How Dolt stores table data," 2020 (cited as [8] and [13]; the Dolthub prolly-tree implementation directly benchmarked against in this paper — retrieve the original design description to verify the paper's characterization that Dolthub lacks an anchor-node concept).
- competing: Gustafson (Canvas). "Merklizing the key/value store for fun and profit," 2023 (cited as [11]; the Canvas/okra prolly-tree implementation directly benchmarked against, and the source of the Table 1 Canvas creation-time figures reused rather than independently measured here).
- competing: IPLD prolly-trees specification, 2022 (cited as [12]; a third prolly-tree implementation discussed but not benchmarked in this paper).

## [REDDY-RFC-20] Traversal Using Relays around NAT (TURN): Relay Extensions to Session Traversal Utilities for NAT (STUN)

**Citation:** Tirumaleswar Reddy, Alan Johnston, Philip Matthews, Jonathan Rosenberg. "Traversal Using Relays around NAT (TURN): Relay Extensions to Session Traversal Utilities for NAT (STUN)." IETF RFC 8656 (obsoletes RFC 5766 and RFC 6156), 2020. DOI 10.17487/RFC8656.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8656
**Source URL:** https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8656
**Domain:** L

### What it does
TURN (Traversal Using Relays around NAT) lets two hosts that each sit behind a network address translator (NAT) exchange application data through a third-party relay when direct hole punching between them fails, by having one host (the TURN client) obtain a public IP address and port on the relay server (the "relayed transport address") and directing the server to forward data between that address and the remote host (the "peer"). The client authenticates to the server (typically with STUN's long-term credential mechanism) and sends an Allocate request; the server creates an allocation, a server-side data structure recording the relayed transport address, its expiry timer, and its permission list, and returns the allocated address in its response. The client keeps the allocation alive by periodically sending Refresh requests before the allocation's lifetime expires; TURN deliberately uses a distinct method (Refresh, not a repeated Allocate) so the client is told explicitly if the allocation has vanished, rather than silently getting a second, different allocation. A single relayed transport address can carry traffic to and from multiple peers, distinguishing TURN from relay protocols such as SOCKS that require one relayed address per remote destination; this multi-peer property traces to TURN's origin supporting SIP (Session Initiation Protocol) call forking.

Before the server relays any inbound peer traffic to the client, the client must install a permission for that peer's IP address (via a CreatePermission request or implicitly via a ChannelBind request); the server checks every inbound UDP datagram's source address against the allocation's permission list and silently discards traffic from an unlisted address. This mimics the address-dependent filtering behavior an RFC-4787-compliant NAT already performs, so a TURN server does not open an inbound path any address-dependent NAT or firewall between client and Internet would not already permit once the client has spoken first. Data can move over the relay through either of two mechanisms: Send/Data indications, which wrap each payload in a full STUN-formatted message (36 bytes of overhead), or channels, which bind a 4-byte channel number to a specific peer via a ChannelBind request and then use a lighter 4-byte-header ChannelData message for each subsequent payload, reducing per-packet overhead for bandwidth-sensitive applications such as VoIP (Voice over IP).

### Measured results
None. This document is a protocol specification defining message formats and normative client/server behavior; it contains no experimental measurement, testbed trial, or deployment dataset. The one numeric result present is an arithmetic derivation, not a measurement: a described amplification attack (Section 21.4) computes that an IPv6-over-TURN-over-IPv4 tunnel packet loop can achieve at most a four-to-one amplification out of a 1500-byte Ethernet MTU packet, because the IPv6+UDP+TURN header overhead is stated as 334 bytes per hop.

### Parameters
- Default allocation lifetime: 10 minutes (600 seconds); the client may request a longer value in the Allocate or Refresh request, and the server states the actual granted lifetime in its response; a Refresh request with lifetime 0 explicitly deletes the allocation, and the server MAY grant a smaller maximum than the default to limit resource consumption.
- Permission lifetime: fixed at 300 seconds (5 minutes), not client-configurable; expires automatically if not refreshed by a further CreatePermission or ChannelBind request, and there is no explicit permission-deletion message. This value is stated to be chosen to match RFC 4787-compliant NAT behavior.
- Channel binding lifetime: fixed at 10 minutes, refreshed by re-sending a ChannelBind request; like permissions, there is no explicit deletion message, only expiry. This lifetime is stated to be chosen to exceed the permission lifetime.
- Per-message overhead: Send/Data indication mechanism adds 36 bytes of STUN framing per payload; the ChannelData mechanism reduces this to a 4-byte header, offered specifically as a bandwidth reduction for applications such as VoIP.
- Tunnel-amplification bound: up to a 4-to-1 packet-size amplification, bounded by a 1500-byte path MTU against a 334-byte IPv6+UDP+TURN per-hop header size (both figures given in the spec text, not separately measured).

### Stated limitations
TURN is stated to require a high-bandwidth server-side connection, described as a high cost to whoever operates the server, so the document recommends using a TURN relay only when a direct path cannot be found — when TURN is combined with ICE (Interactive Connectivity Establishment), ICE performs hole punching first and falls back to TURN only on failure. Send and Data indications cannot be authenticated at all, because STUN's long-term credential mechanism does not support authenticating indications; the document states this is only a partial problem because the client-to-server leg of the path is not the whole path to the peer, and recommends that applications wanting end-to-end confidentiality or integrity encrypt the data themselves rather than relying on TURN to provide it. The document states TURN servers introduce several attacks not present in NAT-based address-dependent filtering, and describes each with its mitigation rather than declaring it solved: a TURN Loop Attack (an attacker spoofs Allocate and ChannelBind requests between two TURN servers to make data loop indefinitely between them) is mitigated by requiring authenticated requests and/or randomized relay port allocation, plus a per-username bandwidth limit and, where the OS permits, TTL decrementing on relayed packets; a Tunnel Amplification Attack (spoofed Allocate/ChannelBind requests turn a TURN server plus an IPv4/IPv6 tunnel endpoint into a packet-looping amplifier) is mitigated by the RECOMMENDED policy that a TURN server not accept allocation or channel-binding requests from addresses known to be tunneled, and MUST NOT accept Teredo or 6to4 addresses specifically. TURN servers are stated to provide "a degree of anonymization" letting a client send data to peers without revealing its own IP address, which the document flags as attractive to an attacker wanting to relay malicious traffic through chained TURN servers without detection; the only stated countermeasure is administrative logging of the actual client source address and installed permissions for later forensic tracing, not a protocol-level prevention. IPsec Authentication Header in transport or tunnel mode is stated not to operate properly through a TURN-allocated relay address, though tunnel-mode IPsec Encapsulating Security Payload is stated to still work.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The client must have some way, out of the scope of the TURN protocol itself, to communicate its relayed transport address to its peers and learn each peer's own server-reflexive transport address; the document names email exchange or a dedicated rendezvous protocol (ICE, with SIP carrying the ICE candidates in its message body) as examples, but the mechanism itself is external. Relaying data requires the server to authenticate the client, typically via STUN's long-term credential mechanism or RFC 7635's third-party authorization extension, meaning the deployment must supply a credential-issuance and verification system the TURN server can check against. Every message that installs or refreshes a permission (CreatePermission, ChannelBind) must be authenticated for TURN's firewall-emulation property to hold; an unauthenticated Send indication cannot itself install a permission, so a peer cannot receive relayed data from the client until an authenticated request has explicitly authorized that peer's address. The server must track a distinct 5-tuple (client transport address as seen at the server, server transport address, and protocol) per allocation, and creating a second allocation requires a different 5-tuple, which places a constraint on how many concurrent relayed addresses a single client-server socket pair can obtain. The relay depends on the server operator provisioning enough allocation and bandwidth capacity per client to withstand the insider-attack case where a legitimately authenticated client floods its own allocation; the document's only stated mitigation is a server-side recommendation to cap per-username bandwidth and per-username allocation count, which the deployment must configure, not TURN itself.

### Contradicts
None found.

### References worth retrieving
- Srisuresh, Ford, Kegel, "State of Peer-to-Peer (P2P) Communication across Network Address Translators (NATs)," RFC 5128, 2008 — foundational, cited as the source for hole-punching failure modes (address-dependent and address-and-port-dependent NAT mapping) that motivate falling back to TURN.
- Audet, Jennings, "Network Address Translation (NAT) Behavioral Requirements for Unicast UDP," RFC 4787, 2007 — foundational, defines the address-dependent filtering behavior TURN's permission mechanism is explicitly designed to mimic.
- Mahy, Matthews, Rosenberg, "Traversal Using Relays around NAT (TURN): Relay Extensions to Session Traversal Utilities for NAT (STUN)," RFC 5766, 2010 — superseded-by (this document obsoletes it, along with RFC 6156).
- Camarillo, Novo, Perreault, "Traversal Using Relays around NAT (TURN) Extension for IPv6," RFC 6156, 2011 — superseded-by (this document obsoletes it).
- Petit-Huguenin, Salgueiro, Rosenberg, Wing, Mahy, Matthews, "Session Traversal Utilities for NAT (STUN)," RFC 8489, 2020 — foundational, the base protocol TURN extends; already in this batch as PETIT-HUGUENIN-RFC-18.
- Keranen, Holmberg, Rosenberg, "Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE): A Protocol for Network Address Translator (NAT) Traversal," RFC 8445, 2018 — foundational, the larger traversal procedure TURN is designed as one component of.
- Reddy, Patil, Ravindranath, Uberti, "Session Traversal Utilities for NAT (STUN) Extension for Third-Party Authorization," RFC 7635, 2015 — foundational, an alternative to long-term credentials for client authentication.
- Leech, Ganis, Lee, Kuris, Koblas, Jones, "SOCKS Protocol Version 5," RFC 1928, 1996 — competing, cited as the prior relay protocol lacking TURN's multi-peer-per-allocation feature.
- Martinsen, Reddy, Wing, Singh, "Measurement of Round-Trip Time and Fractional Loss Using Session Traversal Utilities for NAT (STUN)," RFC 7982, 2016 — foundational, cited as a STUN-based measurement extension relevant to relay path quality, not itself a TURN measurement.

### Verbatim extracts
- "the relayed transport address" and permissions "mimic the address-restricted filtering mechanism of NATs"
- "the default lifetime of an allocation is 10 minutes"
- "the Permission Lifetime MUST be 300 seconds (= 5 minutes)"
- "channel bindings last for 10 minutes unless refreshed"
- "TURN servers provide a degree of anonymization"
- "a four-to-one amplification out of a 1500-byte packet is possible"
- "TURN should not weaken the protections afforded by firewalls"
