## [REVUELTA-DLT-24] Message Latency in Waku Relay with Rate Limiting Nullifiers
**Citation:** Alvaro Revuelta, Sergei Tikhomirov, Aaryamann Challani, Hanno Cornelius, Simon Pierre Vivier. "Message Latency in Waku Relay with Rate Limiting Nullifiers." Distributed Ledger Technology Workshop (DLT), 2024. DOI: not recorded in registry.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://ceur-ws.org/Vol-3791/paper25.pdf
**Source URL:** https://ceur-ws.org/Vol-3791/paper25.pdf
**Domain:** I

### What it does
The paper measures the message-propagation latency added by attaching a Rate Limiting Nullifier (RLN) zero-knowledge proof to every message gossiped over Waku Relay, a GossipSub-based publish-subscribe layer. RLN enforces a shared publishing rate limit without identifying publishers: a publisher registers a commitment c = H(sk) (H is the Poseidon hash) against an on-chain smart contract, paying a one-time on-chain registration fee that raises the cost of creating multiple identities; every relaying node maintains a local Merkle tree of all currently valid commitments, kept in sync through Ethereum RPC calls. To publish, a node computes an epoch value from the current time divided by the rate-limiting interval, an external nullifier from a hash of the epoch and an application-specific rln_identifier, an internal nullifier from a hash of its own secret key and the external nullifier, and a zero-knowledge proof that it holds a valid membership for the current epoch; it attaches the proof, both nullifiers, the epoch, and the Merkle root to the message. Each relaying node accepts a message only if the proof verifies, no other message relayed within the last g seconds (g = 20 s in the deployed configuration) carried the same internal nullifier, and the epoch is within g seconds of the node's own clock; a node that forwards an invalid message has its GossipSub peer score lowered until it is eventually isolated, which the paper states discourages a node from relaying on a spammer's behalf. The paper's own contribution is measurement, not the RLN mechanism: it builds an analytical latency model splitting end-to-end delay into proof-generation time at the publisher, per-hop transmission time, and per-hop validation (proof-verification plus decoding) time at each relay, then checks that model against a 1,000-node single-host simulation and a five-node real-world multi-host deployment.

### Measured results

| Measurement | Result | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| RLN proof generation / verification time, by hardware | MacBook M1 Pro 16GB: 85.7 ms / 2.7 ms; Bare Metal 256GB AMD EPYC 7502P 32-Core: 171.6 ms / 7.9 ms; Digital Ocean 8GB/4CPU: 276.3 ms / 4.5 ms; Digital Ocean 2GB/2CPU: 329.5 ms / 4.4 ms; Raspberry Pi 4B 4GB: 766.8 ms / 18.7 ms | nwaku reference implementation, Merkle tree depth 20, single-run-per-platform benchmark |
| Keccak256 hashing plus BN254 field-element conversion time | 2 KB message: 0.0055 ms; 25 KB: 0.061 ms; 100 KB: 0.244 ms; 500 KB: 1.222 ms | go-zerokit-rln library, darwin/arm64, cited as insignificant relative to overall latency |
| Multi-host end-to-end latency, 4-hop geographically distributed path | Average total latency across five runs: 2 KB message 477 ms, 25 KB 945 ms, 100 KB 1,689 ms, 500 KB 2,468 ms | 5 nwaku nodes on Digital Ocean (8 GB RAM, 4 vCPU), statically linked in order Singapore-Bangalore-San Francisco-New York-Frankfurt, degree 1 at the two endpoints and 2 at intermediaries, NTP-synchronized clocks, each figure averaged over 5 runs |
| Ping RTT between deployed node pairs | Ranged 59-236 ms across the 5x5 pair matrix (for example Bangalore-San Francisco 220 ms one direction, 218 ms the other) | Average of 5 ping requests within a 15-minute span, using the libp2p ping protocol and the wakucanary tool |
| Single-host simulation, 1,000 nodes, total latency distribution | Average total latency: 2 KB 497 ms, 25 KB 756 ms, 100 KB 900 ms, 500 KB 1,358 ms; 95th percentile: 2 KB 597 ms, 25 KB 930 ms, 100 KB 1,076 ms, 500 KB 1,665 ms; max: 2 KB 604 ms, 25 KB 993 ms, 100 KB 1,221 ms, 500 KB 2,468 ms | Shadow discrete-event simulator, 1,000 nwaku nodes, target mesh degree D=6 plus 25 gossip-only peers per node, 100 Mbps up/down bandwidth per node, 150 ms simulated network latency, 10 publisher nodes each sending 1 message, 9,990 total message-received events counted, first two messages excluded to avoid TCP-window-negotiation bias |
| Delivery-time headline claim | Messages of 25 KB or smaller delivered in under 1 second in both the simulation and the multi-host measurement; 95% of 500 KB messages delivered in under 1.7 seconds | Same simulation and multi-host datasets above |
| Path length (hop count) needed to reach all nodes | 4 hops sufficed in the 1,000-node simulation, versus 5 hops predicted by the paper's own closed-form best-topology formula for N=1000, D=6 | Attributed by the authors to variable node degree in the simulation versus the formula's fixed-degree assumption |
| Fraction of total latency attributable to RLN proof generation | About 10% of total latency for 500 KB messages, about 50% for 2 KB messages, in a 4-hop multi-host path | Derived from the same multi-host measurement (Table 3); proof generation is a one-time publisher-side cost independent of message size, so it forms a larger fraction of the (small) total latency for small messages |

### Parameters
Merkle tree depth for the RLN membership set: 20, fixed across all experiments per the RLN protocol specification the paper cites, described as a trade-off between anonymity-set size and proof-generation/verification cost. Maximum epoch gap g (rate-limit window and nullifier-collision window): 20 seconds, stated as the current deployed value. GossipSub mesh degree bounds in deployed Waku: D_low = 4, D_high = 12; typical target D = 6 (cited from libp2p documentation as "the ideal network peering degree"). Single-host simulation: N = 1,000 nodes, target mesh degree D = 6, 25 additional gossip-only peers per node, 100 Mbps upstream/downstream bandwidth per node, 150 ms simulated per-link latency, 10 publisher nodes. Multi-host deployment: N = 5 nodes, static linear topology (no peer discovery), Digital Ocean 8 GB RAM / 4 vCPU machines, path length h = 4 hops, message sizes tested 2, 25, 100, and 500 KB, 5 runs per message size.

### Stated limitations
The paper states its analytical model assumes a stable, regular-degree full-mesh topology and explicitly excludes node churn (nodes joining and leaving), naming investigation of churn's effect on propagation latency as future work. The paper states its measurements cover only low message-publishing rates and explicitly excludes the effect of higher rates, which the authors expect to increase GossipSub control-message overhead and processing load; this is stated as unexamined, not measured. The current nwaku implementation is stated not to support the economic slashing-of-deposit punishment for malicious publishers described in the original RLN proposal, so a misbehaving publisher whose messages are dropped for reused nullifiers faces no on-chain financial consequence in the deployed system, only network-level isolation via lowered GossipSub score. The paper states the RLN membership Merkle tree must currently be constructed and maintained locally by every publisher and verifier, which it states may be impractical for resource-restricted nodes, and reports the authors are investigating (not yet built) a design where the tree lives entirely on-chain to allow delegated proof generation. The paper states its 4-hop-suffices simulation finding used only 10 of 1,000 nodes as publishers and did not test adversarial conditions, node faults, network failures, or clock desynchronization, naming these as future work rather than tested cases. The simulation is stated to underestimate latency for 100 KB and 500 KB messages because the Shadow framework does not model CPU time for message decoding (only the benchmarked proof-verification time is injected), and conversely to overestimate latency for small (2 KB) messages, a discrepancy the authors attribute to this same CPU-time-modeling gap rather than to a flaw in the underlying RLN mechanism.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Every relaying node must maintain a locally synchronized copy of the current RLN Merkle tree of valid commitments, which requires either an Ethereum RPC provider connection (the paper names Infura and Alchemy as examples) or the node running its own Ethereum execution client; a node lacking this synchronization cannot validate incoming proofs correctly. The rate-limit and replay-detection mechanism (the nullifier-collision check) requires every participating node's local clock to stay within the fixed epoch-gap window (20 s in the deployed system) of the network's shared time reference, which the paper's own multi-host experiment satisfies only by adding NTP synchronization; a node whose clock drifts beyond that gap will reject valid proofs or accept expired ones. The rate-limiting property depends on GossipSub's separate peer-scoring mechanism to enforce the consequence of relaying invalid messages (score reduction leading to eventual isolation); RLN itself only supplies the validity check; a network without a scoring/isolation layer underneath RLN gets proof verification but no consequence for relaying-node misbehavior. The measured latency figures assume TCP transport with an already-negotiated window and established handshake between neighboring nodes (the first two published messages were excluded from measurement to remove this effect); a system with a different transport or high per-hop connection churn would not inherit these latency figures unmodified. The underlying spam-resistance property depends on the on-chain registration step remaining an actual (non-zero) cost to acquire a membership commitment; the paper states this fee, not the zero-knowledge proof itself, is what deters an attacker from registering unlimited identities.

### Contradicts
None found. No other entry in this batch measures Waku, RLN, or GossipSub latency, and this paper's central claim (RLN proof-related overhead is not the dominant cost, and is tolerable relative to end-to-end message latency) is not disputed by anything else here.

### References worth retrieving
- Whitehat, Taheri, Thoren, Kilic, Dimovski, "Rate Limit Nullifier," vacp2p RFC (rln-v1), cited [18] — foundational: the RLN protocol specification this paper's implementation follows and whose original economic-slashing design nwaku does not yet implement.
- Grassi, Khovratovich, Rechberger, Roy, Schofnegger, "Poseidon: A new hash function for zero-knowledge proof systems," USENIX Security 2021 — foundational: the hash function used for RLN's commitment and nullifier construction.
- Decker, Wattenhofer, "Information propagation in the bitcoin network," P2P 2013 — competing: prior latency-measurement methodology for a different gossip-based P2P network, cited as related work this paper's methodology follows.
- Neudecker, Andelfinger, Hartenstein, "Timing analysis for inferring the topology of the bitcoin peer-to-peer network," IEEE ATC 2016 — competing: independent latency/topology measurement on a comparable gossip network.
- Zhang, Lee, Ye, Qiao, "Evaluation of ethereum end-to-end transaction latency," NTMS 2021 — competing: comparable latency-measurement study on a related GossipSub-based network (Ethereum).
- Gluhovsky, "EIP-627: Whisper specification," 2017 — attack/superseded-by: prior proof-of-work-based spam-rate-limiting scheme for general-purpose messaging that the paper states "has not gained popularity," relevant as the direct predecessor mechanism RLN replaces.
- Unger, Dechand, Bonneau, Fahl, Perl, Goldberg, Smith, "SoK: Secure messaging," IEEE S&P 2015 — foundational: cited survey of decentralized/federated messaging protocol properties, relevant to comparing Waku's design goals against federated alternatives (ActivityPub, Matrix, Nostr, XMPP, AT Protocol, Farcaster) named in the same section.

"Currently, g is set to 20 s"
"Each registration incurs on-chain transaction fee"
"nwaku implementation does not yet support economic punishment"
"proof generation... requires under 300 ms per proof and does not depend on message size"

## [REYNOLDS-MIDDLEWARE-03] Efficient Peer-to-Peer Keyword Searching
**Citation:** Patrick Reynolds, Amin Vahdat. "Efficient Peer-to-Peer Keyword Searching." ACM/IFIP/USENIX Middleware, 2003. DOI 10.1007/3-540-44892-6_2.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://piki.org/patrick/papers/search.pdf
**Source URL:** https://piki.org/patrick/papers/search.pdf
**Domain:** B

### What it does
The system answers multi-keyword boolean-AND queries over a distributed inverted index built on a distributed hash table (DHT), so that a peer-to-peer file-storage or archival system gets keyword search without a central index. Each keyword maps, via the DHT's hash function, to the single node responsible for storing the full list of document IDs containing that keyword (a vertically partitioned index — one node per keyword, as opposed to a horizontally partitioned index in which every node holds a shard of every keyword's list and every query must contact every node). Vertical partitioning bounds the number of nodes an n-keyword query must contact to n, independent of network size, while horizontal partitioning requires contacting every node regardless of query size.

Resolving a single-keyword query means contacting the one node holding that keyword's document-ID list. Resolving a multi-keyword AND query naively requires transferring an entire document-ID set from one keyword's node to another to compute the intersection, a transfer whose size scales with the number of documents containing the more common keyword, not with the size of the final answer. The paper's core mechanism replaces most of that transfer with a Bloom filter — a bit-array structure that lets a receiver test set membership with a tunable, one-directional error rate (false positives possible, false negatives never) — computed by the sending node over its own document-ID set and sent in place of the full set. The receiving node tests every member of its own set against the filter, sends back the (smaller) set of matches, and the false positives introduced by the filter's error rate are stripped out by the originating node by re-intersecting against its full local set. Sending only the filtered candidate matches directly to the client instead of returning them to the originating node for filtering trades correctness (some false positives reach the client) for eliminating one message round trip, with the tradeoff made at run time once the false-positive-rate parameters are known.

Three further mechanisms reduce cost. Caching lets a node store another keyword-node's Bloom filter or partial filter locally, so a repeated query for a keyword pair can skip a network round trip entirely on a cache hit; sending filters in fixed contiguous hash-space chunks lets a cache store and reuse partial filters. Incremental results retrieve only as many document IDs as the client actually wants (starting from an initial small batch M and doubling it if too few results survive intersection), rather than the full match-list, which the paper argues reduces cost to a constant per query when the requested result count is small relative to the true match count — except when the true match count is itself smaller than requested, in which case incremental retrieval degenerates to fetching the entire search space, and its benefit disappears. Virtual hosts address capacity heterogeneity by mapping each physical node to a number of DHT positions (virtual host IDs) proportional to that node's network and CPU capacity relative to a fixed baseline, concentrating more of the keyword-to-node assignment load onto more capable machines; an optional scaling factor multiplies the number of virtual hosts per node further to reduce the chance any one node is assigned a disproportionate share of the keyword-ID space.

### Measured results

| Result | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| End-to-end query time, headline claim | under 1 second average, under 1 KB average bandwidth | simulated, across the paper's default heterogeneous network-speed distribution and CPU distribution, with all optimizations (Bloom filters, caching, virtual hosts) enabled |
| Scaling of bytes sent with network size | flat beyond ~100 hosts; below 100 hosts, small networks benefit from queries landing on a single host by chance | simulated networks from 1 to 10,000 hosts, heterogeneous network-speed distribution (modeled on Saroiu et al.'s Gnutella measurements), Bloom filters and caching off, virtual hosts on/off compared |
| Virtual hosts effect on bytes sent | ~18% reduction from enabling virtual hosts; a further ~18% from adding virtual-host scaling | same network-scaling simulation |
| Virtual hosts effect on network transmission time | up to ~60% reduction from virtual hosts, with a small further reduction from scaling | same simulation |
| Optimal Bloom filter invocation threshold | ~300 documents (sets smaller than this sent as a full list rather than a Bloom filter) | IRCache search trace (see dataset below), default 6 bits/entry Bloom filter |
| Optimal Bloom filter size and caching interaction | optimal size shifts from 18 bits/entry (no caching) to 24 bits/entry (with caching); at those respective optima, caching gives >50% reduction in total bytes transmitted per query | same trace; false-positive rate allowances of 0%, 1%, 10% tested, with 1%/10% allowances letting some false-positive-removal round trips be skipped entirely |
| Modem-network end-to-end query completion | all queries completed in <=1 second | all-modem network-speed distribution (56 Kbit/s, 6 KB/s best-case transfer), all optimizations enabled reducing per-query bytes to <1,000 bytes |
| Heterogeneous-network response-time reduction, caching + virtual hosts together | 59% reduction in average per-query response time; virtual hosts alone give 48% reduction in the network-transmission component; caching alone gives 47% reduction in the latency component | heterogeneous network-speed distribution, optimal Bloom threshold (300) and optimal Bloom sizes (18/24 bits) |
| WAN-network caching effect | 48% reduction in latency, 30% reduction in CPU time from caching alone | homogeneous high-speed WAN network-speed distribution; CPU heterogeneity still present per the paper's CPU-speed distribution |
| Bloom filter compression factor (general) | approximately one order of magnitude (roughly 10:1) | stated as a general property of the technique in the discussion section, consistent with the 18-24 bits/entry optimal sizes measured |
| Incremental-results bandwidth reduction | up to 30% in the best case, for the paper's own target document set | not separately plotted; the paper states the document set was not large enough to generate many hits per query for most queries, so this technique's full results are not reported in this paper |

Dataset: a real crawled document set of 1.85 GB of HTML, 1.17 million unique words across 105,593 documents (crawl depth 5 from 100 seed URLs); a real search-query trace of 95,409 searches with 45,344 unique keywords, drawn from a 10-day January 2002 IRCache proxy log. Document IDs assumed 128-bit hashes. Simulated host characteristics: three network-speed distributions (all-modem, all-backbone/WAN, and a heterogeneous mixture based on Saroiu et al.'s measured Gnutella population); CPU speeds drawn from a bell curve centered at 750 MIPS; local storage from 1 MB to 100 MB (heavy-tailed); hosts placed at random on a simulated 2,500-mile-square grid with signals assumed to propagate at 100,000 miles/second. CPU costs modeled as 1,500 simple operations per index-lookup hit, 500 per element intersected, 10,000 per document ID inserted into or checked against a Bloom filter — the paper states these are chosen as upper bounds on real CPU cost. Simulator validated by hand-calculated small traces and by comparing simulated Bloom-filter-size curves against the paper's own closed-form analytical prediction (stated as closely matching).

### Parameters
- Document identifier size: 128 bits (assumed content-hash length).
- Bloom filter false-positive formula used: p_fp = 0.6185^(m/n), m = filter bits, n = set size (from Fan et al.'s Summary Cache analysis, cited).
- Bloom filter size sweep: 0 to 40 bits/entry; optimum found at 18 (no caching) or 24 (with caching) bits/entry.
- Bloom filter invocation threshold sweep: 1 to 100,000 documents; optimum found at ~300 for the IRCache trace.
- Allowed false-positive rate in returned results: 0%, 1%, 10% tested.
- Baseline host for virtual-host assignment: 57.5 MIPS CPU, 30 Kbit/s network links (chosen as the speed needed for 5,000 Bloom operations/second).
- Virtual host scaling factor: tested at 1, 10, 100 (multiplies each node's baseline-relative virtual host count).
- Network size swept: 1 to 10,000 simulated hosts.
- Network-speed distributions compared: all-modem, all-WAN/backbone, heterogeneous (Saroiu et al.'s Gnutella measurement-based mixture).

### Stated limitations
The simulator does not model network contention; the authors state that per-query averages would be worse than reported if any individual node's network connection becomes saturated, and note this limitation is mitigated (not eliminated) under network conditions where individual nodes have more spare bandwidth or where virtual hosts spread load away from underprovisioned hosts. Incremental results provide no benefit, and can increase both bytes sent and latency, when a query's true result count is nonzero but smaller than the number of results the client requested — a case the paper illustrates with a multi-keyword query where each keyword individually matches millions of documents but only a handful of documents match all keywords together, forcing the full search space to be considered regardless of the incremental-retrieval optimization. Bloom filters and caching alone (without incremental results) leave both bytes sent and end-to-end query time roughly proportional to the number of documents in the system — they are described by the authors as constant-factor, not asymptotic, improvements. Bloom filters complicate result ranking: because a Bloom filter only conveys set membership and not auxiliary data (such as within-document word position or ranking score), sending only the compressed filter loses the information needed to rank results on the criteria of the keyword whose set was filtered; the authors state ranking is more important than the marginal savings from full Bloom compression, but leave the choice a runtime tradeoff rather than resolving it. The combination of incremental results (sending non-contiguous hash-space chunks ordered by rank) and the CPU-saving optimization of testing only contiguous hash-space chunks against a filter are described as mutually exclusive — a system cannot have both simultaneously. Load balancing under vertical partitioning is uneven because keyword appearance popularity and search popularity are both roughly Zipf-distributed, unlike the more even distribution a horizontally partitioned index would produce; virtual hosts only shift more load onto more capable nodes, they do not make the underlying load distribution itself more even, and the authors' claim that this is acceptable rests on the assumption that peer-to-peer networks are generally over-provisioned, which the paper does not itself measure. The paper's results are drawn from one document set and one search trace; the authors state they do not expect other workloads to change the benefits significantly but do not test any other workload to confirm this. Update discovery (detecting new, removed, or modified documents) is assumed to use a "push" model in which clients notify the index directly, rather than crawling; the paper does not evaluate a workload with high update rates, since it assumes queries will dominate updates for its target file-storage and archival-storage use cases.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
- The mechanism requires a DHT layer beneath it to map each keyword to the node responsible for that keyword's document-ID list; the paper explicitly treats content/document placement as an orthogonal problem the DHT and storage layer solve separately, and assumes no benefit from co-locating a document with the keyword entries pointing to it.
- Vertical partitioning requires that the number of participating nodes exceed the average number of keywords per document for its claimed insert/update cost advantage over horizontal partitioning to hold; below that ratio, horizontal partitioning's single-node update cost becomes cheaper.
- The false-positive-elimination step (sending B intersect F(A) back to the originating node sA rather than directly to the client) requires an extra round trip that the mechanism trades off explicitly against sending unfiltered, partially-incorrect results straight to the client; a component further downstream that needs an exact result set must keep this extra round trip, while one that tolerates a bounded false-positive rate can drop it.
- Ranking of results using a keyword's own auxiliary data (word position, per-document score) requires transmitting document-level detail alongside the Bloom-filtered candidate set; a design that keeps the compressed-filter-only path for bandwidth reasons gives up the ability to rank on that keyword's contribution, and the paper does not supply a mechanism that gets both.
- The system assumes queries vastly outnumber document updates and that most files change rarely if at all; a deployment with high update rates relative to query rates was not modeled and the cost trade-off between vertical and horizontal partitioning would need to be re-derived for it.
- Caching's benefit is contingent on repeated queries or repeated keyword pairs in the workload; the measured >50% bandwidth reduction from caching is specific to the IRCache trace's actual query-repetition structure and is not derived as a property that holds for an arbitrary or adversarially chosen query distribution.

### Contradicts
None found against other entries in this corpus. Relevant for cross-referencing against BRIEF.md's open-problem 1 (ranked full-text search across peers at web scale, "~6 MB per query for 3 billion documents" per Li et al.): this paper reports under 1 KB per query, but at a far smaller scale (105,593 documents, 1.17 million unique words) and using boolean-AND matching with no ranking on the compressed path, not the ranked full-text retrieval Li et al.'s bound addresses — the two figures describe different problems and are not a direct contradiction.

### References worth retrieving
- **[6] Dabek, Kaashoek, Karger, Morris, Stoica, "Wide-area Cooperative Storage with CFS," SOSP 2001** — foundational: the Chord File System (CFS) this paper's DHT-based file-storage motivation is built around, and the source of the virtual-hosts technique this paper adopts and cites directly.
- **[19] Stoica, Morris, Karger, Kaashoek, Balakrishnan, "Chord," SIGCOMM 2001** — foundational: one of the three DHTs (with CAN and Pastry) this paper's architecture is designed to layer keyword search on top of.
- **[7] Fan, Cao, Almeida, Broder, "Summary Cache: A Scalable Wide-Area Web Cache Sharing Protocol," SIGCOMM 1998** — foundational: source of the Bloom-filter false-positive-rate formula this paper uses directly (p_fp = 0.6185^(m/n)).
- **[3] Brin, Page, "The Anatomy of a Large-Scale Hypertextual Web Search Engine," WWW7, 1998** — competing: the centralized Google architecture this paper's distributed design is explicitly contrasted against throughout.
- **[20] (Yang, Garcia-Molina), cited for reducing nodes contacted in Gnutella search** — competing: an unstructured-search-cost-reduction technique for Gnutella-style broadcast search, the horizontally-broadcast alternative to this paper's vertically-partitioned DHT approach.
- **[1] Bernstein, Chiu, "Using Semi-joins to Solve Relational Queries," JACM 28(1), 1981** — foundational: the database semijoin-reduction concept this paper's Bloom-filter intersection technique is explicitly derived from.
- **[13] Mullin, "Optimal Semijoins for Distributed Database Systems," IEEE TSE 16(5), 1990**, and **[12] Mackert, Lohman, "R* Optimizer Validation and Performance Evaluation for Local Queries," SIGMOD 1986** — foundational: the "Bloom join" database literature this paper's set-intersection protocol is built on.
- **[5]/[9] Clarke, "A Distributed Decentralised Information Storage and Retrieval System" (Freenet), 1999; Hong, "Freenet," ICSI Workshop 2000** — competing: cited as providing no search mechanism at all, relying instead on well-known names, a direct contrast to this paper's keyword-search contribution.

## [RHEA-USENIXATC-04] Handling Churn in a DHT
**Citation:** Sean Rhea, Dennis Geels, Timothy Roscoe, John Kubiatowicz. "Handling Churn in a DHT." USENIX Annual Technical Conference, 2004.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://usenix.org/legacy/events/usenix04/tech/general/rhea/rhea.pdf
**Source URL:** https://oceanstore.cs.berkeley.edu/publications/papers/pdf/bamboo-usenix.pdf
**Domain:** A

### What it does
The paper isolates three independent design choices that determine whether a distributed hash table (DHT), a structured overlay that maps keys to nodes for lookup, keeps completing lookups correctly and quickly while nodes continuously join and leave (churn), and measures each choice's separate contribution using a purpose-built DHT called Bamboo. Bamboo uses Pastry's routing geometry: every node keeps a leaf set (its numerically nearest neighbors in the identifier ring, which guarantees correctness) and a routing table (neighbors chosen to share increasingly long identifier prefixes, which gives O(log N) hop counts).

Reactive vs. periodic neighbor-failure recovery: reactive recovery replaces a leaf-set or routing-table entry immediately when that neighbor is detected as failed (via a missed periodic liveness probe or a lookup-message timeout); periodic recovery instead has each node share its leaf set with its own leaf-set members on a fixed schedule regardless of observed failures. The paper shows reactive recovery can enter a positive feedback loop under congestion: a timeout misattributed to node failure (a "false suspicion of failure") triggers a recovery message, which consumes bandwidth, which increases congestion, which causes more false timeouts.

Timeout calculation for lookup messages: the paper studies a fixed 5-second timeout, a TCP-style timeout computed per-neighbor from an exponentially weighted mean and variance of observed round-trip time (RTO = AVG + 4·VAR), and a timeout derived from Vivaldi virtual coordinates (a distributed algorithm that assigns each node synthetic coordinates so that coordinate distance approximates network latency, letting a node estimate round-trip time to nodes it has never directly probed).

Proximity neighbor selection (PNS): the practice of choosing, among multiple candidate nodes that would each satisfy a given routing-table slot's identifier-prefix requirement, the one with lowest measured network latency. The paper separates correctness (any node satisfying the prefix requirement makes a lookup "efficient," i.e., O(log N) hops) from performance (choosing the nearest such node lowers "stretch," the ratio of lookup latency to the direct round-trip time between source and destination) and compares four ways to discover low-latency candidates: global sampling (issuing DHT lookups for random identifiers with the needed prefix), sampling a routing-table neighbor's own neighbors, sampling a neighbor's inverse neighbors (nodes that have the local node as their neighbor, discovered because the local node tracks who probes it), and a recursive algorithm (modeled on Tapestry's nearest-neighbor algorithm) that walks the routing-table hierarchy level by level, retaining only the k closest candidates found at each level.

### Measured results
| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| FreePastry fails to complete a majority of lookups under heavy churn, though completed lookups are mostly consistent | 1,000-node FreePastry 1.3 network, default 24-node leaf sets, log base 16, ModelNet-emulated 10,000-node wide-area topology, churn rate doubling across successive 30-minute periods (session times 6.2h, 3.1h, 1.6h, 47min, 23min), 10-minute no-churn gaps between periods |
| MIT Chord completes and returns consistent results for almost all lookups, but mean lookup latency grows sharply as churn increases; Bamboo (with PNS) shows the smallest latency growth, Bamboo (no PNS) intermediate | Same 1,000-node ModelNet topology and churn schedule; MIT Chord CVS snapshot 8/4/2003, default 10-node successor lists, location cache disabled |
| Bandwidth use under churn | Bamboo used "slightly under 750 bytes/second/node," Chord "slightly under 2,400 bytes/second/node," across all tested churn rates in the same experiment |
| Reactive vs. periodic recovery bandwidth, no churn | Reactive recovery used less than half the bandwidth of periodic recovery | Bamboo, large leaf sets, two 20-minute churn periods with median session times of 47 and 23 minutes |
| Reactive vs. periodic recovery bandwidth, under churn | Reactive recovery's bandwidth use "jumps dramatically," exceeding periodic recovery's, attributed to contention between extra reactive-recovery messages and lookup messages for available bandwidth | Same experiment |
| Timeout calculation, fixed 5-second timeout | Mean latency pulled to "more than twice that of the other configurations," even under light churn | Bamboo, PNS enabled with separate direct-probing latency measurements (not virtual-coordinate-derived) |
| Timeout calculation, TCP-style vs. Vivaldi virtual-coordinate | Comparable mean latency at low churn; Vivaldi stays within a factor of 2 of TCP-style down to a 23-minute median session time, then diverges, but keeps mean latency under 2 seconds down to a 12-minute median session time | Same experiment, recursive routing used for both (isolating the timeout-calculation variable from routing-style differences) |
| PNS technique comparison, single techniques | Global sampling alone: mean latency drops from 450 ms (no PNS) to 340 ms with "virtually no increase in bandwidth"; simple sampling of neighbors'-neighbors or inverse-neighbors: "not terribly effective"; recursive (Tapestry-style/Pastry-optimized-join-style) versions of both: at least as effective as global sampling, "not much more so" | 1,000-node network, 47-minute median session time, bandwidth measured in bytes/second/node against mean lookup latency |
| PNS technique comparison, combinations | Global sampling plus neighbors'-neighbors sampling: small further latency decrease without much added bandwidth; other combinations gave similar results, with "no clear reason to prefer one over another" | Same experiment |
| Lookup consistency benchmark for Bamboo and MIT Chord | At least 99.9% consistency (majority-agreement across 10 simultaneous same-key lookups) | 47-minute median session time, cited from the authors' companion technical report [23] |
| Observed peer-to-peer session times (from prior deployed-system studies, cited not measured by this paper) | Saroiu: Gnutella/Napster, 50% ≤ 60 min; Chu: Gnutella/Napster, 31% ≤ 10 min; Sen: FastTrack, 50% ≤ 1 min; Bhagwan: Overnet, 50% ≤ 60 min; Gummadi: Kazaa, 50% ≤ 2.4 min | Table 1, secondary citation of five prior empirical measurement studies |

### Parameters
- Test cluster: 40 IBM xSeries PCs, dual 1 GHz Pentium III, 1.5 GB RAM, Gigabit Ethernet, Debian GNU/Linux or FreeBSD.
- Network emulation: ModelNet, Inet-generated 10,000-node wide-area AS-level topology, 500 client nodes on 1 Mbps links to 250 distinct stubs; each physical client node runs 2 DHT instances for a total of 1,000 DHT nodes (12.5 DHT instances/CPU).
- Churn model: Poisson node-death process, node selected uniformly at random on each death, immediately replaced to hold network size at 1,000; median session time t_med = N·ln2/λ; tested churn rates 8/second to 4/minute, corresponding to median session times 1.4 minutes to 3 hours.
- Lookup workload: each live node issues lookups for uniformly random identifiers via a Poisson process at rate 0.1/second, aggregate 100 lookups/second across the network; each lookup executed simultaneously by 10 nodes to measure consistency (majority result = consistent, no majority = all inconsistent).
- FreePastry configuration: default 24-node leaf sets, routing-table logarithm base 16; proximity-to-gateway not enforced at join (noted as affecting only neighbor proximity, not routing efficiency).
- MIT Chord configuration: default 10-node successor lists, location cache disabled (`-F` option), because the cache "causes poor performance under churn."
- TCP-style timeout formula: RTO = AVG + 4·VAR (average and variance of observed round-trip time to that neighbor).
- Vivaldi virtual-coordinate timeout formula: RTO = v + 6σ + 15 ms (v = predicted round-trip time, σ = average coordinate-prediction error, 15 ms constant added to prevent unneeded retransmission to the local host).
- PNS latency-record storage: 8 bytes per measured node (an exponentially weighted average of past latency measurements), stated to scale comfortably to large systems.
- Recursive PNS sampling algorithm: bounded to at most 3 outstanding messages (neighbor requests or latency probes) at any time.

### Stated limitations
The authors state the study is limited to a single DHT implementation (Bamboo) on a single network topology using "a relatively simple churn model," and that building and testing a complete DHT implementation on an emulated network is a major effort that constrained the scope. They state they have not studied whether alternate routing-table-neighbor schemes, as used in Kademlia and Tapestry, or the choice between iterative and recursive routing, change the churn-handling results — both are named explicitly as future work. They state their ModelNet topology's inter-node latency distribution is "more Gaussian than the distribution of latencies measured on the Internet," and that available measured Internet latency datasets lack the topology information needed to simulate the network cross-traffic their study found important, so they could not simply substitute a more realistic latency distribution. They state their churn model (Poisson node death, uncorrelated and memoryless) is a simplification of real churn, and cite an anonymous reviewer's suggestion to instead scale traces of observed session times from deployed networks; they had not done this at time of writing. They state the paper only demonstrates resilience of the Bamboo routing layer to churn, calling this "an important first step" but explicitly not addressing security or anonymity, whose relationship to churn they state they are "unclear about." They state they had implemented Chord's Simple Timer-based Protocol (STP) congestion-control algorithm for iterative-routing experiments but "do not yet have definitive results about its performance" at time of writing. For the specific consistency measurements, they state their custom 10-way-agreement consistency metric is "more strict than that required by some DHT applications," so a real deployment tolerating looser consistency could see different, less alarming failure rates than reported here. For PNS neighbor-discovery techniques, they state that active management of inverse-neighbor lists (tracking who has probed the local node) requires additional probing bandwidth in the current Bamboo implementation and had not yet been optimized (an approximation using recent liveness-probe senders was proposed but not implemented) at time of writing.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A DHT that wants to use TCP-style per-neighbor timeout estimation for lookup messages needs recursive routing, because the technique depends on a node communicating almost exclusively with its own logarithmic-size set of direct overlay neighbors and maintaining a response-time history for each; a DHT using iterative routing (where the lookup source itself must estimate timeouts to arbitrary nodes throughout the network, not just its direct neighbors) instead needs a mechanism like Vivaldi virtual coordinates that can estimate latency to a previously unprobed node, at the cost of only being competitive with TCP-style timeouts down to moderate churn levels, and diverging in accuracy at higher churn. A design relying on periodic leaf-set-sharing for failure recovery, rather than reactive recovery, requires that the leaf-set size be large enough that periodic-recovery's per-neighbor overhead stays low relative to the churn rate; the paper's own conclusion is that periodic recovery becomes preferable specifically "when leaf sets are large, as they would be in a large system," making leaf-set size a precondition rather than a free parameter. Any proximity-neighbor-selection scheme built on the sampling techniques studied here (global sampling, neighbor-of-neighbor sampling, inverse-neighbor sampling, or the recursive combination) requires that the routing table's correctness be maintained independently of proximity optimization — the paper's stated design principle is that a routing-table slot should be filled quickly with any node satisfying the required identifier prefix, deferring latency-based replacement to a lower-priority background process, so a design that instead blocks routing-table population on finding a low-latency neighbor would forfeit the O(log N)-hop guarantee under churn that this separation provides.

### Contradicts
None found regarding a claim commonly attributed to this paper.
The paper's own related-work section states a specific disagreement with Mahajan et al.'s automatic maintenance-rate-tuning algorithm for Pastry: this paper states that algorithm's design (increasing maintenance traffic in response to observed losses) risks the same positive-feedback cycle this paper identifies in reactive recovery, and separately states Mahajan et al.'s failure model is "pessimistic" because it does not model hop-by-hop lookup-message retransmission.

### References worth retrieving
- Rowstron, Druschel, "Pastry: Scalable, distributed object location and routing" (cited as [24]) — foundational, the routing geometry (leaf set + routing table) Bamboo directly reuses.
- Maymounkov, Mazières, "Kademlia: A peer-to-peer information system based on the XOR metric" (cited as [20]) — foundational (already in corpus per BRIEF section 7); this paper cites its alternate-routing-table-neighbor design as unstudied future work.

- Gummadi, Gummadi, Gribble, Ratnasamy, Shenker, Stoica, "The impact of DHT routing geometry on resilience and proximity" (cited as [12]) — foundational, source of the "~16 samples gives near-optimal proximity" claim this paper's global-sampling results corroborate.
- Liben-Nowell, Balakrishnan, Karger, "Analysis of the evolution of peer-to-peer systems" (cited as [17]) — foundational, source of the continuous-churn theoretical lower bound this paper's churn model is stated to follow, and source of the "false suspicion of failure" concept this paper observes empirically.
- Mahajan, Castro, Rowstron, "Controlling the cost of reliability in peer-to-peer overlays" (cited as [19]) — competing, an automatic maintenance-rate-tuning approach this paper argues risks the same feedback cycle reactive recovery exhibits.

## [RICHARDSON-ECIR-13] Ranked Accuracy and Unstructured Distributed Search
**Citation:** Sami Richardson, Ingemar J. Cox. "Ranked Accuracy and Unstructured Distributed Search." ECIR, 2013. Pages 171-182. DOI 10.1007/978-3-642-36973-5_15.
**Retrieved:** full text via http://www0.cs.ucl.ac.uk/staff/ingemar/Content/papers/2013/ECIR2013.pdf
**Source URL:** http://www0.cs.ucl.ac.uk/staff/ingemar/Content/papers/2013/ECIR2013.pdf
**Domain:** B

### What it does
The mechanism defines a rank-weighted correctness metric, rank-accuracy, for probably-approximately-correct (PAC) search over an unstructured peer-to-peer network, and derives a document-replication policy that raises this metric above what document-popularity-based replication alone achieves. PAC search finds documents by sending a query to z nodes sampled uniformly at random out of n total network nodes, each node holding a fixed-size local index (rho documents per node), and combining whatever matching documents those z nodes report into a top-k result list. Prior work (Cohen and Shenker) measured only rank-unaware accuracy: the fraction of an exhaustive search's result set that a constrained z-node search recovers, treating every recovered document as equally valuable regardless of its position in the ranked list. Rank-accuracy instead assigns each document d_i in the exhaustive top-k list a rank-dependent weight w_j(i), summing to 1 across the k positions, and scores a query's constrained-search result as the sum of weights of the documents it actually recovered; when every weight equals 1/k, rank-accuracy reduces to the original rank-unaware accuracy measure. The paper adopts a rank-biased-precision-style weight, W = (1-p)*p^(y-1) for a document at rank y, where p is a persistence parameter modeling the probability a user examines the next-ranked result; smaller p concentrates weight more heavily on the top-ranked positions. The replication policy computes, for each document, a weighted retrieval rate v_i that sums, over every query that returned that document in its top-k list, the query's issue rate times the document's rank weight in that query; three replication rules are then compared: uniform (equal replica count per document), rank-aware proportional (replica count proportional to v_i), rank-aware square-root (replica count proportional to the square root of v_i, echoing the square-root-optimal rank-unaware result from Cohen and Shenker), and rank-aware optimal (an integer-programming solution obtained by the same convex-optimization method a prior PhD thesis, Fu 2012, used for the rank-unaware case, with v_i substituted for plain retrieval rate).

### Measured results
Theoretical analysis (closed-form, not simulated): parameters n=10,000 nodes, rho=500 documents/node, m=47,480 distinct documents, 4,748 distinct queries following an inverse power-law query-rate distribution with exponent theta (query rate of query j proportional to j^-theta), total query volume 10,000, query fanout z=100, disjoint top-10 result lists assumed per query. Average expected rank-accuracy A was computed across theta in [0, 1.5] for three rank-biased-precision persistence values, p=0.3, 0.6, 0.9 (Figure 1). Findings: the gap between rank-aware and rank-unaware replication policies is largest at low p (heavily skewed rank weighting) and shrinks as p rises toward 0.9; the gap between replication policies also shrinks as theta rises, because a highly skewed query distribution lets a few popular queries dominate rank-accuracy regardless of policy; even at a uniform query distribution (theta=0), all three rank-aware policies (proportional, square-root, and optimal) show a rank-accuracy improvement over uniform replication, attributed to the disjoint-top-10 assumption giving documents at rank 1 systematically higher replication than documents at rank 2, etc.; the rank-aware square-root policy outperforms the rank-aware proportional policy, and the rank-aware optimal policy performs best of all three, consistent across all three p values tested. Per-query analysis at theta=0.7, p=0.6 (Figure 2) showed the rank-unaware proportional policy gave the best rank-accuracy for the handful of most popular queries but left many other queries performing worse than plain uniform replication, while the rank-aware optimal policy was the only one to keep every query's rank-accuracy above the uniform baseline. Simulation Experiment 1 (idealized, matching the theoretical assumptions exactly: query distribution known in advance, top-10 result lists disjoint, correct replication pre-applied before search): m=47,480 documents, rho=500 documents/node, n=10,000 nodes, 10,000 queries issued of which 4,748 were distinct, power-law theta=0.7, z=100 nodes per query. Average rank-accuracy, rank-unaware / rank-aware: 0.71/0.93 at p=0.3 (+31.0%), 0.71/0.83 at p=0.6 (+16.9%), 0.71/0.72 at p=0.9 (+1.4%). Simulation Experiment 2 (real query data: first 1,000,000 queries from an anonymized Yahoo! web search log, non-disjoint top-10 result sets, m=461,788 distinct documents, rho=1,500 documents/node, R=15,000,000 total network storage capacity, query-distribution knowledge and pre-applied replication still assumed): rank-unaware / rank-aware average rank-accuracy 0.72/0.86 at p=0.3 (+19.4%), 0.69/0.76 at p=0.6 (+10.1%), 0.64/0.65 at p=0.9 (+1.6%); the paper attributes the smaller gains relative to Experiment 1 to the Yahoo! query distribution being more heavily skewed toward extremely popular queries than the idealized theta=0.7 power law used in Experiment 1, despite both having theta approximately 0.7. Simulation Experiment 3 (same Yahoo! data and network parameters as Experiment 2, but no prior knowledge of the query distribution: documents start uniformly distributed and each query's returned top-10 documents are replicated onto up to 20 additional nodes according to the policy under test as queries are issued): rank-unaware / rank-aware average rank-accuracy 0.62/0.78 at p=0.3 (+25.8%), 0.58/0.69 at p=0.6 (+19.0%), 0.54/0.56 at p=0.9 (+3.7%); absolute rank-accuracy for every policy was lower than in Experiment 2 because rank-aware and rank-unaware proportional replication are only approximated as queries accumulate, rather than pre-computed exactly.

### Parameters
- n (network size): 10,000 nodes in all theoretical analysis and simulations.
- rho (per-node storage): 500 documents/node in the theoretical analysis and Experiment 1; 1,500 documents/node in Experiments 2 and 3.
- z (nodes queried per search): 100.
- p (RBP persistence parameter): 0.3, 0.6, 0.9 tested; the paper cites a prior study finding p around 0.6-0.7 approximates typical user behavior.
- theta (query power-law exponent): swept 0 to 1.5 in the theoretical analysis (Figure 1); fixed at 0.7 for the per-query analysis (Figure 2) and all three simulation experiments; the paper cites prior web-search-log studies finding theta typically between 0.7 and 1.5.
- Document collection size m: 47,480 in the theoretical analysis and Experiment 1; 461,788 (extracted from the Yahoo! log) in Experiments 2 and 3.
- Replication-onto count in Experiment 3's incremental scheme: up to 20 additional nodes per query-triggered replication event.

### Stated limitations
The paper states the analysis assumes an idealized network in which all nodes operate correctly with no malicious behavior, explicitly following the same assumption used in the original PAC search framework, and states that node failure and security threats are beyond its scope. The paper states that bandwidth and storage overhead of the search and replication mechanisms are outside its scope, following the same exclusion made in the PAC framework it builds on. Experiment 1's disjoint-top-10-result-list assumption is stated by the authors to be "a rather artificial environment"; results using real, non-disjoint result sets (Experiments 2 and 3) show smaller rank-accuracy gains. The paper states that computing the exact document distribution required by rank-aware proportional or square-root replication needs prior knowledge of the full query distribution, which the authors state may be infeasible to obtain in practice for a large-scale system with a large document collection and many queries; this is why Experiment 3 (incremental, query-triggered replication with no prior knowledge) is presented, and the authors state that improving that incremental technique is left as future work. Due to space constraints, the paper states that it does not report simulation results for the square-root and optimal rank-aware replication policies (only for proportional), though it states rank-accuracy for both can also be improved by making them rank-aware.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Rank-aware proportional and square-root replication (Section 3.2, Equations 11-12) require the system to compute, per document, the weighted retrieval rate v_i, which requires observing which query results (with their ranks) each document appeared in and at what query rate; this is the same "learn what a search found" signal square-root replication (Cohen and Shenker; Lv et al.) needs, extended here to also require the returned document's rank position, not just its identity. Experiments 1 and 2 additionally require the full query-rate distribution to be known before replication is applied; Experiment 3 relaxes this to an online scheme that instead requires each querying node to actively push copies of the top-10 documents it retrieves onto up to 20 additional randomly selected nodes after every query, so the replication mechanism needs write access to other nodes' local indexes, not only read access via search. The rank-accuracy metric itself is independent of any specific information-retrieval ranking model, but assumes the ranking model used to compute the exhaustive top-k list is identical to the one applied at each queried node; the paper states this assumption "may not always be valid" when a ranking model requires collection-wide statistics unavailable to individual peers, in which case rank-accuracy becomes an upper bound rather than an exact prediction of achievable performance.

### Contradicts
None found against other entries in this evidence corpus. The paper states an internal contrast with Cohen and Shenker's finding that square-root replication (rank-unaware) is optimal for minimizing expected search length: the rank-unaware PAC framework instead found square-root replication is not optimal under a fixed search length, with the true rank-unaware optimum given by a convex-optimization solution from a separate PhD thesis (Fu, 2012); the paper does not treat this as an error in either source, only as two different objective functions (minimizing search length versus maximizing accuracy at fixed search length) giving different optimal replication policies.

### References worth retrieving
- Cox, Fu, Hansen, "Probably Approximately Correct Search," ICTIR 2009 — foundational; defines the PAC search framework, its independence and non-disjoint-indexing assumptions, and the rank-unaware accuracy metric this paper extends.
- Cohen, Shenker, "Replication Strategies in Unstructured Peer-to-Peer Networks," SIGCOMM 2002 — foundational; source of the square-root-replication result already in this evidence corpus, cited here as the rank-unaware baseline this paper's rank-aware square-root policy is built in analogy to.
- Fu, "The Quality of Probabilistic Search in Unstructured Distributed Information Retrieval Systems," PhD thesis, University College London, 2012 — foundational; source of the convex-optimization method for the rank-unaware optimal replication policy this paper reuses (with the weighting term added) to derive its rank-aware optimal policy (Equation 14).
- Neumann, Bender, Michel, Weikum, "A reproducible benchmark for P2P retrieval," ACM Wkshp. Exp. DB, 2006 — foundational; a P2P-IR benchmark framework cited as an example of comparing distributed search results against a centralized baseline.
- Witschel, Holz, Heinrich, Teresniak, "An Evaluation Measure for Distributed Information Retrieval Systems," ECIR 2008 — competing rank-aware P2P evaluation metric (ARRR), cited as similar in purpose to this paper's rank-accuracy metric.
- Lu, Callan, "User modeling for full-text federated search in peer-to-peer networks," SIGIR 2006 — competing rank-aware P2P evaluation metric (MAOP), cited alongside ARRR as a prior rank-sensitive P2P-IR measure.
- Chapelle, Metzler, Zhang, Grinspan, "Expected reciprocal rank for graded relevance," CIKM 2009 — foundational; source of the p approximately 0.6-0.7 user-persistence estimate this paper uses to justify its RBP parameter range.
- Baeza-Yates, Gionis, Junqueira, Murdock, Silvestri, "The impact of caching on search engines," SIGIR 2007 — foundational; cited as the source for the typical 0.7-1.5 range of the query power-law exponent theta used in this paper's experiments.

"the rank-accuracy is improved even for a uniform query distribution"
"r-opt exhibits the best performance, with all queries having better rank-accuracy"
"increases of 19.4%, 10.1% and 1.6%"
"it may be infeasible to compute the required document distribution based on prior queries"

## [RICHARDSON-SIGIR-14] Estimating Global Statistics for Unstructured P2P Search in the Presence of Adversarial Peers
**Citation:** Sami Richardson, Ingemar J. Cox. "Estimating Global Statistics for Unstructured P2P Search in the Presence of Adversarial Peers." SIGIR, 2014. DOI 10.1145/2600428.2609567.
**Retrieved:** full text via http://www0.cs.ucl.ac.uk/staff/ingemar/Content/papers/2014/sigir2014.pdf
**Source URL:** http://www0.cs.ucl.ac.uk/staff/ingemar/Content/papers/2014/sigir2014.pdf
**Domain:** B

### What it does
The mechanism lets a node ranking documents under BM25 or a language model with Dirichlet smoothing compute the collection-wide statistics those rankers need (document frequency, average document length) inside a Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) peer-to-peer search architecture, where each of n nodes indexes only a random subset of the document collection and a query samples z random nodes. Each queried node u, besides returning its top-k' matching documents (Ru) with per-document scoring fields, also returns a vector of local statistics derived from its own index (Gu) — for BM25 these are per-term local document-frequency counts and local average document length; for the language model, local collection-probability estimates. The querying node combines the Gu values from all z responding nodes into an estimate of the true global statistic and rescoring the returned documents with it before forming the final top-k list. Because a query already contacts z nodes to retrieve matching documents, the statistics estimate is a byproduct of the existing query traffic and adds no round trip. Because responses from a large sample of nodes are combined, the estimate can be biased by malicious responders; the paper's defense has each querying node compute a skewness statistic Kt (Groeneveld-Meeden measure) over the z returned values for each query term, and repeatedly discard the value contributing most to skew until |Kt| falls under a threshold tau, before computing the global-statistic estimate from the surviving values.

### Measured results
Simulated network: n = 10,000 nodes, document collection C from the WT10g web corpus with m = 1,692,096 documents, documents distributed uniformly at random so each node indexes rho documents. Fifty queries drawn from the TREC 2009 Million Query track, each repeated 10 times, averaged. z and rho are chosen jointly so the PAC framework's theoretical expected accuracy P(di) = 1-(1-rho/m)^z equals 0.9 (z = 1; 2000; 4000; 6000; 8000; 10000, with corresponding rho = 1,692,096; 1,946; 973; 649; 486; 389).

| Condition | Result |
|---|---|
| BM25, global statistics from full collection, any z (n=10,000, WT10g) | average accuracy about 0.9 for all tested z |
| BM25, document-frequency term estimated from querying node's own index only | accuracy drop up to nearly 35% as z rises to 10,000 |
| BM25, average-document-length term estimated from querying node's own index only | accuracy drop up to about 10% |
| Language model, collection-probability term from querying node's own index only | accuracy drop up to about 20% |
| BM25 with the global-statistics estimation technique (statistics pooled from z=10,000 nodes' Gu, k'=rho=389 or k'=10) | accuracy close to the 0.9 theoretical value at all tested z |
| Language model with the technique, k'=rho | accuracy close to 0.9 theoretical value |
| Language model with the technique, k'=10, z up to 10,000 | accuracy drops to about 0.8, about 10% below theoretical |
| BM25 with technique, z=10,000, rho=389, k'=10 | about 95% of the 50 test queries reach accuracy >= 0.7, versus 15% when using only the querying node's local index |
| Language model with technique, same setting | about 65% of queries reach accuracy >= 0.7 (versus about 90% with full-collection statistics, 60% with local-only); over 95% of queries reach accuracy >= 0.3 (versus under 80% local-only) |
| No adversary, PAC baseline vulnerability to a censorship attack (excludes target document, correct global statistics available at each node) | z=1,000 nodes queried, f=0.3% malicious nodes gives 0.95 probability at least one malicious node is sampled, hence up to 95% of queries manipulable at the query-routing level even before the global-statistics extension is added |
| Censorship attack via corrupted global statistics, no defense (query T='small dog', target D2, z=2,000, rho=1,946 nodes each) | target document rank moves 5 -> 9 -> 582 -> 2166 as malicious-node fraction f rises 0% -> 10% -> 20% -> 30%; at f=20% the document falls out of a top-10 list |
| Same attack, PAC baseline where only document exclusion (no statistics corruption) is available and correct global statistics are known at every node | at f=20%, retrieval probability of D2 is still 84% (from the closed-form P'(di) = 1-(1-rho/m)^(z(1-f))) |
| Promotion attack via corrupted global statistics, no defense (same query/target D1, z=2,000, rho=1,946) | target rank moves 20,778 -> 84 -> 11 -> 9 as f rises 0% -> 10% -> 20% -> 30%; under 30% malicious nodes suffices to bring it into a top-10 |
| Promotion attack, exclusion-only baseline with correct global statistics at each node | over 95% of nodes must be malicious to bring the same document into a top-10 |
| Disruption attack via corrupted global statistics, no defense (z=2,000, rho=1,946, 50 TREC queries, k=k'=10) | average accuracy falls from a theoretical baseline of about 0.9 to about 0.6 at only 10% malicious nodes, a nearly 35% relative fall |
| Same attack setting, with the skewness defense active (threshold tau = +/-0.1) | attacks have very little effect while the malicious-node fraction f < 40%; the defense breaks down as f approaches 50% because malicious and non-malicious responses become statistically indistinguishable |
| Baseline requirement for random node sampling (cited from Bortnikov et al., not this paper's own measurement) | Brahms, a gossip-based secure peer-sampling service, is stated to withstand up to 20% malicious nodes before sampling bias becomes significant; the authors state this — not their own skewness defense — is what actually bounds the tolerable adversarial fraction in a deployed system |

### Parameters
- n (nodes in simulated network): 10,000, fixed across all experiments.
- m (documents in collection): 1,692,096 (WT10g corpus), fixed.
- z (nodes queried per search): varied over {1, 2000, 4000, 6000, 8000, 10000}; also fixed at 2,000 for the adversarial-attack simulations.
- rho (documents indexed per node): paired with each z to hold theoretical accuracy at 0.9; values {1,692,096; 1,946; 973; 649; 486; 389}; fixed at 1,946 for most attack simulations.
- k' (documents returned per queried node): tested at k'=rho (return everything indexed) and k'=10.
- k (final result-list length considered): 10 in most experiments; attack-manipulation figures (Fig. 4/5) use no top-k restriction so the full range of achievable rank is visible.
- BM25 free parameters: k1 = 2.0, b = 0.75 (paper states these are typical published choices, not tuned by this paper).
- Language-model smoothing parameter: mu = AVGDL (average document length).
- Skewness defense threshold: tau = +/-0.1, used in the reported defense simulations; no other tau value is reported as tested.
- Malicious-node fraction f: varied continuously from 0 to 1 in the theoretical curves (Figures 3, 6-8) and at discrete points {0, 10%, 20%, 30%} in the worked rank examples (Figures 4-5).
- Query set: 50 queries from the TREC 2009 Million Query track, each repeated 10 times and averaged.

### Stated limitations
The authors state the analysis assumes a peer's local collection is a uniform random sample of the global collection, and state that future work is needed for non-uniform sampling, such as sampling weighted by document popularity, suggesting hash sketches (cited to Bender et al.) as a possible basis. The paper assumes malicious nodes cannot forge a document's content well enough to score highly under an honest ranker, attributing that assumption to a requirement that documents be signed by a trusted third party — a requirement this paper does not itself supply or evaluate. The skewness defense is stated to depend on the underlying node-sampling mechanism (Brahms) tolerating enough malicious nodes that its own sampling bias stays below significance (20% for Brahms); if node sampling is more compromised than the statistics-estimation defense can tolerate (40%), sampling failure — not statistics forgery — becomes the binding constraint. The defense is stated to fail as the malicious fraction approaches roughly 50%, because at that point the skewness measure cannot statistically distinguish malicious from honest values.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Requires a secure, gossip-based random peer-sampling layer to select the z queried nodes per query and to bound the fraction of malicious nodes actually reachable by a query, because the entire accuracy analysis is conditioned on the assumption that node selection is unbiased; the paper cites Brahms as the concrete example and states Brahms's own 20% malicious-tolerance bound, not the statistics defense's 40% bound, is what would set the deployed tolerance. Requires each node's local document set to be a uniformly random subset of the global collection, drawn independently of document popularity or any other selection criterion, because the coverage argument (expected number of distinct documents sampled equals P(di)*m) depends on that uniformity; a popularity-weighted or otherwise correlated sampling process is stated as unanalyzed. Requires a mechanism external to this paper — content signing by a trusted third party is the one named — to prevent a malicious node from returning a forged document body that scores well under the honest ranking function; without it, the attacks analyzed here (which corrupt only summary/statistics fields) would need to be extended to cover forged document content. Requires every node to index the same fixed number of documents, rho, so that no node has disproportionate influence on global-statistics estimation; the paper notes a higher-capacity node can be split into multiple rho-capacity virtual nodes, which then must be defended against as a Sybil attack using a mechanism outside the scope of this paper.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus at time of writing. The paper's own baseline results contradict any assumption that PAC-style unstructured search is inherently resistant to a small adversarial minority once collection-wide statistics are attached to the query protocol: the paper explicitly shows the technique moves the tolerable-adversary threshold for effective manipulation from roughly 70% malicious nodes (exclusion-only censorship, correct global statistics known everywhere) down to under 20% (same attack, statistics estimated from the query, no defense).

### References worth retrieving
- Foundational: H. Asthana, R. Fu, I. J. Cox, "On the feasibility of unstructured peer-to-peer information retrieval," Advances in Information Retrieval Theory, Springer, 2011 — the PAC P2P web-search feasibility paper this work builds on.
- Foundational: I. J. Cox, R. Fu, L. K. Hansen, "Probably approximately correct search," Advances in Information Retrieval Theory, Springer, 2009 — defines the PAC framework and its accuracy formula this paper extends.
- Competing: F. M. Cuenca-Acuna, C. Peery, R. P. Martin, T. D. Nguyen, "PlanetP: Using gossiping to build content addressable peer-to-peer information sharing communities," HPDC 2003 — compact per-node index summaries and TF-IPF as an alternative to estimating document frequency directly.
- Competing: J. Lu, J. Callan, "Federated search of text-based digital libraries in hierarchical peer-to-peer networks," ECIR 2005 — hierarchical hub/leaf alternative that maintains exact global statistics at hub nodes.
- Competing: H. Chen, J. Yan, H. Jin, Y. Liu, L. M. Ni, "TSS: Efficient term set search in large peer-to-peer textual collections," IEEE Transactions on Computers 59(7), 2010 — hybrid structured/unstructured design gathering global statistics via a gossip protocol.
- Competing: H. F. Witschel, "Global term weights in distributed environments," Information Processing & Management 44(3), 2008 — random-sampling estimation of global statistics combined with a local reference corpus; the closest prior technique to this paper's own.
- Foundational (peer sampling security): E. Bortnikov, M. Gurevich, I. Keidar, G. Kliot, A. Shraer, "Brahms: Byzantine resilient random membership sampling," Computer Networks 53(13), 2009 — the secure peer-sampling service this paper's threat model depends on and whose 20% malicious-tolerance bound the authors state is the actual system-wide constraint.
- Attack/foundational: J. Douceur, "The Sybil attack," IPTPS/Peer-to-peer Systems, 2002 — cited as the attack model for virtual-node capacity splitting.
- Competing (bias-reduction technique): M. Bender, S. Michel, P. Triantafillou, G. Weikum, "Global document frequency estimation in peer-to-peer web search," 9th Int. Workshop on the Web and Databases, 2006 — hash-sketch document-frequency estimation addressing collection-overlap bias, not adversarial bias; suggested by the authors as a possible basis for handling non-uniform sampling.
- Foundational (dataset): P. Bailey, N. Craswell, D. Hawking, "Engineering a multi-purpose test collection for web retrieval experiments," Information Processing & Management 39(6), 2003 — defines the WT10g corpus used in the simulations.

### Verbatim extracts
- "an adversary controlling fewer than 10% of peers can censor or increase the rank of documents, or disrupt overall search results"
- "global statistics estimation is viable even when up to 40% of peers are adversarial"
- "it would be Brahms that imposes the limit on the maximum number of malicious nodes tolerated"
- "Our work assumed that a peer's local collection consists of a uniform random sample"
- "we assume that malicious nodes cannot construct and return corrupt documents that will score highly"
