## [RICHTER-IMC-16] A Multi-perspective Analysis of Carrier-Grade NAT Deployment

**Citation:** Philipp Richter, Florian Wohlfart, Narseo Vallina-Rodriguez, Mark Allman, Randy Bush, Anja Feldmann, Christian Kreibich, Nicholas Weaver, Vern Paxson. "A Multi-perspective Analysis of Carrier-Grade NAT Deployment." ACM Internet Measurement Conference (IMC), 2016. DOI 10.1145/2987443.2987474.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.prichter.com/imc176-richterA.pdf
**Source URL:** https://doi.org/10.1145/2987443.2987474
**Domain:** L

### What it does
The paper measures how many Internet access networks place a Carrier-Grade NAT (CGN), an address translator an Internet service provider (ISP) operates inside its own network rather than at the customer premises, between a residential or mobile subscriber and the public Internet, and characterizes how those CGNs behave. A CGN operates transparently to the endpoints it serves, which the paper states is what makes detecting and measuring one from outside difficult: no packet a CGN forwards carries evidence that translation occurred, and a sender cannot tell how many times, if any, its own source address will be rewritten on the path to a destination.

Two independent detection methods are used, combined rather than relied on singly. The first crawls the BitTorrent Distributed Hash Table (DHT), a peer discovery protocol, and exploits the fact that some peers behind a CGN mistake their internally assigned, non-routable address (drawn from address ranges reserved for private use, such as 10.0.0.0/8 or the CGN-specific 100.64.0.0/10 block) for a publicly reachable one and announce it into the DHT; other DHT peers that separately query that same host and observe its real, routable source address then "leak" both addresses together into peer lists the crawler collects, letting the paper associate one internal address with one external, routable address, and hence with an Autonomous System (AS, a network operated under one administrative routing policy). The second method extends Netalyzr, the authors' pre-existing network-troubleshooting tool users invoke voluntarily, adding: a device-reported local address compared against the address the Netalyzr server observes as the packet's source, revealing any translation; a User Plug and Play (UPnP) query to the customer's own router for its externally learned address, letting the paper distinguish translation performed by the customer's own equipment from translation performed further upstream; a TTL (Time To Live)-limited keepalive probing technique that forces the mapping state of one hop at a time to expire while others are kept alive, precisely locating which hop on the path is a stateful NAT and how long its mapping persists before timing out; and an implementation of the STUN (Session Traversal Utilities for NAT) protocol that determines the most restrictive NAT mapping type present on the path, because STUN's probe-and-reply exchange reports the behavior of whichever on-path NAT is least permissive.

### Measured results

| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| CGN penetration: 13.3% of all non-cellular routed ASes deploy CGN; 17-18% of non-cellular eyeball ASes (ASes that connect end users, defined two ways: Spamhaus Policy Block List ASes with at least 2,048 end-user addresses, and APNIC Labs AS Population entries with at least 1,000 samples); over 92% of cellular ASes | Combined result across both detection methods; dataset covers roughly 52,000 routed ASes total, 6.0% of all routed ASes but over 60% of eyeball ASes, because both methods depend on voluntary user-run tools (BitTorrent clients, Netalyzr) |
| BitTorrent DHT crawl: 21.5M peers directly queried across 18.8K ASes; 192.0M peer records learned (from peer-list responses) across 26.7K ASes | One-week crawl starting March 3, 2016 |
| Peers reporting a reserved (non-routable) address, by range: 192.168.0.0/16 range 565.9K total / 11.2K unique IPs; 172.16.0.0/12 range 336.6K total / 85.0K unique IPs; 10.0.0.0/8 range 1.3M total / 328.5K unique IPs; 100.64.0.0/10 (CGN-specific) range 1.5M total / 251.5K unique IPs | Same one-week DHT crawl; "leaking" peers that separately propagated both the internal and external address for the same host numbered, respectively, 186.8K/162.2K IPs/4.1K ASes, 52.9K/33.9K/1.0K, 283.9K/194.4K/2.2K, and 192.0K/165.8K/723 |
| Netalyzr non-cellular sessions: 12.5% of device-reported addresses unrouted, 5.7% routed-and-matching (no translation detected), 3.0% routed-mismatch (translation detected) | breakdown by address-range category, Table 4, cellular vs. non-cellular reported separately |
| Netalyzr cellular sessions: 94% show a translated address (all categories except "routed match") | same Netalyzr dataset |
| AS detection coverage and CGN-positive rate by method (Table 5): BitTorrent detects CGN in 5.2% of all routed ASes / 9.40% of Spamhaus eyeball ASes / 10.8% of APNIC eyeball ASes; Netalyzr non-cellular detects CGN in 2.6% / 14.3% / 17.4% respectively; the two methods combined detect CGN in 6.0% / 13.3% / 17.1% respectively; Netalyzr cellular detects CGN in 0.4% of all ASes but 92.6-94.2% of cellular-specific AS populations | Combined coverage across both data sources, same collection window |
| Regional CGN penetration: APNIC and RIPE regions show more than double the CGN penetration of other regions; AFRINIC shows the lowest non-cellular penetration and roughly two-thirds cellular penetration | Breakdown by the five Regional Internet Registries (RIRs); the paper attributes the pattern to APNIC and RIPE having exhausted their IPv4 address allocations first (2011 and 2012) and AFRINIC not yet having exhausted its supply |
| Internal address space usage: 10.0.0.0/8 is the most common CGN-internal range, followed by the CGN-specific 100.64.0.0/10 block; roughly 20% of CGN-deploying ASes use multiple reserved ranges simultaneously; some ISPs use publicly routable address ranges (not always announced by another AS) internally within their CGN, confirmed by direct contact with one such ISP as resulting from a shortage of internal (private) address space | Per-AS breakdown from combined BitTorrent and Netalyzr detection, cellular and non-cellular reported separately |
| Port allocation strategy: pure port-preservation, sequential, or random strategy observed for about a third of non-cellular CGN ASes and about half of cellular CGN ASes; the rest show heterogeneous (mixed) behavior across sessions of the same AS | Determined from 10 sequential TCP flows per Netalyzr session to an echo server on an unlikely-to-be-proxied high port; port-preservation classified when at least 20% of ports are preserved, sequential classified when consecutive port differences stay below 50 |
| Port allocation strategy breakdown (Table 6): non-cellular ASes 41.2% port-preservation, 22.2% sequential, 35.6% random (of which 9 ASes, 4.6%, show fixed-size chunk allocation); cellular ASes 27.9% port-preservation, 26.0% sequential, 44.7% random (of which 8 ASes, 3.7%, show chunk allocation) | Same session-based classification across all detected CGN-positive ASes |
| Chunk-based port allocation: 17 ASes identified using fixed port-block ("chunk") allocation; 6 of these assign a chunk smaller than 1,024 ports per subscriber, 3 of them specifically 512 ports; a 512-port chunk implies up to 128 subscribers sharing one public IP address (the paper's text states 64 subscribers for a 1K/1,024-port chunk, implying the doubled figure for the half-size 512-port chunk) | Detected in ASes with at least 20 sessions of random port translation, all falling within a port range narrower than 16,384; example given, AS12978, allocates 4,096 ports per subscriber |
| NAT pooling: majority of CGN-positive ASes show paired pooling (a subscriber's sequential TCP sessions bind to the same public IP address); 21% of CGN-positive ASes instead show arbitrary pooling (Netalyzr observed more than one global IP address across more than 60% of a test's sessions) | Per-AS classification from Netalyzr session data; arbitrary pooling is stated to be discouraged by IETF guidelines because it complicates protocols such as SIP and RTP that use multiple ports on one host without separately negotiating IP addresses per port |
| TTL-driven NAT enumeration: 38K sessions collected (deployed September 2014); after filtering to networks with at least 3 sessions, 18K sessions remain, covering 608 ASes of which 259 (43%) are CGN-positive; an expired mapping (evidence of a stateful hop) was found in 67.6% of CGN-detected tests and 30.9% of non-CGN-detected tests, with a pure-stateful-firewall-without-translation result in under 0.5% of tests | Idle time tested up to 200 seconds (the practical ceiling given overall Netalyzr session-length constraints); NATs with a mapping timeout exceeding 200 seconds are undetected by this method, understating true NAT prevalence |
| STUN-based mapping-type test: 23K sessions collected (deployed October 2015); after filtering, 20K sessions remain, spanning 720 ASes of which 170 (24%) are CGN-positive; 20K sessions split 87% non-cellular / 13% cellular | Same Netalyzr platform, separate test deployment date |
| UDP mapping timeout: 74% of detected CGN NATs expire idle UDP state within 60 seconds or less, with observed values ranging from 10 to 200 seconds (the test's ceiling); median timeout for cellular CGNs is 65 seconds versus 35 seconds for non-cellular CGNs; customer-premises equipment (CPE) NATs predominantly show a 65-second timeout | Measured only for sessions where the detected NAT sits three or more hops from the client, to exclude CPE-level NAT timeouts from the CGN-specific figure; the method cannot detect timeouts above 200 seconds, so the reported CGN-vs-CPE gap may not generalize |
| NAT distance from client: 92% of NATs in CGN-negative (no-CGN) ASes sit exactly one hop from the client (i.e., at the CPE); CGNs sit two to five hops away in 64% of non-cellular ASes and 73% of cellular ASes; cellular CGN distance ranges one to twelve hops, with 10% of cellular ASes placing the CGN six or more hops from the client; the paper's overall maximum observed CGN distance is 18 hops | TTL-driven NAT enumeration dataset described above |
| STUN mapping-type distribution: fewer than 2% of CPE NATs show the most restrictive (symmetric) mapping type; 11% of non-cellular CGN-positive ASes show symmetric as their most permissive observed mapping type (including several major European ISPs); cellular CGN ASes show a bimodal split, roughly 40% symmetric and roughly 20% full-cone | STUN test dataset described above; the paper reports the most permissive mapping type observed per AS as the CGN's own behavior, reasoning that when several NATs sit on one path, STUN reports the most restrictive of them, so the most permissive AS-level result is the best available approximation of the CGN's own (least restrictive on top of any CPE) type |

### Parameters
- BitTorrent DHT crawl duration: one week, starting March 3, 2016.
- Netalyzr TTL-enumeration test idle-time ceiling: 200 seconds (a session-length practical limit, not a protocol limit).
- Port-preservation classification threshold: at least 20% of ports preserved across a session's 10 sequential TCP flows.
- Sequential-allocation classification threshold: consecutive port differences under 50.
- Chunk-based allocation classification: at least 20 sessions showing random port translation, all falling within a port range under 16,384 (16K).
- Eyeball-AS definition 1 (Spamhaus Policy Block List): AS holding at least 2,048 addresses in end-user address blocks.
- Eyeball-AS definition 2 (APNIC Labs AS Population list): AS with at least 1,000 recorded samples.
- Minimum session count per AS for TTL-enumeration and STUN filtering: at least 3 sessions from the same AS/CGN-classification combination.

### Stated limitations
The paper states its methods together give only a partial, not exhaustive, view of CGN deployment, because each depends on voluntary user-run software: the BitTorrent-DHT method does not illuminate mobile-carrier CGN use, since mobile devices rarely run BitTorrent clients; the Netalyzr method depends on users choosing to run the tool, which the paper states makes its measured population smaller than the DHT crawl's but under the authors' direct control (letting them add explicit tests such as UPnP probing that the DHT method cannot supply). The TTL-driven NAT enumeration test cannot detect a NAT whose idle-state mapping timeout exceeds 200 seconds, the practical ceiling imposed by overall Netalyzr session-length limits, which the paper states leads to underestimating the true number of stateful NATs present (30.9% of tests in Table 7 found no expired mapping, some unknown fraction of which are undetected long-timeout NATs rather than true absences). The enumeration technique also cannot by itself distinguish a NAT from any other stateful middlebox, such as a stateful firewall performing no address translation, though the paper states this ambiguous case affects fewer than 0.5% of tests and those cases are excluded from the reported figures. The paper states it remains out of scope for this work to precisely measure the effect of CGNs on end-user application performance; that measurement is left to future work.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Neither detection method requires cooperation from the ISP or CGN operator: the BitTorrent method depends only on the DHT protocol's existing peer-list propagation behavior and a crawler that can issue DHT queries and record replies; the Netalyzr method depends only on end users voluntarily installing and running the tool, and on the tool's own server distinguishing the packet's observed source address from the address the client software reports locally. The TTL-driven enumeration technique specifically depends on both the client and the measurement server being able to send TTL-limited packets and observe whether a given hop still forwards traffic after an idle period, which requires a stable number of hops on the path for the duration of one test (the paper filters out results from paths whose hop count changes mid-test). The STUN-based mapping-type test depends on a publicly reachable STUN server capable of replying from a different port and/or address than it received the probe on, per the STUN protocol (RFC 3489, already in this batch as ROSENBERG-RFC-03), and reports only the most restrictive behavior among all on-path NATs, so it cannot by itself attribute a given restriction to a specific hop; the paper compensates for this by taking the least-restrictive AS-wide result as its estimate of CGN-specific (as opposed to CPE-specific) behavior. Any design relying on NAT mapping type or timeout to predict connectivity (for example, a peer-to-peer hole-punching scheme) must treat the CGN's own restrictiveness as independent of, and potentially more restrictive than, the customer's own CPE NAT, since the paper measures CGNs frequently applying stricter (for example, symmetric) mapping and shorter timeouts than commonly deployed home routers.

### Contradicts
None found in this batch. The paper's own comparison (Section 6.5) states CGN mapping is frequently more restrictive than CPE-router mapping, a claim the paper backs with its own STUN measurement rather than a comparison against an external source's figure.

## [RIPEANU-IPTPS-02] Mapping the Gnutella Network: Properties of Large-Scale Peer-to-Peer Systems and Implications for System Design
**Citation:** Matei Ripeanu, Ian T. Foster, Adriana Iamnitchi. "Mapping the Gnutella Network: Properties of Large-Scale Peer-to-Peer Systems and Implications for System Design." IPTPS 2002 (also IEEE Internet Computing 6(1), 2002).
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/abs/cs/0209028
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/cs/0209028
**Domain:** B

### What it does
The mechanism is a distributed network crawler that discovers the live application-level topology of the deployed Gnutella query-broadcast network, so its connectivity structure, generated traffic, and mapping onto the physical Internet can be measured directly rather than assumed. The crawler joins the network as an ordinary Gnutella node (a "servent," meaning a node performing both server and client roles) and uses the protocol's PING-PONG membership messages: it sends a PING to each node on a working list, receives PONG replies naming that node's neighbors, records each discovered node's IP address, port, shared file count, and shared storage volume, and adds newly found neighbors to the list. A first, sequential implementation of this crawl took about 50 hours to complete even on a 4,000-node network, which the authors state was too slow, both because it did not scale and because Gnutella's node population changes during that time, so the resulting graph was not close to a single-instant snapshot. The authors then built a client/server distributed crawler, where a server assigns each of up to 50 clients a small set of starting points and each client explores the topology around those points; the server assembles the client results into one graph. This reduced crawl time to a few hours even for graphs exceeding 30,000 active nodes. The paper's measurement excludes any node reported by another node's PONG but that the crawler itself could not connect to (for example, a node already at its configured connection limit, or one that left the network before being reached), which the authors state is a deliberately conservative definition of network membership.

### Measured results
Crawls run in three windows over a 6-month period: November 2000, February/March 2001, and May 2001. Largest connected component size grew from 2,063 hosts (November 2000) to 14,949 hosts (March 2001) to 48,195 hosts (May 2001), a roughly 25x increase; the largest connected component held more than 95% of all discovered active nodes in each crawl. A modified version of the crawler eavesdropped traffic across one randomly chosen link and classified it by Gnutella message type; results were verified by measuring traffic at multiple, randomly chosen additional nodes. In November 2000, after adjusting for message size, 36% of traffic bytes were user-generated QUERY messages, 55% was PING/PONG membership-maintenance overhead, and 9% was non-standard or PUSH-protocol traffic from older client versions; by after June 2001, the same breakdown had shifted to 92% QUERY and 8% PING, with other message types described as insignificant. Node-to-node shortest-path distribution, measured across multiple crawls: 95% of node pairs were within 7 hops of each other, matching the message time-to-live (TTL) of 7 in general use, and the largest observed network diameter was 12 hops. Because traffic on any given link is proportional to the number of connections under this flooding/TTL-7 regime (verified by direct multi-node traffic measurement), the authors estimate total Gnutella-generated traffic (excluding file-transfer payload) for a 50,000-node network at approximately 1 Gbps, computed as 170,000 total connections times 6 Kbps per connection, equal to about 330 TB/month; this figure is stated to represent about 1.7% of total US Internet backbone traffic as of December 2000 (citing a separate traffic-growth study). Average per-node connectivity remained constant at 3.4 connections/node across the full network-size range measured (roughly 2,000 to 48,000 nodes), despite the network scaling by almost two orders of magnitude over the 7-month observation period. Node connectivity distribution in November 2000 fit a power law on a log-log plot (fraction of nodes with L links proportional to L^-k); by March 2001 (and similarly in May/June 2001) the distribution had become multi-modal: nodes with more than 10 connections still followed a power-law tail, while nodes with 10 or fewer connections followed an almost constant (flat) distribution rather than continuing the power-law trend. The subset of highly connected, server-like nodes was measured to be about 50% more likely than an average node to still be present across two successive crawls (a stated churn/availability measurement, not further quantified with a base survival rate in the extracted text). Dynamic-membership measurement: about 40% of nodes left the network in under 4 hours, and only 25% remained connected for more than 24 hours. Internet-mapping experiment 1 (Autonomous System, AS, granularity): only 2-5% of Gnutella connections linked two nodes located in the same AS, even though more than 40% of measured nodes were located within the top 10 ASs by node count, indicating most Gnutella traffic crosses AS boundaries. Internet-mapping experiment 2 (domain-name clustering): the Gnutella topology graph was partitioned into clusters using a hub-plus-neighbors heuristic (clusters sharing more than 25% of their nodes were merged), and an information-theoretic entropy measure (Shannon entropy, as defined in Cover & Thomas) compared the resulting clustering against a partition by DNS domain name, run on 10 topology graphs from February/March 2001; the clustering-induced entropy decrease from the unclustered baseline was always under 8%, which the authors interpret as showing the Gnutella overlay's self-organized clustering is effectively independent of the underlying domain-name/Internet structure.

### Parameters
- Crawler distribution: up to 50 parallel clients, chosen by the authors specifically to limit crawl invasiveness even though "easily...hundreds" were available to use.
- Sequential-crawler baseline: roughly 50 hours to crawl a 4,000-node network before the distributed crawler was built.
- Distributed crawler: reduced crawl duration to a few hours for graphs above 30,000 active nodes.
- Message TTL in general Gnutella use during the study: 7 hops.
- Cluster-merge threshold in the domain-mapping entropy analysis: two clusters merged if they shared more than 25% of their nodes.
- Traffic-estimate inputs for the 330 TB/month figure: 50,000-node network, 170,000 total connections, 6 Kbps/connection.

### Stated limitations
The authors state their crawler's output is not an exact instantaneous snapshot, because node churn during the crawl (about 40% of nodes leave within 4 hours) means the discovered graph reflects nodes observed across the crawl's duration, not a single instant; they state their view that the graph is close to a snapshot "in a statistical sense" (aggregate properties such as size, diameter, average connectivity, and connectivity distribution) but do not claim per-edge accuracy at a single moment. The authors state that computing an exact mapping between the Gnutella virtual topology and the true Internet router-level topology was prohibitively expensive, both because Internet topology itself is hard to extract and because of the scale of the computation, so both mapping experiments (AS-level and domain-name-level) are stated as high-level approximations rather than an exact mapping. The domain-name-clustering experiment explicitly assumes that domain-name hierarchy tracks physical network locality (the authors state this as an assumption, offering the ".uchicago.edu"-to-".sdsc.edu" example, rather than a measured fact). The paper states that easily obtainable topology information (the same kind their crawler collects) would permit efficient denial-of-service attacks against Gnutella and that the network at the time of study had no mechanism to prevent an intruder from gathering it, which the authors flag as an open security gap rather than something the paper resolves. The explanations offered for the multi-modal connectivity distribution (a technically sophisticated user base with above-average broadband access, and a lack of any protocol incentive to limit connection count) are explicitly labeled by the authors as speculation ("we speculate"), not as a measured causal finding.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The traffic-proportional-to-connection-count relationship the authors rely on for their bandwidth estimate depends on the TTL-7, flood-based query-routing scheme in use at the time; the measurement and the resulting 330 TB/month estimate apply to that routing regime specifically and the paper does not claim the relationship holds under a different routing or replication scheme. The crawler's own methodology (unauthenticated PING/PONG membership discovery available to any participant) is the same capability the paper states could be exploited for denial-of-service targeting, so any redesign that keeps this membership-discovery mechanism open to all participants inherits the mapping-based attack surface the authors describe, without the paper proposing a mitigation beyond noting the gap. The domain-name/AS mismatch findings assume the crawled connections are a faithful sample of the deployed overlay's actual routing paths, which requires the same conservative-membership crawl methodology (excluding unreachable reported nodes) used throughout the paper.

### Contradicts
None found against other entries in this evidence corpus. The paper's own November 2000 measurement (Figure 5) found the Gnutella connectivity distribution to be a clean power law, which the authors state agrees with two prior studies (Adamic et al.; DSS Group), but their own March/May 2001 crawls (Figure 6) found this had shifted to a multi-modal distribution; the authors present this as a real change in the deployed network over time, not a disagreement between measurements of the same state.

### References worth retrieving
- Adamic, Lukose, Puniyani, Huberman, "Search in Power-Law Networks," Physical Review E, 2001 — foundational; independent confirmation the authors cite for early Gnutella networks following a pure power-law connectivity distribution, contrasted with this paper's later multi-modal finding.
- Saroiu, Gummadi, Gribble, "A Measurement Study of Peer-to-Peer File Sharing Systems," University of Washington TR UW-CSE-01-06-02, 2001 — competing/independent measurement study of P2P file-sharing systems, cited for the Gnutella user modem-versus-broadband connectivity breakdown this paper uses to explain its multi-modal distribution.
- Barabási, Albert, "Emergence of Scaling in Random Networks," Science 286(509), 1999 — foundational; the general power-law network model this paper tests Gnutella against.
- Albert, Jeong, Barabási, "Attack and Tolerance in Complex Networks," Nature 406, 2000 — foundational; source of the robustness-to-random-failure-but-vulnerable-to-targeted-attack property this paper's Gnutella analysis is built on.
- Sripanidkulchai, "The Popularity of Gnutella Queries and Its Implications on Scalability," 2001 — foundational; cited for the Zipf's-law query-popularity distribution motivating this paper's proxy-caching suggestion for future P2P designs.
- Ratnasamy, Francis, Handley, Karp, Shenker, "A Scalable Content-Addressable Network," SIGCOMM 2001 — competing structured-overlay alternative (CAN), cited as a system proposing semantic query routing this paper contrasts with preserving Gnutella's unstructured power-law character.
- Rhea, Wells, Eaton, Geels, Zhao, Weatherspoon, Kubiatowicz, "Maintenance-Free Global Storage in OceanStore," IEEE Internet Computing 5(5) — competing structured storage system (Tapestry-based), cited in the same category as CAN.

"only 2-5% of Gnutella connections link nodes located within the same AS"
"all decreases were within less than 8% from the initial entropy value"

## [ROSENBERG-RFC-03] STUN - Simple Traversal of User Datagram Protocol (UDP) Through Network Address Translators (NATs)

**Citation:** Jonathan Rosenberg, Joel Weinberger, Christian Huitema, Rohan Mahy. "STUN - Simple Traversal of User Datagram Protocol (UDP) Through Network Address Translators (NATs)." IETF RFC 3489, March 2003. DOI 10.17487/RFC3489.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3489
**Source URL:** https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3489
**Domain:** L

### What it does
STUN (Simple Traversal of User Datagram Protocol Through Network Address Translators) lets a client behind a network address translator (NAT) discover the address and port the NAT has substituted for its own, and additionally determine which of four behavioral categories the NAT falls into, by sending UDP requests to a public STUN server and comparing what address the server reports receiving against what address the client actually sent from. The four categories, in order from least to most restrictive, are: full cone (every external host can reach the internal host at its one mapped address, regardless of which external address the internal host has contacted); restricted cone (only an external host the internal host has previously sent a packet to, identified by IP address alone, can reach it back); port restricted cone (the same restriction, but matched on the external host's IP address and port together); and symmetric (the NAT assigns a distinct external mapping to every distinct destination address-and-port pair the internal host contacts, so a mapping learned by contacting the STUN server cannot be reused to receive traffic from any other peer).

The client determines which category applies through a sequence of up to three tests built on two request variants the server supports: an ordinary Binding Request, answered from the same server address and port the request arrived on, and a Binding Request carrying a CHANGE-REQUEST attribute asking the server to answer from a different IP address, a different port, or both. Test I (an ordinary request) reveals whether the client sits behind any NAT at all, by comparing the client's own socket address against the MAPPED-ADDRESS the server reports receiving; if they match, the client is unNATed, and a further test (requesting a response from a changed address and port) distinguishes open Internet access from a symmetric UDP firewall (a firewall that requires replies to originate from the address a request was sent to, without performing any address translation). If the addresses differ, the client is behind some NAT, and requesting a response from the changed address and port distinguishes full cone (response received) from the three more restrictive types (no response). Among those, repeating Test I toward the server's alternate address, then comparing the newly returned mapped address against the first test's result, distinguishes symmetric NAT (different mapping per destination) from the two cone types; a further request asking only for a changed port then distinguishes restricted cone from port restricted cone. Because the NAT closest to the public Internet along the path is the one that determines actual reachability, when several NATs sit in series between the client and the server, this procedure reports the behavior of whichever of them is the most restrictive, not necessarily the one nearest the client.

### Measured results
None. This document is a protocol specification defining message formats, the classification algorithm, and normative client and server behavior; it contains no experimental measurement, testbed trial, or deployment dataset of any kind. Any figure describing NAT-type prevalence in a real deployment must come from a separate measurement paper (for example RICHTER-IMC-16 in this batch, which applies this document's own four-way taxonomy and its STUN mapping-type test to measured deployments), not from this specification itself.

### Parameters
- Binding Request retransmission schedule: retransmit starting at a 100 ms interval, doubling on each retransmit until reaching 1.6 s, then continuing at 1.6 s intervals until a response arrives or 9 requests total have been sent; requests are sent at 0 ms, 100 ms, 300 ms, 700 ms, 1500 ms, 3100 ms, 4700 ms, 6300 ms, and 7900 ms, and the client declares the transaction failed if no response arrives by 9500 ms (1.6 s after the final retransmit).
- Shared Secret Request / Binding Request transaction failure timeout: 9.5 seconds after the first request is sent (matches the retransmission-schedule endpoint above).
- Post-response listen window: after receiving one response, the client MUST keep listening for further (duplicate) responses to the same request for 10 seconds.
- Username validity window for a shared secret obtained via a Shared Secret Request: 9 minutes.
- Recommended interval between repeating the full discovery process from the same local address and port: at least half an hour, stated as sufficient for prior NAT bindings from an earlier discovery run to have expired and stop interfering with a repeated test; alternatively, the client can use a different local address and port for each repeated run to avoid the issue entirely.
- Transaction ID: 128 bits of randomness per request, used by the client to reject any response not matching an outstanding request.

### Stated limitations
The specification states its own applicability limits explicitly at the outset: STUN does not enable incoming TCP connections through a NAT at all; it does not enable incoming UDP packets through symmetric NATs, described as common in large enterprises; its discovery procedure rests on assumptions about how NATs treat UDP that the document itself flags as liable to become invalid as new NAT devices are deployed; it does not work when the peer a client wants to reach sits behind the same NAT as the client; and it does not work if the STUN server itself is not reachable within a shared public address realm common to both communicating clients. Section 14 (framed as the IAB's required brittleness discussion for any "UNilateral Self-Address Fixing," UNSAF, proposal) lists further concrete failure conditions: the binding-acquisition technique yields a usable address for any application only behind a full cone NAT, requires application-specific handling behind restricted or port restricted cone NATs, and yields no usable address at all behind a symmetric NAT; NAT binding refresh intervals are described as highly implementation-specific and therefore not reliably determinable, so a client waiting for an incoming message rather than actively receiving traffic wastes bandwidth on refresh traffic it cannot size correctly; using STUN adds at least one round-trip time of latency to call setup for a real-time application; and binding-lifetime discovery itself is described as "prone to error" because it assumes one lifetime applies uniformly across a NAT's bindings, an assumption a NAT using dynamic lifetimes under load, or one that reboots mid-discovery, can violate. Two topological failure conditions are stated explicitly: an address obtained from a STUN server is not usable by a peer if that STUN server does not sit in an address realm that is a common network ancestor of both communicating clients, and even when it does, some NATs refuse to accept a packet sent from inside their own network back to a public address that maps back into that same network (a case this document states requires additional, unspecified protocol mechanisms or configuration to detect). The document states its central security limitation directly: STUN "introduces potential security threats which cannot be eliminated," calling the underlying problem "provably unsolvable" given what STUN attempts, and describes only mitigating heuristics, not a resolution, deferring the full description to its Security Considerations section.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The mechanism requires a STUN server reachable over UDP by the client and located in a public address realm that both communicating peers can treat as a common topological ancestor; if the client's application later shares its discovered mapped address with a peer, correct operation depends on that ancestor condition holding, which STUN itself has no way to verify or detect a violation of. The classification procedure requires the STUN server to support the CHANGE-REQUEST attribute, meaning the server must itself have more than one public IP address and more than one listening port available to answer from, since two of the three tests ask the server to reply from an address, a port, or both, that differ from where the request arrived. Any application depending on the discovered mapped address remaining valid must independently track and refresh the underlying NAT binding, at an interval the application must determine for itself since this document states NAT binding timeouts are implementation-specific and not discoverable with certainty; the document's companion "Binding Lifetime Discovery" procedure (Section 10.2) offers only an approximation, degraded further under a NAT with dynamic, load-dependent lifetimes. A client repeating the discovery procedure must either wait roughly half an hour or use a fresh local address and port each time, or risk a leftover binding from the prior run corrupting the new classification result. Any protocol built on top of STUN's discovered address for peer-to-peer rendezvous must independently defend against the injected-fake-mapped-address attacks this document describes (Section 12.1): it names Distributed Denial of Service against a third-party target, silencing a legitimate client, identity assumption, and eavesdropping, and states the transaction-ID randomness (128 bits) as the only structural defense STUN itself supplies, which is effective only against an attacker who cannot observe the client-to-server traffic.

### Contradicts
None found.

### References worth retrieving
- Daigle (Editor), "IAB Considerations for UNilateral Self-Address Fixing (UNSAF) Across Network Address Translation," RFC 3424, 2002 — foundational, the framework this document's Section 14 brittleness and limitations discussion is structured to satisfy point by point.
- Srisuresh, Kuthan, Rosenberg, Molitor, Rayhan, "Middlebox Communication Architecture and Framework," RFC 3303, 2002 — competing, the MIDCOM (Middlebox Communication) protocol this document contrasts itself against, citing MIDCOM's requirement for upgraded NAT/firewall hardware and an explicit control relationship as reasons STUN instead works with unmodified NATs.
- Senie, "Network Address Translator (NAT)-Friendly Application Design Guidelines," RFC 3235, 2002 — foundational, cited as the existing NAT-friendly design guidance many peer-to-peer protocols cannot follow, motivating STUN's existence.
- Holdrege, Srisuresh, "Protocol Complications with the IP Network Address Translator," RFC 3027, 2001 — foundational, cited as documenting the online-game and similar protocol complications STUN's discovery techniques are partly derived from.
- Rosenberg, Schulzrinne, Camarillo, Johnston, Peterson, Sparks, Handley, Schooler, "SIP: Session Initiation Protocol," RFC 3261, 2002 — foundational, the primary application protocol STUN's Voice over IP usage examples (RTP/RTCP keepalive behavior) are drawn from.
- Rosenberg, Mahy, Matthews, Wing, "Session Traversal Utilities for NAT (STUN)," RFC 5389, 2008 — superseded-by, obsoletes this document; itself later obsoleted by RFC 8489 (already in this batch as PETIT-HUGUENIN-RFC-18).
- Ferguson, Senie, "Network Ingress Filtering: Defeating Denial of Service Attacks which employ IP Source Address Spoofing," BCP 38, RFC 2827, 2000 — foundational, cited as a normative reference for source-address-spoofing defenses relevant to the reflector/amplification attacks this document analyzes.

## [SAFARPOOR-DEHKORDI-AAMAS-25] More Efficient Sybil Detection Mechanisms Leveraging Resistance of Users to Attack Requests
**Citation:** Ali Safarpoor Dehkordi, Ahad N. Zehmakan. "More Efficient Sybil Detection Mechanisms Leveraging Resistance of Users to Attack Requests." AAMAS, 2025. DOI 10.5555/3709347.3743572.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.16624
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.16624
**Domain:** F

### What it does
This mechanism improves an existing Sybil (fake-account) detector's accuracy by running two
graph-algorithm preprocessing steps before that detector runs, using the concept of a benign
user's resistance to an attack request — whether that user rejects a friend/connection request
from a fake account. Resistance r(v) of a user v is 0 (accepts any incoming request) or 1
(rejects). Revealing a user's resistance means testing it directly, described as sending a
friend request from a dummy Sybil account to that user and observing accept/reject.

Preprocessing step one, Maximizing Benigns (MB), selects a budget of k users whose resistance
to reveal so that revealing them provably or heuristically identifies the largest expected count
of additional users as benign. A user is newly discoverable as benign if a path exists from it to
a user already known to be benign, where every user on that path (except possibly the endpoint
itself) has been revealed to have resistance 1 (a resistant user only accepts requests from users
it already trusts, so an unbroken chain of resistant users back to a known-benign anchor rules
out a Sybil origin for that path). The paper proves this maximization problem is #P-hard to
compute exactly (via a reduction from the a-b Connectedness for Induced Subgraphs problem) and
that no polynomial-time (1-1/e)-approximation exists unless NP ⊆ DTIME(n^(O(log log n))) (via
reduction from Maximum Coverage). It gives two algorithms: a Monte Carlo Greedy algorithm that
estimates the objective by repeated random sampling (its sample count is derived from Hoeffding's
inequality to bound estimation error within ε at confidence α), and a Traversing algorithm that
greedily picks, at each step, the not-yet-revealed user with highest (resistance probability ×
count of not-yet-benign in-neighbors), updating in-neighbor counts as each reveal resolves.

Preprocessing step two, Discovering Potential Attack Edges (PAE), identifies edges likely to run
from a Sybil into the benign region. A potential attack edge is defined as an incoming edge to a
known-benign user whose resistance equals 0 (accepts requests indiscriminately), from a user
outside both the known-benign and known-Sybil sets. Because no two candidate reveals' discovered
edge-sets overlap in this formulation, selecting the k benign users with the highest expected
value of (1 − resistance-probability) × (count of qualifying in-neighbors) is provably optimal,
computed in linear time using a median-of-medians top-k selection. Downstream, the discovered
potential attack edges are used to reduce the edge weight given to them in a detection algorithm
that relies on homophily (the tendency of connected users to share a benign/Sybil label).

The paper also introduces a synthetic-dataset generation framework that overlays a Sybil region
onto a real benign social graph, offering three named attack strategies for how a Sybil "copies"
a benign subgraph and forms attack edges into it: Random (uniform request targeting), Preferential
Attachment (a modified Barabási-Albert model that also weights by a target's history of accepting
prior attack requests), and BFS (breadth-first traversal outward from each Sybil's paired benign
node, falling back to Preferential Attachment when BFS cannot reach enough targets).

### Measured results

| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| Traversing algorithm completes in 119 milliseconds vs. 52 minutes for Monte Carlo Greedy, at budget k=30 | Facebook dataset (SNAP), Preferential Attachment attack strategy |
| Traversing and both Monte Carlo Greedy variants "significantly outperform" Random, Highest-Resistance, and Highest-Resistance-and-Degree baselines on discovered-benigns count; Traversing outperforms both Monte Carlo variants | Facebook dataset (4,039 nodes, 88,234 undirected edges, avg in/out-degree 43.69), budget k ranging 1 to unstated max, three attack strategies; qualitative claim from Figure 2, no numeric gap stated in the main text |
| Proposed PAE algorithm outperforms Random selection at discovering potential attack edges, at all tested budgets | Facebook dataset; proven optimal by construction, not merely observed |
| ~20% of the PAE algorithm's discovered potential attack edges are true attack edges (Sybil-to-benign), for various budgets; this ratio approaches that of a Full-Knowledge algorithm (which knows the true resistance values, unavailable to the proposed algorithm) as budget grows | Facebook dataset, all three attack strategies |
| Sybil-detection AUC (Area Under the Curve) after MB preprocessing (Traversing) rises for all three detectors and all three attack strategies over no preprocessing (Init): SybilSCAR 0.924→0.988 (Random), 0.876→0.954 (Preferential Attachment/BA), 0.986→0.995 (BFS); SybilWalk 0.966→0.998 (Random), 0.929→0.972 (BA), 0.985→0.996 (BFS); SybilMetric held at 1.00/1.00 (Random), 1.00/1.00 (BA), 0.97→0.99 (BFS) | Facebook dataset, known-benign training set of 80 users (2% of benigns, matched by an equal count of Sybils), Sybil fraction fixed at 10% of the network, MB+PAE preprocessing budget fixed at 1% of benigns |
| Adding PAE discovery after MB (MB+PAE) changes AUC inconsistently versus MB alone: e.g. SybilMetric under BA drops from 1.00 to 1.00 (no change), under Random unchanged at 0.988/0.998, under BA SybilSCAR drops slightly from 0.954 to 0.944, under BFS SybilMetric rises from 0.99 to 1.00 | Same setup as above; the paper states PAE-based weight reduction "enhances the AUC in some cases, but not always" |
| Sybil fraction fixed at ~10% of network size in synthetic attacks, non-resistant fraction fixed at 25% of benign users, based on external prevalence figures the paper cites (not measured in this paper) | Applies to all reported experiments; cited external figures: ~16% Sybil rate on Facebook per one study, ~10% fake-account rate on Twitter per a 2013 study, 18% immediate accept / 52% undecided after two weeks / 30% decline in a university fake-friend-request study |

### Parameters
- Budget k: varied from 1 to an unstated maximum in the MB and PAE experiments (Figures 2–3); fixed at 1% of the benign-set size for the classification-preprocessing experiments (Table 1).
- Known-benign/training-set size: 2% of the benign set, matched by an equal count of known Sybils; concretely 80 (Facebook), 200 (Pokec), 150 (LastFM), 200 (Twitter) users.
- Sybil-set size: fixed at approximately 10% of the network, a pick attributed to the cited 16% (Facebook) and 10% (Twitter) real-world Sybil-rate studies, not derived from this paper's own measurement.
- Non-resistant fraction: fixed at 25% of benign users, a pick attributed to the cited university fake-friend-request study (18% immediate accept, 52% undecided after two weeks).
- Resistance-probability generator: p_r(v) = (1 − r(v))·x³ + r(v)·(1 − x³) for x drawn uniformly on [0,1]; the paper states that for r(v)=1 this gives P(p_r(v) ≥ 0.5) = 0.79 and an average probability value of 0.75, with no derivation offered beyond restating the formula's output at that one input.
- Random-strategy multiplier c: set to 4 in all attack strategies, chosen so that the expected accepted-attack count matches the desired non-resistance ratio of 25%.
- Monte Carlo Greedy sample count R: set to ⌈k²·Δ_in²·ln(1/(1−α)) / (2ε²)⌉ via Hoeffding's inequality, for a caller-chosen error margin ε and confidence α; no specific ε/α values are stated as used in the reported experiments.
- Datasets: Facebook (4,039 nodes, 88,234 undirected edges, avg degree 43.69, source SNAP), Twitter (10,000 nodes, 350,600 directed edges, avg degree 35.06, source SNAP), LastFM (7,624 nodes, 27,806 undirected edges, avg degree 7.29, source SNAP), Pokec (10,000-node induced subgraph of benigns, 94,066 directed edges, avg degree 9.4).

### Stated limitations
The paper states its own greedy-preprocessing objective function for Maximizing Benigns is not
submodular (proved in an appendix), so the standard (1−1/e) approximation guarantee for greedy
algorithms does not apply to it, despite empirically strong performance. It states exact
computation of the Maximizing Benigns objective is #P-hard, forcing reliance on either Monte
Carlo estimation (computationally far slower, 52 minutes vs. 119 milliseconds at k=30 on
Facebook) or the heuristic Traversing algorithm, which carries no proven approximation ratio.
It states current sybil-detection methods, including its own preprocessing approach, are
"vulnerable to dataset biases, especially when preprocessing reveals new benigns and skews the
dataset," and lists developing bias-robust algorithms as future work. It states that reducing
discovered potential-attack-edge weights (rather than directly incorporating potential-attack-edge
information into the detection algorithms) produces an inconsistent AUC benefit, and identifies
direct incorporation as an open avenue rather than a solved problem. It states that finding a
Maximizing Benigns algorithm with a proven theoretical approximation guarantee (given the proven
non-submodularity) remains future work. It states its own preprocessing algorithms assume the
attacker (Sybil accounts) does not itself exhibit resistance and do not model an attacker that
selectively rejects requests to other suspected Sybils to reduce detectable homophily, though the
paper notes this is a real possibility for attackers to exploit.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Requires an ability to directly test a specific user's resistance to an attack request — the
paper's operational definition is sending a friend request from a dummy Sybil account and
observing whether it is accepted — which consumes a "budget" the paper treats as scarce (avoiding
"bombarding all users"); the rest of the system must supply this test channel and bound its use.
Requires a pre-existing set of known-benign and known-Sybil users to seed the graph traversal
(2% of the benign population, matched one-to-one with an equal count of known Sybils, in the
paper's own experiments); the algorithms do not initialize from zero external labels. Requires
the underlying social graph's edges (accept/reject relationships) to be observable to the
component running the preprocessing, including in-degree and neighbor-set structure, to compute
the per-node scores both algorithms use. The downstream detection algorithms (SybilSCAR,
SybilWalk, the logistic-regression classifier the paper calls SybilMetric) must expose either an
extra set of newly discovered benign labels (for the MB preprocessing output) or an edge-weighting
input (for the PAE preprocessing output) for the composition to take effect — the paper measures
benefit only through those two specific injection points.

### Contradicts
None found among the papers in this corpus. The paper's own dataset-generation critique
(Section 2) states that prior synthesized Sybil datasets (citing SybilBelief's synthesized Sybil
region and another cited framework's uniform-random-edge assumption) are less realistic than its
own resistance-based attack strategies — an attributed methodological critique of those specific
prior works, not a disagreement about a shared measured quantity.

### References worth retrieving
- Q. Cao, M. Sirivianos, X. Yang, T. Pregueiro. "Aiding the detection of fake accounts in large scale social online services." NSDI 2012 — competing (SybilRank; already in this batch, CAO-NSDI-12)
- Prior work introducing SybilWalk (cited [20]) — competing (one of the three detection algorithms this paper's preprocessing is measured against)
- Prior work introducing SybilSCAR (cited [38]) — competing (unifies random-walk and belief-propagation detection; one of the three detectors measured against)

## [SAFARPOOR-DEHKORDI-ARXIV-25] Graph-Based Fake Account Detection: A Survey
**Citation:** Ali Safarpoor Dehkordi, Ahad N. Zehmakan. "Graph-Based Fake Account Detection: A Survey." arXiv preprint, 2025. DOI 10.48550/arXiv.2507.06541.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/pdf/2507.06541
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.06541
**Domain:** F

### What it does
The paper classifies published methods for fake-account detection (FAD) in online social networks (OSNs) by the graph mechanism each method uses to separate real accounts from fake accounts. It groups methods into three families: classical graph algorithms (random walk and loopy belief propagation), traditional machine-learning methods on hand-built graph features, and graph neural network (GNN) methods, and further subdivides the GNN family by how each method handles heterophilic edges (edges joining nodes of different classes), multiple edge or node types, added content features, contrastive training, reinforcement learning, temporal dynamics, mixture-of-experts routing, federated training, and adversarial robustness.

Every method the survey covers relies on one of two structural assumptions stated formally. The homophily assumption states that real accounts predominantly connect to other real accounts while fake accounts are pushed into connecting mostly with each other, because their attempts to connect to real accounts are frequently rejected. The small-cut assumption states the number of edges directly joining the real region to the fake region (attack edges) is small relative to the two regions' internal edge counts. The survey treats these as the same underlying claim — a structural separation between real and fake regions — and states both formally as a homophily ratio, the fraction of edges connecting same-label node pairs.

The classical random-walk family (SybilGuard, SybilLimit, SybilRank, SybilInfer, SybilDefender, SybilWalk) runs traces (random walks) from known real accounts and either classifies a node by whether traces starting from it stay trapped in a small region, or ranks nodes by the frequency with which real-seeded traces land on them. The belief-propagation family (SybilBelief, SybilFrame, SybilSCAR, SybilHP) represents the graph as a Markov random field and propagates a posterior probability of being fake between neighboring nodes over multiple iterations until the probabilities stabilize.

### Measured results
This is a survey; it runs no experiments of its own. The only numeric results it states are descriptive statistics of the benchmark datasets the surveyed methods use, reproduced here as a measured property of the field's evaluation data rather than of any single detection method.

| Dataset | Nodes | Fake accounts | Real accounts | Edges | Text features |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cresci-15 | 5,301 | 3,351 | 1,950 | 7,086,134 | yes |
| TwiBot-20 | 229,580 | 6,589 | 5,237 | 33,716,171 | yes |
| TwiBot-22 | 1,000,000 | 139,943 | 860,057 | 170,185,937 | yes |
| MGTAB | 10,199 | 2,748 | 7,451 | 1,700,108 | numerical vector encoding |
| MGTAB-large | 410,199 | 2,748 | 7,451 | 97,997,710 | numerical vector encoding |

Cresci-15's human accounts were collected from volunteers who passed CAPTCHA verification plus a manually labeled political dataset; its fake accounts were obtained from three online markets. TwiBot-20's labels came from five active Twitter accounts annotating each node by consensus (at least four of five agreeing), with unresolved cases reviewed manually or discarded.

The survey cites one independent empirical finding against the homophily assumption: Yang et al.'s large-scale study of fake accounts on Renren (a Chinese OSN) found fake accounts embedded within real communities rather than isolated, meaning coordinated fake-account behavior can follow patterns not captured by structural separation between a real region and a fake region.

### Parameters
Not applicable in the sense of a single mechanism's tuned constants — the survey reports the parameter choices of surveyed methods individually (e.g., trace-length choices for SybilLimit versus SybilGuard, iteration counts for belief propagation) rather than a single set of its own. No survey-level parameter is stated.

### Stated limitations
The authors identify the following gaps as unresolved in the field, stated as future-work directions: benchmark datasets are drawn almost entirely from Twitter and expanding to other platforms with different structures is unaddressed; labels are binary (fake/real) though finer categories (spammer, robot, data collector) would better capture the diversity of fake-account behavior; heterophilic edges (edges joining accounts of different classes) cause feature mixing during message passing in graph neural networks and no principled causal method for identifying which edges are heterophilic yet exists for the fake-account detection setting specifically; few-shot and zero-shot learning, well explored for general node classification, have not been adapted to fake-account detection; cold-start nodes (newly joined accounts with few connections) remain difficult to classify with existing graph-based methods, and this maps directly onto early detection since fake accounts are typically poorly connected when created; explainability for deep-learning-based detectors is largely unaddressed, limiting deployment in settings requiring accountable decisions; and adversarial-attack research specific to fake-account detection is limited to a small number of studies, so realistic attack strategies for benchmarking detector robustness remain underdeveloped.

Synthesized datasets used to evaluate many methods do not fully capture the complexity of real-world fake-account behavior, per the survey's own statement in the datasets section, though they permit controlled, repeatable experiments that real data cannot.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Any detection method the survey covers requires that the deployer already possess a social graph with edges between accounts (following, friending, or message relationships) — none of the surveyed graph-based methods can classify an isolated account with no observed edges. Random-walk and belief-propagation methods additionally require a seed set of accounts already labeled real (and, for some variants such as SybilBelief and SybilWalk, also a seed set already labeled fake) from which traces or propagated beliefs originate; the survey does not describe a graph-based method in this family that operates with zero labeled seeds. Methods relying on the homophily or small-cut assumption require that the deployment's actual attack pattern keeps attack edges (edges directly joining fake accounts to real accounts) a small fraction of total edges; the Yang et al. Renren finding cited by the survey establishes that this requirement is not guaranteed to hold and its failure degrades detection built on that assumption.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus. The survey itself records that the homophily assumption, on which the majority of methods it covers depend, is contradicted by field data from at least one deployed platform (Renren, per Yang et al., cited as reference [30] in the source bibliography).

## [SATHIAMOORTHY-VLDB-13] XORing Elephants: Novel Erasure Codes for Big Data

**Citation:** Maheswaran Sathiamoorthy, Megasthenis Asteris, Dimitris Papailiopoulos, Alexandros G. Dimakis, Ramkumar Vadali, Scott Chen, Dhruba Borthakur. "XORing Elephants: Novel Erasure Codes for Big Data." Proceedings of the VLDB Endowment, Vol. 6, No. 5, 2013. Pages 325-336. DOI 10.14778/2535573.2488339.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol6/p325-sathiamoorthy.pdf
**Source URL:** https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol6/p325-sathiamoorthy.pdf
**Domain:** C

### What it does
A locally repairable code (LRC), in the family this paper calls Xorbas, reduces the number of blocks read to repair one lost block below what a plain Reed-Solomon code requires, at the cost of storing extra parity blocks. The paper's explicit (10, 6, 5) LRC starts with 10 data blocks encoded by a standard (10, 4) Reed-Solomon code over a binary extension field to produce 4 global parity blocks (the same code Facebook's production clusters used at publication time), then adds local parity blocks computed as fixed linear combinations of subsets of data blocks (for example S1 = c1*X1 + c2*X2 + c3*X3 + c4*X5, using coefficients chosen so every relevant linear system stays invertible): a single lost data block is reconstructed by downloading only the other blocks in its local group and its group's local parity, rather than the larger set a plain Reed-Solomon repair requires. The paper implements this code in a Hadoop Distributed File System (HDFS) module named HDFS-Xorbas, extending Facebook's existing HDFS-RAID module, and adds two decoders: a light decoder invoked for single-block failures using local parities, and a heavy decoder invoked when a failure pattern the local parities cannot resolve requires the underlying Reed-Solomon decode.

### Measured results
| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| HDFS-Xorbas reads 41%-52% the HDFS bytes RS reads to reconstruct the same number of lost blocks | Amazon EC2, two 51-instance Hadoop clusters (m1.small, 1.7 GB memory each, ~7.4 TB total capacity per cluster), 200 files of 640 MB each (64 MB blocks, single-stripe files of 14 RS / 16 Xorbas full blocks), 8 triggered failure events per cluster (four single-DataNode terminations, two triple-DataNode terminations, two double-DataNode terminations) |
| Average blocks read per lost block: 11.5 for RS, 5.8 for Xorbas, a 2x reduction | Same EC2 setup, combined measurements across three experiments (50, 100, 200 files), linear least-squares fit of HDFS bytes read versus blocks lost |
| Network traffic roughly equal to twice HDFS bytes read, for both systems | Same EC2 setup, measured continuously via Amazon AWS CloudWatch at 5-minute resolution during the 200-file experiment |
| Xorbas finishes repair 25%-45% faster than RS | Same EC2 setup, repair duration measured as interval from first to last repair job across all three file-count experiments |
| Under simulated repair-time workload interference, additional job-completion delay from missing blocks is 9 minutes for Xorbas versus 23 minutes for RS | Two 15-slave-node EC2 clusters, five identical 3 GB text files, WordCount jobs, ~20% of required blocks made missing versus all-blocks-available baseline; total bytes read 43.88 GB (RS) vs 74.06 GB (Xorbas) at ~20% missing against 30 GB with all blocks available; average job execution time 92 min (RS) vs 106 min (Xorbas) at ~20% missing against 83 min baseline |
| On Facebook's test cluster, repairing one random terminated DataNode: RS lost 369 blocks, read 486.6 GB total (1.318 GB/block), repair took 26 minutes; Xorbas lost 563 blocks, read 330.8 GB total (0.58 GB/block), repair took 19 minutes | Facebook test cluster, 35 nodes, 370 TB total capacity, 3,262 existing files (~2.7 TB logical data, 256 MB blocks, ~94% of files at 3 blocks and the rest at 10 blocks, average 3.4 blocks/file); paper notes Xorbas stored 27% more than RS in this run (versus an ideal 13%) because of the small average file size, and states this dataset is not representative of Facebook's production cluster |
| Mean Time to Data Loss (MTTDL), analytic Markov model: 3-replication 2.3079E10 days, RS(10,4) 3.3118E13 days, LRC(10,6,5) 1.2180E15 days | Markov reliability model, N=3000 disk nodes, total cluster data C=30 PB, disk mean time to failure 4 years, block size B=256 MB, cross-rack repair bandwidth capped at 1 Gbps (Facebook cluster measurement), stripe size k=10, n=14 (RS) or n=16 (LRC); assumes independent node failures and exponential inter-failure and repair times; data loss defined as 3 erasures for replication, 5 erasures for both RS and LRC |
| Storage overhead: replication 2x, RS(10,4) 0.4x, LRC(10,6,5) 0.6x, relative to the amount of logical data (repair traffic 1x/10x/5x respectively in the same table) | Same Markov model parameters, Table 1 |
| A (9,4) RS code has approximately six orders of magnitude higher reliability than 3-way replication | Cited from reference [9] (Ford et al.), not independently re-measured in this paper; given as a consistency check against this paper's own reliability comparisons |
| A 3000-node Facebook production cluster stores approximately 230 million blocks of 256 MB each; only 8% of data is RS-encoded; 20 or more node failures per day trigger repair; repair traffic is estimated at 10%-20% of the cluster's average 2 PB/day network traffic; RS(10,4) repair requires approximately 10x more network overhead per bit than replicated blocks | Cited as production-cluster measurement in the paper's introduction, motivating the design, not an experiment this paper itself ran |

### Parameters
- LRC code parameters used: (n=16, k=10, r=5) written as (10, 6, 5)-LRC in the paper's own notation, meaning 10 data blocks, 6 total parity blocks (4 global Reed-Solomon parities + 2 local parities, with an implied third local parity derivable from the others), and local repair groups of 5 blocks each.
- Baseline compared against: (10, 4) Reed-Solomon, the code the paper states was in production use at Facebook at the time.
- Block size: 64 MB in the EC2 experiments, 256 MB in the Facebook-cluster experiment (the paper states 256 MB as Facebook's production default).
- Storage overhead: 14% more storage than plain RS in the idealized case (Table 1 and abstract); the paper states this overhead is information-theoretically optimal for the locality obtained, citing its own theoretical result (referenced but not re-derived as a numeric bound in the extracted sections).
- Markov model repair-bandwidth cap: cross-rack communication capped at 1 Gbps, derived from Facebook cluster measurements, used uniformly across all three compared schemes in the MTTDL calculation.

### Stated limitations
The Facebook-cluster experiment's dataset (94% of files at 3 blocks) is stated by the authors as not representative of Facebook's production cluster's actual dataset, and the storage overhead observed there (27%) exceeded the code's ideal 13% because of this small-file skew; the paper flags both facts explicitly rather than presenting the numbers as production-representative. The reliability (MTTDL) comparison assumes independent node failures and exponential inter-failure and repair-time distributions; the paper states repair times may not actually be exponential and that this assumption is made only to simplify the analysis. The paper states the absolute MTTDL values are not meaningful in isolation, useful only for relative comparison between the three schemes under the same model. The EC2 experiments do not saturate available network bandwidth (traffic peaks differ between the two systems), so the paper states the measured repair-time gains understate the gains expected at larger scale, where the authors expect network saturation to delay RS repairs further relative to LRC; this is stated as an expectation, not a further measurement.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The light-decoder single-block repair path requires the block's full local repair group (the other blocks sharing its local parity) to be simultaneously available for download; the paper's Markov model explicitly computes separate probabilities for invoking the light decoder versus falling back to the heavy (full Reed-Solomon) decoder when more blocks are lost from a stripe than the local-parity structure alone can resolve. The coefficients ci used to build each local parity must be chosen so that every linear system a repair could need to solve stays invertible over the finite field used (the paper states this coefficient-selection problem is the main theoretical challenge and defers the construction to an appendix), so an implementer cannot pick arbitrary coefficients and expect the guaranteed fault tolerance. Cross-rack bandwidth-limited placement (each stripe's coded blocks placed in different racks) is assumed by the paper's reliability model as the source of the 1 Gbps repair bandwidth cap; a placement policy that instead colocates a stripe's blocks within one rack would invalidate that specific numeric cap, though the paper does not re-derive the model under that alternative.

### Contradicts
None found.

### References worth retrieving
- Gopalan, Huang, Simitci, Yekhanin. "On the locality of codeword symbols." CoRR abs/1106.3625, 2011 — foundational (also cited by PAPAILIOPOULOS-TIT-14 in this corpus; proves the locality-versus-distance tradeoff this paper's LRC is analytically shown to meet).
- Dimakis, Godfrey, Wu, Wainwright, Ramchandran. "Network coding for distributed storage systems." IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, 2010 — foundational (introduces regenerating codes and the repair-bandwidth metric this paper's locality metric is positioned against).
- Ford, Labelle, Popovici, Stokely, Truong, Barroso, Grimes, Quinlan. "Availability in globally distributed storage systems." USENIX OSDI, 2010 — foundational (source of the six-orders-of-magnitude RS-versus-replication reliability figure this paper cites as a consistency check, and of the 90%-of-failures-are-transient figure motivating degraded-read repair).
- Khan, Burns, Plank, Pierce, Huang. "Rethinking erasure codes for cloud file systems: Minimizing I/O for recovery and degraded reads." USENIX FAST, 2012 — competing (an alternative repair-I/O-minimizing code design cited in this paper's related work).
- Cadambe, Jafar, Maleki, Ramchandran, Suh. "Asymptotic interference alignment for optimal repair of MDS codes in distributed storage." Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, 2011 — competing (an alternative repair-bandwidth-optimal MDS repair approach, listed in this paper's references).
- Papailiopoulos, Dimakis. "Locally Repairable Codes." — foundational/self (also in this corpus as PAPAILIOPOULOS-TIT-14, overlapping authors; states the general information-theoretic locality-distance-storage tradeoff this paper's explicit (10,6,5) construction instantiates and deploys).
- Huang, Chen, Li. "Pyramid codes: Flexible schemes to trade space for access efficiency in reliable data storage systems." NCA, 2007 — foundational (an earlier local-parity code construction cited as prior work on trading storage for access efficiency).
- Greenan, Plank, Wylie. "Mean time to meaningless: MTTDL, Markov models, and storage system reliability." HotStorage, 2010 — foundational (methodological basis and caveat source for this paper's own statement that its MTTDL values are meaningful only in relative comparison).

## [SECKIN-ARXIV-25] The Rise of Bluesky

**Citation:** Ozgur Can Seckin, Filipi Nascimento Silva, Bao Tran Truong, Sangyeon Kim, Fan Huang, Nick Liu, Alessandro Flammini, Filippo Menczer. "The Rise of Bluesky." arXiv preprint, 2025. arXiv:2504.12902.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.12902
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.12902
**Domain:** J

Note on match: the registry record lists seven authors (Seckin, Silva, Truong, Kim, Huang, Flammini, Menczer); the retrieved arXiv v1 text lists an eighth author, Nick Liu, between Huang and Flammini. Title, remaining seven author names, venue, and institutional affiliation (Observatory on Social Media, Indiana University) all match the registry record; treated as the same paper with an updated author list.

### What it does
The paper measures how Bluesky (a microblogging platform structurally similar to Twitter/X but built with decentralized governance and user-controlled data) grew from August 2023 to February 2025, and tests whether growth driven by discrete migration events from other platforms settled into a stable, self-sustaining user base rather than the sign-up-and-abandon pattern common to new social platforms. The authors assign every account to one of four groups based on which of four public migration-triggering events preceded its signup — the February 6, 2024 switch from invitation-only to open public access; the August 30, 2024 blocking of X in Brazil; the October 16, 2024 X policy change letting blocked users still see the blocking account's posts; and the November 4, 2024 US Presidential election — plus a residual group for accounts joining outside those windows. For each group they track daily post/repost/reply/like activity, and separately reconstruct a directed follower network from observed follow actions (singleton accounts with no follower and no followee excluded) to compute, as the network grows, average out-degree, clustering coefficient (the tendency of two users sharing a mutual connection to also be connected to each other), giant-component size, and two measures of in-degree inequality: the Gini index (0 to 1, higher meaning followers are concentrated on fewer accounts) and the Kappa index (kappa = <k^2>/<k^2>, the second moment of in-degree divided by the squared mean in-degree, with values above 1 indicating hub-driven fluctuation in the distribution). Growth is analyzed along "network time," meaning quantities are plotted against the cumulative number of users at each point rather than against calendar time, to align the comparison across events that occurred at different absolute user-count scales.

### Measured results

| Quantity | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Total accounts | 30 million | End of January 2025 |
| Users with at least one friend or follower, used for network-time panels (d-i) | 26 million | Snapshot as of 7 February 2025; the paper notes user counts can occasionally decrease due to account deletion or suspension |
| New accounts after Brazil's August 30, 2024 X ban | nearly 500,000, majority Portuguese-language | Measured shortly after the ban date |
| Daily active user share at steady state | approximately 15% of all existing accounts (implying approximately 85% inactive/lurking) | Measured after the November 4, 2024 US election event, once activity reached a steady state |
| Average per-user daily activity at steady state | stabilized above 10 actions per day | Same post-election steady-state period |
| Giant-component (largest connected component) size | approximately 70-80% of all users | Emerged before the February 2024 public-access opening and remained fairly stable in relative size through the full measurement window; exact network size at each measurement point not given in the retrieved text (stated as "not shown") |
| Clustering coefficient | orders of magnitude higher than an equivalent random network with the same node and edge count | Measured on the undirected version of the follower network, across the full growth period plotted in network time |
| Gini and Kappa index trend | both indices show strong growth during the post-election user influx | Measured on the in-degree (follower-count) distribution across network time |

The paper's figures (average out-degree, average activity per active user, active-user count, Gini index, Kappa index, clustering coefficient) are plotted continuously against network size rather than reported as discrete before/after values with stated conditions; the retrieved text gives no numeric axis values for these curves beyond the ranges visible in the figure descriptions (out-degree axis to 80, clustering-coefficient axis 0.10-0.20, Gini axis 0.65-0.90, activity-per-user axis 0-17.5), so no specific measured number from these curves is recorded here beyond the discrete figures stated above.

### Parameters
No explicit collection parameters (API used, sampling rate, crawl frequency) are stated in the retrieved text beyond a reference to code and data being available at a GitHub repository and a Zenodo record; the retrieved text does not itself describe the data-collection method (e.g., which Bluesky API or firehose feed was polled, or at what interval). The follower-network visualization in Figure 1c uses a stated 1% sample of users; all other network statistics (giant component, clustering coefficient, Gini, Kappa) are computed on the full reconstructed follower graph after excluding singleton nodes.

### Stated limitations
The retrieved text states no explicit limitations or future-work section; the Discussion section states an expectation, not a measured finding, that as Bluesky reaches mainstream adoption it will attract "bad actors and harmful content," and calls for future research on abuse and manipulation without presenting any such measurement itself. The paper does not report the actual network size (user count) at which the giant-component measurements were made, describing the connectivity analysis as "not shown" in the retrieved figure. The paper draws its four-group event attribution from account creation timing alone, which the paper does not validate against explicit self-reported migration reasons or platform-of-origin data for individual accounts.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
None stated as a mechanism requirement — this is a measurement study of an existing deployed system's growth and network structure, not a description of a mechanism another component could implement or depend on. Any citation of the giant-component or clustering-coefficient figures elsewhere in this corpus should be scoped to a federated/decentralized microblogging platform with open follow-graph data and a burst-driven, migration-event-triggered growth pattern, since the paper's own event-group framing is specific to Bluesky's observed 2024 migration waves.

### Contradicts
None found.

### References worth retrieving
- David Easley, Jon Kleinberg, "Network effects," in Networks, Crowds, and Markets: Reasoning about a Highly Connected World, 2010, pp. 509-542 — foundational (network-effect framing the paper's stability question rests on).
- Wei Gong, Ee-Peng Lim, Feida Zhu, "Characterizing silent users in social media communities," Proceedings of the International AAAI Conference on Web and Social Media, vol. 9, 2015, pp. 140-149 — foundational (the lurker-population comparison the paper's 85%-inactive figure is checked against).
- Alessia Antelmi, Delfina Malandrino, Vittorio Scarano, "Characterizing the behavioral evolution of twitter users and the truth behind the 90-9-1 rule," Companion Proceedings of the 2019 World Wide Web Conference, 2019, pp. 1035-1038 — foundational (the comparable lurker-ratio finding on Twitter, cited alongside the Bluesky figure).
- Lilian Weng, Filippo Menczer, Yong-Yeol Ahn, "Virality prediction and community structure in social networks," Scientific Reports 3(1), 2013 — foundational (the clustering-coefficient-and-virality mechanism the paper's clustering result is interpreted through).
- Wentao Han, Xiaowei Zhu, Ziyan Zhu, Wenguang Chen, Weimin Zheng, Jianguo Lu, "A comparative analysis on weibo and twitter," Tsinghua Science and Technology 21(1), 2016, pp. 1-16 — competing (the independent Gini/Kappa hub-concentration measurement on Weibo and Twitter the paper's own indices are compared against).
