## [SINGH-INFOCOM-06] Eclipse Attacks on Overlay Networks: Threats and Defenses
**Citation:** Atul Singh, Tsuen-Wan Johnny Ngan, Peter Druschel, Dan S. Wallach. "Eclipse Attacks on Overlay Networks: Threats and Defenses." IEEE INFOCOM, 2006. DOI 10.1109/INFOCOM.2006.231.
**Retrieved:** full text via http://rowstron.azurewebsites.net/MS/eclipse.pdf
**Source URL:** http://rowstron.azurewebsites.net/MS/eclipse.pdf
**Domain:** A

### What it does
An eclipse attack surrounds one correct node with colluding malicious nodes so that every, or nearly every, message the victim sends or receives passes through an attacker. A modest fraction of malicious nodes can eclipse a much larger number of correct nodes by supplying biased neighbor referrals during ordinary overlay membership maintenance, because correct nodes propagate whatever neighbor information they receive without verifying it.

The paper's defense bounds each node's in-degree (the number of other nodes referring to it as a neighbor) and out-degree (the size of its own neighbor set) to a value close to the overlay's expected per-node degree, without depending on a centralized service to track degree. It proves that if the out-degree and in-degree of every node are bounded to the overlay's expected neighbor-set size (bound multiplier t=1), the expected fraction of malicious entries in a correct node's neighbor set is bounded by f/(1-f), where f is the fraction of malicious nodes in the overlay.

Degree bounds are enforced by distributed auditing rather than a trusted authority: each node x maintains a backpointer set, the list of every node currently listing x as a neighbor. Periodically, x anonymously challenges each of its own neighbors z by requesting z's backpointer set through a randomly selected intermediate node, called an anonymizer, so that z cannot tell which node is auditing it and cannot selectively suppress its response to that specific auditor. If z's returned backpointer count exceeds the in-degree bound, or z's response omits x from that backpointer set, x treats z as suspicious. The anonymizer must itself be unpredictable to z and cannot be trivially spoofed; the paper analyzes three anonymizer-selection techniques and derives, for an overlay with malicious fraction f, the minimum anonymizer-set size n such that the probability at least half the anonymizer set is malicious falls below a target threshold — at f=0.2, only 1% of anonymizer sets of size 16 have at least half their members malicious. The scheme assumes each participating node carries a certificate binding its node identifier to a public key (defeating identifier forgery, though not addressing Sybil identity creation itself) and that the overlay supports a constrained-routing-table (CRT) secure-routing primitive as a fallback path when the primary proximity-neighbor-selection (PNS) routing table fails.

### Measured results

| Result | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Eclipse effectiveness with PNS disabled | Over 70% of routing-table entries malicious at 1,000 nodes; over 80% at 5,000 nodes; top-row (least-constrained) entries over 90% at 1,000 nodes, approaching 100% at 10,000+ nodes | MSPastry packet-level discrete-event simulator, f=0.2 malicious fraction, malicious nodes maintain out-degree 16 per routing-table row (the attacker-optimal strategy per the paper's own simulations), GT-ITM transit-stub topology of 5,050 routers, PNS disabled |
| Eclipse effectiveness with PNS enabled, synthetic topology | Full-routing-table malicious fraction drops to under 30% within 10 hours for all sizes tested; top-row fraction for a 10,000-node network drops from 78% to 41% within 10 hours | Same setup, PNS enabled, GT-ITM topology, network sizes 2,000/5,000/10,000 nodes |
| Eclipse effectiveness with PNS enabled, real Internet delays | PNS defense is significantly less effective than under the synthetic topology; effectiveness decreases further as overlay size increases | Same setup but latencies from King-tool measurements of up to 10,000 real Internet hosts (network sizes 1,740/5,000/10,000 nodes), rather than GT-ITM |
| Idealized (oracle-enforced) in-degree bounding, average malicious fraction in routing table | Bound 16: 0.24 at all sizes (1,000/5,000/10,000/20,000 nodes); bound 32: 0.24/0.29/0.31/0.37; bound 48: 0.24/0.31/0.35/0.45; bound 64: 0.24/0.33/0.38/0.48; unlimited: 0.24/0.35/0.42/0.50 | Oracle-enforced degree bound (no auditing protocol overhead modeled), f=0.2, matches the theoretical f/(1-f)=0.25 bound closely at t=1 (bound=16, the expected per-row degree) |
| Delay-stretch cost of degree bounding | About 25% delay-stretch increase at in-degree bound 16 per row (no attackers present); drops to about 8% at bound 32 | 20,000-node overlay, PNS enabled, no malicious nodes |
| Auditing convergence to full compliance | Every node in the system, correct or malicious, reaches in-degree at or below the bound of 16 after about 10 hours | 2,000-node network, static membership, anonymizer-set size n=24 (chosen so probability of an anonymizer set being at least half malicious is below 1 at f=0.2), audit interval about once per 2 minutes per neighbor |
| Malicious-fraction reduction after auditing starts | Before auditing: ~40% of correct nodes' routing-table entries point to malicious nodes (versus 20% of nodes being malicious). Within 2 simulated hours of auditing starting: fraction drops below 30% (top row) and 25% (overall) under static membership, 5% churn/hour, and 10% churn/hour; at 15% churn/hour the top-row fraction stays above 30% | 2,000-node network, auditing begins 1.5 simulated hours after the attack starts, correct nodes enforce in-degree bound 16/row from the start, malicious nodes do not self-limit |
| Effect of doubling audit rate under high churn | Top-row malicious fraction stabilizes around 27% (a 3-percentage-point improvement); auditing once per minute at 15% churn/hour matches the effect of auditing once per 2 minutes at 10% churn/hour | Same 2,000-node setup, churn 15%/hour, audit interval halved to once per minute |
| Communication overhead of the full defense | Auditing cost ~2 msg/node/sec, secure-routing (CRT) cost ~0.2 msg/node/sec, total maintenance cost ~4.2 msg/node/sec | 2,000-node network, audit rate once per 2 minutes, measured over 5 simulated hours |
| False-positive rate of auditing | About 100 of roughly 96,000 total connections between correct nodes incorrectly marked suspicious and removed, a rate of about 10^-3, after 10 hours of auditing | 2,000-node network, static membership, anonymizer-set size n=24 |
| Total network overhead vs. constrained-routing-table (CRT) defense (Castro et al.) | Auditing-based defense has lower total overhead than the CRT-only defense unless the application sends fewer than about 4.75 msg/node/min, and reduces reliance on (and thus overhead of) the CRT fallback path by more than half in most tested cases | Audit rate once per 2 minutes, churn 5%/hour, both techniques route primarily through PNS-based tables, falling back to CRT-based secure routing on failure |
| Communication-delay comparison vs. CRT defense | Average delay 3.05 s with degree bounding versus 5.4 s without (CRT-only); 90th-percentile delay 5.8 s with degree bounding versus 16 s without | Same 2,000-node, 5%-churn, once-per-2-minutes-audit setup |
| Adversary alternative-response-strategy gain | A malicious node that always returns a fixed maximal-size subset of its true neighbor/backpointer set (rather than a randomly chosen subset) can achieve total degree up to 12% higher than under the random-subset strategy; neither strategy lets malicious nodes reach a degree significantly above the overlay average | Analytical/simulated comparison of the two response strategies under the same auditing scheme |

### Parameters
- Overlay: MSPastry with routing base b=4, leaf-set size ℓ=16.
- Malicious node fraction f: 0.2 (20%) unless stated otherwise.
- Malicious out-degree per routing-table row: 16 (attacker-optimal — the paper states its own simulations show a larger out-degree causes quicker detection and reduces attack impact).
- In-degree/out-degree bound (correct nodes): 16 per routing-table row and backpointer-set row, swept 16/32/48/64/unlimited in the idealized experiment.
- Anonymizer-set size n: 24, chosen so the expected number of anonymizer sets with at least half malicious members is below 1 at f=0.2 (needing at least 12 of 24 correct challenge responses to pass an audit iteration).
- Audit interval: once every 2 minutes per neighbor (halved to once per minute in the high-churn sensitivity test), each audit timed at a random instant within the interval.
- Churn rates tested: 0%, 5%, 10%, 15% per hour, corresponding to average node lifetimes of indefinite, 20, 10, and 7 hours respectively; the paper notes these rates exceed the 37.7-hour average session time Bolosky et al. measured in a corporate environment but are much lower than rates reported for some file-sharing networks.
- Network topology models: GT-ITM transit-stub, 5,050 routers; King-tool-measured real Internet latencies among up to 10,000 hosts.
- Network sizes tested: 1,000/1,740/2,000/5,000/10,000/20,000 nodes, depending on experiment.

### Stated limitations
The defense detects malicious nodes independently at each auditing node and has no mechanism for one correct node to produce a verifiable proof of misbehavior that other correct nodes could act on; the paper states this would require complex cryptographic operations or Byzantine agreement and could interact badly with auditing false positives, so it is not attempted. The mechanism is not directly applicable to overlays that deliberately use asymmetric node degree for performance, such as KaZaA superpeers, because the defense's signal is precisely a degree deviation from the overlay average; the paper states securing such heterogeneous overlays is an open research problem requiring different solutions. Auditing in unstructured overlays needs a separate mechanism to securely select anonymizer sets, which the paper does not build; it sketches maintaining an additional structured overlay purely for anonymizer discovery as one option. Localized eclipse attacks — an adversary concentrating on surrounding a small set of victims rather than the whole network — are not detected by degree bounding, because a localized attacker need not exceed the average degree; the paper states this requires the colluding nodes to have low network latency to the victims specifically (since row-zero eligibility under PNS depends on measured proximity) and states defending against it is an open research problem. The defense assumes the overlay already supports a certified node identifier binding to a public key and a constrained-routing-table secure-routing fallback; it does not itself solve Sybil-identity creation. The target operating regime is stated explicitly as low-to-moderately-high churn — at 15% churn/hour the top-row malicious fraction does not drop below about 30% even after auditing runs, because newly joined malicious nodes have not yet accumulated enough audit history to be caught.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Every node needs a certificate binding its node identifier to a public key before the defense can be deployed; the paper does not supply or evaluate an identity-issuance mechanism, only assumes one exists. The overlay needs a working constrained-routing-table (CRT) secure-routing primitive as a fallback path used whenever primary PNS-based routing fails; the measured overhead figures (about 0.2 msg/node/sec for CRT maintenance) are additive on top of this defense's own auditing cost, and the delay-comparison figures assume this two-tier routing structure is in place. The auditing protocol requires each node to maintain a backpointer set (the list of nodes that currently list it as a neighbor) and to answer anonymized challenges for that set, so any change to how neighbor relations are recorded or discovered elsewhere in the system must preserve this bidirectional bookkeeping. The anonymizer-selection mechanism requires the overlay to supply a way to pick a random relay node whose identity is unpredictable to the node being audited before the challenge is issued; the paper's own analysis (Section IV-C) makes the anonymizer-set-size choice a function of the malicious-node fraction f, so a system deploying this defense needs an independent estimate of f to size that set correctly. The defense needs a nonzero churn-tolerant time window (the paper's simulation requires roughly an hour of node lifetime for 24 audit challenges to accumulate meaningful data) — a system with node lifetimes shorter than this will not collect enough audit rounds to detect an over-degree node before it can complete its attack window, which the paper flags as requiring a correspondingly higher audit rate and proportionally higher overhead.

### Contradicts
None found — no other entry in this corpus reports a conflicting eclipse-attack or degree-bounding figure under matching conditions. The paper itself contradicts the value judgment (attributable to Hildrum and Kubiatowicz, and re-tested here) that proximity neighbor selection alone is a sufficient eclipse defense: measured under real Internet (King) latencies rather than the synthetic GT-ITM topology, PNS's defensive effectiveness is stated to be "significantly reduced," and the paper concludes a PNS-only defense "will not be effective in the real Internet."

### References worth retrieving
- foundational: M. Castro, P. Druschel, A. Ganesh, A. Rowstron, D. S. Wallach, "Secure routing for structured peer-to-peer overlay networks," OSDI 2002 (defines the constrained-routing-table primitive this paper's defense builds on and compares against directly in Section V-E).
- competing: K. Hildrum, J. Kubiatowicz, "Asymptotically efficient approaches to fault-tolerance in peer-to-peer networks," DISC 2003 (the proximity-neighbor-selection eclipse defense this paper measures and finds ineffective under real Internet latencies).
- competing: T. Condie, V. Kacholia, S. Sankararaman, J. Hellerstein, P. Maniatis, "Induced Churn as Shelter from Routing-Table Poisoning," NDSS 2006 (an alternative defense based on periodic identifier change and rate-limited table updates, contrasted directly in Related Work).
- foundational: M. Castro, P. Druschel, Y. C. Hu, A. Rowstron, "Proximity neighbor selection in tree-based structured peer-to-peer overlays," MSR-TR-2003-52 (defines PNS as implemented in the MSPastry simulator used here).
- foundational: K. P. Gummadi, R. Gummadi, S. D. Gribble, S. Ratnasamy, S. Shenker, I. Stoica, "The impact of DHT routing geometry on resilience and proximity," ACM SIGCOMM 2003 (already in this corpus as GUMMADI-SIGCOMM-03; cited for the observation that many Internet hosts fall within a narrow proximity band, undermining PNS-only defenses).
- attack-or-critique: B.-G. Chun, B. Y. Zhao, J. D. Kubiatowicz, "Impact of neighbor selection on performance and resilience of structured p2p networks," IPTPS 2005 (cited for showing proximity- and capacity-based neighbor selection increases vulnerability to targeted attacks — a direct tradeoff against this paper's PNS-compatible defense).
- foundational: E. Sit, R. Morris, "Security considerations for peer-to-peer distributed hash tables," IPTPS 2002 (proposes iterative routing as a defense; contrasted in Related Work).

## [SIRINAM-CCS-18] Deep Fingerprinting: Undermining Website Fingerprinting Defenses with Deep Learning
**Citation:** Payap Sirinam, Mohsen Imani, Marc Juarez, Matthew Wright. "Deep Fingerprinting: Undermining Website Fingerprinting Defenses with Deep Learning." ACM CCS, 2018. DOI 10.1145/3243734.3243768.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/abs/1801.02265
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/1801.02265
**Domain:** G

### What it does
Deep Fingerprinting (DF) identifies which website a Tor user is visiting by analyzing the pattern of encrypted packet timing and direction on the link between the user and Tor's entry node, without decrypting any traffic. The adversary is local (observes only that one link, for example an internet service provider (ISP) or a local network eavesdropper) and passive (records but does not modify, delay, or drop packets). DF represents each observed connection as a fixed-length sequence of packet directions (5,000 cells long, the input length the paper found gives the best classification accuracy) and feeds that sequence into a convolutional neural network (CNN), a deep-learning architecture that scans a signal with learned filters to detect local patterns regardless of where in the sequence they occur. The DF architecture uses four convolutional blocks with a mix of ELU and ReLU activation functions, max pooling (rather than average pooling), two fully connected layers, batch normalization after every convolutional and fully connected layer, and dropout regularization tuned to different rates at different depths (0.1 after pooling layers, 0.7 and 0.5 after the two fully connected layers) — all more numerous and more heavily regularized than the prior CNN-based automated website fingerprinting (AWF) model by Rimmer et al. The full hyperparameter search space and final selected values are given in the paper's Table 1. In the open-world evaluation, the classifier outputs a probability for each monitored site; if the highest probability exceeds a chosen threshold and belongs to a monitored site, the trace is classified as a visit to that site, otherwise it is classified as unmonitored, with the threshold tunable to trade precision against recall.

### Measured results
| Result | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Closed-world accuracy, undefended traffic, DF vs. prior attacks | DF 98.3%; k-fingerprinting (k-FP) 95.5%; CUMUL 97.3%; k-nearest-neighbors (k-NN) 95.0%; AWF 94.9%; stacked denoising autoencoder (SDAE) 92.3% | closed-world dataset of 95 sites with 1,000 visits each (Alexa top 100 minus discarded sites), k-fold cross-validation, tor-browser-crawler used to drive Tor Browser |
| Closed-world accuracy against defenses (Table 3) | BuFLO: DF 12.6%, SDAE 9.2%, AWF 11.7%, k-NN 10.4%, CUMUL 13.5%, k-FP 13.1%, at 246% bandwidth / 137% latency overhead. Tamaraw: DF 11.8%, SDAE 11.8%, AWF 12.9%, k-NN 9.7%, CUMUL 16.8%, k-FP 11.0%, at 328% bandwidth / 242% latency overhead. WTF-PAD: DF 90.7%, SDAE 36.9%, AWF 60.8%, k-NN 16.0%, CUMUL 60.3%, k-FP 69.0%, at 64% bandwidth / 0% latency overhead. Walkie-Talkie (W-T): DF 49.7%, SDAE 23.1%, AWF 45.8%, k-NN 20.2%, CUMUL 38.4%, k-FP 7.0%, at 31% bandwidth / 34% latency overhead | closed-world dataset, WTF-PAD and BuFLO/Tamaraw simulated by author-provided scripts, Walkie-Talkie collected via a real half-duplex crawl using a modified Tor Browser Bundle 7.0.6 |
| Impact of dataset size on closed-world accuracy | DF and CUMUL reach 90% accuracy with 50 training traces per site; k-NN, k-FP and AWF need 250 traces to reach 90%; SDAE needs 750 traces; accuracy for all but SDAE saturates after 550 traces | closed-world dataset, non-defended traffic |

| Open-world results, non-defended traffic, standard model | DF 0.957 true positive rate (TPR) / 0.007 false positive rate (FPR) at 20,000 unmonitored training sites; overall 0.99 precision / 0.94 recall | training set 85,500 monitored traces (900 instances x 95 sites), unmonitored training sites varied 900 to 20,000, test set 9,500 monitored traces + 20,000 unmonitored traces (disjoint from training unmonitored set) |

| Closed-world DF accuracy against W-T under an asymmetric-collision implementation (guideline violation) | 87.2%, compared to 49.7% under correct symmetric collisions | same closed-world W-T dataset, defense implemented without pairing decoy sites symmetrically |
| Open-world DF results when 10% of users violate W-T's symmetric-collision guideline | TPR 0.85 / FPR 0.23, compared to TPR 0.80 / FPR 0.76 when all users comply | open-world W-T dataset |
| ROC operating points, DF vs. non-defended traffic | 0.98 TPR at 0.03 FPR (tuned for high TPR); 0.94 TPR at 0.004 FPR (tuned for low FPR) | open-world dataset, standard model |

| Parameter | Value used | Range / search space tested |

| Optimizer | Adamax | candidates: Adam, Adamax, RMSProp, SGD |
| Learning rate | 0.002 | search range 0.001-0.01 |

| Filter/pool/stride sizes | [8, 8, 4] | search range 2-16 |
| Activation functions | ELU (first two convolutional layers), ReLU (rest) | candidates: Tanh, ReLU, ELU |
| Number of filters per convolutional block | Block 1: [32,32]; Block 2: [64,64]; Block 3: [128,128]; Block 4: [256,256] | search ranges [8-64], [32-128], [64-256], [128-512] respectively |
| Pooling type | Max | candidates: Average, Max |
| Number of fully connected layers | 2 | search range 1-4 |
| Hidden units per fully connected layer | [512, 512] | search range 256-2048 |
| Dropout rates | pooling layers 0.1; FC1 0.7; FC2 0.5 | search range 0.1-0.8 |
| k in k-NN and k-FP open-world evaluation | 6 | tested k=2 to 10; TPR/FPR did not change significantly above k=5 |
| Closed-world dataset size | 95 sites, 1,000 visits each, minimum 1,000 visits retained per site | -- |
| Open-world dataset size | 40,716 traffic traces, Alexa top 50,000 excluding the closed-world top 100 | -- |

### Stated limitations
The paper states that the crawler models a simplistic sequential visiting pattern (round-robin batched visits), not real user browsing behavior, because modeling actual Tor user behavior is not possible given that Tor collects no user statistics for privacy reasons; it notes virtually all prior website fingerprinting (WF) datasets share this limitation. Data collected for training becomes stale: the paper cites that accuracy of WF attacks degrades significantly after 10-14 days of data age (attributing this measurement to Wang and Goldberg and to Juarez et al., not measuring it itself in this paper). Attack cost is nontrivial: collecting a large dataset requires multiple machines running for several days, which the paper states as a practical barrier for a weaker attacker. Traffic parsing (isolating one page-load's packets from concurrent Tor activity) is assumed already solved, following prior work's same assumption. The paper states that improving open-world classification via deeper architectures, more training data, or added timing features is left unexplored. It states that a semi-open-world targeted attack using auxiliary user profile information (for example, known language) is a possible extension not implemented here. Adversarial-machine-learning-based defenses are noted as a promising but unimplemented direction, complicated because Tor traffic streams live (the defender cannot see the full trace in advance) and Tor's transformation options are restricted to adding or delaying packets, not deleting or speeding them up.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
DF requires a labeled training dataset of traffic traces for every site the attacker wants classified in the monitored set, collected either from the same defense configuration the target will use or from data the attacker deliberately gathers under that defense; the closed-world evaluation retrains DF separately on defended and undefended datasets, so a defense's evaluation must specify whether the classifier was retrained on defended traffic. It requires the attacker to control the traffic-parsing step, either by running a Tor entry node (selecting a domain's traffic by its Tor circuit ID) or by using packet-parsing techniques on multiplexed Transport Layer Security (TLS) traffic; both cases are assumed solved, not built by this paper. It requires GPU or substantial CPU time for training (single-digit hours on a consumer GPU, roughly 10 hours without one), which any defense evaluation must account for as attacker overhead when comparing against classifiers with lower training cost such as k-FP. The open-world precision/recall interpretation requires an unmonitored-to-monitored traffic ratio consistent with the paper's own construction (more than two orders of magnitude); a differently structured base-rate assumption changes what precision and recall mean operationally, since the paper explicitly ties precision usefulness to avoiding the base-rate fallacy under a heavily imbalanced monitored/unmonitored split.

### Contradicts
The paper's own results (Table 3, closed-world) directly contradict a claim that WTF-PAD is an effective defense against a modern deep-learning classifier: DF reaches 90.7% accuracy against WTF-PAD, versus the much lower accuracy WTF-PAD was reported to hold prior non-deep-learning attacks to. The paper's discussion section states that Walkie-Talkie's own claimed effectiveness (bounded near 50% accuracy for symmetric collisions) depends on strict client-side adherence to symmetric decoy pairing; the paper's own asymmetric-collision experiment shows accuracy jumping to 87.2% (closed-world) or TPR 0.85/FPR 0.23 (open-world, 10% non-compliance) when that assumption is violated, so any claim that Walkie-Talkie's protection holds independent of implementation compliance is not supported by this paper. WANG-USENIXSEC-14 in this batch is the source of the k-NN attack and the BuFLO/Tamaraw-class provable defense referenced in this paper's Table 2 and Table 3 comparisons — it is not the Walkie-Talkie paper (Wang and Goldberg 2017, cited by Sirinam et al. as reference [41], distinct from reference [38] which is WANG-USENIXSEC-14).

### References worth retrieving
- Foundational: V. Rimmer, D. Preuveneers, M. Juarez, T. Van Goethem, W. Joosen, "Automated website fingerprinting through deep learning" (AWF paper, cited as [31]) — the direct architectural baseline this paper builds on and outperforms.
- Foundational: T. Wang, X. Cai, R. Nithyanand, R. Johnson, I. Goldberg, "Effective Attacks and Provable Defenses for Website Fingerprinting," USENIX Security 2014 (cited as [38]; = WANG-USENIXSEC-14 in this batch — the k-NN attack).
- Competing: T. Wang, I. Goldberg, "Walkie-talkie: An efficient defense against passive website fingerprinting attacks," USENIX Security 2017 (cited as [41]; the actual Walkie-Talkie paper, distinct from [38]).

## [SIRIVIANOS-IPTPS-07] Free-riding in BitTorrent Networks with the Large View Exploit
**Citation:** Michael Sirivianos, Jong Han Park, Rex Chen, Xiaowei Yang. "Free-riding in BitTorrent Networks with the Large View Exploit." Proc. 6th International Workshop on Peer-to-Peer Systems (IPTPS), 2007.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://users.cs.duke.edu/~xwy/publications/largeview-iptps.pdf
**Source URL:** https://users.cs.duke.edu/~xwy/publications/largeview-iptps.pdf
**Domain:** I

### What it does
The large view exploit lets a BitTorrent client achieve a high download rate while uploading no data, by obtaining a swarm view (the tracker's list of active peers for a torrent) far larger than the roughly 50-peer view a compliant client requests and connecting to every peer in that larger view. Connecting to more peers than the protocol specifies raises the probability of being one of the peers a remote leecher optimistically unchokes (BitTorrent's periodic, unconditional grant of upload bandwidth to one connected peer regardless of reciprocation, intended to let newly joined peers with nothing to share begin downloading) and raises the chance of discovering seeders (peers holding the complete file, who upload to requesters in round robin regardless of reciprocation). The authors built this exploit by modifying an existing BitTorrent client (Enhanced CTorrent) rather than writing one from scratch, changing only three behaviors: it never uploads any file chunk to any peer; it re-contacts the tracker every 15 seconds, mimicking a client that keeps rejoining the swarm, to keep requesting fresh partial swarm views; and it connects to every peer named in every view it receives, accumulating a view much larger than the tracker's per-request limit. A fourth, separately tested variant additionally disconnects from a leecher immediately after that leecher has unchoked it, uploaded data, and choked it again, then reconnects to the same leecher under a fresh connection, erasing that leecher's record of past reciprocation with this client (the authors term this whitewashing). The paper proposes, but does not implement or measure, a countermeasure: synchronize all clients and the tracker to a shared time interval T, give every newly joined client the complete swarm membership as of the end of the prior interval, and have each client use a pseudorandom function seeded by its own IP address and the current interval to compute which N peers it is entitled to connect to; a peer receiving a connection request recomputes this function for the requester's claimed IP and refuses the connection if the requester's IP does not appear among its own valid N targets, with N set larger than the standard 50-peer view specifically so that multiple compliant clients behind one NAT (Network Address Translator, a device that lets several devices share one public IP address) can still be assigned disjoint peer sets.

### Measured results
| Setting | Result |
|---|---|
| PlanetLab-hosted private swarm, one initial seeder, approximately 300 leechers (mix of compliant Enhanced CTorrent clients and large-view free-riders) on distinct PlanetLab nodes, 12 MB file, every client (compliant and free-rider) rate-limited to 30 KB/s upload and download, 8-10 completion-time measurements collected per PlanetLab node, no whitewashing, free-riders reaching an average view of approximately 250 clients after approximately 150 seconds | 10% free-riders: mean completion time 823 s (free-rider) vs 872 s (compliant); free-riders faster. 40% free-riders: 1299 s (free-rider) vs 1290 s (compliant); nearly equal, with compliant clients showing higher variance. 60% free-riders: 1720 s (free-rider) vs 1581 s (compliant); compliant clients faster. A baseline swarm with no free-riders under the same setup had mean completion time 741 s, below all three mixed-population cases. |
| Same PlanetLab setup, approximately 300 leechers, 12 MB file, 30 KB/s rate limit, 10% free-riders, this time performing whitewashing (disconnect/reconnect to leechers after being unchoked) | Mean completion time 852 s (free-rider) vs 903 s (compliant); free-rider still faster than compliant, but both slower than the corresponding non-whitewashing 10% case (823 s / 872 s above). At a separately noted 1% free-rider fraction (figure not plotted), large-view-only free-riders reached 644 s mean completion versus 680 s for free-riders that additionally whitewashed, so whitewashing degraded the free-rider's own performance at that population level too. |
| 15 public BitTorrent torrents (drawn from torrentportal.com, file sizes approximately 500 MB-2 GB, swarm sizes roughly 50-650 peers, average seeder counts ranging 8.48-242.18 and average leecher counts ranging 41.21-492.01 per torrent per Table I), one compliant and one free-riding CTorrent client per torrent on separate machines in the same LAN, joining simultaneously, not rate-limited, one run per torrent | The free-riding client completed faster than the compliant client in 12 of 15 torrents. In the 3 torrents where it did not win (torrents 2, 3, 13), those had among the smallest average seeder counts (9.88, 14.19, 8.48) and comparatively small swarms, which the authors attribute to the larger view providing little benefit when the tracker's standard 50-peer response already covers most of a small swarm. Torrent 7 had a small overall swarm (51.89 average leechers) but a comparatively high seeder count (30.83 average, with the authors noting approximately 31 seeders total discoverable), and the free-rider won there specifically because its larger view let it discover nearly all available seeders. |

### Parameters
- Rate limit applied to all PlanetLab clients (compliant and free-rider), both directions: 30 KB/s, chosen to give all clients equal resources.
- File size for PlanetLab experiments: 12 MB, shared across all PlanetLab trials (Figures 1 and 3).
- Free-rider tracker re-announce interval: every 15 seconds.
- Free-rider average acquired swarm view: approximately 250 clients, reached after approximately 150 seconds into the download, against a compliant client's standard limit of connecting to at most 50 peers.
- Measurements per PlanetLab node: 8 to 10, varying with node availability.
- Countermeasure design parameters T (interval duration), a (post-interval connection delay, stated only as "much less than T"), and N (per-client allowed peer-connection count, stated only as "greater than 50"): none given numeric values; the paper states determining good values for T, a, and N empirically is future work.

### Stated limitations
The authors state the proposed countermeasure (synchronized interval-based pseudorandom peer assignment) is unimplemented and unmeasured: assessing its added load on the tracker, and empirically determining working values for its T, a, and N parameters, are both named explicitly as future work. The authors state their technique for identifying a peer by IP address is undermined by clients sharing one IP behind a NAT, and their proposed fix (setting N above the standard 50-peer view so NAT-sharing compliant clients can still receive disjoint peer assignments) is a design sketch, not a validated solution with a chosen N. The paper explicitly separates its own single-run, unaveraged public-torrent measurements (one run per torrent, 15 torrents) from its averaged PlanetLab measurements (8-10 runs per node), so its 12-of-15 public-torrent win count for the free-rider does not carry the same statistical confidence as the PlanetLab means. The authors state they observed no correlation between file size and the exploit's effectiveness, without further quantifying that null finding. The authors state whitewashing (disconnect/reconnect to erase reciprocation history) reduces overall swarm throughput and degrades even the whitewashing free-rider's own completion time relative to a free-rider that does not whitewash, concluding a rational free-rider has no incentive to whitewash, a conclusion the authors state follows directly from their own measured 1% and 10% comparisons above.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The exploit as measured requires only the standard tracker announce protocol and the standard practice, which the authors note is already implemented in mainstream compliant clients for tracker-failure resilience, of accepting and merging additional peer lists from other peers, so no protocol change or credential is required to mount it. The authors' proposed countermeasure requires every client and the tracker to share a synchronized time reference (interval boundaries of duration T) and requires the tracker to actively push membership-change updates (joins and departures) to all currently connected clients at each interval boundary, which the paper states may be assessed for tracker load but is not measured in this paper. The countermeasure requires clients to authenticate connection requests by IP address as the sole identifier, so it provides no defense, and the paper does not claim one, against a client that can present multiple distinct IP addresses. The countermeasure's disjoint-peer-set guarantee for NAT-sharing compliant clients depends on the tracker choosing N larger than the standard 50-peer view; the paper does not state a lower bound relating N to the number of clients expected behind a single NAT.

### Contradicts
None found in this paper's own claims. Cross-reference within this batch: LOCHER-HOTNETS-06 (BitThief) and this paper both report free-riding constructions against BitTorrent's tit-for-tat mechanism using materially different swarm compositions and metrics (BitThief reports relative download-time multiples against a reference client across 7 named public torrents and one controlled testbed; this paper reports absolute mean completion times across a controlled PlanetLab population sweep and a 15-torrent public sample with a win-count metric), so the two papers' numbers are not directly comparable as a single figure, though both independently conclude that a client that uploads nothing can match or beat a tit-for-tat-compliant client under common conditions. This paper explicitly distinguishes its own free-rider definition (zero upload) from Jun and Ahamad's cited PlanetLab study (approximately 150 leechers, 75 free-riders capped at 4 KB/s upload against a 100 KB/s cap for others, so a "free-rider" there still uploads at reduced rate), so a synthesis must not merge the two papers' free-rider population figures as measuring the same condition.

### References worth retrieving
- Cohen, "Incentives build robustness in BitTorrent," P2PEcon 2003 -- foundational (the original description of BitTorrent's tit-for-tat mechanism this exploit targets).
- Axelrod, "The Evolution of Cooperation," Basic Books, 1984 -- foundational (the iterated-prisoner's-dilemma game-theoretic framework the paper uses to explain why tit-for-tat is exploitable when the game has a finite, client-controlled number of rounds).
- Jun, Ahamad, "Incentives in BitTorrent induce free riding," P2PEcon 2005 -- competing (an independent PlanetLab measurement of BitTorrent free-riding under a weaker, reduced-upload-rate definition of free-rider, explicitly contrasted against this paper's zero-upload definition).
- Liogkas, R., Kohler, Zhang, "Exploiting BitTorrent for fun (but not profit)," IPTPS 2006 -- competing/foundational (shows peers that connect only to discovered seeders can raise download rate without contributing bandwidth; cited as related prior evidence for this paper's design rationale).
- Locher, Moor, Schmid, Wattenhofer, "Free Riding in BitTorrent is Cheap," HotNets 2006 -- competing (the near-concurrent BitThief paper, retrieved in this same batch as LOCHER-HOTNETS-06; this paper explicitly enumerates four ways its own experiments differ from and complement BitThief's).
- Piatek, Isdal, Anderson, Krishnamurthy, Venkataramani, "Do incentives build robustness in BitTorrent?," NSDI 2006 -- competing (shows careful peer and per-peer-upload-rate selection can raise download rate while substantially cutting uplink use, a related but distinct exploit from the large-view technique).
- Andrade, Mowbray, Lima, Wagner, Ripeanu, "Influences on cooperation in BitTorrent communities," P2PEcon 2005 -- competing (shows free-riders can attain better sharing ratios than compliant peers in seeder-heavy swarms).
- Shneidman, Parkes, Massoulie, "Faithfulness in internet algorithms," PINS 2004 -- attack (conjectures a Sybil-based optimistic-unchoke-frequency attack via multiple presented identities, explicitly distinguished by this paper from the large-view exploit, which requires no multiple identities).
- Douceur, "The Sybil Attack," IPTPS 2002 -- foundational (cited for the multiple-identity attack the paper explicitly notes its own exploit does not require).
- Li, Clement, Wong, Napper, Roy, Alvisi, Dahlin, "BAR Gossip," OSDI 2006 -- foundational (source of the verifiable pseudorandom peer-selection technique this paper's proposed countermeasure adapts, originally assuming certifiable per-client key pairs and a leave-only churn model this paper explicitly relaxes).
- Feldman, Papadimitriou, Chuang, Stoica, "Free-riding and whitewashing in peer-to-peer systems," IEEE JSAC 2006 -- foundational (source of the term "whitewashing" this paper adopts for its disconnect-and-reconnect technique).

## [SIRIVIANOS-USENIXATC-07] Dandelion: Cooperative Content Distribution with Robust Incentives
**Citation:** Michael Sirivianos, Jong Han Park, Xiaowei Yang, Stanislaw Jarecki. "Dandelion: Cooperative Content Distribution with Robust Incentives." USENIX Annual Technical Conference, 2007. Pages 157-170.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.usenix.org/legacy/events/usenix07/tech/full_papers/sirivianos/sirivianos.pdf
**Source URL:** https://www.usenix.org/legacy/events/usenix07/tech/full_papers/sirivianos/sirivianos.pdf
**Domain:** I

### What it does
Dandelion incentivizes peer-to-peer clients to upload content to each other by withholding the decryption key for a content chunk from a downloading client until that client's upload activity has been credited by a central server, so that a client gains no benefit from downloading without also uploading, regardless of whether its peers hold content it wants in return. A file is split into fixed-size chunks; each chunk is distributed encrypted, and a client must obtain the corresponding decryption key from the server to use it. The server maintains a per-client credit balance: a downloading client B spends delta_c credit units to acquire a chunk from an uploading client A, and A earns delta_r credit units for correctly serving that chunk, with delta_c set equal to delta_r so two colluding clients cannot inflate their combined credit by falsely claiming to have exchanged chunks with each other. The protocol runs as a three-party fair exchange for every chunk transaction: client A encrypts the chunk fresh for each request and sends it to client B along with a signed ticket; B, upon receiving the encrypted chunk, immediately requests the decryption key from the server rather than waiting to verify the chunk's integrity itself; the server authenticates the request (HMAC), verifies the ticket (HMAC), decrypts the server-held copy of the decryption key (symmetric encryption), updates both clients' credit, signs the decryption key response, and returns it. Because the server is a mandatory party to every single-chunk exchange, and because the server can check a client's credit balance before releasing a decryption key, the paper proves (Lemmas 4.1-4.4 in the paper, proofs deferred to a companion technical report [51]) that a selfish client cannot claim credit for chunks it never delivered, cannot claim credit for corrupted chunks it delivered, cannot impersonate another client's ID, and cannot replay old signed messages to fraudulently charge or blacklist another client. If a client cannot retrieve a chunk from peers in time, it falls back to requesting the plaintext chunk directly from the server for a higher, delta_s > delta_c credit charge, or receives an error if the server is overloaded, so the pipeline degrades gracefully rather than stalling.

### Measured results

| Condition | Result |
|---|---|
| Per-chunk server cryptographic operation timings, dual Pentium D 2.8 GHz / 1 MB CPU, 1 GB RAM, 250 GB/7200 RPM HDD, Linux 2.6.5, getrusage(RUSAGE_SELF) over 10,000 executions, HMAC-SHA1 (128-bit key) for auth/ticket/signing, 8-byte-block Blowfish-CBC (128-bit key, 128-bit IV) for chunk/key encryption, SHA-1 for chunk hashing | Authenticate decryption key request (98 bytes): 0.018 ms; generate ticket (78 bytes): 0.018 ms; encrypt/decrypt decryption key (32 bytes): 0.056 ms; sign decryption key response (46 bytes): 0.017 ms — total CPU-centric cost for operations 1-4: 109 microseconds. Encrypt/decrypt a 128 KB chunk: 0.715 ms; hash a 128 KB encrypted chunk: 0.487 ms |
| Credit-file operations, gettimeofday() over 10,000 executions, 10,000-entry file with 44-byte entries | Query credit file: ~0.004 ms; update without forcing disk commit: ~0.02 ms; update with fsync() disk commit (HDD caching disabled): ~9.25 ms; update with disk commit every 100 updates (amortized): ~0.27 ms |
| Server-side decryption-key-request throughput, ~200 clients on distinct PlanetLab hosts, server rate-limited at the application layer to 1-5 Mb/s, per-client request rate swept 1-14 req/sec, 10-minute runs averaged over 10 repetitions | At 1-3 Mb/s, throughput scales with bandwidth (bandwidth-bound); at 4-5 Mb/s, throughput plateaus at approximately 1,200 decryption-key responses per second (CPU-bound, server CPU utilization approaches ~100%); with 128 KB chunks, this supports approximately 1,200 simultaneous clients each downloading at 128 KB/s from each other; memory utilization stays low throughout |
| Chunk-size sensitivity, ~40 leechers, one initial seeder, PlanetLab, file sizes 10/100/250 MB, chunk sizes 64/128/256/512/1024/2048 KB | For a 10 MB file, 64 KB chunks give the best mean download completion time, with performance degrading as chunk size grows; for a 250 MB file, 128 KB chunks outperform 64 KB chunks; the paper adopts 128 KB chunks for the rest of its evaluation based on this tradeoff |
| Seeder-probability impact, ~200 leechers, one initial seeder, PlanetLab, seed-after-completion probability a in {25%, 100%}, file sizes from 0.5 to 250 MB, 10 repetitions per configuration, 95% confidence intervals reported | For a 250 MB file, mean swarm-wide download completion time was 674 seconds at a=100% versus 837 seconds at a=25%; the relative benefit of full seeding shrinks as file size grows, because larger files keep leechers online (and thus contributing uplink) longer regardless of a |
| Comparison against BitTorrent, ~200 CTorrent 1.3.4 tit-for-tat-compliant leechers with all leechers remaining online after completion (a=100%), same PlanetLab conditions and file-size sweep | Dandelion (a=100%) achieves download completion times comparable to, and for some file sizes better than, BitTorrent; the paper states it does not claim general superiority, since both protocols' performance depends on numerous unexplored parameters |
| Credit distribution, single 250 MB file, ~200 leechers, one initial seeder, all clients start with 100% of the credit needed and all become seeders on completion | Product-moment correlation coefficient between a client's average download rate and its final credit ratio: 0.72 (the fastest downloaders/uploaders accumulate the most credit); 25.8% of clients ended with less than 70% of their initial credit, i.e. they uploaded substantially less than they downloaded |
| Prior free-riding measurement cited from the authors' own earlier work [50] | A modified "large view" free-riding CTorrent client downloaded faster than a tit-for-tat-compliant client in 12 of 15 randomly selected public torrents, file sizes 500 MB-2 GB, swarm sizes 50-1,000 peers; in a PlanetLab swarm of ~300 leechers rate-limited to 30 KB/sec plus one seeder at 120 KB/sec, when compliant clients made up 90% of the swarm, free-riders downloaded faster than compliant clients in the same (mixed) swarm and only slightly worse than compliant clients in a swarm with no free-riders |

### Parameters
- Credit unit values: delta_c (cost to download a chunk) set equal to delta_r (reward for uploading a chunk), specifically to prevent two colluding clients from inflating their combined credit through mutual false claims.
- Server fallback charge for direct plaintext-chunk delivery when the server is moderately busy: delta_s, set greater than delta_c to discourage clients from preferring the server over peers.
- Chunk size: swept at 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048 KB; 128 KB adopted for the main evaluation.
- Cryptography: HMAC-SHA1 with 128-bit keys for authentication, ticket verification, and response signing; 8-byte-block Blowfish-CBC with 128-bit key and 128-bit IV for chunk and key encryption; SHA-1 for chunk hashing.
- Test hardware for profiling: dual Pentium D 2.8 GHz/1 MB CPU, 1 GB RAM, 250 GB/7200 RPM HDD, Linux 2.6.5-1.358smp.
- Test hardware for the system-performance (Section 6.3) experiments: Xeon 3 GHz/2 MB CPU, 2 GB RAM PlanetLab VServer, server rate-limited to 2 Mb/s; TCP sender/receiver buffer size set to 120 KB to cover PlanetLab's bandwidth-delay product.
- Deployment scale evaluated: up to ~200-300 PlanetLab-hosted clients (leechers) per experiment; the profiling-based projection (not a direct load test at this scale) states a server on the tested commodity hardware with a 4-5 Mb/s access link can support "a few thousand clients."

### Stated limitations
The paper states its threat model explicitly excludes bandwidth or connection-flooding denial-of-service attacks ("we consider bandwidth or connection flooding attacks outside the scope of this work"); the non-manipulability proofs cover only protocol-message-level attacks. Observation 4.8 states a malicious client can always abandon a protocol run partway through, denying the counterparty resources already spent, and the paper's only mitigation is that this costs the attacker resources roughly proportional to the victim's, calling the attack "not particularly practical" rather than prevented; a further, partial mitigation (short-lived tickets issued only to accounts in good standing, and an option for the server to charge for ticket issuance) is described as deterrence, not elimination. The security proofs for Lemmas 4.1-4.4 are stated but not proved in this paper; the paper states the proofs are deferred to the Appendix of a companion technical report. The paper explicitly declines to claim general superiority over BitTorrent, stating performance of both protocols depends on unexplored parameters. The design assumes "weak security of the IP network": clients can eavesdrop but the paper assumes they cannot corrupt or interfere with routing/forwarding at the network layer, and separately assumes communication errors may occur during message transmission; a network model departing from this (active tampering with routing, not just message content) is outside what the paper's guarantees cover. The 1,200-clients-per-server figure and the "few thousand clients" scalability projection are extrapolated from a 200-client PlanetLab throughput measurement and single-machine CPU/bandwidth profiling, not from a load test actually run at thousands of concurrent clients; the paper's own Section 6.1 states the per-operation profiling "does not consider the parallel processing of I/O and CPU operations" and "does not include the cost of system calls and the cost of TCP/IP stack processing," and explicitly states "we refrain from deriving conclusions on the throughput of the server" from that profiling data alone. The scheme's non-manipulability rests on centralizing every single-chunk exchange through one server that checks credit balances synchronously; the paper's own Section 5.1 states this server, though logically separable from the credit base, is combined into a single machine in the actual prototype, and single-server involvement in every chunk exchange is the design choice the paper explicitly trades for scalability ("we trade scalability for the ability to provide robust incentives").

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The provable non-manipulability property depends on each client holding one authenticated, paid account with the content provider; the paper states explicitly that "a user cannot boost its credit by presenting multiple IDs (Sybil attack) and claiming to have uploaded to some of its registered IDs" precisely because "each user maintains an authenticated paid account with the provider" and "essentially purchases its initial credit." This means the fair-exchange proof depends on a centralized, identity-verifying, paid-registration process external to the peer-to-peer protocol itself; the paper does not analyze or claim the proof holds for clients that can obtain fresh, unauthenticated identities at low or zero cost. The mechanism requires a single server (or a server cluster acting with a shared, consistent credit ledger) to be reachable and responsive for every chunk exchange between any two clients, since decryption keys are withheld until the server processes and settles a credit transaction for that specific chunk; a design in which client pairs can complete a chunk exchange without contacting a shared arbiter is incompatible with this proof structure. It requires clients to encrypt each served chunk freshly per request (stated in Lemma 4.2's precondition) rather than caching one encrypted copy, so that credit crediting and content delivery stay bound to the exact request being served. It requires the server to issue short-lived, per-transaction tickets to prevent abandoned-protocol-run denial-of-service attacks from unauthorized or blacklisted clients, meaning ticket-issuance state (validity windows, per-account status) must be tracked centrally alongside the credit ledger. The design assumes the content provider can price accumulated virtual credit such that "the benefit that a selfish client gains from acquiring virtual currency for content it uploads exceeds the cost of utilizing its uplink to upload it" — an external pricing decision the protocol itself does not make or verify, and without which the stated incentive-compatibility (Nash equilibrium of cooperation) argument does not follow.

### Contradicts
None found. No other paper in this batch reports a conflicting measurement of the same quantity.

### References worth retrieving
- Cohen, B., "Incentives Build Robustness in BitTorrent." P2P Econ, 2003. — foundational (defines BitTorrent's rate-based tit-for-tat incentive mechanism that this paper's incentive design is built to improve on)
- Douceur, J. R., "The Sybil Attack." IPTPS, 2002. — foundational (defines the Sybil attack the paper's centralized-paid-account requirement is stated to prevent)
- Locher, T., Moor, P., Schmid, S., Wattenhofer, R., "Free Riding in BitTorrent is Cheap." — competing (near-concurrent independent experimental demonstration of the same BitTorrent free-riding weakness this paper's own prior work also measured)
- Liogkas, N., Nelson, R., Kohler, E., Zhang, L., "Exploiting BitTorrent For Fun (But Not Profit)." — attack (prior BitTorrent-exploitation work the paper's own "large view" free-riding client builds on)
- Jun, S., Ahamad, M., "Incentives in BitTorrent Induce Free Riding." — attack/critique (prior critique of BitTorrent's tit-for-tat incentive scheme cited among the sources motivating this paper's design)
- Li, J., Kang, X., "Proof of Service in a Hybrid P2P Environment." ISPA. — competing (a proof-of-service fair-exchange scheme the paper directly contrasts its own design against, noting the prior scheme did not provide an experimental evaluation and is vulnerable to selfish clients obtaining content from other selfish peers without sufficient credit)
- Vishnumurthy, V., Chandrakumar, S., Sirer, E. G., "KARMA: A Secure Economy for Peer-to-Peer Resource Sharing." — competing (a distributed, non-centralized virtual-currency incentive scheme, part of the design space this paper's centralized-server approach is positioned against)
- Yang, B., Garcia-Molina, H., "PPay: Micropayments for Peer-to-peer Systems." — competing (a peer-to-peer micropayment scheme relevant to the paper's virtual-currency incentive design)
- Fan, B., Chiu, D.-M., Lui, J. C., "The Delicate Tradeoffs in BitTorrent-like File Sharing Protocol Design." — foundational (analyzes the performance/free-riding-susceptibility tradeoff the paper cites as the reason BitTorrent does not implement strict chunk-level tit-for-tat)

## [SIT-IPTPS-02] Security Considerations for Peer-to-Peer Distributed Hash Tables

**Citation:** Emil Sit, Robert Morris. "Security Considerations for Peer-to-Peer Distributed Hash Tables." IPTPS, 2002. DOI 10.1007/3-540-45748-8_25.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://pdos.csail.mit.edu/papers/chord:security02/chord:security02.pdf (candidate URL from registry; local file matches title/authors/abstract)
**Source URL:** https://pdos.csail.mit.edu/papers/chord:security02/chord:security02.pdf
**Domain:** A

### What it does
The paper classifies liveness attacks against distributed hash table (DHT) lookup systems — attacks that prevent participants from finding data, as distinct from data-authenticity attacks, which the authors state are already addressed by cryptographic techniques such as self-certifying path names. It defines the adversary model, enumerates attack classes against routing and against storage, and derives six design principles from the defenses discussed for each class. The paper contains no implementation and no experiment; it is an analytical taxonomy applied to three published DHT designs, Chord, Pastry, and CAN (content-addressable network).

The adversary model: a malicious node can generate packets with arbitrary content, including forged source IP addresses, but can only receive packets addressed to its own IP address. This lets a node use IP address as a weak identity check: a node receiving a packet from address X can confirm the sender controls X by sending a confirmation request to X. Malicious nodes may conspire, each individually bound by this same constraint. Malicious nodes cannot overhear or modify traffic between other nodes.

The six design principles the paper derives: (1) define verifiable system invariants and verify them; (2) let the querier observe lookup progress hop by hop, so it can detect a lookup that fails to converge toward the target key; (3) assign node identifiers to nodes in a verifiable way, for example by deriving the identifier from a cryptographic hash of the node's IP address and port, so another node can check a claimed identifier against the claimant's network address; (4) treat routing-table entries chosen by a latency- or performance-based server-selection rule as attacker-influenceable, since an adversary can offer itself as the lowest-latency or best-ratio option and thereby bias which nodes get chosen; (5) cross-check a node's own routing table by issuing random queries through previously-trusted nodes and comparing results, to detect that a node has been diverted into a parallel, internally-consistent malicious network (a partition attack); (6) avoid single points of responsibility in the storage layer — replication must be organized so that no single node governs whether a client obtains a replica, and clients must independently determine the correct replica set rather than asking one node for it.

Attack-specific mechanisms discussed: incorrect lookup forwarding (a node forwards a query to a wrong or non-existent node) is detected when the querier can verify that each hop's identifier distance to the key strictly decreases, which requires an iterative-lookup design where each hop reports back to the querier — this check is stated to be impossible under CAN's proposed recursive-forwarding round-trip-time (RTT) optimization, where a node forwards to whichever neighbor has the best progress-to-RTT ratio without involving the querier. Incorrect routing-table updates (a node injects false entries into another node's routing table) are mitigated by requiring each update to satisfy a checkable structural rule (Pastry requires each table entry to share the correct address-prefix length) and by requiring reachability verification before an update is incorporated. Partition attacks (an adversary builds a self-consistent parallel network and diverts a joining or rejoining node into it) are mitigated by bootstrapping new nodes only from an out-of-band trusted source, and by an already-joined node periodically cross-checking against previously-used nodes with random queries. Storage-denial (a node claims not to hold data it is responsible for, or claims to hold data but refuses to serve it) is mitigated only by replication combined with the single-point-of-responsibility principle: querying clients must consult at least two independent replica sites before concluding data is truly missing, because consulting only the node structurally responsible for replication (as DHash does) leaves the client unable to distinguish "data missing" from "the one node that controls replica lookup is lying." Inconsistent behavior (a node behaves correctly toward nearby-in-identifier-space nodes and incorrectly toward distant ones) is stated to be undetectable by distant nodes reporting the bad behavior to near ones unless responses are signed, because an unsigned complaint cannot be distinguished from a false complaint meant to discredit a benign node. Node overload (packet flooding against a targeted node or its replicas) is mitigated by assigning node identifiers independently of network topology and by physically dispersing replicas, so a topologically localized attack cannot take out an entire portion of the key space. Unsolicited/forged responses (a node that referred a querier to a next hop forges a reply purporting to come from that next hop) are mitigated with a per-query random nonce that the genuine respondent must echo back.

### Measured results
None. This is an analytical/taxonomic paper; it contains no experiment, no simulation, and no reported numeric result of any kind. No figure in this paper may be cited as measured evidence.

### Parameters
None stated. The paper introduces no tunable parameter of its own; it discusses design choices made by the systems it analyzes (Chord's successor-list replication, Pastry's prefix-verification rule, CAN's RTT-ratio neighbor selection) without stating specific numeric configurations for any of them.

### Stated limitations
The paper explicitly scopes itself to liveness attacks only, stating that data-correctness and data-authenticity attacks are considered already addressed by existing cryptographic techniques (citing self-certifying path names) and are out of scope. The adversary model explicitly excludes a node's ability to overhear or modify traffic between two other nodes; an adversary with that capability is not analyzed. The paper states that trust metrics built on IP address are dangerous in a network with high churn and weak identity, because a Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP)-assigned address can belong to a malicious node one day and a benign node the next. For the inconsistent-behavior attack, the paper states plainly that without public-key signatures on responses, "each node must make its own determination as to whether another node is malicious," i.e., no cross-node verification mechanism is offered. For the verifiable-node-identifier defense, the paper states that deriving a node's identifier from a hash of its IP address, port, and virtual-node number (as Chord does) still leaves a single physical host able to run many virtual nodes and thereby exercise some choice over which keys it becomes responsible for, so Chord's approach only partially closes the attack DHash remains exposed to. The rapid-join/-leave rebalancing attack is stated to be unavoidable in general: any DHT, with or without adversaries, must already handle rebalancing triggered by ordinary churn, so the paper offers no defense beyond noting that the adversary's model here (no ability to fake liveness of a node cheaply, and rebalancing requiring acknowledged data transfer) limits how cheaply an adversary can trigger excess rebalancing.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
For principle 2 (observable lookup progress) to be enforceable, the lookup protocol must be iterative (each hop reports the next hop back to the querier) rather than fully recursive/relayed, because the paper states this check is impossible under CAN's proposed RTT-optimized recursive forwarding. For principle 3 (verifiable node identifiers) to be enforceable, the identifier-derivation function must bind the identifier to something the querier can independently check against the network, such as the claimant's IP address and port; a system letting a node choose its own identifier arbitrarily (as the paper states CAN allows) cannot support this check. For principle 5 (cross-checking via random queries) to work, a node must maintain a set of other nodes it has successfully used in the past, obtained through an out-of-band trusted bootstrap the first time, and query randomness must be preserved so a malicious partition cannot distinguish a verification probe from a real query it wants to intercept. For the storage/replication defenses (principle 6) to work, the system must let a client independently compute or discover the full replica set for a key rather than obtaining it through one designated node, and must support the client querying at least two replica sites per lookup. For the inconsistent-behavior and unsolicited-response defenses, the system needs either digital signatures on all node responses (to let a third party verify a complaint about a node, and to let a querier verify a reply's claimed origin) or, absent that, a per-query random nonce that a legitimate respondent echoes back, which defends only against response forgery, not against a node lying about its own state.

### Contradicts
None found among the papers in this batch (W1-5). This paper predates and is foundational to later disjoint-path and puzzle-based Sybil-resistance work (e.g., S/Kademlia, already in the corpus per BRIEF.md section 7); it does not itself measure a lookup-success rate under attack, so it cannot be checked against S/Kademlia's 99%-success figure for disagreement — the two papers operate at different levels: this one is a taxonomy, S/Kademlia is a measured defense.

## [STEFANOV-CCS-13] Path ORAM: An Extremely Simple Oblivious RAM Protocol
**Citation:** Emil Stefanov, Marten van Dijk, Elaine Shi, Christopher W. Fletcher, Ling Ren, Xiangyao Yu, Srinivas Devadas. "Path ORAM: An Extremely Simple Oblivious RAM Protocol." ACM CCS, 2013. DOI 10.1145/2508859.2516660.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://eprint.iacr.org/2013/280.pdf (arXiv:1202.5150 original construction, later published at CCS 2013)
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2013/280.pdf
**Domain:** G

### What it does
Path ORAM (Oblivious Random Access Memory) hides which data a client reads or writes from an untrusted storage server, so that the server observes only a sequence of physical storage accesses statistically indistinguishable from any other access sequence of the same length, regardless of the client's actual logical read/write pattern. The security definition it satisfies (Definition 1) requires that for any two request sequences of equal length, an outside observer cannot distinguish the resulting physical access patterns, and that the protocol returns correct data with overwhelming probability. The mechanism: server-side data is organized as a binary tree of height L, where every node is a "bucket" holding up to Z real data blocks (padded with dummy blocks to always appear full at size Z). Each data block is currently assigned, in a client-held position map, to one uniformly random leaf of the tree; the protocol's invariant is that every block resides either in some bucket along the path from that leaf to the root, or in the client's local "stash." To read or write a block, the client looks up its assigned leaf x in the position map, downloads every bucket along the path from leaf x to the root into its stash, reassigns the block to a freshly and independently chosen random leaf, updates the position map, then writes the path back to the server — greedily placing blocks from the stash (including the requested block) as deep down the path toward their newly assigned leaves as bucket capacity allows, so that stash occupancy stays low. Because the requested block is re-randomized to a new leaf on every access, repeated accesses to the same block do not produce a repeated physical access pattern. To keep the position map itself small (it grows linearly with the number of blocks N in the naive construction), the paper applies a recursion technique: the position map is itself stored as a sequence of smaller ORAMs, each holding the position map for the next level, so that only a constant amount of position-map state remains on the client after recursion.

### Measured results
| Result | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Proved asymptotic bandwidth cost, small blocks | O(log^2 N) blocks moved per access | block size B = Omega(log N) bits, recursive Path ORAM, failure probability N^-omega(1) (negligible in N) |
| Proved asymptotic bandwidth cost, moderate blocks | O(log N) blocks moved per access | block size B = Omega(log^2 N) bits (e.g. 4 KB blocks), recursive Path ORAM using block size Theta(log N) during recursion, failure probability N^-omega(1) |
| Proved client storage | O(log N) . omega(1) blocks | recursive Path ORAM, both block-size regimes above |
| Per-access bandwidth formula (non-recursive, exact) | 2 . Z . log(N) blocks per load/store operation (read the path down, then write it back) | bucket size Z held constant, tree height L = ceil(log2 N) |
| Concrete stash-overflow failure bound (worked example, non-recursive) | for stash capacity R log N blocks, server storage 20N blocks, bandwidth 10(log N)^2 blocks/operation, over s load/store operations, failure probability at most 14 . s . log N . 0.625^-R | bucket size Z=5, tree height L=ceil(log N); choosing R = Theta(log s + log log N) . omega(1) drives failure probability to negligible |
| Empirical stash size vs. security parameter lambda (Figure 3/4) | required stash size grows linearly with lambda and is empirically independent of N (verified up to lambda=26) for Z=4 | simulated a single run of ~250 billion accesses after a 1-billion-access warm-up, worst-case round-robin access pattern {1,2,...,N,1,2,...}, measured at N=2^16, bucket size Z=4 |
| Extrapolated max stash size for larger security parameters (Table/Figure 5) | at Z=4: lambda=80 needs stash 89; lambda=128 needs stash 147; lambda=256 needs stash 303. At Z=5: lambda=80 needs 63; lambda=128 needs 105; lambda=256 needs 218. At Z=6: lambda=80 needs 53; lambda=128 needs 89; lambda=256 needs 186 | extrapolated from empirical results for lambda <= 26 (practical security parameters such as lambda=128 cannot be directly simulated, since a feasible-time observed failure would contradict the target security level); worst-case round-robin access pattern; stash size excludes the transiently fetched path |
| Average bucket load per tree level (Figure 6) | for Z in {4,5}, expected bucket load near the root is about 1 block (about 25% full for Z=4, about 20% full for Z=5); Z=3 shows a qualitatively different, worse distribution | worst-case round-robin access pattern, measured across tree levels |
| Hardware secure-processor overhead (cited from Ren et al. and Maas et al., not measured in this paper) | approximately 1.2x to 5x performance overhead on benchmarks including SPEC traces and SQLite queries | on-chip caches used, Path ORAM requests issued only on last-level cache misses |

### Parameters
| Parameter | Symbol | Value used | Notes / range tested |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bucket capacity | Z | small constant; theorem proved for Z>=5; Z=4 used as the practical default | empirically tested Z in {3, 4, 5}; Z=3 gives markedly worse (larger) stash occupancy and the paper states it is unclear how likely stash overflow is at Z=3 |
| Tree height | L | ceil(log2 N) in theoretical bounds; ceil(log2 N) - 1 sufficient in the experiments | -- |
| Block size (non-recursive small-block regime) | B | Omega(log N) bits | yields O(log^2 N) bandwidth |
| Block size (moderate regime) | B | Omega(log^2 N) bits (paper's example: 4 KB blocks) | yields O(log N) bandwidth |

| Simulated total accesses | -- | ~250 billion, after 1 billion warm-up accesses | single run, N = 2^16 |

### Stated limitations
The security proof and construction explicitly exclude the timing channel: the paper states that, like all related prior ORAM work, it does not consider information leakage through when or how frequently the client makes data requests, only which physical locations are accessed. Integrity against a malicious (as opposed to honest-but-curious/untrusted-but-passive) server is not the paper's main focus; it is addressed only as an extension in Section 6.4 using a Merkle-tree hash over each bucket, and the paper states it does not focus on integrity in its main presentation. The theoretical stash-overflow bound (Theorem/Main Theorem in Section 5) is proved only for bucket size Z>=5; the paper's own empirical results show Z=4 performing well in practice but state this is not proven, and Z=3 is empirically markedly worse with an unresolved overflow-probability trend. Practical security parameters (for example lambda=128) cannot themselves be validated by direct simulation, because observing a failure at that parameter in feasible simulation time would itself indicate insufficient security; the reported large-lambda stash sizes are extrapolations from empirically measured values only up to lambda=26.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Path ORAM requires the client to hold a stash (local storage measured empirically as usually near-empty, with worst-case size growing linearly in the security parameter lambda and, per the proof, O(log N) . omega(1) asymptotically) and, in the non-recursive construction, a position map whose size grows linearly with the total number of blocks N; the recursive construction removes this linear-growth requirement by storing the position map itself as smaller ORAM instances, at the cost of additional bandwidth (an added O(log N) multiplicative factor for small blocks). It requires every access — whether a logical read or a logical write — to perform the identical download-path/re-randomize/write-back sequence, so the mechanism gives no way to serve a read at lower bandwidth cost than a write, and any layer built on top of it inherits a fixed per-access bandwidth cost regardless of whether the underlying operation needed to move the data. It requires the client to generate an independent, uniformly random leaf label on every access to that block, and requires the server-side bucket capacity Z to be fixed in advance; choosing it too small (Z=3, empirically) produces materially worse stash-overflow behavior. It assumes an honest-but-curious server model for its core privacy guarantee — the server is untrusted but not assumed to tamper with results — and treats defense against a maliciously tampering server as a separable, additional mechanism (Merkle-tree bucket hashing) layered on top rather than a property the base protocol provides. It requires the client itself (its processor, memory, and disk) to be trusted; no part of Path ORAM protects data or access patterns from an adversary that can observe the client's own internal state.

### Contradicts
None found within this batch.
