## [TRAUDT-ICDCS-21] FlashFlow: A Secure Speed Test for Tor
**Citation:** Matthew Traudt, Rob Jansen, Aaron Johnson. "FlashFlow: A Secure Speed Test for Tor." IEEE ICDCS, 2021. DOI 10.1109/ICDCS51616.2021.00044.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.robgjansen.com/publications/flashflow-icdcs2021.pdf
**Source URL:** https://www.robgjansen.com/publications/flashflow-icdcs2021.pdf
**Domain:** I

### What it does
FlashFlow measures the true forwarding capacity of a Tor relay so the Tor network can assign load-balancing weights that a relay cannot inflate by lying about its own bandwidth. Tor relays currently self-report bandwidth to Bandwidth Authorities (BW Auths), which combine the self-report with a small active download test (TorFlow); a relay controls the self-reported number and prior work showed this self-report can be forged to inflate a relay's assigned traffic share. FlashFlow replaces the self-report with a load test large enough to force the relay to carry all the traffic it claims to be able to carry. A FlashFlow team, which constitutes one BW Auth, has a coordinator and one or more measurers. The coordinator opens an authenticated connection (keyed by a public key distributed in the Tor consensus) to each measurer and to the target relay, then divides the total measurement traffic across m measurers, each running k_i = max(1, c_i/p_i) modified Tor processes, where c_i is the measurer's CPU-core count and p_i is its expected number of parallel measurements that period. Each measurer sends and receives normal-looking Tor cells to and from the target over measurement circuits; sent cell contents are randomly generated and a fraction p of returned cells are checked byte-for-byte, so a relay that forges a response (skips decryption, or replies before receiving) is caught with probability approaching 1 as more responses are checked, and a relay forging k responses evades detection with probability only (1−p)^k. The team measures a candidate capacity z; if z is small enough relative to the team's allocated capacity a_i (specifically z < Σ_i a_i (1−ε1)/g), the measurement is accepted as accurate because the true capacity x must then lie in the interval ((1−ε1)x, (1+ε2)x); otherwise the allocated capacity is at least doubled (z0 = max(z, 2z0)) and the relay is remeasured. New relays without a prior estimate start from the 75th-percentile capacity observed across the network in the preceding month. Because the target relay also carries its normal client traffic during the load test, the design caps the relay's self-reported normal traffic at a ratio r of the total measured traffic during the measurement window, so a relay cannot claim high capacity by counting client traffic it never actually forwarded beyond that ratio. Measurement timing per relay is drawn from a schedule known only to the BW Auths and generated from a shared random seed each 24-hour measurement period, so a relay cannot predict when it will be tested and inflate capacity only during that window; results from a majority of BW Auths are aggregated by taking the median, following Tor's existing directory-authority trust model.

### Measured results
| Metric | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Malicious-relay capacity inflation bound (analytic) | At most 1.33x true capacity, versus a demonstrated 177x for TorFlow | Derived from the traffic-ratio cap 1/(1−r) with recommended r = 0.25; the 177x figure is cited from the PeerFlow paper's demonstrated attack against TorFlow |
| Measurement accuracy, Internet experiments | Within 11% of ground truth (0.89-1.11x capacity) in 95% of experiments; within 20% in 99.8% of experiments | Real Internet hosts in Fremont CA, Santa Rosa CA, Washington DC, Bangalore, and Amsterdam; target relay throughput limits of 10, 250, 500, 750 Mbit/s and unlimited; each configuration run 7 times over 24 hours, 30-second measurement slots, multiplier g = 2.25 |
| Ground-truth capacity, single relay | 890 Mbit/s maximum median throughput, consuming 95-100% of one CPU core | Lab-controlled relay on the US-SW host measured by supporting Tor processes on the remaining lab machines |
| Tor single-relay processing ceiling | 1.25 Gbit/s maximum, using 20 TCP sockets, Tor reaching 100% CPU on one core | 120-second lab measurement designed to minimize network, TCP, and Tor flow-control limits; consistent with the fastest publicly claimed relay capacity, 998 Mbit/s in July 2019 |
| Background-traffic ratio cap behavior | When r <= 50/250 = 0.2, background traffic during measurement is consistently held to 250r; above that ratio background traffic stays at its unconstrained rate of ~50 Mbit/s | Real Tor relay run for 60 days to earn the Guard flag and attract genuine client traffic, capacity-limited to 250 Mbit/s, measured by one FlashFlow measurer in Amsterdam, ratios r tested between 0.1 and 0.5 |
| Full-network measurement speed (simulation) | Median 5 hours (599 30-second slots; min 4.9, max 5.1 hours) to measure the entire network, median 6,419 relays (min 6,355, max 6,528), median total capacity 608 Gbit/s (min 592, max 621) | Simulated using archived Tor consensuses/descriptors for each day of July 2019, greedy scheduler, one team of 3 measurers at 1 Gbit/s each, excess factor f = 2.84 |
| New-relay measurement speed (simulation) | Median 30 seconds to measure new relays in a consensus (min 0 minutes, max 13 minutes); median of 3 new relays per consensus (min 0, max 98) | Same July 2019 consensus replay; new-relay capacity estimate set to the 75th-percentile advertised bandwidth from June 2019 descriptors, 51 Mbit/s |
| Added network load | 5.89 TiB/day per FlashFlow team, about 0.3% of the ~1,965 TiB/day the Tor network forwarded in June-August 2019 | Computed as f * C * t with f = 2.84, C = 608 Gbit/s network capacity, t = 30 s measurement duration |
| Network capacity/weight error (Shadow simulation) | FlashFlow: 14% network capacity error, 4% network weight error; TorFlow: 29% network weight error (86% relative reduction by FlashFlow); median and interquartile relay capacity error for FlashFlow both 16% | Shadow discrete-event simulator, private test network 5% the size of the public Tor network: 3 Directory Authorities, 328 relays sampled from January 2019 consensus, 397 TGen clients modeling 40k Tor users' traffic, plus 40 benchmark clients |
| Transfer-time improvement | Median transfer time decreases by 15% (50 KiB), 29% (1 MiB), 37% (5 MiB) versus TorFlow at 100% traffic load; standard deviation decreases by 55%, 61%, 41% respectively | Same Shadow simulation, three load levels tested (100%, 115%, 130% of normal client traffic), timeouts set to 15/60/120 seconds for the three file sizes |
| Transfer timeout rate | Median rate of transfer timeouts decreases by 100% (effectively eliminated) for FlashFlow at all three load levels, versus 5%, 10%, 23% timeout rates for TorFlow at 100%, 115%, 130% load | Same Shadow simulation |
| Throughput scaling under added load | Increasing client load by 15%/30% increases median Tor network throughput by 15%/29% under FlashFlow weights but only 12%/18% under TorFlow weights | Same Shadow simulation |

### Parameters
- Excess capacity factor f = g(1+ε2)/(1−ε1); used value f = 2.84 for the July 2019 simulation, derived from g = 2.25, ε1 = 0.20, ε2 = 0.05.
- Number of measurement sockets s = 160 (value that maximized throughput on the slowest lab host; determined empirically, range not stated).
- Capacity-estimate multiplier g = 2.25 (smallest g found sufficient for accuracy in the paper's own tuning experiments).
- Measurement duration t = 30 seconds (chosen as, in the authors' words, a reasonable balance of time-to-result versus accuracy).
- Error-bound parameters ε1 = 0.20, ε2 = 0.05.
- Background-traffic ratio r: recommended value 0.25; range tested 0.1-0.5 in the client-background-traffic experiment.
- Measurement period p = 24 hours.
- Response-check probability p (fraction of returned cells verified byte-for-byte): a design variable, no single numeric default stated in the extracted text.
- Measurement team capacity in the simulation study: 3 measurers, 1 Gbit/s each (3 Gbit/s total).
- New-relay initial capacity estimate: 75th-percentile advertised bandwidth among all relays over the preceding month (51 Mbit/s in the July 2019 dataset).

### Stated limitations
The authors state a malicious relay controlling multiple IP addresses on one physical machine can be measured separately at different times and obtain a capacity estimate equal to the shared machine's full capacity for each of its aliases, a Sybil-style limitation FlashFlow shares with TorFlow; their proposed mitigation is to measure suspected co-resident relays simultaneously and average the result, not yet built into the described system. A second stated limitation: because measurement slots are short (30 seconds), FlashFlow may capture a host's burst throughput rather than its sustainable capacity where an ISP or hosting provider throttles sustained rates below burst rates; the authors argue the median of separately scheduled measurements from different BW Auths mitigates this when the burst is due to shared-resource congestion, and that a rate limit applied faster than 15 seconds would still be caught. The threat model explicitly excludes an adversary that controls an autonomous-system-level network position, an adversary that runs a Sybil attack, and an adversary that can change its relay's capacity quickly; the security analysis is stated to hold only under an honest majority of BW Auths (and, transitively, of Directory Authorities that each trust their own BW Auth). The authors state FlashFlow measures capacity, not whether a relay actually forwards real client traffic, and note a relay could send little to no client traffic on non-measurement circuits while reporting accurate self-measured capacity; they call this an additional limitation shared with TorFlow and leave detecting such misbehavior as future work. Future work sections list the unresolved problem of detecting co-resident relays automatically (by IP address or autonomous-system-number heuristics) and combining FlashFlow's secure capacity floor with additional, insecure dynamic measurements (per-relay CPU or network utilization) to further refine weights without reopening the inflation vulnerability.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
FlashFlow requires the same Directory Authority (DirAuth) and Bandwidth Authority (BW Auth) infrastructure Tor already runs: DirAuths distribute the coordinator's public key in the network consensus, and a majority of DirAuths (and, in the paper's recommended configuration, their associated BW Auths) must be honest for the security bound to hold. It requires the BW Auths to hold sufficiently synchronized clocks to coordinate a shared, secret measurement schedule generated from a jointly produced random seed (the paper points to Tor's existing secure-randomness protocol as the source of that seed). It requires the measurement team's aggregate bandwidth capacity to exceed the highest capacity among target relays by the factor f = g(1+ε2)/(1−ε1), meaning the rest of the system must provision and fund measurer bandwidth (3 Gbit/s per team in the deployed-scale simulation) as an ongoing operational cost, separate from relay bandwidth. It requires the target relay to run modified Tor software able to accept authenticated measurement connections and to be reachable simultaneously by the number of measurers a given test allocates. It requires an existing weight-consumption mechanism — Tor's v3bw file format and consensus-voting process — to accept FlashFlow's capacity and weight outputs unchanged, since FlashFlow only replaces how a BW Auth produces those numbers, not how DirAuths use them.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus. Against the specific claim it is designed to supersede: the paper's own related-work section cites PeerFlow's demonstrated 177x weight-inflation attack against TorFlow and PeerFlow's own analytic self-inflation bound of 4.5x for its recommended parameters, both of which FlashFlow's inflation bound of 1.33x is measured against directly in Table II of the source; this is the authors' own comparison, not a disagreement between independent measurements of the same system.

### References worth retrieving
- **Foundational**: Tor project. "TorFlow" [28] — the currently deployed system FlashFlow replaces; described in the paper's Background section rather than cited as a separate retrievable paper.
- **Competing**: PeerFlow, cited as reference [23] — reports the 177x TorFlow weight-inflation attack and its own analytic inflation bound of 4.5x under recommended parameters and 2/τ in general (τ = trusted relay-weight fraction); produces capacity lower bounds via peer-reported byte counts, needs 14+ days to measure the largest 96.8% of relays.
- **Competing**: Snader, Borisov. EigenSpeed peer-measurement system, cited as reference [32], plus a demonstrated attack achieving 21.5x weight inflation with 20% trusted relays (by number or weight), and separately a "targeted liar attack" reaching 7.4-28.1x depending on trusted-relay fraction.
- **Competing**: Reference [33], Snader and Borisov — a simpler median-of-pairwise-speed variant of EigenSpeed, stated to be vulnerable to a Sybil attack because it uses an unweighted median.
- **Competing**: Reference [9], "SmarTor" — decentralizes BW Auth operation via blockchain and trusted execution environments but keeps TorFlow's file-download measurement technique, so it is stated to remain vulnerable to the same bandwidth-inflation attacks as TorFlow.
- **Competing**: Reference [25], "Simple Bandwidth Scanner" — an easier-to-maintain reimplementation producing the same results as TorFlow, addressing none of its security weaknesses.
- **Competing**: Reference [13], "TightRope" — assumes capacity weights already exist and instead optimizes path selection for load balancing using differential privacy over current relay load.
- **Competing**: Reference [36], Wang et al. — client-side lightweight active latency measurement to detect and avoid congested relays, an alternative mechanism to server-side capacity measurement.
- **Attack**: References [10, 12, 23, 34] — collectively cited as prior work demonstrating TorFlow's self-report and weight-inflation vulnerabilities; [34] and [23] specifically demonstrate 89x and 177x inflation attacks respectively.

### Verbatim extracts
- "FlashFlow limits a malicious relay to obtaining a capacity estimate at most 1.33 times its true capacity."
- "we find that FlashFlow measures relay capacity with ≥89% accuracy 95% of the time."
- "FlashFlow can measure the entire Tor network in less than 5 hours using 3 measurers with 1 Gbit/s of bandwidth each."
- "network weight error decreases by 86%."
- "the median rate of transfer timeouts decreases by 100%."
- "an adversary that has access to multiple IP addresses on the same machine can surreptitiously run multiple relays."
- "FlashFlow is designed to measure Tor capacity and not to detect if client traffic is actually relayed."
- "We require that a majority of BW Auths are honest."

## [TRAUTWEIN-ARXIV-26] Large-Scale Measurement of NAT Traversal for the Decentralized Web: A Case Study of DCUtR in IPFS

**Citation:** Dennis Trautwein, Cornelius Ihle, Moritz Schubotz, Corinna Breitinger, Bela Gipp. "Large-Scale Measurement of NAT Traversal for the Decentralized Web: A Case Study of DCUtR in IPFS." ACM Internet Measurement Conference (IMC), 2026. DOI 10.1145/3777912.3809138 (also arXiv:2604.12484; an earlier four-author preprint of the same underlying study is arXiv:2510.27500).
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.12484
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.12484
**Domain:** L

### What it does
DCUtR (Direct Connection Upgrade through Relay) upgrades an already-established relayed connection between two libp2p peers behind Network Address Translators (NATs) to a direct connection, without a centralized STUN/TURN/signaling server. It runs over three precursor libp2p protocols: Identify (each peer learns its own externally observed address from a connected peer, replacing a separate STUN lookup), AutoNAT (a peer asks others to dial back its advertised address to learn whether it is publicly reachable), and Circuit v2 (a private peer holds a bounded, time- and data-capped reservation at a relay, so any public peer can serve as a relay without unbounded resource exposure — this is the mechanism VYZOVITIS-SPECS-23 specifies). One peer (the initiator, which accepted the relayed connection) first attempts Connection Reversal: if the other peer (the listener) appears publicly reachable from Identify data, the initiator dials it directly, skipping hole punching entirely. If that fails or the listener is private, the initiator sends a CONNECT message with its candidate addresses over the relay, measures the relayed round-trip time (RTT), and sends a SYNC message; the initiator then waits half the measured RTT before dialing while the listener dials immediately upon receiving SYNC, aiming for near-simultaneous packet arrival at both NATs so each side's outbound packet opens a NAT mapping before the peer's inbound packet arrives. The coordination phase exchanges under 500 bytes per direction over two round trips through the relay; if the first synchronized attempt fails, synchronization and dialing are retried up to two more times. DCUtR is shipped as a default component of go-libp2p, rust-libp2p, and js-libp2p, so it runs automatically in every application built on those stacks, including IPFS (InterPlanetary File System) and Ethereum nodes.

### Measured results
| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| Conditional hole-punch success rate: 70% ± 7.1% | 6.25 million hole-punch results across 212 API keys / 148 sign-ups, measurement campaign December 1, 2022 – January 1, 2023; figure is a linear fit across per-network daily success rates on the subset (4.43 million of 6.25 million results, 70.9%) unambiguously assignable to a single client network, filtered to networks contributing over 1,000 data points, no pre-existing port mapping, outcome SUCCESS or FAILED only |
| This 70% rate is conditional on relay reservation (Circuit v2) and public-address discovery (Identify) already having succeeded, which themselves fail for approximately 29% of attempts | Same campaign; the 29% figure covers data points excluded from the network-identification step because no unambiguous single-network association could be made |
| TCP and QUIC hole-punch success rates are statistically indistinguishable at approximately 70% each, when hole punching is restricted to a single transport by a server-assigned "protocol filter" | Same campaign; when transport is unrestricted, roughly 80% of resulting connections use QUIC, attributed to QUIC's lower connection-establishment latency rather than to a hole-punch-success difference |
| 97.6% of successful hole punches complete on the first of up to three attempts; 1.8% on the second; 0.6% on the third | Sample sizes 1,200,947 / 21,612 / 7,366 successful hole punches respectively, same campaign |
| Success is largely independent of relay round-trip time and of the relay's fractional position along the path between client and remote peer (binned in 5% increments) | Same campaign; failed attempts show slightly higher RTTs than successful ones (weak negative correlation), but the two outcome-conditioned RTT cumulative distribution functions remain closely aligned (sample sizes 897,747 successes / 684,376 failures) |
| Direct-path RTT after a successful hole punch: 50% of peers see it drop to 70% or less of the pre-hole-punch relayed RTT; approximately 10% of peers see a higher RTT after hole punching; approximately 90% see a reduction | Same campaign, computed over all successful hole punches with both relayed and direct RTT recorded |
| Connection Reversal effectiveness: a substantially higher share of CONNECTION_REVERSED outcomes occurs when the client reports an active port mapping (e.g., via UPnP or PMP) than when it does not | Same campaign; port-mapping status is self-reported by the 212 volunteer clients, whose network configurations the authors state may not represent the broader population |
| Over 90% of relay-mediated RTT measurements (client to remote peer via relay) show a standard deviation under half the mean RTT | Same campaign, each RTT measurement an aggregate of up to ten ping samples, split into three scenarios (client→relay, client→remote via relay, client→remote direct after success) |
| 859 distinct client networks and 86,769 distinct remote-peer networks identified; clients deployed from 39 countries, hole-punched remote peers in 167 countries; over 60% of clients operated from a single network throughout the study, one highly mobile client from 28 distinct networks | Same campaign; network identity inferred from public IP address, or from unchanged private-IP-address set within the same Autonomous System when the public IP changes |
| Prior independent NAT-traversal success-rate measurements: 64% of peers behind a NAT/firewall with hole punching expected to work, over 80% of attempts between such peers succeeding (Halkes et al., 2011); 88% average TCP-connection-establishment success rate with NATs in the wild (Guha and Francis, cited via this paper's related-work discussion) | Halkes et al. dataset age 2011, fewer than 2,000 peers; Guha and Francis figure drawn from measurements of 93 home NATs, cited by this paper as the only comparable prior "in the wild" success-rate measurement |

### Parameters
- DCUtR retry count: initial synchronized attempt plus 2 retries (3 total), each retrying both synchronization and synchronized dialing
- Coordination-phase message size: fewer than 500 bytes per direction over the relay
- Wait time before dialing after SYNC: half the measured relayed RTT (T_wait = 1/2 · RTT_relayed), a fixed synchronization strategy in the deployed protocol; the paper's own §7.2 proposes but does not deploy a refined formula, T_wait = 1/2(RTT_Listener-Initiator + RTT_Listener-NAT − RTT_Initiator-NAT)
- Hole-punch stream open timeout: 15 seconds (client reports NO_STREAM if the /libp2p/dcutr stream is not opened within this window)
- Network-inclusion threshold for the H1 success-rate analysis: client must have contributed more than 1,000 data points from a given network
- Default Hop Limit used in a birthday-paradox port-collision proposal (§7.1, proposed not deployed): 256 or 2,048 ports probed/opened, yielding respectively a proposed 64% or 99.9% success probability against one Endpoint-Dependent-Mapping (EDM) NAT and 0.01% when both peers are behind EDM NATs (source: Anderson 2020, cited, not independently measured by this paper)
- Endpoint-Dependent-Mapping NAT prevalence used to project the birthday-paradox improvement: approximately 11% of peers (Halkes et al. 2011, cited, not measured here); projected mixed EDM/EIM combination rate approximately 19.6%, both-EDM combination rate approximately 1.2%, yielding a projected overall DCUtR success-rate improvement of 12.5% if the birthday-paradox technique achieves 64% success on the mixed-combination subset — this projection is explicitly derived from the cited 2011 figures, not from this paper's own campaign

### Stated limitations
Client sampling is drawn from volunteers in the IPFS and libp2p communities, a group the authors state is likely more technically proficient and on more stable networks than the general P2P user base, which may overestimate the measured success rate. The honeypot discovery method only finds NATed peers reachable through a relayed connection, systematically excluding peers behind NATs or firewalls restrictive enough to block even relayed connections, which the authors state may inflate the observed success rate. The measurement observes only the outcome (success or failure) of a hole punch, not the internal NAT mapping/filtering behavior, so individual failures cannot be attributed to a specific NAT type (Cone, Symmetric, or Carrier-Grade NAT specifically); this is stated as a direction for future work. The reported 70% figure characterizes only the hole-punching stage conditional on relay reservation and address discovery already succeeding; the unconditional end-to-end success rate from scratch is lower once the roughly 29% prerequisite-stage failure rate is included. The Connection Reversal analysis (H4) is based on port-mapping self-reports from the 212 volunteer clients only, whose configurations the authors state may not be representative. The authors state the dataset cannot distinguish a single NAT layer from a Carrier-Grade NAT (an additional NAT layer some ISPs insert), because both classify identically under the outcome-only measurement.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
DCUtR requires that a relayed connection through a Circuit v2 relay already exists between the two peers before hole punching begins, so it depends on Circuit v2's own reservation and connection-establishment succeeding first (VYZOVITIS-SPECS-23); this paper's 29% prerequisite-failure figure is exactly the rate at which that dependency is not met. It requires the underlying transport to support both the initiator and listener attempting near-simultaneous outbound connection attempts to each other's advertised address (TCP simultaneous open, or QUIC's dummy-UDP-packet NAT-state priming), so a transport without a simultaneous-open-equivalent cannot use this synchronization mechanism as specified. It requires each peer to expose its externally observed address through Identify, so a peer that cannot establish even one connection to obtain this observation (i.e., is fully unreachable, not merely NATed) cannot participate. The RTT-based synchronization assumes approximately symmetric one-way network delay between the two peers' paths to each other; the paper states that when path asymmetry is significant, the synchronization margin shrinks, which the authors offer as a partial explanation for part of the residual approximately 30% failure rate. During the CONNECT exchange both peers disclose their public IP address and port to whichever peer initiates the exchange, and the paper states this creates a route for systematic address collection via repeated probing, plus a trust boundary at the relay, which can observe and correlate both parties' addresses and connection timing over time.

### Contradicts
This paper's own H3b result contradicts the commonly stated belief, which the paper itself attributes to the field's conventional understanding, that "UDP hole punching is easier than TCP" — DCUtR shows statistically indistinguishable success rates for TCP and QUIC (both approximately 70%), which the authors attribute to DCUtR's RTT-based synchronization removing the timing unpredictability that ordinarily disadvantages TCP hole punching. No other paper in this corpus reports a conflicting DCUtR-specific measurement as of this batch.

## [TRAUTWEIN-INFOCOM-24] IPFS in the Fast Lane: Accelerating Record Storage with Optimistic Provide

**Citation:** Dennis Trautwein, Yiluo Wei, Yiannis Psaras, Moritz Schubotz, Ignacio Castro, Bela Gipp, Gareth Tyson. "IPFS in the Fast Lane: Accelerating Record Storage with Optimistic Provide." IEEE INFOCOM, 2024. DOI 10.1109/INFOCOM52122.2024.10621404.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://gipplab.uni-goettingen.de/wp-content/papercite-data/pdf/trautwein2024.pdf
**Source URL:** https://gipplab.uni-goettingen.de/wp-content/papercite-data/pdf/trautwein2024.pdf
**Domain:** A+J

### What it does
Optimistic Provide shortens the time a Kademlia-based InterPlanetary File System (IPFS) node takes to store a provider record (a PUT operation: publishing that this node holds a given piece of content) by ending the record-placement process as soon as it is statistically confident it has found the right peers, instead of waiting for every peer contacted to confirm. The unmodified (classic) PUT operation runs in two phases: a DHT walk that queries progressively closer peers until the three currently-closest-known peers have all responded, and a follow-up phase that pushes the record to the 20 peers closest to the target key found during the walk. The paper's own measurement (section III) finds the DHT walk consumes over 90% of total PUT latency in most cases, because the walk's own termination rule waits for confirmation from the three closest known peers even after the eventual 20 recipients have already been discovered; an unreachable peer among those three stalls the whole walk while the algorithm backtracks to more distant peers (a behavior the paper calls DHT Walk backtracking). Optimistic Provide replaces this rule with three changes. First, it computes, using an estimate of the total DHT population size, a maximum XOR distance from the target key such that any peer discovered inside that distance is a member of the true closest-20 set with probability p_individual; a peer discovered within that distance is stored to immediately, without waiting for the walk to finish. Second, it computes a second maximum average distance for the currently-known set of 20 closest peers such that, with probability p_set, that set already equals the true closest-20 set; once the known set's average distance falls under that threshold, the walk terminates early instead of waiting for the three-closest-peer confirmation. Third, since ending the walk early skips backtracking and can leave a slow or unreachable peer among the 20 recipients in the follow-up phase, the follow-up phase itself returns control to the caller once k' of the 20 contacted peers have responded (k'=5 chosen in this paper's evaluation, tunable), while the remaining queries continue asynchronously in the background rather than being canceled. The distance thresholds behind steps one and two require a live estimate of the total number of peers in the DHT; the paper derives this from Kademlia's own XOR-distance order statistics (the expected distance to the i-th-closest peer among N total peers is 1/(N+1) times i, so measuring several order-statistic distances and fitting a line through the origin yields an estimate of N), sampled for free from the routing-table-refresh lookups every node already performs, corrected for a keyspace-density bias that would otherwise skew the estimate.

### Measured results

| Result | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Baseline PUT latency percentiles, IPFS, classic algorithm (done strategy: wait for all 20 follow-up responses) | 50th 6.3 s, 90th 20.6 s, 95th 49.8 s | Two servers in central Europe, two-day measurement window; classic sample size 8,502 |
| Baseline PUT latency, first measurement (walk + follow-up breakdown) | 8,503 measurements | One host in eu-central-1 AWS region, 2023-06-06 to 2023-06-07; DHT walk accounts for over 90% of total latency in the majority of cases |
| Optimal (theoretical minimum) DHT walk termination | Terminates several seconds earlier than the actual walk in most cases; only 4.3% of PUT operations experience no delay at all between discovering all 20 closest peers and the follow-up phase | Same eu-central-1 measurement |
| Median time to discover final PUT recipients (before follow-up phase begins) | 1.3 s | Same measurement, cited as motivation for the design in section IV |
| PUT latency, IPFS, Optimistic Provide vs. classic (done strategy) | 50th: 5.1 s (vs 6.3 s classic), 90th: 8.7 s (vs 20.6 s), 95th: 15.4 s (vs 49.8 s); speed-ups 1.2x/2.3x/3.2x | Two servers in central Europe, two-day window; optimistic sample size 11,964, classic 8,502 |
| PUT latency, IPFS, Optimistic Provide (return strategy, k'=5) vs. classic (return strategy, 15th of 20 responses) | 50th: 0.51 s (vs 5.8 s classic), 90th: 0.80 s (vs 15.8 s), 95th: 0.92 s (vs 43.0 s); speed-ups 11.3x/19.7x/46.7x | Same setup |

### Parameters
- p_individual (probability threshold for immediately accepting a single discovered peer as a member of the closest-20 set): chosen as 0.9 in evaluation; stated as freely tunable.
- p_set (probability threshold for accepting the current known 20-closest-peer set as the true closest-20 set, computed via the expected distance of the hypothetical 10.5th-closest peer): chosen as 0.9 in evaluation; stated as tunable.
- k' (number of the 20 follow-up-phase peers whose responses are awaited before returning control to the caller, remaining queries continuing asynchronously): chosen as 5, based on a cited prior study finding that lowering k to 15 in classic IPFS record replication has negligible impact on availability; stated as configurable.
- Network size estimation rolling window t_window: 2 hours.
- Network size estimation minimum/maximum sample counts S_min / S_max: 16 / 192 lookups (S_min corresponds to one full routing-table refresh; S_max corresponds to one full refresh every 10 minutes for 2 hours); both stated as tunable and affecting estimation accuracy.
- Kademlia identifier length L: 256 bits (used in the order-statistic-based network-size derivation).
- Maximum bucket level k_max for the bias-correction weighting function: 20 for IPFS.
- Routing-table refresh depth in the deployed Kubo and Lotus clients: the first 16 of 256 possible buckets, each refresh issuing 16 lookups.
- DHT walk timeout (both approaches, regional experiment): 3 minutes.
- Kubo (IPFS reference implementation) version supporting Optimistic Provide: v0.20.0 and later.

### Stated limitations
The authors state as future work an investigation of how severe network conditions — network partitioning, high churn, and Sybil attacks — affect Optimistic Provide and its component mechanisms; none of these conditions are evaluated in this paper. They state as future work a deeper investigation into the cause of the observed difference in RPC success-rate variation between the IPFS and Filecoin networks, which this paper does not explain. The network-size estimation method systematically underestimates true network size (6.0% for IPFS, 13.5% for Filecoin, both relative to a full-crawl baseline) because it reuses routing-table-refresh lookups that are biased toward the requesting peer's local keyspace neighborhood and excludes peers made undialable by the same backtracking behavior the paper's mechanism is designed around; the authors state this underestimate does not measurably harm PUT performance in their results but note that a deployment needing more accurate absolute counts would need a separately-derived scaling factor, since the underestimate is consistent across measurement points rather than fully corrected. The full network-size crawl used as the accuracy baseline is itself described only as covering the peers the crawler could find and dial, not as a verified ground truth; the paper treats it as the best available comparison rather than an exact count.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Every participating peer must implement the same threshold-based termination logic to be optimistically stored to during another peer's DHT walk, which the paper achieves by upstreaming the change into the shared go-libp2p-kad-dht implementation used by both the IPFS reference client Kubo and the Filecoin reference client Lotus; the paper states full backward compatibility is maintained, meaning a peer without the update still participates correctly in a walk initiated by an updated peer, but does not state what performance a walk initiated by an updated peer against entirely non-updated peers would achieve. Every peer must independently estimate the live network size to compute the distance thresholds; this estimate is derived only from data the peer's own routing-table-refresh queries already produce, so a peer skipping refreshes or refreshing fewer than the S_min=16 lookups per rolling 2-hour window operates on state accuracy the paper does not evaluate. Both the p_individual and p_set thresholds assume DHT peer identifiers are uniformly randomly distributed across the identifier space (stated explicitly in section IV-B); a system where identifiers cluster non-uniformly (through adversarial identifier selection or a non-uniform assignment scheme) would compute unreliable proximity thresholds, and the paper's stated future work on Sybil-attack impact has not yet examined this. Reducing k' below 20 in the follow-up phase requires accepting that a record's full 20-way replication is asynchronous rather than confirmed at return time; a caller that needs the paper's own PUT operation to guarantee replication before returning must use the done strategy, whose latency the paper measures separately and which is markedly slower.

### Contradicts
None found. This paper's own comparison to Trautwein et al.'s earlier IPFS measurement study (cited as reference [5], "Design and evaluation of IPFS: a storage layer for the decentralized web") is presented as complementary, not contradictory: this paper describes that earlier study as reporting GET performance as "already satisfactory" while this paper's contribution addresses PUT latency specifically. That earlier paper is the source of the 112-second 90th-percentile content-storing latency figure cited secondhand in ZHANG-FC-23 in this corpus; ZHANG-FC-23 should be checked against the original IPFS measurement paper directly rather than against this Optimistic Provide paper, which measures a modified protocol and different latency figures (6.3-49.8 s baseline).

## [TRAUTWEIN-SIGCOMM-22] Design and Evaluation of IPFS: A Storage Layer for the Decentralized Web

**Citation:** Dennis Trautwein, Aravindh Raman, Gareth Tyson, Ignacio Castro, Will Scott, Moritz Schubotz, Bela Gipp, Yiannis Psaras. "Design and Evaluation of IPFS: A Storage Layer for the Decentralized Web." ACM SIGCOMM, 2022. Pages not stated in retrieved text. DOI 10.1145/3544216.3544232.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://doi.org/10.1145/3544216.3544232
**Source URL:** https://doi.org/10.1145/3544216.3544232
**Domain:** C+J

### What it does
The InterPlanetary File System (IPFS) locates and retrieves content by its cryptographic hash rather than by its storage location, so a requester can verify what it receives without trusting who served it. IPFS builds a Content Identifier (CID) for each piece of content: a self-describing structure that states the encoding, the hash function used (default SHA2-256), and the hash digest itself. On import, content is split into chunks (default 256 kB), each chunk gets its own CID, and IPFS links the chunks into a Merkle Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) — a tree-like hash structure that allows a node to have multiple parents, which lets identical chunks shared across files be stored once. To publish content, a node computes a provider record mapping the CID to its own PeerID (the hash of its public key) and stores that record on the k = 20 peers whose PeerIDs are numerically closest to the CID's hash under the XOR distance, using the Kademlia distributed hash table (DHT) — a peer-to-peer index that routes lookups toward the peer whose identifier is closest to the target key. Provider records expire after 24 hours by default and are republished every 12 hours so churned-out peers get replaced. To retrieve content, a requester first asks its already-connected neighbors using the Bitswap block-exchange protocol (a 1-second opportunistic timeout), and only then performs two sequential Kademlia lookups over the DHT: one to map the CID to a hosting PeerID (a "DHT walk," forwarding each request to α = 3 closest-known peers per round), and a second to map that PeerID to a network address (a Multiaddress). It then connects to that address and fetches the content over Bitswap. IPFS distinguishes DHT Server peers (publicly reachable, store and serve records) from DHT Client peers (behind NAT, only request) using AutoNAT: a new peer starts as a client, asks other peers to dial it back, and upgrades to server status once three peers succeed in connecting to it. Anyone that retrieves content can optionally begin serving it themselves by publishing their own provider record for the same CID. IPFS gateways bridge the peer-to-peer network to plain HTTP: a gateway runs a DHT Server node alongside an nginx web server with a Least-Recently-Used (LRU) cache, so a browser with no IPFS software can fetch content via a normal GET request.

### Measured results

| Measurement | Value | Conditions |

| Peer reachability | 253,198 (54.5%) reachable at least once; 211,105 (45.5%) never reachable | same crawl dataset |
| Geographic concentration of peers | US 28.5%, China 24.2%, France 8.3%, Taiwan 7.2%, South Korea 6.7% | same crawl dataset, "Detailed Analysis" time window |
| Reliable peers (>90% uptime) | 1.4% (2,747 peers); largest single country (US) holds 0.3% of all peers | same crawl dataset |

California, Frankfurt, São Paulo), each running go-ipfs v0.10.0 as a DHT Server, 3,281 total publication operations across regions, each publishing a fresh 0.5 MB object |

### Parameters
- CID chunk size: default 256 kB, used to split imported content before building the Merkle DAG.
- Hash function for CIDs: default SHA2-256, 32-byte digest.
- DHT key space: 256-bit, using SHA256 hashes of PeerIDs and CIDs (the paper states this replaces the original Kademlia 160-bit SHA1 key space, citing anticipated advances in deliberate hash collisions).
- Kademlia bucket structure: i = 256 buckets of k = 20 nodes each.
- Transport for DHT operations: TCP and QUIC, not UDP, cited as a deliberate deviation from the original Kademlia specification made "to make connection management in the implementation more straightforward."
- Provider-record replication factor: k = 20 closest peers by XOR distance, described as a practitioner-chosen compromise between replication overhead and record loss under churn, also referencing a recommendation in the original Kademlia paper.
- Provider-record republish interval: 12 hours (default).
- Provider-record expiry interval: 24 hours (default).
- DHT lookup parallelism (α): 3 peers queried per round during a DHT walk, per the original Kademlia specification.
- AutoNAT server-upgrade threshold: 3 successful inbound connection attempts from other peers.
- Address book size: up to 900 recently seen peers cached locally per node, to skip repeated peer-record lookups.
- Bitswap opportunistic-discovery timeout before falling back to the DHT: 1 second.
- Performance-benchmark object size: 0.5 MB, fixed for every publication/retrieval measurement round.
- Performance-benchmark deployment: 6 AWS t2.small virtual machines, one per region (Bahrain, Sydney, Cape Town, N. California, Frankfurt, São Paulo), each running go-ipfs v0.10.0.

### Stated limitations
The overall publication and retrieval delay measurements are described by the authors as the closest achievable to a controlled experiment on the public IPFS network, but not a true controlled experiment, because peer churn, CPU load, and traffic load on the rest of the network cannot be replicated in a simulation and are outside the authors' control. The performance benchmark used only a fixed 0.5 MB object size; the authors state that content-exchange duration depends on the amount of data exchanged, so retrieval-duration figures at other object sizes are not established by this paper. The stretch metric approximates the equivalent HTTPS retrieval time by subtracting the DHT discovery step from the measured IPFS time, rather than performing an independent HTTPS measurement. Retrieval measurements were run from AWS data centers, and the authors state explicitly that last-mile performance experienced by home users will differ. The authors state they have not evaluated IPFS's resilience or its capacity to withstand information attacks such as censorship, and describe this as future work. Moderation and misuse on IPFS, including a reported instance of the Storm botnet operating over the network, had not been investigated at the time of writing; the authors state their initial monitoring found no abusive behavioral signals but call further investigation future work. The Hydra Boosters DHT-augmentation component was explicitly excluded from the study due to space constraints and what the authors describe as its limited adoption. Content-import latency (as opposed to provider-record publication latency) is stated as already covered by a separate cited paper and not reevaluated here.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Content retrieval requires a functioning Kademlia DHT populated with enough long-lived DHT Server peers to answer two sequential lookups (CID-to-PeerID, then PeerID-to-Multiaddress) inside the 24-hour provider-record expiry window; if fewer than k = 20 peers close to a CID remain reachable, the provider record for that CID can be lost. Any consumer of IPFS retrieval-latency figures needs to account for the mandatory 1-second Bitswap opportunistic-discovery timeout baked into every retrieval reported here, because the authors' experimental setup guaranteed a Bitswap miss on every trial. Nodes behind NAT cannot serve content as DHT Servers under the AutoNAT scheme described, so a deployment relying on those peers for storage capacity needs a separate hole-punching mechanism (the paper notes one was under development but not yet deployed) or third-party pinning services to host content on their behalf. The self-certifying CID scheme requires every consumer to independently recompute and check the content hash against the received CID; nothing in IPFS enforces this except that a mismatch is externally detectable. Because CIDs are immutable, any system built on top that needs mutable references must add a separate mapping layer (the IPNS scheme described maps a PeerID-derived CID to a signed pointer, itself requiring key management the paper does not detail here).

### Contradicts
The comparison in Related Work states that IPFS's median record-lookup latency (under 1 second for half of probes) contrasts with prior operational-DHT measurement studies of BitTorrent's Kademlia implementation reporting latencies exceeding a minute; the authors attribute this gap to excessive dead nodes and slower links in the earlier deployments rather than to a property of Kademlia itself, and this paper's own DHT still exhibits an 87.9%-of-delay DHT walk cost during publication, so the low-latency finding applies specifically to the two-hop retrieval walk, not to the 20-way publication RPC batch. No entry in this corpus reports a disagreeing IPFS-network-scale measurement (searched: no other IPFS deployment-measurement paper is in this batch).

### References worth retrieving
- Maymounkov, Mazières, "Kademlia: A peer-to-peer information system based on the XOR metric," IPTPS 2002 — foundational (already verified in this corpus per BRIEF.md §7)
- Wolchok, Halderman, "Crawling BitTorrent DHTs for Fun and Profit," WOOT 2010 — attack/critique (measured BitTorrent's Kademlia deployment showing lookup latencies exceeding a minute, the paper's own comparison point)
- Stutzbach, Rejaie, "Improving lookup performance over a widely-deployed DHT," INFOCOM 2006 — competing (independent Kademlia performance measurement and proposed fixes, cited as showing substantially worse performance than IPFS)
- Stutzbach, Rejaie, "Understanding Churn in Peer-to-Peer Networks," IMC 2006 — foundational (source of the long-session churn-correction methodology this paper's churn analysis reuses)
- Wang, Kangasharju, "Measuring large-scale distributed systems: case of BitTorrent Mainline DHT," P2P 2013 — competing (independent operational-DHT measurement study, cited as reporting churn rates similar to this paper's findings but slower lookups)
- Raman, Joglekar, De Cristofaro, Sastry, Tyson, "Challenges in the decentralised web: The mastodon case," IMC 2019 — competing (federated, non-content-addressed decentralization architecture used as the paper's cloud-hosting-share comparison point, 6% Amazon-only for Mastodon versus <2.3% any-cloud for IPFS)

## [TYAGI-EUROCRYPT-22] A Fast and Simple Partially Oblivious PRF, with Applications
**Citation:** Nirvan Tyagi, Sofía Celi, Thomas Ristenpart, Nick Sullivan, Stefano Tessaro, Christopher A. Wood. "A Fast and Simple Partially Oblivious PRF, with Applications." EUROCRYPT, 2022. DOI 10.1007/978-3-031-07085-3_23.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://eprint.iacr.org/2021/864.pdf
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2021/864.pdf
**Domain:** I

### What it does
A partially oblivious pseudorandom function (POPRF) lets a client obtain a keyed function output on a private input `x` bound to a public input `t` (called a tag), while the server that holds the key learns neither `x` nor which output resulted from which request. "Partially oblivious" distinguishes the tag `t`, visible to both parties, from `x`, hidden from the server. The paper's construction, 3HashSDHI, computes `Ev(sk, t, x) = H2(x, H1(x)^(1/(sk+H2'(t))))`, combining the 2HashDH oblivious pseudorandom function (OPRF) of Jarecki, Kiayias, and Krawczyk (JARECKI-ASIACRYPT-14) with the Dodis-Yampolskiy pseudorandom function. To request an evaluation, the client blinds its input as `B = H1(x)^r` for random `r`, sends `B` and the public tag `t`; the server returns `B' = B^(1/(sk+H2'(t)))`; the client unblinds by computing `(B')^(1/r)` and finishing with `H2`. The server additionally produces a Chaum-Pedersen non-interactive zero-knowledge (NIZK) proof of discrete-log equality so the client can verify the response was computed under the claimed public key, without which a malicious server could return arbitrary values undetected. Security is proved in the random oracle model by reduction to a new assumption, one-more gap strong Diffie-Hellman inversion, itself shown implied by the q-discrete-log assumption in the algebraic group model.

Applied to Privacy Pass token issuance, binding a token to a public tag `t` (for example a coarse timestamp such as the current day, or a client autonomous system number) lets a server enforce that a client's tokens are scoped to that tag without needing per-scope secret keys or client-verified key rotation.

### Measured results
All measurements from a Go implementation using the CIRCL cryptographic library, ristretto255 group (bn256 curve for the pairing-based Pythia baseline), on a 2.6 GHz 6-core Intel Core i7 with 32 GB RAM, macOS 10.15.7, averaged over 1000 measurements per operation, input size L fixed at 16 bytes, tag size T varied at 1, 8, and 64 bytes.

| Scheme | T (bytes) | KeyGen (µs) | KeyVerify (µs) | Req (µs) | BlindEv (µs) | Finalize (µs) | Full Ev (µs) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2HashDH | 1 | 0 | 0 | 73 | 222 | 392 | 77 |
| 2HashDH | 64 | 0 | 0 | 84 | 256 | 447 | 89 |
| 3HashSDHI | 1 | 0 | 0 | 85 | 369 | 527 | 125 |
| 3HashSDHI | 64 | 0 | 0 | 75 | 328 | 471 | 110 |
| Pythia | 1 | 168 | 0 | 849 | 4068 | 6070 | 2871 |
| Pythia | 64 | 171 | 0 | 809 | 3922 | 5849 | 2768 |
| ABVOPRF | 1 | 294 | 292 | 74 | 517 | 684 | 370 |
| ABVOPRF | 64 | 15053 | 19196 | 80 | 15305 | 19702 | 15163 |

Excluding precomputable operations (the KeyGen/KeyVerify columns above), 3HashSDHI Finalize cost at T=64 bytes is 472 µs against 447 µs for 2HashDH (approximately 25% relative overhead, per the paper's own framing including all operations), 5843 µs for Pythia, and 19721 µs for ABVOPRF — an order of magnitude above 3HashSDHI at large tag size, attributed by the authors to ABVOPRF's tag-length-linear proof cost.

### Parameters
- Group: ristretto255 for 2HashDH, 3HashSDHI, ABVOPRF; bn256 pairing-friendly curve for Pythia.
- Input size L: fixed at 16 bytes across all measurements.
- Tag size T: 1, 8, 64 bytes, the tested range.
- Averaging: 1000 measurements per operation, on the stated single-machine hardware.

### Stated limitations
3HashSDHI does not support key rotation: distributing per-tag rotation tokens analogous to Pythia's compact rotation token trivially reveals both the old and new secret keys, because the tag hashes are publicly computable. The authors state finding a pairing-free POPRF that also supports key rotation is an open problem. The one-more gap strong Diffie-Hellman inversion assumption's tightness under the algebraic group model reduction is stated as open to further tightening. Binding a token to a public tag reduces the anonymity set of redemption to only the clients issued tokens under that same tag value, a property the authors state holds for the key-rotation alternative as well; the authors state that choosing how to use the tag "requires care and further work to identify best practices." Extending the construction to also carry a private metadata bit (indistinguishable-but-server-decodable, as in Kreuter et al., KREUTER-FC-22's antecedent construction) is left to future work; the authors state a randomized variant would likely be needed, since a deterministic pseudorandom function cannot achieve indistinguishability between private-metadata values.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Verification of a POPRF response requires the client to have the server's public key `pk` in advance and to run the Chaum-Pedersen zero-knowledge proof check on every response; without this check a malicious server can return an arbitrary value. Any protocol using tag-scoped tokens (for example a rate-limiting scheme selecting `t` as an autonomous-system number or time window) needs a mechanism, external to the POPRF itself, for client and server to agree on the tag value before the request — the POPRF does not negotiate or authenticate the tag. Because binding to a tag narrows the anonymity set to clients sharing that tag, any system composing this primitive with an unlinkability requirement must independently bound how coarse-grained the tag partition is; the paper does not supply that bound. The random-oracle-model proof requires hash functions `H1`, `H2` in the construction to be modeled as random oracles; a real deployment must instantiate them with cryptographic hash functions believed to behave as such.

### Contradicts
None found.

### References worth retrieving
- **JARECKI-ASIACRYPT-14** [JKK14] — already in this corpus; 2HashDH OPRF, foundational.
- **[JKX18]** Jarecki, Krawczyk, Xu, "OPAQUE: an asymmetric PAKE protocol secure against pre-computation attacks," EUROCRYPT 2018 — foundational, one of this paper's three target applications.
- **[DGS+18]** Davidson, Goldberg, Sullivan, Tankersley, Valsorda, "Privacy Pass: Bypassing Internet Challenges Anonymously," PoPETs 2018(3) — foundational, defines Privacy Pass and the hoarding/farming attack this paper addresses.
- **[ECS+15]** Everspaugh, Chatterjee, Scott, Juels, Ristenpart, "The Pythia PRF Service," USENIX Security 2015 — competing pairing-based construction, directly benchmarked against.
- **[HIJ+21]** Huang et al. (Facebook), "PrivateStats: De-Identified Authenticated Logging at Scale," 2021 — competing attribute-based VOPRF (ABVOPRF), directly benchmarked against.
- **KREUTER-FC-22** [KLOR20 in this bibliography, listed as CRYPTO 2020 "Anonymous tokens with private metadata bit"] — already in this corpus; competing construction for private-metadata tokens.
- **[SS21]** Silde, Strand, "Anonymous tokens with public metadata and applications to private contact tracing," ePrint 2021/203 — concurrent independent work describing the same 3HashSDHI-equivalent construction with an incomplete security analysis; superseded-by relationship is the reverse (this paper's proof supersedes SS21's incomplete one for the same construction).
- **[JKX21]** Jarecki, Krawczyk, Xu, "On the (in)security of the Diffie-Hellman oblivious PRF with multiplicative blinding," Public Key Cryptography 2021 — attack/critique, on multiplicative-blinding variants of 2HashDH-style OPRFs.
- **[TPY+19]** Thomas et al., "Protecting accounts from credential stuffing with password breach alerting," USENIX Security 2019 — foundational for the breach-alerting application discussed.

## [TYAGI-SOSP-17] Stadium: A Distributed Metadata-Private Messaging System
**Citation:** Nirvan Tyagi, Yossi Gilad, Derek Leung, Matei Zaharia, Nickolai Zeldovich. "Stadium: A Distributed Metadata-Private Messaging System." ACM SOSP, 2017. DOI 10.1145/3132747.3132783.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://people.csail.mit.edu/nickolai/papers/tyagi-stadium.pdf
**Source URL:** https://people.csail.mit.edu/nickolai/papers/tyagi-stadium.pdf
**Domain:** G

### What it does
Stadium delivers point-to-point messages while hiding metadata (which users communicate with which) from a network-level adversary, scaling the work of doing so across hundreds of independently operated, low-cost servers rather than concentrating it on a small trusted pair as Vuvuzela does. It bounds what the adversary learns using differential privacy: cover ("noise") traffic is added so that the observable traffic pattern for any two distinct communication patterns is statistically close, quantified by a privacy parameter epsilon (information leaked) and a failure probability delta. Servers are organized into "mixchains" — small ordered groups of servers, each belonging to a different, presumed non-colluding provider — and every message passes through one input mixchain and one output mixchain. Within a chain, each server permutes and re-encrypts (mixes) the batch of messages it receives using Bayer and Groth's verifiable shuffle protocol (a zero-knowledge proof that a claimed permutation and re-encryption were performed correctly), made non-interactive via the Fiat-Shamir heuristic and instantiated over the Curve25519 elliptic-curve group; this lets every other server in the chain — honest or not — check that the shuffle was executed correctly, without needing to trust the shuffling server itself. A message travels through seven processing phases per round: input, input-chain mixing, distribution (all-to-all exchange between input and output chains), output-chain mixing, an exchange step where messages are dropped at shared per-conversation "dead-drops" hosted by the output chain, and the reverse path back to the two conversing users, undoing each chain's permutation. Two users exchange messages only if they route to the same output chain and dead-drop, a restriction the paper states is required by its privacy analysis. Noise is generated in a distributed way (§8, not detailed in this extraction) so that no single server, honest or corrupt, needs to inject all the cover traffic Vuvuzela's two-server design requires. Verifiable processing lets a single honest server per chain detect corrupted or improperly mixed messages and abort or flag the round; the protocol's differential-privacy guarantee, and hence Stadium's metadata privacy, holds only if this per-chain honest-server condition is met.

|---|---|---|

### Parameters
| Parameter | Value used | Range tested |
|---|---|---|
| Chain length (ell) | 3, 6, 9 in the main latency/throughput benchmarks | 3 to 14 in the compromised-chain-probability analysis (Figure 8); 3 to 9 in the latency-vs-chain-length benchmark |
| Number of servers | 25, 50, 75, 100 measured directly; 200-800 extrapolated | up to 800 in the noise-requirement analysis (Figure 5, analytic) |

| Message batch load per server (chain-length experiment) | 100K, 300K, 500K messages/server | -- |

### Stated limitations
The paper explicitly states that, due to time and cost constraints, it did not evaluate configurations larger than 100 servers directly; figures beyond 100 servers are extrapolations that assume Stadium's observed near-linear latency scaling continues, obtained by proportionally halving per-server load and linearly interpolating. It states that individual servers lacked sufficient memory to support very large message batch sizes at small server counts, so small-server-count deployments could not be fully benchmarked, and the paper separately notes that small numbers of servers are impractical for deploying Stadium. The prototype does not support real client message input — server-side message generation is simulated by having each server generate its own share of "client" messages — and the implementation excludes verifiable decryption and has no fault tolerance. Stadium is explicitly not resistant to wide-scale denial-of-service: the paper states this follows unavoidably from its own assumption that an adversary can block traffic on any network link, though it guarantees that a denial-of-service attack does not compromise the privacy guarantee. Stadium's core security property (metadata-privacy through differential privacy) depends on every mixchain containing at least one honest server; the paper evaluates only the probability of this condition holding under a random-assignment policy and an assumed upper-bound adversarial-server fraction f, not a proof that any particular real-world deployment satisfies it. The paper assumes a public-key infrastructure already exists (server public keys known to users) and assumes two communicating users already share a secret key, citing Alpenhorn as an external candidate mechanism for establishing that shared secret rather than building one itself.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Stadium requires servers to be organized into mixchains such that servers within one chain belong to providers assumed unlikely to collude, and requires at least one server per chain to be honest and to follow the verifiable-shuffle protocol — the differential-privacy guarantee does not hold, and the paper does not claim it holds, if every server in some chain is adversarial. It requires two communicating users to independently select the same output chain and dead-drop for their messages to be exchanged, which the paper states is a restriction imposed directly by its privacy analysis, not an incidental implementation detail — any application layered on Stadium must supply or agree on this shared routing coordinate out of band. It requires a public-key infrastructure delivering authentic server public keys to users, and requires users to already hold a shared secret key with their communication partner before using Stadium — key establishment is out of scope and delegated to an external system (the paper names Alpenhorn). It requires standard cryptographic primitives under the random oracle model: public-key and symmetric encryption, key exchange, digital signatures, and hash functions. Chain length is a security-performance trade-off that must be set by the deployment: a longer chain lowers the probability that every server in some chain is adversarial (falling exponentially in chain length under the stated union-bound analysis) but raises per-message latency with a quadratic term from all-to-all proof verification within the chain, so any composed system choosing a chain length is trading measurable latency against a measurable compromise probability, not a free parameter.

### Contradicts
None found within this batch. The paper's own comparison figures for Vuvuzela (10 million users at 200 s latency, "more than nine minutes" for 30 million users) are drawn from Vuvuzela's own reported best-projected performance rather than an independent re-measurement by this paper's authors, which should be noted when this paper's comparative claims are cited as evidence about Vuvuzela's behavior specifically.

## [UNGER-SP-15] SoK: Secure Messaging
**Citation:** Nik Unger, Sergej Dechand, Joseph Bonneau, Sascha Fahl, Henning Perl, Ian Goldberg, Matthew Smith. "SoK: Secure Messaging." IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (S&P), 2015. DOI 10.1109/SP.2015.22.
**Retrieved:** full text
**Source URL:** https://www.ieee-security.org/TC/SP2015/papers-archived/6949a232.pdf
**Domain:** H

### What it does
This paper is a Systematization of Knowledge (SoK): it does not propose a new mechanism, and its contribution is an evaluation framework that decomposes secure messaging into three near-orthogonal problems and scores every known approach to each against a fixed set of properties, so a reader can compare mechanisms on a common basis rather than each paper's own claims. The three problems are trust establishment (verifying that a long-term cryptographic key is actually associated with the intended real-world party — for example, key directories, Trust-On-First-Use, or out-of-band fingerprint verification), conversation security (protecting message confidentiality, integrity, and authentication once trust is established — for example, static asymmetric encryption, Diffie-Hellman ratcheting, or deniable group key exchange), and transport privacy (hiding who is communicating with whom from network and server observers — for example, onion routing, Dining Cryptographer networks (DC-nets), broadcast, or Private Information Retrieval). For each problem the paper defines security/privacy properties, usability properties, and adoption properties, then rates every catalogued approach (and named example tool or protocol) against every property using a three-value scale (provides / partially provides / does not provide), assembled into three tables (Tables I, II, III). The threat model considers a local network adversary, a global network adversary (each active or passive), and service-provider operators as potential adversaries, all of whom are also assumed to be legitimate participants in the messaging system able to start conversations and send messages; endpoint compromise (malware, hardware attacks) is explicitly out of scope. Usability scoring is derived from expert cognitive walkthroughs of actual implementations against Nielsen's usability principles, not from user studies with human subjects.

### Measured results
This paper reports no quantitative measurements from an experiment, testbed, or implementation the authors ran. Its evaluation is a qualitative property-satisfaction rating (full / partial / none) assigned by the authors' own expert review to each catalogued protocol design, published as Tables I (trust establishment), II (conversation security), and III (transport privacy). No node counts, latencies, message sizes, or other quantities with stated experimental conditions appear; per the extraction rule that a figure without experimental conditions is not usable evidence, no numeric result from this paper is recorded here as measured fact. Where the paper does state comparative outcomes for named systems (for example, that a broadcast transport system, Bitmessage, uses proof-of-work or fees to limit spam), these are qualitative design descriptions the authors extracted from those systems' own specifications, not measurements this paper's authors performed.

### Parameters
Not applicable — this is a systematization/survey with a property taxonomy, not a mechanism with tunable parameters.

### Stated limitations
Endpoint security (malware and hardware attacks) is explicitly excluded from the threat model. The paper does not audit implementations for software exploits and assumes cryptographic primitives are correctly implemented, only penalizing a scheme if it lets end users misuse primitives in ways the design permits. Higher-level group-chat features — invitation mechanisms, removing users, chat-room moderation — are stated as out of scope because they operate above the secure-messaging protocol layer. The paper's own conclusion states that no conversation security protocol in Table II provides all desired properties simultaneously, and that no transport-privacy approach in Table III provides strong privacy against global network adversaries while remaining practical for synchronous use. The authors state group conversation security is unresolved: "the situation is less clear for secure group conversations; while no approach is a clear answer." Multi-device support is identified as broadly unaddressed: only the least secure protocols in Table II support multiple devices without a pairing procedure. The authors state it "remains unclear exactly what consistency properties are required to match users' expectations" for group protocols, and call for usability research to guide future group-protocol design — an open question the paper does not resolve. Usability results come from expert cognitive walkthroughs of the authors' own choosing, not controlled user studies; the authors distinguish this from — and cite as inspiration but not replacement for — prior user studies of specific tools (Whitten and Tygar's "Why Johnny Can't Encrypt" and its several follow-ups).

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
As a systematization, this paper does not itself impose runtime requirements on a system; it states, as a finding rather than a design requirement, what other papers' mechanisms need. Its most load-bearing structural claim for downstream design is that the three problems (trust establishment, conversation security, transport privacy) are "nearly orthogonal" and their solutions "can largely be chosen independently" — a composition claim that licenses selecting one mechanism per layer, but the paper simultaneously cautions that layering an anonymity-preserving transport under a conversation-security layer that leaks key identifiers "undermines" the transport's anonymity guarantee (the paper's own "Anonymity Preserving" property), so a selection at one layer can still destroy a guarantee claimed at another and the two layers are not fully independent in practice. The paper's recommended trust-establishment combination — central key directories, transparency logs for global consistency of directory entries, and optional out-of-band verification for security-conscious users — requires an operational key-directory service and a transparency-log infrastructure that neither this paper builds nor specifies in implementable detail; it is presented as the authors' judgment of the best available trade-off, not a proven or measured result, and must be attributed to the authors as a value judgment rather than treated as an established property of any single mechanism in the corpus.

### Contradicts
None found. This paper's claims are broad qualitative judgments (attributed here to the authors, per the extraction rule on value judgments) rather than quantitative results, so no cross-paper numeric disagreement with another key in this corpus applies.

### References worth retrieving
- Foundational: Whitten, Tygar, "Why Johnny Can't Encrypt: A Usability Evaluation of PGP 5.0," USENIX Security Symposium, 1999 — the seminal usability study the paper's own usability framework is built in response to.
- Foundational: Wendlandt, Andersen, Perrig, "Perspectives: Improving SSH-style Host Authentication with Multi-Path Probing," USENIX Annual Technical Conference, 2008 — cited as the origin of Trust-On-First-Use (TOFU), a trust-establishment baseline this paper's Table I evaluates.
- Competing: the DGKE-based mpOTR protocol (deniable group key exchange, cited as references [67],[68]) — a group conversation-security approach the paper evaluates in detail against Table II's properties, a direct comparison point for any deniable group key agreement mechanism considered in this corpus's synthesis.
- Competing: GOTR (2013), a "hot-pluggable" group key agreement protocol using circle keys (cited as reference [69]) — evaluated as achieving message unlinkability and flexible group membership, properties the paper's mpOTR evaluation finds lacking; worth retrieving to check its own measured costs.
- Competing: Dissent and Verdict, shuffle-based DC-net systems providing group anonymity with global-adversary resilience (cited as references [88]-[91]) — the paper's transport-privacy comparison identifies these as addressing DC-nets' collision/denial-of-service weakness through a verifiable shuffle, worth retrieving for their own measured scalability figures.
- Attack/critique: unspecified statistical deanonymization analyses of onion routing by global network adversaries referenced in Section V — the paper states such analysis can use content size, transmission direction, packet counts, and timing, but does not itself cite a single paper by name for this claim in the passage extracted; a full-text pass over the reference list is needed to identify the specific citation.
- Foundational: the FS-IBE (Forward-Secure Identity-Based Encryption) scheme discussed in the paper's Section IV-C3, cited as [57] — stated by the paper to resolve server-complexity and denial-of-service problems the TextSecure prekeys approach has, at the cost of new scalability and performance issues, and to have "received a considerable amount of follow-up research," making it a high-value forward-mining target.
