## [URDANETA-CSUR-11] A Survey of DHT Security Techniques
**Citation:** Guido Urdaneta, Guillaume Pierre, Maarten van Steen. "A Survey of DHT Security Techniques." ACM Computing Surveys 43(2), 2011. DOI 10.1145/1883612.1883615.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.distributed-systems.net/my-data/papers/2011.acm-cs.pdf
**Source URL:** https://www.distributed-systems.net/my-data/papers/2011.acm-cs.pdf
**Domain:** A

### What it does
This paper classifies published defenses for distributed hash tables (DHTs — overlay networks in which each node holds a small routing table and a lookup for key k is routed hop by hop toward the node responsible for k) against three attack categories and states each defense's mechanism and disadvantage. It runs no experiments of its own; every quantitative figure below is a figure the survey reports from the paper it discusses, not a measurement performed by Urdaneta, Pierre, and van Steen. The three categories: the Sybil attack (one physical attacker creates many logical identities), the Eclipse attack (an attacker occupies enough of a correct node's routing-table entries to isolate that node from the honest network, also called routing-table poisoning), and routing/storage attacks (a poisoned routing table or a colluding storage-set causes a lookup to fail or return forged data).

Sybil defenses fall into six mechanism families: centralized certification (a trusted authority signs one certificate per identity), distributed registration (nodes vet each other's join requests without a central authority), physical-network-characteristic fingerprinting (network coordinates or measured latency distinguish physical hosts), social-network-based verification (SybilGuard, SybilLimit — described below), computational puzzles (a node must solve a proof-of-work puzzle to obtain or keep an identity), and game-theoretic mechanisms (an economic penalty for operating Sybil identities).

Eclipse defenses fall into two families: constrained routing tables, where the only entries a node may hold are determined by a public function of node identifiers (defeats Eclipse by construction but forecloses proximity-based neighbor selection), and defenses that keep a proximity-optimized table alongside a constrained fallback table, switching to the fallback when a routing-failure test signals that the optimized table has been poisoned.

Routing/storage defenses combine redundant storage (replication or erasure coding across multiple nodes so that no single compromised node controls a key) with redundant routing (sending a lookup along multiple paths or through multiple candidate next-hops per step, so a single malicious node on one path does not block the lookup). Replicas placed at numerically close identifiers ease consistency maintenance for mutable data; replicas spread across the identifier space are harder for a spatially concentrated attacker to capture, but the paper argues this is not a large improvement because placement functions are public and an attacker can target all relevant locations for a given key. Redundant routing takes one of three forms: wide paths (each routing hop attempts several candidate next-hops in parallel; the hop advances if any one candidate is honest), multiple disjoint paths (independent full paths from source to destination; success requires a majority of paths to be entirely honest), or multiple wide paths (successive attempts at a full wide-path route).

### Measured results
All figures below are as reported by this survey about other authors' experiments; none is this survey's own measurement. Retrieve the cited primary source before using a figure in a selection.

| Reported finding | Conditions (as stated in survey text) | Source discussed |
|---|---|---|
| 15% malicious nodes produces approximately 80% malicious entries in standard Pastry routing tables | Pastry proximity-based routing table, no defense | Condie et al. 2006, cited by Urdaneta section 4.6 |
| Probability of successful single-path routing ≈ 0.24 | f = 0.25 fraction malicious, path length 5, formula (1−f)^5 | Worked example in the survey's own text, section 4 |
| Redundant-routing false-positive probability 0.77 under a node-suppression attack vs. 0.12 without attack | Fraction of colluders f = 0.3, γ = 1.23, 256 samples for the distance test, target false-negative rate 0.001 | Castro et al. 2002, section 5.2 |
| Checked iterative routing adds 2.7 extra hops on average | Castro et al.'s simulation, exact node count and topology not given in this survey's text | Castro et al. 2002, section 5.2 |
| Probability of reaching all correct replicas ≈ (1−f)^(1+log_b N) | f = fraction malicious, b = identifier base, N = expected node count | Castro et al. 2002 formula, section 5.2 |
| SybilGuard: 99.96% of nodes have at least 10 route intersections at group size w=300 (no malicious nodes) | Kleinberg synthetic social-network model, up to 1,000,000 nodes, degree 24 | Yu et al. 2006, section 3.7 |
| SybilGuard: probability that all routes remain in the honest region stays near 100% for attack edges g ≤ 2,000, dropping to 99.8% at g = 2,500 | 1,000,000-node network, w=300 (route length parameter reported elsewhere in the text as needing to be as large as 2,000 for a million-node network) | Yu et al. 2006, section 3.7 |
| SybilLimit accepts between 10 and 20 Sybil nodes per attack edge | Synthetic Kleinberg network of 1,000,000 nodes / 10.9 million edges (w=10, r=10,000); Friendster 932,000 nodes / 7.8 million edges (w=10, r=8,000); LiveJournal 900,000 nodes / 8.7 million edges (w=10, r=12,000); DBLP 106,000 nodes / 626,000 edges (w=15, r=3,000) | Yu et al. 2008, section 3.8 |
| Myrmic: 97th/90th percentile lookup times 346 ms / 281 ms; 93% of lookups solved within 6 hops plus verification | PlanetLab testbed, 120 nodes, all correct, certificate size l=3, 500 lookups per node at 1 request per 3 seconds | Section 5.7 (referenced from surrounding text; source paper not separately keyed here) |
| Myrmic: 0.0122% of lookups fail | LAN environment, 1,000 nodes, 30% malicious, verification procedure assumed infallible | Same as above |
| KAD DHT estimated size: 1.5 million nodes (Steiner et al. 2007) vs. 4 million nodes (Crosby and Wallach 2007) | Two independent measurement studies of the same deployed network, methodology not detailed in this survey | Section 6 |

### Parameters
No parameters are this survey's own; each value above belongs to the cited primary paper and is listed under Measured results with its source.

### Stated limitations
The survey states that none of the reviewed Eclipse or Sybil defenses is evaluated against an adversary that attacks a small subset of nodes, a specific key, or specific routing-table rows, or that poisons slowly by behaving correctly most of the time — these are called more subtle attacks left unaddressed by every proposal it reviews. Singh et al. 2006 (cited within) explicitly states that defending against localized attacks, where an honest node is geographically surrounded by malicious nodes, remains an open problem. The survey states that no reviewed transactional DHT design tolerates malicious nodes. The survey states that Rodrigues and Liskov's study of erasure coding versus replication does not model mutable data or malicious nodes, so its bandwidth-parity finding may not hold once both are considered. The survey concludes that current deployed DHTs (KAD, BitTorrent, LimeWire, the Storm botnet, OpenDHT) are not designed to tolerate malicious nodes, and that Kademlia (used by all of them) remains vulnerable to Sybil and Eclipse attacks because nodes generate their own identifiers.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The survey's own conclusion (section 7) states four preconditions the reviewed literature treats as jointly necessary for a secure DHT: secure assignment of node identifiers (an identifier a node cannot freely choose), a bound on the fraction of malicious nodes, malicious nodes spread across the identifier space rather than concentrated, and data replication combined with a routing mechanism that reaches a correct replica set with high probability. Centralized-certification Sybil defenses require an online or offline certification authority trusted by all participants and a certificate-revocation mechanism. Social-network Sybil defenses (SybilGuard, SybilLimit) require every participant to hold a genuine social relationship with some other participants, offline distribution of a symmetric key per social edge, and low churn in the social graph, since registry and witness tables update only on social-graph change. Computational-puzzle Sybil defenses require every honest node to continuously spend computing resources on puzzle solutions and require the puzzle difficulty to be set low enough for the least-capable honest node to keep solving puzzles while retaining spare capacity for other work; the survey cites a measurement (Anderson and Fedak 2006) that the most powerful nodes in a real peer-to-peer system have several orders of magnitude more CPU capacity than the least powerful, which bounds how high that difficulty can be set. Redundant-routing schemes based on multiple disjoint paths require paths to actually be disjoint for the stated success probability to hold; the survey states this disjointness is not guaranteed in practice. Eclipse defenses based on constrained routing tables require stable, randomly assigned node identifiers and foreclose proximity-based neighbor selection as a performance optimization.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus. The paper is itself a secondary source over the papers it discusses (Castro et al. 2002 [CASTRO-OSDI-02 in this corpus], Yu et al., Singh et al., and others); a downstream synthesis step should prefer the primary source's own reported conditions over this survey's paraphrase where the two differ.

## [VAJHA-FAST-18] Clay Codes: Moulding MDS Codes to Yield an MSR Code

**Citation:** Myna Vajha, Vinayak Ramkumar, Bhagyashree Puranik, Ganesh Kini, Elita Lobo, Birenjith Sasidharan, P. Vijay Kumar, Alexander Barg, Min Ye, Srinivasan Narayanamurthy, Syed Hussain, Siddhartha Nandi. "Clay Codes: Moulding MDS Codes to Yield an MSR Code." USENIX Conference on File and Storage Technologies (FAST), 2018. Pages 139-153. DOI not stated in retrieved text.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.usenix.org/system/files/conference/fast18/fast18-vajha.pdf
**Source URL:** https://www.usenix.org/conference/fast18/presentation/vajha
**Domain:** C

### What it does
A Clay code (Coupled-Layer code) reduces the network traffic and disk reads needed to repair one failed storage node in an erasure-coded system, compared to a Reed-Solomon (RS) code of the same size, by letting the repair process download only a fraction of each surviving node's data rather than that node's full content. An erasure code divides an object into k data chunks and computes m = n − k parity chunks, storing all n chunks on separate nodes so that any failure of up to m nodes is recoverable; a Maximum-Distance-Separable (MDS) code achieves this at the lowest possible storage overhead n/k for a given fault tolerance. Under conventional RS repair, restoring one failed node requires downloading k times as much data as the failed node held, because each of the k surviving nodes must send its entire chunk. A Minimum-Storage-Regenerating (MSR) code is a sub-class of MDS codes designed to avoid this: to repair a node, the system selects d helper nodes (k ≤ d ≤ n − 1) and downloads only β = α/(d − k + 1) bytes from each, where α is the sub-packetization level — the number of bytes grouped into one indivisible unit ("superbyte") per node, so the total repair download dβ is smaller than the kα bytes a conventional approach would move. The paper's own normalized-repair-bandwidth formula is dβ/(kα) = d / (k(d − k + 1)), which for d = n − 1 reduces to (n − 1) / (k(n − k)), showing repair traffic falls as the number of parity chunks (n − k) grows.

Clay codes construct an MSR code from any existing MDS code (scalar or vector) by stacking α independent copies of that MDS code in "layers," then applying a pairwise linear transformation between two bytes drawn from paired layers — a transform the paper calls Pair-wise Forward Transform (PFT) and its inverse Pair-wise Reverse Transform (PRT). This coupling lets each repair operation recover a failed byte by decoding the underlying scalar MDS code plus one elementary two-byte linear operation, rather than requiring a new theoretical code family. The construction builds directly on Ye and Barg's 2017 theoretical MSR code, re-expressing it from a coupled-layer perspective that the paper states makes an implementation more direct, generalizes it to work with any scalar MDS code (not only Vandermonde-RS codes), and extends it to a generic multi-node-repair algorithm covering more than one simultaneous failure — properties the original Ye-Barg construction did not include. The paper also modified Ceph, a distributed object-storage system, to support vector codes (multi-byte superbytes per node) rather than only the scalar codes it previously supported, and implemented Clay codes as a Ceph plugin; this Ceph modification became part of Ceph's upstream master codebase.

### Measured results

| Result | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Repair network traffic reduction, code C1 (RS-comparable (6,4,5), storage overhead 1.5x) | 25% reduction vs. RS | fixed-object-size workload W1 (64 MB objects), Ceph Jewel 10.2.2, single placement group (PG) |
| Repair network traffic reduction, code C2 ((12,9,11), overhead 1.33x) | 52% reduction vs. RS | same setup |
| Repair network traffic reduction, code C3 ((20,16,19), overhead 1.25x) | 66% reduction vs. RS, a factor of 2.9x | same setup; this is the paper's headline figure |
| Repair disk-read reduction, codes C1/C2/C3 | 37.5% / 59.3% / 70.2% reduction vs. RS, a factor of 3.4x for C3 | fixed-object-size workload W1, same setup |
| Repair time reduction, code C3 | factor of 3x reduction vs. RS | single-PG setting, fixed workload W1 |
| Degraded I/O throughput, code C3 vs. matching (20,16) RS | write throughput +106%, read throughput +27% | standard Ceph read/write benchmark, degraded state (repair running in background); normal-state throughput is stated as identical between Clay and RS |
| Encode computation time | higher for Clay than RS (exact factor not given as a number in the read sections) but total encoding time (compute + disk I/O + network transfer) "remains close to" the RS code's | workload W1, attributed to the extra multiplications in the PFT/PRT transform |
| Worst-case disk-read amplification, code C3 under workload W2 | 4x more disk data read than data actually needed for repair (16 KB needed, 4 KB granularity times 4 fragments = worst case) | stripe size S = 1 MB, chunk size L = S/k = 64 KB, sub-chunk fragments of 64 bytes each under parity-node failure |
| No disk-read penalty, codes C1-C3 under workload W1 | disk read equals the theoretical minimum, no fragmentation penalty | stripe size S = 64 MB, sub-chunk fragment size (S/kα) aligned to 4 KB SSD read granularity |

Experimental setup for all measurements above: a Ceph cluster of 26 Amazon EC2 m4.xlarge instances (16 GB RAM, 4 CPU cores each), one dedicated to the Ceph MON daemon and 25 running one OSD (Object Storage Daemon) apiece, each attached to a 500 GB SSD volume, giving roughly 12.2 TB total cluster capacity. Node failures were injected by removing OSDs; the failure domain was one node (one OSD per node). Measurements were taken with the nmon and NMONVisualizer tools, in both a single-PG configuration and a 512-PG configuration (the multi-PG figures for network traffic and disk read during single-node repair are shown separately in the paper, averaged across 3 runs, and are described as showing inferior performance in some cases because Ceph can dynamically reassign an already-participating OSD as the replacement, which the paper treats as effectively two failures). Two object-distribution workloads were used: W1, all objects fixed at 64 MB (8,192 total objects, 512 GB); W2, a mix of 64 MB (82.5%), 32 MB (10%), and 1 MB (7.5%) objects (820-6,758 objects depending on size, 448 GB total), chosen to match a distribution reported for the Facebook data-analytics cluster in a separate cited paper. Repair comparisons for the multiple-node-failure case (codes C4, C5, C6, all (14,10,d) parameters for d = 11, 12, 13, matching a Facebook-cluster (14,10) RS deployment) were run under workload W1 in the 512-PG setting, injecting between 1 and 4 simultaneous node failures; the paper states the average multi-failure network-traffic figures assume every failure pattern of a given size is equally likely, and it separately reports a purely theoretical (non-measured) average-network-traffic curve for f = 1 to 4 failures in Figure 17.

### Parameters
- Six evaluated code instances and their (n, k, d), sub-packetization level α, storage overhead, and normalized repair bandwidth β/α: C1 (6,4,5), α=8, overhead 1.5, β/α=0.5, chosen to match the RDP (Row-Diagonal Parity) code; C2 (12,9,11), α=81, overhead 1.33, β/α=0.33, chosen to match the locally repairable code used in Windows Azure; C3 (20,16,19), α=1024, overhead 1.25, β/α=0.25, chosen to match the (20,17)-RS code used at Backblaze; C4 (14,10,11), α=128, overhead 1.4, β/α=0.5; C5 (14,10,12), α=243, overhead 1.4, β/α=0.33; C6 (14,10,13), α=256, overhead 1.4, β/α=0.25 — C4-C6 all chosen to match the (14,10)-RS code used in Facebook's data-analytics clusters.
- Finite-field size: the paper's simplified presentation assumes a field of size 2^8 (one byte per field element) but states the construction works over a field only approximately as large as n, "significantly smaller" than 2^8 if desired.
- Ceph version used: Jewel 10.2.2.
- Cluster size: 26 EC2 m4.xlarge nodes (1 MON + 25 OSD), 500 GB SSD per node, ~12.2 TB total capacity.
- Workload W1: fixed 64 MB objects, stripe size S = 64 MB (chosen to avoid zero-padding).
- Workload W2: mixed 64 MB / 32 MB / 1 MB objects in 82.5% / 10% / 7.5% proportion, stripe size S = 1 MB.
- The construction requires q = (d − k + 1) to divide n for the base parameter set; the paper describes a "shortening" extension (padding n up to the next multiple of q with zeroed systematic nodes) for parameter sets where this does not hold, and states this extension is included in their implementation.

### Stated limitations
When the design parameter d is less than n − 1, single-node repair requires that, whenever a failed node's "y-section" (its layer-group in the coupled-layer grid) contains other failed nodes, all surviving nodes in that y-section must also be used as helper nodes; if no valid choice of d helper nodes satisfying this exists, the failure pattern is not repairable with bandwidth savings and the paper's algorithm falls back to a plain decode operation instead (Remark 1: this occurs, for example, when q failures land in the same y-section). Repair-bandwidth savings for multiple simultaneous failures hold only for what the paper calls "repairable failure patterns"; patterns outside that set are recovered through decoding, at a higher bandwidth. The encode computation time for a Clay code is higher than for the matching RS code, attributed to the extra pairwise linear-transform multiplications; the paper treats this as an acceptable trade against the larger measured savings during repair, without quantifying the encode-time increase as a number in the sections read. The paper explicitly frames its Clay-Ye-Barg comparison as showing Clay's advantages (any scalar MDS code as a building block, multi-failure repair, coupled-layer implementability) but does not claim Clay improves the Ye-Barg construction's theoretical repair-bandwidth bound itself — Clay is presented as a practical realization of that existing bound, not a new bound.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The storage system must support vector codes — multi-byte "superbytes" grouped per node — because Clay codes require sub-packetization level α > 1; the paper states plain Ceph did not support this and had to be modified (upstreamed into Ceph's master codebase) to add sub-chunking through interleaving. A repair operation needs the coordinator (in the paper's Ceph implementation, the primary OSD, "p-OSD") to be able to select and contact d distinct helper nodes out of the surviving n − 1, and, when d < n − 1, to identify and include every surviving node sharing the failed node's y-section as a helper — this requires the coordinator to know the code's layer/grid structure, not just node liveness. Disk-read savings depend on the storage medium's read granularity matching the sub-chunk fragment size (S/kα): the paper's own measurement shows that when this alignment fails (workload W2, code C3), 4x more data is read from disk than is needed, so a deployment must choose stripe size and α relative to the underlying disk or SSD block size to realize the disk-I/O benefit, not just the network-traffic benefit. The construction assumes an MDS code already exists to serve as the per-layer building block; Clay codes do not replace that MDS code, they wrap it.

### Contradicts
None found against another entry in this corpus. The paper's own Table 1 comparison states that the prior product-matrix MSR implementation (Rashmi, Nakkiran, Wang, Shah, Ramchandran, FAST 2015, citation [24] in this paper's bibliography) is disk-I/O-optimal but has higher storage overhead, of the form (2 − 1/k) — this is presented as a design trade-off between two published systems, not a numeric disagreement to be resolved.

### References worth retrieving
- Rashmi, Shah, Kumar, "Optimal Exact-Regenerating Codes for Distributed Storage at the MSR and MBR Points via a Product-Matrix Construction," IEEE Trans. Inf. Theory 57(8), 2011, pp. 5227-5239 — competing (the product-matrix MSR construction this paper's Table 1 compares against on storage overhead; this is the target RASHMI-TIT-11 the registry identifies Clay codes as needing to be checked against)
- Ye, Barg, "Explicit constructions of optimal-access MDS codes with nearly optimal sub-packetization," IEEE Trans. Inf. Theory 63(10), 2017, pp. 6307-6317 — foundational (the theoretical MSR construction Clay codes implement and extend)
- Rashmi, Nakkiran, Wang, Shah, Ramchandran, "Having your cake and eating it too: Jointly optimal erasure codes for I/O, storage, and network-bandwidth," FAST 2015, pp. 81-94 — competing (product-matrix MSR implementation, disk-I/O-optimal but higher storage overhead, listed in Table 1)
- Pamies-Juarez et al., "Butterfly" code implementation paper — competing (Table 1 entry, limited to n−k=2, sub-packetization 2^(k−1))
- Kralevska, Gligoroski, Jensen, et al., HashTag codes paper — competing (Table 1 entry, evaluated in Hadoop, requires large finite field and helper-node computation)
- Rashmi, Shah, Gu, Kuang, Borthakur, Ramchandran, "A hitchhiker's guide to fast and efficient data reconstruction in erasure-coded data centers," SIGCOMM 2014, pp. 331-342 — foundational (piggy-backed RS codes, retain MDS property but do not reach MSR-level savings, per this paper's Related Work)
- Sathiamoorthy, Asteris, Papailiopoulos, Dimakis, Vadali, Chen, Borthakur, "XORing elephants: Novel erasure codes for big data," PVLDB 6(5), 2013, pp. 325-336 — competing (Xorbas locally repairable code, cited as trading the MDS property for repair efficiency)
- Tamo, Wang, Bruck, "Zigzag codes: MDS array codes with optimal rebuilding," (Zig-zag codes) — foundational (first non-explicit low-overhead MSR construction for all n,k at d=n−1)
- Rashmi, Shah, Gu, Kuang, Borthakur, Ramchandran, "A Solution to the Network Challenges of Data Recovery in Erasure-coded Distributed Storage Systems: A Study on the Facebook Warehouse Cluster," HotStorage 2013 — foundational (source of the cited 0.2-petabytes/day median repair-traffic figure for the Facebook warehouse cluster used to motivate the paper)

- "the median amount of data transferred ... is in excess of 0.2 petabytes per day"
- "the disk read is 4 times the amount of data needed for repair"
- "the degraded write, read throughput ... is observed to be more than the (20,16) RS code by 106% and 27%"
- "it is not a repairable failure pattern"
- "Ceph supports scalar erasure codes such as RS codes. However, it does not support vector codes."

## [VALAPU-ARXIV-25] Towards a Non-Binary View of IPv6 Adoption

**Citation:** Sulyab Thottungal Valapu, John Heidemann. "Towards a Non-Binary View of IPv6 Adoption." ACM Internet Measurement Conference (IMC), 2025. DOI 10.1145/3730567.3764467.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/pdf/2507.11678
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.11678
**Domain:** L

### What it does
The paper measures how much of a dual-stack participant's actual Internet Protocol version 6 (IPv6) traffic is used, at three levels — client, server, cloud/CDN (content delivery network) provider — instead of measuring only whether IPv6 is supported at all. At the client level, commodity routers running OpenWRT with a custom flow monitor record every inbound/outbound flow's protocol version, byte count, and timing at five residences, without inspecting payload content, to compute the day-by-day and site-by-site fraction of traffic that is IPv6 rather than IPv4. At the server level, the OpenWPM web-privacy-measurement framework drives a real Firefox browser to load each of the Tranco top 100,000 websites' main page plus five randomly chosen same-domain internal links, recording every HTTP request, DNS result, and connection IP address for the main page and every embedded (including third-party) resource, then classifies each site by whether its main page has an IPv6 (AAAA) DNS record (else IPv4-only), whether every embedded resource is IPv6-reachable (IPv6-full) or only some are (IPv6-partial). At the cloud level, the same server-side crawl's resource fully qualified domain names (FQDNs) are attributed to a hosting organization via CAIDA's AS-to-Organization dataset, and IPv6 readiness is compared per organization; to separate a cloud's own IPv6 support from a tenant's choice to enable it, the paper isolates "multi-cloud tenants" (one eTLD+1 domain whose subdomains are split across two or more different cloud organizations) and compares the same tenant's IPv6-full fraction of subdomains across the different clouds serving it, using a two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test per cloud pair.

### Measured results
| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| External IPv6 byte-fraction varies 0.07-0.68 and flow-fraction varies 0.09-0.82 across five residences; internal (LAN-to-LAN) traffic varies 0.17-0.99 by bytes and 0.19-0.98 by flows, with internal and external IPv6 shares not well correlated across residences | Five residences (A-E) in the Los Angeles area, 17 individuals total, nine-month observation (November 2024-August 2025), ~21.5 TB total traffic; four residences use Spectrum (native IPv6), Residence B uses Frontier (IPv4-only ISP, IPv6 via university tunnel) |
| Daily fraction of IPv6 bytes at Residence A drops sharply during a known unoccupied period (university spring break, March 16-19) and shows a recurring evening-to-midnight peak with a secondary mid-morning peak; no strong weekly (weekday-vs-weekend) pattern | Multi-Seasonal Trend Decomposition using LOESS (MSTL) applied to March 2025 daily IPv6 byte fraction at Residence A; similar decomposition pattern observed at Residences B and C |
| 57.6% of reachable Tranco top-100,000 websites are IPv4-only (no AAAA record); 29.8% are IPv6-partial (main page reachable via IPv6, some embedded resources IPv4-only); 12.6% are IPv6-full (main page and every embedded resource IPv6-reachable); of the IPv6-full sites, only 11.1% of all reachable sites actually used IPv6 for every resource in the browser's real Happy-Eyeballs race | Tranco top 1M list (2024-10-16, ID Z3Z3G), top 100,000 sites, July 2025 measurement; 81,822 of 100,000 sites reachable (18,178 excluded for DNS/HTTP/TLS loading failure); OpenWPM/Firefox crawl of main page plus up to five same-eTLD+1 internal links, from one residential and one academic vantage point in the western U.S. |
| Comparing October 2024 to July 2025: IPv4-only share decreased 0.6 percentage points, IPv6-full share increased by the same 0.6 points | Same Tranco top-100,000 methodology, three measurement rounds (October 2024, April 2025, July 2025) |
| Top 100 sites: 30.1% IPv6-full, more than double the 12.6% rate across the top 100,000 | Same July 2025 crawl, stratified by Tranco rank bucket (100 / 1k / 10k / 100k) |
| Restricting analysis to only the main page and its directly embedded resources (no internal-link crawling) raises the IPv6-full share from 12.5% to 14.1%, a change over twice the size of the 0.6-point, nine-month organic growth | Same July 2025 dataset, comparing full five-link crawl against main-page-only subset |
| IPv6-partial sites carry a median of 7 IPv4-only resources (p25=3, p75=21) accounting for a median 21% of that site's resources (p25=9%, p75=41%) | 24,384 IPv6-partial sites from the July 2025 crawl |
| Cloud/CDN IPv6-full domain share ranges 3%-85% across the top 15 providers by domain count (which collectively host 76% of the 265,248-FQDN dataset); Cloudflare 85.2%, Google 67.7%, Amazon 24.6% (stated in text; figure shows Amazon's overall IPv6/IPv4-only split as part of a stacked bar) | Same server-side crawl (265,248 FQDNs), cloud attribution via BGP-prefix-originating AS mapped to organization using CAIDA's AS-to-Organization dataset |
| Bunnyway/bunny.net CDN: 99.5% IPv6-only across 1,203 domains, with IPv6 addresses served from Bunnyway's own address space but IPv4 addresses attributed by the AS-to-Org dataset to a separate partner organization, Datacamp Limited/CDN77 | Same dataset; the authors note this reflects an organizational/AS-to-Org attribution artifact, not two independent providers |
| 67 of 78 possible cloud-provider pairs have at least two shared multi-cloud tenants differing in IPv6 support, enabling a per-pair two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank comparison | 21,314 identified multi-cloud tenants (eTLD+1 domains whose subdomains span two or more cloud organizations) drawn from the expanded Tranco crawl dataset |

### Parameters
- Tranco list snapshot used: top 1M list dated 2024-10-16 (list ID Z3Z3G), top 100,000 sites analyzed
- Internal-link crawl depth: main page plus 5 randomly chosen same-eTLD+1 links (fewer if a page has too few links)
- Measurement rounds for server-side crawl: October 2024, April 2025, July 2025 (nine-month span)
- Client-side flow-monitoring duration: 9 months (November 2024-August 2025) across 5 residences
- OpenWRT version on measurement routers: 22.03.3, Linux kernel 5.10
- Misclassification check for Happy-Eyeballs-driven protocol-dependent resource selection: found 106 potentially misclassified sites, 0.4% of all IPv6-partial sites (FQDNs containing substrings such as "v4", "ipv4", "px4")

### Stated limitations
The client-side residence study covers only five residences in a single metropolitan area (Los Angeles), with partial traffic visibility at two of the five residences because some individuals opted out; the authors state they make no claim that this small sample represents the Internet or even users in their region. The client-side dataset contains only flow-level information (five-tuple, byte/packet counts, timing), with no visibility into specific websites accessed or payload content, a restriction the authors state was required by their Institutional Review Board (IRB) agreement to protect study-participant privacy. The server-side analysis inherits known limitations of any top-list-based study: results can vary by choice of list, list age, and list size; the authors state they chose Tranco for its use of multiple ranking sources and its wide adoption but note no list perfectly reflects popularity. A site's set of embedded resources can differ depending on which IP protocol wins the browser's Happy Eyeballs race, which can misclassify an otherwise IPv6-full site as IPv6-partial if IPv4 wins the race and the page then dynamically selects IPv4-only resources; the authors estimate this affects at most 0.4% of IPv6-partial sites via a substring-based check and state this rare edge case is unlikely to affect overall conclusions. The paper treats all third-party resources as one category despite functional differences (a broken ad versus a missing JavaScript library), which the authors state may overlook differences in real-world impact. The cloud-adoption analysis evaluates only default-policy differences (default-on versus opt-in) and does not evaluate secondary factors such as a provider's operational history or pre-existing customer configurations that could also explain adoption-rate differences between providers sharing the same default policy; the authors state they leave a more detailed investigation of these differences to future work.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A design that treats "the client has IPv6" or "the destination has IPv6" as a fixed, binary property of a participant or service is contradicted by this paper's own measured variance: external IPv6 byte-fraction at a single residence has a daily standard deviation exceeding 15% (Table 1's per-residence daily standard deviation column ranges roughly 0.09-0.42 across residences), so any component that hard-codes an assumed protocol availability for a peer must instead re-check or re-negotiate protocol capability per session or per day rather than caching a one-time determination. A design relying on full IPv6 reachability of a named web resource (not just its main page) must budget for the finding that only 12.6% of top-100,000 sites are IPv6-full end to end, and that this fraction was measured to rise only 0.6 percentage points over nine months, so a network deployed against an assumption of near-universal IPv6 destination reachability needs an IPv4 fallback path for the majority of named web-scale destinations for the foreseeable future. A design that depends on a cloud or CDN provider's default configuration to determine tenant IPv6 support cannot assume uniform behavior across providers, because the paper measures a 3%-85% range in per-provider tenant IPv6-full adoption largely attributable to whether that provider enables IPv6 by default versus requiring explicit opt-in.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus. The paper's own within-study comparison shows a common assumption is not supported by its data: the belief that a dual-stack host, which prefers IPv6 via the Happy Eyeballs algorithm, will show IPv4 traffic only for genuinely IPv4-only services is complicated by the finding that the majority of bytes remain IPv4 at 3 of 5 residences even though the majority of flows are IPv6 at those same residences — large-volume flows (downloads, streaming) more often remain IPv4 even where flow-count-based adoption looks high.

### References worth retrieving
- Czyz, J., Allman, M., Zhang, J., Iekel-Johnson, S., Osterweil, E., et al. — foundational (cited [15]; prior work reporting 96% of top-10k websites IPv4-only in 2014, this paper's ten-year baseline comparison)
- Bajpai, V., Schönwälder, J. "A Longitudinal View of Dual-Stacked Websites." — competing (cited [6]; prior smaller-scale, single-year server-side IPv6 adoption measurement this paper explicitly expands on, 1000x smaller dataset)
- Baltra, G., Song, X., Heidemann, J. "Ebb and Flow: Implications..." — foundational (cited [7]; source of the MSTL decomposition methodology applied to client-side IPv6 traffic)
- Bandara, K., Hyndman, R.J., Bergmeir, C. "MSTL: A..." — foundational (cited [8]; the Multi-Seasonal Trend Decomposition using LOESS method itself)
- Le Pochat, V., Van Goethem, T., Tajalizadehkhoob, S., et al. — foundational (cited [31]; the Tranco top-list methodology)
- Englehardt, S., Narayanan, A. "Online tracking: a 1-million-site measurement..." — foundational (cited [20]; OpenWPM, the web-privacy crawling framework this paper's server-side measurement is built on)
- Stowes, S.D. "Diurnal and Weekly Cycles in IPv6 Traffic." — competing (cited [51]; prior server-side diurnal-pattern measurement this paper's client-side diurnal finding is compared against)
- Richter, P., Gasser, O., Berger, A. "Illuminating large-scale IPv6..." — competing (independent large-scale IPv6 measurement methodology, relevant cross-reference for the corpus's IPv6-reachability domain; also cited in XIE-ARXIV-26)

"the fraction of IPv6 traffic a user sends varies greatly...with a standard deviation of over 15%"

## [VISHNUMURTHY-P2PECON-03] KARMA: A Secure Economic Framework for Peer-to-Peer Resource Sharing
**Citation:** Vivek Vishnumurthy, Sangeeth Chandrakumar, Emin Gün Sirer. "KARMA: A Secure Economic Framework for Peer-to-Peer Resource Sharing." Workshop on Economics of Peer-to-Peer Systems (P2PEcon), 2003.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.cs.cornell.edu/people/egs/papers/karma.pdf
**Source URL:** https://www.cs.cornell.edu/people/egs/papers/karma.pdf
**Domain:** I

### What it does
KARMA discourages participants in a peer-to-peer system from consuming more resources than they contribute, without a central accounting server. Each participant holds a single scalar balance, called karma, that rises when the participant contributes a resource (a file, a message, a computation result) and falls when the participant consumes one. A resource-consuming operation is refused if the consumer's karma balance is below the price of the operation.

The balance for a node A is not held by A itself. It is held redundantly by a bank-set: the k nodes whose node identifiers are closest, in a circular identifier space, to the hash of A's own identifier. A distributed hash table (the paper builds on Pastry) maps A's identifier to this set of k closest nodes, so the bank-set assignment is a deterministic function of A's identifier rather than a choice A or anyone else makes. Each bank-set member independently stores A's signed balance, the last transaction sequence number, and a recent transaction log.

A karma transfer from consumer A to provider B proceeds as follows. A sends B a message, signed with A's private key, stating the balance A would hold after the transfer and a sequence number that prevents replay. B forwards this to its own bank-set, whose members query BankA. BankA members check that the signed balance A supplied matches their stored balance; if so, they acknowledge, deduct the amount from A's account, and inform A. BankB members that receive a majority of positive acknowledgements from BankA credit B's account and inform B, at which point B transfers the resource to A. Bank-set members act independently and do not run a Byzantine agreement protocol among themselves: commutativity of addition guarantees that once a node stops issuing new transactions, the members of its bank-set converge on the same balance regardless of the order in which they observed credits and debits. A balance may dip transiently negative at one member if that member sees a debit before a credit that a majority of the bank-set saw in the opposite order; the balance is corrected once the credit propagates, so this transient underflow is contained to less than half the bank-set.

A new node obtains its identifier through a cryptographic puzzle: it selects a public/private key pair and a value x such that MD5(public key) matches MD5(x) in the low n digits, then sets its identifier to MD5(public key, x). This ties identifier assignment to a proof of computation the node cannot precompute for a chosen identifier, and n controls the difficulty of that computation. On joining, a node's prospective bank-set members exchange signed account records for it; if more than k/2 of them agree on a balance and sequence number, that balance is adopted, otherwise the node is initialized with a fixed system-wide starting balance and sequence number zero.

To bound long-run inflation or deflation of the total karma supply, the system recomputes a correction factor rho at the end of each epoch (a period the paper describes as typically spanning several months): rho equals (karma_total_at_epoch_start times nodes_active_now) divided by (karma_total_now times nodes_active_at_epoch_start). Each bank-set node broadcasts, at epoch end, the count and unused balances of nodes that went inactive and the count of nodes that joined; every node then computes the new totals and applies rho to the accounts for which it is a bank-set member.

For a file-sharing application built on KARMA, a file is hashed to a rendezvous node, which providers advertise to and seekers query; the seeker runs an auction over the karma bid providers submit and picks the lowest bidder. File delivery itself uses a Certified Mail scheme: the provider sends the file encrypted with a symmetric key, and the consumer receives the decryption key only in exchange for a signed receipt, so a karma transfer completes if and only if the file transfer completes, and vice versa.

### Measured results
The paper is a design paper with one analytic (not experimental) probability computation, no implementation or simulation is reported.

| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| Probability that an attacker who has compromised 10% of the nodes in a 1,000,000-node network controls a majority of some single 64-member bank-set is under 5.6 × 10^-12 | Closed-form calculation, not measured: attacker controls 10% of 1,000,000 nodes; expected attacker-controlled members of a given 64-member bank-set is 6.4 (10% of 64); bound derived via a Chernoff-style tail bound P(X > 32) = P(X > (1+4)·6.4) < (e^4/5^5)^6.4 |
| Probability that the attacker controls a majority in at least one bank-set across the whole network is under 5.6 × 10^-6 | Same setting, multiplied by the total number of bank-sets in a 1,000,000-node network at k=64 |
| Simply having peers announce their held content produces "less than a tenth of a percent" bandwidth overhead | This figure appears in the companion BitTorrent paper (COHEN-IPTPS-03), not in KARMA; do not attribute it to this paper |
| Currency-correction protocol requires O(N^2) messages per epoch, where N is the number of nodes in the system | Stated as an asymptotic message-count bound, not measured; the paper argues the cost is acceptable because an epoch spans several months, without stating what "several months" is derived from |

### Parameters
| Parameter | Value used in the paper | Tested range |
|---|---|---|
| Bank-set size k | Used symbolically throughout; the one worked numeric example uses k=64 | No range tested; the paper states only that the system needs "at least k nodes in the system at all times" |
| Node-identifier puzzle difficulty n | Left as "a parameter that can be used to limit the difficulty of the puzzle" | Not specified numerically |
| Epoch length | Described as "typically several months" | Not derived or measured; stated as a design assumption used to argue the O(N^2) correction cost is acceptable |
| Fraction of malicious nodes tolerated by the underlying secure-routing layer | Cited from Castro et al.'s secure routing for structured peer-to-peer overlays as tolerating up to 25% of nodes not adhering to the routing protocol | This bound is imported from the cited secure-routing paper, not derived within KARMA |
| Adversarial fraction in the worked bank-set-corruption example | 10% of a 1,000,000-node network | Single point example, not a range |
| Compensation dampening threshold for bank-node service karma | Example given: award extra karma only after a bank node has performed 10^4 transactions on behalf of others | Presented as an example fix, not a derived or tested value |

### Stated limitations
The paper states that KARMA relies on the identifier-to-bank-set mapping remaining secure, and its own tamper-resilience bound is conditioned entirely on the security of that underlying DHT routing layer: the authors write that "the limiting factor to KARMA's tamper-resilience lies in the p2p routing substrate, and not in the higher level protocols." It leaves the resource-pricing mechanism (how many units of karma a given resource in a given application costs) entirely to the application built on top of KARMA. It states that KARMA cannot prevent Sybil attacks in a peer-to-peer setting without external identifiers, and only limits the rate at which new identifiers can be manufactured through the cryptographic-puzzle join procedure; the authors write they "permit Sybil attacks but limit the rate at which they can be launched." The paper also identifies, without resolving beyond a sketch, a second-order incentive problem: bank-set members themselves have no built-in incentive to perform bank-node work honestly and consistently for other nodes, and the paper's proposed compensation (awarding karma for bank-node service) is presented with the caveat that it risks a runaway chain reaction of compensatory transactions unless a dampening rule is added, and risks violating the zero-sum property of the currency, which the paper says a taxation-based alternative might address instead, without specifying the tax mechanism.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
KARMA requires an underlying secure-routing DHT (the paper builds on Pastry with the Castro et al. secure-routing extension) that tolerates a bounded fraction of adversarial nodes and can map a node's hashed identifier to the k nodes closest to that hash; KARMA's own security bound against bank-set corruption holds only conditional on that routing layer's own bound holding. It requires every participant to hold a persistent public/private key pair, established once at join time through the identifier-generation puzzle, and requires all subsequent balance and transaction messages to be signed by that key. It requires the DHT to notify a newly joined or newly failed bank-set member of which accounts now fall under its responsibility, so that node can retrieve those accounts' balances by majority vote from the account's other current bank-set members. It requires an application layer to supply the actual exchange semantics (what resource a transaction concerns, and how many karma units it costs); KARMA supplies only the balance-transfer and file-delivery-atomicity primitives, not pricing. It requires that the fraction of malicious members within any single node's bank-set stay below one-half at the moment of a transaction decision, since the transfer protocol resolves consumer-side and provider-side approval by majority vote within each bank-set. It requires application-level periodic delivery of epoch-boundary join/leave counts and balances between all bank-set members to keep the inflation-correction factor consistent, and tolerates temporary inconsistency between nodes in different epochs only by rescaling in-flight payments with the correction factor.

### Contradicts
None found. No other entry in this batch measures or discusses the karma/bank-set credit-scheme mechanism.

### References worth retrieving
- foundational: A. Rowstron, P. Druschel, "Pastry: Scalable, distributed object location and routing for large-scale peer-to-peer systems," IFIP/ACM Middleware 2001 — the DHT KARMA layers its bank-set assignment on top of.
- foundational: M. Castro, P. Druschel, A. Ganesh, A. Rowstron, D. Wallach, "Secure routing for structured peer-to-peer overlay networks," OSDI 2002 — supplies the 25%-adversarial-node routing-resilience bound KARMA's own security argument depends on.
- attack: J. Douceur, "The Sybil attack," IPTPS 2002 — the attack KARMA states it does not prevent, only rate-limits.
- competing: T. Ngan, D. S. Wallach, P. Druschel, "Enforcing Fair Sharing of Peer-to-Peer Resources," IPTPS 2003 — a fairness mechanism for spatial (storage) resources verified by random audit, which the KARMA authors argue does not extend to temporal resources like bandwidth.
- competing: J. Shneidman, D. Parkes, "Rationality and Self-Interest in Peer to Peer Networks," IPTPS 2003 — mechanism-design framing for incentivizing globally beneficial peer behavior, cited as a parallel approach to KARMA's accounting approach.
- foundational: S. Saroiu, P. K. Gummadi, S. D. Gribble, "A measurement study of peer-to-peer file sharing systems," MMCN 2002 — source of the cited 20-40% Napster / ~70% Gnutella freeloading figures that motivate KARMA.
- foundational: E. Adar, B. Huberman, "Free riding on Gnutella," First Monday 5(10), 2000 — the other cited source for the freeloading motivation, also cited directly by COHEN-IPTPS-03 in this batch.

## [VISWANATH-SIGCOMM-10] An Analysis of Social Network-Based Sybil Defenses

**Citation:** Bimal Viswanath, Ansley Post, P. Krishna Gummadi, Alan Mislove. "An Analysis of Social Network-Based Sybil Defenses." ACM SIGCOMM, 2010. DOI 10.1145/1851182.1851226.
**Retrieved:** full text
**Source URL:** http://ccr.sigcomm.org/online/files/p363.pdf
**Domain:** F

### What it does
The paper shows that four published social-graph Sybil-defense schemes (SybilGuard, SybilLimit, SybilInfer, SumUp) all reduce to the same underlying graph operation despite differing algorithms and stated goals: each, given a trusted node, produces a ranking of every other node by trustworthiness, and each scheme's tunable parameters only move a cutoff point along that fixed ranking rather than changing which nodes rank near the top. The paper establishes this by running every scheme's algorithm at many parameter settings and observing that partitions grow or shrink monotonically (nodes added to the Sybil set are never later removed as a parameter is swept in one direction), which lets the authors convert every partitioning-based scheme into a single ranking for direct comparison. The paper then measures mutual information between pairs of schemes' rankings at every cutoff position and conductance (the ratio of edges leaving a candidate set to edges inside it) of each candidate partition, and finds the rankings agree most strongly exactly where conductance has a local minimum — the boundary of a locally tightly connected node cluster around the trusted node, i.e., a local community. It substitutes an explicit off-the-shelf local community-detection algorithm (Mislove's greedy conductance-minimization method) for each scheme's own ranking procedure and finds it performs comparably. It then shows the negative consequence of that structural equivalence: a network whose honest population is itself split into multiple tightly-knit sub-communities is harder for every one of these schemes to defend, and an adversary who chooses which specific honest nodes to attach Sybils to (rather than attaching uniformly at random) is far more effective than the schemes' own published evaluations assumed.

### Measured results
| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| All four schemes' rankings agree most strongly (highest pairwise mutual information) at the same cutoff point, which coincides with a local minimum (trough) in conductance | Synthetic network from a cited prior study (rewired to have controllable community structure), and repeated on real-world Facebook (Rice University graduate-student network) and Astrophysics co-authorship networks (dataset sizes in Table 2: Facebook 514 nodes/3,313 links avg. degree 13; Astrophysicists 14,845 nodes/119,652 links avg. degree 16; also YouTube 446,181/1,728,938 avg. degree 7.7; Advogato 5,264/43,027 avg. degree 16) |
| An off-the-shelf local community-detection algorithm (Mislove's, minimizing conductance) achieves accuracy comparable to SybilInfer and higher than SybilGuard/SybilLimit, all improving as more Sybils are added, on a synthetic scale-free topology | 1,000-node scale-free non-Sybil network (Barabasi-Albert), 10% (100 nodes) compromised uniformly at random into Sybils, additional Sybil identities added in a matching scale-free topology, swept 30 to 1,000 additional Sybils, averaged over 100 runs, mean 789 attack edges connecting Sybil and non-Sybil regions; SybilGuard and SybilLimit under-detect because they cap accepted Sybils at O(log N) per attack edge and the injected Sybil count stays below that bound |
| The same four schemes plus community detection all achieve markedly lower absolute accuracy on a real social graph than on the synthetic topology of similar density, though community detection remains comparable to or better than the explicit schemes | Facebook graduate-student network (514 nodes, half the size of the synthetic test), additional Sybils swept 0-400 |
| Community detection substituted for SumUp's voting-envelope construction produces more stable vote accuracy (fraction of counted votes that are genuinely non-Sybil) across three real networks than SumUp's original envelope method, whose accuracy varies widely by network | Advogato, Astrophysics, YouTube networks; 100 attack edges injected via 10 Sybil nodes each linked to 10 random non-Sybil nodes, each Sybil further attached to many additional Sybil identities by single links, non-Sybil voter fraction swept from 0.001 to 1 of total non-Sybil nodes, averaged over 5 runs, methodology matching SumUp's original evaluation |
| Detection accuracy (AUC/A', probability a random Sybil ranks below a random non-Sybil) of all four schemes falls from near 1.0 toward 0.5 (random) as the non-Sybil region's community structure increases, holding node count, link count, and degree distribution fixed | Synthetic Barabasi-Albert network of 512 nodes rewired in 5-link increments from no community structure to two 256-node communities joined by 5 links; a 256-node Sybil region attached by 40 links at each rewiring step |
| The same degradation pattern holds on real networks: a correlation coefficient of -0.81 is measured between network modularity (a community-structure metric, range -1 to 1) and detection accuracy (A') | 8 real datasets (Table 3: Facebook undergrad 1,208 nodes/43,043 links modularity 0.278; Advogato 5,264/43,027 modularity 0.318; Wikipedia votes 7,066/100,736 modularity 0.350; email 1,133/5,451 modularity 0.504; Astrophysicists 14,845/119,652 modularity 0.621; Facebook grad 514/3,313 modularity 0.644; High-energy physics 8,638/24,806 modularity 0.690; Relativity 4,158/13,422 modularity 0.790), each given a power-law Sybil region sized to one-quarter its non-Sybil node count, attached with random links equal to 5% of non-Sybil-internal link count |
| Restricting Sybil attack edges to target only the k nodes closest (by community-detection ranking) to the trusted node, instead of placing them uniformly at random, monotonically decreases detection accuracy as k shrinks, for a fixed total number of Sybil-to-non-Sybil links | Synthetic network from the community-structure experiment (rewired to 40 inter-community links), k swept 0 to 500 |
| On the Facebook graduate-student network, the same targeted-attachment experiment drives accuracy first to 0.5 (random) and then below 0.5, meaning Sybils are ranked higher than non-Sybils | Facebook graduate-student network (514 nodes), k swept 0 to 500 |

### Parameters
- Synthetic scale-free non-Sybil network for the community-detection comparison (Section 4): 1,000 nodes, Barabasi-Albert generator, 10% (100 nodes) turned Sybil uniformly at random, additional Sybils added in matching scale-free topology, swept 30-1,000, 100 runs averaged, mean 789 attack edges
- Synthetic network for community-structure sensitivity (Section 5.1): Barabasi-Albert, 512 nodes, initial degree parameter m=8 (about 3,900 links), rewired in increments of 5 links down to 5 remaining inter-community links between two 256-node halves; attached Sybil region of 256 nodes via 40 links
- Real-network community-structure experiment (Section 5.1): Sybil region sized to one-quarter of non-Sybil node count per network, attached with links equal to 5% of non-Sybil-internal link count
- Targeted-attack experiment (Section 5.2): same rewired synthetic network fixed at 40 inter-community links; k (number of nodes nearest the trusted node, by community-detection ranking, among which Sybil links are randomly placed) swept 0-500 on both synthetic and Facebook (514-node) networks
- SumUp-comparison attack model: 100 attack edges via 10 Sybil nodes each linked to 10 randomly chosen non-Sybil nodes, each Sybil further attached to additional Sybil identities via single links, 5 runs averaged
- SybilGuard/SybilLimit theoretical acceptance bound cited: O(log N) accepted Sybils per attack edge, where N is total non-Sybil network size

### Stated limitations
The paper states its own analysis deliberately strips each scheme of its application-specific optimizations (e.g., SybilGuard/SybilLimit's decentralization-specific design features, SumUp's voting-specific mechanisms) to compare the shared graph-partitioning core, meaning results describe that core algorithm and not necessarily every deployed variant's full behavior. It states it did not formally prove that every parameter of every Sybil-defense scheme induces a monotonic node ordering, only that this held for every scheme, environment, and parameter setting the authors tested. It states its focus on local (as opposed to global) community-detection algorithms was a deliberate choice justified by a cited prior finding that global and local algorithms share similar properties, and explicitly leaves verifying this equivalence for community detection under Sybil attack to future work. It states, as an open question, whether the core assumption every examined scheme makes — that Sybils can only form a bounded number of links to non-Sybils — holds in any of today's real online social networks, citing evidence that in at least one real network it does not. It states that identifying communities reliably across a wide range of real-world networks is itself a difficult, unsolved problem in the community-detection literature, an additional limitation beyond the ones the paper directly measures. The paper's discussion section raises, as unresolved value questions rather than measured findings, whether the mere existence of Sybil (multiple) identities should be treated as evidence of misbehavior at all, and whether Sybil-tolerance (limiting a Sybil's effect, as SumUp does) is preferable in principle to explicit Sybil identification — the paper does not claim these are settled.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Any system built on one of these four schemes, or on community detection as a substitute, needs a designated trusted node (or trusted-node set) from which the ranking is computed, since every measured ranking here is defined relative to that node's position in the graph. It requires the input social graph to be undirected or convertible to an undirected weighted graph, since the paper's own conductance and modularity computations, and the schemes they analyze, operate on undirected graphs (Table 3 states this explicitly for the real-world datasets used). The paper's finding that accuracy depends on community structure and on the adversary's ability to target specific honest nodes means any consuming system needs an independent estimate of its social graph's modularity, or of an adversary's link-placement capability, to know whether the deployed scheme's accuracy is anywhere close to the near-1.0 AUC measured on low-modularity synthetic graphs rather than the near-random or below-random AUC measured on high-modularity or targeted-attack conditions. Because detection accuracy is measured relative to a trusted node and a fixed graph snapshot, any system needs a process for selecting and updating that trusted node and for refreshing the input graph, neither of which this paper specifies or evaluates.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus as of this batch regarding this paper's own reported numbers. This paper is itself the primary source for the finding, later reused and extended in ALVISI-SP-13 (also in this corpus), that community-structured honest regions and targeted attack-edge placement both degrade social-graph Sybil defense; ALVISI-SP-13's own targeted-attachment measurements (probabilities of 0.34-0.49 across five schemes under the RenRen-observed attack pattern) are a distinct, later experiment on a different attack model and should not be conflated with this paper's k-nearest-node targeting experiment (Figures 14-15), which measures a different construction. Cross-reference for later composition checking against GONG-TIFS-14 in this corpus: SybilBelief's own evaluation in that paper uses uniformly random attack-edge placement, not the targeted-attachment model this paper shows is materially more damaging; that gap is not closed by GONG-TIFS-14's results.

### References worth retrieving
- Yu, Kaminsky, Gibbons, Flaxman. "SybilGuard" — foundational (one of the four schemes analyzed)
- Yu, Gibbons, Kaminsky, Xiao. "SybilLimit" — foundational (one of the four schemes analyzed)
- Danezis, Mittal. "SybilInfer" — foundational (one of the four schemes analyzed)
- Tran, Min, Li, Subramanian. "SumUp" (Sybil-resilient online content voting) — foundational (one of the four schemes analyzed)
- Douceur. "The Sybil Attack." IPTPS 2002 — foundational
- Mohaisen, Yun, Kim. "Measuring the mixing time of social graphs" — attack/critique (cited to support the real-world modularity findings)
- Bilge, Strufe, Balzarotti, Kirda. "All your contacts are belong to us." WWW 2009 — attack (cited as evidence the bounded-attack-edge assumption may not hold)
- Mislove, Viswanath, Gummadi, Druschel. Local community-detection algorithm paper (the "Mislove's algorithm" substituted for scheme-specific rankings) — foundational

- Newman. "The structure of scientific collaboration networks" — foundational (source of the Astrophysicists dataset)

## [VORICK-SIA-14] Sia: Simple Decentralized Storage

**Citation:** David Vorick, Luke Champine. "Sia: Simple Decentralized Storage." Nebulous Inc. technical report, 2014-11-29. Pages 1-8. DOI not stated.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://sia.tech/whitepaper.pdf
**Source URL:** https://sia.tech/whitepaper.pdf
**Domain:** C

### What it does
Sia lets a storage provider (a "host") and a client agree on a storage arrangement and enforces that agreement through a blockchain, without a third party escrowing funds or verifying storage on the network's behalf. Sia is built as a fork of Bitcoin's transaction model: it replaces Bitcoin's scripting system with an M-of-N multi-signature scheme for all transactions, and adds a new transaction type, the file contract, that both parties sign.

A file contract states the Merkle root hash of the file to be stored (computed by splitting the file into fixed-size segments and hashing them into a Merkle tree — a tree of hashes where each parent node is the hash of its children, letting one root hash commit to the entire file), a duration, a challenge frequency, and payout parameters: the amount released to the host for a valid storage proof, the amount released elsewhere for a missing or invalid proof, and the maximum number of proofs the host may miss before the contract becomes invalid. The challenge frequency divides the contract duration into discrete challenge windows, one storage proof required per window.

A storage proof works as a proof of retrievability: the host reveals one segment of the file plus the list of Merkle-tree hashes needed to verify that segment against the committed root hash. Which segment is demanded is unpredictable in advance: for challenge window W_i, the random seed is the hash of the contract ID concatenated with the hash of the block immediately preceding the start of W_i, so the host cannot know which segment will be checked until that block is mined. Because the seed derives from a specific prior block, submitting a proof of possessing only a fraction of the file succeeds only in that same fraction of challenge windows — the paper states a host storing 50% of a file fails roughly 50% of proofs. A valid proof submitted inside its window triggers an automatic blockchain transaction crediting the host, enforced by network consensus alone; an unmet window instead directs the contract's held funds toward an unspendable "missed proof" address, so a client never needs to personally check host behavior. A contract can also be edited if it carries pre-agreed "edit conditions," with any edit's effect deferred to a future challenge window so it cannot retroactively invalidate an in-flight proof.

The design assumes a single host provides poor availability alone, so the paper recommends clients split a file across multiple hosts using an erasure code — specifically regenerating codes, splitting the file into n pieces recoverable from any m of them — encrypting each piece before distributing it, so that availability depends on the m most reliable hosts among those holding a piece rather than on the average host's reliability, and download latency or throughput can be optimized by choosing the closest or fastest m pieces to fetch, in parallel.

Because a storage proof only demonstrates that a host still holds the file, not that the host will transfer it on request, Sia has no protocol-level mechanism forcing a host to serve downloads. The paper's proposed fix inverts the usual download-fee relationship: instead of a client paying for a download, a client offers a reward for the host sending it a file (an "upload incentive"), so an uncooperative host can simply be ignored in favor of one of the other m-of-n hosts, and hosts compete on responsiveness for the reward. Actual per-segment rewards for this scheme are expected to move through pre-existing micropayment channels, exchanging small amounts of currency for small transferred segments in rapid succession to bound each party's exposure to being cheated mid-transfer.

Sia mitigates a Sybil attack against host reputation — a host fabricating a storage history for itself by repeatedly forming self-contracts over fabricated data — by having clients require that a host's self-announcement (posted in the blockchain's arbitrary-data field) include a volume of coins locked for a future date; the paper defines a lock's value as coins × days-until-unlock (10 coins locked 14 days out creates a lock valued at 140 coin-days), and recommends clients favor hosts presenting higher-value locks, on the reasoning that a valuable lock is not inexpensive to fabricate.

Sia funds its developer, Nebulous Inc., through a separate token, siafunds, rather than through currency premining: when a file contract is created, 3.9% of the contract's committed funds is diverted to whoever holds siafunds at that time, with Nebulous Inc. initially holding roughly 88% of all siafunds and early backers holding the remainder. The paper frames this as tying Nebulous's revenue to the total value of contracts actually created on the network rather than to currency-supply appreciation.

### Measured results
None. This is a design whitepaper: it presents the protocol and its incentive reasoning, with no implementation benchmark, deployment measurement, or simulation. The one quantitative claim resembling a measured result — "a host storing only 50% of the file will be unable to complete approximately 50% of the proofs" — is a probabilistic argument from the random-sampling proof design, not a number from a run system, and carries no experimental conditions.

### Parameters
- File-contract Merkle segment size: described as "constant size," with no specific byte value stated in the retrieved text.
- Challenge-window random seed: H(contract ID || H(block immediately preceding the window)).
- Contract fee routed to siafunds holders: 3.9% of the contract fund, deducted at contract creation.
- Initial siafund distribution: approximately 88% held by Nebulous Inc., the remainder by early crowd-fund backers.
- Block-reward schedule: first block mints 300,000 siacoins; the reward decreases by 1 coin per block until reaching a floor of 30,000 coins per block; target block interval 10 minutes.
- Stated annual currency-supply growth at that schedule: 90% (year 1), 39% (year 2), 21% (year 3), 11.5% (year 4), 4.4% (year 5), 3.2% (year 8), 2.3% (year 20) — these are the paper's own derived figures from the block-reward schedule above, not independently measured.
- Arbitrary transaction data field: nodes accept up to 64 KB of arbitrary data per block, used for host self-announcement and other out-of-band coordination.
- Erasure-code redundancy (n pieces, recoverable from any m): left as a design choice for the client; the paper illustrates with an example of m = 10 out of n = 100 but states this is only illustrative ("as an extreme example").

### Stated limitations
The authors state the protocol contains no mechanism enforcing host uptime and no provision requiring a host to transfer a file to the client on request; both properties depend entirely on an out-of-band incentive layer the paper proposes but does not make part of the protocol. Block-withholding attacks let a miner controlling a share of hashing power bias the random segment-selection seed in its own favor; the paper states an attacker controlling 50% of hashing power can manipulate roughly 50% of challenges but still fails the remaining unmanipulated half, and the paper's recommended defense (high challenge frequency, large missed-proof penalties) is stated to deter only a financially motivated attacker below the 50% hashing-power threshold, not a Byzantine attacker acting without financial motive. Closed-window attacks let a miner refuse to include a host's storage-proof transaction in a block, or extort a large transaction fee for doing so, forcing a proof failure; the paper's defense is a larger challenge-window size so more miners have an opportunity to include the proof, which reduces but does not eliminate the exposure. A host reputation still depends on clients configuring their own selection criteria (price, lock value, storage volume offered, missed-proof penalty); the paper explicitly leaves any more complex host-selection method, including human review, to out-of-band and more centralized systems. The currency's price volatility is stated as a risk to hosts mid-contract, expected to raise prices on long-term contracts as a hedge, with a two-way peg to other crypto-assets described as future work rather than a present mitigation.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Every consumer of a storage proof needs only to read the blockchain, since proof validity is fully checkable from public data (the Merkle root committed in the contract, the revealed segment, and the accompanying hash path) — no direct interaction between client and host is needed for proof verification itself. The random-sampling proof-of-storage design requires a source of unpredictable randomness the host cannot control in advance; the paper supplies this from block hashes, which means the scheme's unpredictability is only as strong as the blockchain's own resistance to hashing-power concentration (stated explicitly as the 50%-hashing-power boundary above). Achieving actual file availability, not just provable possession, requires a client-side erasure-coding and multi-host placement layer that Sia's contract mechanism does not itself provide — the paper is explicit that a single-host contract "guarantees little in the way of availability, bandwidth, or general quality of service." Achieving actual download service from hosts requires a separate, client-configured incentive layer (micropayment-based upload rewards) that is not part of the protocol Sia enforces; a system relying on Sia for storage without also implementing this layer has no guaranteed way to retrieve stored data. Sybil-resistant host selection requires clients to independently evaluate a host's locked-coin value and other self-reported metrics; the protocol supplies the locking primitive but not a policy for how much lock value is sufficient.

### Contradicts
None found. This is a design proposal with no deployment or measurement claims that a later source could confirm or dispute; no other entry in this corpus reports a disagreeing measurement of the same mechanism, and this paper does not claim to overturn a competing design (it frames the erasure-coded multi-host strategy and the storage-proof mechanism as new proposals, not as improvements on measured prior numbers).

### References worth retrieving
- Nakamoto, "Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System" — foundational (the transaction and blockchain-consensus model Sia forks)
- Shacham, Waters, "Compact Proofs of Retrievability," Asiacrypt 2008, pp. 90-107 — foundational (the proof-of-retrievability primitive Sia's storage-proof algorithm implements a blockchain-native variant of)
- Rashmi, Shah, Kumar, "Optimal Exact-Regenerating Codes for Distributed Storage at the MSR and MBR Points via a Product-Matrix Construction" — foundational (the regenerating-code family the paper recommends clients use for multi-host erasure coding; already retrieved in this corpus as a competing reference in VAJHA-FAST-18)
- Back, Corallo, Dashjr, Friedenbach, Maxwell, Miller, Peolstra, Timon, Wuille, "Enabling Blockchain Innovations with Pegged Sidechains" — foundational (the two-way-peg mechanism Sia's planned Bitcoin connection depends on)
- Maxwell, "Proof of Storage to make distributed resource consumption costly," bitcointalk.org — foundational (an earlier informal proposal of a blockchain-verifiable proof-of-storage scheme, direct precursor to Sia's storage-proof design)
- Hearn, "Rapidly-adjusted (micro)payments to a pre-determined party," bitcoin.it wiki — foundational (the micropayment-channel mechanism the paper's upload-incentive scheme relies on for per-segment reward transfer)

### Verbatim extracts
- "a host storing only 50% of the file will be unable to complete approximately 50% of the proofs"
- "clients do not need to personally verify storage proofs"
- "storing data on a single untrusted host guarantees little in the way of availability"
- "the 'download fee' becomes an 'upload incentive'"
- "clients are advised to plan around potential Byzantine attacks"
- "3.9% of the contract fund is removed and distributed to the holders of siafunds"
