## [VYZOVITIS-SPECS-23] Circuit Relay v2 (libp2p specification)

**Citation:** Dimitris Vyzovitis (@vyzo), with interest-group review by Max Inden, Steven Allen, Raúl Kripalani. "Circuit Relay v2." libp2p/specs repository, recommendation-stage specification, revision r3, 2023-02-28.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://raw.githubusercontent.com/libp2p/specs/master/relay/circuit-v2.md
**Source URL:** https://github.com/libp2p/specs/blob/master/relay/circuit-v2.md
**Domain:** L

### What it does
Circuit Relay v2 lets a peer that cannot receive unsolicited inbound connections (a "private" peer, typically behind a NAT) become reachable by routing a connection through a third, publicly reachable peer (the relay), while keeping the relay's resource exposure bounded and explicit instead of open-ended. The protocol splits into two subprotocols: `hop`, which a client speaks to a relay to reserve relay capacity and to request that the relay open a connection to another peer, and `stop`, which the relay speaks to the connection's ultimate endpoint. A private peer A first opens a connection to relay R and sends a `hop` `RESERVE` message; if R accepts, it returns a `STATUS:OK` reply carrying a `Reservation` (an expiration time, R's public relay addresses, and a signed voucher) and, optionally, a `Limit` (a maximum relayed-connection duration in seconds and a maximum data volume in bytes per direction). A is expected to keep its connection to R alive and to refresh the reservation before it expires; the reservation becomes invalid if A disconnects. A now advertises a circuit multiaddress of the form `/p2p/QmR/p2p-circuit/p2p/QmA`, discoverable out of band (e.g., via a Distributed Hash Table or a rendezvous point). A second peer B that wants to reach A connects to R, opens a `hop` stream, and sends `CONNECT` naming A; R checks that it holds an active reservation for A, opens a `stop` stream to A carrying a `CONNECT` message naming B, and if A responds `STATUS:OK`, R relays `STATUS:OK` back to B and bridges the two streams — the `hop` stream between B and R, the `stop` stream between R and A — into one relayed connection, over which A and B then negotiate their own end-to-end security and stream multiplexing exactly as they would over a raw TCP connection. If the connection exceeds the negotiated data or duration `Limit`, the relay resets both the B-side and A-side streams. A now-deprecated "active relay" mode, in which a `hop` `CONNECT` request itself supplies a target address for R to dial rather than requiring a pre-existing reservation, is retained in the wire format but flagged as deprecated for security reasons in public relays. Reservation vouchers are cryptographically signed certificates (a Signed Envelope with domain `libp2p-relay-rsvp`, multicodec `0x0302`) by which R testifies it is willing to serve A; the spec states vouchers are advisory only, since dialing a relay address is not currently required to carry one.

### Measured results
None. This is a protocol specification document, not an experimental paper; it contains no deployment measurement, no reservation-duration default, no per-relay concurrent-reservation cap, and no per-circuit data-cap value. The `duration` and `data` fields of the `Limit` message are defined as protocol fields whose numeric values are set by each relay implementation and communicated per-reservation; the specification text states no default numbers for them. (TRAUTWEIN-ARXIV-26's measured DCUtR hole-punch dataset, which runs over Circuit v2 relayed connections as its precondition, is the measurement counterpart to this specification within this corpus, but it measures hole-punch outcomes, not relay resource-limit values.)

### Parameters
- `Limit.duration`: maximum relayed-connection duration in seconds; value 0 means no limit applied; no default numeric value stated in this document — set per relay implementation and communicated to the client in the reservation/connection response
- `Limit.data`: maximum bytes transmitted per direction over the relayed connection; value 0 means no limit applied; no default numeric value stated in this document
- `Reservation.expire`: reservation expiration as a UTC Unix timestamp in seconds; no default lifetime value stated in this document
- Protocol IDs: `/libp2p/circuit/relay/0.2.0/hop` and `/libp2p/circuit/relay/0.2.0/stop`
- Reservation-voucher envelope domain: `libp2p-relay-rsvp`; multicodec code `0x0302`

### Stated limitations
The `limit` field, when omitted from a relay's response, "indicates that the relay does not apply any limits" — the specification does not require a relay to bound duration or data volume; a relay operator that omits the field runs unbounded relaying for that reservation. Reservation vouchers are stated to be advisory only: "the intention is to eventually require the use of reservation vouchers for dialing relay addresses, but this is not currently enforced." Active relay functionality (a `hop` `CONNECT` that itself supplies a dial target rather than requiring a pre-existing reservation) is retained in the wire format "for the rare cases where it is actually desirable... in a controlled environment" but is explicitly flagged "deprecated for security reasons, at least in public relays" without the specification stating what that security reason is. The specification states that implementations "should not" accept a new reservation or a new connection-initiation request over a connection that is itself already a relayed connection, but this is stated as a should-not, not an enforced protocol rule. A relay retains discretion to drop a connection with an active reservation "if a relay server becomes overloaded" and doing otherwise "would prevent it from maintaining its resource quotas," meaning the expiration time in a `Reservation` is not a guarantee against earlier termination under relay-side resource pressure.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A private peer depending on Circuit v2 for reachability must maintain a live, continuously refreshed connection to at least one relay holding its reservation, because the specification states the reservation becomes invalid immediately if the reserving peer disconnects — so any component that assumes a private peer stays reachable through a relay across that peer's own connection churn is unsupported by this mechanism as specified. A peer that wants to reach a private peer through a relay must already possess that private peer's circuit multiaddress (naming both the relay's peer ID and the target's peer ID) obtained out of band — the specification names a DHT or a rendezvous point as examples but does not itself supply address discovery, so any calling system must supply its own mechanism for publishing and looking up which relay(s) a given private peer currently holds a reservation with. Because reservation vouchers are advisory and not currently enforced for dialing, a system that needs cryptographic proof that a relay actually agreed to serve a specific peer, rather than trusting an unauthenticated `p2p-circuit` address, cannot rely on this specification's default behavior to supply that proof — it would need to add its own voucher-verification step before treating a relayed connection as authorized. DCUtR (TRAUTWEIN-ARXIV-26), the mechanism used to upgrade a Circuit v2 relayed connection to a direct one, requires this reservation-and-connection sequence to succeed first as its own precondition; TRAUTWEIN-ARXIV-26 measured that precondition failing for approximately 29% of its campaign's attempts, a figure this specification document does not itself state or bound.

### Contradicts
None found. This document makes no experimental claims that could disagree with another corpus entry's measurement; it is the mechanism specification TRAUTWEIN-ARXIV-26 measures downstream of.

### References worth retrieving
- AutoNAT specification (referenced in-text as the reachability-determination step that must precede a public host mounting relay service; cited by URL as libp2p/specs issue 180, not a standalone paper). — foundational
- Circuit Relay v1 specification (the predecessor protocol this document explicitly departs from — no unbounded resource reservation, conflated hop/stop functionality). — foundational
- libp2p Signed Envelope RFC 0002 (the cryptographic-envelope format reservation vouchers use). — foundational

## [WALLEZ-SP-25] TreeKEM: A Modular Machine-Checked Symbolic Security Analysis of Group Key Agreement in Messaging Layer Security
**Citation:** Théophile Wallez, Jonathan Protzenko, Karthikeyan Bhargavan. "TreeKEM: A Modular Machine-Checked Symbolic Security Analysis of Group Key Agreement in Messaging Layer Security." IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (S&P), 2025. DOI 10.1109/SP61157.2025.00228.
**Retrieved:** full text
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/410.pdf
**Domain:** H

### What it does
This paper proves the security of TreeKEM, the group-key-agreement core of the Messaging Layer Security (MLS) standard (RFC 9420), against a bit-level precise, executable specification of the protocol rather than against a simplified abstract model, so the proof covers the exact serialization formats, tree operations, and cryptographic encodings an interoperable implementation must produce. TreeKEM organizes a group's participants as leaves of a binary tree and derives, at each protocol epoch, a fresh epoch secret known only to the current membership. A participant updates the group by generating a new secret at its leaf and re-deriving every node on the path from that leaf to the root — the path update — encrypting each new node secret so that only the participants below it can decrypt; the topmost derived value, the commit secret, feeds a key schedule (§2.3 of the paper) that combines it with the group's prior init secret to produce the new epoch secret, giving forward secrecy (an epoch's secret stays hidden even after a later compromise) through key erasure and post-compromise security (a corrupted participant's secrets recover once they perform an update) through the tree structure. The protocol distinguishes proposals (individually constructed add/remove/update operations), commits (a bundle of proposals applied together, possibly with a path update), and epochs (the group state after a commit is processed); messages are relayed through an untrusted Delivery Service that receives commits from participants and rebroadcasts them, with the ordering of concurrent competing commits handled by that external service, not by TreeKEM itself. The proof is written using the DY* framework (a Dolev-Yao style symbolic model implemented as an F* verification methodology, where Dolev-Yao treats cryptographic operations as unbreakable black boxes that can only be defeated by an attacker who already holds the relevant key) applied directly to an executable F* specification that doubles as a reference implementation testable against interoperability test vectors. The paper's confidentiality theorem for TreeKEM is stated to compose with the prior authentication theorem for TreeSync (the MLS sub-protocol governing group-membership authentication, already in this corpus as WALLEZ-USENIXSEC-23), together giving a modular guarantee for the combination of the two components of the published standard.

### Measured results
| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| Specification size: 1.5 thousand lines of F* code | The executable, interoperable TreeKEM specification proved in this paper |
| Proof size: 4 thousand lines of F* | The machine-checked security proof, built on the DY* framework, for the specification above |
| One protocol weakness found: an active network attacker who also compromises one participant's initialization key (or controls one malicious participant) can cause a newly invited participant to join at a later epoch than the one they were actually invited to, without their knowledge | Traced mechanically through the executable specification (Appendix A): exploits that only the GroupInfo object is signed during the Welcome procedure while the encrypted group secrets sent alongside it are not bound to any specific epoch by that signature; the paper states this attack does not break TreeKEM's proven confidentiality guarantees (§4.4) |

The paper reports no runtime, memory, or proof-checking-time performance figures — the "1.5k" and "4k" line counts are the only quantitative results in the paper, and they characterize specification and proof size, not runtime performance.

### Parameters
Not applicable in the sense of tunable numeric parameters — this is a formal-methods proof over a fixed specification of the published MLS standard, not a system with configurable operating points. The one structural distinction the proof exploits, relative to a predecessor computational proof (Alwen, Coretti, Dodis, Tselekounis, cited as [6]) of MLS draft 12, is that the published MLS standard separates the initialization key from the leaf node key, whereas draft 12 did not; the paper states this separation "yields a stronger theorem in our case" for forward secrecy because new participants no longer need to retain the medium-term initialization key after joining.

### Stated limitations
The paper's threat model does not include bad randomness as a possible attacker capability, unlike the prior computational proof [6] it is compared against, which does model bad randomness. TreeKEM as analyzed relies on an untrusted Delivery Service that receives and rebroadcasts messages; the paper explicitly states that how competing concurrent commits from two different participants are resolved "falls outside the scope of the MLS protocol" and is not covered in this paper — that resolution is a property the delivery service, not TreeKEM, must provide. The proof does not cover TreeDEM, the third MLS sub-protocol responsible for group message encryption once an epoch secret is established; the authors state completing a machine-checked proof of TreeDEM, to finish verification of the full MLS standard, is future work. Post-quantum security of TreeKEM is stated as a second direction of future work, not addressed by this proof. The proof is symbolic (Dolev-Yao model, treating public-key encryption as an unbreakable black box short of key compromise) rather than computational; the paper states symbolic and computational models "have their strengths and weaknesses" — symbolic models yield stronger proof tooling and can handle more low-level protocol detail, but computational cryptographic assumptions are more precise about what an attacker with bounded computing power can and cannot do, a precision this proof does not provide. The Welcome-procedure epoch-authentication weakness found in Appendix A is stated by the authors not to affect TreeKEM's proven confidentiality guarantees, so it is a documented gap in a property (epoch binding at join time) the paper does not claim to close, not a break of the paper's central theorem.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Requires an untrusted Delivery Service external to TreeKEM that receives commit messages from every participant and rebroadcasts them to the rest of the group; MLS as analyzed here is explicitly not peer-to-peer — messages are not sent directly between participants. Requires that service, or some other external mechanism, to resolve the ordering of concurrent competing commits submitted by different participants, since TreeKEM's own specification and this proof do not define or verify that resolution. Requires each participant to process the sequence of commits it receives from the delivery service in the order delivered — the paper states MLS "assumes that each participant receives a sequence of commits from the delivery service and attempts to process them in order." Requires participants to perform key erasure as specified — the paper notes that in its formalization the epoch secret "is never actually stored" by an honest participant precisely because retaining it would break TreeDEM's forward secrecy, meaning any real implementation must erase this and related secrets promptly to obtain the guarantees this proof establishes. Requires the TreeSync component's authentication guarantee to hold for TreeKEM's confidentiality theorem to compose into a full guarantee for the published standard — this proof's result is stated as valid in combination with TreeSync's prior authentication theorem specifically, not as a standalone guarantee for TreeKEM in isolation. The Welcome-procedure weakness means a caller relying on strict epoch-binding for newly joined participants (a guarantee that a participant knows precisely which epoch they were invited into) needs an additional mechanism beyond what TreeKEM as specified provides, since the paper documents this gap as unresolved by its own theorems.

### Contradicts
None found. This paper's finding that the published MLS standard's initialization/leaf-node key separation yields a strictly stronger forward-secrecy theorem than the computational proof over MLS draft 12 (reference [6]) does not contradict [6] — it identifies a specification difference between the drafts, not a disagreement over a measurement of the same object.

### References worth retrieving
- Foundational: Wallez, Protzenko, Beurdouche, Bhargavan, "TreeSync: Authenticated Group Management for Messaging Layer Security," USENIX Security 2023 (reference [21] — already held in this corpus as WALLEZ-USENIXSEC-23) — the paper this work's confidentiality theorem is stated to compose with, and the source of the DY* methodology and the earlier-found MLS signature ambiguity attack this paper references.
- Foundational: Alwen, Coretti, Dodis, Tselekounis, "Security Analysis and Improvements for the IETF MLS Standard for Group Messaging," CRYPTO 2020 (reference [3]) — proves TreeKEM as specified in MLS draft 7 is a valid CGKA (Continuous Group Key Agreement); direct predecessor whose coarse-grained compromise model this paper's finer-grained model is compared against.
- Foundational: Alwen, Coretti, Dodis, Tselekounis, "Modular Design of Secure Group Messaging Protocols and the Security of MLS," CCS 2021 (reference [4]) — decomposes MLS into CGKA (TreeSync+TreeKEM) plus a stateful group AEAD (TreeDEM); the modularity precedent this paper's own TreeKEM/TreeSync composition follows.
- Foundational: Alwen, Coretti, Jost, Mularczyk, "Continuous Group Key Agreement with Active Security," TCC 2020 (reference [5]) — defines the CGKA security notion this paper's TreeKEM proof targets.
- Competing/predecessor computational proof: analysis of MLS draft 12 against malicious group members focusing on TreeSync integrity mechanisms (reference [6]) — the specific pen-and-paper proof this paper directly compares its compromise granularity and forward-secrecy theorem strength against; retrieve for its own coarse-grained-compromise theorem statement to check against this paper's finer-grained one.
- Foundational: Cohn-Gordon, Cremers, Garratt, Millican, Milner, "On Ends-to-Ends Encryption: Asynchronous Group Messaging with Strong Security Guarantees," ACM CCS 2018 (reference [16]) — introduces the Asynchronous Ratcheting Tree (ART) design TreeKEM was proposed as a more efficient KEM-based alternative to.
- Attack/critique: Cremers, Hale, Kohbrok, "The Complexities of Healing in Secure Group Messaging: Why Cross-Group Effects Matter," USENIX Security 2021 (reference [17]) — studies post-compromise security for group messaging protocols including MLS; a critique-adjacent source worth checking for measured cross-group healing failures.
- Foundational: Brzuska, Cornelissen, Kohbrok, "Security Analysis of the MLS Key Derivation," IEEE S&P 2022 (reference [15]) — analyzes the MLS key schedule this paper's key-schedule description (§2.3) builds on.
- Foundational (semi-automated tool precedent): reference [13], symbolic F* analysis of the original TreeKEM design comparing its security to alternate designs, and reference [18], Tamarin-prover analysis of a simplified TreeKEM for forward secrecy only (explicitly not post-compromise or post-remove security) — both cited as partial precedents this paper's full machine-checked proof supersedes in scope.

## [WALLEZ-USENIXSEC-23] TreeSync: Authenticated Group Management for Messaging Layer Security
**Citation:** Théophile Wallez, Jonathan Protzenko, Benjamin Beurdouche, Karthikeyan Bhargavan. "TreeSync: Authenticated Group Management for Messaging Layer Security." USENIX Security Symposium, 2023. Pages 1217-1233.
**Retrieved:** full text
**Source URL:** https://www.usenix.org/system/files/sec23fall-prepub-372-wallez.pdf
**Domain:** H

### What it does
TreeSync guarantees that every honest member of a Messaging Layer Security (MLS) group holds a consistent, authenticated view of who is in the group and which cryptographic keys they hold, so that an attacker cannot silently add, remove, or move a participant without every honest member's next processed commit detecting the inconsistency. The paper identifies TreeSync as one of three independent sub-protocols composing MLS — TreeSync (group state, membership operations, consistency/integrity/authentication), TreeKEM (group key agreement, already analyzed in this corpus as WALLEZ-SP-25), and TreeDEM (message encryption) — and proves TreeSync's guarantees hold independent of whatever TreeKEM and TreeDEM do, so a broken or replaced key-agreement or encryption layer cannot undermine TreeSync's membership-authentication property, though TreeSync's guarantee is in turn a stated precondition both other layers need. Each MLS group maintains a binary tree whose non-empty leaves hold member credentials and public keys; group membership operations (add, remove, update) modify this tree, and every modification a committing member makes is bound together by a parent-hash mechanism: each internal node's hash covers the content of its child subtrees, so tampering with any node's content or position changes the hash chain up to the root and is detected by any member re-deriving it. Each leaf's credential — the cryptographic binding between a member's identity and their signing key — is issued out-of-band by a trusted Authentication Service (AS), and the tree operations rely on a separate, only mostly-trusted Delivery Service (DS) that stores and relays messages and defines one global order for group modifications; a malicious DS can withhold or selectively deliver messages (partitioning the group) but cannot forge or read them. The paper's formal specification is written in F* (a dependently typed proof-oriented programming language) at byte-level precision — covering exact message serialization, not an abstract protocol model — verified with the DY* symbolic (Dolev-Yao) protocol-analysis framework, and the specification is also directly executable, compiled through F*'s OCaml extraction into a runnable reference implementation tested against the RFC's own test vectors and against two independent industrial MLS implementations for interoperability.

### Measured results
| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| Specification size: 4,914 lines of non-blank, non-comment F* code total, broken down as Library code 836, TreeSync 1,274, TreeKEM 396, TreeDEM 1,384, High-level API 1,024 | Measured as source lines of code (LoC) of the complete formal specification |
| Proof size: 5,188 lines total, broken down as Library proofs 1,170, TreeSync proofs 4,018, Tests 2,782 | Same codebase; TreeSync's own proof (4,018 lines) is roughly 3x the size of the TreeSync specification itself (1,274 lines) |
| Verification time: 11 min 15 s to verify the total specification, 15 min 15 s to verify all proofs; TreeSync proofs alone take 13 min 30 s | Measured on an Intel Xeon CPU E5-2620 v4 @ 2.10 GHz with 32 GB memory |
| Reference-implementation size comparison: this paper's F*-derived implementation, 4,914 LoC; mlspp (industrial C++ implementation), 4,250 non-blank non-comment lines; OpenMLS (industrial Rust implementation), 15,000 non-test non-blank non-comment lines | Same LoC-counting methodology applied by the authors to all three codebases for comparison |
| Performance (cumulative computation time across all group participants) for three workloads: Adds — 2.7 s (this paper) vs. 1.2 s (mlspp) vs. 0.7 s (OpenMLS), adding 10 participants one by one with 20 messages from each after every add; Messages — 3.2 s vs. 0.6 s vs. 0.2 s, adding 3 participants with 400 messages from each participant after each add; Removes — 5.5 s vs. 0.9 s vs. 0.7 s, adding 15 participants with 1 message each after each add, removing every odd-position participant, re-adding to 15 participants with 1 message each after each re-add | Measured on the same Intel Xeon E5-2620 v4 @ 2.10 GHz, 32 GB memory; the authors state all three implementations are in different languages/toolchains so only a broad conclusion is drawn — all three execute "within the same order of magnitude" |
| One protocol vulnerability confirmed and fixed by the standards body: the "signature confusion attack," in which TreeSync and TreeDEM signatures under the same signing key collided after byte-level serialization because the two protocols used the same signature format with no disambiguating label | Found only by modeling bitstring-level serialization in the executable specification — the paper states "this attack only appears if one models bitstring-level serialization... since the two signatures would otherwise appear to be on different MLS types"; presented to the MLS working group and fixed in draft 13 by adding uniform disambiguating labels to every MLS signature, a fix required for the paper's own authentication proof to complete |
| Additional protocol defects found and fixed in the IETF standard as a direct result of this work: the parent-hash mechanism originally authenticated only TreeKEM-related tree content, not leaf credentials (fixed in draft 13 by extending it to the full tree content); four previously unenforced well-formedness conditions for parent-hash links under unmerged leaves and filtered paths (identified during the proof, some unenforced in the RFC); one missing well-formedness check for unmerged leaves on group join, which could break the parent-hash invariant (fixed in draft 15) | All found through the process of completing the proof, with the authors constructing concrete protocol traces that break the property in each case before the corresponding RFC fix |
| Independent implementation bugs found through interoperability testing: serialization errors in the authors' own implementation (for example, a field serialized as uint8 instead of uint16) and separate bugs in both mlspp and OpenMLS | Found via cross-implementation interoperability testing against RFC test vectors, reported to and fixed by the respective projects |
| Skype integration proof-of-concept: reference implementation compiled to WebAssembly via js_of_ocaml and linked against HACL-WASM, deployed in an experimental branch of the Skype client adding a "secure group chats" feature, with successful message exchange across endpoints and no noticeable UI slowdown | A one-time collaboration with a Microsoft team; the paper reports the qualitative outcome (successful cross-endpoint conversation, no noticeable slowdown) and does not state a specific group size, message count, or timing figure for this integration, so no numeric performance claim from the Skype test is usable as measured evidence beyond what is stated above |

### Parameters
Not a system with tunable numeric parameters — this is a formal specification and proof of a fixed protocol version (MLS draft 16, the version nearing IETF standardization at the time of writing). The one architectural choice the paper states explicitly is to materialize TreeSync and TreeKEM as two separate trees internally, "favoring clarity and readability over conciseness," a design trade-off the authors state recurs throughout the specification wherever readability was chosen over a more concise or optimized implementation.

### Stated limitations
The paper's security proof covers only TreeSync; TreeKEM and TreeDEM are formally specified (so the interaction between all three is accounted for structurally) but their own comprehensive security analysis is explicitly left as future work — the paper states "we do not analyze TreeKEM and TreeDEM in this paper." The TreeSync authentication guarantee holds only as long as enough honest, uncompromised members continue creating commits — a group with too few active honest members does not receive the guarantee, though the paper does not quantify "enough" as a numeric threshold. The proof assumes leaf credentials have already been validated and issued out-of-band by a trusted Authentication Service before a leaf enters the tree; this issuance process itself is outside what TreeSync specifies or proves. The Delivery Service is assumed only "mostly" trusted: it can withhold messages or partition the group by selective delivery, and the paper's guarantees do not cover recovery from or detection of such partitioning beyond what the underlying commit-ordering property provides. The performance comparison against mlspp and OpenMLS is stated by the authors to support only a broad, order-of-magnitude conclusion, not a precise ranking, because the three implementations use different languages and toolchains with no controlled-for confound removal. The Skype integration is described as a one-time proof-of-concept "tested and benchmarked... on small groups exchanging a handful of messages," not a scaled evaluation, and the paper reports no numeric figures from it beyond the qualitative outcome. The authors state that MLS's growth into "a large protocol standard" makes even understanding the full protocol "a challenge... even for cryptographic developers and protocol experts," and suggest — as their own retrospective judgment, not a measured fact — that TreeSync/TreeKEM/TreeDEM's modular separation should have been built into the standard from the start.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Requires a trusted Authentication Service (AS) external to TreeSync that attests to the binding between a member's real-world identity and their authentication credential, issued out-of-band before that member's leaf enters the tree — TreeSync's proof assumes this binding already holds and does not itself establish it. Requires a Delivery Service (DS) that stores and relays messages between participants and enforces one globally unique order for all group modifications; the DS need not be fully trusted (it may withhold or selectively deliver messages) but must not be able to forge or read message content, and TreeSync's guarantees depend on this ordering property being supplied by the DS rather than by TreeSync itself. Requires TreeDEM (or whatever protocol occupies that role) to use signature formats disambiguated by purpose-specific labels from any signatures TreeSync itself produces under the same signing key — the paper's own authentication proof could not complete until this labeling fix (adopted in MLS draft 13) was in place, so any composition reusing a signing key across sub-protocols needs an equivalent disambiguation mechanism. Requires every honest group member to re-derive and check the parent-hash chain on receiving a commit, since the integrity guarantee is enforced by members performing this check, not by any property the delivery mechanism verifies on their behalf. States as a structural fact — not merely an assumption of this paper but something the paper proves as a dependency — that TreeSync's authentication guarantee is "a necessary precondition" for both TreeKEM and TreeDEM, because both layers rely on group members agreeing on the tree; a system substituting a different, weaker membership-authentication layer beneath a TreeKEM-like key-agreement mechanism inherits this same precondition and needs an equivalent guarantee from whatever layer replaces TreeSync.

### Contradicts
None found regarding this paper's own measured results. The paper cites Unger et al. (already in this corpus as UNGER-SP-15) as concluding that, as of that 2015 survey, "conversations between larger groups still lack a good solution" — this is quoted here as an attribution of Unger et al.'s own stated conclusion, not a finding of this paper, and is consistent with, not contradicted by, this paper's own scope (TreeSync addresses group membership authentication specifically, not the full space of group-conversation-security properties Unger et al. survey).

### References worth retrieving
- Foundational: Wallez, Protzenko, Bhargavan, "TreeKEM: A Modular Machine-Checked Symbolic Security Analysis of Group Key Agreement in Messaging Layer Security," IEEE S&P 2025 — already held in this corpus as WALLEZ-SP-25, the direct follow-up proof of the TreeKEM component this paper explicitly leaves unanalyzed.
- Foundational: Alwen, Coretti, Dodis, Tselekounis, cryptographic analysis of TreeKEM draft 7 against a passive, non-adaptive attacker, defining Continuous Group Key Agreement (CGKA) (reference [3]).
- Foundational: Alwen, Jost, Mularczyk, on tree-based CGKA insider security (reference [5]) — cited in the main text as a source of prior authentication attacks on new MLS members that this paper's TreeSync formalization better explains.
- Attack/critique: Bhargavan, Beurdouche, Naldurg, "Formal Models and Verified Protocols for Group Messaging: Attacks and Proofs for IETF MLS" (reference [14]) — cited as the source of the "welcome message attack" this paper's tree-tampering-attack prevention theorem is checked against.
- Attack/critique: reference [5]'s "tree signing attack," where an attacker changes leaf positions in the tree to fool a new member — a second named prior attack this paper's integrity theorem is stated to prevent.
- Competing/related formal analysis: Cremers, Hale, Kohbrok, "The Complexities of Healing in Secure Group Messaging: Why Cross-Group Effects Matter" (reference [24]) — same author group as cited in WALLEZ-SP-25's bibliography, worth retrieving for cross-checking healing-property claims against TreeSync's authentication guarantee.
- Foundational: Cohn-Gordon, Cremers, Garratt, Millican, Milner, Asynchronous Ratcheting Trees (ART) cryptographic proof (reference [23]) — the original tree-based design MLS's TreeKEM was proposed as a more efficient replacement for.

## [WANG-ARXIV-26] Whose Posts Get Ranked: Identical-Text Exposure Gaps in Bluesky Custom Feeds
**Citation:** Yipeng Wang, Mohit Singhal. "Whose Posts Get Ranked: Identical-Text Exposure Gaps in Bluesky Custom Feeds." 20th ACM Conference on Recommender Systems (RecSys '26), September 27-October 02, 2026, Minneapolis, MN, USA. 3 pages. DOI 10.1145/3773078.3841250.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13879
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13879
**Domain:** K

### What it does
The paper measures whether Bluesky's user-published custom feeds — independently operated
recommendation services the platform distributes alongside each other, roughly 40,000 of them from
18,000 creators at the time of writing — return byte-identical post text at equal rates across
different authors, using only naturally occurring duplicate posts already in the feeds' ranked
output, without creating test accounts or injecting content.

Data collection: the authors polled the public Top-50 output of Bluesky custom feeds roughly every
10 minutes through the `app.bsky.feed.getFeed` API endpoint, keeping only "complete" snapshots — one
poll of one feed that returned exactly 50 distinct ranks mapped to 50 distinct posts after
deduplication. From this stream they formed "matched sets": groups of posts sharing byte-identical
text but different authors, all present in the candidate pool for the same feed at the same snapshot
time, each post published no more than 7 days before that snapshot, with the group's creation-time
span and age span both capped at 120 minutes (with 60- and 30-minute caps used as robustness checks),
and each group required to contain at least two distinct authors. Byte-exact text matching removes
text content itself as an explanation for any exposure difference within a set.

Exposure was scored per copy by two rank-based weighting functions: reciprocal rank (1/r, the paper's
primary metric) and discounted cumulative gain weight (1/log2(r+1)); a copy absent from the returned
Top-50 list receives zero exposure under both. The authors regressed each copy's reciprocal-rank
exposure on author-history, profile, media, and post-type feature blocks, using matched-set fixed
effects (which absorb every factor common to all copies in a set — the feed, the snapshot time, the
text itself), with standard errors clustered by text group (the set of all posts across all snapshots
sharing that byte-identical text), and controlled the false discovery rate across tests with the
Benjamini-Hochberg procedure, reporting both within-block (q_blk) and across-all-tests (q_all)
corrected significance.

### Measured results

| Finding | Figure | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Raw Top-50 posts observed before filtering | 7.3 million distinct posts | Full snapshot stream, unfiltered |
| Complete snapshots retained | 297,093, covering 1,366 distinct feeds | February-April 2026 collection window |
| Matched sets in the main sample | 64,853 | 120-minute creation/age-span cap, byte-exact text matching, at least 2 distinct authors per set |
| Matched sets span | 250 feeds | Same sample |
| Sets where one copy is returned and another is missing | 33% | Main 64,853-set sample |
| Sets where one copy reaches Top-10 and another does not appear at all | 6.8% | Same sample |
| Two-post matched sets with at least one returned copy | 58,318 (89.9% of all 64,853 sets) | Used for Figure 1's rank-pair visualization, same 120-minute cap |
| Average DCG-weight gap between paired copies | 0.102 (mean); up to 0.25 in the most unequal decile | Same two-post-set sample; a 0.25 gap is stated as equivalent to a post's entire DCG weight at rank 15 |
| Better-ranked copy's share of total exposure in its matched set | 66% on average | Same sample |
| Exposure-gap robustness to tighter time-span caps | 0.095 at 60-minute cap, 0.085 at 30-minute cap (versus 0.102 at 120-minute cap) | Same DCG-gap metric, same sample re-filtered at each cap |
| "New author on feed" reciprocal-rank penalty | -0.061 RR (SE 0.020), p=0.003, q_blk=0.023, q_all=0.047, permutation p=0.007 | Fixed-effects regression on the 64,853-set sample; "new" = feed had returned none of that author's posts in the collection logs before this snapshot |
| Prior-exposure effect on current RR | +0.032 RR per natural-log unit of prior same-feed exposure (SE 0.012), p=0.007, q_all=0.078, permutation p=0.012 | Same regression |
| Return-probability penalty for first-time authors under strictest cap | -27 percentage points, q_blk=0.007 | 30-minute time-span cap specification |
| New-author penalty after controlling for copy arrival order | -0.049 RR, p=0.016 | Robustness check adding arrival-order as a control |
| Leave-one-feed-out robustness | all 250 per-feed refits remain negative; 99.6% satisfy p<0.05 | Each of the 250 feeds dropped one at a time and the regression rerun |
| Robustness to excluding the single most-duplicating author | -0.063 RR, p=0.003 (versus -0.061 baseline) | Same regression, that author's posts removed |
| New-vs-previously-returned author head-to-head win rate | new author's copy ranks better only 16% of the time | 6,768 matched sets pairing a new author against a previously returned author |
| New author with more followers, head-to-head loss rate | new author's copy still ranks lower 74% of the time | Subset of 746 matchups where the new author has strictly more followers than the competing author |
| Content/media feature significance | 0 of 304 tested media and post-type features (e.g. has_image, is_reply, hashtag count) pass FDR correction | Same fixed-effects framework, feature-block tests |
| Multiway-cluster p-values for the new-author estimate | exact text: 0.003; +author: 0.007; +feed: 0.028; text+author+feed: 0.024 | Robustness across four clustering specifications |
| Family-wise max-T permutation p-value | 0.017 | Robustness check |
| Frequency concentration within the matched-set sample | most frequent single text: 0.5% of all matched sets; largest single contributing feed: 11% of all matched sets | Descriptive check that no single duplicate text or feed dominates the sample |

### Parameters
| Parameter | Value used | Range tested |
|---|---|---|
| Snapshot polling interval | ~10 minutes | Not varied |
| Snapshot completeness requirement | exactly 50 distinct ranks mapped to 50 distinct posts | Fixed |
| Matched-set text-matching rule | byte-exact match | An unspecified alternate "text-matching rule" is mentioned as one of the robustness checks the two headline estimates were tested against, without the alternate rule's definition given in this 3-page paper |
| Matched-set creation/age-span cap | 120 minutes (main) | 60 and 30 minutes as robustness checks |
| Maximum post age at snapshot time | 7 days | Not varied |
| Minimum distinct authors per matched set | 2 | Not varied |
| Exposure weighting functions | reciprocal rank (main), DCG weight (secondary) | Both reported; RR used for the regression |
| Multiple-comparison correction | Benjamini-Hochberg FDR, both within-block (q_blk) and across all tests (q_all) | Applied to all reported feature-block tests |
| Collection window | February-April 2026 | Not varied |

### Stated limitations
The authors state that most of the custom feeds in their dataset run algorithms that are black boxes
to the observer, so confounding variables affecting exposure cannot be ruled out. They state author
history is left-censored: it is observed only within the collection window, so an author's true prior
history on a given feed before the study began is unknown and any author's measured "new" status may
undercount actual prior exposure that occurred before data collection started. They state that,
although byte-identical text rules out the text itself as an explanation for exposure differences,
copies within a matched set may still differ in media attachments, thread position, or moderation
status, and that the paper examines only observable media factors, finding none of the 304 tested
features statistically significant after correction — leaving unobserved factors (thread position,
moderation status) as an acknowledged possible confound the paper does not measure.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The measurement method requires nothing from Bluesky's protocol beyond the already-public
`app.bsky.feed.getFeed` endpoint returning a feed's current ranked Top-50 list; it requires no
platform cooperation, no test-account creation, and no injected content, because it relies entirely
on duplicate posts that already occur naturally on the platform. The fixed-effects fair-exposure
audit method depends on identical text recurring across multiple authors at comparable ages within
the same feed's candidate pool — a system with no duplicate-post traffic at all (e.g., one enforcing
canonicalization or global deduplication at the protocol layer) would supply this method with no
matched sets to compare, so the technique's applicability is conditional on the target system
tolerating duplicate content. Any component of a "ranking without a global index" architecture that
uses per-author history — return counts, prior appearances on a specific feed — as an input signal
inherits the finding's failure mode directly: this paper shows that signal produces persistent,
statistically robust exposure inequality for otherwise-identical content, independent of follower
count, and independent of the specific feed (the effect holds across all 250 feeds tested
individually).

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus. The paper does not claim its measured penalty reflects intentional
discrimination by feed operators; it presents the correlation between prior exposure and current
exposure as the finding, explicitly comparable in the authors' own words to "popularity-bias feedback
loops observed in centralized recommendation systems," attributed as the authors' own interpretive
framing rather than a separately established causal mechanism in this paper.

### References worth retrieving
- **Balduf, Sokoto, Ascigil, Tyson, Scheuermann, Korczyński, Castro, Król, "Looking AT the Blue Skies of Bluesky," IMC 2024** — foundational/competing measurement of the Bluesky network and feed ecosystem, cited [1]; the paper states this prior work maps the platform and feed ecosystem but does not measure exposure allocation, which is the gap this paper fills.
- **Kleppmann, Frazee, Gold, Graber, Holmgren, Ivy, Johnson, Newbold, Volpert, "Bluesky and the AT Protocol: Usable Decentralized Social Media," DIN 2024** — foundational protocol description, cited [7]; the source for the custom-feed-generator mechanism this paper audits, already flagged from QUELLE-PLOSONE-25's bibliography.
- **Huszár, Ktena, O'Brien, Belli, Schlaikjer, Hardt, "Algorithmic amplification of politics on Twitter," PNAS 2022** — competing/foundational algorithm-audit methodology on a centralized platform, cited [6]; directly comparable amplification-measurement methodology from a non-decentralized system.
- **Singh, Joachims, "Fairness of Exposure in Rankings," KDD 2018** — foundational fair-ranking framework this paper's exposure metric derives from, cited [12].
- **Biega, Gummadi, Weikum, "Equity of Attention: Amortizing Individual Fairness in Rankings," SIGIR 2018** — foundational fair-ranking framework, cited [3].
- **Diaz, Mitra, Ekstrand, Biega, Carterette, "Evaluating Stochastic Rankings with Expected Exposure," CIKM 2020** — foundational exposure-metric methodology, cited [5].
- **Sandvig, Hamilton, Karahalios, Langbort, "Auditing Algorithms: Research Methods for Detecting Discrimination on Internet Platforms," ICA 2014** — foundational algorithm-audit methodology this paper extends to social feeds, cited [11].
- **Singhal, Ling, Paudel, Thota, Kumarswamy, Stringhini, Nilizadeh, "SoK: Content Moderation in Social Media," EuroS&P 2023** — foundational, cited [13] for moderation-status as an unmeasured potential confound; co-authored by this paper's second author.

### Verbatim extracts
"in 33% of sets, one copy appears on the list while another does not" (abstract).
"A new author with more followers than the competing author still loses 74% of head-to-head comparisons" (abstract).
"none are statistically significant" (Section 3, Content features).
"Author history is observed only within our collection window (left-censored)" (Section 3, Limitations).
"resembles the popularity-bias feedback loops observed in centralized recommendation systems" (Section 4, Conclusion).
"feed operators can also apply this method to their own logs to monitor such gaps" (Section 4, Conclusion).

## [WANG-GLOBECOM-12] Real-World Sybil Attacks in BitTorrent Mainline DHT

**Citation:** Liang Wang, Jussi Kangasharju. "Real-World Sybil Attacks in BitTorrent Mainline DHT." IEEE GLOBECOM, 2012. DOI 10.1109/GLOCOM.2012.6503215.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://doi.org/10.1109/GLOCOM.2012.6503215
**Source URL:** https://doi.org/10.1109/GLOCOM.2012.6503215
**Domain:** J

### What it does
The paper identifies two routing-table attacks against BitTorrent's Mainline distributed hash table (MLDHT), a 160-bit Kademlia-based key-value store in which peer and content identifiers share one address space and each node keeps a k-bucket routing table (a fixed-size list of contacts grouped by numeric distance from the node's own identifier). A horizontal attack spreads a small number of forged identities (Sybils, meaning falsely distinct identities controlled by one attacker) widely across the network by answering every PING message with a random identifier and every FIND_NODE message by claiming sole ownership of the queried identifier, so querying nodes and the nodes those nodes tell about the attacker both come to treat the attacker as authoritative; the derivation the authors give is that a horizontal attack needs only N / max(k, log(N)) Sybils to intercept messages for an N-node network with bucket size k, because average lookup path length is O(log N) and eventually exceeds k as the network grows. A vertical attack instead inserts k Sybil identifiers numerically adjacent to one target identifier (a specific node or a specific content info hash), which lets the attacker intercept every query and every stored key-value pair addressed to that one target; the authors state this is a broader form of the previously known eclipse attack (an attack that fills a victim's routing table entirely with attacker-controlled entries) because it can also target a content identifier, not only a node. The authors detect real instances of both attacks with three honeypots: a detector that queries random, near-certainly-nonexistent node and content identifiers and marks any node that falsely claims ownership as an attacker; an MLDHT honeypot that places crafted content identifiers immediately adjacent to its own identifier so that any node performing a vertical attack against those identifiers is drawn toward the honeypot and revealed; and a BitTorrent-protocol honeypot that completes the BitTorrent handshake with any node that follows up a DHT-level probe with an actual download attempt, to confirm the probing node is truly monitoring content rather than only probing at the DHT level.

### Measured results
| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| Estimated Sybil count in MLDHT increasing throughout 2011, currently around 300,000 | Monitoring since December 2010, sampling a randomly selected 12-bit zone (a set of nodes sharing a 12-bit identifier prefix) every 30 minutes; per-attacker time series shown for the whole of 2011 with standard deviation, not a single point estimate; detailed methodology stated to be in a companion technical report not examined here |
| One identified attacker ("Mr. 50," IP prefix traced to Amazon EC2) injected an estimated 80,000 to 290,000 Sybils across 2011, holding roughly steady near 100,000 from mid-January through July before rising after August | Estimated from the same 30-minute zone-sampling monitoring system plus honeypot logging, not from a controlled experiment; identity based on shared, identically erroneous protocol implementation with a second, less active entity ("Mr. 184") |
| Attribution of observed Sybils in 2011: Mr. 50 56%, Mr. ISP 27%, other 14%, Mr. 184 3% | Same monitoring period and methodology as above |
| Traffic-localization test: for 6 popular files (top files on The Pirate Bay), the fraction of same-ISP ("native") nodes returned to an insider client connecting through a proxy inside the suspected ISP's network peaked at over 90%, versus a markedly lower fraction for an outsider client on the authors' own network; for 2 unpopular files (from a Chinese file-sharing site) both clients received a low native-node fraction, with the insider client still slightly higher | 8 total torrents tested (6 popular, 2 unpopular), one insider and one outsider instrumented client per file, requesting only the initial peer set from the suspected attacker ("Mr. ISP") without joining the actual file distribution |
| A cited prior result (Timpanaro et al., not this paper's own measurement): inserting 20 Sybils near a target causes a client to receive over 90% Sybils in its returned peer set | Attributed to reference [11] (Timpanaro, Cholez, Chrisment, Festor, IFIP NTMS 2011); reported here as a supporting citation, not reproduced experimentally in this paper |

### Parameters
- Node and content identifier length: 160 bits (MLDHT identifier space)
- Zone sampling granularity for the monitoring system: 12-bit zones (nodes sharing a common 12-bit identifier prefix), one zone selected at random per 30-minute sampling round
- Monitoring interval: fixed 30-minute sampling rounds, running from December 2010 through the 2011 measurement period reported in the figures
- Honeypot deployment start: September 2011 for the MLDHT and BitTorrent honeypots (so no direct observational record exists for "Mr. ISP" activity before that date, though "Mr. 50" traffic first appeared in the authors' logs in January 2011)
- Minimum Sybils for a successful horizontal attack, as derived (not separately measured): N / max(k, log(N)), where N is total network size and k is the routing table's bucket size

### Stated limitations
The authors state explicitly that they observed no overtly malicious behavior from either identified attacker and have no concrete proof of actual malicious activity; the paper's claim is that the scale of the observed activity is large enough to be a concern, not that harm occurred. The identity of "Mr. 50" and "Mr. 184" as the same controlling party rests on both nodes implementing an identical, protocol-incorrect message-handling pattern; the authors state they attempted to detect coordination between the two by feeding each a different fake info hash and observing whether the other later requested it, and never observed such sharing, so the shared-identity claim remains a conjecture, not a demonstrated fact. The authors do not know how various BitTorrent client implementations react to a Sybil's protocol-incorrect replies, so they cannot state how much real query traffic a horizontal attack actually captures in deployed clients as opposed to what the protocol alone would allow. The paper reviews defenses (a centrally issued identity authority, monetary or IP-based identity certificates, physical-network-fingerprint identity binding, social-network-based Sybil defenses, and statistical distribution analysis to detect anomalous node density) and states each has a specific weakness: a central authority raises processing and administrative overhead and creates a barrier to legitimate nodes joining; an IP-based certificate scheme needs a separate mechanism for nodes behind firewalls or network address translators; physical-network-fingerprint schemes fail when network conditions change; social-network-based defenses require a social graph to already exist in the deployment; and distribution-analysis detection can be evaded by an attacker who monitors the same statistic and stays under the alarm threshold, and in any case cannot detect a horizontal attack because that attack raises node density uniformly rather than locally. The authors state there is no complete solution among these, only ways to raise the resource cost of mounting the attacks.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Any content-location or measurement system built on MLDHT that assumes a node's claimed identifier reflects a genuine distinct participant is false in this deployment, because MLDHT lets a node choose its own identifier and never requires the identifier returned in a PONG message to match the one requested in the preceding PING; a system safe against this needs an explicit consistency check between the requested and returned identifier plus a per-request challenge value, which the authors propose as a low-overhead protocol fix but which is not present in deployed MLDHT. Measurement studies of MLDHT session lengths or churn that infer online duration from repeated responsiveness to the same identifier will be biased upward wherever a horizontal attacker is present, because the attacker answers every probe regardless of the identifier's real owner; the authors state they are unaware of any prior MLDHT measurement study that accounts for this. A system relying on a k-closest-neighbor response to locate content assumes those neighbors are not colluding to intercept the query; the vertical attack shows that assumption fails whenever an attacker can insert k adjacent Sybils near a target identifier, which the current protocol does not prevent.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus at the time of writing. Cross-check candidate: WOLCHOK-WOOT-10 crawls the separate Vuze DHT (not MLDHT) using a Sybil-based technique with a different goal (content-search bootstrapping and IP-to-content monitoring rather than routing-layer traffic interception); the two papers target different DHT instances and should not be merged into one combined MLDHT-plus-Vuze Sybil-vulnerability figure.

### References worth retrieving
- foundational: Douceur, "The Sybil attack," IPTPS 2002 — defines the identity-forgery attack this paper's horizontal and vertical attacks both instantiate (already in corpus per BRIEF §7 baseline)
- foundational: Sit, Morris, "Security considerations for peer-to-peer distributed hash tables," IPTPS 2002 — cited as the origin of the free-identifier-choice vulnerability this paper exploits
- foundational: Urdaneta, Pierre, van Steen, "A survey of DHT security techniques," ACM Computing Surveys 43(2), 2011, pp. 8:1-8:49 — the survey this paper draws its defense catalogue from (already named as a dense bibliography in BRIEF §4.4)
- competing/attack: Timpanaro, Cholez, Chrisment, Festor, "BitTorrent's mainline DHT security assessment," IFIP NTMS, Feb. 2011 — the source of the "20 Sybils yields over 90% of a peer set" figure this paper cites without reproducing, and the distribution-analysis vertical-attack detector this paper argues is evadable
- competing: Varvello, Steiner, "Traffic localization for DHT-based BitTorrent networks," IFIP/TC6 Networking 2011, and Steiner, Varvello, "Peer-to-peer traffic localization as a service," INFOCOM Demo 2011 — the traffic-localization methodology "Mr. ISP" is compared against, described by the authors as less aggressive than what was observed in the wild
- competing: Le Blond, Legout, Lefessant, Dabbous, Kaafar, "Spying the world from your laptop," USENIX LEET 2010 — prior demonstration of user-privacy compromise via BitTorrent portal monitoring, cited as showing this paper's attacks enable the same violation more easily and at larger scale
- foundational: Castro, Druschel, Ganesh, Rowstron, Wallach, "Secure routing for structured peer-to-peer overlay networks," ACM SIGOPS Operating Systems Review 36 (SI), 2002, pp. 299-314 — proposes charging for identity certificates and embedding IP address in the certificate, cited as a candidate defense with a stated weakness for nodes behind firewalls
- competing/attack: Danezis, Lesniewski-Laas, Kaashoek, Anderson, "Sybil-resistant DHT routing," ESORICS 2005, pp. 305-318; Yu, Gibbons, Kaminsky, Xiao, "SybilLimit," IEEE S&P 2008; Yu, Kaminsky, Gibbons, Flaxman, "SybilGuard," ACM SIGCOMM 2006 — social-network-based Sybil defenses the authors state only apply where a social graph already exists in the deployment
- attack: Naoumov, Ross, "Exploiting P2P systems for DDoS attacks," InfoScale 2006; El Defrawy, Gjoka, Markopoulou, "BotTorrent: misusing BitTorrent to launch DDoS attacks," USENIX SRUTI 2007; Liang, Naoumov, Ross, "The index poisoning attack in P2P file sharing systems," IEEE Infocom 2006 — prior demonstrations that a compromised P2P routing layer enables denial-of-service, cited as the risk this paper's attack scale makes newly practical against MLDHT

### Verbatim extracts
- "the number of sybils in the Mainline DHT network is increasing and is currently around 300,000"
- "the minimum sybils needed to perform a successful horizontal attack is in fact N / max(k, log(N))"
- "the attacker only needs to insert 20 sybils to make a client receive over 90% of sybils"
- "the number of sybils injected by Mr. 50 varied between 80,000 and 290,000"
- "we have not observed any malicious behavior. However, causing considerable damage would be easy"
- "distribution analysis cannot protect against a horizontal attack, which increases the node density uniformly"

## [WANG-SIGCOMM-11] An Untold Story of Middleboxes in Cellular Networks

**Citation:** Zhaoguang Wang, Zhiyun Qian, Qiang Xu, Zhuoqing Morley Mao, Ming Zhang. "An Untold Story of Middleboxes in Cellular Networks." ACM SIGCOMM, 2011. Pages 374-385 (as paginated in text pp. 374-386). DOI 10.1145/2018436.2018479.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://conferences.sigcomm.org/sigcomm/2011/papers/sigcomm/p374.pdf
**Source URL:** https://conferences.sigcomm.org/sigcomm/2011/papers/sigcomm/p374.pdf
**Domain:** L

### What it does
NetPiculet is a measurement tool that infers a cellular carrier's Network Address Translation (NAT) and firewall policies end-to-end, without administrative access to carrier equipment, by coordinating probes between an Android client running inside the carrier's network and a dedicated server on the open Internet. For NAT mapping, it opens 12 back-to-back connections to 4 destinations using the same local port (following prior methodology) plus, as this paper's own addition, 12 more connections to a single destination using different local ports, to classify how a NAT box assigns external (IP, port) endpoints to internal connections: Independent (same external endpoint reused for every connection), Address-and-Port-dependent (external endpoint changes when the destination changes), or Connection-dependent (external endpoint changes for every new connection), each further classified by whether the port increments by a fixed value or a random value. For endpoint filtering, the client first establishes a connection to the server (creating a NAT mapping), then the server varies its own source address/port when sending unsolicited SYN packets back to that mapped external endpoint, and the client checks which packets it receives, to determine whether the NAT filters inbound packets by destination-endpoint match only or also checks the source. For firewall behavior, NetPiculet separately probes IP spoofing tolerance (client modifies the source-IP field of outgoing packets), TCP state-machine transitions (probing which sequences of SYN/SYN-ACK/ACK/DATA/FIN/RST packets are permitted, inferring a state diagram), TCP idle-connection timeout (multiple parallel connections held open without keep-alive, timed until reset), and out-of-order-packet buffering (whether packets outside the expected sequence window are dropped, buffered, or immediately delivered). Both server and client are implemented in C and Java, approximately 3,000 lines of code total, released as a free Android application to recruit a broad user base across carriers the authors could not access directly.

### Measured results
| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| NAT mapping: 30 of 72 carriers Independent, 15 Address-and-Port(fixed increment), 19 Connection(random increment), 5 Connection(time-dependent increment), 3 both Address-and-Port(time-dependent) and Connection(time-dependent) | 72 cellular carriers deploying NAT boxes, from ~400 users in 107 carriers total, two weeks of data collected January 2011 |
| 19 of 72 carriers (26.4%) exhibit random-port (Connection-random) NAT mapping, versus a 0.5% figure the authors cite for home NAT boxes from prior work | Same 72-carrier NAT-mapping dataset |
| A previously undocumented time-dependent NAT mapping (external port increments linearly with elapsed time, wrapping after reaching a maximum) found in 8 of the 72 carriers; controlled validation showed external port increasing linearly with time over a 30-minute session | Controlled experiment in Carrier B's network: one mobile client creating new connections at random 0-60 second intervals, each to the same destination port but a different local port, over 30 minutes |
| Endpoint filtering: 20 of 20 carriers (100%) use Address-and-Port filtering (most restrictive), versus 82% reported for home NATs in cited prior work | 20 cellular networks, subset of users running the client with root privilege (required for raw-socket-based tests) |
| TCP state tracking: 18 of 20 carriers allow an incoming SYN after an outgoing SYN; 18 of 20 allow an outgoing SYN-ACK after an outgoing SYN; one carrier (Hungary) disallows both sequences | Same 20-carrier root-privilege subset |
| Filtering response: 19 of 20 carriers silently drop unsolicited incoming SYN packets; 1 carrier (France) responds with RST | Same 20-carrier root-privilege subset |
| Packet mangling: 0 of 20 carriers modify TCP sequence numbers | Same 20-carrier root-privilege subset |
| A NAT-traversal scheme exploiting the time-dependent mapping (predicting external port from increment rate and elapsed time, then probing a window of ±15 ports around the predicted value) achieved 80% success within 12 seconds (12 trials at ~1-second timeout each) | 1,000 runs of an Android implementation, established between one phone on Carrier A (independent mapping) and one on Carrier B (time-dependent mapping); two unmodified commercial P2P video-chat apps (Fring, Tango) failed to establish a direct connection in the same environment |
| IP spoofing allowed by 4 of 60 carriers tested (6.7%); all 4 are large cellular ISPs in the U.S. and Europe; each of the 4 allows spoofing of a full /24 and /16 range | 60 cellular networks where the IP-spoofing test could run (requires root privilege) |
| Controlled IP-spoofing scan of one carrier found in the wild: 2-3 seconds for spoofed SYN packets to reach the external server, 3-4 more seconds for the server to scan and await responses; spoofing throughput bottlenecked at approximately 90 packets/second; 54 hosts on average responded per /24 scan | 10 repeated trials, controlled local experiment against one carrier previously identified as allowing IP spoofing |
| TCP inactivity timeout distribution: of 73 carriers measured, 4 have a timeout of 5 minutes or less, 7 in (5,10] minutes, 6 in (10,20] minutes, 8 in (20,30] minutes, 48 above 30 minutes | 73 carriers, NetPiculet timeout-inference test |
| Carrier A's firewall: ESTABLISHED-state inactivity timeout 1,800 seconds; TCP sequence-number acceptance window as large as 1G (sometimes 128K) depending on which firewall path a packet traverses; out-of-order packets buffered rather than dropped, for over an hour in controlled tests | Local controlled experiments plus wide-scale inference against Carrier A, a named U.S. nationwide cellular provider |
| Carrier B's firewall: ESTABLISHED-state inactivity timeout 255 seconds; SEQ window 128K; does not buffer out-of-order packets; a looser SYN-ACK-RCVD/SYN-RCVD-to-ESTABLISHED transition than Carrier A (accepts an ACK whose SEQ falls within ±128K of the previous SEQ); port 5228 (used by Google's push-notification service) observed with an extended 1,600-second timeout instead of the default 255 seconds | Local controlled experiments against Carrier B |
| Estimated energy cost of periodic keep-alive to hold open an idle TCP connection: over 17% of a 1,350 mAh smartphone battery's daily capacity consumed when the firewall timeout is under 5 minutes, dropping to under 2% for a 30-minute timeout | Derived using an existing cellular-interface power model (cited, not built by this paper) applied to the measured 73-carrier timeout distribution above |

### Parameters
- Test parallelization budget: all tests except TCP-timeout inference complete within 10 seconds on the client, to save user time and device battery
- NAT-mapping-type discovery probe count: 12 connections to 4 destinations (3 each) on the same local port, plus 12 additional connections to one destination on different local ports (24 total)
- IP-spoofing scan range tested: /24 and /16 address ranges
- Time-dependent-NAT port-prediction search window: ±n around the predicted port, with n=15 by default
- Time-dependent-NAT traversal retry interval: 1-second timeout between consecutive dial trials
- Measurement period: two weeks, January 2011
- Deployment scale: ~400 users, 107 carriers total (with smaller sub-populations for tests requiring root privilege or private-IP assignment)

### Stated limitations
NAT tests apply only to carriers that assign private IP addresses to devices (72 of 107 carriers in the dataset); carriers assigning only public IPs are excluded from this analysis entirely. Several probes (IP spoofing, TCP state-machine inference, packet-mangling detection) require raw-socket access, which needs root privilege not available on every phone, so those results are reported for a smaller subset (20-60 carriers) than the full 107-carrier or 72-carrier NAT-capable population. The full TCP state-machine diagram is measurement-intensive and time-consuming, so it was inferred only in local controlled experiments for two named U.S. carriers (A and B); the publicly released tool substitutes a simpler TCP-connection-timeout measurement rather than the full state diagram. The authors state their classification of a given policy as "NAT" or "firewall" is only a convenience label and may not correspond to the carrier's actual implementation, since a single network device can implement both functions, and their end-to-end black-box probes can infer only the existence of a policy, not its internal mechanism. The paper's NAT-load-balancing analysis (deriving that Carrier B splits traffic across two NAT boxes by the parity of source+destination port sum) is described by the authors as "2-way balancing solely based on our measurement observation"; the authors state a more complex hash function, or n-way balancing with n>2, would be "much more challenging" and explicitly leave this for future work. The authors state their findings, though drawn from cellular networks, likely generalize to wired-network middleboxes (e.g., time-dependent NAT mapping or out-of-order buffering could also occur there) but explicitly leave verification of that generalization as future work — they did not measure wired-network middleboxes in this study.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Any peer-to-peer NAT-traversal scheme that assumes a client sits behind exactly one NAT box with one consistent mapping type is unsupported for the 3 of 72 carriers this paper measured assigning a client's connections to two different NAT boxes (with two different mapping types and sometimes two different external IP addresses) depending on a hash of the connection's five-tuple; a traversal scheme must first discover and hold constant whichever five-tuple property the carrier's load-balancing hash keys on (in Carrier B's case, the parity of the summed source and destination port numbers) before it can assume a single, predictable NAT mapping applies. A traversal scheme relying on port-prediction (as this paper's own time-dependent-NAT traversal scheme does) requires knowing the specific NAT's port-increment behavior (fixed-value versus time-dependent versus fully random) in advance, obtained here only by first running NetPiculet's own 24-connection discovery probe against that specific carrier; a scheme lacking this per-network characterization step cannot distinguish a time-dependent mapping from the harder Connection-random case the paper found in 19 of 72 carriers, for which the authors state no traversal technique existed prior to this paper's own contribution (and which the birthday-paradox approach of NATBlaster, cited by this paper, needs 439 connections and root access to attempt). A component depending on a long-lived idle connection to a cellular endpoint (e.g., for push-based delivery) must either issue periodic keep-alives at an interval no larger than the carrier's inactivity timeout — measured here to be under 10 minutes for 11 of 73 carriers and under 5 minutes for 4 of 73 — or accept that the connection will be silently reset by the firewall and must be re-established, which the paper's own tested example (MSN Talk under Carrier B's 255-second timeout) confirms happens in practice. A design assuming firewall-level TCP state enforcement (e.g., relying on the firewall to reject connections with out-of-spec sequence numbers as a security boundary) cannot assume this holds broadly, since the measured acceptance window reaches up to 1G in Carrier A's firewall, which the paper's own security-implication discussion (§4.3.3, not itself reproduced here in full) uses as the basis for a feasible TCP RST-injection/hijacking attack surface.

### Contradicts
The paper's own finding directly contradicts a prior study cited within it: Makinen and Nurminen (cited [28] in this paper's related work) measured NAT properties from one vantage point in each of six cellular networks and concluded existing NAT-traversal techniques would work in cellular networks without modification; this paper's own 316-user, 72-carrier measurement instead finds 19 of 72 carriers (26.4%) use a Connection-random mapping type that existing techniques of the time could not handle, and identifies an entirely new time-dependent mapping type absent from prior classification schemes. No other paper in this corpus directly disagrees with this paper's own measured figures as of this batch; TRAUTWEIN-ARXIV-26 measures a different, later-generation, decentralized-relay-based traversal mechanism (DCUtR) rather than the direct port-prediction NAT traversal this paper studies, so the two are not measuring the same mechanism.

### References worth retrieving
- Guha, S., Francis, P. "Characterization and Measurement of TCP Traversal through NATs and Firewalls." ACM SIGCOMM IMC, 2005. — foundational (source of the ~100-commercial-NAT-box baseline this paper's 0.5%-random-port-mapping and 82%-Address-and-Port-filtering comparison figures are drawn from; also cited independently by TRAUTWEIN-ARXIV-26 as [13] Guha, "in the wild" 88% TCP success figure)
- Biggadike, A., Ferullo, D., Wilson, G., Perrig, A. "NATBLASTER: Establishing TCP Connections Between Hosts Behind NATs." ACM SIGCOMM Asia Workshop, 2005. — competing (birthday-paradox traversal scheme for random-port NAT, requiring 439 connections and root access, contrasted against this paper's lighter time-dependent-NAT traversal)
- MacDonald, D., Lowekamp, B. "NAT Behavior Discovery Using STUN." IETF draft-ietf-behave-nat-behavior-discovery-08. — foundational (defines the mapping/filtering/binding-time attribute taxonomy this paper's NAT classification builds on; also cited independently by TRAUTWEIN-ARXIV-26)

## [WANG-USENIXSEC-14] Effective Attacks and Provable Defenses for Website Fingerprinting
**Citation:** Tao Wang, Xiang Cai, Rishab Nithyanand, Rob Johnson, Ian Goldberg. "Effective Attacks and Provable Defenses for Website Fingerprinting." 23rd USENIX Security Symposium, 2014. Pages 143-157.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.usenix.org/system/files/conference/usenixsecurity14/sec14-paper-wang-tao.pdf
**Source URL:** https://www.usenix.org/system/files/conference/usenixsecurity14/sec14-paper-wang-tao.pdf
**Domain:** G

### What it does
This paper does two separate things: it presents a website fingerprinting (WF) attack based on a k-nearest-neighbors (k-NN) classifier, and it presents a family of provably private WF defenses built on packet-sequence supersequences. It is not the Walkie-Talkie paper — the registry's own retrieval-justification note misattributes this citation as "the Walkie-Talkie paper"; that paper is a separate 2017 USENIX Security publication by Wang and Goldberg (see Contradicts, below), which this paper cites only as a related technical report ("Comparing website fingerprinting attacks and defenses," CACR 2013-30) predating the actual Walkie-Talkie publication. The k-NN attack works as follows: for each candidate site, the attacker collects packet-sequence traces and computes distances between traces using a large feature set covering timing, packet-count, and packet-size statistics; feature weights are adjusted iteratively (over R rounds) to shrink the distance between traces of the same page and grow the distance between traces of different pages, and classification requires all k nearest neighbors to agree on a page label before that label is assigned, otherwise the trace is classified as non-monitored — a design choice the paper states reduces false positives at small cost to true positives. The provable defense works as follows: a defense is "simulatable" if it can be written as a function from a packet sequence to a padded output sequence with no side channel beyond that function, and "deterministic" if the function has no randomness; the paper proves that a simulatable, deterministic defense that pads every packet sequence in an anonymity set to a single shared supersequence (the shortest sequence that contains every member sequence as a subsequence) gives a formal upper bound on any attacker's classification accuracy over that set, because every output the defense produces observationally overlaps across every sequence in the set. Because computing an exact shortest common supersequence (SCS) over more than two sequences is NP-hard, the paper gives a polynomial-time approximation: at each step, an outgoing packet is emitted if more than one quarter of the remaining sequences have an outgoing packet next, otherwise an incoming packet is emitted, and each sequence's position pointer advances only when its next element matches the emitted direction. Anonymity sets are chosen by clustering packet sequences under one of four information levels available to the client at send time (no information, sequence-end information, class-specific/page-identity information, or full information), trading a smaller number of shared supersequences (lower client-side foreknowledge, higher padding overhead) against a larger number (more foreknowledge required, lower overhead).

### Measured results

|---|---|---|
