### Stated limitations
The attack assumes an oracle that identifies the start and end of a single page-load's packet sequence, and assumes the user does not interrupt the load or interleave other web activity; the paper offers heuristics (an initial burst of outgoing packets roughly three times the later rate) rather than a solved general mechanism. The paper states the attack is not effective at finding one sensitive page access among millions without a very low false-positive rate, and that attack usefulness depends heavily on the base incidence rate of monitored-page visits; at incidence below 0.1%, false alarms would overwhelm true positives with this classifier. It states that no attack is known to beat the accuracy upper bound of the new defense on this specific data set, but explicitly does not claim optimality against defenses not evaluated or against future attacks: "we do not know if there exist better attacks for these defenses." The polynomial-time supersequence approximation is stated to admit unboundedly poor cases in the worst case, citing a hardness result for approximating shortest common supersequences. Anonymity-set selection under partial information (sequence-end or class-level) is stated to be less efficient (higher bandwidth overhead) than full information, and the paper states its clustering strategy for class-level information may not be optimal — "a clever clustering strategy... could achieve lower bandwidth overheads" is left open.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The provable defense requires the client to determine, before or during a page load, which anonymity set (which shared supersequence) a load belongs to; the paper's four information levels bound what is realistic (full information, the strongest guarantee, requires knowledge of the load's entire future packet sequence in advance, which the paper states is "not generally of practical interest except for serving as a bound"). It requires the client to avoid storing extraneous browsing history to assist set selection, because on Tor Browser (no disk cache) such storage is itself a privacy risk distinct from the WF threat. It requires an attacker-side classifier trained on the specific defended distribution to be evaluated meaningfully — the paper always retrains and re-tests its k-NN attack directly against each defense's simulated output rather than assuming transferability across defenses. The defense's formal privacy bound holds only under the paper's simulatable/deterministic defense model; it does not extend a guarantee to random or non-simulatable defenses, and the paper explicitly separates BuFLO (not provably private on its own) from its own construction.

### Contradicts
This paper is not the Walkie-Talkie paper. The retrieval registry's justification field for this key states "This is the Walkie-Talkie paper," which this full text does not support: Walkie-Talkie is Wang and Goldberg, USENIX Security 2017, cited within this paper's own bibliography only as an earlier 2013 CACR technical report ("Comparing website fingerprinting attacks and defenses"), not as this paper's own contribution. Any figure in this corpus attributed to "Wang, Walkie-Talkie, USENIXSEC-14" under this key is misattributed; the actual Walkie-Talkie defense numbers (49.7% accuracy under symmetric collisions, 31% bandwidth / 34% latency overhead) appear as externally-cited results inside SIRINAM-CCS-18 in this batch, sourced to the true 2017 Walkie-Talkie paper, not to this one.

## [WEI-INFOCOM-12] SybilDefender: Defend Against Sybil Attacks in Large Social Networks
**Citation:** Wei Wei, Fengyuan Xu, Chiu C. Tan, Qun Li. "SybilDefender: Defend Against Sybil Attacks in Large Social Networks." IEEE INFOCOM, 2012. DOI 10.1109/INFCOM.2012.6195572.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.cs.wm.edu/~liqun/paper/infocom12_1.pdf
**Source URL:** https://www.cs.wm.edu/~liqun/paper/infocom12_1.pdf
**Domain:** F

### What it does
SybilDefender decides whether one specified suspect node in a social graph is a Sybil identity, and separately finds the whole cluster of Sybil nodes surrounding a known Sybil node, using only a bounded number of random walks rather than by processing the entire graph. It also proposes two measures for limiting how many attack edges (a link between a real user's node and a Sybil node) a real-world social network permits.

Mechanism, sybil identification: the social graph has a small cut of attack edges separating a large honest region from a smaller Sybil region. A random walk of a fixed length that starts inside the Sybil region tends to stay trapped inside it, so it visits (traverses) fewer distinct nodes than a same-length walk starting in the honest region. A pre-processing phase (run once per graph) picks a known honest node h, performs f short random walks of length log(n) from h to obtain f additional nodes that are honest with high probability under a fast-mixing assumption (defined below), and treats h plus those f nodes as judge nodes. For each candidate walk length l from a minimum l_min to a maximum l_max in steps of 100, the algorithm performs R random walks of length l from every judge node, counts for each judge node the number of nodes visited at least t times (t a small constant), and records the mean and standard deviation of that count across judges — producing one tuple (l, mean, stdDeviation) per length. To then test a suspect node u, the algorithm performs R random walks of length l starting from l_0 and doubles l on each iteration up to l_max; at each length it compares the suspect's own count of nodes visited at least t times against the judges' recorded mean for that length, and declares u a Sybil the first time the shortfall exceeds stdDeviation times a scaling constant alpha; if no length up to l_max triggers this, u is declared honest.

Mechanism, sybil community detection (finds the whole cluster around one already-known Sybil node s, rather than testing nodes one at a time): first estimate a suitable partial-walk length by repeatedly doubling a starting length and running R partial random walks from s at each candidate length until the fraction of "dead" walks (walks that exhaust the graph's reachable local region before reaching the target length) reaches a threshold beta close to 1. Then perform R partial random walks of that length from s, tally how often each node is visited, sort nodes by visit frequency, and greedily grow a candidate set S by adding nodes from the sorted list whenever doing so does not increase the set's conductance (the fraction of edge-endpoints in S that cross to outside S, a measure of how tight the boundary cut around S is); repeat sweeping the list until conductance stops improving across two full passes, and output the resulting S as the detected Sybil community.

Mechanism, limiting attack edges (two proposed techniques, evaluated only by a user survey, not by an attack simulation): (1) let users rate each of their existing relationships as "Friend" or "Stranger" through a purpose-built application, and drop "Stranger"-rated edges before running Sybil defense; (2) restrict the graph used for defense to an "activity network," where an edge exists only between users who have actually interacted (not merely declared a relationship), which is argued to naturally exclude unused attack edges.

### Measured results
All experiments use two full real-world social-graph data sets: Orkut (3,072,441 nodes, 117,185,083 edges, average degree 76.28) and Facebook (3,097,165 nodes, 28,377,481 edges, average degree 18.32) — described in the paper as the largest data sets ever used to evaluate topology-based Sybil defenses at the time. Sybil regions were synthetically attached to these real graphs using either a Preferential Attachment (PA, scale-free) model or an Erdos-Renyi (ER, random) model; the PA sybil region's average degree matches the host data set's average degree, while the ER sybil region's average degree ranges from 8 to 11 (a sparse topology by comparison). All experiments used the full published data sets with no small-degree-node pre-filtering (unlike some prior evaluations the paper cites).

| Experiment | Conditions | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Random-walk coverage difference, honest vs. Sybil origin | PA-model Sybil region of 10,000 nodes, 1,000 attack edges, 1,000 random walks per source node, mean of 20 experiments per point, random-walk length swept to 10,000 hops | At walk length 10,000, the honest-origin curve exceeds the Sybil-origin curve by more than 200,000 nodes visited at frequency >= 5; observed standard deviation of the judge-node counts stayed under 1,500 |

| t (visit-frequency threshold) | 5 | fixed |

| f (number of extra judge nodes derived from h) | 100 | fixed |
| R (random walks per node tested, sybil identification) | swept over {1000, 1500, 2000} | this is the one parameter varied across the main result table |
| l_0 (starting length, community detection) | 100 | fixed |
| beta (dead-walk-ratio threshold, community detection) | 0.95 | fixed |
| R (partial walks, community detection) | 2000 | fixed |
| Number of attack edges (main sybil-identification experiments) | 1,000 | held fixed while sybils-per-attack-edge was varied |
| SybilLimit comparison parameters | w=20 hops, r=10,000 random routes | taken from SybilLimit's own paper's stated optimum for this data set |
| Gatekeeper comparison parameters | m=100, f_admit=0.2 | taken from Gatekeeper's authors' recommendation |

### Stated limitations
SybilDefender is explicitly a centralized mechanism: "the administrator knows the social network topology," justified only by the observation that all current online social networks are already under centralized administrative control — it is not designed to run without a central party with full graph visibility. It assumes at least one node in the network is already known with certainty to be honest, as the starting point for the whole identification algorithm; the paper does not test what happens if that assumption is violated. It assumes the size of the Sybil region is not comparable to the size of the honest region, and states this is reasonable only by appeal to the large user bases of networks like Facebook, Twitter, and Orkut at the time and to account-creation friction (email verification, CAPTCHAs); the paper provides no bound on how close the two region sizes can get before the identification algorithm breaks down. It assumes the honest region is fast-mixing (a random walk of length Theta(log n) converges to the graph's stationary distribution with probability at least 1 - 1/n), citing prior work (Yu et al.) as having shown real social networks are fast-mixing, without re-validating that claim itself. It assumes the number of attack edges is limited, and the paper's own survey data shows this assumption is not automatically satisfied on real online social networks (Bilge et al.'s prior finding that roughly 20% of bogus friendship requests on Facebook are accepted, cited by the authors, and the authors' own survey finding 19.8% of rated relations are "Stranger"). Nodes that lie directly on the small cut (compromised nodes connected by attack edges) are the ones the algorithm systematically fails to identify correctly, in both the identification and community-detection algorithms — this is stated as the source of essentially all observed errors, not merely a hypothetical edge case. Finding the true minimum-size cut between honest and Sybil regions is NP-hard, which the paper states as the reason the community-detection algorithm approximates the cut with the greedy conductance heuristic instead of solving it exactly.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Requires a single administrative party (or a coalition acting as one) with complete, current knowledge of the social graph's full edge set; the algorithm cannot run against a graph only partially visible to the party running it. Requires that party to already hold, from some external source, at least one node identity it is certain is honest, since the whole judge-node bootstrap in the pre-processing phase is derived by walking outward from that single node — the mechanism supplies no way to establish that certainty internally. Requires the graph to remain fast-mixing on the honest side, which depends on the honest population not being fragmented into many small, weakly-interconnected communities (the paper notes but does not test this failure mode; it is the same failure mode later measured directly against a related family of methods in GAO-CNS-18). Requires that the number of attack edges stays small relative to network size for the small-cut/conductance signal to exist at all — a network that does not maintain this (as the paper's own survey suggests real online social networks may not) removes the basis for both the identification and the community-detection algorithms. Supplies, but does not itself enforce, two techniques (manual relationship rating, or restricting to an interaction-derived activity network) intended to keep the attack-edge count low; each requires either a separate user-facing rating application or an independently available interaction log, neither of which SybilDefender's core algorithms provide.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus regarding SybilDefender's own reported figures. This paper's own re-implementation and measurement of SybilLimit produce substantially higher false-negative rates for SybilLimit (up to 85.3% at low sybils-per-attack-edge) than SybilLimit's asymptotic O(log n)-sybils-per-attack-edge claim might suggest in isolation — a case where an independent re-measurement (by a competing paper's authors) diverges sharply from the originating paper's own framing, illustrating exactly the kind of re-measurement disagreement this corpus is built to preserve; no direct textual figure from the original SybilLimit paper is quoted here to compare against, so the two cannot be set side by side numerically without retrieving SybilLimit (Yu et al., IEEE S&P 2008) directly.

- "there is at least one known honest node in the social network."
- "the size of the sybil region is not comparable to the size of the honest region."
- "finding small cuts in a graph is an NP hard problem."
- "the algorithm alone cannot be used to identify the sybil nodes."
- "the average percentage of strangers among all the relations is 19.8%."

## [WEI-NSDI-24] The Eternal Tussle: Exploring the Role of Centralization in IPFS
**Citation:** Yiluo Wei, Dennis Trautwein, Yiannis Psaras, Ignacio Castro, Will Scott, Aravindh Raman, Gareth Tyson. "The Eternal Tussle: Exploring the Role of Centralization in IPFS." USENIX/ACM NSDI, 2024.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.usenix.org/system/files/nsdi24-wei.pdf
**Source URL:** https://www.usenix.org/conference/nsdi24/presentation/wei
**Domain:** A+J

### What it does
The paper, written by IPFS (InterPlanetary File System) core maintainers at Protocol Labs, reports on three centralized components deliberately added to the deployed IPFS system to compensate for measured weaknesses of the pure Kademlia-DHT (distributed hash table) design, and measures each component's effect using operational data from the live network. It is a measurement-and-engineering-experience paper, not a proposal of a new decentralized mechanism.

InterPlanetary Network Indexers (Indexers): a server-based key-value store that receives an announcement message from a content provider (containing a batch, or "advertisement," of many content-identifier-to-provider mappings, possibly 16,000-20,000 records at once) and answers CID-or-multihash lookup queries over a RESTful HTTP API, bypassing DHT traversal entirely. Advertisements form a hash-linked chain per provider, so an Indexer can reconstruct all of a provider's records by walking the chain and can audit what a provider has published. Indexers gossip announcement messages among themselves (over Gossipsub) and cache query results at a frontend server ahead of the backing Pebble database.

Hydra Boosters: a set of DHT-server nodes ("Hydra Heads") deliberately positioned across the Kademlia identifier space so that, in expectation, every ordinary peer has at least one Hydra Head within its 20-peer XOR-proximity bucket. All heads share one backing database (Amazon DynamoDB), so a query answered by any head can return provider records collected by every other head, collapsing what would otherwise require multiple DHT hops into fewer hops.

HTTP Gateways: a small set of HTTP-to-IPFS bridge servers that let an ordinary web client fetch IPFS content without installing IPFS software. A gateway runs Nginx with default web caching in front of a co-located IPFS node's own block-storage cache, so already-fetched or already-stored content is served without any DHT lookup.

### Measured results
| Metric | Figure | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Total provider records held | Indexer: 173,998,039,712 (~0.17 trillion); DHT: over 100x fewer | Indexer dataset snapshot 2023-04-24 UTC, from the Protocol-Labs-operated Indexer at cid.contact; DHT count from the paper's own Hydra Booster database |
| Number of distinct publishers | Indexer: 604 major providers (mostly NFT or storage services); DHT: ~56,000 providers | Same datasets |
| Query rate | Indexer: 2.5k lookup requests/second; DHT: ~5k GET-PROVIDER requests/second (estimated from Hydra Booster logs) | Operational logs |
| Advertisement synchronization time vs. DHT publication time | Indexer ~2x faster at the 50th percentile; per-record indexing time ~500 microseconds because most advertisements batch 16K-20K records | Sample of 16,757,817 provider records ingested 2023-04-24, out of ~5.3 billion processed/day; DHT publication time from separate active-measurement dataset |
| Indexer query performance | 62,611,156 successful HTTP requests over one day (2023-04-18 09:05 UTC to 2023-04-19 09:05 UTC), 246.77 GB served; average cache hit rate 65.22%; cache hits ~100x faster than DHT lookup at the 50th percentile; even the 34.78% cache-miss requests outperform DHT lookup | Amazon CloudFront request logs for the Indexer frontend |
| Overall Indexer lookup time vs. DHT | ~10x faster than DHT at the 50th percentile | Comparison of Indexer CloudFront logs against DHT lookup time from the six-region active-retrieval experiment |
| Hydra Booster content lookup time improvement (median), with vs. without shared database | us-west-1 +36.5%, af-south-1 +25.1%, ap-southeast-2 +16.4%, sa-east-1 +11.7%, me-south-1 +3.8%, eu-central-1: no improvement | Six AWS regions, one IPFS DHT server node each (Kubo v0.16.0), 0.5 MB object published from one randomly-selected node and retrieved by all others each iteration, nodes disconnected between iterations to force DHT-based (not Bitswap-based) resolution; "with" window 2022-11-25 15:27 UTC to 2022-12-01 17:30 UTC; "without" window (database unplugged from Hydra Boosters, heads kept but reconfigured) 2022-12-01 17:30 UTC to 2022-12-08 20:00 UTC; retrieval counts per region ranged 9,590-10,375 (with) and 12,084-13,233 (without) |
| Single-hop DHT walk rate, with vs. without Hydra database | af-south-1 41.45% vs. <5%; ap-southeast-2 27.81% vs. ~2%; eu-central-1 26.68% vs. ~2%; me-south-1 29.79% vs. ~2%; sa-east-1 17.04% vs. ~2%; us-west-1 46.64% vs. ~2%; without Hydras, ~20% of walks in every region need 3+ hops | Same six-region experiment |
| Hydra Head proximity coverage | 96.6% of 16,208 measured peers have at least one Hydra Head in their 20-proximity; mean number of Hydra heads within a peer's 20-proximity is 2.36; 99.5% of peers have at most 5 | DHT routing-table snapshot, 2,015 total Hydra heads across 135 Hydra Booster instances (10-15 heads each) on Amazon ECS in us-east-1 |
| Gateway content lookup time vs. DHT | ~100x faster than DHT at the 50th percentile for cached content; 24 ms at the 95th percentile for cached objects; non-cached content lookup time comparable to raw DHT lookup, plus added forwarding overhead | Gateway dataset: all HTTP GET requests on 2023-03-15 UTC, 69,339,954 successful requests from 1,645,611 IP addresses, 91,869 GB served |
| Gateway cache hit rates | Nginx cache hit rate 50.3%; co-located IPFS node storage hit rate 27.6% | Same gateway dataset |
| Gateway retrieval-performance improvement rate | Better than DHT lookup time in ~95% of cases (gateway); Indexer better than DHT in ~90% of cases | Aggregate of the above comparisons |
| Gateway client adoption | 771,977 users via mobile user-agents, 776,286 via desktop user-agents, 195,854 via net tools/libraries (each unique IP counted as one user); 18.8% of requests / 31.8% of traffic from mobile, 29.8% of requests / 32.9% of traffic from desktop | Same gateway dataset, one day |
| Gateway referral-driven traffic | 51.6% of traffic and 29.8% of requests carry an HTTP Referer header pointing to another site; 70.23% of referred requests originate from just 23 of the top-100 referral sites; referred requests come from 1,312,066 users vs. 405,087 users for non-referred requests | Same gateway dataset |
| Estimated Indexer server cost | Capital expenditure $5,000-10,000; operating expenditure ~$1,000/month | Author-stated operational figure, no measurement methodology given |

### Parameters
- DHT replication factor for provider records, cited as the baseline the Indexer departs from: k=20 peers (paper cites Maymounkov and Mazières, [30]).
- Hydra Booster deployment: 135 nodes on Amazon ECS in us-east-1, 10-15 heads per node, 2,015 total heads.
- Active-retrieval test object size: 0.5 MB per published CID.
- Hydra-disabled condition (used as the "without" baseline): ADD-PROVIDER queries to Hydra Heads ignored (heads make up ~10-15% of the network, so this is described as "artificially decreasing the k-replication to 19"); GET-PROVIDER queries answered with closer-peer lists only, no provider records, because the shared database is disconnected.
- Nginx and IPFS-node caching layers at each gateway: default Nginx web cache in front of a co-located IPFS node's own block cache; no explicit cache-size or eviction-policy parameter is stated in the reviewed text.
- Number of publicly known Indexers at time of writing: 7. Number of gateways: over 80.

### Stated limitations
The authors state the Indexer introduces a single point of failure: some provider records exist only in the Indexer and are not replicated in the DHT, so a centralized Indexer failure can make "significant volumes" of provider records inaccessible; they state this risk is only partially mitigated by inter-Indexer Gossipsub announcement sharing, which "offers no hard guarantees on real-time synchronization." They state the Indexer's monetary operating cost ($5,000-10,000 capital, ~$1,000/month) contrasts with the DHT's load-spreading design, which needs no comparable individual hardware investment. They state Hydra Booster failure (of the shared DynamoDB database, or of the routing function itself) degrades performance (they measured up to 36.5%) but does not reduce content availability, because peers fall back to ordinary DHT routing; they state they observed no failed retrievals when Hydra Boosters were excluded from routing entirely. They state a centralized entity operating multiple Hydra Heads could theoretically attempt result poisoning or eclipse attacks, but argue (not measure) that IPFS's self-validating content identifiers (CIDs) limit a Hydra Head to, at most, forcing a re-query rather than delivering falsified content, and that the low mean Hydra-Head density in any single peer's proximity set (2.36) limits routing-manipulation leverage. They state gateways sacrifice IPFS's end-to-end cryptographic content validation, creating a man-in-the-middle exposure that would require additional client-side hash verification to close, which they say "may undermine the goal of improving adoption." They state that as centralized instances, Indexers, Hydra Boosters, and gateways let their operators monitor which content identifiers are queried by which clients, and that most clients' reliance on Protocol-Labs-operated instances of these three components is "not a sustainable solution" given the resulting dependency. They state privacy and censorship attacks are independently possible in the pure decentralized DHT routing layer as well (citing Balduf et al. [10] and Sridhar et al. [37]), so the centralized components are not the sole source of that exposure, though the paper does not quantify the DHT-only attack surface itself. They state none of the three types of incentive they identify for third-party Indexer/Gateway operators (storage-service self-interest, application self-interest, ecosystem-alignment interest) is a "formal incentive model," and that it is undetermined whether third-party uptake will be wide without one.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A content-identifier-to-provider indexing layer that adds a centralized fast path (as the Indexer does) requires the content addressing scheme underneath it to be self-validating (a hash-derived content identifier) so that a compromised or malicious index operator cannot substitute false content, only false or withheld provider pointers — this paper's own security argument for Hydra-Booster safety depends specifically on that property and does not hold for an indexing layer sitting in front of a non-self-validating naming scheme. A fallback-to-DHT design for availability (as used for both Hydra Boosters and, implicitly, gateways) requires the DHT to remain independently reachable and populated at all times; the paper's own robustness argument for Hydra Boosters rests entirely on ordinary DHT routing continuing to function when the centralized accelerator is absent, so a design that lets the DHT's own participant population shrink (for example, by deprecating DHT-server responsibilities in favor of only using the Indexer) would remove the fallback this paper relies on for its no-availability-loss claim. Any accounting of "decentralization" for this class of system needs to state which of at least four separate observable channels it measures — content-provider count, publication volume, query volume, or entry-point traffic — because this paper's own data shows these four diverge sharply (56,000 DHT publishers vs. 604 Indexer publishers, but the Indexer holding over 100x more provider records).

### Contradicts
No claim commonly attributed to this paper was found unsupported by its text; the paper is explicit that Indexers "do not replace the DHT" and that the DHT "still plays a larger role" by publisher count and query volume even though the Indexer holds the numerical majority of provider records — a nuance a headline restatement of "one centralized indexer holds over 100x the DHT's location records" (as flagged by the target registry's why_needed note) risks flattening if the publisher-count and query-volume figures are dropped.
Disagrees with BALDUF-IMC-23 on IPFS cloud/DHT-node-hosting share: this paper does not itself report a DHT cloud-hosting percentage in the sections reviewed, but is the direct target of BALDUF-IMC-23's methodological critique — BALDUF-IMC-23 attributes the 2022 Trautwein-et-al. figure of "less than 3% of cloud nodes" (a predecessor measurement by overlapping authors, cited in this paper's own bibliography as [41], Trautwein et al., ACM SIGCOMM 2022) to a counting-methodology difference, not to network change; this NSDI-24 paper by largely the same author group does not revisit that cloud-hosting percentage, so the two papers' cloud-centralization findings are not directly comparable on the topology channel, only on the indexing/traffic channels this paper covers.

### References worth retrieving
- Maymounkov, Mazières, "Kademlia: A peer-to-peer information system based on the XOR metric" (cited as [30]) — foundational (already in corpus per BRIEF section 7).
- Trautwein, Raman, Tyson, Castro, Scott, Schubotz, Gipp, Psaras, "Design and evaluation of IPFS: a storage layer for the decentralized web," ACM SIGCOMM 2022 (cited as [41]) — foundational, prior measurement by an overlapping author group, source of the <3% cloud-node figure disputed in BALDUF-IMC-23.
- Balduf, Henningsen, Florian, Rust, Scheuermann (cited as [10]) — attack/critique, cited by this paper as showing privacy attacks are possible in the decentralized DHT routing subsystem independent of Indexers/gateways.
- Sridhar, Ascigil, Keizer, Genon, Pierre, et al. (cited as [37]) — attack/critique, cited by this paper as showing censorship is possible in the purely decentralized IPFS DHT.
- Vyzovitis, Napora, McCormick, Dias, et al. (cited as [42], likely the libp2p GossipSub specification/paper) — foundational, the protocol used for inter-Indexer announcement gossip.
- Singh, Castro, Druschel, Rowstron, "Defending against Eclipse attacks on overlay networks" (cited as [36]) — attack/critique, cited by this paper regarding the theoretical Hydra-Booster eclipse-attack concern.
- Kaashoek, Karger, "Koorde: A simple degree-optimal distributed hash table" (cited as [26]) — foundational, listed among prior DHT structures in related work.
- Rowstron, Druschel, "Pastry: Scalable, decentralized object location and routing" (cited as [34]) — foundational, listed among prior DHT structures in related work.

## [WEI-PACMNET-25] An Empirical Analysis of the Nostr Social Network: Decentralization, Availability, and Replication Overhead

**Citation:** Yiluo Wei, Gareth Tyson. "An Empirical Analysis of the Nostr Social Network: Decentralization, Availability, and Replication Overhead." Proceedings of the ACM on Networking, 2025. DOI 10.1145/3768994.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.05709
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.05709
**Domain:** J+K

### What it does
The paper measures Nostr, a decentralized social network in which users publish signed posts to any number of independently operated relays (open storage-and-forward servers holding no shared state with each other), and clients connect directly to whichever relays they choose to read from and write to, with no server-to-server federation protocol between relays. Because a user is not bound to one server, the same post can exist as identical copies (replicas) on many relays simultaneously, and a client seeking a given user's posts must independently connect to and query every relay that user is known to use. The authors build two datasets over a six-month window: a relay dataset, giving each relay's metadata, hosting Autonomous System (AS, the routing-visible network block a server is hosted within), and 15-minute-interval availability snapshots; and an event dataset, obtained by connecting directly to every crawled relay and recording, for every unique post, users, and micropayment ("zap") record, exactly which relays hold a copy. From these they compute relay-level, country-level, and AS-level concentration of posts and users; relay uptime and outage-duration distributions; relay income from admission fees and zap payments against an estimated operating cost; per-post replication counts; simulated censorship-style relay and AS removal and its effect on the fraction of posts still reachable from at least one surviving relay; and, from a reconstructed follower graph, the volume of duplicate download traffic caused by a client independently fetching the same post from every relay it shares with the post's author. The paper then proposes two client-side-only mechanisms — capping the number of relays each post is pushed to (optionally weighted to spread across ASes) and a top-N relay-selection rule for retrieval — and evaluates each by replaying the same removal simulation against the capped dataset.

### Measured results

| Quantity | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Relays discovered online at least once | 911, of which 712 yielded usable event data | Daily crawl of the nostr.watch relay index, 2023-07-01 to 2023-12-31; the 199 excluded relays had no published events (58% of exclusions), went permanently offline shortly after appearing (41%), or required payment to read (1%) |
| Free vs. paid relays | 625 free, 87 paid (of 712) | Same dataset, classified from each relay's self-published relay information document |
| Posts collected | 17,851,871 | Crawled from all 712 relays, 2023-07-01 to 2023-12-31 |
| Unique users (pubkeys) | 1,558,891 | Users who posted at least once in the same window |
| Zap (micropayment) transactions | 252,905 transactions, totaling 305,427,302 Satoshi (~137,000 USD at measurement-period exchange rate; 1 Bitcoin = 100,000,000 Satoshi) | Same crawl window; 52% of zap transactions did not publicly disclose their amount |
| Post concentration at single top relay | 73% of all posts present on the single top relay | Same 17.85M-post dataset; the authors note this alone overstates centralization because a post can exist on multiple relays simultaneously |
| Mean replication factor | 34.6 relays per post, and 12.4 ASes per post | Computed over the full 17.85M-post dataset |
| Country-level concentration | US hosts 85% of posts and 30% of users; ~52% of countries host fewer than 2 relays; most of the top 15 countries by relay count each still hold >=20% of posts, with Canada, France, Germany, Finland each above 40% | Same dataset, IP-geolocated via the IP-API service |
| Comparison to Mastodon country concentration | Mastodon: 89.1% of toots concentrated in Japan, US, France combined (cited from Raman et al., IMC 2019) vs. Nostr's more distributed pattern above | Cross-paper comparison, both measurements from the respective papers' own full datasets |
| AS-level concentration | 64% of ASes host only 1 relay; all of the top 15 ASes (ranked by relay count) each host >15% of posts | Same dataset |
| Relay uptime | 50% of relays available >99% of the 2023-10-01 to 2023-12-31 window; ~20% of relays down >40% of the time; after excluding 132 relays classed "dead" (offline continuously for over a week through the end of measurement), 90% of remaining relays operational >80% of the time | 15-minute-interval availability polling, 3-month window |
| Outage duration | 56% of outages last under 15 minutes; 10% last over 100 minutes; free and paid relays show nearly identical outage-duration distributions; relays with >1M posts have only 1% of outages lasting over 1000 minutes, versus 88% for relays with <100 posts | Same 3-month polling window, outage durations grouped by relay post count |
| Admission fee for paid relays | 35% of paid relays charge under 1,000 Satoshi (~$0.45 USD); 15% charge over 10,000 Satoshi (~$45 USD) | From relay information documents, same dataset |
| Zap income distribution | 64% of relays receive zero zaps; among those that do, the 90th percentile receives 471 zap transactions totaling 150,000 Satoshi (~$67 USD) | Same 6-month zap dataset |
| Income vs. estimated operating cost | Most free relays with >10 users fail to cover an estimated 6-month operating cost (estimated by analogy to the published cost of running a similarly sized Mastodon instance); most paid relays with 50-1,000 users do cover it | 6-month income estimated from admission fees times active users plus zap income, projected to 184 days where a relay's observed lifetime was shorter |
| Post availability under relay removal | Remains near 90% after removing the top 50 relays ranked by user count; ranked by post count, stays above 90% until the top 30th relay removed, then drops to 71% by the top 50th | Simulated sequential removal of top-X relays by post count or user count; a post counted available if replicated on at least 1 surviving relay |
| Post availability under AS removal | Over 80% of posts remain available after removing the top 10 ASes | Same simulation, AS-level removal; contrasted against Mastodon's federation graph, where the equivalent Raman et al. figure is under 10% availability after removing the top 10 ASes |
| Replication redundancy | 50% of posts replicated across >14 relays; 25% across >49 relays; capping maximum replication at N=20 eliminates 380 million (61.7%) post replications; capping at N=10 eliminates a further 100 million, for 480 million (77.9%) total | Computed over the full 17.85M-post dataset by summing, for every post P with replica count M_P > N, the excess M_P - N |
| Duplicate-retrieval traffic waste | Average optimal retrieval count per follower edge (each post fetched once) is 1,130 posts; actual estimated retrieval count is 62,839 posts per edge; 98% of traffic is wasted for over 50% of follower edges; overall 98.2% of download traffic is wasted, totaling 144 TiB | Computed over a reconstructed follower graph of 3.5 million follower relationships, assuming a client retrieves every followed user's posts from every relay it shares with that user |
| AS-diversity replication-cap strategy vs. random-selection baseline | For N=10 replicas: AS-aware selection gives average availability difference from the uncapped original of -0.39% after removing the top 50 relays and -0.53% after removing the top 30 ASes; random selection gives -1.15% and -8.38% respectively for the same removal counts | Simulated using the same relay/AS removal method as the uncapped case, applied to a dataset modified so each post's replica set is first reduced to N=5, 10, 15, or 20 (plus N=2 as a low-replication illustration), using either random relay selection or AS-spanning selection for the retained replicas |
| Retrieval-side top-N relay selection (post coverage) | Retrieving only from the top 4 or top 5 relays (ranked by how many of a given sender's posts they hold) gives 90% of senders 100% post coverage | Computed over the same 17.85M-post dataset and the per-user relay usage sets |
| Retrieval-side top-N selection (following-edge completeness and traffic saved) | At N=5 retained relays per followed user: 99.4% post completeness achieved, retrieval count reduced by 93% versus the uncapped case, wasting 10.2 TiB (7.1%) of the traffic instead of 143.9 TiB | Table 1 in the source, computed over the 3.5M-edge follower graph; results also given for N=2 (99.0% completeness, 1.7% wasted), N=3 (99.2%, 3.5% wasted), N=4 (99.3%, 5.4% wasted) |

### Parameters
Relay-removal simulation swept top-X removed relays from 0 to 50 and top-X removed ASes from 0 to roughly 30, ranked separately by post count, user count, and (for ASes) relay count. Replication-cap evaluation swept N in {2, 5, 10, 15, 20}. Retrieval-side top-N relay selection swept N in {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}. Relay availability measured every 15 minutes over a 3-month window (2023-10-01 to 2023-12-31); event and relay-list crawling ran over a 6-month window (2023-07-01 to 2023-12-31). A relay is classified "dead" once continuously offline for more than a week through the end of the measurement window; 132 relays met this criterion.

### Stated limitations
Excluding offline and paywalled relays from the dataset may skew results toward the behavior of publicly accessible relays only. Relay-availability findings depend on third-party monitoring data from nostr.watch rather than independent probing by the authors, though they state this also avoids bias from a relay banning their own probing infrastructure specifically. Geolocation and IP-to-AS mapping depend on the IP-API service and may carry mapping errors. The estimate of relay operating cost is derived by analogy to published Mastodon hosting prices, not from surveying Nostr relay operators directly. The censorship-simulation only models relay-level and AS-level attacks, not country-level censorship, which the authors state has been documented elsewhere (citing measurement studies of censorship in China and Turkmenistan). The proposed AS-spanning replication-cap strategy is stated to potentially create a new attack surface: a relay that is the sole relay hosted in its AS becomes a high-value, easily identified single point of failure for every post the AS-spanning strategy assigned to it, and the paper's own resilience evaluation only models whole-AS failure, not this more targeted single-relay attack, leaving Nostr's resilience under such targeted adversarial relay selection an explicitly stated open question. The evaluation of the client-side retrieval optimization measures bandwidth savings only and does not measure the resulting effect on user-perceived latency or on content consistency during a query fallback (when the top-N relays do not hold a wanted post). The simulation assumes uniform adoption of the proposed client behavior and does not model users adaptively circumventing the replication cap or strategically choosing which relay subset to use. The proposed mechanisms address only the operational-cost side of relay sustainability; the authors state they introduce no new revenue mechanism, and cite exploring micropayments or tokenization as future work to address the underlying lack of financial incentive. The six-month dataset (ending late 2023) represents one point in a rapidly evolving network, and the authors state relay stability, user base, and client behavior may since have changed; a longitudinal follow-up and a comparative study against Bluesky are cited as future work.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A content-location or discovery layer consuming Nostr-style multi-relay replication needs a mechanism for a client to learn which relays hold a given user's or a given post's replicas, since the paper's own duplicate-retrieval measurement shows that without such a mechanism a client defaults to querying every relay it shares with an author, producing the measured 98.2% wasted-traffic outcome. A replication-capping mechanism that targets AS diversity requires, before it can select a spanning subset, prior knowledge of each candidate relay's hosting AS; the paper computes this via the IP-API third-party service and states this dependency introduces potential geolocation error. Any component relying on the paper's censorship-resilience figures (near-90% availability after 50-relay or 10-AS removal) inherits an assumption that failures occur at the granularity of whole relays or whole ASes; the paper explicitly does not model or bound resilience against an adversary that targets specific relays chosen for their structural position (e.g., the sole relay in a small AS), and states this is an open question for its own proposed AS-spanning capping strategy. A relay-sustainability mechanism built on the paper's income analysis needs an external revenue source beyond admission fees and zap payments to keep free relays with more than roughly 10 users solvent, since the paper's own cost-vs-income comparison finds most such relays do not cover an estimated operating cost from those two revenue sources alone.

### Contradicts
Common misattribution: none identified in the retrieved text that the paper itself flags as a misreading of its own results.
Cross-paper: this paper's post-availability-under-AS-removal figure (>80% availability after top-10 AS removal, Nostr) directly contrasts with RAMAN-IMC-19's Mastodon figure (availability collapsing to <10% after top-10 AS removal), which the paper cites explicitly as the comparison baseline; both figures are measured, not claimed, and the difference is attributed by this paper to Nostr's more uniform relay distribution across ASes versus Mastodon's instance-hosting concentration in a few major providers.

- Leonhard Balduf, Saidu Sokoto, Onur Ascigil, Gareth Tyson, Ignacio Castro, Andrea Baronchelli, George Pavlou, Björn Scheuermann, Michał Król, "Bootstrapping Social Networks: Lessons from Bluesky Starter Packs," arXiv:2501.11605, 2025 — competing (Bluesky bootstrapping/growth mechanics, relevant to cross-platform comparison).

## [WESOLOWSKI-EUROCRYPT-19] Efficient verifiable delay functions
**Citation:** Benjamin Wesolowski. "Efficient verifiable delay functions." EUROCRYPT, 2019.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://eprint.iacr.org/2018/623.pdf
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2018/623.pdf
**Domain:** I

### What it does
This paper constructs a verifiable delay function (VDF): a function that takes a specified number of sequential steps to evaluate and produces an output any observer can check far faster than that evaluation took. The construction builds a trapdoor VDF first: a version in which a party holding a secret key (the trapdoor) can compute the output quickly, while anyone without the trapdoor needs the full sequential computation. Deriving a plain VDF from it means running the trapdoor-VDF setup in a way that discards or never generates the trapdoor, so nobody, including whoever ran the setup, can compute the output faster than the stated delay. The trapdoor construction works over a group of unknown order G (an RSA group, or the class group of an imaginary quadratic field, chosen because nobody can efficiently compute that group's order without extra secret information). Evaluation on input x for delay parameter t computes y = x^(2^t) mod the group's modulus by t sequential squarings; someone holding the trapdoor (knowledge of the group's order, i.e. Euler's totient for an RSA modulus) can compute the same 2^t-th power directly via modular exponentiation of the exponent reduced modulo the order, skipping the sequential squarings. The proof of correctness is a single group element pi computed as follows: the verifier or, via the Fiat-Shamir transform, a hash function derives a random prime number l from the statement (g, y); the prover computes pi = g^floor(2^t / l); the verifier computes r = 2^t mod l and checks that y equals pi^l times g^r. Producing this proof takes O(t / log t) group operations using a precomputation algorithm the paper gives explicitly (Algorithm 5), rather than the naive O(t) operations of recomputing every intermediate squaring, by grouping the exponent's bits into blocks of size kappa and combining a table of gamma = sqrt(t) precomputed powers. A bandwidth-saving variant transmits (l, pi) instead of (y, pi), since l is far shorter than a group element, and lets the verifier recover y = pi^l * g^(2^t mod l). A separate technique splits the sequential computation into n segments so a second computation thread produces the proof for each earlier segment while the first thread continues evaluating, reducing the residual work needed after evaluation finishes from O(t/log t) to O(t/omega^n) at the cost of a proof that grows to n group elements plus n-1 short primes, where omega is a small constant (the paper's example uses omega = 20). The same construction supports proof aggregation across several VDF evaluations sharing the same base and delay, and a watermarking variant that ties a proof to an evaluator's identity by deriving the challenge prime from a hash that includes that identity, at no extra sequential cost to an honest evaluator holding the intermediate values but at the cost of a full VDF re-evaluation for anyone forging a different identity's watermark.

### Measured results
This is a construction and security-proof paper; its numeric figures are algorithmic complexity bounds and one worked concrete example, not deployed-system or empirical benchmark measurements.

| Figure | Conditions |
|---|---|
| Proof size: 1 group element, vs. Pietrzak's O(log(delta)) group elements | Both constructions compared in the same RSA-group setting; the paper states this directly as its own construction's advantage |
| Verifier cost: essentially 2 group exponentiations, vs. Pietrzak's O(log(delta)) group exponentiations | Exponents in both cases are of bit-length equal to the security level k; stated as a direct comparison in the same setting |
| Concrete worked example: RSA modulus of 2048 bits, delay parameter set to 2^40 sequential squarings | Under these parameters, the paper states Pietrzak's proof is 10 KB long, while this paper's proof is 0.25 KB long, a 40x size reduction for the identical (modulus, delay) pair |
| Proof-computation overhead ratio using the paper's Algorithm 5 with omega treated as a constant such as 20 | Total evaluation time with s parallel cores is stated as approximately (1 + 1/(20s)) * delta, i.e. the extra proof-computation work adds roughly epsilon = O(1/log(delta)), "in the order of 0.05" for practical parameters, on top of the sequential evaluation time |
| Two-thread overhead reduction | Splitting into n segments reduces the proof-computation overhead remaining after evaluation completes from T/omega to at most T/omega^n, at the cost of a proof of n group elements plus n-1 short primes instead of a single group element |
| Class-group order-computation hardness, cited from prior algorithmic number theory results | Best known algorithm for computing the class-group order of an imaginary quadratic field of discriminant d runs in time L_{|d|}(1/2) under the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, where L_t(s) = exp(O(log(t)^s log(log(t))^(1-s))) — a stated asymptotic complexity bound, not a wall-clock measurement |
| Illustrative distance-bounding example for the paper's timed-identification protocol | For deniability against a judge standing 100 meters away, the paper computes a required delay of approximately 0.66 microseconds, using the speed of light (c ~= 3.00 x 10^8 m/s) as the sole physical input; the paper itself states this precision level is currently unreasonable to achieve without trusted hardware |

### Parameters
- Delay parameter: t (or Delta), the number of sequential group-squaring steps; example instantiation t = 2^40.
- Security level k: stated typical values 128, 192, or 256 bits; controls the bit-length of the random Fiat-Shamir challenge prime l, sampled from Primes(2^k).
- Precomputation-algorithm tuning parameters for proof generation: block size kappa and table-count gamma, with the paper's suggested choice kappa = log(t)/3 and gamma = sqrt(t), giving about t * 3/log(t) group operations and storage of about sqrt(t) group elements.
- RSA setup example: 2048-bit modulus N, product of two safe primes, group G = (Z/NZ)* / {+-1}.
- Segment count n for the overhead-reduction technique: a tunable integer trading proof length (n group elements plus n-1 primes) against residual post-evaluation work (T/omega^n).

### Stated limitations
The paper states that generating an RSA modulus with a strong guarantee that nobody knows its factorization is hard in practice: sampling a random number large enough to be divisible by two large primes with high probability "severely damages the efficiency of the construction" and increases the opportunity for parallel arithmetic optimization or specialized hardware to speed up an attacker; a secure multiparty RSA key-generation protocol avoids this but requires a third party to trust that the participating parties did not collude to recover the secret factorization. The paper's proposed alternative, the class group of an imaginary quadratic order, avoids the trusted-setup problem but its security rests on a generalized time-lock assumption (Assumption 2) that is not known to reduce to a standard, well-studied hardness assumption; the paper states this explicitly, contrasting it with the RSA setting where the analogous assumption can be reduced toward the difficulty of factoring or the RSA problem, though the paper notes even that RSA-setting reduction is not itself established to a standard problem in the strict security-reduction sense described in the proof section. The paper states that achieving precise real-world timing guarantees "is unlikely to be achievable without resorting to trusted hardware," so applications built on this VDF are described as needing to tolerate the small constant-factor timing slack (about 5% for practical parameters) between guaranteed sequential work and total work, rather than relying on the two being identical. The deniable timed-identification protocol described in Section 8 requires an accurate real-world estimate, in seconds, of the delay parameter needed to prevent a near-optimal adversary from forging a response before that estimate can be converted into a physical distance bound via the speed of light; the paper states obtaining such an accurate real-time estimate is a non-trivial open task related to the general difficulty (discussed in the paper's Section 3.2) of calibrating an abstract sequential-step count against real-world seconds.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The plain (non-trapdoor) VDF requires a public setup procedure that generates a group of unknown order without producing a known trapdoor; the paper states this is most efficiently done using the class group of an imaginary quadratic order rather than an RSA modulus, because RSA-modulus generation with a provably-unknown factorization either damages efficiency (public random sampling) or requires trusting a multiparty computation's participants not to have colluded. The Fiat-Shamir non-interactive variant requires a secure cryptographic hash function H mapping to {0,1}^(2k) and, separately, a hash-to-prime function Hprime used to derive the challenge prime l; the paper's soundness proof is stated in the random oracle model, meaning the security argument requires this hash to behave as an ideal random function, not merely a standard collision-resistant hash. The construction's sequentiality proof for the RSA setup rests on the classic time-lock assumption of Rivest, Shamir, and Wagner: no polynomially bounded algorithm without the factorization of N can compute the delayed exponentiation faster than the stated cost function, an assumption the rest of the system must accept as a computational premise rather than a proven-hard problem. The watermarking extension requires the honest evaluator to retain an intermediate value from its own computation (the second-to-last squaring result) to compute a certificate efficiently; a system that discards intermediate state after producing the final output cannot use the cost-effective watermarking method described. The two-thread overhead-reduction technique requires the evaluator to run two computation threads in parallel with a specific handoff of intermediate values between them; a purely single-threaded evaluator cannot reduce the post-evaluation proof-computation overhead below O(t/log t).

### Contradicts
None found. This paper's related-work section (Section 1.2) explicitly distinguishes its own construction from BONEH-CRYPTO-18's polynomial-GCD-based candidate (stated as needing more-than-polylogarithmic parallelism to run in the target delay, one of "these disadvantages" this paper avoids) and from the bounded-pre-computation exponentiation construction in the same paper (stated as "insecure against an adversary that can run a large (but feasible) pre-computation"), but these are the earlier paper's own stated properties for its weaker constructions, not a factual disagreement between the two papers' measurements.

### References worth retrieving
- Pietrzak, K., "Simple verifiable delay functions." Cryptology ePrint Archive, Report 2018/627. — competing (the paper this one directly and repeatedly benchmarks against for proof size and verifier cost; retrieved separately elsewhere in this corpus would give the primary-source figures for the comparison)
- Rivest, R. L., Shamir, A., Wagner, D. A., "Time-lock puzzles and timed-release crypto." 1996. — foundational (originates the repeated-squaring time-lock puzzle and the classic time-lock assumption this paper's sequentiality proof rests on directly)
- Boneh, D., Bonneau, J., Bünz, B., Fisch, B., "Verifiable delay functions." CRYPTO 2018. — foundational (the paper that formalizes the VDF definitions this paper adopts; retrieved separately in this corpus as BONEH-CRYPTO-18)
- Lenstra, A. K., Wesolowski, B., "Trustworthy public randomness with sloth, unicorn and trx." International Journal of Applied Cryptology, 2016. — foundational (the slow-timed hash function work this paper's introduction states was later formalized as VDFs)
- Buchmann, J., Williams, H. C., "A key-exchange system based on imaginary quadratic fields." Journal of Cryptology, 1988. — foundational (introduces class groups of imaginary quadratic fields to cryptography, the group family this paper proposes for trustless setup)
- Boneh, D., Naor, M., "Timed commitments." CRYPTO 2000. — foundational (introduces the timed-commitment primitive cited as related time-sensitive cryptography)

## [WILCOX-OHEARN-STORAGESS-08] Tahoe – The Least-Authority Filesystem

**Citation:** Zooko Wilcox-O'Hearn, Brian Warner. "Tahoe – The Least-Authority Filesystem." ACM Workshop on Storage Security and Survivability (StorageSS), 2008. Pages not stated in retrieved text. DOI 10.1145/1456469.1456474.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://doi.org/10.1145/1456469.1456474
**Source URL:** https://doi.org/10.1145/1456469.1456474
**Domain:** C

### What it does
Tahoe stores a file across multiple untrusted servers such that possession of one short string (a capability) is both sufficient to access the file and necessary — no separate access-control server or list exists anywhere in the system. A capability is a bit string, at least 96 bits long to resist guessing, that identifies one file or directory; holding it is both necessary and sufficient to exercise the access it grants. This follows the Principle of Least Authority: a process should hold no more access than the specific task requires. Tahoe defines three capability levels per file with a strict hierarchy: a write capability (read-write-cap) can derive a read capability (read-cap), which can derive a verify capability (verify-cap), but the derivation is one-directional — a verify-cap holder can check a file's integrity without being able to read its plaintext, and a read-cap holder can read the file but not modify it. Producing a weaker capability from a stronger one is called diminishing.

Every file is erasure coded with Reed-Solomon codes over the finite field GF(2^8): a writer chooses N, the total number of shares written across N distinct servers, and K, the number of shares sufficient to reconstruct the file (K ≤ N ≤ 256), and any K of the N shares suffice for recovery regardless of which K. For an immutable file (written once, read many times), the client picks a symmetric key, encrypts the plaintext with AES-128 in counter mode, erasure-codes the ciphertext into N shares, and writes one share to each of N servers. Two separate Merkle trees (binary hash trees where each parent commits to both children, letting any subset of leaves be verified without downloading the whole structure) are built: one over the erasure-code shares, so a client that detects corruption knows which specific share to discard and reconstruct from the others, and a second over the ciphertext itself, so a client can verify and stream part of a file without fetching all of it, and so no single erasure-code-share Merkle tree alone could let a malicious writer plant shares from two different files under one nominal identifier. The read-cap is the verify-cap plus the symmetric decryption key; the verify-cap is the secure hash (SHA256d, meaning SHA256 applied twice, chosen to prevent length-extension attacks) of a small "Capability Extension Block" holding both Merkle roots, stored on every server alongside that server's share rather than embedded in the capability itself, keeping the capability string short.

A mutable file (contents can be overwritten) is bound to an RSA key pair generated at file creation. From the RSA signing key SK, the client derives a 16-byte write key WK = truncated-SHA256d(SK), and from WK derives a 16-byte read key RK = truncated-SHA256d(WK) — so holding WK lets a party compute RK, but RK alone reveals nothing useful about WK, giving the required one-directional hierarchy without needing three independently generated secrets. To write, the client derives an encryption key from RK and a fresh random salt, encrypts, erasure-codes, distributes shares, builds a Merkle tree over the shares, and signs the Merkle root, the salt, the erasure-coding parameters, the file size, and a monotonically increasing sequence number with SK; the corresponding RSA public key (the verifying key VK) is stored unencrypted alongside the shares on every server, and the verify-cap is the hash of VK. The signing key SK itself is stored on the servers too, but encrypted under WK, so only a write-cap holder can decrypt and use it. To defend against a server (accidentally or maliciously) returning a stale, validly signed earlier version, the read protocol queries K + E servers for share metadata first (in the deployed client, K = 3 and E = K = 3), and only proceeds to download once it either confirms at least K shares of the highest sequence number it has found, or exhausts the servers it can query — a scheme the authors state reduces the chance of a stale read given that enough queried servers are honest and current, but does not by itself guarantee freshness. Directories are themselves mutable files holding (child name, capability) pairs; to preserve a transitive read-only property — a holder of read-only directory access can obtain only read-only capabilities to children, never write access — each child entry stores two separately encrypted capability slots, one for read-write and one for read-only, with the read-write slot "super-encrypted" (encrypted again, on top of the directory's own encryption) so a read-only directory holder cannot recover it.

### Measured results

| Result | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Deployed erasure-coding parameters | K = 3, N = 10 (each file split across 10 servers, any 3 sufficient to reconstruct) | allmydata.com production backup service, as of the paper's writing (October 2008) |
| Deployment scale | 64 servers; ~340 clients typically connected at any time; ~300 users accessing via the web front-end per 24-hour period; ~6.5 million user files stored; ~9.5 TB aggregate stored size | allmydata.com production service, measured October 17, 2008, service launched with first beta April 3, 2008 and first shipped product May 5, 2008 |
| Convergent-encryption file-sharing rate | less than 1% of stored files (measured by aggregate file size, not file count) are shared between users | measurement of files stored on the allmydata.com service; exact sample size and date not given in the retrieved text |
| RSA-2048 key-pair generation time | between 0.8 and 3.2 seconds | "modern commodity PC hardware" (no specific model, CPU, or count of trials stated) |
| DSA key-pair generation time (comparison figure, not used in the deployed system) | under 1 millisecond | same unspecified commodity hardware, cited as the motivation for the paper's proposed future semi-private-key construction |
| Erasure-coding computational cost | measured to be lower than the cost of the encryption and secure-hash operations in the same pipeline | production Tahoe deployment, using the "zfec" Reed-Solomon implementation; no absolute timing figure or hardware specification given in the retrieved text |

### Parameters
- Capability length: minimum 96 bits, chosen to be unguessable while remaining short enough to embed in a URL.
- Erasure-code field: GF(2^8), Reed-Solomon, with the constraint 1 ≤ N ≤ 256 and 1 ≤ K ≤ N; the byte-wise implementation over this field is what keeps encode/decode efficient despite Reed-Solomon's stated O(N^2) worst-case computational complexity.
- Deployed (K, N): K = 3, N = 10 in the allmydata.com production service — the paper's own stated production default, not a value it claims is universally optimal.
- Symmetric encryption: AES-128 in CTR mode, used for both immutable- and mutable-file content encryption.
- Hash function: SHA256d (SHA256 applied twice) throughout, with purpose-specific tag prefixes on every hash input to prevent cross-purpose collisions.
- Mutable-file signature key: 2048-bit (256-byte) RSA key pair, one generated per mutable file.
- Derived secrets for mutable files: write key WK and read key RK each 16 bytes (128 bits), each a truncated SHA256d output.
- Mutable-file freshness read protocol: queries K + E servers before proceeding to download shares; deployed setting E = K, so with K = 3 the client queries at least 6 servers for metadata before commit.
- Convergence secret: an additional secret mixed into the convergent-encryption key derivation, scoped per group of users who share that secret, to limit which users' identical files converge to identical ciphertext.

### Stated limitations
Tahoe's freshness-read protocol reduces, but the authors state does not eliminate, the chance of an accidental or malicious stale read, and only "provided that enough of the servers are honest and have fresh data" — the paper gives no numeric bound on how many dishonest or stale servers the K+E query can tolerate. The system makes no attempt to enforce any consistency property beyond single-file freshness; the authors state explicitly that it does not enforce linearization of operations spanning more than one file, unlike the Byzantine fault-tolerant filesystems they cite for comparison. Convergent encryption (deriving a file's encryption key from a hash of its own plaintext, so identical files by different users produce identical ciphertext and can be stored once) is stated to be able to undermine confidentiality in some cases, citing a separate paper by one of the authors; Tahoe's mitigation (a convergence secret scoping which users converge) is described but not claimed to close every such case. The two nonstandard cryptographic constructions used or proposed — encrypting the RSA signing key under a key derived from a hash of that same signing key, and the proposed semi-private-key scheme for future ECDSA-based capabilities — are both explicitly described by the authors as resting only on heuristic security arguments, not proofs, with the paper stating it would be surprising if a weakness existed that did not also break the underlying standard primitive (RSA, AES-128, SHA256), which is an expectation, not a proof. The paper states a Proof of Retrievability protocol (downloading and checking a randomly chosen subset of ciphertext rather than the whole file) was designed but explicitly not deployed in the current Tahoe release at time of writing, described as a work in progress. RSA-2048 key generation taking up to 3.2 seconds per mutable file is presented by the authors as a performance problem motivating their proposed (undeployed) DSA/ECC-based semi-private-key alternative described in the Future Work section.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A reader needs to contact at least K of the N servers holding a file's shares to reconstruct it, and the freshness protocol additionally needs at least K + E servers to be reachable during the metadata-query phase for the staleness defense to function at all; a deployment with fewer than K+E reachable servers per file falls back to whatever subset it can reach, with the paper's stated freshness guarantee no longer applying at full strength. The one-directional capability hierarchy (write-cap → read-cap → verify-cap) requires every derivation to be computable forward (via a one-way hash) and infeasible backward without the higher-level secret; any component that needs to grant a weaker capability without ever exposing the stronger one must perform that hash-based diminishment locally, since Tahoe places no server or protocol step in the way of a party diminishing its own capability at will. For mutable files, correctness of the freshness scheme depends on servers correctly reporting the highest sequence number and share count they hold when queried in the metadata phase; the paper does not describe any independent mechanism forcing honest reporting, so the scheme's holding is conditional on the "enough honest servers" assumption above being met by whatever server-selection or diversity policy the surrounding system supplies. Directory transitive read-only requires every directory entry, not just the directory's own encryption, to carry the extra super-encryption layer on its read-write slot; a system storing directory entries any other way (for example a flat mutable file per child rather than an encrypted-slot pair) would not preserve this property.

### Contradicts
None found against another entry in this corpus (no other Tahoe deployment-measurement paper is in this batch). The paper's own conclusion states that Reed-Solomon codes "have been characterized as being asymptotically inefficient in the literature" — attributing that characterization to unnamed prior literature rather than presenting it as Tahoe's own finding — while reporting that in Tahoe's own deployment the erasure-coding cost measured lower than the encryption and hashing cost in the same pipeline; this is the paper's own qualification of a claim it attributes to others, not a disagreement with a specific paper elsewhere in this corpus.

### References worth retrieving
- Rivest, Shamir, Adelman, "A method for obtaining digital signatures and public-key cryptosystems," MIT/LCS/TM-82, 1977 — foundational (the RSA construction mutable-file write capabilities are built on)
- Merkle, "A digital signature based on a conventional encryption function," CRYPTO 1987, pp. 369-378 — foundational (the Merkle tree construction used for both share verification and streaming-download verification)
- Juels, Kaliski, "PORs: proofs of retrievability for large files," CCS 2007, pp. 584-597 — foundational (the proof-of-retrievability protocol the paper states is designed but not yet deployed in Tahoe)
- Douceur, Adya, Bolosky, Simon, Theimer, "Reclaiming space from duplicate files in a serverless distributed file system," ICDCS 2002, p. 617 — foundational (the convergent-encryption technique Tahoe optionally uses, with its confidentiality caveat)
- Grothoff, "Crisp advisory 2008-01: URIs do not refer to unique files in allmydata Tahoe," 2008 — attack (a specific reported flaw motivating the ciphertext-level Merkle tree the paper describes, cited directly in Section 4.3 as the reason a single share-level Merkle tree is insufficient)
- Goodson, Wylie, Ganger, Reiter, "Efficient byzantine-tolerant erasure-coded storage," 2004, pp. 135-144 — competing (a Byzantine fault-tolerant erasure-coded filesystem cited as enforcing stronger consistency, e.g. cross-file linearization, than Tahoe does)
- Li, Mazières, "Beyond one-third faulty replicas in byzantine fault tolerant systems," NSDI 2007 — competing (another Byzantine fault-tolerant filesystem cited in the same comparison)
- Plank, Xu, Luo, Schuman, Wilcox-O'Hearn, "A performance evaluation and examination of open-source erasure coding libraries for storage," 2009 — foundational (the performance evaluation underlying the paper's claim that its "zfec" Reed-Solomon implementation is fast; co-authored by this paper's own author)
