## [WILKINSON-STORJ-18] Storj: A Decentralized Cloud Storage Network Framework

**Citation:** Shawn Wilkinson and Storj Labs, Inc. "Storj: A Decentralized Cloud Storage Network Framework." Storj Labs technical report, v3.1, 2024 (original v3.0: 2018-10-30). Pages 1-84 (whitepaper, unpaginated by chapter). DOI not stated.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://github.com/storj/whitepaper
**Source URL:** https://github.com/storj/whitepaper
**Domain:** C

### Retrieval note (rule 3 check)
The registry target record cites the v3.0 edition dated 2018-10-30. The text on disk is v3.1, dated 2024-03-07 (both editions are published from the same repository at the same URL, with v3.1 stated in its own changelog to be an update of v3.0, not a different paper). Title and lead contributor (Shawn Wilkinson, listed by name among the contributors) match the registry record. The v3.1 changelog states it replaced Kademlia-based node discovery with a direct node-to-Satellite indication scheme and simplified the audit/containment design relative to v3.0; entries below describing node discovery and audits describe the v3.1 mechanism, not the 2018 one the registry record cites. This is flagged inline where it matters rather than as a mismatch, since the document is a later edition of the same named source, not a different paper.

### What it does
Storj lets a client store an object across many independently operated, mutually distrusting storage nodes with high durability and without simple replication's bandwidth overhead, coordinated by an operator-run "Satellite" that tracks metadata, schedules repairs, and settles payments, rather than by a fully peer-to-peer consensus mechanism. An object is broken into segments (a whole small file may be a single "inline" segment stored directly with its metadata if it is smaller than the metadata itself), each large segment further divided into stripes (sub-segment units on the order of a couple of kilobytes, the granularity at which erasure encoding and audit both operate), and each stripe erasure-coded with a Reed-Solomon (k, n) code: n erasure shares are generated per stripe, any k of which reconstruct it, so each share is 1/k the size of the stripe. Same-indexed erasure shares across all the stripes of a segment are packed together into one "piece," so a storage node holds one piece per segment rather than many small per-stripe shares; a piece is 1/k the size of its segment, and only k of the n pieces are needed to reconstruct the whole segment.

The system extends the standard two Reed-Solomon numbers (k, n) to four: k ≤ m ≤ o ≤ n. k is the minimum pieces needed for reconstruction and n the total pieces generated. m is the repair-trigger threshold: when a segment's live piece count falls to m, the Satellite immediately schedules a rebuild, so m − k is the safety margin against data loss between detecting the need for repair and completing it. o is the piece count considered "optimal": during upload or repair, once o of the up-to-n pieces have finished uploading, the remaining upload attempts (up to n) are canceled, so o − m is the number of nodes that can go simultaneously offline without forcing a repair, and n − o is the number of slow ("long-tail") nodes the system tolerates without waiting on them — the mechanism the paper credits with letting every read or write proceed at the speed of the fastest responding nodes in the selected set rather than the slowest.

A per-Satellite node-discovery cache (in this v3.1 edition, replacing the earlier Kademlia distributed hash table (DHT) used in the 2018 edition) tracks each storage node's current address, available space, and other metadata; a node announces itself to every Satellite on its trustlist, checks in periodically (the paper suggests roughly once per hour), and a Satellite that cannot reach a node stops recommending it to clients. Audits verify that a storage node still holds what it claims: a Satellite requests a randomly chosen stripe's erasure shares from every node responsible for it and runs the Berlekamp-Welch error-correction algorithm across the returned shares, which both detects which specific responses are missing or wrong and lets the Satellite reconstruct the correct data from whichever responses are correct, without needing to have pre-generated the challenge and expected response ahead of time (which the paper states was a weakness of the Merkle-tree-based proof scheme used in Storj's earlier, 2016 design — a storage node could pass most audits without holding all the data simply by memorizing which pre-generated challenges existed and caching only their expected responses). A node that responds to an audit dial but not with the requested data within the expected time is placed into "containment mode" and retried until it succeeds, actively fails, or is disqualified for prolonged unavailability, rather than immediately marked as failing.

Repair operates against the same m threshold: when the node-discovery cache observes a node transitioning from online to offline, a reverse index over the Satellite's metadata identifies every segment that had a piece on that node; any segment whose live-piece count drops to m is downloaded, reconstructed from its surviving pieces, re-encoded to replace the missing pieces, and the replacement pieces are uploaded to newly selected nodes, with the segment's pointer (the metadata record listing which nodes hold which pieces, plus encryption and erasure-coding parameters) updated accordingly. Bandwidth accounting between an Uplink (client-side software) and a storage node uses a scheme the paper derives from Neuman's proxy-based accounting protocol: the Satellite issues a signed "bandwidth allocation" capping the resources an Uplink may use in an operation, the Uplink sends the storage node successively larger restricted sub-allocations (each one covering only the data transferred so far, using the same non-reusable check number so only the largest one can ever be redeemed), and the storage node periodically forwards its largest received allocation to the Satellite for later payment — a design intended to bound the loss either party is exposed to if the exchange is interrupted partway through, rather than depending on both peers' end-of-operation reports being honest.

Payment moves from clients to Satellites in any medium a Satellite accepts, and from Satellites to storage nodes exclusively in the Ethereum-based ERC-20 STORJ token, calculated monthly per node from the Satellite's own stored-piece and bandwidth-usage accounting; a Satellite withholds part of a storage node's earnings until the node has sustained good uptime for a period the paper states is on the order of "greater than half a year," reclaiming the withheld amount if the node departs early. The design explicitly avoids Byzantine fault-tolerant consensus and blockchain-style global coordination for its metadata and control plane, on the stated reasoning that systems requiring less inter-node coordination scale in throughput more directly with added resources; the paper cites this as the reason the current design places the Satellite, rather than a decentralized consensus mechanism, at the center of metadata authority, repair scheduling, and payment settlement.

### Measured results
Most quantitative content in this paper is derived from stated mathematical models or from Monte Carlo simulation, not from measurement of an operating network; the few network-scale figures given are point-in-time deployment statistics without a stated measurement date or methodology beyond "at the time of writing."

| Result | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Durability under erasure coding, varying (k,n) at fixed 2x expansion factor | 99.207% (k=2,n=4) rising to 99.999999999990544% (k=32,n=64) | closed-form: Poisson-distribution cumulative distribution function (CDF) with mean λ = pn, monthly node churn rate p = 10%, durability = P(at most n−k pieces lost in a month); a derived formula, not a simulation or a network measurement |
| Durability under simple replication, varying redundancy at fixed churn | 90.48% (1 copy) rising to 99.999999998% (16 copies) | same p = 10% monthly churn model, replication instead of erasure coding, same Poisson-CDF formula |
| Durability at varied expansion factors | 97.69% (k=4,n=6, 1.5x) up to 99.999999999999548% (k=20,n=50, 2.5x) | same p = 10% churn model and formula, illustrating that durability depends on both k,n individually and on the expansion factor n/k, not on the ratio alone |
| Repair bandwidth ratio and durability across churn rates | see table below | Monte Carlo simulation, 10,000-node network, 1000 repeated 24-month simulation runs per row, mean-rebuilds/month taken at the 99th percentile of the observed rebuild-count distribution across runs; the paper states network size does not affect the per-segment mean-rebuilds/month value under its constant-monthly-loss-rate assumption |
| Audit success-probability estimate vs. number of consecutive successful audits | Uniform prior: 0.5 (0 audits) → 0.9878 (80 audits) → 0.99505 (200 audits); Jeffrey's prior: 0.5 (0 audits) → 0.9938 (80 audits) → 0.99751 (200 audits) | Bayesian estimator P = (a+n)/(a+b+n) under a beta(a,b) prior, evaluated for the Uniform prior β(1,1) and Jeffrey's prior β(0.5,0.5); a closed-form calculation given the assumption that every audit so far succeeded, not a measurement of an actual node population |
| Bandwidth cap constraint on usable storage per node | a node with 1 TB available space and a 500 GB/month bandwidth cap can store at most 333 GB, if 50% of its data is expected to require repair in a month | worked numerical example from the paper's repair-cost model, not an observed measurement |
| Deployment scale, "typical scenario" | files distributed across 40 disk drives (a 20/40 Reed-Solomon setup) in a network the paper states has "over 100,000" independently operated storage nodes; the paper states the previous (2016) version of the network had "over 150,000" independently operated nodes | stated without a specific measurement date, sampling method, or citation; presented in Appendix C ("Primary user benefits"), a section framed as marketing rather than the paper's technical evaluation |

Repair bandwidth ratio / durability table (Table 7.2 in the source), all rows from the same 10,000-node, 1000-iteration, 24-month Monte Carlo simulation described above, with a constant monthly piece-loss rate as the churn model:

| MTTF (months) | k | n | m | Repair bandwidth ratio | Durability (nines) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 20 | 40 | 35 | 9.36 | 0.9999 (8 nines) |
| 6 | 20 | 40 | 30 | 0.87 | 0.9999 (17 nines) |
| 12 | 20 | 40 | 25 | 0.31 | 0.9999 (13 nines) |
| 1 | 30 | 60 | 35 | 3.40 | 0.9999 (4 nines) |
| 6 | 30 | 70 | 40 | 0.60 | 0.9999 (15 nines) |
| 12 | 30 | 80 | 45 | 0.31 | 0.9999 (25 nines) |
| 1 | 40 | 80 | 60 | 5.21 | 0.9999 (4 nines) |
| 6 | 40 | 120 | 50 | 0.52 | 0.9999 (14 nines) |
| 12 | 40 | 120 | 45 | 0.24 | 0.9999 (11 nines) |

MTTF is Mean Time To Failure, the mean node lifetime in months (equivalently, the churn rate α = 1/MTTF); "repair bandwidth ratio" is the paper's own BR quantity, the fraction of total network data volume expected to be moved as repair traffic per unit time, not an absolute bandwidth figure.

### Parameters
- Erasure code family: Reed-Solomon.
- Reed-Solomon working example throughout the paper: (k=20, n=40), used repeatedly for illustration but the text does not state this as the production default in the v3.1 edition read here.
- Extended parameter set for long-tail tolerance: (k, m, o, n) with k ≤ m ≤ o ≤ n, where m − k is the safety buffer before data loss risk, o − m is the number of nodes tolerated offline without triggering repair, and n − o is the number of slow uploads tolerated without waiting.
- Illustrative object-size assumption used in one bandwidth calculation: average object size 50 MB, n = 40.
- Design assumption on typical object size: the initial product targets objects of 4 MB or larger; smaller objects are supported but the paper states they may be more costly to store.
- Bandwidth-cap example (US ISP): Comcast's stated residential cap of 1 TB/month, which the paper computes bounds sustained throughput to no more than 385 KB/s averaged over a month.
- Node check-in interval: suggested roughly once per hour (v3.1 node-discovery cache design).
- Storage node payment withholding period: on the order of "greater than half a year" of sustained good uptime before a Satellite releases withheld earnings in full.
- Bayesian audit-estimator priors evaluated: Uniform β(1,1) and Jeffrey's β(0.5,0.5).
- Simulation scale for the repair-bandwidth decision tables: 10,000-node simulated network, 1000 independent 24-month runs per parameter row, mean-rebuilds/month read at the 99th percentile of the observed rebuild-count distribution.
- Payment token for Satellite-to-storage-node transfers: Ethereum-based ERC-20 STORJ token (client-to-Satellite payment may use any mechanism the Satellite accepts).

### Stated limitations
The paper states plainly, in its own Future Work chapter, that "we place significant burdens on the Satellite operator to maintain a good service level with high availability, high durability, regular payments, and regular backups," and that eliminating Satellite control of metadata via a workable Byzantine fault-tolerant consensus algorithm is a long-term goal not yet achieved — "should one arise" is the paper's own qualifier. Data repair depends on the Satellite process running continuously: the text states explicitly that if a user's Satellite stops running, repairs stop and data will eventually be lost to node churn, an acknowledged single-point-of-failure dependency the paper compares to the requirement in Kademlia that a value's original publisher must periodically republish it or the value expires. The bandwidth-measurement and payment-accounting system tracks only bandwidth used during storage and retrieval operations; the paper states it explicitly does not cover node-discovery traffic or other maintenance overhead, so total network bandwidth exceeds what is measured and paid for. Reed-Solomon-based audit error-correction (the Berlekamp-Welch algorithm) is stated to depend on the assumption that most storage nodes behave rationally and store data faithfully; the paper frames this as an assumption underlying the mechanism, not a guarantee the mechanism itself enforces. The Honest Geppetto attack (an adversary operating many nodes that accumulate reputation before defecting simultaneously) is stated to have no complete defense; the paper's best answer is that the attack becomes ineffective only at sufficient network scale, backed partially by Bayesian relatedness analysis across node behavioral signals, not by a mechanism that eliminates the exposure. The hostage-bytes attack (a node withholding data to extort added payment) is stated to be defeated by Reed-Solomon redundancy only when malicious nodes do not collude to control multiple pieces of the same file; collusion is explicitly identified as the residual case the redundancy does not cover. A faithless Satellite or storage node modified to serve any paying requester is stated not to compromise data privacy, because client-side encryption is independent of Satellite behavior, but the paper states explicitly that "Storj is not designed to protect against compromised clients."

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The Satellite must run continuously for repair to occur at all; a design that depends on Storj for durability therefore inherits an availability requirement on a specific centralized-per-user-or-organization process, not just on the storage-node population, which is a materially different assumption from a system whose repair logic runs from any node's local view (the paper's own comparison point is Kademlia, where republishing similarly depends on the original publisher staying online). The audit and repair pipeline requires the erasure code to operate at the stripe granularity (not the whole-segment or whole-piece granularity) so that a Berlekamp-Welch challenge-response can run against a single small stripe rather than downloading a full segment for every audit; a storage backend that only exposes whole-piece reads could not reuse this audit mechanism without modification. Data repair additionally requires a separate per-piece hash, stored alongside each piece and validated against the pointer, because the paper states Reed-Solomon decoding alone is insufficient to confirm correctness when only the minimum k pieces are downloaded for a repair — so a system relying purely on the erasure code's own error-correcting property during repair, without this extra hash layer, would not have the same correctness guarantee the paper claims. The bandwidth-allocation accounting scheme requires every Uplink to already hold a public/private key pair as part of its node identity, since restricted bandwidth allocations are authenticated with that existing key rather than a newly issued one; any client identity system without persistent asymmetric keys would need to add one before this accounting mechanism could apply. The described payment settlement requires the Satellite to hold an accurate day-by-day accounting of which pieces each storage node stores; a storage node that misses a delete command while offline continues holding data the Satellite no longer credits it for, which the paper states is cleaned up later by garbage collection, not by an accounting reconciliation at the time of the missed command.

### Contradicts
None found against another entry in this corpus. Internally, the paper's Appendix C states the network has "over 100,000" independently operated storage nodes while noting the prior (2016) version of the network had "over 150,000" — a decline the paper does not explain or attribute to any specific cause in the retrieved text, and states without a measurement date, so it cannot be checked against a specific point in time. This is a paper-internal unexplained figure, not a disagreement with another source in this corpus.

### References worth retrieving
- Giroire, Monteiro, Pérennes, "Peer-to-peer storage systems: A practical guideline to be lazy," IEEE GlobeCom, 2010 — foundational (source of the mathematical framework for durability and repair bandwidth as a function of Reed-Solomon parameters, node lifetime, and reconstruction rate, which this paper states "much of our work follows from")
- Blake, Rodrigues, "High availability, scalable storage, dynamic peer networks: Pick two," HotOS 2003 — foundational (source of the churn-versus-redundancy-versus-bandwidth relationship this paper repeatedly cites for its durability and repair-bandwidth reasoning)
- Rhea, Geels, Roscoe, Kubiatowicz, "Handling Churn in a DHT," USENIX ATC 2004 — foundational (source of the cited real-world peer-to-peer median-session-length figures motivating the paper's churn-tolerance design)
- Maymounkov, Mazières, "Kademlia: A Peer-to-Peer Information System Based on the XOR Metric," IPTPS 2002 — foundational (already verified in this corpus per BRIEF.md §7; the DHT the v3.0 edition of this paper used for node discovery and that v3.1 explicitly replaced)
- Bowers, Juels, Oprea, "HAIL: A High-availability and Integrity Layer for Cloud Storage," (venue not given in excerpt) — foundational (source of the per-stripe erasure-coded audit technique this paper's audit mechanism is built from)
- Juels, Kaliski, "PORs: Proofs of Retrievability for Large Files," (already retrieved in this corpus per WILCOX-OHEARN-STORAGESS-08's bibliography) — foundational (the proof-of-retrievability concept this paper's audit design is a variant of)

## [WILLIAMS-ARWEAVE-19] Arweave: A Protocol for Economically Sustainable Information Permanence
**Citation:** Sam Williams, Viktor Diordiiev, Lev Berman, India Raybould, Ivan Uemlianin. "Arweave: A Protocol for Economically Sustainable Information Permanence." Arweave technical report (yellow paper), 2019.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arweave.org/yellow-paper.pdf
**Source URL:** https://arweave.org/yellow-paper.pdf
**Domain:** C

### What it does
Arweave gives a single upfront transaction fee that funds storage of a piece of data indefinitely, replacing the per-contract renewal model other decentralized storage networks use. A block producer earns a mining reward only if it holds a copy of one specific prior block, the "recall block," selected deterministically but unpredictably from a hash of the previous block and its height. To build or verify a new block a miner must present the recall block's full content as input to the proof-of-work hash, a construction the paper calls Proof of Access (PoA). Blocks link to two predecessors, the previous block in sequence and the recall block, forming a graph the paper calls the blockweave rather than a linear chain. Because the recall block is chosen uniformly at random from block history, a miner maximizes its win probability by storing a larger share of the full blockweave, and rarely held blocks give the miners holding them a competitive edge over a smaller pool of rivals also holding that block, so PoA rewards storing scarce data more than storing already-abundant data. Each new full node need not download the entire blockweave: block headers memoize a Block Hash List and a Wallet List sufficient to verify and process new blocks, so a joining node can operate by holding only the current block and progressively verifying backward proofs of work, trading verification trust for the amount of history it fetches. Block propagation sends a compact "blockshadow" — a hash of the Wallet List and Block Hash List plus a list of transaction hashes — rather than the full block; a receiving node that already holds those transactions locally reconstructs the block itself, following the compact-block design of Bitcoin's BIP-152 and the Graphene protocol. Storage cost accrues through a formula for the price of storing one gigabyte on one hard disk drive for one hour, PGBH = HDD_price / (HDD_sz * HDD_mtbf); the perpetual price of storing a data item is modeled as the infinite sum of this per-period cost as the cost is projected to decline over time. Transaction fees fund a storage endowment; each block's total miner reward combines instantly-released transaction fees, a fixed inflation schedule declining with block height, and a top-up drawn from the endowment only when the first two do not cover the modeled storage burden for that block. Node-to-node bandwidth allocation is governed by "wildfire," a reference implementation of an "Adaptive Interacting Incentive Agent" (AIIA) meta-game: each node ranks its peers by a rolling average of response speed and accuracy and by observed generosity in forwarding transactions and blocks, then serves higher-ranked peers first and prunes low-ranked peers probabilistically.

### Measured results
| Figure | Conditions |
|---|---|
| Average annual decline in GBh (cost of storing one gigabyte for one hour) storage cost: 30.57% | Computed from a hard-disk price/capacity/MTBF dataset spanning approximately 50 years, given in the paper's appendix 10.1 (a linked Arweave transaction, not reproduced in the body text) |
| Network-wide transaction replication rate exceeds 97% | Reported as the state of the live Arweave network at time of writing, no date given beyond "current" |
| Network capacity for approximately 310 million typically-sized data transactions per year | Stated as of block height 223,280 on the live network, under "the current architecture" prior to the proposed Succinct Proofs of Access change |
| Approximately 750 replications of each piece of data in the network | Reported "at the time of writing" on the live network |
| The permaweb had been live for 500 days and was growing at approximately 2,500 web applications and pages per day | Reported at time of writing, live network measurement, no independent methodology given beyond the authors' own count |
| Maximum consumer storage-media data density observed: 1.66×10^12 bits/cm^3; maximum achieved in research: 2.5×10^25 bits/cm^3; theoretical maximum: 1.53×10^67 bits/cm^3 | Cited figures, not measurements performed by this paper; used to project 434, 697, or 1,329 years to reach the theoretical maximum at 30%, 20%, and 10% annual growth rates respectively |

The AIIA meta-game simulation (Section 6.4) reports qualitative convergence behavior only — that agent characteristic vectors converge toward common biases over "a long enough time period" when the rate of bias-perception change does not exceed the rate of bias expression — with no stated agent count, iteration count, or numeric convergence rate, so it does not meet this batch's usability bar for a quantitative result.

### Parameters
- 1 AR = 1,000,000,000,000 Winston (the sub-unit).
- Genesis supply: 55,000,000 AR, created 8 June 2018; a further 11,000,000 AR (20% of genesis supply) released gradually as block mining rewards, for a maximum circulation of 66,000,000 AR.
- Inflation reward per block: R_inflation = GAR * 0.2 * ln(2) * 2^(-BH/By), with GAR = 55,000,000 (genesis AR) and By = 262,800 (blocks per year).
- Total miner reward per block: R_total = R_fees + R_inflation + R_endowment, where R_fees sums the per-transaction instant reward across all transactions in the block.
- Endowment draw is nonzero only when R_inflation + R_fees fall short of (block_size * PGBB), the modeled per-block-period storage cost of the block; the drawn amount is scaled by Prop(), which weights it by the ratio of the required recall block's size to the network's average block size, so miners forced to hold larger-than-average recall blocks are compensated proportionally more.
- Transaction pricing: TX_cost = TX_size * sum over future block periods of PGBB[i] (price to store 1 GB for one block period at height i); TX_reward = TX_cost * C_fee, a constant fraction; TX_total = TX_cost + TX_reward is what the user pays.
- No numeric value for C_fee is given in the retrieved text.

### Stated limitations
The AIIA/wildfire adaptive mechanism-design layer has three limitations the authors state directly. First, it can only reinforce behavior that a majority of participating agent designers already favor; it cannot compute pro-social behavior independent of that majority, and is exposed to the same class of majority-collusion attack as blockchain Sybil-resistance games generally. Second, AIIA games can adjust only off-chain reputation-like peer rankings; they cannot shift network-wide consensus rules. Third, the speed at which the network adapts to a changing environment is bounded by how much short-term utility nodes are willing to sacrifice to express a pro-social bias; excessively selfish nodes slow that adaptation. The paper reports that as of writing, the only two deployed AIIA agents are wildfire and a second agent called Weaver, and that Weaver nodes are a minority, de-prioritized by the majority of wildfire nodes. The paper's proposed Succinct Proofs of Access mechanism (future work, unimplemented at time of writing) trades away Proof of Access's proof-of-distribution guarantee: it lets a large dataset enter the blockweave by storing only its Merkle root, so consensus about the transaction's inclusion no longer implies the data was ever fully replicated to the network. The paper states this mechanism is intended only as an optional feature for large low-redundancy-requirement datasets. ArQL, the transaction-tag query mechanism, returns results only from the single servicing node's locally held data; the paper states explicitly that a query gives no certainty of completeness across the network. The authors state they do not expect the Arweave network to mine blocks "in true perpetuity," anticipating that the mechanism-design-driven network itself will eventually stop, after which they expect data preservation to depend on social incentives and prior replication rather than the protocol's financial incentives.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A verifying or mining node must be able to fetch the specific deterministically-selected recall block for the current height on demand, so the network requires enough live nodes holding a spread of historical blocks that any given recall block is retrievable within the block-time window; the paper gives no quantified bound on how sparse blockweave replication could become before recall-block retrieval starts failing. Block validation depends on the miner receiving a Wallet List and Block Hash List consistent with the block being validated; a node must synchronize these two structures before it can verify new transactions or blocks, so any indexing or serving layer built on Arweave needs those structures kept current locally rather than fetched per query. Blockshadow-based block reconstruction requires a receiving node to already hold the referenced transactions locally before the compact shadow arrives; a node that does not will fail to reconstruct the block from the shadow alone and must fall back to fetching full transaction data, so any transport layer serving Arweave must propagate individual transactions ahead of, or independent from, block propagation. The storage-endowment pricing model requires the projected decline in PGBH (storage cost per gigabyte-hour) to hold over the multi-decade span needed to fund perpetual storage from a one-time payment; if the actual decline rate falls below the rate priced in at upload time, the endowment underfunds later storage periods, a risk the paper acknowledges only by citing the historical trend's 50-year consistency, not by any margin analysis. ArQL and any application built on transaction tags must tolerate node-local, incomplete query results, since no node is required to hold the full blockweave.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus at time of writing.

- Competing: A. Pinar Ozisik, Gavin Andresen, George Bissias, Amir Houmansadr, Brian Levine, "Graphene: A new protocol for block propagation using set reconciliation," 2017 (blockshadowing explicitly builds on and claims to improve upon this).

## [WILLOW-SPEC-23] Willow: 3d Range-Based Set Reconciliation (protocol specification)
**Citation:** Sam Gwilym, Aljoscha Meyer, and the Earthstar/Willow project contributors. "Willow: 3d Range-Based Set Reconciliation (protocol specification)." willowprotocol.org, protocol specification (not a peer-reviewed paper), funded in part by NLnet, 2023.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://willowprotocol.org/specs/rbsr/index.html
**Source URL:** https://willowprotocol.org/specs/rbsr/index.html
**Domain:** D

### What it does
The mechanism lets two peers holding entries in a three-dimensional coordinate space (a namespace subspace, a path, and a timestamp) identify which entries the other peer lacks, without either peer transmitting its whole entry set. Each Willow entry is wrapped into a `LengthyAuthorisedEntry`: the entry plus a count of how many consecutive bytes of its payload, from the start, the peer already holds. This wrapping merges two separate synchronization problems (missing entries, and entries whose payload is only partly held) into one problem: a peer either holds a `LengthyAuthorisedEntry` or does not.

Reconciliation proceeds recursively over a `3dRange`, a three-dimensional range that bounds a set of entries by subspace, path, and time. A peer that wants to compare a `3dRange` against another peer's holdings computes a `Fingerprint`, a hash over every `LengthyAuthorisedEntry` it holds inside that range, and sends a `3dRangeFingerprint` message naming the range and the fingerprint. The receiving peer computes its own fingerprint over the same range. If the fingerprints match, the peer replies with an empty `3dRangeEntrySet` for that range, signaling that reconciliation of the range is complete and no data needs to change hands. If the fingerprints differ, the receiving peer takes one of two actions: it splits the range into multiple sub-ranges and sends a `3dRangeFingerprint` for each, so the mismatch localizes recursively; or, once the range holds few enough entries, it replies with a `3dRangeEntrySet` containing every entry it holds in that range and sets a `want_response` flag, prompting the other peer to reply with its own entries (omitting anything just received) and complete the exchange for that range. A peer splitting a range must divide it so each sub-range holds close to the same number of entries the peer locally has, not so each sub-range spans equal numeric width of subspace, path, or time; splitting by numeric width defeats the recursion's efficiency because a peer cannot know in advance how its holdings are distributed across the coordinate space.

Fingerprint computation supports incremental assembly: a range's fingerprint is computable by combining the fingerprints of its sub-ranges, avoiding a full rescan on every split. Each `LengthyAuthorisedEntry` is mapped to a `PreFingerprint` by a `fingerprint_singleton` function sensitive to every field of the entry (namespace, subspace, path, timestamp, payload digest, payload length, and bytes held). `PreFingerprint`s combine pairwise through an associative and commutative `fingerprint_combine` function with a neutral element `fingerprint_neutral`, so a range's combined `PreFingerprint` can be computed in any grouping or order — commutativity is required here because the specification does not prescribe a linear order over three-dimensional coordinates, unlike the one-dimensional range-based set reconciliation this generalizes. A final `fingerprint_finalise` function maps the accumulated `PreFingerprint` to the transmitted `Fingerprint`, and the specification recommends this be a standard cryptographic hash so the wire-transmitted value stays small even if the `PreFingerprint` representation is large.

Because a peer cannot cheaply determine, from the set of ranges it has received so far, whether their union covers a range it originally asked about, the specification has the splitting peer attach metadata to the final sub-range in a split batch, stating which of the other peer's original ranges is now fully covered by the sub-ranges sent. Both peers rely on this metadata being accurate to track reconciliation progress without maintaining coverage-tracking data structures; a peer supplying inaccurate metadata degrades reconciliation, but the specification treats this as tolerable because a malicious peer already has other ways to disrupt reconciliation.

### Measured results
None. The document is a protocol specification with no reported experiment, benchmark, node count, or dataset. It states an asymptotic property only: reconciliation "collaboratively drill[s] down to the differences... in a logarithmic number of communication rounds," inherited by construction from the recursive halving, without measuring round count, message count, or bandwidth on any concrete topology.

### Parameters
- Split factor: unspecified as a fixed number. The specification states a peer "can actually split sets into arbitrarily many subsets in each step," and that splitting into more subsets per step decreases the number of communication rounds, but gives no recommended value or tested range.
- Threshold for switching from further splitting to direct entry transmission ("if the set is sufficiently small"): unspecified — no numeric threshold given.
- Fingerprint size (`Fingerprint` type): unspecified — left to the implementation, with the sole constraint that `fingerprint_finalise` must not map distinct inputs to equal outputs.

### Stated limitations
The specification states that fingerprinting is "not mandatory for Willow, but it probably is a good idea," marking the entire fingerprinting construction as optional rather than a requirement of the reconciliation protocol itself.

The metadata mechanism used to track which ranges have been fully covered has a stated failure mode: "a malicious peer could provide wildly inadequate metadata," which corrupts a peer's own view of reconciliation progress. The specification does not describe a countermeasure beyond noting that a malicious peer already has other means to disrupt reconciliation, so this is treated as an accepted exposure rather than a solved problem.

The specification defers commutativity of `fingerprint_combine` as an extra requirement not present in the one-dimensional predecessor, because it declines to prescribe a linearization of the three-dimensional coordinate space; this is stated as a design choice rather than a defended proof that no acceptable order exists.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Reconciliation operates over `AuthorisedEntry` objects that already carry a `namespace_id`, `subspace_id`, `path`, `timestamp`, `payload_digest`, and `payload_length` — the rest of the system must supply and authenticate these fields before reconciliation can run, since the fingerprint function is defined over exactly this tuple.

The protocol assumes each peer can enumerate, for an arbitrary `3dRange`, the `LengthyAuthorisedEntry` set it holds inside that range, and can split that range into sub-ranges holding an approximately equal share of its local entries. This requires a local index over entries keyed by the three coordinates (subspace, path, timestamp) that supports efficient range queries and range splitting by entry count, not by coordinate-space width.

The protocol assumes each peer can determine how many consecutive bytes from the start of a given entry's payload it holds locally (the `available` field of `LengthyAuthorisedEntry`), which requires a storage layer that tracks partial payload receipt per entry rather than only complete/absent status.

Correctness of the whole scheme depends on `fingerprint_singleton` sensitivity to every entry field, together with a `fingerprint_finalise` function that maps distinct `PreFingerprint` values to distinct `Fingerprint` values with high probability even against maliciously crafted input. This is a requirement placed on whichever concrete hash function an implementation selects, not something the specification proves generically.

The `want_response` protocol state depends on message delivery and ordering being reliable enough that both peers agree on which range a given `3dRangeEntrySet` answers; the specification does not state a transport-layer requirement (e.g., ordered or reliable delivery) explicitly, leaving this implicit in the message-exchange description.

### Contradicts
None found.

### References worth retrieving
- Meyer, Aljoscha: "Range-Based Set Reconciliation." 2023 42nd International Symposium on Reliable Distributed Systems (SRDS), IEEE, 2023, pp. 59–69. — foundational (already in this corpus; this document is the direct generalization of Meyer's one-dimensional range-based set reconciliation to three dimensions).
- Minsky, Yaron; Trachtenberg, Ari; Zippel, Richard: "Set reconciliation with nearly optimal communication complexity." IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, vol. 49, Nr. 9, 2003, pp. 2213–2218. — foundational (states the general set reconciliation problem this protocol solves).

### Verbatim extracts
- "In the scientific literature, this problem is known as set reconciliation (Minsky et al., 2003)."
- "peers collaboratively drill down to the differences between their two sets in a logarithmic number of communication rounds"
- "it is crucial for overall efficiency to not split based on volume... but to split into subranges in which the peer holds roughly the same number of AuthorisedEntries"
- "a malicious peer could provide wildly inadequate metadata, but in general this is tolerable"
- "What we describe now is not mandatory for Willow, but it probably is a good idea."

## [WOLCHOK-WOOT-10] Crawling BitTorrent DHTs for Fun and Profit

**Citation:** Scott Wolchok, J. Alex Halderman. "Crawling BitTorrent DHTs for Fun and Profit." USENIX WOOT, 2010.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.usenix.org/legacy/events/woot10/tech/full_papers/Wolchok.pdf
**Source URL:** https://www.usenix.org/conference/woot10/crawling-bittorrent-dhts-fun-and-profit
**Domain:** J

### What it does
The paper demonstrates that a single machine can reconstruct which peers are downloading which content from an unmodified, widely deployed distributed hash table (DHT), by inserting many fake identities into the DHT and reading the data that legitimate replication delivers to them. A distributed hash table is a decentralized key-value store built as a peer-to-peer network in which every node and every stored key share one numeric address space, and each node holds a replica of the key-value pairs whose keys are numerically close to its own address. The authors reuse an existing crawler, ClearView, a from-scratch reimplementation of the Vuze DHT's Kademlia protocol that performs a Sybil attack (inserting many falsely distinct identities into a system that assumes one identity per participant) by running thousands of DHT client identities inside a single process. After the DHT's own periodic replication delivers nearby content to these planted identities, the crawler moves its identities to a new region of the address space and repeats, so a small number of processes cover a large fraction of the keyspace over successive rounds. Applied to search, the crawler extracts "torrent description" records (metadata records some Vuze clients create linking a torrent's info hash to its name, size, and seeder/leecher counts) and peer-list records (which list of IP addresses is currently exchanging a given torrent, keyed by a hash of the info hash), and stores them in a relational database with a full-text inverted index, so a rebuilt torrent search site (the authors' SuperSeed prototype) can be brought back online after a legal takedown of a centralized search site. Applied to monitoring, the same crawl (the DHT does not expose a way to permit content location without also exposing peer identity) is run repeatedly over time and the resulting peer-list and torrent-description records are joined on info hash to build content-to-IP-address and IP-address-to-content mappings, giving a content owner a per-IP-address history of what that address downloaded, without touching any centralized tracker or torrent discovery website.

### Measured results
| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| SuperSeed indexed 1,019,701 torrents on average per crawl | Vuze DHT only; each crawl = 2 hops of 4,000 Sybil identities each, 30 minutes per hop; crawls run 5 AM/1 PM/9 PM EDT daily to align with Vuze's 8-hour value-expiration time; averaged over 47 completed crawls out of 48 attempted over 16 days (May 10-25, 2010); single University of Michigan machine, 4-core Intel Xeon, 1 TB SATA disk at 3 Gb/s, 12 GB RAM |
| Estimated coverage: about 13% of all torrents estimated to exist in the Vuze DHT (7.5 million estimated total) | Estimate derived from recovering ~1.5 million peer lists per crawl, dividing by the crawler's estimated 20% keyspace coverage (from a prior analytic model, not measured directly in this paper), and multiplying by 5 assuming uniform peer-list distribution across the keyspace |
| Full SuperSeed bootstrap: about 100 minutes without .torrent-file retrieval, 153 minutes (2.55 hours) with it | Same 47-crawl setup; component breakdown: 81 min ClearView crawl, 13 min database import, plus optional 23 min peer refresh + 30 min .torrent retrieval + 6 min inverted-index build; crawl time could be reduced to 35-45 minutes at the same coverage if network bandwidth allowed |
| .torrent file retrieval succeeded for 56,590 of 249,371 torrents that had both a description and a peer list (22.7%) | Same 47-crawl average, single-machine setup as above |
| Monitoring over 16 days: 15,113,700 peer-list records, 10,354,067 unique IP addresses, 14,756,483 unique IP:port pairs; 1,538,522 torrents with both a description and a peer list, mapped to 7,934,945 IP addresses in 45,762,064 IP-torrent pairs | Same 16-day, single-machine crawl; IP-torrent pair count described by the authors as roughly the number of observed downloads |
| .torrent retrieval for monitoring: succeeded for 400,908 of 1,538,522 torrents by torrent count (26.1%), but for 37,682,371 of 45,762,064 IP-torrent pairs by peer-weighted count (82%) | Same 16-day crawl; the authors note the un-retrieved torrents skew toward very low peer counts (343,983 had only one peer) |
| Top ten torrents by observed IP count ranged from 33,089 to 47,612 downloads and represented under 1% of total observed downloads; 9 of 10 were video, half were recent TV episodes | Same 16-day crawl, ranked by number of distinct IP addresses associated per torrent |
| Manual inspection of the 1,000 most popular torrents with retrieved .torrent files (13% of observed downloads) found only one apparently non-infringing file, ranked 925th | Same dataset; classification performed manually by the authors, not by the automated classifier |
| Automated content classification by file extension: video 216,178 (53.9%), audio 92,128 (23.0%), unclassified archive 29,050 (7.2%), software 17,837 (4.4%), books 16,658 (4.2%), unclassified disk image 8,390 (2.1%), games 7,444 (1.9%), unclassified 5,316 (1.3%), images 4,216 (1.1%), other 3,691 (0.9%) | Rule-based classifier over filenames/extensions from all torrents for which a .torrent file was recovered during the 16-day monitoring crawl |
| Four outlier IP addresses in the same /24 subnet, identified as belonging to an SSL VPN provider (anchorfree.com), showed a distinctive linear relation between number of torrents joined and number of distinct ports used, among the top 10,000 IP addresses by torrent count | Same 16-day crawl; used to distinguish proxy/NAT aggregation points from individual heavy downloaders |

### Parameters
- ClearView hop interval: 30 minutes (increased from an original 3-minute interval after Vuze removed replicate-on-join behavior in response to a related earlier attack against the Vanish system)
- Sybil identities per hop: 4,000 (10x the identity count used in the earlier 3-minute-hop configuration, to compensate for the longer hop interval and preserve roughly the same coverage)
- Hops per crawl: 2, each 30 minutes, for a total crawl duration of about 1 hour of active hopping per crawl (81 minutes measured including startup)
- Crawl schedule: three crawls per day (5 AM, 1 PM, 9 PM EDT), aligned to the Vuze DHT's 8-hour key-value expiration time
- Database: PostgreSQL 8.3, used for storage and full-text search via its built-in keyword search facility
- Vuze DHT size relative to Mainline DHT: 25-50% as many nodes as Mainline, stated as background, not separately measured in this study

### Stated limitations
The authors explicitly did not measure what fraction of indexed torrents could actually be downloaded (some indexed torrents may have zero seeders). The coverage estimate of 13% of all torrents rests on an assumption that peer lists are uniformly distributed through the DHT keyspace and on an unverified analytic coverage model carried over from a prior paper, not on ground truth. The Vuze DHT is chosen over the larger Mainline DHT solely to avoid the added engineering complexity of supporting two DHT protocols in the crawler; the authors state the same technique should extend to Mainline but did not implement or measure it. Torrent description records exist only because a specific Vuze client feature creates them when a user downloads two torrents in the same session, so the search technique depends on that client feature's continued presence and is not a property of the DHT protocol itself. Peer identification from IP address is degraded by proxy and NAT aggregation, which the authors detect but cannot fully resolve into individual users. The paper is exploratory and offers no defense or countermeasure against the crawling attacks it demonstrates; the conclusion recommends increasing legal and content-poisoning pressure on individual infringers rather than proposing a technical fix to the DHT.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A DHT that supports distributed content tracking by storing (info hash, peer address) pairs as key-value records cannot prevent a participant from reading those records once it holds a numerically nearby identity, because DHT replication delivers stored values to any node whose address is close enough in the keyspace, honest or not; the paper's central finding is that search-enabling replication and monitoring-enabling exposure are the same mechanism and cannot be separated ("BitTorrent DHTs cannot allow one and prevent the other"). Any system relying on this class of Kademlia-style DHT for content location must assume that any sufficiently resourced observer can enumerate a large fraction of active (content, IP address) pairs within days, using commodity hardware, without cooperation from any tracker or discovery site. A design that wants to prevent this needs either admission control that makes Sybil identity insertion costly, or a mechanism that does not deliver full peer lists to arbitrary nearby nodes.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus. Cross-check candidate: WANG-GLOBECOM-12 measures Sybil identities actually observed in the live Mainline DHT (not Vuze) and should be checked against this paper's Sybil-insertion technique (which targets Vuze, not Mainline) for whether the two DHTs show comparable vulnerability, since they are different DHT instances with only architectural similarity.

### References worth retrieving
- foundational: Maymounkov, Mazières, "Kademlia: A peer-to-peer information system based on the XOR metric," IPTPS 2002, pp. 52-56 — the routing protocol both BitTorrent DHTs implement (already in corpus per BRIEF §7)
- foundational: Douceur, "The Sybil attack," IPTPS 2002, pp. 251-260 — defines the identity-forgery attack this paper's crawler performs
- foundational: Wolchok, Hoffmann, Heninger, Felten, Halderman, Rossbach, Waters, Witchel, "Defeating Vanish with low-cost Sybil attacks against large DHTs," NDSS 2010, pp. 37-51 — the authors' own prior paper introducing the ClearView crawler this paper reuses; contains the analytic coverage model this paper's 20%/13% coverage estimate depends on
- competing: Grunthal, "Efficient indexing of the BitTorrent distributed hash table," unpublished manuscript, Esslingen University of Applied Sciences — a concurrently developed Mainline DHT crawler using tens of low-footprint nodes rather than thousands of Sybils, reported by this paper as retrieving 500,000 new .torrent files in one week versus this paper's 400,000 in 16 days
- competing: Le Blond, Legout, Lefessant, Dabbous, Kaafar, "Spying the world from your laptop -- identifying and profiling content providers and big downloaders in BitTorrent," USENIX LEET 2010 — centralized-tracker-based monitoring the authors call most similar to their own work, collecting 148 million IP addresses and about 2 million torrents over 103 days from Pirate Bay and Mininova
- competing: Zhang, Dhungel, Wu, Ross, "Unraveling the BitTorrent ecosystem" — independent large-scale BitTorrent measurement via centralized sites; reported comparable content-category results and a 4.6-million-torrent crawl of five discovery sites used as this paper's coverage comparison point
- competing: Piatek, Kohno, Krishnamurthy, "Challenges and directions for monitoring P2P file sharing networks," USENIX HotSec 2008, pp. 1-7 — prior monitoring work via discovery sites and trackers
- attack/critique (self-referential): Geambasu, Kohno, Levy, Levy, "Vanish: Increasing data privacy with self-destructing data," USENIX Security 2009, pp. 299-314 — the system the authors' earlier Sybil-crawling technique was originally built to attack

### Verbatim extracts
- "It can efficiently host thousands of DHT clients in a single process."
- "BitTorrent DHTs cannot allow one and prevent the other."
- "key-value pairs are still replicated every 30 minutes, so for this work, we configured ClearView to wait 30 minutes"
- "we estimate that there are 1.5 million x 5 = 7.5 million torrents in the Vuze DHT on average"
- "Only one file was obviously non-infringing"
- "DHT-based monitoring can let us watch the watchers!"

## [WORLDCOIN-WP] World (Worldcoin) Whitepapers — "Building World," "Achieving Proof of Human," "Advancing Decentralization," "Designing for Scale"

**Citation:** Tools for Humanity (collective; not peer-reviewed). "World Whitepapers." Project whitepaper, updated March 25 2026. No DOI.
**Retrieved:** full text via candidate URL `https://whitepaper.world.org/`
**Source URL:** https://whitepaper.world.org/
**Domain:** E

### What it does
World issues a per-person credential (World ID) that lets a relying party check a presented proof against a public registry and learn only a single bit — unique-human member of the set, yes or no — without learning which person. The registry membership check runs as follows. At enrollment, a purpose-built infrared camera called the Orb captures iris images inside a trusted execution environment (TEE) on the device, derives a fixed-length code from the iris texture using multi-scale Gabor wavelet filtering and phase quantization of the filter output, and never uploads the raw image for the uniqueness check. The Orb splits that iris code into multiple encrypted fragments before the uniqueness check runs, so no single party holds a decodable code; this fragment scheme is called Anonymized Multi-Party Computation (AMPC). Multiple independent operators each hold one fragment and jointly compute whether the new code's Hamming distance to every previously enrolled code falls below a match threshold, without any party learning the distance values — the joint computation returns only a match/no-match bit. If no match is found, a World ID secret (a random byte string) is generated, its hash is added to a public registry (a Semaphore identity set implemented as an Ethereum smart contract, replicated to other chains through state bridges), and a Proof of Human (PoH) credential is returned to the user's device. To authenticate later, the user's app produces a zero-knowledge proof (zk-SNARK, via Semaphore, using Poseidon hashing over the BN254 scalar field) that it holds a secret whose hash sits in the registry, paired with a nullifier that prevents that same secret from producing multiple valid proofs for the same relying-party action; the relying party checks the proof against the public registry and learns only that the presenter is a unique registered human, not which one.

### Measured results
| Metric | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| False match rate (FMR) target | 1×10⁻¹² system-wide | Design target so a genuine new signup, checked against a billion enrolled identities, has a 1-in-1000 chance of false rejection |
| FMR required per iris comparison to reach the system target | 1×10⁻⁶ per iris | Stated as the per-comparison rate needed to reach the 1×10⁻¹² system-wide target at billion-identity scale |
| False non-match rate (FNMR) target | below 5×10⁻³ | Same billion-identity design target |
| FMR achieved in pre-launch testing | 2.25×10⁻¹⁴ | "Extensive, purpose-built test sets conducted prior to launch," at approximately 1×10⁻³ FNMR — no dataset size, demographic composition, or independent-lab identifier is given in the text |
| FMR in real-world operation (stated, not a controlled test) | approximately 1×10⁻¹² | Described as "the measured error rate of the system for confusing any two people to be the same" in real-world operations, translated to roughly 99.999% true acceptance and 0.001% false rejection at billion-person scale; no measurement methodology, sample count, or time window is given |
| Face-biometric FMR for comparison | "far below" iris FMR, no figure given | Stated qualitatively only — the paper asserts face recognition is not accurate enough for exclusion-free billion-scale deduplication but gives no comparable numeric rate |
| Sybil arithmetic for credential resale | 1% of the US population selling 9 of 10 acquired credentials lets one actor pose as 31 million Americans | Illustrative arithmetic in the paper's own text (0.01 × ~310M × 10), not a measured attack — included here as the authors' stated reasoning for requiring strict one-credential-per-person uniqueness, not as an observed incident |

No independent, third-party-reproducible benchmark harness, dataset identifier, or peer-reviewed test methodology is given for any of these figures; every number above is self-reported by the issuing organization.

### Parameters
- False match rate design target: 1×10⁻¹² system-wide (billion-identity scale), requiring 1×10⁻⁶ per-iris FMR.
- False non-match rate design target: below 5×10⁻³.
- Two hardware-burned cryptographic keys per Orb unit: one provisioned into the main system-on-chip during manufacturing, one in a hardware secure element that cannot be exported; the device refuses to operate unless both keys validate and their execution environments are intact.
- Identity-set commitment scheme: Poseidon hash over the BN254 scalar field, used as the hash function whose output populates the Semaphore membership set.
- Zero-knowledge proof system: Semaphore, built on Groth16-verifiable zk-SNARKs, deployable to any chain capable of verifying Groth16 proofs.
- Personal Custody Package (PCP) currently contains: iris and face embeddings, raw iris and face images, and the AMPC fragments — each field individually encrypted (each MPC fragment with the public key of its specific AMPC party), then the whole package encrypted again on the Orb with a user-supplied key before leaving the device.

### Stated limitations
The paper states biometric verification is inherently probabilistic and carries nonzero error rates at any threshold choice; it does not claim a zero-error system. Some severe eye conditions reduce iris-biometric accuracy (common conditions such as cataracts are stated not to matter meaningfully); the paper proposes specialized verification centers using facial biometrics as a fallback but states this extension "would need careful design to preserve the system's integrity" and has not built it. Smartphone and existing consumer iris cameras are stated to lack the imaging resolution, multi-angle capture, and active illumination needed for reliable presentation-attack detection, which the paper gives as the reason a purpose-built device (the Orb) is required rather than a phone. Without an on-device trusted execution environment enforcing that image capture originates from a compliant device, the paper states attackers could spoof both image capture and enrollment requests to create unlimited fraudulent credentials — a control the paper says many smartphones cannot provide because on-device secure enclaves are inconsistently available or accessible only to the phone manufacturer. Uniqueness without a strict one-credential-per-person guarantee is stated to be vulnerable to relay attacks, where a small group of humans repeatedly authenticate on behalf of many automated agents. The paper states that "any hardware system interacting with the physical world requires continual enhancements" and describes third-party audits (Theori, Trail of Bits, Least Authority) and a bug bounty program as ongoing responses, not a closed problem. AMPC's roadmap section states current work is to reduce compute requirements and to add trusted execution environments to the compute nodes, which are not yet in place. World ID 4.0, described as a future protocol upgrade, is stated to introduce a distributed oblivious pseudorandom function (OPRF) network for nullifier computation and enforced one-time-use nullifiers — implying the nullifier scheme described elsewhere in the current text does not yet have these properties.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A relying party that wants to check a PoH credential must be able to verify a Semaphore zk-SNARK proof (Groth16) against a public registry commitment; the paper assumes the verifier can read that on-chain (or state-bridged) commitment. The uniqueness check requires every enrollment to reach at least one live AMPC compute node operated by one of the named independent institutions (Nethermind, University of Erlangen-Nuremberg, UC Berkeley RDI, with KAIST and UTEC stated as joining); no fragment holder alone can complete a match. The one-registry-per-person invariant that the whole scheme depends on assumes iris images are captured only by hardware meeting the paper's stated multispectral, TEE-backed, tamper-monitored specification — a general-purpose camera or phone is stated to be insufficient for the false-match-rate target. The paper assumes each enrolling person has functioning eyes matching the biometric modality; it names no complete alternative-verification path already built for people who cannot use iris capture. The nullifier mechanism assumes relying parties supply an action-scoped context so that the same person's proof produces different nullifiers per context, preventing cross-context linkage — the mechanics of nullifier scoping are referenced but not specified in the excerpted text. The whole registry-membership approach assumes the identity-set commitment (the Merkle-style set of secret hashes) is kept synchronized across every chain a relying party might verify against, through the state-bridge mechanism the paper names but does not detail.

### Contradicts
The paper's own claim that "no biometric data ever leave the user's device" is qualified elsewhere in the same text: the Personal Custody Package, which does leave the Orb (it is sent to the user's device, not retained on the Orb, but the raw iris and face images and iris/face embeddings are the biometric data in question, packaged and encrypted, not withheld from ever being formed off the sensor into a transportable artifact). This is the paper's own internal tension between "processed locally" language and the explicit list of raw images and embeddings inside the PCP; it is not a claim from another source. No other paper in this corpus makes a directly conflicting measurement — this is the only source in the batch on iris-based proof of personhood.

### References worth retrieving
The whitepaper carries no numbered academic bibliography; it names sources inline without full citations. From the text:
- Iris recognition foundational method — John Daugman, 1993, cited by name only ("Iris recognition was first developed in 1993 by John Daugman") — foundational, needed for the actual false-match-rate literature this paper's figures are compared against.
- Semaphore protocol (Ethereum privacy layer using zk-SNARKs / Groth16) — named, no citation given — foundational, needed to verify the nullifier and set-membership mechanism claimed here.
- The paper's companion whitepapers ("Achieving Proof of Human," "Advancing Decentralization," "Designing for Scale") are referenced as separate documents in the same series — competing/complementary, worth retrieving as they are stated to contain the uniqueness-mechanism detail and decentralization-roadmap detail this document defers to them.

### Verbatim extracts
- "a FMR of 1x10-6 per iris" needed to reach system-wide "1x10-12" at billion scale.
- "These targets were exceeded ... an FMR of 2.25×10⁻¹⁴ at approximately 1×10⁻³ FNMR."
- "AMPC ... reveals only a single bit per invocation: whether the individual has previously verified."
- "no code can run without a valid cryptographic signature."
- "a single malicious actor could masquerade as 31 million Americans."
- "Without such protections, attackers could spoof both image capture and enrollment requests."

## [XAVIER-ARXIV-24] An evidence-based and critical analysis of the Fediverse decentralization promises

**Citation:** Henrique S. Xavier. "An evidence-based and critical analysis of the Fediverse decentralization promises." WebMedia 2024 (arXiv preprint), 2024. arXiv:2408.15383.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.15383
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.15383
**Domain:** J

### What it does
The paper argues, from a mix of protocol analysis and traffic measurement, that the Fediverse (the network of independently operated social media servers, called instances, that interoperate through the ActivityPub protocol) does not by itself prevent concentration of users onto a small number of instances or capture by for-profit companies. It examines what ActivityPub, the protocol governing inter-instance communication, technically enforces versus what it merely permits: a post made on one instance only propagates to a second instance if the second instance has not blocked the first and at least one user on the second follows the author, an account is bound to a single home instance and cannot post through another instance's identity, and nothing in the protocol prevents an instance from running proprietary code, injecting advertisements or algorithmic recommendations, or being operated by a for-profit or Big Tech entity. The paper then measures the actual current distribution of Fediverse users across instances using a public crawler dataset, compares monthly visit traffic between prominent Fediverse-connected domains, and draws a structural analogy to two older, similarly permissionless decentralized protocols — email (SMTP) and the World Wide Web (HTTP) — arguing from those systems' measured traffic concentration that a protocol allowing anyone to run a server does not, on its own, prevent traffic and user concentration in practice.

### Measured results

| Quantity | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Instances in dataset | 21,146 | Collected from fediverse.observer on 2024-08-02; fediverse.observer builds its index via crawlers that start from known instances and trace connections through user-following relationships |
| Instances with fewer than 5 active users | 82% of 21,146 | Same dataset |
| Instances with zero active users | 24% of 21,146 | Same dataset |
| Largest single instance (mastodon.social) monthly active users | approximately 225,000 | As of August 2024, same crawler dataset |
| User concentration on top instances | 50% of all active Fediverse users on the top 20 instances; 80% of all active users on 189 instances (0.9% of the 21,146-instance dataset) | Same crawler dataset, cumulative distribution over instances ranked by active user count |
| Total FOSS-based (non-Threads) Fediverse active users | approximately 1 million | Same dataset, August 2024 |
| Meta Threads active users, for comparison | 150 million | As of April 2024, cited from a TechCrunch report of a Mark Zuckerberg statement, not independently measured by this paper |
| Most-followed ActivityPub accounts, June 2024 | four highest-follower accounts on the Fediverse all hosted on Threads: Barack Obama (4.5M), Mark Zuckerberg (4.1M), Joe Biden (3M), the White House (1M) | Reported from a cited web archive snapshot, not independently measured by this paper |
| Average monthly visits, Mar-May 2024 (Table 1) | threads.net: 303.4 million; gab.com: 5.0 million; baraag.net: 2.9 million; mastodon.social: 2.6 million | SimilarWeb traffic-estimation data, March-May 2024 |
| Webmail traffic concentration | live.com and mail.ru accounted for 44.8% and 25.9% of the "Email" industry's global traffic, Aug-Oct 2023, among 2,406 SimilarWeb-classified email domains; live.com had 2.19 billion monthly visits vs. mail.google.com's 10.88 billion (mail.google.com excluded from the industry ranking as a subdomain, so the paper states true concentration is likely understated by this figure) | SimilarWeb traffic data |
| Outsourced email-service concentration | 28.5% and 10.8% of the most popular domains (Alexa top 1 million, 2017-2021 sample) had email service provided by Google and Microsoft respectively; among a random sample of .com domains, GoDaddy served as email provider for 29% | Cited from Liu et al., IMC 2021, not independently measured by this paper |
| Web traffic concentration | approximately 3,000 of over 100 million web domains account for 50% of global web traffic; the "Social Networks and Online Communities" category (one of SimilarWeb's top 5 industries by traffic out of 187 tracked) received 50 billion monthly visits Aug-Oct 2023, with Meta (Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp combined) capturing 52% of that category's traffic; mastodon.social ranked 282nd in the same category, under 0.01% of its traffic | SimilarWeb data, same reporting period |

### Parameters
No experimental parameters in the sense of a simulation or system implementation; this is a measurement-and-argument paper drawing on two external third-party datasets: fediverse.observer (crawled Fediverse instance/user counts, snapshot date 2024-08-02) and SimilarWeb (commercial web-traffic estimation service, reporting periods March-May 2024 for the instance-traffic comparison and August-October 2023 for the email- and web-industry concentration figures).

### Stated limitations
The paper states its own future work explicitly: to survey Fediverse instances directly rather than relying on third-party crawler data (fediverse.observer), to examine ActivityPub's and the AT Protocol's selective implementation and vulnerability to manipulation in more depth, and to connect the Fediverse's anticipated evolution to broader social harms (hate speech, disinformation, mental health effects, behavioral manipulation) which this paper raises as open questions rather than measures. The paper itself notes a methodological caveat on its own webmail concentration figure: SimilarWeb excludes mail.google.com from its "Email" industry ranking because it treats it as a subdomain, so the reported industry-share concentration for Google understates the true figure, evidenced by mail.google.com's own visit count (10.88 billion) exceeding the reported industry leader live.com's count (2.19 billion). The paper notes unique-visitor counts (used for the SimilarWeb non-Fediverse comparison) are not the same measure as monthly active users (used for the fediverse.observer Fediverse figures), since active users require an authenticated login while unique visitors do not, and states the two are "close enough" to support a directional comparison without claiming numeric equivalence. Threads (Meta's ActivityPub-connected platform) is described as only one-way connected to the Fediverse: Fediverse users can follow Threads accounts, but Threads users cannot follow or view content from other Fediverse instances, so a plain sum of "Fediverse users" that includes Threads' 150 million active users overstates the interoperable population; the paper does not itself compute an adjusted combined total accounting for this asymmetry.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
None — this is an argument-and-measurement paper about an existing deployed protocol's observed concentration, not a description of a mechanism with implementable preconditions for another system to satisfy. Its measured concentration figures (82% of instances under 5 active users; 50% of users on the top 20 of 21,146 instances) are directly relevant as a base rate against which any newly designed federated or peer-to-peer social system's own concentration should be compared, since they establish that permitting anyone to run an independent server does not, without an additional enforced mechanism, prevent the emergence of a small number of dominant nodes.

### Contradicts
The paper explicitly states that a specific popular claim about the Fediverse — that a user can post using an account from any instance the way one might expect from a fully peer-to-peer system — is inaccurate, and clarifies that posting requires an account specific to the instance being posted from, with cross-instance visibility gated by both the receiving instance's block list and its users' follow relationships. This is presented as a correction of a claim commonly made about the Fediverse's flexibility, not a disagreement with another paper in this corpus. No disagreement with another entry in this corpus found.

### References worth retrieving
- Christine Lemmer-Webber, Jessica Tallon, Erin Shepherd, Amy Guy, Evan Prodromou, "ActivityPub," W3C Recommendation, 2018 — foundational (the protocol specification the paper's technical analysis is built on).
- Enze Liu, Gautam Akiwate, Mattijs Jonker, Ariana Mirian, Stefan Savage, Geoffrey M. Voelker, "Who's got your mail? characterizing mail service provider usage," ACM Internet Measurement Conference (IMC), 2021, pp. 122-136, DOI 10.1145/3487552.3487820 — foundational (the source of the paper's email-outsourcing concentration figures; worth retrieving directly for its full methodology and raw numbers rather than relying on this paper's citation of it).
- Danielle Allen, Eli Frankel, Woojin Lim, Divya Siddarth, Joshua Simons, E.
