## [XIE-ARXIV-26] Revisiting and Expanding the IPv6 Network Periphery: Global-Scale Measurement and Security Analysis

**Citation:** Zixuan Xie, Zitao Yang, Shurui Fang, Zhaoyang Li, Wenxing Xie, Nannan Fu, Liangyu Dong, Xiang Li. "Revisiting and Expanding the IPv6 Network Periphery: Global-Scale Measurement and Security Analysis." arXiv preprint (CoRR); under review, IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security, 2026. DOI 10.48550/ARXIV.2604.19487.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/html/2604.19487v2
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.19487
**Domain:** L

### What it does
The paper measures how many end-host devices sit reachable at the "periphery" of the global IPv6 network — the boundary devices (home routers, gateways, last-hop equipment) that terminate an Internet Service Provider's routed prefixes — rather than measuring only how many IPv6 prefixes or Autonomous Systems are routed. To make Internet-scale active scanning of the sparse IPv6 address space tractable, the paper introduces Response-Guided Prefix Selection (RGPS): starting from Border Gateway Protocol (BGP)-announced prefixes for selected Internet Service Providers, RGPS keeps prefixes between /28 and /48 directly, and for shorter (larger) prefixes it first runs an exploratory scan, collects the source addresses that actually respond, and derives active /28 sub-prefixes from those responses rather than scanning the full shorter prefix; during scanning of any candidate prefix, RGPS terminates early if no new device responds for τ=2 minutes, on the reasoning that XMap's randomized (non-sequential) address-generation order makes a stretch of silence informative about the remaining a prefix's density. XMap (a ZMap-derived high-speed IPv6 prober using GNU Multiple Precision arithmetic to permute large address ranges) performs the network-layer probing; ZGrab2 then performs application-layer fingerprinting (service banners, TLS certificates, HTTP responses) on hosts XMap finds responsive. Built on the discovered device population, the paper runs three further measurements: a service-exposure scan (checking DNS, NTP, FTP, SSH, TELNET, HTTP/80, TLS, HTTP/8080 on each discovered device and matching returned software-version banners against Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) records), a routing-loop detection probe (sending an ICMPv6 Echo Request with Hop Limit 32 to an address in an unassigned subnet, and confirming a loop only if both that Hop Limit and a retransmission at Hop Limit+2 each independently elicit an ICMPv6 Time Exceeded reply, which the paper argues distinguishes a genuine forwarding loop from an isolated routing anomaly), and a case study applying a three-stage Hierarchical LLM (Large Language Model) Exposure Verification (HLEV) framework — transport-layer port reachability, then application-layer response-signature matching, then model-identifier confirmation via tool-specific query endpoints — to check whether any discovered periphery device exposes a local LLM-serving tool's unauthenticated API.

### Measured results
| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| 281.9M total IPv6 network periphery devices discovered globally | 73 countries/regions, 164 ISPs across all 5 Regional Internet Registries (RIRs); APNIC region alone contributes 249.51M (88.50%) across 17 regions/43 ISPs, RIPE NCC contributes 22.05M (7.82%) across the broadest span (35 regions/63 ISPs), ARIN 5.76M (2.04%), LACNIC 4.52M (1.60%), AFRINIC 87.40k (0.03%) |
| Device count across the 15 original ISP blocks in India, China, and the U.S. rose from 52.6M (2021 baseline) to 244.8M (2025 revisit), a 364.8% increase; Bharti Airtel mobile (India) rose from 22.5M to 205.6M (approximately 9-fold); BSNL broadband (India) rose more than 75-fold | Direct comparison against the same 15 ISP blocks measured by the 2021 baseline study (Li et al., DSN 2021), using one representative prefix per block in the 2025 revisit versus the full block coverage used in 2021; 9 of 15 blocks show growth (49.6% to 7440.4% increase), 6 show a decrease the authors attribute to reduced (single-prefix) 2025 scan scope rather than genuine decline, since even the reduced-scope single-prefix counts reach at least 8.6% of the corresponding full-block 2021 counts |
| 2.5% (approximately 7.1M) of discovered devices expose at least one of eight measured services; SSH most common at 1.0%, HTTP/80 at 0.7% | Global scan; per-RIR average exposed-service count per device: ARIN 1.040, APNIC 0.249, LACNIC 0.120, RIPE NCC 0.016, AFRINIC 0.008 — ARIN has the highest exposure density despite APNIC having far more total devices |
| Within the 15 original 2021-baseline blocks, total exposure across the 8 tracked services dropped even as device count rose roughly 5-fold: HTTP/8080 3.5M→78k, HTTP/80 1.3M→138k, DNS 741k→210k, TLS 144k→31.2k | Same 15-block longitudinal comparison; 9 of 15 blocks (2,3,4,5,6,7,10,11,12 per the paper's numbering) show exposure not growing proportionally with device count, which the authors attribute to tightened ISP filtering; some blocks show growth in specific services (e.g., Comcast in HTTP/80, TLS, HTTP/8080; China Telecom in FTP, TELNET, HTTP/8080) |
| HLEV case study confirmed exactly 1 exposed local-LLM-tool instance (an Ollama deployment) among the discovered IPv6 periphery devices | Applied to the full 281.9M-device discovered population, using default-port probing for Ollama, LM Studio, GPT4All, Jan.ai, vLLM, Xinference, and LobeChat |
| 4,517,099 devices (1.6% of all scanned) show routing-loop behavior globally; within the 15 original 2021-baseline blocks, the affected proportion fell from 11.04% (2021) to 1.43% (2025 revisit), an absolute device-count drop from 5.8M to 3.5M | Global figure: 281.92M devices scanned total, breakdown by RIR: AFRINIC 0.62%, APNIC 1.59% (3.96M of 249.51M), ARIN 0.54%, LACNIC 6.01% (highest regional rate, 0.27M of 4.52M), RIPE 1.15% (0.25M of 22.05M); China alone contributes 3,375,219 of the globally affected devices, with AS9808 alone contributing 2,341,168 |

### Parameters
- RGPS prefix-length range for direct scanning: /28 to /48 (upper bound /48 chosen as the longest commonly routable IPv6 prefix; lower bound /28 chosen for scanning efficiency)
- RGPS early-stop threshold τ: 2 minutes of no new response before terminating a candidate prefix's scan early
- Routing-loop probe Hop Limit: 32, chosen on cited evidence that 99% of Internet paths involve fewer than 32 hops, validated by the authors against recent Route Views BGP data
- Routing-loop confirmation retransmission: Hop Limit incremented by 2 (h+2) on a repeat probe; a loop is confirmed only if both the original and the h+2 probe each independently elicit an ICMPv6 Time Exceeded (Type 3) message
- Regions/ISPs covered: 73 countries/regions, 164 ISPs, spanning all 5 RIRs, selected using public country-level IPv6 deployment statistics from APNIC Labs and Google as a prioritization signal (which the authors state biases the sample toward denser, more active IPv6 deployments)
- Total discovered periphery-fingerprint dataset used for cloud/service attribution: not separately reported for this paper (compare VALAPU-ARXIV-25's independent 265,248-FQDN dataset, a different measurement)

### Stated limitations
The paper's region, ISP, and prefix selection prioritizes observable/active IPv6 deployment, so the authors state the 281.9M figure is not a complete census of the IPv6 Internet and is biased toward denser, more active networks. The sparse IPv6 address space means some active devices or exposed services may go undetected regardless of scanning strategy. Service-fingerprinting-to-CVE mapping via software-version banners indicates potential vulnerability, not confirmed exploitability, because of incomplete version strings, vendor-specific modifications, or backported security patches the CVE database cannot detect from a banner alone — the authors state this explicitly for the CVE-count table. The HLEV LLM case study confirmed only one exposed instance among IPv6 periphery devices specifically, which the authors state should not be read as evidence that LLM-tool exposure is negligible across the broader IPv6 Internet, since periphery devices (gateways, routing infrastructure) are not where local LLM services would typically run; the authors state the same HLEV methodology needs to be applied to broader IPv6 end-host address space or to IPv4 to assess LLM exposure meaningfully. The 6 (of 15) ISP blocks showing an apparent 2021-to-2025 device-count decrease reflect the 2025 revisit's reduced single-prefix-per-block scanning scope rather than a claimed real decline, and the authors state that exhaustive rescanning would likely show further growth in those blocks too.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A component that assumes exposed-service prevalence tracks total device-population growth is contradicted by this paper's own longitudinal comparison: total exposure across the 15 original blocks dropped even as the device count in those same blocks grew roughly 5-fold, so a design must not infer growing attack surface directly from growing IPv6 deployment scale without an independent exposure measurement. A component relying on ICMPv6-based loop or reachability diagnostics must account for path lengths up to the Hop-Limit-32 threshold this paper validated against current Route Views data as covering 99% of paths; a diagnostic using a materially smaller Hop Limit risks false negatives on longer paths, and one using a materially larger Hop Limit risks amplifying any loop it does detect (more packet repetitions per detection attempt). RGPS's prefix-selection method depends on the target ISP's BGP-announced prefixes already being discoverable through a BGP-data source (the paper uses the Hurricane Electric BGP Toolkit) and on that ISP's devices being reachable enough to produce responses to an exploratory scan within the RGPS early-stop window; an ISP or deployment that filters ICMP/scan probes at the border, or that concentrates its live hosts in prefixes shorter than /28 without producing responsive addresses under exploratory scanning, would be underrepresented by this method regardless of true device population. A design treating IPv6-periphery-device exposure or CVE-banner counts as a proxy for confirmed exploitable vulnerability inventory needs its own independent version-confirmation step, since the authors state banner-to-CVE matching only indicates potential, not confirmed, exploitability.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus as a direct measurement disagreement. The paper's own data complicates a plausible prior expectation (not itself a claim commonly attributed to a specific prior paper in this corpus) that rapid IPv6 deployment growth necessarily increases the absolute exposed-service attack surface: within the same 15 blocks the 2021 study measured, device count rose roughly 5-fold while total tracked-service exposure fell by roughly an order of magnitude, which the paper attributes to tightened ISP-side filtering introduced alongside expansion rather than to any inherent property of IPv6 itself.

## [XU-ARXIV-25] Distributed Retrieval-Augmented Generation
**Citation:** Chenhao Xu, Longxiang Gao, Yuan Miao, Xi Zheng. "Distributed Retrieval-Augmented Generation." arXiv:2505.00443, 2025.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.00443
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.00443
**Domain:** B

### What it does
Distributed Retrieval-Augmented Generation (DRAG) answers a user query by combining a large language model (LLM, a machine-learned text-generation model) running locally on a device with knowledge fetched from other devices over a peer-to-peer network, instead of drawing on one centralized knowledge base. Each device (peer) holds a local knowledge base, a local LLM, and a communication module. On a query, the querying peer's local LLM first checks whether its own knowledge base answers the query, by comparing semantic similarity between the query and local content against a threshold (or by using explicit or implicit user dissatisfaction signals). If local knowledge is insufficient, the peer starts a network search using the paper's routing algorithm, Topic-Aware Random Walk (TARW). Once a peer along the search path returns a relevant knowledge snippet, that peer applies a privacy filter (rule-based or LLM-driven) before releasing the snippet, so raw local data does not leave the source peer. The querying peer's local LLM combines the returned snippet(s) with its own local context to generate the final answer, and caches the result locally, along with which peers held which topics, to speed and reduce the cost of future queries on similar topics.

TARW is a random walk over the peer graph, modified to prefer neighbors that past experience suggests hold relevant knowledge. Given a query, the querying peer's LLM first extracts a set of topics from the query text. The walk keeps a visited-peer set and a queue of (peer, hop-count) pairs, starting from the querying peer at hop 0, and a cache of peer expertise built up as the walk (and past walks) proceed. At each step the algorithm dequeues one (peer, hop-count) pair; if the hop count has reached the maximum `H_max` it drops that branch. Otherwise it queries the dequeued peer's local knowledge base and computes a relevance score between the returned knowledge and the original query. If that score meets or exceeds a threshold `θ`, the walk stops, the peer's identity and the query's topics are added to the expertise cache, and the returned knowledge is passed through the privacy filter and returned as the result. Otherwise the algorithm looks at the dequeued peer's not-yet-visited neighbors, scores each neighbor using the cached expertise history against the query's topics, and enqueues only the top `k` scoring neighbors (rather than all neighbors, as an unweighted random walk or query broadcast would) at hop-count+1. If the queue empties before any peer meets the relevance threshold within `H_max` hops, the walk returns no result.

### Measured results

Network simulated with the NetworkX Python library using the Barabási-Albert preferential-attachment topology model to approximate Internet- or social-media-like connectivity. Three question-answering datasets: MMLU (a multiple-choice general-knowledge benchmark), Medical Extended (a synthetic dataset of generated patient questions and doctor answers), and News (approximately 210,000 HuffPost news headlines, 2012-2022, task is identifying the article's author from its headline). Default LLM Llama 3.2-3B (3-billion-parameter model), with Gemma 2 2B and Qwen2.5 3B also tested. Default network: 20 peers, connectivity 4 (Barabási-Albert attachment edges per new node), `H_max`=6, neighbor-selection count `k`=4, relevance threshold `θ`=0.8. All figures below are averages; the paper does not state the number of independent simulation runs per data point.

| Comparison | Result | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| DRAG-TARW vs. DRAG-Flooding (DRAG-FL), message count | TARW: 6.87 messages (MMLU), 8.82 (Medical), 7.82 (News); FL: 10.91 (MMLU), 9.72 (Medical), 10.99 (News) | Default 20-peer network, Llama 3.2-3B, connectivity 4, H_max=6, k=4, θ=0.8 |
| DRAG-TARW vs. DRAG-FL, accuracy (EM/F1/Precision/Recall) | TARW slightly below FL on every dataset: e.g. MMLU F1 83.92% (TARW) vs. 85.45% (FL); Medical F1 90.58% (TARW) vs. 91.58% (FL); News F1 74.73% (TARW) vs. 76.54% (FL) | Same setup as above |
| DRAG-TARW vs. DRAG-Random-Walk (DRAG-RW), hit rate | TARW 98.11% vs. RW 23.46% | MMLU, default 20-peer setup |
| DRAG-TARW vs. Centralized RAG (CRAG) | TARW EM 83.90% vs. CRAG EM 85.73%; TARW F1 83.92% vs. CRAG F1 85.75% | MMLU, complete centralized knowledge base assumed for CRAG, default DRAG setup |
| DRAG vs. CRAG under an incomplete centralized knowledge base | At 70% of centralized samples available (CRAG-0.7S), CRAG F1 drops to 61.54% on MMLU, versus DRAG's 83.92% with the same distributed knowledge total | MMLU, default DRAG setup, CRAG knowledge base artificially truncated to 70% of samples or 70%/50% of topics |
| Network-size sensitivity, F1 | MMLU F1 falls from 83.92% (20 peers) to 79.72% (100 peers); Medical Extended falls from 90.58% to 86.66% | TARW, Llama 3.2-3B, peer counts 20/40/60/80/100, other defaults held |
| Network-size sensitivity, messages, and comparison to flooding | At 100 peers: TARW 27.67 messages (MMLU) vs. FL 53.34; TARW 23.71 (News) vs. FL 48.83 — roughly a 50% reduction | Same peer-count sweep as above |
| Network-size sensitivity, DRAG-RW collapse | RW F1 falls from 19.97% (20 peers) to 3.57% (100 peers) on MMLU | Same sweep, DRAG-RW variant |
| Query-volume convergence of message cost | Average messages per query, 100-peer network, starts at 34.73 over the first 500 queries and falls to 27.67 after 10,000 queries (over 20% reduction), attributed to accumulating cached peer-expertise data | MMLU, TARW, 100-peer network, cumulative query counts 500 to 10,000 |
| Peer-connectivity sensitivity | F1 stays within roughly 80%-83% as connectivity varies 2/4/6/8; message count at 100 peers rises from 26.64 (connectivity 2) to 29.37 (connectivity 8) | MMLU, TARW, 100-peer network |
| LLM-choice sensitivity | MMLU F1: Llama 3.2-3B 83.92%, Qwen2.5 3B 82.86%, Gemma 2 2B 77.13%. News: Llama 3.2-3B F1 74.73% at 7.82 messages, Gemma 2 2B F1 76.12% at 6.90 messages | Default 20-peer setup, MMLU and News datasets, three LLMs substituted with all other settings held |
| Neighbor-selection-count (k) sensitivity | 20-peer network: F1 jumps from 56.27% (k=2) to 83.92% (k=4). 100-peer network: F1 rises from 79.72% (k=4) to only 85.33% (k=8) while messages rise from 27.67 to 28.71 | MMLU, TARW, k swept over 2/4/6/8, other settings at default |

### Parameters
- `H_max` (maximum walk hops): fixed at 6 for all reported experiments; not swept.
- `k` (neighbor selection count, top-k neighbors forwarded to per hop): default 4; swept over 2, 4, 6, 8.
- `θ` (relevance threshold to accept a peer's local answer): fixed at 0.8 for all reported experiments; not swept.
- Network size (number of peers): default 20; swept over 20, 40, 60, 80, 100.
- Network connectivity (Barabási-Albert attachment edges per new peer): default 4; swept over 2, 4, 6, 8.
- LLM: default Llama 3.2-3B; Gemma 2 2B and Qwen2.5 3B also evaluated.

### Stated limitations
The paper states DRAG-TARW trades a small amount of accuracy for lower message count relative to query broadcast (DRAG-FL): "there is a slight trade-off in accuracy, with DRAG-FL generally exhibiting marginally higher EM, F1, Precision, and Recall scores." The paper states TARW itself is vulnerable to deanonymization if an adversary observes network traffic and infers query topics and peer expertise from the routing pattern, and lists candidate but unevaluated defenses: adding noise to topic extraction, mix networks to obscure routing paths, and access-control restrictions on peer visibility. The paper states knowledge-quality control is unresolved: because peer knowledge bases vary in expertise and data quality, the system can propagate misinformation or stale knowledge, and the paper only proposes unimplemented mitigations (peer rating of snippet quality, consensus mechanisms for conflicting snippets, reputation tracking of peer history) rather than evaluating any of them. The paper states peer connectivity does not reliably improve either accuracy or message cost in its simulations, attributing this to "the inherent randomness in knowledge distribution across the peer-to-peer network" interacting unpredictably with topology. The paper states, as future work, that the knowledge-search algorithm needs further optimization for very large and dynamic networks, without giving results at scales beyond 100 peers. The paper never evaluates incentive mechanisms for peer participation; it only lists token-based, reputation-based, and knowledge-marketplace approaches as unimplemented candidates.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Requires each peer to run a local LLM capable of two functions used inside the routing algorithm itself: extracting topics from the query text, and scoring semantic relevance between a returned knowledge snippet and the query, against threshold θ. The routing decision at every hop therefore depends on local LLM inference quality — the LLM-substitution results above show F1 varying by more than 6 percentage points (77.13% to 83.92% on MMLU) purely from swapping the local LLM, with no change to TARW itself. Requires every peer to maintain a persistent local expertise cache, keyed by topic, of past-successful peer contacts, because TARW's per-hop neighbor scoring reads this cache (`RelevanceScore(N_i, E, T)` in the paper's Algorithm 1); the message-cost convergence result (34.73 to 27.67 messages over 10,000 queries) is a direct consequence of this cache accumulating entries, so a deployment that resets or does not build this cache will not obtain that convergence. Requires a privacy filter (rule-based or LLM-driven) that can be applied to a knowledge snippet before it leaves the holding peer; the paper does not specify or evaluate this filter's false-negative rate — how often it fails to remove sensitive content. Requires an underlying peer graph with fixed, discoverable neighbor sets per peer (the paper's simulations use a static Barabási-Albert graph generated once per experiment); the paper does not evaluate TARW under peer churn (peers joining or leaving during a walk). Assumes queried peers answer truthfully about their own local knowledge-base content and relevance scores; the paper's threat model addresses only traffic-observation deanonymization, not a peer that misreports relevance to attract or divert queries.

### Contradicts
None found against other entries in this corpus as currently extracted.

### References worth retrieving
- Lewis, Perez, Piktus, Petroni, Karpukhin, Goyal, Küttler, Lewis, Yih, Rocktäschel, et al. "Retrieval-augmented generation for knowledge-intensive NLP tasks." NeurIPS, 2020. — foundational (origin of the RAG mechanism this paper distributes).
- Wang, Khramtsova, Zhuang, Zuccon. "FeB4RAG: Evaluating federated search in the context of retrieval augmented generation." SIGIR, 2024. — competing (federated, not fully peer-to-peer, RAG architecture the paper cites as still relying on a centralized request mediator).

Workshop on Privacy in NLP, 2024. — competing (a distributed private-search approach to the same retrieval problem, using cryptographic similarity search rather than topic-routing).

- Xue, Zheng, Hu, Liu, Chen, Lou. "BadRAG: Identifying vulnerabilities in retrieval augmented generation of large language models." arXiv:2406.00083, 2024. — attack (poisoning attack on RAG, complements ZHONG-EMNLP-23's poisoning attack on dense retrieval already in this corpus).

## [YANG-ICDE-03] Designing a Super-Peer Network
**Citation:** Beverly Yang, Hector Garcia-Molina. "Designing a Super-Peer Network." IEEE ICDE, 2003. DOI 10.1109/ICDE.2003.1260781.
**Retrieved:** full text via http://infolab.stanford.edu/~byang/pubs/superpeer.pdf
**Source URL:** http://infolab.stanford.edu/~byang/pubs/superpeer.pdf
**Domain:** B

### What it does
A super-peer network reduces the cost of query broadcast in a peer-to-peer file-sharing system by having a small subset of nodes (super-peers) answer queries on behalf of a larger set of weaker nodes (clients) that connect to exactly one super-peer each, so that only super-peers route messages to each other while clients are shielded from all query traffic. A super-peer and its clients form a cluster; cluster size is the node count in a cluster including the super-peer. A pure peer-to-peer network (every node routes for itself, as in Gnutella's baseline design) is the degenerate case where cluster size is 1. Every other node in the pure network model has an outdegree (a count of open neighbor connections it maintains) and messages travel hop by hop only along these open connections; a query carries a time-to-live (TTL) that is decremented at each hop and stops the query once it reaches 0, and the reach of a query is the number of nodes that end up processing it.

In a super-peer network, a client sends a query only to its own super-peer; the super-peer answers on the client's behalf by consulting an index it keeps over its clients' data (built by having clients send file metadata to their super-peer at join, update, and leave time), then forwards the query to its neighboring super-peers exactly as if it were the super-peer's own query, and relays back any results. This converts client-to-super-peer traffic into a client-server pattern while leaving super-peer-to-super-peer traffic as an unstructured overlay routed as in a pure peer-to-peer system (the paper studies the baseline Gnutella flooding rule specifically: forward to every neighbor until TTL reaches 0).

k-redundancy adds k nodes ("partners") that jointly serve as one virtual super-peer: every partner holds a complete index of the cluster's clients and of the other partners, clients send queries to partners in round-robin rotation, and incoming queries from neighboring super-peers are distributed evenly across partners. This lowers each partner's per-query load by roughly a factor of k relative to a single non-redundant super-peer with the same clients, at the cost of the aggregate cost of every client-join action increasing by a factor of k (because a joining client must send its metadata to every partner) and the number of open super-peer-to-super-peer connections increasing by a factor of k^2 (because every neighbor super-peer must connect to every partner). The paper restricts its analysis to k=2 because connection count grows too fast beyond that.

### Measured results
The paper's numbers come from an analytical cost model (an event-driven mean-value simulation over generated network topologies), not a live deployment; the per-action bandwidth and processing-cycle costs feeding that model were measured (bandwidth costs specified by the Gnutella wire protocol; processing costs measured on a Pentium III 930 MHz processor running Linux kernel 2.2, with one "unit" defined as the roughly 7,200-cycle cost of sending and receiving a Gnutella message with no payload), while file-count, lifespan, and query/match-probability distributions were taken from independent Gnutella measurement studies (Saroiu, Gummadi, Gribble, 2002; Yang and Garcia-Molina, 2001, for OpenNap query/match probabilities). All headline results below are expected-value outputs of this cost model over generated topologies, with 95% confidence intervals shown in the paper's figures where applicable.

| Result | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Aggregate load vs. cluster size | Aggregate bandwidth decreases sharply as cluster size grows from 1, with a "knee" around cluster size 200 (strongly connected topology, TTL=1) or cluster size 1000 (power-law topology, average outdegree 3.1, TTL=7); expected result count held constant across cluster sizes | Graph size 10,000 nodes (default); strongly connected topology used as a best-case bandwidth scenario; power-law topology (generated via the PLOD algorithm) used to reflect measured Gnutella topology |
| Individual load vs. cluster size | Individual super-peer incoming bandwidth roughly doubles going from cluster size 50 to 100 in the strongly connected system; individual incoming bandwidth is proportional to f*(1-f), where f = cluster size / total network size, giving a maximum at f=1/2 (cluster size 5000 of 10,000) and minima at f=0 and f=1 | Same default topologies and graph size as above; this f*(1-f) relationship is derived analytically from the model, not read off a plotted curve |
| Effect of super-peer redundancy (k=2) on load, cluster size 100, strongly connected | Aggregate bandwidth increases by about 2.5%; individual bandwidth per partner decreases by about 48%, to the level of a non-redundant super-peer with cluster size 40; aggregate processing load increases by about 17%; individual processing load decreases by about 41% | Strongly connected topology, TTL=1, cluster size 100, k=2 redundancy applied |
| Effect of increasing average outdegree from 3.1 to 10, power-law topology | Aggregate bandwidth improves over 31%; a super-peer with 3 neighbors (outdegree=3.1 system) has expected load ~9.6 x 10^5 bps and receives ~750 results per query; a super-peer with 7 neighbors (outdegree=10 system) has expected load ~9.9 x 10^5 bps and receives ~890 results per query; Expected Path Length (EPL, mean hop count of a response back to its source) decreases from 5.4 to 3.0 | Power-law topology, cluster size 20 in both compared systems (paper states result is the same for any cluster size) |
| Cost of one super-peer unilaterally increasing outdegree | A single super-peer raising its outdegree from 4 to 9 sees its own load rise from 1.18 x 10^6 to 3.58 x 10^6 bps, a 303% increase | Power-law topology with average outdegree 3.1 as the surrounding system (i.e., only one node deviates) |
| Cost of every super-peer raising outdegree together | The same super-peer that saw a 303% increase when acting alone instead sees a 14% reduction in load (to 1.01 x 10^6 bps) when every super-peer raises its outdegree so the network average becomes 10 | Power-law topology, uniform outdegree increase from 3.1 to 10 |
| Effect of reducing TTL while preserving full reach | A system with average outdegree 20 and TTL=4 uses about 9.95 x 10^8 bps aggregate incoming bandwidth for full reach; reducing TTL to 3 (which the paper states still achieves full reach) cuts this to about 6.30 x 10^8 bps, a 19% reduction | Power-law topology, average outdegree 20, full-reach condition (TTL=3 vs. TTL=4) |
| Global design procedure applied to a Gnutella-scale scenario | Rebuilding a 20,000-node, cluster-size-1 (i.e., no super-peers), average-outdegree-3.1, TTL=7 topology (representing then-current Gnutella, reach approx. 3,000 of 20,000 nodes) into a super-peer topology with cluster size 10, TTL=2, and average outdegree 28 achieves the same reach (3,000 nodes) with over 79% improvement across incoming bandwidth, outgoing bandwidth, and processing power, plus a lower EPL (1.9 vs. 6.5) and slightly higher result count (270 vs. 269) | Individual per-node constraints imposed on the redesign: at most 100 Kbps expected upstream and downstream bandwidth, at most 10 MHz expected processing load, at most 100 open connections |
| Individual-load distribution, redesigned topology vs. original | For the lowest 90% of ranked individual loads (corresponding to clients in the new topology), individual load is one to two orders of magnitude lower in the new design than in the original; the top 10% of loads still improve, from about 40% at the 90th percentile up to a full order of magnitude for the top 0.1% heaviest-loaded nodes | Same redesign scenario and constraints as the row above; loads taken from one representative generated topology instance per configuration, not averaged over multiple runs |
| Redundancy applied to the redesigned topology | Average super-peer load (top 20% of ranked nodes with redundancy, vs. top 10% without) is 41% lower with k=2 redundancy than without; average client load is 2-3x higher with redundancy but remains on the order of 100 bps | Same redesign scenario, k=2 redundancy added |
| Cost of outdegree beyond the point where it still shortens EPL | Increasing average outdegree from 50 to 100 decreases Expected Path Length by only 0.14 when the desired reach is 500 nodes, while individual load still rises because redundant queries increase with outdegree; a system with average outdegree 100 is shown to underperform one with average outdegree 50 at matched TTL=2 and matched target reach | Power-law topology, TTL=2, target reach set to the total number of super-peers in the system |

### Parameters
- Graph Type: strongly connected or power-law; default power-law, generated via the PLOD algorithm to match measured Gnutella topology.
- Graph Size: default 10,000 peers (used 20,000 in the global-design-procedure worked example, matching a reported Gnutella network size at the time of writing).
- Cluster Size: default 10; swept across the full range in experiments (1 to Graph Size).
- Redundancy: boolean, default off; only k=2 evaluated, because open-connection count among super-peers grows as k^2.
- Average Outdegree: default 3.1 (measured from a June 2001 Gnutella network crawl); swept up to 100+ in experiments; actual per-node outdegree follows a power-law distribution around this average, reflecting observed voluntary variation in peer capability.
- TTL: default 7; swept from 1 upward.
- Query Rate: default 96.26 x 10^-3 queries per user per second (paper's own general statistic, source cited to a prior Gnutella measurement study).
- Update Rate: default 1.68 x 10^-2 updates per user per second (same source).
- Atomic action costs (bandwidth and processing) drawn from the Gnutella wire-protocol specification and from processing-time measurements on a single Pentium III 930 MHz / Linux 2.2 machine; the paper states these processing-cost values are "meant to be representative, rather than exact" because they will vary across machines and implementations.
- Open-connection overhead model: derived from a cited measurement of select()-call scan cost (about 3 microseconds per file descriptor on a Pentium 100 under Linux 2.1.x) and a cited finding that per-call select() overhead grows linearly with open-connection count up to roughly 1,000 connections, after which it levels off; the paper states none of its own reported results exceed 1,000 open connections, so only the linear-growth regime applies to its figures.

### Stated limitations
The paper states its performance model does not capture absolute response time, only relative response time inferred through Expected Path Length (mean hop count of a response's return path), and explicitly excludes "relevance of results" as a quality metric because it is "subjective and application specific." The bootstrapping problem — how a joining node discovers already-connected nodes, which determines the actual distribution of cluster sizes in practice — is stated to be "an open problem in pure and super-peer networks, with many potential solutions," and the paper sidesteps it by assuming any well-constructed discovery method is fair or random, using a normal distribution for cluster-size variation rather than deriving one from a specific discovery mechanism. The global design procedure is stated explicitly not to be provably optimal: "we can not prove the procedure yields the 'best' topology," only that empirical evidence shows it usually returns a topology that cannot be improved without violating the designer's stated constraints. Rule #3 (maximize outdegree) is stated to have a caveat in extreme cases: once increasing average outdegree stops reducing Expected Path Length for a given target reach, further increases only add redundant-query overhead and harm performance, so outdegree should be increased only as long as it continues to shorten EPL. The local-decision-making guidelines (Section 5.3) are stated to rely on a "limited altruism" assumption — that every super-peer is willing to accept load up to a self-set limit purely to reduce load for the rest of the network — and the paper notes this assumption does not address the possibility of freeloading or malicious non-participation, citing separate ongoing research on detecting and punishing such nodes as outside its own scope. The choice of cluster size involves a stated unresolved tension the paper does not fully resolve numerically: individual load favors small clusters, aggregate load and the "knee" effect favor large ones, and reliability (fewer single points of failure) favors small ones, with the paper stating only that "the answer to this question is specific to the application and situation."

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The mechanism requires every client to maintain metadata synchronization with exactly one super-peer: on join, a client must transmit metadata for every file it holds; on any update (insertion, deletion, or modification of a shared item), it must resend the corresponding delta; and on leave, its super-peer must remove its metadata — without this discipline the super-peer's index (which is the sole basis on which it answers queries for that client) becomes stale relative to the client's actual holdings. The design assumes clients are reachable through exactly one super-peer at a time (no client multi-homing in the base design), so a super-peer's failure disconnects every one of its clients until they locate a replacement, which is the specific failure the k-redundancy extension is built to reduce, not eliminate. Any routing protocol run at the super-peer-to-super-peer layer is treated as an orthogonal, pluggable choice — the paper states explicitly that "the use of super-peers and the choice of routing protocol are orthogonal issues" and only evaluates the plain Gnutella flooding rule, so its cost figures do not carry over automatically to a structured-overlay routing layer (e.g., a distributed hash table) run among super-peers instead. The k-redundancy mechanism requires every neighboring super-peer to open and maintain a connection to every one of the k partners (not just one representative), which is the source of its stated k^2 connection-count growth, and requires clients to be able to address multiple partners in round-robin fashion rather than a single fixed super-peer address. The global design procedure requires the designer to know or estimate several system-wide properties in advance — total network size, desired reach (equivalently, desired result count per query), and per-node limits on bandwidth, processing power, and open-connection count — and the paper notes obtaining these accurately before the system runs can be difficult, offering periodic re-evaluation by a centralized decision-maker as the fallback rather than a way to avoid the requirement.

### Contradicts
None found against another entry in this batch. Section 5.1's finding that raising average outdegree from 3.1 to 10 lowers both individual and aggregate load is stated by the paper itself to hold only if adopted uniformly across all super-peers; the same change made by a single super-peer acting alone is stated to increase that node's own load by 303% — an internal qualification the paper states directly, not a contradiction between two different results.

### References worth retrieving
- Saroiu, Gummadi, Gribble, "A Measurement Study of Peer-to-Peer File Sharing Systems," Multimedia Computing and Networking, 2002 — foundational (source of the file-count, lifespan, and capability-heterogeneity distributions used to parameterize the cost model; the "up to 3 orders of magnitude" bandwidth heterogeneity claim is attributed here).
- Yang and Garcia-Molina, "Comparing Hybrid Peer-to-Peer Systems," VLDB, 2001 — foundational/competing (source of the OpenNap query/match-probability model reused as the default query distribution, and the paper's own prior work comparing hybrid P2P systems).
- Crespo and Garcia-Molina, "Routing Indices for Peer-to-Peer Systems," ICDCS, 2002 — competing (alternative to flat query broadcast that directs queries toward likely-productive neighbors rather than restructuring the topology into super-peers).
- Lv, Ratnasamy, Shenker, "Can Heterogeneity Make Gnutella Scalable?," IPTPS 2002 — competing (a pure-peer-to-peer alternative in which nodes redirect message flow away from themselves toward higher-capacity nodes, addressing the same capability-heterogeneity problem without introducing super-peers).
- Ratnasamy, Francis, Handley, Karp, Shenker, "A Scalable Content-Addressable Network," ACM SIGCOMM, 2001 — foundational (CAN, cited as a structured routing protocol that could be layered onto the super-peer-to-super-peer overlay, orthogonally to this paper's contribution).
- Stoica, Morris, Karger, Kaashoek, Balakrishnan, "Chord," ACM SIGCOMM, 2001 — foundational (same role as CAN above).
- Rowstron and Druschel, "Pastry," Middleware 2001 — foundational (same role).
- Zhao, Kubiatowicz, Joseph, "Tapestry," UCB/CSD-01-1141, 2001 — foundational (same role).
- Palmer and Steffan, "Generating Network Topologies That Obey Power Laws," GLOBECOM 2000 — foundational (the PLOD algorithm used to generate the power-law topologies in this paper's experiments).
- Adar and Huberman, "Free Riding on Gnutella," First Monday, 2000 — foundational (measurement study establishing the free-riding problem the paper's "limited altruism" assumption sidesteps).
- Cooper, Bawa, Daswani, Garcia-Molina, "Protecting the Pipe from Malicious Peers," Stanford Technical Report, 2002 — attack/competing (cited as ongoing work on detecting freeloaders and malicious nodes, explicitly outside this paper's own scope).

## [YANG-IMC-11] Uncovering Social Network Sybils in the Wild
**Citation:** Zhi Yang, Christo Wilson, Xiao Wang, Tingting Gao, Ben Y. Zhao, Yafei Dai. "Uncovering Social Network Sybils in the Wild." ACM Internet Measurement Conference (IMC), 2011. DOI 10.1145/2068816.2068841.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/pdf/1106.5321
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/pdf/1106.5321
**Domain:** F

### What it does
The paper reports a measurement of Sybil accounts on a real, deployed online social network (OSN),
Renren (120 million users at the time, the largest OSN in China), using account data the operator
supplied under a research collaboration. It builds a real-time detector from behavioral signals
observable at the OSN operator and evaluates whether the graph-topological assumption behind
published decentralized Sybil defenses (SybilGuard, SybilLimit, SybilInfer, SumUp) holds for Sybils
actually operating in the wild, rather than for Sybils synthetically injected into a real social graph.

Detector mechanism: for each account the operator computes three per-account signals directly from
friend-request logs — invitation frequency (friend requests sent per fixed time window), the
fraction of an account's outgoing friend requests that are accepted, and the fraction of its
incoming friend requests it accepts. It adds one graph signal, the clustering coefficient of an
account's first 50 friends (added in time order), computed from invitation edges alone, which
requires no waiting on recipient responses. A threshold rule — outgoing-acceptance ratio < 0.5 AND
invitation frequency < 20 per window AND clustering coefficient < 0.01 — flags an account as a
Sybil. The paper also trains a support vector machine (SVM) on the same four signals and compares
its accuracy to the threshold rule.

Topology analysis mechanism: build a graph restricted to the 667,723 detected Sybil accounts and
the edges among them ("Sybil edges"), separately from edges connecting a Sybil to a normal account
("attack edges"). Decompose the Sybil-only graph into connected components and measure, per
component, the ratio of Sybil edges to attack edges — the quantity community-detection Sybil
defenses require to exceed 1 for a community to be separable by a graph cut. Reconstruct, per
account, the chronological sequence of edge creation from timestamps to test whether Sybil-Sybil
edges are created together (deliberate) or interleaved randomly with edges to normal accounts
(accidental).

### Measured results

| Result | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Sybil accounts identified and banned by the deployed detector | 100,000 | Renren production deployment, August 2010 to February 2011 |
| Total Sybil population analyzed | 660,000 (100,000 detector-caught + 560,000 caught by Renren's prior techniques, 2008–Feb. 2011) | Same Renren dataset |
| Threshold-rule detector accuracy | True Sybil classified Sybil 98.68%, classified non-Sybil (false negative) 1.32%; true non-Sybil classified non-Sybil 99.5%, classified Sybil (false positive) 0.5% | 1000 ground-truth Sybil + 1000 ground-truth normal accounts, verified by a volunteer team examining profile data; threshold rule = outgoing-acceptance < 0.5 AND frequency < 20/window AND clustering coefficient < 0.01 |
| SVM classifier accuracy on the same signals | True Sybil classified Sybil 98.99%/1.01% false negative; true non-Sybil 99.34%/0.66% false positive | Same 2000-account ground truth set, 5-fold split (4 folds train, 1 fold test) |
| Average outgoing friend-request acceptance ratio | Normal accounts 79%; Sybil accounts 26% | Same 2000-account ground-truth set |
| Incoming friend-request acceptance | 80% of Sybils accept all incoming requests | Same ground-truth set |
| Average clustering coefficient over first 50 friends | Normal accounts 0.0386; Sybil accounts 0.0006 | Same ground-truth set |
| Fraction of ground-truth Sybils that are recorded as female | 77.3% | Same 1000-Sybil ground-truth set (overall Renren population is 46.5% female) |
| Threshold separating most Sybils by invitation frequency | >20 invitations per time window flags as Sybil; a 40-requests/hour threshold catches approximately 70% of Sybils at zero false positives | Same ground-truth set, both 400-hour and 1-hour windows |
| Sybils with at least one edge to another Sybil | 20% of the 667,723 detected Sybils | Full 660,000-account Sybil population, Renren social graph |
| Sybils with no Sybil-Sybil edge at all | more than 70% | Same population |
| Number of connected components in the Sybil-only subgraph | 7,094 | Same population |
| Component size distribution | 98% of components have fewer than 10 members | Same population |
| Largest Sybil component | 63,541 Sybil accounts, 134,941 Sybil edges, 9,848,881 attack edges, 6,497,179 distinct normal-account "audience" reached | Same population, Table 2 |
| Ratio of attack edges to Sybil edges, all five largest components | every one of the five largest components has more attack edges than Sybil edges (Table 2: ratios of approximately 73:1, 903:1, 116:1, 307:1, 361:1) | Same population |
| Position of every Sybil component on the attack-edge-vs-Sybil-edge scatter plot | all components fall above the line attack edges = Sybil edges | Same population, Figure 7 |
| Degree distribution within the largest component | 34.5% of member Sybils connect to exactly 1 other Sybil; 93.7% connect to 10 or fewer | Largest component (63,541 accounts) only |
| Fraction of Sybil accounts formally connected to other Sybils via a single large accidental component | 69% of the 30% connected minority (approximately 65,000 accounts) belong to one component | Same population |

### Parameters
Ground-truth labeled set: 1000 Sybil accounts and 1000 normal accounts, manually verified.
Cross-validation split: 5 subsamples, 4 for SVM training, 1 for test. Clustering-coefficient window:
each user's first 50 friends by time order. Threshold-detector cutoffs: outgoing-acceptance ratio
0.5, invitation frequency 20 requests per fixed time window, clustering coefficient 0.01 (these
three values are the deployed detector's chosen operating point; the paper does not report a range
swept over them, only the resulting accuracy at this operating point). Adaptive online tuning of the
deployed detector's thresholds is mentioned but its mechanism is withheld at Renren's request for
confidentiality and security.

### Stated limitations
The paper withholds the deployed detector's adaptive threshold-tuning mechanism, citing Renren's
security and confidentiality requirements, so the operational detector is not fully specified. The
analysis covers one OSN (Renren) over one measurement window (accounts banned through February
2011) and the authors do not claim the found proportions (20% Sybil-Sybil connectivity, more attack
edges than Sybil edges in every measured component) generalize numerically to other social networks,
though they state the qualitative conclusion — that community-based defenses' core assumption is
untested and appears false in this deployment — as general grounds for new detection approaches.
The four signals depend on friend-request logs an OSN operator holds internally; the paper notes
that on networks where only public follower/followee data is available (Twitter), the equivalent
detection has previously worked, but that Facebook- and Renren-style OSNs expose no equivalent
public signal, so their detector requires operator-side data access it does not describe as portable
to a peer without that access.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A deployment of this detection approach needs a party that observes, for every account, its full
inbound and outbound friend-request stream with timestamps and per-request accept/reject outcomes —
data available only to the OSN operator itself in the studied deployment, not to any external
observer or peer. Community-graph Sybil defenses (SybilGuard, SybilLimit, SybilInfer, SumUp) that
this paper evaluates require, to succeed, that the ratio of Sybil-Sybil edges to Sybil-normal
(attack) edges exceed 1 within some cut of the social graph; the measured population here violates
that precondition in every one of the largest observed components, so a design relying on those
defenses for Sybil identification must not assume the precondition holds against an unconstrained
snowball-sampling attacker recruiting from the honest population, since honest recruitment strategy
alone (not deliberate Sybil-Sybil linking) is what created the small fraction of Sybil-Sybil edges
observed.

### Contradicts
The paper's own result contradicts the assumption underlying SybilGuard, SybilLimit, SybilInfer, and
SumUp — that Sybil accounts form communities where intra-Sybil edges outnumber Sybil-to-normal
edges — for the Renren deployment; the authors state this as their central finding, not as an
attributed claim to be doubted. No claim commonly attributed to this paper needs correction here.
Cross-paper: None found in this batch.

### References worth retrieving
- Douceur, "The Sybil Attack," IPTPS 2002 — foundational (defines the Sybil attack).
- Yu, Kaminsky, Gibbons, Flaxman, "SybilGuard: defending against sybil attacks via social networks," SIGCOMM 2006 — competing (one of the four community-detection defenses evaluated here).
- Yu, Gibbons, Kaminsky, Xiao, "SybilLimit: A near-optimal social network defense against sybil attacks," IEEE S&P 2008 — competing.
- Danezis, Mittal, "SybilInfer: Detecting sybil nodes using social networks," NDSS 2009 — competing.
- Tran, Min, Li, Subramanian, "Sybil-resilient online content voting," NSDI 2009 — competing (SumUp).
- Viswanath, Post, Gummadi, Mislove, "An analysis of social network-based sybil defenses," SIGCOMM 2010 — attack/critique (shows the four algorithms generalize to community detection, which this paper then tests against real data).
- Newsome, Shi, Song, Perrig, "The sybil attack in sensor networks: Analysis & defenses," IPSN 2004 — foundational (Sybil attacks outside OSNs).
- Lian, Zhang, Yang, Zhao, Dai, Li, "An empirical study of collusion behavior in the maze p2p file-sharing system," ICDCS 2007 — foundational (empirical Sybil/collusion measurement in a different deployed P2P system).
- Gao, Hu, Wilson, Li, Chen, Zhao, "Detecting and characterizing social spam campaigns," IMC 2010 — foundational (companion large-scale OSN abuse measurement, same research group).
- Grier, Thomas, Paxson, Zhang, "@spam: the underground on 140 characters or less," CCS 2010 — competing (independent large-scale OSN spam measurement, Twitter).
- Stringhini, Kruegel, Vigna, "Detecting spammers on social networks," ACSAC 2010 — competing.
- Webb, Caverlee, Pu, "Social honeypots: Making friends with a spammer near you," CEAS 2008 — competing (honeypot-based detection, contrasted directly against this paper's findings on incoming-request acceptance).

"only 20% of Sybils are friends with one or more other Sybils."
"All components are above the 45° line, meaning that they have more attack edges than Sybil edges."

## [YANG-SIGCOMM-24] Practical Rateless Set Reconciliation
**Citation:** Lei Yang, Yossi Gilad, Mohammad Alizadeh. "Practical Rateless Set Reconciliation." ACM SIGCOMM 2024 Conference (ACM SIGCOMM '24), 2024. 18 pages. DOI 10.1145/3651890.3672219.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/pdf/2402.02668
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.02668
**Domain:** D

### What it does
Rateless IBLT (Invertible Bloom Lookup Table) lets two parties, each holding a set of fixed-length bit strings, learn the symmetric difference between their sets — the items each has that the other lacks — while transmitting an amount of data proportional to the size of that difference rather than to the size of either set, and without either party knowing the difference size in advance.

The sender encodes its set into an infinite sequence of coded symbols s_0, s_1, s_2, ... A coded symbol holds three fields: a `sum` (the bitwise exclusive-or, XOR, of every source symbol mapped to it), a `checksum` (the XOR of the hashes of those source symbols), and a `count` (the number of source symbols mapped to it). A deterministic mapping rule decides, for any source symbol x and any coded-symbol index i, whether x maps to the i-th coded symbol; the mapping probability for index i is rho(i) = 1/(1+alpha*i), so earlier coded symbols receive more source symbols on average than later ones. Because both parties derive coded symbols with the same mapping rule, subtracting (XOR) the two parties' coded symbol sequences pairwise cancels every source symbol held by both parties and leaves only the symmetric difference encoded. The receiver decodes with a peeling procedure: a coded symbol is "pure" when exactly one source symbol maps to it (detectable by comparing checksum against the hash of sum); the receiver recovers that source symbol, removes it (by XOR) from every other coded symbol it maps to, and repeats until no pure symbols remain or all difference items are recovered. The receiver requests additional coded symbols only until decoding succeeds — it needs no prior estimate of the difference size, and the sender needs no prior estimate either, distinguishing this scheme from a regular (non-rateless) IBLT, whose parameters m (symbol count) and k (symbols per source item) must be fixed in advance and which fails outright if the realized difference exceeds m.

The scheme sets alpha = 0.5 in its final design, chosen because computing the inverse mapping function under alpha = 0.5 requires only a square root rather than raising a value to an arbitrary non-integer power, which the authors found substantially slower on older CPUs; simulations show alpha = 0.5 costs only 3% more communication overhead than the numerically optimal alpha = 0.64.

Against adversarial input — a party able to craft items it inserts into its own or a counterparty's set, for example a rogue post in a distributed social-media application — the mechanism uses a keyed hash function (SipHash) with a secret key shared between the two reconciling peers, rather than a long, unkeyed hash. A short unkeyed hash lets an adversary who does not know the key still search for a hash collision against a known item computationally, but cannot target the collision at a specific peer pairing because the peer-specific key is unknown to the adversary; each additional peer key the sender uses adds a separate checksum-computation cost.

An extension, Irregular Rateless IBLT, partitions source symbols into c mutually exclusive subsets by hash value and applies a distinct alpha_j to each subset (regular Rateless IBLT is the special case c=1, alpha_0=0.5), lowering communication overhead further at additional encoding and decoding cost.

### Parameters
- alpha (mapping-probability decay parameter, rho(i) = 1/(1+alpha*i)): set to 0.5 in the final design; optimal value found by search is 0.64 (gives 3% lower overhead but is computationally more expensive per symbol).
- Item length: tested from 8 bytes to 32 KB.
- Set difference size d: tested from 1 to 10^5-10^6 items across different experiments.
- Set size N: tested from 10^4 to 10^8 (Fig. 10) and fixed at 1,000,000 for the main communication-overhead comparison (Fig. 7).
- Hash function for checksums under adversarial workloads: SipHash, a keyed hash function with 64-bit (short) output, keyed per peer pair.
- Irregular Rateless IBLT: c=3 subsets, weights 0.18/0.56/0.26, alpha values 0.11/0.68/0.82 (found by brute-force search, not derived in closed form).
- Regular IBLT and MET-IBLT comparison baselines: 8 bytes allocated for checksum and count fields each, per each scheme's own recommended parameters.

### Stated limitations
Irregular Rateless IBLT has no closed-form parameter derivation; its (c, w_j, alpha_j) configuration was found by brute-force search over simulations, and the authors state they "leave further optimizations of the parameters and the implementation to future works."

The scheme does not address reconciliation across more than two parties simultaneously; the authors list "designing efficient solutions for reconciliation across more than two parties" as future work.

The scheme as analyzed assumes each party's set is static during a reconciliation session; "considering scenarios where Alice and Bob's sets change in the middle of reconciliation" is listed as future work, not solved.

The adversarial-workload defense (keyed hashing) requires the two reconciling peers to share a secret key coordinated in advance; the paper does not specify a key-distribution mechanism, and using a distinct key per peer pair increases the sender's per-peer checksum-computation cost.

Regular (non-rateless) IBLT and MET-IBLT, used as comparison baselines, are stated to fail to decode probabilistically even when correctly parameterized, and MET-IBLT requires selecting a small number of target difference sizes in advance, with 4-10x higher overhead for difference sizes not among those selected.

PinSketch, a comparison baseline, achieves lower communication overhead (the paper reports 37-60% lower) but has quadratic decoding complexity in the number of coded symbols, becoming, in the authors' words, "intractable even at moderate" set and difference sizes.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The transport between the two reconciling peers must preserve ordering of coded symbols, because the receiver reconstructs an implied index i for each coded symbol from position in the stream (after the sender transmits set size N with the 0th symbol) rather than the sender attaching an explicit index to each symbol; this is stated as an assumption for the variable-length count-field compression specifically.

Both peers must independently compute the same deterministic source-to-coded-symbol mapping (same rho(i), same hash functions) for subtraction of their coded symbol sequences to correctly encode the symmetric difference; any divergence in this shared mapping rule breaks the linearity property the scheme depends on.

Defense against adversarial workload requires the two peers to share a secret key for the keyed hash function (SipHash) before reconciliation; without a shared key, an adversary who can inject items into either party's set can construct a hash collision against a target item and permanently block reconciliation of that item (the paper states this failure mode explicitly for the unkeyed case).

The mechanism assumes items are fixed-length bit strings ("bit strings of the same length ℓ"); the paper does not address reconciling variable-length items directly, only fixed-length symbols, so the rest of the system must fix or pad item length before invoking reconciliation.

The receiver must be able to determine when it has recovered every item in the symmetric difference (decoding termination) in order to signal the sender to stop transmitting; the paper's protocol relies on this termination signal traveling back to the sender (Bob "notifies Alice to stop"), requiring a return channel from receiver to sender even though the main data flow is one-directional.

### Contradicts
The paper's own comparison shows PinSketch achieves strictly lower communication overhead (overhead of exactly 1, the information-theoretic optimum, versus Rateless IBLT's 1.35-1.72x) for the same difference sizes (1-400 items, 1,000,000-item sets, 32-byte items) — a reader crediting Rateless IBLT with unconditionally superior performance to all prior schemes would be wrong on the communication-cost axis specifically; the paper's claim is unconditional superiority on computation cost (2-2000x lower) traded against 0-60% higher communication cost depending on scheme compared.

None found against other entries in this corpus.

## [YEN-EPRINT-26] BeeKEM: Decentralized, Secure and Efficient Group Key Agreement
**Citation:** Derek Yen, Andrés Fábrega, Liangrun Da, Martin Kleppmann, John Mumm, Sunoo Park, Brooklyn Zelenka. "BeeKEM: Decentralized, Secure and Efficient Group Key Agreement." IACR ePrint Archive, Report 2026/1434.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1434
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1434
**Domain:** H

This paper is listed in `BRIEF.md` section 7 as already verified in a prior pass ("do not
re-retrieve, do extend"). The summary there is confirmed against the full text on disk; this entry
extends it to the full evidence schema.

### What it does
BeeKEM lets a group of users establish a shared symmetric secret for end-to-end encryption, and
keep updating that secret over time for forward secrecy and post-compromise security, without any
of the users' devices going through a central server, and without requiring the group's messages to
arrive at every device in the same order. This mechanism is called continuous group key agreement
(CGKA): a protocol family that lets a group add members, remove members, and periodically refresh
the shared key. The standardized CGKA protocol underlying Messaging Layer Security (MLS, an IETF
standard used by RCS on iOS and Android, Cisco Webex, and Wire) is TreeKEM, which achieves
logarithmic-in-group-size update cost but requires a central delivery service to impose a single,
total order on every group operation so that every member processes operations in the same
sequence. A prior decentralized CGKA (DCGKA) scheme by Weidner, Kleppmann, Hugenroth, and Beresford
removes the central-server dependency but pays for it with update cost linear in group size.
BeeKEM is the first DCGKA scheme the paper is aware of that matches TreeKEM's logarithmic update
cost in the common case (no concurrent updates), while degrading gracefully — not catastrophically
— to linear cost as the rate of concurrent updates increases, and while carrying a full security
proof.

BeeKEM represents the group's key material as a perfect binary tree, following the general
TreeKEM/MLS design: each leaf corresponds to one group member and holds that member's current
public key; each inner node holds a public key and one or more encrypted copies of the
corresponding private key, encrypted so that either child of that node can decrypt it from its own
secret key and its sibling's public key. The decryption step uses a non-interactive key exchange
(NIKE): a scheme letting two parties who each know only the other's public key compute a shared
symmetric key with no protocol messages exchanged (elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman is the concrete
instantiation used in the paper's implementation). A member can therefore recover the group secret
at the root by walking from her own leaf to the root, deriving one shared key per level from her own
current secret key and the public key of the sibling node at that level.

Membership changes and key refreshes are recorded as an append-only hash-linked graph of operations
(an operation graph, structured as a hash-based directed acyclic graph analogous to a Git commit
history), rather than a single linear log; each user's device stores its own local copy of both the
tree and the operation graph, and applies a deterministic materialization function to compute the
current tree state from whatever subset of the operation graph it has received. Because different
devices may receive operations in different orders during a network partition, the materialization
function is designed for strong convergence — any two devices that have observed the same set of
operations compute an identical tree, regardless of the order they arrived in — together with three
further named properties: remove-liveness (a removed member is absent after any merge that includes
their removal), add-liveness-under-remove-wins (an added member is present after merge unless
concurrently removed, in which case the removal takes precedence), and no-secret-after-merge (only
an explicit Update operation, never a merge of concurrent operations by itself, establishes a new
group secret). The paper states that a reader familiar with conflict-free replicated data types
(CRDTs, a family of data structures designed so that independent replicas that have applied the same
set of updates always converge to the same state, regardless of the order those updates were
applied in) will recognize this vocabulary, and states plainly that BeeKEM itself is a CRDT.

When updates happen concurrently on different branches of a network partition, the same tree node
can end up with more than one valid version — one per branch — which the paper calls a conflict
node. Rather than requiring agreement on which version is authoritative, BeeKEM has every member who
"ought" to have access to a conflict node's secret compute their own encryption of that secret under
each of their currently known public keys, so a later member who applied a causally subsequent
update supersedes the conflict and re-establishes a single version. A subsequent Update operation
(not the passive act of merging) is what collapses a conflict back into a single defined group
secret; until an Update happens, the group secret at the root of a still-conflicted tree is treated
as undefined.

| Asymptotic classification of sender and recipient public-key-primitive invocation counts, message size, and persistent storage, sequential execution, all three systems instrumented to count Diffie-Hellman/HPKE/signature/keypair-generation calls | Table 1: OpenMLS (TreeKEM/MLS) — Update/Remove sender O(log n), recipient O(1), message O(log n) broadcast, storage O(n); Add sender O(log n), recipient O(1), message O(log n) commit plus O(n) welcome. BeeKEM — Update/Remove sender O(log n), recipient O(1) for an existing recipient, message O(log n) broadcast, storage O(n + h_B) where h_B is the size of the operation history; Add sender O(log n), existing-recipient cost O(1), new-recipient cost O(h_B), message O(log n + h_B) including welcome history. ### Stated limitations
BeeKEM does not achieve full forward secrecy; it achieves a parameterized, weaker form (κ-FSU and
κ-CFS) for two reasons the paper states explicitly. First, a member who has not updated in a long
time must, by the protocol's own correctness requirement, retain access to every group secret
established since her last update, so compromising that member exposes all of those secrets — a
limitation the paper states also affects centralized TreeKEM (there addressed by a definition called
Forward Secrecy with Updates, FSU) and which BeeKEM inherits, generalized to the decentralized
setting. Second, and stated as specific to the decentralized setting: a member who deletes an old
personal secret to strengthen her own forward secrecy loses the ability to decrypt group secrets
defined on a different branch of a network partition once that partition heals, so BeeKEM's ability
to recover secrets after a partition heals (Correctness Under Concurrency, CUC) is in direct tension
with deleting old secrets promptly. The paper states it "conjectures" — its own word — that this
tradeoff between CUC and forward secrecy "may be inherent in decentralized settings," and states
that its alternative construction sketch, BeeKEM^FS, resolves the tradeoff in the opposite direction
(full forward secrecy, at the cost of losing the ability to recover any group secret defined on a
branch a member did not directly participate in). BeeKEM^FS and BeeKEM^PQ (a post-quantum variant)
are both stated as sketches only: the paper writes "we defer a full treatment to future work" for
both, and neither is benchmarked in the evaluation section. The evaluation section explicitly does
not compare BeeKEM's partition-handling behavior (Section 6.2) against the other two systems,
stating MLS cannot operate under partition at all and that Weidner et al.'s DCGKA behaves largely
the same under partition as in the no-partition case, so no partition-specific number for either
comparison system is reported. The paper's security proofs assume the messaging layer supplies
authenticated causal broadcast (ACB) — a communication primitive guaranteeing causally-ordered,
reliable, and authenticated message delivery — while the paper states its actual implementation
constructs ACB from a strictly weaker primitive, a reliable broadcast protocol (RBP, such as a
gossip network), using a hash DAG and digital signatures; the gap between what the proofs assume and
what the implementation is built on is bridged by a construction the paper cites to prior work
rather than proves itself in this paper.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
BeeKEM requires a public key infrastructure (PKI) external to the protocol, treated as a black box,
that lets a user obtain another user's initial public key before adding them to a group; the paper
does not itself supply identity verification or key distribution. It requires a reliable broadcast
protocol (RBP) — the paper's example is a gossip network all group members participate in — as the
minimum communication substrate its implementation depends on, and requires that substrate to be
extended (via a hash DAG plus digital signatures, per the paper's citations) into an authenticated
causal broadcast (ACB) for the formal security proofs to apply as stated: causally-ordered,
eventually-reliable, sender-authenticated delivery, with no requirement of a single total order
across all group members. It requires every group member's device to keep a persistent local copy
of both the BeeKEM tree and the full operation graph (or enough of it to replay from a known-valid
starting point), since a new member's join cost is dominated by replaying the O(n)-sized operation
history, and a device that discards its operation-graph history cannot independently verify or merge
concurrent branches it did not witness firsthand. It requires an underlying non-interactive key
exchange (NIKE) scheme and a symmetric authenticated-encryption scheme whose key spaces are
compatible with each other, and the paper's security reduction depends on the specific security
notion the paper calls HKR-CKS for the NIKE, not merely generic NIKE correctness. The retention
parameter κ is a system-wide (or at minimum per-deployment) policy choice that trades cross-branch
recovery against forward secrecy; the paper does not supply a default or a derivation for what value
of κ a given deployment should use, leaving that choice to whoever deploys the system. Adding a
member requires that member's initial public key be obtainable through the external PKI at add time;
BeeKEM's Add operation itself only blanks the direct path to the new leaf and does not perform any
identity check on the added public key beyond what the PKI already vouches for.

### Contradicts
None found within this batch. `BRIEF.md` section 7's prior summary states BeeKEM "requires only
causal broadcast" as a blanket requirement; this full-text pass finds the paper distinguishes two
levels — the security proofs are stated over authenticated causal broadcast (ACB), while the actual
implementation is built over a strictly weaker reliable broadcast protocol (RBP) with ACB
constructed on top via a separate, cited mechanism. This is a refinement of the brief's summary, not
a contradiction of a measured claim: no other entry in this batch reports a number that disagrees
with a number reported here.

### References worth retrieving
- foundational: M. Weidner, M. Kleppmann, D. Hugenroth, A. Beresford. "DCGKA: Decentralized Group Key Agreement for Secure Messaging." (cited as `[34]`, "WKHB") — the O(n)-update-cost prior DCGKA scheme BeeKEM is benchmarked directly against in Fig. 4 and Table 1.
- competing: J. Alwen, M. Mularczyk, Y. Tselekounis. "Fork-Resilient Continuous Group Key Agreement." (cited as `[8]`) — the centralized-delivery-service scheme the paper states independently achieves logarithmic cost and cross-fork-attack security, but "has not been accompanied by an implementation"; this is the direct comparison point for whether BeeKEM's O(log n)/cross-fork-security combination is unique to the fully decentralized setting or achievable in general.
- foundational: J. Alwen, S. Coretti, Y. Dodis, Y. Tselekounis. (cited as `[7]`) — the source of the FSU (Forward Secrecy with Updates) definition and the UPKE-based TreeKEM-to-full-forward-secrecy fix that BeeKEM^FS is stated to be analogous to.
- foundational/formal-verification: K. Bhargavan, R. Barnes, E. Rescorla. (cited as `[13]`) — a formal (F*/DY*) treatment of the MLS membership sub-protocol; the administered-group-membership guarantee a decentralized replacement must reproduce, per this paper's own framing in its related-work discussion.
- competing: R. Barnes, B. Beurdouche, R. Robert, J. Millican et al. — the MLS/TreeKEM RFC (cited as `[10]`/`[12]`) — the centralized standard BeeKEM is positioned as a decentralized alternative to, and whose OpenMLS implementation (`[30]`) is the direct performance comparison in Section 6.
- foundational: M. Kleppmann, H. Howard. "Byzantine Eventual Consistency and the Fundamental Limits of Peer-to-Peer Databases." (cited as `[25]`) — cited alongside the hash-DAG/signature construction of ACB from RBP that the paper's implementation relies on without reproving.
- foundational: M. Kleppmann. "Making CRDTs Byzantine Fault Tolerant." (cited as `[24]`) — cited for the same ACB-from-RBP construction; directly relevant to how BeeKEM's CRDT convergence claim extends to an actively malicious (not just crash-faulty or partitioned) setting, which this BeeKEM paper's stated threat model (honest-but-partition-prone users) does not itself cover.
- attack/adjacent: M. Albrecht, J. Blasco, R. Bjerg Jensen, L. Mareková. "Mesh Messaging in Large-Scale Protests: Breaking Bridgefy." CT-RSA 2021. (cited as `[3]`) — cited for the claim that group chats of thousands of members are used in real protest contexts, the motivating deployment scenario the paper cites for why O(n) DCGKA update cost is "prohibitive."
