## [ZHOU-EPRINT-24] Pacmann: Efficient Private Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
**Citation:** Mingxun Zhou, Elaine Shi, Giulia Fanti. "Pacmann: Efficient Private Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search." IACR Cryptology ePrint Archive 2024/1600, 2024.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/1600.pdf
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/1600
**Domain:** B

### What it does
Pacmann lets a client run approximate-nearest-neighbor (ANN) search over a server-held vector database while the server learns nothing about the query vector. The client, not the server, runs the graph traversal: it holds a private-information-retrieval (PIR) hint built during a one-time preprocessing pass, and at each hop of the search it issues PIR queries to fetch only the neighbor list and vectors of the current graph vertex, computes distances locally, and picks the next vertex itself. Because the server never sees which vertex indices are fetched, it cannot infer the query's topic from access patterns.

The graph the client searches is built by the server from a customized construction, not an off-the-shelf HNSW (hierarchical navigable small world) or DiskANN graph. The construction enforces a directed, exactly-C-out-regular graph, because a non-uniform out-degree would leak information about a vertex's cluster from the number of PIR queries a hop causes. Build proceeds in three parts: for each vector, find 2C approximate neighbors with an existing ANN library, trim to C with the sparse-neighborhood-graph (SNG) heuristic (sorted by distance, discarding a candidate that lies closer to an already-kept candidate than to the vertex itself, for diversity), add edges in both directions, then re-balance in-degree by keeping each directed edge (x -> y) with probability C / InboundDegree(y) and re-filling or re-trimming each vertex's outbound edges to exactly C.

Retrieval uses Piano, a single-server PIR scheme from the client-preprocessing PIR family: the client streams the whole encoded database once during preprocessing (linear cost, amortized across all later queries) and in exchange gets sublinear per-query computation and communication of order the square root of the database size, with client storage of the same order. The paper adds three optimizations on top of the base construction: beam search (m parallel graph paths per query instead of one, cutting the hops needed for a given recall), fast starting (sqrt(n) precomputed starting vertices the client downloads once, instead of one fixed entry point), and batched PIR (a single round issues all of one hop's neighbor-list queries together, splitting the database into B partitions and querying Q/B times per partition to keep per-query privacy). Together the paper reports a 76% reduction in computation and a near-70% reduction in end-to-end latency from these three optimizations on the ablation configuration below.

### Measured results

| Metric | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Search-success-rate improvement over clustering baseline | 63% vs 29% (2.1x) | MS-MARCO dataset, finding the single most relevant document, Pacmann vs. Tiptoe/Wally-style clustering-based private ANN |
| Recall@10 improvement over Tiptoe | 2.5x | 100-million-vector SIFT dataset |
| Quality reached vs. non-private baseline | ~90% of NGT's recall/MRR | both SIFT and MS-MARCO, non-private baseline is NGT (Neighborhood Graph and Tree), a state-of-the-art non-private graph ANN library |
| Latency at 100M records, LAN | 1.6 s (Pacmann) vs >=4 s (Tiptoe), 60% reduction | LAN setting = 5 ms round-trip time (RTT), single 2.4 GHz Intel Xeon E5-2680 CPU, 256 GB RAM, single thread |
| Latency at 100M records, WAN | 3.1 s (Pacmann) vs >=4 s (Tiptoe), 22% reduction | WAN setting = 50 ms RTT, same hardware |
| Crossover point where Pacmann beats the linear-scan latency baseline | database >5M vectors (LAN), database >50M vectors (WAN) | SIFT dataset scaled from 2M to 100M vectors, quality held fixed at 0.90 recall@10 |
| Detailed cost breakdown, WAN setting, 90% quality target | see table below | MS-MARCO = 3.2M documents reduced to 768-dim sentence-BERT then PCA to 192-dim; SIFT = 100M 128-dim vectors; 16 threads for graph build, 1 thread otherwise |

Detailed breakdown (Table 1 of the paper, WAN setting, both at ~90% of non-private quality):

| Stage | MS-MARCO (3M) | SIFT (100M) |
|---|---|---|
| Graph build time (server, one-time) | 8.5 min | 343.5 min |
| PIR preprocessing time (per client) | 9.1 s | 271.6 s |
| PIR preprocessing communication | 2.7 GB | 59.6 GB |
| Online query latency | 1.1 s | 3.0 s |
| Online query computation time | 0.10 s | 1.48 s |
| Online query communication | 3.1 MB | 14.4 MB |
| Rounds per query | 20 | 32 |
| Per-query maintenance time | 0.19 s | 1.99 s |
| Per-query maintenance communication | 60.1 MB | 399.4 MB |
| Client storage | 0.6 GB | 2.9 GB |
| Quality achieved | 0.266 MRR@100 | 0.90 recall@10 |
| Beam width m | 3 | 4 |

Ablation on a 10-million-vector SIFT subset (WAN setting): beam search alone cuts the rounds needed for 0.90 recall@10 by 3x; adding fast-starting cuts rounds a further 20%; adding batched PIR cuts per-round computation time 4x but introduces query failures that trade off against a small increase in round count.

Alternative-PIR comparison, 10-million-vector SIFT subset: substituting SimplePIR for Piano drops preprocessing communication from about 6 GB to about 300 MB but the paper's own estimate raises online per-query latency from 1.5 s to about 90 s (measured SimplePIR throughput ~10 GB/s on the same server, 25 rounds of 96 parallel queries against a 6 GB per-partition sub-database with 16-way batching).

### Parameters
- Graph out-degree C = 32 (fixed for both datasets in the main evaluation).
- Piano PIR security parameter: 128-bit.
- Batched-PIR partition count B = 16, batch size Q = 32 queries per round.
- Beam search width m = 3 (MS-MARCO) or m = 4 (SIFT-100M), tuned per dataset to hit the 90%-of-non-private-quality target.
- Exploration rounds (max hop count H, tuned per data point to reach target recall): 20 for MS-MARCO, 32 for SIFT-100M; the paper states round count grows roughly logarithmically with database size from 2M to 100M vectors.
- Fast-start vertex count: sqrt(n) preprocessed starting vertices, sampled once and downloaded by the client.
- Network settings tested: LAN = 5 ms RTT; WAN = 50 ms RTT.
- Database sizes tested: SIFT scaled from 2 million to 100 million 128-dimensional vectors (1,000 top-10 test queries per configuration); MS-MARCO fixed at 3.2 million documents (5,000-plus test queries, reported over the first 1,000).

### Stated limitations
The scheme requires the client to download the entire indexing-graph database during preprocessing in a streaming fashion (linear communication even though later per-query cost is sublinear), so the authors state it is unsuitable for network-constrained clients. It does not support dynamic updates to the database — insertions or deletions after the preprocessing pass — which the authors describe as an open problem in the PIR literature generally, not one this paper solves. The construction assumes the database itself is public (every client may learn its contents); it provides no server-side privacy, i.e., no protection of the database contents from the client. The security proof covers only a semi-honest (honest-but-curious) server; extension to a malicious server is left as future work. Preprocessing throughput assumes a good network connection (the paper's own preprocessing-time figures assume roughly 1 Gbps).

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
- The graph the client searches must be built server-side with a fixed, uniform out-degree C for every vertex; an ANN index with irregular vertex degree (as ordinary HNSW or DiskANN indexes have) leaks information through the PIR access pattern and cannot be substituted without first regularizing it by the paper's build procedure.
- The underlying retrieval primitive must be a client-preprocessing single-server PIR scheme (the paper uses Piano) that supports batched multi-query rounds; this requires every client to complete a linear-cost, linear-communication preprocessing pass — a full streaming download of the encoded graph — before making any query, and to refresh that preprocessing state once its stored hints are exhausted.
- The database is assumed static during the query phase; any component that mutates the vector database (adds or removes vectors) after clients have preprocessed invalidates client-held PIR hints, and the paper supplies no mechanism to reconcile that.
- The privacy guarantee holds only against a single, semi-honest server; a design that needs protection against an actively malicious server, multiple colluding servers, or protection of the database contents themselves (not just the query) cannot rely on this mechanism as specified.
- Achieving the paper's latency figures assumes a good-bandwidth client link (the paper's own numbers assume approximately 1 Gbps); a client on a constrained or metered link faces the multi-gigabyte-to-tens-of-gigabytes preprocessing download stated above.

### Contradicts
None found against other entries in this corpus. Internally, the paper corrects its own earlier draft: an initial version of its cost table reported MS-MARCO online communication as 1.5 MB/query; the corrected figure recorded in the released table is 3.1 MB/query (stated in the paper's own correction note).

### References worth retrieving
- **HDCG+23** — Henzinger, Dauterman, Corrigan-Gibbs, Zeldovich, "Private Web Search with Tiptoe," SOSP 2023 — competing: the paper's main baseline for private search quality and latency; Pacmann's own numbers are calibrated against Tiptoe's reported figures.
- **ABG+24** — Asi et al., "Scalable Private Search with Wally," arXiv 2406.06761, 2024 — competing: relaxes Tiptoe's cryptographic privacy to differential privacy using batches of anonymous queries; a direct alternative point in the privacy/efficiency tradeoff space.
- **SSLD22** — Servan-Schreiber, Langowski, Devadas, "Private Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search with Sublinear Communication" (Preco), IEEE S&P 2022 — competing: uses locality-sensitive hashing and a two-non-colluding-server assumption; a different trust-model point.
- **ZPZP24** — Zhu, Patel, Zaharia, Popa, "Compass: Encrypted Semantic Search with High Accuracy," ePrint 2024/1255 — competing: solves a related but distinct problem (client-supplied encrypted database with per-client server-side state, using HNSW plus Path ORAM) rather than a public shared database.
- **ZPSZ24** — Zhou, Park, Shi, Zheng, "Piano: Extremely Simple, Single-Server PIR with Sublinear Server Computation," IEEE S&P 2024 — foundational: the PIR primitive Pacmann builds on directly.
- **BIM00** — Beimel, Ishai, Malkin, "Reducing the Servers' Computation in Private Information Retrieval: PIR with Preprocessing," CRYPTO 2000 — foundational: proves the Omega(n) lower bound for PIR without preprocessing that motivates the whole client-preprocessing approach.
- **HHCG+22** — Henzinger, Hong, Corrigan-Gibbs, Meiklejohn, Vaikuntanathan, "One Server for the Price of Two" (SimplePIR), ePrint 2022/949 — competing: an alternative single-server PIR the paper benchmarks as a substitute for Piano, with a measured 20x preprocessing-communication reduction traded against a ~60x online-latency increase.
- **MY18** — Malkov, Yashunin, "Efficient and Robust Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search Using Hierarchical Navigable Small World Graphs" (HNSW), TPAMI 2018 — foundational: the non-private graph-ANN family whose blueprint Pacmann's graph search follows before privacy is added.
- **JSDS+19** — Jayaram Subramanya et al., "DiskANN: Fast Accurate Billion-Point Nearest Neighbor Search on a Single Node," NeurIPS 2019 — foundational: another graph-ANN baseline; source of the "distant neighbor for diversity" edge-selection idea Pacmann's graph-build procedure cites.
- **DGM+24** — Diwan, Gou, Musco, Musco, Suel, "Navigable Graphs for High-Dimensional Nearest Neighbor Search: Constructions and Limits," arXiv 2405.18680, 2024 — foundational: theoretical navigable-graph degree/hop bound the paper's own theoretical-implications section builds on.

## [ZHOU-SP-24] Piano: Extremely Simple, Single-Server PIR with Sublinear Server Computation
**Citation:** Mingxun Zhou, Andrew Park, Wenting Zheng, Elaine Shi. "Piano: Extremely Simple, Single-Server PIR with Sublinear Server Computation." IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy, 2024. DOI 10.1109/SP54263.2024.00055.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/452.pdf
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/452.pdf
**Domain:** G

### What it does
Piano lets a client fetch one entry from a server-held database of n entries while hiding from the server which entry it fetched, without the server running a scan whose cost grows linearly with n on every query. Piano is single-server private information retrieval (PIR): one server holds the whole database in the clear and the privacy guarantee holds against that one server, unlike multi-server PIR schemes that split trust across several non-colluding servers. Piano uses the client-specific preprocessing model: before making queries, the client downloads a linear-size stream of the database once and derives from it a set of "hints," compact enough to store client-side, that let later individual queries be answered with sublinear server work.

Mechanism. The database indices 0..n-1 are divided into sqrt(n) chunks of sqrt(n) entries each. A "hint" is a randomly chosen set S containing exactly one index from every chunk, together with the parity (XOR) of the database bits at those sqrt(n) indices. The client's local state (learned during one linear streaming pass over the database) is three tables: a primary table of order sqrt(n) such hints (compressed to a short pseudorandom-function, PRF, key per hint rather than the raw index set, cutting client storage from O(n) to order sqrt(n)); a set of order-1 replacement entries per chunk, each storing one raw (index, value) pair; and a backup table of order-1 spare hints per chunk for reuse across future queries. To answer a query for index x, the client finds the primary-table hint whose set S contains x, sends the server a modified set (S with x replaced by a fresh random index drawn from x's own chunk), and the server returns the parity of the database bits at exactly that modified set — one round trip, one message each way. The client then recovers DB[x] by XORing the returned parity against the parity it already held for its original, unmodified set, using its own replacement-entry value for x's chunk. After the query, the client consumes one backup-table entry to refresh the hint that was spent, so it is never queried twice with the same set — this refresh is what keeps the distribution of sets the server sees indistinguishable from uniformly random across many queries, which is the privacy argument (Theorem 3.2, proof sketched in the paper, full proof in its Appendix C).

The privacy definition (Definition 3.1) is against a server acting as a probabilistic polynomial-time adversary that may deviate arbitrarily from the protocol and adaptively choose each next query — not merely an honest-but-curious server that follows the protocol.

The preprocessing pass to learn the hints takes O(n) server and client computation but is amortized over the roughly sqrt(n)·ln(n) queries the resulting hint set supports, giving amortized order sqrt(n) computation per query on both sides, order sqrt(n) online communication per query, and order sqrt(n) client storage. The paper proves this matches, up to poly-logarithmic factors, the Corrigan-Gibbs–Henzinger–Kogan lower bound that client storage S and amortized server computation T must satisfy S·T = Omega(n) for any PIR scheme (a bound the paper cites as [CHK22], not reproved here). The only cryptographic primitive Piano needs is a pseudorandom function, which the implementation instantiates with AES via AES-NI hardware acceleration; the paper states this is the first single-server PIR scheme with sublinear server computation built from one-way functions alone, without homomorphic encryption or privately programmable/puncturable PRFs.

Section B.2 (appendix) describes extending the static scheme to a dynamic database supporting Insert, Update, and Delete, using a hierarchical multi-level structure in which the client always keeps the most recent Q updates locally and at the server, merging levels periodically; the merge and rebuild costs are amortized over the update stream the same way preprocessing is amortized over queries.

### Measured results

| Metric | 1 GB (n=2^27, 8-byte entries) | 2 GB (n=2^28, 8-byte entries) | 100 GB (n≈1.68×10^9, 64-byte entries) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Preprocessing client time, SimplePIR vs Piano | 293s / 629s (1 thread), 111s (8 threads) | 608s / 1471s (1 thread), 257s (8 threads) | 425 min / 192 min (1 thread), 32 min (8 threads) |
| Preprocessing communication, SimplePIR vs Piano | 123MB / 1GB | 173MB / 2GB | 1.2GB / 100GB |
| Online time per query, SimplePIR vs Piano | 131.6ms / 3.0ms | 219.5ms / 3.4ms | 10.9s (extrapolated) / 11.9ms |
| Online communication per query, SimplePIR vs Piano | 238KB / 32KB | 338KB / 64KB | 2.3MB / 100KB |
| Client storage, SimplePIR vs Piano | 123MB / 61MB | 173MB / 71MB | 1.2GB / 839MB |

Conditions: two AWS m5.8xlarge instances, 128GB RAM each; local-area-network figures run on a single machine; SimplePIR figures use the open-source implementation from Henzinger et al.; the 100GB SimplePIR column is extrapolated, not measured, because the open-source SimplePIR implementation does not support a database that large or cross-machine connections; online-time figures are averaged over 1,000 queries; amortization is over Q = sqrt(n)·ln(n) queries. For 1GB/2GB, Piano is 43.9x-64.6x faster than SimplePIR on online query latency; at 100GB, the gap widens to about 915x (11.9ms vs the extrapolated 10.9s).

Wide-area-network experiment: server on the US west coast, client on the US east coast, TLS over a 2Gbps link, round-trip time about 60ms, 1,000-query average. For the 100GB database (64-byte entries): non-private baseline 61.0ms online time, SimplePIR 10.9s (extrapolated), Piano 72.6ms online time, 100KB online communication, 839MB client storage. Piano's online time is a 7%-20% latency overhead versus the non-private baseline across the tested sizes; SimplePIR's overhead over the same baseline is 4.6x-178.7x. In the paper's headline figure for this setup, Piano achieves 73ms response time for the 100GB database at 60ms RTT, versus an 11s-or-more extrapolated figure for SimplePIR, a claimed 150x+ speedup, and a 1.2x slowdown relative to the non-private baseline.

Comparison against TreePIR (two-server, non-colluding-server model, not single-server): for an 8GB database with 2^28 entries, TreePIR's best reported amortized online time is 23ms (non-recursive variant) or 84ms (recursive variant with poly-logarithmic communication); Piano reports an amortized 8ms per query under the same database size, at 4x TreePIR's local client storage (the paper attributes the extra storage to Piano's backup hints and setup-phase deamortization, both required only in the single-server setting).

### Parameters
- Chunk size: 2·sqrt(n), rounded up to the nearest power of 2 (for efficient modulo). Set size follows from chunk size; the paper states performance is more sensitive to set size than chunk size, and chunk size does not change the asymptotics.
- Q (queries supported per preprocessing round): sqrt(n)·ln(n).
- Statistical security parameter kappa = 40.
- Computational security parameter lambda = 128.
- PRF keys: 128 bits, instantiated with AES (AES-NI hardware acceleration).
- M1 (primary table size) = sqrt(n)·ln(kappa·alpha(kappa)); M2 (backup entries per chunk) = 3·ln(kappa·alpha(kappa)), where alpha(kappa) is any super-constant function of kappa — used in the correctness proof (Theorem 3.3/C.3) to bound failure probability by 2^-kappa across all Q queries, matching SimplePIR's target failure probability.
- Optimization tested: a single lambda-bit master PRF key plus a unique 32-bit tag per hint (instead of one full PRF key per hint), measured to cut client storage by 30% and give a 2-3x concrete speedup in PRF evaluation.
- Database index width in the implementation: 64-bit integers.
- Implementation size: about 800 lines of Go for the full scheme; about 160 lines for a separate tutorial-only reference implementation.
- Preprocessing parallelization: client-side preprocessing parallelized across 8 threads in the reported experiments (server-side and online computation stay single-threaded).

### Stated limitations
The paper states Piano's main limitation is communication cost: the client must download the entire database once during setup, and per-query online communication is order sqrt(n), worse than prior theoretical schemes ([ZLTS23], [LP22], cited by the paper as achieving order-1 (up to poly-logarithmic factors) communication per query). The paper states this tradeoff is deliberate: avoiding fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) during the offline phase, and avoiding privately programmable PRFs (needed by the order-1-communication schemes and, the paper states, known only in theory, not as a practical primitive), are what make Piano concretely implementable. The paper states that a single-server PIR scheme with order-1 communication that is also practical is an open question for future work.

Batch PIR schemes (an alternative approach the paper compares against but does not implement) are stated to have two limitations Piano avoids: they need many parallel queries submitted simultaneously to amortize server cost (only at about sqrt(n) parallel queries does the amortized time match Piano, per the paper's analysis), and they still require the server to run homomorphic-encryption evaluation over the full database per batch, an O(n) server operation, versus Piano's order-sqrt(n) plaintext-only server operation.

The dynamic-database extension (Appendix B.2) is described as "not hard" to build via a hierarchical structure but is not evaluated experimentally in this paper — no measured figures are given for update throughput or dynamic-scheme performance.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
- A single server holds the full database in the clear; Piano's privacy guarantee is a property of client-server interaction, not of splitting the database across non-colluding servers, so anything that requires multi-server non-collusion assumptions (e.g., two-server PIR) is a different deployment model with different trust requirements.
- The client must complete a one-time (and periodically repeated) linear streaming pass over the entire database — full download or full network scan — before any query benefits from the sublinear-computation property; a client that cannot download order-n data at setup (or every ~sqrt(n)·ln(n) queries thereafter) cannot use this scheme as described.
- Client-side storage of order sqrt(n) (839MB for the 100GB/1.68-billion-entry configuration tested) must be available and persist between queries; losing the local hint tables between queries forces a fresh preprocessing pass.
- The scheme assumes queries within one preprocessing window are not repeated/duplicated (the correctness proof, Theorem C.3, explicitly assumes the client does not make duplicate queries among the Q queries covered by one preprocessing round); a system that needs to re-query the same index inside one window is outside what the stated correctness bound covers.
- The database is treated as static bits indexed 0..n-1 for the core scheme; a caller needing inserts, updates, or deletes must adopt the separate hierarchical dynamic-database construction in Appendix B.2, which the paper does not benchmark.
- Preprocessing communication equals a full database download (100GB for the 100GB-database test), so the network and storage budget for the initial (and periodic) sync must accommodate transferring the entire dataset, not just per-query traffic.

### Contradicts
None found. The 100GB SimplePIR figures used for comparison are the paper's own extrapolation, not a measurement of a run SimplePIR actually completed at that size — that qualifier is stated in the paper's own footnote and is preserved above rather than presented as a direct measurement.

### References worth retrieving
- foundational: Beimel, Ishai, Malkin, "Reducing the Servers' Computation in Private Information Retrieval: PIR with Preprocessing" [BIM00] — proves the linear-server-computation lower bound for PIR without preprocessing that motivates this entire line of work.
- foundational: Chor, Goldreich, Kushilevitz, Sudan, "Private Information Retrieval" [CGKS95] — originates the PIR problem.
- competing: Henzinger, Hong, Corrigan-Gibbs, Meiklejohn, et al., "One Server for the Price of Two: Simple and Fast Single-Server Private Information Retrieval" (SimplePIR) [HHCG+22] — the paper's own primary experimental baseline throughout, state-of-the-art linear-server-computation single-server PIR.
- competing: Corrigan-Gibbs, Henzinger, Kogan, "Single-Server Private Information Retrieval with Sublinear Amortized Time" [CHK22] — source of the S·T = Omega(n) lower bound Piano claims to match, and a competing sublinear-server-computation scheme using linear homomorphic encryption at worse asymptotics (order n^(2/3) client storage/server computation).
- competing: Zhou, Lin, Tselekounis, Shi, "Optimal Single-Server Private Information Retrieval" [ZLTS23] and Lazzaretti, Papamanthou, "Single-Server PIR with Sublinear Communication and Computation" [LP22] — theoretical schemes achieving order-1 communication per query that Piano explicitly trades away for practicality.
- competing: Lazzaretti, Papamanthou, "TreePIR: Sublinear-Time and Polylog-Bandwidth Private Information Retrieval from DDH" [LP23] — two-server model competitor with the closest measured online-time figures (23ms/84ms at 8GB) cited directly against Piano's 8ms at the same size.
- competing: Corrigan-Gibbs, Kogan, "Private Information Retrieval with Sublinear Online Time" [CK20] — introduces the client-side-preprocessing idea in the two-server model that Piano's single-server scheme is compared against.
- foundational: Lin, Mook, Wichs, "Doubly Efficient Private Information Retrieval and Fully Homomorphic RAM Programs from Ring LWE" [LMW22] — global-preprocessing-model breakthrough cited for its server-storage/communication tradeoff.
- attack (lower bound, not an attack on a deployment but a negative result relevant to any order-1-communication claim): the [CHK22] lower bound already listed above.

### Verbatim extracts
- "Piano is the first practical single-server sublinear-time PIR scheme"
- "we outperform the state-of-the-art single-server PIR by 40x-900x"

## [ZIA-ARXIV-25] Collaborative Content Moderation in the Fediverse
**Citation:** Haris Bin Zia, Aravindh Raman, Ignacio Castro, Gareth Tyson. "Collaborative Content Moderation in the Fediverse." arXiv preprint arXiv:2501.05871, 2025. DOI 10.48550/ARXIV.2501.05871.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.05871
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.05871
**Domain:** K

### What it does
FedMod lets Mastodon instances build a better local content-moderation classifier than any one instance could train alone, without any instance disclosing its labeled posts to another instance or to a central server. It runs three steps, repeated on a configurable interval t (default 24 hours):

1. Model initialization: each instance fine-tunes a local classifier (multilingual BERT, mBERT, 172M parameters, 714 MB storage) on its own small labeled set, for one of three moderation tasks — harmful-content detection, bot-account detection, content-warning assignment.
2. Peer selection: each instance picks k other instances to collaborate with. The paper's proposed selection method, hashsim, has each instance periodically fetch every other instance's weekly trending-hashtag list (via each instance's public Trends API) and compute Jaccard similarity between its own trending-hashtag set and each other instance's set, then picks the k instances with highest similarity as peers. A random-k baseline is also evaluated.
3. Parameter exchange: each instance requests model parameters from its k selected peers directly, peer to peer, with no central aggregator, and applies FederatedAveraging (McMahan et al.) locally to combine its own parameters with its peers' into an updated local model. Differential-privacy clipping (via the Flower federated-learning framework) is available to bound any one instance's influence on a peer's aggregated model.

For scalability, an optional pre-sampling step restricts the Jaccard-similarity computation to the top i instances by follow-count overlap (the number of the other instance's users followed by the local instance's own users) before computing hashtag similarity within that smaller set, avoiding all-pairs computation across every instance in the network.

### Measured results
Dataset: 50 Mastodon instances sampled from an 11,516-instance index (Fediverse Observer), split evenly between above-average and below-average user count (average across the full index: 1,162 users/instance); 219,577 unique posts by 44,840 users, collected March 1-June 21, 2023, across 17 languages (75.29% English, 17.73% German). Harmful-content labels came from the Perspective API (post flagged harmful if any of six emotional-attribute scores exceeded 0.5, a threshold matched to prior literature; a stricter 0.8 threshold gave similar relative results). Bot-content and content-warning labels were the platform's own self-declared/self-tagged metadata fields, not model-generated. Every reported model result used only 128 labeled posts per instance per task (8 online-learning steps of 16 posts each), chosen to represent what a volunteer administrator could plausibly label.

| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| 7.48% of all 219,577 posts classified harmful at the 0.5 Perspective threshold (2.71% at the 0.8 threshold); worst single instance 19.43% (0.5 threshold) / 7.92% (0.8 threshold) | Full 50-instance dataset |
| 19.38% of posts from self-declared bot accounts; worst instance 45.65% | Full 50-instance dataset; 13 of 50 instances explicitly disallow bots in policy yet all 50 contain bot posts |
| 5.04% of posts self-tagged with a content warning; worst instance 20.16% | Full 50-instance dataset |
| Local model (mBERT, per-instance, 128 labeled posts): harmful-content macro-F1 0.63; bot-detection macro-F1 0.69; content-warning macro-F1 0.53 | 80:20 stratified train/test split per instance per task; per-instance variance reported directly: harmful-detection macro-F1 ranged from 0.36 (cryptodon.chat) to 0.76 (social.eiden.ch) |
| Local model with 25%-per-step label-noise ("perturbed" set, harmful-content task only): macro-F1 drops 12.69% (p<0.001) relative to the clean-label local model at N=128 | Same setup, 4 of 16 posts per step relabeled with flipped harmful/non-harmful label |
| FedMod (k=2 peers) vs. local, at N=128 labeled posts: harmful-content +12.69% macro-F1 with hashsim peer selection (p<0.001), +9.52% with random peer selection (p<0.001); content-warning +9.43% with hashsim (p<0.001), +3.77% with random (p<0.01); bot-detection hashsim reaches 0.73 vs. random's 0.70 (p<0.05) | Same 50-instance dataset, k=2, all three tasks, no pre-sampling; random-k trial repeated 10 times with different seeds and averaged |
| FedMod (hashsim, k=2) on the perturbed harmful-content set: +14.54% macro-F1 over local at N=128 (p<0.001) | Same perturbed-label setup as the local-model noise test |
| Effect of increasing k (peer count) from 2 to 10 on harmful-content macro-F1: +4.22% at N=128 (p<0.001) but +19.60% at N=16 (p<0.0001) | k swept over {2,3,4,10}; effect of more peers is much larger when each instance has contributed only a few labeled posts |
| Pre-sampling to i=5 most-followed instances before hashsim similarity: macro-F1 degrades only 2.81% for harmful content (p=0.11, not significant), 1.36% for bot detection (p=0.07), 1.72% for content-warning (p=0.73) at N=128, versus computing similarity against the full 50-instance pool, while cutting hashtag-similarity computations (and the data exchanged to compute them) by 90% | k=2, i in {5,10}; 56% of the 50 instances had their single most-similar instance already inside their own top-5-by-follow-overlap pre-sample |
| Moderate policy divergence (a random 25% or 50% of instances raise their harmful-content threshold from 0.5 to 0.8): FedMod macro-F1 for the unchanged-threshold instances drops only 2.73% at N=128 (p=0.37, not significant) when 50% of instances differ | Same 50-instance corpus, harmful-content task only; 68% of the 0.5-threshold instances had at least one 0.8-threshold peer |
| Opposing policies (a random 25% or 50% of instances have their harmful/non-harmful label definition fully inverted): at 25% opposing, the other 75% of instances' FedMod macro-F1 drops 8.21% (p<0.01) at N=128 relative to a same-policy run, but is still 4.68% better than their local-only models (p<0.05); at 50% opposing, FedMod's advantage over local models disappears entirely | Same corpus, harmful-content task, N=128; the authors describe this scenario as deliberately unrealistic, constructed to probe the failure mode, not as an observed condition |

### Parameters
- Peer count k: default/primary evaluation k=2; also tested at k in {3, 4, 10}.
- Federation round interval t: 24 hours (default; not swept).
- Labeled posts per instance per task: 128 total (8 steps of 16), reported explicitly as an arbitrary, not derived, choice made to approximate what a volunteer administrator could realistically annotate.
- Base model: mBERT (172M parameters, 714 MB on disk); DistilmBERT and XLM-R (base) were compared in an appendix ablation and mBERT was selected for best macro-F1 among the three at matched training steps.
- Training: 2 epochs, learning rate 5e-5, batch size 16 (values are the original BERT paper's suggested fine-tuning hyperparameters, not independently tuned for this task).
- Pre-sampling set size i: {5, 10}, compared against no pre-sampling (similarity computed against the full instance pool).
- Perspective API harmfulness threshold: 0.5 (primary), 0.8 (robustness check, appendix).
- Label-noise rate for the "perturbed" harmful-content training set: 25% of posts per training step (4 of 16) relabeled.

### Stated limitations
The authors state that using the Perspective API to generate ground-truth harmful-content labels imposes a single, centrally defined notion of harmfulness on every instance, whereas real administrators would label according to their own, possibly inconsistent, judgment; they address this specific gap only by injecting synthetic label noise, not by using real per-administrator labels. The authors state the bot-detection and content-warning tasks rely on self-declared/self-tagged user metadata, which they did not independently verify. FedMod's peer-selection mechanism (hashsim) requires each instance to periodically fetch every other candidate instance's trending-hashtag list, which the authors state does not scale past roughly 10,000 instances without pre-sampling (all-pairs Jaccard similarity across 10,000 instances requires about 100 million computations); pre-sampling addresses the compute cost but the authors report it can miss the truly most-similar peer for some instances. The authors state that FedMod's performance degrades once instances with opposing moderation policies federate with each other, and that at 50% opposing-policy instances FedMod no longer outperforms training locally; they state this failure was deliberately provoked as a worst case, note it plausibly maps to a malicious actor deliberately federating with opposing-policy instances to degrade others' models, and list a reputation scheme or an alternative peer-selection strategy to defend against it as unimplemented future work. The authors state they have not evaluated FedMod over a real deployment among live instance administrators, nor over a longitudinal period spanning multiple months of continued collaboration; both are listed as future work. In an appendix, the authors state that relying directly on the Perspective API for moderation (rather than the FedMod approach) would deepen the Fediverse's dependence on a single centralized third-party service (operated by Jigsaw/Google) and offers only a fixed, non-customizable set of harmfulness attributes, misaligned with per-instance policy needs — presented as the authors' own reason for choosing the FedMod design over a Perspective-API-only alternative, not as a measured cost.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
FedMod requires each participating instance to expose two API surfaces to peers: a Trends endpoint (`<instance>/api/v1/trends/tags`) returning weekly trending hashtags, used for hashsim similarity, and a way to serve model parameters to selected peers on request. It requires each instance to maintain its own labeled training set locally; no instance is required to disclose its raw labeled posts to any peer or central party, only trained model parameters — the privacy property rests specifically on parameter exchange substituting for data exchange. Peer selection (hashsim) requires a follow-graph observation for the pre-sampling optimization: each instance must know, for every other instance it is considering, how many of that instance's users its own users follow — data drawn from the federation/follow relationships already visible to an ActivityPub-federated instance, not an added protocol requirement, but a dependency on that visibility existing. The federated-averaging aggregation step assumes participating peers are not adversarially poisoning their submitted parameters; the paper's own opposing-policy experiment demonstrates that a peer with an inverted labeling definition degrades the aggregate, and the paper states no defense against this beyond an unimplemented future reputation scheme — so any deployment needs either trusted peer selection or an added Byzantine-robustness mechanism the paper does not supply. The scheme assumes each instance can independently fine-tune a 172M-parameter transformer model (mBERT) locally on some interval (default 24 hours); this is a computational requirement on the hosting instance, not evaluated at low-resource extremes in this paper.

### Contradicts
None found. The commonly cited summary that "federated learning across instances solves Fediverse moderation" overstates this paper's own finding: the paper's measured result is that FedMod helps when instances' policies are broadly compatible and degrades or reverses its benefit once a large fraction of peers hold opposing policies — the paper states this itself and frames it as unresolved future work, not as a solved case.

### References worth retrieving
- foundational: Anaobi, I. H., Raman, A., Castro, I., Bin Zia, H., Ibosiola, D., Tyson, G., "Will Admins Cope? Decentralized Moderation in the Fediverse," ACM Web Conference (WWW) 2023, pp. 3109-3120 — prior measurement of Fediverse administrator moderation burden and a semi-automated policy-generation tool; foundational context this paper builds on.
- competing: reference [7] in this paper's bibliography (title not resolved from the excerpt read) — a prior Pleroma content-moderation system that shares fully trained local models (logistic regression, bag-of-words features) between high-resource and low-resource instances; the paper's own direct point of comparison, explicitly described as requiring thousands of labeled samples and assuming high-resource instances exist to train them, versus FedMod's partially-trained-parameter exchange.
- foundational: McMahan, H. B. et al., FederatedAveraging — the aggregation algorithm FedMod uses locally at each instance (cited as [21] in this paper; exact venue not confirmed from the excerpt).
- foundational: Beutel, D. J. et al. / Porto Buarque de Gusmão et al., "Flower: A friendly federated learning..." — the federated-learning framework FedMod's parameter exchange is implemented on (cited as [6]).
- attack/critique: Davidson, T. et al., hate-speech/offensive-language classifier on 25K labeled tweets (multi-class logistic regression) — cited as a centralized-platform baseline this paper contrasts with FedMod's label-scarce setting.

## [ZOU-USENIX-25] PoisonedRAG: Knowledge Corruption Attacks to Retrieval-Augmented Generation of Large Language Models
**Citation:** Wei Zou, Runpeng Geng, Binghui Wang, Jinyuan Jia. "PoisonedRAG: Knowledge Corruption Attacks to Retrieval-Augmented Generation of Large Language Models." 34th USENIX Security Symposium, 2025. Seattle, WA, August 13-15, 2025.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.usenix.org/system/files/usenixsecurity25-zou-poisonedrag.pdf
**Source URL:** https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity25/presentation/zou-poisonedrag
**Domain:** B

### What it does
PoisonedRAG makes a large language model (LLM) generate an attacker-chosen answer to an attacker-chosen question, by inserting a small number of crafted texts into the knowledge database that a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system searches before answering. RAG has three components: a knowledge database of texts, a retriever that embeds a question and the database's texts into vectors and returns the top-k texts most similar to the question, and an LLM that generates an answer using the retrieved texts as context. The attack requires each malicious text to satisfy two conditions at once: the retrieval condition (the retriever's similarity score between the malicious text and the target question must be high enough for the text to land in the top-k retrieved set) and the generation condition (the LLM must output the attacker's target answer when that malicious text is used as its context).

The mechanism splits each malicious text P into two concatenated parts, P = S + I, so the two conditions can be engineered separately instead of fighting each other in one string (the paper shows that making a text maximally similar to the question, e.g. copying the question itself, achieves retrieval but not generation). I is generated first: the attacker prompts an LLM (GPT-4 in the experiments) with the target question and target answer and asks it to write a short passage of a stated length that would produce the target answer if used as context; if the RAG-side LLM does not produce the target answer when tested against this passage, the passage is regenerated, up to a maximum number of trials. S is then crafted to satisfy the retrieval condition without breaking I's effect. Two settings are defined by what the attacker knows about the retriever: in the black-box setting (no access to retriever parameters or queries), S is simply set equal to the target question itself, on the reasoning that a question is most similar to itself; in the white-box setting (retriever parameters known), S is instead solved for by gradient-based adversarial-text optimization (the paper uses HotFlip) to directly maximize the embedding similarity between S+I and the target question's embedding under the retriever's own encoder.

HotpotQA: 0.99, 0.98, 0.93, 0.98, 0.98, 0.94, 0.97, 0.96 (same LLM order). ### Parameters
- N: number of malicious texts injected per target question; default 5.
- k: number of texts the retriever returns per query; default 5, swept up to 50 in the Knowledge Expansion defense test.
- L: maximum number of regeneration trials allowed when crafting I; default 50, with saturation of effectiveness observed by L=10.
- V: target word length of the generated passage I; default 30.
- LLM decoding temperature: 0.1 for the RAG-side answering LLM; 1 for the GPT-4 call used to generate I.
- Retriever: Contriever by default; Contriever-ms and ANCE also tested; similarity measured as the dot product of question and text embedding vectors by default.
- White-box optimization method for S: HotFlip (a discrete gradient-based adversarial-text search method), used to solve Equation 5 in the paper (maximizing embedding similarity between S+I and the target question).
- Target-question selection: 10 close-ended questions per dataset per trial, repeated 10 times excluding already-used questions, giving 100 target questions total per dataset.

### Stated limitations
The paper states PoisonedRAG does not reach a 100% attack success rate and defers a per-case failure analysis to an appendix rather than characterizing the failure condition in the main text. The authors state their own paraphrasing defense does not paraphrase the knowledge-database texts themselves, only the incoming question, "due to high computational costs," so the defense as tested is a partial mitigation by the authors' own design choice, not a ceiling on what paraphrasing could achieve if applied to the corpus. The authors state it is "still an open challenge to develop a perfect metric" for automatically judging whether a generated answer matches an attacker's target answer (their substring-matching proxy is validated only against the authors' own manual judgments, not independent annotators). Listed future work: extending optimization-based methods (such as adapting the GCG jailbreak-suffix method) to craft I itself, jointly optimizing a single malicious text against multiple target questions at once (currently each malicious text targets one question), and developing new defenses, since all four defenses evaluated in Section 7 (paraphrasing, perplexity detection, duplicate-text filtering, knowledge expansion) are stated to fail to fully stop the attack.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The attack requires write access to the RAG system's knowledge database — an attacker who can insert texts that the retriever will later index and search. It requires the retriever to support a fixed similarity function between a question embedding and a text embedding (dot product in these experiments); the black-box variant needs no further access, but the white-box variant requires the attacker to know the retriever's parameters (specifically its two encoders, one for questions and one for texts) well enough to run gradient-based optimization against them. The black-box variant additionally requires access to some LLM (not necessarily the one used by the target RAG system) capable of following an instruction to write a short passage that entails a given answer to a given question; this LLM-generation step is itself iterative and needs a way to test whether a candidate passage, used alone as context, causes an LLM to output the target answer, which the paper implements by querying an LLM up to L times and checking the output. The attack's retrieval condition assumes the retriever ranks by embedding similarity to the question and returns a bounded top-k set; a retrieval method that does not expose or is not well-approximated by such a scoring function (for instance, a privacy-preserving retrieval channel that returns a match without exposing similarity scores or embeddings) is not evaluated here as either a target or an obstacle. The knowledge-expansion defense result implies that any system relying on “retrieve enough texts to dilute the attacker's texts” must trade retrieval-set size against the LLM's context-window computation cost, since the paper states this defense “incurs large computation costs for an LLM to generate an answer due to the long context.”

### Contradicts
None found against another entry in this batch.

### References worth retrieving
- Liu, Jia, Geng, Jia, Gong, "Formalizing and Benchmarking Prompt Injection Attacks and Defenses" — competing (the prompt injection attack baseline compared against in Table 4; also a defense reference).
- Zhong, Huang, Wettig, Chen, "Poisoning Retrieval Corpora by Injecting Adversarial Passages" — competing (the Corpus Poisoning Attack baseline compared against in Table 4; requires white-box retriever access and is described as achieving a very low attack success rate here because it does not solve the generation condition).
- Zou, Wang, Kolter, Fredrikson, "Universal and Transferable Adversarial Attacks on Aligned Language Models" (the GCG jailbreak paper) — attack, foundational (the optimization method extended and compared against as the GCG Attack baseline in Table 4).

- Lewis, Perez, Piktus, Petroni, Karpukhin, et al., "Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks" — foundational (defines RAG, cited as the reason the paper's evaluation focuses on question answering).

## [ZUO-ICWSM-24] Understanding and Improving Content Moderation in Web3 Platforms
**Citation:** Wenrui Zuo, Raul J. Mondragón, Aravindh Raman, Gareth Tyson. "Understanding and Improving Content Moderation in Web3 Platforms." Proceedings of the International AAAI Conference on Web and Social Media (ICWSM), Vol. 18, 2024. DOI 10.1609/ICWSM.V18I1.31431.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/ICWSM/article/view/31431/33591
**Source URL:** https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/ICWSM/article/view/31431
**Domain:** K

### What it does
This paper measures user-controlled moderation on memo.cash, a microblogging platform built on the Bitcoin Cash (BCH) blockchain with no instance operators, community moderators, or admins of any kind. Every user interaction (posts, follows, likes, and the moderation primitive itself, mutes) is recorded as a transaction in the blockchain's OP_RETURN field, so every action, including every mute, is permanent and publicly visible. Muting hides a target user's posts from the muting user's own timeline only; it does not unfollow the target, delete their posts, or affect any other viewer's timeline. A muting user's mute list is displayed publicly on their own profile, so the record of who muted whom is fully transparent. A muted user's only recourse is a direct message or a public post appealing the mute to the person who issued it; there is no platform-level appeal or override mechanism.

The paper does three things with this measured population. First, it trains classifiers on 406 per-user features (9 platform-activity features plus 397 content features, including 384-dimension BERT sentence-embedding averages) to predict which users get muted, and ranks feature importance. Second, it detects follower-graph communities (Louvain method) and measures whether mutes stay inside or cross community boundaries, using the Massey-Denton isolation index compared against an Erdos-Renyi random-mute baseline. Third, it builds a mute-recommendation system: given a mute-issuer/mute-receiver pair's six shared attributes (follower count, like count, and mutes-received count, for each of the two users), it predicts a 1-4 graded "willingness to mute" label and ranks candidate accounts for a personalized top-N mute list, comparing Random, Most-Popular, SVD, UserKNN, LightFM, and four CNN variants as the ranking model.

### Measured results
Dataset: memo.cash crawl, April 2018 (platform inception) to June 2023 — 27,630 users, 391K posts, 375K likes, 6,240 mutes (1.5M total social actions). 417 users issued at least one mute; 2,215 users received at least one mute.

| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| 91.3% of muted users had received at least one like on their posts; muted users averaged 384.7 likes (median 85) | Full dataset, all 2,215 muted users |
| Among users muted by more than 5 distinct people, 35.4% still received likes on their posts | Full dataset |
| 8.4% of users had been both muted and liked by the same individual user | Full dataset, mute-pair level |
| Mute-prediction classifier (user muted vs. not, binary, 2,215 positive / 25,415 negative, i.e. roughly 8% positive rate): best F1 = 0.62 (Random Forest); Logistic Regression F1 = 0.53, SVM F1 = 0.42, GBDT F1 = 0.49, Graph Convolutional Network F1 = 0.46. Accuracy for all non-GCN models = 0.98; GCN accuracy = 0.93 | 406 features (9 platform-activity + 397 content/BERT), 80:20 train:test split, hyperparameters grid-searched per model (ranges given in the paper's Table 3) |
| Feature importance (Random Forest): platform action count ranks 1st; hate-word count ranks 26th; Perspective-API-derived scores rank lower still | Same Random Forest model as above, top-30 features reported |
| Muted users show more concentrated, short-interval posting than non-muted users; muted users receive engagement (likes, tips, or replies) on 60.5% of their posts versus 47.0% for non-muted users | Full dataset, post-level engagement comparison |
| Followership network: 12,676 nodes, 60,809 directed follow edges; Louvain community detection (resolution 1.0) identified 72 communities total, 11 "main" communities after excluding unaffiliated singleton nodes, largest three holding 2,950 / 2,490 / 1,891 users | Full followership graph derived from the same crawl |
| 60.9% of all mutes occur between two users in the same detected community; 9 of the (paper states 12, elsewhere 11) communities' real isolation-index (RI) values exceed the corresponding random-simulation isolation-index (SI) values | Massey-Denton isolation index, compared against an Erdos-Renyi random baseline simulating the same number of mutes with no community preference |
| Mute-recommendation (top-10 list) best model, LightFM: F1 = 0.76, MAE = 1.62, nDCG = 0.91, MRR = 0.56. SVD F1 = 0.28 (worst non-CNN model). Best CNN variant (CNN-normalized+preprocess) F1 = 0.28; worst CNN variant (CNN-baseline) F1 = 0.16 | 6,242 labeled mute events, 4-level graded label (1-4, defined by combining self-mute, follower-mute, and like presence/absence — see Parameters), 80:20 hold-out with 5-fold cross-validation, top-N in {5,10,20}, six shared pairwise features (follower count, like count, mutes-received count for each of the mute-issuer and mute-receiver) |
| Per-user CDF of recommendation quality (top-10, LightFM as reference against comparison models): only 38.8% of users had F1 <0.5 with LightFM (i.e., most users are well above 0.5); with SVD around 43.7% of users had low F1 (specific SVD threshold value given in-text is partly garbled in the extracted text) | Same experimental setup as above |
| CNN variants: 80% of users experienced F1 <0.4; 23% of users had RMSE <0.5 | Same setup, all four CNN variants |
| Random baseline model: over 80% of users had accuracy and F1 both under 0.2; only 9.8%-11.3% of users had RMSE <0.5 | Same setup |
| The recommendation system is stated to be trained on data covering only 50.7% of memo.cash users | Same 6,242-event dataset — a cold-start condition the paper attributes LightFM's relative advantage to |

### Parameters
- Mute-prediction task: 406 features total (9 user/platform-activity features: creation days, profile-set flag, action count, followers, following, topic count, mutes issued, BCH wallet balance, transaction count; 13 text-derived features including VADER sentiment compound score, toxicity/profanity/threat/sexually-explicit scores, hate-word count via the HateBase API; 384 BERT sentence-embedding dimensions averaged per user, zeroed for users with no posts).
- Classifier hyperparameter search ranges (grid search): Logistic Regression penalty in {l1, l2}, C in {0.001-100}; SVM gamma in {1e-3, 1e-4} (RBF kernel), C in {1-200} (RBF) or {1-100} (linear); Random Forest n_estimators in {50,200,300,700}, max_features in {auto, sqrt, log2}; GBDT learning_rate in {0.05-0.2}, max_depth in {3,5,8}, subsample in {0.5-1.0}; GCN epochs in {100,200,500}, learning_rate in {0.01,0.05,0.1}, node embedding dimension in {100,200,300}.
- Community detection: Louvain method, resolution parameter = 1.0 (chosen because the authors cite prior work finding this value gives a satisfactory community count; not independently derived here).
- Mute-recommendation label scale: 4 discrete levels built from three observed behaviors (self-mute, follower-mute, like presence) — label 4 (very negative, self-mute + follower-mute + no like, 525 events), label 3 (moderately negative, self-mute only + no like, 1,825 events), label 2 (somewhat negative, self-mute + follower-mute + at least one like, 896 events), label 1 (slightly negative, self-mute + at least one like, 2,996 events).
- Recommendation top-N evaluated: N in {5, 10, 20}.
- Recommendation evaluation: 80:20 hold-out, five-fold cross-validation, metrics accuracy/precision/recall/F1, nDCG, MRR, RMSE, MAE.

### Stated limitations
The authors state the mute-recommendation system is built on a limited memo.cash-specific dataset and that generalizing the findings requires comparison against other Web3 platforms in future work. The authors state the recommendation models are trained on data covering only 50.7% of users, producing a cold-start condition that they identify as the reason LightFM (designed to handle cold start) outperforms the alternatives tested. The authors state the CNN-based recommenders underperform because CNNs require larger training sets than the roughly 6,000-event memo.cash mute dataset provides. The authors state their features and analysis are based on interaction counts (following, liking, muting) rather than post content or topic, and describe this as making the approach feasible and scalable for other user-controlled moderation systems, framed by the authors as a design choice rather than as a limitation the paper apologizes for. In the AI/ethics checklist at the end of the paper, the authors state they addressed limitations and biases as future work in the conclusion but did not separately discuss broader societal impact.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A per-user moderation signal of this kind (a mute) requires each mute to be attributable to a specific issuing user and a specific target user, and requires that record to be either directly observable (as on-chain data, in memo.cash's case) or otherwise obtainable in bulk for training — the mute-prediction classifier and the recommendation system are both trained on the full historical mute record, not a sample a single user could see. The follower-community localization result (60.9% of mutes stay within-community) requires a followership graph to already exist and be observable; the isolation-index measurement is computed directly from that graph, so any design relying on community-based mute propagation needs the same graph structure available to compute community membership. The recommendation system's six pairwise features (follower count, like count, mutes-received count, for both the issuing and the receiving user) require that both users' aggregate activity counts are visible to whatever component computes recommendations — on memo.cash this is true by construction because all of it is on-chain and public, but a design with private follow/like/mute state would need an alternate channel to supply these features. The paper measures no false-positive cost or appeal-outcome data: mute appeals happen through unstructured direct messages or public posts on memo.cash, with no measured resolution rate, so a design substituting an automated recommendation for user-initiated muting has no evidence in this paper about how often a recommended mute would be later reversed or contested.

### Contradicts
None found. The paper's own finding — that platform activity count, not hateful content, is the strongest predictor of being muted — runs directly against an intuitive assumption (that toxic/hateful content is what drives moderation action), which the paper states explicitly as its central finding rather than a contradiction of another paper in this corpus.

### References worth retrieving
- foundational: Anaobi, I. H., Raman, A., Castro, I., Bin Zia, H., Ibosiola, D., Tyson, G., "Will Admins Cope? Decentralized Moderation in the Fediverse," ACM Web Conference (WWW) 2023, pp. 3109-3120 — federated (admin-based) decentralized moderation, the direct architectural counterpoint to memo.cash's admin-free, user-controlled model measured here.
- foundational: Massey, D. S., Denton, N. A., 1988 — origin of the isolation index this paper applies to mute-community localization.
- competing: Li, C., Palanisamy, B., 2019 — cited for blockchain-linked social media platforms (SocialX among them), a competing Web3-moderation design point.
- competing: Walia, K., Raghwa, A. — SocialX, cited as another Web3 platform lacking centralized moderation capacity, a direct architectural comparator to memo.cash.
- foundational: Zuo, W. et al., 2023b — the same first author's prior work characterizing memo.cash's blockchain-stored data format (OP_RETURN field usage), foundational to this paper's data-collection method.
